Firms developing a strategy for servitization are thus more likely to develop one for digitization, and vice versa. This finding supports other studies that show digitization can be an enabler for servitization (Cenamor et al., 2017; Coreynen et al., 2017), become an integral part of the total offering (Kohtamäki, Parida, et al., 2019; Vendrell-Herrero et al., 2017), and that services in the future will be categorized as‘non-digital’, ‘digitally-enabled’and fully ‘digital’(Raddats et al., 2019). Second, we find that exploitation and exploration areboth associated with digitization and servitization. In other words, either strategy is likely to be pursued by firms emphasizing both distinct capabilities. We assume that exploitativefirms are likely attracted by the ‘quick wins’of digitization, such as increasing efficiency through ICT (Gastaldi & Corso, 2012), whereas explorativefirms are more likely interested in its long-term benefits, such as developing new insights through IoT applications (Blanchet et al., 2014). Contrary to our expectations, not only explorative but also exploitativefirms are oriented towards servitization, even though it is a much riskier business strategy with more uncertain returns (Fang et al., 2008; Visnjic et al., 2016). A possible explanation is the variety of potential service strategies available to firms. Earlier work pointed towards the link between exploration and radical service business development, on the one hand, and exploitation and incremental service business development, on the other (Fischer et al., 2010). Rather than exploring new business models with customers, such as performance-based contracts, somefirms become ‘industrializers’, which means that they exploit in-house knowledge and resources to achieve scalability in offering previously customized solutions (Kowalkowski, Windahl, Kindström, & Gebauer, 2015). Yet, when both capabilities are present, exploration consistently overshadows the effect of exploitation. One explanation is the significant, positive correlation between exploration and exploitation, which supports earlier findings that both capabilities are complementary rather than substitutes (Bierly & Daly, 2007). Firms that explore business opportunities are therefore also more likely to exploit them, which is in line with earlier assumptions on exploration and exploitation in service business development (Fischer et al., 2010). Third, wefind that both exploitation and exploration are associated with digital servitization as well. From a servitization viewpoint, we just argued that exploitative and explorativefirms may prefer different service strategies, such as standardizing previously developed solutions and experimenting with new service-driven business models (e.g., making products available for use, or performance-based contracts), respectively (Kowalkowski et al., 2015). Through a digital servitization lens, it has been found thatfirms with different service strategies adopt different technologies to facilitate their service transformation. For example, ‘industrializers’often rely on cloud computing to achieve cost efficiency in mass-customization, while‘availability providers’opt for IoT to continuously localize and monitor connected products (Ardolino et al., 2018). Considering this study'sfindings in light of the literature, we suspect that both exploitative and explorativefirms are likely to pursue a digital servitization strategy, albeit different ones – this provides avenues for further research, which we discuss later. Fourth, we did notfind a significant relation between ambidexterity – i.e., the ability to both exploit and explore opportunities– and digital servitization. Ambidextrous firms are thusnot more likely to pursue a digital servitization strategy. Yet, wefind that oncefirms have reached a medium level of exploitation, the effect of exploration on digital servitization grows significantly stronger. In other words, without exploitation, explorative firms are not more likely to pursue digital servitization. A potential explanation is that once explorativefirms have sufficiently exploited the opportunities provided by basic services and technologies, they will further accelerate their digital servitization transformation by moving into more advanced services and technologies as well. This relates to earlier insights thatfirms gradually expand their offering, from basic services to value-added solutions (Brax & Visintin, 2017; Kowalkowski et al., 2015), by linking different technologies (Ardolino et al., 2018; Porter & Heppelmann, 2014). An illustration is the case of the metal component supplier thatfirst implemented 3-D printing to produce customized components more efficiently, and later started providing fully digital and connected production systems at customers' own location (Coreynen et al., 2017). Fifth, we find that these relationships are further accelerated or weakened by different environmental conditions. For one, wefind that technological turbulence is associated with digitization, regardless of firms' emphasis on either exploitation or exploration. In other words, firms active in environments characterized by rapid and impactful technological change, are more oriented towards digitization. As a moderator, we find that in average to high technologically turbulent environments, exploitativefirms are increasingly more associated with digitization. This is in line with prior studies, which pinpointed competitive intensity as an antecedent for the development of industrial services (Gebauer, 2007; Morgan et al., 2019). Explorative firms are more likely aware of the urgency to differentiate from competitors by moving into servitization. On the contrary, exploitative firms are less associated with servitization when competition becomes more intense. This relates to the literature on‘deservitization’ (e.g., Kowalkowski, Gebauer, Kamp, & Parry, 2017a ; Valtakoski, 2017), which considers the conditions under whichfirms decide that it is more beneficial to move away from service. One possible explanation is that exploitative firms prefer to deal with an increasingly competitive environment by focusing on their core business, thus spending less efforts on developing new ideas for integrated offerings. 6. Conclusions 6.1. Theoretical contributions Despite the increasing attention to digital servitization (Kohtamäki, Parida, et al., 2019), little is known about the factors that drivefirms to develop a digital servitization strategy. To date, the literature has focused on the convergence of servitization and digitization (Frank et al., 2019), their combined impact on firms' business models (Coreynen et al., 2017), and theirfinancial performance (Kohtamäki et al., 2020). Yet, the servitization literature still lacks the theoretical foundation to explain why firms venture into digital servitization in thefirst place (Kowalkowski, Gebauer, & Oliva, 2017b). This study offers new insights to the digital servitization literature by investigating its drivers from both an internal perspective (i.e., dynamic capabilities;Teece, 2007) and external perspective (i.e., contingency theory;Miller, 1981). Based on the consulted literature and our analysis of the data collected for this study, we offer the following theoretical contributions. Concerning the internal drivers, wefind that both exploitation and exploration (March, 1991) are associated withfirms pursuing a digital servitization strategy. Though operational skills, such as the ability to analyze data and make quick decisions, are useful to turn servitization into a success (Lenka et al., 2017; Paiola et al., 2012), dynamic capabilities are necessary to continuously adjust firms' strategy (Teece et al., 1997). Without the ability to either exploit or explore, for instance by refining current or adopting breakthrough technologies,firms are less likely to change through digitization, servitization, or a combined digital servitization strategy. This makes them vulnerable for environmental changes, such as shifting technologies that may jeopardize their position in the value chain (Finne et al., 2013; VendrellHerrero et al., 2017) and other suppliers competing to serve customers' increasingly heterogeneous demands (Eggert et al., 2014;Raddats et al., 2016). Concerning the external drivers, wefind that different environments moderate the identified dynamic capability-strategy relationships. The context in whichfirms operate, indeed, does matter (Dmitrijeva et al., 2019), asfirms deal with environmental change differently depending on their dynamic capabilities. For instance, wefind that exploitative firms are more likely to pursue digitization when the technology in their sector is turbulent, and explorativefirms are more likely to venture into servitization when competition is intense. Firms will thus adjust their strategy not only depending on their dynamic capabilities, but also on the environment in which they are active (Teece et al., 1997). Therefore, looking into digital servitization from a dynamic capabilities lens offers only a simplified perspective offirms' strategic transition, and the influence of the environment in which they are active should also be recognized. In summary, in order to fully understandfirms' strategic transition towards digital servitization, both firm-internal and external factors should be considered. This study contributes to the literature by pinpointing two strategic capabilities– i.e., exploitation and exploration– for digital servitization (Kohtamäki, Parida, et al., 2019), as well as the influence of two environmental factors– i.e., technological turbulence and competitive intensity– on this strategic change (Fliess & Lexutt, 2017). 6.2. Managerial implications From a business perspective, servitization and digitization have been described as two“megatrends” that “make business model transformation a key strategic priority for many leaders” (Linz et al., 2017,p . 5). Based on this study's results, we offer several implications for managers. Most notably, we highlight the importance of developing dynamic capabilities for the purpose of strategic change in general, and digital servitization in particular. Either by actively exploiting or exploring opportunities, firms are more likely to adapt their service strategy, which is necessary to maintain a sustainable competitive advantage (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000). In practice, this meansfirms need to frequently adjust their technologies and procedures to improve efficiency, and also create time to discuss and experiment with new ideas that challenge conventional wisdoms. For example, traditional manufacturers can think about which production processes would benefit most from digitization, and how they can further support customers by moving into services. In a later stage, they can explore opportunities for digital servitization, for instance by adding sensors to their products, which unlocks the possibility to connect with customers and provide data-driven services (e.g., remote monitoring and preventive maintenance). Without such dynamic capabilities,firms are likely unable to adapt their strategy to an increasingly digital, customer-driven and competitive business environment. Furthermore, by developing such dynamic capabilities,firms are more likely to take into account the changes of the environment in which they are active. Finding a rightfit with the environment is important, because this may lead to different services strategies that better match different environments (Gebauer, 2008) and ultimately increase firm performance (Eggert et al., 2014;Fang et al., 2008). As this study shows, when there is much technological change,firms are more likely to digitize, especially if they are focused on exploitation; when the competition is intense,firms are likely to servitize when they are focused on exploration. Therefore, we suggest thatfirms pay close attention to their environment, and that developing dynamic capabilities is even more important to adapt in highly evolving and turbulent sectors. 6.3. Limitations and suggestions for future research This study has several limitations. First, the single-item variables for servitization and digitization offer only limited insights in the drivers of different types of digital servitization. Our study, though one of thefirst to contribute to the theoretical underpinnings of digital servitization, therefore only scratches the surface of the drivers of digital servitization. Second, the data stems from a single survey completed by single respondents. To avoid potential CMV, we made sure the respondents were well-informed about the firm's strategy, capabilities and environment. We also used several techniques when developing the W. Coreynen, et al. Industrial Marketing Management xxx (xxxx) xxx–xxx 10 survey to prevent single-respondent bias, such as the inclusion of reverse-coded items. Third, technological turbulence and competitive intensity are based on respondents' perception of the environment that their firm is active in. Such subjective measures are open to interpretation and may not reflect the actual rate of technological change and competition acrossfirms and sectors. As opportunities for further research, a potentially fruitful next step is to consider the drivers of different types of digitization, servitization and digital servitization. For instance, future studies could draw from previous scales from the literature, such as the one developed by Partanen, Kohtamäki, Parida, and Wincent (2017)on different service offerings, andJayachandran, Sharma, Kaufman, and Raman (2005)on different levels of digitalization, which have also been used recently to investigate the relationship with firms' financial performance (Kohtamäki et al., 2020). Such studies may provide further insights into the relationship between dynamic capabilities andfirms' orientation towards different types of service offerings (Kowalkowski et al., 2015) and digitization levels, respectively. Another opportunity is to further look into the effects of digital servitization on performance, taking into account the relationship between different capabilities and environments. For example, it might be more beneficial for firms to develop incremental digital service opportunities through exploitation inless dynamic environments and develop radical opportunities through exploration in more dynamic environments. A combined configurational and contingency approach (e.g.,Flynn, Huo, & Zhao, 2010; Kohtamäki, Henneberg, Martinez, Kimita, & Gebauer, 2019) may shed further light on the most optimal conditions for digital servitization. Digital servitization and sustainability through networking: Some evidences from IoT-based business models Marco Paiola a , Francesco Schiavone b , c , * , Roberto Grandinetti a , Junsong Chen c a Department of Economics and Management, University of Padova, Via del Santo, 22, 35123 Padova, Italy b Department of Management Studies & Quantitative Methods, Parthenope University of Naples, Via Generale Parisi, 12, 80132 Naples, Italy c Emlyon Business School, Ecully, France ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Digital servitization Business model innovation Sustainability Networks ABSTRACT In the last few years, the widespread of digital technologies, such as the Internet of Things, in manufacturing industries and servitization became so strong that, recently, a growing research stream has begun to focus on how digital technologies enable service development, ushering in digital servitization as a specific research stream. Notwithstanding the prospective academic and managerial importance of explaining how digital servi - tization leads to sustainability, this research direction is still poorly investigated in the literature. The present article aims to fill such research gaps by answering the following research question: How do digitally based business model innovation and networking in manufacturing servitization impact sustainability? In order to answer this research question, we performed a multiple case study about technology-driven business model innovation and networking that has been implemented over the last few years by four small and medium manufacturing Italian companies. 1. Introduction In the last few years, the widespread of digital technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT), in manufacturing industries and servitiza - tion became so relevant that, recently, a growing research stream has begun to focus on how digital technologies enable service development, ushering in digital servitization (DS) as a specific research stream ( Paschou, Rapaccini, Adrodegari, & Saccani, 2020; Sklyar, Kowalkow - ski, Tronvoll, & S örhammar, 2019 ). DS refers to the utilization of digital tools for transformational processes whereby a company shifts from a product-centric to a service-centric business model and logic ( Kowal - kowski, Gebauer, Kamp, & Parry, 2017 ). The impact of such a phe - nomenon on firms ’ behaviors, operations and strategies has been extensively studied in the last few years (e.g. Grandinetti et al., 2020; Paiola & Gebauer, 2020 ). Therefore, DS is a key driver for the radical transformation of manufacturers ’ business models and business model innovation (BMI) ( Suppatvech, Godsell, & Day, 2019; Kohtam äki, Par - ida, Oghazi, Gebauer, & Baines, 2019 ). One potential and desirable outcome of such technological industry trends, very likely to be achieved in conjunction with strategies of cir - cular economy, is sustainability ( Parida & Wincent, 2019 ). Notwith - standing the multitude of definitions ( Glavi ˇc & Lukman, 2007 ), essentially the concept of environmental sustainability refers to a “ development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. “ ( Bruntland, 1992 ). The prolificacy of the research stream about sustainable BMI shows how much scholars are currently paying attention to the ability of companies to create and capture value in ways that do not impact negatively on the environment and society ( Geissdoerfer, Vladimirova, & Evans, 2018; Nosratabadi et al., 2018 ). Notwithstanding the above-mentioned contributions, and the prospec - tive academic and managerial importance of explaining how DS leads to sustainability ( Gebauer, Paiola, Saccani, & Rapaccini, 2020 ), this research direction is still poorly investigated in the literature ( Koh - tam äki et al., 2019; Gebauer et al., 2020 ). Indeed, there “ is a need for further research on outcomes in these business models ( e.g. energy savings) and the increasing role of sustainability in these business models ” ( Koh - tam äki et al., 2019, p. 389 ). In particular, within this domain the role and added value of partnerships, which are well-known drivers of sus - tainability ( Elkington, 2004 ) and essential building blocks of BMI in technology-intensive sectors ( Metallo, Agrifoglio, Schiavone, & Mueller, 2018 ), are even more neglected, especially as regards the relation be - tween sustainable business modeling and inter-organizational relation - ships ( Evans et al., 2017 ). The lack of specific research about this point is quite surprising since DS, sustainable BMI, and the circular economy lead to both firm-level and network-level transformations ( Rosa, Sassanelli, & Terzi, 2019 ), that a) revise both corporate business models and network-related value integration ( Yang & Evans, 2019 ) and learning collaborations ( Bocken, Schuit, & Kraaijenhagen, 2018 ) and b) contribute to the achievement of sustainability at corporate, societal, and environmental levels ( Parida & Wincent, 2019 ). Such research gaps are even more critical and evident in highly resource-consuming industrial contexts (e.g. Labuschagne, Brent, & Van Erck, 2005; Raut et al., 2019; Yadav, Luthra, Jakhar, Mangla, & Rai, 2020 ), where stakeholders and value systems face relevant barriers in collectively pursue circular approaches ( Ozkan-Ozen, Kazancoglu, & Mangla, 2020; Luthra & Mangla, 2018 ) and sustainability can be ach - ieved or improved only thanks to the isolated initiatives of a few indi - vidual firms. The present article aims to fill such research gaps by answering the following research question: How do digitally-based business model innovation and networking in manufacturing servitization impact sus - tainability? In order to answer this research question, we performed a multiple case study about IoT-driven BMI and networking that has been implemented over the last few years by four small and medium manufacturing Italian companies. Based on our findings we develop a general reflection on the main impact of such drivers on the sustain - ability of firms, industries, and the environment. We contribute to the vast streams of research about DS and BMI (e.g. Parida & Wincent, 2019; Paschou et al., 2020; Paiola & Gebauer, 2020 ) and their links with sustainability and sustainable business models ( Evans et al., 2017; Geissdoerfer et al., 2018 ) by offering an inductive perspective about the new goals, priorities, and challenges for sustainability in the age of IoT and the role of networking in this context. 2. Literature review 2.1. Digital servitization and business model innovation DS has enjoyed widespread attention by scholars in the last few years ( Paschou et al., 2020; Paiola & Gebauer, 2020; Sklyar et al., 2019 ). The number of scholarly citations about this phenomenon have been boosted in the last ten years ( Kohtamaki et al., 2019 ). DS merges together two different industry trends: digitization and servitization. The first notion refers to “ the increasing use of digital technologies for connecting peo - ple, systems, companies, products and services ” ( Coreynen, Matthys - sens, & van Bockhaven, 2017 ). Servitization commits manufacturers in the move towards solutions ( Paiola, Saccani, Perona, & Gebauer, 2013 ), involving also medium-sized capital equipment producers ( Gebauer, Paiola, & Edvardsson, 2010 ) and leading to inter-organizational networking ( Gebauer, Paiola, & Saccani, 2013 ); it refers to “ the com - pany moves from providing pure stand-alone products and add-on services to maintenance contracts, operational services and, finally, to outcome- or performance-based offerings ” ( Kohtam äki, Parida, Patel, & Gebauer, 2020, p. 3 ). In general, prior research widely acknowledges that the interaction between these two concepts is considered very strong since digitization supports the development and marketing of services ( Vendrell-Herrero, Bustinza, Parry, & Georgantzis, 2017 ). Several last-generation digital technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT), cloud platforms, and big data, provide good opportunities to firms that are interested in the development of DS solutions. These technologies are central in recent studies related to technology-based servitization ( Paschou et al., 2020 ). IoT technologies enable a dra - matic expansion of service innovation opportunities, increasing the relevance of the transition of manufacturing firms toward service-based strategies ( Kiel, Arnold, & Voigt, 2017 ). BMI is a process through which firms realize changes in the activities and functions within their BMs and explore new architectural designs: it consists in exploring new possibilities related to value proposition, value creation, distribution and capture for customers, suppliers, and partners ( Casadesus-Masanell & Zhu, 2013; Gambardella & McGahan, 2010; Kraus, Filser, Puumalainen, Kailer, & Thurner, 2020; Amit and Zott, 2012 ). Via the latest digital technologies, DS obliges firms to intensively modify BM component configurations over time via the optimization of customer segmentation, positioning, and pricing strategies ( Santos et al., 2017 ); to enhance the products ’ development and the design of inno - vative product-service systems (PSSs) ( Frank, Mendes, Ayala, & Ghezzi, 2019 ); and to expand result-oriented propositions in manufacturing BMs ( Paiola & Gebauer, 2020 ). In the current technological scenario firms are now leveraging ser - vices in order to create entirely new BMs, migrating from product- centric approaches to service-oriented ones ( Adrodegari & Saccani, 2017; Coreynen, Matthyssens, & van Bockhaven, 2017 ). Indeed, thanks to these technologies, manufacturing firms can: unlock value from ma - chines ( Ehret & Wirtz, 2017 ); reconceptualize value innovation ( Mat - thyssens, 2019 ); exploit the potential of PSSs ( Lerch & Gotsch, 2015 ); and leverage their position in the supply chain ( Vendrell-Herrero et al., 2017 ). While a product-oriented Product-Service System (PSS) fits perfectly into the manufacturing firm ’ s classic repertoire, use-oriented and result-oriented ones are more distant from the traditional BMs that are adopted and calls for major redefinitions of firms ’ BMs ( Paiola & Gebauer, 2020 ). Also, the empirical study by Laudien and Daxb öck (2016) shows how a full utilization of IoT requires a radical innovation of the firms ’ BM. In particular, IoT-based use-oriented and result- oriented PSSs imply a radical shift in the fundamental revenue models of firms, introducing usage-based, performance-based, and value-based revenue models ( Bonnemeier, Burianek, & Reichwald, 2010 ). The abilities to effectively establish and manage inter-organizational networks and ecosystems relationships ( Kohtamaki et al., 2019; Sklyar et al., 2019; Parida & Wincent, 2019 ), together with a sound social and environmental orientation ( Eggers, Niemand, Filser, Kraus, & Berchtold, 2020 ), are crucial for DS and BMI. Digital servitization gradually pushes firms ’ value propositions from pure products toward pure services, in the form of use-oriented and result-oriented offerings, and it supports the creation of advanced forms of market relations ( Grubic, 2014 ). Capital equipment manufacturers, used to achieving profitability from conventional services such as spare parts, are changing their value propositions toward PSSs ( Hypko, Tile - bein, & Gleich, 2010 ), and updating their mechanisms of revenue gen - eration (along with costing structures, risk assessment, and reciprocal liabilities among partners), moving from a transactional perspective to a relationship-based one ( Visnjic, Jovanovic, Neely, & Engwall, 2017 ). DS can be implemented via five types of BM within ecosystems, each one based on different combinations of pricing, customization, and digiti - zation ( Kohtamaki et al., 2019 ): product-oriented service provider, industrializer, customized integrated solution provider, platform pro - vider, and outcome provider. Sustainability and sustainable business models DS is often associated, among others, with the notion of sustain - ability (e.g. Kohtam äki et al., 2019; Paschou et al., 2020 ). In the “ in - dustry 4.0 ” (I4.0) paradigm, technologies like Internet of Things (IoT), cloud platforms, and big data enable service-oriented, digitalized and sustainable BMs, and companies are able to design and implement more effective and efficient value propositions ( Bouncken, Kraus, & Roig- Tierno, 2021 ). According to the well-known framework of the triple bottom line sustainability can be economic, societal, and environmental ( Elkington, 1994 ). The link between digital technologies and sustain - ability has become so deep and strong over the last few years that recently George and his co-authors (2020) coined the notion of digital sustainability, which refers to all “ the organizational activities that seek to advance the sustainable development goals through creative deployment of technologies that create, use, transmit, or source elec - tronic data ” . With specific reference to DS, the findings of the recent systematic literature review by Paschou and her co-authors (2020) report that there are several benefits of such a phenomenon for society and the environment: reduction in energy consumption, less environ - mental impact, a positive impact on social sustainability, delivery of value for the entire society, and the building of sustainable production processes. The extant theory about BMI paid great attention to sustainability and sustainable BMs are an important and emerging stream within BMI ( Filser, Kraus, Breier, Nenova, & Puumalainen, 2021 ). Within this domain some scholars focused on the general notion of sustainable business models (e.g. Evans et al., 2017 ) to explain how companies can create and capture value in sustainable ways. Sustainable business models refer to “ business models that incorporate pro-active multi-stake - holder management, the creation of monetary and non-monetary value for a broad range of stakeholders, and hold a long-term perspective ” ( Geissdoerfer et al., 2018, p. 403 ). A specific segment of such a domain relates to BMI within the context of the circular economy (e.g. Geissdoerfer, Savaget, Bocken, & Hultink, 2017 ), which has also become an important and fast- growing research domain over the last few years ( Ferasso, Beliaeva, Kraus, Clauss, & Ribeiro-Soriano, 2020 ). The circular economy, along with other industry trends such as digitization and servitization, is currently pushing the transformation of manufacturing firms toward sustainability ( Parida & Wincent, 2019 ). As shown by Fig. 1 , at network level these trends push co-creation with partners and ecosystem orchestration. At firm level, the transformation takes place via the update of corporate resources and capabilities and BMI. Over the last few years an evident outcome of such transformations was, for instance, the growing adoption of both digitization and green servitization, a strategic approach in which corporate business models are designed not only for the achievement of value creation and profits but also to consider and fix some environmental issues ( Agrawal and Bellos, 2017 ). The application of this strategy in the automotive sector, if based on the exploitation of digital technologies, is positively associated with higher productivity outcomes. More generally, the development of PPS is likely to promote sustainability-oriented BMI ( Evans et al., 2017 ). The UNESCO Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) made the link between digitization and sustainable strategies and BMs even stronger ( Del Río Castro et al., 2021 ). Prior research provides some general insights about the role of strategic partnerships and, more extensively, networks for the achieve - ment of sustainability via digitally based BMs. Parida and Wincent (2019) , in their theoretical framework (see Fig. 1 ), suggest network transformation, such as firm transformation, is crucial for achieving economic, environmental, and societal sustainability for manufacturing companies ’ operations. An effective network transformation implies the need for robust capabilities of ecosystem orchestration and co-creation with ecosystem partners. This network transformation is a precondi - tion for sustainable BMI ( Evans et al., 2017 ). A suitable business model for achieving sustainability is the so-called “ platform provider ” model, in which the company offers a fully-fledged digitally-enabled service and connects various providers and customers ( Kohtamaki et al., 2019 ). Prior research about the circular economy also acknowledges the value network ( Amit & Zott, 2012 ), which in this context is defined as “ a set of roles and interactions in which organizations engage in both tangible and intangible value exchanges to achieve economic or social good ” ( Evans et al., 2017, p. 601 ), and which designs various options for value creation, delivery, and capture. Given these assumptions, a range of speculations can be developed about the value, impacts and roles played by partnerships, alliances and networks for the implementation and success of digitally-based BMI on sustainability. For instance, referring to the interconnection between network transformation and firm transformation ( Parida & Wincent, 2019 ), it would be important to understand if different approaches of BMI and BMs (e.g., service provider vs. platform provider) and networking by firms implementing DS lead to different or specific sus - tainability performances. Second, despite the fact that prior research stresses that BMI based on DS can improve sustainability ( Paschou et al., 2020 ), more evidence should be provided about how inter-firm net - works and alliances, which are a crucial building block of BMI in technology-based industries ( Metallo et al., 2018 ), contribute to spreading the benefits of sustainability across the environment, firms, Fig. 1. Research method and setting As the impact of IoT technologies on firms ’ business models is still an emerging and puzzling phenomenon to be explored in depth ( Paschou et al., 2020; Paiola & Gebauer, 2020 ), a qualitative research setting is deemed preferable by the well-known specific literature ( Voss, Tsik - riktsis, & Frohlich, 2002 ). We designed multiple case-study research, in order to provide detailed data and examine current managerial chal - lenges ( Yin, 2018 ). This methodology has been used by a number of recent empirical works investigating how emerging technologies impact business models ( Laudien & Daxb öck, 2016; Müller, Buliga, & Voigt, 2018; Yin, 2018 ), since it gives more robust results than the single case study, allowing a cross-analysis of collective case studies ( Eisenhardt & Graebner, 2007 ). Aiming at privileging the representation of variety over statistical representativeness ( Miles & Huberman, 1994 ), we opted for a sampling process based on a purposive approach, selecting cases that differ in terms of key characteristics relevant to the research question ( Bryman, 2012 ), and on the basis of their convenient accessibility and proximity to the researcher ( Mason, 2002 ). The research design encompasses different phases and data collection efforts. In line with other similar investigations ( Laudien & Daxb öck, 2016 ), we prompted a preliminary investigation phase interviewing ten industry experts (independent technology and strategy consultants), in order to have some orientation in the field of research and hints that are useful to identify interesting case studies ( Littig & P öchhacker, 2014 ). We were looking for business- to-business (B2B) manufacturing companies headquartered in Italy, engaged in IoT-related projects providing new B2B services with a sig - nificant impact on their BM, willing to commit to the research work and provide congruous access to information. Crossing experts ’ suggestions with secondary data and information, we constructed an initial list of firms and knowledgeable informants, ceasing the sampling process at theoretical saturation ( Glaser & Strauss, 1967 ). Between the end of 2016 and the end of 2017, we contacted 25 Italian firms located in the north of Italy, of different sizes and different value chain positions, belonging to different industries, and which were frequent leaders in the respective market or niche. We had several in- depth face-to-face structured interviews with both top managers and specific function managers (general managers or managers in charge of service-related, technology- and IoT-related activities) with the aim of getting detailed information on the type of I4.0 technologies used by the firms, their current impact on the industrial service offering, and emerging changes in the BM. Consistently with acknowledged methodological indications ( Ahl - strom, Blackmon, & Voss, 1998; Voss et al., 2002 ), the in-depth analysis of gathered data (interviews, transcriptions, and coding) supported our theoretical sampling approach, leading us to exclude firms for not complying with one or more of the research criteria. Eventually only four firms featured sophisticated uses of technologies and major changes in the BM. This proportion is consistent with previous literature (e.g., the “ Full IIoT business model ” in Laudien & Daxb öck, 2016 ), and in line with the specific difficulties of equipment manufacturers in adopting the new I4.0 approach ( Rafael, Jaione, Cristina, & Ibon, 2020 ). These companies were chosen to be the base of the work described in this study. Subsequently, between the end of 2017 and mid-2018, follow-up meetings and interactions with these firms were arranged in order to obtain supplementary information, deal with any unclear topic, and avoid any misinterpretation. Two specific industries facing increasing pressure to improve their environmental sustainability are involved in the empirical research. First, the packaging industry is under pressure from different stake - holders, such as regulators and customers, to improve its ecological and social responsiveness ( Verghese, Lewis, & Fitzpatrick, 2012; Sumrin et al., 2021 ). Packaging machinery producers – notwithstanding that they feel lower pressures than other packaging lifecycle actors, such as packaging producers and packaged food producers - have participated in this evolution, designing increasingly smart products that help cus - tomers to reduce energy consumption and favor the introduction of alternative and more sustainable materials, also ones that are recycled and reused ( Pauer, Wohner, Heinrich, & Tacker, 2019; Mahalik & Nambiar, 2010 ). Second, commercial refrigeration is exposed to signif - icant tensions in order to reduce waste, energy consumption, and in - crease sustainability, also having to cope with the evolution of food distribution techniques, increasingly relying on the free renting of mo - bile refrigerators. The food retail stores sector amounts to about 3% of EU members ’ electricity consumption. Specifically, commercial refrig - eration is responsible for 35% of EU-27 CO2-eq emissions related to refrigerants: fluorinated gases, which are the most used refrigerants for space conditioning and refrigeration systems, involve 2% of EU emis - sions, having risen since 1990 by 60% ( Gimeno-Frontera, Mainar- Toledo, S áez de Guinoa, Zambrana-Vasquez, & Zabalza-Bribi án, 2018 ). For these reasons the selected firms have increased their attention to the enabling effect of technologies for new programmes and initiatives aimed at progressively reducing the environmental impact and to improving efficiency in the use of resources, both at the plant and at the product level ( Ben-Daya, Hassini, Bahroun, & Banimfreg, 2021 ). The following section provides a detailed and in-depth description of how IoT is fueling BMI in the four sampled companies. 4. Findings 4.1. Case description As shown in Table 1 , all the selected firms leverage a fully-fledged set of digital technologies for service development strategies. They are all original equipment manufacturers (OEM) with a customized or modular product and a direct sales model, which operate in highly competitive markets serving international and global multinational enterprises. On the whole, the selected firms produce and sell variably complex and frequently customized products (single machines, complete lines, and turn-key systems). So far, they have adopted a quite traditional BM for manufacturers, based on the ability to differentiate their product in terms of quality and performances, and with a pay-per-own revenue model. However, fierce global competition and increasingly hard product-based differentiation have put their premium price strategies at stake, leading them to explore technologies as enablers of new service- oriented BMs, in order to sustain price levels and customer loyalty, also creating additional recurring revenues. Companies A and B operate in the packaging industry, and in particular in the production of packaging machines. Both have a strong and long-standing reputation in quality, innovation, and customer ser - vice, and are leaders in their respective industry segment. The product has a typical lifecycle of 10 – 15 years, whose energy consumption is considerable, even if not extreme, dealing with complex, automated, extremely fast, and efficient machines. Downtimes, anomalies, and Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) are the major cost items of a yearly Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) that can range from 6% to 10% of the equipment price, with a relevant variance due to the type of ma - chines that comprise the line. Industry ’ s products have long since been equipped with dedicated software, but it is the current IoT and cloud- based connectivity that is acting as a game changer, allowing effective remote control of the customer ’ s equipment performance and enabling new value propositions and business models. Companies C and D are leader companies in the design, manufacture, and installation of complete equipment for the retail sector. They are both focused on the production of furniture for global leaders in food retail, to whom they offer personalized systems and turn-key solutions. Discussion and implications 5.1. Discussion Our study contributes to various streams of literature. First, it con - firms and contributes in various ways to the rising body of literature linking DS and sustainability ( Parida & Wincent, 2019 ). In line with the model of Parida and Wincent (2019) our empirical study confirms that new digital services provided by manufacturers have inherent valuable impacts on the sustainability of their customers. The four case studies reported here confirm that in current DS and BMI in manufacturing, relevant sustainability gains can stem from using technology for shifting the focus from manufactured products to customers ’ processes and leveraging network relationships transformation. They also show that sustainability cannot be achieved without the simultaneous and aligned exploitation and evolution of DS and networking. Our findings, pri - marily, contribute to this body of knowledge by showing that sustain - ability, the key outcome of such a process, can be achieved via both dyadic and small network configurations and not only via large business ecosystems. The study also contributes to the stream of literature about digital sustainability and sustainable BMI (Evans, 2017; Geissdoerfer et al., 2018; George, Merrill, & Schillebeeckx, 2020 ) by providing evidence of how manufacturing firms in highly resource-consuming sectors imple - ment DS and transform their BMs and value networks to also offer to customers, among others, positive sustainability-related outcomes and benefits. Smart digital applications provided by the sampled firms are in fact able to produce significant impacts on the overall efficiency of a customer ’ s processes, allowing them to effectively obtain lower energy consumption rates, better resource utilization, and reduced waste of materials and consumable products. This evidence, furthermore, shows that the notion of value network is also meaningful in industries where the need for a circular economy and sustainability is not yet felt by industrial players. Indeed, our study shows that firms in highly resource-consuming contexts know well that the effective management, design, and exploitation of inter- organizational networks (consisting of both suppliers and industrial customers) are crucial for achieving and offering more sustainable performance for their customers. Referring to suppliers, networking relations with suppliers are critical in crafting advanced DS solutions and sustaining customers ’ performances, including those related to sustainability. In fact, the supplier ’ s value proposition is a fundamental criterion for the network design and is profoundly affected by customer participation. The new PSS concept - and in particular the new tech - nological requirements it underlines - affects the supplier ’ s network construction following process-related needs emerging from critical re - lations with key clients and pilot customers. Drivers of green digital servitization include: achieving efficiency improvements and main - taining competitive advantage, accessing digitally-ready and green- oriented customers, leveraging collaborations with stakeholders. In line with the most recent contributions ( Del Río Castro et al., 2021 ) our study shows that BMI that aims at leveraging digital tech - nology and services in order to attain sustainability requires specific and intentional design capabilities, regarding both digital servitization and network construction. Furthermore, this paper extends the literature that underscores the intersection of business modeling and inter- organizational relationships ( Evans et al. (2017) , pointing out that value networks influence BMI when digitization and sustainability are concerned, highlighting the specific role and relevance of digital servi - tization networks, which require specific purpose, design, and gover - nance. In addition, our cases show that external relationships in green digital servitization are collaborative experimentations that also allow medium-sized firms to learn and build precious capabilities and orchestrate external networks for specific value proposition purposes ( Bocken et al., 2018 ): The four cases explored in this study share the same approach as regards network construction, all having a selective and dyadic approach to manage external contributions. Finally, the study confirms and extends to green digital servitization the importance of producer - owner - user integration for realizing environment-friendly BMIs, especially with regard to digitally enabled result-oriented PSS archetypes, and their enhancements in resource utilization, and efficiency in production ( Yang & Evans, 2019; Rosa et al., 2019 ). In particular, our cases draw attention to the potential of digital servitization in terms of longer product life, increased resource and energy efficiency, increased product usage, and reduced carbon emissions and reduced wasted materials. 5.2. Theoretical implications The present study offers relevant academic implications for an increasingly relevant stream at the crossroads of different research lines, which we referred to here as green digital servitization. This is an emergent topic crossing sustainable Business Models Innovation and Digital Servitization, which explores the sustainability of business models, enabled by digitally based advanced manufacturing services. First, the study offers original empirical evidence to an increasingly relevant topic, answering the recent call for investigation inherent to the specific digitalization-related effects on sustainable BM ( Del Río Castro et al., 2021 ). It highlights the relevant impact of digital PSS provided by manufacturers to their customers ’ sustainability performances. This contributes to position the interplay between digitalization and sus - tainability within the perspective of stakeholders relations, where technological services providers, equipment suppliers, and final user clients are fundamental elements of the BMI-related network. Second, our study highlights the underestimated role in sustain - ability BM transitions of digitally oriented partnerships within sustain - ability networks ( Ordieres-Mer é, Prieto Rem ón, & Rubio, 2020 ). In fact, literature regarding the relationship between digitization and sustain - ability has so far overlooked the sustainability effects of digitally based service-oriented solutions that are increasingly frequent in supplier- customer relationships ( Grandinetti, Ciasullo, Paiola, & Schiavone, 2020; George et al., 2020 ). Third, the study confirms and extends previous studies highlighting the direct outcomes of service-based BMI ( Parida & Wincent, 2019 ) and digital green services ( Opazo-Bas áez, Vendrell-Herrero, & Bustinza, 2018 ). It underlines how research on the direct and indirect effects of DS should be integrated into the mainstream research related to product and process sustainability. Our research shows that DS is a constitutive element of firms ’ transition towards a circular view of relationships within value systems, since it guarantees significant economic and environmental sustainability and implies a specific design and gover - nance of variably complex networks. In other words, sustainability benefits have to become an inherent constitutive element of new value propositions in BMI, founded on advanced digital services that allow unprecedented performance in machines and equipment energy effi - ciency, material consumption, and waste reduction. 5.3. Managerial implications Relevant management implications emerge from the findings of the present study, that may be useful for B2B manufacturing firms willing to take full advantage of the opportunities offered by digital technologies for sustainability but still uncertain about the way forward. First, our findings stress the need for companies interested in offering a positive sustainability performance to adopt DS-driven BMs focused on medium/high levels of customization. Indeed, only BMs as the customized service provider or the outcome provider could be effective in the co-creation of solutions well-suited for the specific sustainability needs of customers (e.g. energy savings or resource erosion). In other words, firm value creation is based on the design of BMs which can offer customer-centric, technology-based, and sustainability-focused solutions. Second, firms interested in successfully implementing sustainability- oriented DS initiatives and BMI should hold and integrate a variety of organizational capabilities, such as strategic planning, technology management, marketing and service innovation, business networking, and stakeholder management. Such heterogeneity of the competencies needed for designing such types of DS and BM should require, at orga - nizational level, the creation of a dedicated organizational unit able to effectively manage the synergies and potential conflicts that can emerge within the business ecosystems of the firm, and adopt effective customer management procedures and strategies ( Princes, 2020 ). Such a unit should be led by a senior manager and receive the full legitimation of the Top Management Team. Third, ecosystem orchestration and co-creation with customers are important elements for the effective design and implementation of BMI, providing positive sustainability performance. This relates in particular to two stakeholder categories, namely technology providers (IoT and software related products and services) and customers. As regards sup - pliers, the commitment in manufacturers ’ DS projects represent a valuable co-learning experience precious in facing current BMIs ( Filser et al., 2021 ). As regards customers, notwithstanding whether the firm adopts a reactive or a proactive approach in starting DS projects, the knowledge base that customers contribute as leading firms in their in - dustries significantly supports experimentation. Moreover, as in result- oriented PSSs actual performances also depend on the customer ’ s M. Paiola et al. Journal of Business Research 132 (2021) 507–516 515 cooperation and ability in doing its part of the job, our contribution detects a particularly selective use of the customers that are involved in the supplier ’ s BMI. Our study shows that the new value proposition ig - nites a process of partner selection and collaboration that are specifically related to the new capabilities and resources needed by the firm and that also foster internal learning processes that are fundamental to the firms ’ BM renewal. 5.4. Limitations and future research This study does not come out without limitations. First, the B2B manufacturing firms and industries analyzed in this paper are only a fraction of the B2B landscape. Different approaches to green digital servitization may be adopted in different firms and industries, calling for a wide-spectrum quantitative investigation on the topic. Second, since we are investigating firms involved in transition pro - cesses, we cannot tell what the outcome of the experimentation will be, and if it will be the same for every firm. Future observation of the same companies through a longitudinal analysis would tell whether and how they have managed to achieve full DS sustainability potential. This paper aims at identifying the pathways that companies are undertaking in the digital servitization and recognize what are the competences relevant for the development and management of new service offerings based on Industry 4.0 technologies. Through the development of a conceptual model and a multiple case-study, the digital servitization journeys of eight industrial companies and the related competences are discussed, suggesting that various categories of competences enable different digital servitization paths, but proper combination of technical, methodological, personal and social skills, is required to succeed in the digital servitization. © 2021 CIRP. Introduction The introduction of digital technologies and their integration with operational technologies are one of the core elements characterizing the digital transformation of manufacturing firms and it represents a preliminary stage to embrace the more holistic concept of Industry 4.0 (I4.0) [1]. This transformation is reshaping the industry competition [2], and technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT), Cloud computing or Big data and analytics, are supporting companies to enhance their product-service offering, both providing advanced infrastructure to deliver services and creating the potentiality to extend the service offering [3,4]. The trend of servitization, which can be defined as the paradigm of offering customers a combination of goods, services, support selfservice and knowledge [5], is not new [6]. However, digital technologies promote and facilitate new and different types of service innovation, also defined as servitization pathways [7]. The adoption of digital technologies in the servitization domain is, therefore, changing the way services are delivered completely [8], facilitating new sophisticated service offerings [9] and enabling new servitized business models [10]. The convergence of these trends, namely digital servitization [11,12] is not only reshaping the competitive landscape but is rapidly changing the working environment, forcing companies to develop new specific competences [13,14]. In fact, in this fastchanging landscape, workers need to acquire higher and diversified competences [15]. As an example, employees are required to outfit with skills ranging from data analysis to communication and team working, to face complex and interactive tasks and make data-driven decisions [16]. To deal successfully with the digital servitization phenomenon, it is crucial to identify the core competences that an organization at large should have to fully implement this transformation. Capabilities related to the implementation of Industry 4.0 technologies are considered relevant to the provision of advanced product-service offerings [17,18]. Since specific competences for the servitization transformation have already been addressed by literature, investigating the relevant skills in the field of Industry 4.0 to support digital servitization is of utmost importance. Although the relevance of this topic, there are few models [19], which explore the merging point between servitization and digital technologies to understand these competences better. In this avenue, our research explores the most relevant I4.0 skills that support the digital servitization transformation of manufacturing companies that are already servitized and analyses how different digital servitization strategies affect the competence mix. Literature review Digital servitization In the realm of manufacturing, advances in technology continuously support the development of industrialization [22]. Nowadays, there is an increasing emphasis on the transition of the Fourth Industrial Revolution from manufacturing to service industries domain [23]. I4.0 is a comprehensive concept whose characteristics are strongly correlated with a set of modern technologies that enable integrated product-services [24]. In the analysed literature, it is consent that manufacturing companies increasingly introduce technologies to digitalise their business and intensify their service orientation [25]. Both scholars and managers agree that technology has been a major driving force behind the evolution of service offerings [19], since “the service revolution and the information revolution are two sides of the same coin” [26]. Fast-evolving digital technologies offer opportunities for enabling novel product-service offerings [27], developing customised value propositions [28], with higher quality services and deeper customer relationships. New technologies’ adoption can be crucial in moving towards more serviceoriented business models [29– 31], and accelerating the servitization process [32]: manufacturers introduce digital technologies to increase their service delivery efficiency [33] and raise their service offerings’ value [34,35]. At the same time, according to Weking et al. [36], servitization is one of the main patterns of the business model in the era of Industry 4.0, since IoT connections enhance the product-service offering of firms, which are increasingly becoming solutions providers. Therefore, servitization and digitalisation are considered two of the most relevant trends affecting industrial companies [37], and their convergence, called “digital servitization” [11,32], has been studied in different industrial cases such as General Electric and Rolls-Royce. Today, it is crucial to map this transformation to understand the potential of technologies as enabling factors for different types of service strategies. Over time, many scholars, among different research streams, published different classifications and categorizations of service offerings [38] to describe the transition from product to solution conceptually. These service offerings typologies have often been applied to describe a variety of service options within a particular industry or for a specific manufacturer. Even though the literature shows an increasing interest in digitally-enabled servitization [11,38], there is a lack of classification models that consider the role of digital technologies in the service offering. As companies have different approaches in embedding I4.0 technologies in their service offerings, new servitization paths can be envisaged and increasing levels of technological capability gradually enable more sophisticated paths, entailing new evolutionary scenarios and higher complexity in service management. Moreover, as argued by Baines et al. [39], the servitization process also requires a transformation of the enterprise, including the evolution of organizational variables, such as change skills and competences, which are relevant to ensure a competitive advantage to firms [40]. Chiu et al. [41] proposed a new classification model of product-service offering embedding the analysis of the core competences of the enterprise, suggesting the importance of identifying relevant competences to succeed in the servitization process. In this context, a reference framework to map and identify the opportunities of the digital servitization journeys properly is needed. In fact, the above discussed traditional approaches of service offerings classification do not refer specifically to the technology enabling the service offering. At the best of our knowledge, only Allmendinger & Lombreglia [30] propose four basic business models for product makers that decide to embrace smart services and Porter and Heppelmann [42] discuss how new technologies enable service capabilities. These two last frameworks have been used as a basis for the development of the model presented in detail in Section “Digital Servitization Model”. Digital competences The transformation of the enterprises towards I4.0 will bring changes in the job profiles and required competences to the employees [43]. Developing proper competence frameworks for I4.0 is a priority for both researchers, policymakers and practising managers [44]. Researches show that improving only the products and processes from a technological point of view is not sufficient to be competitive, but specific investments in the development of the workforce’s competences are needed [45]. However, the formulation of general competence frameworks for I4.0 is still underresearched, and a more in-depth discussion about competences for the digital world is required [46]. Currently, in literature, some models have been presented, proposing different sets of the so-called “digital competences”, which entail both “soft” and “hard” skills to perform activities in a digital workplace [47]. Davies et al. in 2011 [48] identify six drivers of change, which should have a disruptive effect on the future of work, including both technological advancement and social trends. Related to them, a set of ten soft skills is provided, encompassing social intelligence, transdisciplinary, sense-making, adaptive thinking, and so on. Gehrke et al. [49] propose a more broad perspective including both technical and personal skills in their model. Another holistic approach, including a wider variety of skills, is presented in Hecklau et al. [21], where starting from C. Cimini, F. Adrodegari, T. Paschou et al. CIRP Journal of Manufacturing Science and Technology 32 (2021) 447–460 448 challenges and trends externally affecting industry, a competence model, in which competences are grouped into four classes: technical, methodological, social and personal competences, is suggested. Similarly, Erol et al. [50] divide the competences into personal, social/interpersonal, action-related and domain-related ones, distinguishing at the same time the required competences for different workers’ level, such as engineers or managers. Other scholars developed some competence models by referring to precise job profiles of specific enterprise areas. Moreover, I4.0 skills overall overviews are provided by van Laar et al. [51] and Janis [52]. It is worth highlighting that among the above contributions, few hints refer to the digital servitization phenomenon. Despite this, the literature suggests that the journey towards servitization and I4.0 requires a clear roadmap to transform the workers’ competences as well [53]. Digitalization capabilities, such as the advanced ability to use smart and connected physical products, are considered relevant to the provision of advanced product-service offerings [54]. Sklyar et al. [55] suggest that the development of IT competences is of high relevance in service ecosystems as well. In particular, digital servitization is significantly supported by IoT and the importance of IoT core capabilities (such as digital business model development, IoT value selling, IoT value delivery) has been studied to demonstrate their relevance in providing customers with high-value IoT-based services [56]. Rymaszewska et al. [57] remark on the importance of IoT capabilities to develop digital services and suggest a balancing between the competences that organisations should develop-in-house and those that can be outsourced. Moreover, in the service sector, customer orientation skills, communication and digital literacy are recognised to be crucial [58]. A framework for digital servitization competences is provided by Paschou et al. [47] and identifies four relevant categories: data analysis and management, digital content creation, soft skills and innovation appetite. In parallel, digital competences related to the stakeholders in product-service systems are explored in research by Süße et al. [59]. From a relational perspective, developing digital competences is recognised as crucial to maintaining a successful digital servitization partnership [60]. Nevertheless, in literature there is a lack of frameworks or competence models regarding the joint transformation towards digitalization and servitization of companies. An in-depth investigation of this topic is required. Also, in industrial implementation of digitalization applied to the service offering, the lack of competences and skills to manage this transition is one of the major challenges that companies are facing [7]. Among all the above mentioned contributions, the competence framework by Hecklau et al. [21] has been chosen as a reference framework to conduct a case study analysis (described in Section “Data analysis: competences patterns”) and collect some empirical evidence about the I4.0 competences useful to undertake the digital servitization successfully. Hecklau et al. [21] developed a new strategic approach for holistic human resource management aiming at supporting manufacturing companies to cope with knowledge and competence challenges related to digital technologies, by maintaining a well-qualified workforce. Moreover, this framework is considered one of the very few competence models that consist of both hard and soft skills. Other scholars supported the strength and relevance of this specific competence model. For instance, Longo et al. [61] state that it is a holistic reference framework to support the worker qualification strategies, while Ghobakhloo [62] supports the idea of developing such a complete competence model as a first step for the Human Resource Strategy in his roadmap for the Industry 4.0 transition. In the framework, reported in Table 1, there are four categories of competences, namely technical, methodological, social and personal ones. Research design and methodology The research flow used to develop this work is depicted in Fig. 1 and described hereafter. The research involved two main phases. Conceptual model development and competence identification In literature, scholars suggest that to design and conduct empirical research, a first step of conceptual development is fundamental and helpful to clarify the main aspects that have to be studied [63,64]. For this reason, the first phase focused on the identification of a conceptual framework useful to describe the digital servitization and to investigate the manufacturing companies’ competence development. Along with this, the most relevant competences have been identified. This phase involved several steps. Firstly, a literature review was conducted to identify relevant theoretical areas related to our research object. A review of journal articles, conference papers, books, and material available on the Internet was conducted from interdisciplinary search engines such as Google Scholar, SCOPUS, etc. “Industry 4.0”, “servitization strategies”, “smart services”, “competences”, “digitalization”, “smart technologies” have been used as keywords. Useful guidelines to develop systematic literature in servitization can be found in Rabetino et al. [65]. The actual gaps in the context of digital servitization, the lack of service offerings classification models that also consider the role of new technologies have been identified. The literature review also aimed at identifying the available competence models related to I4.0. Secondly, to fill the identified literature gap, the Digital Servitization Model (DSM) was proposed. The model is used as a template to understand how companies are approaching their digital servitization journey in the era of I4.0. The model takes into consideration two aspects of digital servitization: the technological maturity related to the products and the company strategy in developing and offering smart services. Thirdly, we performed the Digital Servitization Model verification. Empirical application According to the research aim, the model has been used to explore and analyse the current practices in eight leading industrial firms, which have already started a servitization journey. Due to the nature of the research aim and exploratory intent of the study, multiple case studies empirical research has been chosen [20]. Case studies are specifically suitable when dealing with complex adaptive systems, since researchers should address “insider” and “participatory” approaches to research [66] to capture depth, nuance, and complex data during the interviews [67]. The case research encompassed several phases, from the design of the case study to the development of the empirical investigation to collect and analyse data. To carry out the empirical application, in order to guarantee the reliability of our study, we followed the guidelines provided by Voss et al. [64]. The main phases are described hereafter. Case selection In this first phase, we selected the companies participating in the study adopting a judgmental sampling [68] selecting cases according to different criteria [69,70]. The participation in the interviews was proposed to companies taking part in the ASAP Service Management Forum (www.asapsmf.org), an Italian-based community of researchers and practitioners dealing with servitization. Companies were selected according to the following criteria: a) they should be well acknowledged servitised firms, b) they operate in the machinery sector or value chain, c) they should have shown interest in the research objectives and trust towards the research team. Some of them are multi-national companies, their Italian subsidiary has been chosen as the unit of analysis. In addition to these criteria, the sample was built on the authors’ experience and their knowledge of the Italian machinery sector. Totally, 8 representative companies were selected. Research protocols and instruments development To conduct the investigation in the selected cases, a welldesigned research protocol for the interviews, which is particularly important in multi-case research [71] has been defined. In particular, we chose to conduct semi-structured interviews based on a guideline made of 12 open questions, which have been used with a twofold objective: i) gathering data related to the way companies are approaching servitization and digitalization, in terms of current practices and planned developments, and ii) indepth exploring which are the competences that are considered most relevant to support their servitization and digitalization strategies and which are the ones they are willing to acquire. Reliability and validity As hinted before, the research validity and reliability have been achieved through a number of measures taken in the research development. As explained by Yin [70], the data collection and the research design phases are the most crucial to achieve a suitable level of validity and reliability. In this perspective, in addition to the protocal design, we decided to integrate each interview with secondary data retrieved from the companies’ websites, reports and internal documents to triangulate the information collected during the interviews [74]. A specific coding based on the proposed Digital Servitization Model and the competence framework by Hecklau et al. [21] has been conducted. Finally, the interviewed companies have been mapped in the proposed DSM, in terms both of their actual position about servitization and digitalization, and the strategies they will implement in the future. The map shows the main trajectories and supports the analysis of the competences, which companies are developing or acquiring to support the ideal strategy to face the I4.0 challenges. Digital Servitization Model Coping with the increasing complexity of the digital servitization phenomenon matching the technologies’ potentialities concerning the servitization strategies is a research priority. For this purpose, the Digital Servitization Model has been developed to accurately arrange technologies-based service offerings and at depicting associated digital servitization paths. DSM development The model is based on two classification dimensions, as depicted in Table 3, which rely on well-established literature models. The x-axis represents the four smart servitization strategies that can be adopted thanks to digital technologies, which have been presented by Allmendinger and Lombreglia [30]. These four strategies have been widely adopted and discussed in the servitization literature [77,78]. They are distinguished by looking at the product lifecycle, checking out adjacencies, or getting perspective on the whole opportunity [77]. The first strategy, called “Embedded innovator”, represents the most product-centric perspective and consists of introducing connectivity in the product to get data and information useful to provide additional services. The second strategy, named “Solutionist”, searches for new business opportunities in activities performed in the whole lifecycle of the product or concern adjacencies. “Aggregator” and “Synergist” strategies take advantage of products’ connectivity to network information from different sources and offer services based on a high-value body of data. The distinction between them relies on their different data management approaches. In the case of “Aggregator”, the service provider makes available its own device data for a third-party usage (for instance, for global optimization); conversely, “Synergist” strategy leverages on data from different sources to provide functionality to other devices as well actively. The y-axis includes capabilities that are endowed with smart products, grouped in four incremental stages, as presented by Porter and Heppelmann [42]. Literature extensively supports this classification [79– 81]. The first step, “Monitoring”, includes the products' capabilities related to the real-time communication of the information about their location and condition. In the second step, “Control”, the product is embedded with software that allows product functions’ remote control. DSM verification Starting from the analysis of the two dimensions chosen for the DSM, the model was verified by evaluating the possibility of filling each intersection between the two axes with service offerings already described in the literature. The literature examples have been used to provide a more coherent definition of each box of the model, according to real applications of digital servitization in industrial companies. Therefore, an iterative process for filling the DSM with suitable definitions has been conducted, both based on the axes definition and involving a literature search about applications. In Table 4, the resulting DSM is represented, while in Table 5 the most representative literature examples used to define the DSM are reported. First, it was found that by definition, some boxes are inconsistent: smart product capabilities included in the “Autonomy” level cannot be reached in the first two strategies, “Embedded Innovator” and “Solutionist”. One of the main assumptions reported by Porter and Heppelmann [42] is that autonomous operations and self-configuration are directly influenced by the possibility of coordinating with external products and systems, while in the “Embedded Innovator” and “Solutionist” strategies, the focus is on the single product and adjacent activities of the product lifecycle. In this case, communication and coordination with other devices are excluded. For these reasons, the two boxes that represent the abovementioned intersections are not considered available to classify digital service offering. Second, literature case studies and application examples concerning real offerings of service providers have been identified and classified according to the model dimensions (Table 5). As reported in the methodology, the examples reported in Table 5 have also been used to refine the definition of the DSM proposed in Table 4. In general, several applications of these offerings refer to the shift from traditional maintenance services to advanced services, such as preventive maintenance, based on monitoring and control of product data. In this field, literature presents many examples of machine producers, which exploits the possibility of retrieving data from products to acquire knowledge about the customer’s usage and provide customised services. In recent years, it emerges that companies adopted monitoring and control technologies widely to improve their products, pursuing a smart service strategy, which fits with the “Embedded Innovator” and “Solutionist” strategies, focusing only on products and related activities’, such as maintenance operations. Companies have recently started to approach the cloud technologies’ potentialities to make all collected data from digital ecosystems available and use them to support analytics and, consequently, improve decision-making. Finally, few cases in literature present applied technological solutions that can be identified under the “Autonomy” capability, proposing a theoretical framework for self-aware and self-maintaining machines to explore the feasibility of such service solutions. It is worth noticing how, along with these two main paths, it is possible to depict a combined horizontal-vertical trajectory, consisting of a joint transition towards the “Synergist” strategy and the “Autonomy” capability. Instead, merging the two paths can bring major benefits to companies because each path can take advantage of the improvement in the other path’s direction. For instance, while developing optimization strategies for product utilization, it could be better to include in the optimization model data which are external to the product itself (e.g., data about customers, location, etc.). However, this is not possible since the company adopts an “Embedded Innovator” or “Solutionist” strategy, while it could be very profitable to draw data from an ecosystem.
