Therefore, dynamic capabilities are introduced as another perspective on competitive advantage.Teece et al. (1997) defined “dynamic capabilities” as follows. The term“dynamic” refers to the capacity to renew competences so as to achieve congruence with the changing business environment. The term“capabilities” emphasizes the key role of strategic management in appropriately adapting, integrating, and reconfiguring internal and external organizational skills, resources, and functional competences to match the requirements of a changing environment. To delineate the difference between RBV and dynamic capabilities,Wang and Ahmed (2007)hierarchical depiction of competitive advantage is used. It is stated that Resources (assets) are the foundation and can be a source of competitive advantage when demonstrating the four necessary conditions for sustaining competitive advantage. However, in dynamic market environments, such resources do not persist over time and hence cannot be a source of sustainable competitive advantage. Therefore, there is a need for“capabilities”, which are to result in improved performance, whenfirms demonstrate the ability to deploy resources to attain a desired goal and also for“core capabilities”, which are the ones that are strategically important to the enterprise. Though, when the core capabilities become obsolete due to the changes in the environment, it can create a competency trap (Levitt and March, 1988). Hence, dynamic capabilities are introduced as a constant pursuit of the renewal, reconfiguration and re-creation of resources and capabilities to address the environmental change and are seen as the“ultimate” organizational capabilities that are conductive to long-term performance. As already seen, servitizing within an MSE has a positive effect on an enterprise’s competitive advantage. The output of the Big Data Strategy framework in servitization comprises data and information which, from the RBV perspective, represent, for a manufacturing enterprise, new assets and resources, which can potentially have the four characteristics needed for sustained competitive advantage. Data are generated by the virtualization procedure, by management of I/T assets and by automatic collection during the P–S usage. Some of those I/T assets will be used to compose new P–S, where some core assets will be owned by only one specific MSE partner and, due to factors like causal ambiguity ( Reed and Defillippi, 1990), will be imitable only with difficulty and, finally, where there is otherwise no direct substitute for such an asset. The information generated during the exploitation phase, as the result of data analysis, also constitutes new assets. Compared with a manufacturing enterprise that is servitizing without generating and exploiting the Big Data, it has greater potential to sustain competitive advantage. However, the Big Data Strategy framework does not provide only static assets, but also processes to constantly generate new assets and to exploit them, hence to give them value. The need to compose a new P–S or to ideate or simply to reconfigure an existing P–S can come from the analysed information that has been collected during the P –S usage. This means that the manufacturing enterprise can quickly predict and sense the changes in consumption habits, needs or simply optimize its P– S to maximize revenues. Consequently, the Big Data Strategy framework undergird the dynamic capabilities of a manufacturing enterprise to reconfigure, more quickly and more efficiently, its capabilities (core or non-core) in congruence with the need of a dynamic environment. However, reaching congruence with the environment does not indicate that a manufacturing enterprise must solely follow the existing needs of the market, thus innovating incrementally and being too path dependent. Hence, from a Schumpeterian perspective, a manufacturing enterprise should also innovate radically in order to create new needs and not just follow existing ones. The MSE, in relation with the informatization process, provides to each partner the possibility to combine different resources with different needs, thus improving the possibility to step out of path dependency. 7. Discussion and paths for future research Generating profitf r o mP–S is not self-standing, especially if taking into account the servitization paradox (Neely, 2008). Nonetheless, more and more manufacturing enterprises are servitizing their products and in the future there will be a need for a new evolvement of the servitization strategy. One such possibility is proposed herein. Through the article we have shown that the hypothesis of this article is accepted, meaning that Big Data exploitation can be the next step of the value creation after a manufacturing enterprise has servitized its products within an MSE. Understandingly, it does not mean that servitization and the exploitation strategies as integrated within the Big Data Strategy framework exclude each other, but conversely they do reinforce each other. The more a manufacturing enterprise servitizes its products, the more users they have, the more data can be collected and information exploited through resell and/or reuse. Thus, a novel hierarchy of bases for competitive advantage, from a servitization perspective, is proposed: (a) a manufacturing enterprise servitizes standalone or with ad hoc partners; (b) servitization within an MSE; (c) servitization within an MSE applying a Big Data Strategy framework. This means that a manufacturing enterprise do not differentiate itself solely d on the basis of its products, nor of the services that are related to the products (P–S), but foremost on the type of Big Data exploitation strategies and their efficient incorporation into the servitization process, so to spur the most important of the Big Data’s five “Vs”—Value. The limitations of this work are at least twofold. First, although some parts of the Big Data Strategy framework in servitization have already been operationalized successfully within industry, the entire model still rests a conceptual one. To avoid potential fallacies, rigorous theories have been employed and conceptual simulation performed in stages. Second, one of the most relevant impediments for effective utilization of Big Data for supporting decision making arises from “organizational silos”, meaning that data are connected to certain organizational functions and are often not made available to the other departments within the organization. If there is a problem in the data flow inside an enterprise, than the question is how theflow of Big Data would behave between multiple partakers and organizations. Strict regulations and governance would have to be put in place, however this perspective is not within the scope of this article. 8. Digital servitization, which represents the transition from providing products to offering smart product-service systems, is currently seen as a black box by companies confronting them with major challenges. Current literature has not yet investigated which capabilities are required for the development and provision of smart PSSs. To address this gap, an exploratory multiple case study was performed using semi-structured interviews with 18 representatives of four manufacturing companies and six representatives of companies in a supporting role. A socio-technical systems perspective was adopted to cover the interconnectedness and complementarity of internal and external elements relevant for providing a smart PSS. The study identified 46 capabilities of digital servitization to offer and perform smart PSSs and systemically classified these within the dimensions of the socio-technical systems theory, thus providing companies with numerous insights into successful digital servitization. The re - sults contribute to the practical and academic understanding of digital servitization by outlining capabilities to offer and perform smart PSSs and providing support for the use of socio-technical systems theory to frame these capabilities systematically. 1. Introduction The increasing societal discourse and demand for sustainable goods and solutions as well as disruptive events such as COVID-19 puts pres - sure on manufacturing companies to innovate their offerings, processes, and business models ( Ruggieri et al., 2016 ; Sousa-Zomer et al., 2018 ; Chen et al., 2019 ; Schuh et al., 2019 ; Dolgui et al., 2020 ; Ivanov, 2020 ). Two major intertwined trends currently affect companies in this respect: Industry 4.0 and servitization ( Frank et al., 2019b ). Industry 4.0 aims for higher efficiency and productivity levels and represents the first key topic that is widely discussed in current literature ( Kusiak, 2018 ; Luthra and Mangla, 2018 ; Okorie et al., 2018 ; de Sousa Jabbour et al., 2018 ; Chen et al., 2020b , 2020a ; Ghobakhloo, 2020 ; Yu et al., 2021 ). Tech - nological advances such as big data and analytics, the Internet of Things, cloud computing, robotics, 3D printing, and automated guided vehicles mark this new paradigm shift ( Rü ß mann et al., 2015 ; PwC, 2016 ; G ölzer and Fritzsche, 2017 ; Roden et al., 2017 ; Chiarini et al., 2020 ). Machines, equipment, and products form smart systems that are interconnected and can adapt in order to respond quickly and flexibly to market changes, manufacture customized products, shorten development pe - riods, and reduce waste ( Lasi et al., 2014 ; Wei et al., 2017 ; Frank et al., 2019b ). The emergence of Industry 4.0 and its underlying technologies has also fueled the servitization of manufacturing companies ( Bustinza et al., 2015 ; Frank et al., 2019b ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Chiarini et al., 2020 ; Culot et al., 2020 ; Tian et al., 2021 ). The term ‘servitization ’ was coined by Vandermerwe and Rada (1988) and describes the transition from being a traditional product provider to offering customer-oriented ‘bundles ’ of goods, services, support, and knowledge ( Paschou et al., 2020 ). Through these product-service systems (PSSs; Tukker, 2004 ; Pirola et al., 2020 ), manufacturers are able to differentiate themselves from their competition and build an advantage ( Kastalli and van Looy, 2013 ; Qi et al., 2020 ). To jointly consider both servitization and In - dustry 4.0, we use the term digital servitization ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Paschou et al., 2020 ). Despite the theoretical promises of servitization in general and suc - cessful practical examples of servitization projects such as IBM, Alstom, and Rolls-Royce ( Davies et al., 2006 ; Spohrer, 2017 ), many companies struggle with the transition to service-oriented business models ( Finne et al., 2013 ; Kowalkowski et al., 2015 , 2017 ; Lütjen et al., 2017 ) and still see servitization as a black box ( Coreynen et al., 2018 ; Kamal et al., 2020 ), leading to various difficulties. As a result, recent research has examined servitization from numerous perspectives ( Reim et al., 2015 ; Uuskoski et al., 2018 ; Schuh et al., 2019 ; Dmitrijeva et al., 2020 ; Koh - tam äki et al., 2020 ; Riesener et al., 2020 ; Schuh et al., 2020 ; Feng et al., 2021 ; Kim and Lee, 2021 ; Koz ł owska, 2021 ). One major research theme concerns an organization ’ s capabilities ( Raddats et al., 2019 ; Kamal et al., 2020 ), defined as “ complex bundles of skills and accumulated knowledge, exercised through organizational processes that enable firms to coordinate activities and make use of their assets ” ( Day, 1994 , p. 38). Several studies have been conducted on capabilities in the context of servitization (e.g., Ceci and Masini, 2011 ; Storbacka, 2011 ; Parida et al., 2015 ; Raddats et al., 2015 ; Gebauer et al., 2017 ; Kanninen et al., 2017 ; Story et al., 2017 ; Hasselblatt et al., 2018 ; and Jovanovic et al., 2019 ), showing significant progress regarding the understanding of the neces - sary capabilities. However, the advent of digital servitization has created new challenges. Not only has a digital component been added, which increases the efforts necessary for the coordination of service, product, and digital components, but service delivery is also increas - ingly approached from a collaboration and network perspective that crosses company boundaries ( Lusch and Nambisan, 2015 ; Frey et al., 2019 ; Marx et al., 2020 ). Within this perspective, value is created in intra-organizational systems of actors – consisting of providers, cus - tomers, and additional actors – who provide resources, interact with each other, and maintain complex relationships of collaboration and competition ( Kohtam äki and Rajala, 2016 ). Recently published articles have advocated for more consideration of the digital perspective ( Lenka et al., 2017 ; Hasselblatt et al., 2018 ; Huikkola et al., 2020 ) and for viewing service-offering organizations as systems embedded in higher-order networks or systems ( Jovanovic et al., 2019 ; Lütjen et al., 2019 ; Raddats et al., 2019 ). Still, research on digital servitization, especially in the business-to-business context, is in its infancy ( Frank et al., 2019b ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Paschou et al., 2020 ; Gebauer et al., 2021 ). This study aims to contribute to current research on the capabilities organizations must develop in the course of digital servitization to offer and perform smart PSSs. In addition, we paint a portrait for companies of what to expect at the end of digital servitization - including altered processes, organizational structures, strategy, and the business model in general - to better prepare, track, and verify the progress and outcome of the transition. This study investigates the following research question: What capabilities does a company need to develop in the course of digital servitization to offer a smart PSS, and how can these be structured into systemic thinking? To answer this question, an exploratory multiple case study is used. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 18 representatives of four companies that offer several smart PSSs, in addition to six repre - sentatives of companies in a supporting role ( Yin, 2017 ). To systemati - cally cover capabilities of digital servitization - including social and organizational capabilities - from a systemic perspective, we adopt the socio-technical systems lens initially proposed by Trist and Bamforth (1951) . This perspective facilitates the consideration of the intercon - nectedness and complementarity of internal and external elements relevant for providing a smart PSS ( Voss and Hsuan, 2009 ; Alter, 2012 ), focusing on the complex interplay between human agents and resources such as technologies and physical assets ( B öhmann et al., 2014 ). The applicability of the socio-technical system as theoretical underpinning has already been confirmed in numerous studies and scientific contexts, such as multiplatform ecosystems ( Zhang and Williamson, 2021 ), in - dustry 4.0 technologies ( Kumar et al., 2022 ), new energy vehicles ( Wu et al., 2021 ), digital multimedia broadcasting ( Shin, 2006 ), urban water sector ( Fuenfschilling and Truffer, 2016 ), or e-governance systems ( Kompella, 2017 ). Hence, the contribution of this study to academic research is twofold. Firstly, we contribute to the recent research stream on digital serviti - zation. Since research on digital servitization is still limited ( Frank et al., 2019a ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Paschou et al., 2020 ; Gebauer et al., 2021 ), this article provides exploratory research based on case studies and investigates capabilities of digital servitization. Secondly, the study uses a socio-technical systems perspective to understand digital servi - tization. This perspective provides digital servitization literature with an expanded view of smart-PSS-based business models as socio-technical systems and considers both the interactions between social and tech - nical components as well as the embedding of the system into the environment. In this way, we respond to Sony and Naik ’ s (2020) call by extending the theoretical insights of socio-technical systems with empirical findings and connecting a theoretical foundation with the problems faced by decision-makers in the real world ( Kowalkowski et al., 2017 ; Li et al., 2020a ). The study is structured as follows. After giving an overview of digital servitization and socio-technical systems theory, the research method - ology is described. A case study in the manufacturing industry is carried out, and the results are presented in Chapter 4, followed by the discus - sion and conclusion in Chapter 5. 2. Theoretical foundations 2.1. Servitization, Industry 4.0, and digital servitization For decades, the shift from product-centric to service-centric busi - ness models has been an important market strategy for manufacturing firms ( Visnjic et al., 2018 ; Chiarini et al., 2020 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ). In this process, companies move away from standalone products to - wards results- or performance-based all-in-one solutions such as main - tenance contracts or operating services ( Windahl and Lakemond, 2010 ; Parida et al., 2014 ; Kowalkowski et al., 2015 ; Huikkola and Kohtam äki, 2018 ; Visnjic et al., 2018 ). To describe this phenomenon, Vandermerwe and Rada established the term ‘servitization ’ in 1988, and it has since attracted increasing interest from companies and researchers ( Baines et al., 2017 ). Several definitions have been proposed (e.g., by Vander - merwe and Rada (1988) , Baines et al. (2009) , and Kowalkowski et al. (2012) ), but this paper utilizes the definition of Baines et al., (p. 555) : “ servitization is the innovation of an organizations ’ capabilities and processes to better create mutual value through a shift from selling products to selling product-service systems. ” While servitization de - scribes a transition process, the PSS is the output of this process ( Frank et al., 2019b ). PSSs are marketable combinations of services and prod - ucts that aim to satisfy individual customer needs sustainably and bal - ance environmental, economic, and social factors ( Goedkoop et al., 1999 ; Tukker, 2004 ; Beuren et al., 2013 ; Reim et al., 2015 ). Usually, the share of products and services can vary ( Goedkoop et al., 1999 ; Mont, 2002 ) but, particularly in the industrial sector, there is evidence that the distinction between product and service no longer exists and that new approaches to integrative planning, design, and implementation are necessary ( Mourtzis et al., 2020 ). To highlight this change, some re - searchers use the alternative term industrial PSS (IPSS; Meier et al., 2010 ; Mourtzis et al., 2020 , 2021 ). With Industry 4.0 and the accompanying digital transformation, servitization has gained momentum ( Frank et al., 2019b ; Chiarini et al., 2020 ). Since digital technologies can be dynamically reprogrammed and digital content can be stored, transmitted, processed, and displayed on any digital device ( Waltermann and Hess, 2020 ), content is decoupled C. Thus, the technologies associated with the fourth industrial revolution are leading to a trans - formation of traditional value chains, facilitate the development of innovative products and services, and create completely new business models that enable a higher level of interaction ( Kagermann et al., 2013 ; Adrodegari et al., 2017 ; Bleicher and Stanley, 2018 ; Ustundag and Cevikcan, 2018 ; Horv áth and Szab ó, 2019 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ). New options for results-oriented revenue streams such as pay-per-feature, pay-per-use, or pay-per-output models are only possible in a meaning - ful way by collecting detailed usage data ( Xu, 2012 ; He and Xu, 2015 ; Müller et al., 2018 ). The large amount of behavioral and product usage data can be analyzed using appropriate algorithms and can lead to optimal and sustainable industrial processes ( Frank et al., 2019b ; Pauli et al., 2020 ). New digital channels such as websites and mobile devices present new opportunities for customer interaction ( Coreynen et al., 2020 ). Because of the mutual benefits of servitization and Industry 4.0, recent studies have begun to examine the interplay between the con - cepts and in this context use the term ‘digital servitization ’ ( Opresnik and Taisch, 2015 ; Rymaszewska et al., 2017 ; Martín-Pe ña et al., 2019 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ). 2.2. Digital servitization capabilities Unlike products, services are characterized by their interactive na - ture ( Barras, 1990 ). Services depend on “ people, human behavior, human cognition, human emotions, and human needs ” ( Maglio, 2015 , p. ii) and focus on organizational and human capital factors rather than on physical assets ( Sirilli and Evangelista, 1998 ; Hipp and Grupp, 2005 ; Vargo and Lusch, 2008 ; Gallouj and Savona, 2009 ). As such, smart PSSs require stronger customer and business partner involvement in both development and delivery as well as an understanding of customers ’ needs and circumstances ( Gann and Salter, 2000 ; Fosstenl ø kken et al., 2003 ; Dougherty, 2004 ; Mina et al., 2014 ; Engel and Ebel, 2019 ; Paiola and Gebauer, 2020 ). Because of this, smart PSSs are characterized by greater fuzziness, complexity, and riskiness compared to pure products ( Nijssen et al., 2006 ; Storey et al., 2016 ; Benedettini et al., 2017 ; Schultz et al., 2019 ). Past research has recognized that former product-centric firms need to reconfigure their resource bases (e.g., physical, organiza - tional, and human resources; Barney, 1991 ; Penttinen and Palmer, 2007 ; Ulaga and Reinartz, 2011 ), build new capabilities ( Oliva and Kallen - berg, 2003 ; Gebauer and Friedli, 2005 ; Ceci and Masini, 2011 ; Baines and Lightfoot, 2014 ), and even change their strategy and culture ( Avlonitis et al., 2001 ; Danneels and Kleinschmidt, 2001 ; Schultz et al., 2013 ) for servitization to be successful ( Fliess and Lexutt, 2019 ). Research on capabilities often draws from the resource-based view that emphasizes the significance of valuable, rare, inimitable, and sub - stitutable resources for a company ’ s sustained competitive advantage ( Barney, 1991 ). This positive effect on competitive advantage does not result from resources alone but rather from the appropriate use of re - sources achieved through the application of specific capabilities ( Ulaga and Reinartz, 2011 ). Considering servitization in general, studies have examined established conceptualizations of capabilities, such as dy - namic capabilities ( Kanninen et al., 2017 ; Lütjen et al., 2019 ; Linde et al., 2021 ), operational capabilities ( Gebauer et al., 2017 ), and stra - tegic capabilities ( Ulaga and Reinartz, 2011 ; Huikkola and Kohtam äki, 2017 ). Following a more inductive approach, studies have also devel - oped their own categorizations by referring to service concepts dis - cussed in the literature (e.g., Ceci and Masini, 2011 ; Storbacka, 2011 ; Parida et al., 2015 ; Raddats et al., 2015 ; Story et al., 2017 ; Hasselblatt et al., 2018 ; and Jovanovic et al., 2019 ). For example, Jovanovic et al. (2019) highlight the importance of front-office capabilities such as service customization as well as back-office capabilities such as service process standardization. Parida et al. (2014) identify several global service innovation capabilities and categorize them under collaboration, integration, and orchestration (see also Raddats et al. (2019) thematic review of servitization research streams, including capabilities). More - over, Industry 4.0 has necessitated the development and expansion of digital capabilities ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Coreynen et al., 2020 ) such as the ability to collect and analyze data, which improves interaction with customers and co-creates value with them ( Lenka et al., 2017 ), and adequate knowledge of data security methods ( Horv áth and Szab ó, 2019 ). Articles that offer a combined view of service and digital capa - bilities – which is necessary for digital servitization – are rare. Due to the increasing coordination of products, services, and digital technologies as well as the increasing collaboration between customers and partner companies, several service researchers have taken a network- or (eco-)system-centric perspective on value creation ( Frey et al., 2019 ). These researchers refer to a service (eco)system ( Blau et al., 2009 ; Maglio et al., 2009 ; Alter, 2012 ; Badinelli et al., 2012 ; Lusch and Nambisan, 2015 ; Beverungen et al., 2019 ) as a “ socio-technical system that enables value co-creation guided by a value proposition, ” including “ not only data and physical components, but also layers of knowledge, communication channels and networked actors ” ( B öhmann et al., 2014 , p. 74). This perspective facilitates the consideration of the intercon - nectedness and complementarity of internal and external elements relevant for providing a smart PSS ( Voss and Hsuan, 2009 ; Alter, 2012 ), focusing on the complex interplay between human agents and resources such as technologies and physical assets ( B öhmann et al., 2014 ). At the same time, such a perspective raises the need to re-examine the re - sources and capabilities required for digital servitization, particularly regarding orchestrating resources and activities ( Chandler and Vargo, 2011 ). Accordingly, Raddats et al. (2019) have called for more research on capabilities with a focus on networks. 2.3. Socio-technical systems theory Organizations are complex and need to be studied in their entirety ( Sony and Naik, 2020 ), as Industry 4.0 and related technologies require consideration of all aspects of organizations ( Avis, 2018 ; Li et al., 2020b ), including people and culture as well as processes and technol - ogies ( Clegg, 2000 ; Zhang and Williamson, 2021 ). To understand an organization through a combination of social and technical perspectives that consider behavioral aspects in the development and implementa - tion of technologies, it is necessary to consider digital servitization as a socio-technical system ( B öhmann et al., 2014 ; Zheng et al., 2019 ), hence this paper ’ s use of socio-technical systems theory ( Trist, 1981 ; van Eij - natten, 1998 ; Davis et al., 2014 ; Walker, 2015 ). The socio-technical systems theory extends the views of complexity research, the focus of which is on internal elements such as tools and machines that convert inputs into outputs by considering interrelated social and technical as - pects ( Emery and Trist, 1960 ; Bogg and Geyer, 2007 ). Initially estab - lished by Trist and Bamforth (1951) , socio-technical systems are systems that involve complex interactions between people (i.e., the social com - ponents), machinery (i.e., the technical components), and the environ - mental components of a socio-technical work system. The social dimension focuses on people, relationships, organizations, incentives, and performance measures, while the technical dimension comprises technology, innovation, knowledge, processes, and methods ( Trist, 1981 ; Appelbaum, 1997 ). Both social and technical factors must there - fore be considered when implementing new technologies or business changes ( Cherns, 1976 ; Clegg, 2000 ; Maguire, 2014 ). Since an organi - zation is made up of various interdependent parts that come together in complex ways ( Walker et al., 2010 ), it is essential to consider potential impacts when designing or changing one part of the system; otherwise, systems will be created that limit effectiveness ( van Eijnatten, 1998 ; Sony and Naik, 2020 ). Socio-technical systems theory builds on the social-technical model proposed by Leavitt (1965) , which involves four interacting and coor - dinated dimensions - people, task, structure, and technologies - as important components of an organizational work system. This initial framework was later modified to a six-dimensional interconnected C. Münch et al. These elements are embedded in an external environment consisting of several stakeholders, economic circum - stances, and regulatory frameworks ( Davis et al., 2014 ). Socio-technical systems theory and its associated six-dimensional framework were used as the theoretical underpinning of this paper for several reasons. As outlined, socio-technical systems theory provides a comprehensive framework for examining emerging issues with interre - lated social and technical dimensions. Because service systems include both technical and social components ( B öhmann et al., 2014 ), socio-technical systems theory best describes the development of digital servitization. Additionally, socio-technical systems theory is based on the assumption of an open system ( Baxter and Sommerville, 2011 ); unlike closed systems that have no interactions with the environment, information is effectively shared across boundaries in open systems, especially for service systems influenced by different actors, such as customers, the government, and the legislative environment ( Ng et al., 2011 ; B öhmann et al., 2014 ). Furthermore, socio-technical systems theory has already been applied in Industry 4.0 research studies to investigate similar phenomena (e.g., Davies et al., 2017 ; Avis, 2018 ; Ghaffari et al., 2019 ; Beier et al., 2020 ; Mohamad and Songthaveephol, 2020 ; Sony and Naik, 2020 ; Zhang and Williamson, 2021 ; and Kumar et al., 2022 ). 3. Case selection Using a theoretical sampling approach ( Eisenhardt, 1989 ; Birks et al., 2013 ; Yin, 2017 ), case firms were primarily identified through databases, industry association reports, and newspaper articles. In selecting the firms, the following sampling criteria were applied: (1) the company had to be well established in its market, (2) the smart PSS business model had to have a high maturity level ( Markides and Char - itou, 2004 ), and (3) the company had to belong to the manufacturing sector. Case selection continued until no new information was expected and we reached a point of theoretical saturation ( Eisenhardt, 1989 ). Theoretical saturation was reached when a total of three cases were selected, and the associated interviews conducted. An additional case with one interview was added to confirm theoretical saturation and to verify that no further cases were needed. In total, the final sample consisted of four manufacturing companies, meeting Creswell, (2012) recommendation of four to five cases for case study research and providing an adequate empirical base ( Eisenhardt, 1989 ). 3.2. Data analysis The analysis of data comprised two major steps. Within-case analysis allowed for a deeper understanding of individual company approaches, while cross-case analysis aimed to identify common patterns among the cases. To analyze the data, a systematic coding procedure was used in which the gathered primary and secondary data were analyzed in three consecutive coding cycles by two researchers ( Corbin and Strauss, 2015 ). The process launched with open coding of the interviews and subsequently consolidated the codes into a common coding scheme, with iterative discussion and adjustment of the codes until consensus was reached ( Harry et al., 2005 ). Following Salda ña (2013) , no quan - titative rating was created to measure intercoder agreement because we aimed to obtain comprehensive coverage of the material from multiple perspectives and group consensus. Once group consensus was reached, axial coding followed, which allowed for a deeper understanding of the underlying phenomenon by comparing and identifying relationships between codes ( Corbin and Strauss, 2015 ). In addition, this cycle allowed for better data reliability by grounding the data analysis in theory and refining the concepts. The cycle also involved moving from within-case to cross-case analysis to compare results across cases. In this step of the analysis, we looked for both commonalities and differences between cases. Finally, selective coding was used to identify core cate - gories to which the categories identified in axial coding were system - atically linked ( Corbin and Strauss, 2015 ). Appendix A illustrates our coding procedure as part of the data analysis. In each step, a research team member who was not involved in the first round of data analysis reviewed the identified themes and patterns. Discrepancies in percep - tions between research team members were discussed until a final agreement was reached. For data analysis, Microsoft Excel software was used to reduce and code data ( Kelle, 1997 ; Welsh, 2002 ). Cases were coded in separate spreadsheets, which were then used to further extract the codes and to make comparisons across cases (see Appendix B for within-case analysis). 4. The required capabilities which need to exist at the end of digital servitization are also presented for each dimension. 4.1. Internal perspective 4.1.1. People Several interviewees emphasized the importance of an open mindset among the workforce, which is reflected by the absence of intrinsic barriers to co-creating value: “Employees need to develop a certain mindset where they are open to new things, and they also need to understand that a new business model is not necessarily something negative, it’s just something done differently.” – Interviewee E4 It was also noted that digital affinity is a crucial characteristic of the employees supplemented by a competence shift towards a consulting- oriented skillset, especially in the customer-facing departments; this is also because new structures and departments must be created and have a customer-oriented, cross-functional organizational structure embedded in them. The building of knowledge and skills for developing smart PSSs, including by hiring new employees, was also addressed. Similarly, tar - geted transfer of this knowledge into the organization through employee training was identified as a necessary capability, as outlined in the following quotation: “We need to show its importance, and we also need to train [employees] and get them comfortable with it, with everything from explaining the strategy, the talk track, the KPIs, and the metrics they need to focus on.” – Interviewee B6 In addition to training in one direction, employees should be actively involved in the change process, which has a positive effect on employees’ acceptance and the feeling of appreciation. 4.1.2. Culture Interviewees highlighted that the shift in focus from product to software has meant that agility and agile working methods for speeding up the development of the smart PSS are important capabilities: “So, you must prove it every day, and this, of course, drives us to make our products better every day. This is agility, which is not really a buzz - word but reality.” – Interviewee B4 In this context, customer-oriented value is of central importance to achieving long-term customer loyalty as the provider is also successful through the success of the customer. As one expert emphasized: “With the first subscription contract, we have five years to create so many features and tools that the customer can only get with a subscription that it hurts when they want to stop the subscription afterward.” – Interviewee B1 This process of improvement should be enriched by the consideration of customer feedback. This new approach is accompanied by an error culture, which is particularly significant in the manufacturing sector given its historically long time-to-markets: “It’s better to do something and then apologize later instead of defining everything down to the smallest detail, going through a hundred rounds of coordination, and then never implementing it.” – Interviewee A3 Interviewees in case Alpha also noted that cross-company networking and the sharing of knowledge, open innovation, and inter - nal communication are essential capabilities. Equally important is gen - eration alignment, whereby an understanding of the respective backgrounds and goals of employees must be created to enable effective and efficient collaboration. 4.1.3. Goals Several interviewees emphasized the importance of management commitment, which can only be driven from the top down due to the profound changes for the whole organization, described as follows: “You absolutely need the commitment of a top manager. Grassroots ini - tiatives from the bottom up don’t work.” – Interviewee A1 According to the interviewees and the supplementary material, the target and bonus systems must be geared towards smart PSSs to measure the achievement of objectives. Due to the change from transactional to recurring revenues, the logic of the key performance indicators must be adapted, which also impacts the target system based on the key perfor - mance indicators and the incentivization of employees (bonus system). As one interviewee noted: “Are you going to focus on selling a machine worth five million euros where you get a nice commission, or are you going to focus on selling a € 22,000 piece of software? Where are you going to spend your time?” – Interviewee B2 4.1.4. Processes Both through the interviews and the supplementary material (busi - ness model analysis), the continuous improvement of processes, especially with a cost focus, was identified as a capability. The cost focus is reflected, for example, in the new role of service, which is evolving from a pre - viously strong revenue driver to a cost factor to be minimized: “I have practically made a bet with the customer that I can deliver this output for this price. And whether I do it with these costs or with fewer costs makes a difference for me, not for the customer, who pays the fixed price anyway.” – Interviewee B1 “Times have changed, and less service rather than more service is now good for us.” – Interviewee B5 Other areas also need to be repositioned or expanded during digital servitization. Strengthening customer management was identified as a core component that drives digitalization and process optimization on the customer side to enhance productivity and production efficiency, thereby increasing output. In addition, machinery fleet management is considered necessary to maintain a (global) overview of the assets. The aftermarket sector is also essential as a resource as the reversal of the machines after the end of the contract entails increased complexity: “Once the machine is up and running at the customer’s site, the issue is far from over. When the contract expires, the machine must be collected again, and that’s not the end of it. The machine must be overhauled and then either installed at the next customer site or sold on the aftermarket.” – Interviewee E5 Risk management also gains importance because risk is redistributed in the new partnership and largely shifts customer risks (utilization, failure, supply of commodities/spare parts) to the provider. Regarding consumables and spare parts, the principle of vendor-managed inventory is recommended to ensure transparency regarding consumption and all the associated processes that need to be rebuilt. Service-oriented pricing and billing processes also need to be re-engineered from the ground up and aligned with smart PSSs. The interviews highlighted the opportunity for data monetization, with corresponding processes of data preparation, as well as the acquisition and support of new customers with a will - ingness to pay for data. The aim of the company should be to achieve market transparency through expanded customer data to derive targeted measures for each customer. Continuous change management was considered important for the ongoing transition of processes following digital servitization and should ensure continuous development of the smart PSS. C. Technologies The industrial Internet of Things integration (IIoT) of machines was mentioned both in interviews and in internal company documents as the basis for smart PSSs. To merge the data generated, a digital platform is needed combining the data of different stakeholders: “ The machine generates an infinite amount of data that are available at once and has to be managed. To then process the data in a meaningful way, you need a platform to unite the various stakeholders. ” – Inter - viewee A3 To make the generated data accessible and usable, data analytics tools are an important capability for various processes, such as real-time an - alyses for maintenance: “ There we could get really smart with dashboards, which helped us as a headquarters to be more proactive. ” – Interviewee B2 Contract management tools are mentioned as another essential capa - bility for keeping an overview of various customer agreements. 4.1.6. Infrastructure In terms of infrastructure, the interviews revealed the use of existing resources in the first step, especially regarding the cost factor. One expert explained: “ Trying to take what you have so as not to build up unnecessary costs. ” – Interviewee G3 It was also noted that increasing customer orientation should result in geographic customer proximity , especially regarding service options and service partners, which may be accompanied by centralization of the sales department. Furthermore, open workspaces that enable cross-functional collabo - ration were recommended. 4.2. External perspective 4.2.1. Stakeholders Digital servitization is accompanied by new customer segments through customers gained by data monetization. Within the existing customer base, it is essential to have customers who are involved as lead users and who thus contribute to further development through feedback, highlighted by one expert: “ It is necessary to have customers who bring a certain flexibility and are willing to help the products mature; in other words, the customers serve as guinea pigs. ” – Interviewee E1 In addition to new customer groups, interviewees highlighted the value of support through new key partners , such as banks, insurance providers, information technology service providers, and consultancies. An interviewee observed: “ An ecosystem is developing in which a wide variety of actors are joined together. In this ecosystem, there is a certain prosumer mentality, which means that one moment they [a company] are offering the machine, acting as sellers, and the next moment they are buying the data analysis and acting as buyers. ” – Interviewee A1 Best practice sharing within the ecosystem emerged as an important capability whereby actors contribute specialized knowledge from different subject areas and from other ecosystems in which they are active. 4.2.2. Economic circumstances From the perspective of the interview partners, pre-financing of the machines poses a central challenge that must be solved. Pre-financing should be negotiated with a financier or machinery operator who con - siders the machines within a balance sheet; the resulting transparency of this operation raises the possibility for the manufacturer to increase financial security for the financier. As one expert described: “ This additional step means we have to take things on our own books. How do I get these things off my books? Well, maybe by just giving the financier a little more security beyond the security of the machine that they ’ ve always had. I ’ m saying watch out, you can see or drive this customer a lot more on sight like in the past. ” – Interviewee B4 Interviewees also stated that digital servitization aims at further serving customers and moving in the direction of recurring revenue; as such, shareholder commitment is crucial. 4.2.3. Regulatory frameworks Interviewees highlighted the importance of clear regulations regarding data ownership , highlighted by one expert as follows: “ The whole system only works with the machine data because the manufacturer or operator always needs data such as temperature, oscil - lation, current consumption, and so on. However, the question then be - comes who owns the data at all – do they belong to the user, the operator, or to a third party? ” – Interviewee E2 Furthermore, the interviewees and the internal documents empha - sized the provision of mechanisms to guarantee data security . In addition to the topic of data, the experts believed that clear regulations are necessary regarding the warranty for the machines. An expert pointed out: “ We are talking about a total package – from repair to rework to war - ranty issues. With a warranty, a defective part must be replaced. The supplier is no longer in the supply chain at all, but we are obliged to find a replacement. ” – Interviewee D1 5. Discussion and conclusion Digital servitization is still seen as a black box by many companies, especially regarding the capabilities needed to achieve digital serviti - zation. In light of this research gap, our paper aimed to extend the literature by investigating the capabilities of digital servitization that firms need to develop smart PSSs. Using an exploratory multiple case study, 18 semi-structured interviews were conducted with representa - tives from four companies offering multiple smart PSSs, and six addi - tional interviews were executed with representatives from supporting companies. To cover capabilities of digital servitization, including social and organizational capabilities, from a systemic perspective, we grounded our research in socio-technical systems theory. This perspec - tive facilitates the consideration of the interconnectedness and complementarity of internal and external elements relevant for providing a smart PSS ( Voss and Hsuan, 2009 ; Alter, 2012 ), focusing on the complex interplay between human agents and resources such as technologies and physical assets ( B öhmann et al., 2014 ). 5.1. Theoretical contributions The contributions of this study are twofold First, our study is one of the first to provide a structured empirical investigation of digital servi - tization. As digital servitization is still a recent phenomenon, the research focus of existing literature has mainly been on servitization in general and has not specifically considered the digital dimension (e.g., Ulaga and Reinartz (2011) ; Huikkola and Kohtam äki (2017) , and Huikkola et al., (2020) ). Of the studies that do address digital serviti - zation, they have largely concentrated on conceptual approaches (e.g., Kohtam äki et al., (2019) , and Pirola et al., (2020) ), and little in-depth empirical evidence exists regarding digital servitization (e.g., Lenka et al., (2017) , Gebauer et al., (2017) , and Hasselblatt et al., (2018) ). In this study, we examined four real-world cases to open the black box of C. Münch et al. We complement existing research by deepening the discussion of digital capabilities as part of servitization, outlining the impact of In - dustry 4.0 on business models, and identifying which capabilities are needed to successfully navigate digital servitization ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ). Our results confirm the findings of existing studies regarding the capabilities needed for digital servitization. Like Lenka et al., (2017) , we identified customer value, customer-centric solutions, and customer integration as important capabilities, and our findings support Hasselblatt et al., 2018 emphasis on key customers, top management commitment, the use of pre-existing structures, cross-functional teams, and open innovation as essential capabilities. Compared to capabilities in the setting of traditional (non-digital) servitization (e.g., Gebauer et al., 2017 ; Huikkola and Kohtam äki, 2017 ; Kanninen et al., 2017 ; Jovanovic et al., 2019 ; and Lütjen et al., 2019 ), our findings indicate that digital servitization capabilities do not replace or contradict the traditional ones. Instead, they would complement them or lead to a more efficient application. In this sense, some digital ser - vitization capabilities are identical to their traditional counterpart (e.g., Fig. 3. Beyond this, new capabilities must be established during digital servi - tization. This observation is in line with other digital servitization studies that conceptualize digital servitization as an extension or natural progression of servitization ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ). On the one hand, traditional servitization capabilities are expanded by Industry 4.0 ca - pabilities (e.g., digital affinity, data security, and IIoT integration) that apply to industrial enterprises that digitalize their products and process without the adjustment of their business model ( Lenka et al., 2017 ; Horv áth and Szab ó, 2019 ). On the other hand, capabilities are acquired that are only relevant in the combination of Industry 4.0 and servitiza - tion (e.g., machinery fleet management and machinery operators). Second, our research contributes to the increasing body of knowl - edge regarding capabilities and digital servitization (e.g., Kohtam äki et al., (2019) ) by adopting a socio-technical systems perspective to examine the interrelationships between social, technical, and environmental issues. While a few studies have investigated the different capabilities needed for digital servitization (e.g., Lenka et al., (2017) ), there is no overarching classification of these capabilities. We based our research on the assumption that a smart PSS should be seen as a socio-technical system ( B öhmann et al., 2014 ; Zheng et al., 2019 ). In this way, we strengthened the robustness of our smart PSS research by linking theory (i.e., socio-technical systems theory) to the problems that business practitioners face in the real world ( Kowalkowski et al., 2017 ; Li et al., 2020a ). We thus go beyond the technically oriented perspective of digital servitization and focus on the interrelationships between technology and the social and organizational environment. Our findings demonstrate that technical changes transcend domain boundaries and have an impact on other domains inside and outside a company. This observation is in line with the existing literature on service science, which depicts service systems as complex socio-technical systems that enable joint value creation through the configuration of actors and re - sources ( Ng et al., 2011 ; B öhmann et al., 2014 ). However, this under - standing of service systems has not yet been applied in research on digital servitization capabilities. In this spirit, our case study revealed the importance of new capa - bilities related to the social dimensions of goals, people, and culture. For example, internal communication as well as error culture were mentioned as important cultural capabilities of digital servitization. Both capabilities provide employees with a certain degree of confidence through information and latitude without restricting creativity. In terms of people, digital affinity and a competence shift were identified as essential capabilities of digital servitization. In the dimension goals, we also found that a new or changed KPI logic as well as new target systems are an important capability of digital servitization. In the technical dimension of the socio-technical system perspective, our findings imply that successful digital servitization requires a process-centric way of working. More specifically, we found that digital servitization is associated with a variety of new processes, such as risk management, customer management, and processes regarding the aftermarket. This finding was also noted by Horv áth and Szab ó (2019) in the general context of Industry 4.0. Additionally, Paiola and Gebauer (2020) and Pirola et al., (2020) observed that change to organizational processes is necessary in the context of digital services. Our results also extend previous research in the area of capabilities of digital servitiza - tion by showing that digital technologies cannot be seen solely as re - sources. Previous studies have often assumed that digital technologies, such as the Internet of Things, cloud computing, and data analytics, are resources for the development of a smart PSS (e.g., Belvedere et al., (2013) , Ardolino et al., (2016) , Coreynen et al., (2017) , Ardolino et al., (2018) , and Hasselblatt et al., (2018) ). However, these studies neglect the fact that these technologies also require new capabilities in addition to existing technological capabilities. Our results confirm the impor - tance of certain pre-existing capabilities. For example, in line with Lenka et al., (2017) , we identified the need for a company to develop capabilities in the area of Internet of Things integration, digital plat - forms, and data analytics. Finally, our results indicate a significant increase in the importance of the business environment, especially regarding the interactions be - tween different stakeholders. The importance of stakeholders results from a company ’ s lack of expertise in driving digital servitization ( Kowalkowski et al., 2013 ; Kindstr öm and Kowalkowski, 2014 ). As technology becomes increasingly complex and industries reach higher levels of maturity ( Müller et al., 2018 ), it is unlikely that such special - ized assets will be owned by one company ( Petrick and Echols, 2004 ). As such, companies must adopt a long-term perspective and collaborate with other companies that have complementary capabilities to achieve value innovation ( Adner and Kapoor, 2010 ; Ren et al., 2013 ; He and Xu, 2015 ; Kafouros et al., 2020 ; Pauli et al., 2020 ). Our findings support the network perspective in numerous respects, from surpassing organiza - tional boundaries to service delivery ( Frey et al., 2019 ). Practical implications Currently, two challenging trends put manufacturing companies under pressure. On the one hand, a growing societal discourse and de - mand for sustainable goods and solutions can be observed ( Ruggieri et al., 2016 ; Sousa-Zomer et al., 2018 ; Schuh et al., 2019 ) that also led to the Sustainable Development Goals defined by the United Nations and implemented by national and international authorities ( United Nations, 2015 ; Mathiyazhagan et al., 2021 ). This flourishing shift towards sus - tainability necessitates that manufacturing companies innovate their products, processes, and business models ( Ruggieri et al., 2016 ; Cal - abrese et al., 2021 ; Gebauer et al., 2021 ). On the other hand, global disruptive events such as the COVID-19 pandemic hit the world in an unprecedented way ( Boccaletti et al., 2020 ). National and international measures such as lockdowns, social distancing, border closures, and quarantines ( Amankwah-Amoah et al., 2021 ) led to the stagnation of business and everyday life activities worldwide and the collapse of entire supply chains ( Rapaccini et al., 2020 ). Supply chains need to become more resilient and search for innovative approaches ( Chen et al., 2019 ; Dolgui et al., 2020 ; Ivanov, 2020 ). Companies that display service-based business models and have invested in digital technologies have been shown to have an advantage in both cases, sustainability ( de Sousa Jabbour et al., 2018 ; Parida et al., 2019 ; Paiola et al., 2021 ) and COVID-19 ( Rapaccini et al., 2020 ; Brem et al., 2021 ; Zhang and Qi, 2021 ). On the one hand, those enterprises can respond quickly and flexibly to market changes, manufacture custom - ized products, shorten development periods, and reduce waste ( Lasi et al., 2014 ; Wei et al., 2017 ; Frank et al., 2019b ). On the other hand, companies assume greater responsibility for their smart PSS through take-back, recycling, and refurbishment, which reduces waste ( Mont, 2002 ; Baines et al., 2007 ). However, manufacturing companies currently see digital servitization as a black box that presents them with major challenges. This study opens this black box and offers several implications for managers of manufacturing companies. First, we provide a list of capabilities of digital servitization resulting in the ability of a company to offer and perform smart PSSs. With this list, we provide managers with a framework to help them prepare their companies for the coming transformation of the manufacturing industry. The framework summarizes the various domains in which companies need to develop capabilities to successfully offer and operate smart PSSs. It can serve as a guide for managers to determine which capabilities are already present in the company to deduce those that need to be estab - lished. Missing or lagging skills are thus systematically identified. With this information as a basis, companies can build up capabilities in a targeted manner. The capabilities presented in this article are not only applicable to sustainability or COVID-19 but are relevant to digital servitization in general. Second, the study demonstrates the importance of considering social aspects in addition to technological components in digital servitization by examining digital servitization from a socio-technical systems perspective and therefore combining numerous internal and external dimensions; this enables managers to access multiple viewpoints. The proposed framework offers an overview of key social, technical, and environmental capabilities, thereby providing managers with the requisite knowledge to derive concrete measures for developing these capabilities. In addition to the technical capabilities, such as a digital platform or IIoT integration, managers must also consider the com - pany ’ s values and culture. The results further highlight that people, in the form of employees, play an equally important role. Companies must prepare employees for digital servitization, for example, by building up the relevant knowledge and skills and changing the mindset of em - ployees. In addition to the internal dimensions, the results also show managers that the corporate environment plays a decisive role, e.g., in the form of stakeholders, which are always taken into account in digital servitization. 5.1.3. Limitations and further research As with any research, this study has certain limitations that open up various opportunities for further research. Firstly, the study only investigated cases of large, multinational manufacturing companies. Transferring the results to the context of small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) is possible, but SMEs often face far more numerous and diverse challenges in adopting digital technologies ( Müller et al., 2018 ). For example, SMEs often fail in implementing Industry 4.0 and present a low level of maturity ( Buer et al., 2021 ). In addition, SMEs usually are financially constrained, mostly lack technical resources and expertise, and have different orga - nizational cultures ( Rafael et al., 2020 ). Due to a varying manifestation of social and technical aspects, e.g., technical, financial, and human resources, knowledge, competencies, as well as an often limited degree of maturity of Industry 4.0, the context for SMEs differs and requires a separate consideration. The situation is similar in the business envi - ronment, as large companies are often involved in value networks and partnerships, while SMEs have some catching up to do here. Secondly, the study identified various capabilities from the case data. The findings both confirm previously identified capabilities and also identify new capabilities. Thus, the results serve as a starting point for further investigations that could be conducted in other organizations and service scenarios to increase generalizability. There is also the possibility of adding a temporal dimension. While this study has iden - tified the necessary skills that must be in place by the end of digital servitization, we have not considered the evolution of those skills. It is clear that certain capabilities are needed from the start, while other capabilities become relevant later in the digital servitization process. Future studies should take this temporal aspect into account and eval - uate the development of different capabilities over time. Similarly, further studies could also analyze and rank the relevance of these ca - pabilities as well as their interrelationships. Thirdly, the study applied the socio-technical systems framework and theorized the roles of the various dimensions internal and external to the organization. Thus, we respond to recent calls in the literature to apply socio-technical systems theory to other research domains ( Davis et al., 2014 ) and demonstrate that this theoretical underpinning is an appropriate approach to explore technologically driven innovation at the systemic level. Nevertheless, some challenges associated with socio-technical systems theory emerge, requiring more detailed inves - tigation in future research. The first challenge is the ongoing develop - ment of technologies and the resulting inter-company use of these technologies. Whereas the results of this study are company-specific and interpreted from the perspective of the participating smart PSS pro - viders, future work should take a broader perspective, as digital servi - tization in general and smart PSSs in particular often involve a range of companies ( Bj ø rn-Andersen and Raymond, 2014 ). A further challenge is the system boundary which needs to be addressed in future studies. The basic assumption is that socio-technical systems are open systems influenced by the environment ( Emery and Trist, 1965 ). This C. Münch et al. However, it is noted that boundary selection is difficult ( Klein, 2014 ), so future studies will need to take a narrower and broader boundary perspective when examining digital servitization and smart PSSs. Specifically, the authors focus on changes in the business model (i.e. the value proposition, the value delivery system and the value capture mechanism) for digital servitization. Once the ecosystem relationships are well aligned, the manufacturer gains value with multiple value capture mechanisms (i.e. efficiency, accountability, shared customer value and novelty).
