Literature review The literature on the feature fatigue effect is divided in two streams, empirical research and theoretical models. In both streams, we identi - fied one main limitation, which consists of the static approach used to investigate the feature fatigue effect. This limitation is clearly evident according to Rust et al. (2006) , who define a feature as “ ..one more thing to learn, one more thing to possibly misunderstand, and one more thing to search through when looking for the thing you want.. ” . Using this definition, Rust et al. (2006) identify the feature fatigue effect in the misperception of the impact of features on consumers ’ utility. When purchasing a product, consumers are fascinated and impressed by the features ’ potential, perceiving that the rich-feature product grants the highest overall utility. These sentiments emerging during the purchasing phase contrast with the discouraging and frustrating sentiments emerging in the usage phase, during which the consumers ’ utility is governed by the product ’ s usability ( Spacey, 2016 ). The latter is compromised by the presence of multiple features, which induces the consumers to understand that adding features increases the usability penalty they end up paying. According to Thompson et al. (2005) , this mechanism created in the consumers ’ minds is called the feature fatigue effect, induces a disaffection due to the product complexity, and leads to negative emotional reactions, such as anxiety and stress, that push the consumers to abandon the use of the product. Therefore, as De Giovanni (2019a) argues, the feature fatigue effect originates from the attempt to R. Cesaretto et al. While the literature offers a rich overview of feature fatigue and its implications for consumers ’ purchasing intentions, one clear element deserves further attention, that is the separation between the purchasing phase (during which the consumers are driven by the enthusiasm of buying a rich-feature product) and the using phase (during which the consumers are driven by anxiety, stress, and dissaffection of using a complex product). The separation between the two moments, purchas - ing before and product usage afterwards, imposes the adoption of a dynamic approach that captures the switch from positive sentiments emerging during the purchasing phase to negative sentiments emerging during the using phase. This separation, which is a critical ingredient, has been fully disregarded by previous research in the feature fatigue effect domain. Therefore, we aim to contribute to the literature by adopting a dynamic approach to feature fatigue that allows us to capture the dynamics behind it. By doing so, we model the effect of feature fa - tigue on the goodwill dynamics (brand value) with the intent to develop an additional definition of feature fatigue. That is, feature fatigue is a dynamic effect, which influences the current business and sales by creating great consumers ’ expectations during the purchasing phase while leading to negative sentiments in the long term, exemplified by the inability to use the full product potential, reluctance to buy such complex products, and decreasing willingness to purchase goods from the same brand. The extant research has estimated the amplitude of the feature fa - tigue effect in terms of possible sales loss. Li and Wang (2011) propose an empirical analysis in which the feature fatigue effect emerges when complex products are offered. By developing an application to the mo - bile phone industry, a Bayesian Network model allows one to detect the major sources of feature fatigue, and the findings suggest to firms which feature to avoid to defeat feature fatigue. By working with the same application, Li, Wang, and Wu (2013) investigate the feature fatigue effect as a multi-dimensional phenomenon that is composed of a cate - gory feature (e.g.. MP3) and some additional features linked to the category features (e.g.. features linked to the category feature MP3 are: A-B repeat features, MP3 splitter, custom equalizer settings, bookmark, and volume limiter). By combining a multi-objective genetic algorithm and a Bayesian Network approach, Li et al. (2013) determine the maximum consumer perceived product ’ s capability and the minimum consumer-perceived complexity. De Giovanni (2019b) proposes the concept of feature-based production capability, which represents the firms ’ capacity to make products with multiple features and options. By using Structural Equation Modeling techniques, he shows that the firms acquiring the feature-based production capability are highly exposed to the feature fatigue effect, which imposes an analysis of the entire busi - ness model to alleviate the negative effect of feature fatigue on perfor - mance. A follow-up study by De Giovanni (2020) estimates the recursive relationships existing between the feature-based production capability and some exogenous forces like the competition and the supply chain network relationships. Hereby, these two external forces impose firms to invest in innovation and technology to acquire fatigue-based production capability. However, the recursive effects existing among these in - gredients intensifies the competition and makes supply chain collabo - ration more challenging, thus inducing a deterioration of the overall sales. Stock (2011) carries out an analysis of the relationship between innovation strategies and customer satisfaction, which is investigated through non-linear estimations. In the analysis of innovative products, Stock (2011) finds that feature fatigue exists when goods are too inno - vative, since customer satisfaction increases linearly in the innovation with a linear term (the linear coefficient is 0.16) as well as with a square term (the square coefficient is 0.19). Accordingly, there exists a parabolic relationship between customer satisfaction and innovation, in which the latter increases to a certain point and then decreases when innovation is too high. Regarding the second stream of research that uses theoretical models, the feature fatigue effect has been characterized by non-linear relationships between features and sales, in which the features are directly linked to investments in quality, innovation, and technology. De Giovanni (2019a) proposes a game theory model based on the feature fatigue effect in a supply chain framework. Feature fatigue is modeled in a static form and instantaneously influences the demand function by using both a linear and a square component, that is, following the empirical results obtained in Stock (2011) . Although firms within a supply chain can initiate some collaborative service-based programs with the expected outcome to alleviate the feature fatigue effect, the presence of servitization can induce an increasing investment in tech - nology and then to a wider feature proposition that makes the feature fatigue effect more prominent. Thompson et al. (2005) argue that feature fatigue can be detrimental to firms, and they would be better off focusing on the product ’ s main features. They propose a quadratic effect of quality (and features) on demand, and the linear effect of quality on sales as well. Accordingly, increasing the number of features can be beneficial up to a certain level; and beyond that, increasing the number of features leads to lower sales and then feature fatigue. Rust et al. (2006) followed a similar approach to study the importance of quality decisions in the long run, compelling firms to discount the possible negative initial effects of technology and innovation investments. To deal with the feature fatigue problem, Chai, Li, Zheng, Wang, and Yu (2014) propose a static optimization model in which capability and complexity are regarded as two conflicting objects. Using a multi- objective optimization algorithm, they search for a Pareto solution that satisfies the maximization objectives of increasing the product capability while minimizing the product complexity at the same time. This combination allows the decision maker to list the features and select the best ones mitigating the feature fatigue effect. Chen, Carrillo, Vakharia, and Sin (2010) propose an optimization model to solve the issue of product fusion, which is exemplified by products embedding too many features and generating issues of feature fatigue along with cannibalization and product proliferation. By developing an algorithm that searches for the best parent-child relationship, Chen et al. The feature fatigue effect consists of a complex phenomenon according to which consumers are very much attracted by the product quality, fea - tures, and technology during the purchasing phase. Accordingly, the higher the number of features and options, the higher the consumers ’ willingness to purchase smart products. At the same time, a smart product, which is highly complicated by default and requires some learning time for consumers, can entail a feature fatigue effect in the long run; that is, when consumers use a smart product, they can realize that the product is very complicated to use because the number of fea - tures embedded in it is not necessary to satisfy their basic needs. These products then create frustration and stress for consumers, who regret the purchase. These uncomfortable situations lead consumers to experience negative feelings and sentiments, including regret about their choices, the desire to return the product, provision of negative feedback on social networks, and reluctance to purchase the product in the future. Thus, smart products can induce increasing sales in the short run due to the product ’ s attractiveness, but they might lead to anxiety and frustration in the long run due to their complexity, difficulty in use, missing knowledge on how to connect with other goods, and technical barriers. Managerial implications Exposure to feature fatigue can considerably compromise modern business models that aim at developing and selling smart products. The latter requires new commitments from all involved parties. On the one hand, consumers need to develop skills and capabilities, change habits, and rethink product usability. On the other hand, companies need to invest in the latest technologies to create smart products that comple - ment their current value proposition with new features, insights, and applications. Overall, releasing smart products can entail serious busi - ness implications if consumers are reluctant to change and update their knowledge and if companies invest in technologies (e.g.. Industry 4.0) without a real plan of action and an analysis of the value proposition. The electronics industry is the best example of smart products that can generate feature fatigue, since technology development has been so rapid and radical that it leaves very little room for consumers to un - derstand the changes and for companies to demonstrate their full po - tential. Clearly, other sectors are also affected by this wave; thus, we mention some recent further applications. In the automotive sector, Tesla launched several projects to develop smart cars enabling autono - mous driving ( Mider, 2019 ); in the agriculture sector, firms use drones and sensors to detect the presence of insects and minimize the use of pesticides ( Song et al., 2019 ); in the energy sector, the National Hy - drocarbons Authority (ENI) developed smart clothes for workers to improve work safety (Safety 4.0 project - www.eni.com ); in the healthcare sector, the use of digital technologies allows consumers to inform and firms to detect the presence of new diseases ( Javaid & Haleem, 2019 ); in the logistics sector, DHL in the Netherlands uses intelligent cobot systems to carry out repetitive jobs faster and more efficiently ( AMFG, 2019 ). These few examples are connected by a digital transformation, which necessitates a change in firms ’ and workers ’ op - erations and routines as well as the development of new skills to use new releases properly. The rebound effect of these smart applications is the feature fatigue effect, which is exemplified by consumers ’ frustration and discouragement with using these high-tech solutions. Since feature fatigue is a serious concern that firms cannot disregard in the era of digital transformation, we formulate two optimal control models to capture these aspects in unique frameworks characterized by technology investments leading to smart products, digital servitization, price, brand value, and the possible business damage from the presence of feature fatigue. Our findings highlight the challenge that firms face when their business is exposed to feature fatigue associated with smart products. Digital servitization is the key to overcoming any negative effects induced by feature fatigue. When digital servitization efforts are combined with pricing and technology strategies, the feature fatigue effect always harms the business. Thus, firms should balance their dig - ital servitization efforts with all implications of pricing and technology for sales, profits, and brand value, resulting in a complex decision- making process that leads to a focus on short-term goals. The latter are exemplified by lowering the technology investments along with the price to enhance sales of traditional products rather than to pursue business through smart products. An alternative available to firms involves setting the digital serviti - zation efforts independent of the pricing and technology strategies to fully mitigate the negative effects induced by feature fatigue. In other words, firms should set a budget to prevent the feature fatigue effect. The latter is present inde - pendent of the real features of the smart products because consumers are reluctant to purchase and use smart products. This is highlighted in several marketing studies ( Rijsdijk & Hultink, 2009 ). Digital servitiza - tion should then support and favor the transaction for digital technol - ogies and remove all barriers between old and new technological paradigms. This policy enables firms to develop successful smart prod - ucts and nullify all negative effects linked to feature fatigue. 8. Conclusions This research introduces a framework in which a manufacturer can develop its business by producing and selling smart products. Con - sumers who are exposed to smart products can be highly attracted by their potential applications during the purchasing phase; however, they can experience feelings of disaffection, frustration, and anxiety during the usage phase, exemplified by the feature fatigue phenomenon. Smart products can be complicated and complex, the interfaces with other devices having different technologies can be problematic, and the core value for consumers can depend more on traditional features (a smart - phone connected to the internet) than on smart features (a smart phone connected to the washing machine). These negative effects can have important implications on the value of brands (goodwill) and thus require ad hoc strategies to be resolved. In this paper, we explore the implications of a digital servitization strategy, through which digital technologies like artificial intelligence services, chatbots, and predictive models support consumers during the usage phase. We explore two optimal control models. In the first model, we allow the manufacturer to observe feature fatigue and then set its optimal strategies. Hereby, we find that digital servitization is not an effective tool to mitigate the issues of feature fatigue. In fact, the manufacturer simply decreases its digital servitization efforts when feature fatigue is prominent, looking for myopic (short-term) gains obtained through traditional actions (decreasing the price increases the sales). In the second model, we allow the manufacturer to search for digital serviti - zation investments that are set independent of the feature fatigue effect. In such cases, digital servitization helps to mitigate the feature fatigue effect and increase profits; thus, it turns out to be a successful strategy. We develop a procedure that allows firms to target profits and adjust their budget spending in digital servitization according to the negative effect induced by feature fatigue. This procedure improves the decision- making process and guides firms to identify the policy to pursue for digital servitization in three cases: When it is not needed, when it serves to mitigate severe effects of feature fatigue, and when it can be used as a flexible decision-making tool to determine whether to target either short- or long-term goals. Although this paper is the first to investigate the feature fatigue effect in the context of smart products, further extensions can be pursued in the future. The manufacturer can interact with upstream and downstream suppliers before reaching consumers. Each supplier can have an impact on technology development as well as on the mitigation of feature fa - tigue by using other levers (e.g.. training, communication campaign, promotion, in-store services). Furthermore, firms compete in developing and selling smart products; therefore, the complexity of smart products can depend on the technology development of the entire industry. Consumers who are attracted by new smart products should make in - vestments to exploit the full potential of these products (e.g.. changing habits, using other products, training). All of these elements can increase knowledge in this frame. Finally, it would be interesting to verify the robustness of these findings by conducting either empirical research or clinical case studies. References AMFG (2019). Tensions in AI-driven digital servitization in the banking industry: a socio-technical view Nirosha Nilmini Sathiskumar and Poul Houman Andersen The Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities, Aalborg University Business School, Aalborg University, Aalborg, Denmark Abstract Purpose – The rapid integration of AI into customer advisory processes has transformed traditional service delivery in the banking industry. There is a critical gap in our understanding of how interactions between structures, banking employees, AI and work tasks in banking socio-technical systems give rise to tensions. Thus, this study explores how interactions and interdependencies between these elements in socio-technical systems manifest tensions in AI-driven digital servitization efforts in customer advisory and sales in banking. Design/methodology/approach – Based on 25 expert interviews with banking employees working in customer advisory and sales, this study offers a multifaceted perspective on emerging tensions in banking, underlined by interactions and interdependencies between structures, people, AI and tasks. Findings – The findings illustrate how interactions and interdependencies in banks’ socio-technical systems manifest four key tensions in AI-driven digital servitization: structural control vs bank employee adaptability, data governance structures vs technology innovation, AI-augmented decision-making vs human intuition in decision-making and role evolution vs job security. Practical implications – This study advances the theoretical understanding of digital servitization by providing a socio-technical system view on emerging tensions in AI-driven digital servitization (DS) in banking. It highlights the complex interactions and interdependencies between technological and social elements that manifest such tensions. Furthermore, the study proposes tension management strategies for managers leading AI-driven DS initiatives in banks to proactively navigate and manage the four tensions. Originality/value – This study provides a comprehensive empirical account of emerging socio-technical tensions in the banking industry due to socio-technical interactions in AI-driven digital servitization. Keywords Socio-technical, STS view, Tensions, AI, Digital servitization, Banking industry, Service industry Paper type Research article Introduction The integration of digital technologies to enhance product and service offerings, known as digital servitization (DS), is spurred by the rapid advancements of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies (Silber et al., 2025; Payne and Peltier, 2020). AI’s unique capabilities to learn, sense, reason, and communicate with users position it as a transformative force in today’s business landscape (Huang and Rust, 2018), offering a wide array of benefits, such as enhanced efficiency, reduced error rates at the operational level, and improved strategic outcomes at the organizational level, thereby bringing a new way of working into the organization (Davenport et al., 2020). Despite its promise, AI-driven DS often fails to deliver anticipated efficiency gains and improvements in employee well-being. Recent research has highlighted the adverse effects of AI integration into work processes, such as job displacement and algorithmic control (Berente et al., 2021; M€ohlmann et al., 2021). Scholars attribute these shortcomings to competing demands among organizational actors, which give rise to tensions that hinder the realization of AI’s potential (Sarker et al., 2019). Tensions, defined as competing demands or contradictions among organizational actors, are salient in DS contexts (Tronvoll et al., 2020; Smith and Lewis, 2011). As a globally standardized but locally regulated industry, such transformations position the banking industry as a compelling context for exploring how AI-driven DS manifests tensions (Smith and Lewis, 2011). Although AI is highly promising for banking, concerns persist around data privacy, regulatory compliance, and the propensity for unintentional biases in decision-making (Moharrak and Mogaji, 2024; Mogaji, 2018). This study seeks to explore how tensions manifest among actors in the banking industry due to AI-driven DS. A context-based understanding of how tensions unfold in banking is essential, as the potential organizational impact and trajectories of change from introducing new technologies vary across industries and manifest differently across organizational roles, reflecting organizational actors’ diverse experiences and expectations (Micallef et al., 2024; Dosi and Nelson, 2010). Hence, we explore how implementing AI technologies in traditional customer advisory and sales processes in banking challenges existing work practices, thereby manifesting tensions (Payne and Peltier, 2020). The following research question guides our study: How do AI-driven digital servitization tensions manifest among employees in customer advisory and sales functions in the banking industry? We incorporate the socio-technical systems (STS) view, which offers a comprehensive lens for understanding the interactions and interdependencies between the technological and social systems of organizations (Orlikowski, 2007; Colombari et al., 2024). It conceptualizes organizations as comprising two interconnected sub-systems: a social and a technical system, where new technologies, work practices, organizational structures, and human actors interrelate, and underscores how the dynamic interactions and interdependencies among these elements mutually shape and transform organizational relationships across job roles and workflows (Orlikowski, 2007; Fischer and Staykova, 2021). Following the STS view, we argue that AI’s disruptive nature triggers tensions in both social and technical systems as employees try to navigate the implications of adapting to new work environments. Tensions surface when AI is used in ways that challenge conventional workflows, areas of expertise, and managerial supervision practices. To explore this phenomenon, we conducted 25 expert interviews with senior managers, middle managers, software developers, branch managers, and customer advisors in the banking industry to gain insights into their experiences with AI-driven DS, exploring how socio-technical interactions and interdependencies in the banking context manifest tensions. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. First, we provide a theoretical background to position the study’s focus. Second, we explicate the research context and the method utilized. We then present and discuss the study’s key findings, and conclude by providing theoretical and managerial contributions, limitations, and suggestions for future research. Theoretical background To offer a systematic conceptualization of how interdependencies between social and technical elements in AI-driven DS in banking give rise to tensions, this section draws on the sociotechnical systems (STS) theory to explicate the nature of organizational tensions. Thereafter, we review relevant literature on tensions in DS and develop a conceptual framework grounded in the STS view that supports illustrating how such tensions manifest in AI-driven DS in banking. Organizational tensions and the socio-technical systems view Organizational tensions reflect the coexistence of intertwined opposites, such as stability vs flexibility, autonomy vs control, and exploration vs exploitation (Farjoun, 2010; Smith and IJBM 44,8 1518 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijbm/article-pdf/44/8/1517/10862271/ijbm-05-2025-0353en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 Tracey, 2016). This coexistence reflects the principles of “contradiction and complementarity,” wherein opposing elements are interrelated and mutually shape each aspect, as described by Gaim et al. (2018) in defining tensions: “relationships between competing demands, forces or logics” (Gaim et al., 2018, p. 3). As underscored in the STS view, organizations consist of two interdependent subsystems—social and technical—that require continuous realignment between the two elements (Orlikowski, 1993). The social system comprises strategic business processes (structures) and people, whereas the technical system comprises technologies and work tasks (Sarker et al., 2019; Orlikowski, 1993). These components interact and mutually shape each other, forming new work routines and transforming relationships, job roles, and workflows across the organization, and tensions manifest when changes in one sub-system challenge the other’s equilibrium (Orlikowski, 2007; Sklyar et al., 2019). For instance, tensions manifest in socio-technical systems when intentional transformation efforts or emergent changes in everyday work disrupt the balance between interdependent social and technical sub-systems. Herein, the STS view offers a comprehensive lens for understanding DS’ complexities (Fischer and Staykova, 2021), bringing to our attention the importance of considering the interplay between the two sub-systems as a dialectical process, thereby transcending beyond technology-deterministic perspectives on organizational change. Digital servitization tensions in socio-technical systems Tensions in DS are especially pronounced in service-driven industries, such as banking, where localized customer responsiveness is critical (T�oth et al., 2022). Structural reconfigurations, such as strategic coordination units, separate service entities, or front/back end splits (Kowalkowski and Ulaga, 2017; Cenamor et al., 2017; Oliva et al., 2012; Davies et al., 2006), enable modularity, customization, and flexible digital solution delivery (Coreynen et al., 2017). However, such configurations also intensify tensions between centralization and decentralization by marginalizing the voices of organizational actors capable of interpreting localized service demands, reinforcing professional identity issues (Bartlett and Beamish, 2018; € Oberg, 2016; Bartlett and Ghoshal, 2000). Recent literature on banking has asserted that such central structures often fail to accommodate contextual knowledge held by frontline employees and regional branches, limiting banks’ ability to respond adaptively to local market demands (Ulrich-Diener et al., 2023). To navigate these frictions, the DS literature stresses the value of employee embeddedness—both structurally within the organization and relationally in customer interactions (Gebauer et al., 2010; Brashear Alejandro et al., 2011). To this end, Diener and � Spa�cek (2021) suggest that inclusive innovation environments within banks empower employee involvement, improve their identification with DS goals, and foster adaptability. Beyond structural dynamics, DS also exacerbates tensions around data governance (Smania et al., 2024a). Data serve as the backbone of DS initiatives (Favoretto et al., 2022), particularly in the banking industry in AI-driven DS initiatives (Mogaji and Nguyen, 2022; Fourie and Bennett, 2019). A key feature of DS is the decoupling of data from physical devices, enabling modular reuse across organizational boundaries (Lusch and Nambisan, 2015). The modular use of data in DS requires cross-organizational partnerships (e.g. digital infrastructure providers, software developers, and third-party technology vendors) and triggers tensions over data ownership, control, privacy, and ethical usage (Smania et al., 2024a; Kahle et al., 2020; Sklyar et al., 2019). While strict data governance structures ensure the regulation of access to data, usability, and security, they limit partnership flexibility and reinforce power asymmetries, as actors with greater access and control may acquire disproportionate bargaining power over others (Dalenogare et al., 2022; T�oth et al., 2022; Korkeam€aki et al., 2022; Visnjic et al., 2022). These types of partnership collaborations with technology firms are salient in banking, where AI-driven DS relies heavily on external technology partnerships, but is constrained by strict data regulations due to the risk-averse nature of the banking industry (Ulrich-Diener International Journal of Bank Marketing 1519 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijbm/article-pdf/44/8/1517/10862271/ijbm-05-2025-0353en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 et al., 2023; Iheanachor and Umukoro, 2022; Barra and Ruggiero, 2023; Diener and �Spa�cek, 2021). The DS literature emphasizes the need for interoperability, accountability, and formal data-sharing protocols among actors involved in data partnership collaborations (Mosch et al., 2021). Nonetheless, evolving regulatory requirements, such as GDPR, and ethical concerns over using customer data for AI solution development and training continue to heighten governance tensions in banking (Moharrak and Mogaji, 2024; Fourie and Bennett, 2019). Studies have highlighted that data-related tensions can spark innovation tensions in DS initiatives (Sj€odin et al., 2023). For instance, in AI solution development, data cleaning and analysis play a vital role in obtaining high-quality, contextually relevant information (Sj€odin et al., 2023). In the banking industry, innovation tensions are further driven by high development costs, AI integration challenges with existing processes, and legacy IT infrastructures that hinder AI compatibility (Mogaji and Nguyen, 2022; Ashta and Herrmann, 2021). To gain a competitive edge in AI, organizations need to balance the exploration (new opportunities) and exploitation (refining existing capabilities) of internal and external data (Clauss et al., 2020; Paschou and Papaioannou, 2023). However, strict data governance hinders these mechanisms by limiting data access for experimentation and slowing down the flow of internal data vital for innovation (T�oth et al., 2022; Andriopoulos and Lewis, 2009). Technology integration into business processes also reshapes decision-making (Grisot et al., 2017; Huang and Rust, 2018). Particularly, integrating AI into business processes reshapes decision-making by replacing tasks once reliant on human judgment, raising concerns over transparency and control (Tekic and F€uller, 2023; Makarius et al., 2020). These shifts generate tensions as employees face uncertainty about job roles and trust in AI systems—especially critical in banking, where trust-based relationships and regulatory demands heighten these concerns (Kokshagina and Schneider, 2022; Sheth et al., 2022; Hentzen et al., 2022; Pirkkalainen et al., 2022). AI tools such as emotion recognition systems raise ethical concerns about surveillance, autonomy, and reduced human interpretation, especially when their logic is opaque to users or decision-makers, emphasizing the need for situational awareness in AI-supported decisionmaking (Boustani, 2022; T�oth et al., 2022; Duggan et al., 2020). The literature on banking has asserted concerns about bias, fairness, and discrimination embedded in AI models that have drawn attention from regulators (Fourie and Bennett, 2019; Lui and Lamb, 2018). To this end, Moharrak and Mogaji (2024) caution that biased AI-driven insights can disproportionately affect employee evaluations, undermining perceived fairness in evaluation systems. Previous DS studies have further asserted how AI-driven decision-making can heighten internal competition by tying performance metrics to individual incentives, which undermines collaboration (Kocabasoglu-Hillmer et al., 2023; Rietveld and Schilling, 2021). Prior studies have emphasized the impact of AI-driven DS on reshaping job roles, responsibilities, and work practices, triggering learning tensions as employees face skill demands alongside fears of losing expertise and professional identity (T�oth et al., 2022; Kohtam€aki et al., 2020; Makarius et al., 2020). Skill gaps further reinforce these concerns, creating uncertainty around job security, task ownership, and the perceived value of work (Axelsson et al., 2024; Rietveld and Schilling, 2021). In banking, such tensions manifest in employees’ limited readiness to work with AI—especially among older employees in customer-facing and back-office roles—due to low AI literacy and inadequate communication from managers about AI’s value for work tasks (Ridzuan et al., 2024; Sheth et al., 2022; Dwivedi et al., 2021). Resistance is further fueled by fears of redundancy in job roles and inconsistent upskilling efforts (Rahman et al., 2023; Lazo and Ebardo, 2023). This is further complicated when AI integration leads to productivity declines or when automation expands task scope without reducing workload (Cagliano et al., 2019; Kopp et al., 2019). Thus, while AI can shift employee focus toward higher-value tasks (Chen et al., 2021; Tronvoll et al., 2020), it also introduces ambiguity, performance pressure, and identity shifts (Jarrahi et al., 2022; Lenka et al., 2018). To this end, Lazo and Ebardo (2023) emphasize that strong leadership, strategic human resources (HR) support, and employee buy-in are crucial IJBM 44,8 1520 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijbm/article-pdf/44/8/1517/10862271/ijbm-05-2025-0353en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 for AI-driven DS in banking, as their absence fuels resistance, especially when upskilling is viewed as a threat rather than an opportunity (T�oth et al., 2022; Clauss et al., 2020). Conceptual framework Building on the above theoretical discussion, we present the following conceptual framework (see Figure 1) to guide our empirical inquiry. It illustrates the two interrelated sub-systems—social (left circle) and technical (right circle)—encompassing the key elements: structures, people, technologies, and tasks. The interactions between these elements are shaped by and shape broader transformation processes. This framework is applied to the banking industry context, where AI technologies are increasingly integrated into customer-facing and operational functions. In the framework, bidirectional (thick) arrows between structures, people, technology, and tasks represent the mutual influence between the elements within each sub-system. For instance, in the technical sub-system, integrating AI into existing work processes (e.g. automation of advisory processes) may influence employees’ work tasks. The two bidirectional arrows (with dashes) illustrate the mutual influence of the four elements between the two sub-systems. For instance, while AI integration influences work tasks and transforms the way existing work is carried out, how employees respond to the transformation may also be influenced by AI (e.g. resistance, adaptation). The shaded area where the two sub-systems intersect signifies the socio-technical interactions in which tensions will likely emerge due to the aforementioned interactions and interdependencies between the four elements. It represents the space where social and technical elements converge and compete (see Figure 1). Research design We based this study on semi-structured interviews with industry experts. The objective of conducting semi-structured interviews was to gain broader industry insights on emerging tensions due to AI implementation in socio-technical systems of banking institutions, allowing us to provide an enriched understanding of the tensions associated with DS. Given the novelty of DS (Raddats et al., 2022) and AI-driven digitalization research in banking, it is feasible to base this study on expert interviews. Experts have technical, process, and interpretative knowledge about their areas of expertise, and possess deep knowledge about specific experiences due to their job responsibilities and obligations within the organization (Bogner et al., 2009). This method also enables the recognition of implicit knowledge in a specific field or domain, which might be challenging to collect by employing quantitative data collection techniques, such as surveys (Mergel et al., 2019). Similar methodological approaches have been adopted in recent banking studies to explore AI-driven DS in banking (Moharrak and Mogaji, 2024; Diener and �Spa�cek, 2021). This approach further aligns with the core assumption held in the STS view by garnering insights into how actors in different job roles engage with and make sense of AI based on interactions and interdependencies between structures, people, tasks, and technology. Expert selection Selecting participants with substantial insights into AI strategizing and operational implementation at both the strategic and operational levels in the banking industry was crucial for ensuring the study’s internal validity. We were mindful to include employees working in banking, such as senior managers overseeing AI implementation initiatives, middle managers and software developers involved in the development of AI solutions (internally to the banks or externally as partners), and end users utilizing AI tools in local customer advisory roles in the banks’ front and back offices. We employed an information-oriented sampling technique to choose the most relevant participants for the study. Information-oriented selection of interview subjects allows the researcher to select participants based on their significance to the study. First, we utilized our LinkedIn network to identify relevant subjects based on their job descriptions and work experience (more than 2 years), and identified 35 experts. We then contacted these experts on LinkedIn messaging, explaining the purpose of our study and inquiring about their willingness to participate, and 25 confirmed their interest in participating. The majority of the interviewees (21 out of 25 interviewees) are employed in the Danish banking industry, representing three large retail and commercial banks [1]in Denmark. Data collection On average, each interview lasted between 45 min and one hour. After obtaining the experts’ verbal consent to ensure data privacy, all the interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim. Our theoretical pre-understanding of tensions in STS guided our conversations with the interviewees. An interview guide helped navigate the interviews and ensured that we gathered comparable data from all interviewees. The first part of the interview guide consisted of introductory questions about the experts’ background—e.g. current work position, previous work experience, etc.—and the second part contained questions regarding AI tools integrated into customer advisory and sales, as well as the internal work processes of employees and challenges associated with using these technologies, particularly regarding employees’ adaptation to the changes brought forth by AI into their work routines. The semi-structured approach allowed us to dig deeper when interviewees revealed interesting insights. We also used follow-up questions to obtain further information and to clarify interviewees’ perspectives. As illustrated in Figure 5, structural rigidity negatively influences front- and back-office banking employees’ readiness to adopt AI effectively in their daily work, highlighting the tension between efficiency-driven AI rollouts and practical usability (Ridzuan et al., 2024; Sheth et al., 2022; Kohtam€aki et al., 2020). This reinforces a key contradiction: while top management aims to standardize and control AI implementation to ensure efficiency and strategic alignment, employees are left to integrate these technologies into their workflows with minimal guidance or support. The absence of clear guidelines, training, or follow-up mechanisms has led branch managers and customer advisors to self-experiment with AI tools. As indicated in the data analysis, they spend working hours learning basic functionalities of the implemented AI tools, preventing them from fully realizing the systemic benefits envisioned by the AI hubs. Several interviewees also noted that they use AI tools for personal tasks or casual exploration, as the tools appear only marginally relevant to their core responsibilities, underscoring learning-related contradictions in AI-driven DS in banking (Lazo and Ebardo, 2023). This has led to uneven adoption patterns, where centrally controlled AI implementation does not necessarily facilitate employees’ practical needs and expectations. By adopting a socio-technical systems (STS) lens, the findings reveal four empirically grounded tensions uniquely experienced by banking employees in different job roles. We illustrated that these tensions are not abstract organizational challenges but deeply embedded in the banking industry’s highly regulated, relationship-driven, and risk-sensitive context. Structural control vs bank employee adaptability: misalignment between strategic goals and operational execution Our findings revealed a misalignment between banks’ centralized AI implementation strategies and the operational realities of employees in customer advisory and sales. Aligned with the socio-technical systems perspective (Fischer and Staykova, 2021; Feenberg, 2006), we illustrated that centralized AI hubs—established to drive strategic alignment and efficiency in AI implementation within banks—often exclude key actors, such as customer advisors and IT professionals, whose role-specific expertise is vital for effective AI implementation decisions. This finding mirrors the perspectives offered by Kowalkowski and Ulaga (2017) and Davies et al. (2006), who argue that organizations engaging in DS often establish strategic coordination units to streamline implementation efforts. Aligned with Sklyar et al. (2019) and Oliva et al. (2012), we confirmed that while centralized AI hubs aim to enhance implementation efficiency, they also create tensions with the decentralized, context-specific needs of front- and back-office employees. Toward this end, our findings highlighted how centralized control exerted by AI hubs in the banking sector can hinder the responsiveness of employees across departments and at the branch level, constraining overall AI adoption. This observation aligns with the insights offered by Bartlett and Ghoshal (2000), who emphasize that centralization can impede local adoption, particularly in service-oriented industries where adaptability and responsiveness to local customer needs are critical, which is highly relevant in the banking industry, where customer relationships are rooted in trust building and personalization. Although banks operate within globally standardized structures, their daily operations are localized in branch-level service delivery (Ulrich-Diener et al., 2023). Branch managers and customer advisors tailor their customer engagement strategies based on specific customer needs, regulatory constraints, and relationship dynamics. Our findings also highlighted this dynamic: customer advisors and branch managers often adapt, modify, or even resist centrally mandated AI solutions, exercising their autonomy and agency, deviating from the standardized AI use envisioned by the AI hub. This echoes the perspectives of Kohtam€aki et al. (2020), who argue that misalignments between implemented technologies and a lack of context-specific use limit work efficiency. Our study further illustrated that centralization via AI hubs in banking can create divisions even within the same department (e.g. IT) by differentiating access to strategic involvement and limiting collaborative opportunities among employees. Thus, by following Gebauer et al. (2010) and Brashear Alejandro et al. (2011), we emphasized the necessity of employee embeddedness in AI implementation decisions orchestrated through AI hubs in the banking industry. Governance structures vs technological innovation: ensuring data security and managing technical complexity Our findings highlighted a critical data-related tension in AI-driven DS in banking: the tradeoff between adhering to strict data governance regulations while enabling the development of effective AI solutions that rely on rich, high-quality data. We illustrated how data governance structures salient to the banking industry shape AI innovation. Banks operate in a heavily regulated environment where compliance with GDPR and industry-specific policies is non-negotiable (Mogaji and Nguyen, 2022). These regulations are designed to protect customer data, ensure ethical handling of sensitive information, and mitigate institutional risk. Our findings showed that strict governance structures and internal banking policies requiring legal and IT approvals in data sharing and use create regulatory bottlenecks that hinder AI development. This finding resonates with prior DS literature identifying data as both an enabler and a source of tension in AI innovation efforts when actors within and outside organizational boundaries must collaborate over strict data infrastructures (T�oth et al., 2022; Kahle et al., 2020). The decoupling of data from its originating sources (Lusch and Nambisan, 2015) increases the need for data recombination and reuse in DS initiatives. Our findings indicated that in the banking industry, this is constrained in AI-driven DS by the inability of software developers— both internal and external—to access or experiment with customer interaction data due to legal and compliance restrictions, which hinders AI solution development (Iheanachor and Umukoro, 2022; Barra and Ruggiero, 2023). This supports prior studies in DS that have emphasized how restrictive data governance can impede internal data flows essential for effective technology development (T�oth et al., 2022; Andriopoulos and Lewis, 2010). In line with Smania et al. (2024a), we showed that formal mechanisms to balance control and flexibility (e.g. through legal compliance, NDAs, data-sharing protocols) foster tensions between external technology partners and banks’ IT and legal departments during AI development. Thus, we underscored the complexity that regulatory constraints introduce into banking ecosystem partnerships, as actors often pursue divergent interests and goals in DS initiatives (Kolagar et al., 2022; Korkeam€aki et al., 2022). While managing data governance challenges, banks also need to navigate the technical complexities inherent in AI technologies. A key challenge is that AI models rely on static historical datasets and struggle to capture macroeconomic shocks crucial to the banking industry. AI models trained on outdated or narrow datasets fail to provide customer advisors with reliable, context-sensitive insights for informed decisions (Moharrak and Mogaji, 2024; Ulrich-Diener et al., 2023). This underscores the critical role of high-quality, up-to-date data in sustaining AI relevance and responsiveness in the banking industry (Smania et al., 2024b; Favoretto et al., 2022). Thus, we argue that banks need to implement exploration and exploitation mechanisms to balance the flow of internal and external data sources within and outside organizational boundaries to develop AI solutions that are technically robust and practically effective for customer advisory and sales (Clauss et al., 2020; Paschou and Papaioannou, 2023). Conclusions Theoretical implications This study advances the emerging banking literature on AI-driven DS by offering a nuanced, role-sensitive view of how tensions manifest as conflicting demands within socio-technical systems (Moharrak and Mogaji, 2024; Sheth et al., 2022; Ulrich-Diener et al., 2023; Diener and �Spa�cek, 2021). Our conceptualization of the four tensions provides a theoretical framework for understanding interdependencies among structures, people, tasks, and AI in banking, giving rise to tensions. Our classification of tensions (e.g. role evolution vs job security, AI-augmented decision-making vs human intuition in decision-making), reveals their paradoxical nature—contrasting yet interdependent—adding to the emerging research on tensions in AI-driven DS (e.g. Smania et al., 2024a; Sandvik et al., 2021; T�oth et al., 2022; Sklyar et al., 2019). By extending the extant DS literature on manufacturing firms (e.g. Sklyar et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2021), our study—to the best of our knowledge—is a pioneer in its use of the STS theory as a lens to explore tensions in banking. We illustrate how tensions are nested and interconnected, with one tension often triggering or reinforcing others—addressing calls from Smith and Lewis (2011) to explore such nested dynamics. Hence, this study adds nuance to the tensions literature on DS (T�oth et al., 2022; Smania et al., 2024a) by illustrating that tensions do not manifest in isolation. We show that AI-driven DS in banking unflods as a non-linear process shaped by role-based experiences. Furthermore, we extend STS literature on technological change by underlining how microlevel frictions in AI-driven DS in banking, such as ambiguity in job roles, redistribution of AIfreed-up time, and explainability of AI-driven insights, are manifestations of deeper sociotechnical misalignments (Pasmore et al., 2019; Feenberg, 2006). Thus, we emphasize that AIdriven DS is not merely a technical upgrade but a reconfiguration of the entire socio-technical systems of banks. By integrating the perspectives of external software developers, we highlight the critical role of inter-organizational collaborations in data utilization and governance, unique to AI-driven DS in banking. Thus, we illustrate how intra-organizational tensions in data partnerships for AI solution development in sales and customer advisory in banking can produce indirect but critical inter-organizational impact. Thereby, we contribute to the extant banking literature on partnership collaborations in AI-driven DS (Iheanachor and Umukoro, 2022). Managerial implications This study identifies four socio-technical tensions that AI-driven digital servitization (DS) brings to customer advisory and sales processes in banking. These tensions, central to the highly regulated, risk-averse, and relationship-based banking industry, need to be proactively managed to realize the full value of AI initiatives. Addressing these tensions is crucial for managers in the banking industry, as unresolved socio-technical tensions can undermine effective AI adoption, erode employee trust, and hinder operational efficiency. The tension of AI-augmented decision-making vs human intuition arises from how AI insights are used in decision-making, mainly when branch managers monitor and evaluate customer advisors, and the level of transparency regarding how AI-generated insights are used. To manage this, branch managers in the banking industry should clarify with customer advisors that the AI tools used to monitor their performance are intended as complementary decision aids, not as substitutes for human judgment. Clear protocols for using AI in evaluations and regular training on AI transparency and explainability can build trust among customer advisors. Importantly, ethical guidelines on AI surveillance need to be co-created with front- and back-office employees to reduce fear and mistrust. The final tension concerns evolving job roles and blurred task boundaries due to AI, causing uncertainty about careers in the traditionally human-centric banking sector. To address this, HR and branch managers should develop workforce transition strategies that include skills audits, targeted reskilling programs, and role design workshops. HR and branch managers should together implement workforce transition strategies that allow front- and back-office employees in banks to experience hybrid AI-human roles or assign AI-facilitator roles that bridge domain expertise with AI applications. Together, these coping strategies offer managers in the banking industry a roadmap for navigating AI-driven DS by turning tensions into opportunities for learning and innovation, facilitating alignment between AI and human capabilities. Limitations and future research By bridging the STS view with tensions in DS, we identified four tensions associated with AIdriven DS in the banking industry. Despite its contributions, this study has its limitations. The data utilized in this study are limited to customer advisory and sales in banking. Thus, it does not account for tensions that emerge in other departments in the banking industry. Hence, we recommend that researchers explore this phenomenon in other departmental contexts of banks, as well as other industry contexts. For example, future studies could explore socio-technical interactions and interdependencies that manifest tensions in manufacturing industry contexts and other service industries, such as tourism and healthcare. Furthermore, employing a casebased research approach could help uncover inter- and intra-organizational tensions at a broader level in AI-driven DS. The results of this study were based on the subjective perceptions of the experts we chose. Although we utilized an information-oriented sampling technique, our results included expert biases. Therefore, we suggest employing quantitative approaches to operationalize different types of tensions and their moderating and mediating effects. Our study offers some empirical insights in this regard, providing a stepping stone to develop a quantitative study to explore the phenomenon. Particularly, we invite researchers to investigate the mediating effect of AIdriven insights on managers’ decision-making regarding customer advisors’ performances, thereby assessing the cause-and-effect relationship between the influence of AI-driven insights and advisors’ professional identity. To guide such quantitative research, we propose a set of research propositions that stem from our qualitative findings and highlight key relationships to be empirically tested.
