The research protocol for the risk analysis was based on the EXPLOITT methodology of industrial exploitation ( https://www.focuso nfof.eu/downloads/results/methodology-industrial-exploitation-ta ke-up.pdf ), which was adapted to fit the context of this project. There is a shortage of resources that protect companies from mistakes and risks faced in the development of new technologies, particularly SMEs, a gap already identified and attempted to cover in literature by Schuh et al. in 2014 [76] ; however, there is a perceived lack of focus in the industrial risks of digital services. On the other hand, the EXPLOITT methodology has the main objective of driving and finetuning technology develop - ment of effective industrial exploitation, prioritising innovation, ex - ploitability, and industrial impact. This methodology is an outcome of a Horizon2020 project called Focus ( https://www.focusonfof.eu/results. asp ) and was found particularly useful as it was designed to under - stand the potential for exploitation of research-based developments in real industrial environments. Further, the European context of its development proved to be easily transferrable to this project. The stage “ collect ” included technical activities and a risk analysis. As part of the technical activities, three digital services were developed by collecting inputs from the companies about their needs and goals, including some objectives related to sustainability and eco-efficiency [77] : (1) reduce defects, (2) avoid overproduction, and (3) reduce waiting times. The digital services are based on the use of principles of digital twins for process, machine, and production flow optimization, relying on servitization principles [78] to deliver value through digital services. The description of the digital services is included in Section 4.1 . As part of the risk analysis, the digital services were tested by experts from the project Consortium, based on the EXPLOITT methodology. The experts answered the digital questionnaire in two rounds. In the first round, the risks perceived were identified using a questionnaire with responses on a Likert scale [79] from 1 to 4 for risk likelihood and impact. The risks were categorized by three researchers into the following nine categories, which are part of the EXPLOITT methodology but adapted to fit the purpose of this research: (a) business, (b) project, (c) strategic, (d) legal, (e) team, (f) technical, (g) integration, (h) quality and (h) planning risks. Then, the responses were averaged to ensure anonymity between the industrial partners and presented in a risk ma - trix. The second round of the questionnaire identified the mitigation and contingency actions for the highest risks (based on likelihood and impact scores). In the stage “ analysis ” , the results were compared, and the risk matrixes were developed based on the feedback from the main actors. The average scoring and synthesis of the results were performed after the first round of data collection. This provided the basis for the second round of data collection through the digital questionnaire to identify risk mitigation and contingency actions. Last, the stage “ share ” involved the documentation of results and communication to the main actors. 4. Results This section is divided into two parts: Section 4.1 provides a description of the digital services, which are an output of the technical activities previously described. Then, Section 4.2 presents the identified risks associated with the implementation and use of the three digital services. The order of the activities aims to address the identified gap in the literature regarding the lack of documentation of risks of digital servitization in context-specific environments. 4.1. Applying servitization and digitalization in the machine tool industry The three digital services developed are software-based and built through simulation models for processes, machines, and flow optimization, with the main objective of conceptualizing and designing them to align with some of the main sustainability and eco-efficiency objectives [77] : (1) reduce defects, (2) avoid overproduction, and (3) reduce waiting times. The prioritized principles were highlighted in the initial discussions with the project consortium as useful measures to address sustainability problems that could potentially be supported through digital services. The development process of these services in - volves performance evaluation, with the prospective plan of developing the models into digital twins. The multidisciplinary modelling approach enabled a holistic view to evaluate how a manufacturing system can work towards sustainability goals by interlinking data in the same modelling environment. The digital services developed and offered to the companies are described in Table 2 . The first digital service focuses on Zero Defect Manufacturing (ZDM), a concept that finds its origin in the long history of simulation of sub - tractive manufacturing processes. In this digital service, corresponding predictions are utilized for planning, validation, and optimization of CNC machining processes. With the advancements in computational and algorithmic capabilities, the simulation of the coupled machine-process behaviour for complex machining processes and large workpieces is within reach. The output of the process-level forces is used in the machine-level simulation framework, figuratively the virtual machine "feels and senses the process", behaving as if it was in real operation Table 2 Description of the digital services. Digital service Description Zero Defect Manufacturing (ZDM) ZDM uses a framework that combines process and machine simulations to help achieve established quality goals of machine tool manufacturers and end-users, optimizing the machining processes. The service is based on a model representing the actuation system of the machine tool drive, which estimates the positioning error of the machine considering the mechanic parameters of the machine, the drive, and the controller. A web-based application was developed for the use of setup engineers. The mechanical parameters to be introduced are the mass of the drive, the mass of the element to be moved, and the stiffness and damping between the moving mass and the drive. The digital service evaluates the trajectory of the controller, considering the dynamic properties of the system. This digital service evaluates many signals in a short time span, rapidly detecting the source of the problem. First Time Right (FTR) This digital service is a cost-effective for collision avoidance system (CAS) focusing on small-series and single-part manufacturing. In this context, it is especially relevant to ensure the first produced part is a good part, with minimal effort for setting up and human supervision. By focusing on the first-time right principle, the quality of the workpieces will be increased with support of simulation-based accurate process planning, leading to less resource waste. This digital service is based on a model that uses polygonal meshes generated by a vision system and defines collision areas for the CAS in a machine CNC controller, ensuring first time right production. Lean Production (LP) This digital service optimizes production flow connected to the physical assets and simulation tools via an IoT platform. The architecture of this digital service is composed of 1) asset, 2) IoT gateway, 3) digital cloud, 4) modelling tool and 5) optimization tool. One of the objectives of this digital service is to find the best sequence of parts given an initial production plan, composed of certain references and batch size, assuming the setup activities (i.e., jaw chucks, centering, calibration, tools) and time differ, depending on historical references. The functionalities of the solution are visualization of production data, definition and simulation of the production plan, visualization of simulation results and optimization. C.A. The second digital service, First Time Right (FTR), was developed as an in-process mechanism for those cases where the simulations fail in their attempts to guarantee ergonomics, safety, and efficiency. This digital service aims to combine the advantages of simulation and vision- based approaches in a cost-effective solution for collision avoidance focusing on small-series and single-part manufacturing. FTR can address European machine tool builders ’ sustainability, competitiveness, and social challenges, by enabling the offerings of more attractive machine tools that require lower operator skills along with reduced risk of damage during machining process and preventing resource waste. Collision evaluation usually consists of incremental steps that incur increasing costs. Identifying or discarding potential collisions through a simple and non-costly early step can reduce the need for high-cost evaluations. The third digital service, Lean Production (LP), is based on the idea that lean approaches used in the design and operations of manufacturing systems are needed to adopt new digital technologies and face new manufacturing challenges. The aim of this digital service is to provide a simulation tool for production process managers that showcases con - nected machine tools and production line simulation tools, enabling automatic adjustments in the line simulation model based on the data generated by machines and providing functionalities that improve the management of production lines. 4.2. Further, it reflects on the im - plications of the risk analysis and compares it to the literature findings. 5.1. Digitalization and servitization as support for the machine tool industry ’ s objectives The three digital services developed and presented in this study showcase the potential of adopting servitization and digitalization in the machining tool sector. Sustainability, eco-efficiency and circular econ - omy principles were used as an axis for the conceptualization of the digital services, with goals that include: zero defect manufacturing, optimization of machine tool processes, collision avoidance, ensuring first-time right and improving production flows. The potential impact of these digital services is timely, being the automotive sector one of the main stakeholders in these case studies, digital services can help address the material availability crisis at European and global level, benefiting from maximizing the usage of resources and scrap-avoidance. This study identifies that machine tool companies have become increasingly interested in environmental issues, aiming to limit the amount of scrap and waste production to meet governmental quotas. Machine energy consumption modelling is a pre-requisite for energy saving in manufacturing [53] , and in the context of this research, firms expressed that although they do not always adopt the sustainability discourse in their main product or service description, having environ - mental priorities has been in the raise. Risks associated with digital servitization in the machine tool industry The machine tool industry is a large supplier of pieces for many products of several actors in the manufacturing industry and severe potential errors could be solved through good communication. The highest-rated risk among the ones considered unacceptable by the in - dustrial practitioners was identified in the legal category, posing the concern of having the partners fail to discuss all relevant terms of the digital service. Data sharing across a complete supply and value chain is often required, and complete product lines could be disrupted if the partners have not dedicated the required time and efforts to agree on mutual objectives and business models [ 65 , 81 ]. Good communication and trust-based relationships between stake - holders have become increasingly relevant, as resilient value chains are urgent and not yet achieved in the manufacturing industry. Many global organizations have addressed the post-pandemic manufacturing in - dustry as vulnerable, facing the need for additional tools to avoid dis - ruptions upstream and downstream [82] . Further, the category considered high included risks from six out of the nine categories presented in the results, including business, project, strategy, legal, team and technical. From the business category, the major concerns relate to integrating the digital services with the currently existing ERPs and MES (risk A2). Most firms experience that it could take months or years for ERP systems to be fully integrated, delaying the realization of benefits, and limiting their acceptance across organizations [83] . Also, the expected results could be compromised due to the unavailability of connected machines and the potential lack of data and hardships when emulating failures (risk B9). Further, having several industrial sectors in one value chain could represent a risk, as there is no understanding yet of whether digital services can be adapted for each actor, which could mean a lack of necessary output data (risk C3) and it is important to address the lack of available data and the top-down approach that involves the design of service-added offerings as it could lead to an underestimation of the price required to make services profitable [84] . The results of this study show the need for future research where quantitative methods explore the economic feasibility of new business case adoption with risk-sharing strategies in place. Recommendations based on the risk analysis The risks identified, most specifically those that were considered of potential unacceptable and of high impact, as presented in Fig. 2 , were further discussed with the industrial experts and researchers to create a list of activities that could be performed both to mitigate or prevent the risks. These activities are described in Table 4 . While the questions posed in this research work are answered in a case-specific manner and the authors do not claim complete generaliz - ability, the validity of many of these expressions can be supported by similar observations in comparable or tangential studies. To address the unacceptable risk regarding the lack of under - standing of the terms of the digital service among the partners, some actions are recommended which include create joint-ownership agree - ment between partners, with accurate definitions of the results produced by each of the actors and explicitly describe the conditions of ownership of the data. Also, define IP strategies for how the results and data outputs will be protected, define frequent meetings to re-evaluate the agreed conditions, and define penalty fees in case the agreements are broken. Then, to address the risks considered high some strategies are also suggested. To deal with concerns about integration with currently existing ERPs and MES, the suggestion is to evaluate data formats, develop audits about documentation and assess matches and standards of interoperability at all the stakeholders ’ facilities, as well as estab - lishing closer relationships with the ERP and MES software providers to push towards interconnectivity and standardization, enabling the fore - casting of future disruptions. Further, it is important to evaluate the simplicity of the implementation and start with small wins, avoiding disruptions in the most critical part of the systems. 5.4. Theoretical and managerial implications From a theoretical perspective, this study showcases the gathering of industrial expertise by following qualitative research methods that support the classification of risks on digitalization and servitization in the machine tool industry. The research work identified a lack of case studies that document the risks associated with specific digital services in relation to connected value chains. Although the generalizability of the results is a complex statement, the risks identified and classified in this study can be transferrable to similar digital services that require high availability of technical skills, trust relationships among stake - holders and a clear definition of shared responsibilities for new business model design. From a managerial perspective, the results of this study contribute to the identification of potential risks which can be helpful when designing and defining new business models within the machine tool industry. An understanding of commonly perceived risks which are also reflected in literature brings value to manufacturers and other companies in a value chain to understand what situations must be fool-proofed and co-create solutions to avoid shifting problems from one life cycle stage to another. Further, this study provides a list of possible mitigation activities which can enlighten manufacturers to not only focus on situations that could not go according to plan, but also by equipping them with ideas of how to address such risks through mitigation and contingency activities. 6. Research limitations This study experienced some limitations which can highlight the next research steps that could contribute to further covering the iden - tified research gap. • This study finds a limitation in the number of digital services developed and the timeline in which this analysis is performed, which is mainly at the beginning-of-life cycle stage. This can be seen from two perspectives, on the one hand, beginning-of-life cycle stage is the most influential when it comes to planning business models, particularly with sustainability agendas in mind. On the other hand, an analysis how risks express and materialize in later lifecycle stages could provide interesting results. • The number of companies involved is limited to three firms, which allows an in-depth analysis of their perceptions of risks. The fact that the companies are of different sizes provides valid points to firms ’ reactions towards similar risks regardless of their size but limits generalizability. 6.2. Recommendations for future research Future research is suggested to address more of the eco-efficiency and sustainability principles, capturing more sustainable value from unexplored research avenues. Also, the exploration of the implementa - tion stage can materialize further the results. Last, the analysis of how the mitigation and contingency actions impact the process of the firm can provide valuable research insights to academics and practitioners. In conclusion, this study contributes to bridging the gap between theory and practice by identifying risks and mitigation activities, providing insights from empirical cases and insights from real industrial contexts. Digital versus non-digital servitization for environmental and non-financial performance benefits Yancy Vaillant a , * , Esteban Lafuente b a Department of Strategy, Entrepreneurship and Innovation, TBS Education, France b School of Business, Costa Rica Institute of Technology (ITCR), Cartago, Costa Rica ARTICLE INFO Handling Editor: Cecilia Maria Villas B ˆoas de Almeida JEL classification: L2 M21 Keywords: Digital servitization Digitalization Product-service systems Environmental performance Non-financial performance ABSTRACT The goal of this study is to identify if digital servitization contributed to firms ’ environmental performance, and if it does so beyond the impact of servitization alone. The study ’ s proposed model also analyses if digitalization improves the impact of servitization for other non-financial operational, competitive, and customer-oriented performance outputs. The regression analysis uses a unique sample of 213 firms for 2023 drawn from a self- devised survey. The main findings indicate that digital servitization is a significant contributor to the environ - mental performance of firms. This contrasts with the lack of a significant positive impact found when limiting the analysis to non-digital servitization practices. 1. Introduction Despite the current popularity among producers of servitization — i. e., the transition from basic goods and services to integrated offerings — , its relationship with performance is not clear-cut ( Davies et al., 2023 ). Servitization alone may be insufficient to generate the performance ef - fects that companies need to offset and justify injections and investments aimed at augmenting service capabilities ( Rabetino et al., 2021 ). There is ample empirical research indicating the presence of a servitization paradox ( Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ), whereby the relationship between servitization and firm performance is found to be non-linear ( Wang et al., 2018 ) and even negative under certain circumstances ( Bustinza et al., 2018 ). A similar situation arises with digitalization — the improvement of processes by means of digital solutions — where com - panies aiming to improve their yield often invest in digital capacity but paradoxically fail to enhance their performance accordingly ( Gebauer et al., 2021 ). The solution to both paradoxes, however, may come from jointly implementing servitization and digital strategies together ( Favoretto et al., 2022 ). Digitalization can act as an enabler of support service provision and can evolve into a driver for advanced service delivery ( Martín-Pe ña et al., 2019 ). Hence, it is a mechanism that unlocks the benefits of servitization to enhance firm performance ( Coreynen et al., 2017 ). Inversely, when servitization is introduced to digitalization, it is found to help upgrade products to more advanced smart solutions and value delivery based on product-service-software systems ( Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ). Therefore, when servitization and digitalization are developed together, greater business possibilities are opened from expanded capability frontiers ( Favoretto et al., 2022 ). The resulting joint strategy, termed ‘digital servitization ’ , is the use of digital technologies to create and appropriate value from product-service offerings ( Koh - tam äki et al., 2022 ). Kohtam äki et al. (2019 , 2020) have called for further studies on the complex relationship between digitalization, servitization, and firm performance, which is still in its infancy ( Favoretto et al., 2022 ). The studies that do exist have mainly focused on the financial and economic performance benefits of adopting a digital servitization strategy ( Abou-Foul et al., 2021 ; Gebauer et al., 2021 ; Kharlamov and Parry, 2021 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ; Martín-Pe ña et al., 2019 ; Visnjic et al., 2019 ; Yang et al., 2023 ). These studies have mostly found positive correlations between digital servitization and financial performance, with Kharlamov and Parry (2021) specifying that the impact of * Corresponding author. However, Kohtam äki et al. (2019) proposed that digital servitization could potentially provide different types of gains other than economic benefits. As such, digital servitization has been described as a means for value-creation rather than revenue-generation ( Martín-Pe ña et al., 2019 ; Sklyar et al., 2019 ). Servitization on its own has been identified as an essential tool for firms to attain many non-financial outcomes ( Lex - utt, 2020 ). It is therefore pertinent to question whether the performance benefits of digital servitization transcend economic results and embody various types of interrelated non-financial outcomes. Could the opera - tional ( Kowalkowski et al., 2013 ), competitive ( Oliva and Kallenberg, 2003 ) and customer-oriented ( Sj ödin et al., 2019 ) performance benefits associated with servitization be enhanced by digital technologies, as has been found to be the case with financial benefits ( Bustinza et al., 2018 ; Chen et al., 2021 )? Servitization and digitalization together provide significant oppor - tunities to boost firms ’ performance ( Schroeder et al., 2019 ). Firms that adopt such combined strategies are likely to improve their operational, competitive, and customer-oriented performance, as these are highly interrelated and likely correlated. However, with the possible exceptions of Opazo-Bas áez et al. (2018) and Lafuente and Vaillant (2023a) , who investigated how digitalization influences green outcomes, the literature does not seem to have addressed the possible impact of digital serviti - zation on environmental performance (input resource efficiency and output waste management) beyond its impact within a circular economy scenario ( Bressanelli et al., 2018 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2018 ). Green strategy adoption has been linked to servitization in terms of its impact on the competitive efficiency of companies ( Lafuente and Vail - lant, 2023b ). However, service innovation and sustainability-oriented strategies are often perceived as competing approaches within com - panies ( Mu ñoz-Villamizar et al., 2018 ; Visnjic et al., 2019 ). Would combining digitalization with servitization help drive greater environ - mental performance? To answer these questions empirically, the study presented in this paper not only attempts to ascertain whether digitalization improves the impact of servitization for non-financial operational, competitive, and customer-oriented performance outputs, but also contrasts whether digital servitization contributes to the environmental performance of the firm, and if it does so beyond the impact of servitization alone. Non- digital servitization — i.e., physical maintenance visits, people-operated helplines, and other similar traditional value-adding complementary service provisions — is still very much present in many industrial firms that often face competitive pressures that drive them towards serviti - zation, but do not necessarily have the internal digital capabilities to introduce digitally-based service innovations on their own — i.e., digitally-enabled remote monitoring and autonomous maintenance services, or AI operated customer service chatbots ( Kharlamov and Parry, 2021 ; Lafuente et al., 2023a ). By deliberately segmenting digital from non-digital servitization, this study aims to identify their differ - entiated impacts and thus explain some of the inconsistencies found in the literature when linking servitization and performance. The empirical exercise employs a series of OLS regressions on a unique sample drawn from a self-devised survey from 2023 covering 213 Spanish companies. The main findings indicate that digital serviti - zation is a significant contributor to all non-financial performance var - iables under study, including environmental performance. This contrasts with the lack of significant positive impact when limiting the analysis to non-digital servitization practices for all analyzed outputs other than customer-oriented performance. As for the environmental performance benefits of digital servitization, the results indicate that these are especially significant for manufacturing firms, whose green transition seems to be particularly enhanced by its implementation. The remainder of the paper is as follows. Section 2 presents the theory-based argument that led to the study ’ s hypotheses. The data, variables, and method used to test these hypotheses are described in section 3 . The results of this quantitative analysis and their relation to the study ’ s research objectives are presented in section 4 . Finally, sec - tion 5 discusses the implications of these findings for research, policy, and practice; with indications of potential future research avenues that would help to complement and build upon the study presented herein. 2. Theoretical and hypotheses development The findings of Coreynen et al. (2020) confirm that digitalization is different from servitization, but “ both constructs are to some extent related ” ( Coreynen et al., 2020 , p. 273). Servitization without digitali - zation is often devoid of personalized value propositions, and in many cases remains based on simple service add-ons to standardized products ( Hsuan et al., 2021 ). This is because at low levels of digitalization there are important value leakages, reducing the attainable performance po - tential of servitization ( Sj ödin et al., 2019 ). Resource-demanding ser - vitization-related capabilities, together with the excessive complexity of servitization processes for manufacturers, may consume much of the potential service-based value-added if conducted without a corre - sponding digital strategy ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ). Digitalization therefore provides capable technologies that can be utilized for improved value creation and appropriation on the part of companies implementing servitization ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Wamba et al., 2017 ). As such, digitalization, when used as a means of value-generation and optimization as part of the firm ’ s production process, or as a means of value-delivery as part of the firm ’ s integrated product-service offer, can be an enabler of servitization-based val - ue-added ( Coreynen et al., 2017 ; Raddats et al., 2019 ). As for the financial performance of firms, despite the mixed findings in the literature ( Gebauer et al., 2005 ), servitization has been linked to greater profitability ( Neely, 2008 ; Gebauer et al., 2011 ), higher profit growth ( Gebauer et al., 2006 ), and more stable revenue sources, helping firms to be more resistant to economic cycles ( Gebauer and Fleisch, 2007 ). However, none of these studies isolated the impact on their re - sults of digitalization from that of servitization. Doing so may well have revealed that digitalization serves as the core enabling factor for servi - tization to attain its financial performance goals ( Davies et al., 2023 ). Kohtam äki et al. (2020) specified that servitized companies with higher levels of digitalization achieved positive results but that the reverse was also true, in that servitization was necessary in order to obtain a financial return from digitalization. Digital servitization, in combina - tion, is repeatedly found to lead to positive financial outcomes ( Abou- - Foul et al., 2021 ; Gebauer et al., 2021 ; Kharlamov and Parry, 2021 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ; Visnjic et al., 2019 ; Yang et al., 2023 ). The reasons for this relationship are linked to the lower coordination and implementation costs of endowing highly customized offerings with digital servitization ( Hsuan et al., 2021 ). The findings of Sj ödin et al. (2019) indicate that operational, competitive, and customer-oriented performance are themselves tightly linked to financial performance. Environmental performance, however, may fall outside of these interrelated non-financial performance mea - sures. Whereas recent studies have found links between the adoption of environmentally oriented strategies and performance ( Arag ón-Correa et al., 2008 ; Opazo-Bas áez et al., 2024 ), others have highlighted the incoherence that green practices often introduce to company strategy as well as the trade-offs required to achieve set environmental objectives ( Delmas and Blass, 2010 ; Mu ñoz-Villamizar et al., 2018 ). Below, we look into the potential links between digital servitization and environmental performance, as well as with other non-financial performance outputs, to construct the argument that these are positively impacted by digital servitization, and can therefore be enhanced through the implementa - tion of such a strategy. Environmental performance The adoption of ecological practices and green strategies have been found to positively impact the social, economic, and operational per - formance of companies ( Çankaya and Sezen, 2019 ) as well as their sales and financial performance ( Bhatti et al., 2023 ), innovativeness ( Lafuente and Vaillant, 2023a ) and competitiveness ( Lafuente and Vaillant, 2023b ; Zhu and Sarkis, 2007 ). Links between servitization and the environmental performance of companies have also been found to be positive in nature ( Doni et al., 2019 ). Servitized offerings that imple - ment such measures as more efficient use of energy resources and better waste management can offset the increase in environmental costs and boost environmental and economic performance ( Xing et al., 2023 ). Digitalization, however, could help to even further mitigate the value leakages of servitization practices when aimed at the achievement of green performance objectives. The potential gains in the efficiency of operational resources through the use of digital servitization have been proposed in the past ( Opazo-Bas áez et al., 2018 ; Zheng et al., 2018 ), the suggestion being that digital platforms could assist with the monitoring, control, and optimized allocation of resources in ways that reduce consumption, manage waste better, and achieve environmental gains ( Favoretto et al., 2022 ; Lindstr öm et al., 2018 ; Papazoglou et al., 2020 ). Additionally, digital services have been associated with extended product life ( Vendrell-Herrero et al., 2022 ) and have been found to facilitate the implementation of circular economy practices (Bresssanelli et al., 2018; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ), all of which also lead to potentially greater environmental performance gains. As such, it is hypothesized that. H1 . Digital servitization positively impacts the environmental performance of the company to a greater extent than non-digital servitization. 2.2. Operational performance Operational performance, defined as improvements to production processes, including upstream coordination with suppliers as well as downstream value-chain efficiency in supply and recall management, can potentially be significantly improved through digital servitization. Digitalization enhances and helps capture the value of servitization ’ s solution offerings ( Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ). The integration of digitali - zation and servitization offers an optimal approach for balancing the design of high-value integrated personalized solutions with the optimum scalability of efficient production ( Vendrell-Herrero et al., 2017 ). Digital servitization opens up the operative possibility for the production and delivery of scalable solutions through the enhanced monitoring, control, optimization, and autonomous capacities that it can provide in order to boost the operational performance of the company. The use of digital technologies improves the efficiency and effec - tiveness of service operations ( Kantis et al., 2023 ; Kindstr öm and Kowalkowski, 2014 ; Kowalkowski et al., 2013 ). Digitalization of servi - tization also enables modular service provision that not only facilitates user-managed customization, but also allows for greater operational efficiency and productive adaptability. Kharlamov and Parry (2021) found a positive and significant impact of digital servitization on oper - ational productivity. Based on these arguments, we propose the following hypothesis. H2 . Digital servitization positively impacts the operational performance of the company to a greater extent than non-digital servitization. 2.3. Competitive performance Servitization is an important source of differentiation that leads to greater competitiveness ( Oliva and Kallenberg, 2003 ). Enhanced value generation and capture through servitization helps servitized companies to gain a competitive advantage over their rivals. But for Porter and Heppelmann (2014) , smart digitalization of products is paramount for maximizing the competitive advantages of commercializing products as a service. Digitalized and servitized smart product-service systems not only generate value-added solutions that help to stand out from the competition but can also create the exclusivity whereby digitally servi - tized firms gain bargaining power over buyers, whilst at the same time diminishing any threat of entry or substitution ( Porter and Heppelmann, 2014 ). Digital servitization generates greater customer lock-in, leading to a pseudo-monopolistic position that diminishes customer price- sensitivity, thus resulting in lower overall competitive intensity as well as improved market attractiveness and competitiveness ( S ánchez-Montesinos et al., 2018 ). It can also lead to competitor lock-out, which diminishes rivalry and competitive intensity for the firm, thus improving the potential competitive performance of a digi - tally servitized firm. Hence, digital servitization is likely to boost competitive performance, which can be viewed as the ability to generate comparatively greater value than the competition, to rapidly respond to changes in the competitions ’ offer, to extend contractual relationships with clients, and to increase the volume sold to each client. It is therefore hypothesized that. H3 . Digital servitization positively impacts the competitive performance of the company to a greater extent than non-digital servitization. 2.4. Customer-oriented performance Servitization has played a key role in manufacturers ’ migration from simple product business models to the delivery of higher value customer-oriented solutions. As such, customer-oriented performance relies on the company ’ s adeptness at solving customer problems by harnessing its greater capacity to anticipate changes in technology and customer preferences, but also its capacity for preventive and corrective maintenance, which tends to be the outcome of developing close rela - tional capital ( Storbacka et al., 2013 ). Service provision can therefore lead to greater customer orientation and the forging of longer-term re - lationships in order to better ingrain the firm with customers and ecosystem partners in value creation processes ( Sj ödin et al., 2019 ). Greater customer-oriented abilities are likely to help draw customers into longer-term trust-based relationships that potentially lead to greater cumulative performance. As for customer-oriented performance gains, digital capabilities can complement servitization and enable better interaction between firms and customers to create value ( Lafuente and Vaillant, 2023b ; Lenka et al., 2017 ; Martín-Pe ña et al., 2019 ; Rojas-Segura et al., 2023 ). Digi - talization directly improves customer orientation through access to richer and more reliable data and analytics for customer-related deci - sion-making ( Hasselblatt et al., 2018 ). This helps improve customer satisfaction and retention ( Chen et al., 2020 ). Digital servitization can also improve the customer interface in terms of production, sales and delivery to offer customized solutions for a wider range of applications and markets ( Coreynen et al., 2020 ). Digitalization helps servitizing firms to extend their value chains and better serve their customers ( Rymaszewska et al., 2017 ), and also to reduce transaction costs while directly improving the provision of customer value ( Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ; Sj ödin et al., 2019 ). The benefits of digital servitization for a firm ’ s customer-oriented performance are embedded within its enhanced preventive and curative maintenance capabilities as well as the ability to better anticipate and cater to changing customer prefer - ences. It is therefore hypothesized that. H4 . Digital servitization positively impacts the customer-oriented perfor - mance of the company to a greater extent than non-digital servitization. Y. Data The data used to test the proposed hypotheses comes from a unique dataset of Spanish businesses in the manufacturing and business service sectors for 2023. As part of a broader research project, the questionnaire was designed specifically for the purposes of this study. The firm is the unit of analysis and the data were collected via structured interviews in which executive managers were asked to answer what were essentially closed questions. The survey was conducted by a leading professional market research and public opinion firm that was selected and moni - tored directly by the researchers. Following the standards recommended in the literature ( Colton and Covert, 2007 ), and with the assistance of the professional surveying company, the questionnaire was subject to a pre-test in order to correct potentially ambiguous or confusing ques - tions, which were fine-tuned until the most effective instrument for the specific aims of our study had been constructed. A total of 2936 Spanish businesses operating in the manufacturing and business service sectors were invited to participate in the first stage of the study. The targeted respondents were limited to executives and top management familiar with their company ’ s strategic and techno - logical profile. The data were collected between June and September 2023. The final sample comprises information from 213 valid ques - tionnaires, which represent an effective response rate of 7.26%, com - mon rate among corporate surveys limited to top management where only fully completed survey sets are accepted. A Harman one-factor test confirmed the absence of common method bias. Non-response bias was not an issue as the professional surveyors ensured that all participants gave a complete set of responses. Conversely, early response was tested to compare the variance between the first and last 20% of respondents, and the results supported the overwhelming consistency and negligible variance across early and late respondents to the survey. An analysis of the sampled firms reveals that firm size measured by the number of employees ranges between 31 and 675, with 82.85% of firms being small businesses with up to 50 workers. Most of the sampled businesses operate in manufacturing industries (92%), while the remaining 8% are in business service sectors (i.e., computer consul - tancy, computer programming, information technology and computer services, and research and development on natural sciences and engi - neering). Table 1 further segments the economic activities of the firms included in the sample. 3.2. Description of variables Dependent variables . — Organizational performance is a multidimen - sional construct that is operationalized in this study by means of four variables, namely: environmental performance, operational perfor - mance, competitive performance, and customer-oriented performance. Specifically, to generate the study ’ s performance metrics, managers were asked to evaluate on a seven-point Likert scale (1 = total disagreement and 7 = total agreement) the possible performance ben - efits resulting from the firm ’ s business model. In line with, among others, Zhu and Sarkis (2004) , Cheng and Shiu (2012) , Castellacci and Lie (2017) , García-Granero et al. (2018) , envi - ronmental performance is measured via two items that are directly related to energy consumption and waste management: improvements in energy management (e.g., energy consumption), and improvements in waste management (e.g., reduction in waste and residue) derived from the production process. Strictly connected to the benefits generated by the firm ’ s business model, managers were asked to score four items used to measure operational performance: improvements in upstream coordination with suppliers and raw material management, improvements in production processes (e.g., resource allocation, bottleneck reductions), update of production processes, and improvements in downstream delivery sys - tems including recall reduction controls. These variables have been widely used in previous work (see, e.g., Zhu and Sarkis, 2004 ; Sharma et al., 2017 ). Four variables were considered to identify the firms ’ competitive benefits ( Gebauer et al., 2013 ; Visnjic et al., 2017 ; Zhou et al., 2020 ): increase in the firm ’ s service offering to improve product differentiation, response time to external change leading to improvements in the firm ’ s offering, approval of contract extensions with customers, and increase in sales (volume). Finally, customer-oriented performance is measured by means of three variables: regular maintenance work to prevent unexpected fail - ures (preventive maintenance), identification of failures in the product/ service to inform the customer that maintenance work needs to be done (corrective maintenance), and the firm ’ s capacity to anticipate modifi - cations to its offer due to technological updates or the identification of changes in customer preferences (e.g., Storbacka et al., 2013 ). We ran a factor analysis to test the overall fit of the observed vectors of variables with the analyzed constructs. A summary of the results is presented in Table 2 . The values of the reliability test (Cronbach ’ s Alpha) for the four factors range between 0.8191 and 0.9128, con - firming that the constructs extracted from the factor analysis are inter - nally consistent across items to measure the underlying categories under evaluation. Given that the Cronbach ’ s alpha assessments of the consis - tency of the environmental performance construct could be questionable due to its low number of items, this was complemented by the calcula - tion of composite reliability using Raykov ’ s rho coefficient (RRC) ( Raykov, 1997 ). This was done for factors from confirmatory factor analyses after SEM, a measure that is commonly deemed more accurate than Cronbach ’ s alpha, which is computed based on the assumption of tau-equivalent measures ( Raykov, 2001 ). The construct ’ s reliability was confirmed as robust by the RRC analysis ( Table 2 ). The results of Bar - tlett ’ s test of sphericity (p < 0.001) confirm that the correlation between the analyzed variables does not contaminate the results. The result of the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) index of sampling adequacy is above the recommended cut-off point of 0.50, corroborating that the sample is factorable. These results confirm that our approach to factor analysis is robust ( Nunnally and Bernstein, 1994 ). Servitization . — Similar to previous work on servitization (e.g., Huik - kola et al., 2016 ; Bustinza et al., 2018 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ; Ven - drell-Herrero et al., 2022 ; Shleha et al., 2023 ), managers were asked the following questions to identify servitized firms: 1) ‘In reference to the business ’ offering, describe whether it is a manufacturer, a service provider, or both ’ , and 2) ‘indicate the percentage of revenue generated by its products and complementary services ’ . This information was used to create a dummy variable to identify servitized firms. Descriptive statistics and the correlation matrix are presented in Table 3 . In the study ’ s sample, 44% of firms are servitized (integrated product-service offering). Digital servitization . — To measure digital servitization, we asked managers if the business offers a smart (software supported) product- service offering that enables value creation through connectivity within the firms ’ offering (i.e., products and services) and between the business and its customers. Control variables . — We control for firm size, firm age, labor produc - tivity, and industry in all model specifications. In all models, the variables firm size, age and labor productivity are logged in order to reduce skewness. 3.3. Method To evaluate the relationship between the analyzed organizational performance metrics and (digitized and non-digitized) servitization, we employ OLS regression to compute the following full model: Performance i = β 0 + β 1 Digitalservitization i + β 2 Non digitalservitization i + β 3 Controls i + ε i (1) where i indexes firms, ε is the error term, and β is the vector of co - efficients for the set of independent variables. Based on equation (1) , two model specifications were computed for each dependent variable (i. e., environmental, operational, competitive, and customer-oriented performance). We first ran a baseline model (model 1) which regresses performance against the servitization dummy. The full model (model 2) presented in equation (1) distinguishes between firms with a digitized product-service offering and those without (the reference category is non-servitized offering). In all models, control variables are firm size (ln number of employees), firm age (ln years of market experience), labor productivity (ln sales by employee), and the manufacturing dummy (the omitted industry category is business services). In terms of the study ’ s hypotheses, we expect β 1 > 0 and β 1 > β 2 to corroborate that digital servitization is positively correlated with the different performance measures analyzed in this research ( β 1 > 0 ) , and that the positive effect of digital servitization on performance is greater than that observed for firms with a non-digitized product-service of - fering ( β 1 > β 2 ) ( H1 - H4 ). 4. Robustness check This section presents the results of a robustness check evaluating the suitability of our empirical approach based on OLS models compared to an alternative estimation method using structural equation modeling (SEM) ( Hair et al., 2019 ). Specifically, because of the nature of the data used in this study and the design of our empirical model (equation (1) ) ( Acock, 2013 ), for the SEM model we first used confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to build the dependent variables linked to non-financial performance. In a second step, the structural model was estimated via maximum likelihood following the linear paths presented in equation (1) . To verify that the OLS estimations testing the proposed correlations between digitalization and non-financial performance are reliable viz- `a-viz the results extracted from the SEM model, we ran a series of tests of equality of coefficients to compare the coefficients estimated via OLS and SEM. Summarized results are presented in Table A1 of the Appendix. Overall, the findings shown in Table A1 indicate that the absolute values of SEM parameters are larger than those estimated via OLS. However, despite the differences in magnitude, the key result emerging from Table A1 is that the coefficients produced by the SEM models are qualitatively similar to those computed via OLS. Therefore, the proposed OLS models draw accurate conclusions regarding the connection between digital servitization and non-financial performance, and the reported findings presented in section 4.1 are validated by the SEM results: non-financial performance is positively impacted by digital servitization to a greater extent than by non-digital servitization. At this point, an important consideration is in order. To complement the analysis, we also computed a Hausman test, the results of which lead to mixed conclusions concerning the validity of the OLS results. How - ever, the Hausman test statistic is specific to each estimation method ( Davidson and MacKinnon, 1993 ), and estimation differences give rise to at least two problems that might question the reliability of the results of the Hausman statistic when comparing OLS and SEM estimates. Concluding remarks The goal of this study was to identify whether digital servitization contributes to the environmental performance of the firm, and if it does so beyond the impact of servitization alone. The study ’ s proposed model also analyzed whether digitalization improves the impact of servitiza - tion for other non-financial operational, competitive, and customer- oriented performance outputs. These research objectives were met by the study ’ s finding that digital servitization is indeed a potent contrib - utor to firms ’ environmental performance. Digital servitization is also found to be a significant contributor to all other non-financial perfor - mance variables under study. This contrasts with the non-observance of a significant positive impact when limiting the analysis to non-digital servitization practices for all but customer-oriented performance. As such, the study has answered the calls by Kohtam äki et al. (2019 , 2020) and Favoretto et al. (2022) , among others, for further research into the complex relationship between digitalization, servitization, and company performance. From the postulates quickly taking root within the digital servitization literature, it was hypothesized that servitization and digitalization together provide significant opportunities to boost firms ’ performance beyond profits and revenue ( Schroeder et al., 2019 ). To test these assumptions, the study performed a series of OLS re - gressions to evaluate the relationship between the analyzed non-financial output indicators and (digitized and non-digitized) servi - tization. The model was run using data from a purpose-made self- - devised survey from 2023 covering 213 Spanish companies. 5.2. Academic contributions The study ’ s results help to fill the gap in the literature on the incipient line of research into the links between servitization, digitali - zation, and firm performance. While current studies have mostly investigated financial performance metrics, this one diverged by analyzing the relationship between digital servitization and environ - mental performance measures, as well as other non-financial outputs. The paper also used a large sample for a quantitative study in a field that has to date been strongly dominated by exploratory and qualitative studies using small samples. This paper offers indications that the service paradox, whereby greater servitized-based value injections do not necessarily lead to better performance outputs ( Brax et al., 2021 ), is not solely limited to financial metrics but also affects other non-financial performance indicators. However, similar to the case of financial output, digitalization is found to play a key role in generating non-economic performance improve - ments from servitization. The study introduced environmental perfor - mance as a non-financial output measure functioning in much the same way as other more common organizational performance metrics when crossed with digitalization. Although some authors argue that servitization has essentially become fully digital in nature, thus rendering the ‘digital ’ prefix of digital servitization unnecessary ( Harrmann et al., 2023 ), this study ’ s findings clearly show that researchers should continue differentiating the specificities of ‘digital ’ from those of non-digital servitization. The latter is still very much present in many firms, including SMEs, which often face competitive pressures that drive them towards servitization, but do not necessarily have the internal digital capabilities to introduce digitally-based service innovations on their own ( Lafuente et al., 2023a ). The low performance gains of the transition towards a servitized busi - ness model for these firms can be linked, according to the study ’ s results, to the insufficient digital nature of their servitization. Past research has identified the importance of sourcing digital capabilities from technology-oriented knowledge-intensive business service firms to enable a successful transition towards servitization and to fully capture its competitive potential ( Vaillant et al., 2021 ). The results of the study help to explain the mechanics of why this may be so. 5.3. Managerial and policy implications The practical implications of the study ’ s findings are based on the confirmation that servitization and digitalization go hand in hand. Implementing one without the other limits the company ’ s output po - tential, and this is not only in the case of short-term financial returns, but also in more permanent and strategically significant non-financial goals, including environmental ones. From a policy perspective, an understanding of the requisites for proper service-based value creation among industrial firms is essential for support to be adequately delivered. Many incumbent industrial re - gions have been struggling to transition towards productive product- service innovation ecosystems ( Vaillant et al., 2023 ). In order for pol - icy to facilitate such a transition of their local firms and industrial fab - rics, the results of this study suggest that they need to conjointly attend to service and digital capability needs, opening-up servitization-based innovation to local industry ( Lafuente et al., 2023b ). Many incumbent productive firms are attempting to make the transition from product business model to servitization-based solution delivery ( Storbacka et al., 2013 ; Vendrell-Herrero et al., 2022 ). The study ’ s findings suggest that these companies also need to actively transform digitally in order to empower their digital servitization capacity if they are to reach their performance expectations. The study also provides evidence that a firm ’ s environmental per - formance is intricately tied to digital servitization, as well as to other organizational outputs, both financial and non-financial. Environmental gains are made in much the same manner as other performance mea - sures and are affected by similar factors. The use of technology and digitalization is essential for the environmental gains of companies as it potentiates the impact of servitization on such outcomes. As for the Y. Vaillant and E. Lafuente Journal of Cleaner Production 450 (2024) 142078 8 environmental performance benefits of digital servitization, the findings suggest that these are especially significant for manufacturing firms, whose green transition seems to be particularly facilitated by the implementation of digital servitization. 5.4. Future research This study not only contributes to the growing digital servitization literature, but its findings also open up new avenues for further research. To build on the current study, research could introduce new non- financial performance measures and possibly fine-tune the multi-item performance constructs used in this study. Further analysis using more objective measures of performance could compliment the study ’ s find - ings, as they essentially reflect the respondents ’ (subjective) view of their companies ’ strategies and output. But probably more interestingly, new studies could take a closer look at the complementarity of different performance measures to see how digital servitization might be considered a multifunctional tool that contributes to various different firm outcomes at the same time. Or, whether these outputs work against one another when they are achieved through digital servitization. This is especially so in the case of environmental outputs that have been identified by some as potentially detrimental to performance, particu - larly financial performance measures ( Delmas and Blass, 2010 ). As this is a cross-sectional study, our results only offer a snapshot of reality. More longitudinal analysis could offer a more complete view of the short- and longer-term impacts of digital servitization on environ - mental performance and other performance metrics. And although some control was included within the study ’ s model to better understand the potential influence of firm-specific characteristics on the obtained results, larger datasets would allow for much more in-depth analysis from a micro-foundational perspective, or possibly include this in a more holistic multi-level approach. The relationship between digital serviti - zation and performance will likely change across different contexts and settings. It is therefore important to replicate this study in different national, industrial, firm size and other frameworks. Artificial intelligence-driven digital servitization: The importance of platform characteristics and firm-level factors Minna Saunila * , Tero Rantala , Juhani Ukko LUT University, School of Engineering Sciences, Department of Industrial Engineering and Management, Mukkulankatu 19, FI-15210 Lahti, Finland ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Artificial intelligence AI Digital servitization Digital platform SME ABSTRACT This study explores the connection between artificial intelligence (AI) platform characteristics and digital ser - vitization. The study further investigates how firm-related factors influence this connection. The AI platforms that firms utilize are industrial digital platforms that employ AI-based tools to support their operations. Digital servitization has become a common transformation in several industries collaborating with platforms and seeking ways to establish ecosystems. AI provides substantial opportunities for digital servitization to create revenue streams and improve performance by reducing costs and enhancing customer outcomes. However, the underlying characteristics of the AI platforms that support firms ’ digital servitization have seldom been explored among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Based on survey data collected from 179 SMEs, this study conceptualizes five characteristics as drivers of AI platform utilization and investigates their impact on digital servitization using multiple regression analyses. First, this study develops an AI platform characteristic construct. Second, the study builds a theoretical framework showing which AI platform characteristics leverage digital servitization. Ultimately, this research contributes to the understanding of the connections between AI platform characteristics and digital servitization. 1. Introduction Digital servitization has become common in several industries through collaboration among platforms and attempts to establish eco - systems ( Kohtam äki, Rabetino, Parida, Sj ödin, & Henneberg, 2022 ). The central topic of discussion in digital servitization is how industrial dig - ital platforms can promote digital servitization ( Jovanovic, Sj ödin, & Parida, 2022 ; Kohtam äki, Parida, Oghazi, Gebauer, & Baines, 2019 ; Rantala, Ukko, Nasiri, & Saunila, 2023 ). Artificial intelligence (AI) provides possibilities for remarkable transformations and adds complexity to firm operations, requiring specific organizational re - sources and capabilities ( Brock & Von Wangenheim, 2019 ). Industrial digital platforms have become increasingly common in business-to- business (B2B) contexts ( Budde, Haenggi, Laglia, & Friedli, 2024 ; Mancuso, Petruzzelli, & Panniello, 2024 ). These are software-based platforms typically tailored to enhance and support industrial opera - tions ( Rantala et al., 2023 ; Suuronen, Ukko, Saunila, Rantala, & Ran - tanen, 2024 ). These platforms integrate various digital technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT), and advanced sensor technology, for data collection, analysis, and sharing with internal and external stakeholders ( Jovanovic et al., 2022 ; Rantala et al., 2023 ). They can also integrate intelligent agents that support information retrieval, business optimization, and e-commerce ( Adamopoulou & Moussiades, 2020 ; Kushwaha, Kumar, & Kar, 2021 ). Moreover, these industrial digital platforms can support predictive maintenance in internal use or opti - mize supply chain performance when utilized together with suppliers ( Rantala et al., 2023 ). The artificial intelligence platform explored in this study is an industrial digital platform embedded with an AI-driven algorithm that exploits AI-based tools to support platform operations ( Caiazzo, Murino, Petrillo, Piccirillo, & Santini, 2023 ). In the literature, the firm Sandvik offers a practical example of an AI platform consoli - dating operational data and producing valuable insights into mining and planning operations ( Madanaguli, Sj ödin, Parida, & Mikalef, 2024 ). Similarly, the Siemens MindSphere combines industrial IoT and AI platforms for real-time data collection from industrial machines and equipment (e.g., turbines and robotics), allowing it to predict mainte - nance needs, optimize energy consumption, and reduce downtime.
