For example, a sensor network may provide data that enable greater connectivity of industrial assets, while data aggregation and analytics may open up new opportunities for value creation with external parties ( Jovanovic et al., 2022 ). Digital industrial platforms utilizing AI can promote digital serviti - zation, for example, through augmentation and automation ( Sj ödin, Parida, Palmi é, & Wincent, 2021 ). According to Hadi et al. (2023) , large language model (LLM) AI tools provide wide-ranging opportunities for digital servitization, varying from vision application and pattern un - derstanding to data processing. As an example, the IBM Watsonx pro - vides firms opportunities to build customized AI agents by combining LLMs with traditional ML to support chain forecasting and risk analysis. Sj ödin et al. (2021) also demonstrated that AI platforms, such as Ship - corp, are effective at promoting digital servitization by reducing trans - action costs and allowing users to customize application interfaces by building on AI algorithms and structured data. Kushwaha and Kar (2020) further pointed out that ML as a subset of AI provides opportu - nities for machines to learn from historical data and produce real-time predictions, which can also enhance digital servitization. As an example, Uptake combines industrial analytics with ML while collecting data from heavy machinery (e.g., trucks and locomotives) to optimize fuel usage or logistics through AI-driven recommendations. Chaves and Gerosa (2021) and Kushwaha et al. (2021) also note that AI can support servitization through dynamic and personalized interactions with external parties, to enhance customer service and marketing aspects. Although AI platforms are increasingly adopted in B2B industrial settings, much is still to be learned about their characteristics (cf. Liu, Zhang, Zheng, & Kamal, 2025 ; Veile, Schmidt, & Voigt, 2022 ). In the literature to date, Veile et al. (2022) give examples of the industrial digital platforms considered in this study, defined as platforms embedded with AI algorithms and tools supporting and optimizing op - erations ( Caiazzo et al., 2023 ). In addition, the importance of developing AI capacities and capabilities has been recognized in the literature ( Sj ödin, Parida, & Kohtam äki, 2023 ). AI capacities refer to leveraging technology, such as advanced algorithms ( Sj ödin et al., 2023 ) or increased connectivity, whereas AI capabilities refer to a firm (or employee) achieving business advantages through AI, as investment in AI technology (capacity) alone is unlikely to result in business benefits ( Chowdhury et al., 2023 ). Recent studies have focused on the in - terconnections among generative AI capabilities, service innovation, and competitive advantage under environmental dynamism ( Li, Xu, Zhang, Liu, & Li, 2025 ), although the main emphasis of these studies has not been on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Ayala, da Silva, Tinoco, Saccani, and Frank (2025) further identified, through six case studies, AI capabilities developed for different types of digital serviti - zation in both back- and front-office settings. Interactions between AI platform users and platforms, through different modular structures, have been explored in SMEs by Wei and Pardo (2022) under various conditional factors. Thus, while the importance of AI capacities and capabilities has been recognized, the underlying characteristics of AI platforms that support firms in implementing digital servitization ( Reim, Sj ödin, & Parida, 2021 ) have not been extensively investigated in the context of SMEs. Wei and Pardo (2022) highlight that the servitization processes in SMEs may influence their AI implementation processes, suggesting that further research is needed across different industrial and service contexts, such as digital servitization. Prior studies ( Ayala et al., 2025 ; Marcon et al., 2022 ) have also shown that, beyond human-related capabilities, digital servitization often requires a wide range of more detailed capabilities and technical characteristics, which should be further explored through research. While there is a lack of studies on the characteristics of AI platforms underlying SMEs ’ successful digital ser - vitization, this study addresses the gap by adopting a quantitative approach in a cross-industrial setting. Building on prior calls for deeper understanding of AI platform utilization in digital servitization, this study extends both theoretical and managerial perspectives by examining the characteristics of AI platforms. This study ’ s objective is to explore the connection between AI plat - form characteristics and digital servitization, and the influence of firm- related factors on this connection. Accordingly, the research questions are as follows: (1) Which AI platform characteristics are related to digital servitization? (2) How does firm productivity affect the relationship between AI platform characteristics and digital servitization? To answer those questions, we utilize a survey study of SMEs engaged in AI adoption. Based on data collected from 179 SMEs, this study concep - tualizes five characteristics as drivers of AI platform utilization and in - vestigates their impact on digital servitization using multiple regression analyses. First, we develop an AI platform characteristic construct. Second, this study builds a theoretical framework showing the AI plat - form characteristics that leverage digital servitization. The construct of AI platform characteristics is built on previous literature on AI plat - forms. As theoretical justification, extensive literature on servitization and digital servitization has been utilized. Ultimately, this study con - tributes to the understanding of the connections between AI platform characteristics and digital servitization in the context of SMEs. 2. Servitization research contributes toward a greater understanding of digital servitization Since Vandermerwe and Rada (1988) published the first article on servitization, the shift in manufacturing toward the integration of products and services has received increasing attention ( Kohtam äki et al., 2021, 2022 ; Rabetino, Kohtam äki, Brax, & Sihvonen, 2021 , Rabetino, Kohtam äki, Kowalkowski, Baines, & Sousa, 2021 ). Servitiza - tion refers to firms transitioning from selling basic products and services to selling advanced services, customer solutions, and product – service systems ( Baines, Lightfoot, Benedettini, & Kay, 2009 ; Rabetino, Koh - tam äki, Kowalkowski, et al., 2021 ). These advanced offerings typically include life cycle services and changes in firms ’ business logic ( Rabetino, Harmsen, Kohtam äki, & Sihvonen, 2018 ; Rabetino, Kohtam äki, & Gebauer, 2017 ; Rabetino, Kohtam äki, Kowalkowski, et al., 2021 ; Sousa & da Silveira, 2017 ). Servitization is now a widely used term, and numerous definitions have been presented, among which Kohtam äki et al. (2021) comprehensively define it as follows: “ Servitization is about the transition from product to service logic, often involving a complex inte - gration of product-service-software systems, where the ideal-typical form of service logic can be understood as a customer paying for the realized value in use. ” The definition above fits well with this study, which extends the literature by addressing the lack of emphasis noted by researchers (e.g., Kohtam äki et al., 2021 ) on digitalization in the extant servitization literature, which may correspond to a lack of advanced digital tech - nologies. Today, manufacturing firms are increasingly seeking oppor - tunities to capture the prospects of digitalization by renewing their operations in ways that direct those toward digital servitization ( Kohtam äki et al., 2022 ; Kolagar, Parida, & Sj ödin, 2022 ; Rabetino, Kohtam äki, Brax, & Sihvonen, 2021 ). That idea of digital servitization has emerged in the last ten years and brought new potential to combine advanced services enabled by digital technologies and platforms, which requires adopting an ecosystem perspective ( Jovanovic et al., 2022 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Paschou, Rapaccini, Adrodegari, & Saccani, 2020 ; Sklyar, Kowalkowski, Tronvoll, & S örhammar, 2019 ). Kohtam äki et al. (2019) have defined digital servitization as follows: “ The transition toward smart solutions (product-service-software systems) enables value creation and capture through monitoring, controlling, optimizing, and auto - matic functioning. Digital servitization emphasizes value creation through the interplay of products, services, and software. ” According to Kohtam äki et al. (2019) , the interplay between digi - talization and servitization was active in the early phases of constructing digital servitization strategies. Sensor technologies have been high - lighted as part of the resulting smart solutions and product – service systems, whereas software seems to have been underemphasized in early M. Saunila et al. Industrial Marketing Management 130 (2025) 35–45 36 servitization research (e.g., Kohtam äki et al., 2021 ). Digitalization aids servitization in industrial firms by providing new opportunities for intelligent products, platforms, and services ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019, 2022 ; Rabetino, Kohtam äki, Brax, & Sihvonen, 2021 ). As a concept, digital servitization describes the development of smart solutions that will fundamentally change traditional products, services, and software by combining them with industry structures ( Kohtam äki et al., 2021, 2022 ; Kowalkowski, Gebauer, Kamp, & Parry, 2017 ). For this reason, according to Kohtam äki et al. (2019) , digital servitization is increasingly considered a driver and enabler of value creation in servitization research (e.g., Parida, Sj ödin, & Reim, 2019 ; Rabetino et al., 2018 ). The transformation of most industrial firms ’ businesses toward digital ser - vitization is enabled by the rapid development of technologies revolu - tionizing their services, products, and processes ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2021 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2022 ; Sj ödin, Parida, Koh - tam äki, & Wincent, 2020 ). Examples of advanced digital servitization can be found in the transportation and shipping industries. Moreover, industries such as manufacturing, logistics, forestry, and farming are either developing or already using products and services with some autonomy and are increasingly seeking to develop fully autonomous functionalities through AI-enabled digital servitization ( Kohtam äki et al., 2022 ). This study is founded on the definition presented above, where digital servitization refers to the process of moving toward smart solu - tions that transform traditional firm offerings in conjunction with in - dustry structures. AI is understood to be the most advanced type of digital servitization ( Kohtam äki et al., 2022 ; Parida et al., 2019 ; Sj ödin et al., 2021 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ), with firms engaged in digital serviti - zation transforming their businesses to leverage the great prospects of AI ( Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). While the authors in the existing literature provide examples of advanced AI use, they point to a need for greater under - standing of a firm ’ s journey and practices in transforming toward AI- driven digital servitization. Similarly, Caiazzo et al. (2023) propose that we must better understand AI characteristics in the context of advanced digital servitization. Therefore, this research ’ s goal is to examine the characteristics of an AI platform promoting digital serviti - zation. This study design responds to Rabetino, Kohtam äki, Kowal - kowski, et al. (2021) call for researchers to add management topics to future servitization research and centers the research carried out on the most frequently covered topics in this field — digital servitization (including AI, VR, and autonomous solutions) and platforms. With that as the starting point, the next section introduces the role of AI platforms in digital servitization. 3. AI platforms in digital servitization 3.1. AI platforms One of the most significant trends in the development of AI platforms is the expansion of business ecosystems ( Moore, 1993 ) into digital business ecosystems ( Senyo, Liu and Effah, 2019 ; Suuronen, Ukko, Eskola, Semken, & Rantanen, 2022 ). The latter typically create value collaboratively by sharing costs, risks, responsibilities, resources, and expertise; furthermore, they enhance innovation capabilities and improve flexibility, customer satisfaction, production efficiency, pro - ductivity, and performance ( Chekfoung, Sunil, & Binita, 2020 ; Golnam, Ritala, & Wegmann, 2014 ; Lusch, Vargo, & Gustafsson, 2016 ; Rantala et al., 2023 ). Within these ecosystems, platforms play a dominant role as technological infrastructures that enable member firms to develop, adapt, and deliver advanced services efficiently and on an unprece - dented scale ( Ransbotham & Kane, 2011 ; Suuronen et al., 2022 ; Yoo, Boland Jr, Lyytinen, & Majchrzak, 2012 ). Platforms here are “ modular structures that consist of tangible and intangible components (resources) and facilitate the interaction of actors and resources (or resource bundles) ” ( Lusch & Nambisan, 2015 , p. 162). Digital platforms are transforming traditional value-creation mechanisms by increasing vertical and horizontal interactions among organizational ecosystems ( Rantala et al., 2023 ; Veile et al., 2022 ). While digital platforms have previously focused primarily on consumer business, recent studies have highlighted their growing interest in them and their growing relevance in B2B contexts ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Rantala et al., 2023 ; Ritala & Jovanovic, 2024 ; Trabucchi, Muzellec, Ronteau, & Buganza, 2022 ). These industrial digital platforms — employing various technologies, such as AI — are reshaping the B2B sector through inte - gration into both firms ’ internal operations and the external business environment to raise productivity ( Caiazzo et al., 2023 ; Jafari, Azarian, & Yu, 2022 ). Industrial digital platforms typically start with internal applications, where solutions support industrial firms ’ internal func - tions. As knowledge, technologies, and platform architectures evolve, the interfaces of industrial digital platforms are then opened up to supply chain partners (suppliers and customers) ( Randhawa, Wilden, & Gudergan, 2018 ; Rantala et al., 2023 ). In the B2B context, AI technol - ogies are considered focal to these platforms ( Baabdullah, Alalwan, Slade, Raman, & Khatatneh, 2021 ; Wei & Pardo, 2022 ). As stated by Kohtam äki et al. (2019) , firms are shifting their focus from remote monitoring to process optimization and control, and in the most advanced cases, to autonomous systems supported and operated by AI. In this advanced stage, industrial digital platforms may be referred to as AI platforms. Wei and Pardo (2022) define an AI platform as “ a modular structure that comprises tangible and intangible components (resources) and facilitates the interaction of actors and resources (or resource bundles) and where some resources are AI technologies. ” According to Caiazzo et al. (2023) , it is an industrial digital platform with an AI-driven platform algorithm embedded to apply AI-based tools in its operations. These platforms support a variety of AI functionalities, such as ML, natural language processing (NLP), computer vision, and predictive analytics, often to process large datasets and perform complex computation ( Collins, Dennehy, Conboy, & Mikalef, 2021 ). The platforms ’ multi-layered modular structures often comprise three layers of interactions: coordi - nation, integration, and capability levels ( Wei & Pardo, 2022 ). In the context of SMEs, Wei and Pardo (2022) describe these firms as inter - acting with AI platforms in different roles, such as users, designers, ideators, innovators, and intermediaries. In summary, AI platforms are industrial digital platforms that employ AI-based tools to support their operations. AI platforms are often strategically positioned as value-creating infrastructures that enable firms to introduce smart functionalities to their services, products, and processes. However, the effective utilization of AI platforms requires various inputs, such as large amounts of data, and suitable organiza - tional structures ( Berente, Gu, Recker, & Santhanam, 2021 ; Lafuente & Sallan, 2024 ). According to Kar and Kushwaha (2023) , their adoption depends on two important factors: an overall value addition of AI compared to investments in capability building, and AI ’ s effective uti - lization by employees. When these factors are absent, AI platforms may have limited potential to create tailored solutions for customers via a solution-based model ( Lafuente & Sallan, 2024 ). Thus, the wider context of AI platform adoption is key in driving digital servitization. Next, AI platform characteristics are introduced in the following section. 3.2. AI platform characteristics First, AI platforms can be characterized by their ability to optimize service processes ( Kunz & Wirtz, 2024 ). For instance, by possessing the characteristic of ‘optimization ’ , smart sensors can enhance the timeli - ness of services while also increasing information flow, which can improve services ’ quality and content. According to Sj ödin et al. (2021, 2023) , the main advantage of AI lies in supporting decision-making by transforming data into a manageable form. For example, developing data-driven capacities and capabilities provides significant opportu - nities for industrial firms to improve their resource efficiency, enhance diagnostics, automate operations, and manage resources ( Sj ödin et al., M. Saunila et al. Industrial Marketing Management 130 (2025) 35–45 37 2021 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). To those ends, AI platforms can interconnect various internal and external operators and simplify communication and coordination between them. When supported by AI platforms, decisions can be made based on real and historical data ( Woo, Shin, Seo, & Mei - lanitasari, 2018 ) and with either AI assistance or control ( Caiazzo et al., 2023 ). Collectively, these points highlight AI platforms ’ optimization characteristic. Second, AI provides industrial digital platforms with automation ( Raisch & Krakowski, 2021 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). For example, by pos - sessing the characteristic of ‘automation ’ , AI can automate routine as - signments, thereby reducing costs and enhancing efficiency ( Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). Moreover, AI platform tools such as ML can be used to successfully execute organizational tasks such as monitoring, sched - uling, detecting failures, and assessing quality ( Nassehi, Zhong, Li, & Epureanu, 2022 ). According to Javaid and Haleem (2020) , ML in AI platforms can be used to analyze data on the production process, and human critical thinking then complements its outputs, serving to improve their accuracy and supporting industrial automation based on those data. In addition, AI platforms may identify novel, cost-effective solutions that support sustainable long-term operations and ensure employees ’ well-being ( Caiazzo et al., 2023 ; Mourtzis, Angelopoulos, & Panopoulos, 2022 ). Nonetheless, Müller (2020) notes in this context that human-centricity is crucial to increasing productivity while safeguard - ing employees ’ rights. In that spirit, Caiazzo et al. (2023) propose that on AI-algorithm-driven platforms, human and machine operators should coexist cooperatively in production environments for maximum effi - ciency. In sum, AI platforms are characterized by their ability to auto - mate operations in order to reduce costs and enhance the efficiency of people and equipment. Third, AI platforms can ensure the security and privacy of people and processes. For example, platforms can be used for monitoring by combining digitalization and AI tools ( Caiazzo et al., 2023 ). Monitoring platforms such as neural networks may increase the security of machines and humans in working environments ( Dong et al., 2019 ). For instance, data-based fault diagnosis methods ( Xu, Liu, Jiang, Shen, & Huang, 2019 ) offer a tradeoff between data accuracy and employee capability development that allows for a reduction in training time. In the mining industry, as a specific example, AI platforms can enhance efficiency by enabling autonomous vehicles to execute underground operations ( Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). All these reflect the ‘security and privacy ’ char - acteristic of AI platforms. Fourth, AI platforms can be characterized by their planning capa - bilities in terms of facilitating design, forecasting risk, and managing complexity. By possessing the characteristic of ‘planning ’ , AI platforms can act as intermediaries that can increase the interconnection between a firm ’ s internal and external stakeholders for purposes such as infor - mation sharing and supply and demand management (cf. Rantala et al., 2023 ; Veile et al., 2022 ). This can assist in risk management in terms of design and testing. Sj ödin et al. (2023) further demonstrated that in platform environments, predictive, perceptive, and prescriptive AI ca - pabilities allow industrial firms to enhance resource efficacy by aug - menting and automating data-driven decisions and analyses. According to Jarrahi (2019) , planning augmentation can leverage the power of AI to drive human productivity and decision-making. AI can further intensify the testing and use of products through enhanced optimization, design, and real-time data analysis ( Sj ödin et al., 2021 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). Collectively, these statements highlight the planning character - istics of AI platforms. Fifth, AI platforms enhance organizational innovation by importing ideas and knowledge from external environments. Kar and Kushwaha (2023) highlighted that many firms invest in AI and build related ca - pabilities in order to access its potential for innovation. AI platforms are thus gaining importance in interactive marketing as they offer new ways to utilize information and knowledge outside organizational boundaries, serving to engage customers in value creation and innovation processes based on wider interaction, participation, and communication ( Veile et al., 2022 ; Wang, 2021 ). By possessing the characteristic of ‘innova - tion ’ , in the B2B context, AI advances and the increasing availability of data across platforms ( Haefner, Wincent, Parida, & Gassmann, 2021 ) have enabled the scaling of knowledge searches and efficient recombi - nation, which increase platforms ’ customer value ( Gregory, Hen - fridsson, Kaganer, & Kyriakou, 2021 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, AI not only purveys firms ’ external environments but also transforms traditional manufacturing by combining digitalization ’ s advantages with employees ’ expertise, while connecting up traditional work envi - ronments ( Caiazzo et al., 2023 ). In doing so, AI platforms combine the uses of the physical environment with employees ’ intelligence and knowledge, thereby providing opportunities and flexibility in work management ( Nahavandi, 2019 ) as an ingredient of ‘innovation ’ characteristic. In sum, AI platforms can be characterized in five ways: 1) optimi - zation (enhancing service processes), 2) automation (making both people and processes more efficient), 3) security and privacy (ensuring safety for both people and processes), 4) planning (enhancing capabil - ities for resource efficacy), and 5) innovation (improving agility). The next section introduces this study ’ s hypotheses regarding the contribu - tions of these five AI platform characteristics to digital servitization. 4. Hypothesis development: AI platform characteristics and digital servitization The first hypothesis in this study is broken down into five parts based on the characteristics outlined in the previous section. The first sub - hypothesis corresponds to the optimization characteristic of AI plat - forms and its connection to digital servitization. The introduction of smart technologies such as AI is increasing the power of platform openness, offering firms the chance to leverage external data origins and expose hidden insights ( Rantala et al., 2023 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). This type of technological development requires operational changes to improve the reliability or availability of services ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Visnjic, Neely, & Jovanovic, 2018 ), where firms must move from remote monitoring to optimization, control, and eventually, to autono - mous systems, where progressive functions based on AI to offer more reliable, higher-quality, and more versatile services as part of digital servitization (cf. Jovanovic et al., 2022 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ). In line with optimization characteristic of AI platforms, Jovanovic et al. (2022) found that onboarding quality data is a crucial step in constructing in - dustrial digital platforms that promote digital servitization. An inflow of quality data is needed in order to fully utilize AI algorithms, and securing that inflow requires open and interconnected systems. Jova - novic et al. (2022) accordingly suggested that platform sponsors should open up their interfaces in an authorized manner to raise the platform ’ s value and meet customers ’ needs, resulting in advanced platform ser - vices. In summary, industrial digital platforms utilizing AI can optimize the autonomy, availability, and customizability of services and products and promote digital servitization. Based on the above assertions, the following hypothesis is proposed: H1a . . Optimization characteristic of an AI platform is positively related to digital servitization. The second subhypothesis in this study relates to how the automation characteristic of an AI platform links to digital servitization. Industrial digital platforms are central to the utilization of AI, as they enable increased automation via the connection of various compatible ma - chines, the collection of equipment and operational data, and the implementation of high-level analytics, to offer progressive platform services such as fleet management, preventive maintenance, and site optimization ( Rantala et al., 2023 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). In particular, the progress of AI and the increasing availability of comprehensive data from platform operators enable the rapid scaling of information searches and more efficient data integration ( Alaimo, Kallinikos, & Valderrama, 2020 ; Haefner et al., 2021 ; Jovanovic et al., 2022 ; Savino, Messeni M. Saunila et al. Industrial Marketing Management 130 (2025) 35–45 38 Petruzzelli, & Albino, 2017 ). Rantala et al. (2023) suggested that AI enablement could drive automation and thus enhance advanced plat - form architectures in the future. Their study on industrial manufacturers and industrial digital platform providers indicated that utilizing AI al - gorithms that support automation in data collection, analysis, and simulation capabilities lowers operating and staff-related costs and in - creases the fleet ’ s productivity and effectiveness. These opportunities also support the development of more versatile and scalable services that enhance the platform ’ s value for customers ( Cennamo, 2021 ; Gregory et al., 2021 ; Rantala et al., 2023 ). In summary, industrial digital platforms that utilize AI to increase the automation of people and equipment promote digital servitization. Thus, we propose the following hypothesis: H1b . . Automation characteristic of an AI platform is positively related to digital servitization. The third subhypothesis in this study addresses the connection be - tween the security and privacy characteristics of the AI platform and digital servitization. AI platforms should provide security and privacy for employees, machines, and data to facilitate digital servitization ( Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). The importance of these actions lies in AI ’ s ability to improve routine task automation and overcome constraints on the handling of significant amounts of data ( Kushwaha et al., 2021 ; Wamba, 2022 ). Regarding employee safety, Sj ödin et al. (2023) found that, at least in the mining industry, AI solutions can automate and optimize ventilation systems to direct air effectively to specific areas of an un - derground mine, facilitating employee safety and energy efficiency. Regarding machine safety, AI can enhance operational efficiency and provide novel data for the continued life cycle ( Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). In terms of privacy, a relevant aspect of AI use is secure data sharing. This should underpin moves to broaden the scope of accessible data and combine information from various sources with relevance in running AI platforms ( Sj ödin et al., 2021 ). Certainly, a significant aspect of ensuring the data pipeline lies in linking up assets and machines to establish extensive datasets that AI can effectively utilize ( Sj ödin et al., 2021 ). Thus, AI security and privacy likely contribute to digital servitization. In accordance with previous studies, we hypothesize the following: H1c . . Security and privacy characteristics of an AI platform are positively related to digital servitization. The fourth subhypothesis in this study addresses how the AI plat - form ’ s planning characteristic, associated with design and testing, sup - ports digital servitization ( Abou-Foul, Ruiz-Alba, & L ópez-Tenorio, 2023 ; Paiola & Gebauer, 2020 ; Suppatvech, Godsell, & Day, 2019 ; Wang & Wang, 2018 ). The adoption of AI to predict future trends will be useful in delivering value through digital servitization, for example, in asset management, predictive maintenance ( Wang & Wang, 2018 ), and pro - cess optimization and control ( Paiola & Gebauer, 2020 ). The risks associated with planning design and testing can be reduced by creating routines for adopting AI. When embedded in industrial digital platforms, AI possesses the transformative potential to recognize and address ab - stract and intricate problems ( Sj ödin et al., 2021 ). According to Sj ödin et al. (2021) , it is crucial to manage this complexity by clarifying the potential applications of AI in specific areas and defining its role in design and education. This plays a pivotal role in establishing trust and transparency during AI adoption among employees and highlights that people are hesitant to trust an AI platform when they are unable to comprehend how it works or understand its contributions ( Sj ödin et al., 2021 ). In addition, with respect to the planning characteristic, AI can assist in identifying anomalies and discrepancies in the common mode of action, enabling anticipation, prediction, and responsive measures to support the optimal resource allocation ( Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). Sj ödin et al. (2023) showed that these AI techniques allow past data trends to be deduced, which supports efforts to forecast future behaviors, in turn producing actionable insights that should be applied to guide coordi - nating processes (e.g., maintenance stops and route planning). Thus, different planning activities facilitated by AI likely contribute to digital servitization. In accordance with previous assertions, we hypothesize the following: H1d . . Planning characteristic of an AI platform is positively related to digital servitization. The fifth and final subhypothesis in this study concerns the connection between the innovation characteristic of the AI platform and digital servitization. Managing the use of diverse AI technologies and effectively handling the organizational changes accompanying AI adoption are steps that other firms will find challenging to replicate ( Mikalef & Gupta, 2021 ). Thus, AI platforms deliver a spirit of innova - tion that contributes to digital servitization ( Rantala et al., 2023 ). For example, AI can identify activities that will provide the highest chance of accomplishing the firm ’ s intended objectives ( Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). These may be related to work management, in which AI can offer continuous connectivity and enable real-time data flow to remotely track distinct areas of machine operation in real-time ( Sj ödin et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, Sj ödin et al. (2021) refer to AI ’ s democratization, emphasizing the need to make AI approachable across firms and prove its prospects. The aim is to involve employees in discovering and exploring AI ’ s invaluable possibilities in terms of fostering data-driven insights that may be applied to enhance organizational innovation. Merely possessing technical abilities is not sufficient to derive real ad - vantages for a firm; instead, the firm must enhance its organizational proficiency in democratizing AI to ensure that insights acknowledge the behavior of employees and operations, thereby adding value to digital servitization via AI platforms ( Sj ödin et al., 2021 ). Thus, innovation facilitated by an AI platform likely contributes to digital servitization. In accordance with previous assertions, we hypothesize the following: H1e . . Innovation characteristic of an AI platform is positively related to digital servitization. Then, the second hypothesis in this study concerns the connection between AI platform characteristics overall and digital servitization (cf., Caiazzo et al., 2023 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2022 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ; Veile et al., 2022 ), considering whether firm productivity moderates that connection between the two. AI can either promote a firm ’ s digital servitization or cause a modern paradox (cf. Brynjolfsson, Rock, & Syverson, 2018 ). On the one hand, AI may enable firms to discover novel, productive combinations of the present technologies ( Agrawal, Gans, & Goldfarb, 2019 ), thus enhancing their digital servitization. On the other hand, AI may not produce advantages immediately after its implementation ( Jovanovic & Rousseau, 2005 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ; Yang, Luo, Feng, & Pan, 2023 ). This lag in the digital servitization boost of AI may be attributed, for example, to arrangement costs or organizational transformations ( Brynjolfsson et al., 2018 ; Yang et al., 2023 ). The implementation of AI platforms will also have negative consequences, such as leading employees to fear for the future of their jobs or pro - ducing costs or challenges for firms in securing the capabilities needed to implement AI. In other words, the interplay between AI platform char - acteristics and digital servitization may provide advantages for firms with low productivity, for example, by automating routine servitization tasks; however, it may also cause a productivity paradox for firms with high productivity (or low AI capabilities). Thus, we hypothesize the following: H2 . . Firm productivity moderates the relationship between AI plat - form characteristics and digital servitization. Sample and data collection Data collection began by pretesting our questionnaire with five ex - perts from digital servitization firms and three researchers. The following approach was used to construct and pretest the questionnaire: First, the objectives of the questionnaire were carefully defined by clarifying the information that we aimed to collect. Second, a thorough literature review was conducted to identify relevant studies, based on which a questionnaire could be compiled. We then developed potential questionnaire items for each construct based on the literature review. This resulted in an initial draft of the questionnaire, in which items were organized into logical sections and clear, concise wording was ensured. We then utilized expert consultation by sending a web link to eight experts working in industry and academia, who checked the clarity and validity of the items. The test group provided feedback, based on which we revised or eliminated unclear items and refined the overall user experience in the survey questionnaire execution. Data allowing us to test the research model were collected over four weeks, from February to March 2023. The survey questionnaire and a cover letter explaining the research objective were emailed to the CEOs of 7850 randomly selected SMEs. More than 99 % of Finnish firms are SMEs, which generate more than 50 % of Finland ’ s total turnover. After the initial email, three waves of reminders were sent to the target firms. Of the 7850 firms, 245 emails did not reach the firms ’ email addresses and produced return-to-sender messages. After data collection was completed, the responses were pre-checked and the data cleaned accordingly. Responses were eliminated if the majority of the items were left unanswered. From the remaining 7605 firms, 179 valid responses were received. The 179 valid responses met the benchmarks for response rate ( Saunders, Lewis, & Thornhill, 2007 ) and sample size ( Krejcie & Mor - gan, 1970 ) deemed appropriate for this study. According to the litera - ture, for models with up to five latent constructs, each with over three variables and strong communalities among them, a sample size above 100 is acceptable ( Hair, Black, Babin, & Anderson, 2014 ). The final sample size met these criteria. Most respondents ’ firms were small, employing 49 or fewer em - ployees (64 %), but there were also medium-sized firms employing 50 – 249 employees among the responses (36 %). Overall, 62 % of the responses were from manufacturing-oriented firms, while 38 % were service-oriented. 5.2. Measures 5.2.1. Dependent variable Digital servitization. A three-item scale was used to measure digital servitization as the dependent variable. Respondents were asked to assess whether their respective firms utilized smart technologies for the following purposes: service business (e.g., new services, maintenance, and modernization), generating new business, and sales. The following definition of smart technologies was provided in the survey to prevent uninformed responses: “ [Smart technologies] refers to the technology ’ s ability to utilize skills commonly connected with human intelligence, such as reasoning, learning, or planning. ” Respondents were asked to respond on a scale of 1 (totally disagree) to 5 (totally agree). 5.2.2. Independent variables AI platform characteristics . This scale conceptualizes five AI platform characteristics: optimization, automation, security and privacy, plan - ning, and innovation. Scales of four, five, six, three, and two items were used to measure optimization, automation, security and privacy, plan - ning, and innovation, respectively. Respondents were asked to assess the different elements that smart technologies have enabled in their respective firms on a scale of 1 (totally disagree) to 5 (totally agree). The following definition of smart technologies was provided in the survey to prevent uninformed responses: “ [Smart technologies] refers to the technology ’ s ability to utilize skills commonly connected with human intelligence, such as reasoning, learning, or planning. ” All scale items are listed in Table 1 . 5.2.3. Moderator variable Firm productivity . Firm productivity was measured using a one-item scale in which respondents were asked to rate their firm ’ s productivity compared to their competitors ’ performance on a scale of 1 (much worse than competitors) to 5 (much better than competitors). This variable captures firms ’ performance in relation to various operational-level factors, including order fill capacity, information systems support, and advanced shipping notification. 5.2.4. Control variables Three controls were included in the survey to control for alternative explanations of the studied relationships. We then controlled for a competitive intensity and predictability in the market. The respondents were asked to assess the intensity of competition over a three-year timeframe. Responses were provided on a scale of 1 (not at all intense) to 5 (extremely intense). The respondents were asked to assess predictability in the markets in which they operated over a three-year timeframe. Responses were provided on a scale of 1 = easy to predict to 5 = hard to predict. 5.3. Bias To address common method bias, both procedural and statistical measures were used ( Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003 ). In our procedural measures, anonymity and confidentiality were ensured, preventing respondents from establishing causal relationships between the independent and dependent variables. In our statistical measures, an unrotated factor analysis (Harman ’ s one-factor test) was conducted for all items related to the study variables. This procedure revealed four distinct factors and demonstrated that a single factor accounted for less than 50 % of the variance. Notably, no general factors emerged, sug - gesting that common method bias was not a concern. An ANOVA test was employed to scrutinize the non-response bias. Early respondents who replied within approximately one week of the initial email were compared with later respondents (who replied after the last reminder), resembling non-respondents because of their multi - ple reminders ( Armstrong & Overton, 1977 ). All study variables were compared, including AI characteristics, firm productivity, and digital servitization. No statistically significant differences arose between the early and late respondents, indicating that non-response bias was not an issue. Fig. 1. Research model with hypotheses. M. Saunila et al. Discussion This study explored the impact of AI platform characteristics on digital servitization and the influence of firm-related factors on this relationship. AI-powered industrial digital platforms can enhance digital servitization. However, the AI platform characteristics most greatly impacting digital servitization have not yet been investigated, at least in the SME context. We hypothesized that distinct AI platform character - istics enable SMEs to effectively manage digital servitization — a novel perspective in AI platform research. The main contributions of this study are as follows. First, this study contributes to the literature on digital servitization, which prior research has highlighted as important for developing future servitization research ( Rabetino, Kohtam äki, Kowalkowski, et al., 2021 ). However, empirical studies demonstrating the benefits of advanced digital technologies and explaining how to achieve those benefits are scarce ( Kohtam äki et al., 2021 ). In particular, the potential implications of different AI platform characteristics and specific SME contexts have received little attention. Thus, this study contributes to our understanding of the interplay between AI and digital servitization, which has only recently gained attention ( Caiazzo et al., 2023 ; Lafuente & Sallan, 2024 ; Sj ödin et al., 2021 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). The results show that the optimization, automation, and innovation characteristics of AI platforms are crucial for facilitating digital serviti - zation in SMEs. In particular, the characteristics of an AI platform that optimize the timeliness of services and improve their quality and content play an important role in successful digital servitization. This is in line with prior research that has indicated that the move from remote monitoring to optimization, control, and eventually, to autonomous systems with progressive functions is key to offering more reliable, high- quality, and versatile services as part of digital servitization ( Jovanovic et al., 2022 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ). The results show that when AI is embedded in industrial digital platforms, their optimization of opera - tions can enhance digital servitization. In addition, an AI platform ’ s automation of various tasks plays an important role in successful digital servitization. This is in line with prior research showing that AI plat - forms can be used to successfully execute organizational tasks such as monitoring, scheduling, detecting failures, and assessing quality ( Nassehi et al., 2022 ) and thus can assist in automating routine tasks, driving efficiency, and reducing costs ( Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). All these benefits also facilitate digital servitization in terms of gaining a new service business. Furthermore, they are in line with prior research highlighting the importance of AI for improving routine task automation on existing industrial digital platforms and overcoming constraints on handling significant amounts of data ( Kushwaha et al., 2021 ; Wamba, 2022 ). In particular, the progress of AI and the increasing availability of comprehensive data from industrial digital platform operators enable the rapid scaling of information searches and more efficient data inte - gration ( Alaimo et al., 2020 ; Haefner et al., 2021 ; Rantala et al., 2023 ; Savino et al., 2017 ), leading to more versatile and scalable services, which enhance the value of the platform for customers ( Cennamo, 2021 ; Gregory et al., 2021 ; Rantala et al., 2023 ). Finally, the innovation characteristics of an AI platform, centered on how it renews and man - ages operations, play an important role in successful digital servitiza - tion. AI provides increased flexibility in work environments, allowing more time for the development of ideas related to digital servitization. Second, this study enhances our understanding of the servitization paradox by revealing the moderating influence of firm productivity on the relationship between AI platform characteristics and digital servi - tization. The literature suggests that, on the one hand, AI may enable firms to discover novel productive combinations of the present tech - nologies ( Agrawal et al., 2019 ), thus enhancing their digital servitiza - tion. However, AI may not produce advantages immediately after its implementation ( Jovanovic & Rousseau, 2005 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2023 ). This study deepens our understanding as follows: The firm ’ s productivity level was found to positively moderate the effect of the optimization characteristic of the AI platform on digital servitiza - tion. Therefore, high productivity contributes to the utilization of AI platforms for optimization, for example, in producing higher-quality, timely, and reliable services, in a way that produces new services and increases the sales of various services (digital servitization). In partic - ular, higher productivity seems connected to a firm ’ s ability to utilize and optimize data in a customer-oriented manner, thereby strength - ening digital service delivery. This indicates that high-productivity firms already use AI to create new productive combinations of existing tech - nologies to achieve optimization ( Agrawal et al., 2019 ). Meanwhile, firm productivity seems to negatively moderate the relationship between the automation characteristic of an AI platform and digital servitization. That is, if firm productivity is high, the increased use of AI in industrial digital platforms weakens digital ser - vitization. This lag in the digital servitization boost of AI may be attributed, for example, to arrangement costs or organizational trans - formations ( Brynjolfsson et al., 2018 ; Yang et al., 2023 ). In the case of a high-productivity firm, investing in AI-driven automation is not bene - ficial for digital servitization. This may stem from the firm productivity paradox, where firms with high productivity, when investing in AI tools characterized by automation, may not experience great cost benefits as their digital servitization may already be advanced (cf. Brynjolfsson et al., 2018 ). Although, as Sj ödin et al. (2023) note, the automation capability of AI enables the execution of routine tasks, thereby reducing costs and improving efficiency, in highly productive organizations ser - vitization may have already been advanced through other automation tools. In such cases, the implementation of AI may be regarded as an expensive investment relative to its benefits, particularly if personnel training for AI utilization is required at the same time. In any case, this remains a topic that requires further research. 8. Conclusions This study provides novel insights into how digital servitization is affected by various characteristics of AI platforms. The findings suggest that the moderating influence of firm-related factors depends on those characteristics. Thus, this study contributes to servitization research by enhancing our understanding of the connections between AI platforms and digital servitization. To that end, first, this study developed an AI platform characteristic construct, with an AI platform built on five characteristics: (1) optimization, (2) automation, (3) security and pri - vacy, (4) planning, and (5) innovation. A corresponding measurement scale was developed for this construct. Second, this study developed a theoretical framework for how AI platform characteristics impact digital servitization. While there is abundant research on AI adoption and digital servitization, revealing the significant effects of AI platforms on the latter, research on their inter - play is scarce. This study is among the first to investigate the influence of AI platform characteristics on digital servitization and assess the moderating influence of firm-related factors. Specifically, the results show that three AI platform characteristics contribute to digital servi - tization: optimization, automation, and innovation, whereas the remaining two do not: security and privacy and planning. In addition, the current research is novel in addressing the SME context, as most previous research has studied large firms. In particular, this study re - veals the role of AI platform characteristics in digital servitization using data collected from Finnish SMEs. Through a survey of those SMEs, this study empirically examined the effects of several AI platform charac - teristics on digital servitization, and in that way, it offers new contri - butions to the literature, so far predominantly made up of conceptual and qualitative studies. Third, this study considers firm-related factors and how they mediate the relationship between AI platform characteristics and digital servi - tization, thereby contributing importantly to our understanding of the servitization paradox. The results highlight the role of firm productivity as a crucial factor facilitating digital servitization via AI platforms. The results of this study inspired us to integrate AI platform characteristics, digital servitization, and firm productivity into a single model, where firm productivity can both drive and hinder the relationship between AI platform characteristics and digital servitization. This study points to avenues for further research. First, the empirical evidence for the study was collected in a northern European country, with resulting country- or region-specific characteristics. The focus on Finnish SMEs was chosen to gain contextually coherent sample. Single- country sample provides homogeneous economic, regulatory, and technological environment which increases the internal validity of the study. Finnish SMEs also represent a typical case of SMEs in developed economies, making the insights transferable to similar contexts. Although AI platforms by nature are not necessarily region-specific, but rather operate worldwide, further studies from other regions and sectors would build on the results of this initial contribution. Second, this study has focused on the servitization context and the characteristics of AI platforms, and we welcome further studies with more technology spe - cific approaches. Prior studies have highlighted the roles of intelligent agents, chatbots, and LLMs in AI tool development, and their interplay with AI platform characteristics could be investigated. Third, this study has shed light on the role of firm productivity in creating a paradox between AI platform characteristics and digital servitization, and further studies are needed to explore other firm-related factors involved in this paradox. Fourth, regarding the positive effects of automation and opti - mization highlighted in the current research, future studies can inves - tigate how AI enables fully autonomous organizational processes, where products, services, and platforms interact in real time without human intervention. Additionally, future studies could examine how AI opti - mizes resource use, reduces environmental impact, and supports circular economy models in conjunction with evolving industry structures. Full Length Article The role of transformational leadership in navigating digital servitization Florian Tagscherer , Claus-Christian Carbon * Department of General Psychology and Methodology, University of Bamberg, Markusplatz 3, 96047 Bamberg, Bavaria, Germany ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Digital servitization Transformational leadership Digital transformation Managing complexity Change management ABSTRACT Digital servitization converges two current innovation activities in industrial companies: shifting from product- oriented to service-oriented business models and integrating digital technologies in market offerings. Adding digitalized services offers significant growth and diversification opportunities, but companies have struggled to reap its potential. Establishing digital servitization business models is underpinned by complexity, making it difficult for companies to manage. Digital servitization is a relatively new research stream, especially needing more guidance on how companies should be led to succeed in its implementation. We addressed this research gap and conducted thirty semi-structured interviews with leaders in digital servitization holding ranks ranging from first-level Managers to Vice Presidents and Executives with more than 20 years of leadership experience active in industries such as machinery, electrical equipment, or IT services. We identified transformational leadership as vital to building digital servitization business models and navigating their inherent complexity and change management requirements. Our findings include three focus areas as recommendations for leadership: giving direction, being employee-oriented, and creating an innovative and collaborative environment. Furthermore, transactional leadership aspects should be considered for specific use cases to maintain the business model, for example, improving after a certain amount of time or managing crisis mode. Introduction Digitalization is a megatrend that fundamentally changes existing value chains across industries ( Calderon-Monge & Ribeiro-Soriano, 2024 ). Digitalization in companies creates opportunities for new ser - vices, intelligent products, and business models ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Proksch et al., 2024 ). Servitization is another strategy companies pursue to generate additional growth potential ( Khanra et al., 2021 ). Serviti - zation is an organizational change process, first introduced by Vander - merwe and Rada (1988) , that generates new revenue streams and delivers value through selling integrated products and service bundles ( Baines et al., 2009 ; Bustinza et al., 2015 ; Leoc ádio et al., 2024 ). The introduction of digital technologies to service-oriented business models enables connectivity, monitoring, control, optimization, and autonomy of smart product-service bundles ( Chen et al., 2021 ), resulting in inno - vative business models such as predictive maintenance and remote control systems ( Sklyar et al., 2019 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). This com - bination of both growth opportunities, digitalization and servitization, is called digital servitization and represents an opportunity to increase value creation for companies through digitally enabled services and new business models ( Paschou et al., 2020 ; Shen et al., 2023 ; Sj ödin et al., 2023 ). The reconfiguration of business models through digital servitization involves a complex organizational change process due to the required transition of resources and competencies ( Bustinza et al., 2018 ; Raja et al., 2024 ). Tronvoll et al. (2020) described digital servitization as a process underpinned by transformational shifts. Leaders are essential in implementing organizational change and transforming organizations from their current to their desired future state ( Nging & Yazdanifard, 2015 ; Potosky & Azan, 2023 ). Transformational leadership is a scientific research concept closely associated with change management ( Eisenbach et al., 1999 ; Warrick, 2011 ), where leaders are associated as role models who lead their organizations beyond self-interest with a clear vision and a sense of purpose ( Stewart, 2006 ). Transformational leadership positively correlates with leading companies in times of change ( McCleskey, 2014 ). Despite the expected positive contributions, Pham and Vu (2022) describe companies failing behind their expectations in advancing dig - ital servitization activities, amongst others, caused by the complexity and difficulty of managing them. Theoretical background Digital servitization The concept of servitization was first introduced by Vandermerwe and Rada (1988) . They coined the phenomenon as adding value to companies ’ core offerings through services. More specifically, Vander - merwe and Rada (1988) described servitization as a customer-focused combination of goods, services, support, self-service, and knowledge to offer bundles to the market to sharpen companies ’ competitive edge. The research area of servitization is mainly allocated within manufacturing companies, where manufacturers provide services tightly coupled to their products ( Baines & Lightfoot, 2014 ; Zahoor et al., 2023 ). Practical examples of successful servitization business models can be seen in Rolls-Royce Holdings plc's introduction of guar - anteed flight hours from their aero engines —“ Power by the Hour ” ( Bıçakcıo ğlu-Peynirci & Morgan, 2023 ; Leoc ádio et al., 2024 ) or Xerox's move from providing photocopiers to offering document management ( Ahn et al., 2023 ; Baines et al., 2009 ). While adding services to existing products, companies can gain several advantages. Compared to product-only offerings, services are more resistant to economic cycles ( Oliva & Kallenberg, 2003 ; Ven - drell-Herrero et al., 2022 ), supporting companies to generate more stable and recurring revenue streams ( Bustinza et al., 2013 ; Gebauer et al., 2005 ; Leoc ádio et al., 2024 ). Companies achieve competitive advantages through tailoring product-service bundles and integrated solution packages ( Baines et al., 2007 , 2009 ; Tian et al., 2022 ), which are more difficult to imitate ( Gebauer et al., 2005 ; Oliva & Kallenberg, 2003 ) and help avoid price-based competition ( Baines et al., 2007 ; Leoc ádio et al., 2024 ). Consequently, the business relationship with customers shifts from transactional to more long-term and relationship-based customer relationships ( Kramer et al., 2024 ; Oliva & Kallenberg, 2003 ), locking out the competition and binding customers to the company and its offerings ( Bustinza et al., 2013 ; Chiu et al., 2023 ; Vandermerwe & Rada, 1988 ). Digital as the second component of digital servitization, besides servitization, arises from developing and implementing information and communication technology ( Larjovuori et al., 2018 ). Digitization refers to the technical process of converting analog information into digital bits that can be transferred quickly, accurately, and cheaply ( Brennen & Kreiss, 2016 ; Paul et al., 2023 ). Digital technologies are now incorpo - rated into everyday products such as TVs, watches, or cars, creating intelligent systems based on sensors, networks, and processors ( Yoo et al., 2012 ). Digital technologies are also described with the SMACIT acronym: Social, Mobile, Analytics, Cloud, and Internet of Things ( Samuelson & Stehn, 2023 ; Vial, 2019 ). When companies use digital technologies to alter their existing business processes, offer digital products, or create digital business models, scientific research intro - duced the term “ digitalization ” ( Verhoef et al., 2021 ), which gained increased scholarly attention since 2015 ( Reis et al., 2018 ). Current scientific research sees a strong link between digitalization and servitization. Digital servitization converges the two concepts and enables a new dimension of sophisticated and innovative service offer - ings for manufacturing companies ( Gebauer et al., 2021 ; Paschou et al., 2020 ; Shen et al., 2023 ). Several authors have published definitions of digital servitization. Kohtam äki et al. (2019 , p.4) see it as “ transition toward smart product-service-software systems enabling value creation and capture through monitoring, control, optimization, and autonomous function. ” Paschou et al. (2019) point out the development of new ser - vices or improvement of existing ones using digital technologies by enabling new digital business models, finding ways of co-creating value, and generating knowledge from data. As a result, companies gain competitive advantages through digital servitization, leading to an in - crease in companies ’ operational performance. Digital technologies are the basis for digital servitization activities such as reporting real-time information, monitoring customers ’ usage behavior, responsive and proactive or predictive maintenance, remote control of operations, and equipment availability services ( Ch ávez et al., 2023 ; Paiola & Gebauer, 2020 ). Data availability and analytics are crucial for these digital ser - vices ( Ch ávez et al., 2023 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). These use the installed base of existing customers based on previously sold equipment and products to leverage digital servitization as a customer-oriented busi - ness model for companies ( Paiola & Gebauer, 2020 ; Raja et al., 2024 ). A change in a business model such as digital servitization can significantly impact companies and requires an organizational change effort to benefit from it ( Bustinza et al., 2018 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Momeni et al., 2024 ; Sklyar et al., 2019 ). The increased complexity of digital service offerings is accompanied by changes in involved stake - holders in various areas of the value chain ( Marelli & Dello Sbarba, 2024 ). Companies must interact with hardware and software providers, might have different contacts on the customer end, and a change of departments ’ internal resource and responsibility allocation ( Sklyar et al., 2019 ). Kohtam äki et al. (2019) and Dalenogare et al. (2023) call for collaboration across company boundaries within the ecosystem when implementing smart product-service bundles, as changes in one company's business model affect others due to the interconnectedness of processes, data, and information. A change in a business model must be governed and implemented by leaders within an organization ( Adama & Okeke, 2024 ; Turyadi et al., 2023 ). Digital servitization is a complex change process from various perspectives. On the one hand, new digital technologies and their application is introduced. Trans - formational leadership is a leadership style that scientific research as - sociates suitable for change processes and employee commitment to organizational change ( Anderson, 2017 ; Bagga et al., 2023 ; Ly, 2024 ; Shadraconis, 2013 ), which is further described in the following chapter. Transformational leadership within the full range leadership model Initially introduced in a political context, Burns (1978) first pub - lished ideas on the concept of transformational and transactional lead - ership, which was further developed by Bass (1985) for organizational research ( Eisenbach et al., 1999 ). The Multifactor Leadership Ques - tionnaire (MLQ), developed by Bass and Avolio (1997) , is the most widely used instrument to measure transformational and transactional leadership. Based on a total of 45 questions, the questionnaire distin - guishes between three leadership styles ( Kirkbride, 2006 ; Muenjohn & Armstrong, 2008 ): • Non-leadership (laissez-faire), • Transactional leadership, • Transformational leadership. Laissez-faire leadership is associated with indecisiveness, un- involvement, withdrawal, or reluctance ( Bass & Avolio, 1990 ). Trans - actional leadership builds on agreement and compliance with the leader in return for rewards and recognition, implying close monitoring of deviances and mistakes, resulting in corrective action ( Bass et al., 2003 ). Transactional leadership is achieved by management through exception and contingent reward strategies ( Kirkbride, 2006 ). Thus, transactional leadership seeks to maximize efficiency in well-ordered societies. Transformational leadership is seen as suitable for times of distress and change ( Bass, 1985 ; McCleskey, 2014 ). Transformational leaders elevate the desires of followers for achievement and self-development, increasing followers ’ confidence and gradually moving them from concerns of existing to achievement, growth, and development ( Bass & Avolio, 1990 ). Comparing the three leadership styles, laissez-faire leadership is rated as inactive (passive), transactional leadership is in the middle, and transformational leadership is the most active of the three styles. This classification is depicted in Fig. 1 , which describes the Full Range Leadership Model and explains the continuum of leadership styles ( Humphreys, 2001 ). Moreover, the model ranks efficiency among the three styles, with laissez-faire leadership as the least efficient and transformational leadership as the most efficient ( Kirkbride, 2006 ). Over several decades of research and revisions of the original concept, most authors in this field of research characterize trans - formational leadership with the four common I's — idealized influence, individualized consideration, inspirational motivation, and intellectual stimulation ( Hay, 2006 ). Leithwood and Jantzi (2000) proposed six transformational leadership characteristics — building vision and goals, providing intellectual stimulation, offering individualized support, symbolizing professional practices and values, demonstrating high-performance expectations, and developing structures to foster participation in decisions. We see similarities in both categorizations but continue to use the common four I's as the central concept for future discussions due to its empirical validation in several research works. More specifically focused on the four common I's of transformational leadership, idealized influence means that transformational leaders have a clear vision and a sense of purpose and are role models with whom followers identify. Inspirational motivation is shown through clear communication of expectations and the generation of enthusiasm to demonstrate a commitment to a common goal. Transformational leaders stimulate their followers to be creative and promote new ideas and ways of doing things through intellectual stimulation. This skill set is complemented by individualized consideration, which highlights a supportive climate and the attribute of paying attention to the needs and development of others ( Stewart, 2006 ). We summarized various trans - formational leadership characteristics based on existing research within the dimensions of idealized influence, inspirational motivation, indi - vidual consideration, and intellectual stimulation. The orientation towards the employee is a central element directly described within individual consideration. However, transformational leaders are also concerned with generating a high level of performance from their followers through indirect measures such as creating a clear sense of purpose ( Stewart, 2006 ), motivating and inspiring ( Hay, 2006 ), ultimately leading to increased creativity and innovation capability ( Bass & Avolio, 1990 ). Transformational leaders create the necessary boundary conditions without detailed instructions on how to reach the given goal. Nevertheless, their attitude promotes an environment that motivates employees to achieve those goals based on their distinct ap - proaches. According to Hay (2006) , followers gain confidence in transformational leaders, the baseline for accepting change. Table 2 summarizes our findings to represent the current scientific findings about leadership aspects for digital servitization. Despite many listed aspects, we can identify patterns of frequently mentioned leadership subjects concerning digital servitization. Firstly, several authors emphasize the importance of creating a compelling vision for digital servitization ( Chirumalla et al., 2023 ; Favoretto et al., 2022 ; Marcon et al., 2022 ; Pham & Vu, 2022 ; Sklyar et al., 2019 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). The vision for digital servitization serves multiple purposes, such as legitimization ( Tronvoll et al., 2020 ) and guidance for change ( Sklyar et al., 2019 ), which is also deeply anchored in the defi - nition of a transformational leader ( Kirkbride, 2006 ). Furthermore, extant literature describes significant organizational change processes as a result of the digital servitization journey ( Bustinza et al., 2018 ; Cor - eynen et al., 2020 ; Favoretto et al., 2022 ; Kim & Toya, 2018 ; Marcon et al., 2022 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). Leaders are asked to actively manage the change on a strategic, organizational, and personal level arising from the convergence of the two subjects, digitalization and servitization ( Bustinza et al., 2018 ). These requirements fit the description of a transformational leader ( Hechanova & Cementina-Olpoc, 2013 ). Another aspect frequently mentioned refers to the need for pro - moting internal and external collaboration for organizations in the context of digital servitization ( Cimini et al., 2021 ; Favoretto et al., 2022 ; Marcon et al., 2022 ; Pham & Vu, 2022 ; Sklyar et al., 2019 ; T óth et al., 2022 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). Especially opening up and collabo - rating within ecosystems across organizational boundaries is a critical success factor for digital servitization ( Pham & Vu, 2022 ; T óth et al., 2022 ). Besides the ecosystems perspective, Sklyar et al. (2019) also outline the importance of close intra-firm collaboration between orga - nizational units and departments. An area that has been finding lesser attention in digital servitization research so far is the focus on soft skills. Cimini et al. (2021) recommend finding the right balance between technical and soft skills and argue that underestimating soft skills is a challenge for companies undergoing digital servitization. In their study on transformational shifts through digital servitization, Tronvoll et al. (2020) recognize the close link between applying soft and social skills and the success of change initiatives for digital servitization. Existing research positively relates digital servitization with an innovative ( Marcon et al., 2022 ; Pham & Vu, 2022 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ) and entrepreneurial mindset ( Favoretto et al., 2022 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ) for leadership. Especially the openness to innovation ( Marcon et al., 2022 ) and the ability to create an environment for innovation deployment ( Pham & Vu, 2022 ) are vital aspects that leaders and or - ganizations should recognize for digital servitization. Similar to the previously mentioned leadership aspects, the innovation characteristics also fit the intellectual stimulation dimension of a transformational leader ( Gumusluoglu & Ilsev, 2009 ; Stewart, 2006 ). In summary, despite not being specifically mentioned in the extant literature, we can match several discussed leadership characteristics for digital servitization to transformational leadership attributes. Despite outlining various leadership characteristics promoting digi - tal servitization, existing research lacks specific research emphasis on leadership skills for digital servitization as the primary research objec - tive. Furthermore, as leadership encompasses a wide array of charac - teristics and styles ( Piwowar-Sulej & Iqbal, 2023 ), a more structured approach is required to guide how to succeed in digital servitization. Thus, our research focused on transformational leadership to contribute to the existing research gap. The specific structure and focus on a dedicated leadership style aid in guiding practitioners in overcoming the current complexity and difficulties of implementing digital servitization business models. Methods Data collection The selection process for our research participants for the semi- structured interviews followed the concept of purposive sampling ( Etikan et al., 2016 ). We contacted potential research participants through the business-focused platform “ LinkedIn ” searching for “ digital services, ” “ servitization, ” “ digitalization, ” and “ digital transformation ” in job titles. We ensured they matched our target group by initial questioning. This approach warrants sufficient knowledge and experi - ence to contribute to our qualitative research ( Bernard, 2017 ). One researcher conducted and recorded the interviews from April 2023 to July 2023 via the program “ Microsoft Teams. ” The raw data of the transcripts was enhanced using the intelligent verbatim transcription method ( McMullin, 2023 ) with the support of the MAXQDA program ( VERBI Software, 2021 ). We reached code saturation after thirty interviews. Our interview guideline consists of open-ended questions to answer our research question about which aspects of transformational leader - ship support digital servitization. With open-ended questions, we certify that the answers provide the necessary exploratory background on why the leaders responded this way, as digital servitization is still a new research area. The semi-structured interviews followed the logic of starting with a short introduction to familiarize with the research participant and the inquiry about the demographical background, such as hierarchy level or industry association. Afterward, we created a common understanding of the research subjects of digital servitization and transformational leadership by outlining and discussing their defi - nitions. Thus, this increases reliability and validity by ensuring the researcher and research participant have the same understanding of the research topic. The first substantial question was intentionally kept general, inquiring about the required leadership skills for digital servi - tization. After that, the outlined transformational leadership dimensions (Idealized Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Individual Consideration, and Intellectual Stimulation; see also Table 1 ) served as a baseline to derive the following open-ended interview questions. We included probing questions to deepen the understanding and nuances of the participants ’ responses further ( Adams, 2015 ). Our digital servitization leaders can be attributed to different company levels, ranging from first-level Managers to Vice Presidents and Executives. We considered an even allocation between company levels based on the distribution among the different ranks. For classifying our thirty research participants to the industry, we used the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) as a globally valid standard ( MSCI, 2022 ). Most of our research participants were active in the machinery, automobile, or electrical equipment industry, which can be seen as a focus area of digital servitization. Another category included consultants active in business and IT, supporting their clients in digital servitization activities, classified as professional or IT services. Another criterion for clustering our research participants is their leadership track record, measured in years of leadership experience. Whereas six research par - ticipants were at the beginning of their leadership career ( < 5 years), sixty percent of the respondents had more than ten years of leadership experience. A balanced distribution, including younger leaders, repre - sents recently developed leadership concepts and approaches. Lastly, six of our research participants were female, whereas twenty-six were male. Data analysis We analyzed our data set based on thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke (2006) . More specifically, we applied a hybrid approach of deductive ( Crabtree & Miller, 1992 ) and inductive ( Boyatzis, 1998 ) thematic analysis. We chose this combined approach to analyze the re - sponses to answer our research question ( Fereday & Muir-Cochrane, 2006 ). On the one hand, we used our outlined transformational lead - ership characteristics ( Table 1 ) as a template from a deductive view. We counted the references of the specific attributes of the four I's (idealized influence, inspirational motivation, individual consideration, and in - tellectual stimulation) within the transcripts. On the other hand, we reviewed the data set inductively by adding attributes to the trans - formational leadership categories mentioned during the interviews. The results were structured with a three-stage system summarizing the original codes into themes, which were further aggregated into di - mensions ( Gioia et al., 2013 ). Within the analysis, we excluded initially created codes, which resulted in five or fewer counts due to their sta - tistical relevance. Furthermore, we added a coding in shades of grey based on the number of counts for which the specific code is used in our analyses ( Brauer et al., 2021 ). Lastly, we included a question on the fit of transactional leadership for digital servitization in our questionnaire, in which we summarize the statements inductively as a separate category in the results section. Researcher bias was addressed through an inter - coder check between the research partners, which resulted in agreement on the coding results ( Mayring, 2014 ).
