Strategic emphasis, outsourcing intensity, and financial performance in digital servitization Ornella Benedettini * Department of Mechanics, Mathematics and Management, Polytechnic University of Bari, Via Orabona 4, 70125 Bari, Italy ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Digital servitization Digital services Product-service-systems (PSS) Strategic emphasis Outsourcing intensity Financial performance ABSTRACT The literature on digital servitization calls for more research linking specific organizational choices related to the implementation of digital services to financial outcomes of the providing firm. This study evaluates how two fundamental such organizational choices – i.e., strategic emphasis on value creation activities over value appropriation activities, and outsourcing intensity – affect firm profitability, along with the moderating role of firm size. Analysis of longitudinal archival data, collected for a sample of 176 manufacturing firms engaged in digital servitization, reveals several noteworthy relationships. Greater relative emphasis on value creation activities negatively impacts firm profitability, but to an extent that decreases with firm size. In addition, while outsourcing intensity has a positive direct effect on firm profitability, the relationship is observed to change with the size of the firm; that is, greater outsourcing intensity may lead to lower profitability in the case of large firms. For managers of manufacturing firms, the study provides insights that may help tackle the implementation challenges of digital servitization, enhancing their abilities to determine appropriate resource allocation strategies and configurations of value chain activities to increase financial performance. The appropriate organizational choices vary with the size of the firm. 1. Introduction Over recent years, advancements in digital technologies have radically transformed service industries, offering service sector firms significant new possibilities to create customer value and achieve competitive differentiation ( Porter & Heppelmann, 2015 ; Wirtz & Kowalkowski, 2023 ). The development of digital technologies also represents a prominent drive towards service innovation and expansion for many manufacturing firms that have shifted their business from exclusively providing physical products to developing and selling combined product and service offerings ( Kolagar, Parida, & Sj ödin, 2022 ; Raddats et al., 2022 ). Illustrative examples of this trend, formally conceptualized as digital servitization ( Cenamor et al., 2017 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Sj ödin et al., 2020 ; Sklyar et al., 2019 ), include leading providers like ABB and Volvo – that have been increasingly leveraging sensor technologies and artificial intelligence capabilities to offer innovative digital services, such as fleet management and site optimization based on remotely monitoring, analyzing, and adapting the performance of connected products ( Linde et al., 2021 ; Sj ödin et al., 2021 ; Sj ödin et al., 2022 ). This move by manufacturing firms towards providing digitally enabled services and solutions has been accompanied by a rapidly growing number of theoretical and empirical studies focusing on digital servitization in the marketing, innovation and general management literatures ( Favoretto et al., 2022 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2022 ; Kolagar, Parida, & Sj ödin, 2022 ; Shen et al., 2023 ). The existing research focuses mainly on delineating the overall transformation required of manufacturing firms that venture into the digital service field ( Gebauer, Arzt, et al., 2020 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2021 ; Sklyar et al., 2019 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ), investigating digital service strategies from a broad capability perspective ( Chirumalla et al., 2023 ; Hasselblatt et al., 2018 ; Huikkola, Kohtam äki, & Ylim äki, 2022 ; Lenka et al., 2017 ) and exploring the implications of such strategies for ecosystem relationships ( Kamalaldin et al., 2020 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Sklyar et al., 2019 ) and business model logics ( Ehret & Wirtz, 2017 ; Tabares et al., 2023 ). However, these works provide little insight into specific organizational choices related to the implementation of digital services. While some studies have explored the development of new routines, processes and practices for digital service activities, existing research does not investigate the financial consequences of different implementation approaches. Investigating these consequences is important to revealing how manufacturing firms can actually take advantage of digital service opportunities. Accordingly, the present study explores a firm ’ s strategic emphasis on value creation/ appropriation and outsourcing intensity as organizational choices affecting financial performance in digital servitization. Influencing innovative behaviour and intrafirm collaboration, such choices are critical to the implementation of digital service activities. The strategic emphasis of a firm relates to the relative emphasis that the firm gives to the fundamental processes of value creation (i.e., R & D) and value appropriation (i.e., marketing, branding, and selling activities) for internal resource deployments ( Saboo et al., 2016 ; Sharma et al., 2020 ). Based on the innovation and resource constraints literature (e.g., Mizik & Jacobson, 2003 ), we contend that greater relative emphasis on value creation over value appropriation may indicate lower investment in building customer interest and confidence in new digital service introductions, which in turn leads to comparatively lower sales and returns from such offerings. Outsourcing refers to the pursuit of value chain activities outside the boundaries of the firm, as opposed to vertical integration ( Holcomb & Hitt, 2007 ). Since seizing digital service opportunities requires the adoption of new capabilities and processes in a particularly fast-paced technology environment, we propose that the efficiency and flexibility gains from increased outsourcing intensity tend to exceed the potential control and transaction cost benefits of vertical integration, increasing firm profitability. Additionally, while some prior work has started to investigate digital servitization in the specific context of small- and medium-sized firms (e.g., Kolagar, Reim, et al., 2022 ; Peillon & Dubruc, 2019 ; Rapaccini et al., 2023 ), the possibility of an interplay between firm size and specific organizational choices has so far been only vaguely implied, although it would be expected that interactions might exist. Addressing this gap, we include firm size as a moderator in our hypothesized relationships. We test the proposed effects using a unique sample of 176 servitized manufacturing firms offering digitally enabled services. We collect archival data spanning five years (2017 – 2021) from the Capital IQ database and use a random effects model to explore the direct and moderated effects of strategic emphasis on value creation over value appropriation and outsourcing intensity on firm financial (profit) performance. The paper is structured as follows. First, we offer the theoretical background and the hypotheses of the study. Next, we describe the research methodology, including data collection, construct measurement, and statistical analysis approach. Then, we present our empirical results and supplementary robustness tests. Finally, we discuss the findings and conclude with contributions and limitations of the study. 2. Literature review and hypotheses development 2.1. Digital servitization Digital servitization has received considerable attention in recent academic research ( Favoretto et al., 2022 ; Shen et al., 2023 ). Defined as the convergence of servitization and digital business development ( Frank et al., 2019 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ), it refers to the application of digital tools to support a manufacturer ’ s transformational process from a product-centric to a service-oriented (i.e., servitized) business model and logic ( Sklyar et al., 2019 ; T óth et al., 2022 ). Leveraging the rapid development of various digital technologies, such as the internet of things (IoT), big data, artificial intelligence (AI), and cloud computing, digital servitization presents manufacturing firms with new opportunities for service value creation and innovation ( Coreynen et al., 2017 ; Gebauer, Arzt, et al., 2020 ; Sj ödin et al., 2020 ). In practice, manufacturers that – in their quest for competitive differentiation ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ) and growth ( Sklyar et al., 2019 ) – engage in digital servitization align with current technological advancements by offering digital and digitally enabled services ( Kamalaldin et al., 2020 ; Kolagar, Parida, & Sj ödin, 2022 ). Existing studies have mostly focused on characterizing the overall organizational transformation underpinning a digital servitization strategy, with the profound changes in business identity and structure that it entails ( Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). A first research stream has examined the additional capability requirements that emerge during this transformation ( Huikkola, Kohtam äki, & Ylim äki, 2022 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2022 ; Shen et al., 2023 ), and their role in enabling the implementation of increasingly advanced services ( Sj ödin et al., 2021 ) and comprehensive digital solutions ( Kohtam äki et al., 2021 ). For example, Lenka et al. (2017) suggest a framework of technology-related capabilities (such as intelligence, connectivity, and analytics capabilities) that enable perceptive and responsive mechanisms for value co-creation with the customers, while Sj ödin et al. (2021) identify categories of AI-related capabilities that manufacturing firms must develop to effectively incorporate AI technology into their value offerings. Similar requirements for technical capabilities are identified by several other studies in marketing (e.g., Favoretto et al., 2022 ; Hasselblatt et al., 2018 ; Huikkola et al., 2020 ), innovation (e.g., Huikkola, Kohtam äki, Rabetino, et al., 2022 ; Linde et al., 2021 ), and general management (e.g., Kohtam äki et al., 2021 ). Additionally, Chirumalla et al. (2023) and Huikkola, Kohtam äki, Rabetino, et al. (2022) emphasize the need for transformation (dynamic) capabilities, whereas Momeni et al. (2023) discuss the importance of operational capabilities. Sklyar et al. (2019) argue for the need for a ‘service ecosystem perspective ’ to analyze the socio-technical processes that accompany the pursuit of digital servitization. Harnessing digital technology would require cooperating with external suppliers that may possess digital infrastructures or data expertise and resources; thus, organizing for digital servitization would create new interdependencies between ecosystem actors, calling for relational capabilities. The importance of relational and collaborative capabilities in seizing digital servitization opportunities is a main theme in a number of other studies (e.g., Chen et al., 2021 ; Kamalaldin et al., 2020 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Kolagar, Reim, et al., 2022 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ) and, especially in Schroeder et al. (2020) , is underscored also in relation to the exchange processes with customers. These studies draw on notions from the relational view, resource-based view, embeddedness theory and dynamic capability theory. In another stream of literature, researchers investigate digital servitization as a business model transformation, introducing new digitally enabled logics for developing, delivering and pricing value offerings in manufacturing firms ( Favoretto et al., 2022 ; Shen et al., 2023 ). For example, Gebauer, Fleisch, et al. (2020) suggest a process model of how firms modify business model components as they progress along different phases of converting digital offerings into revenue enhancements, and Chen et al. (2021) similarly identify business model changes underpinning different stages of digital servitization maturity (from standard product-services to smart solutions). Other studies, however, argue for equifinality in digital servitization processes, most notably Kohtam äki et al. (2019) , who use the theory of the firm to delineate five optimal – equifinal – configurations of digital servitization business models. Arguing that these configurations extend beyond firm boundaries into the economic exchanges of the firm with its stakeholders, they additionally propose to conceptualize digital servitization business models ‘within ecosystems ’ . This notion is remarked and explored in other studies, such as Tronvoll et al. (2020) and Sj ödin et al. (2022) , that have explicitly considered the ecosystem-related implications of digital servitization. Although it is important to understand the transformation that takes place in manufacturing firms that start to offer digital services, with the capability and business model challenges it entails, it is equally important to draw attention to the specific implementation issues that accompany this transformation. Since digital services involve revising O. In a recent publication, Huikkola, Kohtam äki, and Ylim äki (2022) focus on the development of smart solutions, suggesting micro-level routines and practices that can help firms co-align their innovation processes for product, service, and software components. Sj ödin et al. (2020) employ a service logic perspective to develop a micro service innovation process model for the agile co-creation of digital services with customers. Studies have also suggested systematic approaches for the development of revenue models ( Linde et al., 2023 ), the analysis of IoT-enabled affordances ( Naik et al., 2020 ), and the orchestration of ecosystem partnerships ( Sj ödin et al., 2022 ). However, a review of these studies reveals an important gap. Researchers have mainly concentrated on identifying new routines, processes and practices to facilitate innovative behaviour and intrafirm collaboration in the pursuit of digital servitization. There is a lack of empirical research linking specific organizational choices concerning the implementation of digital services with the financial outcomes of the providing firm. This paper addresses this gap by examining two critical organizational choices. First, since the creation of value for the customers may not always generate financial value for the provider, a manufacturing firm arguably needs to take appropriate actions to capture value from investments in the development of novel digitally enabled offerings. Against this background, this study explores strategic emphasis on value creation versus value appropriation as an organizational choice potentially influencing the financial performance of a digitally servitized firm. Second, prior research provides only anecdotal evidence of the benefits of involving third parties, such as specialized technology providers, in digital service activities. Thus, this study investigates outsourcing intensity as an additional organizational choice influencing digital service activities and hence financial performance. Further, prior research suggests that firm size can be an important contingency factor in the implementation of digital services. Studies have begun to explore digital servitization from the perspective of smalland medium-sized firms, pinpointing the difficulty of such firms in acquiring digital skills and resources, altering capabilities and processes, securing access to customer data, and gaining legitimacy as a digital service provider (e.g., Kolagar, Reim, et al., 2022 ; Peillon & Dubruc, 2019 ; Rapaccini et al., 2023 ). Yet, empirical research on the interplay between firm size and specific organizational choices concerning digital service activities is lacking. Accordingly, this study examines the ways in which firm size moderates the financial performance effects of decisions regarding strategic emphasis and outsourcing intensity, thereby contributing insights into organizational choices that may help tackle the implementation challenges of digital servitization. 2.2. Hypotheses development 2.2.1. Strategic emphasis on value creation over value appropriation and firm ’ s financial performance As part of their innovation strategies, firms have to allocate organizational resources to the two fundamental processes of value creation and value appropriation ( Han et al., 2017 ; Mizik & Jacobson, 2003 ). Value creation relates to upstream activities (typically R & D) that enable the firm to meet new customer needs or address old ones in new ways, whereas value appropriation primarily focuses on downstream activities (such as advertising and branding) to connect with customers, enhance awareness of innovative offerings, build brand image, and ultimately stimulate purchase behaviour ( Mizik & Jacobson, 2003 ; Saboo et al., 2016 ; Sharma et al., 2020 ). The innovation strategy of a firm is revealed in the trade-off decisions it makes between value creation and value appropriation, that is in the relative emphasis that the firm places on one process over the other for internal resource deployments ( Saboo et al., 2016 ). The more the strategic emphasis of a firm leans towards value creation, the more such a firm will invest in R & D and product/service innovation over marketing, advertising, sales management and relational activities ( Sharma et al., 2020 ; Swaminathan et al., 2008 ). Prior research has evidenced that the level of a firm ’ s strategic emphasis on value creation/appropriation may impact organizational outcomes, such as profitability and idiosyncratic risk ( Han et al., 2017 ; Josephson et al., 2016 ; Mizik & Jacobson, 2003 ; Saboo et al., 2016 ). For a firm engaged in digital servitization, investment in R & D is important for service innovation and performance ( Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ; Korkeam äki et al., 2021 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). While traditional (non-digital) services are typically developed within customer-facing departments, such as sales and service ( Eggert et al., 2015 ; Schaarschmidt et al., 2018 ; Biemans & Griffin, 2018 ), the organization of development activities tends to be much more centred on formal R & D in the case of digital services. Prior research has indicated that R & D plays a key role in enabling firms to bring to the market digital services that provide meaningful differentiation and competitive advantage, increasing ‘clock speed ’ in adaptation to market dynamics and changes in the digital landscape ( Kohtam äki et al., 2021 ; Sj ödin et al., 2020 ). R & D also drives the development of new products with enhanced software, connectivity and sensor features that can support the viability of new digital solutions and offerings ( Martín-Pe ña et al., 2023 ; Porter & Heppelmann, 2014 ). However, although R & D investment affords opportunities for new ways of value creation through innovative and relevant digital services, the capture of economic rents from such offerings depends on the magnitude of a firm ’ s investment in value appropriation activities. Previous studies underscore that customers often struggle to assess the opportunities presented by new digital services, the internal changes required for their implementation, and how best to use the new service features to achieve their personal or business goals ( Cusumano et al., 2015 ; Hasselblatt et al., 2018 ; Kolagar, Reim, et al., 2022 ; Linde et al., 2021 ). Research on innovation adoption indicates that, in such circumstances, activating appropriate information and influence channels plays a key role in shaping the ability of a firm to get customers to understand the value that innovations can bring, enhance customers ’ purchase intentions, and thus generate more sales and revenues. In other words, articulating the advantages and features of new digital services through appropriate communication channels lowers customers ’ perceived risk, thereby enhancing customers ’ interest (willingness to purchase) and raising the firm ’ s sales. In addition to making the scope and purpose of new digital offerings better understood, utilizing compelling communication channels to spread knowledge of such offerings is pivotal to create customer awareness and develop brand recognition ( Eggert et al., 2022 ). Without the necessary communication efforts, many digital service innovations may go unnoticed because, being different from the products and services that are usually provided by manufacturers, they are perceived by customers to fall outside the domain of expertise of the offering firm, which inevitably hurts the firm ’ s ability to generate sales. With respect to our hypothesis development, how actively a firm communicates and promotes its product and service innovations is determined by the investment in value appropriation activities. Therefore, as a firm ’ s strategic emphasis on value creation increases (i.e., for a given level of investment in R & D and value creation through digital services, comparatively less resources are devoted to value appropriation activities), the difficulties associated with attracting customer attention and interest in new digital offerings are likely to lead to lower sales and revenues, which in turn negatively affects the firm ’ s financial performance. Hence, we hypothesize: H1 . For a manufacturing firm offering digital services, greater strategic emphasis on value creation over value appropriation results in lower financial performance. The capacity to capture value from digital service introductions may be affected by the size of the firm. As noted above, customer awareness of new digital service offerings is promoted by ‘demand side ’ (value appropriation) (cf. Saboo et al., 2016 : p.660) activities that communicate the value and existence of these offerings. Larger firms generally O. It is arguable that larger firms can also more easily gain customer trust, due to their typically stronger reputation ( Coluccia et al., 2020 ). This is particularly relevant in the case of digital services, since their inherent data-centricity introduces significant data protection issues, and thus the need for high levels of trust in the supplier-customer relationship (see, e.g., Eggert et al. (2022) for an in-depth discussion). For instance, services such as remote monitoring, predictive maintenance, and optimization of equipment require crucially that the customer shares large amounts of operational data about equipment condition and usage with the service provider. In such situations, trust has been found to affect customer perception of privacy risks and help overcome purchase uncertainty (e. g., Klein et al., 2018 ; Sklyar et al., 2019 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). In addition, larger firms can rely on brand image and reputation to convey information about service quality, reduce customer-perceived risk of service technology, and avoid price-based competition ( Klein et al., 2018 ; Kolagar, Reim, et al., 2022 ; Swaminathan et al., 2008 ). Finally, besides facilitating value appropriation, firm size may arguably increase the productivity of R & D activities, thereby bringing value creation advantages. Prior research notes that larger firms have greater chances to experience scale and scope effects in R & D activities (e.g., Choo et al., 2021 ; Henderson & Cockburn, 1996 ). For firms that complement their product-based offerings with digital services, such effects may be particularly pronounced. Given that their products often have to incorporate additional instrumentation, connectivity and software to enable digital service functions ( Porter & Heppelmann, 2015 ), such firms blur the lines between product and service development processes ( Freije et al., 2022 ), which in turn creates additional opportunities for asset sharing and internal spillovers. Overall, we argue that larger firms require less investment in value appropriation activities to generate sales of new digital offerings and can, as well, more fully exploit their investment in value creation activities to drive digitally enabled product/service innovations and hence sales growth. Both these effects mitigate the negative financial performance consequences of increases in a firm ’ s relative emphasis on value creation. Consequently, we propose: H2 . For a manufacturing firm offering digital services, the negative association between strategic emphasis on value creation over value appropriation and financial performance is positively moderated by the size of the firm. 2.2.2. Outsourcing intensity and firm ’ s financial performance Besides the relative emphasis on value creation over value appropriation, another key organizational choice for a firm that adopts a digital servitization strategy concerns deciding whether and to what extent to use outsourcing. In general, outsourcing refers to the leveraging of resources and expertise from other firms to complement existing capabilities for some or all of the activities in a firm ’ s value chain ( Holcomb & Hitt, 2007 ). In contrast, vertical integration occurs when value chain activities are pursued within the boundaries of the firm ( Rothaermel et al., 2006 ). The resource-based literature suggests that engaging in outsourcing allows for greater adaptability and scalability of the resource deployments associated with the firm ’ s productive output, as well as enabling access to broader sets of competences for the implementation of business strategies ( Holcomb & Hitt, 2007 ; Rothaermel et al., 2006 ; Soto Setzke et al., 2023 ). However, in transaction cost economics theory, outsourcing leads also to higher governance costs and contractual inefficiencies, which in turn result in holdup risks and sub-optimal levels of relationship-specific investments from outsourcing partners ( Holcomb & Hitt, 2007 ; Shenoy, 2012 ). Vertical integration mitigates such issues through common ownership, while also facilitating the integration of know-how and complementary assets across different value chain activities when pursuing innovations ( Rothaermel et al., 2006 ; Teece, 1986 ). These concepts are well established in the operations management and strategy literatures, and considerable empirical research has tested the efficacy of outsourcing as a business practice, trying to connect outsourcing intensity (i.e., the extent to which a firm relies on other firms to carry out value chain activities) to performance-related outcomes. The evidence that emerges from this research is mixed, suggesting that firms may differ as to whether outsourcing intensity can help or hinder firm performance, and hence implying that context may shape the performance consequences of outsourcing. Although there is no research that examines the trade-off between outsourcing and vertical integration in the context of firms that are engaged in digital servitization, we lean towards a generally positive effect of outsourcing intensity on firm financial performance (as measured by profitability). Outsourcing arrangements provide multiple possibilities to enhance a firm ’ s exploitation of the opportunities associated with digital service offerings. First, the delivery of digital services requires the development and implementation of dedicated software, information technology, and data analytics capabilities in a particularly fast-paced, highly dynamic technology environment ( Coreynen et al., 2017 ; Kolagar, Parida, & Sj ödin, 2022 ; Sj ödin et al., 2020 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). Engaging in greater levels of outsourcing may facilitate a firm to accelerate the deployment of the capabilities necessary to deliver novel digital services, as well as allowing for greater agility in updating such capabilities as technology develops and customer demands increase ( Sj ödin et al., 2022 ; Sklyar et al., 2019 ). In turn, such rapid and flexible adaptation of capabilities creates competitive differentiation advantages and can help increase the firm ’ s overall revenues via larger sales volumes of digital services and offerings. Second, the introduction of digital services has been documented to cause resource conflicts that are often difficult to manage (e.g., Gebauer, Arzt, et al., 2020 ; Huikkola, Kohtam äki, Rabetino, et al., 2022 ). Since firms typically have limited resources to support strategic initiatives, pursuing the development and offering of digital services requires the withdrawal of resources from other business activities, thus leading to loss of opportunities. In such circumstances, as the level of outsourcing increases, the likelihood of a firm sub-optimally allocating scarce internal resources to digital service opportunities that have lower payoffs than more established offerings (products and services) plausibly decreases, resulting in lower opportunity costs for the firm. Finally, some digital services (e.g., operations optimization services based on artificial intelligence) represent radical innovations compared to ‘baseline ’ ones (e.g., remote monitoring), and therefore they require quite complex enablers in terms of specialist knowledge stocks that firms need to develop and use ( Raddats et al., 2022 ; Simonsson & Agarwal, 2021 ). Yet, at the same time, given their customized nature and newness to the market, radically innovative digital services provide unique value to customers, which in turn enables premium pricing and thus also higher profit margins. Outsourcing arrangements or other forms of collaboration with specialized technology providers (e.g., analytics providers, connectivity providers, software providers) may be key for manufacturers to compensate for missing competences and capture the profit potential that these services represent ( Kamalaldin et al., 2020 ; Kolagar, Parida, & Sj ödin, 2022 ; Raddats et al., 2022 ; Sj ödin et al., 2022 ). Overall, the above arguments suggest that increasing outsourcing can bring financial benefits to digitally servitized firms in the form of increased revenues, reduced opportunity costs, and enhanced profitability of digital service activities. We therefore hypothesize: H3 . For a manufacturing firm offering digital services, greater outsourcing intensity results in higher financial performance. The relationship between outsourcing intensity and financial performance may be contingent on firm size. A main reason for this is that larger firms likely have more slack resources ( Kowalkowski et al., 2013 ) and thus less need of other firms ’ resources to develop, orchestrate and adapt digital capabilities over time ( Kolagar, Reim, et al., 2022 ). Prior literature has also outlined that larger firms tend to realize higher absorptive capacities than smaller firms ( Schaarschmidt et al., 2018 ), which may lead to superior abilities to assimilate, interpret and exploit outside knowledge to create new digital service innovations. Thus, outsourcing arrangements play a less critical role in compensating for missing competences in the case of larger firms. Taken together, these arguments suggest that the association between outsourcing intensity and lessening of the resource and competence challenges of digital services becomes weaker as the size of the firm increases. Additionally, with their larger endowments of internal resources, larger firms may achieve greater control and transaction cost benefits by emphasizing vertical integration in digital service delivery ( Huikkola, Kohtam äki, Rabetino, et al., 2022 ; Shen et al., 2023 ). For example, they are likely to spend less effort on adapting and managing complex interdependencies among different outsourcing partners as digital technologies and offerings evolve ( Sj ödin et al., 2022 ) while, at the same time, reducing their exposure to partner inefficiencies and accountability gaps as the technical complexity of digital solutions increases ( Chen et al., 2021 ). Likewise, larger firms have greater capacity to invest in specialized and co-specialized assets, which are difficult and costly to obtain through outsourcing ( Momeni et al., 2023 ), but are often necessary for advanced digital services ( Kamalaldin et al., 2020 ). Therefore, increasing vertical integration may allow larger firms to costeffectively provide such services and adapt them to diverse customers ’ needs. Finally, larger firms are typically more diversified ( Josephson et al., 2016 ), and hence they may be more capable of achieving efficiency gains through vertical integration by spreading the cost of digital infrastructure and assets across multiple offerings. In practice, firm size amplifies the potential benefits of vertical integration in digital service provision. Along with the abovementioned effects concerning resource and competence challenges, this reduces a firm ’ s ability to obtain financial benefits by adopting increasing levels of outsourcing. Accordingly, we propose: H4 . For a manufacturing firm offering digital services, the positive association between outsourcing intensity and financial performance is negatively moderated by the size of the firm. Fig. 1 summarizes our theoretical model. 3. Method 3.1. Sample selection Secondary data available from the Capital IQ database are used to test the hypotheses. Obtaining the necessary data through a survey would have allowed the adoption of measures offering high degrees of conceptual overlap with the corresponding constructs and closely matching their domain. However, the survey approach is prone to the problems of low response rates, common method bias, and perceptual measures. A further problem relating to survey methods is that it is quite challenging to obtain longitudinal data, which is necessary to provide stronger substantiation of causal relationship between the constructs of interest. The use of archival data from Capital IQ allows to overcome these issues. Capital IQ includes comprehensive financial statement data on over 62,000 public firms (99% of the world ’ s market capitalization) and 825,000 private ones. Our sampling frame is the set of firms in Capital IQ with primary activities in manufacturing. Accordingly, although all firms that offer any combinations of products and services could potentially be part of our sample, we excluded firms with primary activities in services that may have extended their offerings to products (cf. Choo et al., 2021 ). We characterize firms ’ primary activities based on the Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code identification. Specifically, following other studies of servitization (e.g., Benedettini et al., 2015 ; Davies et al., 2023 ; Visnjic et al., 2016 ), we focus on firms with primary two-digit SIC codes between 10 and 39. These SIC codes represent a wide cross-section of manufacturing industries, including oil and gas, construction, chemicals and allied products, industrial machinery, electronic components, transportation equipment, and measuring and medical instruments. To allow for greater data availability, we required that the firms had a minimum of 100 employees (latest reported number). Among the almost 285,000 firms that matched the above criteria, firms offering digital services were identified by examining the ‘long business description ’ field in Capital IQ. The long business description offers an illustrative summary of a firm ’ s activities, lines of business, strategic intents, and history. Thus, if digital services are explicitly mentioned in the Capital IQ business description, then they are likely to be a relevant component of the firm ’ s market offering. Recent research using business descriptions available in financial databases to infer the service orientation of manufacturing firms (e.g., Benedettini & Neely, 2018 ; Benedettini & Neely, 2019 ; Korkeam äki et al., 2021 ; Visnjic et al., 2016 ) indicates that such descriptions are a reliable source of information on servitization initiatives. 1 The examination of Capital IQ business descriptions was performed in two steps. First, an automated text search was conducted using a comprehensive list of keywords that extant servitization research relates to the digital service offerings of manufacturing firms. 2 Of the initial firms, 1412 firms presented a business description that included one or more of the selected keywords. Next, the business descriptions of these 1412 firms were manually examined to assess the context in which keywords appeared and to determine whether the intended meaning pointed to the offering of digital services. This screening process led to a study sample of 182 unique firms that offered various digital services, such as predictive maintenance, analytics-based optimization of operational processes, web portals for evaluating equipment mechanical condition/ safety and performance, and different types of remote support applications. Most firms (82%) were in durable goods industries (two-digit SIC code from 34 to 39), with industrial machinery and computer equipment (SIC code 35) and electronic and electrical equipment (SIC code 36) being the most prominent industries. Data was collected at the beginning of 2023 and covered the five most recent fiscal years (2017 – 2021). Extending the time frame of the study by including data from earlier years was not advisable since the provision of digital services by product firms is still a recent phenomenon ( Gebauer, Fleisch, et al., 2020 ). 3.2. Independent and moderating variables Consistent with prior literature (e.g., Saboo et al., 2016 ; Sharma et al., 2018 ; Sharma et al., 2020 ), strategic emphasis on value creation/ appropriation is measured as R & D expenses divided by selling, general and administrative (SG & A) expenses. Thus, higher values of the strategic emphasis variable indicate greater relative emphasis on value creation activities over value appropriation activities. Since a firm ’ s financial performance is unlikely to be immediately affected by strategic investments ( Fang et al., 2008 ), strategic emphasis is modelled with a one-year lag. Outsourcing intensity is measured as sales-to-assets ratio (ratio of sales revenues to total assets) ( Banerjee et al., 2008 ). Firms that outsource their activities to suppliers and third parties need to possess few assets and thus should have high values of this ratio, while this ratio should be low for vertically integrated firms. Firm size is measured as natural logarithm of firm total revenues ( van der Borgh et al., 2023 ). Firm size is included in the model both as a moderator and a control variable, since prior studies suggest that financial performance may vary with firm size (e.g., Kohtam äki et al., 2015 ). 3.2.3. Control variables Several other control variables are used to rule out potential extraneous effects related to firm characteristics, industry heterogeneity, and macro-economic conditions. First, we control for firm age (number of years since founding). Second, we control for resource slack. Consistent with other studies of servitization (i.e., Fang et al., 2008 ; Josephson et al., 2016 ), resource slack is computed using factor scores from a principal component analysis of two financial ratios: retained earnings to total assets, and working capital to total assets. Third, we control for the geographic location of firms ’ headquarters (19 different countries) using country dummy variables. Fourth, we use industry dummies to control for industry-specific effects (16 different two-digit primary SIC codes). Fifth, we use year dummies to account for other time effects that affect all firms similarly. 3.3. Data collection The initial data set included 910 firm-year observations (5-year observations × 182 firms). After dropping 107 observations with missing values of the model variables (typically pertaining to firms that were established during the study ’ s time frame or were incorporated by other firms over the same period), 3 there remained 803 observations. These were further reduced to 788 after elimination of 15 observations with either SG & A expenses, total assets, or total revenues equal to zero (to avoid infinite values of the model variables). Finally, in line with Capital IQ, profit margin values below 3 were considered not meaningful and the corresponding observations were eliminated. This resulted in a final unbalanced data set consisting of 762 firm-year observations from 176 unique firms. 3.4. Analytical approach Table 1 provides a summary of the variables used in the study. Either a fixed effects (FE) or a random effects (RE) approach could be used to account for heterogeneity in firms ’ financial performance that is not captured by the independent variables in our model ( Hsiao, 2003 : p.34; Ketokivi & McIntosh, 2017 ; Sharma et al., 2020 ). The FE estimator would allow for arbitrary correlation between such unobserved heterogeneity and the observed independent model variables, while the RE estimator would assume no correlation ( Wooldridge, 2002 : p. 251; Greene, 2002 : p. 293; Certo et al., 2017 ). We adopt the RE specification for our analysis for two reasons. First, the average number of time period observations per panel (firm), T, in our sample is 4.3 and the number of panels, m, is 176. The FE estimator may be inconsistent in the case of short panels ( Hsiao, 2003 : p.41; Abdallah et al., 2015 ) or when T is substantially smaller than m (cf. Leiblein & Madsen, 2009 ; Manikandan & Ramachandran, 2015 ), whereas the RE estimator is not. Second, FE estimation impairs the explanatory power of slowly changing independent variables ( Beck, 2001 ), a condition that our main variables exhibit because of very little within-panel variation as compared to between-panel variation (e.g., 94% of the variation of strategic emphasis in our data is between firms rather than within firms). 4 In such circumstances, prior studies have suggested the choice of a RE over a FE specification (e.g., Mahmood et al., 2017 ; Manikandan & Ramachandran, 2015 ). Given the above, the RE approach is more suitable to our data set. Moreover, the Breusch-Pagan Lagrange Multiplier test for random effects ( Breusch & Pagan, 1980 ) supports the assumption of existence of unobserved effects in the data (p < 0.0001), indicating that panel FE should also be preferred over classic pooled ordinary least squares (POLS) regression ( Antonakis et al., 2010 ). We therefore adopted the Generalized Least Squares (GLS) RE estimator. We relied on clustered standard errors, calculated using the Huber-White ‘sandwich ’ estimation ( White, 1980 ), to adjust for heteroskedasticity ( Baltagi, 2005 : p.79; Petersen, 2009 ). 4. Robustness tests We conducted the following tests to confirm the robustness of our results: a) Sensitivity to outliers.: We repeated our regression analysis on the original data set (with outlying cases included) ( Cohen et al., 2003 : p. 415). The results were very similar to those reported in Table 3 . As an alternative way of dealing with extreme values, we winsorized continuous variables at the 1st and 99th percentiles in the original data set. Again, the results remained consistent. b) Alternative variable operationalization: We used net margin, that is, the ratio of a firm ’ s net income to total revenues, as an alternative dependent variable. Using this alternative operationalization yielded no substantive differences. We also replicated our analysis using twoyear lags of R & D and SG & A expenses to estimate strategic emphasis (assuming that it may take more than one year for strategic actions to affect profitability). We found no substantive differences in results. c) Subsample analysis: We conducted a sub-sample analysis using three randomly selected sub-samples (80% of total observations each time). The results were robust to these sampling effects in terms of significance and support to the hypotheses. d) Alternative estimation approaches: We tested two alternative estimators for our model, the Maximum Likelihood (ML) RE estimator ( Baltagi, 2005 : p.19; Hsiao, 2003 : p.39) and the Between estimator ( Wooldridge, 2002 : p. 269; Baltagi, 2005 : p. 200). While the GLS RE estimator (used for the primary estimation) aims at minimizing the summed squares of the residuals, the ML estimator conducts the likelihood ratio test to examine random effects and computes the model parameters with the highest likelihood of producing the sample data. The Between estimator, instead, uses only the crosssectional component of the data (i.e., variation between firms). The results are shown in Table 4 . The ML estimator was fitted using clustered standard errors. Table 4 further includes the results of a Population Averaged (PA) model, which also represents an alternative specification to the RE for our data. PA models allow to analyze correlated data, such as longitudinal and panel data, relaxing the key assumption of RE models that all predictors are uncorrelated with the random effects ( Ghisletta & Spini, 2004 ; Huang, 2022 ). 5 Robust estimation of standard errors was applied to adjust for heteroskedasticity and violation of the assumption of independent observations. Theoretical contribution As manufacturing firms increasingly engage in digital servitization, studies have begun to explore ways in which digital services can be developed and offered (e.g., Huikkola, Kohtam äki, & Ylim äki, 2022 ; Naik et al., 2020 ; Sj ödin et al., 2020 ; Sj ödin et al., 2022 ). However, there is a paucity of research investigating the financial implications of organizational choices concerning specific implementation issues. By conducting a quantitative analysis of the economic consequences of two fundamental such organizational choices – i.e., strategic emphasis on value creation activities over value appropriation activities, and outsourcing intensity – across firms of different sizes, we contribute to the understanding of the implementation challenges of digital servitization ( Kohtam äki et al., 2021 ; Momeni et al., 2023 ). Our results reveal a negative effect of strategic emphasis on value creation over value appropriation (ratio of R & D expenses to SG & A expenses) on firm profitability and call for particular contingencies, such as visibility and brand image arising from larger firm size, to mitigate this effect. This finding suggests that leveraging the value created by new digitally enabled product/service offerings for higher profits may be difficult without investing adequate resources in marketing, branding and relational activities. Accordingly, our findings underscore the risks associated with market acceptance of new digital offerings ( Gebauer, Fleisch, et al., 2020 ; Klein et al., 2018 ; Linde et al., 2021 ; Raddats et al., 2022 ), particularly for smaller firms. Customers often struggle to evaluate the value of digitally enabled innovations ( Cusumano et al., 2015 ) as they face uncertainty regarding the performance of new functionalities and offerings, the problems and costs of using them, or their fit with particular needs ( Hasselblatt et al., 2018 ; Kolagar, Reim, et al., 2022 ; Linde et al., 2021 ). This suggests that developing digital product/service innovations may not be sufficient to achieve economic rents, as driving customers to purchase and adopt such innovations may not be easy and may require dedicated investment in building customer interest and trust. This study, which is the first to identify a firm ’ s relative emphasis on value creation/appropriation as a relevant contingency factor in digital servitization, therefore contributes to the literature that argues that capturing value from digital services and technologies is not straightforward ( Gebauer, Fleisch, et al., 2020 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ) and requires an appropriate innovation strategy ( Linde et al., 2021 ). In addition, our results demonstrate how greater outsourcing intensity (sales-to-assets ratio) leads to increased profit performance in smaller firms. Prior studies have not examined differences among manufacturers about this issue, making this result particularly insightful. How to acquire the requisite resources and capabilities for generating and capturing value from digital services is an essential question. Momeni et al. (2023) have argued that accessing capabilities from suppliers through collaborative/outsourcing relationships is useful in digital servitization even for large manufacturers. In contrast, our empirical findings pinpoint that the profit impact of increasing outsourcing is positive only in smaller firms; that is, the effective use of outsourcing is heterogeneous across firms (e.g., Huikkola, Kohtam äki, & Ylim äki, 2022 ; Kolagar, Parida, & Sj ödin, 2022 ) and firm sizes (e.g., Kolagar, Reim, et al., 2022 ; Raddats et al., 2022 ; Soto Setzke et al., 2023 ). Finally, ours is one of the very first studies to statistically prove the profit impact of specific organizational choices concerning the implementation of digital services in manufacturing firms. As such, with this study, we respond to recent calls in the literature on digital servitization for more quantitative research that focuses on testing and refining the field ’ s knowledge (e.g., Kolagar, Parida, & Sj ödin, 2022 ; Markfort et al., 2022 ). As a nascent topic, digital servitization has generally been seen as a natural candidate for qualitative descriptive research designs such as explorative case studies, and thus it has attracted little formal theorizing to date. The application of quantitative methods of inquiry is important to enable further theoretical development and validation, which is necessary to make the research field evolve from the nascent stage towards maturity ( Edmondson & McManus, 2007 ). 5.2. Managerial contribution For manufacturing firms, enhancing product offerings with digitally enabled services is a challenging process ( Sklyar et al., 2019 ; T óth et al., 2022 ). Digital services introduce significant implementation issues that are difficult to manage, as they often require revising resource allocation decisions and reorganizing value chain activities ( Huikkola, Kohtam äki, Rabetino, et al., 2022 ). Our study provides empirical sample-based evidence that investing in R & D (so as to create customer value through new or improved digital services and solutions) to the detriment of value appropriation activities, like marketing and advertising, may not be a wise strategy – especially for smaller firms, which in general find it more difficult to gain customer interest and trust in their digitally enabled offerings ( Eggert et al., 2022 ). Managers should not underestimate the difficulties that customers encounter in evaluating the opportunities presented by digital technologies ( Cusumano et al., 2015 ; Linde et al., 2021 ) and should not assume that introducing novel product/service offerings may be sufficient to achieve positive financial returns ( Kohtam äki et al., 2020 ). Based on our empirical results, we further show that the use of outsourcing may be an effective strategy for smaller firms to address the competence and capability requirements of digital service provision. Nevertheless, we suggest that resorting to outsourcing is not always an effective strategy. If larger firms (which can rely on broader internal resources and absorptive capacities) are willing to take the risks from the uncertain returns of investment in digital services (cf. T óth et al., 2022 ), they can achieve greater short-term profits by opting for lower levels of outsourcing. Finally, we highlight that, even though also small firms have begun to embark on digital servitization ( Huikkola, Kohtam äki, & Ylim äki, 2022 ), they need different tactics than large ones if they are to benefits from such strategic moves ( Shen et al., 2023 ). Liabilities of smallness exists with respect to both the intangible and the tangible assets necessary to successfully offer digital services, and managers of small firms should be aware that they will not be able to replicate the success of large, established firms by simply emulating their strategies and approaches. 5.3. Limitations and future directions As with any research, this study has certain limitations. First, our findings are based on a sample of 176 manufacturing firms whose Capital IQ business description includes reference to the offering of digital services. Although we used a comprehensive list of keywords related to digital services to identify and select relevant firms, our sample size is relatively small. As more firms turn to digital services, future research could replicate our findings with a larger sample. Second, we do not explicitly capture the heterogeneity of digital services. Digital services can differ substantially in their complexity, cost, sophistication, customization, ability to create value, and level of risk ( Favoretto et al., 2022 ), but like most empirical research to date, we aggregate firms offering different types of digital services. Thus, we call for future research to focus on the categorization of digital services and to account for service heterogeneity in investigating how digital servitization can best be implemented and managed. Third, we draw on financial statement information to test our hypotheses. While there are significant benefits to using such secondary data (e.g., reliability, objectivity), a main limitation is that secondary data on theoretically relevant variables may simply be unavailable ( Houston, 2004 ). In particular, we lacked the data to determine firms ’ progress in implementing a digital servitization strategy, namely the extent to which their market offerings were oriented towards digital services. Future research could attempt to explore, or account for, this variable, which is clearly an important dimension of digital servitization initiatives ( Antioco et al., 2008 ). Additionally, we could measure only aggregate (firm-level) R & D and SG & A expenditures, and we had no information on the allocation of expenditures on digitalized versus traditional offerings. While Steenkamp and Fang (2011) mention a similar limitation in their study, the lack of fine-grained secondary data precludes efforts to relate the measurement of strategic emphasis more closely to digital developments. However, because firms may choose to create a separate operational segment for digital offerings, and in that case provide disaggregate information on R & D and SG & A expenditures, perhaps future research may be able to adopt sampling approaches that overcome this limitation. Fourth, our sample is limited to firms whose Capital IQ long business descriptions mention the offering of digital services. Such business descriptions are typically extracted from firms ’ annual reports ( Benedettini & Neely, 2018 ), where information on digital service activities represents a voluntary managerial disclosure. In theory, this may create a selection bias because there may be systematic reasons leading some firms not to highlight the digital nature of their services in annual reports. Lastly, we only focused on two – though important – organizational decisions concerning digital services (i.e., emphasis on value creation over value appropriation, and outsourcing intensity), but future research should look into the product innovation strategy ( Chen et al., 2021 ), the degree of service customization ( Schaarschmidt et al., 2018 ), or other implementation choices that may influence the profitability of digital servitization initiatives ( Kohtam äki et al., 2022 ; Linde et al., 2023 ). Moving from servitization to digital servitization: Identifying the required dynamic capabilities and related microfoundations to facilitate the transition Koteshwar Chirumalla a , * , Luna Leoni b , Pejvak Oghazi c a Digital and Circular Industrial Services Research Group, School of Innovation, Design and Engineering, M älardalen University, Box 325, 631 05 Eskilstuna, Sweden b Department of Management and Law, University of Rome Tor Vergata, 00133 Rome, Italy c School of Social Sciences, S ödert örns University, 141 89 Huddinge, Sweden ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Digital servitization Industry 4.0 Digital technologies Product-service systems Business model innovation Systematic literature review ABSTRACT Many manufacturing companies are adopting servitization as a competitive business strategy to offer product- service combinations. The ongoing shift to digitalization and Industry 4.0 provides novel opportunities and benefits to industrial firms in this regard, and researchers termed the adoption of digital technologies to servi - tization as “ digital servitization ” . In order to successfully transition towards digital servitization, fundamental reconfiguration of resources, organizational structures, work practices, infrastructure, culture, etc. are required. Hence, this paper performs a systematic literature review on prior studies covering dynamic capabilities for servitization and digital servitization. The purpose is to identify and compare the dynamic capabilities needed to facilitate a transition from “ traditional ” servitization to digital servitization. In doing so, this paper presents an integrated framework of dynamic capabilities to enable digital servitization, providing 22 micro-foundations for servitization and digital servitization, as well as the key challenges and enablers related to the transition from one to the other. 1. Introduction To survive in the current competitive context, characterized by numerous and rapid changes, manufacturers are adopting servitization as a business strategy to meet consumers ’ renewed needs, thereby attaining sustainable competitive advantages ( Raddats et al., 2019; Vandermerwe & Rada, 1988; Khanra et al., 2021 ). In fact, servitization allows manufacturers to integrate products and services into a unique offering, differentiating themselves from competitors and enhancing their competitive advantage ( Baines et al., 2017; Vandermerwe & Rada, 1988; Taques et al., 2021 ). Despite its widespread use, servitization is still the subject of extensive debate because its implementation is far from simple and manufacturers tend to struggle with it ( Rabetino et al., 2017; Raja et al., 2017; Chirumalla et al., 2019; Donthu & Yoo, 1998; Neely, 2008; Val - takoski, 2017; Zhang & Banerji, 2017 ). This is even truer if we also consider the recent link between servitization and digital technologies, known as digital servitization ( Bustinza et al., 2015; Kohtam äki et al., 2019; Lerch & Gotsch, 2015; Schroeder & Kotlarsky, 2015; Tronvoll et al., 2020; Vendrell-Herrero et al., 2017 ). In recent years, advanced digital or Industry 4.0 technologies (e.g., Rad et al., 2022 ) have been useful means to support manufacturers ’ transformation from product- centric to advanced service-centric (or product – service – software) busi - ness models ( Ardolino et al., 2018; Coreynen et al., 2017; Cenamor et al., 2017 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2021; Suppatvech et al., 2019; Paiola & Geba - uer, 2020 ). Successful transitioning towards digital servitization requires care - fully rethinking resources, organizational structures and processes, work practices, infrastructure, culture, and value chains or ecosystems ( Bus - tinza et al., 2015, 2018 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2021 ; Sklyar et al., 2019a ; Kolagar et al., 2022; Chirumalla, Reyes, & Toor - ajipour, 2022 ). In this vein, recent literature has emphasized how the dynamic capabilities (DCs) theory ( Teece et al., 1997 ) provides an interesting analytical framework for holistically studying strategic organizational changes and transformations ( Coreynen et al., 2020; Chirumalla, 2021; Kohtam äki et al., 2019; Pisano, 2017; Teece, 2018 ). Such capabilities are even more critical in the context of digital servitization, which requires manufac - turers to acquire not only service-related capabilities, but also, increasingly, those relating to digital technologies, the latter being a crucial tool to boost and ameliorate the service provision. Struyf et al. (2021) pointed out that increasing our understanding of what facilitates an effective move towards digital servitization becomes important, and Kohtam äki et al. (2021) and Coreynen et al. (2017) highlighted the significant role of dynamic resource configurations and defining path - ways for digital servitization by practicing change. To this end, it is crucial for firms to identify and subsequently implement the specific processes, procedures, systems, and structures that undergird each DC ( Teece, 2007 ). In other words, by considering DCs ’ lower-level constit - uents, firms should find it easier to build DCs that can facilitate servi - tization and digital servitization strategies, thereby supporting them in a smoother transition from the former to the latter ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ). In this vein, most existing literature discusses different forms of general capabilities, DCs, and microfoundations interchangeably for servitization or digital servitization in a scattered way (e.g., Kindstr öm et al., 2013; Gebauer et al., 2012; Fischer et al., 2010; Gebauer et al., 2017; Coreynen et al., 2017; Adam et al., 2018; Ceci & Masini, 2011; Paiola et al., 2013; Parida et al., 2014; Raddats et al., 2017; Storbacka, 2011 ). These concepts ’ boundaries are not often clear as the term “ ca - pabilities ” is mentioned in an ad-hoc way at different levels in extant literature. Most importantly, there is a lack of research providing detailed overviews on the needed DCs and the underlying micro - foundations for both servitization and digital servitization together. Studies have focused on either servitization (e.g., Kindstr öm et al., 2013; Kanninen et al., 2017; Fischer et al., 2010 ) or digital servitization (e.g., Bustinza et al., 2018; Coreynen et al., 2017; Kamalaldin et al., 2020; Sj ödin et al., 2020 ) from DCs ’ perspective, but not in combination, which lacks the details (i.e., needed DCs and microfoundations, chal - lenges and enablers involved in building DCs) required for analysing and guiding the transition from servitization and digital servitization. Therefore, a study focusing on both servitization and digital servitiza - tion from DCs perspective is needed to provide comprehensive knowl - edge and an overview of DCs in this context and guide companies in the transition by strategically building the required DCs and underlying microfoundations. The purpose of this study is to identify and map the required DCs and related microfoundations as well as key challenges and enablers that can guide the transition from “ traditional ” servitization to digital servitiza - tion. To address this call, two research questions (RQs) are defined to guide the investigation: RQ1: What are the DCs and related microfoundations identified in the existing literature to successfully implement servitization and digital servitization? RQ2: Which key challenges and enablers has existing literature identified related to building DCs and microfoundations for the transition from servi - tization to digital servitization? To answer these RQs, this study systematically analyses the literature addressing DCs in the servitization and digital servitization contexts. In reviewing 24 papers selected through a deductive thematic analysis, this paper identifies the different DCs and microfoundations (activities, processes, etc.) and relates them into an integrative framework, high - lighting the most critical capabilities that manufacturers need to develop to sustain their transition to digital servitization providers. The paper also highlights the key challenges and enablers of such a transition and how they are linked to each other. The results contribute to both servitization and digital servitization literature by offering a more fine-grained view of the required DCs to succeed using these strategies while also highlighting similarities and differences between them, thereby responding to the call to support companies in transitioning more smoothly from one to the other ( Koh - tam äki et al., 2019; Paiola & Gebauer, 2020; Paschou et al., 2020; Kolagar et al., 2022; Kohtam äki et al., 2021 ). By focusing on micro - foundations, this study provides an accurate level of detail, building a firm conceptual foundation for servitization and digital servitization. Moreover, the proposed integrative framework, by extracting distinct microfoundations for servitization and digital servitization, extends the generic DC framework, rendering it more complete and better able to address current features of manufacturing firms and their context. This paper is structured as follows. Following this introduction, a basic conceptual overview of the main topics addressed is provided, establishing the theoretical departure point of this study. The third section details the methodology, describing how the systematic litera - ture review and thematic analysis were conducted. The findings are then presented and discussed. In particular, an integrated framework is pro - vided to highlight the most critical DCs and related microfoundations that manufacturers need, together with the key challenges to and en - ablers of the transition. The final section offers both theoretical and managerial contributions, together with study limitations and future research venues. 2. Theoretical background This section covers three important theoretical foundations related to the topic of investigation: Industry 4.0, the transition from serviti - zation to digital servitization, and DCs and microfoundations. 2.1. Industry 4.0 Industry 4.0 is an umbrella term commonly referring to a broad range of concepts and technological advancements. Digitalization uses digital data or technologies to automate data handling and optimize processes that can facilitate new value-creating and revenue-generating opportunities ( Sj ödin et al., 2020; Urbinati et al., 2019 ). Digital trans - formation affects the entire firm and how it does business ( Rogers, 2016 ), which usually goes beyond digitalization to impact a firm ’ s strategy, activities, processes, structures, competencies, and culture ( Verhoef et al., 2020; Warner & W äger, 2019; Chirumalla, 2021 ). Existing literature has reported various technologies of Industry 4.0 in manufacturing industry. Some underlying technologies include the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, big data technologies, blockchain, augmented reality, automation, advanced robots, additive manufacturing, simulation, and semantic technologies ( Klingenberg et al., 2019; Oztemel & Gursev, 2020; Rad et al., 2022 ). These technologies possess real-time capability, intelli - gence, interoperability, virtualization, decentralization, connectivity, service orientation, modularity, and analytical capabilities ( Oztemel & Gursev, 2020; Chirumalla, 2021 ). Veile et al. (2019) suggested consid - ering seven dimensions when implementing Industry 4.0 in manufacturing industries: corporate culture and communications, personnel, company organization, safety and security, preparation to implement Industry 4.0 solutions, integration of Industry 4.0 solutions, and financial feasibility. 2.2. From servitization to digital servitization A servitization strategy can be considered a transformational journey of product-centred firms toward product-service systems (PSS) ( Kowal - kowski et al., 2017 ). Such transformation occurs gradually, involving all the different organizational aspects (strategy, structure, etc.), and all members within the organization are aware of the transformation ( Oliva & Kallenberg, 2003 ). At the beginning of this journey, manufacturers offer basic/intermediate services (e.g., maintenance, repair) according to a deeper understanding of their customers ’ needs ( Kanninen et al., 2017; Oliva & Kallenberg, 2003 ), gradually shifting to more advanced K. Chirumalla et al. Journal of Business Research 158 (2023) 113668 3 services ( Baines et al., 2020; Kindstr öm & Kowalkowski, 2014; Ulaga & Reinartz, 2011 ). Current literature focuses on the role Industry 4.0 technologies play in manufacturing firms and the link between servitization and digital technologies ( Frank et al., 2019; Vendrell-Herrero et al., 2017; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). In particular, technologies are considered a useful means that can help manufacturing firms struggling to develop a service- oriented business model ( Ardolino et al., 2018; Coreynen et al., 2017 ). Indeed, technologies allow new services to emerge, boosting servitiza - tion through digitalization, thereby giving life to the concept of digital servitization ( Bustinza et al., 2018; Cenamor et al., 2017; Coreynen et al., 2017; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ; Sklyar et al., 2019b ; Vendrell- Herrero et al., 2017 ). Digital servitization refers to the stream of liter - ature examining how digital technologies influence servitization. As a strategy, it basically consists of manufacturing firms ’ provision of digital services embedded in physical products ( Paschou et al., 2020; Schroeder & Kotlarsky, 2015 ). The benefits of adopting such technologies have been investigated by numerous scholars (e.g., Lerch & Gotsch, 2015; Paiola & Gebauer, 2020; Suppatvech et al., 2019 ) and confirmed by different industrial cases, such as Rolls-Royce and General Electric. The literature is unanimous in recognizing that manufacturers have to overcome numerous challenges when adopting a servitization or digital servitization strategy ( Kamalaldin et al., 2020; Reim et al., 2019; Sj ödin et al., 2020; Zhang & Banerji, 2017 ). Servitization and digital servitization are complex, systemic, and lengthy processes that are challenging to manage ( Coreynen et al., 2017 ; Oliva & Kallenberg, 2003 ; Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ). The transition from servitization to digital servitization is even more challenging ( Struyf et al., 2021 ). Scholars have sought to understand how best to address these chal - lenges, and valuable help seems to come from the DCs theory ( Pisano, 2017; Teece, 2007, 2018; Teece et al., 1997 ). In shifting from products to services (as well as digital services), one of the major challenges for manufacturers is to acquire additional capabilities, specifically those centred on tangible products, and to properly manage these capabilities, which are crucial for organizational change in general and service innovation in particular ( Gebauer et al., 2012; Kindstr öm et al., 2013; Leoni, 2015; Raddats et al., 2017; Taques et al., 2021; Teece, 2007 ). Thus, manufacturers need to develop new capabilities, especially if they want to provide advanced technological services ( Baines et al., 2017; Ceci & Masini, 2011; Storbacka, 2011; Valtakoski, 2017 ). DCs represent an ideal perspective for investigating manufacturing firms in servitiza - tion and digital servitization contexts as well as the transition from one to another. 2.3. Dynamic capabilities and microfoundations DCs theory has its roots in the resource-based view (RBV) of the firm ( Barney, 1991; Wernerfelt, 1984 ) – namely, the emphasis on resources and capabilities as crucial elements for a firm ’ s competitive advantage. Basically, DCs emerged to improve the RBV – exceeding the limits of the latter regarding market dynamism and firm evolution over time ( Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000; Helfat, 1997; Teece et al., 1997; Zahra & George 2002; Winter, 2003 ) – emphasizing the firm ’ s search of capa - bilities ’ renewal, reconfiguration, and re-creation to address environ - mental changes and achieve long-term performance ( Wang & Ahmed, 2007; De Silva et al., 2021 ). Teece and colleagues (1997) defined DCs as “ the firm ’ s ability to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external competences ” (p. 516) to address volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA) environments ( Schwarz et al., 2020 ). DCs play a key role in achieving companies ’ competitive advantage and superior performance, enabling firms to identify needs/opportu - nities for change, formulate appropriate responses, and implement suitable actions ( Helfat et al., 2009 ). Teece (2007) identified three DC typologies: • Sensing capabilities : the firm ’ s ability to detect and shape new tech - nological and market opportunities as well as potential threats; • Seizing capabilities : the firm ’ s ability to address technological and market opportunities through new services, sheltering and exploiting new possibilities; and • Reconfiguring capabilities : the firm ’ s ability to recombine and recon - figure resources, processes, and operational skills to match and manage the organization ’ s internal processes with seized opportunities. In order to operationalize the DCs theory, these three DC typologies are all underpinned by specific subdimensions ( W ójcik et al., 2022 ), commonly known as microfoundations. Teece (2007) defined micro - foundations as “ organizational and managerial processes, procedures, sys - tems, and structures that undergird each class of capability, and the capability itself ” (p. 1321). Microfoundations help decompose DCs into micro-actions/processes ( Foss and Pedersen, 2016 ), helping to under - stand how firms can effectively build DCs and how these DCs practically create a competitive advantage, thus enabling firms to survive and stay successful in competitive environments ( Felin et al., 2012; Wilden et al., 2016; Adam et al., 2018; Kindstr öm et al., 2013; Schwarz et al., 2020 ). The role DCs play – and related microfoundations – has proven fundamental for companies aspiring to pursue successful servitization and digital servitization strategies (e.g., Coreynen et al., 2017; Kindstr öm et al., 2013 ) and has emerged as a main thematic area in Khanra et al. ’ s (2021) recent review of the servitization literature. As Kindstr öm et al. (2013) noted, “ the challenge for many firms [ ... ] is to identify and subsequently implement the microfoundations ” (p. 1071). Hence, only by considering DCs ’ lower-level constituents is it possible to obtain a broader and more detailed understanding of servitization and digital servitization. In this respect, for example, Adam et al. (2018) investigated DCs ’ microfoundations related to servitization to under - stand the phenomenon better and, consequently, enhance managers ’ ability to develop and maintain a service-oriented business model. Although scholars have called for more research on DCs/micro - foundations (e.g., Schilke et al., 2018 ) as well as for more comprehen - sive DC frameworks (e.g., Barrales-Molina et al., 2016 ), most studies on servitization and digital servitization still focus on providing ad-hoc DCs for one (e.g., Kanninen et al., 2017 ) or the other strategy (e.g., Sj ödin et al., 2020 ), and sometimes only one DC category is addressed (e.g., Gebauer et al., 2017 ). Based on the discussion thus far, no framework exists to holistically capture DCs and related microfoundations required for servitization and digital servitization, emphasizing similarities and differences among them in order to provide indications not only to pursue one of the identified strategies, but also to transition from one to another, high - lighting the key challenges and enablers related to that transition. Thus, by analysing the servitization and digital servitization literature, “ an effort is made to separate the microfoundations of dynamic capabilities from the capability itself ” ( Teece, 2007 , p. 1321). 3. Methodology This article adopted the systematic literature review (SLR) method, which is the most suitable for the stated goal and to offer clear docu - mentation of the review process, ensuring its replicability and trans - parency ( Tranfield et al., 2003 ). To perform the thematic analysis, a four-stage procedure was fol - lowed: coding, categorising, thematising, and integrating ( Mayan, 2009; Spiggle, 1994 ). The third stage entailed a process of abstraction to establish an “ internal dialogue ” among the different categories, grouping them into themes according to the initial codebook. Finally, the integration stage helped draw a big picture ( Spiggle, 1994 ) – namely, an integrative framework able to map DCs for the identified strategies.
