Thematic analysis In the analysis of the literature, DCs and microfoundations were identified and classified according to Teece ’ s (2007) categorisation: sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring. The sensing, seizing, and reconfi - guring capabilities and microfoundations as well as key transition challenges and enablers are discussed in-depth in the following sub- sections. Finally, an integrative framework combining all results is proposed. 5.1. Dynamic capabilities and related microfoundations for servitization 5.1.1. Sensing ’ s microfoundations for servitization This theme includes the microfoundations (e.g., skills, processes, procedures) that the firm can/must develop internally and externally to properly assess market and technological developments as well as recognize valuable opportunities. Four distinct microfoundations fall into this theme: identifying profitable services; adopting new technologies; exploiting knowledge; and improving relationships . To identify profitable services, the literature emphasizes the impor - tance of manufacturers differentiating their offerings through valuable services. In other words, they need to be able to identify services that consumers are willing to pay for and that will be integrated with the manufacturers ’ tangible products. Fischer et al. (2010) highlighted that manufacturers ’ main sensing activity refers to the use of services to differentiate their total offering, integrating them into the product price. They further noted that these activities are crucial regardless of the service business development approach the manufacturers adopt (i.e., exploration or exploitation). However, Kindstr öm et al. (2013) under - scored that, even when the provided services are embedded into prod - ucts, they must somehow be visible in the financial statements and performance measurement systems to make managers aware of their influence on turnover, profitability, and sales and to properly exploit their potential in this sense. In this vein, Gebauer and colleagues (2012, 2013) stressed the importance of turning customers ’ service needs into new financial opportunities, especially when manufacturers are inter - ested in gaining new customers who recognize the real service value and are willing to pay for them. According to their studies, this micro - foundation refers to the exploitation of additional service revenue streams and service margins throughout the use of tangible products ( Gebauer et al., 2013 ), even though this possibility is better achieved when products and service offerings are unbundled and charged for separately ( Gebauer et al., 2012 ). Moreover, the creation of a new of - fering is linked to the ability to create new markets and new value propositions and constellations through interactions with external ac - tors. In other words, to fully explicate their value, the sensing DCs need to be open to different value chains and beyond industry and existing network borders ( Fischer et al., 2010; Gebauer et al., 2012 ). This pos - sibility is particularly relevant for innovation-oriented companies, which are not limited to the newness of products and services they produce but include innovation in roles and skills in the value-creation process, downstream and/or upstream in the value chain ( Gebauer et al., 2012 ). Concerning the second microfoundation, adopting new technologies, Fischer et al. (2010) investigated 13 manufacturing companies of different sizes and localized in Switzerland and Germany to understand the implementation of specific information mechanisms. In particular, information gathering, filtering, and processing have to become routine mechanisms if firms want to respond to customers ’ needs and compet - itors ’ activities effectively ( Fischer et al., 2010 ). Kanninen et al. (2017) highlighted the importance of sharing services inside the organization. In addition, Kindstr öm et al. (2013) emphasized that properly under - standing if and how the firm systematically captures and relays cus - tomers ’ information is a critical managerial question, especially when the firm is in the initial stages of the servitization process. This micro - foundation allows firms to offer the “ right ” combination of products and services to meet customers ’ demand as well as prepare strategic re - sponses to competitors ’ service actions. Adopting new technologies also involves their exploration through other actors ’ participation. As emphasized by the companies Kindstr öm and colleagues (2013) inves - tigated, effectively sensing technological opportunities requires estab - lishing external cooperation with ICT specialists/experts to shape the service innovation process. In this vein, Lütjen et al. (2019) investigated 133 managers from 28 German firms in the energy utilities sector and concluded that carrying out projects with research institutes and uni - versities is a common and useful practice of service-innovation-intense firms because it may lead to a deeper understanding of new service opportunities. Thus, manufacturers have to develop the abilities to properly communicate with these external actors to understand their technological suggestions/indications. The third microfoundation is exploiting knowledge. Once customers ’ information is collected and made available within the company through ad-hoc technologies, manufacturers can enhance their cus - tomers ’ knowledge ( Fischer et al., 2010; Kindstr öm et al., 2013 ). To exploit this knowledge, it is essential to put into place customers ’ in - formation evaluation mechanisms to incorporate only valuable knowl - edge on them ( Adam et al., 2018 ). Thus, people responsible for interacting with customers play an important role within this micro - foundation ( Kindstr öm et al., 2013 ). Knowledge exploitation is also related to the ability to investigate and understand all partners within an ecosystem as well as external actors to develop capabilities that “ go beyond intra-organizational boundaries and increasingly relate to the broader environment of the focal firm ” ( Lütjen et al., 2019, p. 513 ). This is particularly true when we refer to the manufacturer – suppliers rela - tionship, in which market-sensing opportunities take place only through a strong understanding of each other ’ s capabilities ( Raddats et al., 2017 ). Thus, knowledge exchange among partners within the service network is vital for the provision of advance services, especially when “ neither party had the right mix of capabilities to win the bid on its own ” ( Raddats et al., 2017, p. 12 ). The last microfoundation in this theme is improving relationships . The possibility of succeeding with servitization is conditioned by the existence of a close relationship with consumers; thus, using specific relational skills within firms that make customers comfortable create a relaxed and pleasant atmosphere ( Adam et al., 2018 ). When the firm is able to establish these intimate and long-standing relationships, it is also able to acquire new valuable knowledge that needs to be spread throughout the company ( Adam et al., 2018 ). Thus, this micro - foundation reinforces the previous two, creating a circular, mutual, and interdependent relationship among them. Furthermore, existing litera - ture, especially the most recent works, has recognized the importance of creating an open mindset and skills according to the different set of ecosystem partners (not just customers) in order to evaluate opportu - nities together ( Kindstr öm et al., 2013; Kanninen et al., 2017; Lütjen et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021 ) and develop capabilities that allow for establishing contacts with actors outside the firm and its ecosystem to obtain numerous suggestions and verify the effective feasibility of ideas ( Adam et al., 2018 ). Seizing ’ s microfoundations for servitization This theme includes those microfoundations that allow manufac - turers to address the different opportunities already identified. Five microfoundations fall within this theme: creating a new offering; planning different scenarios; being flexible; exploiting new revenue mechanisms; and becoming a reference point . Creating a new offering has a stronger link with the first sensing microfoundation. According to the identified profitable services, man - ufacturers are called to create a new offering that properly combines tangible products and intangible services. The creation of a new offer - ing, thus conceived, requires interaction between the manufacturing firms and other actors to create something innovative in terms of not only products/services, but also different value chains and beyond existing network borders ( Fischer et al., 2010; Gebauer et al., 2012 ). Concerning defining different scenarios, previous studies have sug - gested that the seizing capability is strictly linked to the firm ’ s capacity to develop potential scenarios and to formulate umbrella strategies accordingly ( Fischer et al., 2010; Gebauer et al., 2012 ). This activity is usually required of managers and is more common in those firms that adopt an exploration approach to the service development; meanwhile, in those that apply an exploitation approach, all efforts and resources are generally devoted to a single scenario and the related strategies ( Fischer et al., 2010 ). When other actors are also invited to seize the different scenarios, it is possible to establish a learning relationship among all the involved actors and – although different scenarios may be reflected in different roles for them – lead them to propose new value constellations that fit better with customers ’ expectations ( Gebauer et al., 2012 ). In terms of being flexible, the literature unanimously states that the ability to seize one or more opportunities is closely linked to the firm ’ s ability to be flexible, from different points of view. This flexibility is mainly expressed by the managers ’ ability to formulate strategies able to explore a broad range of opportunities ( Fischer et al., 2010; Gebauer et al., 2017 ) and to promptly restructure resources (tangible and intangible and at both operational and strategic levels) in line with the services delivery process ( Kindstr öm et al., 2013 ). All of this is strictly linked to the previous microfoundations. In fact, the possibility to explore different scenarios facilitates managerial cognition of a broad range of different business opportunities, enhancing their flexibility and openness. Flexibility also refers to the ability to integrate different ca - pabilities from different sources. In particular, market and technological opportunities can be seized only through an accurate integration be - tween manufacturing firm capabilities and those belonging to other actors (included or not within the service ecosystem) ( Adam et al., 2018; Raddats et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2021 ). This integration can be done through outsourcing activities ( Gebauer et al., 2013; Raddats et al., 2017 ), the involvement of ecosystem actors in decision-making pro - cesses ( Lütjen et al., 2019 ), and the setting up of cross-functional teams ( Fischer et al., 2010 ). Lastly, as Yeniaras et al. (2021) emphasized, developing organization flexibility enables firms to better integrate product and service elements and, consequently, rapidly respond to a multiplicity of customer requirements, thereby reinforcing and sup - porting previous seizing microfoundations (e.g., creating a new offering). The fourth microfoundation, exploiting new revenue mechanisms, consists of verifying the financial benefits previously sensed by assessing whether customers demand and pay for the provided services ( Gebauer et al., 2012 ). This exploitation can be carried out by the firm charging for services previously offered for free ( Fischer et al., 2010 ) or basing the revenue mechanisms on service availability and customer productivity ( Kindstr öm et al., 2013 ). Gebauer and colleagues (2017) investigated pay-per-use services provided by 17 manufacturing firms embracing a variety of industries and products and geographical locations; the re - searchers emphasized the importance, in this phase, of accurately refining the service portfolio and properly managing the customer portfolio to ensure a rapid sales growth and market share expansion. The last microfoundation in this theme is becoming a reference point. Lütjen et al. (2019) asserted that firms offering services, especially highly innovative ones, need to be seen by other actors in the environ - ment as pioneers actively involved in providing innovation because this creates a network stability that positively influences collaboration among all actors. This, in turn, guarantees to the keystone firm that a wide range of actors will try to involve it in new innovation collaboration. 5.1.3. Reconfiguring ’ s microfoundations for servitization This theme identifies microfoundations that allow manufacturers to recombine and reconfigure resources, processes, and operational skills to match previously seized opportunities. Two microfoundations fall into this theme: redesigning tangible and intangible aspects, and visioning and orchestrating activities . Redesigning tangible and intangible aspects mainly refer to bringing new life to the firm. According to the services strategies, the firm ’ s structure and processes need to be redesigned in a way through which the various activities related to products and services may “ talk ” without hindering each other ( Fischer et al., 2010; Kindstr öm et al., 2013 ). This usually involves the creation of a specific unit within the company dedicated exclusively to services ( Fischer et al., 2010 ). However, the firm ’ s capacity to redesign tangible aspects of the firm (e.g., structure and technical requirements) need to be balanced by the capacity to redesign intangible aspects as well. Gebauer et al. (2012), Kanninen et al. (2017) , and Kindstr öm et al. (2013) reported that one of the most difficult but crucial activities is the modification of the corporate culture to re-orient it towards services. The creation of this new culture requires time and managers ’ strong commitment to be successful ( Kindstr öm et al., 2013 ). These changes in the tangible and intangible aspects of the firm influence each other; one is a cause of the other effect and vice versa. Redesign is also expressed by a refining process of multiple actors ’ competencies and capabilities. Gebauer et al. (2013) highlighted the need to create a common language among all involved actors to promote solid relationships among them and, thus, their capabilities integration. Lütjen et al. (2019) advocated the relevance of integrating external knowledge. Adam et al. (2018) further stressed the concept by empha - sizing that the capacity to redesign the tangible and intangible aspects of the firm depends as much on the ability to learn (through a deep and active knowledge sharing among multiple actors) as on the ability to unlearn familiar practices. In fact, as Shen et al. (2021) emphasized, a robust learning capability enables firms to acquire new skills and re - sources, integrate them into their internal capabilities, produce inno - vative products, develop new product markets, reduce costs, and improve innovation performance. The second microfoundation, visioning and orchestrating activities, mainly refers to the internal ability of the firm to face challenges. In fact, servitization usually creates internal resistance and conflicts that need to be overcome ( Fischer et al., 2010 ) through the institution of a service- oriented mental model and flat hierarchies ( Adam et al., 2018 ) and the removal of traditional roots and structures ( Lütjen et al., 2019 ). In this vein, what emerges as critical is the ability to orchestrate the service system. In other words, there is a need to skilfully manage the reconfi - guration of all the firm aspects in a process of continuous alignment between internal and external resources and processes ( Gebauer et al., 2012; Kindstr öm et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2021; Alkalha et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021 ). This reconfiguration mainly passes through to a re- evaluation of the business relationships ( Fischer et al., 2010 ) that al - lows for rearranging the different roles played by the numerous actors, visioning and mobilizing them ( Gebauer et al., 2013 ), as well as to incorporate complementary resources ( Kindstr öm et al., 2013 ). 5.2. Dynamic capabilities and related microfoundations for digital servitization 5.2.1. Sensing ’ s microfoundations for digital servitization The literature analysis found that a set of eleven specific activities is K. Chirumalla et al. Journal of Business Research 158 (2023) 113668 8 necessary to properly develop the DCs needed to successfully implement a digital servitization strategy. In particular, the digitally enabling sensing capabilities refer to the ability to carry out three different ac - tivities: service data exploitation & processing, data interpretation capability to explore new opportunities, and integration of digital competence within the network to map new offerings . Concerning the first microfoundation, data are critically important and an enabler for digital servitization. The initial efforts to install sensors and constantly generate service-related data from the field help firms exploit and further process data ( Coreynen et al., 2017; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ) and to identify any needs or problems. Kohtam äki et al. (2019) stressed the importance of having capabilities in detailed monitoring, control, and optimization for autonomous solutions. Second, data interpretation capability to explore new opportunities refers to firms ’ capacity to interpret the collected data for recognizing customers ’ needs or exploring new opportunities ( Tronvoll et al., 2020; Ulaga & Reinartz, 2011 ). Coreynen et al. (2020) found that high- exploration firms are more likely to be oriented towards digital servi - tization when they have reached a medium level of exploitation. Finally, for the integration of digital competence within the network to map new offerings, firms need to have the right resources or hire employees with data analytics skills to formulate hybrid offerings ( Coreynen et al., 2017 ) and drive new business models around data- related issues ( Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). This requires the integration of business expertise of multiple actors in the network to realize the full potential of digitalization ( Kamalaldin et al., 2020 ). 5.2.2. Seizing ’ s microfoundations for digital servitization The digitally enabling seizing capabilities refer to the ability to carry out four activities: agile co-creation process, partnership governance for business models and risk mitigation, central coordination and integration, and digital platform and visualization capability . Concerning the agile co-creation process, manufacturing firms need to rethink their value-creation process in digital servitization. Rather than maintaining the traditional way of working, firms need to adopt an agile micro-service innovation approach to manage the value co- creation process with customers ( Sj ödin et al., 2020 ). Moreover, stra - tegic agility is considered a prerequisite for digital organizational transformation ( Bustinza et al., 2018 ), helping firms adopt different configurations. In addition, firms need to have a strong service, entre - preneurial, and agile mindset and way of working to productize digital services ( Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). Regarding the second microfoundation, partnership governance for business models and risk mitigation, manufacturing firms need to establish a broader range of external partnerships with different actors in the value chain and in the ecosystem to access specialized compe - tences as well as build a network, such as with third-party software vendors ( Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). Firms also need to redefine business model configurations involving ecosystem actors ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ) as the transformation of a single firm is not enough to realize the digital servitization. This requires relational governance strategies to protect everyone ’ s business interests, cost structures, revenues and in - centives as well as overcome risks and uncertainties ( Kamalaldin et al., 2020 ; Pagoropoulos et al., 2017 ; Ulaga & Reinartz, 2011 ). The third microfoundation, central coordination & integration, in - dicates that the successful organization and transformation to digital servitization requires manufacturing firms to adopt within-firm centralization and integration ( Sklyar et al., 2019a ). The central orga - nization needs to create a common resource pool and a set of digital tools and training methods to support local organizations to strengthen their customer relationships ( Sklyar et al., 2019b ). Finally, for the fourth microfoundation, digital platform and visu - alization capability, firms need to invest in building digital systems and platforms to provide customized digital services to customers and to manage the associated abundance of data ( Kamalaldin et al., 2020; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). Firms also need to allocate dedicated resources and expertise to analyse and visualize massive data for optimizing the operational processes ( Coreynen et al., 2017; Kamalaldin et al., 2020 ). 5.2.3. Reconfiguring ’ s microfoundations for digital servitization Finally, the reconfiguring capabilities for digital servitization are linked to the ability to carry out four specific activities: identity trans - formation with partners, manage front- and back-end coupling, digital- enabled work processes, and legitimize ecosystem embeddedness . Concerning the first microfoundation, identity transformation with partners, firms that are developing digital services need to transform their identity from a product – service-centric company to a digital- centric company. Given the higher dependency among actors in devel - oping digital services, it is not sufficient to transform the identity of a single company; rather, it requires an ecosystem actor ’ s identity trans - formation ( Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). Firms need to search for new skills and a competence base that would be more compatible with the combination of servitization and digitalization by using technologies such as IoT, AI, 5G, and cloud computing ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019 ). Doing so requires a high level of coordination, communication, and relationship among all involved partners ( Sun & Zhang, 2021 ). Regarding the second microfoundation, manage front- and back-end coupling, digital servitization transforms the roles and responsibilities of both front- and back-end units, which need to be tightly integrated ( Coreynen et al., 2017 ; Sklyar et al., 2019a ). Local organizations and digital service centres are more focused on identifying and deploying new digital opportunities and business models whereas back-end units focus on their ability to effectively create solutions with the integration of front-end functions ( Coreynen et al., 2017 ). The third microfoundation, digital-enabled work processes, indicates that manufacturing firms need to develop digital work processes to facilitate the accumulation of and access to data from many different sources within the ecosystem (Kamalaldin., 2020) to improve data transparency and information sharing. Lastly, according to the fourth microfoundation, legitimize ecosystem embeddedness, manufacturing firms need to set a vision of digital-centricity and use this as a frame of reference to be promoted across the ecosystem ( Sklyar et al., 2019b ). It is important to establish trust building and relational and structural embeddedness within the ecosystem through the adoption of a proper legitimization mechanism ( Sklyar et al., 2019a ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). 5.3. Key challenges to and enablers of building DCs and microfoundations for the servitization-to-digital-servitization transition The theoretical analysis identified three categories of key challenges to and five key enablers of building DCs and microfoundations for the transition from servitization to digital servitization. The key challenges related to the transition are the ability to identify and involve partners willing to share their knowledge, competence management and culture gaps, and the lack of data processing and remote monitoring technolo - gies. Meanwhile, the key enablers that support the transition from traditional servitization to digital servitization are entrepreneurial start- up mindset and disciplined management structure, capacity to exploit digital technologies and scalability, clear internal and external gover - nance structures, alignment of the business models within the ecosystem, and network-level change and transformation. The first challenge, ability to identify and involve partners willing to share their knowledge, has been almost unanimously recognized by scholars as the most crucial challenge. Other system actors ’ participa - tion and commitment ( Kindstr öm et al., 2013 ) as well as the possibility to establish a formal partnership with them ( Gebauer et al., 2013 ) are fundamental for creating outside parties ’ willingness to share their knowledge ( Adam et al., 2018 ). Thus, to succeed, firms need to develop a greater focus on other actors ’ resources and capabilities in their network ( Raddats et al., 2017 ). This focus does not have to be related exclusively to the interaction between firms and their customers, but K. Chirumalla et al. Journal of Business Research 158 (2023) 113668 9 should consider all actors in the network, such as supplier partners up - stream and new entrants in the platform network ( Sun & Zhang, 2021 ). When doing this, firms should be aware that customers ’ and competi - tors ’ behaviours as well as other firms ’ past competitive behaviour will most likely act as an additional obstacle to relationship building ( Fischer et al., 2010 ). However, the analysis of the literature suggests that this first challenge can be effectively overcome thanks to the presence of specific enabling factors, such as entrepreneurial start-up mindset and disciplined management structure, clear internal and external gover - nance structures, and alignment of the business models within the ecosystem. The second challenge, competence management and culture gap, mainly refers to the need to properly manage the transition from ser - vitization to digital servitization in terms of required DCs ( Kindstr öm et al., 2013 ). Managers must be able to identify, develop, protect, and deploy valuable resources and capabilities ( Kanninen et al., 2017 ). As the integrative framework ( Fig. 4 ) shows, digital servitization firms have to develop and use – and thus, properly manage – DCs that differ from those used and applied for traditional servitization. In this vein, Raddats et al. (2017) emphasized how managers should also consider the inter - activity effects on capability development and management. Yet cultural gaps must also be considered. It is already incredibly challenging to shift from a product-centric to a service-centric cultural mindset; this chal - lenge is even more significant if we add the digital aspect ( Xu et al., 2021 ). The cultural approach also deeply affects the way in which manufacturers implement digital servitization because culture in - fluences business model adoption and, thus, affects how services are created, made visible, and communicated to customers ( Kanninen et al., 2017 ). However, even for this challenge, it is possible to identify specific enablers that may help, such as clear internal and external governance structures and network level change and transformation. Concerning the final challenges, the lack of appropriate technologies and related capabilities, firms that want to successfully transition from servitization to digital servitization have to adapt to the rapidly evolving nature of digital technologies ( Kindstr öm et al., 2013 ; Xu et al., 2021 ). The mutual relationship between new digital technologies and new customers ’ requirements entails an essential need for the firm to have human resources who possess the technical skills to use the new tech - nologies and, therefore, wisely integrate products and services, satis - factorily responding to the various customer requests ( Yeniaras et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021 ). In this case, there are also ad-hoc enablers that help overcome this challenge: capacity to exploit digital technologies and scalability, alignment of the business models within the ecosystem, and entrepreneurial start-up mindset and disciplined management structure. 6. An integrative framework to guide the servitization-to- digital-servitization transition using DCs and related microfoundations In light on the results presented thus far, further analysis was carried out to identify a guiding path for transitioning from servitization to digital servitization using DCs and related microfoundations as well as the key challenges and enablers. The analysis led to the development of as integrative framework (see Fig. 4 ) to guide this transition. The proposed integrative framework includes 22 microfoundations that permit product-centric firms to build the required DCs (along the categorisation of sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring) for the successful implementation of both servitization and digital servitization. Of these, 11 microfoundations are in servitization and the remaining ones are related to digital servitization. Contributions, limitations, and future research avenues This study has sought to identify and map the required DCs and related microfoundations, as well as key challenges and enablers, to guide the transition from traditional servitization to digital servitization. Guided by two research questions (RQ1 and RQ2), this study identified 24 papers during the systematic search and analysed them using a deductive thematic analysis. To address the first RQ1, 11 DCs and microfoundations were identified for each of the successful imple - mentation of servitization and digital servitization. Answering the sec - ond RQ2 involved identifying three key transition challenges and five enablers for building DCs and related microfoundations in the transition from servitization to digital servitization. 7.1. Theoretical contributions The study provides four important theoretical contributions. Firstly, it identifies 22 microfoundations that companies need to carry out to properly develop sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring DCs for imple - menting servitization and digital servitization. Thus, this paper extends the current literature on servitization and digital servitization, which does not provide exhaustive indications about the needed DCs and their even more detailed level of microfoundations ( Fischer et al., 2010 ; Kindstr öm et al., 2013; Kohtam äki et al., 2019; Raddats et al., 2017; Salonen, 2011 ). Furthermore, this study provides a proper structure to organize and manage the dynamic capability building for servitization and digital servitization in a holistic way as most existing literature discusses such concepts interchangeably in a scattered way (e.g., Fischer et al., 2010; Gebauer et al., 2017; Coreynen et al., 2017; Ceci & Masini, 2011; Paiola et al., 2013; Storbacka, 2011 ). Only a few studies have focused on a holistic approach ( Kindstr öm et al., 2013; Chirumalla, 2021; Lütjen et al., 2019 ). Most importantly, this study considers both servitization and digital servitization together when analysing the necessary DCs and microfoundations, whereas current literature focus on either servitization (e.g., Kindstr öm et al., 2013; Kanninen et al., 2017; Fischer et al., 2010 ) or digital servitization (e.g., Bustinza et al., 2018; Coreynen et al., 2017; Sj ödin et al., 2020 ) from DCs ’ perspective. Considering both in combination is necessary considering the emerging Industry 4.0 and 5.0 technologies ( Oztemel & Gursev, 2020; Rad et al., 2022; Veile et al., 2019 ) and complex challenges involved in imple - menting them (e.g., Rad et al., 2022; Chirumalla, 2021 ). Secondly, this study identifies both key transition challenges and enablers involved when building DCs and related microfoundations for the transition from servitization to digital servitization. Most extant literature discusses challenges and enablers at a general level (e.g., Zhang & Banerji, 2017; Chirumalla et al., 2019; Coreynen et al., 2017 ; Matschewsky et al., 2018; Neely, 2008; Raja et al., 2017 ), but not in relation to building DCs and microfoundations, which is critical considering their role in contributing to the strategic organizational changes and transformations, which is required in the context of servi - tization and digital servitization (e.g., Pisano, 2017; Teece, 2018; Teece et al., 1997 ). Moreover, the study considers both servitization and dig - ital servitization together when analysing the involved transition chal - lenges and enablers in building DCs and microfoundations, which the current literature does not consider, as previously discussed. Thirdly, this study proposed a comprehensive and integrative framework for building required DCs and microfoundations to guide the transition from servitization to digital servitization. Thus, the study contributes to existing literature by offering a more fine-grained and complete view to succeed in these strategies while smoothly moving from the first to the second using DCs and microfoundations as a theo - retical lens. To the best of the authors ’ knowledge, this is the first study of its kind with a specific focus on DCs considering both servitization and digital servitization as part of the investigation. The study highlighted similarities and differences between the required DCs and micro - foundations for servitization and digital servitization under the cate - gorisation of sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring, thereby responding to the call for support for companies more smoothly transitioning from one to the other ( Kohtam äki et al., 2019; Paiola & Gebauer, 2020; Paschou et al., 2020; Kolagar et al., 2022; Kohtam äki et al., 2021; Baines et al., 2020 ). The framework further shows how the key challenges in tran - sitioning from servitization are linked to the key enablers for tran - sitioning to digital servitization. Finally, the approach adopted in the paper aligns perfectly with the views of W ójcik et al. (2022) and Foss and Pedersen (2016), who stressed how adopting a microfoundations lens helps solve the abstract conceptualization of DCs by identifying the specific underlying actions/ processes ( Teece, 2007 ; Felin et al., 2012 ). Thus, the paper contributes to the debate on DCs ’ microfoundations by addressing the call to examine these lower-level factors, rendering it more complete and better able to address manufacturing firms ’ current features. In fact, by focusing on microfoundations, this study provides an accurate level of detail, building a firm conceptual foundation for servitization and dig - ital servitization. 7.2. Managerial contributions The study provides important managerial contributions. Firstly, the study ’ s findings are useful for business development, marketing and sales, aftermarket, (digital) service, and product – service managers and developers seeking to improve performance in servitization, digital servitization, or product – service – software systems, including manage - rial tools and tactics needed for such improvement at the firm level. The ability for organizational transformation depends on managers’ perceptions and the organization’s preparedness to swiftly alter its resource base. The DCs and microfoundations approach provides such knowledge so managers can plan a clear vision for the digital servitization work and a suitable digitalization strategy through targeted modification of resources and capabilities. The find - ings could help managers overcome the constraints in their daily work, such as cognitive limitations and framing biases arising from established practices and norms. This is particularly important as the context of digitalization and Industry 4.0 technologies are challenging firms’ traditional approach to strategizing and the nature of the building dy - namic capabilities. Thus, managers must choose and develop only those DCs and microfoundations that appropriately fit the specific situation. Lastly, the framework sheds light on the importance of the DCs and microfoundations developed through external actors. Accordingly, practitioners’ ability to adequately select partners within their service ecosystem as well as effectively relate with external actors (e.g., in - stitutions, universities) plays a crucial role, especially in terms of knowledge exchange. In this regard, companies and servitization work stakeholders can use the framework as a boundary object in a capability- building exercise to initiate a dialogue within the firm and outside the firm in order to achieve a systematic transformation. 7.3. Limitations and future research avenues Although this study makes important theoretical and managerial contributions, some limitations need to be acknowledged. The SLR was conducted in a rigorous manner, but the selected keywords and database as well as the applied inclusion and exclusion criteria may have led the authors to identify a final sample that other researchers may not have identified. Thus, a different sample (e.g., a final dataset not limited to academic journal articles) could enrich (or contradict) the framework presented in this study. Accordingly, further research could improve the framework by also considering, for example, conference publications and grey literature. Moreover, this work relies on DCs and micro - foundations theory at a general level; thus, further (empirical) in - vestigations are encouraged to examine how manufacturing firms identify microfoundations of sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring both individually and in collaboration with external actors. In this vein, particularly interesting future studies could consider the complementary view of all actors involved (at different levels) considering an ecosystem setting in the services creation and delivery processes, bringing out a more punctual analysis of the roles and abilities of each of them and how they can complement, contribute to, or contradict each other’s DCs and microfoundations in the ecosystem. Future researchers can also conduct confirmatory studies of the whole proposed framework or make a detailed analysis of each single microfoundation (or specific category, such as sensing, seizing, or reconfiguring) related to servitization/digital servitization. We also encourage researchers to define and empirically test possible theoretical propositions based the proposed integrative framework (e.g., at the level of sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring) by considering either servitization or digital servitization specifically or both in tandem; a comparative analysis of sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring between servitization and digital servitization; interdependencies of key transi - tion challenges or key enablers; and interdependencies between key transition challenges and key enablers. As different firms may develop and implement the identified microfoundations in different ways, future studies should investigate the actual process of generation as well as the subsequent development of the DCs and microfoundations in different contexts (e.g., in a small firm, in a multinational company, in the early stages of servitization or digital servitization, during the transition process). The struggle of sensor-based digital servitization: analysis and perspectives for organizational digital transformation in SMEs Thomas Trabert, Luca Doerr and Claudia Lehmann Chair of Digital Innovation in Service Industries, HHL Leipzig Graduate School of Management, Leipzig, Germany Abstract Purpose – The organizational digital transformation (ODT) in companies presents small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)– who remain at the beginning of this transformation– with the challenge of offering digital services based on sensor technologies. Against this backdrop, the present paper identifies ways SMEs can enable digital servitization through sensor technology and defines the possible scope of the organizational transformation process. Design/methodology/approach – Around 21 semi-structured interviews were conducted with experts from different hierarchical levels across the German manufacturing SME ecosystem. Using the Gioia methodology, fields of action were identified by focusing on influencing factors and opportunities for developing these digital services to offer them successfully in the future. Findings – The complexity of existing sensor offerings must be mastered, and employees ’ (data) understanding of the technology has increased. Knowledge gaps, which mainly relate to technical and organizational capabilities, must be overcome. The potential of sensor technology was considered on an individual, technical and organizational level. To enable the successful implementation of service offerings based on sensor technology, all relevant stakeholders in the ecosystem must network to facilitate shared value creation. This requires standardized technical and procedural adaptations and is an essential prerequisite for data mining. Originality/value – Based on this study, current problem areas were analyzed, and potentials that create opportunities for offering digital sensor services to manufacturing SMEs were identified. The identified influencing factors form a conceptual framework that supports SMEs’future development of such services in a structured manner. Although integrating and using sensors (specifically, sensor technology) is an attractive solution to access data, companies need help with the complexity of the prevailing systems and the heterogeneity of the operating systems (Tantscher and Mayer, 2022). Data is connectivity medium to enable new value propositions for manufacturing companies, fostering opportunities for customer engagement throughout the product lifecycle (Jacobides et al., 2018; Kiel et al., 2017; M€uller et al., 2018). Therefore, products are increasingly enriched with data to facilitate emerging data-driven business models and provide innovative services (Ancillai et al., 2023). In this context, it should be noted that data itself does not create value. Instead, value emerges through a process of integration, analysis, visualization and interpretation (K€uhne and B€ohmann, 2019). Nonetheless, creating value-added services through increased digitalization is a significant challenge for the manufacturing industry. It is not merely a choice but an imperative for maintaining competitiveness (Raddats et al., 2022). Considering dynamic and highly volatile markets, manufacturing companies must understand and rethink the processes of product and service innovation to position themselves favorably (Chuang and Chen, 2022; Visnjic et al., 2016). The focus of this analysis extends to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) characterized by having fewer than 250 employees and a revenue of less than EUR 50 million (Federal Foreign Office, 2020). The decision to analyze SMEs was partly due to how the existing literature has predominantly centered on digital servitization within large-sized companies. This bias can be related to the perception that SMEs often seen as followers rather than early adopters of digitalization, face higher risks and resource constraints when undertaking DT initiatives (Paschou et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2023). It is important to emphasize that SMEs are predominant in many economic areas, constituting over 99.4% of all companies in Germany and 99% in the European Union (EU), particularly in the service and manufacturing sector, thereby making research indispensable ( Bettiol et al ., 2023 ; Commission of the European Communities, 2003 ; European Commission, 2022, 2023; Statistisches Bundesamt, 2022a, 2022b). The fundamental organizational transformation processes to realize digital services are vast and complex. They often require multiple organizational changes, including business processes, work practices and new knowledge and capabilities (Baines et al., 2009; Queiroz et al., 2020 ; Sj€odin et al., 2020). In order to describe this transformation process, this study uses the term “organizational digital transformation ” (ODT), which refers to a strategic intervention aimed at improving an organization’s digital capability to enhance its processes, services and business models in line with the framework proposed by Mhlungu et al. (2019). Furthermore, the study addresses the concept ofdigital servitization, which has attracted significant attention in recent research (Chuang and Chen, 2022; Gebauer et al., 2021; Raddats et al.,2 0 1 9; Shen et al., 2023). The term combines the two megatrends of digitization and servitization. It characterizes the expansion of the service business of traditional product-oriented companies with the help of digital technologies to analyze data and realize competitive advantages (Baines et al., 2009; Gebauer et al., 2021; Lamperti et al., 2023; Vandermerwe and Rada, 1988). In this context, the interplay between these two paradigms must be recognized as they collectively shape the business strategy. It reflects a strategic shift in business paradigms where companies not only embrace DT internally but also use these digital capabilities to enhance their external service offerings through digital servitization, thereby redefining their competitive positioning in the market (Chirumalla et al., 2023). However, most SMEs still need a digital strategy in place and a plan to implement one in future (Bouncken and Schmitt, 2022; North et al., 2020). One fundamental research gap is the need for an in-depth understanding of the process of business model transformation in SMEs (D€orr et al., 2023; Lamperti et al., 2023; North et al., 2020). For example, it remains unclear how SMEs can effectively identify new service offerings and develop the capabilities required to deliver and integrate these services into their existing (product-focused) business model (Iriarte et al., 2023). Therefore, this paper aims to provide opportunities for SMEs to enable digital servitization through sensor technology. As a first step, it is necessary to understand the difficulties SMEs face regarding sensor technology as a driver of digital value creation in a data-driven economy (Verhoef et al., 2021). Second, the conditions and perspectives of ODT must be assessed to identify opportunities and ways to overcome difficulties and thus enhance competitiveness (Mhlungu et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2023). Accordingly, a qualitative research approach was chosen to systematically and comprehensively explore the relationship between digital servitization and ODT, focusing on facilitating factors of digital servitization in SMEs. The following research questions (RQ) were defined: RQ1. What are the impacts of digital servitization for SMEs, and how can SMEs manage the transition from product-oriented to service-oriented value creation? RQ2. Which influencing conditions need to be considered for ODT in this context? The paper analyzes action areas and recommendations for SMEs to develop sensor-based digital service activities in order to shed light on the relationship between digital servitization and ODT. 2. Theoretical underpinnings 2.1 Organizational digital transformation According toMhlungu et al. (2019), ODT is defined as the strategic intervention that enhances digital organizational capability, which in turn improves an organization ’s processes, services and business models to the satisfaction of its customers. Due to ODT being a strategic rather than a technical issue, a clear strategy for the adoption and use of digital technologies and services is critical to enable future business success (Mhlungu et al., 2019). Several studies have indicated organizational structure, culture and customer centricity in improving customer experience and customer service as significant factors for ODT (Ram/C19 ırez-Dur/C19an et al., 2021). The challenge for companies is to strive for the functionality and effectiveness of technologies and service offerings to enable shared value creation for all stakeholders within the ecosystem (Winby and Mohrman, 2018). To successfully implement digital technology and enable interactions between individuals, teams and organizations, it is fundamentally important to understand the complexity of the innovation ecosystem (Pasmore et al., 2019; Piantoni et al., 2023; Winby and Mohrman, 2018). Given the limited resources of SMEs, ecosystems can provide support and opportunities for collaboration to overcome these limitations and restrictions (Benitez et al., 2020a; Ghobakhloo and Iranmanesh, 2021; Toth et al., 2020). It is crucial to consider the role of employees in the organizational transformation and to foster their willingness to learn and openness to change as these are fundamental digital capabilities (Ghobakhloo and Iranmanesh, 2021; Zoppelletto et al., 2020). There is an increasing need for the technical capabilities of employees, such as in software development or in using different digital tools (Brown and Souto-Otero, 2020; Brunetti et al., 2020; Harteis and Goller, 2014; Sousa and Rocha, 2019b). It needs to be more represented (at best) in current Industry 4.0 research (Neumann et al., 2021). Highlighting the added value for the entire company and demonstrating the benefits of technologies and services is crucial to achieving high employee engagement (Agostini and Nosella, 2020; Mukherjee et al., 2018). In summary, ODT refers to using digital technologies to transform organization’s internal processes, systems and culture and consequently improving its performance, competitiveness and agility (Burchardt and Maisch, 2019; Troise et al., 2022). Digital servitization, on the other hand, relates to the use of digital technologies tooffer value-added services that complement a company’sc o r ep r o d u c t s(Gebauer et al., 2021). In other words, ODT is a broader concept that includes digital servitization as a potential application of digital technologies (Tronvollet al., 2020). 2.2 Sensor-based digital servitization in SMEs As mentioned inSection 2.1, strategic service orientation is essential to product-centered markets (Mhlungu et al., 2019; Saarikko et al., 2020; Sch€uritz et al., 2017). Digital servitization refers to the transformation toward offering digitally enabled advanced services that are directly linked to manufacturers’products (Chuang and Chen, 2022; Gebauer et al., 2021). The interdependencies of ODT and digital servitization are crucial for success (Gebauer et al., 2021; Satzger et al., 2022; Tronvoll et al., 2020). In particular, technology-oriented SMEs with a product-centric mindset explore a transition that requires a series of changes regarding technologies, processes, human capabilities and offerings to create value (Kolagaret al., 2022; Kowalkowskiet al., 2022; Peillon and Dubruc, 2019). Evolving digital servitization demands an information and communication infrastructure as the backbone of the process, enabling the extraction of data, which is a key resource in the valuecreation process (Dong and Yang, 2020; Mukherjee, 2018). SMEs face technological challenges (e.g., missing sensors) in obtaining data about their products (North et al., 2020). One possible method for preparing existing machines to mine data and thus enable digital servitization is retrofitting: Existing machines, referred to as legacy equipment, can be upgraded by integrating sensors to support the transition towards Industry 4.0-capable shop floors. Hence, it can extend the lifecycle of machines in a feasible, time-saving and low-investment way (Jaspertet al., 2021). As such, retrofitting allows SMEs to integrate digital solutions into their existing infrastructure, thus enabling access to shop-floor data without costly and disruptive equipment replacements (Javaid et al., 2021). This approach empowers SMEs to stay competitive while minimizing the financial barriers associated with DT (Alqoud et al., 2022). Furthermore, the replacement of working legacy equipment with Industry 4.0-capable machines to withstand the DT is also questionable from the perspective of sustainability (Garc/C19 ıa et al., 2022). Selamat and Windasari (2021)argued that a deeper understanding of customers’needs and processes is essential for creating the value proposition of complex services. Close customer relationships can be helpful in this process, as customers would be more willing to provide data and information. Hence, it is necessary to clarify and redesign existing processes and workflows to pivot toward digital servitization strategically (Alkhatib et al., 2019; Khan et al., 2016; Martinelli et al., 2021). 3. Finally, ODT relies on interdisciplinary perspectives and employee capabilities, i.e., a cross-section of technical professions combined with management skills to create a vision of added value. 4.4 Excursus retrofitting The interviewees commented on the sensor-based use case of retrofitting. Retrofitting describes integrating of new technologies (especially sensors) into existing legacy equipment to extend the life cycle of existing machinery (Jaspert et al., 2021). The following second-order themes were defined. First, the interviewees explained that only some solutions fit all retrofitting approaches. Moreover, there is a high need to manage complexity, which refers to such technological and infrastructural constraints as accessibility and space in machines or a variety of signals. Complexity also relates to the concentrated definition of the problem in line with the use case. Second, the possibility of gaining knowledge and experience without purchasing new machinery is an advantage of retrofitting. Iterative tests can enable an understanding of the system and the gathering of experience. Third, the implementation and overall retrofitting can be cost-intensive due to the system’s complexity. Therefore, costbenefit calculations for weighing the effort are essential for every project. Fourth, all stakeholders must be integrated into the process to be successful. Hence, it is recommended to achieve awareness within all levels of the hierarchy by promoting progressive thinking and showing added value. Lastly, thriving flexibility is an advantage of SMEs that can be promoted by retrofitting. Flat hierarchies facilitate the starting of retrofitting projects and gaining the above-listed advantages. Discussion The discussion is based on the conceptual framework (seeFigure 1). Concerning the first RQ, the results present an in-depth understanding of the process undertaken by SMEs to identify and create new digitally service-oriented values (Iriarte et al., 2023; Lamperti et al., 2023). Furthermore, various factors influencing the creation of digital value-adding services in manufacturing SMEs were identified. The introduction of sensor technologies triggers these factors. The creation of digital services are multifaceted processes that are influenced by human, technological and organizational factors (Oppl and Stary, 2019). The results indicate that the surveyed SMEs are aware of the struggle of sensor-based digital servitization but remain in the initial phase of the transformation (D€orr et al., 2023; Jaspert et al., 2021). This shift results from the fact that digital servitization is not yet anchored in company strategy (Hess et al., 2016; Oppl and Stary, 2019; Wu et al., 2021b). However, while most companies already have ideas about how to integrate sensor technologies to improve and expand their offerings, there is a lack of knowledge about their implementation (Franket al., 2019). The respondents cited the complexity of the technologies available on the market as a major reason for the difficulties in digital servitization. This fact demonstrates the different scales of engagement of SMEs in the available technology (G€otz, 2019; Pfister and Lehmann, 2021). The interviewees clarify that they need to master the complexity and create an understanding of the technology among the employees before the implementation of ODT into the strategy and the alignment of the business models can occur (Mukherjee, 2018; Tronvollet al., 2020; Wu et al., 2021b). This approach contrasts with previous studies, which have called for strategy alignment followed by the search for and implementation of appropriate technologies (Bosman et al., 2020; Sinha and Fukey, 2021). Likewise, the respondents suggested that it needs to be clarified how to create value-adding services from data. This problem was also mentioned bySj€odin et al. (2020). Limited capacities hinder the companies’ability to focus on digital servitization as the daily business must be served simultaneously (North et al., 2020). Furthermore, it is essential but complicated to estimate the investment and resulting benefit. Investing in new technologies is associated with high risk (Buer et al., 2021; Sinha and Fukey, 2021). There is a lack of financial resources to test technologies in several projects. Hence, limited financial resources must be used in a targeted manner to mitigate risks (Pfister and Lehmann, 2021). Another reason why SMEs are struggling is the lack of transparency. In most cases, the machines are sold, and the manufacturers cannot collect data about their use. Hence, the interviewees highlighted retrofitting as a solution to gain data for already-sold legacy equipment to create more transparency (Jaspert et al., 2021). In summary, the barriers to facilitating digital servitization in SMEs are complex and must be considered in a structured process so that small steps can be taken toward ODT (Buer et al., 2021; Ram/C19 ırez-Dur/C19an et al., 2021). The second RQ aimed to identify conditions that need to be considered for ODT in SMEs. Consequently, the perspectives that influence ODT in organizations were examined. In essence, ODT is more of an organizational than a technological issue (Mhlungu et al., 2019). Without a sufficient change in operations and learning, organizational performance has less of an impact on ODT (Matt et al., 2015; Mhlungu et al., 2019; Tabrizi et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2021a). It became apparent that functioning processes and standardization are essential components of digital servitization in terms of making data uniformly available, evaluating and exchanging data and making data comprehensible (Pasmore et al., 2019; Winby and Mohrman, 2018; Wu et al., 2021a). This is possible when proceeding in the direction of shared value creation. Thus, data exchange can be pursued in a cross-company ecosystem (Winby and Mohrman, 2018). Accordingly, it needs to be more thoroughly considered in the strategic alignment of organizations (Oppl and Stary, 2019). Ultimately, the change associated with introducing new technologies should not be viewed as a one-time event but rather as a continuous process (Winby and Mohrman, 2018). Essentially, more activities regarding continuous change and adaptation must be conducted by SMEs in order to heighten their capacities to quickly respond to the realities of the marketplace (Benitez et al., 2020b). Based on our results, SMEs encounter difficulties adapting to changing market conditions in time because the interfaces with necessary stakeholders still need to be created. These activities are executed mainly by one person due to a lack of resources. Given the under-representation of the human factor in Industry 4.0 research (Neumann et al., 2021), interdisciplinary human capabilities, in addition to digital ones, are essential. These findings are congruent with the existing literature (Crupi et al., 2020; Sousa and Rocha, 2019a). Indeed, within the context of SMEs, where human resources are often limited, we found that these capabilities typically relate to a single individual. Furthermore, the development of digital services requires not only technical capabilities but also economic ones to establish them in the market (Soluk and Kammerlander, 2021). Many SMEs continue to rely on the experience of their workforce, highlighting the importance of subjectivity in strengthening SME resilience (Sgarbossa et al., 2020). In essence, fostering a culture of continuous learning is highly relevant for preparing for future challenges (Schwarzm€uller et al., 2018). For example, such a culture can mitigate people’s fears of change and provide them with new perspectives to ultimately improve interaction with technology – a finding confirmed in the existing literature ( Ghobakhloo and Iranmanesh, 2021). A functioning network of partners is required to master problems in the ecosystem. Hence, it is important to have a deep understanding of the general demands of the customer and the ecosystem (Winby and Mohrman, 2018). However, there is a close relationship between ODT and digital servitization. To effectively implement digital servitization strategies, companies often need to undergo organizational changes and transformations that are part of ODT (Mhlungu et al., 2019). Companies should develop capabilities in data mining to offer value-added services and restructure their processes to support their delivery (Ghobakhloo and Iranmanesh, 2021; Zoppelletto et al., 2020). ODT and digital servitization may be conceptually distinct but are closely related in practice. They often work in tandem as companies seek to leverage digital technologies to transform their operations and business models (Tronvoll et al., 2020). 6. Conclusion 6.1 Theoretical implications The proposed framework offers theoretical recommendations illuminating the current requirements and problems of digital servitization for SMEs. Furthermore, the framework answers the call within the existing literature for an in-depth understanding of the conceptualization and planning processes for digital servitization and value creation (Iriarte et al., 2023; Lamperti et al., 2023). Given the limited human and financial resources of SMEs, they must open up to the implementation of such complex servitization activities (North et al., 2020). Finally, SMEs often rely on the experience of their employees. However, the development of capabilities for human-machine interaction is required in order to reap the benefits of digitization (Sousa and Rocha, 2019b). Therefore, the proposed framework provides for overcoming the knowledge gap and managing the complexity, for example, regarding sensor selection (Tantscher and Mayer, 2022). It was evident that understanding ODT and digital technologies is necessary for successfully implementing digital servitization projects. Moreover, it is imperative to highlight the added value of technologies and services for companies to promote and retain (Agostini and Nosella, 2020; Mukherjee et al., 2018). The results emphasize the potential of sensor applications as they support SMEs to focus on sustainable solutions, such as retrofitting (Jaspert et al., 2021). In order to successfully implement connected products and services, SMEs need to think in ecosystems and enable data exchange with other actors via standardized interfaces. Thus, data could be uniformly available, analyzable, shareable and understandable (Pasmore et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2021b). Accordingly, data sharing should be established in terms of a cross-enterprise ecosystem that enables shared value for all stakeholders (Bettiol et al., 2023; Winby and Mohrman, 2018). In the future, SMEs must incorporate this approach into their strategic direction to respond to changing market conditions (Benitez et al., 2020b). In addition, the human factor must be considered as a design element in ODT (Mhlungu et al., 2019; Neumann et al., 2021). This step is necessary because each stakeholder, whether at the individual or organizational level, must be involved to consistently promote ODT, especially in SMEs (Winby and Mohrman, 2018). 6.2 Practical implications The present study has high practical relevance for SME managers and consultants, and it offers concrete recommendations for companies seeking to enhance their business performance through digital servitization. The study highlighted the apparent need to understand ODT and to design digital innovation projects transparently. It was recognized that the use and integration of sensor technology as an essential tool enriches the strategic orientation toward the digital servitization of SMEs. Significant potentials and fields of action were highlighted in the study. In this context, the proactive involvement of customers, as well EJIM 27,9 62 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ejim/article-pdf/27/9/52/9605056/ejim-05-2023-0434.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 as all stakeholders in these projects, is highly relevant (Bettiol et al., 2023; Winby and Mohrman, 2018). Further to the deficits in terms of competence requirements, SMEs may not be able to map the lack of human resources fully (Ram/C19 ırez-Dur/C19an et al., 2021; Soluk and Kammerlander, 2021). It is becoming increasingly clear that interdisciplinary capabilities will play a pivotal role in addressing this challenge in the future (Crupi et al., 2020). Moreover, it was recognized that the role of employees in the design of transformation projects should receive more attention (Neumann et al., 2021). Furthermore, SMEs must focus on expanding ecosystems to pursue shared value creation through partnership networks (Di Mininet al., 2019; Sklyar et al., 2019). In addition, standardized interfaces need to be created to simplify data exchange and further reduce the complexity of servitization projects. The acquired knowledge can be used to improve the process further and to drive sensor-based servitization in SMEs in the future. The presented findings can assist companies that require a structured overview for the use case of sensor technology. The framework also provides an overview of the capabilities needed to achieve digital servitization within the presented use case. Finally, sustainable business opportunities were identified to ultimately boost and optimize the ODT of SMEs through sensor-based digital servitization. The opportunities primarily lie within data analysis to simplify processes and make them more transparent. In addition, sensor technologies represent a lucrative way, especially for SMEs, to modernize existing machines to extend their longevity. 6.3 Limitations and further research The results presented in this paper are subject to certain limitations and require further investigation regarding the following points: First, the sample size of the surveyed companies of n 521 appears comparatively small. We expect that larger samples will yield more reliable results. Second, the sample was geographically limited to companies in Germany. Exploring other nations that boast many SMEs would likely yield intriguing insights. These include Italy, France and Spain, which have the highest number of European SMEs (European Commission, 2022). An international comparison between different countries would also influence and challenge the results of this work positively. Third, new studies could apply a quantitative framework for validating and strengthening the identified implications. This would require the collection of measurable results over the longer term to facilitate a quantitative comparison. In addition, the transferability of the results should be examined as the companies surveyed are still in the early stages of developing sensor-based digital services. For this purpose, it would be interesting to observe companies over a more extended period and examine the transformation process against the background of the developed recommendations. Finally, it is worth mentioning that SMEs need help to keep up with the pace of change on their own due to their limited resources and the rapid transformation of digital technologies. Therefore, SMEs are advised to focus on ecosystems, as partners can complement their resources, capabilities and technologies to enable digital servitization. Barriers to the adoption of digital servitization: a case of the Sri Lankan manufacturing sector Weerabahu Mudiyanselage Samanthi Kumari Weerabahu, Premaratne Samaranayake, Dilupa Nakandala and Henry Lau Western Sydney University, Sydney, Australia, and Dasun Nirmala Malaarachchi Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Australia Abstract Purpose – This research aims to identify, examine and evaluate barriers to the adoption of digital servitization in manufacturing firms in the case of the Sri Lankan manufacturing sector and analyze the inter-relationships among digital servitization barriers. Design/methodology/approach – Based on the comprehensive literature review, 13 barriers were identified. The grey decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory (grey-DEMATEL) approach was used to uncover and analyze the relationships among barriers in terms of their overall influence and dependencies. Findings – A prominent barrier to the success of adopting digital servitization in the Sri Lankan manufacturing sector is the lack of digital strategy in developing activities related to the design of digital service packages, organizational structures and processes. Supply chain integration is the most influential factor, which plays an important role in developing a competitive advantage by encouraging innovation process capabilities in servitized companies. Practical implications – Industry practitioners can develop guidelines for adopting digital servitization practices based on the importance and interdependencies of different barriers and thereby prioritize projects within a program of digital servitization adoption in their organizations. Originality/value – Research studies on barriers to digital servitization are limited to exploratory nature and have adopted mainly the qualitative approach, such as in-depth interviews. No empirical study has investigated the inter-relationships among digital servitization adoption barriers in the manufacturing sector. This study provides a holistic view of different barriers to the adoption of digital servitization in the manufacturing sector as a basis for developing comprehensive digital servitization strategies to manage and leverage complexity in digital transformation. Keywords Digital servitization, Industry 4.0, Manufacturing, Barriers of digital servitization Paper type Research paper 1. Introduction Many organizations have shifted from traditional manufacturing and associated business models to innovative business models which offer integrated solutions to achieve greater customer satisfaction (Hoch and Brad, 2020). Manufacturing organizations focus on service-led growth with digital technologies as customers are expected to combine the product with highquality services (Coreynen et al., 2020). This process is referred to as “Digital Servitization” (Raddats et al., 2019). The paradigm shifts from manufacturing organizations’ product-centric business models to service-centric ones created new technological and market opportunities. The term digital servitization is conceptualized as “the development of new services and/or the improvement of existing ones through the use of digital technologies” (Paschou et al., 2020, p. 284). The growing interest in digital servitization in all these mature economies reflects that servitization in manufacturing is an attractive strategy to gain a new competitive advantage (Paschou et al., 2020; Costa et al., 2020; Wirtz and Kowalowski, 2022). Furthermore, developed countries formulated national digitalization strategies, whereas developing countries have adopted Industry 4.0 (I4) technologies on a corporate level rather than the national level. I4 technologies enable manufacturing firms to develop new business models, exploiting the potential of digital servitization. Therefore, many manufacturing organizations in developing countries are increasingly attempting to move beyond pure manufacturing and seek new business models to offer services and solutions delivered through their products (Tripathi and Gupta, 2021). Although developed countries encounter servitization as a widely adopted practice, manufacturing firms in developing countries are concerned about service success as there are inconsistencies between service provision and financial returns (Sz /C19 asz et al., 2017). However, developing countries may still benefit from the opportunities to be first-movers in servitization and experience relevant increases in financial returns (Moreno et al., 2019). Tronvoll et al. (2020) and Sklyar et al. (2019) have emphasized the importance of investigating different barriers that hinder the adoption of digital servitization in developing countries, particularly if organizations need to be competitive in the global supply chain environment. Paschou et al. (2020) discussed the influence of competitive, environmental and social aspects of digital servitization in emerging economies and emphasized servitization as a key future research direction. Several research studies have reported barriers to adopting I4 and servitization independently. On the other hand, research studies on barriers to servitization have adopted literature review (Hou and Neely, 2013) and in-depth interviews (Confente et al., 2015) as primary data collection approaches. Furthermore, research studies on barriers to digital servitization are limited to exploratory nature and have adopted mainly the qualitative approach, such as in-depth interviews (Peillon and Dubruc, 2019) and focus groups (Marcon et al., 2019). Most digital servitization research studies are based on one or a few case studies (Paschou et al., 2020; Kamalaldin et al., 2020), and limited research address the cumulative effect of technologies on digital servitization (Paschou et al., 2020). Therefore, the need for confirmatory research investigating the cumulative effect of digital technologies on the digital servitization domain and the prerequisite for digital servitization (drivers and barriers) to support decision-making was emphasized in previous studies (Paschou et al., 2020). The framework referred to as the technology, organization and environment (T–O–E) model (Tornatzky and Fleischer, 1990) is selected as the basis of this research since it has been adapted and used for implementation and post-adoption issues (Masood and Egger, 2019). In this context, the T–O–E framework is mainly used for explaining the barriers to the adoption and implementation of innovation (Awa and Ojiabo, 2016), and recently it has been widely used for I4 technology adoption and implementation (Aboelmaged and Hashem, 2018; Dewi et al., 2018). The application of the T–O–E model in this research is important and rationalized since barriers to the adoption of digital servitization are directly related to technology, organization and environment (Marcon et al., 2019; Peillon and Dubruc, 2019). Furthermore, the direct and indirect relationships between the factors and the priorities of individual factors describe the situation far more accurately than the assessment of individual factors in isolation (Raj et al., 2019). In this context, grey-decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory (grey-DEMATEL) has an advantage over other multi-criteria decisionmaking (MCDM) methods and previously used qualitative approaches due to its capability of exploiting interdependencies of variables, disclosing hierarchical relationships between the criteria and prioritizing them based on the nature of these relationships (Si et al., 2018). The Sri Lankan manufacturing sector was selected as the research context because it represents a typical manufacturing sector of emerging economies. Therefore, the findings of the research can be used to develop guidelines for adopting digital servitization in other similar types of emerging economies. The Sri Lankan manufacturing sector is currently in the digital transformation process to improve business performance and user experiences (EDB, 2017). Based on the analysis conducted by McKinsey, the Sri Lankan manufacturing sector has a higher digital maturity score, and it is slightly higher than the global median (De Bustis et al., 2018). Many large Sri Lankan manufacturing companies are driven by digitalization, yet there are many barriers to overcome in digitalization (Bigdeli et al., 2021). Therefore, this study adopted the grey-DEMATEL method to examine the barriers to implementing digital servitization practices in the Sri Lankan manufacturing sector and explore relationships among barriers. To address the broader research problem outlined above, this research aims to answer the following research questions: RQ1. What are the barriers to the adoption of digital servitization practices in the manufacturing sector in the Sri Lankan manufacturing sector? RQ2. What are the causalities and dependencies between these barriers? Barriers to digital servitization were identified and selected based on a comprehensive literature review and inputs from manufacturing industry experts. The causal relationships between barriers were established using the grey-DEMATEL approach. Required data for the second stage of using the grey-DEMATEL approach were taken from seven Sri Lankan manufacturing industry experts from three different manufacturing sub-sectors. Furthermore, the analysis based on the grey-DEMATEL approach offers insights into priorities and relationships among those barriers as a basis for developing guidelines by manufacturing practitioners for the successful adoption of digital servitization practices.
