Research methodology 3.1 Case selection This paper uses an in-depth, longitudinal single-case study ( Crotty, 1998; Voss et al., 2002) to advance the current knowledge about the role of KIBSfirms in supporting the DS of SMEs, as case-based inductive research is appropriate when dealing with a new topic (Welch et al.,2 0 1 1). In line with the principles of theory-building empirical research (Meredith, 1993; Meredith, 1998; Melnyk and Handfield, 1998), we used a case study to collect empirical material and explore the phenomena under investigation (Tronvoll et al., 2020). We adopted a longitudinal perspective that brings additional insights and counterbalances the limitations due to lack of replication (Eisenhardt, 1989; Pettigrew, 1990; Yin, 2006). The eligible case had to comply with the following criteria (Seawright and Gerring, 2008): being a small- or medium-sized manufacturer involved in the DS move; collaborating with a KIBS firm in a long-term goal-oriented project, which allows for longitudinal exploration and retrospective reconstruction; willing to disclose in-depth information from primary and secondary sources; and providing access to acknowledgeable informants (Pettigrew, 1990). In line with similar studies (Grandinetti et al.,2 0 2 0; Paiola and Gebauer, 2020), the combination of these criteria drastically narrowed the number of eligible firms. A small manufacturing company (hereafter ALPHA; being the names of the firms anonymized for confidentiality reasons) complying with the mentioned criteria was identified. Thisfirm was collaborating with a technology partner (hereafter BETA) that had been entitled to introduce an industrial internet platform through which ALPHA intended to connect the equipment of its customer base. This digital platform would in addition enable the delivery of advanced digital services such as condition monitoring and predictive maintenance. 3.2 Framing the case and the methods for data collection and analysis According to Leonard-Barton (1990, p. 249),“a case study is a history of a past or current phenomenon, drawn from multiple sources of evidence. It can include data from direct observation and systematic interviewing as well as from public and private archives”. Therefore, we collected data from different sources. Firstly, we used primary data and gathered information from meetings and interviews with managers of ALPHA and BETA. In line with our objectives, the unit of analysis of this paper is represented by the interplay between ALPHA and BETA (Waluszewski, 2011), and the focus is on the contributions made by KIBS (seeTable 3) to push forward this complex transformation (Visnjic et al.,2 0 1 7). At the beginning of the research, the authors established a relationship with the ALPHA director, who was informed about the research aims. We were introduced to some co-workers, such as the managers of the sales, of the service and of the engineering departments. In the case of BETA, which is also a smallfirm, we interacted with the director/owner and with the software engineer in charge of the ALPHA project. Then, we identified other sources of information such as company presentations, financial reports, sales and maintenance contracts. Finally, in line withWouters (2009), we obtained other information by the discussion with an MSc Management Engineering student. The following section presents thefindings of the case study. 3.3 Case description ALPHA is a small Italian manufacturing company with approximately e6m of revenue and 30 full-time employees. It produces generators for technical gas (e.g. hydrogen, nitrogen and zero/dry air). Founded 30 years ago, ALPHA has already achieved a steady scale: the yearly growth, on average, has been less than 3% during the years of this research. ALPHA’s products are mostly sold to industrial customers operating in food and beverage industry and for packaging applications. Irrespective of its small size, the company has a good international reputation and counts over 20,000 installations in 30 different countries. Besides a few smaller German and Italian companies, its rivals are large companies such as Hitachi (335,000 employees), Parker (57,000) or Atlas Copco (34,000). Competition comes also by producers of technical gases sold in cylinders such as the giant Air Liquide (66,000 employees worldwide). To defend its market position, ALPHA has put in place the typical pre- and post-sales offering and provides services such as commissioning, maintenance contracts, warranty extensions and quality certifications. In the early 2018, ALPHA started this ambitious project to connect its installed base with a digital platform and start delivering digitally enabled advanced services. For this aim, ALPHA entered into a partnership with BETA, a small software company but rapidly growing, that has deployed this proprietary platform for DS. This platform can be used by original equipment manufacturers as well by third-party service networks to connect industrial equipment and control remotely their status, check faults, order consumables and spare parts and activate workflows forfield services. Adopting the platform requires no particular investments, as this is sold in the form of Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) (i.e.pay-as-you-go). In addition, the platform comes with standard/built-in modules (e.g. navigation panels, menus, dashboards, reports and workflows). 4. Findings Empirical evidence showed that the DS journey was structured in four stages according to a multi-year roadmap (seeFigure 1). This roadmap has been jointly developed by ALPHA and BETA during their initial interactions. More precisely, the sequence of activities to be carried out was proposed by BETA on the base of its previous experiences. ALPHA adapted this sequence tofit with the context. The structure of this roadmap greatly influenced the interplay between ALPHA and BETA, as explained in the following sub-sections. 4.1 Stage 1: strategic road-mapping As supported by our empirical material, the strategic intentions and commitment of the managing director of ALPHA were key to setting up the stage for the DS project. His decision was boosted by the tax savings granted by the Italian Government to companies investing in connected equipment and Industry 4.0 technologies. The DS manager and the company director analysed the benefit of having real-time data from connected machines. These benefits were explicated in terms of potential reduction of the costs of contractual maintenance. At the light of the consistent savings, the director developed a proposal for selling packages of digitally enabled maintenance services to the buyers of new units, if these would have accepted to connect the new equipment to ALPHA4YOU. Similarly, some customers were offered extended warranty coverages. As said, the pay back of these digital services was evaluated by the DS manager who used his knowledge about the ALPHA4YOU functions to conceive the data that the platform could have provided in short, as far as the base of connected machines grows. This information was used to formulate hypotheses about the performance of the digitized service process, in terms of both efficiency (e.g. reduced intervention time, higher productivity) and effectiveness (e.g. increasedfirst-time-fix). It was possible to estimate also the reduction of the delivery costs from the use of ALPHA4YOU. At the end, this leads to setting the prices of this new digital service offer. In addition to supporting the deployment of the platform (for which it was crucial the training released to the DS manager at previous stages), BETA contributed with indications about the actions to put in place to promote such digital offering towards the existing base of customers, as well as to avoid pitfalls with the dealers’network. 4.4 Stage 4: develop and activate new digital productservice offerings The objective of this last– still ongoing– stage is to develop further the offering of advanced digital services. As mentioned, the BM at this stage includes the digital sales of consumables and spare parts, and the provision of digital services such as process optimization, productivity management and gas certification. The corresponding e-commerce feature has been recently implemented through the activation of a specific ALPHA4YOU module. This pushed ahead the total sales of ALPHA, which in the lastfiscal year reached their highest value (1e6m). Conversely, other advanced services are still under development, and their development is still an early exercise. This latter activity has been in fact delayed due to the impact of COVID-19. The company manager said that they want to accurately assess thefinancial implications of such advanced offering, before moving further. Analogously, attempts to sell the equipment as a-service have not yet been made. This is indeed the declared target of the DS roadmap originally elaborated. In this last stage, however, the contributions from BETA become more and more rarefied. ALPHA prefers, in fact, to be autonomous in its decision to hold on or move further. 5. Discussion This case study sheds light on the processual nature of DS in SMEs and shows the contribution made by KIBS to this journey. Empirical evidence confirms that partnering with a firm that provides both professional and technology-based services can facilitate the DS of a smaller manufacturer. This is in line with the extant literature ( Miles et al., 1995; D’Antone and Santos, 2016). Tables 5and 6 generalize our casefindings and connect them to the theoretical framework of Section 2. Concluding remarks 6.1 Conclusions Despite their role in world economy, SMEs are frequently excluded from mainstream research ( Brunswicker and Vanhaverbeke, 2015). In particular, the challenges faced by smaller manufacturers in the transition to digital services have been frequently overlooked ( Uden and Naaranoja, 2009 ; Paiola et al.,2 0 1 3). Against this background, this paper investigates the problems that SMEs must address in their move to digital services and acknowledges the contributions made by KIBS firms to this transformation (Muller and Doloreux, 2009; Shearmur and Doloreux, 2013; Zhou et al., 2017). We integrate two literature streams and collect empirical material from a longitudinal, in-depth single case study to shed lights on the interplay between a KIBSfirm and a small manufacturer that are partners in a DS initiative. We unveil the mechanisms through which novel knowledge and capabilities are generated to address the problems of DS in SMEs. This paper has both theoretical and managerial implications that the next section illustrates. 6.2 Theoretical and managerial contributions Our findings confirm the relevance of KIBSfirms in customers’ innovation claimed by previous studies in the industrial marketing relational perspective (Aarikka-Stenroos and Jaakkola, 2012) and enhance the extant literature maintaining that KIBS firms contribute significantly to the DS journey of SMEs. On one side, customization allows exploring the ill-structured challenges of DS that are context- and industry-specific( Coreynen et al., 2017). On the other, the provision of standard services and prearranged solutions reduces the operational complexity connected to the impact of digitalization and servitization. As a result, the contribution of KIBS appears rather negligible due to the reluctance of the SMEs to share sensitive data Setting up a clear roadmap can facilitate the balance between servitization (e.g. Stages 1 and 4 in our case) and digitalization (e.g. Stages 2 and 3 in our case) Culture and organization A long-term roadmap facilitates cultural and organizational changes. KIBSfirms contribute to this process by providing digital competences and collaborating to put in place the organizational interventions Limited resources and knowledge gaps A KIBS partner that integrates professional and technological services is of great help in overcoming the limitation of resources of SMEs and fulfilling the numerous knowledge gaps of the DS challenges Access to customer’s data In the preliminary stages, KIBS contribute to exploring customer needs and market opportunities for DS. The use of a readyto-go/easy-to-use digital platform can increase the reputation of smaller manufacturers as provider of digital services. With a branded platform, customers can be more easily convinced to connect their equipment and share their data Operational complexity The provision of a digital platform that incorporates standard packages and pre-arranged workflows can reduce the operational complexity stemming from the move to digital services Business ecosystems KIBS can contribute to orchestrating third parties, setting the ground for the creation of new digital service ecosystems Digital servitization journey Mario Rapaccini, Marco Paiola, Lino Cinquini and Riccardo Giannetti Journal of Business & Industrial Marketing Volume 38 · Number 6 · 2023 · 1362– 1375 1370 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/jbim/article-pdf/38/6/1362/1372119/jbim-01-2022-0008.pdf by guest on 23 September 2026 We also noticed that customized services from the KIBS partner are mostly requested in the early stage of this transformation, while standard services and pre-arranged solutions are more requested in the following stages. For instance, having a ready-to-go digital platform to connect the equipment with IoT technologies can reduce to a great extent the time to market of the basic offering of digital services when advancing through the DS roadmap. It also turned out that smaller firms prefer pay-as-you-go approaches (e.g. SaaS) in respect to the adoption of the mentioned technologies, as this requires lower investments. This seems particularly significant for radical innovations that– such as DS– have higher risks of failure ( Consoli and Elche-Hortelano, 2010). Anotherfinding from this research concerns the fact that KIBSfirms, at a certain stage of this transformation, can be asked to directly orchestrate some customer’s partners that have to perform some crucial but not strategic tasks. Therefore, we claim that KIBS can also contribute to the creation and orchestration of digital business ecosystems. Lastly, our study confirmed that KIBS firms simultaneously operate as carrier (e.g. previous experiences about DS roadmap) and source (i.e. the digital platform already in place) of knowledge (den Hertog, 2000). Although less frequent, KIBS can give also access to stocks that are existing and required for DS (e.g. speci fications and protocols to connect the equipment) (He and Wong, 2009). Lastly, the study confirms that KIBS can be notably attracted by the opportunity of learning from the case company. The reciprocity among the collaborating counterparts can be thus key for the success of DS. 6.3 Limitations and further research This paper has some limitations. Ourfindings come from a single-case study. This affects to a large extent their analytical generalizability. Expanding the given theoretical insights in any contexts and situations is somehow questionable. Therefore, a first avenue for future research is to apply our research framework in wider case settings to compare and validate these findings. Samples could include also largefirms, and in this case, it could be to address how much the company size moderates the contributions by KIBS firms with respect to the problems and stages of DS. Another avenue is to integrate the empirical investigation with quantitative data to appreciate the statistical relevance of the phenomena under study. Using case-based or survey-based research, further studies could investigate the SME contexts in which the journey to digital services progressed with apparently little or no contributions from external partner. Because of the longer time span required to show the financial implications of DS, our case does not provide evidence on these aspects. Thus, we cannot infer anything about whether SMEs can reduce the risk of incurring negative results from DS, and how much of this mitigation is due to partnering with KIBS. This is a topic for further developing the research. The last consideration concerns regulatory and environmental factors. We confirm the importance of public funding in creating favourable contexts for innovation (i.e. digital hub, fiscal incentives for investing in digital technologies). Received 1 October 2024 Revised 29 April 2025 10 August 2025 2 October 2025 Accepted 6 October 2025 Abstract Purpose – This study aims to examine how digital servitization can help manufacturing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) advance circularity in service ecosystems. Design/methodology/approach – This qualitative study interviewed managers from 18 manufacturing SMEs in Norway to explore digital servitization and circularity in their service ecosystem. The interview data were analyzed using a Gioia-inspired approach consisting of inductive first-order codes followed by an abductive coding process based on current literature. Findings – The empirical findings of this study indicate that manufacturing SMEs can advance service ecosystem circularity through digital servitization. A framework was developed illustrating three different pathways, navigating four identified enabling conditions for advancing circularity: service ecosystem adjustment; optimized resource utilization; collaborative resource focus; and smarter process management. Research limitations/implications – The study examined Norwegian manufacturing SMEs, with other competing grounds that might not be comparable to countries outside Europe, such as different data security requirements, digitalization levels and economics. The study also emphasizes managerial focus, neglecting a broader focus on customers and intermediaries. Originality/value – The paper offers insights into how manufacturing SMEs can advance service ecosystem circularity, responding to service ecosystem circularity requirements and emphasizing internal production processes. The study also emphasizes the importance of collaborating with service ecosystem actors on recycling, substituting and rethinking resources to close the loop eventually. This requires strategic planning and following circularity pathways suited for the SMEs’ resources, production, competencies and needs. Introduction The increasing governmental focus on circularity (e.g. European Commission, 2020; UN, 2023a) reflects a commitment to retain the economic value of materials and resources for as long as possible to minimize resource consumption and waste generation (Kjaer et al., 2018). Achieving this transition requires not only technological innovation but also new business models and socio-institutional changes related to norms, beliefs and standards (Potting et al., 2017). This circularity transition can be enabled by digital servitization (Sinha, 2022), defined as “the transition toward smart product-service-software systems that enable value creation and capture through monitoring, control, optimization, and autonomous functions” (Kohtamäki et al., 2019, p. 390). By facilitating circularity by promoting new forms of value co-creation with ecosystem actors (e.g. Paiola et al., 2021; Paschou et al., 2020), digital servitization has become an essential tool for increasing circularity (Hidalgo-Carvajal et al., 2021) by supporting reductions in environmental impact, increasing efficiency and extending product and service life cycles through digital solutions (Mishra et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2021). In manufacturing, digital servitization enables resource efficiency and circularity through remote monitoring, control, optimization and autonomous processes (e.g. Kohtamäki et al., 2021; Porter and Heppelmann, 2015). However, it is essential to incorporate small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the circularity transition, as they account for approximately 50% of national GDP (Nadeem et al., 2023). SMEs face structural barriers to circularity, including a limited number of employees and resources (Arroyabe et al., 2024; Dörr et al., 2023) and less influence over other service ecosystem actors (e.g. Le-Dain et al., 2023). As such, they must adopt a strategic approach to digital servitization, which adopts a holistic perspective, rethinks service provision and encompasses platforms for recycling and resource reduction in collaboration with service ecosystem actors (Fehrer et al., 2024; Konietzko et al., 2020). SMEs struggle to navigate digital servitization and circularity because of numerous challenges, which often require more inter-organizational collaboration (Schöggl et al., 2024; Khan et al., 2024a, 2024b) and even an ecosystem approach (e.g. Helmefalk et al., 2023). However, further research is needed to understand how manufacturing SMEs can leverage digital servitization to advance circularity. Given that both digital servitization and circular 79 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/jbim/article-pdf/41/1/79/10831474/jbim-10-2024-0736en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 production are costly, and that governments are increasingly mandating circular practices in manufacturing, greater insights are required into how manufacturing SMEs can navigate this transition. In particular, research should identify which digital servitization mechanisms, such as specific technologies or organizational practices, should be implemented ( Paschou et al., 2020 ). While recent studies have explored the relationship between servitization and circularity, additional research remains necessary ( Johl et al., 2024 ; e.g. Kühl et al., 2023 ), particularly in light of growing governmental emphasis on manufacturing circularity (e.g. UN, 2023a ). This study aims to explore how digital servitization can help manufacturing SMEs to advance circularity. This is challenging because of the increasing demand for efficiency and the fact that SMEs tend to have fewer resources and less power to decide which materials and services they must provide. For example, recycling typically involves cooperation with other actors to gather discarded products and rethink the use of resources. A further issue is that customers must be willing to accept this shift in resource use or product quality; if not, they may migrate to a competitor. This study provides a framework for navigating the digital servitization process for manufacturing SMEs to advance circularity. The paper is structured as follows. The next section outlines the conceptual background underpinning digital servitization and circular manufacturing. Following a description of the qualitative methodology in Section 3, the findings are presented in Section 4. Section 5 proposes a framework for advancing circularity in manufacturing SMEs. Finally, Section 6 addresses the theoretical and managerial implications of the present study, along with its limitations and opportunities for future research. 2. Conceptual background 2.1 Circular manufacturing Traditional linear business models typically emphasize the taking, making, using and wasting of products and materials ( Khan et al., 2021 ). This way of thinking is now considered unsustainable, and Earth Overshoot Day (when the planet’s annual resources are used up) comes earlier every year ( UN, 2023b ). The need to handle products and waste more sustainably has increased the public’s focus on circularity, in which discarded materials and products are recycled and reused. This means that no additional natural resources or materials are needed for production, and discarded products no longer become waste (e.g. Potting et al., 2017 ; Velenturf and Purnell, 2021 ). Many manufacturers follow the circular economy – a broad concept with different meanings – as an approach to promoting responsibility and the cyclical use of resources ( Homrich et al., 2018 ; Moraga et al., 2019 ). In a well-known definition, the Ellen MacArthur Foundation characterized the circular economy as an industrial system that is restorative or regenerative by intention and design. It replaces the ‘end-of- life’ concept with restoration, shifts toward the use of renewable energy, eliminates the use of toxic chemicals, which impair reuse, and aims for the elimination of waste through the superior design of materials, products, systems and, within this, business models ( MacArthur Foundation, 2013 , p. 7) In manufacturing contexts, circularity typically focuses on eliminating toxic chemicals, using renewable resources, rethinking materials and optimizing processes and resource utilization to minimize waste generation (e.g. Mesjasz-Lech et al., 2024 ). In this regard, Ogunmakinde et al. (2021) stressed the importance of extending product life cycles. One key aspect of circularity is closing the loop – ensuring that materials are reused and recycled rather than left hanging in the cycle ( Ogunmakinde et al., 2021 ). In practice, it is difficult to fully close the loop ( Potting et al., 2017 ). According to Corvellec et al. (2022) , the circular economy literature can be criticized for ignoring established knowledge (e.g. thermodynamics, which asserts that we cannot create or destroy matter). They contend that used resources necessarily end up in environmental systems; even when recycling materials, new resources are still needed. This view implies that a closed loop (without waste) is almost impossible, although others have argued for different levels of closing the loop (e.g. De Pascale et al., 2021 ). Resource efficiency is essential in manufacturing because circularity depends on reducing production inputs ( Ogunmakinde et al., 2021 ). The R-frameworks are widely referenced as core circularity principles and strategies ( Kirchherr et al., 2017 ), from the 3R (reduce, reuse and recycle) ( Ogunmakinde et al., 2021 ) to the 10R framework (refuse, rethink, reduce, reuse, repair, refurbish, remanufacture, repurpose, recycle and recover) (e.g. Potting et al., 2017 ). While the latter approach is more nuanced, it also renders research more complex. Following a 4R framework, Alizadeh et al. (2023) suggest using the four most common terms – recycle, reuse, reduce and recover – although they note that the composition of the 4R framework varies across the literature. Recycling is found to be the most used term among the R framework ( Alizadeh et al., 2023 ; Kirchherr et al., 2017 ). In the context of digital servitization in manufacturing SMEs, a 4R framework focusing on refuse, rethink, reduce and recycle may offer fewer nuances than a 10R framework but provide more suitable strategies for the SME context. Refuse, rethink and reduce are essential for smarter product use and manufacture and often require innovation in core technology and product design ( Potting et al., 2017 ) – developments that typically occur during digital servitization and provision of new services and solutions. Some R-strategies can be considered as subcategories of others depending on the context. For example, in digital servitization, repair, refurbishment, remanufacture and repurpose can be subsumed under rethink or reduce because of optimization of service and digital solutions, predictive maintenance during production and smarter usage of digital solutions. Given the size and limited resources of manufacturing SMEs ( Arroyabe et al., 2024 ), such strategies can be too costly and require technical processes and market structures manufacturing SMEs lack. Nevertheless, refusing, rethinking and reducing are key strategies for increased circularity through smarter product manufacture and use ( Potting et al., 2017 ). However, recycling discarded materials to keep them in the loop for reuse is crucial for circularity ( Ranta et al., 2018 ). In manufacturing contexts, the 4R approach seems necessary: refuse to “make product redundant by abandoning its function or by offering the same function with a radically different product,” rethink to “make product Advancing circularity Bjørn Ronny Vien Journal of Business & Industrial Marketing Volume 41 · Number 1 · 2026 · 79–98 80 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/jbim/article-pdf/41/1/79/10831474/jbim-10-2024-0736en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 use more intensive (e.g. through sharing products, or by putting multi-functional products on the market),” reduce to “increase efficiency in product manufacture or use by consuming fewer natural resources and materials,” and recycle to “process materials to obtain the same (high grade) or lower (low grade) quality” ( Potting et al., 2017 , p. 15). As resource scarcity is a global problem, recycling helps protect the environment by reducing landfill waste ( Khan et al., 2024 a, 2024b ). Kjaer et al. (2018) categorized servitization-based enablers of resource reduction as follows: operational efficiency (e.g. operational support, performance monitoring, maintenance), product longevity (e.g. maintenance, reuse, recycling), intensified product usage (e.g. product sharing) and product system substitution (e.g. product sharing, reuse, recycling, optimization of results). Operational efficiency can be enhanced through user training, maintenance support and upgrades, while ensuring product longevity extends the use stage and minimizes consumption through longer use of resources ( Kjaer et al., 2018 ). In digital servitization for circularity, cloud-based platforms for tailored real-time monitoring and control are essential ( Kim et al., 2022 ). To recycle smarter and close the loop, manufacturing firms must rely on the Internet of Things for product take-back, using relevant data to decide when products should be recycled ( Alcayaga and Hansen, 2024 ). Digital servitization can also contribute to high-level circularity strategies by facilitating solutions that use fewer resources while providing the same functions based on sharing, renting, leasing and pay-per-use business models (e.g. Ciasullo et al., 2021 ). Digitalization can expedite solutions for manufacturing circularity and reduce waste ( Mesjasz-Lech et al., 2024 ). 2.2 Digital servitization in small and medium-sized enterprises Digital servitization is commonly implemented in manufacturing to seize new opportunities for changing business models and creating value (e.g. Kohtamäki et al., 2019 ; Sklyar et al., 2019), for example, through sharing, renting, leasing, or adopting pay-per-use – in turn affecting resource utilization (e.g. Ciasullo et al., 2021 ). Manufacturing processes must incorporate digitalization because it is key to achieving sustainability ( Bressanelli et al., 2024 ) and circularity ( Kim et al., 2023 ). Digital servitization emphasizes value co-creation through remote monitoring, control, optimization and autonomous functions ( Kohtamäki et al., 2019 ). In this context, Sjödin et al. (2023) explained the importance of artificial intelligence (AI) in enabling circularity. AI’s perceptive capacities benefit manufacturers when customers use solutions and sense the environment through data gathering to co-create value in new ways. AI’s predictive capacities facilitate forecasting of environmental changes and future events (e.g. maintenance issues, resource usage), again based on the collected data. Finally, AI’s prescriptive capacities can help manufacturing SMEs to identify solutions that maximize sustainable value co-creation and optimize usage, based on relevant data and analytics. While servitization enables the transition to circularity and sustainable value creation ( Upadhayay et al., 2024 ), Arroyabe et al. (2024) found high digitalization levels to be essential for circularity in SMEs. Digital servitization and the focus on circularity are imperative for manufacturing SMEs for several reasons. For example, because SMEs account for around 50% of the national GDP globally ( Nadeem et al., 2023 ) and most of the world’s economic development, they must be involved in achieving the European Union’s (EU’s) carbon neutrality target by 2050 ( Dey et al., 2022 ). Circular economy practices are found to have positive effects on the economic, environmental and social performance of SMEs ( Dey et al., 2022 ). However, undergoing digital servitization and aiming to increase circularity in manufacturing are challenging, even more so for SMEs, requiring their long-term commitment ( Rapaccini et al., 2023 ). SMEs are more affected by technical barriers, lack of digital skills and change management than larger firms but less affected by the volatile technology environment, corporate culture and communication because of their agility ( de Jesus Pacheco et al., 2019 ). Internal organization, culture and data security are vital areas that are problematic for manufacturing SMEs ( Peillon and Dubruc, 2019 ). SMEs also find it difficult to implement digital technologies ( Dörr et al., 2023 ) and allocate resources for service development ( Tauqeer and Bang, 2018 ). As SMEs have fewer employees, it is daunting to focus on digitalization and environmental activities and requirements ( Arroyabe et al., 2024 ). SMEs are more affected by digital servitization barriers such as data security issues, lack of digital competencies and culture; however, other barriers, including ecosystem networks, insufficient human capabilities and operational factors, change as digital servitization evolves ( Le-Dain et al., 2023 ). High initial costs and the demand for resources pose significant barriers to SMEs’ implementation of circular economy practices, often because of limited resources (e.g. money, competencies) ( Arroyabe et al., 2024 ). 2.3 Circularity in manufacturing small and medium- sized enterprises as part of a system Digital servitization requires interorganizational and service ecosystem collaboration (e.g. Kohtamäki et al., 2019 ; Sjödin et al., 2021 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). Interorganizational collaboration, which is needed to adapt to uncertain market conditions ( Schöggl et al., 2024 ), and ecosystem collaboration are essential for implementing circular economy practices (e.g. Khan et al., 2024 a, 2024b ). A service ecosystem is “a relatively self-contained, self-adjusting system of resource-integrating actors connected by shared institutional arrangements and mutual value creation through service exchange” ( Vargo and Lusch, 2016 , pp. 10 – 11). Circularity practices must be implemented at the organizational (micro) level but should also be emphasized at the meso level to gain economic and environmental benefits between firms, as well as at the macro level, to extend boundaries and demonstrate how to rethink and use resources efficiently ( Kamble and Gunasekaran, 2023 ). Likewise, to increase service ecosystem circularity, recycling infrastructure through interorganizational collaboration is vital, but micro, meso and macro levels must be included as well ( Vellesalu et al., 2023 ). Focusing on service ecosystems is important because many actors will be affected during the transition to circularity. Furthermore, many manufacturers face pressure to adopt circularity for recovering used products and commercializing Advancing circularity Bjørn Ronny Vien Journal of Business & Industrial Marketing Volume 41 · Number 1 · 2026 · 79–98 81 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/jbim/article-pdf/41/1/79/10831474/jbim-10-2024-0736en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 circular ones for novel uses in existing markets or by creating new markets ( Kreye, 2023 ). Digital servitization can enhance service and life cycle management by providing maintenance and upgrading monitoring ( Mishra et al., 2023 ) and platforms for recycling ( Kurniawan et al., 2022 ); facilitating remote monitoring, control, optimization and automation of processes ( Porter and Heppelmann, 2014 ); improving resource utilization; and reducing waste and scrap generation ( Schiavone et al., 2022 ). As a collaborative process among ecosystem actors ( Chen et al., 2024 ), digital servitization can help manufacturing SMEs to reduce resource usage through optimized and efficient processes. Platform-based digitalization also expedites recycling among actors, leading to higher-quality products ( Kurniawan et al., 2022 ). Circularity in service ecosystems requires high-quality delivery by integrating industrial systems, technologies such as real-time monitoring, the Internet of Things, processes and effective performance metrics ( Khan et al., 2024 a, 2024b ). Digitalization is essential in the transition to circularity ( Kamble and Gunasekaran, 2023 ; Romero et al., 2021 ). Increasing ecosystem circularity requires collaboration and firms’ understanding of systemic value co-creation among multiple actors ( Konietzko et al., 2020 ), mutual value creation and collective efforts in shaping such ecosystems, which is an iterative process across micro, meso and macro levels ( Fehrer et al., 2024 ). Digital servitizing and increasing circularity can thus be challenging and complicated by socio-institutional changes that need actors’ contributions, but enabling technologies can help facilitate the process ( Potting et al., 2017 ). Using service platforms ( Fehrer et al., 2024 ; Kurniawan et al., 2022 ), phone applications and the Internet of Things, digital servitization can support the necessary mental shift from ownership to sharing, renting adopting pay-per-use and embracing new service delivery options such as augmented reality for programming or reading books. In a similar vein, Sjödin et al. (2021) discussed how traditional value chain inertia made digitalization challenging because of resource or knowledge deficits, change-related delays or actors’ resistance to change. To increase circularity in service ecosystems, firms must create digital platforms for knowledge-sharing and collaboration among actors to build solutions that benefit the ecosystems ( Fehrer et al., 2024 ). Furthermore, for service ecosystem circularity, firms must concentrate on recycling, channeling information between actors and managing different types of resources ( Helmefalk et al., 2023 ). In addition to handling such tasks, actors should learn to use new services, as well as how customers and firms can co-create value. 3. Research method 3.1 Research approach and informant selection In this study, we explored how digital servitization can advance circularity in manufacturing SMEs and how different approaches can do likewise in service ecosystems by shifting perspectives on value co-creation (e.g. Paiola et al., 2021 ; Paschou et al., 2020 ). However, as the transition may be impeded by barriers related to socio-institutional change or an undue focus on efficiency, we identified the need for a deeper investigation into these issues. The selected firms were part of the same service ecosystem, sharing value propositions as both customers and providers. Inspired by the Gioia methodology ( Gioia et al., 2012 ), the research process was abductive but incorporated inductive coding for qualitative rigor. Our Gioia-inspired approach followed these main steps: First, we built on the theoretical understanding of digital servitization and circularity in service ecosystems to develop the semi-structured interview guide (elaborated in Section 3.2). Second, we created empirical, inductive first-order codes and applied an abductive approach when coding for the aggregated dimensions, building on the theoretical knowledge (elaborated in Section 3.3). Finally, we went back and forth between the empirical data and the theoretical literature during the coding process and conceptualized our framework. Our interviews with managers from 18 manufacturing SMEs in Norway ensured better external validity and helped to minimize observer bias, although this approach provided less depth in each firm’s context ( Voss et al., 2002 ). The firms operate in the steel, glass, wood, furniture, energy, food, construction, automotive, aftermarket and publishing markets. All are B2B providers, and nine also deal with B2C markets (see Appendix 1 ). 3.2 Data collection The data were collected from 18 interviews conducted with 21 managers (three interviews included two managers) in 2022, ranging in duration from 54 to 85 min (see Appendix 1 ). An industry cluster partner with relevant knowledge from manufacturing SMEs and their digitalization collaborated with the research team to recruit informants based on the selection criteria. The first criterion was that the firms should be manufacturing SMEs that engaged in digital servitization and mainly performed processes, which could also be ongoing, because these are often continuous. Following the definition of digital servitization, the firms must have been engaged in a process where significant changes in their business models, products, systems, or processes have altered how they create and capture value (e.g. recycling routines through remote monitoring, optimizing the production process and providing digital solutions and applications). Second, the firms should be focused on sustainability or circularity (e.g. clean production, recycling, optimizing resource usage or waste generation). Third, the firms should belong to the same service ecosystem, with different industries involved in value co-creation (e.g. collaboration in recycling, digital application, using another firm’s waste as a resource and providing solutions to make another firm more resource-efficient). A semi-structured interview guide (see Appendix 2 ) was designed to explore the digital servitization process and how manufacturing SMEs were working toward sustainability and circularity within the service ecosystem. Open-ended questions were used to address the research themes, including digital servitization, sustainability, circularity, strategy and service ecosystem. While the study was abductive, an inductive element allowed the informants to steer the interviews in exciting directions ( Yin, 2018 ). As digital servitization is often an uncommon term for firms, the interview questions were asked/discussed as digitalization in the context of digital servitization, such as the following: Can you describe how digitalization contributes to a sustainable solution or process in the business? To what extent do you collaborate with other players when it comes to digitalization and sustainability? Secondary data, including accounting figures, other relevant documents and company websites, were used to prepare for the interviews. The interviews were recorded and transcribed for analysis by NVivo software. Data was also collected in meetings and in two workshops exploring digital servitization and circularity. Representatives from four service platform providers participated, facilitating the discussion and validation of the findings. During the workshops, the firm representatives were divided into three groups, each including a researcher and a service platform provider. 3.3 Data analysis The analysis was based on interpretations of the interview transcripts, field notes from the workshops and other documents. In the Gioia-inspired methodology, the first-order analysis focused on informant terms and empirical codes, where multiple codes often become overwhelming and researchers can feel lost ( Gioia et al., 2012 ). The analysis and coding process was abductive, going back and forth between empirical data gathering and coding connected to the understanding of the relevant literature (e.g. refuse, rethink, reduce, recycle, micro, meso, macro). Each interview transcript was read and analyzed several times, highlighting phrases that helped elucidate the role of digital servitization in manufacturing SMEs’ transition to circularity. In this phase, 367 first-order codes were extracted; after merging similarities and finding and reducing differences, 53 first-order codes (labeled using informant terms) emerged from the data ( Gioia et al., 2012 ). Building on existing theory, the abductive coding process also led us to categorize the first-order codes at internal and external levels. Following Gioia et al. (2012) , Appendix 3 summarizes examples of the key features of the approach and includes quotations that illustrate the second-order themes as core elements of the aggregated dimensions and the proposed framework. The first-order concepts were then analyzed and categorized as 13 second-order themes to capture the phenomena referred to in the first-order concepts. Building on the empirical first-order concepts and the second-order themes, four aggregated dimensions were generated at a higher level of abstraction. Figure 1 shows the coding structure and illustrates how the concepts were created from the empirical data; the aggregated dimensions are structured and elaborated in the Findings section. The four aggregated dimensions are the main approaches to advanced circularity through digital servitization. Finally, to assess construct validity, internal validity, external validity and reliability, we followed the process described by Voss et al. (2002) . 4. Findings 4.1 External influences Among the external influences promoting circularity, two key enabling conditions dealing with the service ecosystem, comprising governments, regulations, institutions, industry standards and customers, were identified by the interviewed managers. As described below, service ecosystems also influenced collaboration for circularity. 4.1.1 Service ecosystem adjustment The first enabling condition and a key contributor to advancing circularity is service ecosystem adjustment, which can be facilitated by digital servitization to respond to external requirements. Service ecosystem adjustment appears to focus on how manufacturing SMEs can advance circularity through practices, routines and strategies. For example, the interviewed representatives of the manufacturing SMEs clearly stated that they must follow external requirements for resources, as specified by government directives, regulations, industry standards and rules. Manufacturing SMEs must follow prominent actors’ and customers’ specifications regarding products and service, which influence the use of resources and materials. A CEO from the steel industry provided this example: “Our customers require a solution for a product that should maintain a certain temperature in water. Accordingly, we must calculate which materials to use, depending on whether the air is dry, whether it is fresh or seawater, and what temperature is required.” Many rules govern production processes, including the use of chemicals and resources, in turn requiring firms to report environmental metrics and undergo annual audits. In pursuit of circularity, manufacturing SMEs felt the pressure to co-recycle with other service ecosystem actors. To that end, several interviewees commented that their firms had changed how they focus on circularity practices and implemented return schemes for resources and products in response to external requirements. Adjusting recycling to external requirements and existing take-back channels did not, in these cases, create the need for new shared infrastructures, pooling resources across firms, or new external channels. Some of the incorporated recycling practices used sensors for product tracking, with functions linked to the end user and intermediaries (e.g. stores). When adjusting internal recycling practices and strategies to intermediaries, a marketing manager in the vehicle industry explained, “Recycling is also related to transportation and how we think about packaging, aiming for the simplest possible packaging that transports as little air as possible. Our customers don’t want plastic boxes. We use recyclable bags and wooden crates.” According to several representatives of the participating firms, while recycled environmentally friendly resources can be used to provide sustainable products, customers sometimes want cheaper solutions, which makes co-recycling challenging. Some materials are scarcer when recycled, and some customers require recycled materials because of environmental measures and requirements from governments and projects. In any event, firms must recycle what they can and be encouraged to develop a more holistic view of recycled materials rather than prioritizing their own interests, as expressed by a factory manager in construction: “The sustainability perspective should extend beyond one’s construction site. If a customer wants all the recycled steel worldwide, neighboring buildings would have to be erected with unrecycled steel [. . .] which would not help the climate.” Clearly, collaboration is needed to rethink resource usage in the service ecosystem, emphasizing how firms work with circularity practices, routines and strategies. A further benefit for intermediaries is that their operation becomes more sustainable. For example, some manufacturing SMEs use augmented reality for services such as programming robots and machines or as substitutes for books, instruction manuals, or other information sources. According to a CEO in the construction elements industry, “The products we make help buildings to use less energy [. . .]. We deliver a product that helps others to reduce energy consumption.” Some firms deliver sustainable products that last longer because they choose greener resources that extend the product life cycle. For manufacturing SMEs that take on government projects, sustainability and carbon footprint data are vital. 4.2 Internal influences The interviewed managers experienced external influences (Section 4.1) from service ecosystems and service ecosystem actors that affected the focal SME, leading to internal influences on circularity during digital servitization. This led to two enabling conditions for advancing circularity, concentrating on implementing circular processes in the focal SME to maintain smooth factory operations and gather production data for specific purposes. This is a fundamental step for how focal SMEs can optimize resource utilization. Smarter process management focuses on how practices, routines and strategies advance circularity, emphasizing process routines to secure production stability and reduce waste and resource inefficiency by applying digital tools, measurement systems and strategic structures. On the other hand, optimized resource utilization focuses on what resources are used or reconfigured, emphasizing the implementation of digital technologies (e.g. 3D software, robots, lasers, scanners and sensors) to obtain key performance indicators (KPIs), measurements, track material use and reconfigure resources – thereby determining which resources are used to advance circularity and how the resources are optimized during production. The two areas influence and reinforce each other; however, the former is a prerequisite to the latter. 4.2.1 Smarter process management When manufacturing SMEs pursue digital servitization, a key approach to advancing circularity is smarter process management. Specifically, the strategies and practices for the use of appropriate digital tools enable manufacturing SMEs to secure production through predictive analyses, ensuring that each factory remains operational during its scheduled time. As a technical manager in the food industry noted, “It is important to generate and use more automated production data to streamline processes, capture stop causes and times, and measure efficiency.” By capturing production errors and measurements, manufacturing SMEs can gather insights and look for correlations that facilitate predictive maintenance, contributing to an understanding of how to implement circularity practices and strategies, rather than being surprised by machine errors during factory operations. The collected data (e.g. measures of downtime, scrap production or productivity) are included in practices, visualized on dashboards and screens, and can be combined with QR codes for easy access and system integration. Data gathering for control and measurement (e.g. water consumption, electricity, gas, raw materials, CO 2 emissions, stoppage causes and production rate) is essential for smarter process management and the use of KPIs. Resource management can be enhanced through practices and strategies for how to advance circularity using digital tools such as QR codes, barcodes, RFID and platforms for system integration. A CEO for an equipment supplier explained the importance of internal resource management and control: “Digitalization and the related systems help us to buy the right things, have the right things in stock and set the right prices in and out to customers, which is important for resource management because we have so many customers.” 4.2.2 Optimized resource utilization Another circular approach through digital servitization involves optimizing internal resource usage, focusing on what resources are used or reconfigured to advance circularity. First, by using digital tools such as laser cutters for smart waste reduction, manufacturing SMEs can achieve nearly 100% accuracy in waste reduction. Most faced external pressure to increase circularity but also emphasized the importance of prioritizing circularity internally because of growing service ecosystem requirements. However, the pathway from external service ecosystem pressure to internal circularity efforts typically followed distinct routes, as outlined below. It was not feasible to address all circularity requirements simultaneously, as doing so would necessitate changes in digital technologies, resources, collaborations, processes and practices at the same time. As such, SMEs are often required to choose specific pathways based on their context. 4.3.1 Compliance-driven optimization All managers reported experiencing external influence related to circularity requirements and compliance-driven optimization. These requirements influenced how SMEs approached resource selection and utilization, waste management, production methods, product delivery and sustainability reporting. A marketing manager in the steel industry remarked, “We have some suppliers who ask for details about sustainability, where we must show compliance with several directives on sustainability.” In some areas, SMEs had technological flexibility or were already invested in technologies or platforms, where they simply needed to comply with external requirements to advance their circularity. Compliance-driven optimization often resulted in incremental changes aimed at meeting minimum standards, rather than achieving transformative circular outcomes. A CEO in the wood industry noted, “When large governmental actors require us to provide documentation on the lowest carbon footprint emission, to win governmental construction contracts, we had to change and make a new environmental declaration generator to make this efficient.” Several managers mentioned that suppliers were required to submit monthly sustainability reports and document KPIs. Common compliance actions included reducing chemical use, initiating environmental reporting and minimizing scrap, often enabled by existing technologies or routines. As compliance-driven optimization was perceived as easier for managers to follow (e.g. they were already invested in suitable technologies or structures), other firms had to adopt alternative pathways for collaboration or process orientation. 4.3.2 Collaborative circularity Many managers expressed the need to navigate digital servitization and circularity through collaboration with external partners such as hospitals, schools, or other manufacturers. In particular, the collaborative circularity pathway involves interorganizational actors in integrating resources, recycling and providing new digital solutions. This was essential during radical change, particularly in SMEs that lacked the resources, digital technologies and competencies to implement these changes independently. A technical manager in the food industry emphasized the importance of collaboration for internal circularity, “We are completely dependent on good partners to deliver services such as this 3D tool. When building and moving things, we scan the entire factory in 3D for all installation projects. But we must hire the expertise for 3D modeling because we don’t have it ourselves.” Collaboration was also crucial for implementing digital tools such as recycling platforms, sustainability tracking systems and customer- specific solutions for resource use. Managers highlighted how collaboration with service ecosystem actors enabled the co- creation of circular solutions rather than simply meeting the bare minimum standards. 4.3.3 Operational circularity The managers noted that in some instances, the SME had successfully implemented necessary digital tools (e.g. recycling platforms, systems and external competencies) and fostered collaboration or had the flexibility to invest independently, enabling them to concentrate on internal circularity strategies. In such cases, SMEs could develop circular processes, practices and routines. Nonetheless, responding to service ecosystem requirements remained important. A CEO in the wood industry explained, “The public authorities require documentation that the timber has been sufficiently dried to be used and exported because of the risk of infection. Then you need systems for monitoring and data warehouses for documentation to prove that the wood has been warmer than 598 degrees for 30 min.” To meet such expectations, reporting sustainability, KPIs and goals requires the SMEs to gather data and invest in digital technologies to advance their circularity in production. In some areas, SMEs need to develop circularity strategies and focus on new processes and practices to advance circularity, which in turn impacts the internal precision of resource utilization and waste generation, measurements and KPIs. Digital servitization and the use of digital tools, such as process automation for machines, data collection and data utilization, were essential for implementing circular practices. Discussion: advancing circularity through digital servitization in manufacturing SMEs and their service ecosystems The proposed framework ( Figure 2 ) illustrates various pathways through which digital servitization contributes to advancing circularity in manufacturing SMEs. Based on the aggregated dimensions from the empirical analysis ( Figure 1 ), the framework builds on existing accounts of the circular economy, particularly the 4R strategy (rethink-refuse-reduce- recycle) (see, e.g. Kirchherr et al., 2017 ; Potting et al., 2017 ). Figure 2 identifies three pathways that manufacturing SMEs can choose to advance circularity: compliance-driven optimization, operational circularity and collaborative circularity. The pathways navigate between the locus of engagement and value-creation mechanisms versus resource reconfigurations. The locus of engagement is divided into internal engagement, referring to SMEs’ intraorganizational initiatives to manage and optimize their circularity activities, and external engagement, involving interorganizational dynamics. Value- creation mechanisms capture processes, practices, routines and digital strategies enabling circularity, highlighting how circularity is operationalized through digital servitization. The findings section highlighted the service ecosystem adjustment and smarter process management, focusing on how processes, practices and strategies impact the work of manufacturing SMEs in advancing circularity. Nevertheless, resource reconfigurations refer to what resources are used or reconfigured to enable circularity, as the findings section shows, focusing on collaborative resource focus and optimized resource utilization. The pathways navigate four conditions for advancing circularity through digital servitization: service ecosystem adjustment, collaborative resource focus, smarter process management and optimized resource utilization. Although several pathways are possible, the focus is on the three mentioned above. As service ecosystems self-adjust for resource integration ( Vargo and Lusch, 2016 ) and the interviewees highlighted ongoing external pressure, the framework uses pathways originating from service ecosystem adjustment. They all lead to optimized resource utilization because firms must concentrate on internal circularity and their responsibility. The framework shows an arrow pointing back to service ecosystem adjustment because firms commonly adapt to this ecosystem and make changes and other actors change, which can lead to service ecosystem adjustment, creating new rules, regulations and pressure from customers. Manufacturing SMEs could choose different pathways for various products and services. They can pursue collaborative circularity with recycling platforms and digital solutions or focus on operational circularity, data collection and waste management. 5.1 Compliance-driven optimization pathway This pathway directly responds to external requirements (e.g. regulations, directives, demands from customers, suppliers and external actors) with investments in machines, technologies or production systems without necessarily going through platform construction or process transformation first. Manufacturing SMEs following this path use digital servitization to optimize resources internally without first focusing on internal process transformation or collaboration with external actors. This is often the case for SMEs that have the capacity or agility to act fast, with capital, technological flexibility or infrastructure and digital technology in place; act reactively and incrementally; and focus on minimum requirements and legitimacy. While some manufacturing SMEs are slower in pursuing circularity, service ecosystem adjustment often forces them to commit to digital servitization to maintain competitiveness by advancing circularity, reducing their carbon footprint and using natural resources. Such adjustment focuses on external resource requirements, co-recycling and collaborative rethinking of resource usage. Thus, service ecosystem adjustment builds on rethink and refuse from the 4R framework, which further impacts the need for recycling and reducing resources through the pathways. External resource requirements from service ecosystem actors and institutions affect how SMEs address circularity. As external actors can specify regulations and rules for using materials and chemicals, as well as prescribe how products are manufactured and provided, digital servitization is necessarily a collaborative process ( Chen et al., 2024 ), involving orchestrated ecosystem relationships ( Sjödin et al., 2021 ). Along with the need to adapt to customer demands and expectations, this encourages further digital servitization and a shared focus on circularity and customers’ reduced energy use. To drive co-recycling, manufacturing SMEs often adjust to external requirements (e.g. from customers or regulations) and coordinate existing return arrangements with intermediaries without creating new shared infrastructures or resource sharing. When manufacturing SMEs have the necessary skills, infrastructure and systems, they can collect or reuse discarded and recycled products from service ecosystem actors. By enabling manufacturers and customers to share information, these platforms promote high-quality recycled products and reduce waste ( Kurniawan et al., 2022 ). Public projects often receive higher grades when using recycled materials. However, some industries struggle to supply everyone with recycled materials because of limited sources, making it difficult to close the loop and highlighting the importance of smarter process management and optimized resource utilization. As service ecosystem actors use these platforms more, digital servitization will likely incorporate sensors for remote monitoring and recycling. This shift may transition from an adjustment to the service ecosystem and relying on internal channels and processes to a collaborative circularity pathway (see Section 5.3). Fully engaged actors will enable manufacturing SMEs to focus on product lifecycle management. The last element of service ecosystem adjustment is collaborating to rethink resources, including how circularity informs actors’ perspectives on resources and value co- creation. Because service ecosystem actors and institutions have differing requirements, value co-creation is necessarily dynamic as actors adapt to each other and the service ecosystem evolves ( Vargo and Lusch, 2016 ). Some industries have strict rules governing carbon footprint, recycling schemes and waste generation; manufacturing SMEs sometimes encounter customers who reject sustainable and recyclable products because of higher costs. While national and international regulations for environmental certification may force manufacturers’ and customers’ adaptation (e.g. European Commission, 2020 ), customer acceptance also influences industry and regulatory perspectives. This situation drives constant service ecosystem adjustment or self-adjustment ( Vargo and Lusch, 2016 ) because firms must address inertia among service ecosystem actors in response to socio-institutional change ( Potting et al., 2017 ; Sjödin et al., 2021 ). The end key enabling condition for manufacturing SMEs to advance circularity is optimization of resource usage, focusing on internal locus of engagement and resource reconfiguration (what resources are used or reconfigured to advance circularity, such as digital technologies). This is highly connected to reduce in the R-framework. The internal focus on optimizing production through smarter waste reduction and efficient resource utilization is essential. This often requires energy and production data, so manufacturing SMEs can achieve and extend energy goals from customers, regulations and service ecosystem actors using digital technologies with high accuracy. These are optimized for smarter waste reduction and product quality, helping reduce scrap and enhance operational efficiency (e.g. Kim et al., 2023 ; Kjaer et al., 2018 ). In the case of complex products, digital technologies support the assessment of product quality and optimal use of materials. Through digital servitization, factories can become energy- efficient through remote monitoring, control, optimization and automation ( Porter and Heppelmann, 2014 ), decreasing water, electricity, gas and material usage in production ( Potting et al., 2017 ). Furthermore, manufacturing SMEs can use virtual and augmented reality and 3D programs for better product visualization, reducing the need for physical prototyping of customized products. Using advanced machines, robots and other digital technologies helps ensure less energy consumption during the production process and contributes to enhanced circularity across the service ecosystem. This direct pathway is possible for manufacturing SMEs with agility, competencies, digital maturity and infrastructure. However, SMEs lack digital skills ( de Jesus Pacheco et al., 2019 ) and face challenges when implementing digital technologies ( Dörr et al., 2023 ). Adopting circularity practices is also burdensome for SMEs because of high initial costs and resource needs ( Arroyabe et al., 2024 ). Thus, compliance- driven optimization often becomes reactive, adapting to the service ecosystem’s minimum requirements (e.g. customer demand, regulations, industry standards). The process often becomes incremental, making small shifts in SMEs’ circular production because of these issues, they usually need to choose one of the other two pathways to advance circularity. 5.2 Operational circularity pathway This pathway involves strengthening internal processes in response to external demands. Here, digital technologies can gather data, set KPIs and use predictive analytics to build internal processes before optimizing resource usage. This often requires knowledge development and strategic planning to focus on metrics and internal production operations, which are easier for manufacturing SMEs that are digitally mature but not deeply integrated into external platforms. Agile and digitally mature SMEs that respond to service ecosystem adjustment and want digital servitization – beyond complying with the minimum sustainability requirements – should focus on internal production processes. They need smarter process management for value co-creation – focusing on value creation mechanisms and how practices, routines and strategies can advance circularity. This internal process focuses on practices and strategies that are a prerequisite for efficiency in optimizing resource utilization. Besides identifying trends and improving forecasts, AI’s prescriptive capacities can help specify optimal actions based on available data ( Sjödin et al., 2023 ). By implementing practices of using barcodes, QR codes and sensors for monitoring, SMEs can improve control of raw materials and resources. Regarding customized products, AI programs can list appropriate materials for better resource utilization. Smarter process management lays the groundwork for optimized resource utilization, as practices, routines and strategies influence how manufacturing SMEs work to advance circularity through KPIs, gather and use production data and report measurements. However, optimized resource utilization, focusing on what resources are used and reconfigured, also influences practices, routines and strategies in smarter process management (e.g. implementation of 3D applications or AR solutions leads to new and unintended practices and strategies), but not enough to claim its pathway in this framework. Nevertheless, digital competencies often pose barriers to SMEs, requiring system integration and investments, which can compel them to take the collaborative circularity pathway. 5.3 Collaborative circularity pathway On this interorganizational pathway, manufacturing SMEs collaborate with customers, suppliers and service ecosystem actors to jointly manage resources, establish new infrastructures, develop recycling platforms and create shared solutions, resulting in resource-use and internal-optimization changes. This pathway depends on trust, infrastructure and often digital platforms and is commonly pursued by industries with high external complexity. The circularity focus often stems from and is reinforced by other ecosystem actors, regulations and customer demands. How manufacturing SMEs manage intraorganizational circularity will likely affect how external actors co-create value. Understanding this dynamic facilitates concentrating on circularity with external actors and partners during value co- creation, foregrounding the collaborative resource focus. The latter involves resource reconfigurations or what resources are used or reconfigured to advance circularity, thereby rethinking natural resource usage by providing recycling platforms, substituting physical resources with digital solutions and helping others to use fewer resources. To close the loop, recycling is vital because life cycles for solutions cannot always be extended ( Kim et al., 2022 ; Potting et al., 2017 ). However, gathering, recycling and reusing discarded products and other resources typically require coordination with external actors, including customers, suppliers, manufacturers and regulators. Because manufacturing SMEs need collaboration with intermediaries, it can be done through digital servitization with recycling platforms. Some industries have regulations and schemes for recycling and circularity (e.g. Awan et al., 2021 ). In other cases, recycling platforms must be provided to facilitate collaboration with external actors, which can be costly. Manufacturing SMEs also use digital solutions for resource substitution. Higher levels of digital servitization may include 3D programs, augmented reality and AI software for work planning and communication purposes, again reducing resource use. Integrated systems for measuring carbon footprint, energy usage, chemical usage and production data also expedite reporting and customer responsiveness, helping firms remain competitive. Digital servitization also enables real- time monitoring, control and predictive maintenance ( Kim et al., 2022 ), decreasing resource usage during production and in the longer term (e.g. replacing books with augmented reality or printed papers and manuals with software registration or 3D visualization programs). Following the collaborative circularity path, SMEs aim for optimized resource utilization by reducing resource usage and waste generation during production and implementing recycling routines. During digital servitization, shifting the business model encourages others to become sustainable; for example, providing recycling platforms and replacing some resources with digital solutions makes it easier for other firms to use less energy. In large-scale public projects, actors who use recycled resources or achieve a low carbon footprint are often rewarded, encouraging collaboration around resource usage within the service ecosystem, thus following the collaborative circularity path. As manufacturing SMEs pursue digital servitization and compliance-driven optimization, operational circularity, or collaborative circularity pathways, service ecosystems gradually evolve with new rules, institutions, regulations, customer demands and expectations. Combined with the internal locus of engagement, such as smarter process management and optimized resource utilization, the external locus of engagement – collaborative resource focus – encourages service ecosystem actors to change how they co-create value (e.g. Vargo and Lusch, 2016 ), often by rethinking, refusing and recycling natural resources. The framework suggests that digital servitization can advance circularity in manufacturing SMEs by following these three pathways. These can be implemented and maintained by adapting to the service ecosystem. As the process evolves, service ecosystem adjustment again influences how manufacturing SMEs pursue digital servitization to advance circularity. In this incremental and ongoing process, SMEs can follow several pathways simultaneously for several processes or solutions they provide, albeit with increased complexity. 6. Implications 6.1 Theoretical contributions This study explores how digital servitization can support manufacturing SMEs in advancing circularity, offering two main theoretical contributions. First, it contributes to the digital servitization literature by clarifying how manufacturing SMEs can apply digital servitization to advance circularity during production. While prior research has investigated the role of digitalization for circularity (e.g. Romero et al., 2021 ) and resource reduction during the usage phase (e.g. Ciasullo et al., 2021 ; Kjaer et al., 2018 ), this study focuses on reducing resource use and waste during production. Although meso- and macro-level transformations are essential, circularity practices must be implemented at the firm level ( Khan et al., 2024 a, 2024b ).
