Recycle was more emphasized during collaborative resource focus, while reduce was prioritized during smarter process management and optimized resource utilization. The proposed framework elucidates how digital servitization can advance circularity: compliance-driven optimization, collaborative circularity and operational circularity. These pathways navigate four enabling conditions for advancing the circularity: service ecosystem adjustment, optimized resource utilization, smarter process management and collaborative resource focus. As the Earth Overshoot Day arrives earlier every year ( UN, 2023b ) and policy pressure intensifies around circularity in manufacturing (e.g. European Commission, 2020 ; UN, 2023a ), SMEs must intensify their circularity focus. However, consistent with previous studies, this research confirms that many manufacturing SMEs face substantial challenges in implementing circular practices ( Arroyabe et al., 2024 ; Le-Dain et al., 2023 ) and even implement digital technologies ( Dörr et al., 2023 ) to digital servitize and advance circularity. Consequently, many SMEs become reactive, primarily engaging in compliance- driven optimization to meet minimum circularity standards. The pathway operational circularity emphasizes processes, data gathering, control, monitoring and measurements to optimize resource utilization and reduce waste. Second, this study clarifies how manufacturing SMEs can advance circularity by integrating a service ecosystem perspective with digital servitization and insights from the circular economy literature. Consistent with prior studies (e.g. Helmefalk et al., 2023 ; Khan et al., 2024 a, 2024b ; Konietzko et al., 2020 ), the findings demonstrate the difficulty manufacturing SMEs face in advancing circularity independently, without an inter-organizational or service ecosystem approach. The proposed framework illustrates that all three pathways originate in service ecosystem adjustment, where external requirements (e.g. regulations, requirements and customer demand) pressure manufacturing SMEs to align with circularity goals. The collaborative circularity pathway highlights the importance of collaboration with service ecosystem actors for recycling, aligning with Fehrer et al. (2024) and in developing digital solutions that substitute physical resources or help SMEs to use fewer resources. SMEs operating in complex service ecosystems, particularly those with multiple intermediaries selling their products, increase the need to collaborate for recycling platforms, digital systems tracking product containers and integrating information. Thus, consistent with earlier research (e.g. Kamble and Gunasekaran, 2023 ; Romero et al., 2021 ), this study confirms the critical role of digitalization in advancing circularity within manufacturing processes. Manufacturing SMEs seeking to go beyond compliance-driven optimization must pursue one of the two additional pathways that emphasize digital servitization to advance circularity. In some cases, SMEs have already undergone digital servitization and advanced circularity and are now complying with the external requirements. Thus, the focal manufacturing SMEs can influence the self-adjusting service ecosystem. While Ciasullo et al. (2021) examined digital servitization with a systems approach and service-dominant logic, the present study also addresses government efforts to advance circularity in the manufacturing sector (e.g. European Commission, 2020 ; UN, 2023a ). The findings also underscore the importance of establishing recycling platforms to support a collaborative resource focus among service ecosystem actors (e.g. Fehrer et al., 2024 ; Helmefalk et al., 2023 ). Although closing the loop remains challenging (e.g. Potting et al., 2017 ), recycling efforts must aim to achieve material recovery during the production phase, which can only be done with the cooperation of external actors (e.g. platform providers, customers, sales intermediaries, governments and regulators). The proposed framework suggests that an internal circularity focus, when combined with external collaboration, contributes to a continuous adjustment process as service ecosystems evolve. In line with calls for deeper understanding of how service ecosystems evolve and self-adjust ( Vargo and Lusch, 2016 ), this study offers new insights into the mechanisms underpinning that transformation. Advanced service ecosystem circularity likely relies on multiple strategies that promote collaboration, mutual adaptation and continuous adjustment among actors. While high-level circularity strategies such as refuse, rethink and reduce remain essential ( Potting et al., 2017 ), achieving closed-loop systems also depends on operational strategies such as recycling. The proposed framework highlights the importance of collaboration during digital servitization ( Kohtamäki et al., 2019 ; Sjödin et al., 2021 ) and how actors can adjust to the service ecosystem. 6.2 Managerial implications Despite the increasing importance of circularity (e.g. European Commission, 2020 ; UN, 2023a ), manufacturing SMEs continue to struggle with how to improve circularity. Existing frameworks, such as 10R (e.g. Potting et al., 2017 ), can prove challenging to apply in practice, especially for SMEs with limited resources and tight margins. The proposed framework offers managers guidance on advancing circularity through complementary pathways, outlined below with overarching implications (see also Table 1 ). 6.2.1 Responding to service ecosystem adjustment through strategic circularity choices The findings highlight the importance of adopting a service ecosystem perspective in circular manufacturing. SMEs that fail to commit to digital servitization and circularity risk losing market relevance, as competitors increasingly satisfy customer expectations for sustainable solutions. Outdated offerings and inefficient resource use can lead to higher costs and customer churn. By engaging with the service ecosystem, focal SMEs can use digital servitization to more effectively manage costs associated with recycling, traceability and environmentally friendly materials, while collaborating with partners to meet growing demands. Advancing circularity in isolation is particularly difficult for SMEs because of limited resources, high costs and a competence shortage. Because of these difficulties and the need for focal SMEs to take responsibility for circularity, they often comply with the circularity requirements of service ecosystem actors, leading to the implementation of internal circularity practices. However, compliance-driven circularity usually results in minor incremental adjustments in their daily operations. In situations where manufacturing SMEs experience external pressure for circularity and low internal capacity for radical change, a compliance-driven circularity pathway is recommended where managers should: • monitor ecosystem trends (e.g. customers, suppliers, industry, regulatory expectations) related to circularity; • develop short- and long-term circularity strategies (e.g. finding the minimum standards, focus on operational circularity, collaborative circularity or a combination across offerings); • planning necessary collaboration with partners to meet sustainability requirements, if needed (e.g. traceability, carbon reporting and recycling); • integrate digital tools for resource efficiency to support compliance with industry standards and environmental regulations; and • standardize routines, responsibility, data gathering and reporting. 6.2.2 Leverage the collaborative resource focus for circular value creation In value chains where products are sold through intermediaries, establishing shared responsibility for end-of-life product management and recycling can be challenging. Digital recycling platforms can enable collaboration across the service ecosystem, focusing on recycling, resource recovery and KPI reporting. Through improved monitoring and optimization of recycling processes, they effectively recover discarded materials and keep them in circulation. In situations where manufacturing SMEs experience external circularity pressure, complexity in the value chain and complex end-of-life/return challenges, a collaborative circularity pathway is recommended where managers should: • engage in or initiate collaborative recycling platforms and digital solutions (e.g. systems, platforms, sensors, 3D and AR applications); • co-invest in shared digital infrastructure and tools to access secondary resources or provide resource-efficient solutions to other actors; and • share production and recycling data with ecosystem partners. 6.2.3 Prioritize smarter process management for circularity efficiency Smarter process management is essential for reducing waste and minimizing resource inefficiency. Through digital servitization, SMEs can collect real-time production data from machines and sensors to reduce downtime and errors, improve machine performance and track sustainability measurements and KPIs. This enables more accurate resource allocation, continuous data-driven learning and process adjustments. The importance of data gathering increases as service ecosystem actors require reporting of sustainability measures. In situations where manufacturing SMEs experience external pressure for circularity and a high degree of resource consumption in production, an operational circularity pathway is recommended where managers should: • invest in basic digital tools (e.g. sensors, dashboards and systems) to track production and sustainability KPIs; • develop routines for interpreting production data to support process adjustments; and • align process KPIs and routines with circularity strategies and goals (e.g. scrap reduction, material efficiency and carbon footprint). Manufacturing SMEs may require quick responses because of varying digital maturity levels, recycling platforms, data utilization or demonstrating circularity gains to customers and regulators. Combining pathways can help, but it is costly and resource- intensive. 7. Limitations and further research This paper has several limitations. First, as most of the interviewees were managers, the study neglected the potentially critical insights of other employees and ecosystem actors (e.g. intermediaries). To gain a broader perspective, it would also seem fruitful to explore the views of customers and intermediaries regarding the recycling process and how it might be improved by a platform-based approach. Second, the present study focuses on smart process management and optimized resource utilization in the production phase (e.g. the use of VR and 3D solutions) while neglecting the associated issue of high-level digital servitization and its role in business model innovation. Future research should address how subscription, pay-per-use, renting and sharing models affect product or solution ownership as a vital element in reducing resource usage and advancing circularity. Descriptive Maturity Model for Digital Servitization of SMEs Mohammed Khan, Jelena Milisavljevic Syed and Konstantinos Salonitis Faculty of Engineering and Applied Science, Cranfield University, Cranfield, UK Abstract Purpose – This study develops a descriptive maturity model (MM) to assess and guide the servitization progression of manufacturing SMEs through consensus building with both industry and academic practitioners. Design/methodology/approach – The maturity model was developed through a systematic literature review (SLR), validated via the Delphi Survey Method with experts in servitization, and tested with two SMEs in the manufacturing sector. Findings – The study identifies 7 core maturity dimensions and 21 sub-dimensions, each mapped to basic, intermediate and advanced servitization levels. The resulting model provides a structured and detailed diagnostic framework. Research limitations/implications – Advances existing literature by providing a detailed, empirically tested model that differentiates capabilities across servitization levels. The collaboration between industry and academic practitioners addresses a gap in previous research. Practical implications – The model serves as a diagnostic and strategic planning tool for SMEs aiming to transition towards higher levels of servitization. The model supports this strategic transformation by defining the needed capabilities. Originality/value – This is among the first studies to use a Delphi method to build consensus between academics and industry practitioners for a digital servitization MM. Additionally, results of testing and refinement of the developed model through practical application with two SME businesses are shown, bridging the gap between theory and real-world implementation. Keywords Servitization, Product-service systems, Capability, Maturity model, Delphi method Paper type Research article Interesting because: This study presents the first descriptive maturity model that explicitly maps the capabilities required at each servitization level: Level 0, Basic, Intermediate, and Advanced, providing a structured pathway for digital servitization, particularly for SMEs. While prior studies have explored servitization maturity conceptually, none have used servitization level typologies to guide capability development. Theoretical value: The study contributes to the servitization literature by defining and operationalizing 7 maturity dimensions along with 21 sub-dimensions and detailing how each evolves across four distinct levels. By integrating digital considerations within each maturity dimension, the model extends existing maturity frameworks that have often overlooked digital-specific requirements. Furthermore, the Delphi process revealed differences in how academics and practitioners conceptualize servitization, offering new insights into field-level variation and interpretive alignment. Practical value: For practitioners, the model functions as a diagnostic and strategic planning tool, enabling companies, particularly SMEs, to assess their current maturity level and identify targeted improvement areas. Managers can benchmark their progress and prioritize capability investments based on the defined actions and characteristics at each servitization stage. The inclusion of digital elements within each dimension ensures the model is relevant for guiding digital transformation in service-oriented manufacturing contexts. 1. This model involves integrating a suite of services with their product offering (Vandermerwe and Rada, 1988). Servitization denotes the transition of manufacturing enterprises from a product-centric to a service-oriented business model (Baines et al., 2009) and is designed to tap into new revenue streams. This transformation is frequently delineated into three service tiers: basic services, encompassing maintenance and spare parts; intermediate services, facilitating product utilisation through offerings such as operator training or remote monitoring; and advanced services, wherein the provider ensures performance or outcomes via models like pay-per-use or outcome-based contracts (Lightfoot et al., 2013). Simultaneously, PSSs categorize offerings according to the nature of value provided. Tukker (2004) identified three categories: product-oriented PSS, which facilitates the sale of a product; use-oriented PSS, which grants access to the product (e.g. leasing) and result-oriented PSS, which yields a predetermined consequence. The most comprehensive service level, known as advanced or result-oriented servitization, offers the greatest benefits. Notable examples include Rolls-Royce’s “power by the hour” for aircraft engines (Harrison, 2017) and Xerox’s “pay per page” model for photocopiers (Harris and Wonglimpiyarat, 2020). However, to transition into each of these three different service levels requires different configurations and capabilities within a business (Michalik et al., 2019). Especially small-and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) face a bigger hurdle compared to their larger counterparts, specifically with the lack of financial and knowledge resources (Chirumalla et al., 2024). Previous research has demonstrated that SMEs and large companies differ substantially in terms of firm characteristics, including their sizes, organizational structures and finances. These differences significantly influence their organizational processes and overall performance (Ghobadian and Gallear, 1996; Ates et al., 2013; O’dwyer and Ledwith, 2010; Bos-Brouwers, 2009). A framework/model that allows a holistic and granular approach to transition into each of these service levels is required due to the various configurations required for each service type. Maturity models (MMs) are seen to be a very important and useful tool to guide a business on a step-by-step basis towards its desired maturity level. MM can be used for different purposes, either descriptive, prescriptive, or comparative in nature. Descriptive MM are applied for “as-is” assessments where a business can identify where it currently sits in relation to a specific maturity element, e.g. strategy. It is used as a diagnostic tool (Poeppelbuss and Roeglinger, 2011; de Bruin et al., 2005). Prescriptive MM are used to identify desirable maturity levels and provide specific guidelines for improvement (Poeppelbuss and Roeglinger, 2011). There are already MM developed within the field of servitization, as seen Section 4. However, many of these models are descriptive and either conceptual in nature, not tested with a range of industry and academic practitioners or do not comprehensively consider the “digital” aspect of digital servitization. In addition, existing models fail to identify the required resources and capabilities for each service level (basic, intermediate, advanced) and there are differences in which elements/ constructs constitute servitization. Since the existing literature does not offer a complete Descriptive Maturity Model, with detailed input from both industry and academic experts, this raises the following research questions: “What are the essential elements for an SME to determine it reediness level in order to transition into a digital servitization business model?” To address these gaps, a “Descriptive” MM is developed and is evaluated with industrial and academic experts as well as applying in 2 SME businesses for further validation. The proposed model not only provides a comprehensive framework to identify the required capabilities in each servitization level, but also provides a building block to developing a “Prescriptive” MM in the future. Theoretical background 2.1 Digital servitization transition state of art Digital servitization signifies a comprehensive change for manufacturing enterprises, necessitating a fundamental reorganization of resources, organisational frameworks and procedures to amalgamate digital technologies with service provisions (Chirumalla et al., 2023). A dynamic capabilities perspective emphasises the necessity for ongoing adaptation and reconfiguration of resources and competencies as organisations identify and capitalise on digital opportunities in their service sectors (Chirumalla et al., 2023). Concurrently, institutional theory highlights the influence of external constraints and norms in moulding and legitimising this transition, with recent studies using institutional frameworks to elucidate the intricate dynamics propelling digital servitization (Lee et al., 2024). As technologies like IoT, AI and remote connectivity have advanced, servitization has transformed into digital servitization, wherein digital capabilities are pivotal in service delivery and value co-creation (Kohtam€aki et al., 2020a, b; Lenka et al., 2017). This transformation allows companies to provide predictive maintenance, performance-based contracts and data-informed customer insights (Ardolino et al., 2018). Nevertheless, SMEs encounter unique obstacles in digital servitization, such as restricted access to resources, insufficient digital competencies and lack of strategy alignment (Le-Dain et al., 2023). Studies indicate that digital servitization is non-linear and differs according to company size, industry and digital maturity (Bagni and Filho, 2024; Harrmann et al., 2023).To achieve a digital servitization business model, there are barriers that are needed to overcome in relation to specific aspects as seen in Table 1. These challenges underscore the necessity for developing a robust model to aid SMEs and MNEs towards a servitized business model. There is a clear need for a maturity model that can underpin this framework. A maturity model is a framework that allows an assessment and development of a business capability in a specific domain, e.g. technology development, work processes, etc. The development of a particular domain can be divided into different maturity phases or levels, where the higher the maturity level, the more complete or higher the achieved capability. Maturity models originated from the IT industry and were used as more as a management tool (Paulk, 2009). The capability maturity model integration (CMMI) originated from the Software Engineering Institute of Carnegie Mellon University, which is an offshoot from the capability maturity model (CMM) and aims to provide a framework to guide process improvement across either a project, division or entire organization (ScienceDirect, 2016). There are two types of CMMI models that can be used, staged or continuous. The staged maturity model assesses process maturity through discrete, sequential stages, ensuring structured progression. In contrast, the continuous maturity model evaluates specific process areas independently, allowing organizations to prioritize improvements without a linear sequence. While the staged model offers a structured roadmap, the continuous model provides flexibility for tailored advancements. Discussion and conclusion The descriptive maturity model developed in this study significantly advances theoretical understanding in servitization and digital transformation, particularly within the context of SMEs. Unlike earlier maturity models (Adrodegari and Saccani, 2020; Paschou et al., 2019; H€ackel et al., 2021), this model was explicitly shaped by rigorous consensus-building through the Delphi method. Previous models have largely focused either on conceptual frameworks or specific industrial contexts, often overlooking the nuanced capabilities SMEs require at different maturity levels – basic, intermediate and advanced. By clearly delineating specific capabilities necessary for progression at each stage, this study addresses a significant theoretical gap identified in the literature review, particularly the work of H€ackel et al. (2021), Paschou et al. (2019). The Delphi survey method was particularly instrumental in ensuring the robustness of the model. By systematically incorporating perspectives from both industry and academic experts, the study effectively bridged the gap between theoretical constructs and practical realities, capturing diverse views that typically differ significantly, especially in dimensions such as “Culture”. Industry practitioners emphasized pragmatic and operational considerations, whereas academic experts often highlighted theoretical completeness and conceptual clarity. Novel sub-dimensions introduced, such as “Price Offering” and “Risk Management”, alongside redefined constructs like “Serviceability” and “Employee Commitment”, represent additional theoretical contributions. The following sections discuss theoretical and practical implications, as well as limitations. 5.1 Theoretical implications The descriptive maturity model developed in this research offers theoretical implications for the field of servitization and PSS. Firstly, it advances existing literature by providing a comprehensive review of the capabilities required at each servitization level – basic, intermediate and advanced – crafted through collaboration between industrial and academic practitioners and empirically tested with SMEs. This facet of the model addresses a noted gap in prior research, which typically lacks detailed differentiation of capabilities across servitization levels, thereby enriching the strategic guidance available for firms at different stages of their servitization journey. Secondly, utilizing the Delphi Method – marks a departure from existing approaches by fostering a consensus among a diverse group of experts. This methodological innovation is crucial, as it resolves the ambiguity surrounding the foundational components of servitization, such as strategy and culture, which previous studies have often left undefined. By having a “digital” element for nearly all the maturity dimensions represents an improvement upon previous maturity models, which have limited focus or neglected an important facet of servitization (Andersen et al., 2020; Dmitrijeva et al., 2020). By integrating a structured consensus-building approach, this study not only enriches the theoretical foundation of servitization models but also enhances their practical applicability and validity. 5.2 Managerial implications For practice, the model guides SMEs and MNEs in advancing to their desired level of servitization, especially the advanced level. This strategic transition is facilitated by explicitly delineating the capabilities necessary at each phase of servitization maturity, allowing organisations to devise and execute organised development trajectories. For example, management can use the maturity model to evaluate their status quo and desired target state. This makes it easier for managers to assess the necessary efforts for developing needed capabilities. 5.3 Limitations The descriptive maturity model developed has limitations. Firstly, the sample size for the Delphi Method is within the guidelines; however, a larger sample size can further validate the model and may result in further “dimensions” to be found. There may be dimensions that other researchers have discovered which is not in this model. Response bias is a concern, as SME managers’ views may differ from those of other employees. However, this is mitigated by selecting company directors, who have the most comprehensive understanding of overall operations and strategy. Future research could incorporate perspectives from middle management and operational staff to gain a more holistic understanding of servitization maturity. Additionally, the testing of the descriptive maturity model has been limited to a small sample size, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. Future research could address this by testing the model across a broader array of companies and different sectors. Finally, this model is only a “descriptive” model, and the next phase of the research is planned to address these limitations by evolving the model into a more prescriptive tool. Insights on the role of performance measurement systems in the digital servitization landscape: a longitudinal case study Alessandro Marelli Department of Political Science, University of Teramo, Teramo, Italy, and Andrea Dello Sbarba Department of Economics and Management, University of Pisa, Pisa, Italy Abstract Purpose – The purpose of this paper is to investigate the role of performance measurement systems (PMS) within the context of digital servitization (DS), especially in collaborations involving multiple actors. The paper adopts a bottom-up ecosystem perspective to gain insights into how companies can effectively manage the complexities of digital transformation in the servitization domain. Design/methodology/approach – This research draws upon a longitudinal case study within the wine and spirit supply chain. It focuses on a logistics company,“GR”, which has promoted a DS strategy to offer advanced services and enhance the competitiveness of the entire ecosystem. Findings – The study offers valuable insights into the evolution of PMS roles throughout the DS journey, promoting cooperation, coordination, collaboration and control among ecosystem actors, thereby facilitating the development of a DS strategy. Research limitations/implications – The study is focused on a logistics company with unique capabilities and networks. Future research should include a broader range of contexts. Furthermore, our analysis focuses on the initial stages of ecosystem emergence, particularly the initiation and momentum phases. Further research should explore how DS impacts organizations in the following ecosystem phases. Practical implications – This research offers valuable insights for managers, particularly in the development of DS strategy. It underscores the significance of PMS as key facilitators in crafting DS strategy and in the broader ecosystem evolution. Thefindings demonstrate that PMS is instrumental across different phases of the servitization process, improving aspects such as performance monitoring, resource allocation, collaboration and communication. Moreover, this study emphasizes the importance for small and medium-sized enterprises manufacturers and logistics firms to build and nurture collaborative relationships with various supply chain stakeholders to successfully implement a servitization strategy. Introduction As i g n ificant transformation from product-centric to service-centric business models is designing a new paradigm, emphasizing the benefits and positive outcomes (Baines et al., 2009; Kowalkowski et al., 2017; Kamal et al., 2020; Lightfoot et al.,2 0 1 3; Wang et al., 2023). This paradigm shift, known as“servitization”, is characterized by companies enhancing their core strategies by offering comprehensive customer-focused market packages through service provision (Vandermerwe and Rada, 1988). In recent years, a new phenomenon called“digital servitization” (DS) has emerged, wherein companies adopt digital technologies to expand the boundaries of servitization (Palo et al., 2019; Paschou et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2022; Kohtamäki et al., 2019, 2021). DS involves developing new services or enhancing existing ones through digital technologies, harnessing data, developing new business models, enabling value co-creation and gaining a competitive advantage (Paschou et al.,2 0 2 0). The success of DS often relies on multiactor collaboration, particularly in markets dominated by small and medium-sized manufacturers, such as the agri-food industry. These manufacturers need to establish collaborative partnerships with various actors to pursue their DS strategies effectively (e.g. Coreynen et al., 2017; Rabetino et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2021). In this transformation, the concept of ecosystem has gained prominence as an effective lens to study DS (Jovanovic et al., 2022; Kamalaldin et al., 2021; Sklyar et al.,2 0 1 9; Tronvoll et al., 2020). Ecosystems are characterized by a focal offer or value proposition, multilateralism involving complex relationships among different actors, distributed decision-making, and modularity with nongeneric complementarities (Adner, 2017; Iansiti and Levien, 2004; Jacobides et al. , 2018). Nowadays, different actors that intervene in such kinds of relationships are increasingly organized around platforms, which facilitate the exchange of information and regulation of interorganizational relationships, giving rise to a so-called“platform ecosystem” (McIntyre and Srinivasan, 2017). This notion holds significant relevance in the DS as there is a growing emphasis on the value of data and information over traditional physical products and equipment (Tronvoll et al., 2020). Platforms facilitate DS by promoting cooperation and coordination among actors, providing infrastructure for collaboration and empowering actors to control their businesses effectively (Cenamor et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2022; Jovanovic et al., 2022; Thomas et al., 2014). The success of DS ecosystem relies on the capability of companies to develop and execute a successful ecosystem strategy (Adner, 2017). This strategy involves bringing together actors and activities necessary for a value proposition to materialize (Adner, 2017; Talmar et al., 2020). The literature highlights top-down and bottom-up approaches for ecosystem strategy deployment (Adner, 2017; Datt/C19ee et al., 2018). The top-down method involves intentional design and implementation by an ecosystem designer, focusing on creating a strategic blueprint. While effective in transitioning global companies to serviceoriented models, its application faces challenges in complex settings, like the wine industry due to the involvement of numerous independent actors, and difficulties in designing a clear Performance measurement systems 287 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/qram/article-pdf/22/3/286/10299915/qram-11-2022-0185en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 value blueprint in advance (Baines et al., 2009; Coreynenet al., 2017; Datt/C19ee et al., 2018). Given these challenges, a shift toward a bottom-up approach is suggested, where an ecosystem orchestrator collaborates with participants to co-develop an ecosystem blueprint and architecture that meets all actor’s needs. Understanding the role of performance measurement systems (PMS) is crucial for effectively leveraging the potential benefits of a bottom-up DS ecosystem within this complex context. In thefield of servitization, research on PMS has yielded significant insights across various domains (Cinquini et al., 2018). Despite these studies, the role of PMS in servitization has not been fully explored, even though it plays a crucial role, facilitates the planning and execution of service-based offerings, justifies the adoption of servitization strategies, evaluates progress and effectively manages contracts related to service offerings (Legnani and Cavalieri, 2012; Laine et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2006; Meier et al., 2013; Pascual et al., 2017). The literature concentrates on the traditional role of PMS in the planning and control aspects within companies (Cinquiniet al., 2022; Tenucci and Supino, 2020), perceiving PMS as hierarchical and based on control, characterized by mechanistic attributes (Laine et al., 2012). Nonetheless, when it comes to ecosystem settings, conventional approaches might encounter limitations. Few studies have identified PMS characteristics essential for ecosystem strategies.Micheli and Muctor (2021)emphasized the need for PMS adaptability to support dynamic ecosystems, suggesting PMS should represent diverse ecosystem perspectives.Gomes et al.(2023) proposed a framework for PMS to fully encompass ecosystem complexities, integrating various perspectives for strategic support. Despite these insights, main research has applied a top-down approach to DS ecosystems, overlooking the higher uncertainty levels and the complexity of defining roles and value blueprints (Baineset al., 2009; Coreynenet al., 2017; Datt/C19ee et al., 2018). To address this research gap, the study aims to examine the role of PMS in facilitating the transition toward a DS ecosystem. It highlights the necessity for a bottom-up approach and for PMS to facilitate the development of the DS ecosystem by managing uncertainty and fostering the collaborative discovery of ecosystem strategy ( Autio, 2022; Datt/C19ee et al.,2 0 1 8). A qualitative research design is used, conducting a longitudinal case study of a logistics company within the wine industry. It probes into how PMS contributes to aligning goals, orchestrating activities, fostering collaboration among diverse ecosystem actors and enhancing inter-organizational control. The case study choice is informed by the distinctive features of the logistics sector and the specific context of the company, designated here as “GR”. This company has implemented a DS strategy, introduced advanced services and achieved heightened ecosystem competitiveness on an international scale. The empirical results of this study make significant contributions to the theory. First, this study offers valuable insights into the specific dynamics of PMS in fostering inter-organizational servitization, revealing that PMS serves as a fundamental enabler for seamless coordination and collaboration among different organizations involved in the servitization process. Second, it extends the understanding of factors in fluencing servitization success by highlighting the overlooked role of PMS. This insight emphasizes the importance of PMS in driving innovation and operational efficiency within servitization efforts. Third, numerous scholars have critiqued current PMS practices (e.g.Melnyk et al., 2014; Pekkola and Ukko, 2016), pointing out the need to identify specific features that should be considered within the context of ecosystems (e.g.Micheli and Muctor, 2021; Gomes et al.,2 0 2 3). This study shows that, contrary to expectations, while the metrics used in PMS remain the same, their application has evolved. They now enable ecosystem evolution at different stages by facilitating cooperation, coordination, collaboration, communication and control to bolster the implementation of the DS strategy. Literature review 2.1 Digital servitization and multiactor perspective DS and multiactor collaboration are profound transformational processes, wherein manufacturers are transitioning from a product-centric to a service-centric business model, searching new benefits and positive economics returns ( Baines et al.,2 0 0 9; Kamal et al., 2020; Kowalkowski et al.,2 0 1 7; Lightfoot et al.,2 0 1 3; Wang et al., 2023). This shift marks a significant evolution in the industry’s approach, as it focuses more on delivering value through service that cater to customer needs and preferences, fostering a dynamic and customer-centric business environment. This phenomenon, classified as “servitization”, denotes a trend where companies enhance their core strategy by offering comprehensive customer-focused market packages through service provision (Vandermerwe and Rada, 1988, p. 314) [1]. Recent literature underscores that a growing number of leading manufacturers have embraced the adoption of new digital technologies with a top-down approach (Adner, 2017; Datt/C19ee et al.,2 0 1 8) to expand the boundaries of servitization (Chen et al., 2021; Fu et al.,2 0 2 2; Palo et al., 2019; Paschou et al.,2 0 2 0;). In this context, the authors often refer to the concept of DS, which can be described as the process of: [... ] developing new services and/or enhancing existing ones through the utilization of digital technologies. This includes enabling new (digital) business models, exploring innovative approaches for (co)creating value, harnessing data to generate knowledge, improving operational and environmental performance, and ultimately gaining a competitive advantage (Paschou et al., 2020, p. 284). The value co-creation stems from the so-called“advanced services”, with customer support agreements and outcome contracts, which prioritize extending product lifecycle responsibilities, delivering capabilities through performance and supporting customers’ dynamic and evolving activities ( Baines et al., 2017; Cenamor et al., 2017; Lightfoot et al., 2013;). These services include a diverse portfolio of offerings, such as leveraging data, cybersecurity, risk reduction and innovative business strategy design (Bandinelli et al., 2020; Coreynen et al., 2017; Rabetino et al.,2 0 1 8; Zheng et al., 2021). The advanced services allow companies to engage customers more proactively and offer comprehensive solutions that cater to their evolving needs, ultimately fostering stronger customer relationships and value generation throughout the product lifecycle. DS is a relatively new but rapidly growing lens in recent years, when the convergence between digitalization and servitization emerges (Wang et al.,2 0 2 3). According toStruyf et al.(2021), the literature on DS can be categorized into two main streams: one focuses primarily on internal, company-specific challenges, while the other predominantly investigates external challenges associated with changing dynamics of stakeholder relationships and the necessity of adapting to evolving multiactor collaboration. While acknowledging the significance of a holistic approach that Performance measurement systems 289 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/qram/article-pdf/22/3/286/10299915/qram-11-2022-0185en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 considers a multilevel view of DS (Struyf et al.,2 0 2 1), this study specifically focuses on the latter. The multiactor perspective holds particular significance, especially in those contexts dominated by small and medium-sized manufacturers (e.g. agri-food context, especially in Italian wine industry). In fact, given that offering advanced services demands a diverse range of knowledge and expertise, such kind of businesses have the need to nurture collaborative partnerships with various actors to pursue their DS strategies. These actors typically include logistics suppliers, general agents, distributors, retailers and third-party service providers (Coreynen et al.,2 0 1 7; Rabetino et al.,2 0 1 8; Zheng et al.,2 0 2 1). These partnerships can take the form of one-to-one interactions or, more commonly, many-to-many collaborations. Through these multiactor collaborations, different actors combine their resources and expertise, empowering small and medium-sized agri-food manufacturers to enhance their advanced service offerings, provide comprehensive solutions and effectively cater to the evolving demands of their customers (Fu et al., 2022). Leveraging growth opportunities stemming from digital technologies and advanced services comes with challenges due to the plethora of solutions and service providers available in the market (Eloranta et al., 2021; Kapoor et al.,2 0 2 1). 2.2 Digital servitization as an ecosystem strategy Extensive research has been conducted to address the increasing need for a comprehensive understanding of DS from a multiactor perspective, focusing on exploring the challenges and distinctive elements of multiactor collaboration to attain successful outcomes in DS ( Wang et al.,2 0 2 3). This has led to the employment of several theories or theoretical perspectives into thisfield (e.g. network theory, service-dominant logic and value theory) to investigate the mechanisms, outcomes and influential factors that characterize DS (Wang et al.,2 0 2 3). In recent years, the theory of ecosystems has gained prominence, with several authors emphasizing that DS is fundamentally embedded within it (Jovanovic et al., 2021; Kamalaldin et al.,2 0 2 1; Sklyar et al.,2 0 1 9; Tronvoll et al.,2 0 2 0). Although there is no universally agreed-upon definition of an ecosystem, the authors argue that ecosystems share certain common characteristics. First, there is a“focal offer” or “value proposition” that defines the (endogenous) boundaries of the ecosystem itself (Adner and Kapoor, 2010). Secondly, ecosystems exhibit “multilaterality”, involving not only a diverse range of partners but also a set of complex relationships that cannot be simply reduced to an aggregation of bilateral interactions (Adner, 2017, p. 42). Thirdly, they are not unilaterally or hierarchically controlled, meaning that decision-making processes are, to some extent, distributed, although a hub often establishes standards, rules and interfaces (Jacobides et al., 2018). Moreover, ecosystems are enabled by modularity and held together by partners’ investments that are not fully interchangeable (Jacobides et al., 2018). Actors within ecosystem deal with nongeneric complementarities, necessitating the creation of specific relationship structures and alignment to generate value (Jacobides et al.,2 0 1 8, p. 2263). Nowadays, different actors that intervene in such kinds of relationships are increasingly organized around platforms, which facilitate the exchange of information and regulation of inter-organizational relationships, giving rise to a so-called“platform ecosystem” (McIntyre and Srinivasan, 2017; Kapoor et al., 2021). The concept of a “platform ecosystem” encompasses the creation of “a shared architecture that facilitates the division of an ecosystem into a stable platform and a complementary set of modules, while also governing the interactions among these diverse components” (McIntyre and Srinivasan, 2017: 143). This notion of a “platform ecosystem” holds significant relevance in the DS as there is a growing emphasis on the value of information over traditional physical products and equipment (Tronvoll et al., 2020). Within the ecosystem, actors known as“writers” hold a QRAM 22,3 290 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/qram/article-pdf/22/3/286/10299915/qram-11-2022-0185en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 pivotal role as complementors, as they actively contribute essential information crucial for the successful implementation of the platform’s objective, such as delivering advanced services. Conversely, “readers” are empowered to access a diverse array of information pieces contributed by each actor. The actors even have the autonomy to select and combine these information pieces according to their specific requirements (Jacobides et al.,2 0 1 8). A platform approach facilitates manufacturers’implementation of servitization, encompassing the following aspects: cooperation and coordination, collaboration and control (Jacobides et al., 2018). Firstly, a platform comprises both organizational and technological structures that fostercoordination and cooperationamong actors working together toward a common goal sharing information, resources and efforts (Cenamor et al.,2 0 1 7; Jovanovic et al.,2 0 2 1). Based on a modular architecture, a platform provides a structure on which actors can develop compatible standards and coordination processes to search, identify, combine and share information and resources in the ecosystem in a way that leverages value co-creation (Thomas et al.,2 0 1 4). Second, the platform ecosystem provides infrastructure and mechanisms for actors to continually expand and strengthencollaboration (Fu et al., 2022). A platform ecosystem leverages architecture technologies to enable seamless interaction, offering a common system for collaboration among actors in diverse industries (Jovanovic et al., 2021; Tian et al.,2 0 2 1). Finally, platform empowers actors to enhance their abilities in controlling their business (Fuet al. in, 2022). In fact, platform acts as connector between actors and consumers, tackling challenges related to service capacity management, cost control and quality assurance (Fu et al., 2022). While much has been written about the benefits that new technologies can bring to the domain of DS, the literature agrees that a crucial element in an ecosystem is the capability of companies to develop and execute a successful ecosystem strategy (e.g. Adner, 2017). To this end, companies need to bring together actors and activities that are necessary for a value proposition to “materialize” and, ultimately, to reap the bene fits of business ecosystems (Adner, 2017; Talmar et al.,2 0 2 0). The implementation of this strategy encompasses both technological and social aspects, leading to a comprehensive and complex transformation journey (Tronvoll et al., 2020). In this context, ecosystem orchestration presents unique governance challenges because it relies heavily on voluntary contributions from participants who are hierarchically independent, aiming for the co-production of value and the facilitation of benefits across the ecosystem. Effective ecosystem governance must find a balance between standardization and variation, autonomy and control, individualism and collectivism (Wareham et al., 2014). According to the literature, two basic approaches have been suggested to address these challenges in ecosystem strategy deployment: thetopdown and bottom-up (Adner, 2017; Datt/C19ee et al., 2018). In thetop-down approach, as outlined by Adner (2017), the ecosystem architecture is deliberately designed and implemented by an ecosystem designer. From this perspective, the primary responsibility of the platform owner and the ecosystem implementor is to create an“ecosystem value blueprint”. This blueprint is a strategic plan for the ecosystem’s architecture aimed at realizing the ecosystem value proposition by specifying roles and delivery mechanisms to the customer. The ecosystem designer then executes this blueprint in a top-down manner, by selecting ecosystem participants and allocating specific roles to them. While DS has been widely adopted, particularly through successful transitions of global leading companies from a product-centric to a service-oriented approach via top-down implementation, its application in complex settings such as the wine industry appears more challenging ( Datt/C19ee et al.,2 0 1 8; Yadav et al.,2 0 2 2). This context is characterized by the presence of numerous independent actors, including producers, logistics suppliers, general agents, distributors, retailers and third-party service providers. Such a diverse array of Performance measurement systems 291 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/qram/article-pdf/22/3/286/10299915/qram-11-2022-0185en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 actors complicates the ability of focal companies to enforce the roles they have designated for others. Furthermore, the focal company may not be able to design a clear value blueprint in advance (Baines et al., 2009; Coreynen et al., 2017). Consequently, the effectiveness of a top-down approach in designing and implementing an ecosystem strategy seems increasingly limited in situations marked by high uncertainty (Datt/C19ee et al., 2018). This complex reality of ecosystem creation appears to call for a more bottom-up approach, wherein the ecosystem orchestrator initiates multisided conversations with prospective ecosystem participants to co-discover an ecosystem architecture that is palatable to all those concerned. In this vein, Autio (2022)identifies three key phases that unfold in an ecosystem following a bottom-up approach: initiation, momentum building and maturity. In the“initiation stage”, the focus is on creating a technology framework that encourages participation and provides guidance on ecosystem roles (designing interfaces for connectivity and a modular structure for complementary offerings), as well as creating strategic and financial incentives for attracting participation is vital. During the “momentum stage”, the focus shifts to maximizing generativity within the ecosystem by attracting participation and facilitating their contributions. Economic orchestration promotes ecosystem benefits through selective promotion of applications. During the ecosystem maturity stage, the focus is on maximizing appropriation through technological orchestration. Ecosystem benefits are established, roles defined and self-sustainability achieved. Technological bottlenecks are managed, and data resources used. 2.3 The role of performance measurement systems in digital servitization ecosystem strategy In the field of servitization, PMS have received significant attention, providing valuable insights across diverse domains[2]. Researchers have thoroughly explored the impact of servitization on performance, considering bothfinancial and nonfinancial indicators (e.g. Ambroise et al.,2 0 1 8; Visnjic Kastalli and Van Looy, 2013; Kohtamäki et al.,2 0 1 3). They have also investigated new performance metrics and management control tools that aim to provide information about the emerging business objects in the servitization context, such as the balanced scorecard (BSC) (e.g.Chirumalla et al.,2 0 1 3; Pan and Nguyen, 2015), costing and life cycle assessment (e.g.Datta and Roy, 2010; Settanni et al.,2 0 1 4) and performance measurement itself (e.g. Bustinza et al.,2 0 1 9; Meier et al.,2 0 1 3; Pascual et al.,2 0 1 7). Additionally, researchers have explored various customer-related aspects in servitization, such as pricing, bidding, and value creation (e.g.Ng et al.,2 0 1 2; Pasch et al.,2 0 1 6), as well as customer-perceived quality and satisfaction (e.g.Ghasemian et al.,2 0 1 1; Hirons et al.,1 9 9 8; Kimita et al.,2 0 0 9; Pasch et al., 2016; Pan and Nguyen, 2015). Sustainability aspects have also been examined (e.g.Chou et al.,2 0 1 5; Yang and Evans, 2019). Despite these extensive explorations, the role of PMS in the context of servitization remains underexplored, even though it holds critical importance in this domain (Cinquini et al., 2018). Existing research that has explored this topic emphasizes that PMS play various functions in servitization. PMS play a pivotal role in facilitating the planning and execution of service-based offerings, ensuring efficient service delivery (Meier et al., 2013). Moreover, PMS provide the necessary tools for justifying the adoption of servitization strategies, defining the scope and nature of services and maintaining effective control over the servitization process (Laine et al.,2 0 1 2). They enable companies to evaluate their progress in the servitization journey, comparing their performance internally or against external benchmarks to drive continuous improvement (Legnani and Cavalieri, 2012 ). Finally, PMS effectively manage contracts related to service offerings, providing valuable insights for assessing contract performance and ensuring the fulfillment of contractual obligations (Kumar et al.,2 0 0 6; Pascual et al., QRAM 22,3 292 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/qram/article-pdf/22/3/286/10299915/qram-11-2022-0185en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 2017). These studies have been conducted in the context of conventional servitization and do not consider the role of PMS in servitization from a multiactor perspective (Cinquini et al., 2022; Tenucci and Supino, 2020). The literature on servitization and PMS primarily focuses on the conventional role of PMS in planning and control within the company (e.g.Meier et al., 2013). Moreover, they portray PMS as a hierarchical and control-oriented system, characterized by mechanistic features (Laine et al., 2012). The effectiveness of hierarchical and control-oriented PMS, characterized by its mechanistic approach (Laine et al., 2012), seems increasingly constrained in the ecosystem setting (Adner, 2017). In this vein, a limited number of studies have delineated specific characteristics of PMS pertinent to ecosystems (e.g.Gomes et al., 2023; Micheli and Muctor, 2021; Ruggeriet al.,2 0 2 3). Ruggeri et al.(2023) study how digitalization, promoting the ambition of creating centralized knowledge for all actors, may lead to the risk of de-contextualizing that knowledge. The empirical research is focused on the performance measurement of the new product development process in a multidivisional company. The case highlights the possibility to align in a digital platform and promote a corporate accounting language game for the whole organization, favored the combination of divisional accounting language games.Micheli and Muctor (2021)undertook empirical research to investigate PMS’s role in executing strategies within ecosystems. They highlighted the necessity of continually adapting PMS to align with the dynamic ecosystem strategy. Furthermore, they argued that PMS should transcend their traditional role as data collection tools to instead capture and represent diverse perspectives within the ecosystem. Concurrently,Gomes et al.(2023) developed an empirically grounded framework that expanded the scope of PMS to address ecosystem strategies comprehensively. They underscored the importance of incorporating different perspectives, such as integrative, interdependence, regulative and phased learning, into the PMS to accommodate the complexities of ecosystem strategies. By doing so, the PMS can effectively support and enhance the pursuit of strategic goals within the ecosystem context. While these studies offer a valuable starting point for exploring the role of PMS in DS ecosystems, all these have predominantly adopted a top-down perspective when approaching ecosystem strategy. The complex reality of DS ecosystem, marked by the presence of higher levels of uncertainty (Datt/C19ee et al.,2 0 1 8), complicates focal companies’ efforts to enforce predefined roles and to develop a clear value blueprint beforehand (Baines et al., 2009; Coreynen et al., 2017). This complex reality of DS ecosystem creation calling for a more bottom-up approach,underlines the need for PMS to embody unique characteristics crucial for managing the DS ecosystem effectively (Autio, 2022). Specifically, PMS should be capable of supporting the entire DS ecosystem development process – encompassing initiation, momentum building and maturity phases– by managing uncertainty. This entails facilitating multisided dialogues and participatory decision-making processes, thereby enabling a collaborative and organic co-discovery of an ecosystem value blueprint and architecture that aligns with the needs and interests of all actors involved (Datt/C19ee et al.,2 0 1 8). 3. First, when developing a DS strategy, managers should consider the importance of PMS as potential enablers to the development of the DS strategy and of the ecosystem itself. Greater consideration should be given to the roles played by PMS in different stages of the servitization process in term of cooperation and coordination, collaboration and control ( Jacobides et al., 2018). Second, small and medium enterprises, such as those in the wine industry, should positively adopt a multiactor perspective. This is because offering advanced services requires a diverse range of knowledge and expertise. These services need to establish and foster collaborative partnerships with various actors within the supply chain to effectively pursue a servitization strategy. Through these collaborative efforts, they can pool their resources and expertise, thereby enhancing their capacity to provide advanced service offerings, offering comprehensive solutions and effectively meeting the evolving needs of their customers ( Fu et al., 2022). Leveraging multiactor platforms offers them the opportunity to bolster their visibility and competitive position within the globalized and digitized landscape. GR’s unique value proposition centers around providing integrated logistics solutions specifically tailored for the wine market. They offer advanced services including freight forwarding, warehousing and distribution, customs services and information technology. Their approach emphasizes customization and specialization, ensuring products are maintained in their original condition through a worldwide network. GR services are designed to offer secure, competitive access to the market with features like online monitoring, temperaturecontrolled facilities and dedicated handling techniques. Finally, the traditional approach to servitization views producers as the focal company leading the process through a top-down approach, assuming they can intentionally design the ecosystem. However, in contexts involving numerous small and independent actors, like the agri-food supply chain, this approach is less feasible due to the challenges of coordinating roles. Global leaders have successfully adopted a top-down implementation of DS, transitioning from a product-focused to a service-oriented approach. However, in complex contexts, like agri-food supply chains, a bottom-up approach is more suitable, as it allows for organic discovery of a collaborative architecture through open conversations among participants. This approach requires new actors to conceive strategy differently and acknowledges that ecosystems can emerge unpredictably with loosely connected actors. Traditional “plan-and-execute” strategies may be ineffective in such scenarios and new players as logistics companies can play a relevant role. First, we conducted a longitudinal case study of a specific logistics company as the primary focus, which has unique capabilities and networks with identifiable nodes and relationships. To enhance generalizability, future research could validate thefindings by including other actors and exploring diverse contexts. Confirmatory case studies could be used to test and validate the results. Second, while this study explicitly considered aspects related to multiactor collaboration, such as the ecosystem, we chose to analyze the promoter of one platform ecosystem as our unit of analysis. Future research could focus on a broader examination of the perspectives of other relevant organizations within the ecosystem, exploring not only the impact of DS on an organization’s PMS but also the collaborative dynamics among ecosystem partners. Third, it is important to note that this study does not explicitly investigate the specific impacts of servitization on the operational andfinancial performance of wine producers. While we have observed GR’s improvement infinancial results and its capability to expand into new markets and even acquire competitors in the same sector, further research is needed to gain a more comprehensive understanding of how various phases of servitization can impact performance outcomes for other actors within the ecosystem. Such future studies could shed more light on the relationship between servitization and the overall performance of these companies. Fourth, our study primarily focused on the initial stages of ecosystem emergence, specifically initiation and momentum. As ecosystems evolve through different lifecycle phases, particularly the maturity stage, different results and dynamics may emerge. Therefore, future research could delve into the impact of DS on organizations within mature ecosystems to gain a comprehensive understanding of their development and performance. Finally, the insights derived from this case study could serve as a foundational step in advancing the understanding of the role of PMS within emerging research areas. These include (i) the intersection of agri-food supply chain dynamics and PMS (Yadav et al., 2014), (ii) the correlation between collaboration and sustainability initiatives (Beske et al., 2014; Zhu et al.,2 0 1 8), (iii) the implications of uncertainty and risk management (Behzadi et al.,2 0 1 8; Borodin et al., 2016) and (iv) the exploration of resilience factors (Davis et al., 2021). The role of performance measure systems in DS landscape through multiactor collaboration has garnered significant interest across various domains including management, management accounting and service studies, yet the corresponding research is still in its nascent stage. IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON ENGINEERING MANAGEMENT, VOL. 71, 2024 4619 Digital Servitization and Business Model Innovation in SMEs: A Model to Escape From Market Disruption Sofia Lamperti , Angelo Cavallo , and Claudio Sassanelli Abstract—The progress and the adoption of digital technologies can rapidly make products, processes, and business models obsolete, until disrupting entire markets. In this context, small–medium enterprises (SMEs) operating in manufacturing are especially challenged due to their limited resources and smallness liabilities. Firms can implement, design, and deliver new smart and connected products that change the way they compete and trigger the provision of services—until redesigning the entire business model. However, little knowledge is available on how SMEs may effectively trigger and catalyze such transition. Using an interpretative research approach inspired by the design research methodology, in this article, we explore how SMEs may leverage digital servitization to escape from a disrupted market. Based on our findings, an original digital servitization model tailored for SMEs is proposed. Finally, the study provides a set of research and managerial implications on how SMEs can overcome market disruption in the manufacturing context through digital servitization and business model innovation. Index Terms —Business model innovation (BMI), digital servitization (DS), digital transition, lean start-up, small and medium enterprises (SMEs). I. INTRODUCTION O VER the years, digital technologies have pervasively affected the way through which companies operate and support their business model (BM)[1], altering the very nature of products, processes, and strategies[2] and disrupting market structures [3]. The integration and embedding of digital technologies often involve the core business of many companies, bringing into managers’ agendas a wide spectrum of business opportunities [4]. In this regard,Digital Servitization (DS) represents a possible answer to these ongoing challenges[6]. In the literature, DS has been defined as digital-enabled services relying on digital components embedded in physical products that enable new digital BMs [7], find novel ways of value cocreation, generate knowledge from data, improve the firm’s operational performance, and gain a competitive advantage over rivals[8], [9]. To support DS, manufacturing firms need to change their culture[10], adopt a more customer-centric view[11], change the design approach of these new systems[12], and adjust the other mechanisms of their BMs[13], [14], [15]. This promising, although emergent, research stream can already count on valuable research contributions. Some scholars have analyzed how DS may impact the supply chain[16]. Others have argued the adoption of a platform strategy for better use of DS (e.g.,[17]), while some have stressed the role of organizational change to accommodate such a new way to create value (e.g., [10], [18]). Still, other studies have called for additional research, in specific contexts [19], of the role of DS as an important driver for adapting, changing, and innovating a firm’s BM [20]. DS often goes along with business model innovation (BMI) intended as “designed, novel, nontrivial changes to the key elements of a firm’s BM and/or the architecture linking these elements” [19, p. 201]. Notwithstanding the promising efforts, the field currently shows a limited understanding of the relationship between the DS and BMI. This is especially true with reference to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) engaged in manufacturing[21], [22] that are facing the serious challenges of market disruption, intended as a market in decline, drastically altered by a new entry (i.e., new technologies and BMs) that has changed its competitive dynamics and structure[23], [24]. Despite SMEs being generally considered the engine of countries’ economies[25], scholars have been paying major attention to large corporations[26]. Enhancing the understanding of how manufacturing SMEs may undertake DS and BMI is important, given the following points. 1) Little is known about manufacturing SMEs specifically engaging with DS to cope with market disruption[23]. 2) Research is needed about the outer context that influences the time to adopt a service strategy[27], such as drastic changes in market structure. © 2023 The Authors. Given the above arguments, this article examines how DS can become an opportunity for an SME to escape from a disrupted market and how DS and BMI are connected to each other. To this aim, and by employing the design research methodology (DRM) [29], a model to guide SMEs through the DS journey to escape disrupted markets is proposed. An application case was conducted for its validation. Specifically, we investigated an SME located in Italy, originally operating in the (disrupted) broadcasting sector, that is beginning to provide new product–service solutions based on the Internet of Things (IoT) technologies. With this study, we provide two main contributions. First, we propose a DS model, extending previous research with reference to a specific and underinvestigated context: SMEs operating in a disrupted market. Second, this study contributes to the ongoing debate on the link between DS and BMI, showing how each step of the DS journey may involve BM changes. The rest of this article is organized as follows. In SectionII, the research context is presented as the basis of the investigation. In SectionIII, after showing the research methodology, the case is described. SectionIV introduces the results and SectionV discusses them. Finally, SectionVI provides a conclusion, focusing on the research’s value and its limitations. II. RESEARCH CONTEXT A. Digital Servitization First introduced in the seminal work of Vandermerwe and Rada [30], the term servitization refers to the process where firms set out to create greater value by developing new services and/or improving the existing ones. Servitization enables companies to move from a product-centric perspective toward the provision of integrated bundles consisting of both physical goods and intangible services—in the literature, often named product– service systems (PSSs)[31]. In this context, digital technologies constitute a strategic lever to foster knowledge exploitation along the PSSs’ lifecycle [32]. In particular, servitization finds, in the dynamicity of IoT analytics and artificial intelligence, the potential for innovative PSSs on an unprecedented scale[33]. Along with this evolution, a part of the servitization literature has moved toward the study of service provision enabled by digital technologies, giving rise to a substream of research known as DS [34], [35], [36], which is differentiated for the digital aspects and features of the services introduced. TableI collects some definitions of DS selected from the extant literature. Considering the objective of this research, the more inclusive definition is the one outlined by Paschou et al.[9]. It expresses DS as the development of new services and/or the improvement of the existing ones using digital technologies that can enable new BMs. B. The service transition is a complex matter for SMEs[38], [39], [40]. It is acknowledged that undertaking a servitization journey is less common in SMEs than in large firms[41].D u et o their smallness, SMEs (often) do not possess the knowledge or resources to successfully undertake this journey[13].O n the one hand, introducing or extending the service business may not generate the expected returns (service paradox)[42], discouraging manufacturing SMEs to undertake this journey. On the other hand, pursuing a digital transformation is not an easy matter, as the initial investment may appear unaffordable for an SME, together with the risk of overestimating the related benefits (digitalization paradox)[43]. In the literature, some scholars have provided different models to facilitate the (digital) servitization journey and help managers in their decision making[44]. For instance, Oliva and Kallenberg [45] discussed the product–service continuum and the process model for developing installed base service capabilities. Kindström and Kowalkowski [46] developed a four-stage model that drives companies through new services development in the manufacturing context. In addition, Sjödin et al.[43] proposed an agile cocreation process for DS in order to tackle the risk of digitalization. However, these models are not specifically targeted for manufacturing SMEs. Considering the complexity of the transition and the fact that SMEs represent 90% of businesses [47], more research is needed on how SMEs may go through the DS transition. DS and BMI A BM is the value architecture through which an organization creates, delivers, and captures value in a relationship with a network of exchange partners [20], [48], [49], [50].T h ei n - troduction of services enabled by digital means might change the manufacturing company’s value proposition and impact the other value mechanisms of the BM[51], [52]. Since the 1960s, practitioners have listed the distinctive ontological features of services, such as the traditional intangibility, heterogeneity, inseparability, and perishability [53], to which coproduction with customers and simultaneity have been added[54]. Some researchers highlighted the differences between new-service development and new product development. First, service innovation produces the enablers for the service and not the service itself [55]; second, it is important to make the new-service fit with the existing business architectures[56]. The literature seems to agree on the fact that DS may have disruptive effects on the BMs of product-oriented firms: it may affect the firm’s internal and external processes and interdependences, involving the reconfiguration of internal capabilities, value and pricing models, revenues and cost structures, and power and collaboration in the value system. From this perspective, Paiola and Gebauer [28] described how DS requires innovation in the firm’s BM. Moreover, considering the external context of analysis in this study, the innovation of the BM can result as an important factor in responding to crises linked to market disruptions as well as the recent COVID-19 pandemic[57], [58], [59], [60]. However, the literature shows that manufacturing SMEs rarely understand how they should reconfigure the elements of their BM to pursue this innovation[61] and offer digital services. Therefore, we deem that it can be relevant for practice to advance our knowledge on methods that can support SMEs in DS[27]. Advancing our understanding of DS and BMI for SMEs will provide important implications for research and practice. III. RESEARCH METHODOLOGY In this section, the research design is first presented, showing how the journey toward DS has been designed. Later, the methodology for the literature review and the market and case selection are explained. Finally, a section regarding the data collection and analysis outlines the logic used for connecting practical evidence to theoretical concepts. A. Research Design To address the main gaps dealing with the DS transition of SMEs supporting BMI, a research methodology was set and made appropriate for different research traditions[62] in the developmental process of creating the DS journey. Adapting the research approach used in the previous research in the servitization domain[12], [63], [64], this research is classified as interpretivism, entailing qualitative methods and inductive reasoning [65]. This approach is inspired by action research and aspires to contribute to theory development. Indeed, this research can be categorized as applied engineering based[66], implying theory/concept building, together with practice-based testing in an interactive way[67]. The model proposed by this research was tested in a real-world setting, following the guidelines of the systems development field[62]. Different methods (theory building, observation, and experimentation) have been adopted to develop the prototype of the model that constitutes, along the research process, both a proof-of-concept and a starting point for carrying on research in a qualitative iterative process[65]. Wrapping up the design of this research, leading to the proposition of a six-phase journey for DS supporting BMI, can be depicted, as shown in Fig.1, where the correspondence among the phases of this research approach and both the DRM framework [29] and design science research[68] that are used as main references is clarified. Three main stages, as shown in Fig.1, constitute the research process: the conceptualization stage, the theory-building and model development stage, and the validation stage. First, in the conceptualization part (which corresponds to the research clarification and the descriptive study I phase of DRM), an analysis of the current literature was conducted. It has to be noted that the objective of the study is not to provide a systematic literature review on the subject. Two valuable literature reviews already exist about DS: Paschou et al.[9], who specifically focused on defining the concept of DS and the convergence between servitization and digital technologies and Pirola et al.[33], who studied DS in the PSS domain and proposed a research agenda. Yet, these works were lacking in providing an overall and detailed vision of a DS journey. Therefore, both contributions, together with other studies, were instrumental to identify research gaps and to outline the major steps that are present along the journey to DS. These literature gaps were presented to the company selected for conducting this research. The company expressed a clear need for practical guidance toward the DS paradigm. Based on this need emerging from practice and on the literature analyzed, the three main streams of the research domain were identified, leading to the conceptualization of the DS journey model. More details on how the analysis was conducted and how the three research streams were identified are presented in SectionIII-B. In addition, an application case was conducted. We interviewed employees belonging to the same manufacturing company selected at the beginning of this research to explore their practical needs. The company renovated its BM through DS to escape from a critical scenario caused by a market disruption. Throughout the entire research, this company was selected as an appropriate purposive sample[69], as suggested by interpretative tradition, representative of a particular population, and allowing an idiographic (intensive) study of an individual case [65]. Details about the market and case selection are discussed in Section III-C, showing, also, how data were collected and analyzed. Through an interpretative study of the literature results, together with interactive analysis of the interviews, a six-phase model was created in the theory-building and model conceptualization stage (which corresponds to the prescriptive study phase of DRM). Finally, in the validation phase (which corresponds to the descriptive study II phase of DRM), this model was tested by interpreting the data from the application case and verifying and triangulating them with the theory on DS and BMI.
