According to Lorange (2009), the reality of contemporary shipping is that companies must possess a portfolio of value offerings that pay substantial attention to risk management and the reduction of operational costs, and which are based on the needs and demands of clients. For a maritime equipment manufacturer, such as the case company, these issues have several implications when approaching the maritime shipping industry with novel digital solutions. First, understanding the drivers of value becomes more important than before, as only a few dominant players control the majority of the value chain. Second, identifying who bears the operational costs or how they are distributed in the value chain incorporating digitalization into new value offerings. Third, incorporating a product–service systems logic into the company’s business model will facilitate advanced control and monitoring of stand-alone system solutions with a revenue stream based on systems sales (products sales) combined with spare parts and maintenance contracts (Kraus et al. 2022; Ziajka-Poznańska and Montewka 2021). To summarize (Fig. 2), we have identified three key historical events (development of automation system technologies, system integration solutions, and organizational change) that triggered path lock-in for the case company. We have also demonstrated how lock-in mechanisms, such as customer- and company-specific norms, routines, and practices combined with successful economic growth, were hinder - ing the case company’s capacity to choose an alternative path for future economic growth. 4.2 Path‐breaking mechanisms via digital servitization The findings discussed in this section progress from the data analysis of de-lockin events and actions taken by the case company that occurred from 2016 onward. The emergent data structure and progression of the data analysis are depicted in Fig. 3. The analysis identified four de-lock-in mechanisms: organizational reconfiguration, reconfiguration of value offerings, opportunity exploration, and knowledge reconfiguration. The emergence of these mechanisms and the actions taken by the company should be interpreted in light of the rapid transition of the maritime industry to a new digital operational paradigm. This digital paradigm is termed “shipping in the era of digitalization” (Ichimura et al. 2022), which is assumed to be more ground-breaking and volatile for the maritime industry than for other industries. Evidence for this argument is based on the assumption that vessel sensorization (Ichimura et al. 2022) and product-service-software systems (Solem et al. 2021) are providing a large array of data that can be used to optimize processes and operations (performance 397 1 3 Overcoming barriers to transformation in manufacturing firms.... management, capacity optimizations) that are assumed to transform the broader part of the maritime logistic value chain as well as the logic of the singular firm (Munim 2019; Sanchez-Gonzalez et al. 2019). Another aspect of the digital transformation of the shipping industry is the rapid increase of connectivity by information and communication technologies (ICT), which enable new forms of business logic that open up avenues for the novel use of shipping data, thereby demanding more networkbased work forms in which actors learn and co-create new knowledge and values (Ichimura et al. 2022; Tsvetkova and Hellström 2022). In addition to digitalization as a driving force, sustainability has received significantly increased attention, with the acknowledgment that new solutions must contribute to solving sustainability challenges. As one digital solutions manager stated during a webinar: So, talking about maritime, it is not a question of whether digitalization will impact our industry; it is commonly accepted that the adoption of digital solutions will drive us toward more efficient, safer, and greener operations. ... Green shipping is for sure one of the main drivers of this technology development. You have the adoption of technology related to alternative fuels, electrification, energy efficiency, and logistics. We have only just begun to see the start of the green shipping wave, and this will drive the adoption of digital solutions in our industry. The shipping industry is facing the need to reduce its global footprint by lower - ing its dependence on fossil fuels by investing in zero-emission energy. Digitalization is seen as important for achieving the green shift, with the focus on sustainability viewed as creating new business opportunities (Parida et al. 2019). Below, we present events and actions taken by the case company that represent path-breaking mechanisms of digital servitization. 4.2.1 Organizational reconfiguration In 2016, the case company created a new branch devoted to digital software ventures and simulator solutions as a deliberate tactic to interrupt its inherited routines and competencies following its product-oriented logic (Chen et al. 2011). The business logic of the case company was formed over decades of successfully introducing new products for the global maritime and offshore markets driven by in-house developments combined with offerings of new product features for a lower price than its competitors. The intention was to regain its scope of options by establishing a new company entity as a step toward the development of the next generation of digital products and services (Corporate Report, 2015). The new entity was also regarded as playing a significant role in breaking free from the dominant product-oriented organizational practice, as explained by a company manager: ... remember people are used to selling service agreements and propellers. Selling digital solutions is a whole other industry. The new entity was responsible for developing new digital solutions and associated technology alliances based on an already existing portfolio and revenue from 398 T. Brekke et al. 1 3 advanced data, software, and simulation products. The entity was staffed with people from the engineering software departments of the case company and was supported by a group of experienced sales people. The intention was to create better resource synergies (Sydow et al. 2012) between the case company and the new entity by utilizing its global customer support network to identify potential customers and use inherited routines and competencies from the parent company. In addition to these actions, the new company became responsible for building better connectiv - ity between analytics and product systems by permitting the large amount of shipsensor data to be used for more advanced analytical purposes and value offerings. Enabling automation sensor data was also seen as a necessary action in terms of developing the next generation of autonomous ship solutions, such as remote operational centers (ROC) and advanced predictive software analytics. This was noted by one sales manager: Well, we believe it will start by connecting the vessels. There is a lot of data being generated onboard vessels today. If captured, aggregated, and used in decision making, it can help owners and operators with significant cost sav - ings. The company’s effort to improve integration between software analytics and product systems was followed by the development of an ecosystem of software platforms for an emerging market of maritime applications. According to the case company, there are more than 500 maritime software applications targeting the shipping market, most of which fail to provide real business value for customers. There are several reasons for the low level of adoption. One reason highlighted by the case company is the lack of a data-sharing infrastructure between ship owners and operators that would enable faster digitalization of vessel operations. Other reasons are concerned with low data quality and functionality, which can in turn create cybersecurity risks and low reliability of operational management and decision making. According to the company CEO: We invest a lot of money to be within the latest compliances, we are one of the first companies to develop a type of approval for remote operations and data transfer, and we are always working for a safe setup to collect and share the data or enable a customer to share the data with whom they want to share them with. ... In this marketplace, we want to have a full toolkit with a variety of applications that cover all the needs a shipper has. The above quote emphasizes the company’s ambition to become the main digital connectivity provider for the maritime industry by offering a toolkit for utilizing data for software analytics based on company-specific competencies and routines for approved data-sharing methods. The quotation also highlights the company’s efforts to regain its scope of actions by organizational reconfiguration (e.g., new business units) and the transition from a product–service-logic to a product–service-software systems logic. 399 1 3 Overcoming barriers to transformation in manufacturing firms.... 4.2.2 Reconfiguration of value offerings The second identified path-breaking mechanism concerns the capability of the company to invent and introduce new value offerings for the maritime market within autonomous shipping. According to Munim (2019), major ship actors look for innovative solutions that can increase the demand for shipping by penetrating new mar - kets through a modal shift of cargo from road to sea. Autonomous ships are regarded as playing such a significant role as they allow ships to independently control their own actions while transporting goods from one port to another and also reduce operational costs (Ziajka-Poznańska & Montewka 2021). Findings from the analysis show that several events and actions taken by the company increased its maneuverability toward creating a new path trajectory based on autonomous ship solution offerings. Informants highlighted several research reports and analyses in the mid-2010s from which they drew lessons concerning the introduction of autonomous vehicles in the car market and the extent to which introducing such autonomy to the maritime industry could be significant. Based on these reports, a small group of engineers within the case company began exploring autonomy in the context of shipping by building some pilot tests and conducting a concept analysis. The group of engineers discovered that the company’s existing domain of knowledge and technologies formed an excellent foundation for integrating existing system solutions with new autonomous features. However, the group received little support from the company’s middle management, as autonomous solutions were regarded as an immature technology with no real customer cases and were many years away from being commercialized. However, despite reluctance on the part of middle management, news about the pilot tests caught the attention of a national retailer and logistics company, which asked the case company for help in building and operating an autonomous short shore carrier vessel. The retailer’s initiative was based on its zero-emission strategic ambition to reduce its carbon footprint by investing in new sustainable and zero-emission solutions. The request for assistance from such a large logistic retailer increased attention to and support from the company’s top management and justified the significantly larger investment in autonomy and digitalization by the case company. This, in turn, laid the groundwork for actions taken by the case company to assume a leading developmental role as a system integrator of autonomous solutions. As one business manager explained: ... we saw that we had a lot around dynamic position and navigation, and we had the communication systems as well. We saw that we maybe were the company that was best suited to go into this area. Our analysis demonstrated how forward-looking customers play a significant role in promoting the implementation of new technology. Gradually, a new path opportunity emerged as the case company began collaborating with a new and progressive customer—not a conservative maritime customer, but one focused mostly on cost reduction and risk management as the key driver of change. Identifying such early adopters became more critical for the case company, as doing so might confirm the reliability of the technology 400 T. Brekke et al. 1 3 and the existence of a market as well as serve as a means to explore unique value offerings for digital customers. According to Munim (2019), autonomous ship solutions consist of next-generation modular control systems and communications technology that enable wireless monitoring and control functions both on and off board. They also include advanced decision support systems that provides the capability to operate ships remotely under semi or fully autonomous control. It seems apparent that digitalization in terms of building autonomous solutions is a complex and demanding process, one that the following business manager char - acterized as a challenge related to the development of their current organizational routines and practices: ... just in the last year, we have made dramatic changes in the organization, autonomy is just one mechanism. Autonomy requires us to be leaner, better integrated, and adapted to be able to meet the demands of the future. Big change is happening internally; autonomy is a catalyst for that. The above quote underscores that autonomy is causing organizational change in the company by reconfiguring organizational routines and practices and fostering new forms of cross-departmental learning and knowledge-sharing activities aligned with unique customer needs (Kohtamäki et al. 2019; Sjödin et al. 2020). Skills required to adapt to changing demands and integrate new knowledge or insights into the broader organization seem to be essential for the case company to maintain its competitive advantage regarding the reconfiguration of value offerings (Solem et al. 2021). 4.2.3 Opportunity exploration In addition to these above-described path-breaking mechanisms, the analysis revealed how the case company explored new opportunities by forming an industrial ecosystem aimed at developing, testing, and implementing advanced digital product–service solutions (Adner 2017). According to Kohtamäki et al. (2019), digital servitization calls for better collaborations (accessing resources) and the integration of value offerings across the boundaries of firms to more comprehensively explore new market opportunities, which a singular firm cannot do alone. Another aspect concerns the regulatory acceptance of a different level of autonomy (from manned to fully autonomous) and competencies within ship compliance, such as monitoring and reporting national and international requirements. The development and introduction of autonomous systems proved to be a very demanding and complex process when it came to laws, national and international regulations, security, compliance, and operational risk management. As a maritime technology manufacturer, the case company did not possess the requisite knowledge nor did it have sufficient approval (compliance). Therefore, it launched a joint venture with a ship operator and compliance company. As one manager argued: ... the joint venture company was established to handle autonomous ships to operate them. It is a joint venture between the ship operator and us because we had to bring in some knowledge from shipping. They were supposed to feed 401 1 3 Overcoming barriers to transformation in manufacturing firms.... the back-office services through the shore control center, the body holding the certificates, the complement rules, and regulations. They would also feed the people working in the shore control center with knowledge. They have experienced ship officers and a logistic network throughout the world. So that was also something to take advantage of through that cooperation. Another action taken was the orchestration of an industrial ecosystem of actors. As the speed of digitalization of maritime shipping logistics was increasing and more competitors were entering the market, the case company decided, after a few years, to open its digital infrastructure and platforms to other users by signing a strategic partnership with several prominent maritime players. Its purpose in doing so was to increase the network effect of its digital infrastructure platforms by increasing data access to create more business opportunities. Still, the digital transformation and, in particular, ship autonomy remains in a very early phase of development. It has yet to be scaled into commercial activity, and most related initiatives are still in the pilot testing phase (see Munim 2019), which is aimed at addressing who is in the best position to build and scale autonomous solutions. According to the case company, there are only a few actors who have the capacities, knowledge, and skills needed to build, test, and implement such complex and advanced systems. The case company saw itself as well positioned to assume the leading role as an ecosystem orchestrator for autonomous solutions. This issue was highlighted by a sales director: ... so, we are one of those who are trying to take that position. Both in the form of system integration, but also in relation to digitalization ... data collection, data sharing, data analysis, that we also have a grip on the infrastructure. But we see that we will be wasting much time if we try to do everything ourselves without collaborating, and that means we need to go into open source, providing an open and common platform. This statement shows how successfully introducing digital solutions depends on the willingness of actors to share resources and their experience of getting something in return (Kamalaldin et al. 2021; Leminen et al. 2022), which demonstrates the delicate role played by the company in balancing and ensuring joint success. 4.2.4 Knowledge reconfiguration As mentioned in previous analyses, the maritime market primarily consists of conservative customers who mostly focus on cost reduction and risk management as the main value offerings. The case company quickly realized that selling advanced digital service solutions was different from selling products and maintenance contracts in a conservative maritime market. First, the main differences concern the high complexity of other systems collecting data from the vessel and building a new ROC that can operate and maneuver ships. Second, there were several different actors, such as technology suppliers, shipbuilders, ship owners, harbor owners, and operators, and different types of authorities who had to work together to solve many of 402 T. Brekke et al. 1 3 the challenges that accompany new innovative autonomous solutions. Overall, the complexity of the technology and the coordination of industrial actors and regulatory authorities necessitated the application of an experimental learning approach, one in which customer needs were foregrounded in the learning process as a source of reflection and adjustment of proposed solutions. As one sales manager stated: ... because no one has done that much digitalization yet, they understand they need to do something, but they do not understand what to do. Another challenge experienced by the partners was that the regulations and those who enforced them needed to be sufficiently prepared and mature to be able to take the full step from a manned ship to a fully unmanned ship. Regarding this issue, the sales director stated the following: There is no doubt, this is a maturity process both for the regulations, technology, sales, and deliveries. Vessels without people is something else than vessels with people. Building acceptance from authorities and regulatory bodies became a critical juncture for the project. A stepwise trial-and-error process was applied to gain experience, to learn, and to make necessary adjustments. The purpose was to test and validate the solutions on each level of autonomy (fully manned, crew on board, and unmanned) before being put into commercial use. The step-bystep approach allowed authorities to grant limited dispensations from the legislation so that testing could be carried out in a real environment. This process was reflected upon by a product manager: It is a long period of testing with real-life scenarios with a crew onboard and gradually allowing the automated systems to take over more and more of the operation, until the legislative bodies feel satisfied that it is a safe operation, and they will grant approval for the vessel. The step-by-step approach was also important for enabling the customers and actors to become engaged and co-create value, as well as to learn and correct errors from each of the development phases, as one sales director emphasized: It is a bottom-up process where you get together with the customer and enable them to create added value to get a sort of return on the investment. ... This is a step-by-step process. We build the different functions and operations based on experience, and of course we are making a lot of mistakes, but we try to learn from them. The case company, the partners, and the customers co-created a digital service innovation (Sjödin et al. 2020; Solem et al. 2021) by applying an experimental development process based on the step-by-step piloting and testing of solutions in close collaboration with customers and stakeholders. Such an experimental development process requires the actors to adapt their solutions in line with those of others for the purpose of both anticipating and complying with future laws and regulations so that the solution can meet the requirements of the customer. Such a co-creative 403 1 3 Overcoming barriers to transformation in manufacturing firms.... work arrangement affords participants a richer base of experience in that they are able to discuss and reflect on different perspectives concerning the best possible solutions (Westling et al. 2019). Furthermore, the quotations of this section emphasize how the company is reconfiguring its knowledge and learning processes by adapting and adding customer and stakeholder experiences into an co-creative work arrangement. Knowledge reconfiguration does not necessary modify the company’s underlying structure, such as technology platforms, customer segments, or business functions. Instead, knowledge reconfiguration increases the company’s capability to disrupt its “sticky” routines and practices that undermine growth—or to change strategic direction in the face of major industry transformation. Apart from the fact that the shipping market is characterized by conservatism, the shipping industry is also heavily regulated by national and international laws and regulations intended to guarantee the safety of crew and personnel. Accordingly, all new solutions must comply with these laws and regulations before they can be implemented. Therefore, introducing autonomy would entail significant changes and adaptations to existing laws and regulations before a higher level of autonomy (from manned to unmanned vessels) can become a reality. We employed an in-depth single case study to analyze a product-service-software company’s path dependencies and path-breaking mechanisms to answer the following research question: How does digital servitization enable path-dependent organizations to obtain new path formation? Our findings highlight several aspects of digital servitizationbased transformation and path-breaking mechanisms, and thereby contribute to sev - eral streams of literature. 6.1 Theoretical contributions First, we contribute to the digital servitization literature by applying the pathdependency lens to explain some of the challenges faced in implementing a digital servitization strategy in product manufacturing companies (Kamalaldin et al. 2021; Kohtamäki et al. 2022; Thomson et al. 2021). Second, our study explicated four path-breaking mechanisms of a manufacturing company: (1) organizational reconfiguration, (2) reconfiguration of 0 value offerings, (3) opportunity exploration, and (4) knowledge reconfiguration. These mechanisms are deployed to break free from the past focus solely on product manufacturing. The transition is far from easy, and manufacturers are advised to find their own effective ways to initiate such critical path-breaking mechanisms. By identifying path-breaking mechanisms in the context of digital servitization, we provided a micro-foundation-based explanation (Vergne and Durand 2011) for successful implementation of a digital servitization strategy, which is not very well understood and analyzed either in the digitalization servitization (Kothamäki et al. 2019; Rabetino et al. 2018) or path-dependence literature (Sydow et al. 2012). Third, our study revealed mechanisms that reinforce path dependency, such as historical events related to the creation of the product manufacturing business logic and the self-reinforcing mechanisms that generate lock-in (Arthur 1994; Grabher 1993; Sydow et al. 2012). Lastly, we contribute to the path dependency literature by identifying underlying mechanisms responsible for triggering a new path development, which explains in detail some of the evolving dialogue of path change as deliberate collective action (Garud et al. 2010; Sydow et al. 2012) or an external shock of some kind (Arthur 1994; David 2005). 408 T. Brekke et al. 1 3 6.2 Managerial implications Overall, product manufacturing is an industry that has faced significant digitalization during the past 2 decades. The transition is still ongoing—and accelerating. New digital technologies are providing expanded and novel opportunities for manufacturers to explore and exploit. The shift toward digital servitization has been challenging, with many companies continually struggling to change their strategies, business models, organizational structures, and culture. This study helped provide an under - standing of the events and actions that culminate in path dependency, from which it is difficult for manufacturing companies to break free. The study also outlined a clear framework for how manufacturing companies can adopt the identified pathbreaking mechanisms to help implement their own digital servitization strategy. The findings of this study yielded insights that may be of great value to practitioners and managers in seeking to understand the mechanisms of both path lock-in and path de-lock-in—not only on the level of individual firms but also at the interfirm and branch levels as well. Such enhanced understanding may also be crucial in terms of solving major sustainability-related challenges, some of which require faster digital transformation, such as transitioning from fossil fuels to zero-emission sources. Policymakers may also find the findings and contributions of this research useful, especially in conceptualizing how digital servitization might be employed to achieve climate goals and also which historical events could affect the capacity of the company to adapt and become more sustainable. 6.3 Limitations and suggestions for future research The present study was based on a case study of digital servitization within a single maritime manufacturing company. Although the empirical basis for our findings is fairly broad, we acknowledge that future research on autonomous solutions may be contingent on, for instance, industry differences. Cultural disparities and differing regulations between companies, company branches, and countries may all play a role in the design of business models aimed at delivering autonomous solutions. Consequently, we recommend that further research should account for such variations. In addition, we hope that future research will validate the path-dependence framework we have developed to lend support to our findings. Studying the mechanisms of path dependence (lock-in and path breaking) with respect to the development of autonomous solutions and the associated business model concept in other contexts could provide additional or novel insights that allow the generation of a more generalizable framework. Likewise, regulatory issues concerning the acceptance and implementation of autonomous solutions should be further investigated to better understand the transformational challenges involved in such processes. Furthermore, our study laid the foundation for future research on how to develop a path dependence-based understanding of digital servitization as well as why some companies may fail to develop a new path direction, while others succeed. Capturing the path phases and activities that equipment manufacturers undertake when more advanced digital transitions are to be achieved, such as complex systems of autonomous 409 1 3 Overcoming barriers to transformation in manufacturing firms.... solutions, will equip managers with more decisive knowledge and valuable insights into path-breaking mechanisms. Similarly, the actions required to reconfigure and transform a dominant business logic within an ecosystem of business communities can be further investigated in future studies. Doing so would open up new and interesting research avenues with regard to the ways in which actors can collaborate and co-create value offerings, and how constellations of ecosystems can capture value by balancing the roles of different ecosystem actors. However, there is limited understanding of the conditions under which small and medium- sized enterprises (SMEs) develop specific digital servitization busi - ness models, owing partly to the lack of an appropriate business model typology. In this study, we develop a generalizable and operationalizable classification of digital servitization business models and identify the environmental and organizational factors that drive such business model innovation. We apply a multinomial logistic regression framework to analyze a dataset of 326 responses from UK manufacturing SMEs, providing insight into how the seven studied factors differentiate among SMEs following different digital servitization business models and more traditional ones (pure product or “just” servitized). The study contributes to the scarce empirical research on digital servitization in SMEs and provides implications for policy and practice. KEYWORDS Digital servitization; digitalization; SMEs; business model typology; business model innovation (BMI) Introduction Since the emergence of the servitization concept in the late 1980s (Vandermerwe & Rada, 1988 ), the corresponding research stream has gained significant traction (Baines et al., 2009 ; Kowalkowski et al., 2017 ; Rabetino et al., 2018 ). Recently, the integration of digital technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), predictive analytics, and “smart” manufacturing, has enabled firms to develop sophisticated, “con - nected” products (Aliasghar et al., 2023 ; Kohtamäki et al., 2019 ; Porter & Heppelmann, 2014 ). In effect, these digital technologies foster servitization through digitalization (Coreynen et al., 2017 ). This emergent trend is increas - ingly being referred to as digital servitization . The growing research into this phenomenon has primarily focused on the process of digital servitization, identifying internal and external enablers and barriers, and the capabilities CONTACT Jawwad Z. There is a prevalent assumption that digital servitization amalgamates two interdependent yet inherently disruptive pro - cesses—servitization and digitalization (Chen et al., 2021 ). As such, it may entail a fundamental shift in the firm’s entire business model (Albats et al., 2023 ). This is often assumed in relevant definitions of digital servitization, such as that of Sjödin et al. ( 2020 ), who define it as the “transformation in processes, capabilities, and offerings within industrial firms to progressively create, deliver, and capture increased service value, arising from a broad range of enabling digital technologies” (p. 479). Despite increasing research interest, from a theoretical standpoint, it remains unclear which organizational and environmental contingencies are conducive to higher levels of digital servitization and to what extent they drive the development of different digital servitization business models (Coreynen et al., 2020 ; Favoretto et al., 2022 ; Kohtamäki et al., 2022 ). Additionally, the literature is far from conclusive about which service-based business models, and by extension, digital servitization business models, are more suitable under different conditions (Raddats et al., 2019 ). This lack of clarity may stem from the absence of an accepted, clear, and operationalizable typology of digital servitization business models. Furthermore, from a methodological standpoint, owing to the nascent stage of this line of research, there is a dearth of large-scale quantitative studies (Calabrese et al., 2019 ; Rabetino et al., 2021 ), a shortcoming that impedes a holistic understanding of the phenomenon. Finally, there is scholarly consensus that most insights generated to date are primarily relevant to large organizations (Rabetino et al., 2021 ), with their applicability to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) remaining ambig - uous. Despite a few notable exceptions (Coreynen et al., 2017 ; Kolagar et al., 2022 ; Lamperti et al., 2024 ), this oversight is concerning, particularly given that SMEs vastly outnumber large enterprises in almost all economies, accounting for 99 percent of manufacturing firms and 58 percent of employ - ment in the United Kingdom (Make, 2021 ), for instance. The literature suggests that the resource-constrained environments in which SMEs tend to operate have a bearing on business model development (Eggers, 2020 ). Resource scarcity reflects a key limitation of small firms and is commonly referred to as a “liability of smallness” (Aldrich & Auster, 1986 ). Scarcity is restrictive for business development, since it impedes investments toward innovative activities and venture growth (Choi et al., 2022 ). Liabilities of smallness may also constrain the development of new capabilities necessary for the realization of value-adding service activities, including the creation of distinct service organizations (Oliva et al., 2012 ) and the corresponding development of service-based business models (Albats et al., 2023 ). The processes and impact of digitalization and servitization are subject to considerable variation in SMEs (see Kowalkowski et al., 2013 ). For example, JOURNAL OF SMALL BUSINESS MANAGEMENT 2645 the pace of digitalization adoption is rather inconsistent (Li et al., 2018 ), suggesting that it requires a combination of complementary resources and capabilities (Eller et al., 2020 ; Nguyen et al., 2015 ). Regarding servitization, Böhm et al. ( 2017 ) found that size is an organizational precursor of service orientation and that smaller firms should not take service success for granted. Nonetheless, servitization offers SMEs the potential to counteract the influ - ence of environmental pressures that are, in theory, amplified due to their small(er) size (Ambroise et al., 2018 ). Given the lack of a comprehensive, widely accepted, and operationalizable typology of digital servitization business models, and against the backdrop of a limited focus on manufacturing SMEs, the aim of this work is to understand how certain environmental and organizational contingencies differentiate among SMEs following different digital servitization business models. To this end, we advance a business model typology that is based on the role of digital technologies in creating, delivering, and capturing value from product- service offerings and address the following research question: What environ - mental and organizational factors drive the development of different digital servitization business models by SMEs? We approach digital servitization from a business model innovation (BMI) perspective (Frank et al., 2019 ; Lamperti et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2023 ) and advance a generalizable and operationalizable digital servitization business model typology. We then theoretically motivate the relevance of seven salient contextual factors (two environmental and five organizational) that might play a role in the development of different business model types by manufacturing SMEs. To answer the research question, we apply a discrete choice modeling technique (multinomial logistic regression) using a dataset of 326 SME responses. This work makes the following contributions. First, it advances a typology of digital servitization business models and tests it in a quantitative study of UK manufacturing SMEs. It thus deepens our understanding of how specific organizational and environmental factors might influence the development of different business models, contributing to the emerging literature on digital servitization in SMEs. Second, it highlights nuanced distinctions in digital servitization adoption between micro businesses on the one hand and SMEs on the other. This study’s implications also inform managers in manufacturing SMEs when evaluating the feasibility of digital servitization, while policy - makers may be able to leverage these findings to develop inclusive policies aimed at empowering micro businesses and bridging the “digital divide” experienced within UK manufacturing. Theoretical background Background to servitization Since the introduction of the term “servitization” (Vandermerwe & Rada, 1988 ), the academic discourse surrounding the concept has expanded signifi - cantly, incorporating diverse perspectives over the last three decades (for comprehensive overviews, see Khanra et al., 2021 ; Kowalkowski et al., 2017 ; Rabetino et al., 2018 ; Raddats et al., 2019 ; Zhang & Banerji, 2017 ). Closely related to servitization, and occasionally used interchangeably, is the concept of product-service systems (PSS) (Tukker, 2004 ), typically used within engi - neering management. Both concepts emphasize the strategic bundling of goods and services to enhance customer value (Baines et al., 2007 , 2009 ; Vandermerwe & Rada, 1988 ). The underlying motivations for servitization are typically framed within competitive, economic, and demand-based imperatives (Cusumano et al., 2015 ; Oliva & Kallenberg, 2003 ; Raddats et al., 2016 ). However, despite its potential, servitization entails substantial invest - ment, with financial returns often remaining ambiguous or unrealized (Benedettini et al., 2017 ; Neely, 2008 ). This phenomenon, described as the “service paradox,” highlights the challenge of manufacturers to make services profitable (Gebauer et al., 2005 ). Building on the foundations of servitization and its emphasis on integrating goods and services, the advent of digital technologies has led to the emergence of digital servitization, which enables the delivery of remote, cost-effective digital services and further expands the potential for manufacturers to redefine value creation and delivery (Gebauer et al., 2021 ; Kohtamäki et al., 2019 ; Kowalkowski et al., 2022 ; Paschou et al., 2020 ). The nascent research on the phenomenon of digital servitization is growing rapidly, with several academic papers and journal special issues attempting to map and order the evolving domain (for example, Gebauer et al., 2021 ; Shen et al., 2023 ). Among the theoretical perspectives applied to digital servitization research, BMI stands out since it highlights the transformative role of digital technologies in rede - fining manufacturers’ business models (for example, Paiola & Gebauer, 2020 ). Business Model Innovation Business model innovation (BMI) is a holistic concept that reflects changes in the firm’s activity systems of value creation , capture , and delivery (Foss & Saebi, 2017 ). JOURNAL OF SMALL BUSINESS MANAGEMENT 2647 BMI posits that change may be driven by modifications in any activity, resulting in systemic adaptation across all systems (Clauss, 2017 ). This is particularly impor - tant in SMEs, since the convergent processes of digitalization and servitization may entail a redefinition of the firm’s entire business model (Chen et al., 2021 ; Gebauer et al., 2020 ). The outcome of this transition allows firms to revise the offering of an existing product or service, attract new customers, or expand the value provision to existing ones (Markides, 2006 ). As such, BMI expresses the firm’s interpretation of customer needs, and how these could be better satisfied (Randhawa et al., 2021 ). The importance of BMI for SMEs is depicted in research that examines its relevance in enabling strategic agility (Clauss et al., 2021 ) and strategic goal implementation (Heikkilä et al., 2018 ), with recent findings con - necting BMI to firm-level outcomes such as scaling (for example, Cavallo et al., 2019 ; Mihailova, 2023 ; Palmié et al., 2023 ). Moreover, BMI represents a redirection from product offerings to offerings with an increased service focus (Cheng & Wang, 2022 ; Kindström & Kowalkowski, 2015 ). In turn, the transition of SMEs to digital servitization can also be approached from a BMI perspective (Kolagar et al., 2022 ; Lamperti et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2023 ), while the provision of “smart” products and services might help these firms overcome the disruptive forces of the environment (Cavallo et al., 2023 ). A “suitable” business model is central to attaining desired firm-level outcomes (Foss & Saebi, 2017 ), particularly in SMEs (Candi & Kitagawa, 2022 ). It is commonly assumed that a business model creates value through an efficiency or a novelty focus, giving rise to two anchoring business model archetypes (Amit & Zott, 2001 ). Efficiency-focused business models reflect mechanisms employed by firms that promote transaction efficiencies (Zott & Amit, 2013 ) and decrease costs for all interested stakeholders (Pati et al., 2018 ). Conversely, business models that emphasize novelty introduce new means of economic exchange by exercising new connections with stake - holders and novel combinations of products, information, and services (Chen et al., 2022 ; Zott & Amit, 2007 ). Both design choices can coexist in any business model (Zott et al., 2011 ), as highlighted in the literature studying the firm’s transition to digital servitization (Chen et al., 2021 ). BMI in digital servitization has emerged as a rich thematic research area (Shen et al., 2023 ), with previous research investigating how digital tech - nologies are driving BMI (for example, Sjödin et al., 2021 ), business model change (for example, Friedrich et al., 2022 ) and the resulting benefits from this shift (for example, Moeuf et al., 2018 ; Tian et al., 2022 ). However, the conditions under which SMEs develop certain types of business models as opposed to others remain under-studied. Based on the above points, we adopt a BMI lens to study digital servitization in SMEs. A review of relevant business model descriptions and classifications follows. 2648 A. KARATZAS ET AL. Digital servitization business models Drawing from the product-service continuum, a long research tradition at the intersection of marketing and operations management has offered several typologies of services (see, for example, Mathieu, 2001 ) and product-service system offerings (see, for example, Tukker, 2004 ) of manufacturing firms. When it comes to service-oriented business models of manufacturers, an accepted, empirically derived typology is the one by Gebauer et al. ( 2010 ), who classified manufacturers into after-sales service providers, customer sup - port service providers, customer service providers, development partners, and outsourcing partners. In another attempt, and after synthesizing prior theore - tical and empirical knowledge, Huikkola and Kohtamäki ( 2018 ) defined four types of business models: product, service agreement, process-oriented, and performance-oriented. Although useful, these existing typologies (along with a plethora of others not outlined here) do not explicitly account for the increased technological sophistication of products that has culminated in digital servitization. Tangentially, as Favoretto et al. ( 2022 ) point out, “information and technology are not critical, differentiating elements in these typologies” (p. 116), a feature that poses limitations when considering value propositions that assume “dematerialized” physical goods and a central role for information. However, despite the lack of a widely accepted digital servitization business model typology, there exist two notable attempts in the right direction, describing “the architecture of the value creation, delivery, and capture mechanisms” (Teece, 2010 , p. 172) of digitally servitized manufacturers. The first typology was offered by Kohtamäki et al. ( 2022 ), who defined five business models: product, industrializer, integrated solution provider, out - come provider, and platform orchestrator. They derived their classification after reviewing four (grand) theories of the firm and other attempts to categorize (digital) servitization business models. The second typology was presented by Gebauer et al. ( 2020 ), who, as part of their empirically derived framework of digital servitization business model dynamics, defined four “logics:” hardware-plus, outcome-based, software, and platform. Nonetheless, the criticism of Favoretto et al. ( 2022 ) also applies to these typologies, as they are not centered explicitly on the role of digital technologies in creating, delivering, and capturing value. Another feature that hinders the holistic understanding of the phenomenon is that no typology has been tested and validated empirically in a large-N study, and it is hard to ascertain how one could operationalize them to make this endeavor feasible, by clearly and concisely distinguishing among the different types. Finally, both seem to assume a gradual advancement along the product-service continuum, even though the transition into different digital servitization business models can be nonlinear (Coreynen et al., 2017 ). A typology should allow for companies to JOURNAL OF SMALL BUSINESS MANAGEMENT 2649 become digitally servitized starting from different “vantage points,” an argu - ment advanced by Chen et al. ( 2021 ) based on an in-depth case study of a digitally servitized firm. Intuitively, it is possible for firms providing custo - mized solutions to transition into “smart” services, effectively becoming digi - talized solution providers, but it is also possible for non-servitized firms to digitalize their products and use the technology (like sensors, actuators, antennae) to offer digital services, without ever having offered “traditional” services (for example, repair and maintenance). Relevantly, the study of “plat - forms,” a business model that has garnered increased interest from digital servitization scholars (Cenamor et al., 2017 ), has shown that in certain indus - tries, it might be possible for a firm to become a platform provider without necessarily ever offering other services (like maintenance and repair) prior to this (Beverungen et al., 2021 ). Notwithstanding their constraints, both typologies influence the one we advance in this article. However, the main influence is an attempt with a somewhat different and more limited focus (namely, on the IoT), which we show can be readily extended and reliably operationalized. It was originally developed by Suppatvech et al. ( 2019 ) and stands out in the sense that the authors explicitly delineate the role of technology in enabling value creation and delivery. After an extensive systematic literature review, the authors inductively derived four “archetypes” of IoT-enabled business models (and several sub-types); they labeled them add-on , sharing , usage-based , and solu - tion-oriented . Relevantly, and as the authors’ real-world examples testify, this typology is not based on the assumption of a linear progression along the product-service continuum. Although the typology proposed by Suppatvech et al. ( 2019 ) focuses solely on one technology (specifically, IoT) and has not been empirically tested to date, the clarity with which the role of digital technology is elucidated forms the foundation of our extended, fully opera - tionalized typology. The main extension, inspired by the studies of Kohtamäki et al. ( 2019 , 2022 ) and Gebauer et al. Environmental and organizational determinants of digital servitization The strategy literature advocates that firms need to adapt their strategy to the environment they face (Teece, 2007 ); customer demands and needs, techno - logical shifts, and market dynamics can influence the choice of a business model, while the ability of the firm to adapt and modify its business model in response to environmental changes is crucial for success. Tangentially, 2650 A. KARATZAS ET AL. servitization scholars have also shown that the choice of a firm’s service strategy is dependent on the environment in which it operates (see Ambroise et al., 2018 ; Visnjic et al., 2019 ). For example, Visnjic et al. ( 2019 ) found that environmental uncertainty, reflected by several industry-level fac - tors, determines whether a manufacturer will develop and offer product- oriented or customer-oriented services, while Morgan et al. ( 2019 ) found that market conditions and customer demand need to be considered when building a digital servitization strategy. Given that manufacturing SMEs are likely to be weak vis-à-vis their customers and competitors, in this work, we consider two salient factors that capture these sources of environmental uncertainty: competitive intensity and demand unpredictability . Moreover, according to contingency theory (Lawrence & Lorsch, 1967 ), a firm’s choices are contingent upon the fit between its external environment on the one hand and its organizational structure and capabilities on the other (Coreynen et al., 2020 ; see also Miller, 1981 ). The argument is that there is no universally optimal strategy or business model; the right business model is the one that best aligns with both environmental and organizational contingen - cies. As such, in what follows, we also theoretically motivate the relevance of five organizational factors that might play a role in whether an SME develops a digital servitization business model: size , age , product complexity , digital maturity , and entrepreneurial orientation . Competitive intensity Competitive intensity refers to the level of competition a manufacturing SME faces from its immediate competitors (Bodlaj & Čater, 2019 ), and, according to contingency theory, it is a key driver of strategic decisions (see Hall, 1980 ). Businesses need to continuously assess their competitive landscape and adjust their business models accordingly in response to changes in competition to capture value and avoid growth traps (Berends et al., 2016 ; Saebi et al., 2017 ). This is because after-sales services such as repair, spare parts, and maintenance offer higher margins compared to product sales (Cohen, 2006 ) and constitute standard options for manufacturers seeking cost leadership and operational efficiency (Gebauer, 2008 ). This is even though many manufacturers encounter the “service paradox” (Gebauer et al., 2005 ) and need to amass a certain level of service activity beyond which services become profitable (Visnjic- Kastalli & Van Looy, 2013 ). On the other hand, where the market growth potential is high (so, cost-based competitive intensity is likely low), manufacturers might seek differentiation through customer-oriented ser - vices (Gebauer, 2008 ; Raddats et al., 2016 ; Visnjic et al., 2016 ). SMEs, specifically, are more likely to benefit from a move toward advanced service-based business models in contexts with low competitive intensity (Ambroise et al., 2018 ). Services provide an avenue for further business growth, and in today’s digitalized marketplace, so do digital services (Gebauer et al., 2020 ; Kohtamäki et al., 2020 ). As such, SMEs might consider a digital servitization business model to be suitable in a relatively less competitive environment, to differentiate themselves through innovative offerings (Coreynen et al., 2020 ). Demand unpredictability The second source of environmental uncertainty is demand unpredictability, which refers to the degree to which customer demand can be accurately predicted (Dröge et al., 2003 ). As customer needs evolve, firms must adapt to remain competitive in their environment. A significant challenge faced by many manufacturers is the unpredictability of demand for traditional services (for example, repair and maintenance), as customers tend to seek them only when equipment fails. This increases the unpredictability of product sales, makes it difficult to plan service visits or predict equipment failures, and impairs forecasting of spare parts and capacity planning. The emergence of digital servitization comes with significant advancements in digital technology that promise to circumvent the need for some labor-intensive services while allowing customer proximity at a distance. Advanced digital technologies such as IoT, sensors, digital twins, big data, and AI offer unprecedented opportu - nities to improve the predictability of demand for products and services (Raff et al., 2020 ) and deliver support remotely. Digital servitization can enable insights into customer needs, real-time usage patterns, and service perfor - mance, thereby improving demand forecasting and resource allocation. As such, servitized SMEs facing an unpredictable demand might consider intro - ducing digital technologies and developing a digital servitization business model to achieve a more efficient delivery of value to customers by, for 2652 A. KARATZAS ET AL. example, remotely diagnosing equipment failures and delivering predictive maintenance (Chen et al., 2021 ; Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). Firm size Firm size has been depicted as a critical determinant of managerial and organizational processes in SMEs (O’Regan & Ghobadian, 2004 ) and is of particular importance for business model development (Pucci et al., 2017 ). The “liabilities of smallness” may be more pronounced in smaller, “micro businesses” than in small or medium-sized enterprises (Drnevich & West, 2023 ). Smaller size reflects resource deficiencies and capability disadvantages that might fail to provide the fundamental basis for developing sophisticated business models (Gherhes et al., 2016 ). This suggests that micro businesses may be more selective in orchestrating scarce resources toward evolving opportunities (Sirén et al., 2017 ) and carefully proceed to incremental business model modifications that fit their resource profile (Brinckmann et al., 2010 ; Rosenbusch et al., 2011 ). Conversely, larger (small and medium-sized) man - ufacturers might have the capacity to allocate more productive resources to experiment with advanced business models. Firm age Firm age represents a precursor of innovation in SMEs, reflecting the nature of a firm’s resource stock (Rosenbusch et al., 2011 ). While younger, less established SMEs may be susceptible to the well-documented “liabilities of newness” (Gimenez-Fernandez et al., 2020 ), they may also be able to mobi - lize less specific yet highly deployable resources to develop novel business models (Chen & Hambrick, 1995 ) and use the learning advantage to fully utilize such mobility (Autio et al., 2000 ). On the other hand, mature SMEs may already have an established set of resources and operating routines (Amit & Schoemaker, 1993 ) that can be leveraged to transition toward more sophisticated business models. Yet, such resource and capability stocks may be harder to mobilize (Schreyögg & Kliesch-Eberl, 2007 ). Thus, although interesting theoretically, it is unclear whether younger or older firms are more likely to develop digital servitization business models. Product complexity A product or process is complex if it comprises many parts (or elements) that interact with each other in many ways (Vickery et al., 2016 ). Complex pro - ducts can create lucrative service opportunities, often leading to more profit - able, long-term service contracts due to their demand-based and economic motivations such as cost savings and service quality improvement (Raddats et al., 2016 ). This is due to the higher value and extended life cycle of complex products, necessitating ongoing service and maintenance. Moreover, product modularity in complex products can facilitate scalable, customized, service- JOURNAL OF SMALL BUSINESS MANAGEMENT 2653 oriented solutions, enhancing flexibility and reducing differentiation costs (Jovanovic et al., 2023 ). Complex products are also better candidates to be networked (Haug et al., 2023 ), since they require more information to ade - quately describe and understand, and their failure could severely impact the organization (Allmendinger & Lombreglia, 2005 ). Digital technologies can be used to capture and employ this information, transforming complex products into smart, connected ones (Porter & Heppelmann, 2014 ). By leveraging data capture and analytics, these smart technologies can enhance service offerings and improve overall decision-making capabilities (Raff et al., 2020 ). For SMEs, adopting digital technologies to manage complex product–service systems could lead to innovation in their business models. Such a change could enable SMEs to differentiate themselves in competitive markets, offering digitally enabled, flexible solutions that are tailored to specific customer needs. Digital maturity Digital maturity is synonymous to the degree of digital transformation of an organization. Digital technology adoption has an overarching impact across the organization’s processes, sales, and supply channels (Schwer et al., 2018 ; Urbach & Ahlemann, 2016 ) and entails a critical emphasis on new forms of customer interaction and proactive development of digital skills (Ostmeier & Strobel, 2022 ; Schwer et al., 2018 ). Although business models and technologi - cal innovation are intertwined, the concept of a business model is conceptually distinct from technology (Baden-Fuller & Haefliger, 2013 ). In SMEs, the established operational model is characterized by low levels of digital sophis - tication (Denicolai et al., 2021 ), with recent research suggesting that the success of digitalization initiatives may be contingent on the firm’s prior digital maturity level (Tronvoll et al., 2020 ). Framed in the above premises, in the case of digital servitization, the organization’s degree of digitalization represents a precursory condition that demonstrates the organization’s state to strategically develop and leverage new business models (Mikalef et al., 2019 ). As digital servitization represents a long-term strategy, digitally mature firms should have the processes in place to lead this transformation (Forliano et al., 2023 ; Kane et al., 2015 ). Entrepreneurial orientation Decisions related to business model innovation may be contingent on a firm’s strategic posture (Saebi et al., 2017 ). Entrepreneurial orientation demonstrates how ventures initiate actions in response to changes in the external environ - ment and reflects the propensity to innovate, take calculated risks, and proac - tively anticipate market and competitive behaviors (Wiklund & Shepherd, 2003 ). Varying degrees of entrepreneurial orientation may be pronounced in the manufacturing SME sector, with the most entrepreneurial of them being more likely to transition toward advanced business models. This is 2654 A. KARATZAS ET AL. a reasonable expectation, as the concepts of innovativeness and risk-taking dimensions are interlinked to experimentation (Ferreras-Méndez et al., 2021 ), and a firm’s proactive tendency suggests the capacity to create opportunities by market redefinition (Kreiser et al., 2013 ). JOURNAL OF SMALL BUSINESS MANAGEMENT 2655 The third step was to develop descriptors for each business model type, in lay language, which knowledgeable respondents from SMEs could use to self- classify their firm. Drafts of the model descriptors were reviewed for clarity, relevance, and comprehensiveness by six academic experts, with areas of expertise including servitization, digitalization, and business models. Four SME practitioners with extensive experience in manufacturing and technology firms also provided their views over short interviews. Their feedback helped us simplify the descriptors and make the respective business models clearly distinct, as well as make them directly relevant to SMEs. Crucially, the sharing category was absorbed in the description of the usage-based model, because it was suggested that the value creation and capture mechanisms of the under - lying model were also based on the “usage” of an asset. As such, and after several iterations, we ended up with four digital servitization business model types (and the respective descriptors). In the survey, we also included descrip - tors for a pure product (no services) category denoting SMEs that exclusively manufacture and sell a physical product, as well as a “ just” servitized category to capture manufacturers that offer complementary services, but digital tech - nologies play no role in their provision. All descriptors can be found in Appendix A1 . Upon suggestions from our panel of experts, we directed respondents to self-classify their SME’s “primary or established” business model, so our analysis could focus on the firms’ main line of business. Additionally, recog - nizing that a SME’s primary business model might share features of more than one of the types, we asked respondents to choose the descriptor that “best represents” their model. Finally, to avoid the possibility that participants classify their firm after reading solely the names of the business model types and not fully engaging with the textual descriptors, the names of the business models were hidden. However, there exist numerous different multi-item scales for each construct, so we needed to make a justified choice. Because all constructs had been previously used by servitization scholars, we preferred, where possible, scales that had worked well in past servitization survey-based studies. In addition, we preferred measures that had been used in research investigating SMEs (rather than large firms solely). More importantly, because: a) the mode of data collection was online panels of respondents organized by Qualtrics (see next section); and, b) the population of interest (SME owners and high-level managers) is generally considered to have limited time to reply to research 2656 A. KARATZAS ET AL. surveys, we sought scales that sufficiently captured the underlying concept, which were also relatively short. ( 2003 ), but to make it more relevant to our context, we added an item capturing the extent of predictability of product and/or service failures. Age was measured as the number of years since the establishment of the SME, while size was captured as a categorical variable that distinguished between micro businesses, small businesses, and medium- sized enterprises. All measures were self-reported by managers. Control variables Because some business models might be more feasible or appropriate in certain industries, it is necessary to rule out potential confounding effects that are driven by the industry in which SMEs operate. For example, for SMEs in the IT or telecoms industries, the platform business model might be relatively more feasible and promising (due to the higher levels of digitaliza - tion of the entire industry) than for SME manufacturers of construction equipment or components. At the same time, contextual factors such as the variability of the demand and competitive intensity might differ systematically across industries and, consequently, for the SMEs operating in them. We thus control for industry type in our models. The responses to the “primary industry” options provided in the survey (see Appendix A2 ) were grouped into five categories: transport, industrials, IT & telecoms, healthcare, and consumer goods. Industry type was captured as a categorical variable, entering the model as a set of “dummy” variables. Similarly, it is not uncommon for the business model of a firm to be dictated, or at least partly influenced, by the requirements of one or more of its business customers. Moreover, if a SME does not serve business customers (dealing only with individual consumers), it might be very inefficient for it to develop a sophisticated business model that guarantees a certain level of JOURNAL OF SMALL BUSINESS MANAGEMENT 2657 product performance ( solution-oriented ). At the same time, SMEs that do not cater to business clients clearly operate at the downstream end of supply chains, which suggests that they face a less variable (and possibly more predictable) demand due to the widely studied “bullwhip effect” (Wang & Disney, 2016 ). SMEs that serve business customers might also be different from those operating solely in consumer markets in terms of organizational factors such as product complexity and digital maturity; business customers might dictate relationship-specific investments that involve additional product features and upgrades in IT and digital infrastructure. To ameliorate the confounding influence of customer nature , we included in our models a dummy variable that takes the value of “1” for firms that served business customers and “0” otherwise. Sample and data collection process The entire survey instrument was first reviewed by two academic and two industry contacts with survey experience, and its final version can be found in Appendix A2 . To collect responses from appropriate informants, we commis - sioned Qualtrics, a market research company with access to several online panels of individuals willing to reply to research surveys for a fee. The use of online panels of participants (Porter et al., 2019 ) has increased in popularity in recent years, constituting a convenient way to reach relatively hard-to-get populations, such as managers in SMEs. We specified to Qualtrics that responses must be sourced from panels of business owners and managers (rather than consumer panels) who satisfy the following criteria: they must be owners or “high-level” employees of UK manufacturing SMEs, operating in industries with products of medium or high technology intensity (for example, electrical and electronic equipment, automotive, and so on, excluding industries such as jewelry, food and bev - erages, and paper and packaging). Because Qualtrics cannot guarantee that a research instrument will be exclusively distributed to members of the target population, certain questions in the survey instrument acted as automatic filters. For example, if an individual responded that they were currently work - ing in a company with more than 250 employees, or if they replied that their company operates in any industry other than the specified ones, they were automatically disqualified centrally by Qualtrics. Discussion and conclusions Summary of findings In this study, we advanced and applied a digital servitization business model typology after integrating relevant previous attempts. The four business model types were then operationalized in a way to enable a large-scale quantitative study. Descriptive statistics and a multinomial logistic regression analysis framework, using a sample of 326 responses from UK manufacturing SMEs, revealed that, overall, firms that follow digital servitization business models are larger, more digitally mature, more entrepreneurially oriented, and have built their business model around a relatively more complex product. Detailed analysis of the role of the environment also revealed the stark contrast between the business models followed by typical micro businesses on the one hand and typical small-to-medium sized enterprises on the other. As shown, sophisti - cated digital servitization business models might not be realistic options for most micro-businesses, unless they find themselves operating in a very stable environment with predictable demand and low competition. On the other hand, small and medium-sized enterprises are more likely than not to follow a digital servitization business model. Theoretical implications The findings have clear implications for the study of digital servitization in SMEs. First, the digital servitization business model typology advanced herein, and the textual descriptors developed collaboratively with academic and practitioner experts, comprise theoretical contributions in their own right. Scholars interested in digital servitization can adopt or adapt our typology to empirically study the prevalence of these business models in contexts other than UK manufacturing. Second, the business model typology (and respective descriptors) helped us enhance our understanding of the antecedents of digital servitization in the context of manufacturing SMEs. As such, this work extends the limited (but growing) research in this type of firms (Coreynen et al., 2020 ), answering related calls in the literature (Rabetino et al., 2021 ). More importantly, the methodological approach we followed produced insights of considerable nuance, since it revealed that different organizational and environmental contingencies pertinent to the manufacturing SME might have led them to 2670 A. KARATZAS ET AL. develop different types of business models (including the four digital servitiza - tion ones). By showing how the seven selected factors “differentiate” among the five business models, the findings highlight when and where manufactur - ing SMEs might prefer one type of business model over others. As such, this work can act as a benchmark to guide qualitative and/or quantitative studies in manufacturing SMEs and a starting point toward identifying the underlying mechanisms of digital servitization business model innovation, and, subse - quently, explaining differential SME performance. Third, the substantive differences between micro businesses, on the one hand, and small and medium-sized enterprises, on the other, should be positioned against the extant literature that suggests that manufac - turers tend to embrace digital servitization in response to competitive pressures (Morgan et al., 2019 ; Shen et al., 2023 ). When it comes to the broader SME sector, this claim does not seem to be supported in the case of micro businesses. The latter are more likely to develop a digital servitization business model in a relatively less uncertain environment of low competitive intensity and low demand unpredictability; otherwise, they prefer to remain pure product providers or “just” servitized. These (naturally) constrained firms in terms of resources and capabilities might be willing to risk a transition to digital servitization only when they face low levels of environmental uncertainty, wherein they can first build adequate intrafirm relational capital (Ritala et al., 2021 ) and face no urgency to reap quick returns. In such circumstances, a micro busi - ness may take advantage of the stable conditions to enable a slower, albeit more manageable, transition toward digital servitization, and facilitate the buildup of trust between itself and its customers. It is an open empirical question as to whether this preference of micro busi - nesses translates into performance improvements. Finally, this work theoretically bolsters the view of digital servitization as a form of BMI, in line with previous literature (Gebauer et al., 2020 ; Visnjic et al., 2016 ). The empirical application of the developed business model typology demonstrates the complex nature of business models and confirms that BMI is a valuable theoretical perspective that can further nurture the theory and practice of digital servitization (Shen et al., 2023 ). This comple - ments existing attempts to extend BMI theorization beyond the business model design stage (Cavallo et al., 2023 ; Lamperti et al., 2024 ). Implications for practice and policy Our study can assist practitioners in manufacturing SMEs when assessing the extent to which digital servitization is feasible for their company, given the environmental and organizational contingencies they face. For example, a solution-oriented business model might not make any sense if the product JOURNAL OF SMALL BUSINESS MANAGEMENT 2671 is not of sufficient complexity to be “connected” (Porter & Heppelmann, 2014 ). Meanwhile, SME owners and high-level managers need to evaluate their firm’s digital maturity and invest in initiatives that will digitalize internal processes before modifying the business model in its entirety. Although environmental uncertainty might not necessarily forbid certain digital serviti - zation business models, our work suggests that such models are potentially more feasible for small and medium-sized enterprises or micro businesses that find themselves in an environment with a relatively low competitive intensity and a predictable demand. This suggests that managers in such contexts may be able to direct resources to relatively risky strategic endeavors such as digital servitization and not toward operational-level measures to address competi - tion (like cutting purchasing costs) and demand unpredictability (like advanced forecasting technologies). Our findings also point toward a stark difference in technology adoption between micro businesses, on the one hand, and small and medium-sized enterprises, on the other, indirectly confirming the presence of a “digital divide” (van Dijk, 2020 ). This is consistent with extant literature suggesting that firm characteristics influence technology adoption (Arendt, 2008 ) and, by extension, digital servitization business models. For policymakers, this is of profound importance, since micro businesses represent a rapidly growing segment within UK manufacturing (Make, 2021 ), which is characterized by productivity levels of approximately 60 percent of their larger counterparts (UKRI, 2023 ). Although our study does not suggest that this difference in productivity is solely due to the differences in the rate of digital technology adoption, it suggests the need for a more inclusive policy framework that would allow micro businesses to become familiar with advanced digital tech - nologies and enhance the technological and digital skills of their employees. UK policymakers should empower micro businesses through the provision of training, access to financial capital, and technology support. Limitations and further research This work is not free from limitations. First, using the online panels of Qualtrics for data collection means that we can never be sure that all respondents come from the target population of high-level managers (or owners) of UK manufacturing SMEs. Like previous studies that have used this approach (Davis & Bendickson, 2021 ), we relied on the respondents’ word, the Qualtrics panel filters, a set of control questions, and post-hoc removal of problematic responses to assert membership to the target population. Future studies investigating digital servitization business models of SMEs should combine multiple data sources. This will comprise a good test of the credence of our findings. Tangentially, another direction toward validating and potentially generalizing our 2672 A. KARATZAS ET AL. findings would be by replicating this study in different countries, since our work was by design limited to the UK industrial context. The third limitation relates to the theoretical framing of this work. While we tried to investigate environmental and organizational contin - gencies that have saliently been considered relevant in the literature, there is no doubt that our attempt to maintain parsimony has left other interesting factors unexamined. Scholars should theoretically motivate and empirically test other factors that might play a role in SMEs’ choice of digital servitization business models. For example, certain customers might drive, or even “force,” important SME suppliers to follow a particular business model, which would enable the former to transfer certain risks and optimize their operations. More generally, this work did not directly address the influence that the business ecosystem might have on business model choice. For example, the availability (or lack thereof) of competent partners (technology, logistics, customer service, and so on) in the SME’s environment might, to some extent, determine the feasibility of certain usage-based, solution-oriented, and platform business models. Scholars should explicitly focus on such factors in future studies. Tangentially, scholars can adopt alternative conceptuali - zations (and operationalizations) of the factors that were considered herein. For example, treating EO as an individual- (Clark et al., 2024 ) and/or team-level (Covin et al., 2020 ) construct in the context of digitally servitized SMEs can generate nuanced multi-level insight into the role of entrepreneurship. Methodologically, our study is effectively a “snapshot” in time because it relies on cross-sectional data. As such, our estimates do not represent causal effects, and we have neither theorized upon nor tested any “mechanism” underlying the statistically significant coefficients. A natural extension of our study would comprise a longitudinal approach, compiling data from the same SMEs at certain points over an extended time window. Finally, this work did not focus on the outcomes of the different digital servitization business model types. Further research can investigate how the latter contribute toward scalability and profitability (Korkeamäki et al., 2021 ; Mihailova, 2023 ; Palmié et al., 2023 ) and compare amongst them. An inter - esting question is whether scaling one’s operations through the adoption of certain digital servitization business models can help the SME avoid the service paradox and make services profitable much faster. Keywords: AI | digital servitization | digitalization | socio- technical systems | sustainability | twin transition ABSTRACT As industrial sustainability concerns mount, manufacturers engaged in digital servitization grapple with the twin transition of configuring and implementing digital solutions to meet their customers' sustainability objectives. To address this challenge, a socio- technical systems theory- based framework is proposed. Drawing on case studies with three manufacturers undertaking digital servitization and on the sustainability, digital servitization, and socio- technical systems theory research, our framework highlights key processes in navigating the twin transition. It emphasizes the importance of contextual factors in defining a customer twin- transition roadmap, outlines key steps in reconfiguring technical and social subsystems, and stresses the joint optimization processes based on feedback and metrics. This systematic approach guides manufacturers in supporting their customers through the twin transition, emphasizing socio- technical systems and iterative processes for sustained success. Our findings contribute to the growing digital servitization and sustainability research by conceptualizing underlying processes in the twin transition and offering manufacturers practical insights. 1 | Introduction We want to take the customers on a journey starting with getting insights of the current state ...
