Such conditions make these boundary spanners highly vulnerable to role ambiguity ( Zablah et al., 2012 ), and in particular, ethical ambiguity. Role ambi - guity substantially affects both job stress and job performance ( Ingram et al., 2011 ). However, the holistic relationship between these con - structs and ethical leadership, particularly among customer contact employees in the hospitality industry, has yet to be examined. Given this void in our understanding, a question that remains to be addressed is how specifically does ethical leadership interact with ethical ambiguity and job stress to affect the performance quality of customer-contact individuals in the hospitality industry? Considering the increased call for examining hospitality industry ethics ( Lee and Tsang, 2013 ), coupled with hospitality employees ’ exposure to numerous ethical issues and the high incidence of stress among hospi - tality employees, the purpose of this paper is to examine ethical lead - ership ’ s influence on the ethical ambiguity, job stress and performance quality of customer-contact employees in the lodging segment of the hospitality industry. In the hospitality industry, leadership plays a key role in determining the overall performance and success of properties ( Dimitriou and DiGaetano, 2016 ). In particular, ethical leadership has been suggested as a leadership style for achieving this success ( Dimi - triou, 2018 ; Toytok and Kapusuzoglu, 2016 ) and has received attention in the hospitality industry (e.g., Garba et al., 2018 ; Kim and Brymer, 2011 ; Nicolaides, 2019 ; Qin et al., 2014 ). Yet, our understanding of how ethical leadership leads to positive results in the organization in the hospitality industry is limited. Therefore, this study contributes to the hospitality literature by clarifying the mechanisms by which a particular leadership style, ethical leadership, may be used to mitigate hospitality industry customer contact employee ethical ambiguity and job stress while simultaneously improving performance quality. In addition, by examining the aforementioned relationships, this research contributes to ethical decision-making theory by articulating management ’ s impact in the ethical decision-making process beyond its effects on simply ethical/unethical behavior by explaining how man - agement may also impact both job stress and performance quality. Currently, marketing and management models of ethical decision- making (cf., Jones, 1991 ; Schwartz, 2016 ) conclude with ethical/u - nethical behavior as the end outcome in the ethical decision-making process. Moreover, we contribute to EIT by better understanding a mecha - nism (i.e., ethical leadership) by which job stress may be affected in the context of ethical decision-making and behavior. While EIT claims job stress is an important outcome of unethical behavior in the organization, it does not detail intervening mechanisms for reducing this job stress. We also examine the effect of role ambiguity, more specifically a dimension of it, ethical ambiguity, in determining job stress and ulti - mately performance. Understanding the specific role of ethical ambi - guity provides opportunities for addressing it and subsequently reducing hospitality employee job stress and improving their performance qual - ity. In sum, the purpose of this paper is to better understand the specific leadership style (and accompanying leadership behaviors) conducive to reducing ethical ambiguity and ensuing job stress arising from ethical issues, and subsequently improve job performance among customer- contact employees in the hospitality industry. First, the theoretical foundation is provided, hypotheses are then offered, and the methodology is explained. Results are then provided. Finally, implications are discussed before providing research limitations and concluding with future research directions. 2. Theoretical foundation and research hypotheses This research draws from both ethical decision-making theory (cf., Schwartz, 2016 ) and ethical impact theory ( Promislo et al., 2013 ). Ethical decision-making theory in marketing and management (cf., Jones, 1991 ; Schwartz, 2016 ) explicates factors influencing individuals and the mechanisms by which they go about making decisions when faced with a moral dilemma. According to this theory, managers (considered a “ significant other ” ) can influence the ethical decision-making of employees. This is achieved primarily through the ethical example that managers set. Although the specific type of lead - ership exhibited by these managers is not clarified by ethical decision-making theory, behaviors exhibited by ethical leaders can positively affect subordinates ’ ethical behavior ( Bedi et al., 2016 ). Nor does this theory draw a relationship between ethical decision-making and job stress or performance. This is where ethical impact theory ap - plies. It suggests that unethical behaviors committed by one or more organizational members can impact several individuals (i.e., perpetra - tors, victims, witnesses, associated persons). This results in stress and trauma to these individuals, diminishing the well-being of those affected ( Promislo et al., 2013 ). We suggest (see Fig. 1 ) that perceived ethical leadership will have a negative influence on job stress, both directly and indirectly through ethical ambiguity (a little studied construct, but potentially important role stressor). Further, we believe that ethical leadership may positively impact performance quality both directly and indirectly via its influence on job stress. Given ethical leadership ’ s ability to lessen unethical behavior, we tie ethical leadership to job stress without directly exam - ining unethical behavior. The model suggests that ethical leadership should diminish job stress while enhancing performance quality. Consequently, we developed the hypotheses that follow. 2.1. Ethical leadership Leadership styles vary, with quite a few focusing on the support followers receive from leaders. For instance, by providing followers with intellectual stimulation and individual support, transformational leaders inspire them to sacrifice individual goals in pursuit of group goals ( Burns, 1978 ). Considerate leaders cultivate a supportive and friendly environment through their ability to incorporate the ideas and concerns of employees when providing critical resources, making decisions and collaborating with followers ( Rafferty and Griffin, 2006 ). To ensure followers develop and succeed, servant leaders attend to followers ’ needs before their own ( Greenleaf, 1977 ). Although ethical leadership can be practiced along with other styles of leadership, it is considered its own unique form of leadership ( Brown and Trevi ño, 2006 ; Den Hartog and Belschak, 2012 ). For instance, ser - vant leaders are similar to ethical leaders in that they both use compelling communication, practice role modeling, and are altruistic ( Brown and Trevi ño, 2006 ). Unlike ethical leaders, servant leaders minimize pride through self-reflection and emphasize the success of all organizational stakeholders ( Graham, 1991 ). Spiritual, authentic, transformational, and ethical leaders all possess integrity, each care for others, and all involve role modeling. However, while transformational leaders focus on vision, values, and intellectual incitement, spiritual leaders accentuate hope, faith and visioning, and ethical leaders are moral managers who execute ethical standards ( Brown and Trevi ño, 2006 ). Lastly, considerate leaders, like ethical leaders, can be trusted and listen to employee concerns ( House, 1971 ). Nonetheless, the considerate leader neither serves as a role model nor inspires normatively acceptable behavior among followers. Given the unique nature of ethical leader - ship, it deserves research attention, especially in the hotel industry where the increasing number of ethical scandals and related lawsuits are a clear result of the lack of its existence and implementation. Brown et al. (2005) define ethical leadership as the “ demonstration of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to fol - lowers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and deci - sion-making ” (p. 120). Ethical leaders serve as role models whose C.H. Schwepker Jr. and C.K. Dimitriou International Journal of Hospitality Management 94 (2021) 102860 3 followers view them as fair, honest, principled and trustworthy in - dividuals who are concerned not only about them, but the larger society as well ( Brown and Trevi ño, 2006 ). Free of bias and prejudice, they do not waver from their principles, never compromise their ethics, and continually put the needs of others first ( Brown and Mitchell, 2010 ). They communicate the importance of ethical behavior and then rein - force it by holding followers responsible through rewards and punish - ment ( Brown and Trevi ño, 2006 ). Although limited, ethical leadership has received attention in the hospitality industry (e.g., Dhar, 2016 ; Dimitriou and Schwepker, 2019 ; Garba et al., 2018 ). Below we review relevant research supporting our hypotheses. 2.2. Ethical leadership and ethical ambiguity We propose that ethical leadership is associated with job stress both directly and indirectly through ethical ambiguity. Ethical ambiguity, one of seven aspects encompassing role ambiguity, refers to uncertainty regarding how to deal with ethical situations in the workplace ( Singh and Rhoads, 1991 ). This is a unique aspect of role ambiguity that should be highlighted and understood given the negative impact of unethical service providers ’ actions on customer satisfaction ( Wong, 2000 ), customer loyalty, and retention ( Liang and Zhang, 2012 ). Dealing with various customer needs makes customer-contact employees extremely susceptible to role ambiguity ( Zablah et al., 2012 ), and consequently ethical ambiguity. According to ethical decision making theory, em - ployees are affected on the job by information from others ( Ferrell and Gresham, 1985 ). Managers provide one source of such information and play a pivotal role in shaping employee behaviors via role modeling ( Boekhorst, 2015 ). Through learning and socialization processes, customer-contact employees learn important organizational ethical values and are able to reduce role ambiguity ( Madlock and Chory, 2014 ). With its focus on the ethical aspects of employee behavior, this study isolates one particular subdimension of role ambiguity, ethical ambi - guity. Although ethical ambiguity has received little attention in the literature, its investigation stands to provide key insights to managing an important aspect of role ambiguity that is often overlooked. Leaders who provide followers with clear expectations are able to reduce followers ’ role ambiguity ( Tanner et al., 1993 ). More specifically there appears to be a positive correlation between ethical leadership and role clarifica - tion ( Kalshoven et al., 2011 ). Through discussion and communication with subordinates, leaders clarify ethical expectations, which reduces role ambiguity ( Schwepker and Hartline, 2005 ). Moreover, ethical leaders model appropriate ethical behavior, providing a guide for how followers should react to ethical dilemmas ( Brothers, 1991 ; Koh and Boo, 2001 ). When leaders are honest and trustworthy, characteristics of ethical leaders ( Brown and Trevino, 2006 ), role ambiguity among sub - ordinates is lessened ( Russ et al., 1998 ). Moreover, when leaders permit subordinates to sway decisions regarding their role, a behavior of ethical leaders, role ambiguity is reduced ( Teas, 1983 ; Agarwal and Ram - aswami, 1993 ). Although previous research has focused on the rela - tionship between leadership and role ambiguity, the findings suggest that H1 . Perceived ethical leadership behavior will negatively affect customer-contact employee ethical ambiguity. 2.3. Ethical ambiguity and job stress Job stress consists of physical and psychological responses that occur when an individual perceives personal resources are taxed ( Sager and Wilson, 1995 ), and he or she is unable to successfully cope with either the demands being made of him or her ( Lazarus and Folkman, 1984 ) or the demands of his/her environment ( Erkutlu and Chafra, 2006 ). It re - sults in job pressures, including tension, anxiety, and fatigue ( Jex, 1998 ). Role ambiguity is a key contributor to job stress ( Ingram et al., 2011 ). It is a type of hindrance-related stress ( Cavanaugh et al., 2000 ) which develops from employment circumstances that obstruct goal attainment ( LePine et al., 2005 ). Because of the varying needs of customers, and the challenges faced by firms in providing specific direction for attending to those needs, customer-contact employees are especially vulnerable to Fig. 1. Unclear roles (e.g., service to the customer versus to the organization) can increase job tension (Singh and Rhoads, 1991; Rhoads et al., 1994), which adds to job stress (Ingram et al., 2011). Since employees wish to comprehend expectations, activ - ities, and outcomes of tasks (Sawyer, 1992), job stress is likely to ensue from a lack of transparency in job duties and responsibilities (Ingram et al., 2011). It stands to reason that when clarity is lacking regarding what is ethical/unethical in performing one’s role (i.e., ethical ambi - guity exists), then customer-contact employees may experience job stress. This seems to be confirmed by a study of salespeople that found ethical ambiguity negatively related to job stress (Schwepker and Good, 2017). Consequently, it is expected that H2. Ethical ambiguity positively affects job stress among customer- contact employees. 2.4. Ethical leadership and job stress There is evidence suggesting a relationship between leadership and job stress in the hospitality industry. For instance, Erkutlu and Chafra’s (2006) study of boutique hotels in Turkey found a positive relationship between a leader’s use of positional power bases and subordinates’ job stress. Goswami and Dsilva’s (2019) study of six five-star hotels in Mumbai found that employee stress increases when leaders poorly communicate, show favoritism, and fail to properly recognize performance. Evidence also suggests that ethical leadership may directly affect job stress. Ethical leaders provide direction for how to behave ethically. Research shows that job stress can be reduced by providing clear job expectations (Tanner et al., 1993). Thus, by providing ethical expecta - tions, ethical leaders may reduce job stress. Research also finds that procedural and interpersonal justice are negatively associated with job stress (Judge and Colquitt, 2004). Given that ethical leaders strive to create a just environment, one would expect employees to experience less stress when their leader behaves ethically. Transformational lead - ership, which shares some elements in common with ethical leadership, was found to be negatively related to the job stress of customer contact service employees in the Indian hospitality industry (Gill et al., 2010). Closely related, when leaders hold a shared vision with subordinates, employee stress is reduced (Alimo-Metcalfe et al., 2008). Stronger evi - dence of a relationship between ethical leadership and job stress comes from empirical studies involving salespeople (Schwepker and Ingram, 2016), first-line technical support employees (Zhou et al., 2015), and employees from a variety of occupations in Turkey (Elci et al., 2012) all which found ethical leadership negatively related to job stress. Finally, in a meta-analysis examining ethical leadership, Bedi et al. (2016) found ethical leadership negatively related to follower work stress in the six studies that investigated this relationship in the sample analyzed. Given that customer-contact employees are not always under the continuous supervision of their leaders, particularly at times when they interact with customers, one might question the power of the ethical leader’s influence on subordinates’ job stress. However, because ethical leaders are able to clarify ethical expectations and create a just environment through their honesty and genuine care for employees, they should be able to reduce employee job stress. Therefore, it is suggested that H3. Perceived ethical leadership negatively affects customer-contact employees’ job stress. 2.5. Ethical leadership and performance quality Performance quality deals with the manner by which service is delivered. As service providers, customer-contact employees are ex - pected to express socially desirable emotions required by their employer during service interactions (Ashforth and Humphrey, 1993). Such emotions should help develop trust, show reliability and promptness, and provide a sense of individual attention (Hochschild, 1983). When performance is high, customer loyalty and satisfaction are anticipated to increase (Singh, 2000). Leadership involves activities to influence others to achieve common goals. Because people observe and imitate role models, ethical decision making theory predicts that through their behaviors, leaders can inspire others. Ethical leaders make appealing role models (Brown et al., 2005) whose ethical behavior is emulated by followers. Ethical decision-making theory indicates that individuals learn from and are influenced by those with whom they associate. Consequently, sub - ordinates will take their cues, including ethical cues, from their supe - riors and imitate the behavior they experience. Empirical evidence suggests that ethical leadership is positively related to customer-contact employee job performance. When em - ployees believe their leader is ethical, they generate more effort leading to improved job performance (Piccolo et al., 2010). A study of hospi - tality employees in China found a positive relationship between ethical leadership and customer-oriented behavior (Qin et al., 2014). Ethical leadership is likewise positively related to self-reported helping behavior (Newman et al., 2015). Research finds a positive relationship between ethical leadership and performance among commercial bank employees’ in China (Weng, 2014). However, some researchers have found factors such as psychological capital and follower-leader goal congruence (Bouckenooghe et al., 2015) and leader-member exchange, self-efficacy, and organization identification (Walumbwa et al., 2011) to mediate the ethical leadership performance relationship. Finally, two meta-analytic reviews of ethical leadership each found a positive rela - tionship between ethical leadership and job performance (Bedi et al., 2016; Ng and Feldman, 2015). This suggests H4. Perceived ethical leadership positively affects customer-contact employees’ performance quality. 2.6. Job stress and performance quality The relationship between job stress and job performance likely hinges on whether the stress is emanating from hindrance stressors or challenge stressors. The type of stressor (hinderance or challenge) de - termines its effect on performance through job stress. Challenge stressors are obstacles to be overcome to learn and accomplish, while hindrance stressors are the opposite, stressful demands that stifle growth and achievement (Cavanaugh et al., 2000). In a meta-analysis that included 82 studies involving 101 samples, LePine et al. (2005) found that hindrance stressors negatively affect job performance through their negative affect on strains (i.e., anxiety, exhaustion, depression, and burnout), while challenge stressors positively influence performance via motivation, but negatively through strains. Recall that these strains are the tangible expression of job stress (Jex, 1998). As a hindrance stressor, role ambiguity (and specifically ethical ambiguity) is anticipated to positively affect job stress, which should result in job stress negatively influencing performance quality. Strain can negatively affect job performance. Because strains are physically and emotionally draining, they negatively impact employees’ energy levels (Crawford et al., 2010). Lacking the intellectual and physical energy to effectively meet role obligations results in inadequate performance (Nahrgang et al., 2011). Moreover, hindrance stress di - minishes employees’ desire to continue investing in their employment relationship (Crawford et al., 2010). Particularly relevant to customer-contact employees, research finds that employees exposed to higher pressures (e.g., job stress) tend to become more aggressive and less helpful (Cohen, 1980). Specific to the hospitality industry, stress resulting from hindrance stressors (i.e., “bad” stress) was found to be negatively related to extra-role job performance among frontline em - ployees in the hotel industry in Turkey (Karatepe et al., 2018). Together, the evidence to date suggests that job stress resulting from hindrance stressors, such as ethical ambiguity, should have a negative impact on job performance. Thus, C.H. Methodology 3.1. Sample and data collection Mechanical Turk, a documented source for acquiring quality data ( Buhrmester et al., 2011 ), was used to survey self-identified hotel/motel customer-contact employees from across the United States during Autumn, 2016. These individuals were selected because of their sub - stantial influence on the customer experience. Regarded as “ part of the product ” ( Kotler et al., 2017, p. 269 ) and a way to differentiate one ’ s service ( Tsaur and Tang, 2013 ), customer-contact employees provide the means by which companies and customers interact. In part, their job is to make guests feel appreciated and relaxed ( Powers and Barrows, 2006 ). Participants who were offered to take the survey were provided a small monetary reward. Although 1,348 people accessed the survey, many were not allowed to complete it because they were eliminated by a question used to verify if they were a supervised customer-contact employee working in a hotel or motel. As such, 320 respondents (23.7%) completed the survey. The final sample consisted of 316 hotel/ motel customer-contact employees after eliminating four incomplete questionnaires (see Table 1 for respondent characteristics). The data analyzed in this paper is from a subset of the data collected during this survey. An insignificant finding when comparing early to late re - sponders across demographic and study variables in a time-trend extrapolation test (F = 1.16, significance F = 0.30) suggests nonre - sponse bias is unlikely to be an issue ( Armstrong and Overton, 1977 ). 3.2. Operationalization of study variables The ethical leadership (EL) measure we used was developed by Brown et al. (2005) . It assesses respondents ’ perceptions of the degree to which their supervising manager exhibits “ normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relationships, and the pro - motion of such conduct to followers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and decision-making ” ( Brown et al., 2005, p. 120 ). It is comprised of ten, five-point Likert-type scale items ranging from (1) "strongly disagree" to (5) "strongly agree" with higher scores indicating that respondents perceive their supervisor as practicing ethical leader - ship behaviors. Evidence suggests that customer-contact employees experience greater internal than external ambiguity ( Rhoads et al., 1994 ). This is likely to be true in the hospitality industry where these employees are not working outside the immediate organizational environment. Couple this with the fact that focusing on internal ethical ambiguity isolates ambiguity resulting from specific managerial actions (or lack thereof) that can be internally addressed, we used a four-item scale to assess internal ethical ambiguity (IEA) developed by Singh and Rhoads (1991) . Items are measured with a five-point Likert-type scale ranging from (1) “ very certain ” to (5) “ very uncertain. ” Higher scores signify more ethical ambiguity. A scale created by House and Rizzo (1972) and employed by Jar - amillo et al. (2009) and Netemeyer et al., 2004 , was used to measure job stress (JS). Respondents provided their degree of agreement to four items using a five-point Likert scale ranging from (1) "strongly disagree" to (5) "strongly agree." Performance Quality (PQ) was assessed with a reduced version of an instrument used to assess four components of service performance quality: trust, promptness, reliability and individualized attention ( Singh, 2000 ). Using a scale ranging from (1) “ much worse ” to (5) “ much better, ” respondents rated their recent performance level by evaluating how well they believe they performed in each of the four components relative to employees with a similar job position in their organization. Based on substantial empirical evidence, Schneider et al. (1996) report that employee self-reports of performance have “ validity ... and are significantly correlated with judgments made by observers external to the organization (e.g., customers)" (p. 697). This is particularly true when self-reports are acquired anonymously. Moreover, a meta-analysis by Churchill et al. (1985) came to the same conclusion and suggests that self-report performance measures have smaller error and less restriction of range than many objective performance measures. Several control variables (i.e., age, experience, education, gender) were included in the model. Experience was measured as total years of service experience. Education was assessed as (1) “ some high school ” ; (2) “ high school graduate ” ; (3) “ some college ” ; (4) “ college graduate ” ; (5) “ some graduate work ” , and (6) “ graduate degree ” . For gender, (1) is “ male ” and (2) is “ female ” . Both age ( Waldman and Avolio, 1986 ) and job experience ( McDaniel et al., 1988 ) are related to job performance, while gender, age, experience, and education are related to job stress ( Kavosi et al., 2018 ). Analysis and results To determine if multicollinearity was present, each construct ’ s variance inflation factor (VIF) was calculated. The highest VIF is 1.4 (R 2 = .30) for ethical ambiguity. When the VIF is near one multicollinearity is not considered a problem ( Hair et al., 2006 ). The hypotheses were examined using structural equation modeling with AMOS 25. The model ’ s fit statistics ( Table 5 ) show that the model adequately fits the data ( Hair et al., 2006 ). Results from the model testing indicate that each of the hypotheses should be accepted. H1 proposing that perceptions of ethical leadership negatively affect ethical ambiguity finds support (beta = -0.398, p < .001), indicating that when customer-contact employees perceive their supervisors as practicing ethical leadership behaviors, they experience less ethical ambiguity. As anticipated in H2, customer-contact employee increases in ethical am - biguity result in greater job stress (beta = .278, p < .001). As expected in H3, when customer-contact employees perceive their supervisor ’ s leadership behaviors as ethical, they experience less job stress (beta = -.108, p < .01). Perceptions of ethical leadership behavior positively affect customer-contact employee performance quality (H4) (beta = .375, p < .001), suggesting that the performance of customer-contact employees will improve when they perceive their supervisor practices ethical leadership behaviors. Finally, H5 is confirmed finding that job stress negatively affects performance quality (beta = -.285, p < .01). The performance quality of customer-contact employees experiencing job stress is likely to suffer. In terms of the control variables, females appear to experience less stress (beta = -.826, p < .001) (previous findings have been mixed on this - Kavosi et al., 2018 ), while age is positively related to performance quality (beta = .108, p < .05). Steps were then taken to ascertain if job stress mediates the rela - tionship between either ethical ambiguity and performance quality, or ethical leadership and performance quality, as well as whether ethical ambiguity mediates the relationship between ethical leadership and job stress. This involved conducting chi-square difference tests ( Bagozzi and Yi, 1988 ). For every model where the direct path between variable x 1 and variable y is significant, and the paths from x 1 to the mediator and from the mediator to variable y are significant, the constrained model is then compared to the unconstrained path model. Initially, a path was added to the model between ethical ambiguity and performance quality to ascertain if job stress acts as a mediator between the two variables. Since the path is not significant, the association between ethical ambi - guity and performance quality is mediated by job stress. A comparison was then made between the original model and a model devoid of a path between ethical leadership and performance quality. Having a χ 2 dif - ference of 37.5, 1 df, the models differ statistically significantly (p = .05), indicating the relationship between ethical leadership and per - formance quality is not mediated by job stress. Finally, in comparing models to determine if the relationship between ethical leadership and job stress is mediated by ethical ambiguity, a χ 2 difference of 10.9, 1 df, indicates the two models are statistically significantly different (p = .05), signifying that this relationship is not mediated by ethical ambiguity. 5. Discussion There is a need to reduce job stress among hospitality industry em - ployees to improve employee well-being. Similarly, with unethical behavior being a real concern among hospitality industry employees, measures taken to reduce it should be welcome. With this in mind, this research was conducted to understand if and how ethical leadership interacts with ethical ambiguity and job stress to affect the performance quality of customer-contact individuals in the hospitality industry. Our findings suggest that both job stress and unethical behavior may be reduced while simultaneously keeping the performance quality of hos - pitality industry providers at a high level, producing a win-win-win condition for customers, employees and the company. This research finds that the mechanism by which this may be achieved is ethical leadership. As such, this research provides important theoretical and managerial implications. 5.1. Theoretical contributions The significant finding for H1 has important theoretical implications. It adds to our knowledge of ethical leadership theory by finding that ethical ambiguity is an important outcome associated with ethical leadership behaviors. To our knowledge, ethical ambiguity has not heretofore been examined in the context of ethical leadership. By communicating ethical values and principles to customer-contact em - ployees, supervisors who practice ethical leadership behaviors can improve employees ’ understanding of ethical expectations, thus reducing their ethical ambiguity. Ethical decision-making models (cf., Jones, 1991) show that opportunity (i.e., a lack of ethical codes, ethical pol - icies, and punishment for unethical behavior) influences one’s ethical behavior. It appears that clarity regarding the organization’s ethical stance could play a critical role in this process. Although our results do not tie ethical ambiguity directly to the ethical decision-making process, they do tie ethical ambiguity to job stress. This provides additional insight regarding ethical impact theory that claims that stress results from unethical behavior in the organiza - tion. Lacking clarity regarding appropriate ethical behavior likely en - hances the opportunity for unethical behavior (Ferrell & Gresham 1985). Regardless, we learn that ethical ambiguity is apt to lead to stress in the context of ethical/unethical behavior in the organization, and importantly this stress can be reduced directly by ethical leadership. Thus, not only does unethical behavior impact work stress (as predicted by ethical impact theory), but stress can be reduced when managers demonstrate ethical leadership behavior. Further, this finding shows the effect of a supervisor’s ethical behavior on the mental and psychological state of employees, further contributing to our understanding of job stress. The positive finding in H4 between ethical leadership and perfor - mance quality suggests that outcomes beyond ethical decision-making, such as performance, may be impacted as part of the ethical decision- making process. Although we did not assess ethical/unethical behavior, we know that ethical leadership is positively related to ethical behavior (Bedi et al., 2016). Thus, we might anticipate improved employee performance as a result of more ethical decision-making (or at least in tandem with it). This likewise furthers our understanding of the types of performance that ethical leadership can positively impact by adding customer-contact employee service performance to the list, particularly in the lodging industry. This type of employee is not always under the constant watchful eye of a supervisor suggesting that this type of leadership has the ability to influence performance behavior from more than an “arm’s length” distance. Not only may job stress be harmful to employees, but this study also shows that it can negatively impact employee performance quality (H5), which ultimately negatively impacts the organization. Moreover, we learned that as a hindrance stressor, ethical ambiguity works through job stress to negatively affect job performance. This extends our un - derstanding of hinderance stressors by specifically explicating ethical ambiguity as a source of job stress. 5.2. Implications for practitioners While there are various types of leadership, ethical leaders practice normatively appropriate behavior with followers (Brown et al., 2005). Leaders who practice ethical leadership serve as role models, particu - larly as it pertains to ethical values and principles, by not only embodying these values and principles, but by communicating them to employees. Additionally, ethical leaders hold employees responsible by enforcing ethical policies and punishing unethical behavior. Through these actions, these leaders make their and the organization’s ethical expectations clear to followers. From a managerial standpoint, given the negative influence of role ambiguity on job-related outcomes (Jackson and Schuler, 1985: Singh, 1993), any means for reducing it should be welcome. Our finding for H1 suggests that ethical leadership may provide such a mechanism. Thus, by practicing ethical leadership behaviors, such as conducting oneself ethically, disciplining employees who behave unethically, conversing with employees about business ethics or values, and making sound ethical decisions on the job, supervising managers can reduce lodging industry customer-contact employees’ ethical ambiguity. The key is to put supervisors in place who practice ethical leadership behaviors. This can be accomplished by screening for ethical values and principles when hiring or promoting managers. For instance, assessment scales such as Reidenbach et al. (1991) multidimensional ethics scale could be used as a screening tool as part of the selection process. This tool provides insight regarding the moral judgment of individuals. Moreover, man - agement training should be sure to cover the organization’s ethical principles, codes, and values, and instill in managers the importance of communicating, modeling, and enforcing these among subordinates. The significant finding for H2 suggests that reducing customer- contact employees’ ethical ambiguity may reduce their job stress. Although ethical ambiguity has received little empirical attention, this finding supports a similar finding between ethical ambiguity and job stress among business-to-business salespeople (Schwepker and Good, 2017). From a managerial standpoint, it is important that actions be taken to reduce ethical ambiguity. Employees who are not sure how to handle ethical situations face uncertainty about how to behave, and how their actions might be received by management (e.g., “What if I get reprimanded for that? Will I get written up? Will I lose my job?”). This can result in undue tension. Consequently, customer-contact employees must be taught how to handle ethical issues at work, including the procedures for reporting colleagues’ unethical behavior. This could involve scenario training in which employees are presented with a possible ethical situation that could occur on the job and then asked how they would respond. Beyond simply asking employees how they would respond, they can be put in these hypothetical situations and asked to role-play how they would respond. Although companies often leave customer-contact employees out of the communication cycle (Kotler et al., 2017), as part of this training, the organization’s ethical expec - tations (i.e., ethical policies and codes) must be clearly communicated. Moreover, by posting ethical codes and policies in places that are highly visible to employees, they will be constantly reminded of these expec - tations. Lack of clear policies and rules ties employees’ hands, creates additional problems, and blocks the way to quick and effective responses that provide helpful solutions. Finally, as we learned in H1, ethical leadership behaviors likewise will help reduce employees’ ethical ambiguity. As expected in H3, ethical leadership has a significant negative effect on job stress. Consistent with previous studies (Dimitriou and Ducette, 2018), this finding underscores how much the behavior of hotel super - visors impacts the behavior of their subordinates. When employees know that they are dealing with a boss who values business ethics, does not engage in unethical mind games, does not hold double-standards, and appreciates honesty and integrity, then they have the peace of mind that they are in good hands and that should any issues arise, justice will prevail. Hence, by practicing ethical behaviors, supervisors can have a direct impact on the job stress experienced by customer-contact employees. H4 finds that customer-contact employees’ views of ethical leader - ship behavior is positively related to their performance quality. When customer-contact employees perceive their supervising manager is practicing ethical leadership behaviors they are better at instilling cus - tomer’s trust and confidence in their service, quickly providing service, performing dependably and accurately, and providing individualized attention to customers’ concerns. Because employees trust the ethical leader and believe that he or she will do what is right, they presumably are inclined to model this behavior and reciprocate by providing a quality service experience for their customers. Further, employees are motivated to perform at a high level when they are confident that the relationships between rewards, performance, and effort will be recog - nized (Vroom, 1964), which is likely to happen when employees trust their leader. Importantly then, supervising managers should practice ethical leadership behaviors to improve the performance quality of customer-contact employees. H5 indicates that job stress negatively influences customer-contact employees’ performance quality. Thus, job stress may be lessened and job performance improved by clearly outlining the expected customer- contact employee service behaviors, particularly those relating to behaving ethically. This may be accomplished through periodic training. Employees who are clear regarding ethical expectations will experience C.H. Schwepker Jr. and C.K. Dimitriou International Journal of Hospitality Management 94 (2021) 102860 9 less job stress and subsequently provide higher quality service. Ethical ambiguity, however, will lead to high job stress and poor performance quality, which may be reflected in bad hotel/motel customer reviews, low occupancy percentages, and a serious loss of customers. Hence, customer-contact employee job stress must be carefully managed, and attempts should be made to lessen chronic “bad” stress by clarifying ethical expectations. Besides providing direction for acting at the individual organiza - tional level, the results suggest that the hospitality industry overall could benefit from ethics training at the collegiate level. Dimitriou (2020) contended that the hospitality and tourism curriculum should be multicultural and place emphasis on business ethics education. A suc - cessful hospitality and tourism curriculum, apart from providing stu - dents with strong industry knowledge and experience, and teaching them excellent leadership and communication skills, also should focus on business ethics and professionalism, be aligned with current industry trends, and address the real-life situations that students will encounter as industry professionals. Students must learn to be respectful to one another, conduct their business in a responsible manner, and develop ethical decision-making skills (Dimitriou, 2020). In preparing tomor - row’s ethical leaders, course designers should collaborate with industry professionals to keep abreast of the hotel industry’s needs and prepare students accordingly (Dimitriou, 2014). To accomplish this, hands-on teaching is required where a variety of teaching methods and tech - niques should be implemented. Through case studies and scenario training, for example, collegiate hospitality programs can prepare stu - dents for how to handle commonly occurring ethical situations they may encounter in the hospitality industry. Many of these students will be future leaders in the hospitality industry, so preparing them to be ethical leaders will benefit the hospitality industry overall, as well as the indi - vidual organizations represented within it. 6. Limitations and directions for future research Like many studies, this one is not without certain limitations. This research is limited by its sample. All respondents were from the U.S. and employed by motels/hotels. More specifically, the sample may not accurately represent the feelings and perceptions of all lodging em - ployees, as those employed at the back of the house were not included. Consequently, it is challenging to state with precision the extent to which this study’s sample reflects the larger population of hotel/motel workers. While the characteristics of our sample appear similar to workers in the hospitality industry at large, prudence should be taken in generalizing the results to the hotel/motel industry. In 2016, the U.S. Bureau of Labor statistics reported that the median tenure in the hos - pitality industry was 2.2 years, the median age of accommodations workers was 39.8 years, women comprised 52.3% of workers in the hospitality industry and the median income in the hospitality industry was $27,456. In our sample, the median tenure is 2.0 years, the median age is 30 years, women comprised 47.6% of our sample and the median income is $30,000. Although similar, they are not identical. Second, like any study dealing with ethical issues, there is concern with the truthfulness and sincerity of respondents. However, re - spondents were never questioned about their own ethics, but rather their perception of the ethicalness of their supervising manager, as well as their clarity regarding ethical policies. In addition, by offering ano - nymity, the tendency for respondents to misrepresent their true feelings diminishes (Randall and Fernandes, 1991). Third, we did not examine management’s perspective on these issues (e.g., ethical leadership and performance quality). However, it should be noted that it is employees’ perception of their supervising manager’s behaviors that drives their attitudes and behaviors, regardless of how their manager might classify them. Fourth, this study involved a cross-sectional sample that can only measure a moment in time, limiting its ability to make causal inferences. Thus, the results may not be reflective of responses to a longitudinal study. Fifth, this study did not consider the differential impact that could result from different quality hotels. It is possible that higher quality hotels are more robustly staffed as opposed to lower quality hotels where each staff member may have more roles to complete. As such, future researchers may want to consider the moderating impact of hotel quality on the current findings. Finally, it is possible that the small compensation for completing this study may have attracted a sample that differs from one that is not compensated, or even more highly compensated. Nevertheless, with survey respondents frequently compensated today this would appear to create minimal concern. Further research in various countries, as well as in diverse hospitality and tourism segments, should be conducted to examine if the same re - sults will be yielded. Do customer-contact hotel/motel employees working in different nations or segments view the importance of ethical leadership as a key factor that affects their job stress and behavior? Additional studies should also place emphasis on and closely examine if there are any similarities or changes among the different categories and types of properties, such as comparing employees from four-star to two- star properties. Subsequent studies would be needed to investigate the managers’ perceptions and point of view and check to see if the results are consistent with how subordinates feel. It would also be worth investigating the motivational factors that drive customer-contact em - ployees to remain excited and enthusiastic about their job, regardless of the unethical, and unhealthy circumstances that surround their job. Further studies should also focus on how critical and beneficial teaching hospitality ethics in higher education is in terms of providing the hotel industry with responsible and ethical graduates. This would help hotel/ motel managers understand the damaging effects of unethical leader - ship, and set the path for a better future not only for the hotel/motel industry, but also for hospitality academia itself. Qualitative research studies would be valuable in shedding some light on any additional factors that might intensify and cause ethical ambiguity and job stress to hotel/motel employees and the measures they recommend that man - agers take in order to fix or, most preferably, eliminate these issues. Finally, will this study’s findings hold in other sectors of the hospitality industry, such as theme parks or other attractions? It is possible that employees in segments such as these who face different circumstances may respond differently and therefore should be investigated. sustainability Article Relationship of Ethical Leadership, Corporate Social Responsibility and Organizational Performance Min-Seong Kim and Brijesh Thapa * ID Department of Tourism, Recreation & Sport Management, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611-8208, USA; minseong@hhp.ufl.edu * Correspondence: bthapa@hhp.ufl.edu; Tel.: +1-352-294-1656 Received: 18 January 2018; Accepted: 6 February 2018; Published: 8 February 2018 Abstract: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has become a major part of the foodservice industry due to external forces which encourage enterprises’ responsiveness. In reality, consumers’ social concern influences their attitudes towards foodservice firms’ socially responsible practices and purchase decisions, thereby influencing senior management to react. Considering this issue, this study examines the impact of senior management’s ethical leadership in evaluating operational, commercial, and economic performances along with the mediating role of CSR in the foodservice industry. A conceptual model was formulated and empirically tested based on responses from 196 foodservice franchise firms in South Korea. The results indicated ethical leadership significantly influenced CSR and operational performance, while CSR also had a positive effect on operational and commercial performances. Additionally, operational performance had a significantly positive influence on commercial performance, which subsequently enhanced economic performance. Overall, the findings highlight the role that ethical leadership exhibited by senior management of foodservice franchises influenced initiation of CSR activities, which provide implications for research and industry practice and is outlined. Keywords: ethical leadership; corporate social responsibility; firm performance; foodservice 1. Introduction Corporate social responsibility (CSR) is referred to as “the broad array of strategies and operating practices that a company develops in its efforts to deal with and create relationships with its numerous stakeholders and the natural environment” [ 1] (p. 10). Since its origin, CSR has shifted from community-level activities (e.g., donation to local facilities or communities) to societal level initiatives (e.g., running a business that will not harm the environment or society) [2]. This expansion has been led by ideological thinking that an organization plays a role as a positive force for social change, as well as driven by the return on investment from CSR initiatives [3]. Moreover, CSR activities contribute to a firm’s social legitimacy, and enable appeal to its institutional environment’s socio-cultural norm [4,5]. Accordingly, the flow of sustained support and resources from external and internal stakeholders is ensured by social legitimacy [5], which ultimately enhances social and financial performances [6,7]. Despite the growing volume of research about the business perspectives of CSR, scholars from various business fields, including Strategy, Marketing, and Organizational Behavior have called for more research on internal (i.e., roles of employees or senior management) rather than external components that shape CSR initiatives in the first place [3,8]. Particularly, the role of senior management is central to understand external events [ 9], as they are largely driven by selective attention and interpretation, as well as the firm’s internal environment that includes management system and structure [ 10]. Based on the perceptions of specific events, senior management views social issues as opportunities or threats, and develops certain commitments to address such issues [11]. Sustainability 2018, 10, 447; doi:10.3390/su10020447 www.mdpi.com/journal/sustainability Sustainability 2018, 10, 447 2 of 16 Within the context of a franchise system, senior management plays a more significant role to encourage its franchisor and franchisees to initiate CSR practices than other industries [12], as they are required to comply with the established rules and standards by the franchise contract [ 13]. In essence, senior management’s operating philosophy motivates its franchise business to fulfill social goals and objectives, and advocates business engagement with a socially-oriented perspective [14]. Thus, it is necessary to assess the relationship between leadership possessed by senior management and organizational practices and/or strategies (e.g., CSR initiatives) [15]. Furthermore, recent literature has also highlighted a need to develop leadership theories with regards to the interrelationship among CSR, ethical leadership, and organizational performance [3,16]. A leadership theory based on ethical perspectives broadens notions about the conventional leader-subordinate relationship to the leader-stakeholder relationship. It is contended that “building and cultivating . . . ethically sound relations toward different stakeholders is an important responsibility of leaders in an interconnected stakeholder society” [17] (p. 101). Waldman, Siegel, and Javidan considered the inevitable need to bridge the CSR literature and leadership theory, and called for an integration of various leadership dimensions and practices [18]. Ethical leadership style brings socially-oriented changes and initiatives to an organization as a driver of CSR initiatives [19]. Ethical leadership means to “demonstrate integrity and high ethical standards, considerate and fair treatment of employees, and hold employees accountable for ethical conduct” [20] (p. 130). Even though ethical leadership is considered as a driver of organizational effectiveness (e.g., employee performance [21]; psychological empowerment [22]), there is a paucity of research that investigates how ethical leadership influences CSR’s effectiveness to generate desirable organizational outcomes. Previous studies have conducted the influences of CSR initiatives on stakeholders’ retention, loyalty, task performance, and support [3]. However, little is known about how senior management’s leadership style drives a firm’s CSR initiatives and enhances organizational consequences [ 3,19]. Given the growing interest in CSR as a global corporate priority, the influence of senior management leadership on CSR practices remains limited and needs further examination [ 3,19]. Applying the notions to strategic management and ethical leadership, senior management with strong ethical and responsible leadership tend to more likely create a socially responsible organizational culture. Since the perception of CSR is intangible, and may be vague, it needs to be implemented by tangible policies and processes (i.e., CSR activities) to realize its full performance [23]. The purpose of this study is to investigate how ethical leadership adopted by senior management of a firm influences its CSR activities and organizational outcomes. The study is placed within the context of foodservice franchise industry, and examines the perspectives from the franchise country’s headquarters based in Seoul, South Korea. In the Korean franchise industry, the system is generally comprised of a top-down decision-making process, and its structure is highly centralized and formalized with authority concentrated at the senior management level [24]. The top-down structure is typical in South Korean society as there is a power distance and hierarchy, which differs from those in western societies [25]. Hence, an examination will enhance knowledge and practices of a socially oriented food service franchising business in South Korea. 2. Literature Review 2.1. Franchise Industry Franchise is a business model where a franchisor grants to franchisees a right to distribute, sell, market, as well as produce the franchisor’s services and/or products. To operate a franchise business, the franchisees are in exchange for a fee under permission of the franchisor’s reputation, trademarks, name, and guidance such as techniques and procedures [13]. Franchising businesses are beneficial in the sense that franchisees can easily initiate their business with a small investment along with operational and technical skills learned by franchisors. On the other hand, franchisors can also reach rapid market growth and profitability using franchisees’ capital and labor force [26]. The relationship Sustainability 2018, 10, 447 3 of 16 between a franchisor and franchisee relies heavily on a franchise contract or agreement of two parties so that both should act in the brand’s interest [13,27]. The inter-dependent relationship under the franchise contract mutually benefits two parties (i.e., franchisor and franchisee) to be successful, as well as consider whether CSR activities can enhance performance [27]. Therefore, characteristic of the franchise industry offers a context to explore the influences of CSR activities on organizational performance. 2.2. Ethical Leadership Although organizations’ ethical behavior has shown rapid growth, there is no consensus on how to best study this phenomenon [28,29]. While ethical leadership has been a focal point, the concept still suffers from disintegration and confusion [28]. The research literature has attempted responses from a combination of empirical and philosophical standpoints [ 30], or prescriptive, philosophical perspectives [31]. However, “What exactly is ethical leadership?” has yet to be clearly defined [32]. In management studies, ethical leadership is defined as “the demonstration of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to followers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and decision-making” [20] (p. 120). Based on the approach, a construct of ethical leadership built on a 10-item “Ethical Leadership Scale (ELS)” has been advanced by Brown et al. [ 20]. The construct embraces the dimension of a leader as moral managers (i.e., who discuss ethical norms or standards with subordinates and offer proper punishments and rewards with regards to ethical/unethical behaviors), and a moral person (i.e., a caring, honest, and principled individual who makes balanced decisions) [ 20]. In addition, the construct includes critical aspects of other leadership components, such as integrity [33]. However, a moral-manager’s focus of ethical leadership differentiates it from other styles via its transactional nature [28]. On the basis of a social learning perspective, it has been argued that a leader influences the ethical conduct of subordinates through modelling [34]. Such modelling embraces a wide range of “psychological matching processes” [20] (p. 119) that encompasses observational imitation, learning, and identification. The social learning perspective proposes that anyone who can learn from a direct experience can also learn indirectly via observing the behaviors of others and their consequences [35]. In an organizational context, employees can learn via attention to their leader and emulate their values, attitudes, and behaviors [36]. Hence, ethical leaders can be more of a source of guidance and role model due to style and position. Moreover, employees can be taught about expected behaviors, and rewarded via role modelling. Therefore, a leader is of importance and a likely source of modelling by virtue of assigned status, role, success, and possessed power to influence and enforce behaviors and consequences, respectively [ 36]. The status and power of a leader can also enhance appeal, which makes subordinates pay more attention to the ethical leader’s modeled behaviors [36]. 2.3. Corporate Social Responsibility CSR has been conceptualized as the notion that corporations need to indirectly and directly contribute to the social welfare of a community and society through engagement in activities [37–39]. Although scholars have emphasized a corporate’s economic interest and activity, which benefits social goods over the past three decades (e.g., produce a product for community and consumers, whereas being profitable for the business and its stakeholders) [ 40], several diverse aspects of CSR have emerged [ 41–43]. For example, Carroll [ 44,45] conceptualizes CSR as a multi-dimensional construct model [43]. The pyramid model embraces four responsibilities: “economic, legal, ethical, and philanthropic.” This model considers economic responsibility as the most fundamental aspect of CSR initiatives, and a firm pursues the highest level of CSR aspect with advancement towards philanthropic CSR [44,45]. Based on the multifaceted CSR model, the concept of economic responsibility relates to a firm’s engagement to maximize benefits for the business and its shareholders [46]. Moreover, a firm’s legal responsibility is associated with engagement in a code of ethics or fair rules that “embody moral Sustainability 2018, 10, 447 4 of 16 standards, norms or expectations that reflect a concern for what stockholders view as fair or just” [45] (p. 41). Legal responsibility is based on the principles of utilitarianism and justice [ 45]. Basically, ethical responsibility is related to a firm’s involvement in social morality at a level that exceeds legal responsibility. As the highest order of CSR initiatives, philanthropic responsibility can be voluntary and demonstrate ideal corporate citizenship. Although the environmental dimension of CSR was not included in Carroll’s CSR model, it needs to be considered. Environmental responsibility refers to a firm’s voluntary activities that demonstrate the inclusion of environmental concerns in interactions with various stakeholders (e.g., non-profit organization, government, consumer, etc.) and in business operations [42]. The multi-dimensional CSR model is a beneficial tool as it embraces the different aspects and levels of activities, and provides a comprehensive assessment of initiatives [45]. The model has also been employed to investigate CSR issues in the restaurant industry [43,47,48], while research has not assessed the direct effect on performance of food service franchises, despite the significant influence reported in various contexts [43]. 2.4. Organizational Performance Previous research has used financial, economic, stock market measures, or rate of market share measures to investigate marketing strategies’ influence on organizational performance [ 49]. However, several empirical studies as well as theoretical models have indicated that effective economic performance can be achieved with improvement of two separate aspects of organizational performance—operational (i.e., production stage-oriented) and commercial performance (i.e., market stage-oriented) [50,51]. At the first level of product management, operational performance is considered as a major indicator that incorporate components associated with the improvement of efficiency in procedures (e.g., a firm’s innovation capacity, procedures’ flexibility and time, and product quality [ 49,52]). Thus, the operational performance construct reflects the effectiveness of the operation systems and production with regards to quality, speed, flexibility, costs, etc. [50]. At the second level, organizational performance needs to embrace other indicators, such as firm’s capacity to manage and improve its connections to suppliers, customers, local community, and society [53]. Therefore, a firm’s commercial performance is defined as its commercial function’s effectiveness. It reflects the firm’s ability to meet clients’ demands, and align its behavior and commercial offers with societal values in consideration [54]. Ultimately, the financial and economic performance is a reflection of all the monetary consequences of a firm’s economic activities. As the most traditionally used variable, economic performance reflects measures based on a firm’s profit after tax, economic consequences, sales growth, or market share [55]. This study proposes that a firm’s CSR initiatives may have significant positive results for its procedures that contribute to the enhancement of operational efficiency (i.e., operational performance). This results in improvement of relationships with stakeholders via establishment of responsible attitudes toward society and the environment (i.e., commercial performance). Finally, the operational and commercial performances can improve firm’s economic benefits [49]. Prior research has mainly employed financial performance measures as a consequence of a firm’s socially-oriented activities, which has led to inconsistent results [49]. Hence, more empirical evidence on the interrelationships among the multi-dimensions of organizational performance is needed [55]. Additionally, there is lack of literature with respect to the influence of CSR on product and market-oriented performance, and subsequent implications to adopt initiatives [56]. Consequently, division of organizational performance as independent dimensions can be more effective to examine the hierarchical influences of CSR on organizational performance. 2.5. Research Hypothesis Development Within an organization, a leader focuses attention on ethical codes via frequent communications about the ethical and social aspects of the firm’s business activities [57]. In accordance with the ethical aspects of leadership, senior management may establish clear and relevant societal responsibilities Sustainability 2018, 10, 447 5 of 16 (e.g., CSR activities), and encourage employees to initiate them [58]. Thus, this study assumes that ethical leadership can be a driver of CSR activities based on social learning. The following hypothesis is formulated: Hypothesis 1 (H1). Ethical leadership is positively associated with CSR. A leaders’ strategic choice, which is based on their personalities, values, and experiences influences a firm’s performance [23]. Essentially, leaders’ ethical attributes greatly affect their strategic choices and decisions [23,59]. Thus, a firm and its performances can be seen as reflections of ethical characteristics embodied by the leader [ 60]. Empirical research based on this notion indicates that leaders’ ethical leadership has been significantly associated with organizational performance and in different organizational life cycles [61]. Accordingly, the following hypotheses is outlined: Hypothesis 2 (H2). Ethical leadership is positively associated with operational performance. Hypothesis 3 (H3). Ethical leadership is positively associated with commercial performance. Several empirical studies have examined the impact of CSR on firm performance with a wide range of positive consequences over the past three decades [62,63]. The fundamental notion is that CSR enhances performance with the improvement of relationships with other stakeholders, which affects expenses and revenues [63]. From a revenue perspective (or commercial standpoint), an enhanced stakeholder relationship attracts new investment opportunities and customers that enables a firm to charge a premium price [ 64]. From a cost perspective (or operational standpoint) via enhanced relationship, trust leads to decrease in certain processes and transaction costs. CSR activities enhance financial performance and can induce consumers to purchase products and services [ 63]. More specifically, targeting socially-oriented consumers enables firms to maximize their profits as CSR activities may directly affect satisfaction and loyalty [65]. Therefore, CSR initiatives are advantageous to operational, commercial, and economic performances. The following hypotheses are noted: Hypothesis 4 (H4). CSR is positively associated with operational performance. Hypothesis 5 (H5). CSR is positively associated with commercial performance. Hypothesis 6 (H6). CSR is positively associated with economic performance. Prior literature has investigated CSR initiatives’ organizational outcomes, corporate image, corporate reputation, and core competences [66]. This study is based on a multidimensional approach of a firm’s performance which proposes that CSR activities may have significant positive outcomes and contribute to increase in operational efficiency. A firm may also enhance its relationship with stakeholders with the adoption of socially responsible behaviors. Such operational and commercial performances may allow a firm to enhance its economic consequences. To measure organizational performance, Hubbard [ 67] suggests a hierarchical organizational performance model to link the micro to the macro components of organizational performance (i.e., operational activities to market performance). According to Hubbard [ 67], business activities that embrace social, economic, and environmental perspectives will influence different levels and direction of a firm’s performance since they affect each operation differently due to their complexity. Hence, as demonstrated by Fraj-Andrés et al. [49], this study also seeks to identify the dimensions of organizational performance derived from applying CSR initiatives that benefit firms. The following hypotheses are proposed: Hypothesis 7 (H7). Operational performance is positively associated with commercial performance. Hypothesis 8 (H8). Operational performance is positively associated with economic performance. Sustainability 2018, 10, 447 6 of 16 Hypothesis 9 (H9). Commercial performance is positively associated with economic performance. Under strong ethical leadership, a firm is more likely to engage in CSR practices since leaders not only implement CSR activities with determination and consistency, but also support initiatives with solid actions, which in turn enhances the firm’s performance over time [68]. Since CSR is not a short-term engagement project, hence it needs to be formed from strong ethical leadership. In practice, ethical leaders will invest and implement more in CSR initiatives which can positively affect a firm’s performance [69]. However, if a leader with strong ethical leadership does not engage in CSR activities, his/her leadership style cannot directly enhance firm performance [68]. Based on the notion, ethical leadership will indirectly influence firm performance through CSR activities. Hence, the following hypothesis is formulated: Hypothesis 10 (H10). CSR mediates the influence of ethical leadership on organizational performance. 3. Methods 3.1. Sample and Data Collection The unit of analysis consisted of international and domestic foodservice franchising firms’ country level headquarters (e.g., Olive Garden, Dunkin Donuts, Lotteria, Pizza Hut, etc.) in South Korea. Since the foodservice industry account for 72.4% of the Korean franchise industry [70], this study only focused on foodservice franchise firms. Firms were selected from the 2015 Korean Franchise General Control registry released by the Korea Fair Trade Commission. Only foodservice franchising firms that had implemented CSR practices (e.g., support fair trade practices; support the welfare of communities) were selected. A total of 418 were compiled, and the lead author contacted representatives at each firm. The objectives of the study were explained to each contact, and upon approval were subsequently requested to distribute the questionnaire (i.e., translated from English to Korean by three bilingual professionals) to their middle-level managers at their headquarters. All completed questionnaires were collected after two weeks during October 2015. Following removal of several responses due to missing information, a final sample of 196 respondents was achieved with a response rate of 46.9 percent. The rationale to focus on middle-level management is due to the fact that they are immersed in the operational aspects of business practices, and are also most suited to evaluate senior leadership and organizational performance. Additionally, middle-level managers are usually requested to complete various questionnaires as representatives of their respective companies [ 71]. In the questionnaire, each manager was requested to evaluate their senior management’s ethical leadership style as they are considered to be the primary source to develop and initiate strategies or activities [72]. In addition, participants were asked to assess the business’s performance based on its internal and external reports in terms of finances and CSR. 3.2. Operationalization of Variables Each construct was measured with multiple items adapted from the literature. All items except for organization’s performance were measured on a 7-point Likert-type scale anchored by “strongly disagree” and “strongly agree.” The ethical leadership construct was measured with ten items [20]. The CSR construct comprised of twenty-three items [38] to measure economic (7 items), legal (6 items), ethical (6 items), and philanthropic (4 items). More specifically, the economic CSR dimension was operationalized as indicate how a franchise company perceived its economic performance. The legal CSR dimension was related to a franchise company’s perception of compliance with law and legal standards. The ethical CSR dimension was emphasized as franchise company’s perception of its ethical behavior. The philanthropic CSR dimension addressed a franchise company’s behavior as well as its interest in philanthropic activities. Finally, organization’s performance was measured on a 7-point Likert scale anchored by “with respect to our competitors, our position is much worse” and “with respect to our competitors, our position is much better”—operational (5 items), commercial (6 items), Sustainability 2018, 10, 447 7 of 16 and economic (5 items) [49]. Additionally, operational performance focuses on the overall improvement of efficiency of processes, while commercial performance is associated with the commercial function’s effectiveness. Economic performance refers to monetary consequences from its economic activities. 4. Results 4.1. Profile of Respondents Males accounted for 90.3 percent of the respondents while females were 9.7 percent. This skewed result was reflective of the Korean business climate whereby females accounted for only 9 percent of top management position in 2016 [ 73]. Also, 51.0 percent of the respondents were in their 40 s, and 27.6 percent noted as 30 s, followed by 50 years and above (20.4 percent). Furthermore, 73.5 percent of the respondents were 2- or 4-year college degree holders; 21.4 percent had a graduate degree, and 5.1 percent had a high school diploma. The franchise headquarters varied in size (i.e., numbers of employees), and largely included between 21–40 (33.7 percent) and 41–80 (28.6 percent). 4.2.
