The relationship between technological innovation andfirm performance Innovation as a management term is ubiquitous as it relates to several concepts. Often, it can be described as an“iterative process” initiated by the perception of a new market opportunity for an invention which leads to the development, production, and marketing (OECD, 1991). These opportunities can include developing new ideas on products, methods of production, sources of supply, exploitation of new markets, new ways to organize business ( Schumpeter, 1934), processes of improving capabilities and increased utility ( Drucker, 1985; Farr & Ford, 1990). Recently, with more business processes engaging on the digital platform, research in innovation has increasingly focused on “technical innovation” including areas of management, marketing, economics and production engineering (Eurostat, 2005). Conceptually, technological innovation refers to any incremental or radical change in technology embodied in product and process, including changes in value activities such as service and administration (Teece, 1986). From a resource-based view, this innovative capability, among other capabilities, is seen as critical to afirm achieving strategic competitiveness (Conner, 1991). Specifically, innovations enable afirm to offer a greater variety of valuable, rare, inimitable and differentiated products, and therefore lead firms to higher financial performance (Barney, 1991;Hitt, Hoskisson, & Ireland, 1994; Zahra, Ireland, & Hitt, 2000). In that respect, technological innovation can embody inventions from the industrial arts, engineering and the applied sciences. As a result, technological innovation is crucial to afirm acquiring and sustaining competitive advantage and improving its performance in a dynamic environment (Hannan & McDowell, 1990; Koellinger, 2008). Hence, research has shown that investments in R&D have been on the increase (Koellinger, 2008) as this may lead to increasing the competitive advantage of thefirm. Yet, an investment in technological innovation needs to be justified in terms of long-term economic gains and shareholder value (Srivastava, Fahey, & Christensen, 2001). This is especially true for firms considering investments in the adoption of speci fic technologies, such as IT which plays an important role for innovation through the improvement of processes or enablingfirms to offer new products or services to its customers. Conversely, technology investments that do not result in innovations are considered as sunk costs since these investments will not result in improvedfirm performance (Levin et al., 1987; Teece, 1986). Therefore, the relationship between technological innovation and firm performance is dependent on several factors. First, the ability of firms to transfer technology investments into innovation which tends to be influenced byfirm-specific resources (Sampson, 2007). Second, the type and suitability of innovation that emerges from thefirms' R & D investments to complement its business activities. Third, the intensity of the markets' competition which relates to the stage of thefirm's technology adoption (i.e. whether the firm is an innovator, early adopter, late majority, or a laggard), the price-elasticity of demand of the firm's products or services, thefirm's market share, and the negotiation power the firm possesses with its suppliers and customers. Fourth, choosing an appropriate strategy such as new products if the underlying design was unique, functionally elegant, and difficult to imitate can help thefirm obtain supernormal profits from innovations, suggesting that the success of these tactics is likely to vary across industries and with the type of innovation carried out. Alternatively, the literature mentions that if companies are unable to gain competitive advantages from its innovation, then competitors can gain through open competition (Levin et al., 1987; Teece, 1986). To evade the issue, companies normally seek out earnings through innovation by employing various strategies which include confidentiality, lead time, patents as well as the use of complementary capabilities (Cohen, Goto, Nagata, Nelson, & Walsh, 2002). However, the effect on a firm's performance will depend on the strategy chosen. With regards to the empirical and theoretical findings in the literature mentioned above, a significant relationship between a firm's performance and technological innovation was found (Hitt et al., 1994;McWilliams & Siegel, 2000;Teece, 1986). Thus, we put forth the following hypothesis: Hypothesis 1. Technological innovation is positively related tofirm performance. 2.4. Ethical leadership in the digital economy In the digital economy, two important issues that are currently being examined are enterprise ethics and corporate social responsibility as it is believed that leaders need to establish ethical behaviour to continue operating accountable businesses by implementing more sophisticated technologies (Gerbaudo, 2017; Tu & Lu, 2016).Baker and Craig (2006) have highlighted that some understanding has been gained by the study of leadership and ethics in the past decade because of increased concerns pertaining to ethical issues in business, particularly due to increased activities of misinformation. For sustainable businesses, a critical driver is the presence of ethical leadership, which mostly results in profitability for organisations. A study by the Ethics Research Centre (ERC) in Washington found that the highest quality recruits are attracted tofirms that maintain ethical business practices and management (Fulmer, 2004). Similarly, Mo and Shi (2018)also confirmed the significant role played by ethical leadership in maintaining positive employee performance resulting in higher revenues for the company (Mo & Shi, 2018). With all the recent scandals to hit the tech business (such as the Facebook's Cambridge Analytica Scandal or Yahoo's massive data breach on its users), digital businesses need to establish practices that can balance stakeholder's wealth and organizational profitability in an ethical and socially responsible way. Thus, a better understanding of ethical leadership needs to be gained by organisations when managing technological innovation. Ethical leadership can be described as‘the showcasing of normatively appropriate conduct with the help of interpersonal relationships and personal actions, and employing two-way communication, reinforcement and decision making to promote such conduct to followers’ (Brown et al., 2005, p. 120). Fundamentally, normatively appropriate conduct shows ethical leaders' moral component along with desirable traits like honesty, fairness and trustworthiness to oversee their own actions, as well as to utilize punishments and rewards on subordinates Fig. 1.Theoretical Framework. Punishments are employed to discourage unethical behaviour, while the reward systems are for motivating normatively appropriate behaviour in thefirm (Brown et al., 2005). Both in theory and practice, ethical leadership is said to be capable enough to actively manage morality, sometimes also known as moral identity (Mayer, Aquino, Greenbaum, & Kuenzi, 2012). The key aim for moral identity is to encourage leaders to have a moral schema that guides these leaders in their daily behaviour. It often shows receptiveness to others' expectations and welfares since insincerity could create dissonance and self-condemnation. For instance, moral identity can be considered as a predictor of pro-social behaviours like donations and charity (Reed, Aquino, & Levy, 2007), which can be negatively associated with unethical behaviours like cheating ( Reynolds & Ceranic, 2007). Because ethical leaders understand their responsibility well and live by principles and values, they are more likely to contribute to the betterment of society (Maak & Pless, 2006). From the viewpoint of stakeholders, ethical leaders know how to maintain and build good relations with all key stakeholders as they can create incentives to motivate, foster respectful collaboration, and offer a commitment to establish responsible and sustainable change both outside and inside the organisation (e.g.Maak & Pless, 2006). For instance, ethical leaders tend to offer a healthy, safe and fair working environment for their workers as well as morally obligated to provide safe products and services for their customers. Ethical leaders also ensure transparent communication regarding the possible risks of products and services, if there are any, keeping in mind customers' safety. With regards to communities and societies, it is expected that ethical leaders would be conscious towards the region where they run the business and where they are more likely to evaluate the effects cast by their organisation decisions on the society and its natural environments. This is because the ethical leadership'sfinal goal is to accomplish a mutual good like organizational legitimacy that affords business sustainability (Bass & Steidlmeier, 1999). 2.5. Moderating role of ethical leadership As explained in the previous sections, the technological innovation of firms is fostered through ethical leadership, which further improves and adds to the performance of thefirm. Ethical leaders generally set well-defined and consistent ethical standards for their followers, communicate ethical values, define reward for ethical behaviour, and render punishment for unethical behaviour (Brown & Trevino, 2006). Moreover, ethical leadership could uphold afirm's credibility and reputation by giving importance to ethical decision-making specifically to strengthen stakeholder relations and to make a new technology investment. The firms that are involved in technological innovation practices and procedures under strong ethical leadership are inclined towards building trust-based relationships with their stakeholders. The level to which leaders exhibit their trustworthiness towards new technological innovations becomes the decisive factor in ascertaining whether the technological innovation pursuits are effective or not. That is, the strong ethical leaders of firms need to have a personal contribution and involvement in the firms' long-term commitment to technological innovation pursuits (Damanpour, 1991; Jung, Chow, & Wu, 2003; Jung, Wu, & Chow, 2008). Studies by Eisenbeiss, Van Knippenberg, and Fahrbach (2015)and Chen and Hou (2016)have found a positive relationship between the firm's performance and technological innovation as soon as leaders exhibit ethical leadership (Chen & Hou, 2016; Eisenbeiss et al., 2015). This is because ethical leaders not only encourage their followers to voice their opinions and suggestions on ethical matters but also on work-related processes (Walumbwa & Schaubroeck, 2009). Giving the followers the opportunity to voice their opinions and ideas will foster creativity on the job since such voices would prompt employees to think of new methods of thinking (Chen & Hou, 2016). On the other hand, the existence of a weak ethical leadership alongside technological innovation in an organisation can prove to be destructive and limiting for the organisation's growth (Jung et al., 2008). According to Zhu, Sun, and Leung (2014), ethical leaders pursue and implement technological innovation with determination and committed action, which will eventually lead to the creation of a sustainable value to the stakeholders. Hence, this study then posits: Hypothesis 2. The relationship between firm performance and technological innovation is moderated by ethical leadership in a way that perceived technological innovation positively impacts performance when the leaders exhibit high ethical leadership. 3. In our study, we adopt the accounting-based performance as a proxy tofirm performance (FP). There is not much agreement about which measurement tool is most suitable. It ought to be mentioned that ROA is a measurement of CFP and management competence as it represents in what way competent the management is in making revenues from assets and how effective in handling assets to create income. It is defined as the percentage for determining the profitable nature of the company, related to the total assets. Control variables This study employed three different firm-level control variables to regulate forfirm size, slack resources and risks which were proxied by total assets, free cashflow, and leverage. Firm size was computed as a natural logarithm of afirm's total assets and was controlled to avoid any compounding effect offirm size onfirm performance. Firm size controls for any systematic, size-related effects on the dependent variable; it can influence its decision-making competences, profitability, and structure (Simerly & Li, 2000). For instance, big companies performed better and more effectively than small companies since these companies enjoy economies of scale in the form of costs reduction in operation and greater purchasing power (Riordan & Williamson, 1985). On the contrary, big companies can suffer from higher costs due to their larger and more complex operations and systems (Canback, Samouel, & Price, 2006). Correspondingly, leverage was used to control forfirm risk as it measured a firm's financial risk which is a total debt to total equity ratio. The need for managers of highly leveragedfirms to generate and retain cash to service the debt might reduce their ability to fund technological innovation (Barnea & Rubin, 2010; Reverte, 2009). We, therefore, controlled forfirm leverage. Finally, the slack resource provides a firm opportunity to innovate and make an investment in the operation. The higher the slack, the more resources are accessible for developing future investment choices. We measure free cashflow as slack resources since it is vital to control for slack in our empirical model. These data on total assets and leverage and free cashflow are collected from DataStream. 4. Methodology For this study, a quantitative methodology was used to test the hypotheses developed for this study. We used the dynamic panel data (DPD) “System Generalized Method of Moments (SYS-GMM)” as proposed by Arellano and Bover (1995)and Blundell and Bond (1998). SYS-GMM can eliminate/mitigate the issues of dynamic panel bias and potential endogeneity due to any independent variable correlating with the error term (Zaefarian, Kadile, Henneberg, & Leischnig, 2017). The main objective of utilising SYS-GMM instead of Pooled OLS or Fixed Effect estimates was that both the Pooled OLS and Fixed effect estimates could lead to biased and inconsistent outcomes since these two approaches were not capable in controlling for dynamic biases and endogeneity concerns (Arellano & Bover, 1995; Blundell & Bond, 1998). Second, Fixed Effect considers for the unobserved time-invariant firm-specifice ffects in the DPD model (Hsiao, 2014). In addition, the SYS-GMM is seen to yield efficient and consistent estimates in the regression model, wherein the independent variables were not strictly exogenous, i.e., these variables correlated with past and current realizations of the error, and/or in which heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation within individuals existed ( Roodman, 2009a). Much of these issues on modern leadership surround the notion of ethical leadership and howfirms conduct their marketing activities. In the B2B platform, much of these are generated through direct and relational marketing that is often considered one of the most controversial methods of advertising channels, especially when the approaches included are unsolicited with some pushing the limits of ethical standards and legality in a strong manner. A survey by theEthics Resource Centre (2013) found that 43% of respondents believed that their supervisors lacked ethical integrity. Furthermore, with disruptive innovation, it not only challenges traditional business models but often disrupts the ethics and moral standards by using dubious practices. For example, the use of dynamic pricing tofill capacity and the“bait and switch” where customers are “baited” through the advertisements for some products or services that have a low price is a classic case. In the long term, these unscrupulous practices are considered as non-sustainable business models and are known to“step over the line”. This implies then that managing innovative technology requires some form of ethical leadership as there is much at stake when it comes to enabling a company to optimize its returns to various stakeholders including employees, customers, business partners, local communities and the environment. Hence, organisations should encourage their managers to develop ethical leadership by emphasizing morality, two-way communication, respecting employees' dignity while empowering subordinates to come up with new ideas. It is recommended that managers should develop ethical leadership style by emphasizing morality in workplace, respecting their followers' nature and dignity, empowering and enriching the job significance to encourage their followers to come up with new ideas and put them into practice. Our study explores this relationship and thefindings confirm several of the research aims. First, it demonstrates that technological innovation plays an important part in thefirm's performance. This is almost intuitive as we find increasing numbers of organisations investing heavily into the digital aspects of their operations, from processes to services. Second, we show that ethical leadership has a moderating role in the relationship between technological innovation and firm performance. This suggests that firms that practice good governance and are morally and ethically high in its CSR score tend to have a positive effect onfirm performance. It is important to draw these observations as the study empirically indicates that ethical leadership is critical forfirms wanting to compete in the digital economy. A benefit seen with the implementation of new technologies that enable innovation is recognising the firm and market-specific mechanisms that could result in various consequences affecting the firm that is investing in the same technologies. Moreover, two kinds of technology-induced changes (process vs. product innovation) can be recognised regarding rather diverse economic implications. For instance, a key difference between both innovations is how these could cast an effect on employment. The expansion because of both types of innovations results in generating an extra request for the labour and capital production aspects, suggesting that innovating companies would likely generate additional employment. This is also known as the compensation effect (Pasinetti, 1981). Though, innovations could lead to a labour decreasing effect too. In the case of process innovations, this could happen once productivity growing effects start to materialise. Increase in productivity suggests that a lower production input could induce a given level of output. Thus, should output and demand to continue to remain constant, a reduction of labour would result due to process innovation. This is also known as the replacement e ffect (Edquist, Hommen, & McKelvey, 2001). For product innovations, this consequence is less possible, regardless of these being IT-enabled or not. Industrial Marketing Management xxx (xxxx) xxx–xxx 8 Therefore, our study has two theoretical implications. First, it extends our understanding of technological innovation and B2B studies. It is insufficient for firms to invest in B2B technological innovation if it ignores how these technologies are to be used. Literature suggests that as digital technologies become increasingly sophisticated (Li et al., 2018), so will the wide use of misinformation to gain a strategic advantage. In this respect, B2Bfirms would have to look to ethical leadership in managing how these technologies to not only benefit itself but to look beyond in the interest of society and the environment. For example, a recent article suggested thatfirms are too fixated on statistics to the extent that writing“fake online reviews” have now become an occupation (Hu, Bose, Koh, & Liu, 2012). Although some online firms have committed to weed out these practices, sceptics are not entirely convinced that it is easy to challenge £23 billion spent annually on online reviews (BBC, 2018). In this regard, it appears that ethical leadership is needed to ensure that their organisations are using digital technologies not merely effectively but also to safeguard its use from a marketing perspective. Theoretically speaking, marketing ethics is one of the most complicated and contentious subjects in management theory (Lilien, 2016). The relationship between commercialism, profitability and ethics has been studied by both academics and business leaders for years with little consensus reached, and still, not much insight has been offered on how ethical leadership may affect firm performance. However, our study found that the relationship between technological innovation andfirm performance was stronger with the presence of an ethical leader. Ethical leaders are defined as leaders who demonstrate normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions, interpersonal relationships and by encouraging two-way communication, reinforcement and decision-making (Brown et al., 2005). Hence, followers of ethical leaders are more likely to experience higher levels of job significance and would be more willing to generate new ideas to contribute to organizational goals (Yidong & Xinxin, 2013), thereby encouraging an innovative work behaviour which leads to higher technological innovation. Second, our study adds to a better understanding of ethical leadership with regards to marketing practices on the B2B platform. In the wake of the technology-driven economy, several challenges including the notion that the increasing complexity of society where markets are connected (physically) yet disconnected (proximity) has lead marketing practices astray. For example, data sharing between large corporations on the B2B platform have purportedly infringed on privacy laws (Arqué-Castells, 2012; Bennett & Segerberg, 2013). Such sharing has led to millions and millions of unsolicited marketing messages and furthered compromised the security of individuals as well as businesses. Our research has extended the discussion on the importance of further theoretical research into this area. Finally, our methodology proposes the use of the GMM which has been rarely used in marketing studies. We believe that this is an innovative way to examine marketing performance by demonstrating the relationships between marketing investments and the firm's performance. It also presents an alternative to studying the moderating effects of other important variables in marketing activities. 7. Limitations and recommendations for future studies Although our research model explains the relationships between technological innovation, firm performance and ethical leadership on the B2B platform, there are limitations to the study and additional opportunities for further development. First, other potential factors may change the relative impacts of ethical leadership onfirm performance such asfirm size, structure and culture. Future research needs to consider controlling other types of variables including otherfirm performance measures such asfirm risk or reputation. Second, this study employed secondary date to operationalize the various dimensions of performance; but future research could use primary and objective measures such as data in relation to production cost, market share, and total revenues. ORIGINAL PAPER Corporate Social Responsibility and Ethical Leadership: Investigating Their Interactive Effect on Employees’ Socially Responsible Behaviors Kenneth De Roeck 1 • Omer Farooq2 Received: 29 April 2016 / Accepted: 24 July 2017 /C211 Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2017 Abstract This research investigates the interlinkage between corporate social responsibility (CSR) and ethical leadership in inducing employees’ socially responsible behaviors (SRBs). Specifically, building on organizational identification theory and cue consistency theory, we develop and test an integrated moderated mediation framework in which employees’ perception of ethical leadership moderates the mediating mechanism between their perceptions of CSR (i.e., perceived CSR–environment and perceived CSR–community), organizational identification, and SRBs (i.e., green and societal behaviors). The findings highlight the need for consistency between employees’ perceptions of CSR and ethical leadership to foster their propensity to further social good through relationship-building activities with their organization. The results, which largely verify the theoretical framework, contribute to and have implications for both research and practice. Madoff Investment Securities) have seriously damaged the legitimacy of corporations and their leaders (Bedi et al.2016; Porter and Kramer2011). To bring business and society back together, organizations are increasingly integrating the concept of corporate social responsibility (CSR), consisting of discretionary policies and practices that take into account stakeholders’ expectations for long-term economic, social, and environmental well-being (Dahlsrud 2008; Du et al. 2015), into their management practices and operations (Du et al.2015). CSR investments thus represent a form of competitive initiatives through which firms strive to achieve win–win stakeholders’ relationships (Chen and Miller 2015; Malik 2015). In other words, ‘‘CSR may be more narrowly defined as a discretionary allocation of corporate resources to improving social welfare that serves as means of enhancing relationships with key stakeholder’’ (Barnett2007, p. 801). Literature on stakeholders’ responses to CSR suggests that employees have a decisive role in turning a firm’s CSR investments into business and social value (Aguilera et al. & Kenneth De Roeck kderoeck@bsad.uvm.edu Omer Farooq omer.farooq@kedgebs.com 1 Grossman School of Business, University of Vermont, 55 Colchester Ave., Kalkin Hall, Burlington, VT 05405, USA 2 KEDGE Business School, Domaine de Luminy, BP 921, 13288 Marseille Cedex 9, France 123 J Bus Ethics DOI 10.1007/s10551-017-3656-6 2007; Aguinis and Glavas 2012). To date, the micro (employee)-CSR literature has mainly focused on the impact of perceived CSR on traditional organizational behavior (OB) outcomes such as organizational citizenship behavior (OCB), commitment or task performance (for a review see Gond et al.2017). These findings have contributed to create a strong business case for CSR that legitimizes a firm’s social investment on economic grounds. Such an instrumental focus, though, has left aside the study of CSR’s propensity to promote employees’ socially and environmentally oriented behaviors, and thus to also foster positive social change (De Roeck and Maon 2016; Gond et al. 2017). Echoing this observation, Rupp and Mallory’s review of micro-CSR research (2015, p. 225) highlights that though ‘‘employees are an important stakeholder group, and their reactions to an organization’s CSR efforts are relevant to understand the social good generated by CSR initiatives, the research to date has not exactly taken this position.’’ The handful studies in this research area suggest that CSR policies and actions can affect employees’ socially responsible behaviors (SRBs) (e.g., Erdogan et al.2015; Raineri and Paille ́ 2016; Vlachos et al. 2014). Although this area of research needs additional empirical investigation to support the presumed CSR–SRBs association, a review of this literature also indicates that the theoretical rationales explaining why, how, and when CSR can impact employees’ SRBs still lack integrative and systematic testing and refinement, which further limits the generalizability of existing findings (De Roeck and Maon 2016; Raineri and Paille ́ 2016; Slack et al. 2015). To address these limitations, we develop and test a model that (1) elucidates the role of organizational identification as a mechanism explaining how perceived CSR can relate to employees’ SRBs and (2) explores the moderating role of ethical leadership in this process. To build our framework, we rely on three interrelated and complementary theoretical perspectives. First, we rely on social information processing (SIP) theory (Salancik and Pfeffer 1978; Thomas and Griffin 1989) as a backdrop to explain why employees’ perceptions of CSR can affect their SRBs. Indeed, according to this theoretical perspective, individuals’ attitudes and behaviors essentially result from the cognitive processing of informational cues stemming from their (work) environment rather than from individual characteristics. However, SIP is not clear on the potential mediating mechanisms and boundary conditions explaining how and when contextual cues can influence employees’ beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors in the workplace (Zalesny and Ford 1990). Thus, we complement this framework with organizational identification theory (Ashforth et al. 2008; Pratt 1998) and cue consistency theory (Anderson 1981, 1996; Slovic 1966). On the one hand, organizational identification is a concept that represents the extent to which employees integrate organizational attributes, values, and goals into their selfconcept (Dutton et al.1994), thus providing a way to account for the agency of human action within an organizational framework (Albert et al. 2000). Accordingly, identification appears as a powerful construct to explain how identity and normative cues stemming from CSR can influence employees’ propensity to engage in behaviors consistent with their organizational socially oriented values and objectives. On the other hand, according to cue consistency theory (Anderson 1981 ; Maheswaran and Chaiken1991; Slovic1966), employees rely on multiple contextual cues and assess their consistency to make sense of the organizational milieu and adapt their attitudes and behaviors accordingly. In this respect, we propose to explore the moderating role of ethical leadership, or ‘ ‘the demonstration of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to followers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and decision-making’ ’ (Brown et al.2005, p. 120), in explainingwhen perceived CSR is more likely to foster SRBs through increased level of identification. Specifically, we argue that the contextual cues stemming from CSR and ethical leadership (both of which transmit information about an organization’s ethical stance and social responsibility) need to be consistent to avoid the formation of a negative bias toward the organization’s work context that could potentially dampen CSR’s propensity to foster SRBs. Our study contributes to the micro-CSR literature by delineating some of the mechanisms that explain the psychology of CSR (Aguinis and Glavas 2012; Gond et al. 2017). Concurrently, it also addresses calls to explore the interlinkage between CSR and ethical leadership to shed more light on how companies and their leaders can better contribute to positive social change (Christensen et al.2014; De Roeck and Maon 2016; Groves and LaRocca 2011). Background and Hypotheses Development Although ample research has discussed organizational actions and rationales to advance the social good (i.e., CSR; for a review, see Aguinis and Glavas 2012), scant research has examined employees’ SRBs, defined as employees’ discretionary behaviors that target the social level or, in other words, that intend to enhance the well-being of their organization’s stakeholders, including the natural environment 1 (Crilly et al. 2008; Daily et al.2009; Vlachos et al.2014). Accordingly, we 1 This concept thus differs from related constructs focused on employees’ discretionary behaviors toward coworkers or the organization itself (e.g., OCB, pro-social behaviors). SRB is also cast under the labels of employee engagement in CSR (Slack et al. 2015), extrarole CSR performance (Vlachos et al. 2014), and OCB targeting external stakeholders (e.g., OCB toward the environment; see Daily et al. 2009). K. De Roeck, O. Farooq 123 examine two specific types of SRBs: (1) employees’ engagement in green behaviors, including employees’ actions to perform work in an environmentally friendly way (e.g., recycling, rational use of resources, participation in environmental initiatives, setting of more sustainable policies), and (2) societal behaviors, including employees’ actions that support overall community well-being even outside the work context. In their study on SRBs, Crilly et al. ( 2008) suggest that individual characteristics such as personal values, affect, and modes of reasoning explain differences in employees’ propensity to engage in SRBs. Although these findings are valuable, according to the SIP theory (Salancik and Pfeffer 1978; Thomas and Griffin 1989), individuals’ attitudes and behaviors are foremost determined by their proximal social context. According to this perspective, employees will scrutinize and cognitively process informational cues stemming from their work environment to determine the most appropriate attitudes and behaviors to adopt in the workplace (Maheswaran and Chaiken 1991; Salancik and Pfeffer 1978). In line with this reasoning, some scholars have argued that perceptions of the moral actions of a company, such as its CSR initiatives, can influence the moral concerns of employees and, thus, their behaviors oriented toward others’ well-being (Aguilera et al. 2007; De Roeck and Maon 2016). However, to date, only a handful of studies have found empirical support for this overall rationale (i.e., Erdogan et al. 2015; Raineri and Paille ́ 2016; Slack et al. 2015; Vlachos et al. 2014). Vlachos et al. ( 2014) propose that perceived CSR initiatives can increase employees’ commitment to engage in extra-role CSR performance because CSR sends informational cues about how to act in social groups. Slack et al. ( 2015) confirm these preliminary findings through a qualitative exploratory investigation in which they find that a lack of communication and visibility of CSR is one of the main barriers to employees’ engagement in SRBs. Finally, Raineri and Paille ́ (2016) show that employees who perceive their organization as engaged in environmental policies are more likely to follow its lead by demonstrating more environmental citizenship behaviors. In line with our background perspective based on SIP theory, these findings lend support to the idea that employees are more likely to engage in SRBs when the organization sends, through its CSR engagement, clear informational cues about the importance of contributing to social welfare. However, this line of research is still relatively underdeveloped, and the theoretical mechanisms explaining how and under which conditions informational cues stemming from perceptions of CSR can alter employees’ SRBs are not yet fully understood (Gond et al. 2017; Raineri and Paille ́ 2016; Rupp and Mallory 2015). In an effort to address this gap, we follow recent recommendations in micro-CSR literature to rely on a bi-factor model of CSR (see Glavas and Kelley 2014; Jones et al. 2014) to distinguish organizational actions toward the natural environment (i.e., perceived CSR–environment, such as environmentally conscious investments, pollution prevention, and promotion of sustainable growth) and the community (i.e., perceived CSR–community, such as charitable giving, community development investments, and collaboration with non-governmental organizations). Indeed, extant research suggests that these two CSR aspects have different relationships (in terms of significance or strength) to outcomes (Glavas and Kelley 2014; Jones et al. 2014; Rodrigo et al. 2016). The Mediating Role of Organizational Identification Organizational identification theory emerged as an offshoot in the organizational world of social identity and social categorization theories (Ashforth and Mael 1989; Bergami and Bagozzi 2000). According to the latter two theories (Tajfel and Turner 1986), social identification is an inherent human process that leads individuals to partly define themselves through a social identity, or ‘‘that part of an individual’s self-concept which derives from his/her knowledge of his/her membership of a social group (or groups) together with the value and emotional significance attached to that membership’’ (Tajfel1978, p. 63). In doing so, they try to reinforce their self-concept by affiliating with social groups of reference considered attractive and prestigious because of their positive and socially valued characteristics (Ashforth and Mael 1989; Bergami and Bagozzi 2000). Organizational identification is a particular form of social identification that corresponds to a ‘‘perception of oneness with or belongingness to an organization, where the individual defines him or herself in terms of the organization(s) in which he or she is a member’’ (Mael and Ashforth 1992, p. 104). That is, more than a mere feeling of membership, organizational identification represents the extent to which employees incorporate into their self-definition the descriptive and normative identity cues reflecting the central, distinctive, and enduring attributes of an organization (Ashforth et al. 2008; De Roeck et al. 2016). As such, it serves as a central concept in organizational studies to explain why employees act on behalf of the organization (Albert et al. 2000; Bergami and Bagozzi 2000), as strongly identified employees are more likely to internalize and enact the norms and values of their organization and thereby develop attitudes and behaviors in line with organizational goals (Dutton et al. 1994; Riketta 2005; Vough 2012). Thus, we argue that employees who strongly identify with an organization they perceive as socially Corporate Social Responsibility and Ethical Leadership: Investigating Their Interactive ... 123 responsible will engage in SRBs as a way to support its objectives in the social arena, which in turn helps them reaffirm the values and attributes that underlie their organizational identity and, by extension, their own self-concept. Although no studies have directly tested this proposition, Dutton and Dukerich’s ( 1991) qualitative investigation of employees of the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey offers some support to this idea. They show that identified employees engaged in SRBs to restore the positive social image of their employer, which was affected by a temporary societal issue (i.e., a homeless problem). In addition, the micro-CSR literature suggests that organizational identification helps explain how perceived CSR can influence employees’ work outcomes, such as organizational commitment, job satisfaction, and OCB (De Roeck et al. 2014; Farooq et al. 2014b, 2016). This line of research indicates that CSR (which embodies values institutionalized in society) sends informational cues to employees that positively enhance their evaluations of the organization’s reputation, leading them to bask in the organizational glory through an increased level of identification (De Roeck et al. 2016; El Akremi et al. 2015; Farooq et al. 2016). In the same vein, some studies suggest that cues stemming from CSR can bring more meaning to people’s work (Du et al. 2015; Glavas 2016), leading them to believe that ‘‘what they do has an importance that transcends purely economic aspects’’ (Rodrigo and Arenas 2008, p. 272). As a result, instead of viewing their organization as just a place to work, employees begin regarding it as an institution that shares their values, which in turn fosters their willingness to strengthen their identification with the organization (Rodrigo and Arenas 2008). Finally, research has also argued that perceptions of CSR can provide employees with normative identity cues that serve as a heuristic to assess the organization’s overall fairness and trustworthiness (Aguilera et al. 2007; De Roeck et al. 2014), helping diminish the perceived risk of defining themselves in terms of the organization’s norms and values (De Roeck and Delobbe 2012; Vough 2012). Thus, we propose that CSR initiatives can send informational cues that highlight reassuring, positive, and desirable organizational attributes that ultimately foster employees’ willingness to strengthen their identification, as doing so helps them view themselves in a more positive light and brings more meaning to their lives. Concurrently, the resultant feelings of oneness with their organization should induce them to internalize, enact, and promote the socially valued characteristics of their organization by engaging in SRBs, further helping them to reinforce their self-concept. Therefore, in line with the previous arguments and conceptualizations of CSR and SRBs adopted in this study, we propose the following: Hypothesis 1 Perceived CSR–environment positively relates to employees’ (a) green behaviors and (b) societal behaviors through the mediation of organizational identification. Hypothesis 2 Perceived CSR–community positively relates to employees’ (a) green behaviors and (b) societal behaviors through the mediation of organizational identification. The Moderating Role of Ethical Leadership Building on cue consistency theory (Anderson 1981; Maheswaran and Chaiken 1991; Slovic 1966), we further propose that cues stemming from employees’ assessment of ethical leadership, or their supervisor demonstration and promotion of normatively appropriate conduct (Brown et al. 2005), can moderate the way CSR affects their organizational identification and, therefore SRBs. According to the feminism component of ethical leadership (i.e., the ethics of care), the so-called normative appropriate conduct of ethical leaders is characterized by a deep concern with how their decisions may affect others’ well-being (Knights and O’Leary 2006; Northouse 2009), such that ethical leaders appear to care more about the greater good of their employees, organization, and society rather than their own self-interests (Brown and Trevinõ 2006). Specifically, ethical leaders strive to balance the various needs of stakeholders in a way that serves the interests of all, and therefore they often appear as CSR champions who demonstrate and promote SRBs to followers (Christensen et al. 2014;D e Hoogh and Den Hartog 2008; Lawton and Paéz 2014). So far, few studies have focused on the simultaneous impact of CSR and ethical leadership on employees (Christensen et al. 2014). Existing research has mainly discussed the direction of the potential relationship between the two constructs. For example, Hansen et al. ( 2016) show that perceived CSR influences employees’ inferences about their leaders’ ethical stance which in turn impact their perception of the work climate. By contrast, Wu et al. (2015) argue that employees’ perception of their CEOs’ ethical leadership is positively related to their CSR perception through the mediating role of organizational culture. Although both rationales on the direction of the CSR–ethical leadership relationship are plausible, based on cue consistency theory, we suggest that their potential interactive impact is more crucial for determining followers’ work outcomes, especially in terms of identification and SRBs, which, respectively, reflect the appropriation of their organizational and leaders’ ethical stance within their identity and behaviors. K. De Roeck, O. Farooq 123 Indeed, according to cue consistency theory, employees rely on multiple cues from the organizational context and assess their consistency (i.e., congruency of the different information) to determine which beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors to adopt (Miyazaki et al. 2005; Slovic 1966). When cues provide corroborating information, an employee’s attitudes and behaviors are derived by a straightforward integration of their values (Miyazaki et al. 2005). In other words, when cues are consistent, the employee is more likely to use them jointly (i.e., with equal weight) to determine how to navigate the organizational milieu (Anderson 1981; Miyazaki et al. 2005). However, when informational cues are inconsistent, a negative bias dominates the employee’s cognitive processing of the information, and he or she will give more weight to the negative cue to determine the most appropriate attitudes and behaviors to adopt (Anderson 1981, 1996). In line with this rationale, we expect that when employees hold high perceptions of ethical leadership, the impact of perceived CSR on their SRBs through organizational identification (i.e., their attitude) will be stronger than when they hold low perceptions of ethical leadership. In such a case, cues stemming from their supervisors’ endeavors to demonstrate and promote a caring approach to business that considers the voice and needs of their organizations’ multiple stakeholders should corroborate with the cues stemming from their organizational CSR’s engagement to transmit a meaningful and attractive organizational context that fosters their organizational identification and SRBs. Conversely, we expect that when employees perceive their supervisor as being poorly ethical, the potential for normative identity cues stemming from CSR to favorably affect employees’ organizational identification and SRBs will fade because of the formation of a negative bias toward the organization’s work context. Thus: Hypothesis 3a Perceived ethical leadership moderates the indirect effect of perceived CSR–environment on employees’ green behaviors through the mediation of organizational identification, such that the indirect effect will be stronger when perceived ethical leadership is high. Hypothesis 4a Perceived ethical leadership moderates the indirect effect of perceived CSR–community on employees’ green behaviors through the mediation of organizational identification, such that the indirect effect will be stronger when perceived ethical leadership is high. We selected companies involved in CSR according to the sustainability and CSR-related information publicly available on their websites. We also considered whether the chosen companies encouraged employee engagement and participation in SRBs (e.g., employees’ contribution to the design and implementation of CSR initiatives, participation in social and environmental volunteering programs, donation to charities supported by the organization). For example, most companies are extensively involved in relief efforts in response to disasters that have occurred in South Asia, including the Awaran earthquake, internally displaced people’s crisis due to the Afghan war, and the famine in Tharparkar. These companies also contribute to social initiatives that promote the well-being of local communities (e.g., providing schooling opportunities, improving and developing education facilities, providing clean drinking water and sanitation facilities in the remote areas of South Asia). Employees had the opportunity to directly participate in such activities on a voluntary basis. For example, one of the companies we surveyed contributed a large amount of money to flood relief activities, and its employees could also discretionarily contribute to this cause by either donating a certain percentage of their monthly salary or providing time and physical assistance to the affected areas. Then, using our alumni database, we contacted the targeted companies to receive their permission and support to administer the survey in their respective companies. We visited the companies and handed out paper copies to more than 400 informants willing to take part in the study. The questionnaires were accompanied by a cover letter with the necessary instructions on how to answer the survey. The cover letter also assured respondents that the survey was anonymous and that their answers would be processed with the utmost confidentiality by independent researchers. We also emphasized the anonymity and confidentiality of the study verbally. To reduce social desirability bias, we stressed that there were no right or wrong answers and that we were only interested in respondents’ spontaneous opinions (Randall and Gibson 1990). To maintain anonymity, respondents were invited to drop the completed questionnaire into a drop box placed at the reception desk within a week’s time (Mitchell et al. 2009). We made one reminder telephone call to the respondents during the week to maximize the response rate. We received 359 responses, which corresponds to a response rate of 89.75%. This high response rate rules out any concern about non-response bias. Of this final sample, 62% were men. In addition, 50% of the respondents were between ages 18 and 28 years, 27% were between ages 29 and 40 years, 18% were between ages 41 and 55 years, and 5% were more than 55 years. Respondents had 5.82 years’ tenure on average. Regarding their education, 3% had only a high school degree, 57% held undergraduate degrees, and 40% held a master’s degree. Respondents occupied a wide variety of positions: 23% were senior managers, 25% were middle managers, 28% were in lower management positions (e.g., junior manager, other white-collar positions), and 24% held an operational function without any management responsibilities. We also tested the normality of the data using Finney and DiStefano’s ( 2006) proposed method and calculated the skewness and kurtosis values. Common Method Variance We collected data from single sources on self-report measures by using a cross-sectional design, which may cause common method variance. Therefore, we used multiple methods to determine the threat of common method bias in our data. First, we conducted Harman’s (1967) onefactor analysis through exploratory factor analysis in which we fixed the number of factors to produce a single factor, which extracted only 33% of the variance. Second, we again performed Harman’s factor analysis, but this time we did not fix the number of factors, so they were free to produce multiple factors based on their eigenvalues; this process produced six independent factors that extracted 81.3% of the total variance. Among these factors, the first factor explained only 36.5% of the variance. Third, we compared the fit indices of the six-factor CFA with the single-factor CFA (see Table 1) and found that the singlefactor CFA test yielded a poorer fit with the data. Finally, we used the common latent factor method prescribed by Podsakoff et al. ( 2012) to examine the risk of common method bias in our data. The common latent factor extracted only 18% of the variance, which is less than the median method variance (25%) among studies of self-reported perceptions (Williams et al. 1989). These analyses suggest that common method bias is not a serious threat to our data. Although these findings are crucial to support the relevance of CSR to OB, considering only its impact on employees’ favorable attitudes and behaviors toward the organization provides an incomplete picture of these organizational practices, which normatively and ideologically also aim to increase stakeholders’ well-being (Gond et al.2017; Slack et al.2015). This gap in the literature is quite surprising as CSR initiatives provide many opportunities to sensitize and engage employees in SRBs (e.g., volunteerism programs, donation to charities supported by the organization, or participation in the design, management, and promotion of CSR) (De Roeck and Maon 2016). This research’s objective was thus to address this limitation by building an integrative framework that investigates why, how, and when perceived CSR can affect employees’ engagement in SRBs (i.e., enhance the well-being of civil society and the natural environment). Informed by SIP theory and its extension through cue consistency theory, overall this study’s findings (see Appendix2 for a summary) support that CSR and ethical leadership are two major sources of contextual cues that interact to determine employees’ propensity to identify with their organization and thereby foster their engagement in SRBs. Theoretical Contributions First, our framework focuses on the mechanisms explaining CSR’s impact on employees’ SRBs, thus answering recent calls to expand the nomological network of perceived CSR beyond its focus on traditional OB outcomes (e.g., De Roeck and Maon 2016; Gond et al. 2017; Rupp and Mallory 2015). Specifically, our results show that perceptions of CSR–environment and CSR–community positively relate to employees’ green and societal behaviors. Thus, we confirm the sparse findings that suggest that employees’ perceptions of CSR–environment relate to green behaviors (i.e., Erdogan et al. 2015; Raineri and Paille ́ 2016) or that overall perceived CSR correlates with employees’ CSR performance (Vlachos et al. 2014). Also, we further extend knowledge on the CSR–SRB relationship by showing that (1) perceptions of CSR actions enhancing the natural environment can also affect employees’ societal behavior beyond the impact on green behavior and (2) CSR actions oriented toward community well-being can induce not only employees’ societal behaviors but also green behaviors. In addition, our measure of societal behavior consists of employees’ actions that extend beyond the work environment, showing that organizations can be a strong engine for positive social change by promoting a new and more sustainable way of life to their employees. Finally, our findings extend literature on the relationship between perceived CSR and SRBs by showing that CSR–environment relates more strongly to employees’ green behaviors than other SRBs (i.e., contribution to civil society), whereas employees’ perceptions of their employers’ engagement in the community foster more employee societal than green behavior. These new insights are thus consistent with the multi-target similarity theory, which argues that predictors should account for more variance in matched than mismatched criteria (see Farooq et al. 2016; Lavelle et al. 2007). As such, employees’ evaluations of informational cues stemming from their organizational engagement in CSR help them determine the appropriateness of engaging in SRBs. Second, our study addresses scholars’ calls to more systematically delineate and test the theoretical rationales explaining the potency of CSR on micro-level outcomes (Aguinis and Glavas 2012; Rupp et al. 2013), notably the mechanisms explaining how CSR affects employees’ SRBs (De Roeck and Maon 2016; Slack et al. 2015). Specifically, our findings support the idea that CSR initiatives provide employees with descriptive and normative identity cues that favorably illustrate the organization’s prestige and overall character, thereby leading to increased feelings of oneness or belongingness with their employer (De Roeck et al. 2014, 2016). In doing so, employees internalize and enact the societal values and objectives of their organization and therefore demonstrate increased engagement in SRBs as a way to support their organization’s goals and reinforce their self-concept. These findings thus extend CSR literature on the mediating role of organizational identification, which has largely focused on attitudinal outcomes, such as job satisfaction and affective commitment (e.g., De Roeck et al. 2014; Farooq et al. 2014b). However, attitudes do not automatically transfer to actual behaviors (Ajzen and Fishbein 1977), and thus our research’s findings reinforce the robustness of organizational identification theory in explaining employees’ reactions to CSR. These results also extend the sparse knowledge on the CSR–SRB relationship. Particularly, we extend Vlachos et al.’s ( 2014) suggestion that CSR judgments can affect employees’ CSR extra-role performance because CSR reinforces their attachment to the organization. Indeed, although identification results in greater attachment and affective commitment, it remains conceptually and empirically distinct (Riketta 2005), as it is identification, not commitment, that entails the appropriation of the organization’s attributes and objectives into one’s self-concept (Ashforth et al. 2008). Thus, our findings are groundbreaking for micro-level literature, in that they show that employees’ identification not only helps support a corporation’s primary objective linked to its bottom-line improvement but also those related to the improvement in social welfare. These results confirm research that asserts that identification, as a root construct, provides a way to account for the agency of human action within an organizational framework (e.g., Albert et al. 2000; Ashforth et al. 2008; Pratt 1998). However, our findings also extend this literature by showing that organizational identification can also influence employees’ behaviors outside the work context (i.e., that are not directly linked to an employee’s self-interest in career advancement) because organizational attributes related to its CSR initiatives (e.g., compassion, trustworthiness, frugality) become self-defining and, thus, part of employees’ lifestyle. Third, our study findings on the moderating role of ethical leadership in the mediation between perceived CSR, organizational identification, and employees’ SRBs directly contribute to recent calls to extend knowledge on the boundary conditions that might determine the potency of perceived CSR in determining employees’ outcomes (Aguinis and Glavas 2012; Glavas 2016; Gond et al. 2017; Rupp et al. 2013). In doing so, we concurrently address calls to investigate the interlinkage between CSR and ethical leadership (Christensen et al. 2014; De Roeck and Maon 2016 ; Groves and LaRocca 2011). Specifically, under the cue consistency theory’s premise that individuals search for and assess the consistency of multiple contextual cues to determine which attitudes and behaviors to adopt in the work context (Anderson 1981; Miyazaki et al. 2005), our framework that highlights the interactive effect of both these constructs on employees’ attitude (i.e., organizational identification) and behaviors (i.e., SRBs) significantly extends the sparse and emerging research examining the impact of perceived ethical leadership on CSR or vice versa (Hansen et al. 2016;W u et al. 2015). In so doing, our study also brings empirical support to cue consistency’s assumption that when information is inconsistent, more weight is accorded to the negative cue to determine the attitudes and behaviors to adopt (Anderson 1981). Indeed, it appears that when employees perceive poor ethical leadership, the indirect effects of CSR–environment on their SRBs disappear (i.e., the links become nonsignificant), whereas the indirect effects of CSR–community on employees’ SRBs become significantly weaker than under the condition of high perceived ethical leadership. These findings suggest that when cues are inconsistent, employees might become skeptical about Corporate Social Responsibility and Ethical Leadership: Investigating Their Interactive ... 123 the organization’s ethical stance, integrity and overall character, which in turn should temper their willingness to identify with it. These later results could, therefore, inform literature on the condition explaining the potential backfiring effect of CSR (Wagner et al. 2009). Indeed, considering the increased defiance against the corporate world and the growing skepticism of stakeholders regarding organizations’ claimed contributions to the social realm (Porter and Kramer 2011), it is critical for companies to appear more authentic and credible in their social engagement to reap the beneficial returns of their CSR’s investments (McShane and Cunningham 2012). As such, our results suggest that consistency between perceptions of ethical leadership and CSR is critical to maintaining CSR credibility in the eyes of employees and, thus, to preserve and strengthen CSR’s ability to foster members’ identification and propensity to engage in behaviors supporting their organization’s objectives. Managerial Implications This research also has several implications for management practice. First, organizations that want to boost their social performance by encouraging employee engagement in SRBs need to ensure that employees favorably perceive their CSR initiatives. To do so, organizations could rely on internal communication strategies (e.g., internal memos, intranet, thematic events) to highlight their stance on social (and ethical) responsibility. Second, organization officers should keep in mind that specific CSR initiatives are more likely to generate particular SRBs. Therefore, it is important to carefully plan and strategize about CSR initiatives to obtain good results in terms of the desired type of SRBs. In this respect, organizations should not treat CSR as an add-on activity to their traditional business models but rather as something that should be carefully planned and integrated into the company strategy, culture, and DNA. Only then will employees positively perceive CSR as a strong identity cue that will trigger their identification with the organization and, as a result, foster their engagement in such activities through SRBs. Third, organizations should invest in the training of supervisors regarding social and ethical responsibility to ensure that these leaders transmit and promote a consistent image of the organization regarding its contribution to social welfare. If supervisors do not appear as ethical leaders championing CSR and stakeholder management, a loss of credibility in the organizational stance on CSR could dampen the micro-social returns of such investment. Finally, this study also has some important implications for recruiting and promotion. When making such decisions, organization officers should strive to hire and promote individuals to leadership positions who fit with the company CSR strategy and (ethical) culture, to maintain the credibility of the organization’s social engagement in the eyes of members and thereby foster their engagement in SRBs through enhanced identification with their employer. Limitations and Avenues for Further Research Although we surveyed employees from different organizations in different industries, the generalizability of our findings could be called into question, as we surveyed only employees from one country. As such, studies that replicate our findings in other national and cultural context are warranted to corroborate our conclusions further. In particular, we conducted our study in the developing world, specifically in South Asia. The differences between culture and economic conditions of South Asia and developed countries provide an opportunity to examine this phenomenon in contrasting conditions (Jamali and Karam 2016). Indeed, it has been noticed that current insights about CSR research ‘‘have fallen short in terms of a more nuanced analysis of how CSR manifests itself in markets outside the developed core’’ (Jamali and Karam 2016, p. 1). For example, South Asia contrasts sharply with the developed world on cultural factors such as the individualism–collectivism, and power distance indexes. In this respect, the influence of CSR–community and CSR–environment on employees’ attitudes and behaviors may vary across individualist and collectivist societies (Farooq et al. 2014a, 2016) as well as low- and high-power distance societies (Farooq et al. 2014b). Similarly, economic conditions of South Asia where 22.3% of the population lives below the poverty line (CIA 2016) may also affect the results of this study. Owing to economic disparities, employees may put more importance on economic than social and environmental issues (Burton et al. 2000). Therefore, testing our model in a cross-cultural setting would help to expand our results. Another limitation is the cross-sectional nature of our study based on self-reported data, which might create common method variance bias and uncertainty about the causality between the variables included in our theoretical model. However, we used validated and reliable measurement scales and found an interaction effect that cannot be artificially created by common method variance bias (Siemsen et al. 2010). Moreover, although we cannot methodologically rule out all alternative models with our study design, we endeavor to rigorously develop the theoretical reasoning underpinning the implied causal links among the variable included in our study. As pointed out by some authors, the use of time-lagged design is still very rare in the micro-CSR literature (De Roeck et al. 2016 ; Gond et al. 2017). As such, we recommended to future K. Beyond these methodological limitations, further research could extend our study by examining how other informational cues about an organization’s social responsibility and organizational identity stemming from, for example, coworkers, customers, and family/friends could eventually interact with cues arising from CSR initiatives and ethical leadership to predict employees’ SRBs (see Thomas and Griffin 1989). Our findings on the role of CSR and ethical leadership as antecedents of SRBs could also be analyzed in conjunction with the individual factors previously identified as contributors to SRBs (e.g., mode of reasoning—see Crilly et al. 2008) or with other individual factors moderating the CSR–work outcome relationship (e.g., attitude to CSR and moral identity—see Rupp et al. 2013; Turker 2009b). In this respect, individual characteristics could act as boundary conditions that determine the extent to which perceived CSR and ethical leadership affect employees’ propensity to engage in SRBs. Research could also expand on the potential mediating mechanisms that may translate CSR perceptions into SRBs. Our results suggest a full mediation of organizational identification between CSR–community and green behavior and between CSR–environment and employees’ societal behaviors. However, we also found a direct relationship between CSR–environment and green behaviors and CSR–community and societal behaviors, which indicates a partial mediation of organizational identification in these relationships. These findings suggest that other mediating mechanisms could potentially explain these dynamics. In this respect, a first step would be to rely on the intermediary processes proposed in existing micro-CSR literature, such as work meaningfulness (Glavas and Kelley 2014), generalized social exchange (Farooq et al. 2014b), perceived organizational support and justice (De Roeck et al. 2014; El Akremi et al. 2015). Finally, other moderators that might reflect on the authenticity and credibility of the organization’s engagement in CSR should also be investigated to understand the CSR–SRB relationship better. For example, it might be worth investigating whether employees’ self-centered versus other-centered CSR attributions affect the propensity of perceived CSR to influence their SRBs favorably (see Donia et al. 2016). If employees perceive their organization’s investment in CSR as motivated by self-interest (e.g., search for legitimacy and goodwill) rather than by altruism (i.e., intrinsic motivation to contribute to social welfare), they might question the authenticity of such socially responsible actions and thus disengage from SRBs. Employees might also judge the degree of perceived fit between a CSR activity and the organization’s core activity (see Becker-Olsen et al. 2006) to determine the real intention of the organization to engage in CSR, and therefore a poor CSR fit might dampen the potential positive impact of perceived CSR on employees’ SRBs. In the same vein, a growing body of literature on strategic CSR indicates that to better reap the financial return of CSR, firm’s need to enter in dialogue with stakeholders to develop initiatives that matter to them (e.g., see Michelon et al. 2013; Miles et al. 2006). Extending this rational to the micro (employee)-level through the lens of the cue consistency framework could highlight another boundary condition that might determine employees’ response to perceived CSR. In this respect, if there is a lack of consistency between employees’ perceptions of stakeholders’ demands and the perceived CSR actions of their organization, then employees might conclude that their company is engaging in non-strategic CSR; or in other words, their might consider that CSR is used as a short-term philanthropic tactic to gain general goodwill. Article International Review of Administrative Sciences The need for ethical leadership in combating corruption Mohsin Bashir Lahore University of Management Sciences, Pakistan Shahidul Hassan Ohio State University, USA Abstract In this article, we empirically assess the role of ethical leadership in reducing corruption. We also examine whether the effectiveness of ethical leadership in curbing corruption depends on the quality of the reward system in public organizations. We focus on two related components of the reward system: the use of performance-based rewards and procedural fairness. Using data collected through a survey of 741 employees in 154 government and non-profit organizations in Pakistan, we find a negative association between ethical managerial leadership and reports of corruption. We also find that the use of performance-based rewards is associated with fewer incidences of corruption, and that the negative relationship between ethical leadership and corruption is stronger when employees report low levels of procedural fairness. We discuss the implications of these findings for research on and strategies for combating corruption in public organizations. Points for practitioners Ethical managerial leadership can reduce corruption in public organizations in developing countries. The need for ethical leadership is particularly high in organizations that are yet to establish a fair reward system. Moreover, to reduce incidences of unethical behavior and promote ethical behavior, managers in public organizations in developing countries should communicate ethical standards clearly, encourage subordinates to Corresponding author: Mohsin Bashir, Suleman Dawood School of Business, Lahore University of Management Sciences, Lahore, Pakistan. Keywords corruption, ethical leadership, reward systems Introduction Corruption is a serious impediment to good governance in most developing countries (Pollitt, 2016). It not only weakens the perceived legitimacy and effectiveness of public institutions, but also impairs the moral fabric of a society by lowering incentives for people to value honesty and uphold the rule of law. The economic cost of corruption is also considerable. According to the World Bank, it is estimated at approximately 5% of global gross domestic product (GDP) (i.e. USD2.6 trillion), with over USD1 trillion paid in bribes to public officials each year. 1 Cross-national studies have provided valuable insights, highlighting the importance of governance institutions in curbing corruption. Relatively few studies, however, have examined within-country variation in corruption. As noted by MeyerSahling and Mikkelsen (2016), this is a notable limitation of the extant literature because the prevalence of corruption may vary across sectors and public organizations within a country depending on how organizations are structured and managed. Examining the sources of such variation may also help us to identify effective managerial practices and organizational deterrents against corruption. To provide insight about the proximal causes of corruption, however, several recent studies have considered the role of individual and job-related factors. With survey data from public officials in South Korea, Kwon (2014), for example, found that bureaucrats with limited discretion and higher levels of public service motivation are less susceptible to accepting bribes. De Graaf and Huberts (2008) examined prominent corruption cases in the Netherlands and discovered that public officials’ motives for engaging in corruption, aside from personal gains, included friendship, higher status, and the desire to impress others. Further, an ethnographic study in South Africa revealed that public-sector employees might engage in corruption to protect themselves from intimidation and violence by criminals and colluding colleagues (Sundstrom, 2016). These studies have provided useful insight but more research is needed to identify the specific practices that public managers can use to prevent incidences of corruption. Building upon the extant evidence, we consider broader organizational research on unethical employee behavior to provide insight about the organizational determinants of corruption. We contend that insights from micro-organizational research can be particularly useful in identifying the actionable managerial responses needed to fight against corruption. The micro-organizational perspective 2 International Review of Administrative Sciences 0(0) suggests that unethical behavior is more likely to occur in certain contexts, and can be prevented through instituting appropriate structures, effective reward systems, and ethical managerial leadership (Brown et al., 2005; Trevino, 1986). Accordingly, we examine the influence of ethical managerial leadership in reducing corruption. We also assess how, together, perceptions about the quality of the reward system and ethical leadership are related to reports of corruption. Literature and hypotheses Public administration scholars have begun to investigate the effectiveness of leadership practices in public organizations. The extant research, however, focuses largely on the impact of transformational and transactional leadership practices (Orazi et al., 2013; Van Wart, 2013), with few studies assessing the influence of ethical managerial leadership in public organizations (Hassan, 2015; Hassan et al., 2014). Organizational scholars describe ethical leadership in many ways. Kanungo (2001) notes that ethical leaders not only engage in behaviors that benefit others, but also refrain from behaviors that may cause harm to others. Another study provides a comprehensive perspective and suggests that ethical leadership is “the demonstration of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to followers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and decision making” (Brown et al., 2005: 120). According to Brown et al. (2005), two essential components of ethical leadership are: (1) being amoral person; and (2) beinga moral manager.A sa moral person,a leader may promote good conduct and discourage unethical behavior by exhibiting exemplary behavior and leading in a principled and just manner. As amoral manager, a leader tries to influence followers by providing ethical guidance, clarifying ethical expectations and standards, rewarding ethical conduct, and sanctioning unethical behavior. Both aspects of ethical leadership are likely to be important in shaping the ethical disposition and behavior of followers. We suggest that ethical managerial leadership is likely to play an important role in reducing corruption in public organizations (see Figure 1). This argument is based on theories of social learning (Bandura, 1986) and social exchange (Blau, 1964). Yukl (2013) suggests that leadership is a process of social influence, and ethical leaders attempt to influence their followers by embedding their values and beliefs (Brown et al., 2005). These embedding mechanisms include: the issues and behaviors that leaders pay attention to, monitor, and control; deliberate role modeling; coaching; recognizing ethical behavior; and sanctioning unethical conduct (Brown and Trevi~no, 2006). In addition, subordinates learn about what is appropriate and inappropriate behavior by observing their role models (e.g. supervisors) and peers in the workplace (Bandura, 1986). Several recent studies have provided indirect evidence connecting ethical leadership, or lack thereof, with reports of corruption. De Graaf and Huberts’ (2008) study of Dutch corruption cases, for example, revealed that weak leadership was Bashir and Hassan 3 one of the most important contributing factors. Downe et al. (2016) found that ethical leadership played an important role in promoting and reinforcing ethical conduct in English local governments. In two other public-sector studies, leading by example and role modeling were found to be the most influential means through which public managers fostered ethical behavior in their organizations (Downe et al., 2016; Heres and Lasthuizen, 2012). Based on the accumulated evidence from these studies and aforementioned theoretical arguments, the first hypothesis that we test is as follows: Hypothesis 1:Ethical leadership will be related negatively with reports of corruption. Besides ethical leadership, perceptions about the quality of reward system may have an influence on employees’ decision to engage in or refrain from corruption. The classic study by Becker and Stigler (1974) highlights the importance of an effective reward system in reducing corruption in public organizations. Trevino et al. (1999) identify two components of the employee reward system that are critical for reducing unethical behavior in organizations: (1) job rewards (i.e. pay, benefits, and career/professional advancement opportunities) are tied clearly to employee performance; and (2) the formal procedures used in making decisions about the allocation of job rewards and resources are fair or unbiased. Perceptions about these two related factors inform employees’ judgments of distributive and procedural fairness (Lind and Tyler, 1988). Psychological contract theory provides important insights into how perceptions about the effectiveness of the reward system are likely to be related to incidences of corruption.
