Employee perceptions of procedural and distributive fairness lead to the fulfillment of such expectations, which, in turn, results in higher employee commitment and performance. However, perceived inequity and procedural injustice indicate a breach of this psychological contract, which leads to lower employee performance and may even influence some employees to engage in counterproductive and unethical behavior (Morrison and Robinson, 1997). Similarly, Bandura (1999) suggests that individuals are more likely to engage in unethical behavior when they can easily displace moral responsibility for their actions and rationalize unethical behavior. We contend that distributive and procedural injustice is likely to increase corruption in public organizations by making it easier for public employees to rationalize corruption. There is also some evidence that an organization’s reward system can both facilitate and prevent unethical behavior. A recent public-sector study in South Korea showed a negative link between a performance-based reward system and bureaucrats’ susceptibility to accepting bribes (Kwon, 2013). A cross-national study in post-communist countries indicated that the implementation of a merit-based recruitment process and performance evaluation system reduced incidences of corruption in public agencies (Meyer-Sahling and Mikkelsen, 2016). Following these studies and theories discussed, we test two hypotheses, as follows: Hypothesis 2: Use of performance-based rewards will be associated with fewer incidences of corruption. Hypothesis 3: Procedural fairness will be associated with fewer incidences of corruption. As shown in Figure 1, we suggest that perceptions about the quality of the reward system, in addition to their direct influences, may moderate the deterring effect of ethical leadership on corruption. Specifically, we contend that the relationship between ethical leadership and corruption will be weaker in public organizations with an effective reward system and that it will be stronger in organizations with a poor reward system. This argument is consistent with the substitutes for leadership theory (Kerr and Jermier, 1978; Kerr et al., 1974), which suggests that certain personal characteristics of employees, their job tasks, and organizational norms and practices may counteract managers’ ability to weaken or strengthen their work attitudes and behavior. These substitutes, when fully institutionalized, direct employee behavior to such a large extent that managerial practices have little or no influence (Kerr and Jermier, 1978). Perceptions about the effectiveness of the employee reward system are potential substitutes for ethical leadership. Bandura (1999) suggests that individuals’ propensity to disengage morally is higher when they feel that they have been treated unfairly or they think that they deserve better. As we noted earlier, the likelihood of moral rationalization and disengagement will be lower in public organizations Bashir and Hassan 5 with an effective reward system (i.e. high levels of distributive and procedural fairness). The rationale is that incentives for engaging in corruption in such organizations will be lower and the costs will be much higher. We contend that the need for ethical leadership in such organizations will also be lower because employees’ ethical behavior and decisions will be largely guided by the reward system. By contrast, the need for ethical leadership will be higher in public organizations that have yet to establish an effective reward system. In such organizations, ethical managerial leadership will be more influential in guiding employee behavior and reducing corruption. Accordingly, the last hypothesis we test is as follows. Hypothesis 4: The relationship between ethical leadership and corruption will be weaker in public organizations that distribute employees’ rewards based on performance and where employees perceive a high level of procedural fairness. Data and methods Sample and procedures We tested four hypotheses with data collected through a questionnaire from employees working in various public and non-profit organizations in Pakistan. These employees were participants in a five-year-long institutional capacitybuilding program funded by the United States Aid for International Development (USAID). The breakdown of the trainees selected from USAID partner organizations for survey purposes is as follows: 60 government, 82 nonprofit, and 12 for-profit organizations. The main objective of this program was to assist government and non-profit organizations in Pakistan in developing institutional capacity in order to effectively implement development projects. The training areas were financial management, human resource management, procurement, program monitoring and evaluation, leadership, fiscal decentralization, gender, communication, and forensic auditing. An average training period lasted for three to five days and consisted of 30 participants. Over the course of the program, more than 3000 employees from all four provinces of Pakistan received training in one or more subject areas. Most of the trainees were nominated by their supervisors, while some nominated themselves to join the program. The vast majority were professional employees: 56% were from government agencies, 41% were from non-profit organizations, and 3% were employed in private firms. Most of the trainees (85%) were men. 2 In the fall of 2015, we approached the program’s manager and requested access to the contact details of all trainees. The program manager provided us with email addresses of 2436 trainees. 3 After removing duplicate entries and trainees employed in private companies, the sample size was 2335. Of these, 207 trainees were unreachable or did not have a valid email address, further reducing the sample size to 2128. Using Qualtrics, we invited trainees to take part in the 6 International Review of Administrative Sciences 0(0) study and complete a survey. In the recruitment email, we explained the study’s purpose, maintained that participation was voluntary, and guaranteed anonymity. The survey asked respondents about corruption in their organization, the leadership practices of their supervisor, their organization’s reward system, and their work environment. Both the recruitment email and the survey were in English. The survey remained open for one month and three email reminders were sent to boost the response rate. Altogether 741 surveys were returned for a response rate of 34.8%: 56% of the respondents were employed in public agencies and 44% were employed in non-profits; 13% of the respondents were women; and the average age was between 30 and 39 years. Measures For the purpose of this study, we relied on subjective measures of corruption and asked respondents to report the corrupt behavior of others in their workplaces. We constructed a five-item measure that asked respondents the following question: “Over the past one year, how often have you observed, or heard about, someone in your office 4 engaging in each of the following behaviors? (1) taking or demanding a bribe, (2) receiving a gift or personal favor from a client in exchange for a service, (3) falsifying or misreporting information, (4) misusing or wasting office funds or resources, and (5) giving an unfair advantage to a vendor/contractor.” The items had five response choices (11⁄4never; 51⁄4very often). We constructed the items based on corrupt practices identified by De Graaf and Huberts (2008). Steers’s (1976) Task-Goal Attribute Scales provided the basis for the three-item measure of performance-based rewards. The items have six response choices (1 1⁄4strongly disagree; 61⁄4strongly agree). We measured procedural fairness with the seven-item procedural justice scale developed and validated by Colquitt (2001). The items have five response choices (11⁄4not at all; 51⁄4to a great extent) and asked respondents to rate the fairness of the procedures used in their offices to make jobrelated decisions (i.e. pay, promotion, and performance evaluation). We measured ethical leadership with 10 items from the Ethical Leadership Questionnaire (ELQ) developed and validated by Yukl et al. (2013). The ELQ items capture different aspects of ethical leadership and include both values and behaviors. Respondents rated their supervisors’ honesty, integrity, fairness, accountability, and ethical guidance. All ELQ items had a six-point Likert-style response format (11⁄4strongly disagree; 61⁄4strongly agree). Research shows that public employees with higher public service motivation are more likely to behave ethically and report the ethical misconduct of others in their organizations than those with lower levels of public service motivation (Wright et al., 2016). To isolate the effect of ethical leadership on corruption in public organizations, we therefore included a five-item measure of public service motivation. The items are based on the scale used by Wright et al. (2013) and have six response choices (11⁄4strongly disagree; 61⁄4strongly agree). In addition, we control for organization type (public1⁄41; otherwise1⁄40), respondent gender (female1⁄41; Bashir and Hassan 7 male 1⁄40), age (11⁄420 to 29 years; 51⁄460 years or older), and office tenure (11⁄4less than six months; 51⁄4more than five years) in our analysis. Findings Confirmatory factor analysis We performed confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to assess the construct validity of the study measures. We relied on established measures to evaluate the measurement model, including the Root Mean Squared Errors of Approximation (RMSEA), the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), and the Tucker Lewis Index (TLI). A satisfactory model fit to the data is indicated by CFI and TLI values being greater than .90, and the RMSEA value being smaller than or equal to .08 (Bowen and Guo, 2012). In addition, we examined the convergent and discriminant validity of the measures. Convergent validity is demonstrated when all items have standardized loadings greater than .70 on their respective factor and the average variance extracted (AVE) for each factor is greater than .50 (Bagozzi et al., 1991). Discriminant validity is demonstrated when the AVE of each construct is greater than the shared variance between each pair of constructs (Fornell and Larcker, 1981). The fit indices for the measurement model are as follows: CFI1⁄4.91, TLI1⁄4.90, and RMSEA1⁄4.06. This suggests that the measurement model fits adequately to data. All scale items have significant (p <.01) factor loadings on their respective constructs except for the last two items of the procedural fairness scale (see the online appendix). The factor loadings on these two items are inexplicably low (ks 1⁄4–.06 and .01;p >.10) and they depressed the AVE of the procedural fairness factor to .37. 5 One of the items of the performance-based rewards factor has a weak but significant factor loading (k 1⁄4.22; p <.01). Factor loadings on the two remaining items of scale are high and the AVE of the performance-based rewards factor is .53. The AVEs of the ethical leadership and corruption factors are .70 and .60, respectively. The AVEs of all factors are greater than the shared variance between any pair of factors, indicating that measures have adequate discriminant validity. To assess the discriminant validity of the procedural fairness and performance-based rewards measures further, we estimated an alternative four-factor CFA in which the correlation between procedural fairness and performance-based rewards was set to 1. The fit indices of this measurement model are CFI1⁄4.87, TLI1⁄4.86, and RMSEA1⁄4.09. We also performed a sequential chi-square difference test which indicated that the five-factor model fits the data better than the alternative four-factor model (Dv2 1⁄4420.5; p <.01). Even though the factor loadings on the last two items of the procedural fairness scale were very low, we did not exclude these items when we calculated the composite scale score of procedural fairness. Davis and Stazyk (2017) recommend against deleting items from established scales because that would be contradictory to existing theory and previous efforts that validated the scales. As scores for our dependent measure are right-skewed (251 of the 741 respondents indicated never observing any type of corrupt behavior in their offices), the use of Ordinary Least Square (OLS) regression analysis may introduce a downward bias in the slopes for the coefficients and an upward bias in the estimated intercept. Moreover, because survey responses are nested by organizations, use of an OLS estimator may introduce bias in the estimates for standard errors in regression coefficients. To address these issues, we first estimated two OLS models. The first OLS model included controls and three predictor measures; the second model included two interaction terms and the variables included in the first model. In both models, the standard errors of the coefficients were clustered around organizations. Second, we estimated two censored regression models that are analogous to the OLS models but use Tobit’s (1958) maximum likelihood estimator. The use of a Tobit estimator allows us to assess the robustness of the OLS estimates, as well as fix the specification error introduced in OLS models with truncated data (Heckman 1979). Similar to OLS models, standard errors in Tobit models were clustered around organizations. Finally, we estimated two multi-level Tobit (ME Tobit) models that address both nesting and truncation issues. 6 In all six models, we standardized the values for all predictor measures except for two dummy variables (employee gender and organization type) in order to minimize the likelihood of multicollinearity. Table 3 reports the results of the regression analysis. Estimates reported in the table show similar results across all three types of regression analysis. Looking at the estimates of model 5 that are robust to the data truncation and nesting issues noted earlier, we find higher incidences of corruption in public compared to nonprofit organizations in Pakistan (b1⁄4.39; p <.01). Female employees are more likely than male employees to report incidences of corruption in their organization (b 1⁄4.22; p <.05). We also observe that the connection between ethical leadership and corruption is negative and statistically significant (b1⁄4–.19; p <.01). The use of performance-based rewards appears as a strong deterrent of corruption (b1⁄4–.46; p <.01). However, the connection between procedural fairness and corruption is not statistically significant. Bashir and Hassan 11 Discussion Summary and implications The purpose of this study was to assess the influence of ethical leadership in reducing corruption in public organizations, and whether this relationship is moderated by the perceived fairness of organizations’ reward systems. We assessed these relationships with original survey data and found that incidences of corruption are higher in government than in non-profit organizations in Pakistan. Female employees are more likely than male employees to report corruption. The results also show that ethical leadership reduces incidences of corruption, but this relationship is weaker in organizations with high procedural fairness perceptions. We also found a negative connection between the use of performance-based rewards and reports of corruption in public organizations in Pakistan. The findings have implications for both public management research and practice. The remedies to corruption typically suggested by experts are: increasing surveillance, oversight, and sanctions; improving the transparency of public procurement procedures; the privatization of state-owned enterprises; and improving the wages and benefits of public-sector workers (Rose-Ackerman and Palifka, 2016). However, there are disagreements about the extent to which these measures, particularly external oversight and control, are effective in reducing corruption. Segal (2002) suggests that true reforms often require deinstitutionalizing corruption at the organizational level by changing organizations’ cultures, overhauling Figure 2. Similarly, Trevino et al. (1999) suggest that the organizational practices that seem to reduce incidences of unethical employee behavior are: the fair treatment of employees; ethical managerial leadership; and establishing an open work culture where employees can discuss ethical problems without fear of retribution. Consistent with these suggestions, we find that ethical leadership and performance-based rewards are related negatively to incidences of corruption in Pakistan. This finding is in line with the arguments of Becker and Stigler (1974) and policy advice by international institutions such as the World Bank and International Monetary Fund. It highlights the importance of establishing an equitable reward system to reduce corruption in public organizations. Moreover, it supports the argument that when the performance of employees is not recognized with appropriate rewards and incentives, some employees may displace moral responsibility for their actions, rationalize unethical behavior, and engage in corruption. However, it would be interesting to assess whether this relationship holds in organizations with highly utilitarian reward structures or that emphasize meeting short-term goals over long-term outcomes. There is ample evidence that coupling job rewards too tightly with performance metrics, such as student test scores in public school districts or the number of loans issued by mortgage bankers, can lead to serious ethical problems. One could argue that the global financial crisis in 2008 and the recent scandal involving Wells Fargo were, in large part, due to a highly utilitarian reward system. An important finding of our study is the negative relationship between ethical leadership and corruption in public organizations. This finding highlights the need to recruit and retain ethical managers in public organizations. Our study also offers insights into specific actions that public managers can take to reduce and prevent incidences of corruption in their organizations. These actions include coaching subordinates about ethical issues, communicating clearly about ethical standards and expectations, and holding subordinates accountable for both ethical and unethical behavior. We observe that the link between ethical leadership and corruption is stronger when respondents report a low, as opposed to a high, level of procedural fairness. It is possible that political instability, weak legal controls, and weak regulatory regimes often preclude the establishment of strong governance structures in publicsector organizations in much of the developing world. Our study suggests that the need for ethical leadership is much higher in such organizations. A final contribution of our study is the use of a multi-item behavioral measure of corruption. Prior studies largely employed single-item perceptual measures (e.g. propensity to accept bribes) or focused solely on incidences of bribery. Our study considered incidences of bribery as well as the falsification or misreporting of data/ information, the misuse/wastage of public funds and resources, and favoritism in the organization. Additionally, instead of asking respondents about their perceptions of these behaviors, we asked them about the frequency of observing such Bashir and Hassan 13 behaviors. The factor analysis results showed that items have desirable psychometric properties and high levels of internal reliability. Although we find a significant negative association between procedural fairness and corruption, this relationship disappeared when we controlled for other predictors in the regression analysis. This was somewhat unexpected because two recent public-sector studies found a negative association between the use of a neutral/merit-based recruitment process and incidences of corruption in governments (Dahlstrom et al., 2012; Meyer-Sahling and Mikkelsen, 2016). One potential explanation for our result is that we did not ask respondents specifically about the neutrality of the recruitment procedures in their organizations. Instead, our questions asked respondents about the overall fairness of how decisions regarding their jobs were made in their organizations. Another potential explanation is that respondents confounded ethical leadership with procedural fairness. However, this is unlikely as the correlation between procedural fairness and ethical leadership was not high. The factor analysis results also showed two distinct factors. This relationship needs further investigation. Limitations and directions for future research Our study is limited to Pakistan, but we expect similar patterns to be observed in other South Asian countries like Bangladesh and India. We used single-source data, which is prone to social desirability biases. To counter the issue, we took several precautionary measures in designing our survey instrument. For example, instead of asking respondents about their involvement in corruption, assuming that they were unlikely to admit this, we asked them to report about their coworkers. We also used both positively and negatively worded items in the survey. Moreover, we used different anchors or scale formats for different measures. The results provided some assurance that these precautionary measures were effective in reducing, if not eliminating, social desirability bias in the survey responses. For example, the intercorrelations among the study measures were low to moderate. The principal components analysis also showed that the first or method factor did not explain the majority of the variance in items. Further, the use of relevant controls and a robust estimation strategy also provided some guard against the problems that typically manifest with common-source data. Nevertheless, it is important for future studies to consider using independent sources of data for the dependent variable in order to verify our findings. We used a cross-sectional design in our study. Thus, we cannot infer any causal connection between ethical leadership and corruption. Another limitation of our study is that we used a convenience sample. The participants were employees in government and non-profit organizations that were involved with USAID projects in Pakistan. The use of non-probability samples leads to selection bias, which we are unable to resolve with our data. The prevalence of corruption may, indeed, be much higher in organizations that are not involved with USAID in Pakistan. 14 International Review of Administrative Sciences 0(0) The positively skewed corruption scores observed in this study reflect this problem. Our findings need to be verified with a longitudinal design and a systematic sample. There are several interesting questions that future research should consider exploring. As noted earlier, ethical leaders are not only honest and trustworthy, but also actively shape the behavior of their followers by modeling ethical behavior, clarifying ethical standards, rewarding ethical behavior, and sanctioning unethical behavior. Prior research has largely examined the overall influence of both themoral personand moral managementaspects of ethical leadership, and not their independent and joint effects. It would be interesting to examine, for example, how public managers’ personal attributes, such as ethical reputation, interact with their attempts to influence the ethical behavior of their subordinates, for example, by providing guidance and sanctioning unethical behavior. Future research should also examine variables that may mediate the effects of ethical leadership on corruption. One potential mediating variable is the ethical organizational climate (Victor and Cullen, 1988). Finally, an interesting question that future studies should pursue is how the broader institutional environment and societal values interact with the proximal work context in predicting corruption in public organizations. Influence of Ethical Leadership in Managing Human Resources in Construction Companies Ali Nawaz Khan, Ph.D.1; Naseer Abbas Khan, Ph.D.2; and Mohsin Ali Soomro, Ph.D.3 Abstract: Construction companies are often notorious for high employee turnover and antisocial behavior. In a hazardous work environment, arduous scheduling tasks, unethical supervision, and working with multiple team members put higher stress on employees to reflect antisocial behavior and lead to turnover intention. Therefore, this article attempts to investigate the association between ethical leadership and turnover intention and antisocial behavior through trust in the leader and procedural justice in the construction industry. From the perspective of resource conservation theory, this article assumes that the moderating influence of job embeddedness plays a role in the association between mediators (trust in leaders and procedural justice) and outcome variables (turnover intention and antisocial behavior). This article uses data collected from 275 employees of Hong Kong construction companies. The results indicated a negative association between ethical leadership and employee turnover intention in the construction industry. The results revealed that job embeddedness moderated the link between trust in leader and turnover intention, and the link between procedural justice and turnover intention. Moreover, the influence of job embeddedness was found nonsignificant in the case of antisocial behavior. This article provides useful insights for policy and decision-making authorities, especially site managers, on how ethical leadership can retain employees by strengthening trust and procedural justice in construction companies.DOI: 10.1061/(ASCE)CO.1943-7862.0001919. © 2020 American Society of Civil Engineers. Introduction The construction industry is a challenging industry for employees due to time and cost-intensive difficult schedules and harsh, difficult working conditions (Cheng and Hoang 2015). Dangerous and stressful working conditions have made the construction industry infamous, and employee turnover has long been an important issue for the global construction industry. At present, the US construction industry’s employee turnover rate is estimated at 21.4%, which is one of the highest in all industries (Yildirmaz et al. 2019). It is a great competitive advantage for companies that can retain skilled employees. Most of the management scholars emphasized that hazardous work conditions, high accident rates, work stress, deep dissatisfaction with work, and the poor balance between work and life are common issues in the construction companies (Chih et al. 2016), which leads to a high rate of turnover. However, this article presents another aspect of the construction industry, which is rarely noticed by scholars, and this is the influence of ethical leadership on turnover intention and antisocial behavior of employees. Anwar et al. (2017) defined turnover intention as an employee’s desire to resign depending on their emotional state. In the public domain, the construction industry has a poor record of ethics and social image (Afsar and Shahjehan 2018; Khan et al. 2019b). Leadership faces even greater challenges, as leaders in the construction industry focus more on the job accomplishment than on ways and means to get the job done (Ofori 2008). As a result, they tend to ignore the needs of followers, the organization they work in, and the society in which they live. Besides, conventional performance standards in the construction industry promote increased profits, thereby making a trade-off over employee satisfaction and well-being (Yang et al. 2018). In this regard, leaders in the construction industry have a responsibility to adopt and emphasize ethical practices, which helps increase employee satisfaction while performing complex, risky tasks on site. On the other hand, when employees are forced to perform in an unethical work environment, turnover intention and antisocial behavior can be promoted within the employees, and the consequent loss of talent can lead to the loss of productivity and the market reputation of the construction company (Chih et al. 2016). This article uses the broad term antisocial behavior to state negative behavior in an organization. Antisocial behavior covers a wide range of actions, and the term also encompasses the harmful nature of these actions (i.e., the fact that they could cause damage to the property of individuals and/or organizations) (Giacalone and Greenberg 1997). This dimension of potential harm is the focus of most definitions of related constructs (see details,Robinson and Greenberg 1998). Lingard (2003) and Sherman (1986) argued that poor ethical practices in the workplace not only undermines the team’s work that is required to complete construction tasks in accordance with required standards, but also leads to increased employee turnover. For example, the US construction industry reports an annual employee turnover rate of 28.2%, of which 65% is for small construction companies (Bureau of Labor Statistics 2018; Jackson 2018). Nevertheless, introducing ethical leadership in the construction industry is difficult due to the project-based structure of companies and the trend of temporary contractual relationships with subcontractors. Ethical leadership is a valuable style that emphasizes the ethical aspects of leadership in the management of a construction project. It is, therefore, related to concepts like trust, fairness, honesty, charisma, and consideration (Brown et al. 2005). Ethical leadership is based on appreciation and adoption of ethical beliefs and values and respect for the rights and dignity of others. Thus, it is argued that if a construction manager exhibits ethical leadership to their team/subordinates, it will ensure that the workforce individuals are provided with a safe workplace environment and that their professional as well as personal needs are taken care of. Recognizing the global significance of ethical leadership in promoting employee ethical behavior (Gok et al. 2017; Walumbwa et al. 2011), construction companies also need to implement ethical leadership to improve overall workplace productivity and prevent employee turnover and deviant work behavior. Therefore, this article attempts to assess the influence of ethical leadership on employee turnover intention and employee antisocial behavior. This article focuses on the three main contexts in the construction industry: (1) the role of ethical leaders in improving employee trust in leadership and employee procedural justice; (2) the mediating role of ethical leaders in indirect relationships with employee turnover intentions and antisocial behavior; and (3) the moderating role of the job embeddedness to overcome the adverse effect of outcome variables (as shown in Fig.1). Trust in leadership means employees want their leaders to treat them well, so they are willing to stay open with their leaders (Cheung et al. 2013; Chughtai et al. 2014). In the construction industry, trust in leadership can affect the ability of leaders to motivate and inspire employees (Chughtai et al. 2014; Ding and Ng 2010). When employees trust leaders, they have confidence in their decisions. According to the conservation of resources (COR) theory, ethical leaders support the protection of organizations and employee resources by enhancing employees’ trust and belief in the organization’s environment (Quade et al. 2017). Whereas procedural justice emphasizes fair procedures used in the decision-making process (Srinivasan et al. 2018) of construction companies. Many benefits have been found in the use of justice in the work environment, such as job satisfaction (Sweeney and McFarlin 1993), low turnover (Ayodele et al. 2020), and low absenteeism (Lam et al. 2002). Moreover, previous researchers have studied the role of moral leadership from the perspective of positive outcomes such as job satisfaction (Tu et al. 2017; Hantula 2015), commitment (Neves et al. 2018), performance (Mo and Shi 2017), and creativity (Javed et al. 2018). However, this study examines the psychological aspects that link the ethical approach of leaders to employee turnover and antisocial behavior. Theory and Hypotheses Development According to COR theory (Hobfoll 1989), an employee’s turnover intention may increase with the depletion of the employee ’s psychological resources when performing challenges and complex tasks in construction companies. In these circumstances, the role of an ethical leader is critical to protecting the psychological resources of employees. In addition, COR theory argues that the focus of ethical leadership is to preserve existing resources and find new ones by reducing stress on employees and providing an enabling work environment, which is essential in most construction projects (Thamhain and Wilemon 1977). In the management literature, scholars have reached a consensus that followers often rely on leadership, which typically triggers more positive behaviors and promotes socialization among them, and increases productivity by reducing the depletion of psychological resources (Bowen et al. 2014; Hurst et al. 2017; Khan and Ali 2018). For employees, conserving psychological resources is more important than acquiring new resources in the workplace (Hobfoll 1989). Therefore, ethical leadership through procedural justice and trust in leaders can help minimize the depletion of the psychological resources of the employees and increase job satisfaction. Job embeddedness serves as a framework for predicting the impact of social relationships on voluntary turnover in some situations. Moreover, job embeddedness denotes a broad range of effects, not just emotional ones. As far as we know, past studies (Chih et al. 2016; Ma et al. 2017) mainly focused on the psychological mechanism of interpersonal factors leading to voluntary turnover. Various resource indicators are related to turnover intention. In this regard, there are two main reasons to consider job embeddedness as a boundary condition that limits negative behavior and intentions. First, job embeddedness is a key construct that is originally embedded to predict employee turnover (Mitchell et al. 2001). Second, this construct (job embeddedness) is essentially a broader construct that covers the various factors that lead to job retention. From a COR perspective, job embeddedness indicates the resources that are acquired by employees by investing energy, time, and effort (Burton et al. 2010; Choi et al. 2018; A. N. Khan, N. A. Khan, A. A. Bodla, and S. Gul, personal communication, 2019). In the construction industry, individuals value resource conservation. Generally, employees in the construction industry tend to accumulate resources and experience a high degree of job embeddedness until they maintain contact with the organization and its members, adapt to work and company culture, and have strong psychological health for employees who need to protect resources (Bano et al. 2019; Harris et al. 2011). Ethical Leadership Toward Employee Turnover Intention and Antisocial Behavior Brown et al. (2005) suggest that ethical leadership often motivates leaders to act for the common well-being of their employees and is generally accepted in the communities where they live. Ethical leaders consider the opinions of others (such as colleagues or subordinates) to make a final decision (Treviño et al. 2003). Ethical leaders have the ability to make decisions based on complex ethical principles characterized by integrity and fairness (McCann and Holt 2009). COR theory emphasizes that resources, including human resources, are critical to the productivity of an organization (Gordon et al. 2018). This is very relevant to the construction industry, in which employees not only spend years learning skills to become skilled technicians but also act as custodians of the knowledge accumulated after the company has commissioned project work for many years. Ethical Leadership Toward Employee Trust in Leader, Turnover Intention, and Antisocial Behavior Brown and Mitchell (2010) found that the general content of ethical leadership (including honesty, fairness, and ethical role models) is recognized in different contexts and industries, including the construction industry. As a legitimate role model, ethical leaders have the ability to create a rewarding work environment in the company, in which ethical behavior has been given due consideration, and the clarity of ethical standards is likely to encourage followers and trust of leaders, eventually leading to job satisfaction (A. N. Khan, N. A. Khan, A. A. Bodla, and S. Gul, personal communication, 2019; Khan et al. 2019c; Tu et al. 2017). In the construction industry, the reciprocity of followers’engagement in prosocial behavior may increase when ethical leaders show fairness, impartiality, and trustworthiness, and acknowledges the advice of followers in the decision-making process (Brown and Mitchell 2010). Javed et al. (2018) argued that trust in leaders makes subordinates more willing to rely on their leaders and promotes positive work outcomes. On the other hand, when employee trust breaks down, they become doubtful and suspicious (Cao et al. 2018; De Jong et al. 2009). Lack of trust causes anxiety over the behavior of the leader as a means of self-protection, and despite witnessing unethical behavior, individuals begin to shift resources and observe turnover (Yang and Mossholder 2010). Ethical leadership provides a conducive environment for employees, and employees can build trust in leaders to maintain harmonious relationships with each other, which is necessary to complete challenging tasks. In a construction project, it is often the case that project-site staff has to make decisions pertaining to the site operational tasks in the absence and without the approval of their leaders, keeping in view the necessity of time and the action. The examples of such tasks are commissioning and decommissioning of construction tasks and procurement of materials by assistant engineers, hiring and/or deploying laborers by site supervisors, etc. Employees make such decisions keeping in view the need and pace of the project, given that they have trust in their supervisors that they will fully adhere to their decisions. According to COR, ethical leaders have the ability to build trust and retain psychological resources that can mitigate factors that may increase employee stress. The trust is based on moral grounds (Blau 1964). When leaders and employees behave in a consistent manner, employees will have greater trust with their leaders and show higher productivity. Therefore, the following hypotheses can be proposed: H1c: Ethical leadership enhances trust in leader in construction company employees. H2a: Trust in leader decreases the turnover intention of employees in the construction company. H2b: Trust in leader decreases the antisocial behavior of employees in the construction company. From a multidisciplinary perspective, Rousseau et al. (1998) define trust as a state of mind that includes intentions to accept vulnerability because of the positive expectations of the intention or behaviors of others. Cook and Wall (1980) proposed two major factors for discussing the value of trust in a relationship. The first is the belief in the intentions of the others and the second is the degree of confidence in its reliability and capabilities. On the other hand, McAllister (1995) mentioned this phenomenon, which is a cognitive dimension that trusts someone in some cases based on objective reasons and an emotional dimension driven by interpersonal relationships. Yang and Mossholder (2010) put forward two perspectives to discuss trust in leaders: trust in direct supervisors and trust in management. On the other hand, Podsakoff et al. (1990) described two dimensions by explaining the trust in leaders in term of faith and loyalty. Jung et al. (2009) see loyalty and trust in leader as two separate entities. Overall, trust is a key element in building interactions between employees and supervisors, not only maintaining harmonious working relationships, but also improving organizational effectiveness (Khan et al. 2019a). Therefore, the ethical values of the leader and the trust in the construction companies have enhanced the psychological resources of the employees, who have shown higher satisfaction in completing their daily work. Conversely, employees with low morale due to reduced trust in leader are those with low job satisfaction or low organizational commitment (Chughtai et al. 2014; Shen et al. 2017). In the association between leadership and employee behavior, past studies have discussed the mediating role of trust in leaders. For example, Kelloway et al. (2012) examined the link between transformational leaders and employee well-being through trust in leaders. Afsar and Shahjehan (2018) also looked at the interceding role of trust in leaders in the construction industry. In this regard, this article also assumes that trust in leaders can mediate the link between ethical leadership and turnover intention and antisocial behavior. Hence, this article posits as H2c: The association between ethical leadership and turnover intention in construction company employees is mediated by trust in leaders. H2d: The association between ethical leadership and antisocial behavior of construction company employees is mediated by trust in leader. Ethical Leadership Toward Procedural Justice, Turnover Intention, and Antisocial Behavior Ethical leaders are always in favor of creating and establishing conditions conducive to employees that enable them to observe factors of justice and fairness. Organizational justice is formed by employees interacting with leaders and organizations (Rousseau and Aquino 1993). In the construction industry, ethical leaders are more focused on increasing followers’perception of procedural justice to increase their engagement in assigned tasks (Chan and Chan 2005; Piccolo and Colquitt 2006). It is unavoidable in the construction industry to follow fair practices and procedural justice, as employees working on projects face increasing uncertainty and fragile conditions (Srinivasan et al. 2018; Yang et al. 2018). Ethical leaders can acknowledge and insist on taking the necessary actions to benefit employees (Geistauts et al. 2008). When employees receive the care and support of leaders, they are motivated to do more for the organization and avoid negative behaviors in the workplace (Walumbwa et al. 2011). Similarly, when employees believe that leaders are fair and just in the decision-making process, they tend to be more loyal and satisfied. Moderating Role of Job Embeddedness The concept of job embeddedness has changed dramatically over time, starting with the voluntary departure model (Lee and Mitchell 1994), which provides a good indication of why individuals are looking forward to long-term employment. The construction industry is notorious for high subordinates turnover (Chih et al. 2016), so the leadership of construction organizations is under constant pressure to make arrangements that can retain human resources (Jackson 2018). The inherent characteristics of management practice plays a vital role in the pursuit of reducing subordinates turnover and increasing job embeddedness (Burton et al. 2010; Khan and Khan 2019; Sadiq and Qadeer 2017). However, there is not enough evidence in the management literature to outline how job embeddedness can best be moderated by organizations to reduce turnover intention and employee behavior. International financial institutions issued a report that states that job embeddedness is also driven by employee realization (Burton et al. 2010). Previous studies of job embeddedness in various industries are rare, which explains that job embeddedness explains a number of differences beyond employee engagement (Karadas and Karatepe 2019), job satisfaction (Felps et al. 2009), and organizational commitment (Tanova and Holtom 2008). Bambacas and Kulik (2013) studied job embeddedness as a boundary condition to examine the link between human resource practices and employee work outcomes. Wijayanto and Kimono (2004) found a positive correlation between job embeddedness and prosocial behavior. Mitchell et al. (2001) examined and found that job embeddedness moderated the impact of absenteeism, citizenship, and turnover intention. Therefore, this article proposes the following hypotheses: H4a: Job embeddedness moderates the association between trust in leaders and turnover intention, making this association weaker as job embeddedness increases rather than decreases. H4b: Job embeddedness moderates the association between trust in leaders and antisocial behavior, making this association weaker as job embeddedness increases rather than decreases. H5a: Job embeddedness moderates the association between perception of procedural justice and turnover intention, making this association weaker as job embeddedness increases rather than decreases. H5b: Job embeddedness moderates the association between perception of procedural justice and antisocial behavior, making this association weaker as job embeddedness increases rather than decreases The aforementioned literature provides academic support to the role of job embeddedness for determining the impact of leadership on the behavioral outcomes of followers. Consistent with this, this study also assumes that job embeddedness can significantly serve as as boundary condition in the link between ethical leadership and turnover intention, and the link between ethical leadership and antisocial behavior through trust in leader and perception of procedural justice condition. Therefore, this article assumes the following hypotheses: H6a: Job embeddedness moderates the mediating effect of trust in leader in the association between ethical leadership and turnover intention, making this mediating effect stronger as job embeddedness increases rather than decreases. H6b: Job embeddedness moderates the mediating effect of trust in leader in the association between ethical leadership and antisocial behavior, making this mediating effect stronger as job embeddedness increases rather than decreases. H7a: Job embeddedness moderates the mediating effect of perception of procedural justice in the association between ethical leadership and turnover intention, making this mediating effect stronger as job embeddedness increases rather than decreases. H7b: Job embeddedness moderates the mediating effect of perception of procedural justice in the association between ethical leadership and antisocial behavior, making this mediating effect stronger as job embeddedness increases rather than decreases. Since the original scales were in the English language, the items of these scales were translated into Chinese using standard reverse translation procedures recommended by Brislin (1980). While collecting the questionnaire responses, we targeted such teams and the employee responding to their team leaders. In order to maintain the rigor of the sample, the primary data was collected from multiple building project sites operated by fourteen construction contracting companies having the highest annual turnover among the Hong Kong based contractors. The questionnaires were distributed by hand in sealed envelopes with specific codes assigned for matching leader-follower dyads to 550 employees of different construction companies, of which 309 returned the completed questionnaires. Discussion This article examines the complex effects of ethical leadership, trust in leaders, and perceptions of procedural justice on the turnover intention and antisocial behavior of construction company employees. The results of this article extend the theory and contribute to the literature on ethical leadership for employees of construction companies. Although past studies have linked the leadership to employee behavioral outcomes, this paper emphasizes construction companies to study the interaction between ethical leaders and employees. This may be the first article that explores the impact of ethical leadership on employee turnover intention and antisocial behavior through trust in leader and perceptions of procedural justice, and the moderating role of job embeddedness, especially in the construction industry. As a result, this article expands existing debates about ethical leadership in employee intent and behavior and provides new insights into this emerging concept. The results of this article found that ethical leadership directly and indirectly (through trust in leaders and perception of procedural justice) significantly affects the turnover intention and antisocial behavior of construction company employees. Our findings can be supported by some past studies in the construction industry. For example, Afsar and Shahjehan (2018) found that when there is a high degree of trust in leaders and leader−follower value congruence, there is a strong positive association between ethical leadership and employee behavior. Another important finding of this research is that job embeddedness moderated the association between trust in leaders and turnover intention and the association between procedural justice and turnover intention. However, some distinctive results were noticed regarding the moderating role of job embeddedness. The results showed that job embeddedness has an insignificant moderating effect on the association between trust in leaders and antisocial behavior, and on the relationship between perception of procedural justice and antisocial behavior of construction company employees. Similarly, distinctive results have been found when examining the moderating effect of job embeddedness on the mediating effects of trust in leader and perception of procedural justice on the association between ethical leadership and antisocial behavior. In addition to these distinctive findings, the buffering effect of job embeddedness in these findings does not affect the reduction of antisocial behavior but can reduce the turnover intention of employees in the construction industry. The remaining results complement findings from previous research on organizational behavior in other industries (Jones 1998; Steers and Porter 1991). Employees are primarily inspired by leaders, and if leaders have ethical standards they can help their followers to avoid quitting their jobs. Theoretical Contributions This article has contributed in several distinctive ways. First, our overall contribution is that this article has established and assessed a conceptual model that distinctively combines ethical leadership with turnover intention and antisocial behavior by emphasizing the construction industry in Hong Kong. This article illustrates the important role that ethical leaders play in limiting follower turnover intention and antisocial behavior. Previously, ethical leadership was often seen as a mechanism to curb unethical behavior, but this article has proven that ethical leadership can effectively reduce job turnover intention and antisocial behavior in the construction industry. Second, the study adds substantive mediators (trust and procedural justice) to elucidate the influence of ethical leadership on employee turnover intention and antisocial behavior. Despite concerns, risks, and fears related to complexity in the construction industry and its ethical standards, trust in leaders and procedural justice are key psychological pathways that can help ethical leaders inspire follower job satisfaction and avoid antisocial behavior. The mainstream leadership literature highlights the significance of ethical leadership in fostering positive behaviors and intentions, such as organizational citizenship behavior, organizational commitment, and in achieving higher levels of job performance (Khan et al. 2020; Neubert et al. 2013). However, scholars in the construction industry pay little attention to the value of ethical leaders in curtailing negative attitudes and behaviors, which are often observed in the workplace. To cover this gap in the engineering management literature, this article enriches the existing literature by enhancing a deep understanding of the value of ethical leadership in reducing employee mobility and antisocial behavior. Third, this article investigates the circumstances in which ethical leadership can reduce turnover intentions among construction company employees with high job embeddedness. This article suggests that ethical leadership can efficiently lessen turnover intention when construction company employees are highly embedded in their job. However, when job embeddedness buffered the association between trust in leaders and antisocial behavior, and the association between procedural justice and antisocial behavior, ethical leaders have proven to be not very effective in suppressing antisocial behavior. Similarly, the buffering role of job embeddedness on arbitrating effects of trust in leaders and procedural justice suggests that ethical leadership cannot effectively minimize antisocial behavior. Finally, in response to a previous call for research on the underlying mechanisms linking ethical leadership to employee work outcomes (Kalshoven and Zegveld 2011), this article recognized two distinctive but corresponding employee-centered variables— trust in leaders and procedural justice— which have been proven to connect ethical leadership with employee intention and behavior. From a resource conservation perspective, the results of this article indicate that higher degree of ethical leadership can lead to more psychological resources of employees, such as higher degree of trust in leaders, procedural justice, and job embeddedness for interacting with leaders, which leads to reduce turnover intention and antisocial behavior in the construction industry. Managerial Implications This article puts forward many important practical implications. First, the findings of this article show that ethical leadership has a significant influence on employee turnover intention and negative behaviors. The construction project employees are exposed to a multitude of stress caused by work overload and tight schedules (Zhang et al. 2015) that usually leads to employees behaving antisocially at the workplace and in their daily routine outside the workplace (Ofori 2008). Subjected to such stress, construction employees tend to leave the company (Haupt and Dala 2016). This study has shown that adopting ethical leadership can significantly reduce the turnover intentions of construction employees and improve their behavior. Therefore, it is important for construction companies to find, choose, and encourage people who display required ethical values as leaders. Instead, construction companies can choose to invest in training programs related to ethics to allow existing leaders to strengthen their ethical reasoning and moral behavior. © ASCE 04020125-8 J. Second, this study has shown that if ethical leadership is forged with the trust in leader and procedural justice through the use of defined scenarios to encourage employees through positive or alternative ethical experiences and effective social persuasion. Such trainings can help construction employees and their leaders to envisage the impacts of positive behavior mediated through procedural justice and the trust build by the leaders. Third, construction managers should understand that the ethical leadership approach can promote ethical behavior, not just impeccable logic in this way to reduce the turnover intention, especially for those who align with their values. Trust in leaders and procedural justice make ethical leaders more prominent and effective in reducing employee turnover intention. Emphasis on procedural justice, job embeddedness, and empowerment may increase trust in leaders and thereby increase job satisfaction. Construction employees building trust in their leaders and the procedural justice can better cope with the workplace stress and thereby not only improving their performance but also reducing intentions to quit jobs. Moreover, the ethical values of leadership should be given priority because construction is a global business (Moodley et al. 2008). The evident ethical concerns in construction industry includes bribery, collusion, fraud, negligence, and unfair practices on site (Bowen et al. 2007). For the construction industry, therefore, it becomes essential to provide a mechanism through which ethical issues should be addressed by promoting ethical values in leadership. Finally, leaders must pay particular attention to issues such as how much employees trust them and how well they can express their inner feelings. The construction sector should encourage leaders to work honestly and openly with employees, beyond the“just painted” smile (Hochschild 1983; Raza et al. 2020). When employees feel unfair about leadership and distrust the leader, or are afraid to communicate openly with the leader, it can lead to a variety of negative behaviors and turnover intentions. Therefore, it is recommended that leaders should cultivate ethical values, because in this competitive era, ethical practices in the construction industry have become a key factor for success. Conclusions The growing body of literature (e.g.,Chih et al. 2016; Love et al. 2011) calls for a better understanding of the construction employees’social and psychological attitude in a project environment, to conserve their performance and creativity for their respective organizations. In response to such a call, this study chose to evaluate the impact of ethical leadership on construction sector employees in reducing their turnover intentions and antisocial behavior. This study considered two mediating variables (i.e., trust in the leader and procedural justice) through which the impact of ethical leadership was evaluated. The results indicated that ethical leadership significantly reduced job turnover intentions in construction sector employees and improves their social behavior. Such a significant impact was affirmed through the mediating variables and the direct impact as well. Besides, this study also considered the moderating impact of employees job embeddedness over the outcome variables via their established association with the mediating variables. The results illustrated that job embeddedness significantly moderated the association between trust in leaders and turnover intentions and the association between procedural justice and turnover intention. However, job embeddedness was found to have an insignificant moderating effect on the association between trust in leaders and antisocial behavior, and on the relationship between perception of procedural justice and antisocial behavior of construction company employees. This study demonstrated that ethical leadership can be a pivotal way to conserve human resources in construction organizations. This study also emphasized that along with encouraging construction leaders to be ethical, the existence and fair practice of procedural justice augments the positive impacts of ethical leadership. Limitations and Future Research Directions Like other studies, this study has some limitations. First, due to logistical constraints and the project-based nature of the respondents, data were collected for all variables, namely trust in leader, procedural justice, job embeddedness, employee antisocial behavior, and turnover intention at once. Therefore, these constructs could not be measured at different times. For future research, longitudinal studies are also suggested, by adding some new related variables and to understand the dynamics of the study constructs better. Second, in the current paper, ethical leadership is used as a unidimensional construct by using the definition of Brown et al. (2005). In future research, scholars can analyze different dimensions by examining the influence of ethical leadership on employee outcomes. Third, this research was carried out in a specific country with a particular culture, namely Hong Kong. Results of repeated studies in other regions may differ from this article. Finally, more research is needed to investigate whether specific elements of job embeddedness (such as link, fit, and sacrifice) have different moderating effects on the association between ethical leadership and behavioral outcomes of the employees through procedural justice and trust in leader. Vol.:(0123456789)1 3 Journal of Business Ethics https://doi.org/10.1007/s10551-018-3972-5 ORIGINAL PAPER Status Threat and Ethical Leadership: A Power-Dependence Perspective Guangxi Zhang1 · Jianan Zhong2 · Muammer Ozer3 Received: 20 November 2017 / Accepted: 7 July 2018 © Springer Nature B.V. 2018 Abstract Whether, how and when do leaders engage in ethical leadership as a response to status threat? We propose that leaders facing status threat are likely to develop ethical leadership behaviors toward subordinates. Drawing on power dependence theory, we theorize that experiencing status threat augments leaders’ dependence on subordinates who can provide them with statusrelevant resources (e.g., performance, loyalty and trust). Dependence on subordinates further motivates leaders to absorb the resource constraints through displaying ethical leadership. However, if leaders are able to obtain alternative resources to cope with status threat, their dependence on subordinates is weakened. We conducted two studies to test the predictions. Using a moderation-of-process design, Study 1 found that when participants experienced status threat, they displayed more ethical leadership behaviors, but particularly so when their reward structure was team- rather than individual-based. Study 2 was a field study using a sample of 104 teams from two Chinese firms listed in the “Top 500 private enterprises in China.” We found that leaders who experienced more status threat were perceived to be more ethical by their subordinates, which was mediated by leaders’ perceptions of dependence on subordinates. The mediated effect was stronger (weaker) for leaders who were less (more) skilled in networking. Implications for theory on the contextual factors of ethical leadership, dependence, and status threat are discussed. Keywords Ethical leadership · Status threat · Dependence · Status · Power-dependence theory Introduction There is growing recognition in the public that to maintain a healthy and sustainable economy, good ethics should be strictly maintained. Because leaders are often viewed as representatives of the company and their behaviors generate a more profound effect than that of general employees (Eisenberger et al. 2010), leaders’ ethics has received a substantial amount of attention in both academic and business communities. Researchers have conducted studies to understand ethical leadership (Brown et al. 2005; Treviño et al. 2003), how it influences subordinates (e.g., Walumbwa et al. 2011) and how it can create benefits for groups (e.g., Mayer et al. 2009) or firms (e.g., Eisenbeiss et al. 2015; Pastoriza et al. 2008). Educators in business schools have advocated incorporating more ethical training in undergraduate curriculums and MBA programs (Ryther 2016; Arce and Gentile 2015). Practitioners have endeavored to build an ethical reputation in the eyes of the public, such as hiring the “right” managers and investing in corporate ethics programs (Treviño et al. 1999; Weaver et al. 1999). Collectively, the research, educational, and practical efforts underscore the importance of ethical leadership. Ethical leadership traditionally comprises two components, including moral agent and moral action. Trevinõ et al. (2000, 2003) argue that to be perceived as ethical, a leader must be simultaneously seen as a moral person (agent) and a moral manager (action).
