Zhang et al. 1 3 research on ethical leadership. However, our understanding of its causes is rather limited. While a limited understanding of its causes might make it difficult for educators to design focused curriculums or training programs, it might blind the efforts of organizations’ toward encouraging ethical leadership. As Brown and Mitchell (2010) note, “...obviously, there are many opportunities for investigating the influences on ethical leadership in future research” (p. 587). A handful studies have examined the antecedents of ethical leadership by focusing on the personality traits of leaders, such as higher levels of agreeableness and conscientiousness (Walumbwa and Schaubroeck 2009), moral identity (Mayer et al. 2012; Skubinn and Herzog 2016; Harvey et al. 2014) or advanced stages of cognitive moral development (Jordan et al. 2013), as predictors of ethical leadership. Although several studies investigated contextual factors, such as ethical culture (Fehr et al. 2015), role modeling (Brown and Treviño 2006), and family influence (Rowe 2014), these factors are relatively abstract, and the suggested mechanisms through which they work are mainly based on the social learning process. Taken together, the relatively less attention to contextual factors in the ethical leadership literature is striking given that the importance of contextual factors has surged in many management and organizational studies. Theoretically, person-environment fit theory (Schneider 1987; Kristof 1996) and person-situation interactionist model (Endler and Magnusson 1976) suggest that contextual factors are important considerations in leadership and ethical behaviors. Contextual factors not only generate effects on ethical leadership through a social learning process, but also provide external incentives (e.g., financial reward, respect, status and achieving other desirable outcomes), which motivate leaders to perform ethical behaviors toward subordinates. One desirable external incentive in organizations’ reward system is status, defined as the “respect, admiration, and voluntary deference an individual is afforded by others, based on that individual’s perceived instrumental social value” (Anderson et al. 2015, p. 575). In organizations, the competition for status can be severe and long-lasting (Bendersky and Hays 2012), resulting in status threat to the occupants of status (e.g., leaders). Therefore, status threat, which we define as the challenges to a person’s status that may cause potential loss of status (Kellogg 2012) and that may create a context that can motivate leaders to adopt ethical leadership to protect their threatened status. Thus, our research question is whether, how and when does status threat induce ethical leadership behaviors? The reason for whether status threat leads to ethical leadership is mainly based on research on socially adaptive behaviors under threat and the consequences of ethical leadership. Status threat foreshadows an exclusion risk from the current status hierarchy, which is likely to evoke motivation for social reconnection (Derfler-Rozin et al. 2010) and social conformity (Williams et al. 2000; Phillips and Zuckerman 2001). Because leaders and direct subordinates are embedded in small groups, in which repeated interactions make information on reputation transparent and punishment on unethical behaviors possible (Hammerstein 2003; Boehm 1993), it is rational for leaders to be ethical toward subordinates, given that ethical leadership generates many benefits for followers and organizations. The mechanism of how status threat leads to ethical leadership can be explained by power dependence theory (Emerson 1962). According to this theory, the power of one party on another party is the inverse of dependence on another party, and the dependence is a function of one’s motivational investment in goals mediated by the other (p. 32). For example, if a leader is highly dependent on subordinates’ knowledge, performance or loyalty, he/she will have less power over the subordinates. Because leaders’ dependence on subordinates varies with their motivation to reach valuable goals (i.e., status) through subordinates, status threat creates a context that increases leaders’ dependence on their subordinates and motivates them to display commitment to ethical norms. We further explore when status threat is likely to produce dependence. Based on power dependence theory (Emerson 1962), again, dependence is affected by the availability of alternative resources to substitute the other party. Hence, the dependence of leaders on their subordinates induced by status threat varies with the availability of alternative resources beyond the leader–member relationships. Thus, we propose that the networking ability of leaders, which we define as the skill to develop and use diverse networks of people (Ferris et al. 2005, p. 129), can reduce the positive effect of status threat on leaders’ dependence on their subordinates. We finally propose a moderated mediation model and test our model in a multi-source field study. Our paper makes several theoretical and empirical contributions. First, we contribute to ethical leadership literature by shifting the traditional focus on what motivates ethical leadership from its individual causes to contextual determinants. Unlike past research that has predominantly examined individual preferences as major causes of ethical leadership, we argue that contextual variables may also induce a strategic need for displaying ethical leadership. This perspective makes the theoretical prediction of ethical leadership more complete and thus offers important practical implications. Second, prior studies on status threat have focused on its negative consequences, such as giving up organizational reform (Kellogg 2012), risk taking in tournaments (Bothner et al. 2007) and suffering from physiological response (Scheepers et al. 2009). We documented the unexamined positive consequences of status threat, thus making a unique contribution to the status literature as well. Finally, drawing Status Threat and Ethical Leadership: A Power-Dependence Perspective 1 3 on power–dependence theory, we provide evidence that dependence theoretically explains why and how contextual variables induce ethical leadership. Such a perspective deepens our understanding of how contextualization occurs and represents an authentic incorporation of context into the ethical leadership literature. Theoretical Background Ethical leadership has a short history as an independent leadership style in management studies. Enderle (1987) first advanced the concept of ethical leadership and defined it as a way of thinking with two goals: (1) to clarify and make explicit the ethical dimensions in management-decision and (2) to formulate and justify ethical principles (p. 658). Treviño et al. (2003) conducted 40 semi-structured inter - views and proposed a series of traits of ethical leaders, such as people-orientation, setting ethical standards and accountability, and broad ethical awareness. Empirical research on ethical leadership gradually entered into an active stage after the reliable measurement scales were developed by Brown et al. (2005), who formally defined ethical leader - ship based on the leadership process as “the demonstration of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to followers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and decision-making” (p. 120). We, in this study, argue that leadership process is dynamic and flexible and ethical leadership behaviors are influenced by personality and contextual factors. As a result, we adopted the definition of Brown et al. (2005). According to this definition, ethical leadership is defined and measured in terms of others’ per - ception of leaders’ behaviors, which makes the motivation behind these behaviors less relevant. In most empirical work about the antecedents of ethical leadership, scholars examined internalized preferences of leaders. Overly attributing ethical leadership to individual differences forms a sharp contract with macro-level studies on business ethics, which notes that business ethics are strongly driven by external forces (Joyner and Payne 2002). This tendency is also inconsistent with the definition of leadership as a process of influence to attain mutual goals (Bass 1990; Hollander 1985). Therefore, exploring how contextual factors encourage, shape or maintain ethical leadership behaviors will provide a more comprehensive understanding of ethical leadership and offer alternative practical approaches that can encourage ethical leadership. Two contextual factors, namely, ethical climate and role models, were mentioned in the theoretical framework of Brown and Treviño (2006). However, contextual factors should go beyond factors generating effects through social learning processes. Although a variety of contextual factors may foster ethical leadership through various mechanisms, in this study, we only focus on a specific contextual factor (i.e., status threat), and propose that ethical leadership is more likely to become an adaptive leadership style that could help leaders protect their threatened status. Status Threat and Ethical Leadership Having a high social status has many benefits, including higher chance of survival, greater influence on others and more control over resources (Simonton 2003). Therefore, humans naturally desire to increase status or maintain a high status (Chapais 2015; Maslow 1943; Anderson et al. 2015). As status entirely lies on the conferral from others, the occupants of status tend to have an outward orientation (Hays and Blader 2017): they are sensitive to their relationship with others and how they are viewed by them. The process of obtaining status and the outward orientation of the occupants of status imply that conformity to widely accepted norms, especially ethical norms, is a precondition in status attainment. Status as a social resource in organizations is limited, which easily generates competition for status and creates status threat to those who already have status (e.g., leaders) (Bendersky and Hays 2012; Marr and Thau 2014). Status threat is a potential risk of losing status rather than a real loss of status (Kellogg 2012, p. 1549). For example, leaders may perceive status threat when low-status colleagues compete for the high-status position occupied by the leader, when leaders perceive less acceptance by the high-status group, when the leaders are categorized against his/her will as a low-status member, and when the leader feels that his/ her prestigious position is less distinguishable from the lowstatus group (Kellogg 2012). According to the research on neuroscience, humans are equipped with neural mechanisms that are sensitive to status information (Koski et al. 2015 ). Compared with followers, leaders are more sensitive to status threat, as status are more important to leaders’ self-identification (Spataro et al. 2014), and status threat to leaders may consequently lead them to engage in socially adaptive behaviors aimed at maintaining or increasing their status. There are three distinctive paths toward status attainment: dominance, competence, and morality (Bai 2017). Dominance strategy is the introduction of intimidation and coercion to induce fear. Competence strategy is based on the demonstration of task skills and expertise to gain respect. Morality strategy is to elicit feelings of warmth and admiration and willing deference toward the virtuous actors. The three strategies are independent but not mutually exclusive. However, the dominance strategy is not well liked and accepted in modern societies (Cheng et al. 2013). The morality strategy may play a more important role in shaping desirable impression than the competence strategy (Fiske G. Zhang et al. 1 3 et al. 2007). A wealth of evidence suggests that morality, such as generosity, altruism, or self-scarification, is positively associated with an increase in status (Flynn 2003 ; Grant 2013; Flynn et al. 2006). In addition, in a collectivist culture where sociability and interdependence are strongly emphasized (Triandis 1995), the preference for employing the moral strategy to achieve status is stronger than that in an individualist culture (Torelli et al. 2014). Therefore, we feel that leaders are more likely to choose the morality strategy to resolve status threat in our research setting. 1 The ethical behaviors of leaders provide signals that they are willing to forgo self-interests and advance the welfare of others if a higher status will be conferred. We argue that leaders under a status threat are likely to behave ethically toward subordinates for several reasons. First, people form social cognition of others along two distinct and fundamental dimensions, namely, warmth and competence (Fiske et al. 2007), which may serves as different foundations for obtaining status (Torelli et al. 2014). The warmth dimension (e.g., sociability and morality) captures one’s perceived intentions for good or ill, while the competence dimension (e.g., intelligence and skill) captures one’s perceived ability to pursue these intentions. Warmth-based information is generally believed to play a more central role in forming global impressions of others compared with competence-based information (Abele and Wojciszke 2007), and the moral component of warmth is predominant in social judgments (Brambilla and Leach 2014). Therefore, ethical leadership is very likely to be a preferable strategy to deal with status threat. Specifically, we argue that leaders facing status threat are likely to display their warmth through ethical leadership as a major adaptive approach on the basis of two rationales. On the one hand, warmth judgments precede competence judgments, because from an evolutionary perspective, the favorable/unfavorable intents of others are more important to individual survival than their ability to act on such intents (Fiske et al. 2007, p. 77). On the other hand, while the competence of leaders is relatively stable, warmth is more flexible, which means that moral–social behaviors (i.e., ethical leadership) are more likely to be shaped and changed by social contexts (i.e., status threat in our study) than competence. Secondly, as the value of status is more important to those people who occupy status (Duguid et al. 2012), the threat to leaders’ status may cause insecurity that increases conformity to expected social norms (Phillips and Zuckerman 2001). The positive link between status threat and conformity is rooted in the definition of status and the process of obtaining status: status is obtained through conforming to group expectations (Hollander 1958). Hollander (1958) argues that conformity to group norms serves to maintain and increase one’s status through increasing one’s positive impressions (i.e., “idiosyncrasy credits”) in the eyes of others. Therefore, leaders who face status threat should have strong motivation to increase prestige in the eyes’ of others and conform to ethical norms. For leaders, displaying ethical leadership behaviors provides strong signals of being good exchange partners and good organizational citizens, which will in turn lead to status conferral and hence offer an alternative approach to resolve status threat. Thirdly, leaders facing status threat are exposed to some kind of exclusion risk from their current status hierarchy, which invokes socially adaptive behaviors aiming to resolve status threat. One type of likely adaptive behaviors is to reinforce connections with colleagues (Derfler-Rozin et al. 2010), particularly with those who can provide status-related resources (e.g., subordinates). Recent studies on the risk of social exclusion lends support to our argument with evidence showing that individuals at exclusion risk are motivated to show increased conformity to social expectations (Phillips and Zuckerman 2001), engage in reconnection behaviors (Molden et al. 2009) and display increased reciprocity and trust towards others (Derfler-Rozin et al. 2010). Therefore, because ethical leadership meets group expectations, conveys human orientation, and helps reinforce interpersonal relationships, it might be strategically used as an adaption to status threat. This idea corresponds to the evolutionary ethicists’ view that suggests that ethics are shaped by the environment to resolve adaptive problems (Mesoudi and Danielson 2008). Finally, behaving ethically towards subordinates meets the leaders’ own interests in coping with status threat bet - ter than behaving unethically. If leaders choose to behave unethically towards subordinates, such behavior is inconsistent with the ethical norms expected by group members, which will induce subordinates’ supervisor-directed deviance (Tepper et al. 2009). The deviance will be stronger if subordinates already have an intention to quit or have alternative job opportunities. In extreme cases, leaders’ unethical behaviors may result in “reverse dominance hierarchy” because of subordinates’ strong reprisals and punishment (Boehm 1993). Therefore, behaving ethically is a safer, more rational and long-term orientated route toward status attainment than behaving unethically. Ethical leadership is rewarded with more liking (Walumbwa et al. 2011) and increased contributions by followers (Walumbwa et al. 2011; Den Hartog and Belschak 2012). Ethical leadership results in high-quality relationships with followers that are characterized by loyalty, emotional connection and mutual support (Erdogan et al. 2006; Walumbwa et al. 2011). The benefits of ethical leadership to leaders themselves were recorded in empirical evidence showing that leaders engaging in ethical leader behaviors were increasingly perceived to have the potential of filling senior leadership positions (Rubin et al. 2010) and achieving longer tenures (Rowe 2014). Therefore, ethical leadership can potentially benefit the leaders, followers, and organizations and offers a solution to status threat. A counterargument is that as subordinates’ resources are more critical for leaders’ status production than those of the members outside the group, status threat may encourage the in-group-oriented-behaviors of leaders and thus trigger their unethical pro-organizational behaviors or pro-group unethical behaviors. However, we argue that the leaders facing a status threat should be refrained from performing such unethical behaviors, as their status is rated not only by the members within the focal group but also by the members outside the focal group. In addition, leaders are representatives of the organization; thus, their behaviors are more visible than those of the team members, which may increase the salience and costs of involving in unethical behaviors (Graffin et al. 2013). Therefore, status threat is more likely to encourage the ethical rather than the unethical behaviors of leaders. Taken together, if status threat creates a context that requires leaders to be socially adaptable, and ethical leadership towards subordinates can be a solution to protect or maintain status, then it follows that Hypothesis 1 Leader experiences of status threat are positively related to ethical leadership. Power Dependence Theory Emerson’s power dependence theory ( 1962) provides the theoretical framework for our model. This theory suggests that one party’s power over another party is the reverse of dyadic dependence. One’s dependence is a multiplicative function of the motivational investment in “goals” mediated by another actor and one’s access to alternative exchange partners. Such goals may include any demanded outcomes that are sought consciously or unconsciously. For example, if a leader evaluates status as an attractive outcome, he/she will increase the motivational investment in someone who can help him/her achieve status. However, if this leader is able to construct wide social relationships in which each resource provider can substitute another, then his/her dependence on a single resource provider will be reduced. In a dyadic relationship, if one party controls more critical resources than the other party, the latter becomes more dependent on the former. Then, the dependent party is motivated to resolve the tension in the unbalanced relationship using two tactics: cost reduction or rebalancing operations. The first tactic reduces the pain in serving a powerful partner, whereas the second tactic materially reduces dependence (Emerson 1962, p. 34). It should be noted that although status and power are conceptually and empirically related (for example, a position of power often afford the occupants with status), they are distinct concepts: power is decided by controlling over valuable resources, whereas status describes one’s relative standing in social hierarchy (Anderson et al. 2012 ). Consequently, status and power have different effects on social perceptions and behaviors. Since the key independent variable in our study is status threat rather than status, and because we conceptualize status threat as the motivational investment in the goals mediated by group members based on the core tenet in power dependence theory, we are able to avoid the conceptual confusion between status and power. Power dependence theory is an appropriate framework to explain the mechanism for how status threat gives rise to ethical leadership in two aspects. First, given that dependence is a function of motivational investment and the availability of alternative resources, we conceptualize status threat as a context that increases motivational investment in the relationship with group members and networking ability as the ability to obtain alternative resources, which interact and result in dependence on subordinates. Second, given that dependence on subordinates arising from status threat calls for solutions to reduce dependence, ethical leadership serves two strategically important goals: absorbing resource constraints and working as an approach that is likely to safeguard the threatened status. Taken together, the four key variables (i.e., status threat, networking ability, dependence, and ethical leadership) tightly grasp the tenets and logic of power dependence theory. Dependence on Subordinates as the Mediator Leaders’ dependence on their subordinates occurs when their desired outcomes are contingent on the actions of the subordinates. According to power dependence theory (Emerson 1962), leaders’ dependence on their subordinates varies with the leaders’ motivational investment to realize their goals through their subordinates. Leaders’ motivation to invest in the relationship with their subordinates is influenced by the social context in which the leaders are embedded. Specifically, status threat creates a challenging environment for the relative standing of leaders in a status hierarchy, which motivates them to adopt various strategies to increase or maintain their status. Resolving status threat requires leaders to demonstrate their prestige (Cheng et al. 2013), virtue (Bai 2017), or meet other expectations from organizations G. Zhang et al. 1 3 (Hollander 1958), which are inseparable from the support, respect, and efforts from the followers. Therefore, status threat makes the value of subordinates in producing statusrelevant resources increasingly salient, hence increasing the leaders’ dependence on their subordinates. The importance of subordinates in resolving leaders’ status threat is manifested twofold. First, because status is socially conferred and emergent through others’ evaluation, subordinates are among the audience of leaders’ status. When leaders’ sta - tus is at dispute, leaders are increasingly sensitive to their images as perceived by others, including group members, making them psychologically dependent on their subordinates. Second, subordinates provide critical resources, such as expertise, loyalty, social capital, and good performance. All these factors increase the effectiveness and contributions of leaders to the organization, thus making the leaders materially dependent on their subordinates. Although leaders may seek resources from other sources to consolidate their status, resources and support from their subordinates are more controllable and reachable compared with resources obtained from remote areas or through weak ties, given that leaders have frequent interactions with their subordinates and can influence them through various ways, such as task allocation and rewards (Keller and Szilagyi 1978; Shi et al. 2013). Our logic allows us to infer that leaders who experience a status threat will increase their motivational investment in realizing their goals and obtaining benefits through their relationship with their subordinates, thus making them increasingly dependent on their subordinates. The dependence on subordinates calls for a resolution to reduce the dependence. Materially reducing dependence means increasing control over critical resources that are needed, which further suggests the necessity to cooper - ate with others who possess those critical resources (e.g., Thau et al. 2004). At the macro level, cooperative behav - iors include forming alliances or implementing acquisitions (Pfeffer and Salancik 1978). Similarly, at the micro level, leaders need to initiate exchanges with those on whom they are dependent. To achieve this goal, leaders must show cooperative gestures by following ethical norms in social exchanges and signify their reliability as exchange partners. Demonstrating ethical leadership behaviors provides signals that the leaders are trustworthy exchange partners with certain moral traits, which elicit their subordinates’ admiration for virtue and encourage the subordinates’ commitment to the exchange relationships. Given that the essence of most social behaviors is the exchange of material and non-material goods (Homans 1958), leaders who behave ethically towards their subordinates will receive more resources in return, and such relationships are likely to be enduring. This point is supported by abundant evidence showing that ethical leadership allows leaders to form better relationships with subordinates (Mahsud et al. 2010) and positively relates to many desirable outcomes from the subordinates (e.g., Tu and Lu 2013; Chen and Hou 2016; Wang and Sung 2016). Therefore, our arguments allow us to predict that ethical leadership serves as a way to resolve leaders’ dependence on their subordinates through facilitating better exchange relationships with them. Taken together, because of increasing awareness that subordinates are needed to reinstate status, ethical leadership may become an adaptive strategy to absorb status-relevant resources from subordinates. In sum, our reasoning suggests that Hypothesis 2 The positive relationship between status threat and ethical leadership is mediated by leaders’ dependence on their subordinates. Moderating Role of Leaders’ Networking Ability As our discussion of power dependence theory will suggest, dependence is also a function of the availability of alternative resources in addition to motivational investment; thus, we predict that leaders who face status threat become less dependent on the resources provided by subordinates if they can obtain alternative resources elsewhere. The access to alternative resources is determined by a larger exchange network in which leaders are embedded, particularly three dimensions, including the number, availability, and value of exchange partners (Molm et al. 2001). To reflect these network features more completely, we choose to study leaders’ networking ability, defined as the ability to establish and use diverse relationships with other people (Ferris et al. 2005). Networking ability, by definition, indicates one’s ability to construct resource-rich diverse networks, increase partners’ availability and approach valuable resource providers (Fer - ris et al. 2000). Therefore, leaders’ networking ability adequately reflects their ability to obtain alternative resources as predicted by power–dependence theory. We argue that leaders’ networking ability is likely to offset the positive effect of status threat on the leaders’ dependence on their subordinates for three reasons. Regarding the number of social ties, leaders with a strong networking ability can attain central positions in the social network, which allows them to accumulate diversified resources, including social and intellectual capital (Cole - man 1988; Nahapiet and Ghoshal 1998). A large amount of intellectual and social capital is likely to make leaders more adept in responding to status threat, therefore reducing dependence on subordinates. For example, skilled networkers could develop stable inter-firm managerial or political ties, which increase the leaders’ performance and their contributions to the organization (Li and Zhang 2007; McDonald and Westphal 2003; Nesheim et al. 2017). Hence, if the solution to status threat can be achieved through alternative social ties, the demand from subordinates will be reduced. Status Threat and Ethical Leadership: A Power-Dependence Perspective 1 3 Regarding the availability of partners, leaders with a high networking ability can build and leverage social capital when needed. Because skilled networkers can develop friendships easily (Ferris et al. 2007), they can effectively increase the availability of partners. Leaders skilled in networking are also good at negotiating, making deals, and resolving con - flicts; therefore, they are likely to initiate exchanges with others, and others are likely to respond favorability to the leaders’ requests. With increased availability from partners, leaders will feel safer when a status threat emerges, as their networking ability provides them with more available coping resources. In this case, resources from the subordinates are less needed, and leaders will become less dependent on their subordinates. Regarding the value of partners, leaders with a high networking ability are more capable of identifying and approaching valuable partners than those with no such ability (Brouer et al. 2016). Their ability to accumulate social capital also increases their favorable reputation among tar - geted people, which helps them successfully obtain valuable resources from their network partners (Zinko et al. 2012). For example, networking ability grants leaders with oppor - tunities to approach and influence important decision makers and stakeholders (Fang et al. 2015). Therefore, when leaders face status threat, they can obtain alternative resources of high value and become less dependent on the resources of their subordinates. These arguments suggest that Hypothesis 3 The indirect effect of status threat on ethical leadership via dependence on subordinates is weaker (stronger) for leaders with a high (low) networking ability. Study 1 Study 1 manipulated status threat through others’ disagreement with the status of the leader. We tested the mechanism that explained the impact of status threat on ethical leadership through a moderation-of-process design. As participants may not have a vivid experience of dependence when they are provided with scenarios, or because they may be unwilling to confess their felt dependence, dependence is not easy to be measured accurately in a vignette-based experiment. According to Spencer et al. (2005), when mediators are difficult to measure but easier to manipulate, a mod - eration-of-process design is appropriate. The moderating variable should have an effect on the proposed mechanism, which is the only mechanism that the moderating variable could exert an effect upon (p. 847). Therefore, we manipulated the bonus structure as a moderator, because leaders under different bonus structures (individual-based vs. teambased) should experience different degrees of dependence on their team (Fan and Gruenfeld 1998). If we can observe that status threat causes more ethical leadership behaviors under a team-based bonus structure than that under an individual-based bonus structure, we have evidence proving that dependence is the underlying mechanism. Method Design and participants One hundred and fifty-seven part-time MBA students in an eastern Chinese university participated in the study. Par - ticipants were randomly assigned to a 2 (low-status threat, high-status threat) × 2 (individual-based bonus, team-based bonus) between-subject factorial design. Two student responses to the final task were abrupt and incomplete and were excluded from the analyses. The participants’ ages ranged from 26 to 40 years (38.1% were from 26 to 30, 31.6% were from 31 to 35, and 21.3% were from 36 to 40) and 56.8% were male. The average working experience was 10.17 years, and 63.2% held managerial positions. Experimental Procedures and Materials The experiment materials were presented in Mandarin. Participants were told that they would be joining a study involving managerial problem solving. We told the participants that their responses would be used strictly for research purposes. They were encouraged to immerse themselves in scenarios and to provide genuine responses. The first scenario they read included the status threat manipulation. Then, they answered several questions about two exploratory measures, namely, conformity value (Schwartz 1992) and positive mood (Watson et al. 1988). Including these measures as covariates did not affect the results reported below. Next, the participants read a second scenario to resolve an ethical dilemma. Status Threat Manipulation We manipulated status threat by using peer disagreement with leader status, as challenges in status threat are evident if the sources of threat come from similar peers (Bothner et al. 2007; Edelman and Larkin 2015). Participants in the low (high) status threat condition read the following prompt: Imagine you are a manager in charge of an R&D team in a large IT company. Recently, you were promoted to a more important position. Other colleagues expressed their admiration and most of them felt that your hard work deserved the promotion. [However, privately you heard that two managers of other R&D teams disputed your promotion because they felt their performance was not inferior to yours]. G. Zhang et al. 1 3 Manipulation Check of Status Threat After reading the first scenario (high-/low-status threat), the participants were asked to assess the degree to which they feel status threat using four items on a seven-point scale. These items included, “Some colleagues do not agree with my promotion,” “Some of my colleagues may take sides to challenge my status,” “Other team managers may compete with me for influence,” and “I need to try harder to protect my status in the organization.” We deleted the fourth item to improve the Cronbach’s α score. The α coefficient was 0.71 after this item was deleted. Bonus Structure Manipulation Leader dependence on subordinates is influenced by their bonus structure (Fan and Gruenfeld 1998). A team-based bonus makes leaders more dependent on their subordinates than an individual-based bonus, because their rewards are directly influenced by the performance of subordinates in the former structure. By contrast, an individual-based bonus structure makes subordinate performance less of a concern for leaders (Barnes et al. 2011; Shaw et al. 2002; Bloom 1999). In the team-based bonus condition, participants read the following: According to the salary system of your company, as the R&D team leader, the annual bonus accounts for 50% of your annual income. Actually, 80% of the bonus is decided by the team members, and the remaining 20% is decided by your own performance. In the individual-based bonus condition, participants read the following: According to the salary system of your company, as the R&D team leader, the annual bonus accounts for 50% of your annual income. Actually, 20% of the bonus is decided by team performance, and the remaining 80% is decided by your own performance, which is rarely affected by other team members. Manipulation Check of Bonus Structure Three questions were designed to check whether participants noticed the bonus structure and whether those in different bonus structures perceived different levels of dependence. The principle–principle component analysis of three items resulted in one single factor explaining a 59.42% variance (α = 0.70). The items included the following: “It will be difficult for me to increase personal income without support from my subordinates,” “I feel that I need to rely on my subordinates to achieve good income,” and “If some competent subordinates leave my team, it will be a significant shock for me.” Resolving an Ethical Dilemma Next, participants were told that they needed to resolve a management problem, which was a justice versus mercy dilemma adapted from Flynn and Wiltermuth (2010). The participants were given the role of a leader in charge of testing a new software package. As the product would be launched in 1 month, they would set up a round-the-clock testing. The participants were required to assign people to two teams operating at day and night shifts, respectively. However, five subordinates had their own reasons (physical situation, family issues, or tenure) for wanting to be assigned to the day shift. Given that ethical leaders are people-oriented, they should make a balanced decision in such a scenario (Treviño et al. 2003). Participants were asked to assume the role of the team leader and then required to write an email to subordinates. The email to the subordinates was designed to include five components as follows: (1) What are we going to do? (2) How do you plan to assign the day and night shifts to team members (perhaps including you as the leader)? (3) Are there any reasons that you feel you need to explain the assignment? (4) You need to motivate your subordinate and express your expectation. (5) Any additional information that you need to add in the email (e.g., any support they can get). Note that this outline was suggestive, and participants had sufficient freedom to decide the structure and contents of the email. Finally, participants were thanked and given a token gift (valued at 30 RMB) for their participation. Measure of Ethical Leadership The participants’ emails were assessed by two trained judges using the consensual assessment technique (Amabile 1983). This technique allows subjective viewpoints to be considered by recognizing that everyone has a different view of ethical leadership. Seven items were adapted from the original 10-item ethical leadership scale (Brown et al. 2005) 2 with scores ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). To facilitate ratings, examples were provided for each item in the ethical leadership scale. Discussion Study 1 investigated whether status threat provides a situ - ational incentive for leaders to lead ethically using a scenario Fig. 1 Effect of status threat on ethical leadership moderated by bonus structure G. Zhang et al. 1 3 simulation. We used a moderation-of-process design in an experiment, in which we manipulated the dependence of participants on their subordinates by having them imagine different types of bonus structures. Consistent with our proposed mechanism, we found that participants in the team-based bonus structure were more dependent on team members and that status threat led to behaviors of ethical leadership in an email task. The positive relationship between status threat and ethical leadership was strong in the team-based bonus structure. In the high-status-threat scenario, the team-based bonus structure induced more significant ethical leadership than the individual-based bonus structure, but this difference was less significant in the lowstatus-threat scenario. Although Study 1 provides evidence of a causal relation from status threat to ethical leadership, it did not directly measure dependence, and the ecological validity of the experiment deserves further test. To over - come these limitations, we conducted another field survey to replicate these results with a direct measure of leaders’ dependence on subordinates. Study 2 Sample and Procedures We collected data from a sample of 105 working teams in two companies that were listed among the “Top 500 private enterprises in China.” The first data source consisted of 77 teams working in three subsidiaries of a hotel group in China. The company is ranked among the Top 3 in the Chinese hospitality industry, with more than 170 hotels and 24,000 employees across the country. The majority of the team leaders are frontline and middle-level managers. The second data source comprised of 28 managerial teams located in the headquarters of a large listed company in the petrochemical industry. This company has more than 8000 employees (most of them are blue-collar workers) and is ranked among the Top 3 in the Chinese chemical fiber industry. Team leaders in the second sample have relatively high status, ranging from middle to high levels. The researchers contacted the respective human resource (HR) departments 2 weeks before the survey. We explained the research purpose, definition of the working teams, sample requirements, and the survey process. With help from the HR departments, we received the lists of the teams to prepare for the matched questionnaires. We did not ask participants to indicate their names on the questionnaires. Instead, we assigned a unique number imprinted on the back of the questionnaire to identify their identities. Leaders and subordinates were matched afterwards based on the name lists and the unique numbers we created for each team and the participants. All the surveys were collected on site. The participants were invited to a quiet council chamber during work - ing hours after receiving a notification sent from the HR departments 1 day before the meeting. When participants entered the room, two research assistants distributed the questionnaires to them based on the unique number on each the envelope. Before we distributed the questionnaires to the participants, the researchers explained the research purpose and procedures of completing the questionnaires. We emphasized that the data were independently collected by academic institutions for academic purposes. Their companies would have no chance to access the questionnaires, and their anonymity will be well protected. Once the participants filled the questionnaires, the researchers checked for missing answers, and the participants placed the completed questionnaires in an unmarked sealed envelope. Finally, participants were thanked and given a token gift. For a small portion of participants who were not in their companies on that day, we left the questionnaires with the HR departments and received those questionnaires within 1 week. The overall response rate was 94%. As previous research suggests that three responses is a sufficient number to aggregate to the team level (Klein and Kozlowski 2000), we excluded one team that had two responses from subordinates. The final sample consisted of 541 subordinates embedded in 104 teams. Each team, on average, had 5.20 subordinates. Measures We translated the English-language scales into Mandarin. The items were first translated into Mandarin by a nativespeaking business school professor. A research assistant helped to refine the wordings. The translated items were back-translated to English by an independent translator. Next, one of the researchers compared the English and Mandarin versions of the survey instruments to ensure that the versions were comparable. We asked eight MBA students and two professors in business schools to comment on the appropriateness of expressions used in the measures and the design of the questionnaires. We then made minor modifications based on their comments. Ethical Leadership We measured ethical leadership using the 10-item scale (α = 0.93) of Brown et al. ( 2005 ). We aggregated the responses of subordinates to the ethical leadership measure to obtain group-level ethical leadership. We assessed the degree of agreement with the ethical leadership measure by calculating the r wg statistic. Given that potential response bias might exist in our data (e.g., leniency biases) and leaders being rated might be perceived to have favorable attributes, the null distribution might be violated (LeBreton and Status Threat and Ethical Leadership: A Power-Dependence Perspective 1 3 Senter 2008). Following a prior study (Meyer et al. 2014), we calculated rwg by using the uniform null distribution as the high-end estimate, and then slightly skewed distribution as the low-end estimate. The mean r wg values for ethical leadership was 0.93 for the uniform null distribution and 0.86 for the slightly skewed distribution. In addition, the ICC 1 value was 0.25, thus suggesting a strong agreement within work groups regarding ethical leadership and the appropriateness of aggregation of individual responses to a group-level response (Bliese 2000). The ICC 2 value was 0.64. Status Threat We adapted the scale on status conflict developed by Bendersky and Hays (2012) to measure status threat to leaders within the organization. The four-item scale of status con - flict was initially developed to capture disputes among team members over relative status positions at group level, and thus, the items were framed from the perspectives of group members. However, the individual level status conflict has a two-way manifestation: (1) an actor challenges the status of others, and (2) others challenge the status of the actor. The latter form is the status threat. Given these immanent rela - tions, the status conflict scale provided a suitable foundation for the scale adaption. We reframed the items by using “I” as the subject, and made minor changes to make the contents reflect status threat. Thus, the items included “I felt some colleagues colluded to challenge my status in the firm,” “I felt my domi - nance in work was threatened by other colleagues,” “Some colleagues competed with me to increase their influence in the firm,” and “I felt some colleagues did not agree with the relative value of my contribution to the firm” (α = 0.80). Dependence on Subordinates We adapted the four-item scale used by Shi et al. (2013) to measure the overall dependence of supervisors on subordinates. These items included “Overall, my subordinates have good expertise or overall qualities,” “When I complete tasks, I am dependent on the support of my subordinates,” “I had high expectations of my subordinates,” and “If many of my subordinates leave their jobs, it will be very difficult to find people to replace them.” We deleted the first item to improve the Cronbach’s α score. The α coefficient was 0.70 after this item was deleted. Networking Ability Networking ability was measured using the six-item networking ability scale of the political skill inventory (Ferris et al. 2005). Sample items included “I am good at using my connections and networks to make things happen at work” and “I have developed a large network of colleagues and associates at work who I can call on for support when I really need to get things done” (α = 0.89). Control Variables We controlled for variables that may confound the relationships among status threat, dependence, and ethical leadership. Absolute Status The initial status of individuals in a status hierarchy may influence their behaviors after experiencing status loss (Marr and Thau 2014; Neeley 2013) and relate to their ethical decisions (Piff et al. 2012; Edelman and Larkin 2015). Therefore, we controlled for the absolute status using a subjective rating method (e.g., Neeley 2013; Smith et al. 2012): Leaders were required to mark their status on a hierarchical scale that had five points: low level (22.1%), between low and middle level (39.4%), middle level (26.9%), between middle and high level (10.6%), and high level (1%). Team Size Managers in larger teams may have more resources that make them less dependent on subordinates and less likely to treat subordinates ethically, as the group cohesion is alleviated in large groups (Boehm 1993; Hammerstein 2003). Therefore, we controlled for team size by using information obtained from HR departments. Personal Ethical Orientation According to ethics position theory (Forsyth 1980), individual ethical perspectives influence moral judgments, actions, and emotions in ethical dilemmas, and likely affect the ethical behaviors of leaders and the way they cope with status threat (Wang and Calvano 2015). We used Forsyth’s (1980) 10-item Ethics Position Questionnaire to control for the two dimensions of personal ethical orientation, namely, idealism (7 items, α = 0.83) and relativism (3 items, α = 0.81). Highly idealistic individuals “‘assume that desirable consequences can, with the ‘right’ action, always be obtained” (Forsyth 1980, p. 176). In comparison, highly relativistic people tend to configure their moral judgments based on the context of a particular situation and action they are evaluating. These studies nor - mally apply to ex-ante and ex-post measures suggested by Podsakoff et al. (2003). Following these studies, we applied such ex-ante measures to obtain data for the independent and dependent variables from different sources, thus improving the clarity of the scales through pretests and assuring the participants about the confidentiality of the information they provided. We also applied several ex-post measures. For example, Harman’s single-factor test showed that 10 distinct factors accounted for 73.16% of the total variance, and no single factor accounted for the majority of the variance. In addition, because Harman’s single-factor test is an insensitive test, we retested our hypotheses after controlling for a single unmeasured latent method factor with all measures as indicators to represent common method biases and found consistent results (Podsakoff et al. 2003). Finally, research shows that models involving moderated variables are less sensitive to this bias (Siemsen et al. 2010). Considering all the ex-ante and ex-post measures and given that we studied the moderated mediation model, common method bias was not a major concern in our analyses. Post Hoc Analysis Implicit in our argument is the assumption that ethical leadership will help the leader to obtain status and resolve status threat as a result. We used promotion as an indicator of whether the leaders have elevated their status in the organization. Previous studies suggested that promotion to higher rank is an indicator of status achievement (e.g., Baron et al. 1986; Lyness and Heilman 2006), and the informal deference hierarchy of status in organizations often results in formal distinctions in positions (Sauder et al. 2012). Rubin et al. (2010) provided evidence that ethical leaders were likely to be highly rated by their supervisors, but whether the potentiality is truly realized is untested. We collected additional data on leaders’ promotion (1 = promoted during the time interval, 0 = not promoted during the time inter - val) 1.5 years after the initial survey was conducted, which allows sufficient time lag for casual inference. We run a binomial logistic regression of promotion on ethical leadership, adding the control variables in Fig. 2. The effect of ethical leadership on promotion was positive and significant (β = 0.37, p < .001), providing evidence that ethical leaders are likely to be promoted to higher positions, and therefore, ethical leadership is helpful to resolve status threat. General Discussion This article investigated whether, how and when status threat creates a context in which leaders are motivated to lead ethically. A laboratory study and a field survey using differ - ent measures and manipulations supported our predictions. Fig. 3 Moderating effects of networking ability Status Threat and Ethical Leadership: A Power-Dependence Perspective 1 3 In Study 1, we found initial support for our prediction that status threat caused ethical leadership behaviors. Using a moderation-of-process design, we manipulated the dependence of participants on subordinates by having participants imagine different types of bonus structures. Consistent with our proposed mechanism, the positive relationship between status threat and ethical leadership was stronger in the teambased bonus structure. In Study 2, we analyzed a sample of 104 working teams in two large organizations and found that status threat encouraged ethical leadership behaviors. The mediating role of dependence was significant, and this indirect link was moderated by the networking ability of leaders. These findings support the predictions drawn from power–dependence theory, which posits that dependence is a function of an actor’s motivational investment in the goals mediated by another actor and the availability of alternative resources. Theoretical Implications The most significant contribution of our research is testing a model that shifts the consensus about ethical leadership. Departing from the traditional view that ethical leadership is leaders’ preferences influenced by stable personal factors, we focused on the understudied contextual predictors that provide external incentives for leaders behaving ethically. We investigated a specific contextual factor, namely status threat, and found that it is positively related to subordinates’ perception of ethical leadership. Although the role of the contextual variables was widely recognized in the broader literature of individual ethics (e.g., Flynn and Wiltermuth 2010; Brass et al. 1998) and business ethics (e.g., Joyner and Payne 2002), they were under-investigated in ethical leadership literature, which represents an incomplete theorization. Our review of the literature suggests that researchers seem to focus on different causes when explaining unethical leadership compared with ethical leadership. On the one hand, when researchers explain unethical leadership (e.g., abusive leadership, toxic leadership and tyrannical leadership), they prefer to interpret unethical leadership as an outcome of an unfavorable environment (e.g., Mawritz et al. 2012; Burton and Hoobler 2011; Tepper et al. 2011; Kiewitz et al. 2012). On the other hand, when scholars predict ethical leadership, they predominantly examine internally developed and relatively stable preferences (e.g., Eisenbeiss 2012; Brown and Treviño 2006; Walumbwa and Schaubroeck 2009). Therefore, exploring how contextual factors, particularly factors beyond the social learning processes, shape ethical leadership provides a more complete understanding of ethical leadership. The second contribution is that this study changes the current conversation on status threat. Past studies on sta - tus threat mainly focused on its negative consequences. For example, status threat resulted in failed reforms in hospitals (Kellogg 2012), more crashes in NASCAR racing (Bothner et al. 2007), and stressful physiological responses (Scheepers and Ellemers 2005; Scheepers et al. 2009). We propose that as status threat is a universal phenomenon (as long as there are status hierarchies, there exist status threats), it may have some positive effects that have not been paid much attention in past research. Status threat in organizations as a stressful context may last for a relatively long time, and for someone to adapt to it requires a rational mind and long-term orientation. Status threat also represents exclusion risks from the current status hierarchy that requires reinforcing connections with critical resource providers. Extending this logic, we suggested that when leaders face status threat, they feel uncertain about their positions, and this uncertainty could lead to increased motivational investment in the relationships with their subordinates. Consequently, ethical leader - ship becomes a preferable leadership style that can absorb subordinates’ resources that produce leaders’ status. Finally, we contribute to ethical leadership literature through bringing new theoretical insights to explain what motivates ethical leadership. As previously mentioned, the mainstream studies on ethical leadership focus on leaders’ internal needs toward behaving ethically (e.g., moral preferences and social learning from role models); how - ever, leaders’ external need to behave ethically has been neglected. People sometimes behave ethically because they are dependent on others and have to demonstrate that they are moral (Barclay and Willer 2007). For example, business leaders sometimes donate to charity because they want to increase their prestige in the public. Therefore, studies on ethical leadership need a perspective that can explain how contextual factors evoke dependence and ethical behaviors as an adaption. As power–dependence theory captures forces and incentives imposed by the environment, it is useful in explaining leaders’ adaptive behaviors and complements the social learning theory that has been widely used in ethical leadership literature. Because dependence on the environment has different forms and sources with boundary conditions, power–dependence theory provides a unique framework that can explain a variety of contextual variables encouraging/discouraging ethical leadership, which paves the way to develop and test many hypotheses in future studies. Limitations and Future Research Directions This research has several imitations. First, considering the targets of ethical leadership, leaders may treat their team members ethically when they are facing status threat. However, leaders may also treat members in other teams less ethically, particularly those who belong to the competitors’ camp (Chapais 2015). According to moral balance G. Zhang et al. 1 3 theory (Nisan and Horenczyk 1990), behaving ethically in one domain allows one to behave less ethically in another domain, and such a disparity suggests a combination of ethical and unethical behaviors within the same leader (e.g., Lin et al. 2016). Having said that, we are unable to make a clear differentiation of leaders’ ethical behaviors based on different raters in this study, as the measure of ethical leadership was obtained from subordinates in the same group. Thus, a potentially interesting line of future inquiry would be to investigate how members outside the groups rate ethical behaviors of the leaders and to compare these results with ratings from the leader’s subordinates. Second, we did not measure leaders’ in-group orientation and the tendency to engage in unethical behaviors, which may help to rule out alternative explanations and counter - arguments. Status threat strengthens the motivation of leaders to be liked and respected by group members. Hence, is it possible that status threat encourages in-group orientation and encourages leaders to engage in unethical pro-organizational behaviors or unethical pro-group behaviors? Leaders who are confronted with status threat should hesitate to perform such unethical behaviors because their behaviors are more visible than those of general employees, and the high possibility of being caught will substantially harm their status. The leaders’ status is likewise rated by a broad audience, including members outside the focal group; hence, performing unethical pro-organization or unethical pro-group behaviors is likely to further threaten their disputed status. However, as our data do not contain those measures, we encourage future studies to do additional tests to verify and extend our study. Third, the measure of status threat is an adaption of the scale developed by Bendersky and Hays (2012), which captures the overall phenomenon of status threat without specifying the sources. Because the foundation of status can be built on different pillars, including being a warm person (e.g., good personality and ethics) and a competent person (e.g., competence and good performance), the status threat may come from different sources. Therefore, it is interesting to explore different adaptive strategies to different types of status threat. For example, if the leaders’ status is threatened in terms of warmth, the subsequent adaptive behaviors may be somewhat different if their status is threatened in terms of competence. Another example is that if status threat comes from different levels, leaders’ strategies to resolve it from similar peers may be somewhat different from resolving it from coworkers with lower status. Even in this case, the arguments for the positive link between status threat and ethical leadership are still applicable for two reasons. Firstly, if subordinates are able to threat the leaders’ status, they may have critical resources such as expertise and social capital (Deshpande et al. 2008). If leaders use unethical ways to crowd out such subordinates, leaders will not obtain valuable resources from them and will stimulate rebellions from their subordinates (Boehm 1993). Secondly, leaders’ unethical behaviors toward their subordinates will provide signals to other subordinates that leaders are narrow-minded, which will damage trust and commitment from other subordinates, and hence worsen the situation of status threat. Because our study is the first empirical attempt to explore the effect of status threat on ethical leadership and because the measure of status threat is at the preliminary stage, we did not categorize status threat based on the sources. However, we hope our study can pave the way for future studies on status threat with more detailed considerations. Furthermore, we used a subjective measure of status threat and absolute status, which is debatable (Piazza and Castellucci 2014). Status threat was obtained from the selfreports of leaders, which are likely to be influenced by individual sensibility, tolerance and capability to resolve status threat. In this study, we were unable to obtain a more reliable source other than the leaders themselves. However, the subjective rating of status and status threat may still be reliable, as previous studies indicate that individuals usually perceive status accurately (Anderson et al. 2008) and that leaders themselves have the best information of status threat. Fourth, although we obtained data from multiple sources, which can help to reduce common method bias (Podsakoff et al. 2003), the data testing the model were collected at the same time point, which was cross-sectional in nature. This research design limits the conclusion of a causal relationship: does status threat or dependence on subordinates come before the emergence of ethical leadership? Because of the lack of a strong theoretical foundation explaining that ethical leadership will increase/decrease dependence on subordinates, we think that the casual relationship from ethical leadership to dependence is much weaker than the casual relationship from dependence to ethical leadership. If future studies can bring in time lags (e.g., 3 months) between status threat, dependence, and ethical leadership, the conclusion based on our arguments can be more robust. Finally, we conducted this study in China, which is well known for its collectivist culture and paternalistic leadership style (Pellegrini and Scandura 2008). As status characteristics theory (Berger et al. 1980) suggests, the determinants of status attainment are culturally contingent. People in collectivist oriented cultures emphasize the social–moral dimension of social cognition, whereas people in individualist orientated cultures associate competence traits with status to a greater degree (Fiske et al. 2007; Torelli et al. 2014). Thus, in collectivistic cultures, moral characteristics are more likely to result in admiration for virtue and status attainment, therefore the positive relationship between status threat and ethical leadership is likely to be stronger than that in individualistic cultures. Ancient Chinese philosophers Status Threat and Ethical Leadership: A Power-Dependence Perspective 1 3 also considered being a moral person, which is stated in many ancient books (e.g., “the Great Learning”) as the precondition to being righteous in regulating one’s family and kingdom. Therefore, it is possible that Chinese leaders tend to resort to ethical leadership as a primary way to cope with status threat. In this study, we did not control for cul - tural variables, as the participants were exposed to a similar cultural environment. However, because different cultures have varying interpretations of ethical leadership and the functional value of ethical leadership (Resick et al. 2006) more studies across cultures are needed, and controlling for cultural effect would also be useful. Practical Implications Our research makes several practical contributions for cultivating ethical leadership in organizations. First, we find that ethical leadership could be encouraged by environmental factors, and those factors may generate a compulsive force that requires an adaption through displaying moral behav - iors. Although our study only provides evidence for one specific type of external incentives, namely, status threat, there are a variety of promising approaches (e.g., financial or non-financial rewards) that can be leveraged to encour - age ethical leadership. Organizations traditionally may prefer providing ethical education to the leaders and followers, which bases its theoretical foundation on social learning theory. However, we feel that given the stability of individual moral values, constructing an environment that could control leader behaviors and provide incentives for leaders to behave ethically is a more practical approach than simply relying on ethical education. For example, as status is an external incentive for leaders’ career advancement, an organization can associate the promotion system with ratings of leaders’ ethical behaviors. In the promotion system, leaders who are considered moral persons and moral managers can be given more consideration for promotion to higher rank. As our study indicates, status threat to leaders can also be lever - aged to encourage ethical leadership behaviors. As a result, organizations may try to prevent forming a stable and rigid power structure. Instead, allowing flexibility of moving up and down the status hierarchy will impose more status threat on leaders and evoke their attention to the external appraisal system, which results in leaders’ pro-social behaviors and conformity to ethical norms. At the same time, because status threat has some negative consequences as documented in the literature, organizations should avoid an extremely high level of status threat, as it will create a very stressful situation and make the negative side of status threat salient, such as risk taking and resistance to changes (Bothner et al. 2007; Kellogg 2012). An extremely high level of status threat is very likely to shortly transform into actual status loss, which brings less hope in reversing the situation and making leaders’ adaptive strategies less useful compared with imposing a long-time and mild threat to leaders’ status. Second, we find that the dependence of leaders on subordinates is a strong predictor of ethical leadership. Leader dependence on subordinates is proportionate to the criticality of subordinate resources (e.g., human capital or social capital). Therefore, the HRs management practices should consider increasing leaders’ dependence on subordinates. For example, organizations can encourage employees to develop their skills and competencies, which increase team members’ importance to the leaders’ performance. Leaders’ dependence could be induced by changing team composition or task allocation. For example, if every team member has a unique value and he/she is non-substitutable by others, the leader should be more human-oriented to coordinate the team with diverse capabilities. Furthermore, as leaders’ dependence on subordinates is likely to be reduced if alter - native resources are available, organizations should restrict leaders’ approach to alternative resources that can substitute the effectiveness of subordinates’ efforts or ensure that leaders will seek support from subordinates as the primary choice. Although we propose that the unilateral dependence of leaders on subordinates may make them human-oriented, organizations should enforce mutual dependence between the leader and his/her subordinates, as mutual dependence is the stable force in dyadic relationships (Mohr et al. 2016; Casciaro and Piskorski 2005), whereas power imbalance is the disruptive force (Michaels and Wiggins 1976). Leaders who depend more on subordinates than the subordinates depend on them may be less willing to punish subordinates’ unethical conducts (Deshpande et al. 2008). Therefore, organizations should encourage mutual dependence between leaders and subordinates. Finally, we found that status threat has some positive aspects. Although past studies discovered some dark sides of status threat, organizations should not completely eliminate status threat. Imposing status threat on leaders will increase their outward orientation in status comparison system, which in turn encourages conformity to ethical norms and directs their attentions to formulating good relationships with others (Hollander 1958). Therefore, organizations should wisely take advantage of status threat to leaders. Our study indicates that status threat results in dependence on subordi - nates and ethical leadership behaviors. It also indicates that whether status threat will generate strong dependence on subordinates depends on whether the leaders can access alternative resources to replace the resources of their sub - ordinates. Therefore, to ensure that the status threat to leaders is transformed into dependence on subordinates rather than into the exploitation of subordinates, organizations should ensure that the subordinates’ resources are critical to the leaders’ status production and that those resources G. Zhang et al. 1 3 are not easily substituted. However, this does not mean that organizations should prevent leaders from obtaining other resources through their networking abilities, as leaders’ ability to obtain valuable resources is beneficial for the organizations’ interests. Instead, organizations should encourage leaders to seek group resources as their primary consideration, which requires several preconditions such as a strong team culture, an interdependent team structure and strong capabilities of subordinates. Conclusion In sum, status threat explains ethical leadership by increasing leader dependence on subordinates. These findings not only advance our traditional view of status threat but also deepen our understanding of the formation of ethical leadership. We hope they will inspire more research on ways that ethical leadership can be encouraged within groups and organizations. Journal of Management & Organization, page 1 of 18 © 2018 Cambridge University Press and Australian and New Zealand Academy of Management doi:10.1017/jmo.2017.56 Ethical leadership, trust in leader and creativity: The mediated mechanism and an interacting effect BASHARATJAVED,* MOHAMMEDYAR AWWAS,** SUJATA KHANDAI,§ KAMRAN SHAHID|| AND HAFIZ HABIB TAYYEB¶ Abstract This study examines the relationship between ethical leadership and employee creativity with mediating role of trust in leader and moderating role of openness to experience. Data were collected from 205 supervisor–subordinate small textilefirms across Pakistan. Confirmatory factor analysis confirmed the distinctiveness of variables used in our study. The results confirmed that ethical leadership promotes creativity at workplace, while trust in leader mediates the effect of ethical leadership on creativity. Furthermore, the results did not confirm the moderation of openness to experience on the relationship between trust in leader and employee creativity. The implications are discussed. Keywords: employee creativity, ethical leadership, trust in leader, creative personality Received 27 April 2017. Accepted 29 September 2017 INTRODUCTION O rganizations in the hectic and complex environment of today need to necessarily adopt an adaptive and responsive approach and therefore encourage creative behavior among employees. Organizations today exist in an environment inundated with changing and ever-increasing consumer demands, along with escalating performance standards for employees as a result of globalization and technology changes (Heunks, 1998; Shalley, Zhou, & Oldham, 2004; Belleflamme & Peitz, 2015). Hence, organizational leaders are under a great deal of pressure tofind ways to increase creativity in their organization due to increasing globalization, competition, and pace of technological change. For organizations as these, creativity is thus regarded as a core competence. Needless to say, today, creativity is no longer regarded as an innate quality that only some individuals possess (Amabile, Conti, Coon, Lazenby, & Herron, 1996), but is increasingly being considered as a competence to be further improved and/or developed in all employees through adequate experience and training (Scott, Levitz, & Mumford, 2004). Therefore, at the current time, researchers and practitioners equate organizational survival and success with employees’ creativity (Hirst, Van Knippenberg, & Zhou, 2009; Williams & McGuire, 2010; Xia & Li-Ping Tang, 2011). Creativity, in essence, brings something new into the organization. It results in the attainment of a certain degree of intellectual knowledge and a level of emotional maturity aided by a freedom of expression and the opportunity to use all resources (Townsend, 2000). It is worthwhile to differentiate between the concepts of creativity and innovation. While creativity is defined as ‘the production of novel and useful ideas in any domain,’ innovation is ‘the successful implementation of creative ideas within an organization’ (Amabile et al., 1996: 1155). Since creativity involves generating new and novel ideas at the workplace (Amabile, 1983, 1996), which indicates that employees are encouraged to disagree with the leader and raise their voices to improve the work process (Chughtai, 2016). Therefore, creativity is enhanced in an organizational culture which nurtures and encourages a creative environment (Chua, Roth, & Lemoine, 2015). Leadership as a important part of organizational culture, play an important role with supportive behavior in creating and enhancing creativity (Amabile, Schatzel, Moneta, & Kramer, 2004). Research scholars have paid significant attention to the supportive role of leadership in promoting employees’ creativity (Javed, Bashir, Rawwas, & Arjoon, 2017). Numerous studies have found that supportive behavior of leadership and the leader’s ethical behavior to have a major positive impact on employees’ creativity (Zhu, May, & Avolio, 2004; Brown, Treviño, & Harrison, 2005; Gu, Tang, & Jiang, 2015). While employees’ creativity decreases with leadership controlling behavior (Tierney & Farmer, 2002, 2004; Jung, Chow, & Wu, 2003; Wang & Zhu, 2011; McMahon & Ford, 2013). In every organization, employees are bound to follow certain standardized norms (Javed, Naqvi, Khan, Arjoon, & Tayyeb, 2017). However, creativity is a special case where employees go beyond the standardized norms and challenge thestatus quo, many a times by disagreeing with the leader (Baucus, Norton, Baucus, & Human, 2008; Javed, Khan, Bashir, & Arjoon, 2017). Moreover, generating new ideas does not guarantee success and even creativity can result in ethical dilemmas (Yidong & Xinxin, 2013). Therefore, leaders need to be ethical in their approach for their employees to exhibit creativity (Ma, Cheng, Ribbens, & Zhou, 2013). Ethical leaders with open communication channels promote a supportive environment, which promotes employee creativity (Chughtai, 2016). Moreover, there are various mediated mechanisms that mediates in the relationship between ethical leadership and creativity. Particularly, Javed et al. (2016) called future researchers to check the role of mediated mechanism of trust in leadership in the relationship between ethical leadership and creativity. In order to respond to this call, in the current study, we used trust in the leadership as a mediated mechanism between ethical leadership and employees’ creativity. We found limited evidence to demonstrate how trust in a leader might play a mediating role between ethical leadership and employees’ creativity. Trust indicates the willingness to have dependence on other people (Mayer, Davis, & Schoorman, 1995). Trust also shows the expectation that other people will behave positively if one cooperates with them (Cook & Wall, 1980; Lane & Bachmann, 1998; Rousseau, Sitkin, Burt, & Camerer, 1998; van den Akker, Heres, Lasthuizen, & Six, 2009). Trust plays an important role in the relationship between leaders and their employees and effective trust show positive consequence via cooperation, information sharing and by increasing openness (Mayer, Davis, & Schoorman, 1995; Lane & Bachmann, 1998; Dirks & Ferrin, 2002; Den Hartog, 2003; Deutsch, 1973). Moreover, when employees show trust in their leader, the former exhibit increased willingness to take on the risk of creativity (Zhang & Zhou, 2014). While exhibiting a particular behavior, employees constantly monitor the work environment to decide whether they should repose trust in their leader (Carnevale, 1988; Dirks & Ferrin, 2002; Newman, Kiazad, Miao, & Cooper, 2014). Ethical leadership has been found to significantly influence employees’ trust in their leader (van den Akker et al., 2009; Engelbrecht, Heine, & Mahembe, 2014). Moreover, literature on creativity shows that creativity does not come from all employees (Schilpzand, Herold, & Shalley, 2010; Simmons, 2011). This is because; all employees have not a creativity relevant personality. It is evident that employees with a certain creativity relevant personality trait exhibit creativity (Kim, Hon, & Crant, 2009). Feist (1999) stated that taking thefive factor personality dimensions into consideration, the dimension which is very strongly related to creativity is openness to experience. Employees who demonstrate an openness to experience are those who exhibit creative behavior and‘out of the box’ thinking (Simmons, 2011). Since creativity promotes‘out of the box’ thinking, employees are thus encouraged to develop new and innovative ideas as opposed to old and traditionally prevailing ideas (Shelley, Zhou, & Oldham, 2004; Schilpzand, Herold, & Shalley, 2010). Thus, when employees show trust in their leader then they show more creativity when they are high on openness to experience. This shows the moderation of openness to experience between trust in leader and employees’ creativity. To our knowledge, no study has theoretically and empirically tested the moderation of openness to experience on the relationship between trust in a leader and creativity. The current study contributes, in several ways, to the theoretical development of creativity. First, this study attempts tofind out the effect of ethical leadership on creativity. Second, the current study will test the mediating role of trust in the leader between ethical leadership and creativity.
