The ethical constraints on leaders For scholars interested in leadership ethics, what could be a more fitting place to start than Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s self-described theory of ethical leadership ? According to their definition, ethical leadership is ‘‘the demonstration of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to followers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and decision-making’’ (Brown et al., 2005: 120, original italicized). The dual aspirations of the theory—constraining leaders’ behavior combined with tasking them to lead others to conform their behavior to such constraints—correspond to what they call the ‘‘moral person’’ and ‘‘moral manager’’ dimensions of ethical leadership (Brown and Trevin ̃ o, 2006: 597). Ethical leaders are acting as moral persons when they behave as they should; they are acting as moral managers when they get others to do so. Before saying more about Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s theory, I need to adopt a clarifying strategy. By naming the theory ethical leadership , the authors give the impression that this is the theory of ethical leadership, as opposed to a theory of ethical leadership (Ciulla, 2014: 23). Unfortunately, this confusion has been picked up by others and now runs through the leadership literature, where most talk of ethical leadership now corresponds to this particular theory. It would be a mistake, however, to infer from the fact that a theory is called ethical leadership that it picks out the demands of ethical leadership more generally. Naming something ethical leadership no more settles the matter than does calling something the true leadership theory make it true. I will therefore refer to the theory as Brown and Trevin õ’s EL theory . It is only one among many possibilities and needs to be treated as such until we consider reasons for thinking that it is the correct one, as well as set these reasons against criticisms that might lead us to reject the theory. Let us begin, however, with what Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory gets right. Its two most positive features can be found in its recognition of formal features of an acceptable theory of leadership ethics—namely, that it impose constraints on leader behavior and that it elucidate the nature of the influence process by which leaders get followers to do things. In other words, the theory should tell us what leaders are generally permitted to do (and prohibited from doing) and, more particularly, the conditions under which leaders are justified in shaping the behavior of followers. To its favor, then, Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory identifies two of the most basic challenges that leadership ethics must address. As we shall see, neither of their responses to these challenges is convincing in the end. I take up their account of what it is for a leader to be a ‘‘moral person’’ is this section. In the next section, I consider their account of what it is to be a ‘‘moral manager.’’ Consider the moral constraints that Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory places on leaders. The theory’s advocates propose that leaders should behave in ‘‘normatively appropriate’’ ways. As I earlier pointed out, no acceptable analysis of leadership ethics, much less a conceptual analysis, defines ethics in terms of equally ill-defined concepts. In this particular case, ethical leadership is defined by something even more complicated than ethics itself: normativity. Because there are all kinds of norms—e.g., norms of organizational effectiveness, rationality, manners, sport, etc.—‘‘normatively appropriate conduct’’ need not refer to 4 Leadership 0(0) anything ethical at all. It is broader than the ethical. Ethics must therefore be understood as a subset of the normative. Moreover, when we exclude non-ethical norms and focus only on the norms of morality, admonishing leaders to behave in normatively appropriate ways gives them no more guidance than does simply repeating that they should be ethical. The identified norms for leaders would simply be the ethical requirements and prohibitions on their behavior, what we were trying to figure out in the first place. The advocates of Brown and Trivino’s EL theory do gesture at examples of ‘‘conduct that followers consider to be normatively appropriate conduct’’ (Brown et al., 2005: 120). They offer ‘‘generalities’’ such as ‘‘honesty, trustworthiness, fairness, and care’’ (Brown et al., 2005: 120). One problem worth noting at the outset is that all these terms are nouns and, as such, cannot be used to describe conduct. Of course, we can easily adjust them to convey that normatively appropriate conduct is honest, trustworthy, fair, and caring. However, although conduct can be caring or fair, and maybe even honest, it sounds odd to call behavior ‘‘trustworthy.’’ What the authors really seem to have in mind when they refer to ‘‘normatively appropriate conduct’’ is behavior that exemplifies the honesty, trustworthiness, fairness, and caring of the leader . On this reading of the theory, ethical leaders behave in ways that lead us to think that they have particular characteristics or moral traits—namely, that they are honest, trustworthy, fair, and caring. This reading is also in keeping with their claim that ‘‘the moral person aspect of ethical leadership ... represent[s] observers’ perceptions of the leader’s personal traits, character, and altruistic motivation’’ (Brown and Trevin ̃ o, 2006: 595). Whether we understand Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory in terms of behavior or traits, we are left at the level of generalities, which themselves require further specification. 5 Does honesty require complete transparency? Is a leader trustworthy if he uses dishonest means to achieve the ends the group entrusted him to pursue? Is fairness a matter of desert or equality? How do we deal with inevitable collisions between, for example, honesty and caring? 6 Surprisingly, the advocates of Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory embrace the indeterminacy of the moral constraints: The term ‘‘normatively appropriate’’ is deliberately vague because ... what is deemed appropriate behavior is somewhat context dependent. For example, in some cultures normatively appropriate behavior might include speaking out publicly against some organizational action; in other cultures, such public voice would be considered to be normatively inappropriate. (Brown et al., 2005: 120) This quote might incline us to conclude that the theory endorses a kind of cultural relativism, the view that what is right or wrong will vary across, and be determined by, the cultures of which people are a part (Eisenbeiss, 2012: 793). But a charitable reading of Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory requires that we reject this conclusion. First, cultural relativism is clearly false. Cultures infamously accept norms that defy ethics. This is true of political societies—e.g., Nazi Germany and the antebellum South. There is no reason to think that unethical norms do not also regularly constrain the behavior of individuals in organizations. An ironic case in point is their own example of the prohibition on ‘‘speaking out publicly against some organizational action’’ (Brown et al., 2005: 120). The contingent fact that people face a social prohibition on expressing their opinions and, more particularly, that this prohibition seems to hold even when people believe the organization is on the wrong track, is not a reason to believe that we have discovered anything ethical about that organization or the proper constraints on behavior. It is more Price 5 of a reason to suspect that there is something deeply wrong with that culture, regardless of whether people act as if they have bought into the norm of silence. Second, Brown and Trevin ̃ o frame their overall project in a way that allows them to resist the charge that they are committed to any moral theory, let alone the theory of cultural relativism. They claim, ‘‘Philosophers have answered the question ‘what is ethical leadership’ from a normative perspective, specifying how leaders ‘ought’ to behave. By contrast, our social scientific approach to the topic is focused more on describing ethical leadership as well as identifying its antecedents and consequents’’ (2006: 596, emphasis added). In other words, they aim to tell us what ethical leadership is, without dealing—or dealing primarily—with the thorny normative questions associated with leadership. Whether this is possible remains to be seen. As Bill Clinton famously said, ‘‘It depends on what the meaning of the word ‘is’ is’’ (Clinton, 1998: 510). If Brown and Trevin ̃ o were to discover what ethics is, their findings would tell us something—quite a lot, one would think—about the normative, specifically, the norms of morality. For example, learning that lying is prohibited by ethics gives us a moral reason to think we ought to tell the truth. The fact/value distinction on which the authors implicitly rely, as well as the related is/ought fallacy, applies only when we try to draw normative conclusions from purely descriptive facts. 7 In contrast, ethical facts do have obvious normative implications. How could they not? It would be very odd to accept a claim as a truth about morality and, yet, deny that it offers any behavioral guidance. So the normal rule that social scientists aim to tell us about the world as it is, not as it should be, does not hold true in this particular case. By the meaning of the terms alone, we know that ethical facts tell us what we morally ought to do. This feature of ethics is peculiar, but we must accept it all the same. Brown and Trevin ̃ o might well deny that they are doing normative work by pointing out that they are merely describing people’s beliefs about morality. Indeed, their view moves very quickly, and often without warning, between ethical leadership and perceptions of ethical leadership (Ciulla, 2014: 24). The former is undeniably normative, and the latter is descriptive with no obvious normative implications. If Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory is concerned only with what people think about morality, then it is indeed fair to call the theory descriptive. As such, the theory would be only about what is: what people believe about morality. However, this move comes at significant cost, the most important of which is that it takes the ethical promise out of the theory. The descriptive turn reduces what is referred to the theory of ‘‘ethical leadership’’ to a theory of ‘‘subordinate’s perceptions of ethical leadership’’ (Brown and Trevin ̃ o, 2006: 597). 8 One strategy for connecting the descriptive and normative aspects of Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory would be to suggest that findings about people’s perceptions of ethical leadership serve as legitimate grounds for accepting a particular view of ethical leadership—in other words, that what people think about morality serves as evidence of what ethics really requires. In some circumstances, the fact that people generally believe something gives us a reason to accept, or at least privilege, these views over the alternatives. Of course, popularity in itself cannot give a position metaphysical force; people’s beliefs do not change reality. We know this from the many counterexamples in which people got things badly wrong in both science and ethics. Rather, according to this strategy, consensus serves as an epistemic tool, one that guides our attempts to discover what we have most reason to believe. There is support for this basic approach in the philosophical literature, both for considering what people think about value and for considering what people would think if asked 6 Leadership 0(0) particular questions, say, about justice. In the nineteenth century, the utilitarian John Stuart Mill argued that we could look to the majority to discover which of two experienced pleasures are ‘‘higher’’ (1979: 11), and in the twentieth century, John Rawls famously defended the view that the principles of justice would be those chosen by parties to what he called ‘‘the original position’’ (1971: 17ff). Their methods have at least some passing similarity, then, to ‘‘structured interviews with twenty senior executives and twenty ethics/compliance officers in a variety of industries’’ in which participants are asked ‘‘to think about an ethical leader with whom they were familiar, and to answer broad questions about the characteristics, behaviors, and motives of that leader’’ (Brown and Trevin ̃ o, 2006: 596). Yet neither Mill nor Rawls would think that interviewees in some study get to decide for themselves what morality requires. Mill is very specific about the reasons behind his appeal to people’s beliefs and also about the limits of this appeal. The rationale for looking to people’s views of pleasure is that this is the best way to discover the truth of the matter. Individuals are the most reliable judges of their own interests (knowing and caring the most) and, when ‘‘competently acquainted’’ with different pleasures, the best judges of which ones are most conducive to happiness (Mill, 1978: 74, 1979: 8). But there are definite limits to the trustworthiness of people’s beliefs. For example, Mill would certainly be opposed to letting people determine the principles of morality. His commitment to the truth of utilitarianism, despite whatever the majority thinks about morality, was the foundation for his interest in people’s views of pleasure and, therefore, not itself up for grabs. Rawls’s view is more complicated, but it is particularly worth considering in the context of a critique of Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory. Rawls defends particular constraints that must be placed on people before we can trust their ethical views. According to Rawls, ethical reasoning requires us to imagine that the parties to the original position are behind a ‘‘veil of ignorance’’ when they decide on the principles of justice (1971: 12). Specifically, they do not know particular facts about their race, class, and so on—facts that would distort their choices in favor of their own particular interests. Abstracting away from these interests gives Rawls’s theory the kind of impartiality that we associate with ethics. In fact, the connection to the ethical perspective is so strong that we might say the parties to the original position do more than discover the principles of justice. There is a sense in which people, properly constrained, can be viewed as creating or constructing them. 9 This appeal to the philosophical literature, in particular to Rawls’s insights, should make us wary of any attempt to discover what is ethical by simply looking at subordinate’s perceptions of their leaders. If we are to trust the conclusions people draw about ethical leadership, we need guarantees that they are engaged in their deliberations under the right conditions. Unfortunately, leadership contexts notoriously lack the impartiality associated with this approach to ethics. Leadership functions in large part as a way of serving group interests—often without meaningful consideration of outsiders, and sometimes at their expense. This descriptive partiality is the source of some of the most serious moral problems associated with leadership. It will be difficult, then, if not impossible, to disentangle people’s perceptions of ethical leadership from the views they have of their own leaders, who—by and large—work to serve the interests of group members. 10 Here, my point is not that studies surrounding Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory lend themselves to a charge of empirical bias. These studies may well capture what participants think about ethical leadership. But we will have little reason to conclude that the theory has captured anything meaningful about ethical leadership if the participants are subject to a distinctive form of moral bias—an unfounded preference for their own leaders. Brown and Price 7 Trevin ̃ o themselves unwittingly point to evidence for this kind of bias: ‘‘In one national poll, only 13% of respondents expressed a great deal of confidence in business leaders who are running major companies ... [O]ver 80% of respondents to a national survey in the United States indicated that leaders at all levels in their organization communicate the importance of ethics and set a good example in terms of ethical behavior’’ (Brown and Trevin ̃ o, 2006: 608, emphasis added). 11 Because subordinates are necessarily bound up in the partiality associated with leadership, we cannot take their perceptions to be definitive indicators of what constitutes ethical leadership. The ethics of influence Brown and Trevin ̃ o characterize the proper influence relation between leaders and followers this way: This aspect of ethical leadership represents the leader’s proactive efforts to influence followers’ ethical and unethical behavior. Moral managers make ethics an explicit part of their leadership agenda by communicating an ethics and values message, by visibly and intentionally role modeling ethical behavior, and by using the reward system (rewards and discipline) to hold followers accountable for ethical conduct. Such explicit behavior helps the leader to make ethics a leadership message that gets followers’ attention by standing out as socially salient against an organizational backdrop that is often ethically neutral at best (2006: 597). So, in addition to abiding by basic behavioral constraints (their ‘‘moral person’’ function), ethical leaders get others to do so as well (their ‘‘moral manager’’ function). Here again, to their favor, Brown and Trevin ̃ o point toward a distinctive feature of leadership, one that any theory of leadership ethics must address. A central aspect of leadership, perhaps the central aspect of leadership, is that leaders get followers to do things (Yukl, 2002: 145). It is also potentially the most troubling from a moral perspective because getting people to do things is a departure from letting them do what they want. As such, this special influence relation stands in need of moral justification. To analyze Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s view of the ethics of influence, we must once more return to issues of language. The kind of influence that Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory associates with ‘‘ethical leadership’’—namely, the promotion of ethics in followers—is importantly different from the kind of influence we typically associate with claims about ethical leadership. More commonly, the term ‘‘ethical leadership’’ implies that the leader’s behavior, not the follower’s behavior, is ethical. And for good reason: this meaning is the one in which we have the most interest. We want to understand the morality of getting people to do things. The fact that someone gets others to be ethical is not enough to justify her influence, unless we assume both that promoting ethics exhausts the influence relation between leaders and followers and that the promotion of ethics is itself always justified. By assuming that getting others to be ethical is the defining characteristic of an ethical influence relation, Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory largely avoids what makes most leadership activity questionable in the first place. Simply put, there is a lot more to leadership than simply getting people to be ethical. Some things that need to be done for the sake of goal achievement are neither required nor prohibited by morality. These behaviors are in a kind of moral free space. So an individual could choose to do—or, alternatively, not to do—them and still be well within ethical bounds (Price, 2014: 144). Being an effective follower in such cases might well entail that the individual should do what is asked of him, say, because it is in 8 Leadership 0(0) the service of group goals. But it is simply false that these reasons are always moral reasons. Behaviors can be necessary to serve group goals without being required by morality. Similarly, being an effective leader necessitates getting followers to accede to these requests by motivating them, encouraging them, and so on. The requests from leaders must be consistent with the requirements of morality. But even when the requisite behavior is morally permissible, it will rarely rise to the level of an ethical obligation for followers. One notable exception is when leaders can rely on follower promises. In these cases, there will be clear ethical implications—in particular, an ethical requirement that the follower do what he promised to do. This point helps explain why doing one’s job is normally required by ethics. If someone contracts to do something that morality allows, then ethics provides a very strong reason for making good on that promise. Here, morality lines up with the pursuit of organizational objectives. It would be a mistake, however, to think that a failure to meet leaders’ expectations can always—or even usually—be understood in terms of contractual violations. The things that people are asked to do, indeed got to do, extend well beyond what they are contractually obligated to do. Many leader–follower relationships are hardly contractual in any strict sense. One of the most surprising things about leadership is that people almost invariably follow individuals and work with other group members to get things done without explicit promises, much less formal contracts. Even in employment arrangements, contracts get leaders only so far when it comes to motivating followers. Numerous tasks that need to be carried out are ‘‘above and beyond the call of duty’’ and, therefore, not specified by employment contracts. 12 If we could always rely on contracts, we would have less need for leadership. The influence that characterizes leadership ranges much more widely—and is more ethically contentious—than mere contract enforcement. We must therefore dig deeper and address the morality of leaders getting people to do what it is morally permissible for them to do or not to do. Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory points at most to a necessary condition on the ethics of influence: people can be justifiably influenced to do only what morality allows. Obviously, the things that people are got to do must themselves be ethical. But an account of the ethics of influence hardly ends there. Ethical influence is about more than simply getting followers to work within the bounds of morality. It is also about the permissibility of the means that leaders use to get followers to engage in some morally permissible behaviors and to refrain from engaging in others—for example, not following! So simply using influence tactics in the service of ethical follower behavior is not sufficient to get the leaders off the moral hook. There are moral limits on how leaders can influence followers to do even what morality allows them to do. Moral limits on influence tactics are necessary because getting people to do things—for example, ethically permissible behaviors in the service of organizational objectives—bears some resemblance to ‘‘using’’ people. Philosopher Immanuel Kant articulates these worries in terms of a strict prohibition on treating people ‘‘merely as a means’’ (1964: 95, italics in original). Virtue theorist Alasdair MacIntyre similarly suggests that management contexts are particularly susceptible to the instrumental perspective: ‘‘Others are always means, never ends’’ (1998: 74). According to MacIntryre, The manipulative mode is accorded social respect by modernity through the prestige which the concept of managerial effectiveness enjoys. And this too functions as a moral fiction, a fiction because its application presupposes the availability of a set of social scientific laws, knowledge of Price 9 which will enable managers to control social reality; but we do not in fact know of any such laws. (1998: 70–71) In other words, the instrumental perspective is the result of a failed conception of rationality and modern efforts to separate our understanding of the world from ethics (Knight, 1998: 5– 6). Even if we are not convinced by MacIntyre’s diagnosis of the problem, we should worry that there is something intrinsically manipulative about management and, so too perhaps, about leadership (Learmonth and Morrell, 2016). So we must ask whether Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s ‘‘ethical leaders’’ are at risk of treating people simply as instruments for organizational objectives. The best interpretation of their theory heads off this particular criticism but gives rise to a related problem. The ‘‘moral manager’’ function of the theory suggests that the primary aim of ethical leadership is not the achievement of organizational objectives. This function makes the inculcation of ethics, not organizational success, the real goal of ethical leadership. Ethical leaders are not only ‘‘moral persons’’ but also ‘‘moral managers’’ who help followers become ‘‘moral persons.’’ What could be wrong with leaders using their influence only to get people to be moral? Turns out a lot can be wrong with it. In fact, there is a name for the basic phenomenon of trying to manufacture moral persons according to your own conception of morality: ‘‘ moralistic paternalism ’’ (Feinberg, 1984: 12–13). It is a variant of paternalism, the attempt to get people to act in their own interests, even when they do not want to do so. To call something ‘‘moralistic paternalism’’ is not to say that the paternalism is itself moral or justified but, rather, to point out that the act reflects a paternalistic approach to inculcating morality in others. In ethics, it is not particularly flattering to be called a ‘‘paternalist,’’ and much less so to be called a ‘‘moral paternalist.’’ The leadership context makes it very easy to see why. What it would take to turn people into moral persons is, in principle, limitless and extends well beyond the ethical reach of typical organizations and most any leadership relation. 13 Getting someone to be a moral person is more worrisome, not less, than trying to get people to act in ways that advance organizational goals. I do not mean to suggest that Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory is completely blind to these larger issues about the morality of influence tactics. Indeed, its advocates explicitly favor some methods of ethical inculcation over others. According to Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s ‘‘social learning’’ model, ‘‘[O]bservers can freely select models to observe and emulate’’ (2006: 604). It is well worth noting, however, that even behavior properly characterized as free can be morally problematic on account of the processes used to get people to make these choices. For example, in cases of manipulation, freedom or autonomy is not the main issue (Buss, 2005). The person who is manipulated, say, by appeal to his weakness for flattery, still freely chooses what he is got to do by means of manipulation. It is the freedom that characterizes such choices that distinguishes cases of getting from cases in which people are made to do things (Feinberg, 1970: 176). Getting people to do things is morally troubling precisely because it shares the freedom of letting but nevertheless has something in common with the paradigmatically objectionable case of making people do things. As it turns out, Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s description of these processes is less than reassuring: [I]ndividuals learn by paying attention to and emulating the attitudes, values and behaviors of attractive and credible models. Most individuals look outside themselves to other individuals for ethical guidance. Ethical leaders are likely sources of guidance because their attractiveness and 10 Leadership 0(0) credibility as role models draws attention to their modeled behavior. Power and status are two characteristics of models that can enhance their attractiveness, thus making it more likely that followers will pay attention to the ethical leaders’ modeled behavior. Most leaders possess authority because they occupy positions of status relative to their followers. (2006: 597) In this passage, modeling does not sound so innocent after all. Drawing on leaders’ attractiveness, especially when it is ultimately grounded in perceptions of power and status, is hardly without moral risks (Ciulla, 2014: 24). 14 We might even think that the causal arrow goes in the opposite direction: for example, facial features are precursors to power and status (Kahneman, 2011: 90–91). We cannot simply assume that these avenues of influence are unproblematic from the standpoint of morality. This weakness in Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s account of ethical influence is exacerbated by their claim that ethical leaders ‘‘reward ethical conduct and discipline those who don’t follow the standards’’ (Brown et al., 2005: 120). It appears that if role modeling—based on leader attractiveness when it is effective—is not sufficient to get followers to do the right thing, then ethical leaders resort to sanctions. Followers who are not themselves rewarded or punished get the message through ‘‘vicarious learning’’ (Brown et al., 2005: 120). This mechanism of influence is in keeping with their claim that ‘‘ethical leadership as defined here includes a transactional influence process that distinguishes it from transformational leadership’’ (Brown and Trevin ̃ o, 2006: 599). Transforming or transformational leadership, in contrast, aims to get followers to act on ‘‘higher levels’’ of moral motivation (Burns, 1978: 43). On this theory, doing the right thing to get a reward or avoid a punishment hardly reflects the highest moral development in followers. The practical problem with moralistic paternalism in leadership ethics is that we lack assurances regarding the ethics of leaders. 15 Leaders sometimes use ethics talk just to get followers to obey and, sometimes, to do what is actually unethical (Price, 2008, 2010). When there is disagreement between leaders and followers about what ought to be done, the influence process recommended by the theory will be impossible to distinguish from means Brown and Trevin ̃ o reject—for example, the Machiavellian use of ‘‘[c]oercion and manipulation,’’ both of which, in their own words, ‘‘are generally not regarded as ethical sources of influence’’ (2006: 604). Followers are effectively compelled to act on leaders’ opportunistic, or perhaps mistaken, views of ethics. Admittedly, on the transactional approach, followers have consented to their relationship with leaders (Hollander, 1964: 16). But consenting to this kind of relationship is not the same as promising to abide by leaders’ ethical conclusions. We are therefore left with a conceptual tension, one that takes us back to the earlier issues with the specification of ethical leadership. Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s theory relies on follower perceptions of ethical leadership, yet ethical leaders—in their role as ‘‘moral managers’’—are responsible for promoting ethics among followers. As I argued in the previous section, we cannot rely on follower perceptions to determine what is ethical. But neither can we simply resort to the ethical perceptions of leaders. There is perhaps less reason to trust them than there is to trust followers. Leaders face greater pressures to justify their behavior when they break the rules (Hoyt et al., 2010). The added cognitive, emotional, and physical pressures can also make it harder for them to exercise self-control (Kahneman, 2011: 41–44). 16 For example, ‘‘People who are cognitively busy are also more likely to make selfish choices, use sexist language, and make superficial judgments in social situations’’ (Kahneman, 2011: 41). In addition to being cognitively busy, leaders are often expected to control their emotions Price 11 and function on little rest. Do we really want them determining what is ethical and, based on their decisions, using rewards and punishments to ‘‘teach’’ followers how to behave morally? Critical leadership ethics Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory fails to answer central questions that must be addressed by a critical theory of leadership ethics. First, contrary to what this theory suggests, we cannot establish the moral constraints on leaders by definitional fiat or by an appeal to follower perceptions. Second, the theory’s focus on influencing followers to be ethical, as opposed to getting leaders to exercise influence in ethical ways, makes the leadership context more worrisome, not less. Instead of grappling with the basic kind of influence that characterizes leadership, its advocates take up the ethics of influence in one of the most problematic contexts of all: getting people to be moral. Despite its weaknesses, however, Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory does draw our attention to two distinctive problems in leadership ethics: the need for both moral constraints on leaders and an account of the ethics of influence. Moreover, by applying a critical approach to this theory, we can identify three additional morally troublesome features of leadership: its commitment to partiality, the high tolerance for status and inequality, and a consequentialist logic. Critical leadership ethics takes all five challenges seriously: (1) the problem of moral constraints, (2) the problem of partiality, (3) the problem of status and inequality, (4) the problem of consequentialism, and (5) the problem of influence. A successful treatment of these challenges requires that we address each systematically and provide responses that hang together consistently. This approach is also at pains to ensure that its answers are sufficiently critical of the phenomenon of leadership itself, one respect in which organizational approaches to ethics are often lacking. Fortunately, philosophical ethics lends itself to systematic and consistent application across problems. Virtue ethics, deontological theories such as Kant’s, and consequentialist theories such as utilitarianism are considered theories for precisely this reason. They allow us to confront particular problems and move among them without contradiction. As we shall see, however, the critical recourses of some moral theories will mean that they are better equipped to serve as safeguards against the distinctive challenges of leadership than are others. To address the first challenge, we must ask whether the moral constraints on leaders are at the level of behavior or character. Is the conduct of leaders the primary object of moral concern, or should we focus instead on their ‘‘traits?’’ Here, precision of thought matters for making sense of our judgments about ethical leadership. Specifically, we need to know whether leadership ethics prioritizes means, ends, or virtue. Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory incorporates all three strands of ethical analysis: ‘‘individual characteristics,’’ prohibitions on means such as ‘‘coercion and manipulation,’’ and ‘‘outcomes’’ (Brown and Trevin ̃ o, 2006: 596, 604). But it is much too simplistic to proclaim that we must be concerned with all three. 17 Different moral theories break down roughly along the lines of virtue, deontology, and consequentialism, and they regularly generate different, even competing, ethical conclusions. 18 A critical approach to leadership ethics therefore requires that we make some make hard choices. 19 The centrality of individual characteristics in Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory might suggest an affinity for virtue theory (Brown and Trevin ̃ o, 2006: 599). Notice, however, that the trust its advocates place in follower perceptions is clearly at odds with key tenets of this approach to ethics. For example, Aristotle—the historical champion of 12 Leadership 0(0) this view—assumes that people do not easily, or naturally, know what virtue is (1985: 34, 1103a30). People become virtuous only by habituation, by following the example of those who are virtuous (1985: 34–35, 1103b5-25). Although Brown and Trevin ̃ o similarly hold that it is the primary job of leaders to impart morality to followers, this claim conflicts with their assumption that followers are the best judges of what constitutes ethical leadership—in this case, what individual characteristics ethical leaders have. In other words, advocates of Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory face a conceptual puzzle: if people do not know what virtue is, it seems that they will be unable to identify the virtuous among them. 20 Perhaps followers who do not know what virtue is nevertheless recognize it when they see it.21 Accordingly, even individuals who cannot articulate an understanding of virtue might be able to identify virtuous leaders and to emulate them. The problem with this understanding of virtue theory is that it exacerbates the problem of partiality in leadership ethics and, in so doing, shows why virtue theory does lend itself to a critical approach to leadership ethics. We simply cannot trust people’s opinions about the ethical characteristics of group members. It is a well-established phenomenon that merely sharing group membership is associated with relatively more favorable impressions of other people in the group (Tajfel, 1970). Group members are even more forgiving of their leaders. Followers allow leaders to get away with all kinds of behaviors when leaders get things done for the group (Hollander, 1964: 174). In other words, leaders are rarely held to the same standards as group members. The effects of this kind of partiality combine with other psychological phenomena that distort the ethical attributions we make to leaders (Flanigan, in preparation: 19). Because of the ‘‘halo effect,’’ we quickly infer that individuals with some good qualities also have other good qualities (Kahneman, 2011: 82). So, for example, we assume that the effective leader must be ethical as well. This need for coherence similarly inclines us to infer that positive outcomes must have positive origins (Nisbett and Ross, 1980: 26–27). For the virtue theorist, the relevant inference would be to the presence of positive traits. The problem with this version of virtue theory, then, is that the information we use to identify virtuous leaders is as likely to be the result of group favoritism and historical or situational context as it is to be the result of leaders’ stable, dispositional traits (Doris, 2002; Harman, 1999). Appeals to virtue therefore feed whatever worries we might have about status and inequality , the third distinctive problem associated with leadership. These appeals perpetuate the questionable view that leaders really are better than the rest of us, a view that serves to ground unequal relationships between leaders and followers. The fourth challenge of leadership is the problem of consequentialism. As James MacGregor Burns puts it, leadership is about getting things done (1978: 22). The moral risk of this consequentialist logic, of course, is that a single-minded focus on the ends can encourage leaders to neglect the means. In response to this risk, the strategy in the leadership literature on ethics has been to dodge the moral perils of consequentialism by insisting, much like utilitarianism, that leadership can be justified when aimed at the right end: follower wellbeing. 22 In a review of the literature, Dinh et al. (2014: 57) summarize the work on ethical leadership: ‘‘This thematic category encompasses leadership theories that have in common a core focus on altruistic behaviors.’’ Here, the idea seems to be that consequentialism is not so bad if leaders’ efforts are directed at morally worthy goals such as employee welfare, as opposed to, say, the bottom line. Brown and Trevin ̃ o join this consequentialist chorus, claiming that one similarity shared among their EL theory, authentic leadership, spiritual leadership, and transformational leadership is ‘‘[c]oncern for others ([a]ltruism)’’ (2006: 598). However, as we have seen, Price 13 their theory is not altruistic, at least according to the standard meaning of the term. Altruistic behavior is (1) not self interested, (2) directed toward others, and (3) focused on well-being. Not all behavior that meets the first criterion of altruism will meet the second and third criteria. Behavior that is not self interested can nevertheless fail to be other interested. For example, leadership is often aimed at making an excellent product or winning a match, neither of which need be connected to the welfare of leaders, followers, or anyone else (Price, 2014: 139). Admittedly, ethical leadership, according to Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory, is both (1) not self-interested and (2) other interested. But it fails to meet the third criterion because their notion of ethical leadership is in service of the ethical behavior of followers, not their well-being . 23 In the end, not even altruism gets leadership around the problem of consequentialism. For one thing, what reason is there to think that leaders know what is in the best interests of followers? Keep in mind that altruism does not imply that leaders actually do serve the interests of followers, only that they are motivated to do so. We would also have to assume that when leaders have this special knowledge, they are genuinely motivated to act on it. That is a lot of trust to put in leaders, particularly given their gifts for spinning and selling decisions to make it look as though they are acting in ways that ultimately benefit others. Finally, even if leaders both know the truth about follower interests and are motivated to act on this knowledge, we are still left with the fact that leaders are getting followers to do things. Getting followers to do things, even for the sake of their own good, stands in need of justification. This need for justification is at the root of the problem of influence, the fifth distinctive challenge of leadership. Consequentialism is relatively blind to this problem because it is preoccupied with what gets achieved, rather than how it is achieved. So, like virtue ethics, consequentialist theories, including utilitarianism, tend to make things too easy on leaders by ignoring one of the problematic features of leadership. Both theories contrast with the deontological approach to ethics—an approach that prioritizes the morality of means. The deontological approach is designed specifically to identify the behaviors that can be used to achieve our goals and, equally important, respect the freedom of others whose help we might need in the process. Some actions—for example, lying and promise breaking—are wrong in themselves, and treating people instrumentally, whether in pursuit of their own good or that of group members, is always morally impermissible (Kant, 1964: 83–84, 95). 24 In this respect and others, the deontological approach sets itself up as a critical antidote to leadership. In fact, I believe that it is the only moral theory that can systematically, consistently, and—crucially for leadership ethics— critically take on the distinctive ethical challenges of leadership. Though establishing this claim is outside the scope of my paper, here are some supporting reasons in its favor. First, as noted above, the approach lays out strict constraints on leader behavior. Concrete prohibitions on behaviors such as lying and promise breaking make for a stark contrast with Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s imprecise specification of ‘‘normatively appropriate conduct’’ (2005: 120). Second, unlike virtue ethics, the deontological approach gives no fundamental moral weight to group membership, so it answers the problem of partiality. Any special obligations leaders and followers have toward group members are subject to the behavioral constraints defined by ethics more generally (Price, 2008). Third, because the deontological approach is grounded in the moral equality of all agents, including leaders and followers, it has a built-in theoretical check on status and inequality. For example, organizational hierarchy is justified only to the extent that it is compatible with 14 Leadership 0(0) the fundamental moral status of all group members. Fourth, unlike utilitarianism, the deontological approach focuses our attention on the morality of the means. In so doing, it warns leaders against using the ends to justify their behavior—the problem of consequentialism. One problem with the ill-defined normative theories in the leadership literature is that when combined with consequentialism, their appeal to values such as the good of others can be used to justify almost anything. Finally, the deontological approach provides a framework for responding to questions about the influence process that characterizes leadership. Leaders must treat followers as moral agents with their own ends and projects, not as instruments for the achievement of the goals of others. The deontological approach to leadership ethics certainly deserves a much fuller defense than I have provided here. What I have tried to argue in this final section is that this approach stands out as a promising alternative both to Brown and Trevin ̃ o’s EL theory, as well as to other philosophical competitors in leadership ethics. The first main strength of the deontological approach is that it allows us to engage critically with the leadership literature. Despite the ethicist’s initial inclinations to dismiss empirical work in this area, there is an important sense in which Brown and Trevin ̃ o are on the right track. Deontological ethics makes sense of their search for behavioral constraints on leaders and their fascination with the influence relation. Second, the deontological approach allows us to take a much more critical view of leadership itself. With commitments to strict behavioral constraints, impartiality, equality, means-based reasoning, and the moral agency of followers, this approach suggests that ethics makes room for leadership only if it can be exercised within the bounds of strict moral limits. My goal, however, has not been to establish either that deontological ethics definitively solves the ethical problems associated with leadership or that it is the only moral theory that might work. A comprehensive defense of this theory will require extensive argumentation over several papers as part of a larger research agenda. My goal was rather to use the critical leadership ethics approach to investigate what acceptable solutions to these problems might look like. The first step, then, was to identify the problems and consider an influential attempt to solve them in the leadership literature. To build on this approach, it will be necessary to turn to other prominent leadership theories that purport to address ethical questions. There are also alternative solutions that deserve greater consideration than I can give them in this paper. One, for example, is the virtue approach to ethics, which I dismissed as insufficiently critical of leadership. But there is debate within virtue ethics itself about how critical or accommodating the theory must be (Beadle, 2008). As we have seen, the work of Alasdair MacIntyre (1998) suggests an alternative foundation for engaging in critical leadership ethics. Going forward, other scholars might therefore turn to virtue ethics, or—for that matter—even consequentialism, to carry out the critical leadership ethics project. Regardless of the theory in which scholars ground the project, their work will be very much consistent with the broader aims of critical leadership studies. For example, there is no reason to think that critical leadership ethics would not draw on other philosophical traditions or alternative approaches in the humanities—any more than it ignores the empirical and social scientific literature on leadership. In fact, the starting assumption for the project is that these approaches go hand in hand. And, given the context of leadership, for good reason. As Jackson and Tourish put it, ‘‘Our field is too complex to rely on only one explanation, or to be explored via only a small coterie of methodologies ... [It needs] a broad range of theoretical perspectives and multifarious methodologies ... [and papers that are not] Price 15 reluctant to question established theories and practices’’ (2014: 4). That is just what critical leadership ethics tries to do. A Role-Definition Perspective of Ethical Leadership and Unethical Behavior Ted A. Paterson Oregon State University Lei Huang Auburn University Prior studies have demonstrated that leaders’ ethical behaviors have an impact on followers’ unethical behaviors, and yet the explanatory mechanisms in this relationship have not been fully explored. To further explicate the relationship between ethical leadership and unethical employee behavior, we adopted a role-based perspective and introduced the concept of role ethicality. That is, we explored the impact that leaders’ actions and voice behaviors, particularly regarding ethical issues, have on perceptions of ethical role requirements and in turn the effect such perceptions have on unethical behavior. In a field study involving 394 employees and 68 supervisors and a randomized experiment conducted with 121 working professionals, we find that as predicted, leaders’ behaviors and ethical voice have a significant influence on role ethicality, which in turn impacts unethical behavior. Based on our empirical findings, we describe the implications, limitations, and future directions relevant to this study.
