These institutions need to adapt to changes in order to maintain their existence, provide quality and cost-effective services for the health requirements of the society, ensure patient and employee safety, and increase the satisfaction of service providers as well as receivers.1,2 Healthcare institutions and employees may face many ethical problems regarding such issues. The ethical climate in the institution and the ethical leadership characteristics of the manager play an important role in identifying and maintaining correct behaviors that will determine the resolution of these problems.3,4 The ethical climate theory developed by Victor and Cullen 5 includes the development of a common understanding of how to deal with ethical problems and what is ethically the right behavior. 5,6 Ethical climate is defined as the shared general perception regarding institutionalized organizational values, practices, and processes.2,6–8 In other words, ethical climate is employees’ general observation and opinion of the institution rather than their individual attitudes and thoughts regarding how ethical problems are addressed and possible solutions. Ethical climate which reduces conflicts within an organization is a part of an organization’s culture that promotes ethical standards and gives importance and priority to ethical values.9,10 Ethical climate guide employees in making decisions about acceptable and unacceptable behaviors.2,9,11 The ethical climate of an organization gives clues about the way an organization operates and the behaviors of individuals.11–13 Nurses have responsibilities to the patients they give care, to their colleagues, to the students they guide, to their profession, and to the society. Ethical dilemmas arise in all these relationships, and the solution requires an ethical approach.14 Ethical leadership requires acting in accordance with the requirements of the nursing profession for the benefit of individuals, groups, and organizations in these ethical conflicts that nurses often meet.15 Nurses’ negative perceptions of ethical climate and the ethical characteristics of their leaders may lead to a failure in the care and treatment of the patients they are responsible for. 15,16 In 1998, Olson1 developed a scale for assessing the ethical climate scores of nurses working in hospitals and stated that this scale could be used to understand, recognize, and evaluate the impact of ethical climate on nursing practices. In the study of Hart 17 in which he used this scale, it was reported that positive perceptions of ethical climate for hospitals reduced the tendency of nurses to leave their jobs and profession. In the study of Bulutlar and Oz,16 it was expressed that working in an organization having ethical climate would regulate the ethical behaviors of individuals and prevent them from experiencing psychological burnout while enhancing their organizational commitment so that they would be motivated to contribute to the organization and develop a feeling of security which will help them cope with difficulties more easily. It is determined from the previous studies that when the ethical climate of the institution was perceived negatively, individuals’ motivation and job performance decreased, their job satisfaction 2,6,12,13,18,19 and cooperation20 and organizational commitment12,19 were decreased. Today, when leaving employment and ethical problems are on the increase, the positive ethical climate of an institution has an important place in the maintenance of correct and professional nursing practices.1,10 Especially in Turkey, nurses have problems such as not being able to participate in decision-making mechanisms and informing the patient and the family, lack of autonomy, feeling unworthy in the healthcare team, not being able to act as the spokesperson of the patient, and experiencing an inadequate communication with doctors.21 The causes for these negative feelings are the shortages of nurses, working in intense physical environment and in shifts, inadequate promotion and wage opportunities, lack of fair and uncertainties in management, ambiguities and inequalities in the role and job definition, and inadequate health and institutional policies. Due to these causes, the job satisfaction of nurses decreases in Turkey. 21 The determination of the effect of ethical climate on job satisfaction has great significance in increasing job satisfaction. Ethical leadership is necessary for the creation of an ethical climate environment that would handle such problems. 2 Nursing Ethics XX(X) The responsibility of establishing the ethical principles that govern p eople’s behaviors in institutions or the ethical climate in which norms prevail belongs to the leader. The climate of a virtuous organization perceived as ethical, and in this process, ethical leaders are those who are able to do the best for others and are models for implemen ting ethical behavior. 4,22–25 Today, ethical leadership in nursing is increasingly becoming recognized at local, natio nal, and international levels. 14,26–29 According to Bandura’s definition, ethical leadership is the demo nstration of normatively appropria te conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relations and the promotion of such conduct to followers through communication. 30 In other words, it is defined as the promotion of moral way of thinking in compliance with high ethical standards by the ethical leader to other people.31,32 Ethical leadership should be addressed through a fourdimensional approach. Ac cording to the first dimension, ethical leaders should act as a lens and demonstrate behaviors within a transparent framework. I n the second dimension, the ethical leader should influence the viewers with an effort to raise an aware ness in their behavior. The third dimension is about the ethical leader adopting the basic principles of ju stice and righteousness and demonstrating virtues in their professional and personal lives. In the final d imension, the leader should guide the viewers by protecting social values. 33 Nurses’ expectations from ethical lead ers is that they demonstrate ethical behaviors and establish “a workplace where values are c learly shared, and that these values direct ethical action, and where individuals feel safe to be heard.”31 Ethical leaders act as ethical guides for employees, and it has been stated that employees’ job satisfaction is influenced by the ethical characteristics of leaders.31,32 Therefore, it is necessary to determine how nurses’ perceptions of ethical leaders affect their job satisfaction in Turkey. The ethical principles underlying organizational values and leadership in hospitals are respect for patient autonomy, giving priority to the interests of patients, and fair and equal provision of healthcare.34 In addition, the Faculty of Medicine also states that the provision of healthcare should adhere to six fundamental ethical principles which means the healthcare provided should be equitable quality, effective, patient-centered, efficient, safe, and timely. 35 These values should guide the decisions taken in the hospital. It is these ethical values that are fundamental to today’s healthcare organizations and the success of a hospital, and its leader is measured by the accordance of their decisions and actions with these ethical values. 34 Ethical leaders need to work with care providers in accordance with contemporary leadership approaches in a multidisciplinary way and strengthen them in clinical decision-making, clinical trials, and effective communication with patients. 14,28 It is necessary that ethical leaders set high ethical standards, proactively organize healthcare, ensure coordination, and collaborate with executives to provide patients with safe, effective, and timely healthcare. In this way, mutual expectations of the organization and the nurses would be balanced and the job satisfaction of employees would increase. 36 Even though ethical leadership plays an important role in fulfilling healthcare ethics, nurses have stated that they are not supported by their leaders. 25,37 Even if nurses take the leadership role to develop their ethical practices, they will not be able to provide an ethical working environment unless they are supported by their leaders, thus patient care quality will be affected negatively.30,38,39 Studies conducted in different fields also support the fact that the perception of ethical climate increases, thanks to the perception of ethical leadership.38,39 In the literature, studies that analyze the impact of ethical leadership on ethical climate and job satisfaction have gained importance in recent years. 14,26–29 However, there are a limited number of quantitative studies in this field. Furthermore, there is no study that studies ethical leadership and its relation to ethical climate and job satisfaction in our country. Aim The aim of the study is to determine the ethical leadership, ethical climate, and job satisfaction levels of nurses and to examine the relationship between these variables in Turkey. Oz̈den et al. 3 Method Type of study The study has been conducted as a descriptive and cross-sectional study. The population and sample of the study The population of the study consisted of 500 nurses working in all the departments of Surgery, Internal Medicine, and Intensive Care units of a University hospital and an Education and Research Hospital in Izmir between 15th July and 31st December 2016. These units, which don’t include the outpatient clinic and remote treatment centers of the two hospitals, are chosen because patients receive long-term care. There was no sample selection, so a total of 285 nurses who met the sample selection criteria and agreed to participate in the study were included in the sample. The following inclusion criteria were applied: (1) working actively in these units, (2) willing to participate in a study; and the exclusion criterion was being on annual leave or having a report due to illness. Data collection forms Data were collected using four different forms: Personal Information Form, Ethical Leadership Scale, Hospital Ethical Climate Scale, and Minnesota Satisfaction Scale (MSQ). Personal Identification Form. This form, which was prepared by the researchers after a literature review, consists of 19 questions regarding the socio-demographic and professional characteristics of the nurses. The Ethical Leadership Scale.The Ethical Leadership Scale was developed by De Hoogh and Den Hartog, 40 the validity and reliability of the Turkish version was conducted by Alkan, 33 and the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient was reported to be 0.965. The scale consists of a total of 17 questions in three sub-dimensions; ethics and fairness (6 items), role clarification (5 items), and sharing power (6 items). The scale ranges from 1 1⁄4 “strongly disagree,” 2 1⁄4 “disagree,” 3 1⁄4 “neither agree nor disagree,” 4 1⁄4 “agree,” 5 1⁄4 “strongly agree.” The total score to be received from the scale is minimum 17 and maximum 85. A rise in the total score received from the scale indicates that the ethical leadership perception is positively enhanced.33 In our study, the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of the scale was also found to be 0.91. The Hospital Ethical Climate Survey.The Hospital Ethical Climate Survey (HECS) was developed by Olson41 in the United States in 1995 and was adapted to Turkish with its validity and reliability conducted by Bahcȩcik and O ̈ ztur̈k.3 The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient was found to be 0.91 by Olson,41 while Bahcȩcik and O ̈ ztur̈k3 determined it to be 0.89. The scale consists of a total of 26 items and five sub factors; Hospital (6 items), Colleagues (4 items), Patients (4 items), Managers (6 items), and Doctors (6 items). All the items on the Likert-type scale are positive ranging from 1 to 5 points as “almost never true,” “seldom true,” “sometimes true,” “often true,” “almost always true.” The maximum possible score to be taken from HECS is 130, while the minimum is 26, and the highest score is 130. A rise in the total score received from the scale indicates that the perception of hospital ethical climate is positively enhanced. In our study, the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of the scale was also found to be 0.93. Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire (MSQ).This scale was used to determine the job satisfaction level of the nurses. It was developed by Weiss et al.42 and adapted to Turkish with its validity and reliability conducted by Baycan.43 The Cronbach’s alpha value was found to be 0.77 in this study. Individuals are asked to 4 Nursing Ethics XX(X) determine their level of satisfaction regarding 20 professional needs on a scale ranging from “not satisfied” (1) to “extremely satisfied” (5). To calculate the total satisfaction score, the responses given to 20 items are added. The total score ranges from 20 to 100. The increase in the score indicates an increase in job satisfaction.41 A percentile value above 75 indicates high job satisfaction, while a value below 25 indicates low job satisfaction. A percentile score ranging from 26 to 74 indicates normal job satisfaction. The Cronbach’s alpha value was found to be 0.91 in our study. Procedure The data were collected by face-to-face interviews conducted with participants in their clinics. After written information was given about the study, the forms were given to the nurses, who agreed to participate in the study, and collected after they were filled. It was told that the participation in the study was based on volunteerism, and the data obtained would be kept confidential. Before the collection of data for the study, consent was obtained from Dokuz Eylul̈ University Faculty of Medicine Hospital and Tepecik Training and Research Hospital as well as the Non-Interventional Research Ethics Committee of Dokuz Eylul̈ University. The study was conducted in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration Principles (reference number: 91829616/804-739). Data analysis For the evaluation of data, the SPSS for windows 15.0 (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences) software was used. In addition to descriptive statistical methods (frequency, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, number and percentage), for the comparison of numerical data, significance test for the difference between two means in independent groups, Mann–Whitney U test, Kruskal–Wallis test, and analysis of variance (ANOVA) test were used. Correlation analysis was used to determine the relationship between ethical leadership, ethical climate, and job satisfaction. 44 Limitations of the study Since the study was conducted in the internal medicine, surgical, and intensive care units of two hospitals in a single province, the results are valid for this hospital. In the literature, it has been reported that nurses’ ethical climate scores of their hospitals are influenced by the behaviors of managers which increase job satisfaction.10,45,46 In their study conducted with employees from various institutions, Bulut47 reported that ethical leadership and ethical climate has a positive effect on job satisfaction. Bilgen 48 also stated that there is a positive correlation between ethical leadership and ethical climate. Furthermore, Sonakın49 stated that as the ethical climate score increases, job satisfaction level also increases. Ethical leadership ensures the establishment of ethical values in patient care by resolving the negative factors affecting job satisfaction.24 Our study also supports this information by having revealed a significant positive correlation among the nurses’ ethical climate, ethical leadership, and job satisfaction mean scores (Table 1). Employees are the key persons who determine the service in the service-oriented organizations, so maintaining job satisfaction at a high level is crucial in ensuring the efficiency of the organization. The positive correlation between ethical leadership and job satisfaction confirms Bandura’s theory of social learning. 30 Nurse leaders help to develop an ethical climate in the institution by prioritizing ethical values in their relationships with patients and employees, and acting in compliance with ethical principles while providing care. Ethical climate enables the unification, support, and internalization of professional values. 11,13,16,46 All these findings show that job satisfaction can be affected by the provision of ethical climate in organizations. In parallel with our findings, the literature also shows that there is a strong relationship between a positive ethical climate and organizational ethical behavior and job satisfaction. 2,14,23,46 In our country, where there is a high rate of intent-to-leave and a limited number of nurses, this result is an important finding for increasing the job satisfaction of nurses.21,29 In order to increase the job satisfaction of nurses, further studies may be conducted on increasing ethical climate and ethical leadership. Victor and Cullen5 stated that as the time spent in work life increases, the desire to heal others, that is to say, the perception of ethical climate increases. Furthermore, Bilgen48 revealed that there is a relationship between ethical leadership, ethical climate, and age. However, in our study, we found that the age variable does not have an effect on ethical leadership or ethical climate (Table 2). This finding might have been resulted from the fact that the number of the nurses in age groups was not randomized. Moral development theory points out that the lev el of education has an impact on moral development.13 Hence, our study also revealed that the ethical le adership perceptions of nurses with a high level of education were significantly higher (p < 0.05) and t heir ethical climate scores were found to be higher although there was not a significant difference. Similar to our finding, Goldman and Tabak13 also pointed out that there was a difference between education a nd ethical climate scores. The study conducted by Hashish46 also revealed nurses with a high level of education had a more positive perception of organizational support. As opposed to our findings, Karagoz̈ogl̆u et al.10 reported that the level of education and ethical climate score were inversely proportiona l. This finding may be related with the fact that an increase in the level of education leads to an increa se in professional awareness which consequently leads to higher expectations from the manager and institution. In Turkey, where education has not yet been standardized, the nursing profession is still being practiced by high school or vocational school graduates which may have a negative impact on the ethical climate among employees, cause ethical conflicts, and lead to a decrease in the quality of car e. It may be suggested to increase the standard in university education and in-service trainings. In our study conducted in two different hospitals, it w as found that there was a statistically significant difference between the hospitals in terms of ethical leadership, ethi cal climate, and job satisfaction. Similar to our finding, in her study conduc ted in three different hospitals, Hashish 46 reported that there were significant differences among the ethical climate perceptions and job satisfaction levels of nurses. In the study conducted by Makaroff et al., 36 it was emphasized that corporate mission, vision, and values were influential on the ethical values of employees. This result may be attributed to the organizational and managerial differences in institutions as well as to the different nature of the subunits and sections of each hospital.46 Moreover, in Turkey, the restricted policies o f institutions on ethical standards and their economic position are affecting pa tient care, employee sat isfaction, working hour s, and, therefore, job satisfaction. 21 The ethical standards to be developed throughout the country can serve as a guide in the practice of nurses. In our study, it was found that there were significant differences regarding the ethical leadership, ethical climate, and job satisfaction scores of the nurses according to their working clinics (p < 0.05) and that the ethical leadership and ethical climate scores, consequently the job satisfaction level of the nurses working in internal units, were higher when compared to surgical and intensive care nurses (Table 3). In the literature, unlike our finding, it has been reported that the ethical climate scores of intensive care nurses is higher.3,18 In the study conducted by Bahcȩcik and Oztur̈k3 to determine the hospital ethical climate scores of the nurses working in all the clinics in our country, it was found that the ethical climate scores of intensive care nurses were higher with a statistical significance. Intensive care unit is a stressful environment where patients stay for a long time, and ethical climate is experienced. In Turkey, there are still uncertainties regarding the regulation of ethical issues and treatment support in intensive care units. While making a decision on patient care, nurses experience an ethical dilemma and feel insecure. 21,50 Therefore, it can be argued that intensive care nurses have lower ethi cal climate scores and ethical leadership, which 10 Nursing Ethics XX(X) consequently affects their job satisfaction. Furthermore, recurrent patient admission occurs less in internal services compared to surgical services; thus, nurses, patients, and relatives experience less stress. 51,52 For such different clinics, nurses need their leaders’ support, so they would strengthen the ethical decisionmaking process.31 It was found that as the total length of service increased, the ethical climate mean score was higher and the difference was statistically significant (Table 3). In their study, Goldman and Tabak 13 reported that senior nurses had a higher ethical climate scores. Makaroff et al. 36 reported that nurses did not feel they could fulfill their ethical obligations to their patients during the first 6 months of their profession. This result can be attributed to the lower awareness and expectations of inexperienced nurses from their institutions and managers. Nevertheless, in parallel with the length of service, the increase in nurses’ knowledge and skills, commitment to the institution, and the ability to cope with problems may also be influential on positive ethical leadership perception and ethical climate scores. It is noteworthy that as the nurses’ length of service in their institution increases, the ethical leadership mean scores increase with a statistically significant difference. It could be suggested from this finding that nurses with longer experience mentor the nurses who are new in the profession and that the starters and those with a short length of service are given trainings on ethical leadership and ethical climate. When the position in the institution is considered, it was found that the ethical climate and job satisfaction mean scores of chief nurses were higher than service nurses although the difference was not significant. It was also observed that the ethical leadership mean score did not change. Aitamaa et al.52 reported that the nurses in managerial positions are responsible for dealing with other employees’ ethical problems. Furthermore, they also found it surprising that nurses in managerial positions were using ethical codes considering that service nurses were more likely to work with patients. In their study, Martin and Cullen19 stated that the satisfaction of nurses regarding their managers was influential on ethical climate scores. In their study conducted with nurses in Taiwan, Tsai and Huang 53 stated that managers could create a positive ethical climate environment using ethical principles and supporting the education and development of nurses. Makaroff et al.36 determined that nurses experience many problems in achieving ethical leadership. Nurses are required to work in different shifts, mostly being night shifts. 11 According to the data from Health Resources and Services Administration’s, the nursing shortage is getting worse, which increases the workload of nurses.54 It has been reported in recent reports that the situation is similar in European countries and in Turkey.55 In this study, it was determined that the ethical climate of nurses working in day shifts and working less than 40 h a week was more positive. This finding is supported by the argument that nurses’ organizational climate and work performance are interrelated and that ethical climate plays an important role in the planning of the work environment among different organizations. 11 In the same way, it was determined that nurses working in day shifts and less than 40 h a week had high ethical leadership and job satisfaction scores. It is also noteworthy that nurses who provided care for more than five patients had higher ethical leadership mean scores. Makaroff et al. 36 argue that ethical leadership should be reinforced to support nurses’ ethical practices and provide the most appropriate patient care required. Restrictions on the number of nurses, particularly after the Transformation of Health Program in Turkey, and overtime work may have an adverse effect on both the job satisfaction of nurses and the care given to patients. 51,52 The fact that nurses are satisfied with their profession and their colleagues and the way they perceive their work environment affect their attitudes toward ethical issues and their ethical decision-making processes. Taking ethical decisions that affect patient care in a positive way ensures that ethical climate is perceived as positive. Supportive and empowering ethical climate work environments will also have a positive impact on both nurse and patient outcomes.13,36,46 Our findings, supportive of this information, also indicated that nurses who were satisfied with their working conditions, profession, and relationship with their colleagues had positive ethical leadership and ethical climate scores and that their job satisfaction also increased. In their study, Hart 17 found that there was a strong relationship between ethical climate and Oz̈den et al. 11 reasons for turnover. Nurses’ high ethical leadership and ethical climate scores of work environments will also increase their job satisfaction. 11,36,46–48 Previous studies in the literature are also supportive of our findings. Ethical climate is a professional relationship established between nurses and their patients, colleagues, managers, and other health professionals and is greatly influenced by managerial or leadership practices.36 Studies have shown that collaboration among nurses supports the development of an ethical climate.11,13,18 In the study of Lorber and Skela-Savic ˇ,56 it was also found that the relationship with colleagues was ranked first among the factors affecting job satisfaction. Schluter et al.57 reported that peer support not only plays an important role in making ethical decisions in healthcare services but also influences the moral problems experienced by nurses. Meltzer and Huckabay58 found that nurses supported by colleagues while experiencing problems were more effective in coping and more likely to continue work. As seen in our results, employees’ ethical leadersh ip, ethical climate, and job satisfaction scores are positively influenced by their positive perception of their job, profession, and managers. It was determined that there was not a significant relationship between the nurses’ satisfaction with their wages and their ethical climate and ethical leadership mean scores. Makaroff et al. 36 found that nurses placed greater importance on improving quality of workplaces than increasing wages. This result supports our findings. However, we found that nurses who were satisfied with their wages had higher job satisfaction. Lorber and Skela-Savicˇ56 pointed out that wage was the second mo st important factor affecting job satisfaction. Huang et al. 11 found that ethical principles and care-oriented ethical climate increased organizational commitment, while ethical climate based on individual interests had a negative effect on maintaining commitment. Providing ethical leadershi p and positive ethical climate will contribute to the development of nurse, patient, and institution outcomes. If employees perceive strong support from organizational management for ethical behavior, they will probably have a higher level of job satisfaction. Conclusion In this study, the ethical leadership, ethical climate, and job satisfaction mean scores of the nurses were found to be moderate, and it was determined that there is a significant positive correlation between these parameters. It was determined that the nurses’ perception of ethical leadership is influenced by their gender, level of education, working hospital, working clinic, total length of service in the clinic, the average number of patients they provide care for, and their satisfaction with their profession and their colleagues. It is recommended that different studies would be carried out to evaluate the relationship of ethical leadership and ethical climate scores in nursing with moral distress, institutional commitment, and burnout. In order to increase the job satisfaction of nurses, studies should be carried out on improving the ethical leadership skills and ethical climate of hospitals. Founder and Publisher: Academic Research and Publishing UG (i.G.), Germany Abstract: In the context of growing institutional turbulence and digital transformation of the economy, ethical business leadership is increasingly recognized as a key prerequisite for trust, transparency, and sustainable development in knowledge -intensive professional service sectors, particularly the management consulting market. At the same time, existing studies on consulting market development insufficiently explain how ethical leadership and institutional conditions shape structural differences between consulti ng ecosystems in European transition economies, especially in the case of Ukraine, which remains underrepresented in comparative research on business leadership and professional service industries. The purpose of this study is to identify the institutional determinants of ethical leadership in the management consulting sector and to assess Ukraine's position within the European consulting market structure. The empirical analysis is based on statistical data covering 23 European countries in 2015 –2023, combi ning sectoral indicators of consulting market development from FEACO reports with institutional and macroeconomic indicators from international databases, including the Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI), the Economic Freedom Index, the Digital Economy and Society Index (DESI), as well as data from the World Bank and OECD. The methodological framework integrates hierarchical cluster analysis (Ward’s method), kmeans clustering, principal component analysis (PCA), correlation analysis, and forecasting of the Ethical Leadership Index (ELI). Statistical calculations and data modeling were performed using the R statistical environment (RStudio). The results identify three clusters of European consulting markets characterized by different levels of institutional maturity and ethical business leadership across the 23 analyzed countries. The calculated Ethical Leadership Index (ELI) reveals significant cross -country differentiation, with average values of 70.3 in the most institutionally advanced cluster, 65.4 in co untries with an intermediate level of development, and 52.7 in Ukraine, confirming the hypothesis of a comparatively lower level of ethical leadership in the Ukrainian consulting ecosystem. Comparative institutional analysis also reveals structural asymmetries between Ukraine and structurally comparable European economies, including a 27-point gap in corruption perception indicators, a 16.1 -point difference in economic freedom, and more than a €15,000 difference in average salary levels, which constrain the competitiveness and international integration of the Ukrainian consulting market. The findings extend understanding of the role of ethical business leadership in the development of professional service markets and provide an analytical basis for strengthe ning institutional transparency, improving ethical governance standards, and supporting the development of consulting ecosystems in economies undergoing structural transformation. Western European countries operate within consolidated institutional frameworks supported by advanced ethical stand ards, predictable governance, and sustained demand for high -value strategic advisory services. By contrast, consulting sectors in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) continue to embody characteristics of transitional economies: rapid but volatile growth, regu latory instability, uneven professionalization, and evolving ethical norms. Within this heterogeneous landscape, management consulting functions not only as an economic activity but also as a vehicle of ethical leadership, institutional modernization, and crossborder knowledge transfer. Over the past decade, consulting markets across Europe have undergone a profound transformation driven by three mutually reinforcing forces: digitalization, ethical accountability, and institutional adaptation. The rising demand for technology - intensive, ESG-oriented, and integrity-based advisory services reflects a broader shift toward responsible management and trust-centered business models. As a result, consultants increasingly act as agents of ethical leadership, shaping organizational culture, enhancing transparency, and supporting the development of governance systems that prioritize integrity and societal value. According to FEACO reports, consulting markets in CEE countries, especially within the Visegrád Group (V4: Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia), have demonstrated consistent growth in turnover, employment, and service diversification. However, quantitative expansion does not necessarily translate into institutional maturity. Recent empirical research on idiosyncratic risk patterns in V4 countries confirms that institutional fragmentation increases firm -level vulnerability (Zsigmondová et al., 2025). Significant differences remain across Europe in ethical infrastructure, professional self -regulation, digital competence, and corporate governance practices. These disparities highlight the ongoing challenge of institutional and ethical convergence between Western and Eastern European consulting ecosystems. Ukraine’s consulting industry, although increasingly represented in European benchmarking systems since its integration into FEACO reporting in 2022, remains structurally underdeveloped and insufficiently embedded in EU value chains. Despite making meaning ful progress, such as the establishment of CMC -Ukraine, the development of growing digital capabilities, and expanding participation in international initiatives, the sector is constrained by limited export capacity, low revenue per consultant, and fragmented institutional support. Empirical studies confirm that formal rules are effective only when supported by political and managerial will (Haliah et al., 2025). These challenges mirror broader governance issues typical of emerging markets: weak regulatory enforcement, inconsistent adoption of ethical and professional standards, and delayed integration of digital and quality assurance systems. The central research problem concerns the persistence of asymmetries between Ukraine’s management consulting sector and structurally comparable European economies. These asymmetries arise not only from performance gaps but also from ethical and institution al divergence: differences in transparency, accountability, leadership culture, and digital readiness that shape consulting market maturity. The guiding hypothesis of the study is that Ukraine exhibits a distinct structural and ethical – institutional profile compared to European consulting markets, which is characterized by a lower level of ethical leadership (ELI), limited institutional maturity, and weaker integration into EU consulting ecosystems. These differences are assumed to systematically influence the clustering outcomes, correlation patterns, and convergence trajectories revealed in the empirical analysis. LITERATURE REVIEW The management consulting market is characterized by structural complexity and the absence of a unified measurement methodology, which is a persistent subject of debate among scholars and practitioners. Classic stud y (Gross & Poór, 2008 ) emphasize s the difficulty of distinguishing consulting activities from adjacent professional services such as auditing, IT, recruitment, and marketing. Management consulting encompasses a broad spectrum of services, including IT systems support, project management, and financial advisory services, which complicates the harmonization and comparability of these services across classification systems. These definitional ambiguities are particularly evident in emerging economies, where consulting often intersects with donor -driven programs and informal expert networks. The lack of standardized classification leads to inconsistencies across data sources ( Gross & Poór, 2008). Widely used typologies identify four core service lines: strategy, HR management, operations, and IT consulting. Research agencies (Kennedy Information, IBISWorld, MCA, and Business Research Company) additionally distinguish financial advisory as a standalone segment ( Clark & Kipping, 2012 ; Gross, 2013 ; Sturdy & O’Mahoney, 2018 ). In transition economies, however, hybrid forms frequently emerge, combining organizational design, accounting support, and digital implementation, reflecting institutional experimentation and adaptation. Contemporary research explains the dynamics of consulting through economic, governmental, cultural, organizational, and educational factors (Sturdy & O’Mahoney, 2018). The International Council of Management Consulting Institutes (ICMCI) introduced the National Consulting Index (NCI), which integrates economic, institutional, and cultural variables to assess market maturity (Haslam et al., 2018; Haslam, 2022). Leading analytics firms (Gartner, IDC, ALM Intelligence, and Source Global Research) build upon these frameworks, emphasizing digital transformation trends and global shifts in service delivery. For emerging markets, these models are especially important, as they link digital readiness with institutional quality, which are the two key determinants of consulting market performance. Among comparative frameworks, FEACO remains one of the most established in Europe, combining macroeconomic and sectoral indicators with expert assessments ( FEACO, 2023 ). Poór et al. (2022) developed maturity typologies based on turnover per consultant, export share, and service diversification. These approaches enable the classification of consulting markets as emerging, developing, or consolidated, an analytical lens particularly valuable for transition and post -transition economies, where consulting serves as a sensitive indicator of institutional modernization and market openness. International institutions highlight the role of professional services in structural transformation. The OECD (2024) highlights the importance of institutional support and export -promotion mechanisms for consulting firms in lower -middleincome and transitional economies. Similar perspectives are presented in studies by Meyer and Peng (2016) and Meyer et al. (2011) , which conceptualize consulting as a mechanism for Business Ethics and Leadership (BEL) Volume 10, Issue 1, 2026 ISSN: 2520-6311 https://armgpublishing.com/journals/bel/ https://doi.org/10.61093/bel.10(1).345–366.2026 348 facilitating institutional change and regional convergence through the transfer of capabilities. This convergence process is strengthened through strategic partnerships that allow coordinated capability development across institutional domains (Hrebeshkova et al., 2018). In Ukraine, FEACO indicators have been applied in academic research ( Vinnikova & Marchuk, 2016 ; Burbelo, 2024; Mazur & Nikolashyn, 2021 ). Scholars highlight persistent limitations, including market informality, low SME participation, and the absence of a national classification system (Kosichenko, 2020; Sheremeta & Savchyn, 2021 ; Hrebeshkova et al., 2025). These findings confirm that Ukraine’s consulting market reflects the institutional volatility typical of an emerging economy, underscoring the need for alignment between national and international analytical frameworks. A separate body of literature addresses the digitalization of consulting. Romania has emerged as a regional leader in digital consulting ( Crișan & Stanca, 2021 ), while hybrid and platform -based models are spreading across Europe ( Crișan & Marincean, 2023). These developments illustrate the transition toward interdisciplinary service bundles that integrate strategy, HR, technology, and transformation advisory services ( Sayyadi et al., 2023; Szabla, 2023 ). In emerging markets, digitalization represents not only technological modernization but also institutional leapfrogging, where digital tools partially substitute for weak governance capacity. The ethical dimension of management consulting has gained growing attention in the context of corporate responsibility and transparency. Foundational theories of ethical leadership (Brown & Treviño, 2006 ; Maak & Pless, 2006 ; Kaptein, 2019 ) conceptualize it as a combination of moral example, fairness, and stakeholder -oriented decision -making. Within consulting, ethical leadership functions as an institutional resource that reinforces trust, accountability, and integrity in professional serv ices. Access to professional networks and the quality of relational governance significantly enhance innovation capability, highlighting that consulting ecosystems function not merely as market structures but as trust -based institutional networks ( Fahmi et al., 2025). Recent contributions have expanded this agenda in light of digital transformation and the rising ethical risks it presents. Ughulu (2024) emphasizes that the ethical behavior of leaders and consultants directly influences organizational adaptability and resilience in contemporary economic environments. Kandasamy (2024) examines ethical leadership in the age of artificial intelligence, emphasizing the need for transparent decision -making protocols. These elements of responsible data governance and accountability are becoming increasingly relevant for consulting firms that i ntegrate AI -driven solutions. Digital transformation functions as a catalyst for harmonizing management control and accountability mechanisms (El Massaoudi et al., 2025). Beyond general calls for ethical leadership, recent research in business ethics emphasizes that ethical issues in consulting are enacted through values -inpractice during consulting missions and through consultants’ own normative commitments in advisory do mains such as diversity and inclusion, which makes ethics a measurable dimension of service delivery rather than an abstract principle (Bazdah & Allard -Poesi, 2025 ; Greene & Kirton, 2024). Empirical evidence from Haslam (2022), Poór et al. (2022) , and the OECD (2024) demonstrates that institutional trust, digital competence, and governance quality have a significant influence on consulting market productivity and internationalization. Thus, ethical leadership acts as a mechanism of institutional convergence, as markets with higher standards of transparency and accountability exhibit greater adaptability, competitiveness, and integration into international consulting networks. For Ukraine, aligning international frameworks (FEACO, ICMCI) with national institutional realities is essential for capturing the dynamics of a transitional, EU-oriented consulting market. This study is the first to apply FEACO’s standardized methodology to a cross-country comparative analysis, encompassing Ukraine, and to integrate ethical, digital, macroeconomic, and sectoral dimensions. METHODOLOGY The study employs an integrated, multi -level research design to examine the structural, ethical, and institutional characteristics of management consulting markets across 23 European countries, including Ukraine, over the period from 2015 to 2023. The analysis is limited to 2023 because, at the time of the study, this was the most recent year for which complete and methodologically comparable data were available across all selected international databases and FEACO reports. The methodological framework combines sectoral indicators from FEACO with macroeconomic, institutional, and digital variables from reputable international sources, enabling the construction of a harmonized cross-country dataset. A central element of the analytical design is the Ethical Leadership Index (ELI), developed in this study to capture governance quality, transparency, and digital readiness : dimensions that reflect the ethical and institutional maturity of consulting markets and complement traditional economic metrics. To test the study’s hypothesis regarding institutional and ethical divergence, the analysis proceeds in three stages. First, standardized indicators are used to perform a cluster -based comparative assessment following established multivariate grouping approaches (Hennig et al., 2015). This step identifies groups of countries with similar consulting market profiles and ethical leadership characteristics, positioning Ukraine within the broader European consulting landscape. Second, correlation and structural analyses are applied to explor e the relationship between market performance and institutional conditions within and across clusters. Third, a forecasting component projects the medium-term dynamics of ELI, allowing for the evaluation of expected convergence or divergence trajectories. This forward -looking dimension strengthens the analytical narrative by linking retrospective structural patterns with anticipated institutional developments. Data Sources and Sample Construction 23 European countries for the period 2015 –2023 (Hrebeshkova et al., 2025 ). The dataset integrates sectoral, macroeconomic, institutional, and ethical indicators, compiled specifically for the empirical analysis presented in this article. The primary source of sector -specific consulting indicators is the European Federation of Management Consultancies Associations (FEACO). FEACO provides harmonized data on market turnover, employment, service structure, service-line distribution, and consul tant productivity for European countries. Since Ukraine officially contributed to FEACO only in 2022 via CMC -Ukraine, the authors directly collected and verified national Ukrainian indicators for the FEACO 2023 –2024 reporting cycle ( FEACO, 2023), ensuring, for the first time, Ukraine's consistent inclusion in the European consulting statistics database. Because FEACO does not provide retrospective Ukrainian data for 2015 –2021, these values were reconstructed exclusively for Ukraine using official domestic sources, namely the State Statistics Service of Ukraine for market volume, employment, and service st ructure, and the National Bank of Ukraine and Ministry of Finance of Ukraine for GDP and exchange rates. To ensure comparability across all 23 countries, the authors supplemented FEACO’s sectoral indicators with macro -institutional data from international sources covering every country in the sample, including The Heritage Foundation (2025) – Economic Freedom Index; European Commission (DESI, 2022) – Digital Competence Index; Transparency International – Corruption Perceptions Index; World Bank – Total Tax Burden; OECD – average wage data. All financial values were converted into euros using annual average official exchange rates, and all indicators were harmonized to a unified cross - country format. Forecasting Limitations Several methodological constraints apply. First, limited time depth (nine observations per country) may restrict the precision of trend estimation. Second, institutional indicators may be subject to structural breaks arising from regulatory reforms or geopolitical shocks, which ETS cannot fully capture. Third, forecasts reflect historical variance rather than exogenous policy interventions; thus, substantial reforms could produce trajectories that differ from model projections. Despite these limitations, forecasted ELI trends offer valuable insight into medium-term convergence prospects and contribute to the study’s overarching goal of assessing institutional and ethical maturity within the European consulting landscape. RESULTS Key Trends of the Ukrainian Management Consulting Market (2015–2023) Between 2015 and 2023, the Ukrainian management consulting market demonstrated uneven development, pronounced institutional vulnerabilities, and significant sensitivity to macroeconomic and regulatory shocks. In comparison with 22 European countries, Ukrai ne consistently underperformed across core FEACO indicators: total turnover growth, employment dynamics, revenue per consultant, and the consulting sector’s contribution to GDP. These disparities reflect not only structural weaknesses but also persistent institutional asymmetries rooted in low levels of transparency, limited regulatory coherence, and an underdeveloped ethical infrastructure of professional services. Evidence from professional service settings indicates that AI adoption reshapes clients’ satisfaction mechanisms and disclosure expectations, while consultancy firms’ public discourse on digital transformation may conceal persistent blind spots that constr ain genuine capability -building ( Li et al., 2025; Monod et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024). Despite moderate improvements in the post-2021 period, driven by recovery dynamics and increased demand for digital transformation services, Ukraine’s consulting ecosystem continues to exhibit high volatility. Market downturns in 2017 –2018 and 2020–2021 co incided with periods of political instability and economic recession, confirming the sector’s dependence on institutional resilience. Improvements observed after 2021 parallel broader macroeconomic stabilization and an accelerating shift toward the integra tion of digital advisory services. Employment growth in the consulting sector shows some positive dynamics after 2019, indicating rising demand for external expertise. However, unlike EU markets , where employment growth typically correlates with institutional maturity and an expanding portfolio of high -value services, Ukraine’s trend remains fragmented. Limited SME engagement, dependence on donor - funded projects, and low institutional incentives for consulting uptake constrain the sector’s ability to fully capitalize on human capital improvements (Castro & Ehrl, 2025; Fyliuk & Prytula, 2024). Revenue per consultant remains significantly below European benchmarks, pointing to underpricing, limited service specialization, and restricted access to innovation -driven or export - oriented consulting segments. Although a gradual upward trend is observed after 2021, the magnitude of the gap suggests that Ukraine’s consulting market remains structurally positioned within low-value segments, where project complexity and ethical governance standards are less developed. The broader macroeconomic and institutional context confirms a mixed trajectory. While digital competencies and economic freedom have improved, Ukraine continues to rank low on the Corruption Perceptions Index and faces increasing fiscal pressure. Overall, the Ukrainian management consulting market operates within a context of structural volatility, limited institutional trust, and low ethical and institutional maturity. Despite improvements in human capital and digital readiness, Ukraine’s relatively low ELI score and persistent structural gaps constrain the sector’s ability to converge with European consulting ecosystems. Strengthening transparency, reducing institutional corruption, supporting SME consulting engagement, and enhancing regulatory co herence are crucial prerequisites for the sustainable development of the consulting market. Positioning Ukraine in the European Consulting Landscape: A Cluster -Based Institutional and Ethical Analysis While dynamic trend analysis provides valuable insights into national performance dynamics, it does not adequately capture structural proximity, institutional similarity, or ethical divergence among countries. To address this limitation, the study employs a cluster analysis methodology following established approaches to multivariate grouping in socio-economic research ( Hennig et al., 2015 ). Previous studies on transition economies confirm the relevance of cluster -based comparative frameworks for identifying structural analogues and convergence trajectories in national consulting markets (Yevtushenko & Halimon, 2021 ). Building on this foundation and applying standardized variables (equation (2)), Euclidean distance metrics ( equation (3)), Ward’s pre-clustering procedure (equation (4)), and the k-means optimization criterion ( equation (5)), the analysis positions Ukraine within the broader European consulting landscape, integrating institutional and ethical dimensions through the Ethical Leadership Index ( ELI). Using this multi-step clustering framework, the study identifies three institutional–ethical clusters within the European consulting landscape. The PCA transformation (equation (7)) enables visualization of latent structural similarities across 23 countries based on economic, digital, regulatory, and ethical indicators , each of which contributes to the Ethical Leadership Index (ELI) defined in equation (1). The resulting clusters reflect different degrees of consulting market maturity, institutional quality, and ethical governance capacity, providing a structured basis for positioning Ukraine among comparable European economies. DISCUSSION The findings of this study reveal several structural inconsistencies and paradoxes that deepen the understanding of Ukraine’s management consulting market and its position within the European institutional landscape. First, the empirical results demonstrate that the development trajectory of the Ukrainian consulting sector does not follow classical economic growth models, which typically assume a strong association between macroeconomic stability, professional income, and the integration of business services into national economic systems. The weak or negative correlations between GDP dynamics, employment, digital competence, and consulting turnover indicate that economic indicators alone cannot fully explain market performance in a transformational economy. These results align with earlier evidence on the heterogeneity, instability, and institutional constraints of consulting markets in transition contexts ( Khrapkina & Yatsyna, 2022 ; Yevtushenko & Halimon, 2021). In this context, the findings of the study suggest that the development of consulting markets cannot be interpreted solely through macroeconomic indicators but must also consider relational and institutional dimensions of professional services. In particular, the quality of consulting services should not be understood exclusively as a technical characteristic of professional expertise but rather as a relational construct shaped through the interaction between clients’ expectations and consultants’ professional judgments. This interpretation aligns with recent empirical evidence showing that trust exchange dynamics play a critical role in shaping professional relationships within consulting organizations (Abgeller et al., 2025). Moreover, the importance of relational factors in consulting interactions has been highlighted by studies demonstrating that social bonding between consultants and clients significantly influences perceived service value and long -term cooperation (Krolikowska & Kuenzel, 2024). A similar conclusion emerges in research on communication consulting, where perceived service quality is shown to arise from the interaction between client expectations and consultants’ professional assessments (Ziegele et al., 2025). A second structural paradox concerns the gap between Ukraine’s educated human capital and the low productivity, narrow specialization, and limited export capacity of consulting firms. Improvements in digital competence and participation in international initiatives have not translated into higher revenues or stronger representation in high -value advisory segments. The cluster analysis confirms that even in countries with moderate levels of digital readiness and professionalization, institutional vulnerabili ty Business Ethics and Leadership (BEL) Volume 10, Issue 1, 2026 ISSN: 2520-6311 https://armgpublishing.com/journals/bel/ https://doi.org/10.61093/bel.10(1).345–366.2026 361 persists when transparency, accountability mechanisms, and ethical norms are underdeveloped. These institutional gaps weaken consulting firms’ ability to scale, engage in cross -border projects, or compete with firms from more institutionally mature markets. These findings highlight the limitations of purely economic analysis and justify a shift toward examining ethical leadership determinants of consulting market performance. As emphasized by Brown and Treviño (2006) , ethical leadership strengthens trust, predictability, and the coherence of organizational systems , qualities essential for industries built on expertise, confidentiality, and advisory relationships. Maak and Pless (2006) likewise argues that ethical leadership shapes not only interpersonal norms but also the broader institutional infrastructures in which firms operate. In Ukraine and across Cluster 3, these infrastructures remain fragile, contributing to inconsistent serv ice quality, the prevalence of informal practices, and low institutional trust. The divergence between Groups A and B within Cluster 3 further reinforces this interpretation. The analysis shows that institutional quality, corruption control, regulatory coherence, and the presence of self-regulatory mechanisms are stronger predictors of consulting market maturity than market size, revenue growth, or employment dynamics. This finding is consistent with cross -cultural research on ethical leadership (Meyer & Peng , 2016), which demonstrates that business systems characterized by high trust and robust ethical norms display greater convergence with international standards in professional services. A notable discrepancy also emerges between the formal and informal dimensions of professionalization. Although Ukraine has established a national certification body, CMC - Ukraine, aligned with ICMCI principles, its institutional influence remains limited. N ational legislation, procurement practices, and SME -support programs do not yet incorporate CMC standards, creating a structural barrier to the institutionalization of ethical norms and professional quality. As North (1990) argue, ethical norms are insufficient without congruent enforcement mechanisms, and this disconnect undermines the development of a coherent ethical infrastructure. Finally, the forecasting results of the Ethical Leadership Index ( ELI) provide a forward -looking dimension to these findings. The projected ELI trajectories indicate that institutional and ethical divergence among European consulting markets is likely to persist unless targeted reforms accelerate institutional upgrading. While Group B countries, including Ukraine, exhibit modest upward trends, their levels remain consistently below those of Group A, reflecting a longer -term institutional “catch -up” process rather than rapid convergence. Taken together, these insights suggest that consulting market maturity depends less on economic metrics and more on the ethical and institutional conditions governing interactions among consultants, clients, and public institutions. Ethical leadership, exp ressed through transparency, responsibility, integrity, and predictability, emerges as a fundamental transformation in consulting markets and competitiveness. In this context, the Ethical Leadership Index proposed in this stu dy serves not only as an analytical tool but also as a conceptual contribution to the emerging literature on ethical infrastructures, institutional trust, and governance quality. Theoretical and Practical Implications Theoretical Implications First, the study demonstrates that traditional economic indicators , such as market size, turnover, employment, and productivity , have limited explanatory power in transitional economies. This finding underscores the need for theoretical models that integrate ethical, behavioral, and institutional dimensions as central determinants of consulting market development. Second, the results support and extend existing theories of ethical leadership ( Brown & Treviño, 2006; Meyer & Peng, 2016). The evidence shows that ethical values and leadership practices at the organizational level have systemic implications at the industry level, shaping the maturity and international integration of consulting markets. Third, the study contributes to debates on institutional convergence by demonstrating that alignment with European professional standards does not arise solely from economic growth. Instead, convergence is facilitated through improvements in ethical infras tructures, regulatory transparency, and the coherence of institutional arrangements. Practical Implications From a practical perspective, the findings have direct relevance for policymakers, industry associations, and consulting firms. The results of the study indicate that strengthening institutional governance mechanisms in the consulting sector is essential for improving market transparency and competitiveness. In particular, the findings suggest that reforms in public procurement and professional regulation must be complemented by stronger accountability mechanisms and professional standards within the consulting industry. This interpretation is consistent with recent international evidence showing that procurement regimes and governance frameworks significantly influence the structure and competitiveness of consulting markets (Haslam, 2022; Sundberg, 2024). First, strengthening the competitiveness of Ukraine’s consulting sector requires targeted institutional reforms, including the integration of international ethical standards into national regulatory frameworks and the enhancement of accountability and transparency mechanisms. Second, ELI can serve as a monitoring instrument in SME support programs, EU -funded technical assistance, and public administration reforms , providing a more holistic measure of institutional conditions than traditional performance indicators. Third, the results underline the need to revise the national certification and qualification system by integrating CMC certification into occupational standards, procurement systems, and state -funded advisory schemes. Ultimately, for consulting firms, the findings underscore the strategic importance of investing in ethical competence, transparent governance, and robust internal quality control systems to foster trust among clients, enhance market positioning, and bolster international competitiveness. These theoretical and practical implications provide a basis for formulating the concluding recommendations and outlining future research directions, presented in the next section. CONCLUSIONS The results of this study demonstrate that the Ukrainian management consulting market remains structurally fragmented and institutionally underdeveloped relative to its European counterparts. The analysis confirms the persistence of asymmetries in consulting market maturity, driven not only by economic constraints but also by disparities in ethical leadership, transparency, and institutional robustness. The cluster -based results and ELI values validate the research hypothesis: Ukraine forms part of the Emer ging cluster (Cluster 3), which is characterized by countries with lower ethical maturity, weaker institutional trust, and limited integration into European consulting value chains. Despite episodes of sectoral growth, these factors constrain the market’s ability to convert human capital potential and digital capabilities into sustainable consulting performance. At the same time, the study identifies several drivers that create a foundation for long -term convergence. Ukraine demonstrates gradual improvements in digital competence, growing engagement with European professional networks, and the beginning of profess ional standardization. The forecasted trajectory of the Ethical Leadership Index suggests a potential , but not automatic , pathway toward institutional convergence, contingent on strengthening governance quality, regulatory transparency, and ethical norms. These findings suggest that ethical leadership serves as a crucial lever for transforming the consulting market, influencing not only organizational behavior but also sector-wide institutional outcomes. Unlocking Ukraine’s consulting potential requires a strategic shift toward strengthening the ethical and institutional underpinnings of the sector. Key directions include reinforcing the role of national professional associations, integrating international ly Business Ethics and Leadership (BEL) Volume 10, Issue 1, 2026 ISSN: 2520-6311 https://armgpublishing.com/journals/bel/ https://doi.org/10.61093/bel.10(1).345–366.2026 363 recognized certification schemes (such as CMC) into qualification frameworks and procurement standards, and expanding SME access to consulting services. Embedding consulting within national innovation and export-support programs, facilitating cross-border cooperation with EU markets, and raising awareness of the strategic value of advisory services will further accelerate market development. Enhancing institutional trust, improving sectoral data transparency, and creating incentives for continuous professional development represent essential preconditions for meaningful alignment with mature European consulting ecosystems. This study has several limitations. The retrospective time frame (2015 –2023) restricts the ability to fully capture long -term institutional transformation, particularly given wartime disruptions and postwar restructuring. Cross - country comparisons may be a ffected by differences in data reporting practices, reliance on expert estimates, and FEACO’s exclusion of independent consultants. Moreover, while this study focuses on national-level indicators, Ukraine’s structural weaknesses, such as low certification uptake, limited internationalization, and fragmented institutional infrastructure, largely stem from firm -level constraints, including SMEs’ restricted financial capacity, insufficient awareness of the value of consulting, and unstable business models among small firms. Future research should extend the empirical base through firm-level datasets, sectoral case studies, and surveys among consultants and clients. Further attention should be devoted to analyzing specialization patterns, organizational models, and the role of ethical leadership in shaping client trust and market resilience. Examining how improvements in transparency, accountability, and ethical norms contribute to institutional convergence with European consulting ecosystems will help refine theoretical models and support evidence -based policymaking in transitional economies. Ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality management: A systematic literature review and research agenda Giang Hoang a , * , Mingjun Yang b , Tuan Trong Luu c a RMIT University, Vietnam b La Trobe University, Australia c Swinburne University of Technology, Australia ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Ethical leadership Ethical issues Systematic literature review Tourism and hospitality management ABSTRACT This study reviews the empirical research on ethical leadership, which is an important and relevant leadership construct in tourism and hospitality contexts. A rigorous and systematic search process based on transparent inclusion and exclusion criteria yielded a sample of 33 empirical studies. The analysis and synthesis of these studies revealed that (a) there is a high consistency in defining and measuring ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality; (b) social exchange theory, social learning theory and conservation of resources theory were the most frequently used theoretical lenses to investigate ethical leadership; (c) all studies in the sample were quantitative; no qualitative studies were found; and (d) ethical leadership affected various employee attitudes and behaviors and team and organizational outcomes. An integrated framework for ethical leadership research in tourism and hospitality settings was provided based on these findings. We also provided several research implications for future studies and managerial implications for tourism and hospitality firms to effectively promote ethical leadership at workplace. 1. Introduction The organizations in tourism and hospitality industries are exposed to various ethical issues such as service sabotage, overbooking, over - charging and sexual harassment ( Dimitriou and Schwepker, 2019 ), which may cause customer dissatisfaction and retention, and diminish firm performance ( Dimitriou and Schwepker, 2019; Garba et al., 2018 ). Hospitality and tourism workers also experience ethical problems (e.g., high workload, underpay, bullying), which result in high rates of turn - over and absenteeism in these sectors ( Hefny, 2021; Liladrie, 2010 ). Scholars suggest that these ethical issues can be addressed when the leaders of tourism and hospitality firms apply ethical leadership ( Garba et al., 2018; Mkheimer et al., 2022 ) to become a moral role model for employees and create an ethical work environment where employees are treated with respect, credibility and fairness ( Brown et al., 2005 ). In the past two decades, the number of studies on ethical leadership has been increasing in both general management and tourism and hospitality literature ( Banks et al., 2021; Garba et al., 2018 ). Several reviews on ethical leadership have been conducted; for example, Den Hartog (2015) reviewed ethical leadership in general management to portray some characteristics of this leadership construct, or Bedi et al. (2016) and Ng and Feldman (2015) conducted meta-analytic reviews to examine the effects of ethical leadership on several follower ’ s outcomes. Although these reviews provided a comprehensive picture of ethical leadership in general management, none of them focused on the impacts of ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality sectors. Despite being influenced by broader management research, the implications from the reviews of ethical leadership in general management are not always mirrored within tourism and hospitality research due to the aforementioned specific characteristics associated with these sectors ( Kimbu et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, while ethical concerns are of significance in any in - dustry, these issues are particularly important in tourism and hospitality for several reasons. First, tourism and hospitality workers have to deal with greater pressures from simultaneous production and delivery of services and from demanding customers and changing customer de - mands ( Davidson, 2003 ). In addition, tourism and hospitality workers suffer from greater pressures from uncertainty, job insecurity, and hos - tile work environment with performance pressures from managers that differ from other industries ( Bowen and Ford, 2004; Hertog et al., 2011; Ozdemir et al., 2022 ). These characteristics render workers in tourism and hospitality sectors likely to involve in unethical acts, which have * Corresponding author. E-mail address: giang.hoang@rmit.edu.vn (G. Hoang).
