These unethical issues are negatively im - pactful on individual and team performance, organizational image and competitive advantages ( Dimitriou, 2023 ). Research indicated these ethical issues as the result of lack of ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality sectors ( Eluwole et al., 2022 ). Ethical leadership therefore deserves special research attention in tourism and hospitality manage - ment literature as enhancing our understanding of this leadership style could contribute to preventing deviant behaviors among employees and provide tourism and hospitality managers with practical guidelines to develop this leadership and in turn minimize ethical issues in tourism and hospitality workplaces (Schwepker Jr & Dimitriou, 2021). Due to these important reasons, it is timely to conduct a systematic literature review (SLR) which integrates the findings of empirical studies (including both quantitative and qualitative research) on ethical lead - ership in tourism and hospitality. Such a systematic review is necessary and urgent to provide a broad understanding of the effects of ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality and shed light for future research on this topic. Our SLR contributes significantly to the tourism and hospitality management literature in multiple ways. Firstly, by synthesizing the empirical research on ethical leadership in these contexts, we develop an integrated model that includes mediators, moderators, and outcomes of this leadership style. This framework advances our understanding of the associations of ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality and pro - vides a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners alike. Secondly, based on our findings, we propose a research agenda to identify future research directions and opportunities in ethical leadership research in tourism and hospitality management. Finally, we provide managerial implications for practitioners who are seeking to address ethical issues in their organizations through ethical leadership practices. By offering practical guidance, our study can help managers promote ethical behavior and cultivate a positive work environment in tourism and hospitality organizations. In pursuit of these research aims, and following the approach of prior studies ( Bavik, 2019; Hoang et al., 2021 ), six research questions were formulated as follows. RQ1. How has ethical leadership been defined in tourism and hos - pitality literature? RQ2. What scales have been used to measure ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality literature? RQ3. What research designs and analytical approaches have been employed to study ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality? RQ4. What theoretical lenses have been employed to study ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality? RQ5. What are the specific tourism and hospitality contexts in which ethical leadership has been empirically investigated? RQ6. What are the antecedents, outcomes and mechanisms under - lying the effects of ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality? To identify the scope and findings of the studies in our sample, we adopted a systematic literature review process ( Bavik, 2019; Hoang et al., 2021 ). First, we discuss the distinctiveness of ethical leadership construct and its relevance to tourism and hospitality industries. Next, we present the SLR method that has been adopted in this study. We then report the findings from the review to address the research questions. Finally, our SLR provides a research agenda for future research and propose several managerial implications for tourism and hospitality firms. 2. The importance of ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality sectors The questions about the importance of ethical leadership in contemporary management have been raised in the past decades ( Banks et al., 2021 ). Ethical leadership is defined as “ the demonstration of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and inter - personal relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to followers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and decision-making ” ( Brown et al., 2005 , p. 120). According to Brown et al. ’ s (2005) defi - nition, ethical leaders are individuals who demonstrate high level of ethical values characterized by fairness, justice, honesty, trustworthi - ness, and genuineness. Furthermore, an ethical leader is an ethical manager who influences their employees through ethical leadership behavior and promotes ethical behavioral norms by creating an ethical climate at the workplace ( Brown et al., 2005 ). Although ethical leadership has been widely recognized as an effective leadership style in the tourism and hospitality sectors, several scholars have raised concerns regarding its distinctiveness from other related leadership constructs ( Eluwole et al., 2022 ; Schwepker Jr & Dimitriou, 2021 ). These scholars argue that ethical behavior is a vital component in various leadership styles, including authentic, servant, and transformational leadership ( Eluwole et al., 2022 ). The scholars also note that authentic, spiritual, transformational, and ethical leaders all possess qualities such as integrity, concern for others, and role modeling ( Schwepker Jr & Dimitriou, 2021 ). However, theoretical evidence sug - gests that while ethical leadership can be practiced alongside other styles, it holds its own unique form of leadership that warrants dedicated research ( Brown and Trevi ño, 2006 ; Den Hartog, 2015 ). For example, both servant and ethical leaders exhibit compelling communication, practice role modeling, and prioritize altruism, but servant leaders pri - oritize the success of all stakeholders within an organization while ethical leaders focus more on compliance and alignment with moral standards ( Brown and Trevi ño, 2006; Graham, 1991; Lemoine et al., 2019 ). Transformational leaders focus on vision, values, and intellectual stimulation and spiritual leaders highlight hope, faith, and visionary aspects, whereas ethical leaders, on the other hand, act as moral man - agers, ensuring the implementation of ethical standards ( Brown and Trevi ño, 2006 ). While ethical leaders prioritize moral management, authentic leaders emphasize self-awareness and authenticity. Despite the central role of ethical leadership in the general management liter - ature between 2011 and 2017, as found by J. Zhu et al. (2019) , a recent systematic review on contemporary leadership in hospitality by Huer - tas-Valdivia et al. (2022) reveals that ethical leadership has received limited exploration within the hospitality industry. Considering the unique nature of ethical leadership and its vital importance in the tourism and hospitality sectors, Huertas-Valdivia et al. (2022) suggest that this leadership construct deserves greater research attention in tourism and hospitality sectors, where the rising number of ethical scandals and related lawsuits is a direct consequence of its absence and inadequate implementation. Ethical leadership has been suggested to be particularly relevant to tourism and hospitality ( Garba et al., 2018 ) due to several ethical issues and misconducts associated with these sectors ( Eluwole et al., 2022 ). Prior research indicates that unethical behaviors in tourism and hospi - tality, such as giving misleading information, sabotage, overbooking, overcharging, may negatively impact customer satisfaction and firm performance ( Dimitriou and Schwepker, 2019 ). On the other hand, tourism and hospitality employees also suffer the consequences of ethical issues, as such underpay, long working hours, or irregular work schedule, may result in burnout, insecure, confused, vulnerable feelings of the employees ( Schwepker Jr & Dimitriou, 2021 ). As ethical leaders play an important role in shaping an ethical climate, several scholars G. Hoang et al. In short, ethical leadership has been identified as an important and relevant leadership style for the tourism and hospitality organizations and has been receiving increasing scholarly attention. In the next sec - tion, we present our method in conducting our SLR on ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality contexts. 3. Method 3.1. Systematic review process Our systematic review attempts to identify, analyze, and synthesize the extant literature on ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality. In line with recent SLRs in tourism and hospitality literature (e.g., Hoang et al., 2021 ; Le et al., 2019 ), we follow a five-step process that has been utilized in reviewing tourism and hospitality research, including (1) defining the research questions and objectives for a review; (2) deter - mining keywords, databases and inclusion and exclusion selection criteria; (3) searching keywords in databases and screening initial out - comes; (4) extracting relevant materials and assessing the quality of studies; and (5) synthesizing, interpreting and presenting findings. A flowchart of the search and selection process is exhibited in Fig. 1 . Articles in our SLR were selected from Scopus, a comprehensive database which includes peer-reviewed publications that meet rigorous standards ( Booth et al., 2020 ). The initial searches included the following keywords in title/abstract/keywords: [( “ ethical leader ” OR “ ethical leadership ” ) AND (travel OR tourism OR hotel OR hospitality OR restaurant OR airlines OR accommodation OR event OR catering OR cruise OR recreation OR casino)] ( Hoang et al., 2021 ). The initial search process yielded 255 articles containing the identified keywords. After removing duplicates, there were 173 articles remained. Furthermore, other transparent inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied in the searching process, such that the articles were published in a refereed journal and were written in English. Regarding time limit, the search process was set until end of June 2022. We then downloaded the full-text articles from the database and thoroughly reviewed them to evaluate eligibility. The articles were assessed based on three criteria. First, it must be an empirical study as the primary aim of this review is to integrate the empirical findings on ethical leadership to answer priori-defined research questions ( Kim, 2020; Le et al., 2019; Rudolph et al., 2020 ). Second, the study must examine ethical leadership as a central topic. Third, the study must investigate ethical leadership in a tourism and hospitality setting. The absence of at least one of these criteria would result in the exclusion of the paper. After this round, 70 articles were removed from the list because they did not meet the inclusion criteria of this round (e.g., conceptual papers, editorial notes, questionnaire development papers, articles that had “ ethical leadership ” keyword in the abstract but did not have an ethical leadership theme in the main body). Finally, 33 articles were retained in our final sample and qualified for analysis ( Fig. 1 ). The results showed that studies in our sample were published in 22 journals between 2007 and 2022 ( Fig. 2 ) and all of them employed a quantitative method to examine ethical leadership. Analytical approach In analyzing the empirical findings from 33 studies in our sample, we followed to the content analysis approach suggested by Gardner et al. (2011) . First, we coded the basic information of each article, including author name(s), journal name, year of publication, definitions of ethical leadership, and study contexts (i.e., country, sector). We then coded the underlying theory, hypotheses, sample (i.e., sample size and re - spondents), data collection process, measures, level of analysis, ante - cedents, moderators, mediators, and the outcomes of ethical leadership. The coding process involved two independent researchers in our team, who independently coded the information and critically reviewed the coding results. Defining ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality This SLR explores the degree of consistency in ethical leadership definitions in the tourism and hospitality contexts. The results show a high consistency for the definition of ethical leadership. Specifically, almost all the studies in our sample (n = 32) employed Brown et al. ’ s (2005) definition, which viewed ethical leadership as “ the demonstra - tion of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to fol - lowers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and deci - sion-making ” ( Brown et al., 2005 , p. 120). Only Srivastava and Madan (2022) cited Sharma et al. ’ s (2019) ethical leadership definition. As Sharma et al. ’ s (2019) definition of ethical leadership emphasizes moral/ethical conduct to trigger ethical outcomes in workplaces, it is considered a part of Brown et al. ’ s (2005) definition. This SLR therefore recommends that Brown et al. ’ s (2005) can be used as a common defi - nition of ethical leadership in the tourism and hospitality literature. 4.2. Methods, measures and analytical approaches used to study ethical leadership The findings of this SLR revealed a significant degree of consistency regarding the methods and measures employed to examine the impact of ethical leadership in the tourism and hospitality fields. Specifically, all 33 articles included in the review utilized quantitative research methods to investigate ethical leadership, and employed questionnaire surveys as the primary tool to gather quantitative data. Moreover, the majority of the articles (32 out of 33) relied on Brown et al. ’ s (2005) 10-item scale to measure ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality settings, while only one study ( Sugianingrat et al., 2019 ) employed a modified version of the same scale. In summary, this SLR concludes that quantitative research methods and Brown et al. ’ s (2005) 10-item scale were the most commonly utilized methods and measures, respectively, to investigate ethical leadership in the tourism and hospitality domain. The findings of this SLR highlight that qualitative research methods have not been used to study ethical leadership in the tourism and hos - pitality literature. Future research could employ qualitative or mixed methods to examine ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality or - ganizations to provide in-depth understandings of this leadership style in these industries. In terms of the level of analysis, our sample comprised 23 studies that only examined the relationships between ethical leadership and its related variables at the individual level (e.g., Garba et al., 2018 ; Hoang et al., 2022 ; C.-J. Lee and Huang, 2019 ). Additionally, one study explored ethical leadership and its associations at the organizational level (Y. Zhu, Sun, and Leung, 2014 ). Theories utilized in ethical leadership research in tourism and hospitality The findings of this SLR show that several theories have been used to explain the mechanisms underlying the effects of ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality contexts. Table 1 exhibits the overview of the - ories utilized in ethical leadership research in tourism and hospitality. In our sample, the most frequently utilized theory to explain the impact of ethical leadership in the tourism and hospitality sectors was social exchange theory (n = 11), which was developed by Blau (1964) . According to this theory, employees ’ behaviors and work outcomes are shaped by the ethical conduct of their leaders ( Cropanzano et al., 2017 ). Specifically, when employees perceive that their leaders uphold high ethical standards and treat everyone fairly, they are more likely to reciprocate this behavior by displaying positive work behaviors and achieving better work performance in areas such as customer-oriented citizenship behavior ( Garba et al., 2018 ), service recovery perfor - mance ( Eluwole et al., 2022 ), and affective commitment ( Tarkang Mary and Ozturen, 2019 ). Social learning theory, developed by Bandura and Walters (1977) , was the second most widely used theoretical lens (n = 5) to explain the impact of ethical leadership tourism and hospitality contexts. According to social learning theory, employees are likely to observe, imitate, and learn from their leaders during interactions and communications, thereby influencing their perceptions and behaviors in the workplace ( Li et al., 2021 ). When employees observe an ethical behavior from their leaders, they are more inclined to imitate it and invest more effort into ethical conduct to achieve better work outcomes such as service inno - vative behavior ( Dhar, 2016 ) and organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) ( Srivastava and Madan, 2022 ). Another theory that was frequently employed (n = 4) was COR theory ( Hobfoll, 1989 ). This theory emphasizes that employees tend to make more commitments to acquire and protect valuable resources such as personalities and social relationships ( Hobfoll, 1989 ). In the tourism and hospitality contexts, individuals tend to protect resources and ac - quire more resources for resource gain spirals ( Hobfoll, 1989 ). Ethical leaders who provide employees with fair treatment can serve as a resource with which employees tend to invest to acquire more resources. When employees possess more resources, they are likely to invest in performance and extra-role behaviors such as service performance, work engagement (C.-J. Lee and Huang, 2019 ), and service-oriented organi - zational citizenship behavior ( Luu and Vu, 2021 ). 4.4. Contexts for investigating ethical leadership To provide a comprehensive understanding of the contexts in which ethical leadership is studied, we conducted an analysis of the 33 articles reviewed in this SLR. Our findings demonstrated that ethical leadership was examined across various sectors within tourism and hospitality, as well as in different cultural contexts. Of the articles reviewed, the ma - jority (n = 25) focused on ethical leadership in the hotel contexts, while travel agencies (n = 3) and multi-type tourism and hospitality firms (n = 3) were also examined. Two studies specifically investigated ethical leadership in the context of restaurants. Furthermore, we per - formed an analysis of the cultural contexts represented in the 33 articles reviewed, and found that 31 studies were conducted within a single cultural context, while two studies explored ethical leadership in a cross- cultural context. Specifically, Nazarian et al. (2021) collected data from the United States, the United Kingdom, Italy, and Spain to investigate ethical leadership, and Sarwar et al. (2020) studied ethical leadership using a sample collected from both Italian and Pakistani. Table 2 pro - vides additional details on the cultural contexts explored in studies of ethical leadership within tourism and hospitality. 4.5. Antecedents of ethical leadership The majority of studies reviewed in this SLR did not investigate the antecedents of ethical leadership. Only two articles examined the factors that trigger ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality sectors. Spe - cifically, Zoghbi-Manrique-de-Lara and Su árez-Acosta (2014) reported that interactional justice to peers was a positive antecedent of ethical leadership, while Srivastava and Gupta (2022) found that workplace spirituality enhanced ethical leadership. The findings of this SLR suggest that the antecedents of ethical leadership have not been thoroughly explored in the tourism and hospitality literature. Future studies should focus on investigating the factors that trigger or mitigate ethical lead - ership in tourism and hospitality organizations to gain a better under - standing of this leadership style in this sector. 4.6. Spe - cifically, our analysis indicated that ethical leadership had a positive impact on organizational citizenship in general ( Srivastava and Madan, 2022; Zoghbi-Manrique-de-Lara and Su árez-Acosta, 2014 ), service-oriented/customer-oriented organizational citizenship behavior ( Garba et al., 2018; Luu and Vu, 2021 ), innovative/creative behavior ( Dhar, 2016; Hoang et al., 2022 ; Javed et al., 2017b), other forms of organizational citizenship behavior (i.e., green behavior ( Wood et al., 2021 ), knowledge sharing ( Bhatti et al., 2020 ) and internal whistle - blowing ( Srivastava and Gupta, 2022 )), and feedback seeking ( Qian et al., 2017 ). Our results also showed that ethical leadership had a negative impact on some individual-level behavioral outcomes among tourism and hospitality employees, including deviance behavior ( Tar - kang & Ozturen, 2019 ; Tarkang et al., 2022 ; Zoghbi-Manrique-de-Lara and Su árez-Acosta, 2014 ), service sabotage ( Dimitriou and Schwepker, 2019; Yes ̧ iltas ̧ and Tuna, 2018 ), unethical pro-organizational behavior ( Srivastava and Madan, 2022 ), and social loafing behavior ( Eluwole et al., 2022 ). The present SLR provides insights into the attitudinal outcomes of ethical leadership in the tourism and hospitality sectors. In detail, several studies have found that ethical leadership improves employee loyalty ( Fan et al., 2021 ; Nazarian et al., 2022) and information security policy compliance intention ( Wang and Xu, 2021 ). Furthermore, ethical leadership fosters commitment to service quality ( Dimitriou and Schwepker, 2019 ) and enhances trust among employees ( Tarkang & Ozturen, 2019 ; Wood et al., 2021 ). The results also indicate that ethical leadership is negatively associated with the intention to leave among tourism and hospitality employees (Nazarian et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2015 ). In terms of affective outcomes, two studies in our sample reported that ethical leadership fosters affective commitment among employees in tourism and hospitality industries ( Tarkang & Ozturen, 2019 ; Tar - kang et al., 2022 ). Additionally, ethical leadership has been found to promote psychological outcomes such as job/career satisfaction (Khat - tak et al., 2022; Kim & Brymer, 2011) and employee well-being ( Wood et al., 2021 ). With regard to performance outcomes, ethical leadership has been shown to enhance overall work performance ( Sugianingrat et al., 2019; Tao et al., 2017 ) and performance quality ( Schwepker and Dimitriou, 2021 ), as well as facilitate proactive performance such as service recovery performance ( Eluwole et al., 2022 ) and adaptive per - formance (Javed et al., 2017a). Moreover, our analysis demonstrated that ethical leadership has a negative effect on absenteeism ( Eluwole et al., 2022 ) in tourism and hospitality organizations. Overall, in the context of tourism and hospitality, ethical leadership was found to have a significant impact on individual outcomes. Among the different types of outcomes studied, behavioral outcomes were the most commonly researched, with 20 out of 33 reviewed articles demonstrating that ethical leadership influenced individual behaviors, particularly organizational citizenship behavior. In addition, attitudinal outcomes were also commonly studied, with 11 articles showing that employees ’ loyalty, intention to leave, and trust were significantly affected by ethical leadership in the tourism and hospitality industries. 4.6.2. Group and organizational outcomes Out of 33 articles reviewed by our SLR, only one study focused on group outcomes of ethical leadership. Specifically, Detert et al. (2007) identified that ethical leadership was not associated with counter - productivity and that counterproductivity negatively impacted store-level financial performance and customer satisfaction in the restaurant context. In terms of organizational outcomes, two studies indicated a positive association between ethical leadership and firm performance ( Sarwar et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2014 ). Additionally, our SLR findings demon - strated that justice (including distributive and procedural justice) (Nazarian et al., 2022), corporate ethical values ( Yes ̧ iltas ̧ and Tuna, 2018 ), service climate ( Yes ̧ iltas ̧ and Tuna, 2018 ), and ethical climate ( Gong and Wang, 2022 ) were organizational outcomes of ethical lead - ership in the tourism and hospitality sectors. 4.7. Mediators 4.7.1. Employee-centered mediators The majority of studies in our sample examined the mediating effects of employee-centered factors on the association between ethical lead - ership and its outcomes in tourism and hospitality organizations. We identified six types of employee-centered mediators that influence this relationship, including psychological, relational, cognitive, attitudinal, affective, and behavioral mediators. With respect to psychological me - diators, the findings of this SLR showed that felt obligation ( Garba et al., 2018 ), psychological ownership ( Fan et al., 2021 ), psychological empowerment (Javed et al., 2017b), employee well-being ( Bhatti et al., 2020; Wood et al., 2021 ), and individual job satisfaction ( Qin et al., 2014 ) mediated the association between ethical leadership and its various outcomes among tourism and hospitality employees. Job-centered, leader-centered and organizational-centered mediators The findings of this SLR suggest that job-centered, leader-centered and organizational-centered factors exerted mediating effects on the association between ethical leadership and its outcomes in the tourism and hospitality discipline. For instance, based on social exchange theory, Khattak et al. (2022) found that job embeddedness acts as a job-centered mediator to mediate the association between ethical leadership and career satisfaction. Similarly, Zoghbi-Manrique-de-Lara and Su árez-Acosta (2014) employed social exchange theory to investigate the mediating role of ethical leadership on the effect of interactional injustice to peers on interpersonal deviant workplace behavior and interpersonal organizational citizenship behavior in the Spanish hotel industry. Through the lens of ethical decision-making theory, Schwepker and Dimitriou (2021) discovered that ethical leadership was negatively associated with job stress, which, in turn, decreased perfor - mance quality. Organizational-centered mediators were investigated through the lens of stakeholder theory, leader-member exchange or institutional theory. Specifically, several studies indicated that corpo - rate social responsibility (CSR) played a mediating role between ethical leadership and its outcomes, such as green behavior ( Wood et al., 2021 ) and firm performance ( Zhu et al., 2014 ). Regarding organizational-centered mediators, organizational justice ( Fan et al., 2021 ), organizational virtuousness ( Mkheimer et al., 2022 ), firm repu - tation ( Zhu et al., 2014 ), and ethical culture ( Sarwar et al., 2020 ) also acted as mediators in the association between ethical leadership and its outcomes in the tourism and hospitality organizations. 4.8. Moderators 4.8.1. Ethical leadership as a moderator Out of 33 articles reviewed by this SLR, three studies investigated the moderating effect of ethical leadership in the tourism and hospitality contexts (Javed et al., 2017a; Tao et al., 2017 ; Zhu et al., 2014 ). For instance, in light of stakeholder theory, Zhu et al. (2014) showed that ethical leadership positively moderated the indirect effect of CSR on firm performance through firm reputation in Chinese tourism firms, such as hotels and travel agencies. Ethical leadership was found to act as a positive moderator for the relationship between Islamic work ethic and innovative work behavior based on theory of planned behavior (Javed et al., 2017a). In addition, Tao et al. (2017) provided empirical evidence that ethical leadership served as a moderator to neutralize the negative impact of new employee intention to leave on subsequent work per - formance in the hospitality industry of China. 4.8.2. Other moderators The findings of this SLR show that the relationship between ethical leadership and its outcomes could be moderated by various factors, including individual moderators (i.e., psychological, attitudinal, affec - tive and cognitive factors) and contextual moderators (i.e., cultural and structural factors). Among the individual moderators, psychological detachment (a psychological factor) was found to moderate the impact of ethical leadership on employees ’ customer-oriented citizenship behavior ( Garba et al., 2018 ). Trust in leader served as an attitudinal factor that played a moderating role in the indirect link between ethical leadership and service innovative behavior via intrinsic motivation in Vietnamese hotels ( Hoang et al., 2022 ). Additionally, emotional intel - ligence (an affective factor) served as a moderator on the indirect rela - tionship between ethical leadership and feedback seeking via leader-member exchange in the Chinese hotel context ( Qian et al., 2017 ). Finally, service role identity was a cognitive factor that moder - ated the association between ethical leadership and employees ’ adaptive selling in Vietnamese tourism companies (Luu & Ngan, 2021). Regarding contextual moderators, a cultural factor such as collec - tivistic culture was found to moderate the link between ethical leader - ship and leader-follower value congruence in the Chinese restaurant industry ( Tang et al., 2015 ), whereas power distance orientation attenuated the effect of ethical leadership on psychological ownership and organizational justice in the Chinese hotel industry ( Fan et al., 2021 ). In addition, structural factors, such as work-unit structure ( Qian et al., 2017 ) and job autonomy ( Dhar, 2016 ), were also found to mod - erate the impact of ethical leadership on its outcomes in tourism and hospitality contexts. Our analysis indicated that most of the moderating mechanisms in the studies in our sample were explained by social based theories, such as social exchange theory (e.g., Garba et al., 2018 ; Qian et al., 2017 ), social cognitive theory (e.g., Hoang et al., 2022 ) and social learning theory (e.g., Dhar, 2016 ; Tang et al., 2015 ), and conservation of re - sources theory (e.g., Luu and Vu, 2021 ). 5. Discussion 5.1. Summary of the findings from the reviewed studies This SLR revealed the following findings on ethical leadership studies in the hospitality and tourism sector. First, in terms of study context, this SLR found that reviewed studies collected data from Western as well as non-Western countries, among which China, the US, Pakistan, and India are the contexts for data harvesting in most studies. This SLR further found two articles that cross-culturally examined the effects of ethical leadership. Analyzing the datasets from Pakistan and Italy, Sarwar et al. ’ s (2020) study reported the differences in the impacts of ethical leadership on employee work engagement and well-being. The influence of ethical leadership on work engagement was found to be more pronounced among Pakistani workers, whereas the link between ethical leadership and well-being was found to be stronger among Ital - ian workers. The other cross-cultural study was conducted by Nazarian et al. (2021) in the US, the UK, Italy and Spain. This study observed the impacts of ethical leadership on organizational justice and job satisfac - tion in the US, Italy and Spain, but not in the UK. Second, the current SLR revealed variables associated with ethical leadership in the hospitality and tourism sector. Fig. 3 displays a nomological network regarding ethical leadership and its outcomes, antecedents, mediators, and moderators. When it comes to antecedents of ethical leadership, our SLR found two antecedents, including inter - actional justice to peers ( Zoghbi-Manrique-de-Lara and Su árez-Acosta, 2014 ) and workplace spirituality ( Srivastava and Gupta, 2022 ), for ethical leadership. In terms of ethical leadership outcomes, this SLR revealed that hospitality and tourism studies have concentrated on individual-level outcomes of ethical leadership. As this SLR indicates, the mediation mechanisms behind the effects of ethical leadership in hospitality and tourism organizations are mainly employee-centered mediators rather than job-centered (job stress, job embeddedness) and organization-centered mediators (CSR, organiza - tional virtuousness, organizational justice, ethical culture, firm reputa - tion). Employee-centered mediators in this SLR are categorized into psychological (e.g., psychological ownership, psychological empower - ment), relational (e.g., leader-member exchange), cognitive (e.g., moral courage, ethical values person-organization fit), attitudinal (e.g., trust, customer orientation), affective (e.g., service harmonious passion), and behavioral mediators (e.g., innovative work behavior, adaptive selling, taking responsibility). Leadership contingency perspective has been adopted in some hos - pitality and tourism studies to investigate contingencies consisting of structural factor (work-unit structure), cultural factor (collectivistic culture, power distance orientation), attitudinal factor (trust in leader), cognitive (service role identity), affective factor (emotional intelli - gence), and psychological factor (psychological detachment, job au - tonomy, group job satisfaction). Third, in the current SLR, three theoretical perspectives mostly adopted consist of social exchange theory, social learning theory, and COR theory. Less used theories include social cognitive theory, ethical decision-making theory, attachment theory, planned behavior theory, cognitive evaluation theory, self-determination theory, leader-member exchange theory, stakeholder theory, institutional theory, agency the - ory, and deterrence theory. 5.2. Future research agenda Four crucial gaps that this SLR identifies from ethical leadership studies in the hospitality and tourism discipline comprise: (1) research settings; (2) research designs; (3) outcomes, antecedents, and inter - vening mechanisms of ethical leadership; and (4) theoretical lenses employed to underpin relationships around ethical leadership. From these gaps, four recommendations are outlined as follows: 5.2.1. First recommendation: examine ethical leadership across different contexts Though ethical leadership studies in the hospitality/tourism industry were based on data from both Western and non-Western nations (as shown in Table 2 ), countries from Europe, Africa, and Latin America are seldom considered for examining ethical leadership in this industry. Future research should test ethical leadership models based on datasets from these countries to enhance our understanding of ethical leadership effects in these study contexts. Furthermore, our SLR found two cross- national studies, namely Sarwar et al. ’ s (2020) study across Pakistan and Italy and Nazarian et al. (2021) study across the US, the UK, Italy and Spain. Nevertheless, future cross-national studies of ethical leader - ship in the hospitality and tourism sector should engage countries from Latin America and Africa, as well as more nations from Europe and Asia. Moreover, the two above cross-national studies did not investigate how national cultural values could influence the effects of ethical leadership in these nations. Future research should fill this gap by examining how the effectiveness of ethical leadership is influenced by different national cultural values. Through interpersonal relationships and personal conducts such as responsible, fair, and honest behaviors, ethical leaders can promote normatively appropriate conducts among employees ( Brown et al., 2005 ). Ethical leaders fairly treat employees and care about their interests and conducts towards others in work groups (H. Wang et al., 2017 ). Individuals in a collectivistic culture are also concerned about others and behave appropriately to others in their groups. In other words, there is a match between ethical leadership and beliefs and perceptions of employees in a collectivistic culture, which can facilitate their willing acceptance of ethical standards from ethical leaders. Contrarily, less acceptance of such ethical standards can be observed in employees with self-centered values in an individualistic culture. In high power distance cultures with unequal distribution of infor - mation and autonomy ( Hofstede, 2001 ), ethical leaders ’ fair and responsible behaviors ( Banks et al., 2021 ) are likely to be viewed as attractive role models, valued and accepted by employees ( Peng and Kim, 2020 ), which can translate into their positive behaviors. Therefore, given the differences in employees ’ acceptance of ethical leaders and ethical leadership effectiveness across cultural contexts, future tourism and hospitality studies are encouraged to explore the impacts of ethical leadership on employees ’ acceptance of ethical standards from ethical leaders as well as on their attitudinal and behavioral outcomes across cultures of collectivism versus individualism and high versus low power distance. Since differences in individual behaviors may be accounted for by several other factors beyond cultural values ( Tsui et al., 2007 ), future cross-national studies should consider the impact of other national characteristics on ethical leadership effects on employee behaviors. In addition to cultural aspects, the major contextual factors separating one country from another consist of political, economic, and social aspects ( Golob et al., 2018 ). Future research is encouraged to examine ethical leadership effects across nations with differences in terms of socialism (central government expenditure as a percentage of gross national product), economy (e.g., level of industrialization gauged via energy use), social inequity (GINI index of income), and nation development (educational attainment, per capita income, and life expectancy). 5.2.2. Second recommendation: use different study designs The results of this SLR indicate that all reviewed studies adopted quantitative method. Hence, future hospitality and tourism research is encouraged to undertake qualitative as well as mixed-method approach to conduct an in-depth exploration of causal mechanisms behind the impacts of ethical leaders ’ behaviors that have not been fully unpacked through quantitative studies. Moreover, experimental designs should be used in future research to explore causal effects of ethical leadership on organizational, team, or employee outcomes, as well as the extent to which ethical leadership training interventions can develop supervisors ’ ethical leadership. Third recommendation: Expand associated variables of ethical leadership . Hospitality and tourism leadership studies have examined only interactional justice to peers ( Zoghbi-Manrique-de-Lara and Su árez-Acosta, 2014 ) and workplace spirituality ( Srivastava and Gupta, 2022 ) as antecedents of ethical leadership. This constrains our G. Hoang et al. International Journal of Hospitality Management 114 (2023) 103563 10 understanding of how to develop ethical leadership in organizations in this service context. Studies in general management have identified some individual antecedents embracing leader-specific and follower-specific antecedents although the antecedents of ethical lead - ership perceptions have been modestly studied compared to its out - comes ( Frazier and Jacezko, 2021 ). Future research in the tourism and hospitality setting is encouraged to examine the antecedent roles of some personality traits that have been unpacked in general management studies such as conscientiousness, agreeableness ( Kalshoven et al., 2011; Walumbwa and Schaubroeck, 2009; Xu et al., 2011 ), emotional stability ( Kalshoven et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011 ), and extraversion ( Xu et al., 2011 ). Leaders ’ Machiavellianism and M āori leaders ’ values (e.g., altruism, humility, cultural authenticity, collectivism, long-term orien - tation) should also be taken into account in future tourism and hospi - tality studies since these leader-specific antecedents of ethical leadership were uncovered in Frazier and Jacezko (2021) , W. Wang et al. (2023) , and Haar et al. (2019) in the general management contexts. A work of Ahn et al. (2018) and a study by Mayer et al. (2012) respec - tively revealed that leaders ’ core self-evaluation and their moral identity internalization and symbolization can facilitate their ethical leadership. Tourism and hospitality studies should therefore validate the role of these leader-specific antecedents of ethical leadership. Studies in gen - eral management have further reported that employee perceptions of ethical leadership can be nurtured by leaders ’ perceived behavioral control and favorable attitude towards ethical behavior ( Rahaman et al., 2019 ), cognitive moral development ( Jordan et al., 2013 ), ethical role modelling ( Brown et al., 2005; Frisch and Huppenbauer, 2014 ), as well as less likely to be fostered by supervisor moral disengagement ( Bonner et al., 2016 ). These potential leader-specific antecedents of ethical leadership should be unfolded in future studies in the tourism and hospitality discipline as well. Moreover, some works in general management have found some follower-specific or leader-follower specific antecedents to follower perceptions of ethical leadership comprising followers ’ rank ( Pucic, 2015 ), low leader-follower social distance ( Tumasjan et al., 2011 ), and the leader ’ s more advanced cognitive moral development than the fol - lowers ’ ( Jordan et al., 2013 ). Studies in the tourism and hospitality context are encouraged to investigate if ethical leadership can be affected by these antecedents. Additionally, research in general man - agement reported the impacts of some situation-specific predictors on ethical leadership including the negative impact of leader perceptions of organizational politics on ethical leadership (S. Lee et al., 2021 ), the role of leaders ’ negative perceptions of organizational justice and climate in promoting their ethical leadership ( O ’ Keefe et al., 2020 ), the role of employee perceptions of corporate social responsibility in fostering their perceptions of top management ethical leadership ( Duane Hansen et al., 2016 ), and the effects of owner ’ s values or business strategy on ethical leadership ( Frisch and Huppenbauer, 2014 ). These situational ante - cedents should be examined to provide further insights into how situa - tions can shape ethical leadership among managers. Though studies in our SLR demonstrate a focus on individual out - comes of ethical leadership, more individual-level outcomes should be investigated. Studies on ethical leadership have drawn upon social learning theory ( Bandura and Walters, 1977 to posit and examine pos - itive behaviors among employees as a result of their emulation of ethical leaders ’ behaviors oriented towards others based on ethical standards. Hence, future research in the tourism and hospitality context should investigate more employee behaviors that benefit others and the orga - nization as the whole in the work environment of ethical leadership, such as job crafting, affiliative promotive behavior, challenging pro - motive behavior (voice behavior)), as well as the role of ethical lead - ership in reducing behaviors that may negatively affect others and the organization, such as knowledge hiding, unethical pro-leader behavior, counterproductive work behavior. Ethical leaders not only serve as moral role models for employees to emulate their behaviors but also provide support for employees to undertake such positive behaviors. Therefore, employees in the tourism and hospitality environment incline to reciprocate towards such a support in forms of positive behaviors (through social exchange theory lens ( Blau, 1964 )) as well as utilize support as a contextual resource (through the lens of job demands-resources model, ( Bakker and Demerouti, 2007 )) to craft their job or share rather than hide their knowledge. This further advocates investigations into the above behavioral outcomes of ethical leadership in the tourism and hospitality discipline. Furthermore, Cropanzano et al. (2017) expanded social exchange theory to incorporate the role of emotions in building the social ex - change relationship between leaders and members. This suggests that future works in the tourism and hospitality context delve into affective outcomes such as positive affect, harmonious or obsessive passion, and emotional labor. Research in general management has also revealed the role of ethical leadership in promoting positive attitudinal outcomes (e. g., Charoensap et al., 2019 ; Z. Wang and Xu, 2019 ) and positive psy - chological outcomes particularly employee well-being (e.g., Chughtai et al., 2015 ; C. Yang, 2014 ). In light of social cognitive theory ( Bandura, 1986 ), ethical leaders who treat employees fairly and encourage them to act ethically can influence employees ’ beliefs and cognitions of ethical standards ( Koay and Lim, 2022 ). Taken together, tourism and hospi - tality studies are advised to unpack how ethical leaders can promote employees ’ attitudinal outcomes such as trust in leader, cognitive flex - ibility, and moral belief, as well as their psychological outcomes such as employees ’ different forms of well-being including physical well-being, psychological well-being, and social well-being. In addition, our SLR unveils a gap in relation to work-life interface outcomes of ethical leadership in hospitality and tourism research. Drawing on social learning theory ( Bandura and Walters, 1977 ) and work – family enrichment theory ( Greenhaus and Powell, 2006 ), Liao et al. (2015) found the role of ethical leadership in fostering family satisfaction of employees ’ spouses as well as suggested further in - vestigations into work-family effects of ethical leadership. Future research in the tourism and hospitality discipline is hence advised to examine the impacts of ethical leadership on work-life interface out - comes such as work-family balance, enrichment, or conflict, which are crucial in hospitality and tourism workplaces characterized by high job demands ( Li et al., 2021 ). Moreover, this SLR indicates the less focus of hospitality and tourism studies on group outcomes of ethical leadership. In light of social learning theory ( Bandura and Walters, 1977 ), Mo et al. (2019) posited and revealed that working with an ethical leader as a moral role model, members of a team tend to learn how to treat others ethically and collaborate with others as well as develop interpersonal trust, contrib - uting to team performance in general and team creativity in particular. Future research should therefore expand the set of group/organization-level outcomes of ethical leadership by engaging more fine-grained types of performance (e.g., financial performance, innovative performance, ambidextrous information, open innovation, sustainable performance) as well as other group-level outcomes such as team ethical climate, team job crafting or team ethical decision making. In addition to investigating further individual-, team-, and organization-level outcomes of ethical leadership, future research in the hospitality and tourism discipline should uncover more multiple-level mechanisms and multiple-level outcomes of ethical leadership in hos - pitality and tourism firms to garner further understanding of the nuanced nature of ethical leadership effectiveness. This is suggested by some studies in general management, which have reported multiple-level mechanisms behind the effects of ethical leadership ( Bai et al., 2019; Eva et al., 2020 ), as well as multiple-level outcomes of ethical leadership ( Christensen-Salem et al., 2021 ). As regards mediation mechanisms behind ethical leadership effects, albeit hospitality and tourism studies have investigated a number of employee-centered mediators underlying ethical leadership effects, research in this stream can engage further employee-centered mediation mechanisms. According to social learning theory ( Bandura and Walters, G. Hoang et al. International Journal of Hospitality Management 114 (2023) 103563 11 1977), employees who observe ethical leaders’ behaviors incline to emulate their behaviors and perform well, indicating that some positive behaviors of employees may mediate between ethical leadership and employee performance. Future tourism and hospitality studies are thus encouraged to consider behavioral mediators, such as knowledge sharing, voice behavior, and thriving. Additionally, through social cognitive lens (Bandura, 2001), ethical leadership may shape em - ployees’ behaviors through influencing their beliefs and cognitions of ethical standards (Koay and Lim, 2022). Studies, such as Bouckenooghe et al. (2015) and Men et al. (2020), also drew upon social learning theory to posit that emulating ethical leaders’ behaviors, employees incline to develop interpersonal trust and mutual respect, which can contribute to the formation of psychological factors (e.g., psychological capital, psychological safety) and in turn behavioral or performance outcomes. It is accordingly advisable that inquiries in the tourism and hospitality context investigate the role of cognitive mediators (e.g., cognitive appraisal, cognitive engagement, cognitive flexibility, moral awareness, moral disengaging process, moral reflectiveness, moral attentiveness) and psychological mediators (e.g., psychological capital, psychological attachment/detachment, psychological safety) in trans - lating ethical leadership into employee behaviors or performance. Social exchange theory further postulates that employees are likely to recip - rocate towards the support and fair treatment from ethical leaders by developing a strong relationship with leaders, positive attitudes and emotions towards leaders and the workplace (Blau, 1964; Cropanzano, Anthony et al., 2017). Future tourism and hospitality inquiries should hence examine the mediating role of relational (e.g., relational energy, relational attachment), attitudinal (e.g., trust in leader, learning goal orientation, duty orientation), and affective (e.g., moral anger, emotional distress, emotional attachment) factors behind the effects of ethical leadership. Based on job characteristics model, Piccolo et al. (2010) observed the role of job characteristics in mediating ethical leadership and job per - formance, as well as called for inquiries into job-centered mediators for the ethical leadership effects. Moreover, research in general manage - ment has revealed the mediating role of group-level factors, particularly culture or climate, underlying ethical leadership effects (e.g., Chris - tensen-Salem et al., 2021; S ̧ engüllendi et al., 2023). Due to the scant attention of extant hospitality and tourism research to job-, team-, and organization-centered mediators, future ethical leadership research in this discipline is advised to delve into more job-centered mediators (such as job crafting or quality of work life), team-centered (such as team ethical culture/climate) as well as organization-centered mediation pathways (such as innovation climate, collaborative culture, or organi - zational politics). Furthermore, this SLR reveals that trickle-down effects of ethical leadership appear not to receive attention from hospitality and tourism scholars. General management literature denotes some scholarly atten - tion granted to cascading effects of ethical leadership from higher- to lower-level managers such as Constandt and Willem (2019) and O’Keefe et al. (2020). Thus, the stream of research on trickle-down effects of ethical leadership should be extended to the hospitality and tourism discipline. In addition to moderation mechanisms found in this SLR, future research is advised to extend this repertoire of ethical leadership con - tingencies. Ethical leadership research in general management has indicated the role of individual moderators such as personality traits (Q. Yang and Wei, 2017) and moral identity (Z. Wang et al., 2021) as well as contextual moderators such as climate (Christensen-Salem et al., 2021). This suggests that future inquiries in the tourism and hospitality context engage more individual moderators (e.g., personality traits (extraver - sion, openness, conscientiousness, agreeableness), moral identity, moral values) and more contextual moderators (organizational or team climate). Fourth recommendation: use more theoretical perspectives Though mostly used theories (i.e., social exchange theory, social learning theory, COR theory), as revealed through this SLR, can be further adopted to underpin new mechanisms behind the effects of ethical leadership, other theories should be utilized to shed light on other mechanisms behind the relationships between ethical leadership and new outcomes at individual, team, and organizational levels. In addition to social exchange theory employed to explicate how ethical leaders in the hospitality or tourism organizations influence employee outcomes, leader-member exchange theory integrated with affective events theory, instead of social exchange theory in general, should be adopted to cast light on affective intervening mechanisms for ethical leadership effectiveness, as proposed by Cropanzano, Anthony et al. (2017). Therefore, future hospitality and tourism studies that examine affective mediation pathways (e.g., emotional attachment, emotional distress) should utilize such an integrated theory of leader-member exchange. Besides, future research in the hospitality and tourism domain that unpacks the effects of ethical leadership on team or organizational behaviors or performance can also draw upon collective social exchange theoretical framework (Y. Gong et al., 2010). This SLR indicates that COR theory has been increasingly employed to illuminate the associations of ethical leadership with outcomes of hospitality/tourism employees (e.g., T. Gong and Wang, 2022; C.-J. Lee and Huang, 2019; Luu and Vu, 2021; Tarkang Mary and Ozturen, 2019). However, a derivation of COR theory, namely the job demands-re - sources model (Bakker and Demerouti, 2017), should be used to un - derpin the interaction between job demands (e.g., time pressure, work overload, role ambiguity, job insecurity) and job resources provided by ethical leaders in the hospitality and tourism sector. Furthermore, due to the focus of COR theory on individual outcomes, multiple-level out - comes (i.e., individual, team/organizational level outcomes) of ethical leadership should be explained through a theoretical integration of COR theory with resource-based view (Barney, 2001) in light of the sugges - tion by (Wheeler et al., 2012). Moreover, other theories should be employed to explore more mechanisms through which ethical leaders can shape behaviors among employees. For instance, social cognitive theory or cognitive evaluation theory can be of use to elucidating cognitive mediation mechanisms (e. g., cognitive appraisal, cognitive flexibility, moral awareness, moral reflectiveness, moral attentiveness) that ethical leaders can stimulate to shape employees’ positive behavioral outcomes. Mediation mecha - nisms, such as psychological attachment/detachment and relational attachment, behind the ethical leadership effects can be examined through the lens of attachment theory. Social identity theory can be utilized to cast light on how moral identity or moral identity centrality mediates the effects of ethical leadership, while self-determination theory can serve as an appropriate theoretical framework to explicate the role of harmonious passion or moral disengagement in linking ethical leadership with employees’ ethical or unethical behaviors. 5.3. Practical implications The critical significance of ethical leadership in tourism and hospi - tality sectors has been discussed in the empirical studies reviewed. Our SLR suggests that ethical leadership can be instrumental in promoting positive outcomes at individual, team, and organizational levels. In this section, we offer several managerial implications for tourism and hos - pitality firms. First, tourism and hospitality organizations should make effort to train managers at all levels to develop ethical leadership style. Specif - ically, through providing training programs, tourism and hospitality organizations could improve the manager’s awareness on the impor - tance of ethical leadership and help them hone their skills to demon - strate ethical leadership behaviors in daily practice (Garba et al., 2018). Furthermore, tourism and hospitality firms could also search for several personality traits from candidates, which were found to be predictors of G. Hoang et al. International Journal of Hospitality Management 114 (2023) 103563 12 ethical leadership such as agreeableness, conscientiousness (Walumbwa and Schaubroeck, 2009), emotional stability (Kalshoven et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011), and extraversion (Xu et al., 2011), during the recruitment and selection process (Garba et al., 2018). Second, our findings in this SLR highlight some mediating mecha - nisms that translate ethical leadership into positive outcomes at different levels. We therefore suggest that tourism and hospitality or - ganizations enact the mediators (e.g., enhancing employee’s moral courage or creating an ethical culture) to enhance the effectiveness of ethical leadership. Ethical leaders can realize these goals by sending consistent massages to their followers about ethical conducts through daily interactions. When these goals are achieved, ethical values will be fostered and shared amongst employees. Third, our SLR also reveals the importance of moderating mechanisms that strengthen the effects of ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality contexts. We thus recom - mend that tourism and hospitality organizations should promote the contingent conditions that have been found in the studies in our sample, such as helping employee realize their service role identity or providing job autonomy for employees. 6. Limitations and future reviews Although our SLR yielded important implications for theory and practice, there remain some limitations that should be addressed in future reviews. First, despite following a rigorous reviewing process, we cannot guarantee the completeness of a sample of empirical research on ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality because this SLR only considered articles published in peer-reviewed journals and excluded non-journal publications to ensure the quality of publications reviewed (Le et al., 2019). Second, due to the language barriers of the research team, the search process was filtered down to articles published in En - glish language. The increasing importance of ethical leadership makes us believe that there could be more studies published in other languages that can support or challenge the current findings. Thus, further reviews may take this opportunity to enhance our understandings of ethical leadership in tourism and hospitality. Third, we also suggest that more meta-analytic reviews should be carried out to investigate the effects of ethical leadership on group and organizational outcomes, other than individual outcomes examined by Bedi et al. (2016) and Ng and Feld - man (2015). More systematic reviews on ethical leadership in other sectors, such as manufacturing or healthcare, would also add more values to the management literature. We apply social learning theory and social cognitive theory to suggest that the association is stronger when the employees involved have high (versus low) moral identity and high (versus low) self-control. By testing the model using 375 supervisor-subordinate dyads at a large Iraqi organization, we demonstrated a separate strengthening role of subordinates ’ self-control and moral identity in the positive effect of ethical leadership on their ethical behavior, and that ethical leadership had the strongest positive influence on the ethical conduct of employees with both high moral identity and high self- control. Our findings have important implications as they suggest that harnessing the full benefit of ethical leadership requires attention being paid to the characteristics of both leaders and subordinates. 1. Introduction To address the concern that long-standing approaches to business leadership (e.g., the transformational model) placed too little emphasis on the importance of ethics, several alternatives were developed ( Nassif, Hackett, & Wang, 2021 ), including ethical leadership as reflected by Brown, Trevi ño, and Harrison (2005, p. 120) ethical leadership scale (ELS). The ELS is associated with a wide range of high-value group or organizational outcomes (e.g., group creativity, Keem, Koseoglu, Jeong, & Shalley, 2022 ; circular economy processes, Cheffi, Zahir-ul-Hassan, Farooq, Baqrain, & Mansour, 2023 ) and subordinate-level outcomes (e.g., job satisfaction, organizational commitment, Kim, Jeong, & Seo, 2022 ; task performance, Kalra, Briggs, & Schrock, 2023; Zhu, He, Trevi ño, Chao, & Wang, 2015 ; employee voice, Zhu et al., 2015 ; social media use for work, Kalra et al., 2023 ). Moreover, exposure to ethical leadership tends to be a positive for subordinates ’ ethical or moral behavior ( Al Halbusi, Ruiz-Palomino, Morales-S ánchez, & Abdel Fattah, 2021 ), thanks to the social learning process of employees ’ experience (cf., Brown et al., 2005 ). Indeed, by demonstrating ethics in their per - sonal actions, communicating ethical expectations and enforcing ethical policies and procedures, ethical leaders drive subordinates to acquire ethical behavior as the appropriate way to act ( Ruiz-Palomino & Linuesa-Langreo, 2018 ). Furthermore, the learning process these leaders activate is also explicative of many other positive outcomes found to be generated by ethical leadership (e.g., employee self-efficacy, ethical climate, Bedi, Alpaslan, & Green, 2016 ), and which, according to pre - vious research, are, in turn, positively linked to employee ethical behavior (see Al Halbusi et al., 2021, Owens, Yam, Bednar, Mao, & Hart, 2019 ). Nonetheless, few studies address the links between ethical leadership and moral conduct ( Bedi et al., 2016 ), most of which focus on preventing unethical behavior as opposed to fostering moral action ( Moore et al., 2019; Wang, Xing, Xu, & Hannah, 2021 ), with some recent meta -analytical studies (albeit among nurses) concluding that the effect size of the expected positive impact of ethical leadership on sub - ordinates ’ ethical behavior is weak and non-significant ( Kim et al., 2022 ). More surprisingly, the literature on the conditions that impact the effectiveness of ethical leadership is also limited ( Sosik, Chun, Ete, Arenas, & Scherer, 2019; Wang et al., 2021 ). Thus, time-lagged research designs that reveal the pattern of relationships between ethical leader - ship and other person-related factors in their impact on subordinates ’ behaviors are recommended ( Dust, Resick, Margolis, Mawritz, & Greenbaum, 2018 ). Furthermore, given that moral behavior involves self-regulatory processes ( Chen, Liu, Zhang, & Wang, 2022 ) that are attention-consuming and require cognitive resources ( Joosten, Van * Corresponding author. Using a time-lagged research design, this study aims to better un - derstand the association between ethical leadership and subordinates ’ moral behavior by testing a model involving the individual differences that drive self-regulation and affect the magnitude of the relationship. The first of these is subordinates ’ moral identity, i.e., one ’ s sense of self as moral, as reflected by complex knowledge structures comprising moral values, goals, traits, and behavioral scripts ( Aquino & Reed, 2002; Aquino, Freeman, Reed, Lim, & Felps, 2009 , 2011). Specifically, we contend that the positive influence of ethical leadership on ethical conduct will be heightened among subordinates with high moral iden - tity. This expectation is grounded in the view that these subordinates are more likely to attend to the behaviors modeled by ethical leaders, which is a precursor of the observational learning ( Bandura, 1977 ) thought to underlie the effectiveness of ethical leadership ( Wang et al., 2021 ). It is also grounded in the idea that ethical leadership should motivate sub - ordinates who see themselves as moral because it will encourage them to be consistent in their self-concept ( Wang & Hackett, 2020 ). Finally, this expectation is consistent with social cognitive theory (SCT; Bandura, 1991 ), through which the moral self-influence provided by moral identity and its regulatory function of moral behavior ( Wang et al., 2021 ) can be reinforced by a series of cognitive mechanisms elicited by contextual demands (e.g., ethical leadership) that cause the individual to behave in ways that are consistent with their moral standards ( Chen et al., 2022 ). Another source of moral self-regulation ( Bandura, 1991 ) is self- control, which we also examine as a boundary condition potentially affecting the extent to which ethical leadership fosters employees ’ moral conduct. Defined as the capacity to self-regulate thoughts, moods or emotions and to inhibit undesirable impulses and facilitate persistence to achieve expected performance ( De Ridder, Lensvelt-Mulders, Finke - nauer, Stok, & Baumeister, 2012 ), self-control underlies the self- regulation of cognition and behavior that, following SCT, explains moral thought and action ( Bandura, 1991 ), and is a resource that helps adjust subordinates ’ behaviors to leaders ’ expectations or example ( De Ridder et al., 2012 ). Thus, drawing on the SCT notion that observance of salient role models leads to learning appropriate behavior ( Bandura, 1991 ), self-control may help subordinates engage in the goal-directed behavior ( De Ridder et al., 2012 ) ethical leaders exemplify and encourage ( Banks, Fischer, Gooty, & Stock, 2021; Brown & Trevi ño, 2006; Zhu, Zheng, He, Wang, & Zhang, 2019 ). Finally, we anticipate that the positive influence of moral identity on the relationship between ethical leadership and subordinates ’ ethical behavior will be strengthened when subordinates ’ self-control is high. As a relatively enduring trait, self-control serves as a cognitive resource that enables people to resist short-term temptations and refrain from impulsivity ( Lian, Yam, Ferris, & Brown, 2017 ). It is a moral muscle ( Baumeister & Exline, 1999; Tangney, Baumeister, & Boone, 2004 ) that should augment the positive impact of moral identity in relation to the positive functioning of ethical leadership. This expectation draws on previous research suggesting that self-control enables one to keep promises and accomplish self-imposed goals ( De Ridder et al., 2012 ) and demonstrates that leaders ’ self-control is involved in the effective func - tioning of their ethical leadership ( Sosik et al., 2019 ). As will be explained, much of the theory associated with the effec - tiveness of ethical leadership is grounded in SLT ( Bandura, 1977 ) – as it relates to the leader as a role model ( Wang et al., 2021 ) – and SCT ( Bandura, 1991 ), which especially addresses the role of internal self- regulatory processes ( Sosik et al., 2019 ). Both theories emphasize the strong influence on behavioral outcomes of the reciprocal interaction between the person and the environment. Under an SLT perspective ( Bandura, 1977 ), employees are expected to learn “ what to do in the workplace ” by paying attention to and emulating the values, behaviors and messages of attractive, credible and legitimate role models, such as ethical leaders, who hold desirable personal characteristics (i.e., fair - ness, honesty, Brown & Trevi ño, 2006 ). In addition, following SCT ( Bandura, 1986, 1991 ), the resulting behavior of subordinates is seen as an interplay of both personal and external factors, which operate as interacting determinants and as stimuli of targeted behaviors. Thus, because those who practice ethical leadership are a source of “ situa - tional stimuli ” ( Wang et al., 2021; p. 452 ), the notion that person-based variables (moral identity, self-control) might influence subordinates ’ reactions to ethical leadership, aligns well with both SLT and SCT, and could shed light on the reasons for which the expected positive impact of ethical leadership on subordinates ’ ethical behavior has, in previous research, yielded mixed findings (i.e., Moore et al., 2019; Owens et al., 2019 ) and little explanation of variance (i.e., Wang et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, the consideration of both person-based var - iables could help unmask mixed findings regarding the strengthening role of moral identity in the impact of ethical leadership on sub - ordinates ’ ethical behavior ( Moore et al., 2019, Wang et al., 2021 ), as self-control could reinforce the expected positive effect of moral identity in driving ethical leadership of supervisors towards increased ethical behavior in their subordinates. Thus, the following questions are raised: 1) Are moral identity and self-control each a condition for ethical leadership to be more effective in increasing subordinates ’ ethical behavior? and 2) is self-control a condition that bolsters the power of moral identity in leading to the strongest effect of ethical leadership on subordinates ’ ethical behavior? Answering these questions will expand the literature in two main ways. First, the study of person-related variables in relation to ethical leadership functioning is an emergent and growing field ( Sosik et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021; O ’ Keefe, Son Hing, & Catano, 2023; Mitchell, Reynolds, & Trevi ño, 2020 ), and although subordinate moral identity has been studied as a possible strengthener of the relationship between ethical leadership and subordinates ’ ethical behavior ( Wang et al., 2021; Li, Jia, Seufert, Luo, & Sun, 2022 ), no conclusive findings have thus far been reported. Furthermore, we are the first to test self-control (a sub - stitute for moral identity, Gino, Schweitzer, Mead, & Ariely, 2011 ) as another internal self-regulatory mechanism ( Sosik & Zhu, 2020 ) that may play a similar role in the relationship, which is important to deci - pher, as Mitchell et al. (2020) have called for research on the role of self- regulatory mechanisms for a better understanding of the causes of em - ployees ’ (un)ethical behavior. Second, we are the first to test a model linking ethical leadership to subordinates ’ moral identity and self- control, in ultimately influencing their moral behavior, thus advancing the recent literature ( Sosik et al., 2019, Wang et al., 2021 ). Sosik et al. (2019) focused on how self-control leads managers ’ character strengths to be embedded in their actions, ultimately reflecting strong ethical leadership. Our study, however, advances upon that of Sosik et al. (2019) , testing whether supervisors ’ ethical leadership and the external ethical guidelines it represents impact more strongly on the ethical behavior of subordinates with high self-control. Importantly, we test whether self-control helps embody subordinates ’ moral identity (i.e., the degree to which being ethical is one ’ s sign of identity, Zhu, Riggio, Avolio, & Sosik, 2011; He, Chao, & Zhu, 2019 ) in their daily behavior. Our considering these two person-based variables in the same model is a relevant contribution, as the impact of moral identity has varied depending on the nature of the overall model involved ( Wang et al., 2021 ). Thus, by showing that self-control helps subordinates be true to their moral identity, we can offer a solution (i.e., ensuring that in - dividuals have self-control) in situations where materialistic aspects prevail and, therefore, the effects of moral identity on ethical behavior might be weakened ( Aquino et al., 2009 ). If our model is supported, the main practical implication will be that attaining the full potential value of ethical leadership requires organi - zations attend not only to the capabilities of leaders but also to the characteristics of subordinates. This would mean, for example, that organizational efforts to enhance leadership capabilities also need to be paired with initiatives to build subordinates ’ sense of moral identity and H. Theory and hypothesis development 2.1. The relationship between ethical leadership and subordinates ’ ethical behavior and its contingencies As a form of leadership with a greater focus on moral considerations than other approaches ( Nassif et al., 2021 ), Brown et al. (2005, p. 120) conceptualize ethical leadership as “ the demonstration of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal re - lationships, and the promotion of such conduct to subordinates through two-way communication, reinforcement, and decision-making ” . The theoretical foundation for the effectiveness of ethical leadership ( Brown et al., 2005 ) lies in SLT ( Bandura, 1977 ), which suggests that employees learn appropriate behaviors by looking closely at, and emulating, the behaviors of attractive, credible role models, such as ethical supervisors, who generally present traits that are universally considered attractive (i. e., caring concern for others, kind-heartedness, honesty, etc. Brown et al., 2005; Ruiz-Palomino & Linuesa-Langreo, 2018; Zhu et al., 2019 ) and build up their credibility and likeability ( Ete et al., 2020 ). Addi - tionally, this theory suggests that the behavioral learning process in the workplace is also based on knowing “ what ” is sanctioned, either through one ’ s own experience or vicariously – by observing the consequences of certain behaviors of other workmates. Indeed, ethical leaders are thought to be positive role models of the behaviors desired by the employer due to their hierarchical position and their associated level of influence over subordinates, including their ability to administer work- related rewards and punishments ( Nassif et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2019 ). As such, driven by clear communication of ethical standards, intentional role modeling, and explicit use of rewards and punishments ( Nassif et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2019 ), we, in line with past research ( Bedi et al., 2016; Al Halbusi et al., 2021 ), expect ethical leadership to be a positive for subordinates ’ ethical behavior; the latter is defined here as behavior built on universal moral principles (e.g., integrity, fairness), which aims to be accepted by the wider community and is conducive to positive human growth ( Ruiz-Palomino & Linuesa-Langreo, 2018 ). However, as detailed below, significant variation in the magnitude of the relationship is expected due to individual differences among subordinates, consistent with a person-situation interactionist view that theorizes the impact of situational variables (e.g., supervisors ’ ethical leadership) is contingent on subordinates ’ individual differences ( Trevi ño, Den Nieuwenboer, & Kish-Gephart, 2014; Mitchell et al., 2020 ). Indeed, the literature (see Table 1 ) reports, for example, that the reinforced positive impact of ethical leadership on subordinates ’ ethical behavior is likely to depend, for example, on a number of person-related aspects that lead subordinates to be more in need of a moral compass (low moral awareness, Gok et al., 2017 ), to rely on external cues to guide their behavior (Machiavellianism, Belschak, Den Hartog, & De Hoogh, 2018 ; relativism, Ruiz-Palomino & Martinez-Ca ñas, 2011 ; low self- esteem, Avey, Palanski, & Walumbwa, 2011 ; low conscientiousness, Evans, Davis, & Neely, 2021 ), to perceive their role as followers as abiding by the supervisor ’ s rules or advice (i.e., seeing their follower role as good citizen or as one of subordination, Knoll, Schyns, & Petersen, 2017 ), to be flexible and adaptable to observed norms and values (low right-wing authoritarianism, O ’ Keefe et al., 2023 ), or to be sensitive to ethical cues (i.e., moral attentiveness, Al Halbusi et al., 2021 ). On another note, however, a second group of studies reveals a similar pattern in the relationship when subordinates perceive a fit ( Ruiz-Palomino & Martinez-Ca ñas, 2011 ) or identify with their leader ’ s values ( Wang et al., 2021 ), thus suggesting that working with supervi - sors who encourage and/or role model ethics could act as a reinforcing element among subordinates who also value ethics as important in their lives. Finally, strictly related to this last reflection, the literature (see Table 1 ) shows that the consideration of morality as an important part of self-concept (i.e., moral identity) – which helps to self-regulate behavior in accordance with such a moral schema, Ete et al., 2020 – may also help one to be more positively impacted by external factors that prime ethical behavior ( Aquino et al., 2009 , see Table 1 ), for reasons related to the pursuit of identity-consistent behavior (cf., Aquino, McFerran, & Laven, 2011; Banks et al., 2021 , see Table 1 ).
