(2021) argued that complexities associated with the role modeling process suggest it should not simply be assumed that sub - ordinates will be uniformly influenced by their leaders. For these and other authors (e.g., Banks et al., 2021 ), variations in the level of indi - vidual differences may play a role. Many person-related variables have this potential, although cognitive variables have recently attracted attention ( Trevi ño et al., 2014 ). These include moral conation, “ the capacity to generate responsibility and motivation to take moral action ” ( Hannah, Avolio, & May, 2011, p. 664 ), and moral attentiveness, “ the extent to which morality is chronically contemplated and perceived in daily experience ” ( Al Halbusi et al., 2021, p. 3 ). Another such variable is moral identity, which has attracted the greatest attention regarding its interaction with other variables to explain ethical behavior ( Krette - nauer, 2022 ). As Wang and Hackett (2020) report, the moral identity construct has been defined in various ways. Hardy (2006, p. 215) , for example, sug - gests that moral identity reflects the “ extent to which the elements most central to a person ’ s identity (e.g., values, goals, and virtues) are ethical ... such that when moral virtues are important to one ’ s identity, this yields motivation to behave in line with one ’ s sense of morality ” . Relatedly, Aquino and Reed (2002) provide a cognitive perspective, in which moral identity comprises two complex knowledge structures, i.e., internalization (the being side) and symbolization (the doing side), each consisting of moral values, goals, traits, and behavioral scripts. The importance ascribed to moral identity is consistent with SCT ( Bandura, 1991 ), in which the ongoing exercise of self-influence is a crucial motivator and regulator of moral behavior. Indeed, moral identity is a potential source of self-regulation ( Wang et al., 2021 ), especially from a virtue ethics perspective ( Wang & Hackett, 2020 ). Thus, the extent to which subordinates see themselves as moral ( Aquino et al., 2009, 2011; He et al., 2019 ) is likely to influence the degree to which they align, attend, and are drawn to, the situational stimuli associated with ethical leadership ( Wang et al., 2021 ), as a supervisor who develops strong ethical leadership is typically characterized as also having a high moral identity ( Zhu et al., 2016 ). The knowledge structures associated with ethical considerations are more likely to be primed, assessable and easily activated among those of high (versus low) moral identities ( He et al., 2019 ), such that the behaviors modeled by ethical leaders are especially likely to be noted by subordinates high in moral identity. This is crucial since gaining likeability ( Ete et al., 2020 ) and, therefore, the attention of subordinates, is necessary to generate the SLT-based ( Bandura, 1977 ) observational learning thought to underlie the effectiveness of ethical leadership ( Wang et al., 2021 ). This is also consistent with previous findings confirming that subordinates are more likely to work to meet the leader ’ s performance expectations (e.g., that subordinates behave ethically) when they identify with their leader ’ s values ( Zhu et al., 2015 ) which is, for example, more likely to occur when supervisors practice ethical leadership and, therefore, make salient the aspects that Table 1 ( continued ) Authors (year) Moderator Findings Remarks Banks et al. The amplifying role of self-control Self-control is another individual difference that may shape the in - fluence of ethical leadership. Described as the resource and capacity “ to alter or override dominant response tendencies, and to regulate behavior, thoughts, and emotions ” ( De Ridder et al., 2012, p. 77 ), self- control is a character strength that reflects the virtue of temperance ( Sosik & Zhu, 2020 ) and is another cognitive source of self-regulation (also considered a moral muscle, Trevi ño et al., 2014; Baumeister & Exline, 1999 ) that is needed to self-regulate one ’ s behavior to the behavioral demands of daily life ( Sosik & Zhu, 2020 ), even under the presence of an ethical supervisor. Indeed, when supervisors exercise ethical leadership, they are said to provide clues about the type of behavior that is supported ( Al Halbusi et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2019 ), all of which, in line with SLT ( Bandura, 1977 ) and SCT ( Bandura, 1991 ), should positively impact employee ethical behavior. However, following SLT and SCT, while individuals learn by observing and interacting with salient role models, this occurs through adaptive cognitive processes, whereby individuals adjust their mindsets and behaviors according to the expectations or example of leaders and the signs and clues perceived ( Neubert, Wu, & Roberts, 2013 ). Thus, it is particularly critical for subordinates to have strong levels of self-control, so that the ethical leadership of supervisors can have a more positive impact on their ethical behavior. Indeed, sub - ordinates ’ expected emulation of the behaviors of attractive role models such as ethical leaders (see SLT, Bandura, 1977 ) is likely to occur more easily if these subordinates have self-control, as it will give them strong willpower to resist any temptation to deviate their behavior from the moral values observed in, and mandated or communicated by, ethical leaders (cf., Sosik et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, while the provision of in - formation by ethical leaders may be processed internally by their sub - ordinates in a way such that their self-concept may be accordingly transformed (see SCT, Bandura, 1991; Ete et al., 2020 ), it does not guarantee they will behave in accordance with their self-concept. However, for this behavior to be developed, they need to have previ - ously experienced a self-regulation process. Indeed, prior to developing a behavior, individuals regulate their behavior in accordance with their self-concept (see SCT, Bandura, 1991 ), and, thus, having high levels of self-control should be key for subordinates to behave in line with the previously internalized values from their ethical leaders. In all, the ethical leadership of supervisors is likely to impact the ethical behavior of subordinates more positively if the latter have high self-control. Self-control involves a series of steps (i.e., establishing a goal, planning how to pursue it, exerting the required effort, monitoring progress toward the goal and revising the level of accomplishment of the goal, Johnson, Lin, & Lee, 2018 ), through which employees can increase the effort they make to faithfully follow the ethical guidelines their ethical supervisor sets regarding how to behave in daily routines. Accordingly, H1b . The positive influence of ethical leadership on subordinates ’ ethical behavior is greater among employees with high versus low self- control. 2.4. A three-way interaction: self-control as a moral muscle of moral identity realization As stated, we anticipate that self-control will positively moderate the link between moral identity and the positive relationship between ethical leadership and subordinates ’ ethical behavior. Support for such a three-way interaction requires several types of evidence that we describe below. First, it requires self-control being an important enabler for sub - ordinates to live out the convictions associated with a strong moral identity. This function of self-control is unsurprising because, as described by Plato, human life is a constant struggle between our most natural desires and rationality ( Yam, Lian, Ferris, & Brown, 2017 ), and self-control, as a moral virtue ( Baumeister & Exline, 1999 ), is required for people to achieve their ideal form. Indeed, enabling one to resist undesirable tendencies and impulses and short-term temptations ( Tangney et al., 2004 ) is crucial to be faithful to one ’ s moral identity, given the multiple ways in which the influence of one ’ s moral identity may be challenged, as, for example, when the context involves self- interest-based incentives ( Aquino et al., 2009 ). In fact, unethical behavior, which is impulsive in nature ( Trevi ño et al., 2014 ), is more likely to occur when individuals lack self-regulatory mechanisms ( Sosik & Zhu, 2020 ) due to their probable inability to anticipate and judge their actions in comparison to a set of internal moral standards. Thus, since moral identity may not be as enduring and stable as might be expected, given the wide range of situational cues people encounter daily ( Aquino et al., 2009 ), self-control is required for people to be true to their moral identity and behave accordingly. Indeed, exercising moral virtue is not easy and self-control is required ( Baumeister & Exline, 1999; Hofmann, Baumeister, F örster, & Vohs, 2012 ) as it helps establish effective habits and routines ( De Ridder et al., 2012; Hofmann et al., 2012 ). Thus, while moral identity helps individuals strive to act in ways aligned with their identity ( Wang et al., 2021 ), it does so by helping them resist tempta - tions, thanks to their using the self-regulatory resources ( Aquino & Reed, 2002; Wang, Weng, Kiani, & Ali, 2022 ) that self-control can provide ( Wang et al., 2021, Trevi ño et al., 2014 ). In support of this, Tangney et al. (2004) found, for example, that people with high self-control were less likely to procrastinate, were strong in perspective taking, and had good interpersonal relationships, all of which are involved in the “ hard- H. Bolin (2004) also found that high levels of self-control are associated with negative attitudes toward dishonesty, with honesty being another aspect of moral identity (Aquino & Reed, 2002; Krettenauer & Hertz, 2015; Ete et al., 2020). Additionally, Sosik et al. (2019) found that leaders’ positive character traits were involved in their practice of ethical leadership, but only in those with high self-control. Second, support for this prediction also requires a more powerful impact of ethical leadership on the social learning subordinates are ex - pected to undergo (Bandura, 1977) when employees are high (versus low) in both moral identity and self-control, which is more than feasible. In response to perceptions of high ethical leadership, subordinates high in moral identity are thought to be more likely to develop ethical behavior as a way to achieve alignment between their moral concept and their behavior (Wang & Hackett, 2020; Banks et al., 2021). This is much more likely to occur if these subordinates also have high self- control, as individuals high in moral identity generally use self- regulatory resources (which are not always held at a high level, Wang et al., 2022) when striving to align their behavior with their self-concept (Aquino & Reed, 2002). Indeed, drawing on SCT’s main proposition (Bandura, 1986, p. 2) that “personal factors, [...] moral conduct and environmental factors all operate as interacting determinants that in - fluence each other in determining outcomes”, a three-way interaction between ethical leadership, moral identity and self-control is believed to account for ethical behavior among subordinates. As emphasized by SCT (Bandura, 1986), people continually regulate their behaviors in accor - dance with the contextual cues they observe, and the salience of the message provided by the context (i.e., ethical leadership) is key for so - cial learning to be fully realized. Thus, the role model of ethical leaders will be more worthy of imitation when they also consider “ethics” as key in their lives (Wang et al., 2021). Additionally, it will most likely impact their behavior when they also possess a moral muscle such as self- control, which helps them live a moral life (Baumeister & Exline, 1999) by self-regulating and resisting impulses (Sosik et al., 2019) un - aligned with the traits of their moral identity. Instead, under low levels of moral identity and self-control, the positive impact of ethical lead - ership is least likely to occur (Wang et al., 2021), as subordinates would not be predisposed to consider the message provided by ethical leaders as salient to them (Wang et al., 2021) and would find it difficult to resist impulses leading them to engage in opportunistic behaviors (De Ridder et al., 2012). In all, we expect ethical leadership to have the strongest positive impact on subordinates’ ethical behavior when these have both a high moral identity and a high self-control. Thus, H2. The positive influence of ethical leadership on subordinates’ ethical behavior is greatest when both moral identity and self-control of employees are high versus low. Sample and procedure As noted, much of the research concerning moral identity ( Aquino et al., 2009; Aquino et al., 2011 ) and ethics ( Mitchell et al., 2020 ) has occurred in laboratory settings, so our sample of full-time working adults was intended to advance the literature. We collected data from 450 employees and their 115 supervisors in a large public organization in Baghdad, Iraq, once we had obtained permission to conduct our survey from a senior officer in the human resources (HR) function. Iraq was chosen for various reasons. First, in considering the UN ’ s sustainable development goals, specifically Goal Ten, reducing in - equalities, Iraq is under-researched and underrepresented in the litera - ture ( Budur & Demir, 2019 ). Second, Iraq is an emerging country facing myriad institutional pressures (e.g., from international markets, inter- governmental organizations, and parent companies) that drive increased consideration of ethical issues ( Jain, Aguilera, & Jamali, 2017 ). Finally, Iraq has a culture that stands out for its high levels of power distance, collectivism, avoidance uncertainty ( Center, 1967- 2010 ) and adherence to religious values ( Moaddel & Karabenik, 2010 ), all of which might positively affect reactions to (ethical) leadership perceptions. For example, high power distance affects how employees respond to managerial behavior (i.e., with loyalty and obedience, Cen - ter, 1967-2010 ); high uncertainty avoidance also makes employees anxious to follow the guide of managers ( Miao, Humphrey, & Qian, 2018 ); collectivism also relates to a tendency to engage in “ we ” rather than “ I ” thinking, thus likely leading employees to be more influenced by their supervisors ( Evensky, 2005 ); and strong adherence to religion could make their managers ’ ethics-grounded leadership seem attractive. Because the correlations between variables can be spuriously over - inflated when the data are collected only at one point in time, we adopted a time-lagged data collection method to reduce the occurrence of this potential common method bias ( Podsakoff, MacKenzie, & Pod - sakoff, 2012 ). Thus, the data were collected in two phases, one month apart. In the first phase (Time-1), subordinates were asked to rate su - pervisors ’ ethical leadership and their own moral identity and self- control. In the second phase (Time-2), supervisors rated their sub - ordinates ’ ethical behavior. The surveys were coded so that sub - ordinates ’ and supervisors ’ responses could be matched. Following Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, and Podsakoff (2003 ), Podsakoff et al. (2012 ), several steps were also taken to minimize the potential role of social desirability and evaluation apprehension in the responses. For example, a cover letter emphasized the data collected was for research purposes only, and that anonymity and confidentiality of the responses was guaranteed. Finally, both leaders and subordinates were asked to complete the surveys outside working hours and (anonymously) return them in pre-stamped envelopes to our research team. A total of 421 (93 %) subordinates and 97 (84 %) supervisors returned their surveys. After accounting for missing responses, 375 matched supervisor-subordinate dyads were obtained. In terms of gender, 72.8 % of the participants were male; 27.2 % were female. Most (66.7 %) were < 40 years old; only 10.9 % were 51 or older. Regarding educational level, 12.5 % had completed high school, 59.5 % had a bachelor ’ s degree, and 10.4 % had postgraduate (master, doctorate) training. Finally, most had long service with the organization. Only 3.5 % had worked there for < 2 years and tenure between 3 and 5 years accounted for an additional 17.9 %. Finally, because we had several employees per supervisor, a nested structure by group or department could potentially exist. The several tests we conducted reflected, however, that the group-level effects were unimportant. First, a hierarchical linear model including a supervisor identification number variable as a random effect revealed no significant effects (p = 0.687) in an empty model including our dependent variable. The intra-class correlation (ICC1) calculated in this simplest model also revealed a value of 0.013, far below the recommended cut-off of 0.05 ( LeBreton & Senter, 2008 ), which indicated that the group-level effects account for a near-zero variance of such variable. Thus, an individual- level approach (rather than a multilevel approach) to analyzing the data was the most parsimonious way to test our model ( Aguinis, Gott - fredson, & Culpepper, 2013 ). 3.2. Measurement Table 3 shows the items associated with all the variables, which were part of scales previously validated. We followed the Brislin (1980) back- translation procedure; the items were translated into Arabic and then two bilingual speakers compared the translation to the original to ensure semantic equivalence. Additionally, a panel of six experts in organiza - tional behavior and business ethics were consulted to give feedback regarding the appropriateness of the items in Iraq. After approval by the expert panel, a pilot test with 85 employees from another public orga - nization was conducted to ensure the appropriateness and clarity of the questions, and no significant changes were incorporated. In all cases, a 5-point Likert response format was used (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree), such that higher scores on the scale reflected a stronger value on the attribute. Ethical leadership. Subordinates completed the 10-item ELS designed by Brown et al. (2005) (e.g., My supervisor sets an example of how to do things the right way in terms of ethics). The responses were combined to form a reflective, Mode A first-order composite variable. The scale showed good internal consistency, reflecting a Cronbach alpha of around 0.912. Employee moral identity. This variable was assessed using Aquino and Reed (2002) 10-item scale, which consists of two dimensions, internal - ization (5-items about the extent to which a set of moral traits are core to one ’ s self-concept) and symbolization (5-items about the extent to which one demonstrates these traits to others). Although the internalization dimension is the most used in the literature, we implemented both di - mensions to build a reflective, second-order construct, as this option is the second most used and the best at capturing moderating effects ( Lefebvre & Krettenauer, 2019 ). Respondents were asked to imagine an ethical person (characterized as compassionate, friendly, helpful, generous, sincere, kind, hardworking, fair, caring) to use as a reference in relation to the item content, e.g., “ It would make me feel good to be a person who has these characteristics ” (internalization) and “ I am actively involved in activities that communicate to others that I have these characteristics ” (symbolization). One item from symbolization (i. e., “ the fact that I have these characteristics is communicated to others by my membership in certain organizations ” ) was dropped due to low loading ( Table 3 ). Cronbach ’ s alpha for the scale is 0.816. Employee self-control. This reflective Mode A first-order composite was assessed using 13 items adapted from previous studies ( Tangney et al., 2004; Vitell et al., 2009 ), e.g., “ I am good at resisting temptation ” . Cronbach ’ s alpha for this scale is 0.89. Employee ethical behavior. To assess this reflective Mode A first-order composite variable, we adapted a 12-item scale from previous studies ( Ferrell & Weaver, 1978; Newstrom & Ruch, 1975 ). This scale was used here because it contains items that are in tune with both established organizational norms (e.g., reporting violation of company policies by others, careful performance during work time, honest use of company material and resources) and socially accepted moral norms (e.g., honesty, responsibility, confidentiality). This made it more accurate in measuring the ethical behavior of employees, in contrast to other newer scales that are more specifically designed to measure behavior that is contrary to organizational norms (e.g., deviant behavior, counterpro - ductive behavior, see Trevi ño et al., 2014 ). This scale was also selected here because of its proven psychometric qualities in previous studies conducted in a variety of cultures (e.g., the US, Ferrell & Weaver, 1978 ; H. Al Halbusi et al. Data analysis techniques and results We implemented two methods to test the hypotheses: ordinary least squares regression-based path analysis using PROCESS v.3.1 ( Hayes, 2017 ) and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) using Smart PLS 3.2.8 ( Ringle, Wende, & Becker, 2015 ). PLS-SEM was used because it is appropriate for causal analyses involving both first- and second-order constructs ( Hair, Hult, Ringle, & Sarstedt, 2017 ), making it highly suitable to test H1a and H1b. Given that PLS-SEM does not explicitly incorporate the testing of three-way hypotheses, PROCESS v.3.1. (Model 3) was utilized to test H2 as it has shown to be accurate in testing similar hypotheses ( Hayes, 2017 ). Bootstrapping was used to test the significance of path coefficients using 5,000 replications and a p < 0.05 significance level ( Hayes, 2017; Hair et al., 2017 ). 4.1. Measurement model Item reliability, internal consistency, and convergent and discrimi - nant validity are addressed in Tables 3 and 4 . For item reliability, most of the items exceed the recommended 0.707 level or were above the 0.5 threshold, indicating a medium correlation with the targeted construct ( Hair et al., 2017 ). As mentioned, only one moral identity item (MI10, Table 3 ) had a loading below 0.2 and was dropped. In terms of internal consistency, the composite reliabilities and Cronbach ’ s alphas all exceeded the 0.70 cut-off ( Hair et al., 2017 ). Evidence supporting the convergent validity was also obtained; the average variance extracted (AVE) exceeded the 0.5 threshold ( Hair et al., 2017 ) for all the con - structs. Finally, the AVE for each measure was greater than the variance that each shared with the remaining latent variables, and the heterotrait-monotrait ratio (HTMT) of correlations revealed HTMT values below 0.90 that differed from 1 (i.e., 95 % confidence intervals not including 1), in support of discriminant validity of each pair of constructs ( Hair et al., 2017 ). 4.2. Structural model 4.2.1. Evaluation of common method variance (CMV) concerns The nature of the relationships that interested us required many of the key variables (e.g., moral identity, self-control) being collected from the same source, i.e., subordinates, so CMV was a potential concern ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Harman ’ s one-factor test, however, suggested CMV was not a major concern because seven factors with eigenvalues greater than 1 were required to account for 68 % of the variance, and the first factor accounted for only 32 % of the total variance ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Thus, CMV is unlikely to have inflated our findings, much less those concerning the interaction terms (see Podsakoff et al., 2012 ), the primary interest of our study. 4.2.2. Discussion and conclusions Two main research questions originated this study, which were answered affirmatively. First, both moral identity and self-control are person-based conditions that were found to enhance the positive impact of ethical leadership on subordinates ’ ethical behavior. Second, our findings revealed, as predicted, that ethical leadership has the greatest positive effect on subordinates ’ ethical behavior when both person- based variables are high (versus low), among subordinates. 5.1. Theoretical contributions As noted, research on the impact of person-related variables in relation to the functioning of ethical leadership is only now emerging (see Table 1 ). Thus, our investigation responded to the call of Wang and Hackett (2020) on the need for further research involving full-time employees in organizational settings, while advancing previous ethical leadership literature that has mainly focused on the prevention of immoral behavior (see Table 1 ), leaving aside the promotion of ethical behavior, the true target of the leadership concept developed by Brown et al. (2005) . In particular, our study is supportive of Krettenauer (2022) suggestions that moral identity could function well as a moderator of the influence of variables such as ethical leadership, on employee ethical behavior. In fact, we are among the few to demonstrate that moral identity per se enhances the positive impact of ethical leadership on subordinates ’ moral behavior, which advances the findings of Wang et al. (2021) , who reported that moral identity failed to strengthen the impact of ethical leadership on the prevention of unethical behavior, unless the subordinates involved also identified with the leader. Finally, our findings also combined with others suggesting that the moral identity of both subordinates ( Wang et al., 2021 ) and leaders ( Zhu et al., 2016 ) could be involved in the successful practice of ethical leadership and add to the literature by identifying ethical leadership as part of the group of motivators of moral conduct ( Aquino et al., 2011 ) whose effect is amplified among employees with a high moral identity. Specifically, we advance existing research ( Aquino et al., 2009, Aquino et al., 2011 ) showing that a situation that primes moral schemas (i.e., witnessing acts of moral goodness) increases the cognitive accessibility of a person ’ s moral identity towards favoring prosocial behaviors engagement. We advance these findings by showing that supervisors ’ ethical leadership promotes employees ’ ethical behavior, a type of behavior that differs from the former (prosocial), in that it refers to behaviors consistent with societal or organizational norms that do not exceed formal requirements or are necessarily oriented towards benefitting third parties. This study also furthers our understanding of the important role of employee self-control in the use of ethical leadership by managers. We demonstrate that subordinates ’ self-control per se helps supervisors ’ ethical leadership have a more powerful impact on their ethical behavior. Although new to the literature, this finding is consistent with SCT ( Bandura, 1991 ), as it proves that self-regulating mechanisms (i.e., self-control) play a crucial role in adopting a behavior that produces the rewarding and expected outcomes provided by the perceived environ - ment (i.e., ethical leadership, cf., Bandura, 1991; Brown et al., 2005 ). (2019) , who showed that managers ’ self-control puts their own moral character (internal ethics-related expectations leading one to act morally well) into action, as manifested in developing ethical leadership. Further - more, it is complementary to that of Sosik et al. (2019) , as we reveal that self-control also puts external ethics-expectations provided by the context (ethical leadership) into action, as manifested in behaviors consistent with such (ethical) expectations. Finally, we are the first to propose and demonstrate the joint effects of moral identity and self-control among subordinates and extend pre - vious experimental work involving college students in which self-control was an underlying mechanism that helped account for the relationship between students ’ moral identity and whether or not they engaged in cheating ( Rua, Lawter, & Andreassi, 2017 ). Our demonstration of this three-way interaction effect aligns well with Aquino and Reed (2002) , who suggested that moral identity could be less impactful on ethical behavior when self-regulatory mechanisms are lacking. The role of self- control here (in combination with moral identity) is unsurprising as the importance we attach to moral identity can vary from moment to moment, be displaced by other aspects of self-identity ( Aquino et al., 2009 ) and vary across social contexts ( Krettenauer & Hertz, 2015 ). Thus, although moral values form the foundation of one ’ s self-concept and infuse strong commitment to actions that promote such moral values ( Zhu et al., 2011; Ete et al., 2020 ), the appropriate management of tempting situations – situations in which an individual finds a conflict with the values that define their self-concept – will require exercising choice and volition to avoid giving into them ( Rua et al., 2017 ). Thus, as proven, for such moral identity to be manifested in specific behaviors, the control of the impulse to resist the diversity of beliefs on view and the discipline to follow internal or external regulations is critical ( Sosik et al., 2019 ). In all, our findings, combined with others (for moral identity, see Aquino et al., 2009, 2011; Li et al., 2022; O ’ Keefe et al., 2019 , for self- control, see Sosik et al., 2019 ), suggest that self-control and moral identity are an important consideration in the functioning of ethical leadership for both leaders and subordinates. Moreover, our findings reveal that, as these variables are self-regulators, each of them acts as a substitute for the other, thus exercising a similar strengthening size ef - fect for the expected positive impact of ethical leadership on employee ’ s ethical behavior (see Fig. 5 ); for example, in high moral identity and low self-control situations, this finding confirms previous research indicating moral identity serves as a resource stock that helps restrain self- interested desires, even when self-control is depleted ( Gino et al., 2011; Joosten et al., 2014 ). Notwithstanding the above, our findings reveal that the combined effect of both self-regulators yields the stron - gest effect of ethical leadership on employee ethical behavior, given that self-control is a moral muscle ( Baumeister & Exline, 1999 ) that facili - tates adhesion to moral values (i.e., moral identity) under challenging conditions. Finally, our findings reveal that the positive effect of ethical leadership could be greatly reduced when employee self-control and moral identity are simultaneously low, which could explain why Kim ’ s (2022) meta -analysis yielded null effects of ethical leadership on sub - ordinate ethical behavior. Thus, we show that, for the social learning mechanism involved in linking ethical leadership to ethical employee behavior ( Bedi et al., 2016 ), self-regulation is critical ( Bandura, 1977 ). Indeed, unethical behavior is likely to occur when self-regulatory mechanisms are deactivated ( Trevi ño et al., 2014 ), and, despite the learning process expected to emerge from the ethical role modeling of ethical leaders, subordinates with low moral identity and low self- control will likely find ways to shrink from responsibility for unethical behavior or will be unable to exert willpower to resist temptations to engage in unethical behavior. 5.2. Managerial implications Our core finding that harnessing the full benefit of ethical leadership requires attention be paid to both leaders and their subordinates has important practical implications, i.e., the optimal effect cannot be ob - tained by focusing on leader behavior only. Thus, for example, employee selection systems across hierarchical levels should include components (via interviews, personality tests, etc.) that are potentially reflective of moral identity. For example, personality tests including HEXACO ( Ashton & Lee, 2009 ) have components that assess honesty and humil - ity. Although our study addressed subordinates ’ moral identity, the construct is also relevant to the selection of leaders ( Wang & Hackett, 2020 ). Zhu et al. (2016) found, for example, that leaders ’ self-rated moral identity was positively related to their use of ethical leadership as judged by subordinates. Relatedly, concerning the importance of leader selection, their level of ethical conviction (as perceived by sub - ordinates) moderated the link between their use of ethical leadership and subordinates ’ organizational citizenship behavior ( Babalola, Stouten, Camps, & Euwema, 2019 ). Again, both leader and subordinate characteristics need to be considered in the functioning of ethical leadership. The HR function should also implement efforts to foster the effective use of ethical leadership. More broadly, the training agenda should include building awareness of the cardinal moral virtues (e.g., courage, temperance, justice, prudence) which provide a strong foundation for moral identity among subordinates ( Wang & Hackett, 2020 ). Training and development must be followed up by effective performance man - agement in which there are consequences for (un)ethical behavior, which is embedded within the practice of ethical leadership ( Table 3 , EL2). Some have argued this is crucial in accounting for the link between ethical leadership and subordinates ’ moral behavior ( Nassif et al., 2021 ), although others have also suggested that leader behaviors that promote ethics are more effective than those that focus on preventing unethical behavior ( Bush, Welsh, Baer, & Waldman, 2021 ). Beyond the behaviors associated with individual leader-subordinate dyads, moral identity can be fostered by building a supportive normative organizational culture ( Wang & Hackett, 2020 ). Ethical leaders, by acting as moral managers and being moral persons ( Brown & Trevi ño, 2006 ), signal that ethical behavior is highly expected, thus constituting key sources of information for others regarding the appropriate values to follow. However, they also help shape the work climate, that is, the shared perceptions of those aspects of the work environment that inform members about which behaviors will be supported ( Ruiz-Palomino & Linuesa-Langreo, 2018; Zhu et al., 2019 ). Thus, company-wide slogans and symbols can make moral concerns salient to employees ( Aquino et al., 2009 ), and corporate responsibility initiatives ( Wang & Hackett, 2020 ), policies and procedures that send a moral message, as well as codes of ethics, hotlines and ombudspersons may also be helpful in this regard. Regarding the role of self-control, although it can help prevent people from acting unethically, it can be easily depleted when over- exercised, although self-control can be replenished by designing jobs in a manner that fosters autonomy ( Lian et al., 2017 ). Nonetheless, reasonable goals must also be involved as over-work associated with fatigue is linked to diminished self-control ( Gino et al., 2011; Trevi ño et al., 2014 ). Thus, even in high pressure environments such as Google, employees are encouraged to take relaxing daily lunch breaks in which they are free to engage in hobbies or sports ( Johnson, Muraven, Dolandson, & Lin (J.), 2017 ), and/or use company-provided sleep pods for naps ( Yam et al., 2017 ). Thus, Google exemplifies the manner in which a supportive organizational culture provides a context in which employees feel free to exercise self-control in the promotion of moral behavior. 5.3. Limitations and future research directions Our study has design limitations that suggest future research ideas. For example, as noted, the nature of the relationships that interested us required many of the key constructs be collected from subordinates. H. Al Halbusi et al. Journal of Business Research 165 (2023) 114044 15 Although they were the single most appropriate source for the variables of interest, CMV could have artificially inflated the relationships observed. Nonetheless, our one-factor test findings and our time-lagged research design suggested that CMV was not a serious issue (Podsakoff et al., 2003, 2012). However, further research could use leaders’ as - sessments of subordinates’ self-control and/or ratings of ethical lead - ership reported by superiors or peers. Although the collection of leaders’ judgements of subordinates’ ethical behavior was separated in time from our independent variables, our study does not allow for strong causal inferences because other uncontrolled mechanisms could have influenced the findings. For example, Bedi et al. (2016) and Zhu et al. (2019) indicated that the degree of the impact associated with ethical leadership may vary with societal culture. In our case, Iraq is characterized by strong cultural religiosity (Moaddel & Karabenik, 2010) which could underlie sub - ordinates’ levels of moral identity, self-control, and ethical behavior. Such a strong adherence to religious values could have made our re - spondents report a stronger moral identity, which, combined with the strong power distance, collectivism and uncertainty avoidance in this country (Center, 1967-2010), could have explained the strengthening role of moral identity we found. In effect, in a society with a strong power distance and uncertainty avoidance, employees expect to be told what to do and need a behavioral guide to know “how” to behave in unknown situations (Center, 1967-2010). Furthermore, in a strong collectivistic culture, individuals may be more influenced by the clues provided by others (Center, 1967-2010). Thus, in Iraq, a supervisor who is a role model of ethical behavior is likely to have a powerful influence, especially among religious persons that adhere to moral values per se. Future research could therefore replicate our study in countries where religiosity is less important (Moaddel & Karabenik, 2010) or where the culture differs from that of Iraq (e.g., the US, where power distance, collectivism or uncertainty avoidance are low, Center, 1967-2010). In all, we agree with Wang et al. (2021) that cross-cultural research is called for to refine the role of person-related factors in the functioning of ethical leadership. In addition, we used the scale proposed by Brown et al. (2005) to measure ethical leadership in a Middle Eastern culture such as Iraq. However, future replication studies could use other scales (see Zhu et al., 2019) that have demonstrated high reliability in both Western and Eastern cultures, as well as efficacy in capturing additional nuances of ethical leadership (e.g., moral cognition, creating a moral atmosphere). Furthermore, the scale we used to measure ethical behavior was built from a U.S. perspective, although it has shown similar mean ratings in other different cultural contexts (e.g., Israel, Izraeli, 1988, Russia, Deshpande et al., 2000; Uganda, Ntayi et al., 2010), indicating its suit - ability for use in our study. Notwithstanding, future research could use newer measures for the dependent variable in this study, such as orga - nizational citizenship behavior (OCB, voluntary behavior aimed at benefiting the organization and/or its members, e.g., altruism, cf., Lee & Allen, 2002) or deviant behavior (voluntary behavior directed at harming the organization and/or its members, e.g., theft, cf. Bennett & Robinson, 2000), which are treated as opposites. Future research could benefit from their combined inclusion to reveal whether significant differences arise regarding either the findings of this study or the outcome targeted (i.e., deviant behavior vs OCB), which could give a more comprehensive view of the role of the relationships hypothesized in this study. Additionally, since our hypotheses were tested in a single Iraqi public organization, we recommend testing them across other public organizations so a broader understanding can be obtained. Moreover, future research should use private industries, as they may encompass distinct policies in terms of bureaucracy and innovation (Bysted & Hansen, 2015) as well as in the induction of tension to fulfill established targets, which could engender more situations where self- control is depleted. Finally, our research model ignored the potential mediating mech - anisms that, drawing on SLT (Bandura, 1977), might underlie the relationship between supervisor ethical leadership and subordinates’ ethical behavior. For example, one’s social interactions with an ethical leader who enacts mastery and psychological arousal in others promote employee self-efficacy –the belief one can engage in a behavior successfully– (Bedi et al., 2016), which has been positively related to ethical behavior (Owens et al., 2019). In addition, in line with SLT (Bandura, 1977), ethical leaders, who behave in an ethical manner and formulate policies that reinforce ethical behavior, serve as informational guides for acceptable behavior and help shape an ethical work climate (Bedi et al., 2016), through which ethical behavior is enhanced (Al Halbusi et al., 2021). Thus, future studies should test our model by including ethical climate or self-efficacy as mechanisms by which employee ethical behavior is enhanced. Even in the case of ethical climate, further research could substitute the role of ethical leadership in our model to determine whether employees’ moral identity and self- control may strengthen the impact of an ethical climate on their ethical behavior. 6. Conclusions Much research has been conducted on the benefits of ethical lead - ership on the ethical behavior of employees. However, fewer studies examine the conditions that make this impact as effective as possible. Based on SLT and SCT, our research elucidates that the subordinates’ possession of two person-related variables (moral identity, self-control), which encompass a self-regulatory function, not only separately enhance the effects of ethical leadership, but together help to maximize the effect. Thus, managers should be aware that strategies to promote the ethical quality of their organizations need to focus not only on having ethical leaders but also on having a human resource base with the most suitable characteristics to heighten the effects of these leaders. The influence of organisational justice and ethical leadership on employees’ innovation behaviour Pinghao Ye and Liqiong Liu Wuhan Business University, Wuhan, China, and Joseph Tan Information Systems, McMaster University, Hamilton, Canada Abstract Purpose – This paper aims to explore the influence of organisational justice (including distributional justice, procedural justice and interactional justice) and ethical leadership on employees’innovation behaviour and to analyse the role of ethical leadership in regulating the relationship between organisational justice and employees’ innovation behaviour. Design/methodology/approach – This paper explores the key factors affecting employees’ innovation behaviour from three forms of organisational justice (distributional justice, procedural justice and interactional justice) and ethical leadership. The questionnaire survey method is used to survey Chinese industrial workers. A total of 323 valid questionnaires are collected, and the model is verified by SmartPLS. Findings – The study found that distributional justice and interactional justice in organisational justice had a significant positive influence on employees’innovation behaviour. Ethical leadership had a significant positive influence on employees’innovation behaviour and interactional justice. At the same time, ethical leadership has a significant regulatory effect on the relationship between interactional justice and employees’ innovation behaviour. The study also found that procedural justice had a significant positive influence on distributional justice and interactional justice. Research limitations/implications– This paper is limited to industrial workers in Hubei, China, and the research objects need further expansion. In terms of research methods, future research will use other laboratory research methods, combining experimental environments with real-world situations, enhancing the scientific nature of research methods and increasing the credibility of research results. Practical implications– In management practice, organisations can take various measures to improve the interaction level of employees, improve employees’ perception of organisational distribution justice by establishing a scientific distribution system, give full play to the role of ethical leadership, implement more ethical management and stimulate employees’ innovation behaviour. Originality/value – This research theorises the relationship between distributional justice, interactional justice and employees’ innovation behaviour and enriches the research system of employees’ innovation behaviour. At the same time, it examines the regulatory effect of ethical leadership on the relationship between interactional justice and employees’ innovation behaviour, which helps enrich the mechanism of ethical leadership affecting employees’innovation behaviour path. It clarifies the mechanism of the interaction among distributional justice, procedural justice and interactional justice and expands the research theory of organisational justice. Background 2.1 Organisational justice The concept of organisational justice originates from the social exchange theory proposed by Homans (1958), which refers to individuals in the process of social exchange, expecting a fair distribution of effort and gain.Niehoff and Moorman (1993)divided the organisational justice scale into three dimensions, including (1) distributional justice, which refers to the degree to which employees perceive whether their work tasks and salary distribution methods are fair; (2) procedural justice, which means the degree to which employees perceive whether the organisation’s decision-making procedures and processes are fair; (3) interactional justice is the degree to which employees perceive whether the interactive communication of organisational leaders in the decision-making process is fair. Bies and Moag (1986) first proposed the concept of Interactional Justice based on Distribution Equity Theory, that is, members’ perception of interpersonal interaction and communication during the operation of the organisation. The previous discussion ignored the interpersonal relationship, that is, the latter defined interactional justice and only studied the interpersonal relationship as one of the contents of procedural justice. Thereafter, scholars have conducted several explorations on whether interactional justice can be used as a justice dimension (Bies and Moag, 1986 ). Greenberg (1990) believed that procedural justice, distributional justice and interactional justice are three independent dimensions, which have different correlations with other variables and will independently affect people’s behaviour and attitude. Suzanne et al. (2000) proposed that organisational justice is a three-dimensional structure, and interactional justice is an independent dimension. Colquitt et al. (2001) subdivided interactional justice into interpersonal justice and information justice, and the fourdimensional theory of organisational justice took shape. Later, an increasing number of empirical research results support this view. Interpersonal justice means that managers in the organisation treat employees with enthusiasm, and they treat and respect the needs of each individual (Seepma et al., 2021). Information justice means that managers can convey effective information to employees, explain the relevant procedures and results of the organisation and inform individuals of the reasons and results of this distribution procedure (Colquitt, 2012). Most scholars generally regard interactional justice as the subjective feelings of employees, that is, the perception of justice among members of the organisation about themselves, their colleagues and leaders in the decision-making execution process, interpersonal communication and handling procedures (Gursoy et al.,2 0 1 3; King et al.,2 0 1 7). On the basis of the research of scholars such as Greenberg and Colquitt, combined with the Chinese cultural context, this paper defines the interactional justice of employees as the perception of justice in the interaction between individual employees, especially the perception of justice in interaction with superiors in information transmission and feedback. Ethical leadership refers to the behaviour that leaders show ethical behaviour in their own behaviour and interpersonal communication and stimulate the innovation activities of subordinates via two-way communication, strengthening and decision-making activities (Nazir et al., 2021). Ethical leaders affect the moral behaviour and concepts of employees through their own moral behaviour and concepts and are the model for organisation members to emulate when facing moral dilemmas (Shafique et al., 2020a). Given that ethical leadership has the characteristics of multiple types of leadership, it has received extensive attention from scholars in recent years. Ethical leadership is closely related to employees’active and positive behaviour and is an important factor in promoting employees’ remonstrance and reducing silent behaviour (Liu et al., 2021). Employees’innovation behaviour is a proactive and positive behaviour. Providing suggestions, proactively reporting problems, extra work effort and work commitment and admonition behaviour are the positive behaviours in the innovation process of employees. Leaders are the core elements of an organisation, and their values and behaviour will directly affect the ethical atmosphere of the organisation and the beliefs and behaviour of employees (Ariail et al., 2021). Leaders need to emphasise“ethical thinking” in management because morality has a central position in leadership activities, and leaders who cannot meet ethical requirements in behaviour are not true leaders at all (Banks et al., 2021). In recent years, the concept of ethical leadership has further highlighted the importance of ethics to leadership. Ethical leaders will not only generate more appropriate and ethical behaviours themselves but also encourage followers to ensure that their behaviours meet ethical standards through continuous interaction, effective communication and correct decisionmaking among employees (Ilyas et al., 2020). Research model Distributional justice refers to employees’ perception of the fairness of the organisation’s distribution results. Employees always compare their efforts with their rewards (Kim et al., 2017). The distributional justice of the organisation conveys a message to employees that “more efforts will have more returns”, which affects employees’ attitude and investment in work. When employees feel that the distributional justice of the organisation is high, employees tend to invest more in work. When employees feel that the organisation does not pay attention to fair distribution, they tend to reduce their investment in work (Velez and Neves, 2017). When employees have autonomy in their work, that is, employees can decide how much effort they make for their work, the external reward of“more work, more pay” is a positive feedback for employees; the latter makes employees feel that their work will be recognised and stimulates their sense of job competence (Raub and Liao, 2012). Thus, it improves work motivation, and employees tend to invest more in work, which will promote the generation of active innovation behaviour. Conversely, when employees perceive a low sense of distributional justice, that is, the distribution of remuneration and rewards is not based on the actual level of work performance, individuals will experience tension and will eliminate it by reducing independent behaviours outside their roles. Doing so will damage employees’ initiative, which will reduce the dynamic basis of active work and damage their work motivation. Discussion and conclusion 6.1 Discussion of findings This paper analyses the factors affecting innovation behaviour from two aspects: ethical leadership and organisational justice. The following key conclusions are drawn. Firstly, distributional justice and interactional justice in organisational justice have a significant positive influence on employees’ innovation behaviour. However, the impact of procedural justice on employees’innovation behaviour has not been confirmed. Apparently, distributional justice and interactional justices are important driving forces for employees’ work attitudes and behaviours. Distributional justice can protect employees’ personal interests, mainly manifested in the fact that employees can determine how much work they invest in according to established distribution principles. Long-term deviations in their attitudes towards the company may lead to psychological imbalances and a decline in work passion, which are not conducive to stimulating innovation behaviours (Altuna et al., 2015; Rita Silva and Caetano, 2014). Interactional justice can better reflect the emotional evaluation and justice perception of the members in the organisation to the superior managers. Interactional justice has important value in the communication of organisational content (Bansal, 2017). If the organisation has surplus resources and actively supports the work of employees, employees will form a high emotional attachment to the organisation, they are willing to advance and retreat with the organisation, maintain the image of the company proactively and carry out more innovative works consciously. 5.5 5 4.5 4 3.5 3 Low High Low Ethical Leadership Medium Ethical Leadership High Ethical Leadership Interactional Justice Innovation Behaviour Figure 2. The results show that ethical leadership can make employees feel at ease and make bold innovations in the process of employee innovation behaviour management; moreover, the leaders’ good demonstration and guiding role of ethical norms can fully stimulate employees’innovative ability (Wahid and Mohd. Mustamil, 2017). At the same time, ethical leaders will attach importance to the establishment of honest and mutual trust relationships with employees. Employees can perceive the integrity, ability and kindness of ethical leaders and will not worry that ethical leaders will give unbalanced and unfair punishment when taking risky behaviours such as advice and innovation (Anser et al., 2020; Gotsis and Kortezi, 2013). Therefore, ethical leadership is the most important factor affecting employees’ innovation behaviours in the organisational environment. When employees perceive that ethical leadership supports innovation behaviours, their psychological security will largely be enhanced. Thirdly, procedural justice has a significant positive influence on distributional justice and interactional justice. The research results show that procedural justice, as an information tool reflecting the social status of employees in the organisation, plays a positive role in regulating the internal psychological state of individual employees and can affect individual employees’work attitudes and behaviours for a long time (Bansal, 2017; Lee et al., 2017). At the same time, procedural justice allows employees to feel the respect of the organisation, thereby enhancing their psychological security. When employees are affirmed and supported by the organisation, their psychological security will improve, which can encourage employees to express their opinions and suggestions freely and to participate in the various decision-making processes of the organisation (Arn/C19eguy et al., 2020). Therefore, procedural justice is a supportive organisational environment that has a significant positive impact on the distributional and interactional justice that employees perceive. 6.2 Practical implications This study presents key practical implications for managers, working professionals and academics. The current research indicates that innovative work behaviour in the workplace is less inclined to emerge if the organization does not focus on developing ethical leadership among managers. Findings demonstrate tha t ethical leadership positively impacts employees’ innovative work behaviour. Therefore, managers could use the essence of ethical leadership to improve employees’ innovative work behaviour in the organizational justice context. Ethical leaders on the foundation of optimism and enthusiasm provide intellectual ingredients, make themselves readily available to support their followers and encourage them to work differently to discharge tasks. Firstly, the significant positive influence of interactional justice on employees’innovation behaviour is considered. Organisations can take a variety of measures to improve the level of employee interaction, encourage employees to participate in collective activities, enhance their sense of collective honour and promote emotional exchanges and communication between employees by organising team entertainment activities or conducting team cooperation projects to improve the quality of emotional communication among employees, enhance their sense of team identity and ultimately inspire their innovation behaviour. Secondly, distributional justice has a significant positive influence on employees ’ innovation behaviour. Finally, according to the significant positive influence of ethical leadership on employees’ innovation behaviour, ethical leaders must not only demonstrate good ethical behaviours to all the employees in corporate management practices but must also strive to be more patient, fairer and more concerned with employees whilst frequently listening to their voices. Leaders should not only be ethical but must also implement ethical management to meet the high standard requirements of employees for ethical leadership. 6.3 Theoretical implications In addition to the practical contributions, the study offers important theoretical implications. Compared with past studies (Duan et al., 2018; Javed et al., 2018), this study proposed and tests that ethical leadership and organizational justice are important predictors of creativity. The findings answer“how” ethical leadership and organizational justice influence creativity, thus explaining the underlying mechanisms through which ethical leadership and organizational justice promote creativity. First of all, this study theorises the relationship among distributional justice, interactional justice and employees’innovation behaviour and supplements the theoretical research on the antecedent variables of employees’ innovation behaviour. Following the analysis of the impact mechanism of organisational justice on employees’innovation behaviour, it continues to enrich the research system of employees’ innovation behaviour. Secondly, from the perspective of social identity theory, this study brings ethical leadership into the research of innovation behaviour and investigates the impact of ethical leadership on employees’innovation behaviour. Meanwhile, it examines the regulatory effect of ethical leadership on the relationship between interactional justice and employees’ innovation behaviour, which helps enrich the mechanism of ethical leadership affecting employees’ innovation behaviour path. Finally, this paper discusses the relationship among distributional justice, procedural justice and interactional justice and clarifies the mechanism of the interaction among them, which is helpful when analysing the internal relationship among the three dimensions when the different dimensions of organisational justice have an impact on the innovation behaviour of employees. It further expands the research theory of organisational justice. 7. Limitations and future research directions Firstly, given that organisational justice is the subjective perception of employees, the internal perceptions of organisational justice and objective organisational justice are usually different. The questionnaire survey method used in this paper is the most commonly used research method by scholars. To reduce the problem of homology variance, future research will adopt other laboratory research methods, combine the experimental environment with the actual situation, enhance the scientificity of the research methods and improve the credibility of the research results. Secondly, the research samples in this paper are all from Hubei Province, China. Whether the research conclusions are suitable for enterprises in other countries and regions needs further exploration. Future research will collect data from multiple countries or regions to improve the universality of the research conclusions. At the same time, the author will attempt to investigate other types of enterprises and organisations within a larger sample range to further examine the findings of this paper. Finally, this paper only explores the three factors in organisational justice, i.e. distributional justice, procedural justice and interactional justice. Linking ethical leadership to followers’ innovative work behavior in Pakistan: the vital roles of psychological safety and proactive personality Israr Ahmad College of Management, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China Yongqiang Gao School of Management, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China Fangguo Su College of Management, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China, and Muhammad Kamran Khan School of Management, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China Abstract Purpose – This study examines the link between ethical leadership and innovative work behavior. Also, drawing on the substitute for leadership theory, this study investigates the role of a follower’s proactive personality in the relationship between ethical leadership and innovative work behavior (IWB). Similarly, this study further explores the role of psychological safety in this relationship. Design/methodology/approach – The data for this study were collected from software development companies based in Islamabad, Pakistan. A total of 240 employees and their immediate supervisors were asked to participate in this study. Processes Macro and Amos were used to assess study hypotheses. Findings – Using data from software companies in Pakistan, this study found that ethical leadership can be effective to enhance IWB in followers whose proactive personality is low, while this effect is limited in high proactive individuals. Furthermore, psychological safety mediates the main effect of ethical leadership on IWB as well as the interactive effect between ethical leadership and follower’s proactive personality on IWB. Originality/value – This study is among the first to investigate the moderating role of employees’proactive personality in the relationship between ethical leadership and followers’ IWB. Secondly, draws on the substitute for leadership perspective, this study explains that how the role of ethical leadership can be less effective for high proactive individuals or how individual characteristics can substitute leadership behavior. Thirdly, this study deepens our understanding of the mechanisms linking ethical leadership to IWB by exploring the role of psychological safety as a mediator. Finally, our research is based on data collected from Pakistan might also add some new insights to the existing west-dominated literature. IWB is a complex work phenomenon, involving multiple risks and difficulties, and thus requires effective leadership to gain its benefits (Anderson et al., 2014). The importance of leadership in firm innovation has been well and generally suggested by management scholars. For instance, Waterman and Peters (1982)upheld that the main attributes of excellent companies are innovation, employee empowerment and decentralized control. All these attributes are likely to be associated with effective leadership. Similarly,Druker (1985)treated innovation as one of the key factors to organizational effectiveness, and a vital attribute of entrepreneurial behavior in the ever-changing business environment, and suggested that leadership (entrepreneurship) plays a crucial role in the success of firm innovations. More recently, Tu and Lu (2013)in their study explored the relationship between ethical leadership and employees’IWB in the Chinese context and found that ethical leadership has a positive effect on IWB through intrinsic motivation. Despite the work ofTu and Lu (2013)and the general arguments made by some management scholars, our knowledge about when and how ethical leadership may affect followers’IWB is still rather limited. In this work, we aim to contribute to the ethical leadership– IWB literature by considering the underlying mechanism of employees’psychological safety. Furthermore, recent studies showed that ethical leadership may be less effective in certain contexts (Babalola et al., 2019; Goket al., 2017) and the positive impact of ethical leadership may be dependent upon other factors such as individual proactive personality. Thus, based on substitute for leadership theory this study further investigates the moderating effect of proactive personality. This may act as an important step to deepen our understanding of when and how ethical leadership may enhance employees’ IWB. On the basis of the study ofTu and Lu (2013)and given the characteristics of an ethical leader such as being people-oriented, promoting autonomy, emphasizing morality and encourage speaking up in followers, we first propose that ethical leadership is positively associated with followers’ IWB. Furthermore, existing studies on IWB have shown that employees will more likely to engage in innovative work when they perceive that participation in risk-taking activities is encouraged and that failure will not bring any negative repercussions (Kessel et al., 2012; Newmanet al., 2017a). The psychological state having the characteristics of no risk and/or uncertainty related to the voicing of opinion, proposing new ideas and solutions is referred to psychological safety (Edmondson et al., 2004). This study argues that considering the inherent risks and uncertainty associated with an innovative process, employees look toward their leader as an essential resource to manage risks associated with it and to avoid future repercussions (Tu et al., 2019). Ethical leadership perception can be effective in cases like these as such leader is characterized to value truthful and honest relationships, promote interpersonal trust and mutual respect, which helps in enhancing employees’ psychological safety ( Walumbwa and Schaubroeck, 2009 ) and subsequently persuading them to participate in IWB. Therefore, we argue that employees’ perception of psychological safety is likely to bridge the relationship between ethical leadership and IWB. Likewise, prior studies have suggested that employees personality characteristics play an important role while responding to the leadership behavior (Guenter et al., 2017; Newman et al., 2017b) and thus critical in understanding the conditions in which ethical leadership can be less or more effective for some individuals (Taylor and Pattie, 2015).
