According to this perspective, some contextual factors such as employees’ characteristics can substitute or neutralize specific leader behavior by eliminating the need for leadership across situations (Gok et al., 2017). In general, proactive individuals are more likely to initiate proactive behaviors without waiting for a leader’s instructions in order to fix work-related problems (Li et al., 2013; Bateman and Crant, 1993); while less proactive individuals seek leadership directions to take initiatives and participate in risk-taking tasks (Guenter et al., 2017). Building on this, we contend that since employees with proactive personalities rely less on the instructions and directions from a leader, therefore proactive individuals will act as a substitute for perceived ethical leaders. Consequently, proactive employees will actively participate in risk-taking activities (such as IWB) regardless of ethical leader motivation, however vice versa for the low proactive employees. Individuals with proactive personalities are hardly constrained by situational forces to take initiative and participate in risk-oriented actions (Guenter et al., 2017), therefore for such individuals the impact of perceived ethical leadership on their risk-taking behavior (such as IWB) will be minimal. Hence, this study explores this important underlying mechanism of psychological safety in the relationship between ethical leadership and IWB as well as in the interactive effects of ethical leadership and proactive personality on IWB. This study attempts to make several contributions to the literature. First, this study deepens our understanding of the mechanisms linking ethical leadership to IWB by exploring the role of psychological safety as a mediator. Second, this study is among the first to investigate the moderating role of employees’ proactive personality in the relationship between ethical leadership and followers’ IWB, which offers support for the perspective of substitute for leadership. Finally, our research is based on data collected from Pakistan might also add some new insights to the existing west-dominated literature. Pakistan is a developing country with a Muslim-dominant population. Contrary to some Western countries, Pakistan shares a relatively high power distance and collectivistic culture (Hoftede et al., 2010). Hence, differences in cultural and economic conditions between most Western countries and Pakistan may provide an opportunity to elucidate the effects of ethical leadership on employees’ outcomes in contrasting conditions. Theory and hypotheses Ethical leadership and IWB Ethical leadership is defined as“the demonstration of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to followers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and decision-making” (Brown et al., 2005, p. 120). Two vital aspects of ethical leadership could be identified as“Moral Person” and “Moral Manager” (Trevi~no et al., 2000). Moral persons are fair, trustworthy, selfdisciplined and honest. Similarly, ethical leaders display the behaviors of moral managers by setting an excellent example, demonstrating ethical values, treating subordinates with care and reinforcing ethical standards with rewards and punishment (Brown et al., 2005). An ethical leader perceived to be strong in both moral person and moral manager aspects (Trevi~no et al., 2000), and a leader who is weak in either of the mentioned aspects will be perceived by employees as a hypocrite or a leader who does not care about ethics in the workplace (Brown and Mitchell, 2010). Ethical leadership is distinct from other similar leadership constructs (Ng and Feldman, 2015) and is perceived to be effective in promoting several behaviors and attitudes in followers such as organizational citizenship behavior, performance, voice, commitment and creativity, and deterring employees from negative Linking ethical leadership to followers’ IWB 757 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ejim/article-pdf/26/3/755/270745/ejim-11-2020-0464.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 moral behaviors such as counterproductive work behavior, deviance behavior and organizational incivility (see the review ofHartog, 2015). IWB refers to “individuals’ behaviors directed towards the initiation and intentional introduction of new and useful ideas, processes, products or procedures within a work role, group or organization” (De Jong, 2006, p. 19). IWB is a complex work behavior consisting of generation, promotion and implementation of new and useful ideas (Janssen, 2000; Scott and Bruce, 1994), thus different from creativity which only focuses on the generation of novel ideas (King and Anderson, 2002). IWB is very important for organizations for the reason that it facilitates product development ( Wu et al. , 2014 ), and positively contributes to organizational creativity, effectiveness and survival (Woodman et al., 1993). Given this importance, previous studies have examined numerous antecedents of IWB including job demands, job characteristics, group and organizational climate, personality and leadership (Anderson et al., 2014; Janssen, 2000; Scott and Bruce, 1994; Tu and Lu, 2013; Wuet al., 2014), among which the role of leadership is considered very prominent and important (Javed et al., 2019). Ethical leaders are perceived to advocate two-way communications and promote participation in decision-making processes, encourage followers to express their opinion and emphasize fair treatment (Neubert et al., 2009; Qi and Ming-Xia, 2014). These practices motivate employees to promote and implement new ideas (Javed et al., 2019; Tu and Lu, 2013). Besides, an ethical leader is the one who gives subordinates autonomy and control over their work (De Hoogh and Den Hartog, 2008; Piccoloet al., 2010), which allows subordinates to give inputs and make decisions about their work activities. Finally, perceived ethical leaders provide employees opportunities for the development of work-related skills and knowledge to enhance their abilities to innovate (Tu and Lu, 2013). When employees enjoy more freedom and accrue more ability to explore new ideas, they are more likely to engage in the IWB (Waterman and Peters, 1982). Thus, with the support of the above propositions and following Tu and Lu (2013)findings, we expect a positive relationship between ethical leadership and employees’ IWB. H1. Ethical leadership is positively related to employees’ IWB. The mediating role of psychological safety The high risks associated with IWB (Ellen et al., 2012) suggest that employees may not be willing to engage in it unless they feel that failures will not bring any negative repercussions. We expect that in such a situation ethical leadership can be effective in motivating employees to engage in IWB by shaping their psychological safety; a psychological state in which employees feel comfortable and safe to engage in interpersonal risks (Edmondson, 1999). According toKahn (1990), psychological safety is the state of mind in which employees feel safe to “show and employ one’s self without fear of negative consequences to self-image, status or career” (p. 708). The organizational environment will be perceived psychologically safe by an individual when others in the organization respond positively to their interpersonal risk-taking in the workplace, such as asking questions, admitting and reporting mistakes, seeking feedback and/or providing proactive ideas (Edmondson, 1999; Edmondson et al., 2004). The leadership role is always regarded as crucial in influencing followers’psychological safety (Frazier et al., 2017; Newmanet al., 2017a) because they serve as an important source that shapes their perception of the workplace. We expect that the behaviors displayed by an ethical leader can more likely motivate employees to engage in interpersonal risk-taking, show mutual respect and trust others in the organization (Brown et al., 2005; Chen and Hou, 2016; Qi and Ming-Xia, 2014). An ethical leader is characterized a one who’s caring, truthful, open and socially responsible and believes in two-way communication. Ethical leaders ensure EJIM 26,3 758 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ejim/article-pdf/26/3/755/270745/ejim-11-2020-0464.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 followers that their prime concerns are to serve employees’best interests (Brown et al., 2005). Previous studies draw on social learning theory (Bandura, 1977) exhibit that followers learn and try to emulate the behaviors displayed by ethical leaders (Brown et al., 2005; Menet al., 2020), as they are considered role models. Thus, when an ethical leader displays openness in communication and shows genuine concerns for followers, it helps in promoting mutual respect and interpersonal trust between leader and followers as well among followers themselves (Men et al., 2020), which is beneficial in shaping followers’ psychological safety. Moreover, the ethical leader through open communication ensures followers the importance of risk-taking behaviors and guarantee safety from any negative consequences if it leads to failure (Tu et al., 2019). It liberates followers from interpersonal risks and potential harms to their personal image (Men et al., 2020; Tuet al., 2019) and hence, motivate them to show more willingness to offer novel ideas because they have no fear from criticism for any possible failures (Detert and Burris, 2007). Empirical evidence suggests that employees with high psychological safety perceptions do not fear the expression of novel ideas and respectful disagreements, and thus engage more in creative behaviors ( Newman et al., 2017a; Roussin et al., 2016). Specifically, in a psychologically safe environment individual feel not threating from surrounding (i.e.... coworkers and leadership) and feel confident that experiment and taking the risk will not lead to their humiliation or denigration (Edmondson et al., 2004). Contrary to this, those who do not experience psychological safety is lacking confidence, and therefore be more defensive and feel unsafe to involve in risky tasks such as IWB (Javed et al., 2019). Interpersonal trust and mutual respect have been considered very helpful in promoting IWB among employees (Leung et al., 2014), which stems from psychological safety. As ethical leadership is considered an important factor to augment psychological safety (Men et al., 2020), and psychological safety is proved a strong precursor to IWB (Leung et al., 2014). Therefore, in light of these propositions, this study suggests that psychological safety acts as a mediator in the relationship between ethical leadership and IWB. H2. Psychological safety mediates the relationship between ethical leadership and followers’ IWB. The moderating role of proactive personality Prior research has widely supported the effectiveness of ethical leadership on employee outcomes, and in a similar way, our initial hypothesis argued its association with employees’ IWB. However, recent studies showed that ethical leadership can be irrelevant or less impactful in across certain situations and therefore interesting to be considered (Babalola et al., 2019; Gok et al., 2017). According to substitute for leadership perspective, some contextual factors (individual, task and organizational) may substitute or negate the effects of leadership (Kerr and Jermier, 1978). The substitute in this model is referred to something or someone that mitigates the leadership ability to influence subordinates’ behaviors or/and attitudes (Podsakoff et al., 1993). In other words, substitutes for leadership replace the leader’s influence by eliminating the need for leadership (Gok et al., 2017). Following this line of argument, Gok et al.(2017) found that for individuals with high moral awareness the ethical behavior of a leader will be largely redundant, however, will be effective for those who are low on moral awareness. Thus, based on these arguments and relying on substitute for leadership framework (Dionne et al., 2002; Kerr and Jermier, 1978), we propose followers’ proactive personality as a potential characteristic that may act as a substitute for ethical leadership on its effects on followers’ IWB. According toBateman and Crant (1993), proactive personality represents an individual “who is relatively unconstrained by situational forces and who effects environmental changes” (p. 105). Proactive employees are self-directed, self-reliant and continue efforts to bring change in the organization (Guenter et al., 2017; Morrisonet al., 2015). Employees with proactive personality are less susceptible to social influences (Guenter et al., 2017) and experience more control in work over time (Li et al., 2014). They initiate more proactive behaviors and rely less on cues originated from the leadership in fixing work-related problems (Li et al., 2013). Therefore, we argue that individuals with proactive personality will act as a substitute for ethical leadership as such employees are highly motivated to participate in activities that bring positive change in the organization (Li et al., 2010). As we discussed earlier, employees with proactive personality demonstrate stable character which is mostly unaffected by situational forces (Bateman and Crant, 1993). Therefore, it is argued that the interactive effect of ethical leadership and proactive personality on IWB via psychological safety will be stronger and significant for low proactive individuals as ethical leaders encourage them to involve in interpersonal risk-taking and voice their concerns (Qi and Ming-Xia, 2014; Tu and Lu, 2013 ), but vice versa for individuals with proactive personality. Thus, we hypothesize that: H4. The interactive effect of ethical leadership and proactive personality on followers’ IWB is mediated by followers’ psychological safety. Method Sample and procedure The data for this study were collected fromseven software development companies based in Islamabad, Pakistan. A total of 240 employees and their immediate supervisors were asked to participate in this study. Access to the participants w as gained through companies ’human resource officers. Additionally, utilizing substitute for leadership theory, this study hypothesized that the positive relationship between ethical leadership and IWB is contingent upon subordinates’ proactive personality such that the proactive personality of subordinates weakens this association. The personality psychology researchers argue that the behavior of individuals is contingent on the environmental situation, and their behaviors are sensitive to situational cues (Denissen and Penke, 2008). In the case of proactive personality, less proactive individuals are more susceptible to social cues (Morrison et al., 2015), especially those cues that signal risks or lack of risks (Guenter et al., 2017). Therefore, the positive effect of ethical leadership on IWB will be weakened for subordinates with proactive personality; such that those who are proactive by nature will involve in IWB regardless of the level of ethical leadership behavior displayed by their supervisor (Guenter et al., 2017). The findings of the present study empirically supported the proposed relationships. Further, this study tested the moderated mediation model, such that the interactive effect of ethical leadership and proactive personality on IWB was mediated by psychological safety. The findings of the study indicate that the indirect effect of ethical leadership on IWB through psychological safety is stronger for those employees who are low in proactive personality, while it is weak and insignificant for employees with proactive personality. Theoretical implications This study makes several contributions to the existing literature on ethical leadership and employees’IWB. With existing empirical evidence which emphasized the importance of ethical leadership in promoting employees’positive attitude and behavior such as IWB, there are calls for the need to understand the linking mechanisms and boundary conditions (Babalola et al., 2019; Tu et al.,2 0 1 9). Thus, responding to the call, our study proposed and tested the relationship between ethical leadership and IWB, as well as its linking mechanism of psychological safety. The characteristics of an ethical leader such as openness in communication, caring and showing genuine concerns for followers help promote mutual respect and interpersonal (Brown et al., 2005; Chen and Hou, 2016; Qi and Ming-Xia, 2014) that shapes followers’ psychological safety (Tu et al., 2019). With psychological safety, employees feel safe to express themselves, point out problems, give suggestions and new ideas, which helps to assist the employees in indulging in IWB (Leung et al., 2014). This study proposed and found that the relationship between ethical leadership and IWB is contingent on subordinates’ proactive personality. Based on the substitute to leadership perspective (Kerr and Jermier, 1978), this study proposed subordinates’ proactive personality as a substitute to ethical leadership. This study found that subordinates engage more in IWB when ethical leadership is paired with a low proactive personality of subordinates, but not for those who are high in proactive personality. This suggests that proactive personality gets additional importance for employees when working under low ethical leadership. The proactive employees are being relatively unconstrained by situational forces, and they are self-reliant, self-directed and determined to bring change in the organization (Guenter et al., 2017), which makes them respond more positively to the environment regardless if it suggests otherwise. Furthermore, our results are consistent with previous studies’ findings for other positive leadership styles such as transformational leadership and authentic leadership (e.g. Li et al., 2013; Guenter et al., 2017). In addition to this, our study also investigated the moderated mediation model, such that the interactive effect of ethical leadership and proactive personality on IWB was mediated by psychological safety. Lastly, by testing our assumptions in Pakistan, we provided additional empirical evidence from a developing country to the usefulness of ethical leadership in promoting IWB among employees. Although the effectiveness of ethical leadership is well-studied in Western societies, such studies are scarce in emerging economies like Pakistan. In opposite to Western societies, Pakistan is high in collectivism and power distance orientation (Hoftede et al., 2010), as well as having a Muslim-dominant population and therefore it isn’t easy to literally assume that ethical leadership will be equally effective in societies like Pakistan. However, our results provided direct evidence for the generalizability and applicability of the ethical leadership construct in developing countries, at least in Pakistan. Thus, this study’s findings deepen our understanding about the effectiveness of ethical leadership across social cultures and different development levels of countries. Practical implications Our study also offers important practical implications for managers. First, our findings along with that ofTu and Lu (2013), suggest that ethical leadership behavior facilitates IWB in employees, at least in emerging economies such as China and Pakistan. IWB is very helpful for organizational success in the rapidly changing and highly competitive marketplace (Barsh et al., 2008). Therefore, organizations need to provide a work environment to employees that encourage IWB. Furthermore, leaders need to display an ethical behavior in the organization by treating employees fairly and in ethical manner, and practice ethical role modeling to motivate subordinates. Our study findings show that ethical leadership is very effective in enhancing IWB in subordinates, therefore, organizations need to cultivate ethical leadership behavior for better results. Second, our findings suggest that ethical leadership is more effective for employees with lower proactive personality, because less proactive individuals are more reliant and susceptible to leader-derived cues. Therefore, ethical leaders need to put more efforts into less proactive employees to motivate them to participate in IWB. To encourage employees with less proactive personalities, leadership needs to provide a work environment that is more conducive to speak about new ideas and express their opinions. Third, as IWB is risky for unpredictable outcomes, leaders need to provide such an environment in the organization in which employees feel psychologically safe while engaging in risk-taking behaviors. Thus, due to the important role of ethical leadership in encouraging IWB and enhancing psychological safety in employees, organizations need to promote ethical leadership behavior in the workplace. Limitations and future research directions Our study has several limitations that should be acknowledged while interpreting these results. First, the data for this research is cross-sectional, which does not allow us to draw strong inferences about causality. Therefore, to get a better idea about causality, we need more evidence based on experimental and/or longitudinal research design in the future. Second, we used a sample drawn from employees working in a single sector in Pakistan, which restricts the generalizability of the study results. Therefore, there is a need to reassess and reconfirm the generalizability of our study findings in other organizational and cultural backgrounds, and different work contexts. Third, though we collected data for this study by using multiple data sources, but most of the study variables were obtained from the same source (subordinates). Therefore, there can be the possibility that the study findings may have been influenced by common method bias. However, we empirically assessed this issue in our study, and we believe this is not a serious problem such as all the measures used in this study are widely studied in previous empirical researches. Moreover, the results of CFA also proposed that the study variables were empirically distinct. We also performed the Harman’s single factor test to assess the effects of CMV (Podsakoff et al., 2003), and results for the test indicate that CMV is not a major issue for our study model. However, future studies should attempt to take measures to address these possible problems linked to CMV (Podsakoff et al., 2003). Third, it is expected that some variables may have a certain influence on IWB such as firm size, individual motivation, group motivation, group climate and some other contextual factors (Rogers, 2004; Zhuet al., 2018). Thus, future studies should consider and/or control for these variables while replicating our findings. Finally, previous meta-analytic studies found that ethical leadership is distant but related to other similar leadership styles (Ng and Feldman, 2015). As our study did not control for other related leadership approaches, it would be beneficial for future studies to control for other related leadership styles that have been found positively associated with ethical leadership. In addition, as this research studied the role of employees’proactive personality in the ethical leadership and IWB association, future studies can investigate the role of employees’ proactive personality on employees’ other outcomes such as employee voice behavior or silence (Guenter et al., 2017). In conclusion, this study identifies employees’ proactive personality as an important boundary condition and psychological safety is an important intervening mechanism in the ethical leadership– IWB link. We hope that our research findings appeal to more research on ethical leadership and IWB as well as on intervening mechanisms and boundary conditions in which it is related to important employee outcomes. Ethical leadership, workplace spirituality, and job satisfaction: moderating role of self-efficacy Junaid Aftab and Huma Sarwar Department of Economics and Management, University of Brescia, Brescia, Italy Alina Kiran Fakulti Pengurusan Teknologi Dan Teknousahawanan, Technical University of Malaysia Malacca, Durian Tunggal, Malaysia Muhammad Imran Qureshi Teesside University, Middlesbrough, UK Muhammad Ishtiaq Ishaq Quaid-I-Azam University, Islamabad, Pakistan Sadaf Ambreen Department of Business Administration, Government College Women University Faisalabad, Faisalabad, Pakistan, and Arqam Javed Kayani Department of Business, The University of Lahore, Lahore, Pakistan Abstract Purpose – In the 21st century, spirituality is becoming an interesting phenomenon in the workplace and has been discussed by academicians, researchers, and practitioners alike. This growing knowledge offers important insights and calls for conceptual and empirical studies on workplace spirituality. Accordingly, the current research aims to examine how ethical leadership (EL) helps to foster workplace spirituality and job satisfaction (JS) in the information technology (IT) industry. Additionally, it investigates the mediating role of workplace spirituality and moderating role of self-efficacy (SE) in the relationship between EL and JS. Design/methodology/approach – Using a cross-sectional design, the data were collected from 268 employees in the IT industry and analyzed on SmartPLS 3.2 using structural equation modeling. Findings – The findings indicated that EL promotes a sense of spirituality and increases JS. Additionally, results suggested that workplace spirituality partially mediates, and SE moderates the relationship between EL and JS. Practical implications – The results suggest that the top executives should work on identifying and developing ethical qualities to promote a sense of meaningfulness (workplace spirituality) and increase JS. Originality/value – The research provides an important contribution to the academic literature by exploring the role of EL in fostering spirituality among employees and the moderation of SE on the relationship between EL and JS in the services industry. Introduction Information technology (IT) has assumed a crucial role in the emerging dynamics of a knowledge economy and is one of the key levers of economic development and growth. The IT industry in Pakistan is carving a differentiated position as a source of software development, freelancing, and business process outsourcing, as it ranks fourth worldwide concerning IT exports. The exports of Pakistan’s IT industry for the fiscal year (FY) 2019– 2020 stand at USD 1.23 billion, with a growth of approximately 23% compared to USD 994.84 million for the FY 2018–2019 (Ministry of information technology MOIT, 2020). As the demands and expectations of businesses are changing daily, especially in an emerging economy, such as Pakistan’s, the role of leadership is significant to ensure that the business targets are met effectively and ethically. Aftab et al.(2022) claimed that leaders’qualities, such as ethical conduct, are among the main factors that guide subordinates to put in more effort and achieve organizational goals. Therefore, researchers pay close attention to identifying the specific traits and behaviors that are essential for effective leadership, such as ethical leadership (EL) (Sarwar et al., 2020). EL defines as“the demonstration of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to followers through twoway communication, reinforcement, and a decision-making.” (Brown et al., 2005, p. 120). This definition emphasizes a perceptual and behavioral approach by describing a unique type of leadership that is perceived by subordinates (Aftab et al., 2022). Many believe that ethical leader has a significant impact that goes far beyond simple perception (Freire and Bettencourt, 2020) and influences those who follow them. The ethical conduct of leaders positively affects the lives of their followers (Sarwar et al., 2020). The current literature has called for an understanding of the ethical leader’s role and suggests that ethical leaders influence numerous individual- and organizational-related outcomes in China (Qing et al., 2019; Ren and Chadee, 2017; Tu et al., 2017), the United States (Moon and Jung, 2018), Spain (Ruiz et al., 2011), and Portugal (Freire and Bettencourt, 2020), such as job satisfaction (JS) and workplace spirituality. JS is defined as a positive or pleasurable emotional state due to the job experience. Although the existing literature indicates the positive role of EL on performance, motivation, and JS (Toor and Ofori, 2009), numerous researchers have proposed investigating how EL influences employees’behavior (Bouckenooghe et al., 2015; Qing et al., 2019). We argue that the association of EL and JS has been studied in Western culture or large economies, such as China. However, its generalizability in emerging economies remains unknown, and the effect of EL on JS in the Pakistani context may be different from previous studies. For instance, Sarwar et al.(2020) claimed that the influence of EL is different across cultures; therefore, understanding this concept in emerging economies is important from both theoretical and managerial perspectives. Therefore, the first objective is to explore the impact of EL on JS in the emerging economy. Spirituality is another important factor in the workplace that requires comprehensive empirical and theoretical studies. Workplace spirituality (WPS) involves identifying one’s life purpose, developing a positive connection with colleagues at the workplace, and aligning oneself with the organizational values (Mitroff and Denton, 1999). The nexus of EL–WPS is rarely examined in the academic setting, and it is imperative to know how a leader with ethical values develops meaningful work and a sense of connectedness at the workplace. Hence, the secondand third objectives of this research are to determine EL’s role in influencing WPS and mediating the role of WPS in the relationship between EL and JS. Similarly, the boundary conditions in the EL–JS relationship have rarely been examined (Ren and Chadee, 2017; Sarwar et al., 2020), especially self-efficacy (SE).Bandura (1986) defines SE as one’s belief to perform a particular task successfully and proposed four factors, Moderating role of selfefficacy 5881 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijoem/article-pdf/18/12/5880/2070499/ijoem-07-2021-1121.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 namely vicarious learning, verbal persuasion, physiological state, and enactive mastery experience. Since the studies on EL are currently in development (Aftab et al., 2022; Sarwar et al., 2020), additional studies are required to explicate the myriad of boundary conditions that improve our understanding of the effectiveness of EL at the workplace. Therefore, the fourth objective of this study is to explore the moderating role of SE between the EL and JS relationship in the IT industry. This study addresses important theoretical gaps and provides insightful implications for practicing managers. First, understanding the relationship between EL and JS in the IT industry of Pakistan extends the literature in an emerging economy and makes a unique contextual contribution to the existing research. In addition, our study followed the advice of Engelbrecht et al. (2017), Ko et al. (2018), and Sarwar et al. (2020) on exploring other moderating and mediating constructs in the EL conceptualization. They further argued that supportive behaviors increase commitment, performance, and satisfaction and improve efforts while nurturing engagement, integration, personality, and self-motivation. Research method 3.1 Sampling and data collection We collected the data from non-managerial employees who were working in the IT industry in Pakistan using a highly structured questionnaire. The IT industry has a bright future, as it is brimming with extraordinary individuals and could become the largest export industry in the country (MOIT, 2020). Therefore, despite the COVID-19 pandemic, this sector has continued to grow and provide high-quality services at reasonable prices to local and international customers. In addition, the World Economic Forum placed Pakistan among the top countries in terms of the affordability of information and communication technology services (MOIT, 2020). Currently, there are over 10,000 registered technology firms in the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP), with over 500,000 talented professionals serving the needs of local and international markets. The researchers believe that the productivity of these individuals depends on their level of satisfaction at work. Among all factors that directly and indirectly affect individuals’ JS, spirituality has an undeniable importance. However, it has been underexplored. Therefore, IT industry employees were chosen as our target population. Initially, a list of IT companies was generated from the SECP, which is a financial regulatory agency in Pakistan. Using a simple random sampling technique, 50 companies were selected that were operational in major cities of Pakistan. Next, we approached the human resources department of the selected companies to obtain the formal approval for participation in this research and received consent from 38 companies (e.g. Punjab province: 15, The capital Islamabad: 7, Balochistan province: 2, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province: 3, and Sindh province: 11). A total of 500 questionnaires and cover letters were distributed between July 2020 –October 2020 to randomly selected employees, which requested them to respond within four weeks. We received 292 responses, of which 24 were discarded due to many missing values, and the remaining 268 were selected for subsequent analyses. The response rate was 54%, which exceeded the minimum criteria for the sample size, as suggested byWolf et al.(2013) for structural equation modeling. We used a 7-points Likert scale (“1 5strongly disagree”, and“7 5strongly agree”) to get responses to the questions. (1) Ethical leadership: Brown et al. (2005) proposed a 10-items scale to measure EL. During validation, four items“discusses business ethics or values with employees”, “Listens to what employees have to say”, “define success not just by results but also the way that they are obtained”, and“has the best interests of employees in mind” were deleted due to low factor loading. A sample item reads: In my firm, a leader “conducts his/her personal life in an ethical manner.” (2) Job satisfaction: A 3-items scale of JS from the study ofCammann et al.(1983) was used. A sample item of the JS scale is“all in all, I am very satisfied with my current job.” (3) Self-efficacy: SE was measured from the 6-items scale ofBorgogni et al.(2010). The example of the item includes,“I am confident to keep in a good mood, even in tense situations.” (4) Workplace spirituality:WPS was measured using a 6-items scale from the study by Valasek (2009). A sample item is“feeling self-worth and great when I share my valuable information.” (5) Demographic variables: We also asked questions about the demographic details of each respondent including gender, age group, working experience, and education level. 3.3 Pilot testing We carried out pilot testing to confirm the reliability of the constructs. For that purpose, we randomly contacted three IT companies of the actual population. After obtaining their consent to participate in the survey, we distributed 25 questionnaires and collected 17 of them after one week. After data collection, the reliability of each scale was determined using SPSS v. 26. The reliability (Cronbach’s alpha) for JS, SE, EL, WPS were 0.906, 0.934, 0.912 and 0.925 respectively. 3.4 Common method bias As discussed earlier, we used a cross-sectional design approach, as we collected data on all study variables at a single point in time and from the same source (e.g. employees of IT companies). This resulted in a common method bias (CMB) in the dataset (Podsakoff and Organ, 1986). To confirm that our data did not suffer from CMB, we applied Harman’s singlefactor method in SPSS. The output revealed that as the first factor explained 37.13% of the variance and was under the threshold of 50%, no CMB issue was found. Data analysis and results The “partial least square-structural equation modeling” (PLS-SEM) is the approach that was used to analyze the data using a statistical tool, SmartPLS 3.2. PLS-SEM is a multivariate statistical analysis approach that can assess the relationship between all the study variables simultaneously. In this research, we adopted a two-step approach for data analysis. The first step was evaluating the outer or measurement model, and the second step was assessing the inner or structural model (Hair et al., 2019). 4.1 Assessment of measurement model The first step of the PLS-SEM analysis was the assessment of the measurement model. The PLS algorithm procedure was conducted to get the results of the factor loadings, composite reliability (CR), and convergent and discriminant validities. Hair et al. (2017) defined convergent validity as“the extent to which a measure correlates positively with alternative measures of the same construct” (p. 112). For the item loadings, a value of 0.7 and above is recommended (Hair et al., 2020), and it should not be less than 0.5 (Hair et al., 2017). A CR value of above 0.7 is advisable to check the reliability in PLS (Hair et al., 2020). The convergent validity was assessed with the average variance extracted (AVE) and should be higher than 0.5 (Fornell and Larcker, 1981). In Table 2, the results show an acceptable level of item loadings, except for one item of WPS (e.g. WPS6) and four items of EL (e.g. EL7, EL8, EL9, and EL10), which had loadings of less than 0.5. Therefore, they were removed. The remaining loadings ranged from 0.660 to 0.860 (Figure 2), which fulfills the recommendations ofHair et al.(2017). Similarly, the AVE values of all four constructs were above 0.5 such as EL (0.536), JS (0.690), WPS (0.615), and SE (0.655). Furthermore, the CR of the variables is above the given threshold of 0.70. The CR values of EL, JS, WPS, SE were 0.874, 0.870, 0.889 and 0.919 respectively. The adequate convergent validity allowed us to proceed to the second criteria to evaluate the measurement model through discriminant validity. Discriminant validity is defined as a measurement of different constructs, rather than a replication of other constructs (Hair et al., 2017). Discriminant validity was assessed using the well-known Heterotrait–Monotrait (HTMT) ratio of correlations (Henseleret al., 2015). The recommended HTMT value is less than 0.85 to confirm the discriminant validity (Henseler et al.,2 0 1 5). The results of the HTMT ratio of correlations inTable 3indicate that all values are under the limit of 0.85. Discussion and conclusion The current study was conducted to explore the relationship between EL and JS with the mediation of WPS and moderation of SE in theIT sector of Pakistan. Previously, although the literature demonstrated that EL influenced JS, it was mostlyfocused on western or developed economies. As stated previously,Brown and Trevino (2006)advocated for the generalizability of EL and its consequences across different cultures. Therefore, we decided to investigate the EL and JS nexus in an emerging economy, e.g. Pakistan. In addition, the mediating and moderating effects were examined in these relationships, as per the recommendation ofSarwar et al.(2020). The statistical results suggested that EL positively influences both WPS and JS, anda positive relationship between WPS and JS was established. Furthermore, WPS partially mediates and SE positively moderates the EL–JS nexus. This supports all five proposed hypotheses in the context of Pakistan’sI T industry. 5.1 Theoretical implications Theoretically, the results indicate that EL shares a positive link with JS and confirm the previous studies that showed the leadership effects on subordinate attitude and behavior (Brown and Trevino, 2006) that lead to JS (Freire and Bettencourt, 2020). For instance, the positive relationship between EL and JS has been proved in the professional service providers Figure 3. The study’s findings confirm the positive role of EL in shaping WPS. WPS provides a setting where workers can realize their primary purpose in life, develop a solid bond with colleagues and other coworkers, and align their core beliefs with their organizational values (Haldorai et al., 2020). De Carloet al.(2020)found that the optimistic behavior of leadership positively influences WPS, work engagement, and the performance of employees. In general, previous studies reported a positive relationship between different types of leadership styles and WPS, such as servant leadership to WPS (Khan et al., 2015) and transformational leadership to WPS (Al Amin et al.,2 0 2 0; Islam et al.,2 0 2 0), and spiritual leadership to WPS (Afsar et al., 2016). This finding adds an important contribution to the literature, as it provides empirical support for the relationship between EL and WPS, which has rarely been examined in previous literature. In addition, we noted that WPS is positively related to JS in IT companies in Pakistan. The findings reconfirm the premise that WPS can be used as a tool to drive JS (Lawande and Jadhav, 2020). The study findings support the previous studies (e.g.Gupta et al., 2014; Hassan et al., 2016; Lawande and Jadhav, 2020) that reported a significant positive link between WPS and JS. Belwalkar et al.’s (2018) study reported that the dimensions (i.e. “inner life, interconnectedness, meaning at work”) of WPS are positively related to employees’ JS. Contrary to our findings,Hafni et al.’s (2020)study reported no significant link between WPS and JS. Additionally, we found that WPS mediates the relationship between EL and JS. These results show that when subordinates perceive justice in their leadership, it improves their psychological well-being and encourages WPS (Haldorai et al., 2020), which leads to JS. Furthermore, De Carlo et al. (2020) reported that WPS contributed to explaining the relationship between positive leader behavior and work engagement. Satisfied employees are more engaged in their jobs, which means that WPS can improve leadership and JS relationships. Furthermore, a study byYazdini et al.(2010) reported that spirituality mediated justice (a characteristic of EL) and worker outcomes, including JS and commitment. Finally, the boundary condition of SE in the relationship between EL and JS is an important contribution to the literature, especially regarding the services industry of an emerging economy. According toIlyas et al.(2020), SE tends to influence the relationships that enhance motivation and ability, thus playing a moderating role between EL and JS. Piccolo et al.(2010) stated that the“normatively appropriate”behavior of EL implied that they are fair and principled in involving the subordinates by transactional means (e.g. rewards and punishment), and our study confirmed that the relationship between EL and JS is positively moderated by SE. In conclusion, the literature on EL has broadly recognized that the behavior of leaders and managers can significantly impact employee work outcomes and that subordinates respond to the treatment that they receive from their managers/leaders (Bedi et al., 2016). However, despite the increased academic interest, limited attention has been paid to the core mechanisms by which managers affect the JS (Chughtai et al., 2015). Therefore, the moderating role of SE in the EL–JS nexus is an important contribution to the literature. Through this, the researchers responded to the call asking for more investigations on the intervening variables in the relationship between EL and its individual and organizational outcomes (Chughtai et al., 2015; Ko et al., 2018). 5.2 Managerial implications The top management of IT companies must understand that EL can have a central role in individual development, JS satisfaction, and organizational performance. As our results indicate, EL is vital in developing a framework that encourages employees to be ethical and IJOEM 18,12 5892 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijoem/article-pdf/18/12/5880/2070499/ijoem-07-2021-1121.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 fully involved in their work. Therefore, the ethical skills of leaders are important in motivating their subordinates. It is suggested that the top management should organize training programs for managers/supervisors to develop and improve their ethical skills because subordinates are inspired by the actions and behaviors of their leaders. Furthermore, WPS has become a tremendously salient concept because it involves individual empathy, and the achievement of transcendental goals is necessary for every organization (Madison and Kellermanns, 2013). In the context of this research, the leadership of IT companies can improve WPS and create a win-win scenario for employees by implementing and promoting a humanistic workplace. This environment will enhance teamwork, innovation, and JS (Daniel, 2010). Furthermore, managers should allow their employees to bring their spiritual, intellectual, emotional, and physical attributes to the workplace. With this, the employees can feel a sense of belonging, become intrinsically motivated, and perform their duties to their maximum potential. Furthermore, our research presents the importance of SE by identifying its role as a moderator in the EL–JS nexus. ELs usually deal with their subordinates at two different SE levels, depending on their involvement in their work. Employees with high SE are more prone to work well and are more resourceful for the company than those with low SE. Therefore, to achieve maximum results, the leaders should trust them. However, employees with low SE are affected by external signals; therefore, more direction by ethical leaders and managers would heighten their satisfaction level (Cheng et al., 2014). In conclusion, our research findings help practitioners and human resource professionals of IT companies to develop and promote a work culture that focuses on ethics, honesty, and spirituality, which in turn, lead to JS and sustainable organizational outputs. 5.3 Limitations and future suggestions Despite the several managerial and theoretical contributions, the present research has several limitations. First, although CMB was not an issue in this study, we acknowledge that crosssectional data are considered one of the main sources of CMB. Therefore, longitudinal data are recommended in the future to lower the risk of CMB. Nonetheless, the cross-sectional design has value in providing an accurate picture of how employees feel about their jobs. We believe that no one knows more about the employees’satisfaction at work than the employees themselves. Furthermore, the data were collected from employees of companies that operate across Pakistan, and the citizens of this country are conditioned by similar spiritual values that could affect the generalizability of this study. Hence, it would be interesting to collect data from different geographical locations and cultures to see whether the outcomes are similar or change depending on the context. Consequently, a cultural comparison is recommended. Additionally, the current study uses employee perceptions to estimate EL, which may raise issues regarding whether actual behaviors are measured (Ren and Chadee, 2017). Nevertheless, this practice is in line with the perceptual approach of defining EL (Brown and Mitchell, 2010) and is commonly used in the leadership literature (e.g.Aftab et al., 2022; Qing et al., 2019; Sarwar et al., 2020). Arguably, assessing any type of leadership lies in the hands of the employees who experience such behavior (Ren and Chadee, 2017). Finally, although the focus of our study was on EL, we might also expect WPS to accentuate the positive influence of other leadership styles, such as authentic leadership on employee job outcomes, given that this leadership style also engages supervisors’ role-modeling and expected behavior and would be another interesting and fruitful area for future research. 5.4 Conclusion In conclusion, the current study aimed to contribute to the EL literature through a focused investigation into how and when the influence of EL on JS occurs within the context of the Moderating role of selfefficacy 5893 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijoem/article-pdf/18/12/5880/2070499/ijoem-07-2021-1121.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 Pakistani workplace. For this purpose, we explored the mediating role of WPS and moderating role of SE in the relationship between EL and JS. Relationship of ethical leadership, organizational culture, corporate social responsibility and organizational performance: a test of two mediation models Wafa Awni Alkhadra Department of English Language and Literature, American University of Madaba, Madaba, Jordan Sadam Khawaldeh Department of Business Administration, Damascus University, Damascus, Syrian Arab Republic, and Jehad Aldehayyat Department of Business Administration, Al-Hussein Bin Talal University, Maan, Jordan Abstract Purpose – The sound leadership style can be indicative of organizational success and explanatory of quality performance. Besides this, there are various factors that can impact organizational performance. To this end, this study aims to investigate the effect of ethical leadership on organizational performance, with the mediating role of corporate social responsibility (CSR) and organizational culture. Design/methodology/approach – The service sector in Jordan was targeted by this research, and data were collected from 371 middle-level and top-level managers working in service companies. These responses were analyzed by using analysis of a moment structure. Findings – The result conveyed that ethical leadership does not only influence organizational performance, but it also, and positively so, affects the organizational culture and CSR. In addition, CSR and organizational culture significantly mediate the relationship between ethical leadership and organizational performance. Practical implications – The findings of this study are a guide for managers and owners of service companies who are aiming to enhance organizational performance. If they follow the ethical leadership approach and emphasize CSR initiatives and organizational culture, they can attain, and naturally so, the maximum level of organizational performance. Originality/value – To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this research paper is thefirst to analyze ethical leadership in the context of the service sector in Jordan and highlight its influence on organizational culture, CSR and ultimately organizational performance. Moreover, it examined the mediating effects of organizational culture and CSR between ethical leadership and organizational performance. Implications, limitations and recommendations 7.1 Implications Ethics always remains an important component of business practices, and their practical implications can lead to the enhancement of the performance of the business. The study has discussed several factors correlated to ethical leadership that can strengthen the organizational performance of service-based companies in Jordan. Thus, it has foregrounded several implications for academicians as well as practitioners. Theoretically, this study has diverted the attention of the researcher toward the important organizational factors including ethical leadership, CSR and organizational culture. Moreover, it entails explanatoryfindings that explain the relationship between these factors and their impact on organizational performance. Furthermore, it has provided sufficient literature on ethical leadership, corporate culture, CSR and organizational performance. Comparatively speaking, this research is significantly different from other studies as it analyzes the two mediators (i.e. organizational culture and CSR) between ethical leadership and organizational performance; whereas prior researchers merely emphasize measuring the influence of ethical leadership on specific performance factors. This research is entirely different from prior studies, the majority of which focused on the ethical leadership theory instead of the stakeholder theory. In addition, the literature has mostly discussed ethical leadership in the manufacturing sector. The researchers can consider this research as a guide while discussing ethical leadership or the performance of service-based organizations. Moreover, they can use the results of this research as a reference for future studies. In terms of practical implications, this study is a guide for managers and owners of service companies. The results of this research provided different strategies to enhance organizational performance, which includes: ethical leadership, CSR and better organizational culture. Therefore, to increase organizational performance, the managers of Jordanian service-based organizations can work on the development of ethical leadership, better organizational culture and CSR. 7.2 Limitations and recommendations Although the research has contributed significantly to the literature on CSR, organizational culture, ethical leadership and organizational performance, it has failed to escape the following limitations. Rai Research Scholar, Manipal Institute of Management, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, India, and Navin Kumar Koodamara Manipal Institute of Management, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, India Received 16 June 2023 Revised 14 October 2023 19 February 2024 25 April 2024 Accepted 13 May 2024 Abstract Purpose – This study aims to comprehensively analyse and synthesize existing studies that investigate the relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence. This review also aims to provide a detailed understanding of the impact of ethical leadership on various dimensions of organizational silence. Design/methodology/approach – This study uses a systematic review methodology, adhering to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis guidelines, to explore the relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence. Using the SCOPUS database, the search involved Boolean operators to narrow down relevant papers published in English between 2000 and 2023. Following a meticulous screening process, 10 papers were selected for review after removing duplicates and excluding non-English or irrelevant studies. The selected papers underwent a methodological quality assessment, ensuring focused research questions, precise subject selection methods, representative samples and reliable measurement instruments. Findings – This study has led to two crucial fndings. Firstly, the review has revealed that employees feel secure and motivated to share their opinions when leaders are ethical, which is essential from the perspective of organizational performance. Secondly, in a collectivist culture, employees generally do not express their views (prosocial silence) even though the leaders are ethical. However, in an individualistic culture, employees express their views and opinions on organizational matters even though leaders are ethical. Research limitations/implications – This research has three research implications. Firstly, the papers on the relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence followed quantitative approach. Besides, there is a dearth of qualitative studies. Therefore, qualitative studies are urgently needed to understand the true nature of this relationship. Secondly, the relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence in existing literature is inconsistent. Several studies have reported a non-signifcant relationship between these two constructs, which requires further investigation. Thirdly, most existing literature on the relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence is concentrated in the manufacturing sector. Therefore, it is necessary to test this model, even in the services or other sectors. Originality/value – To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the frst study to have reviewed the impact of ethical leadership on organizational silence. This review provides insights into how ethical leadership can mitigate silent behaviour. In addition, this review suggests future research directions pertaining to the relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence. Therefore, ethical leadership is inevitable for success in the current business world. Besides, ethical leadership boosts employee morale and makes them feel happy. Ethical leadership is “demonstrating and promoting normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relations” ( Brown et al., 2005, p. 120). On the other hand, the notion of “organizational silence” is a newer construct that has attracted organizational researchers lately. Organizational silence is a phenomenon in which members purposefully withhold information and opinions about their organization (Van Dyne et al., 2003 ). Employees intentionally abstained from expressing their views. Consequently, withholding information or knowledge deters overall organizational performance. Otherwise, this knowledge and information can be used to solve complex problems in an organization. In the current literature on organizational silence, the concept of organizational silence is used interchangeably with employee silence ( Brinsfeld, 2013; Hao et al., 2022 ; Knoll and van Dick, 2013 ; Dehkharghani et al., 2022 ). Current literature justifes employee silence or organizational silence as a multidimensional concept that includes acquiescent silence, defensive silence, prosocial silence, opportunistic silence, diffdent silence and indifferent silence ( Dehkharghani et al., 2022 ; Vakola and Bouradas, 2005). Although the current understanding of the relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence is limited, a few studies have highlighted the importance of ethical leadership in infuencing organizational silence (Bormann and Rowold, 2016; Gomezel and Stritar, 2021). Ethical leadership augments teamwork, builds healthy peer relations, eliminates communication gap (Bahadori et al., 2021), maintains morale of employees, builds cordial relation and reduces organizational silence ( Bormann and Rowold, 2016 ). Ethical leadership plays a critical role in shaping the ethical behaviour of employees (Halbusi et al., 2023). Employees proactively disclose their problems when leaders are perceived to be ethical because they perceive them to be more cooperative and respond with greater empathy ( Stouten et al., 2018). Under ethical leadership, employees are encouraged to speak confdently and constructively. Hence, leaders must exhibit ethical leadership in their daily behaviours, choices and actions (Zehir and Erdogan, 2011). In emerging markets, ethical leadership is crucial for encouraging employee innovation by giving employees the freedom to speak up at work (Nazir et al., 2020). Top managers and supervisors can eradicate silent behaviour among employees by fostering a culture where workers express freely their opinions and are encouraged to share their thoughts ( Shojaie et al., 2011). However, additional insights are necessary to understand the factors driving ethical value alignment. It is essential to recognize the signifcance of an ethical organizational culture in the face of the increasing complexity of modern society ( Halbusi et al., 2019 ). Only with the help of ethical leadership are employees encouraged to bring change to the workgroup and refect on their opinions ( Halbusi et al., 2023 ). Despite the signifcant relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence (Bormann and Rowold, 2016; Khan et al., 2021; Zehir and Erdogan, 2011), few studies have reported a non- signifcant relationship between these two constructs ( Bormann and Rowold, 2016). Furthermore, fndings on the relationship between ethical leadership and various dimensions of organizational silence need to be more consistent. Despite the vital need to study ethical leadership and organizational silence, there are no extensive review articles on the relationship between them. Therefore, it is essential to review of the impact of ethical leadership on organizational silence in an organizational context ( Bormann and Rowold, 2016 ; Imam and Kim, 2022 ; Chehraghi et al., 2015 ). Ethical leadership involves displaying morally sound behaviour through individual actions and interpersonal interactions, while simultaneously fostering such conduct in followers via effective communication, reinforcement and decision-making processes ( Brown et al., 2005 ). To be an ethical leader, one must preserve morally and sincerely held principles, exhibit charisma and empower others ( Eisenbeiß and Brodbeck, 2014). Positive impact of ethical leadership. The emulation of ethical leadership increases the leadership quality of followers (Dua et al., 2022). Establishing high ethical standards, setting an example of ethical behaviour and rewarding employees are ways to develop high- performing teams ( Walumbwa et al., 2012). Respect for others’ rights and dignity are at the core of ethical leadership. Nevertheless, the implications of ethical leadership in business go beyond the necessity of safeguarding a company’s reputation from harm. Incremental effects of ethical leadership. Ethical leadership has distinct impacts beyond the benefts of transformational and transactional leadership. Based on the benefts of ethical leadership, organizations must emphasize training programs that impart ethical leadership behaviours (Bormann and Rowold, 2016 ). Leaders have a privileged societal position (Bahadori et al., 2021). How leaders make decisions, their actions and their effects on those around them are the primary concerns of the academic discipline, which is widely recognized as “ethical leadership” ( Resick et al., 2006). To gain an in-depth understanding of the antecedents and consequences of ethical leadership, this study developed a multidimensional model encompassing fairness, integrity, ethical guidance, people orientation, power sharing, role clarifcation and concern for sustainability ( Kalshoven et al., 2011). Organizational silence Multidimensional nature of organizational silence. Organizational silence is a broad notion with many different angles from which employees are vocal, in addition to formal silence (Pinder and Harlos, 2001). Organizational silence is a multidimensional concept that includes acquiescent, quiescent, prosocial, opportunistic, diffdent and indifferent silence. Firstly, acquiescent silence occurs because lack of obedience and power. Secondly, defensive silence is based on self-protection motivation, worrying about negative management consequences or social distancing caused by opinions. Thirdly, quiescent silence occurs when someone withholds essential information to protect themselves because they fear that speaking up could lead to adverse outcomes ( Pinder and Harlos, 2001). Fourthly, prosocial silence occurs because of self-interest and cooperative motivation ( Dyne et al., 2003 ; Pinder and Harlos, 2001). Prosocial silent employees refrain from intervening in matters involving grievances. Fifthly, another type of silence is “opportunistic silence”, in which employees strategically hide their ideas, information and opinions to help themselves ( Bormann and Rowold, 2016; Knoll and van Dick, 2013). High prosocial and opportunistic silence could signify a voluntary effort to maintain a positive perception of social groups ( Knoll and van Dick, 2013 ). Finally, the “diffdent silence” is when people do not say what they think because they fear losing face and reputation if they do ( Brinsfeld, 2013). Origins of organizational silence. Identifying the reasons for silence would provide clarity and help differentiate the mere absence of voice behaviour from silent behaviour (Brinsfeld, 2013). Several causes lead to organizational silence. Firstly, employees are reluctant to establish offcial communication when a silent atmosphere dominates the organization. As people need to communicate to express their opinions, ideas, jobs and even personal problems in such scenarios, they resort to unoffcial communication channels, especially rumours in the organization, to express their opinions, viewpoints, insights and feelings ( Hozouri et al., 2018). Secondly, the tendency to remain silent is strong during organizational wrongdoing because speaking up is risky (Mayer et al., 2013). Finally, organizational silence is the outcome of a negative attitude towards the immediate supervisor or a particular department, which is not necessarily related to a negative attitude towards the company ( Jain, 2015). Consequences of and remedies for organizational silence. Motivated non-behaviour, such as various types of silence, provides insight into the processes that guide an individual’s conscious and unconscious decision-making ( Bormann and Rowold, 2016 ). Consequently, organizational silence leads to several negative consequences in organizations. Firstly, organizational silence motivates the withholding or expression of ideas, information and opinions regarding work-related improvements (Van Dyne et al., 2003 ). Secondly, organizational silence that already exists in an organization can deteriorate into selfreinforcing behaviour that destroys team spirit and negatively affects the ability to adapt to change (Morrison, 2014). Thirdly, maintaining silence is apparent in the workplace, where employee recommendations for solving organizational issues are considered inadequate. Nevertheless, this is detrimental to the service sector, particularly in the hospital and airline industries ( Shojaie et al., 2011 ). Therefore, the appropriate administration of remedies for silence is necessary. Organizations try to discourage organizational silence by providing training platforms for managers’ and supervisors’ relationship skills and presenting an appropriate framework for rewarding creative ideas ( John and Manikandan, 2019; Bai et al., 2017). Theoretical perspective. According to the social learning theory propounded by psychologist Albert Bandura, individuals acquire knowledge by observing the behaviors, attitudes and consequences demonstrated by others. This theory posits that individuals are more likely to adopt behaviours if they witness rewards and less likely to observe punishments. According to Bandura’s (1977) social learning theory, individuals learn by observing, modelling and imitating the behaviour, attitude and emotional reactions of others. This theory points out that leaders are critical in changing the behaviour and views of their people through modelling and reinforcement ( Bormann and Rowold, 2016). Social learning theory and ethical leadership. In various ways, social learning theory serves as a fundamental concept in ethical leadership. Firstly, followers observe and internalize leaders’ behaviors, potentially adopting them into their own conduct. Secondly, followers witness how leaders handle ethical dilemmas, conficts and complex situations. By observing leaders prioritizing ethics, followers are more likely to emulate such behaviour. Thirdly, ethical leaders create environments in which ethical actions are recognized, appreciated and incentivized. When followers see their peers rewarded for ethical conduct, they are more inclined to engage in similar actions. This aligns with the social learning theory, in which behaviours are reinforced through positive outcomes. Fourthly, ethical leaders promptly address unethical behaviour, sending a clear message that such actions are unacceptable. When followers witness the consequences of unethical actions, they are less inclined to engage in similar behaviours because of potential negative outcomes, in line with social learning theory principles. Finally, ethical leaders emphasize the importance of social responsibility and the impact of individual actions on a wider community. Through effective communication and demonstration, followers are encouraged to consider the ethical implications of their decisions on various stakeholders, fostering a sense of shared responsibility and ethical awareness. Thus, social learning theory offers a structure for comprehending how ethical leadership affects followers’ behaviour through a process of observing, imitating, reinforcing and disciplining. Through embodying ethical values and demonstrating ethical conduct while fostering environments that support ethical behaviour, leaders can create an ethical climate within organizations and inspire others to act with integrity and accountability. Social learning theory and the ethical leadership–organizational silence relationship. Social learning theory provides insights into how ethical leadership infuences organizational silence. There are two crucial reasons due to which we posit that the social learning theory provides an adequate theoretical underpinning for explaining the ethical leadership– organizational silence relationship. Firstly, the theory’s postulates imply that ethical leadership may favour organizational silence by serving as an example for others, rewarding ethical actions, promoting learning through observation and creating a workplace where people feel trusted and comfortable enough to speak up. Secondly, employees are more likely to voice their concerns and foster a transparent and ethical organizational culture when leaders constantly demonstrate ethical behaviour and promote open communication ( Nikolova et al., 2019 ; Imam and Kim, 2022 ). In the quality-oriented leader–follower relationship, where leaders exhibit care and concern, an individual is ought to respond with desirable behaviours. Some desired behaviours highlight unethical activities, sharing personal views and suggestions, being creative and maintaining the confdentiality of organizational matters. Therefore, the followers perceiving leader’s characteristics as transparent, integrity and openness to ideas; would easily contribute by sharing sensitive information. Ethical leadership and acquiescent silence Among the four types of silence examined, acquiescent silence is the most infuential and signifcant ( Bormann and Rowold, 2016 ). Acquiescent silence is critical for organizations, but it is also easier to explain methodologically. When leaders communicate what is required to achieve specifc goals and outline individual responsibilities, an environment of obligation to speak up on important matters can emerge ( Bormann and Rowold, 2016). However, task-oriented focus may hinder the development of close interpersonal relationships between leaders and followers, which can increase opportunistic behaviours and decrease prosocial behaviours. Ethical leadership effectively reduces acquiescent silence, and based on these fndings, project managers are recommended to adopt an ethical leadership style to discourage team members from remaining silent during meetings ( Khan et al., 2021). The relationship between organizational silence and ethical leadership is complex and contradictory. This study shows the signifcant impact of acquiescent, defensive and prosocial silence on ethical leadership ( Chou and Chang, 2020 ; Montgomery et al., 2023 ; Parhizgar et al., 2019). In multinational corporations, organizational silence tends to be more prevalent as leaders adopt more assertive ethical behaviour ( Zehir and Erdogan, 2011 ). This study highlights the signifcance of leadership in shaping organizational silence. Also, organizational factors and hierarchical structures play a signifcant role in fostering silence. The quantitative studies that were analysed provided inconsistent results. In some studies, ethical leadership had a signifcant impact on acquiescent silence (Bormann and Rowold, 2016; Khan et al., 2021), whereas in some cases, it has resulted in an insignifcant relationship (Parhizgar et al., 2019). An acquiescent silence is a silence that occurs due to purposeful, inactive and uninvolved behaviours. However, with the help of more quantitative and qualitative studies, more insight into the reasons underlying the impact of ethical leadership on acquiescent silence will be provided. Culture plays a critical role in identifying what induces organizational silence; for example, silence does not necessarily mean unfavourable to the organization in a collectivist culture, whereas in an individualist culture, the meaning of silence is different (Hofstede, 2001; Imam and Kim, 2022). Employees in individualistic cultures tend to voice and share their thoughts. Depending on the organizational culture and industry they work in (public or private), employees have different understandings, ways of thinking and behaviours that impact how people perceive their managers’ ethical leadership (Goswami et al., 2021). People in the private sector perceive their managers as more ethical than those in the public sector do (Khuntia and Suar, 2004). Similarly, organizational silence also affects ethical leadership (Zehir and Erdogan, 2011; Parhizgar et al., 2019). When organizational silence prevails, ethical leadership is adversely affected. The organization must practice a culture of open communication, which can help ethical leaders instil confdence in employees to express themselves without hesitation (Zehir and Erdogan, 2011). A study on the impact of ethical leadership as a mediator specifes that ethical leadership favourably infuences employee performance favourably (Zehir and Erdogan, 2011; Parhizgar et al., 2019). In the presence of ethical leadership triggering the mediating effect of other variables on organizational silence, this study showed partial mediation compared to a direct impact (Khan et al., 2021). In other words, ethical leadership negatively impacts team members’ silent behaviour compared to nonsignifcance in sequential mediation, namely, subordinates’ feeling of trust and loyalty towards the supervisor. Ethical leadership, with its inherent qualities, is a critical element in human resource development (HRD) and its role in facilitating fair and managerial practices that encourage freedom of expression and involvement in decision making is signifcant. The fndings on the direct relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence highlight the complexity of this effect. Trust, organizational culture and human resource strategies also play a pivotal role in enhancing ethical leadership and infuencing silent behaviour, along with its dimensions. Conclusion and implications Organizational silence is an important issue that must be addressed. Organizations need to identify this issue, as it may severely affect overall organizational development. However, identifying the factors that contribute to silent behaviour in organizations is challenging. Ethical leadership has proven instrumental in predicting outcomes, such as followers’ job satisfaction, dedication and willingness to report problems to management. Moreover, it is instrumental in reducing silence behaviour among employees. Therefore, continued research in this area can contribute to the development of effective leadership development programmes and strategies that cultivate ethical leadership practices and ultimately create healthier and more productive organizational environments. In terms of practical implications, this study serves as a guide for supervisors and top- level management of organizations. In the service sector, employees expressing opinions and hardships they encounter will help them overcome diffculties and lead to a win-win situation.
