From a leadership development perspective, leaders’ ability to handle subordinates ethically and to some extent is crucial. Prompt, fair and just leaders who embody ethics in their personal and professional dealings inspire employees to express concern or maintain silence regarding unethical activities. Limitations and suggestions for future research Despite the expectation that ethical leadership would reduce organizational silence, the results consistently showed little relevance to silent behaviour. Limited empirical research has been conducted on the impact of ethical leadership dimensions on organizational silence, and the direct relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence is yet to be adequately considered. In addition, more empirical research is needed to demonstrate ethical leadership as a mediator that infuences silence behaviour. The moderating effect of ethical leadership dimensions remains unexplored, providing future research avenues for organizational behaviour. Further empirical research is needed to examine the diverse fndings surrounding the impact of organizational silence. Further investigation is needed into the dimensions of ethical leadership and its impact on organizational silence. Promoting ethical leadership behaviour and creating a supportive environment for employee voice can lead to positive organizational outcomes ( Halbusi et al., 2021 ). Acquiescent silence dominates the dimensions of silence in the private sector (Lourencia et al., 2020; Deniz et al., 2013). Therefore, further investigations are needed to identify the possible effects of ethical leadership on employees’ silent behaviour of employees. As it is a well-known fact that culture infuences employee behaviour in the Indian context, limited studies have identifed the impact of ethical leadership on silent behaviour. Few studies have measured the impact of culture on the relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence ( Dehkharghani et al., 2022). This subject promises a fruitful avenue for future research ( Imam and Kim, 2022; Goswami et al., 2021). There is a need for more in-depth studies to understand culture and study the impact of ethical leadership on organizational silence ( Imam and Kim, 2022 ) and organizational silence on ethical leadership ( Zehir and Erdogan, 2011 ). Future research could focus on employees’ perceptions of ethical leadership and how they infuence their silent behaviour. Therefore, further research on leadership qualities that motivate employees to express or maintain silence is essential for HRD literature. Although previous studies have explored the manufacturing sector ( Alkhadra et al., 2022; Halbusi et al., 2022a , 2022b), there is much scope to replicate the same study in the service sector to examine how ethical leadership infuences organizational performance. This study provides guidance for future research on the relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence in the service sector. Future researchers can explore the difference between private and public sector companies operating while practising ethical leadership on organizational silence. Future research should focus on conducting empirical studies comparing the private and public sectors, which will contribute to developing strategies for promoting ethical leadership practices that positively affect silence behaviour. Another emerging area of research is the relevance of ethical leadership for employees operating in international corporations. Despite having more ethical leaders and improving employee performance, employees in such settings tend to remain silent. Exploring this phenomenon can provide valuable insights into the complexities of the ethical leadership–silence relationship in a global context. There is a need for empirical evidence to analyse the moderating role of demographics such as age, gender, work experience and designation, on the relationship between ethical leadership and organizational silence. Ethical leadership and public service r ecovery performance: the r oles of thriving at work and moral self-efficacy Long Le Hoang Nguyen University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City , Ho Chi Minh City , V ietnam Abstract Purpose – The study aims to explore the mechanism to strengthen service recovery performance among public sector employees. Delving on the notion that ethical aspects of public leaders could serve as reliable models, the research investigated the role of ethical leadership, thriving at work and moral self-efficacy . Design/methodology/approach – A quantitative approach with two waves of data collection from both supervisors’ and subordinates’ perspectives in public org anizations was conducted. The final sample size was 331. Findings – Ethical leadership has a positive effect on public sector employees’ thriving at work. In turn, the state of thriving at work mediates the association between ethical leadership and service recovery performance. Public servants’ moral self-efficacy moderates both the direct relationship between ethical leadership and thriving at work, as well as the indirect effect of ethical leadership on service recovery performance through thriving at work. Originality/value – The research findings suggest an understanding of how ethical leadership could cultivate public service recovery performance through employees’ thriving. The common values between subordinates and leaders were found to facilitate a better translation of the leaders’ role model into employees’ psychology and behaviors. Keywords Leadership, Self-effi cacy , Behavior change, Ethics Paper type Research paper Intr oduction Shifting from the traditional model, the government systems have been transitioning to a market-oriented approach since the era of new public management (Funck and Karlsson, 2020). Nowadays, public or ganizations are becoming similar to private or ganizations in terms of reforming internal processes to be more effective and ef ficient (Lapuente and V an de W alle, 2020). Hence, there is a tendency for public managers to pay attention to integrating service management practices into public service (D €oring, 2022). Accordingly , public organizations have switched from an “ask-give” mechanism to a more ef fective model by treating citizens like customers in a private service setting (Funck and Karlsson, 2020). Similar to the private sector , customers in the public service sector also gain satisfaction with public service from their expectations (e.g. promotional claims, word of mouth) and service performance (Zhang et al., 2022). Thus, any situation in which public organizations cannot meet the demands of citizens leads to dissatisfaction and is described as a service failure situation. However , unlike failures in private or ganizations that damage the or ganizational image or af fect customer attitudes, failures in public service can have negative ef fects on a broader range of stakeholders, such as harming people’ s lives or reducing confidence in the government (Lee and Kim, 2024; V an de W alle, 2016). Consequently , public service failures could harm the reputation of organizations or even be blamed as red tape (V an de W alle, 2016). In addressing citizens’ demands, public organizations need to implement approaches to improve their effectiveness. For example, public leaders could learn from the best private service practices that employees could play an important role in recovering the service quality in the perception of customers by exhibiting service recovery behaviors such as providing explanations, offering apologies and expressing empathy (e.g. Liao, 2007). Causes of public service failure are mainly due to public sector employees’ lack of engagement in public service ideals (V an de W alle, 2016), the state of thriving at work, which includes a high level of vitality and a desire to learn, is proposed to play an important role for public employees to exhibit public service recovery performance. Drawing from social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1986), we propose that public sector employees can exhibit recovery behavior , fueled by their moral emotions and knowledge of how to perform in moral ways, to correct public service failures. In addition, we posit that the ethical aspect of public leaders could serve as a trigger for thriving at work by translating ethical values to public servants through role modeling and the active practice of ethics at work (e.g. two-way communication, guidance for standardized behaviors). In turn, the state of thriving plays a mediating role in connecting moral values to public service recovery performance. Since thriving at work is activated by an agentic view that individuals can overcome diff iculties with their efforts and are goal-oriented, we propose the degree of moral self-effica cy could strengthen the effe ct of role model (ethical leadership) due to the similarity with the values (Bandura, 1994). Thus, besides exploring how ethical leadership could enhance service recovery performance by promoting employee thriving, the research also aims to investigate when ethical leadership can impact public employees by exploring the moderating effect of moral self-effic acy . In summary , the research makes several contributions. First, by examining public service recovery performance, the research addresses the scientific gap in the public management literature (V an de W alle, 2016) and responds to calls from other scholars to expand the application of service recovery performance into various service settings (e.g. V an V aerenbergh et al., 2019). Second, we propose that the intertwined ef fects of the af fective and cognitive aspects of public sector employees, in terms of thriving at work, could serve as a bridge between ethical leadership and service recovery performance, which is scarcely mentioned in prior management literature. Third, the research of fers a comprehensive framework to better explain how moral self-effic acy can hold a moderating role in the association between ethical leadership and public sector employees’ outcomes. Literatur e rev iew and hypotheses Ethical leadership and thriving at work Since many ethical issues occur in the daily working environment, such as political, environmental scandals or workplace discrimination, moral-based leadership styles such as servant leadership, authentic leadership and ethical leadership have caught the attention of scholars and continue to be explored in contemporary studies (Banks et al., 2021). In the public sector , scholars found a wide range of desirable outcomes among public sector employees when working under moral leaders such as career commitment (Li and Xie, 2022), work engagement (Zahari and Kaliannan, 2023) or public service motivation (Gnankob et al., 2022). Among moral-related leadership styles, ethical leadership has caught the distinct attention of scholars due to its strong predictive power when compared to other leadership styles (Banks et al., 2021). Ethical leadership is defined as a style of leading that simultaneously cares for the benefits and prevents harm that could happen to others (Y ukl et al., 2013). Accordingly , Brown et al. (2005) proposed that ethical leaders need to express both their morality in personal life (moral person) and promote work-related moral practices (moral manager). Drawing from social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1986), individuals can learn and reinforce their behavior by observing and direct experience. An ethical leader is characterized as a moral person who puts ef fort into moral behaviors (e.g. two-way communication), this leadership style could be recognized as a reliable model (Brown et al., 2005) for employees to imitate ethical behavior . Furthermore, by continuously promoting work ethics, ethical leaders encourage employees to engage in discussions on ethical topics by establishing moral practices that guide employees IJOTB 28,2 144 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijotb/article-pdf/28/2/143/9845114/ijotb-05-2024-0096.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 on what should and should not be done (Brown et al., 2005). Subsequently , subordinates under the guidance of ethical leaders may develop related personal processes, as they are triggered to learn moral values from their supervisors. Koay and Lim (2022), for instance, found that ethical leadership could reduce the level of moral disengagement and consequently decrease knowledge-hiding behavior among employees. In the context of the public sector , ethical leadership was also found to play an important role in shaping a variety of employee’ s psychological processes such as motivation (e.g. W right et al., 2016), af fection (e.g. Qing et al., 2020) or cognition (e.g. Miao et al., 2020). Banks et al. (2021) suggested that both cognitions and moral emotions are necessary for ethical leadership to emer ge. Therefore, through the lens of social cognitive theory , ethical leaders possess both cognitive and af fective qualities concurrently and translate values to their subordinates, but are not limited to any sole aspect. Accordingly , the tendency to focus on studying the single ef fect of moral-related leadership on employees’ psychological processes may explain why , in some contexts, the effectiveness of this leadership style remains in doubt (Asif and Rathore, 2021). T o be specific, individuals who only focus on learning (cognitive processes) from the leader ’ s social model without considering af fective aspects (e.g. moral emotions) may become exhausted (Li et al., 2016) and behave negatively (e.g. Dennerlein and Kirkman, 2022; Zhang et al., 2021). In the same manner , employees who empathize with the leaders’ values but lack learning opportunities are limited in transferring these values into consistent learned behavior . For example, public sector employees who perceive an ethical climate and actively contribute to ensuring integrity , yet lack knowledge of how to act according to ethical guidelines when service failures occur (e.g. a public servant follows an incorrect procedure for a citizen), may experience constraints in career growth and begin to view their job as a routine, lacking diverse skills. Since ethical leadership is characterized by both caring for stakeholder benefits and providing guidance for practicing work ethics (Brown et al., 2005), the research focusing on the state of employees’ thriving at work as a consequence of ethical leadership may offer a better explanation of how ethical leadership can be effective. The state of employees’ thriving at work describes an intertwined relationship between vitality (affec tive dimension) and learning (cognitive dimension) (Kleine et al., 2019). Porath et al. (2012) proposed that the combination of both dimensions (vitality and learning) will af fect and strengthen each other leading to a thriving state of employees. Because thriving at work has been found to relate to various desirable outcomes such as innovative work behavior (Nguyen and McGuirk, 2022; W ang, 2023), organizational citizenship behavior (Li et al., 2016; Suryani et al., 2023; W u et al., 2023), promoting employee to thrive is essential to achieve sustainable org anizational performance (Goh et al., 2022). Spreitzer et al. (2005) proposed a comprehensive model of thriving at work in which contextual features enhance agentic work behavior including (1) task focus, (2) exploration and (3) heedful relating. Accordingly , in this research, we propose that ethical leadership can promote the thriving of public sector employees at work by leveraging a sense of agency . In the light of social cognitive theory , ethical leadership which holds the role of external determinant could fuel public servants’ internal determinant (thriving at work) through human agency and vicarious learning mechanism (see Nabi and Prestin, 2017). Specifically , we hypothesize that practicing ethical leadership could enhance the human agentic behavior of public employees which defines thriving at work. Ethical leaders use their reliable models (Brown et al., 2005) to active the learning process through observation (vicarious learning). For example, public servants observe the moral personality of their supervisor and how he/she handles daily work by following moral standards, which could guide them to implement learned behaviors into their values. Furthermore, ethical leaders encourage moral practices at work by implementing reward systems, ef fective communication and guidance for employees. This exposure to ethical situations enhances subordinates’ abilities regarding moral matters, reduces tension when facing moral dilemmas and increases the moral experiences of employees. As such, by gaining moral experience, employees tend to pay more attention and International Journal of Organization Theory & Behavior 145 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijotb/article-pdf/28/2/143/9845114/ijotb-05-2024-0096.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 continuously contemplate morality at work (e.g. Miao et al., 2020) (task focus). Besides, employees also thrive when they possess an exploratory dimension, which can raise their curiosity and make them more energetic (Spreitzer et al., 2005). Under the umbrella of social cognitive theory , ethical leadership translates ethical values to subordinates through vicarious learning, and human agency could build intellectual resources that enable employees to confidently apply and adapt them to fit the working context (Ullah et al., 2021). Finally , ethical leadership, characterized as honest and caring (Brown and T revi ~no, 2006), shares the same values with the heedful relating dimension, which makes individuals more responsible by encouraging participation in learning and enhancing vitality (Spreitzer et al., 2005). Thus, the research proposes that by promoting agentic behaviors, ethical leadership is hypothesized to positively af fect employees’ thriving at work. The following hypothesis was formed: H1. Ethical leadership, thriving at work and service r ecovery performance Public service failures can occur in various forms, such as when public service employees fail to return administrative documents in time or low public service quality from public hospitals or public universities. Unlike failures in the private service sector , which lead to customer dissatisfaction and have negative ef fects on an org anization’ s image, thus causing economic damage to business or ganizations (e.g. Jean Harrison-W alker , 2012; Liu and Xiong, 2023; W ang et al., 201 1), public service failures may result in severe outcomes, such as citizens losing their homes, jobs or even their lives (V an de W alle, 2016). In addition, service failures also harm the reputation of public organizations and are often regarded as inherent to bureaucracy (V an de W alle, 2016). Notably , the causes of service failures mostly stem from the behaviors of public sector employees, rather than from public service systems, and are characterized by a lack of engagement with public service ideals such as ignorance, rigidity and neglect (V an de W alle, 2016). As such, since the sources of public service failures originate from human behaviors, solutions need to be derived from individual behavior to address the reality . Therefore, by adopting the best management practices from the private sector in the period of public administration reform (Funck and Karlsson, 2020), public organizations need to cultivate public service recovery performance among public sector employees to ensure the quality and image of public services (V an de W alle, 2016). Service recovery performance is defined as the direct actions of service employees to address the complaints of customers in order to recover service quality and customer positive attitudes (Liao, 2007). For example, employees could express their concern, empathy or compensation to customers when the service delivery processes fail to meet expectations (Luo et al., 2019; V an de W alle, 2016). Despite the public sector ’ s efforts to shift toward a more market-oriented approach, emphasizing efficiency and treating citizens as customers, similar to the private sector (Funck and Karlsson, 2020), there has been hardly any attention from scholars regarding public service recovery performance (Lid �en and Edvardsson, 2003; V an de W alle, 2016). Thus, the research responds to the call to expand the stream of service recovery performance to other service contexts (e.g. V an V aerenbergh et al., 2019) and aims to shed light on how to trigger recovery behavior among public sector employees. The af fective state of employees was considered requisite for individuals to evaluate and express service recovery behavior (Babakus et al., 2003; Luo et al., 2019). However , since service recovery performance is regarded as a type of extra-role behavior that aligns with the goals of organizations (Liao, 2007), we ar gue that the behavior contains a cognitive dimension as an antecedent. For instance, public sector employees exhibit service recovery performance influenced by their own emotions (affec tive dimension) and intend to fulfill their moral values (cognitive dimension) in order to achieve the public service ideal. As cognition and af fection need to interplay and emerge simultaneously (Dionne et al., 2018), we propose that thriving at work, which is a combination of cognitive (learning) and af fective (vitality) aspects, could serve as a motivator for public service recovery performance. That is, employees need to combine both their knowledge and energy to go beyond the prescriptive role and benefit the org anization. Drawing from social cognitive theory , environmental processes could interact with personal processes, including cognition and emotion (Schunk and DiBenedetto, 2020), leading to behavioral outcomes. Thus, ethical leadership as an external environment, utilizing role modeling and vicarious learning, by exposing public sector employees to ethical guidelines and promoting open communication about morality , could activate the learning processes and moral emotions of public servants. Next, the employees utilize their knowledge about how and why they need to care for the benefit of others, combined with moral emotion, to activate behaviors for recovering service. The assumption is partially in line with previous research about how leadership models could enhance personal’ s psychological process and lead to service recovery performance (e.g. Luo et al., 2019). However , we combine moral cognition with the affective side of employees. In addition, we address the gap in public management literature and ar gue that public employees in a state of thriving could care more about citizens and translate the effects of ethical leadership into actions. Therefore, thriving at work is hypothesized to link the nexus between ethical leadership and service recovery performance among public sector employees. H2. Moral self-efficacy as a moderator Self-eff icacy describes the perception that people believe in their capacity to perform certain tasks at designated levels (Schunk and DiBenedetto, 2021) and is considered a prominent element of human agency within the framework of social cognitive theory (Rullo et al., 2022; Schunk and DiBenedetto, 2021). Accordingly , individuals possessing a sense of agency tend to expand their efforts, make better goal choices, exhibit greater persistence and employ ef fective learning strategies (Schunk and DiBenedetto, 2021). Therefore, self-eff icacy was found to correlate to various cognitive and af fective personal factors such as work engagement (Musenze et al., 2021; Orgamb � ıdez et al., 2020), passion (Cardon and Kirk, 2015) and commitment (Hameli and Ordun, 2022). Drawing from the concept of general self-ef ficacy , moral self-effic acy can be defined as a specific type of self-ef ficacy in which an individual possesses the capacity to implement ethics in order to meet moral standards (Rullo et al., 2022). Since thriving at work is fueled by the agentic view that an individual can overcome workplace difficulties through active engagement and purpose, we propose that moral self-effic acy could strengthen the ef fect of ethical leadership and public sector employee’ s thriving at work under the framework of social cognitive theory . Specifically , ethical leadership, serving as an external factor , can be more ef fective because employees with a higher level of moral self-eff icacy are likely to make moral, goal-oriented choices that reflect their values (Bandura, 1986). In other words, the consistency between the values of leaders and employees can strengthen the ef fect of the moral role model of ethical leaders and translate into active learning for practicing moral behaviors, as well as engaging in a state of moral emotion. In other words, the greater the similarity between the role model and individuals, the higher the chance of success in role modeling for directing individuals’ behavior accordingly (Bandura, 1994). Thus, we also propose that in situations under ethical leadership, public sector employees can build their moral cognition and emotion (thriving at work), and exhibit public service recovery performance that upholds the ethical values learned from ethical leaders. Methods Sampling The dataset was collected from managerial and non-managerial public sector employees working at multiple levels of local government in Ho Chi Minh City , V ietnam. T o address the issue of lacking sampling frame and to maintain the confidentiality of participants, the research employed the snowball sampling method, which is considered suitable for application in leadership studies (e.g. Mashele and Alagidede, 2022; Nguyen, 2023; T ang and Li, 2022). A two-wave online survey was conducted in this research. In the first wave (T1), we invited managerial public sector employees who were alumni of the public management programs to distribute the digital version of the questionnaire to their direct subordinates. The participants of T1 shared their perceptions of ethical leadership and provided general demographic information. All of the questionnaires were assigned a 4-digit code to maintain confidentiality and to match with the second wave (T2) of the survey . The T2 survey was conducted two months after T1. W e distributed questionnaires to the initial managerial employees so they could deliver an electronic version to respondents from T1. At T2, non-managerial employees rated their opinions regarding moral self-ef ficacy and their state of thriving at work. Managerial employees also rated the service recovery performance of their subordinates at T2 in a separate questionnaire. All measurements were evaluated using a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (totally disagree) to 5 (totally agree). Since PLS-SEM approach was adopted, we followed the recommendation of Hair et al. (2021) to determine the required sample size using G*Power version 3.1 (at a power level of 80%). The minimum sample size for this research is 77 observations. Of the participants, 431 non-managerial employees participated in T1, and 343 participated in T2. There were a total of 332 ratings for non-managerial public sector employees from their direct supervisors in T2. After matching data from 2 waves, the sample size is 331, yielding a 76.8% response rate. Among the respondents, 170 were female (51.4%), 157 were male (47.4%) and 4 respondents preferred not to mention their gender (1.2%). The majority of participants hold a bachelor ’ s degree or equivalent (78.9%), 19.3% of non-managerial employees hold a master ’ s degree or higher and 1.8% hold a degree lower than a bachelor ’ s. The average job tenure is 1 1.5 years (SD 5 9.56). Data analysis strategy The hypotheses were assessed by adopting partial least square SEM (PLS-SEM) approach. Although CB-SEM and PLS-SEM are both popular in treating structural relationships, there are several reasons for us to choose the PLS-SEM approach in this research. Firstly , PLS-SEM could ef fectively handle complex models (Astrachan et al., 2014) in which our goals are to test the direct, indirect, moderation and moderated mediation effects. Secondly , when the loading indicator meets the standard (0.708), the accuracy between the two approaches could provide similar results (Reinartz et al., 2009), which addresses the concern about differentiation in evaluation. Thirdly , PLS-SEM is a more preferred approach when the aim of the research is to make a prediction (e.g. proposing managerial implications from the data analysis results) (Dash and Paul, 2021). W e followed the recommendation of Ringle et al. (2020) in applying PLS-SEM in research related to the field of human resource management. Therefore, we evaluated the measurement model and the structural model respectively . Since all of the research constructs were reflective, at stage 1 (assessing measurement model), we examined indicator reliability , internal consistency , convergent and discriminant validity . Then, we appraised the collinearity , predictive relevance, significance and relevance of path coefficients for evaluating the structural model. Common method issue W e employed multiple techniques to address the issue of method bias in the research as suggested by Podsakoff et al. (2003). First, we separated the predictor (ethical leadership), psychological variables (moral self-ef ficacy , thriving at work) and the outcome variable (service recovery performance), and conducted a time-lagged survey with a 2-month interval. Discussion The research findings confirmed the role of ethical leadership in enhancing employees’ thriving at work (H1). Accordingly , the results are partially in line with prior studies regarding the effect of ethical leadership on employees’ cognitive and affective processes (e.g. reflective moral attentiveness, work engagement, etc.) (see Miao et al., 2020; Mostafa and Abed ElMotalib, 2020; Naeem et al., 2020). However , unlike prior streams of research that focus solely on affective or cognitive processes, both of these dimensions are intertwined (Kleine et al., 2019) and take place concurrently . Accordingly , by establishing the nexus between ethical leadership and public sector employees’ thriving at work, comprising both vitality (af fection) and learning dimensions (cognition), the research contributed insights to management literature about the validity of ethical leadership in fostering positive psychological processes among employees. There are no services that are error -free and require employees to exhibit extra-role behavior , such as service recovery performance, to correct service failures in order to maintain org anizational image or customer satisfaction (Mihardjo et al., 2020). Eluwole et al. (2022), for instance, identified a mechanism in which ethical leaders could trigger service recovery performance among employees in hotel service through emotional response (affect-based trust). In this research, we enriched our understanding of how ethical leaders could leverage desirable outcomes for public sector employees through both an emotional channel (vitality) and a cognitive channel (learning). Particularly , thriving at work was confirmed as a mediator in bridging a gap between ethical leadership and public service recovery performance (H2). Under the supervision of ethical leaders, public servants could generate a moral response in the form of moral emotion and actively seek ways (such as learning) to address complaints from citizens related to unsatisfactory service delivery . W ang et al. (2021) found that the sense of becoming oneness with leaders (leader identification) could enhance the perception of an ethical role model. The findings in this study were partially consistent with the research of W ang et al. (2021), which suggests that the likeness in value of individuals and role models could play a vital role in successful learning (Bandura, 1994). However , we added a perspective of personal characteristics that could leverage the validity of ethical leadership. W e recognized that moral self-efficacy among public servants could serve as a moderator in the research context, enhancing the effect of ethical leadership on thriving at work (H3a). Additionally , moral self-efficacy also extends the indirect effect of an ethical leader on service recovery performance through thriving at work (H3b). Resear ch implications There are several theoretical contributions to the research. First, we contribute to public management literature by providing how to enhance thriving at work among public sector employees. Although thriving at work plays a vital role in the workplace, fostering a wide range of desirable outcomes (Shahid et al., 2021), there is hardly any research focusing on the public service setting. Thus, the research provides an understanding in the public sector International Journal of Organization Theory & Behavior 153 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijotb/article-pdf/28/2/143/9845114/ijotb-05-2024-0096.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 context, ethical leadership could be a solution to promote public sector employees’ thriving. A few studies have also found that ethical leadership can transfer moral values to employees, shaping their thoughts about caring for stakeholders’ benefits and exhibiting service recovery performance through promoting an affective aspect (e.g. Eluwole et al., 2022). Therefore, we made a second contribution by identifying that both emotion and cognition could link the gap between ethical leadership and service recovery performance. In other words, the mediating of thriving was confirming to close the gap between moral-related leadership and public service recovery performance. By doing so, we also respond to the call of other scholars for the need to explore service recovery performance in the public service setting (e.g. V an de W alle, 2016). Third, in several research contexts, scholars did not find the ef fect of ethical leadership (e.g. Sarwar et al., 2020) on followers. In the current research, we reinforced our findings by confirming the moderating role of moral self-eff icacy in fostering the validity of ethical leadership in personal determinants (thriving at work). Furthermore, a fourth theoretical contribution was made by exploring the moderated mediation effect of moral self-ef ficacy . A higher level of confidence in performing tasks at a morally designated level (moral selfef ficacy) could strengthen the indirect ef fect of ethical leadership on public service recovery performance via thriving at work. Finally , in the light of social cognitive theory , we constructed a collection of cognitive processes in which the interactions between the moral external factor (ethical leadership), personal determinants (moral self-effic acy and thriving at work) and the aligning behavioral outcome (service recovery performance) were corroborated. Managerial implications From the managerial viewpoint, there are recommendations to be drawn from the results. Firstly , the ethical competence of leaders is crucial for them to cultivate the vitality and learning of followers. Thus, the competence of ethical leaders should be preferred in org anizations and comprise both the moral person (e.g. managerial employees need to demonstrate integrity , fairness, etc.) and the moral manager (e.g. supervisors need to actively communicate ethical guidance and promote two-way interaction, etc.). Accordingly , org anizations could integrate moral criteria in selection processes in both internal and external recruitment. Additionally , periodic training on moral competence such as laws, public ideals and leadership skills, should also be considered. Furthermore, organizations could formalize a code of ethics within the performance feedback system to better guide appropriate behavior and provide clear expectations for leaders and employees. Second, employees’ state of thriving at work was found to link the ef fect of ethical leadership to service recovery performance. Hence, developing ethical leadership competence is essential for or ganizations to foster this recovery behavior among employees, as the data analysis results support the mediation mechanism. In addition to the ethical leadership factor confirmed in the research, since thriving at work has been found to be associated with service recovery performance, we propose that practitioners pay attention to other empirical evidence promoting thriving at work, such as leader– member exchange (Di Milia and Jiang, 2024), workplace civility (Abid et al., 2018), and support from superiors and coworkers (Zhai et al., 2020), in order to promote service recovery performance among employees. Finally , moral self-eff icacy was identified as a vital factor for employees to reinforce the ethical leadership ef fect in the or ganization. Therefore, it is required for managers to gain a further understanding of how to promote moral self-effic acy among their employees. Selfef ficacy is sensitive to contextual factors and can be fueled by four main channels: mastery experiences, vicarious experiences, social persuasion and physiological indexes (Schunk and DiBenedetto, 2021). For mastery experience, individuals can gain moral self-eff icacy from IJOTB 28,2 154 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijotb/article-pdf/28/2/143/9845114/ijotb-05-2024-0096.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 their practices of solving a variety of situations at work. Therefore, we suggest that managers devise organizational policies to strengthen personal experiences, such as job rotation and job enrichment at work, or integrate training programs that focus on applying skills to solve moral dilemma situations. Besides, employees also gain moral self-ef ficacy by observing successful models (vicarious experiences). As such, a solution to enhance the learning of morality could focus on job shadowing, allowing individuals to observe their supervisors or colleagues handling work-related issues in accordance with moral standards. Next, social persuasion is vital in shaping employees’ moral self-ef ficacy because it helps them understand expectations and the right actions at work. Thus, we suggest that practitioners promote communication about morality and issue a code of ethics in the workplace. Finally , there should be encouragement to reduce anxiety among individuals when performing moral acts. Hence, a reward and punishment system that focuses on morality could also be considered. Limitations and suggestions for futur e r esear ch There are some limitations and suggestions for future research directions in this research. First, the research contains limitations in the sampling procedure. This research is a cross-sectional study with two waves of data collection and needs to be developed into a longitudinal approach to better explain the causal relationship between leadership and employees’ behavior . Second, there are limitations in measurements. Even with ef forts to mitigate bias by collecting responses from multiple sources, the measurements are on subjective scales, which may be overestimated or underestimated. For instance, supervisors could miss critical situations in which their employees exhibit recovery behaviors to serve the citizens, resulting in a lack of information for rating. Therefore, further studies could vary sources of evaluation from stakeholders such as co-workers, citizens, etc. when examining public sector employees’ behavior . Third, the data have its limitations in the public setting of one country in Asia, which may not allow for generalizing the ef fect of ethical leadership in other contexts (see Sarwar et al., 2020, for a cross-cultural comparison), future research could retest the model in differe nt countries to make a comparison. Finally , a single study cannot cover all outcomes; there are desirable outcomes that may be related to ethical leadership, such as information security awareness or employee voice, which could contribute to the sustainability of organizations. Future studies could further develop ethical leadership research to enrich the understanding of this leadership style in both public and private contexts. Likewise, future research could expand the current research model to better understand how employees’ traits (moral selfef ficacy) can be incorporated with ethical leadership to define various outcomes, such as moral courage or moral attentiveness. The role of ethical leadership to employees work engagement: a social learning theory perspective Junaidi Junaidi Department of Accounting, Universitas Muhammadiyah Palopo, Palopo, Indonesia Abstract Purpose – This study examines the role of ethical leadership in building employee trust, knowledge sharing (KS), job satisfaction and then influencing employee engagement in the workplace. Design/methodology/approach – The sample included 610 employees of Indonesia Islamic Bank, obtained through an online survey. Structural equation modelling was used to test the research hypotheses. Findings – Ethical leadership actively contributes to the growth of employee trust, exchange knowledge frequent and job satisfaction and then become key points to enhance employees’ engagement. Research limitations/implications – Future research is required to validate across regions and organisations to in light of the findings of the topic study. Practical implications– Organisational leaders and employees obtain a better understanding of ethics and organisation management field, hence employees and leaders must encourage ethical values as code of conduct in the workplace. Originality/value – This study demonstrated the extent of the Khan concept for a combination of employee engagement, ethical leadership and KS. It also incorporates employee job satisfaction and the organisational engagement among employees. Introduction In the modern era, Enron was followed by other ethics scandals in business, government, sports, social organisations and religious organisations. It raised questions about the ethical leadership of the organisation (Mohd Ghazali, 2021). A leader has a crucial role in being the driving force of ethical behaviour for employees and organisations (Ramlawati et al., 2023; Yazdanshenas and Mirzaei, 2023). Therefore, the government and professional organisations should develop clear ethical standards and laws in business and professional organisations for leaders and employees. It embedded stakeholder trust because ethical leadership is a source of wellspring to bring organisation sustainability, competitive advantage and most importantly, to regain people’s trust. Leadership refers to the process of influencing others to understand and agree, and it also facilitates action to achieve personal and organisational goals (Yukl et al., 2009). Indonesians have a particular problem with white-collar crime in government positions such as ministers, governors and auditors through financial report misstatement. In the private and public context, the number of leaders suspected of abusing their power to manipulate their financial reports and corruption indicators has become a critical issue (Rustiarini et al., 2021). A high level of ethical leadership in the workplace is essential to ensure employees act in accordance with the organisation’s goals and ethical codes. The presence of ethical leadership has become a filter within government and also a factor in achieving organisational goals as well as employee trust and work engagement (Koay and Lim, 2022; Rechberg and Syed, 2013). However, in developing countries such as Indonesia, progress in fighting corruption has been slow (Quah, 2020; Rustiarini et al., 2021). As of 2022, Indonesia’s Corruption Perception Index (CPI) score is 34/100 and ranks 110/180 in the world. This score has increased by 2 points since 2012, compared to over thirty-two points in the previous decade (Transparency International, 2023). It’s in line with African countries such as Gambia, Malawi and Sierra Leone, as well as Nepal in South Asia. In addition, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil, Ethiopia and Equatorial Guinea do much better, despite facing political instability and low social capital. Overall, ethical leadership can be seen as an innovative approach to enhancing employee engagement in the workplace by preventing unethical behaviour (Ramlawati et al., 2023). In view of the numerous ethical scandals in numerous private, public, religious and social organisations, there is a lack of ethical leadership. It makes the trustworthiness of the people plummet. From a normative or philosophical standpoint, several academics have written about ethics and leadership and made recommendations for what leaders should do. However, a more developed and integrated social science perspective on ethics and leadership is still lacking (Bavik et al., 2018; Jia et al., 2022; Ramlawatiet al., 2023). Basic queries, such as what constitutes ethical leadership, have been raised in response to ethical scandals. How does trust among employees, information exchange and job satisfaction differs under ethical leadership? How ethical leadership influences employee work engagement toward trust, knowledge sharing, and job satisfaction Therefore, this study conducted a comprehensive ethical leadership framework and linked it to employees’social capital dimensions in order to clarify the current situation and provide insights for future research from the perspective of public and private organisations. Previous research also focused on the social or organisational level based on the impact of organisational characteristics on the effectiveness of ethical leadership (Al Halbusi et al., 2021; Bavik et al., 2018; Engelbrecht et al., 2017). Therefore, this study examines the fundamental aspect of social learning theory (SLT) (Bandura, 1977), which assumes that employees’ personal behaviour is formed by observing the behaviour of the leader and other people. According to the SLT, employee and organisation management is closely related to the personality and ability of the leader to empower other employees and share information and knowledge. In addition, learning from ethical leaders can increase employee job satisfaction and work engagement. Therefore, the main objective of this study was to investigate the influence of leadership ethics on employee work commitment, trust and exchange of knowledge and job satisfaction. In their research,Singh (2022)and Xia and Yang (2020) recommended that future studies validate the effect of ethical leadership on employees’ trust and KS, which could possibly also influence employees’ job satisfaction and work engagement in a private and public organisation context. 2. If the aim is to promote ethical behaviour in organisations, the process becomes essential as role modelling influences the workforce to pick up on the expectations, organisational benefits and consequences of organisation members’ behaviour. Organisational leaders communicate the potential relevance of normatively appropriate behaviour to employees through moral leaders who explain the acquisition and regulation of observational learning (Bandura, 1977). It requires organisational leaders and employees to act as admirable and reliable role models (See Table 1). Ethical leadership has an effect on followers because it provides direction that followers cognitively assimilate to generate critical self-reactions and direct further actions (Ren and Chadee, 2017). This is because leaders now set the tone for the behaviour of their followers. Ethical leaders foster a sense of belonging as team members by discussing the popular issues of the organisation and their opinions and by participating in the decisionmaking process. Actively discussing, exchanging ideas and sharing knowledge may influence job satisfaction (H/C23avold et al., 2021). The main value of trust and the moral component of social learning theory adequately conceptualises the influence of ethical leadership; it has become the result of employee behaviour, job satisfaction and work engagement (€Ozsungur, 2020; Ren and Chadee, 2017; Yazdanshenas and Mirzaei, 2023). 2.2 Ethical leadership, trust, knowledge sharing and job satisfaction Ethical leadership refers to certain activities of employees in the workplace as well as their interpersonal interactions with organisational leaders and their colleagues. It is related to personal qualities such as sincerity, reliability, altruistic motivation, moral obligation and employee competence (Rechberg and Syed, 2013). Ethical scandals in organisations have a strong correlation to ethical leadership because the organisation’s code of conduct plays a central role in driving and guiding employee behaviour (Poma et al., 2023). For example, ethical leadership has a positive and significant impact on employees’trust in their leader and the sustainability of the organisation (Engelbrecht et al., 2017; Kmieciak, 2021). In some organisational contexts, ethical leadership also has positive effects on employees’ attitudes and behaviours (Al Halbusiet al., 2021), KS (Amber et al., 2022; Bavik et al., 2018) and job satisfaction ( Ren and Chadee, 2017 ). The organisation management is based on trustworthiness and willingness to engage in respectful dialogue and interaction among employees. Ethical leadership emerges through two-way communication and trustworthiness to reduce fundamental barriers and pursue KS and trust among members of the organisation, which subsequently influences employee job satisfaction (Amber et al., 2022; H/C23avold et al., 2021; Koay and Lim, 2022; Mason and Leek, 2008 ). Discussion 5.1 Key findings Overall, it can be said that a leader who applies ethical concerns in their activities as well as ethical and moral values in the workplace has a crucial role in influencing employee behaviour as an ethical principle. Clear ethical standards for employees have a strong correlation to developing a positive work environment for employees through the ability and credibility of leaders. Ethical leadership also has a positive role in influencing employees’ sense of belonging to the organisation. Stimulating knowledge-sharing behaviours through ethical leadership and employee trust in leadership: the moderating role of distributive justice Phong Ba Leand Dung Thi Nguyet Nguyen Abstract Purpose – Drawing on social exchange theory, this paper aims to clarify the influences of ethical leadership (EL) on knowledge-sharing (KS) behaviours of employees through the mediating roles of affective- and cognitive-based trust in leadership. This work further offers deeper insight into the moderating mechanism of distributive justice in the EL–KS relationship. Design/methodology/approach – Structural equation modelling (SEM) is used to investigate the influential degree of EL, aspects of employee trust in leadership and distributive justice on employee behaviours towards tacit and explicit knowledge via data collected from 339 participants in 75 Vietnamese firms. Findings – The empirical findings reveal that employee trust in leadership positively mediates the relationship between EL and KS behaviours. In particular, distributive justice significantly fosters the impacts of EL on tacit and explicit KS behaviours. Practical implications – Managers and practitioners should strengthen EL practices to build and maintain employee trust in them for promoting KS behaviours. In addition, research highlights the necessity of establishing distributive justice in organisations to enhance the effect of EL on KS behaviours of employees. Originality/value – This paper is unique in its attempts to advance the insights on the theory of leadership and knowledge management by investigating the different moderated-mediation mechanisms in the relationship between EL and specific aspects of KS behaviours. Introduction In today’s knowledge-based economy, the key factor for prosperity and economic growth is superior knowledge capitalisation. Rather than physical resources such as assets, capital and facilities, the competency and competitive advantage of a firm is mainly determined by its intellectual capital, such as technology, management know-how and knowledge resources ( Le and Lei, 2019 ; Nguyen et al.,2 0 2 1). Many prior studies have pointed out that the knowledge-sharing (KS) processes can foster the flow and integration of knowledge in organisations, arouse creativity and new ideas of employees and actively support the emergence of competitive advantage in firms ( Lei et al., 2021 ; Yang et al., 2018 ). KS helps equip companies with essential skills and knowledge for employees to work efficiently by enabling firms to improve performance and obtain key organisational outcomes ( Son et al., 2020; Tangaraja et al.,2 0 1 5). Therefore, the identification of factors promoting KS among members in an organisation is vital. Current literature reveals that ethical leadership (EL) and employee trust in leadership are the key antecedents to creating an appropriate climate for fostering KS behaviours in employees ( Bhatti et al.,2 0 2 1; Lei et al., 2019a, 2019b). Prior studies indicate that if employees have high trust in the ethical behaviours of leaders and perceive integrity and fairness in their organisation ( Phong and Son, 2020 ; Su et al., 2021 ), they have greater motivation and commitment to actively participate in the activities of KS. Accordingly, this study focusses on exploring the different mechanisms and interactions by which EL affects KS behaviours via the mediating role of employee trust and the moderating role of distributive justice. This study expects to significantly expand the theory of leadership, organisational behaviour and knowledge management from the perspective of various motivational factors. First, leadership behaviour not only affects KS behaviours of employees directly due to the leaders’ decisive roles and comprehensive impacts on all organisational activities but also indirectly affects KS processes by creating an appropriate culture to foster the willingness of employees for sharing knowledge ( Lei et al., 2019a, 2019b; Shariq et al.,2 0 1 9). Scholars have devoted considerable effort to exploring and explaining the leadership –KS relationship; however, most studies examine the effects of transformational leadership ( Phong and Son, 2020 ; Yin et al., 2019 ) while overlooking the essential role of EL despite it being one of the most appropriate leadership styles for enhancing KS activities in an organisation ( Bavik et al, 2018 ; Bhatti et al.,2 0 2 1). Although typical studies have tried to explain the EL –KS relationship ( Bavik et al., 2018 ; Bhatti et al.,2 0 2 1; Tu et al.,2 0 1 9), they have not clarified the mechanism and influence of EL on specific aspects of KS, such as tacit and explicit KS. To address these theoretical gaps, this study applies a moral lens to inspect and explain how EL can shape and foster specific aspects of KS behaviours of employees, namely, tacit and explicit KS, by proposing the first research question: RQ1. Does EL significantly predict tacit and explicit KS? Second, literature on trust suggests that high levels of trust generally create reciprocity among employees and managers while inspiring employees to share formal and informal knowledge (Le et al., 2018; Swift and Hwang, 2013 ). In addition, Wu and Lee (2017) suggested that employees are the main executors of KS processes within an organisation, stressing the importance of understanding psychological behaviours surrounding the KS process, such as aspects of employees’ trust in leadership. Notably, Lei et al. (2019a, 2019b) argued that little to no research has applied a moral lens to examine the effects of EL on employees’ KS behaviours via the mediating role of employee trust. This limits our insight into the different ways EL may positively affect employee trust in leadership to produce better influences on KS behaviours. In other words, further theoretical and practical evidence is required to detect and explain possible mediating effects of attributes of employee trust in the relationship between EL and KS processes. So, the second research question arises: RQ2. Do aspects of employee trust in leadership mediate the impacts of EL on tacit and explicit KS? To address the research questions, this study applies structural equation modelling (SEM) based on data collected from 339 participants in 75 Vietnamese firms to investigate the degree of influence of EL and aspects of employee trust on KS behaviours under the moderating role of distributive justice. Social exchange theory recommends that parties with the expectation of some future return or reciprocity will be involved in and sustain the exchange relationship with others ( Blau, 1964 ; Cropanzano and Mitchell, 2005 ). Drawing mainly on social exchange theory ( Blau, 1964 ), this study suggests that positive perceptions and attitudes about leaders and the organisation lead to high trust and positive KS behaviours of employees. This study is expected to provide theoretical initiatives on organisational behaviours and knowledge management as well as practical implications to foster KS behaviours of employees in organisations. The remainder of this study is arranged as follows. A literature review clarifies the relationship among the latent research factors in Section 2. The methodology section presents the research methods testing the proposed model given in Section 3. Section 4 presents data analysis and results, which are followed by an examination of the empirical findings. Finally, a discussion and conclusions present the theoretical and practical contributions and offer proposals for future research in Section 5. 2. Literature review and hypotheses 2.1 Theoretical background and concepts 2.1.1 Social exchange theory.“Social exchange theory” is considered one of the foremost concepts related to individual behaviour in the workplace ( Cropanzano and Mitchell, 2005 ). The theory suggests that interactions between two parties must involve reciprocal interdependence (Blau, 1964). This theory implies that employees will respond with suitable behaviours if they realise that their organisation is dedicated to them ( Alpkan et al., 2020; Su et al., 2021). Drawing from the principles of social exchange theory, this study purports that expressions of sincere concern and kindness by ethical leaders towards employees while focusing on their collective interests can create employee trust. This display of interest in the welfare of employees from ethical leaders fosters positive reciprocation from employees through engagement in KS activities that benefit their organisation in return. 2.1.2 Ethical leadership.Leadership behaviours play a decisive role in creating appropriate conditions that allow employees to exercise and cultivate their knowledge and skills, and to contribute their private knowledge capital to organisational knowledge resources ( Gui et al., 2021; Wang and Noe, 2010). According to Brown et al.(2005), EL leaders emphasise honesty and integrity and manifest normatively appropriate behaviour through personal actions and interpersonal relationships. Leaders who practice EL further promote such behaviour to subordinates based on two-way communication, reinforcement and decision-making. Bedi et al. (2016) spotlighted that ethical leaders actively promote ethical behaviour through both roles of “moral persons”, and “moral managers” by clearly communicating their ethical standards and requiring followers responsible for ethical behaviour. Although there are certain commonalities in the ethics between EL and other typical leadership styles (such as authentic leadership, transformational leadership and servant leadership), prior studies have pointed out that some leadership styles consider ethics as merely one aspect of leadership behaviour. In comparison, ethical leaders focus entirely and explicitly on ethics and ethically driven behaviour ( Lei et al., 2019a, 2019b; Mayer et al., 2009). 2.1.3 Knowledge-sharing.As a crucial asset for any organisation, knowledge is a special resource that differs from other resources in its frugality ( Du et al.,2 0 0 7). The application and transfer of knowledge in KS processes not only does not consume knowledge but also helps promote knowledge creation by improving the absorptive capacity of organisations ( Yang et al.,2 0 1 8). As Gok̈sel and Aydıntan (2017) stated, “knowledge has no value if it is not used”. Accordingly, to increase the value of knowledge, it must be shared among individuals both inside and outside organisations. Le and Lei (2019) defined KS as the process of exchanging knowledge and experience that helps individuals equip each other with new complementary and valuable knowledge and skills to achieve personal and organisational goals. The literature mainly distinguishes KS behaviours into two main components – explicit and tacit KS – due to its crucial influences on key organisational outcomes, such as organisational productivity and performance, absorptive and innovation capability and sustainable competitive advantage ( Lei et al., 2019a, 2019b; Shao et al., 2015 ; Wang et al.,2 0 1 6). “Tacit KS” involves the process of sharing knowledge possessed by individuals such as experience and expertise, uncommon understandings, insights and intuitions ( Lei et al., 2019a , 2019b; Wang et al., 2016). “Explicit KS” involves the process of sharing codified knowledge and formal information that can be captured and transmitted within an organisation, such as documents and reports, procedures and policies or handbooks ( Lei et al., 2019a , 2019b; Wang et al.,2 0 1 6). 2.1.4 Trust in leadership.Trust is considered a dynamic, interpersonal link between people in the workplace ( Bligh, 2017 ). In particular, trust manifests itself in the degree of confidence an individual has in another’s competence and his or her willingness to act in a fair, ethical and predictable manner ( Nyhan, 2000 ). Developments in the organisational sciences stress the significance of employee trust in the leadership –employee relationship for sustaining individual and organisational effectiveness ( Islam et al.,2 0 2 1; Le and Lei, 2017). In the organisational context, trust in leadership is considered a central feature of leader–follower relationships that affects key outcomes of an organisation ( Bligh, 2017 ). Successful leaders can build and maintain employee trust through practices that create positive employee perceptions of their leadership characteristics and behaviours ( Le and Lei, 2018a, 2018b). According to Schoorman et al. (2007), trust in leadership reflects the willingness of employees to accept vulnerability based on positive expectations of the intentions of leaders. McAllister’s (1995) model of trust separated trust into affective-based trust and cognitive-based trust. “Cognitive-based trust” is rooted in one individual’s logical and objective evaluation of another person’s key personal characteristics, such as her or his VOL. 27 NO. 3 2023jJOURNAL OF KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENTj PAGE 823 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/jkm/article-pdf/27/3/820/1824744/jkm-06-2021-0462.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 competence, reliability and integrity ( Yang et al.,2 0 0 9). “Affective-based trust” is formed by one individual’s feelings based on ongoing socio-emotional exchanges and a sense of reciprocated sentiments ( Zhu et al.,2 0 1 3). To simplify, Chua et al. (2008) described cognitive-based trust as “trust from the head” and affective-based trust as “trust from the heart”. This study uses these two types of trust to measure employee trust in leadership because they are commonly used in empirical studies of leadership and have been validated in a variety of contexts ( Lei et al., 2019a , 2019b). Moreover, McEvily and Tortoriello’s (2011) work measuring trust in organisational research regarded McAllister’s two-dimensional model of trust as a noteworthy instrument, ranking it first out of 27 evaluated models. 2.1.5 Distributive justice. Organisational justice is a traditional subject of research on organisational behaviour that mainly focusses on employees’ perception of justice in organisations ( Le and Lei, 2017 ). “Justice” is defined as the extent to which employees consider that the organisational decisions are fair ( Phong and Son, 2020 ). In general, feelings and evaluations of employees in social interactions flow from their judgment of the fairness of outcomes in interactions others, such as their leaders ( De Cremer et al., 2004 ; Phong and Son, 2020 ). As a significant issue in the field of leadership and organisational behaviour, organisational justice is generally classified into three main categories: distributive, procedural and interactional justice ( Akram et al.,2 0 1 7). Among these, distributive justice is the main component of organisational justice because positive behaviour and working motivation of employees can only be aroused and developed if they receive fair or favourable outcomes ( Alpkan et al.,2 0 2 0; De Cremer et al., 2004 ; Samadi, 2018 ). According to Phong and Son (2020), distributive justice reflects employees’ perceptions of fairness of key outcomes that they received in the process of working in an organisation. To a certain extent, the achievement of the organisation’s goals depends significantly on the degree of fairness or unfairness in the distribution of outcomes such as salary, promotions and welfare ( De Cremer et al.,2 0 0 4; Le and Lei, 2017 ). Distributive justice can serve as a crucial factor that explains employees’ motivation and willingness to share knowledge in organisations ( Phong and Son, 2020 ; Samadi, 2018). Hence, this study focusses on investigating the moderating influence of distributive justice on the EL –KS relationship. 2.2 Effect of ethical leadership on knowledge-sharing KS activities do not come automatically in an organisation – the KS process occurs only when necessary conditions are met. Organisational support and the leadership role have great potential to influence the extent of KS activities ( Le, 2021 ). Leadership behaviours have a strong correlation and are necessary to create and maintain a positive KS climate among employees in organisations ( Le and Lei, 2019 ; Lin and Lee, 2004 ). Many previous studies have shown the positive relationship between leadership styles (such as transactional, transformational and authentic leadership) and KS processes ( Ed/C19uValsania et al.,2 0 1 6; Le and Lei, 2019 ; Rawung et al.,2 0 1 5). Regarding the EL –KS relationship, Tang et al. (2015) showed that EL has positive influences on KS behaviour. Bavik et al.(2017) indicated that EL contributes to stimulating KS behaviours of employees by eliminating the structural barriers hindering KS, fostering the formation of trusting and fair relationships and developing employees’ expectation of fair interchange for their contributions. In particular, Lei et al.(2019a, 2019b) argued that ethical leaders significantly contribute to fostering the engagement and attitude of employees towards KS behaviours based on creating an ethical and ideal environment for KS activities to take place. Their empirical findings revealed that EL is significantly associated with KS behaviours of employees towards tacit and explicit KS. Xia and Yang (2020) argue that employees identify ethical leaders as attractive and credible role models, thus they will follow and actively participate in KS activities for the common benefit of the organisation. The above arguments support the positive relationship between EL and KS behaviours. We therefore propose the following hypotheses. H1a.b. EL is positively related to tacit and explicit KS behaviours of employees. 2.3 Effect of ethical leadership on employee trust in leadership Trust is most meaningful in situations where one party is at risk or vulnerable to another party. For this reason, it becomes especially crucial in leader –employee relationships in the workplace ( Bligh, 2017 ). Le and Lei (2018a , 2018b) exhibited that leadership behaviours and substitutes (such as intrinsically satisfying tasks or employees’ ability, training and experience) account for unique variance in attitudes of employees. The relationship between EL and trust in leadership has recently received significant attention from scholars and practitioners. Indeed, according to Kalshoven and Hartog (2009), employees tend to highly appreciate to ethical behaviours of leadership because such moral behaviours make their leaders attractive and credible models. So ethical leaders are significantly related to the level of employees’ trust in the leadership. Basing a sample of 294 matched leader –employee dyads, Kalshoven et al. (2011) asserted that perceptions of employees towards ethical behaviours significantly contribute to their trust in leadership. In a similar vein, Engelbrecht et al.(2015) indicated that if employees perceived the ethical behaviour of the leaders, their trust in leaders will be set up. Bedi et al.(2016) reveal that ethical leaders positively influence both employees’ cognitive trust in leadership (trust in their leadership capabilities and personal attributes) and affective trust in leadership (trust in socio-emotional exchanges and admiration towards their leaders). According to Mo and Shi (2017) , employees may have a higher degree of trust in ethical leaders keeping promises and behaving consistently due to such leaders usually reward ethical behaviour and discipline unethical behaviour. They inform employees of what is expected from them and how they can positively contribute to the organisation. In a similar vein, Engelbrecht et al. (2017) reported a positive relationship between EL and employee trust in leadership. These scholars argued that ethical leaders’ concern for the best interests of the organisation and fair decision making should result in fostering the trust of employees in their leaders. Using data collected from 269 participants at 65 Chinese firms, Lei et al. (2019a, 2019b) reported that ethical leaders induce positive impacts on cognition-based trust and affect-based trust of employees in their leaders. Bhatti et al.(2021) supposed that when interacting with ethical leaders, employees tend to have high trust in them, worry less about socio-political challenges and focus much attention on tasks leading to fertile outcomes. In particular, literature indicated that ethical leaders enhance employee’s cognitive trust by maintaining consistency between words and actions, and they also strengthen the emotional bond to elicit higher levels of affective trust of employees (Zhu et al., 2013; Iqbal et al.,2 0 2 0). In general, the above arguments support the positive influences of EL on employees’ trust in leadership. Indeed, according to Cheng et al.(2008), employee trust is one of the main factors influencing their decision to share knowledge. In case of having higher trust in relationships with leaders and colleagues, employees will pay more intentions to actively participate in the KS process and are more willing to provide useful knowledge. Using the sample of 202 professionals and managers in the world headquarters of an international organisation, Holste and Fields (2010) stressed that trust acts as an antecedent and lies at the centre of KS. Their empirical findings show both cognitive trust and affective trust significantly affecting the extent to the willingness of professionals for using and sharing knowledge with their colleagues. Ferreira Peralta and Francisca Saldanha (2014) explained that as an aspect of relationships among individuals, trust propensity will serve as a predictor of KS activities due to a trusting interaction established between two or more employees in organisations. Also, Jain et al. (2015) asserted that a higher level of trust among employees will create greater impetus and intentions to engage in KS processes. Their empirical findings showed affective-based trust and cognitive-based trust positively associated with employee behaviours of collecting and donating knowledge. Notably, Le and Lei (2018a , 2018b) claimed that the difference in the trust levels of employees explained the variance in their degree of sharing knowledge with others. Their empirical findings showed that both disclosure- and reliance-based trust in leadership are significantly related to KS behaviours. Lee et al. (2020) suggest and show the key roles of trust and openness in fostering informal and formal KS processes. It is also noted that affective-based trust and cognitive-based trust encourage employees to share their ideas with others because it subtracts the fear of sharing their significant resources with someone else, such as the position in the organisation, job security, time, bonuses and others ( Casimir et al., 2012; Islam et al.,2 0 2 1; Jain et al.,2 0 1 5). Based on the discussion above, this study suggests that when employees have a high level of trust in leadership in terms of cognition and affection, they will feel free and ready to share their expertise and skill with colleagues to obtain greater interests for themselves and the organisation. Thus, the following hypotheses arise: H3a.b. Affective-based trust in leadership significantly affects tacit and explicit KS. H3c.d. Cognitive-based trust in leadership significantly affects tacit and explicit KS. The arguments above suggest the positive impacts of EL on employee trust in leadership that in turn significantly relate to tacit and explicit KS behaviours of employees. Furthermore, Lee et al.(2010) indicated that both trust in leaders and co-workers mediates the effect of leaders on KS behaviours. Notably, Le and Lei (2018a , 2018b) justified that ethical leaders who successively build up employees’ trust in leadership will positively stimulate KS behaviours of employees in an organisation. Their findings manifested that disclosure- and reliance-based employee trust in ethical leaders serve as mediators between the EL –KS relationship. Current literature also reveals that the fairness and moral behaviours of EL not only create reciprocity among employees and managers but also build high levels of employee trust in their leaders, thereby leading to greater willingness and motivation for sharing both tacit and explicit KS ( Bavik et al., 2018 ; Le and Lei , 2018a, 2018b; Lee et al., 2020; Lei et al., 2019a , 2019b). Regarding the impact of distributive justice on KS, Ibragimova (2012) demonstrated that employee perceptions of fairness play an important role in stimulating KS. Akram et al. (2017) suggested that employees will voluntarily share their knowledge with their colleagues if they trust in receiving a fair reward for their KS efforts. Similarly, Le and Lei (2017) pointed out that the awareness of fairness and reciprocity of employees in the KS process is the main drive motivating them to positively share their knowledge and expertise with others ( Le and Lei, 2017 ). Recently, Phong and Son (2020) claimed that the degree of attitude and behaviour of employees towards KS activities is governed mainly by their beliefs and evaluations about expected results and outcomes. Previous studies considered distributive justice as a vital moderating or mediating factor in organisational relationships ( De Cremer et al.,2 0 0 4; Janssen et al., 2010 ; Oh, 2019 ). According to De Cremer et al. (2004), the sense and evaluations of employees in social interactions flow from their assessments of the fairness of their outcomes when dealing with others. Consequently, the impact of ethical leaders on KS processes will be multiplied and stronger if employees perceive fairness in the outcomes arising from their KS activities ( Bavik et al., 2018; De Cremer et al.,2 0 0 4). In particular, recent studies have indicated that employees tend to be reluctant to share key knowledge with others because they dreaded losing their distinctiveness compared with colleagues, especially in cases of a lack of awareness of the integrity and fairness of an organisation ( Le and Lei, 2019 ). Thus, ethical leaders will be more likely to strongly provoke explicit and tacit KS behaviours in an organisation if employees have high trust in the support, integrity and fairness in the outcome distribution ( Bavik et al.,2 0 1 8 ; Le and Lei, 2019 ). To explore the potential moderating role of distributive justice in the EL –KS relationship, the following hypotheses are proposed: H5a.b. Distributive justice significantly predicts tacit and explicit KS. H6a.b. Distributive justice positively moderates EL’s effects on tacit and explicit KS. 3. Research methodology 3.1 Sampling The study applied a survey method based on a questionnaire to collect data. To select participants, this study examined a total of 75 Vietnamese firms. The firms were randomly selected from a list of the top 1,000 service and manufacturing enterprises in Vietnam published by VietNamNet Magazine in 2018. We communicated with representatives of these firms by phone or make personal visits to explain the purpose of the research and ask for their assistance in disseminating and collecting the questionnaires. To meet research needs, the respondents in our research need to be key employees who are team leaders or leaders at departments of administration, R&D, accounting, operation, marketing and sales to ensure the necessary understanding of their firm as well as frequently exchanging strategic information in the organisation. This study used the measurement items that adapted from existing scales in the literature to develop the initial list of items. We then employed backward translation to confirm the consistency between English questionnaire and Vietnamese questionnaire.
