This study has covered up the gap with specific reference to conducting this study in Pakistan. In this study, "bottom line mentality" refers to the role of top management in meeting the bottom line demands and how this can lead to the social undermining of employees. The analysis showed that employees and management sometimes get too involved in achieving the demands of the bottom line that they often forget to follow ethical leadership practices, although ethical considerations are equally important (Greenbaum et al., 2020; Wolfe, 1988). The employees' voice depicted that there is a need for proper ethical leadership in the organizations, and the Standard Operating Procedures should be developed to ensure that all employees are treated equally and ethically. We have analyzed that to meet the demands, the top management ignores the demands of the employees. The same reference can be found in the literature, which states that the focus of the management is just to increase the profits of the organization (Wolfe, 1988). One of the participants stated in the interview that the employees work hand to meet the organization's demands, and all the rewards are taken over by the managers who are supervising them. It can be con - cluded here that the bottom-line goals of the organization are being met at the expense of other employees working within the same organization (Sims & Brinkman, 2002). According to Greenbaum et al. (2012), the success of employees is intentionally hindered by the top management, which leads to social undermining (e.g., providing the wrong informa - tion, competition for status, and delaying work, etc.). As per the literature, such practices of management are harmful to the proper functioning of the organization (Greenbaum et al., 2020). For example, management’s BLM can lead to the social undermining of (Greenbaum et al., 2012) unethical behavior and abusive behavior. The analysis showed that middle managers have the role of acting ethically and ask - ing their subordinates to follow ethics so that the element of social undermining of the employees can be reduced to zero. This role of middle managers has been highlighted in the literature (Singh et al., 2020). As mentioned by one of the interviewers, their middle managers have a role in this. "Definitely, our middle managers follow the ethics and motivate them to follow the ethics." Theoretical Implications The objective of this study was to explore the trust and perception of followers of their middle-level managers and immediate supervisors on how to motivate leaders in the genesis of ethical leadership and to explore the perceptions of top management's bottom-line mentality and how it can lead to the social undermining of middle-level managers in the genesis of ethical leadership. The gap in the literature to understand individual behavior, bottom-line mentality, trust perceptions, and social undermining from the perspective of ethical leadership was covered in this study in the context of an underdeveloped country, Pakistan. The study's main findings relate to its objectives, that the personality and positioning of the leader (middle manager and top manager) are more important in building perceptions in the minds of followers. The results of the study revealed that trust has a significant role in maintaining employees' trust, and that bottom-line demands play an important role in the social undermining of employees. To shift the focus towards the personality of leaders, which current literature has been continuously criticizing. Theorists can incorporate more personality models and theories into ethical leader - ship to create an integrated approach. It turns out that fol - lowers' perceptions are more important than leaders' ethical behavior. The empirical contribution of this study has indicated that employees’ interests are taken for granted, and bottom-line objectives are more important in the eyes of top manage - ment. This study has opened new directions for the scholars and theorists of the social sciences to investigate the model proposed by this study to determine the role of middle-level managers as they are the key source of reducing the social undermining of their subordinates. The model proposed in this study can be tested to strengthen and generalize the findings of this study for the theoretical expansion of LMX and ethical leadership theory. Practical Implications With regard to the implications for human resource man - agement in respect to ethical leadership, the findings of this research offer some pathways. First, the findings of this research offer organizations an opportunity to invest their resources in the implementation and practice of ethical leadership in their organizations. Secondly, the extant lit - erature has highlighted that the bottom-line mentality of the top management leads towards the dysfunctionality of the organizations. The fulfillment of demands and achievement of higher profits narrow down the role of top management. We have mentioned in our research that such mentality leads to the social undermining of the employees. Thus, we studied this aspect from the qualitative lens by listening directly to the employees about such practices. We have contrib - uted to improving managerial practices by bringing light to this issue by conducting research in a developing country. Thus, the findings of this research recommend that better performance and profit maximization expectations from the employees can be enhanced by reducing the bottomline mentality. Organizations should understand that the 16613Current Psychology (2023) 42:16602–16617 1 3 bottom-line mentality can be both beneficial and costly for employees and organizations. Therefore, it is important to incorporate the findings of our research into managerial programs to make the leaders realize that the bottom-line mentality can lead to the social undermining of employees, thus, as a result, poor performance and hence reduced profits. Our findings have practical implications for the ethical leadership practices in organizations. The extant literature has focused mainly on the factors contributing to ethical leadership practices. Ethical leadership practices hinder unethical values and practices at the workplace. Our research has studied the phenomenon of ethical leadership and how unethical leadership practices can be a cause of social undermining of employees. The findings contribute to these managerial issues by giving due importance to ethical leadership practices. Managers should keep moral values and ethics in mind while communicating the bottom-line demands to their employees. The findings of this research highlight the significance of following ethics in the organization. The top management should explicitly state in their strategies the significance of ethical leadership practices, and these practices should be followed while meeting the bottom-line demands of the organizations. However, the focal point here to mention is the formulation of policies, rules, and regula - tions, ethical practices, and the implementation of these ethical practices. This study suggests the pivotal role of ethical leadership in organizations. Additionally, the implementa - tion of such practices should be rewarded and promoted in organizations. Finally, this study offers useful insights for the top man - agement to get the actual picture in terms of employees’ perspectives. The employees' trust perception of top man - agement makes them act ethically and, thus, follow all ethical leadership practices. Our findings suggest that the organization's practitioners avoid abusive behavior to meet the demands of the bottom line. Such demands can be ful - filled by good leadership and by the charismatic personal - ity of the leaders. The top and middle management should devise Standard Operating Procedures (SOP’s) and ethical values to lower social undermining and work pressure on the lower-level employees. As a result, the management can win the trust of their employees. Limitations and Future Research The present study has been conducted considering time and other constraints; hence, it has some limitations. The first limitation is the small sample size. A larger sample size could have explored the opinions and viewpoints of more individuals. As we could get only 2 representatives from each department, more representation might have led to more similarities or differences to develop further in-depth knowledge. Moreover, a cross-industry comparison where more manufacturing companies can understand how the leaders specifically behave: consistent with this, future studies can also consider the services sector, especially in the current COVID situation where most of the services indus - tries are operating online, and teams are connected virtually. It will be interesting to know how ethical leadership has evolved or in the process of evolving with employees’ per - ception and trust in their leaders while connecting virtually. The statistical generalization of qualitative is rather dif - ficult because it is neither about the particular views nor particular location about which the wider applicability of findings can be drawn rather it is the in-depth study of a particular phenomenon, lived experiences and factors that shape the phenomenon being studied (Lewis et al., 2003). The representation generalization of findings does not require how far the findings can be applied to parent population (Lewis et al., 2003). In a traditional sense, the qualitative studies are not generalizable rather they contribute to the community with a more in-depth finding (Myers, 2000). This research has sought to capture how trust and per - ception of followers on their middle-level managers and immediate supervisors motivate leaders in the genesis of ethical leadership and how the perceptions of top manage - ment's bottom-line mentality led to the social undermining of middle levels managers in the genesis of ethical leader - ship. While, limited in sample size, our target population was small because negotiating access to the population was slow and labor intensive due to COVID-19 restrictions, therefore we opted for the telephonic interview to reach the right population. Although, limited in sample size but the method opted for data collection helped us to generate the rich data. Being qualitative in nature, the interviews were opted to establish the in-depth interviews with the respondents and to address the research problem in-depth. The smaller the sample size, the closer is to establish the in-depth relationship with the respondents, therefore, the smaller number of cases has facilitated the researchers to establish the close association with the participants in naturalistic settings. The phe - nomenon being under study usually occurs once therefore, the sample size is often kept small in qualitative research. The saturation of themes is likely to occur within the first six in-depth interviews and saturation point is clearly evi - dent at 12 interviews (Guest et al., 2006). Additionally, in phenomenology approach the sample size is usually kept small because in the view of Gonzalez ( 2009), the sample size is driven on the basis of the main variants of the study and once the start appearing the sample size of less than twenty are common. Cresswell ( 2011) has argued that it is normal “to study a few individuals or a few cases” (pg, 209) in qualitative research studies. The data saturation was achieved, and same themes were appearing therefore, the authors stopped their data collection 16614 Current Psychology (2023) 42:16602–16617 1 3 on 10 interviews. According to qualitative researchers, most of data can be collected from the initial interviews from the participants and sample size of 10 is adequate where the characteristics of the population are homogenous (Sandelowski, 1995). Hence, the sample size adopted for this research was appropriate as per the scope and the nature of the topic (Morse, 2000). The contact time with each participant was enough to get the richer information Marshall et al. ( 2013) and in this research the target population was homogenous working in the same industry and at same level (Trotter, 2012). Additionally, as per aims and objectives of this study the target population selected for the sampling was the truly representative (Bock & Sergeant, 2002). The philosophical stance of this study is constructivism which requires in-depth inquiry of the matter; thus, this indepth understanding of phenomenon can be achieved through smaller number of interviews from the target population (Boddy, 2016). Albeit, as per qualitative researchers there is no hard and fast rule for the minimum sample size requirement for qualitative research. The minimum sample size for this study is justified within the aim, scope and nature of this study. The second limitation is related to the informants; data was collected from subordinates to understand their perceptions and trust. However, future studies could include mid - dle management, department heads, and top management along the same lines. As the results indicated, the role of top management is unclear with respect to the head of depart - ments and, ultimately, middle-level managers. Therefore, future studies can also explore trust and perception by con - sidering the viewpoints of middle managers and integrating them with the views of employees at lower levels. Thirdly, data was collected cross-sectionally from employees prob - ing their past experiences. However, this perception and the trust identified in the study are ongoing. Therefore, future studies can consider exploring the evolution of employees’ trust and perception of their leaders by collecting data dur - ing different time intervals. This perception may evolve as some difficult situations are encountered. It will be interesting to see the evolution and even co-evolution of employees’ trust and perception of their leaders. Finally, we recommend and open the floor for new researchers to incorporate other process theories to conduct a grounded theory. Although ethical leadership is not a novel approach, for further theory advancement, a more qualitative approach such as grounded theory can be of great significance. Conclusion Ethical leadership has gained special attention from scholars and researchers during the last decade. In today’s dynamic work environment where employees are a competitive advantage, their concerns and issues should be addressed fairly by their leaders. This study signifies the ethical behavior of middle-level managers towards their subordinates and how the followers shape their perception. It has been found that leaders’ behavior and personality are more important in building trust and the perception of employees, and this perception does not entail that a leader will act ethically in real life, but they are perceived to be. The findings reported that the bottom-line mentality demands are given priority, and thus to achieve these demands, ethical values are being ignored while the nature of the task and attitude of the supervisor leads towards the social undermining of the employees. Four studies consisting of both qualitative and quantitative were conducted, involving 732 hotel employees from 11 hotels. Study one used literature review, in-depth interviews, and focus group discussion to conceptualize ethical leadership as a four-dimensional construct, including moral person, employee care, moral management, and social responsibility. They find that different societies emphasized different aspects of EL. In the Chinese society, ethical leadership derives from Confucian philosophy (Lin & Huang, 2012 ). The propositions of Confucianism (such as benevolence, righteousness, harmony, loyalty, and humility) utterly reflect the values and ethical codes required of an ethical leader (Qin et al., 2014 ). Confucianism advocates the “rule of virtue,” meaning that the governance of the country depends on the morality of the ruler (Liu & Stening, 2015 ). Indeed, Confucian philosophy encourages leaders to judge and rule on the principle of morality (Pan et al., 2012 ). Over the course of the history, Chinese state leaders have attached great importance to the “rule of virtue.” Perhaps unsurprisingly then, with regard to organizational management in China, the ethics or morality of the leaders are paramount. China’s hospitality industry in recent years has been fraught with ethical issues, such as price gouging, food safety violations, breaches of hygiene standards, deceptive advertising, employee mistreatment, to name just a few. Such unethical acts lead to customer defection and employee turnover, and the dire situation calls for strong ethical leadership in Chinese hospitality firms. However, to date, relatively few empirical studies have investigated EL in the hospitality settings grounded in Chinese culture, partly due to a lack of a tailor-made measurement scale. The majority of the existing measurement scales of EL are developed from the Western perspective. Since cultural differences can greatly influence the connota - tion and structure of EL, it is necessary to examine the concept of EL through the lens of Chinese philosophical foundation. Therefore, this study attempts to develop a measure that captures the aspects of EL from the Eastern cultural perspective in the hospitality context. Literature review Definition of ethical leadership (EL) Kanungo and Mendonca ( 1996 ) highlighted the issue of EL by noting, “One’s understand - ing of leadership is severely incomplete, if not distorted, if one does not also consider the ethics or morality of leadership” (p.234). Kanungo and Mendonca ( 1998 ) continued their 948 B. WEN AND C. G. CHI line of thought and argued in favor of a belief that EL directs and guides organizational members toward goals and objectives that benefit the organization, its members, and society. However, they did not provide a precise definition of EL, nor did they conduct a follow-up empirical study. It was not until the early twenty-first century that scholars began to probe EL systematically. Treviño et al. ( 2000 ) proposed that a “moral person” and a “moral manager” form the substantive basis of EL. The term “moral person” refers to leadership characters and virtues such as honesty, integrity, trustworthiness, concern for people, and fairness (Brown & Treviño, 2006 ). The term “moral manager” refers to a manager who should act as a role model for employees (Brown et al., 2005 ; Rubin et al., 2010 ); communicate with employees about the organization’s code of ethics, principles, and values; and establish a reward system to hold employees accountable to ethical standards (Mayer et al., 2012 ). Adopting a social learning perspective, Brown et al. ( 2005 ) defined EL as “the demonstration of normatively appropriate conduct through personal actions and interpersonal relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to followers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and decision-making” (p.120). This definition emphasized that ethical leaders could influence the ethical conduct of fol - lowers via role modeling (Brown & Treviño, 2014 ). Most research related to EL is grounded in the Western perspectives. Resick et al. ( 2011 ) explored the meaning of EL within both Western and Eastern societies. They identified six main themes of EL: accountability, consideration and respect for others, fairness and nondiscriminatory treatment, character, collective orientation, and openness and flexibility. They also described the convergence and divergence in both the meaning and the impor - tance of EL across cultures. Therefore, it is worth noting that cultural differences exist in EL. Dimensions and measurement of ethical leadership (EL) Prior research has discussed the dimensions of EL from different perspectives and via different approaches. In such studies, the dimensions of EL vary from a single factor to multiple factors. Single dimension Brown et al. ( 2005 ) developed a single-factor scale, the ethical leadership scale (ELS), which includes 10 items based on the social learning perspective. According to this perspective, employees learn (in)appropriate behaviors via leaders’ role modeling and understand the related consequences (Treviño et al., 2003 ). This scale was tested using a sample of employ - ees from a financial firm in the U.S. and showed high validity. Yukl et al. ( 2013 ) developed and tested a 15-items composite scale, the Ethical Leadership Questionnaire (ELQ) using a sample of U.S. graduate students. Their scale included various elements of EL, including integrity, honesty, fairness, altruism, and others. However, other researchers (see below) considered EL as a multi-dimensional construct. Multiple dimensions Kanungo and Mendonca ( 1998 ) conceptualized three dimensions of EL: the leader’s motive, the leader’s influence on strategy, and the leader’s character. In this conceptual model, the leader’s motive must be altruistic; the leader’s influence on strategy must focus on JOURNAL OF HOSPITALITY MARKETING & MANAGEMENT 949 empowerment rather than control; and the leader’s character must incorporate moral principles in his or her beliefs, values, and behavior. Based on the conceptual study of Kanungo and Mendonca ( 1998 ), Khuntia and Suar ( 2004 ) proposed a 22-item scale con - sisting of the following dimensions of EL: empowerment, motive and character. Using the definition by Brown et al. ( 2005 ), De Hoogh and Den Hartog ( 2008 ) conceptualized EL with three dimensions: morality and fairness, role clarification, and power sharing. Instead of developing a corresponding scale, they borrowed the measurement from the Multi-Culture Leader Behavior Questionnaire (MCLQ, Hanges & Dickson, 2004 ). Treviño et al. ( 2003 ) conducted 40 semi-structured interviews with corporate ethics officers (20) and senior executives (20) from medium to large American companies. They conceptualized EL as five dimensions consisting of people orientation, ethical actions and traits, ethical standards and accountability, ethical awareness, and ethical decision-making process. However, no follow-up empirical study tested the validity of this scale. Kalshoven et al. ( 2011 ) also expanded and established a seven-dimensional scale of EL, including morality and fairness, role clarification, power sharing, people orientation, integrity, ethical guidance, and concern for sustainability. However, this scale was considered too broad in EL conceptualization (Zhu et al., 2019 ). Resick et al. ( 2006 ) identified four aspects of EL: character/integrity, altruism, collective motivation, and encouragement. In contrast with other EL scales, this one was developed against a multi-cultural rather than single cultural background. The study showed that the four-dimensional structure had good cross-cultural applicability, but different cultures varied significantly in the degree of endorsement for each dimension, indicating that EL is a culturally embedded concept. A couple of recent studies examined EL in Eastern cultures. A. -C. Wang et al. ( 2017 ) used an indigenous, qualitative approach to investigate behavioral manifestations of EL in the Chinese context and developed the Chinese Ethical Leadership Scale (CELS), consisting of moral courage, openness to criticism, incorruptibility, reliability, fairness, and role modeling. Considering Chinese philosophical teaching, Zhu et al. ( 2019 ) developed a measure of EL consisting of 16 items in four dimensions: moral characteristics, moral cognition, moral role modeling and moral atmosphere. Both studies were conducted in the general business context. Based on the foregoing, researchers clearly did not agree on the structure and dimensions of EL. Two reasons may explain this. First, respondents in prior studies evaluated leaders at different management levels. Some evaluated senior managers (De Hoogh & Den Hartog, 2008 ; Khuntia & Suar, 2004 ; Treviño et al., 2003 ), some evaluated middle level managers (Brown et al., 2005 ; Kalshoven et al., 2011 ; Resick et al., 2006 ), while others evaluated both (Zhu et al., 2019 ). Management at different levels have different job descriptions, roles, authority, responsibilities, and skills; thus, they interpret EL differently. Second, the under - standing of EL is affected by cultural backgrounds and industry contexts, and there needs to be more contextualized research on leadership (A. -C. Wang et al., 2017 ). However, to date, not much research in English has explored EL from the Eastern perspective and few focused on the hospitality industry. This study thus aims to further investigate the structure and dimensions of EL in hospitality industry based on the Chinese culture and compare it with the broadly used EL scale developed from the Western context. 950 B. CHI Conceptual model for ethical leadership (EL) Based on a comprehensive review of previous literature and considering the Chinese cultural context and hospitality organizational practices, this study defines EL as having two aspects. First, the characteristics and behavior of the leader must accord with a code of ethics. Second, the leader must guide employees to follow the code of ethics. The pre - liminary four dimensions of EL are developed as follows: Moral person The Confucian “rule of virtue” dictates that the best way to govern is through virtues, i.e. leaders set high moral examples for the masses to follow. Consequently, the Chinese people have high regard of a leader’s moral standards and consider “morality” as the prime attribute of a leader. In the minds of the Chinese people, a leader’s morality is an independent and the most important part of ethical leadership. This is demonstrated by the study of Liu and Stening ( 2015 ), in which morality is identified to be a pillar in management. This view is also congruent with the Western perspective of EL (Lawton & Páez, 2015 ). Hence, this study adopts “moral person” as a dimension of the EL concept. Employee care Confucius and Mencius philosophy demands that the ruler be benevolent toward their subordinates and love their people (Turner, 2007 ), consistent with the Western view that ethical leaders should be people-oriented (Christensen-Salem et al., 2020 ). The essence of people orientation is to protect the needs and interests of most people. Hospitality profes - sion is in the business of people caring for other people and is thus by nature people oriented. Employees are the most important assets for a hospitality firm, and the leader must care about the wellbeing of the employees. Thus, employee care is included as a dimension of EL. Moral management Confucianism advocates for “moral education,” meaning that a leader should cultivate and enhance the morality of people through education (Liu & Stening, 2015 ). An ethical leader should not only be a “moral person” but also a “moral manager” (Zhu et al., 2019 ). In other words, ethical leadership not only requires a leader to possess lofty morals, but s/he should be able to guide the employees to follow the moral codes. While authentic leadership, spiritual leadership, and transformational leadership all stress “ethics,” “moral manage - ment” differentiates EL from other leadership styles (Sharma et al., 2019 ). Thus, “moral management” should be a crucial part of EL. Social responsibility In recent years in China, corporate scandals, especially food safety related, greatly hurt hospitality company images, and erode customer trust. Companies place profits before customer interests. Such business practices are undoubtedly not sustainable. Leaders thus must attach prime importance to social responsibility to achieve long-term success for their businesses (Eisenbeiss, 2012 ). Treviño et al. ( 2000 , 2003 ) found that ethical leaders should be concerned with social responsibility. Social responsibility is thus included as a dimension of the EL concept. Another round of empirical research was conducted to verify the model. Theoretical background and research hypotheses Employee voice behavior. Employee voice behavior plays a critical role in achieving organizational effectiveness and avoiding crises (A. N. Li & Tangirala, 2021 ), and has thus attracted both practitioners’ and researchers’ attention. Researchers have not agreed on the meaning and the dimensions of voice behavior (Weiss & Morrison, 2018 ; Y. Li & Sun, 2015 ). This study used the voice behavior measurement established by Liang et al. ( 2012 ) because of the Chinese context of their study and the scale has also been widely used in the hospitality literature (e.g., Lu & Lu, 2020 ; Park et al., 2021 ). Further, their definition of voice corresponds well with the purpose of this study; namely, “voice behavior is altruistic, and its purpose is the effective development of an organization rather than personal gain.” Liang et al. ( 2012 ) proposed “promotive voice” and “prohibitive voice.” Promotive voice empha - sizes ways to improve organizations, while prohibitive voice focuses on the discovery of factors that would be harmful to organizations (Svendsen et al., 2018 ). Ethical leadership and employee voice behavior. In accordance with Bandura’s ( 1986 ) social learning theory, people learn from direct experience or from others’ behavior and the corresponding outcomes, i.e. indirect experience. As such, employees learn what behavior is appropriate and expected by observing the behavior of their leaders (Byun Psychological safety Voice behaviorEthical leadership Leader-member exchange Figure 2. Ethical leaders attach importance to organizational interests and tend to point out inappropriate conduct in organizations (Brown et al., 2005 ). Modeling and learning from their ethical leaders, employees are likely to draw attention to problems and offer advice about bettering the organization. Prior research has shown that EL can influence employee voice behavior. Hassan ( 2015 ) stated that EL directly affects employee voice behavior. While more scholars believe that EL indirectly affects employee voice behavior through certain mediating variables (e.g., Lee et al., 2017 ; Mo & Shi, 2018 ). According to Howell and Costley ( 2001 ), a leader’s behavior first elicits employees’ psychological reactions (such as feelings, attitudes, emotions, moti - vations, and expectations), which then influences employees’ behavior. To identify mediat - ing variables can help to explain the underlying mechanism (Valle et al., 2018 ). Thus, this study examined psychological safety and leader-member exchange as two mediating variables. Psychological safety as the mediator. This study investigated psychological safety from an individual perspective, defined as an employee’s “sense of being able to show and employ one’s self without fear of negative consequences to self-image, status or career” (Kahn, 1990 , p. 708). Considered to be honest, upright, trustworthy, and concerned for their employees, ethical leaders make employees feel safe to communicate with them (Men et al., 2020 ). In this regard, ethical leadership contributes to the formation of employees’ psychological safety (Tu et al., 2019 ). In turn, employees’ psychological safety influences employee voice behavior (Xu et al., 2019 ). Employee voice behavior often involves challenging the status quo of organizations, which may be subject to criticism and accompanied by high risk (Xia et al., 2020 ). Consequently, only when employees believe they can freely express themselves, they would exhibit voice behavior (Newman et al., 2017 ). In sum, it is proposed that: H 1 : Psychological safety mediates the relationship between ethical leadership and employee voice behavior. Leader-member exchange as a mediator. Leader-member exchange focuses on the rela - tionship between a leader and each subordinate (Zhao et al., 2019 ). The core idea of leader- member exchange is that leaders develop different levels of relationship with each employee (L. C. Wang & Hollenbeck, 2019 ). A high level of mutual trust, respect, and obligation typifies high-quality leader-member exchange (Seo et al., 2018 ); while the characterization of low-quality leader-member exchange is that leaders control employees mainly by super - vision and contracts (Herdman et al., 2017 ). With ethical leaders’ favorable traits such as being honest, upright, and trustworthy (Brown & Treviño, 2014 ), employees tend to be loyal and develop a good relationship with the leaders (H. Y. Wang et al., 2017 ). Consequently, ethical leadership is conducive to the development of high-quality relationships between leaders and employees (Haar et al., 2018 ). As aforementioned, high risks often accompany employee voice behavior. When employees have high-quality relationships with their leaders, they trust that they can openly express their viewpoints without fearing the consequences. Thus, high-quality leader- JOURNAL OF HOSPITALITY MARKETING & MANAGEMENT 957 member exchange contributes to employee voice behavior (Stinglhamber et al., 2021 ). H 2 was thus proposed: H 2 : Leader-member exchange mediates the relationship between ethical leadership and employee voice behavior. Measures The two-dimensional voice behavior measurement was adopted from Liang et al. ( 2012 ), including five items for promotive voice (e.g.: I proactively develop and make suggestions for issues that may influence the unit) and five items for prohibitive voice (e.g.: I advise other colleagues against undesirable behaviors that would hamper job performance). Psychological safety was assessed with five items in accordance with Liang et al. ( 2012 ) (e.g.: In my work unit, I can express my true feelings regarding my job). Leader-member exchange was measured with eight items adapted from Graen and Uhl-Bien’s ( 1995 ) (e.g., I know where I stand with my leader). All the measurements were anchored with a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Appendix Table 2 shows the measurements. Discussion Theoretical implications There’s no consensus on the dimensions of EL because of different research objectives, contexts, and cultural backgrounds. Currently the EL scales have largely been developed in the Western cultural contexts (e.g., Brown et al., 2005 ; Yukl et al., 2013 ). Few research has broached on the subject from the Eastern perspective in the hospitality industry. Therefore, there is a need of a scale that is more suitable for Chinese hospitality enterprises. Grounded in the Confucius philosophical teachings, this study has developed and tested an EL scale with four dimensions (moral person, employee care, moral management, and social responsibility) via a scientific process. Four studies involving 732 subjects in both qualita - tive and quantitative research design have been conducted and the results have confirmed the reliability and validity (concurrent, convergent, discriminant and nomological validity) of the scale. This research enriches the EL literature and provides a reliable and valid measuring tool for hospitality scholars who are interested in studying leadership in Eastern cultures. CHI Additionally, to test the nomological validity of the proposed scale, this study has put the scale in a framework that examines how EL would affect employee voice behavior. Employee voice behavior requires greater research attention because it is the foundation of organizational competitiveness. In prior studies, scholars have different opinions on the relationship between EL and employee voice behavior (e.g., Hassan, 2015 ; Mo & Shi, 2018 ). This study has examined both the direct and indirect influences of EL on employ - ees’ voice behavior by proposing a dual mediation model. The results show that psycho - logical safety and leader-member exchange play a full mediating role between EL and employee voice behavior. Managerial implications This study provides insights for hotel managers to develop and enhance ethical leadership skills. The four-dimension EL scale offers clear guidance. Firstly, hotel managers should be “moral persons,” i.e., above all, they must hold ethical standards and adhere to the standards. Secondly, hotel managers should care about their employees. They should take employees’ interests seriously, listen to employees, respect employees, and help employees grow. Thirdly, hotel managers should adopt an equitable reward/punishment system, which will help regulate employee conduct and encourage them to behave ethically. Lastly, hotel managers should be concerned with social interests and social responsibility and encourage their employ - ees to be socially responsible too. This study also provides practical implications for hotel organizations as to how to encourage employee voice behavior. Whether used to improve an organization’s circumstances or to highlight problems that have occurred in an organization, employee voice behavior is important to organizational development. In the hospital - ity industry, front-line employees provide services and have direct contact with customers; thus, they understand customers’ needs and wants well. In this regard, front-line employees’ voice behavior is crucial for hotels to improve service quality and secure customer satisfaction and loyalty. This study finds the mechanism of how EL enhances employee voice behavior via psychological safety and leader-member exchange. Because voice behavior often involves challenging or criticizing the status quo of an organization, employees may harbor fears that the management will take reprisals against them. Consequently, employees will only voice opinions when they feel psychologically safe to do so (Newman et al., 2017 ). Ethical leaders value employee views and listen to employ - ees, which makes employees feel safe to speak up. This encourages voice behavior in an organization and builds a favorable organizational climate. By establishing a system of rewarding good advice and allowing for anonymous comments, hotel organizations ensure employee psychological safety, which in turn promotes voice behavior. Ethical leaders care about and have a high-level of social exchanges with employees, leading to high-quality leader-member exchange. This means that the relationship is not limited to the formal contractual relationship but based on mutual trust and respect (Seo et al., 2018 ). According to social exchange theory and the norm of reciprocity (Mo & Shi, 2018 ), employees will then engage in proactive behavior in return, such as voice behavior (Stinglhamber et al., 2021 ). Hotel organizations could improve leader-member exchange JOURNAL OF HOSPITALITY MARKETING & MANAGEMENT 961 through strengthening communication with employees, understanding employees’ poten - tial and providing support to employees. High quality leader-member exchange inspires employees to speak their mind about the organization, which in the long term will benefit organizational growth. Limitations and future research recommendations Although this study follows a rigorous scale development process, it is not without limita - tions. First, the data was collected only from hotels in Southern China, thus the results may not be generalizable. Future research is encouraged to collect a larger amount of data from a wider geographical area. Second, common method bias may be a problem since the data was collected only from employees. Future research is encouraged to collect data also from managers, especially for questions related to ethical leadership and leader-membership exchange. The role of the leader in SMEs is one of the most discussed issues in the field of management and innovation. In this study, the role of ethical leadership and green organizational culture on green innovation was investigated in the context of Turkey with a cross-sectional research study covering 464 SMEs and using structural equation modelling. According to the findings, it was seen that ethical leadership has an important potential in terms of developing a green organizational culture in SMEs. In addition, it has been determined that green organizational culture has a mediating role between ethical leadership and green product and process innovations. As a result, suggestions are given to researchers and managers in the context of leadership and organizational culture in order to create green innovation and a sustainable work environment. Introduction The term“green” has been attracting attention since the 2000s, due to increasing sustainability and environmental concerns (Chen, Lai, and Wen2006). Green Innovation relates to innovation developed by the businesses specifically for the purpose of environmental protection during both production and business processes, so that they can be considered to fulfill their institutional responsibilities (Quet al. 2022). Meanwhile, strategies for green innovation and their outputs provide businesses with a sustainable competitive advantage and enable them to meet the expectations of the society (Albort-Morant, LealMill/C19an, and Cepeda-Carri/C19on 2016). Even though green innovation practices are often considered to be applicable only to large-scale businesses, they can also significantly increase the profitability of small ones. In fact, the limited number of studies that have focused on small-scale businesses and green innovation have proved that effective green innovation practices by small-scale businesses bring higher profitability when compared with large-scale ones (Linet al. 2019). In addition, it has been stated that the effectiveness of green innovation practices depends on the characteristics of the businesses rather than their size (Wysocki2021). The importance and volume of SMEs in the Turkish economy are undoubtedly also realized with the environmental impact of their activities. Green innovation has an important function in minimizing the adverse effects of businesses on the environment (Aguilera-Caracuel and Ortiz-deMandojana 2013). Therefore, many businesses are trying to become oriented towards green innovation as a strategy in terms of environmental awareness (Takalo and Tooranloo 2021). This is also related to the fact that green innovation provides a sustainable competitive advantage to businesses, apart from its environmental protection function (Hur, Kim, and Park2013). It has also been stated that green innovation provides firms with the opportunity to expand their market share, attracting customers and producing green products/services (Gurlek and Koseoglu 2021). Due to its abovementioned contributions, green innovation has recently attracted the attention of both business owners and researchers (Takalo and Tooranloo2021). Scientific studies within the scope of green innovation, in recent years, have focused on revealing the antecedents of the concept (Suet al. 2020). Boiral, Baron, and Gunnlaugson (2014), state that it is only possible to implement any kind of green practices with the contribution and leadership of the administrators. For instance, the effects of green transformational leadership (Begum et al. 2022; Zhang, Xu, and Wang 2020), transformational leadership (Pham, Pham, and Dang 2022; Singh et al. 2020) and environmental leadership (Zhang and Ma2021;S u et al. 2020) on green innovation have been stated under different studies. However, it is observed that the relationship between leadership and green innovation has not been studied sufficiently within the literature. It is also observed that the leadership styles that are directly related to green innovation, such as green transformational leadership and environmental leadership, have been analyzed in the existing studies, whereas the leadership styles that are likely to affect green innovation indirectly have been ignored. In the last five years, some studies have begun to question the effects of ethical leadership and ethical culture on innovation capacity (Van der Wal and Demircioglu2020; Liu and Zhao 2019; Bahzar 2019) and green innovation behavior of employees (Wood, Eid, and Agag2021), but field studies carried out at different organizational levels are required in order to contribute to the abovementioned studies. Although green innovation practices are of critical importance in terms of businesses’ institutional performance, institutional green policies developed by the leaders have an important dimension in increasing public acclaim and enhancing their institutional value (Daily, Bishop, and Govindarajulu2009; Huanget al. 2016). Besides, institutional leadership needs to establish the organizational culture within the context of green practices, so that their green policies can be effective in the long term. This can be achieved through leadership (Graves and Sarkis 2018; Bahzar 2019) and green organizational culture (Banerjee 2002; Wang2019), both of which are assumed to be the most important resources for businesses within the concept of resource-based theory. Green organizational culture expresses the common beliefs and value systems that shape environment-oriented behaviors. In this respect, the discovery and dissemination of a set of values that guide “green goals” can be developed by the leader and his/her team (Gao2017 ). Moreover, employees may consider green innovation as one of the main values of the business and may tend to behave in more environmentally friendly ways (Chen2011b; Chang 2015; Azhar and Yang2022). Within this understanding, ethical leadership is likely to transform business strategies into a more green-innovation-oriented understanding, by attaching Journal of Environmental Planning and Management 1703 greater importance to conserving the environment and by developing values in this direction (Liu and Zhao2019). Although some theoretical facts on the question of whether or not the ethical leadership perception will affect employees’ green behaviors (if yes, when and where) have been suggested, more systematic studies are required to enable generalization of the results (Tourignyet al. 2019). Society also demands institutions to behave more ethically and implement innovative and entrepreneurial behaviors that contribute to sustainability. As observed during Volkswagen’s carbon dioxide emissions scandal, the aforementioned demands by society and the values required might compete with each other in many cases (Van der Wal and Demircioglu2020). Therefore, studying mediator mechanisms through which ethical leadership can lead to green innovation and to understand the process in different sample groups and sectors is considered to contribute to the field of study. Based on previous research and theoretical evidence, this research examines the mediator effect of green organizational culture on the relationship between ethical leadership and green innovation in a sample of SMEs in Turkey. The research model was constructed in the context of social learning theory (Bandura1977), which is a theory that employees learn and imitate by observing the behavior patterns of their managers. 2. Literature review and hypothesis development 2.1. Ethical leadership In the literature, ethical behavior has been previously defined within charismatic and transformational leadership behaviors (Peuset al. 2010; Brown and Trevino2006b). It has been stated that transformational leaders harmonize their followers’ value systems with their own systems (Burns1978) in parallel with moral principles; they also become role models in doing the right thing with high standards of ethical and moral behavior, and they change the behavior of their employees (Avolio1999, 43). During this period, the researchers defined ethical leadership using normative terms. Most of the research has focused on moral principles, while defining ethical leadership, and used them to establish and form ethical decision-making mechanisms. However, studies defining“what ethical leadership is” start with Brown, Trevino, and Harrison (2005) and Bedi, Alpaslan, and Green (2016). Brown and Trevino (2006a) define ethical leadership as showing normatively appropriate behaviors in interactions and introducing those behaviors to followers through mutual communication and reinforcement. In this definition, ethics includes both being moral and being a role model. An ethical leader uses communication, reward-punishment systems, and ethical standards to affect followers’ behaviors. and makes proactive efforts as a role model (Brown and Trevino2006a; Mayer, Kuenzi, and Greenbaum 2010). Thus, ethical leadership, which stands out for the elimination of institutional corruption (Kuenzi, Mayer, and Greenbaum2020), has gained strategic importance in terms of both its positive effects on subordinates and its organizational benefits (Fontrodona, Ricart, and Berrone2018). For an ethical leader, establishing high-quality social relationships with subordinates (Brown, Trevino, and Harrison2005; Thiel et al. 2018); being a legitimate and reliable role model; providing a fair workplace environment; and managing ethics effectively in the workplace are all motivations for his/her followers in developing normative behaviors (Brown, Trevino, and Harrison2005). These attitudes may also enhance employee productivity and lead to them developing helpful behaviors towards society (Liu and Zhao 2019). The former studies confirm that the ethical leader significantly influences 1704 M. F. Most importantly, these two employee behaviors have been directly linked to performance (LePineet al. 2008). 2.2. Green organizational culture Global environmentalism has been considered one of the primary issues for society over the last two decades with the aim of preserving resources for future generations. Therefore, it has become important for firms to become pro-environmental businesses, engaged in environmental management and to consider environmental health during their production processes (Lauring and Thomsen2009). Previously, businesses carried out their activities relating to the protection and improvement of the environment within the scope of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR). Even these projects were considered to be an institutional marketing strategy by some businesses (Kleynet al. 2012). Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) performance emerges as a kind of strategic behavior, particularly in developing markets (Hadjikhani, Lee, and Park2016). In the meantime, they can enhance their performance through environmentally friendly technologies and services (Carroll2000; Orlitzky, Schmidt, and Rynes2003). Using resources efficiently for the sake of a sustainable environment and fulfilling activities and projects in the business sector, industrial sector and service sector with an ecological approach also depends on employee behaviors based on this awareness (Temminck, Mearns, and Fruhen2015). For this reason, businesses guide their employees about what workplace behaviors are suitable from an ecological perspective, how employees should show this motivation and how stakeholders should be treated (Saifulina and Carballo-Penela2017). Green organizational culture is one of the most important elements used for this purpose (Banerjee 2001). Organizational culture expresses a common belief, value, idea and attitude system that shapes organizational behavior. In this sense, it is considered an intangible resource that plays a key role in advancing an organization towards better environmental management for environmental issues and practices (Yanget al. 2017). On the other hand, organizational culture is shaped by regulatory, normative, and cognitive-cultural pressure and the beliefs and values of senior management (Kitchell 1995). The assumptions of the senior management, or the leader, about the business first turn into beliefs and values and then into tangible images that can be viewed by employees and stakeholders (Norton, Zacher, and Ashkanasy 2012). In this way, organizational culture assists progress from the perspective and understanding of senior management towards employee behaviour (Norton et al. 2015). Pro-environmental behaviors and environmental descriptive norms by the leader help employees to display pro-environmental behaviors with the help of organizational culture (Robertson and Barling 2013). In this context, green organizational culture is defined as a set of values and assumptions that support sustainable economic and ecological development within the organization and help integrate ecological understanding into the entire operation of the business (Wang 2019; Garc/C19ıa-Machado and Mart/C19ınez-/C19Avila 2019). According to many researchers, green organizational culture has an important place in the green management and sustainable development of organizations (Quet al. 2022). With the help of green organizational culture, businesses can integrate their sustainability efforts and business processes in a better way and transform employee behaviors (employee green behavior) (Nortonet al. 2015; Van der Wal and Demircioglu2020). Green innovation Concerns about global warming and increasing environmental pollution, international environmental regulations, and environmentally friendly consumer demands by society are intensely increasing (Naghavi2007). Today, both structural sanctions (Huanget al. 2016) and an increase in consumers’ environmental awareness force business administrations to offer environmentally friendly products and services (Chen 2008). Responding to these pressure groups accurately and promptly depends on the resources and capabilities of businesses (Soewarno, Tjahjadi, and Fithrianti 2019). Businesses give “green organizational responses” by using their resources and abilities and focusing on green innovation (Huanget al. 2016). In the related literature, green innovation corresponds to environmentally oriented innovations (Soewarno, Tjahjadi, and Fithrianti2019), (Garc/C19ıa-Machado and Mart/C19ınez- /C19Avila 2019). In addition to this concept, some other concepts such as eco-innovation (Cheng, Yang, and Sheu2014), (Hojnik and Ruzzier2016); environmental innovation (Rennings and Rammer 2011) and sustainable innovation (Lopez-Valeiras, GomezConde, and Naranjo-Gil 2015), (Shen, Sha, and Wu2020) also appear in the studies. Various explanations have been given using different concepts, but research highlights the importance of behavior change in businesses and their stakeholders in relation to environmental problems; the changing organizational culture; the perceived organizational climate; and the fact that the emerging innovations provide a competitive advantage to businesses (Olsen, Sofka, and Grimpe2017). In parallel, firms focus on greener practices that allow them to achieve institutional goals to protect the natural environment (Wang 2019) and take into account the practices of their green competitors in the market (Soewarno, Tjahjadi, and Fithrianti2019). In this study, environmentally oriented policies and practices by businesses are considered green innovation, and the definitions by Chen, Lai, and Wen (2006) are used. According to researchers, green innovation is related to firms’ green products and green processes. It covers energy saving, pollution prevention, waste recycling, green product design, or institutional environmental management through technical innovations in terms of both hardware and software (Albort-Morantet al. 2017; Farrukh et al. 2021). They also analyze the green innovation performance of businesses on the basis of two dimensions. These are product performance and process performance. Concerning green practices such as energy-saving and pollution prevention, while green product innovation includes green product design and production, green process innovation is related to the business process improvements (Chen, Lai, and Wen2006, 534). Within this context, green innovation is defined in this study as the introduction of new processes and products that lead to a noticeable reduction in environmental burdens. It considers green innovation as an important advantage that supports the active actions taken by the business administration in order to minimize environmental pollution and extravagance. In this respect, the existing knowledge of the business is transformed, so that knowledge about environmental protection is developed with the aim that it is internalized by employees (Wang2019). 2.4. Ethical leadership and green innovation In order to create and develop green innovation, employees must have“green-oriented values” (Tuan 2020 ). Green-oriented management styles and environmental organizational culture play a key role in the formation of positive perspectives on green innovation 1706 M. F. Sȩng€ullendi et al. and the success of green innovation practices (Chen, Chang, and Wu2012). In this respect, managers motivate their employees by encouraging green-oriented production and management as their responsibility towards society (Hughes and Terrell2011). They realize this by acting as a bridge between senior management and employees in firms (Liu and Zhao 2019). In parallel, transformational leadership and environmental leadership positively affect green behaviors and green innovation (Chen and Chang2013; Robertson and Barling2013). Additionally, ethical leaders achieve a similar effect with their ethical behaviors and as role models to their employees. According to social learning theory, which is also the basis for the hypothesis for this research, employees learn by observing the behaviors of their managers and acquire their attitudes through mutual interactions (Bandura 1977). In other words, ethical leaders playing a moral role model in society fulfill their social responsibilities by providing green innovation. The literature confirms that issues such as sustainability and green innovation are important for an ethical leader (Liu and Zhao2019). The ethical leader, who displays behaviors such as making ethical decisions, supporting socially responsible activities, and giving importance to environmental protection, is respected by employees because he/she acts in parallel with the interests of the institution and society. These conditions enable ethical leaders and their followers to work more harmoniously and display innovation-oriented behaviors (Demircioglu and Audretsch 2017; Van der Wal and Demircioglu 2020). The findings of the study by Khalili ( 2016) on 1,172 Iranian employees reveal that ethical leadership positively affects the green creativity capacity and eco-innovation of the employees. Within the context of organizational identity and social learning theories, Liu and Zhao (2019) also suggest a model stating that ethical leadership is likely to affect green innovation positively. In consideration of these data, the first two hypotheses of the research are as follows: H1: Ethical Leadership has a positive impact on Green Product Innovation. H2: Ethical Leadership has a positive impact on Green Process Innovation. 2.5. Ethical Leadership and Green organizational Culture Managers are the key components of ecological behavior and green transformation in firms (Jiaet al. 2018). It is stated that the establishment of the right relationship between managers and employees will ensure employee performance, protect the environment and achieve environmental goals for organizations and society (Cheng, Yang, and Sheu 2014). Thus, efforts by managers to create such an environment enables businesses to gain a green identity (Martin, Johnson, and French2011). Chen’s( 2011a) research on SMEs concludes that businesses should develop an environment-oriented organizational culture and environment-oriented leadership behaviors in order to enhance their green organizational culture, identity and green competitive advantage. The studies by Wang, Flood, and Gao (2009) analyze the relationship between responsible leadership and green organizational culture and draw a theoretical frame relating to the effect of this relationship on institutional social performance (Tepe K€uc ̧€uko/C21glu 2014). Ethical leaders have a strong sense of institutional social responsibility focused on sustainable development (Brown, Trevino, and Harrison2005). In this context, they have the characteristics to build a good image in terms of environmental ethics within their businesses. Therefore, when ethical leaders and employees communicate and collaborate on the environment, Journal of Environmental Planning and Management 1707 employees can respond enthusiastically to the ethical leaders’ understanding about protecting the environment. According to organizational identity and social learning theories, the higher the affinity of the employees with the identities of their businesses, the more willing they are to internalize and struggle to achieve organizational goals and objectives (Liu and Zhao2019). Therefore, ethical leaders contribute to the formation of a green organizational culture. Taking these data into account, the third hypothesis has been proposed: H3: Ethical Leadership has a positive impact on Green Organizational Culture. 2.6. Green organizational culture and green innovation Organizational culture creates a set of mental assumptions that guide employee behavior (Chen 2011a). Therefore, organizational culture is vitally important for businesses in terms of accelerating, or conversely abolishing, innovation activities (Kitchell1995; Gurlek and Tuna 2018). Organizational culture is the most prominent factor among green drivers. In addition, one of the important factors for green innovation activities is the creation of the right organizational culture (Gurlek and Koseoglu2021). In this respect, it is stated that green organizational culture is the right cultural model for the success of green innovation practices (Howard-Grenville2006). In order to achieve green innovation, environmental culture must be dominant in the organization (Fern/C19andez, Cala, and Domecq2011). The relationship between these two concepts, namely the idea that green organizational culture can affect green innovation, can be explained using the resource-based view (Gurlek and Koseoglu 2021). In the context of this theory, organizational culture is a valuable and inimitable resource that the business can use to gain competitive advantage (Barney1991). There are studies on the effect of green organizational culture on green innovation. These studies were conducted on both the service sector and the production sector. Wang (2019), states, in the study carried out on 327 businesses in Taiwan, that green organizational culture is the pioneer of green innovation and green performance. In this study, it is also stated that green innovation has a mediator effect in the relationship between green organizational culture and green performance. Another study was conducted on automotive sector employees (Garc /C19ıa-Machado and Mart /C19ınez-/C19Avila 2019). The findings of this study revealed that green innovation had a mediator effect on the relationship between green organizational culture and environmental performance. Other studies in the manufacturing sector also confirm the positive relationship between green organizational culture and green innovation (Chen, Chang, and Wu 2012; Chang 2015). Supporting the previous studies, organizational culture has been found to be related to green innovation (Tajeddini and Trueman2012; Chen 2011b). Chang (2015) also confirms that green organizational culture contributes to the development of green innovation. The results of the research conducted by Gurlek and Tuna (2018), in the service sector, show that green organizational culture has a positive effect on green innovation and competitive advantage. Accordingly, green organizational culture is an important determinant of green innovation and competitive advantage. In consideration of these data the following hypotheses have been proposed: H4: Green Organizational Culture has a positive impact on Green Product Innovation. The mediating effect of green organizational culture A limited number of studies state that administrators are likely to affect either the business culture or its climate through their behavior and attitudes (Van der Wal and Demircioglu 2020; Martin and Cullen2006). Since ethical leadership is more likely to affect the personal values of employees when compared with other leadership types (Trevino, Butterfield, and McCabe 1998), it can affect workplace behaviors towards more pro-environmental and innovative ones (Wood, Eid, and Agag2021). The fact that leadership behaviors increase green innovation tendency, together with green organizational culture, can be explained in the context of social learning theory (Brown, Trevino, and Harrison2005; Liu and Zhao2019). This theory argues that the behaviors of an individual emerge due to individual, behavioral and environmental effects, and learning is fulfilled through either observation or direct learning within the community (Bahn 2001). Administrators who demonstrate innovative work behaviors and ethical leadership are considered role models by followers (Van der Wal and Demircioglu2020). The behaviors of individuals and groups can be transformed as a result of internalizing responsible behaviors by ethical leaders, through the social learning process. It is possible for ethical leadership to stimulate green innovation behavior during this interaction and mutual learning process (Wood, Eid, and Agag2021). When considered within the context of social learning theory, the green innovation behavior of employees can be considerably influenced by leadership behavior (Liu and Zhao 2019). On the other hand, the culture of the organization is another mechanism that can help to explain this mutual relationship in a better way. For this reason, the effects of green organizational culture have been discussed as a mediator mechanism in this mutual relationship. Green ethical culture is a subset of organizational culture that influences and guides the formal and informal behavior of the business and its employees (Van der Wal and Demircioglu 2020, 389). The behavioral patterns and habits that employees acquire by learning from ethical leadership behavioral patterns and by imitating them may emerge more widely by means of a“green-focused” culture in the organization. In consideration of these data the following hypotheses have been proposed: H6: Green Organizational Culture mediates the relationship between ethical leadership and green product innovation. H7: Green Organizational Culture mediates the relationship between ethical leadership and green process innovation. Methodology Since SMEs have important functions in an economic system, they have become the focus of much scientific research in recent years (Jun, Seo, and Son2013; Stekelorum, Laguir, and ElBaz2020; Abbasiet al. 2021). Such kinds of businesses have significant impacts on basic macroeconomic indicators (particularly employment and gross domestic product) (Maranto-Vargas and Rangel2007; Lee, Shin, and Park2012). They also shape the social system of the country to which they belong. The SME sector includes a wide variety of businesses in terms of size, shape, and structure (Svatosova2018). Journal of Environmental Planning and Management 1709 Prause (2019) states that SMEs have closer customer relationships, a greater capability not only of adapting to new technologies but also for entering niche markets as a result of their simple organizational structure; they are able to adapt quickly to changing market conditions and can contribute to the economy with low capital. When Turkey, the focus of the research, is analyzed, it has been observed that SMEs constitute 99.8% of the total number of enterprises, 72.4% of employment, 51.8% of personnel costs, 50.4% of turnover, 44.1% of production value and 44% of factor costs and added value by the year 2020 (TUIK2021). This study aims to test the effect of ethical leadership behaviors on the green innovation trend through green organizational culture. In this context, the aim of the study is to analyze the effect of ethical leadership perceptions of industrial SME employees in Istanbul on green innovation and to test the mediator role of green organizational culture in this relationship. Starting from this point of view, employees working in the same SME for at least 5 years in Istanbul were chosen as the research sample. The reasons for targeting these employees are that they can realize the big picture better than other employees; they are able to understand the organizational culture, information, processes and organizational structure better with the help of their past experiences and social interactions compared to other employees (Kumar, Stern, and Anderson1993). Data have been gathered through surveys using the simple random sampling technique. After legal permission, an electronic survey was sent to 10,000 SMEs that operate in Istanbul by SMEDO (Small and Medium Enterprises Development Organization of Turkey), an institution that supports SMEs and scientific research on SMEs in Turkey. The data gathering process was designed with one participant from each firm. 1,339 firms responded and the response rate was 13%. Inappropriate data and data for employees with less than 5 years’ experience have been excluded. As a result, the minimum sample size has been achieved with data for 464 employees from 464 firms (Kotrlik and Higgins2001). Table 1shows the demographic profile of the participants. We used SEM for validity and reliability analyses and hypothesis testing to examine the estimation of multiple, complex and connected relationships with the possibility of representing unobserved constructs and to take measurement errors into account in the estimation procedure (Hair et al. 2010). The AMOS package program was preferred in SEM because it provides the researchers with interface convenience and allows the bootstrap sampling procedure in analyzing complex structural equation models such as our research model (Arbuckle2008). Measurement instruments The scale developed by Brown, Trevino, and Harrison (2005) has been used to measure ethical leadership behaviors, which is the independent variable for the research. It is a singledimension scale with ten items. The scale includes items to be answered by the employees such as“sets an example of how to do things the right way in terms of ethics”, “can be trusted”, “disciplines employees who violate ethical standards” about the administrators. Green organizational culture, which is the mediator variable in the research, has been measured with the single-dimension scale with 6 items, developed by Wang (2019). The scale includes items such as“our firm links environmental objectives with our other corporate goals”; “environmental preservation is a high priority activity in our firm” and “our firm links environmental objectives with our other corporate goals”. The dependent variable for the research, green innovation, on the other hand, has been measured using the scale developed by Chen, Lai, and Wen (2006). This scale includes 8 items and 2 dimensions; these are product innovation and process innovation. The scale includes items such as“the company chooses the materials for the product that produce the least amount of pollution for conducting the product development or design” and “the company chooses the materials for the product that consume the least amount of energy and resources for conducting the product development or design” to measure the size of green product innovation. The scale includes items such as“the manufacturing process of the company effectively reduces the emission of hazardous substances or waste” and “the manufacturing process of the company recycles waste and emissions that allow them to be treated and re-used” to measure green process innovation. 3.2.
