Discussion and conclusion The aim of this study is to analyze the mediator effect of green organizational culture on the relationship between ethical leadership and green innovation in the context of social learning theory. Green innovation has an important role in enabling businesses to acquire competitive advantage by providing them with opportunities to expand their market share, increase customer appeal, and develop green product manufacturing or services. The fact that green innovation focuses on environmental protection and sustainability increases the interest in it. In this respect, scientific research within the scope of green innovation, in recent years, has focused on revealing the antecedents of the concept (Su et al. 2020). Boiral, Baron, and Gunnlaugson (2014) state that implementing any kind of green actions in business is possible with the participation and leadership of the administrators. In this context, few studies are found in the literature on how green innovation is affected by leadership behaviors (Begumet al. 2022; Zhang, Xu, and Wang2020; Pham, Figure 2. Result of structural model. 1714 M. F. Sȩng€ullendi et al. Pham, and Dang 2022; Singh et al. 2020). Here, it is thought that ethical leadership behaviors, such as making ethical decisions, supporting socially responsible activities and giving importance to environmental protection will transform a business into a green innovation-focused one. In the context of developing countries such as Turkey, the reflection of ethical leadership behaviors such as ethical decision making, is a moral role model; and socially responsible activities may appear as green-oriented practices (Ahmad and Umrani2019). Green organizational culture is also thought to be another antecedent of green innovation, since it represents the common beliefs and value systems that shape environment-focused behaviors and plays a key role in issues such as determining and disseminating a set of values that lead to“green objectives”. According to the findings of this study, it has been concluded that ethical leadership affects green product innovation significantly and positively, whereas it does not affect green process innovation significantly. Therefore, by the behaviors of the managers such as establishing high-quality communication with their employees, being reliable role models, providing a fair workplace environment and actively managing ethics in the workplace, the firms will benefit in energy-saving, designing and manufacturing proenvironmental products and reducing environmental pollution. Additionally, Chen, Lai, and Wen (2006) and Chiouet al.( 2011) state that green process innovation is related to environmental management performance for the sake of environmental protection. Although some SMEs are better able to configure their environmental impacts and have taken action to manage these impacts efficiently, most of the SMEs still have no idea about environmental management. They also lack awareness and the culture to deal with environmental management problems (Iraldo, Testa, and Frey2010). When considered in this respect, it is possible to say that ethical leadership has no direct effect on green process innovation. Nevertheless, these results should be considered in the context of Turkey as a developing country and SMEs. On the other hand, ethical leadership affects green organizational culture significantly and positively. Based on the social learning process, this conclusion is in parallel with the argument that employees respond enthusiastically in understanding environmental protection when ethical leaders communicate and co-operate with their employees when establishing a good image on environmental ethics and with their strong sustainable development-oriented sense of organizational social responsibility (Brown, Trevino, and Harrison 2005). Subsequently, it has been observed that green organizational culture significantly and positively affects green product innovation and green process innovation. The findings are in parallel with the research by Chang (2015), Wang (2019), Garc/C19ıaMachado and Mart/C19ınez-/C19Avila (2019), and Chen, Chang, and Wu (2012). This study has shown that green organizational culture has a mediator role in the relationship between ethical leadership and green product/process innovations. In other words, the factors acquired by employees through imitation and learning from ethical leadership behaviors will lead to the development of a“green-focused” culture over time and, in this way, will contribute to green innovation tendencies. According to Corley and Gioia (2011), the contribution of a scientific research study shows itself in two ways. The first one is the practical-theoretical effectiveness of the research and the second one is the originality of the research in terms of revealing development. When considered in this aspect, the study is effective, since it explains the relationship between ethical leadership, green organizational culture, and green innovation. This makes a practical contribution to SME entrepreneurs and administrators. In the meantime, the study also contributes to the literature by explaining the relationship Journal of Environmental Planning and Management 1715 between the variables. Besides, the study is a unique one, as it is the first research study that reveals a conceptual relationship between ethical leadership, green organizational culture and green innovation. Accordingly, the research has revealed that managers’ leadership style, serves as a model for subordinates and contributes to the development of employees’ green innovation behaviors through the organization ’s culture. This research, therefore, enriches the findings of previous studies within the context of social learning theory (Brown, Trevino, and Harrison2005; Liu and Zhao2019). Moreover, it is suggested in the study by Van der Wal and Demircioglu (2020) that the relationship between the variables should be analyzed in Asian and developing countries. From this point of view, this study has a developing contribution to the literature. 4.1. Practical implications The research has important contributions for managers. First of all, it shows that managers can verify whether ethical leadership behaviors in their firms contribute to green innovation by developing a green organizational culture. The results of the research suggest that ethical leadership behaviors have no direct effect on green process innovation; but do have a direct effect on green product innovation. However, with the presence of green organizational culture, ethical leadership and green organizational culture seem to affect both green process innovation and green product innovation. Therefore, managers should pay attention to green organizational culture in this context. In this way, firms can increase their green innovation performance. Second, the research results show that green organizational culture mediates the relationship between ethical leadership and green innovation. For these reasons, firms should select and promote managers who exhibit ethical leadership behaviors and who are sensitive to environmental issues. If companies want to improve their environmental performance and green innovation levels, they should appoint managers who exhibit ethical leadership behaviors with passion and interest in environmental issues (Eiadatet al. 2008). In fact, such managers should not only be appointed, they should also be given the opportunity to turn their environmental passions into action. Thus, companies with a green organizational culture can increase the green awareness level of other companies. Moreover, employees can reach higher motivation levels to develop innovative ideas about green processes or green products. Therefore, these companies will be able to further develop their innovation capacity (Pipatprapa, Huang, and Huang2017). Another contribution of our research is in shedding light on public policies. Research findings can contribute to understanding the importance of green innovation for many companies in Turkey as a country struggling with environmental pollution. Therefore, companies should pay attention to environmental policy and adopt a green innovation strategy that can facilitate and accelerate their sustainable development capacity. In addition, SMEs that do not have the financial resources for green management can benefit from opportunities that could be created by the government to promote green management practices through ethical leadership behaviors and green organizational culture (Lee and Kim2011). 4.2. Theoretical implications This research explores how ethical leadership behaviors affect green product and green process innovation. Although some studies in the literature describe the antecedents of green innovation, our results show that ethical leadership enhances green innovation 1716 M. F. Sȩng€ullendi et al. through green organizational culture. Our research provides a developing contribution to the existing literature in terms of answering the questions about which leadership model will affect green innovation and which behavioral, individual and institutional concepts have a mediating role; based on SMEs that are neglected in green innovation research; and considering the suggestions by Gurlek and Koseoglu (2021) for future studies. Consequently, this research contributes to the development of the current literature by explaining the antecedents of green innovation in SMEs through social learning theory. Social learning theory can be used in management research to explain organizational interactions by relying on the fact that people’s behaviors and thoughts are learned from the people or role model behaviors in their environment. This theory helps in understanding how members of an organization learn from each other and how this learning affects the culture and behaviors of the organization. Organization members adopt green behaviors by following the example of ethical leaders through social learning. The connection between ethical leadership and social learning theory supports the formation and development of a green organizational culture, leading to a more focused approach on green priorities. Ethical leadership defines the organizational culture in a “green” context, while social learning theory helps organization members to adopt and implement“green” behaviors. In this regard, the research can be considered among the pioneering studies in the literature examining the role of green organizational culture in the relationship between ethical leadership and green innovation in the context of SMEs. 4.3. The limitations of the study The study has some limitations due to being a cross-sectional study. It is only possible for a longitudinal study to completely reveal the green organizational culture and green innovation levels of the employees and the whole business. On the other hand, if the study gains a longitudinal nature, this may pave the way for future studies. Future studies may put forward differences by adding control variables or moderator variables, such as education level, sector, etc. to the model established using the conceptual model tested in this study. Additionally, future studies may analyze the relationship between ethical leadership, green organizational culture, and green innovation by gathering data from different countries and regions. Future research can explore the impact of green servant leadership on green organizational culture and green innovation. However, green servant leadership studies are currently in their infancy (Mansooret al. 2022; Farazet al. 2021). As Mansooret al.( 2022) points out, green servant leadership is still a new concept and is not fully mature, but it has significant potential. For further studies, green servant leadership is suggested as a leadership role that should be investigated in terms of green-oriented outcomes. In this study, we extend the concept of ethical leadership in the context of supply chain, and explore how supply chain ethical leadership (SCEL) affects GSCI via the green image and the moderating role of perceived institutional force drawing on social learning theory. We test hypotheses using hierarchical regression analysis by collecting two-waved data from 317 Chinese firms. Our results reveal that SCEL has signi ficantly positive impacts on three dimensions of GSCI, and the green image partially mediates the impact of SCEL on strategic integration. Introduction As the increasingly prominent of environment issues, the environmental awareness of regulatory authorities, media, consumers and community residents has also increased, which significantly increases the environmental pressure thatfirms are facing (Lo et al.,2018; Turken, Carrillo, and Verter 2020; Zhang et al.,2020b; Zhu et al.,2017). Thus, incorporating the concept of environmental protection into the whole production and operations management process to mitigate emissions and waste throughout the supply chain has become the key to enhancing sustainable competitiveness (Yang, Jiang, and Zhao2019; Zhang et al.2019; Zhang et al.2020a). Since green supply chain integration (GSCI) refers to the extent to which the focalfirm integrates its supply chain partners into environmental practices to seamlessly link internal and external processes to effectively solve environmental concerns (Kong, Feng, and Huo2021; Zhou et al.2020; Wong, Wong, and Boon-itt2020; Yang et al.2020), it has been appreciated by academic and practice. In this study, we segregate GSCI into three dimensions: strategic integration, information integration and operational integration (Flynn, Huo, and Zhao2010; Han and Huo2020; Wong, BoonItt, and Wong2011). Strategic integration refers to the extent to which the focalfirm establishes long-term relationships with supply chain partners to achieve strategic goals (Lee and Whang 2000; Liu et al. 2016). Information integration refers to the extent to which information is © 2022 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group CONTACT Taiwen Feng taiwenfeng@126.com INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF LOGISTICS: RESEARCH AND APPLICATIONS 2023, VOL. 26, NO. 9, 1145– 1171 https://doi.org/10.1080/13675567.2021.2022640 exchanged among members across the supply chain (Kulp, Lee, and Ofek2004; Liu et al.2016). Operational integration refers to the extent to whichfirms exchange decision rights, knowledge and resources across the supply chain to streamline supply chain activities (Liu et al.2013). Several scholars have suggested that the focalfirm can benefit from GSCI (Yang et al.2020;W u2013). However, our existing knowledge of enhancing the degree of three dimensions of GSCI is still limited. Ethical leadership refers to leaders showing proper behaviours and promoting the moral behaviour of others through communication with followers (Brown, Treviño, and Harrison2005). Drawing on social learning theory, which clearly explains how individual or organisation learn norms of conduct by observing others (Bandura1978; Bedi, Alpaslan, and Green2016), previous studies proposed that ethical leadership will motivate employees learn andfinally engage in moral conducts (Babalola et al.2018; Brown and Treviño2006; Mayer, 2012; Zheng et al.2021). However, a few studies have examined the social learning effect brought from ethical leadership in the green supply chain context (Chen et al.2021; Mokhtar et al.2019), which has been practised. For example, in response to environmental protection demands, Huawei commits to practising business ethics by integrating green ideas into the whole product development process and optimising its utilisation of resources in a sustainable way (Li et al.2020). Following Huawei, its suppliers take responsibility for pollution control more proactively, which effectively makes products meet requirements related to the environment (Li et al.2020). Therefore, we are inspired to extend the concept of ethical leadership to the supply chain context (Brown, Treviño, and Harrison2005) and propose supply chain ethical leadership (SCEL). According to social learning theory, the focalfirm with a high level of SCEL serves as a credible role model since it demonstrates integrity and sets high ethical standards for other supply chain partners (Brown, Treviño, and Harrison 2005; Chen and Hou 2016). In other words, supply chain partners tend to learn from the focalfirm with a high level of SCEL and actively participate in green supply chain practices (Dai, Cantor, and Montabon 2015; Han and Huo2020). Therefore, we propose that SCEL has a positive impact on GSCI. Furthermore, unpacking the‘black box’ in the link between SCEL and GSCI is conducive to our better understanding of translating the SCEL of the focalfirm into green supply chain practices. Drawing on the social learning perspective, ethical leadership influences the conduct of followers via modelling (Brown, Treviño, and Harrison2005). The green image represents the green reputation and green credibility of a firm (Chen 2008), which helps the focal firm set an ethical model for supply chain partners. Specifically, the focal firm with a high level of SCEL will impress supply chain partners with its green image by adopting green strategies and establishing a shared value of environmental sustainability (Mitra and Datta,2014). The green image then will help the focal firm win the trust of supply chain partners and change their perception of green value (Chen 2010; Hwang and Kim2019; Wu et al.2015), which may further facilitate supply chain partners actively engage in collaborative green practices. In this manner, the green image may help to transform the SCEL of the focalfirm into GSCI. Social learning theory also indicates that the motivation of social learning may be potentially subject to external forces (Santos-Vijande et al.2005; Song et al.2020). Under a high level of institutional force,firms are more likely to better recognise the green needs of stakeholders (Hyatt and Berente 2017), and understand the necessity and urgency of engaging in green initiatives (Tsai and Liao 2017). In this case,firms would better exert their ethical leadership in the supply chain to establish the green image to respond to institutional force from distinct stakeholders (Xie, Zhu, and Wang 2019). Thus, we propose that perceived institutional force positively affects the indirect effect of SCEL on GSCI via green image. This study aims to explore how and under what conditions SCEL affects GSCI. Specifically, we investigate four research questions. First, whether SCEL is positively related to the three dimensions of GSCI? Second, does the green image mediate the relationship between SCEL and GSCI? Third, do two types of perceived institutional force positively moderate the relationship between SCEL and the green image? Fourth, whether two types of perceived institutional force positively moderate the mediating effect of the green image? The investigation of the above questions would offer four 1146 J. WANG AND T. FENG major contributions to the green supply chain management literature. First, we extend the concept of ethical leadership to the supply chain context, which enriches the literature related to social learning theory. Second, the study endeavours to examine the mediating role of green image in the SCEL-GSCI relationship, which enhances our understanding of how SCEL and GSCI are related. Third, we advance the literature by identifying the boundary conditions that may affect the SCEL-green image-GSCI link. Fourth, by collapsing GSCI into strategic integration, information integration and operational integration, we provide novel insights for enhancing GSCI. 2 Literature review and hypotheses development 2.1 Green supply chain integration Economic globalisation andfierce competition have made supply chain integration play an increasingly important role in business activities (Alfalla-Luque, Marin-Garcia, and Medina-Lopez2015; Erboz, Yumurtacı Hüseyinoğlu, and Szegedi 2021). Compared with supply chain collaboration, which begins with customers and extends back through thefirm to material and service suppliers (Stank, Keller, and Daugherty2001), supply chain integration is needed internally and externally (Leuschner et al.2013). Supply chain integration is believed to be a set of collaboration of supply chain members in intra- and inter-organisational processes (Yang et al.2020), and supply chain collaboration as the element of supply chain integration (Leuschner et al.2013). Supply chain integration can not only helpfirms obtain the capabilities and resources needed to maintain their performance but also enhance formulating development strategies from a higher perspective and further improve core competitiveness (Delic, Eyers, and Mikulic2019; Zhang et al. 2020; Zhao, Feng, and Wang2015). GSCI adds the concept of green development into traditional supply chain integration management practices. It can effectively reduce pollution and enhance the sustainable development offirms. Scholars have commonly developed their definition and dimensions of GSCI based on the research of supply chain integration (Dai, Cantor, and Montabon 2015; Lo et al.2018; Wolf2011; Wong, Wong, and Boon-itt2015;W u2013), but failed to reach a consensus. As Table 1 shows, some scholars divided GSCI into internal and external GSCI (Yang et al.2013), some broke GSCI into green stakeholder integration, green internal integration, and green supplier integration (Mao, Zhang, and Li2017; Wolf 2011;W u 2013), others divided GSCI into internal integration, green supplier integration, and green customer integration (Flynn, Huo, and Zhao2010; Jajja, Chatha, and Farooq2018; Wong, Wong, and Boon-itt2020; Yang et al.2020; Zhao et al.2013). Most literature has divided GSCI based on integration objects, enriching and developing the GSCI theory. However, collapsing GSCI by the integrated content may provide more novel insights. First, in the context of low-carbon, environmental protection, energy-saving and emission reduction, it isn’t easy to measure the degree of GSCI of all the integration objects (Zhou et al.2016). Previous studies generally measure the degree of green supplier/customer integration according to the major supplier/customer. However, the environmental image of focalfirms is affected not only by the major supplier/customer, but also by otherfirst-tier or second-tier suppliers/customers. Second, from the perspective of the ecosystem, GSCI should be a trinity of suppliers, focalfir ms, and customers (Viswanadham and Samvedi2013). Dividing dimensionality based on integration objects implies the focalfirm’s integration with customers and suppliers, which may ignore the interaction between suppliers and customers and fail to reflect the connotation of GSCI accurately. Three components are used to measure supply chain integration to highlight the strategic collaboration between supply chain partners at multiple levels: strategic alignment, information sharing and operational coordination (Flynn, Huo, and Zhao2010; Han and Huo2020; Wong, Boon-Itt, and Wong2011). To the best of our knowledge, a few existing studies on GSCI have incorporated all the three components. Therefore, this research conceptualises GSCI comprising the three dimensions of strategic integration, information integration and operational integration. It means jointly making and revising green plans, strategies and objectives with supply chain partners (Flynn, Huo, and Zhao2010; Vachon and Klassen2008). According to Formentini and Taticchi (2014), each nodefirm of the supply chain is in a complex network relationship. The essence of supply chain management is to govern the network relationship. Maintaining a good strategic cooperation relationship with supply chain partners will effectively minimise opportunistic behaviours (Yuan et al.2010). Information integration refers to the extent to which information is exchanged among members across the supply chain (Kulp, Lee, and Ofek2004; Liu et al.2016). It means that supply chain partners exchange timely valuable information, including obtaining high-quality information from suppliers and delivering it to manufacturers and customers, and obtaining accurate feedback information and dynamic demand information from customers and delivering them to manufacturers and suppliers (Li and Lin2007). The information integration between supply chain partners helps firms obtain more comprehensive knowledge and then make better decisions (Eve, Aleda, and James 2003). It was suggested that the information shared between supply chain partners must be accurate and timely; otherwise, it will lead to the bullwhip effect (Mackelprang et al.2014). Highquality information integration helps improve business performance (Choi, Blocher, and Gavirneni 2008; Gosain, Malhotra, and Sawy2005; Rossin2007; Liu et al.2021; Zhou et al.2014). Operational integration refers to the extent to whichfirms exchange decision rights, knowledge, and resources across the supply chain to streamline supply chain activities (Liu et al.2013). It integrates suppliers and customers into the entire green value chain, strengthens coordination and improves green operational efficiency (Sanders 2007). Several scholars have suggested that interfirm collaboration is required due to the high asset specificity between supply chain partners (Dyer and Singh1998; Simpson, Power, and Samson2007). The operational integration is a supply chain structure that can facilitate a low transaction cost environment and favour suppliers and buyers (Lo et al.,2018). 2.2 Supply chain ethical leadership and GSCI Ethical leadership, referring to leaders showing proper behaviours in personal and interpersonal relationships, and promoting the moral behaviour of others through communication with followers (Brown, Treviño, and Harrison2005), has been confirmed to be one of the key determinants of strategic choices and organisational performance (Hambrick and Mason1984; Qing et al.2020; Wood, Eid, and Agag 2021). A few scholars explored the role of ethical leadership in supply chain management, suggesting that ethical leadership plays an important role in managing purchasing agents’unethical practices (Ko et al.2019), and is one of the main problems for a successful supply chain management system (Aytan and Sayan2019). In the management practice of GSCI, ethical leadership plays an important role within and out of the organisation that cannot be ignored; however, its effect on green supply chain partners has not been fully discussed. Therefore, according to social learning theory, we extend the connotation of ethical leadership and define SCEL as the demonstration of appropriate conduct through personal and organisational actions and inter-personal and inter-organisational relationships, and the promotion of such conduct to followers and supply chain partners through two-way communication, corporation, reinforcement and decision-making. Compared with ethical leadership, which focuses on the ethical influence of managers on employees (Moore et al.2019), SCEL highlights the ethical influence of the focalfirm across the supply chain. From the perspective of followers within the organisation, social learning theory suggests that when subordinates observe positive actions from moral leaders, they will respond correspondingly based on the principles of social learning (Bedi, Alpaslan, and Green2016). Therefore, under a high level of SCEL, employees will regard leaders with ethical qualities as learning benchmarks and take 1150 J. WANG AND T. FENG standardised actions (Brown and Treviño,2006; Mayer et al.2012). When green decisions are made, they shall actively participate in environmental protection activities (Raineri and Paillé 2016), which promotes the formation of green culture in the organisation (Wu et al.2015) and reduces inner barriers of GSCI. From the perspective of supply chain partners outside the organisation, SCEL functions in three ways to promote GSCI. First, as outlined by social learning theory, ethical leadership encourages moral behaviours through role modelling appropriate behaviours (Babalola et al.2018). A focal firm with a high level of SCEL tends to commit to practising business ethics by prioritising the long-term utility offirm development and social benefits and formulating green decisions responsible to stakeholders (Yan, Sun, and Leung2014). By observing and learning behaviours of the focal firm, supply chain partners willfind the focalfirm trustworthy and become more confident in engaging in green actions. Then the focalfirm and supply chain partners will work with each other to improve the quality of cooperation in the long run and build a long-term alliance. In this manner, SCEL contributes to the strategic integration of the green supply chain. Second, drawing on social learning theory, SCEL not only role models appropriate and valued behaviours (Brown, Treviño, and Harrison2005) but also enhances supply chain partners’ green ability by allowing them to learn from social processes. Specifically, a focalfirm with a high level of SCEL will actively provide partners with green knowledge that might help improve their green capacity and green information that is conductive to their sustainable development, such as governments’ regulations, customers’ demand, etc. (Kong, Feng, and Huo2021). Such endeavour that promotes green knowledge sharing and green information dissemination among supply chain partners contributes to the information integration of the green supply chain. Third, social learning theory suggested that SCEL defines success not only in terms of results but also by the processes involved in attaining results (Babalola et al.2018). As such,firms with a high level of SCEL will enhance the implementation of green concepts throughout the process of cooperation (Song et al. 2020; Srinivasan and Swink 2015). To achieve common green performance goals, the focalfirm with a high level of SCEL will coordinate with partners on operational processes, including procurement, order execution, engineering change, new product/ service introduction, service support. In this manner, SCEL enhances the operational integration of the green supply chain. Based on the theoretical analysis above, we propose the following hypotheses: H1: SCEL is positively related to (a) strategic integration, (b) information integration, and (c) operational integration. 2.3. Supply chain ethical leadership and the Green image Green image, representingfirms’ green reputation and green credibility (Chen2008), is an intangible asset forfirms to enhance their competitive advantage. It contributes to the expansion of market share and business performance, and facilitates building and maintaining customer loyalty (Andreassen and Lindestad1998). Under the context of growing environmental awareness,firms with a high level of SCEL tend to make green strategic decisions and implement green practices. Then employees of the focalfirm will be encouraged to emulate ethical leaders and engage in valued behaviour (Babalola et al.2018). Such endeavours will facilitate forming a green organisational culture within the focalfirm. Besides, SCEL is conducive to the effective allocation of green resources (Robertson Barling2017) and integrating green concepts and product processes (Chen2008; Zhang, Shen, and Wu2011), thereby enhancing firms’ green capacity. The green culture and the green capability contribute to shaping the green image for afirm. Hence, we propose the following hypothesis: H2: SCEL is positively related to the green image. INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF LOGISTICS RESEARCH AND APPLICATIONS 1151 2.4. The mediating role of the green image The social learning perspective on ethical leadership proposes that leaders influence the ethical conduct of followers via modelling (Brown, Treviño, and Harrison2005). The green image serves as an approach that exhibits the modelling effect of the focalfirm, and the learning behaviours of employees and supply chain partners. Specifically, by setting high ethical standards and implementing green strategies, the focalfirm with a high level of SCEL becomes an ethical model for followers. Employees of the focalfirm are encouraged to engage in green behaviour through observation and emulation, which contributes to establishing thefirm’s green image. Then green image transfers the signal to supply chain partners that the focalfirm is credible (Chen2010; Hwang and Kim 2019). As a result, supply chain partners are motivated to engage in green action by witnessing and learning the focalfirm’s role modelling behaviours. The consistent endeavour of engaging in green practice willfinally enhance GSCI. Therefore, based on social learning theory, the green image can be seen as a way forfirms to translate SCEL into GSCI. A previous study acknowledges the role of green image as a mechanism linking contextual factors and green practices (Chen et al.2020). We suggest that the green image plays a mediating role in the relationships between SCEL and the three dimensions of GSCI. First, a green image transmits a positive signal that the focalfirm is credible, which provides supply chain partners with the cornerstone of trust in the focalfirm with a high level of SCEL (Chen2010). Then the focalfirm and partners can establish a long-term and stable cooperative relationship (Flavián, Guinalíu, and Torres 2005; Mukherjee and Nath2003). In this vein, green image mediates the SCEL-strategic integration relation. Second, the focalfirm with a good image set an example for supply chain partners. Then supply chain partners will be more convinced of the SCEL of the focalfirm and more actively learn and imitate the green behaviours of the focalfirm (Song et al.2020). Furthermore, the effectiveness of learning depends on the sharing of knowledge and the timely exchange of information (Kong, Feng, and Huo2021); thus, the information integration will be enhanced. In this vein, SCEL will be transformed into information integration through the green image. Third, the green image makes it easier forfirms to gain consumers’ favour, form green product premiums and increase market share (Wallin and Lindestad1998). To meet market demand, the efficiency of supply chain operations needs to be improved (Chang and Tu2005; Emeizan et al. 2016; Martenson 2007). Therefore, the focalfirm with a high level of SCEL will jointly plan the development of demand forecast with partners and work together with partners to optimise the operation process of the supply chain (Liu et al.2013; Sanders 2007). In this vein, the green image mediates the SCEL-operational integration relation. Based on the above arguments, we hypothesise: H3: Green image mediates the impacts of SCEL on (a) strategic integration, (b) information integration, and (c) operational integration. 2.5. The moderating role of perceived institutional force Perceived institutional force refers to general stakeholder pressures that have been perceived by firms exerted by governments (in the form of environmental regulations), media (in the form of supervisions), customers (in the form of green needs), industry rivals (in the form of competitions), etc. Perceived force is identified as an important external contextual factor that influencesfirms’ green actions (Hyatt and Berente2017). Social learning theory clarifies conditions for modelling behaviours; that is, the motivation of social learning may be potentially subject to external forces (Song et al.2020), suggesting perceived institutional force may potentially affect the SCEL-green image-GSCI link. However, the existingfindings are inconsistent, ranging from a positive effect (Liao and Tsai 2018)t on oe ffect (Zhu and Sarkis 2007), indicating that the boundary condition of SCEL 1152 J. WANG AND T. FENG transforms into GSCI via the green image need to be identified. Therefore, in this paper, we clarify the perceived institutional force into perceived business force and perceived social force, and explore whether or not they will amplify the indirect effects of SCEL on GSCI via the green image by enabling and motivating the better use of green resources. Perceived business force includes perceived pressures from customers, suppliers, shareholders, industry rivals andfinancial institutions. Concentrating on these pressures allowsfirms to take better advantage of SCEL to enhance their green image by more accurately recognising business stakeholder needs and then more wisely mobilising relevant green resources (Hyatt and Berente2017). In this vein, the perceived business force acts as an external stimulus that maximises SCEL in the process of green image enhancement. Perceived social force refers to perceived pressures from governments, media, non-governmental organisations, and local public agencies. Under a high level of perceived social force,firms are more likely to understand better the way society is likely to enact regulations and supervisions, enabling firms to more quickly and accurately identify opportunities and challenges and make green strategic decisions (Yang et al.2020). In addition, perceived social force dictates a certain way forfirms to conduct environmental strategies without hesitation (Tsai and Liao2017); therefore, firms with a high level of SCEL will effectively utilise green resources to perform relevant practices and constantly advance their green images as reactions to social policies. In sum, perceived social force may boost the impacts of SCEL on the green image. Hence, we propose the following hypotheses: H4: (a) Perceived business force and (b) perceived social force positively moderate the impact SCEL on the green image. The positive impact will become stronger when the degree of perceived business and social force becomes higher. In sum, we propose a moderated mediation model for GSCI: SCEL is related to GSCI (partially) by enhancing the green image. Yet, a low level of perceived institutional force is proposed to form a prerequisite for SCEL to translate into GSCI via the green image. In contrast, under the boundary condition of a high level of perceived institutional force,firms are more likely to put endeavours into ensuring their green image to achieve GSCI. Thus, we propose the following hypotheses: H5: Perceived business force positively moderates the indirect effect of SCEL on (a) strategic integration, (b) information integration, and (c) operational integration via the green image. H6: Perceived social force positively moderates the indirect effect of SCEL on (a) strategic integration, (b) information integration, and (c) operational integration via the green image. China’s economy is facing increasingly prominent environmental problems (Jiang et al.2018; Wong and van der Heijden2019). Customers in China are recognised for their increasingly green awareness and demand for green products (Chen et al.2015; Wang et al.2019). Under this context, more and more Chinesefirms implement green initiatives, including GSCI, to obtain competitive advantages and customers’ loyalty (Taoketao et al.2018). Therefore, we chose China as our research setting. Since China’s economic development is characterised as unbalanced and diverse (Feng et al. 2019; Zhao, Flynn, and Roth2006), we strategically selectedfirms in Guangdong, Jiangsu, Shandong, Henan and Inner Mongolia to increase the generalisability of our results. Guangdong, Jiangsu and Shandong locate in Pearl River Delta, Yangtze River Delta and Bohai Rim region, respectively, representing a relative high level of economic development. Henan locates in Central China, representing an average level of economic development. Inner Mongolia locates in Northeast and Western China, representing a relative low level of economic development. Firms in thesefive regions reflect distinct levels of GSCI. Based on the published industry catalogue, we randomly selected 200 firms from each region. Then, we contacted thesefirms to seek cooperation with a cover letter explaining our research purpose and ensuring confidentiality. A total of 435firms agreed to participate in the research. Before designing the questionnaire, we conducted interviews with 12firm executives. Based on careful consideration of the information obtained, the questionnaire was developed. Then, another 20 firm executives participated in the pre-test. We collected data in two rounds. At Time 1, the questionnaire was completed by two respondents; one answered questions relating to thefirm’s basic information, SCEL, and green image; the other answered perceived business force and social force. A total of 352 questionnaires were returned. At time 2, 6 months later, data on GSCI were collected from respondents. Finally, we received 317 valid questionnaires involving 634 respondents with an average job duration of 7.19 years in theirfirms. Among the 634 respondents, 64.8% held the positions of CEO, general manager or vice president, 35.2% were operations directors. The operations directors were executive-level managers, who actively engaged in firms’ strategic decision-making; thus, they were expected to be familiar withfirms’ internal operations and interactions with external partners. Our questionnaire effective response rate was 37.1%. Thefinal sample includes 56 firms in Henan, 60 firms in Inner Mongolia, 72 firms in Guangdong, 62 firms in Jiangsu, and 67firms in Shandong. INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF LOGISTICS RESEARCH AND APPLICATIONS 1163 Our findings suggest that SCEL significantly promotes strategic integration, information integration and operational integration, which are consistent with previous studies that highlight the importance of ethical leadership in inter-organisational relationship management (Bedi, Alpaslan, and Green2016). Ourfindings further strengthen the important role of SCEL in integrating supply chain partners into green initiatives, which suggests that social learning effects indeed exist among green supply chain partners. Our results also reveal that the green image partially mediates the relationship between SCEL and strategic integration, which is in line with previous studies (Chen2010; Flavián, Guinalíu, and Torres 2005). This suggests the important role of the green image in winning the trust and support of supply chain partners. Although the mediating effects of the green image in SCEL-information integration and SCEL-operational integration links are insignificant, further research suggests that strategic integration plays a complete mediating role in the impacts of the green image on information integration and operational integration. The green image may affect information integration and operational integration indirectly by facilitating strategic integration. Thesefindings provide novel insights for our understanding of how SCEL promotes GSCI and enrich the existing GSCI literature. As for under what conditions SCEL affects GSCI, we dividefirms’ perceived force into perceived business force and perceived social force, andfind that both positively affect the SCEL-green image and SCEL-green image relationships which is consistent with our research hypothesis. Specifically, a higher business force enables firms to more precisely recognise green needs of stakeholders (Hyatt and Berente2017), and a higher social force makesfirms better understand how society enacts environmental regulations and supervisions (Tsai and Liao2017). Thenfirms should take better advantage of SCEL to enhance the green image by more wisely mobilising relevant green resources to implement green strategies (Hyatt and Berente2017), to achieve the improvement of GSCI. 5.2. Theoretical contributions This study contributes to the existing literature in four ways. First, we extend the concept of ethical leadership to the context of the supply chain and propose that SCEL exhibited by the focalfirm produces the learning effect among supply chain partners. Previous literature on ethical leadership has mainly focused on the impact of ethical leadership within the organisation (Bedi, Alpaslan, and Green 2016; Brown and Treviño2006; Walumbwa et al.2011; Mayer et al.2012; Zheng et al. 2021). Our research contributes to the literature by extending the explanation of social learning theory. Second, we enrich the understanding of how SCEL influences GSCI by exploring the mediating role of the green image. We suggest that SCEL is a governing style of the focalfirm, which will be externalised when transforming internal green practices of the focalfirm into signals such as green reputation and green credibility (Chen2008). The green image provides an approach for successfully translating SCEL into GSCI by effectively conveying the focal firm’s environmental value, enhancing green knowledge learning, and strengthening green cooperation among supply chain partners (Chen2010; Flavián, Guinalíu, and Torres2005). Third, our study clarifies conditions for modelling behaviours by evidencing the moderating effect of perceived institutional force on SCEL-green image-GSCI link. We propose thatfirms’ motivation for green knowledge learning becomes stronger when a high level of institutional force is perceived, explaining how SCEL enhances the green image and GSCI in uncertain environments and extends the interpretation boundary of social learning theory. Fourth, this study enriches the GSCI literature by exploring the relationships among three dimensions of GSCI. Ourfindings suggest that the green image promotes information integration and operational integration by facilitating strategic integration. Thisfinding suggests that strategic integration may be the foundation of information and operational integration. 1164 J. WANG AND T. FENG 5.3. Managerial implications From a managerial perspective, this study provides some guidance for managers. First, managers of the focal firm should take leading roles in promoting GSCI practices among supply chain partners. According to the results of H1a, H1b and H1c, SCEL exhibited by the focalfirm is effective in motivating moral behaviours of supply chain partners, which further enhances the implementation of GSCI. Therefore, strengthening the ethical leadership of the focalfirm would undoubtedly be efficient to encourage its supply chain partners to learn green principles and engage in green practices. Second, H2 and H3 suggest that the green image mediates the relationship between SCEL and strategic integration and promotes information integration and operational integration indirectly through strategic integration. Thisfinding provides a possible way for managers to achieve GSCI from SCEL. Specifically, managers should highlight the role of the green image in winning trust of supply chain partners and adopt green strategies, such as enhancing resource recycling and developing innovative eco-design, to transform SCEL into the green image. Third, Chinesefirms bear different institutional forces when making decisions related to green supply chain practices. H4, H5, and H6 confirm that when focalfirms perceive high business force and social force, they try harder to transform SCEL into GSCI by enhancing the green image. This finding implies that managers should enhance awareness of environmental claims from different stakeholders to the strategic level, enabling them to identify opportunities and challenges precisely. Then led by SCEL, the focalfirm and supply chain partners will be informed of the importance of environmental protection and actively promote environmental protection policies. Fourth, this study also provides novel guidelines forfirms seeking to enhance GSCI by confirming the crucial role of strategic integration. When the focalfirm aims to enhance GSCI, it would be wiser if it made efforts to achieve strategic integrationfirst. Therefore, managers should be careful to formulate the right green cooperation strategies, and guide the focalfirm to cooperate with supply chain partners to carry out executive-level integration. 6. Conclusion and limitations Achieving GSCI is important forfirms to gain a competitive edge and to improve their corporate performance (Yang, Jiang, and Zhao2019; Zhang et al.2019). On the basis of social learning theory, this article enhances our understanding of how and under what conditions afirm’s SCEL can promote GSCI. Specifically, ourfindings suggest that SCEL significantly promotes strategic integration, information integration and operational integration; that the green image partially mediates the relationship between SCEL and strategic integration; that strategic integration completely mediates the green image-information integration and green image-operational integration relationships, suggesting the green image promotes information integration and operational integration indirectly by promoting strategic integration. Thus, the indirect relationship between SCEL and GSCI provides empirical evidence forfirms’ transforming SCEL into GSCI through the green image. Furthermore, this study indicates that perceived business force and perceived social force positively moderate the‘SCEL-green image-strategic integration’ relation. We hope this article will provide theoretical and data support for future research on how SCEL improves GSCI. This study has several limitations. First, we analysed only the influence of SCEL on GSCI. Future scholars should use organisational and leader-level data to create a complete model of consequences of SCEL. For instance, it would be interesting tofigure out the impact of SCEL onfirms’ financial and environmental performance and the behavioural and attitudinal consequences for supply chain ethical leaders. Second, we explored the mediating effect of the green image between SCEL and GSCI. However, the impact of SCEL on GSCI can also be achieved in other ways. In further research, other novel ways of achieving SCEL and enhancing GSCI should be explored. INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF LOGISTICS RESEARCH AND APPLICATIONS 1165 Finally, we studied the effects of perceived institutional force. Future research should examine other potential boundary conditions, such as technology turbulence and cultural tolerance. The impact of SCEL on GSCI may depend on some background factors; thus, setting different adjustments in future research can deepen this research line. RESEARCH ARTICLE Influence of corporate social responsibility and ethical leadership on employees' affective commitment: Evidence from the hospitality industry in Vietnam Nguyen Khanh Hai Tran Faculty of Business Administration, University of Finance–Marketing, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Correspondence Nguyen Khanh Hai Tran, Faculty of Business Administration, University of Finance– Marketing, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Email: khanhhai@ufm.edu.vn Abstract This paper intends to evaluate the relationship between corporate social responsibility (CSR), ethical leadership (EL), job satisfaction (JS), and affective commitment (AC). Filtered and entered Statistical Package for the Social Sciences and Amos is a powerful structural equation modeling software helping support research and theories, the data were gathered from 432 participants in Vietnam's hospitality sector. According to study findings, CSR and EL positively impact AC and JS among employees. Moreover, JS is also a vital component that has influenced employees' AC. The study results have managerial implications for improving JS and strengthening the correlation of employees' AC. KEYWORDS affective commitment, CSR, employees' corporate social responsibility perception, ethical leadership, job satisfaction JEL CLASSIFICATION M14, M54 1 | INTRODUCTION Human resource management (HRM) becomes increasingly pivotal as competition heats up, and human resources are a crucial success factor in a firm's competitive advantages. This is a big challenge for corporations in developing workforce resources that they can devote to their organization in the long term. For that reason, studies investigate the elements that influence a firm's employee commitment (Messner, 2013; Meyer & Allen,1997; Ocen et al.,2017). Allen and Meyer (1990) prioritized affective commitment (AC) since it provided the most significant advantages to the firm and its personnel. As a result, it shows attachment in both attitudes and behaviors of employees toward the organization. The more the AC to their company, the greater their agreement with its aims and readiness to contribute to it (Meyer & Allen, 1997). Therefore, AC has the highest level of employee's commitment to their efforts, enthusiasm, concentration, and willingness to dedicate themselves to the organization. In other words, AC is a strength that creates a competitive advantage that helps an organization to survive, be stable, and be successful over the long term. Recently, organizations have begun to implement internal corporate social responsibility (CSR) measures to address HRM (Jamali et al., 2020), aiming to bolster their employees' sense of security and affiliation with the organization (Chatzopoulou et al.,2022). This approach enables them to gain a competitive edge in an increasingly uncertain and volatile market environment (Munir & Beh,2019; Trivedi & Srivastava,2022). Many empirical studies investigated the relationship between CSR and organizational commitment (Hayat & Afshari, 2022; Papacharalampous & Papadimitriou,2021;T u r k e r ,2009; van der Westhuizen & Malan,2023), organizational identification (Zhao et al., 2019), job satisfaction (JS) (Glavas, 2016; Silva et al.,2022), and organizational engagement (Al Amri et al.,2019). However, several businesses focus on external CSR b u ti g n o r eC S Rf o re m p l o y e e sa n dr ed u c ec o s t sf o re m p l o y e ed e v e l o p - ment activities. Consequently, it is essential that companies and organizations carefully analyze the significance of employee-oriented CSR action plans and their effect on employees' AC. Managers are essential to developing moral guidelines within their companies. By praising moral behavior and punishing immoral behavior, they mold the behavior of those under them (DeConinck, 2015). Through social learning processes, this leadership style teaches its followers how to behave ethically (Babalola et al., 2018). Some researchers have recommended focusing more on understa nding how these influential activities operate in ethical leadership (EL) (Bouckenooghe et al., 2015). Among other leadership philosophies, EL inherently fosters a sense of JS among employees and typically culminates in the achievement of organizati onal objectives (Bouckenooghe et al., 2015). In summary, globalization has intensified societal expectations for corporations to improve their CSR effectiveness, ethical conduct, and leadership (Mishra & Schmidt,2018). Concurrently, ethical leaders are concentrating on developing a moral workplace via human connections (Walumbwa et al., 2012). Prior studies indicate that fundamental corporate factors, including CSR and EL, enhance stakeholder relationships (Arrigo, 2013) and bolster employee satisfaction and commitment (Freire & Bettencourt,2020;I si̧k, 2020; Torlak et al.,2021). Nevertheless, there is a conspicuous dearth of thorough study delving into the unique effects of these elements on employee attitudes and behaviors, especially when it comes to comprehending the subtle effects of CSR on employee commitment (Scheidler et al., 2019; Donia et al.,2019). Given the specific context of CSR, this research zeroes in the hospitality market in Vietnam. This market was chosen primarily because it significantly contributes to Vietnam's economic growth, valued at approximately 35,453.39 trillion VND in 2022 (Statista, 2022). Additionally, the hospitality sector is an essential source of labor in Vietnam, providing about 6 million jobs (Statista, 2022). Regrettably, worker responsibility has not been sufficiently addressed. The hospitality industry is recognized for a high rate of turnover and subpar workplace conditions (Park & Min, 2020). Therefore, it is crucial to identify intervention strategies and mechanisms to promote CSR toward employees. Hospitality resources may be strained by their broad and ambiguous focus on corporate social responsibility, according to academics (Chen, 2019). Additionally, employees are a vital resource in hotels. Consequently, many hotels are adapting and designing CSR expressly for workers. Hence, this research investigates internal CSR's particular and different influences on AC. Notably, while these research streams suggest that JS could elucidate the effect of CSR activities on AC, the simultaneous combination of CSR and EL to explain AC needs to be addressed by previous research. Therefore, to address the significant gaps mentioned above, this study employs a combination of social exchange theory (SET) and social learning theory (SLT) to clarify the correlation between EL, CSR, and work attitudes, which include JS and employees' AC, especially considering the hospitality sector in Vietnam. 2 | LITERATURE REVIEW 2.1 | Theoretical background As per the SET (Blau,1964), responsibilities are generated by a chain of interactions between interdependent entities, implying that an employee who receives benefits feels a moral obligation to reciprocate toward the employer (Haar & Roche,2010). Employees anticipate rewards from their employers in exchange for their labor and vice versa. Consequently, a lack of experienced reciprocity could lead employers to reduce the benefits provided to workers or could lead workers to decrease their work endeavors (Birtch et al., 2016). Based on the SET, which combines aspects of sociology, psychology, and economics, employee participation in different kinds of interactions is based on how they weigh the advantages and disadvantages of doing so in terms of influencing their attitudes and behaviors within the company (Mory et al., 2016). Employers can foster social exchange with their workforce by implementing regulations and activities that indicate a more social exchange connection, encouraging workers to display more positive attitudes and behaviors at work (Cropanzano & Mitchell, 2005). According to the theory SET, if one party is pleasing to the other, the other will probably return the favor. This theory clarifies the idea of reciprocity in a mutual relationship between two entities. Regarding CSR, an employee may feel obligated to repay the business for the benefits they receive (such as freely providing well-being support services to colleagues). CSR inherently possesses the potential to foster social exchange mechanisms within the organization and its employees (Farooq et al., 2014). Therefore, through social exchange, CSR may effect on an employee's mindset and actions. Compared with AC, this line of reasoning implies that job happiness may be a more direct result of perceived CSR. This suggests that JS acting as a mediator may influence AC and perceived CSR. Therefore, this research highlights the use of SET to examine how CSR affects employee attitudes and behaviors like AC. Furthermore, Blau ( 1964) notes that since social exchange requires faith in others to reciprocate, the beginning of exchange relationships requires investments that represent a commitment to the other party. Employees observe and pick up on ethical behavior in their leader. The SLT, which describes how people see and pick up behavior from society, is the foundation for this. Employees consequently exhibit more excellent AC. 2.2 | Development of the hypotheses 2.2.1 | JS and AC JS can be perceived as fulfilling employees' expectations (Lee et al., 2012). The first hypothesis is proposed as follows: H1. JS has positively influenced AC. 2.2.2 | CSR, JS, and AC Rupp and Mallory (2015) divided CSR into internal and external ones. External CSR describes the organizational business and strategic activities toward the related parties, including consumers, suppliers, governments, and society—which comprise the living environment, and internal CSR depicts the organizational action plans toward employees. Internal CSR encompasses those organizational practices aimed at improving working conditions. These practices might include diversity management, training and development, family-friendly policies, and career possibilities (Turker, 2009). In other words, employee-oriented CSR includes training courses, learning organizational readiness, a safe working environment, socialization and integration policies, and other similar programs (Turker, 2009). The findings of Welford et al. (2008) concluded that there are big differences between businesses and their stakeholders that are deprived of specific interests or priorities of that group. Since workers are the key contributors to the survival and development of the firm, responsibility for employees is increasingly focused on companies and employees' perceptions of CSR efforts. Employee perception of CSR is about how an individual evaluates the initiatives and how they feel about what they know about CSR. This could influence an individual's future attitudes, actions, or behaviors connected to CSR (Gkorezis & Petridou, 2017; Gond et al., 2017). Understanding procedures and guidelines about workers' physical and mental health is necessary to perceive internal corporate social responsibility (Rasool & Rajput, 2017). For CSR to be widely implemented, companies must treat their employees fairly. Businesses that do not take employee responsibility seriously will not be held accountable to their clients or the community in which they operate (Asrar-ul-Haq et al.,2017). According to Asrar-ul-Haq et al. (2017), a business's social recognition increases employee JS, and prospective employees find the organization more appealing when it demonstrates a commitment to morality, ethics, and social responsibility. Workers employed by morally and ethically conscious companies are more well-liked by coworkers and have higher JS (Chatzopoulou & de Kiewiet, 2021). Additionally, prior studies have unveiled a range of benefits that employees can derive from a socially responsible corporation, encompassing aspects such as self-assurance and satisfaction (Appiah, 2019). Recent studies have shown that JS is greatly influenced by an organization's CSR activities (Farmaki et al.,2022; Hayat & Afshari,2022; Silva et al.,2023). Internal CSR practices are significantly associated with the enhancement of working conditions. Consequently, these behaviors impact how satisfied a person is with their employment. According to Ting (1997), there is proof that HRM practices and work satisfaction are related. Employees' CSR perceptions positively contribute to work attitudes and behaviors, pride, enthusiasm, enjoyment, and satisfaction (Barakat et al., 2016), implying JS. Furthermore, SET illuminates how a company's CSR perception and satisfaction mutually influence each other; hence, affiliation with an organization of high repute impacts their emotional aspect. Workers who work for moral and socially conscious companies typically have higher moral standards and recognize their affiliation with the company (Asrar-ul-Haq et al., 2017). Research on reputation confirms that a company's status and appeal increase worker commitment (Chatzopoulou & de Kiewiet, 2021). Studies show the correlation between employees' CSR perception and AC (Bouraoui et al.,2018; Papacharalampous & Papadimitriou,2021; Turker, 2009). Therefore, hypotheses are proposed as follows: H2a. CSR has positively influenced JS. H2b. CSR has positively influenced AC. 2.2.3 | EL, JS, and AC According to Brown et al. According to Rivers et al. ( 2018), a leader is a moral manager who sets an example of ethical behavior, communicates ethical standards, and ensures followers accountable for acting morally. Ethical leaders are fair, reliable, and disciplined and actively promote moral conduct among their followers by clearly communicating moral principles and expectations, offering moral guidance, and holding followers accountable for their conduct (Ahmed et al., 2020; Zaim et al.,2021). EL has positively influenced AC. 3 | METHODOLOGY 3.1 | Procedure and sample During the initial phase, the questionnaire was pretested with the participation of 10 employees from the hospitality industry in Vietnam to evaluate their comprehension of the highlighted questions. In light of their combined feedback, a few adjustments were implemented to enhance the clarity and precision of the questionnaire. The Appendix A presents the utilized items. In the second phase, the 500 printed surveys were distributed directly to employees (subordinate employees) who are working in the hospitality industry in Vietnam. The 432 collected questionnaires resulted in a response rate of 86.4%. The research data were gathered using a convenience sampling strategy. The valid number of respondents is 432, in which the relative gender ratio does not differ much. Specifically, there were 188 male (43.5%) and 244 female (56.5%) respondents. In terms of age, 45.2% of the participants were from 22 to 34 years old, and 36.8% were from 35 to 50 years old. Almost all of the participants hold a university degree or higher—including 306 people. In terms of tenure, 90 employees with less than 3 years of seniority, 182 employees with 3 under 5 working tenure, 114 employees with 5–10 years of working, and only 46 people with over 10 years of seniority participated in the survey. This study used Covariance based Structural Equation Modeling (CB-SEM) to analyze the data and test the hypotheses. 3.2 | Measurement The related study's scale was extracted and modified to match the Vietnam market. Specifically, the CSR includes a six-item scale adopted from Turker (2009); the seven items on EL were inherited and amended from the scale of Lin and Liu (2017); the JS comprises three items scale originated from the scale of Vlachos et al. (2013); the AC scale is inherited from Papacharalampous and Papadimitriou ( 2021) including six items. This study examined the influence that employee views of CSR and EL on JS and AC, as well as JS's mediating function in the interaction between CSR, EL perceptions, and AC. By investigating the effect of CSR and EL on the attitudes and behaviors of employees, this paper suggests that CSR managers and EL take action strategically on relevant activities that aim to achieve both macro and microorganizational benefits. This study's distinctive and valuable component is that it helps empirically to affirm the excellent function of CSR toward employees. Instead of perceiving all types of CSR as the same, the article extends the existing literature on green HRM by highlighting diverse CSR activities' beneficial and unique impact on employees. This study utilizes the framework of SET to gain a deeper understanding of how CSR influences JS and AC. This study adds valuable ideas to the theory by pointing out the need to study an individual's subjective perception of CSR to get a holistic view of its influence on people's attitudes and behaviors. The findings stressed that CSR is the strong bond between the corporation and its workforce, and it enhances JS and AC between the employee and the organization. More specifically, the research results reconfirm previous research depicting that employees whose perceptions are positive toward their organization's CSR could have an AC to their organization (Bhatti et al., 2022; Bouraoui et al., 2018; Papacharalampous & Papadimitriou, 2021; Turker,2009); and JS (Glavas,2016; Silva et al., 2022). This is also entirely in line with the results of Gond et al. (2017), who claim that CSR perceptions of employees affect jobrelated decisions, attitudes, and individual behavior in the workplace. Moreover, Bouraoui et al. ( 2018) implied that there is a rare use of SET to test the relationship between CSR and AC. Based on the SLT (Bandura,1977), the presence of ethical managers produces an ethical cycle, culturally and both overtly and implicitly, transferring positive thinking to employees (Xu et al., 2016). Employees trust and rely on their leaders to resolve difficulties ethically and fairly, improving AC. The findings indicate that EL positively impacted JS, which is entirely in line with the research results of Shafique et al. ( 2018), Freire and Bettencourt (2020), and Torlak et al. (2021). At the same time, the study results also present that EL positively influences employee AC in accordance with the studies of Benevene et al. (2018), Isi̧k (2020), Torlak et al. (2021). This finding is consistent with the conclusion of Fu and Deshpande (2014), Zhu et al. (2015), and Imam and Kim (2023) that the ethical environment provided by the leader will increase employee commitment and performance. 6 | MANAGERIAL IMPLICATIONS The present study has many implications for management practice. Investigating the potential impact of CSR and EL on employee attitudes toward work provides valuable insights for academics and practitioners involved in human resource development. The findings indicate that CSR and EL can lead to improved AC and higher JS among employees, which may ultimately improve corporate performance in the long term. Additionally, research suggests that employees with a high level of AC in their organization are more likely to align with its goals and be more willing to contribute to its success. Therefore, businesses should prioritize implementing internal CSR initiatives and strengthen EL to foster positive employee attitudes and improve organizational performance. The research results show a direct link between the workforce and the organization. Proponents of this approach argue that investing in employees' well-being and satisfaction can lead to increased AC to the company. Additionally, the study found that mediating factors, such as job satisfaction, play an important role in the relationship between CSR, EL, and AC. As such, organizations must prioritize workforce satisfaction to remain competitive in the market. To achieve this, companies should implement targeted internal CSR programs and ensure effective implementation. The study's findings hold substantial implications for CSR strategies. Managers should recognize that employees' perceptions of CSR initiatives influence various stakeholders, especially internal ones like the employees themselves. This perception enhances their JS and emotional engagement. The affirmative correlation between CSR and AC implies that organizations should guarantee that employees are informed about their CSR policies and initiatives via corporate communication. In the hospitality industry, managers can increase employee awareness of internal CSR programs by encouraging participation in volunteer activities and skill development, addressing employee needs and desires, and supporting continued learning. Additionally, implementing fair policies to balance work and life for employees can enhance JS and practical commitment to the company. Organizations participating in CSR are likely to adopt similar responsibilities toward their employees by enforcing better policies to protect employee welfare. This study substantiates that EL is crucial in improving employees' level of JS and AC, suggesting that EL is vital in providing proper direction that motivates people to engage more in their work. Given that EL benefits follower outcomes, businesses should endeavor to develop moral behaviors among subordinates and their supervisors. The study also reveals that JS is linked to CSR, EL, and AC. Therefore, managers must understand and investigate these causal relationships. The researchers recommend that organizations invest in appropriate training and development programs for leaders and the implementation of CSR initiatives. This can establish reciprocal relationships between EL and AC in the organization. Furthermore, the results of this study indicate that ethical values are critical for organizational success. Executives and ethical leaders should strive to create a culture of shared ethical values that goes beyond personal interests and financial gain to promote emotional cohesion among employees. 7 | LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE RESEARCH The present study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. The study findings have practical relevance for managers in boosting JS and fostering a favorable relationship between employee AC and the company. Celina (celinap@srmist.edu.in ) Received: 24 October 2025 | Revised: 23 January 2026 | Accepted: 30 January 2026 Keywords: accountability | corporate integrity | employee performance | ethical leadership | trust ABSTRACT Ethical leadership has a significant role in shaping corporate governance practices. The current study determined to examine the impact of ethical leadership on major aspects such as corporate integrity, accountability and employee performance in focus of building trust and commitment through vision, empathy and courage. The study employed a quantitative approach and collected data using a structured questionnaire from 500 respondents. The analysis was performed using SPSS version 27, applying sta - tistical methods such as correlation and regression to examine the relationship between variables. The results revealed a robust positive correlation between a leader's vision and corporate integrity ( r = 0.856), as well as between corporate responsibility and courage (r = 0.854). Regression analysis demonstrated that a leader's vision was a significant predictor of employee performance (β = 0.834, p < 0.001), while empathy emerged as a strong predictor of employee commitment (β = 0.819, p < 0.001). Moreover, both empathy and courage were recognised as pivotal factors affecting organisational trust, with courage having a more pronounced effect within the model. Additionally, a strong correlation was found between organisational trust and employee performance (r = 0.813). These findings underscore that ethical leadership involves multiple aspects, including vision, empathy and courage. The study provided recommendations for organisations to strengthen ethical leadership practices, focusing on developing vision, empathy and courage for cultivating a committed, high- performing workforce and ensuring long- term business success. 1 | Introduction 1.1 | Background of the Study Corporate culture management is one of the pillars of organi - sational success, but the threat of corporate scandals has re - awakened leadership ethical failures (San 2023). International corporate scandals such as Enron and Satyam have become case studies in the global market (Madegowda 2025). Also, it has raised critical concerns about what a leader can do to enhance accountability and integrity in an organisation (Pandey 2023). Corporate integrity is not just the lack of fraud, but rather a company's unwavering commitment to upholding moral and ethical standards in all practices, starting from employees to customers (Tariq 2025). Likewise, corporate accountability re - quires leaders to accept responsibility for outcomes and to en - sure transparency in decision- making (Efunniyi et al. 2024; Muff et al. 2022; Limbore et al. 2025). Together, integrity and accountability shape the ethical foundation of corporate gover - nance (Tanoto and Tangkawarow 2023).
