Positive attitude In a social psychological context, attitude is considered to be the tendency to react in a generally favorable or unfavorable manner in relation to the object of the attitude ( Robinson, Stimpson, Huefner, & Hunt, 1991 ). In order to survive an economic downturn, such as the GFC, the most important characteristic of an SME owner was found to be the positive attitude that they brought to bear on problems within their business. Without exception, all the surviving franchisees and inde - pendent SMEs displayed a positive attitude rather than looking for someone to blame for the prevailing economic conditions. It was recognized that, as their SMEs were performing reasonably well, they were more likely to exhibit a positive response. Common sentiments expressed were: “ People who fail blame everyone but themselves. ” (TB, FeS, Food and beverage) “ I like to see my staff flourish. ” (LR, IS, Food and beverage) There were interesting patterns between the SME owners ’ personal characteristics and their resultant perceptions of the culture of their business. In particular, successful franchisees and independent business owners appeared to share a belief in their own abilities to establish a positive and proactive business culture. Many of these participants developed strategies to counteract negative external forces, “ So we have driven average sale, we monitor it, we communicate it, and we have a culture in place that it ’ s not about what you achieve, it ’ s about your growth in that aspect you have an opportunity to grow your average sale no matter what shift you are on. ” (ML, FS, Food and beverage) In contrast, the SMEs who were now struggling were downbeat and often despondent. They did not appear to take responsibility for their predicament, and instead, tended to blame the economy, customers, the franchisor, competitors, or shopping center management. We did not observe a difference between franchisees and independent SMEs in this regard. 4.3. Resources A theme that emerged in the research centered on the resources that both franchisees and independent business owners perceived to be important to their survival in a time of recession. These were financial resources and time. 4.3.1. Financial resources Financial costs were identified across all cohorts as a constraint that affected debt levels and survival well beyond pre-purchase decisions, supporting previous research such as Smallbone et al. (2012) . However, the ongoing constraints resulting from high start-up costs were consid - ered to be more significant in franchises than independent SMEs. When considering successful franchisees ’ and independent SMEs ’ approaches to financing their ventures, clear distinctions emerge. Overall, successful franchisees possess clear templates for financial monitoring, reporting and have access to established documenting systems. This enabled them to borrow significant amounts from banking institutions, while suc - cessful independent owners recounted difficulties in accessing sufficient finance from financial institutions and tended to finance their own business start-ups, often sourcing private equity investment from friends and family. Successful business owners also indicated the flexibility of how the capital was allocated to business activities to cover the costs and repay debts through well-planned investments and retrenchment strategies such as cutting rental costs by operating from home and reducing prices. With extensive industry experience, SM, FeS in Weight loss and health care found an effective way to deal with capital allocation, similar to JF, a successful food and beverage retailer: “ That was the cost for the franchise, and obviously I needed more for marketing and set up and all that sort of thing ... Then there is the equipment set up. I kept looking ahead at each milestone and trying to get there, and it was all about breaking that down into tiny little milestones and then kind of enjoying every little step. ” (SM, FeS, Weight loss and health care) “ From the day we came into the shop I didn ’ t have to put any more money into the shop. We are drawing wages, not big wages, but enough to keep our head above water and pay our bills. The shop has paid its way since day one, and we ’ ve been able to put a few staff on as well. ” (JF, IS, Food and beverage) A majority of unsuccessful independent business owners had accu - mulated large debts, often utilizing personal assets as equity to secure bank loans. Most suggested that servicing large amounts of debt was the single biggest issue for them, “ Even though I make money each year, I had to put it all into the business just to survive, so the debt is still there ... growing. ” shared JS (IU, Awnings, blinds, shades) who was hit hard by the downturn. 4.3.2. Time management Most SMEs are operated by sole owners or are family-owned. While most successful franchisees acknowledged that they often worked extremely long hours (often constraining their ability to achieve a ‘work- life ’ balance) unsuccessful franchisees routinely reported how their business had impacted their personal health. Nearly a third of all par - ticipants in the successful franchisee cohort reported being able to reduce their hours subsequent to successfully building their franchise businesses. With regard to the independent business cohort, successful owners followed a similar pattern to successful franchisees. Typically, most successful owners would spend considerable time in building their businesses in the first three to five years, after which, many would pull- back from day-to-day operations to accommodate family demands. Though this tendency had been reversed for many on account of the GFC, most managed to gradually improve their lifestyle as SH, a suc - cessful owner of a manufacturing company, who had been in the busi - ness for two years shared: “ Work-life balance? This is where I am getting to now, more of a balance. My kids and family are camping this week, so I went there yesterday to help them set up a tent, but I still had to tell them that I am racing back to a meeting in Sunbury. ” (SH, IS, Manufacturing) Conversely, both unsuccessful franchisees and independent business owners reported working long hours and being extremely stressed, often resulting in mental health problems and breakdowns in personal and business relationships. Some regretted their decision to enter the current business: “ I ’ m great with people, but I just couldn ’ t make it work. And you know, since I ’ ve lost the business, I ’ m seeing a Psychologist. I ’ ve suf - fered agoraphobia, anxiety attacks and depression ... I don ’ t really un - derstand this as I have always been such a strong person. ” (SS, FeU, Food and beverage) “ I ’ ve worked for six years for ... nothing as far as I can tell. Not to mention the pressure it has put on us at home ... it ferments ... if I hadn ’ t been fortunate enough to meet my wife, you know, 33 years on, I don ’ t think anyone else would have put up with this. ” (NN, IU, Food and beverage) Moreover, a majority of unsuccessful franchisees and independent business owners tended to sacrifice their personal life by working longer hours as a way to respond to the worsening market conditions instead of making changes. In many cases, the increased commitment of time at work resulted in high levels of psychological distress ( Cegarra-Leiva, S ánchez-Vidal, & Cegarra-Navarro, 2012 ) and was often proven to be an ineffective business strategy. For instance, one interview participant revealed: “ We don ’ t make any changes to our strategy. To be honest, we can ’ t influence people visiting our area. I just have to work longer hours to keep the doors open. ” (JS, IU, Awnings, blinds, shades). 4.4. Dynamic capabilities during an economic recession Three main dimensions emerged from the interview data in relation S. Weaven et al. Journal of Business Research 128 (2021) 109–123 117 to dynamic capabilities relevant to surviving an economic downturn. They are sensing, responding (seizing) and reconfiguring. 4.4.1. Sensing Sensing refers to how businesses are able to use their resources to better understand the market, realize opportunities and detect threats, especially through obtaining information ( Osiyevskyy et al., 2020 ). There are three sub-themes under sensing, namely business assessment, and information acquisition and market monitoring. 4.4.1.1. Business assessment. Business assessment refers to obtaining information related to business potential and opportunities. In terms of the ostensive routine aspect of this dynamic capability, all business ex - perts indicated that successful business entrants often formalized a process to gather extensive and specialized advice at the pre-entry stages of the business evaluation process. In assessing reported differences between different cohorts, it was apparent that successful franchisees and independent business owners follow a systematic approach to assessing the business opportunity which was not evident in the ap - proaches taken by the unsuccessful SME cohorts. For example, the business appraisal procedures include the identification of the relevant external parties such as lawyers, accountants, and business advisors, and the systematic documentation of any information pertaining to the po - tential business (i.e. reports). This was a key element as to how suc - cessful business operators appraised the information in the pre-entry stages of business ownership. Business experts also observed that many unsuccessful small busi - nesses used subjective reasoning without following an adequate due diligence process. One business expert, a shopping center manager, self- reported: “ Like I say, due diligence is a nice thing, but does it always happen? I would argue that it probably doesn ’ t. It ’ s just staggering how many people will outlay a heap of money, but don ’ t do their due diligence ...” (TB, BFE) Ostensive aspects also manifested through the process of establishing standardized and structured contracts. For independent business owners, their business arrangement promoted their independence from other firms in the supply chain, which has been reported in prior SME research (e.g. Perrigot et al., 2015 ). Regarding franchisees, this requires the specification and assessment of the terms and conditions of their business contract with the franchisor, taking into consideration current and anticipated market conditions based on available information. The degree of understanding the nature of relevant business contracts was identified as the core to SME survival. Most business experts agreed that prospective business owners were often unable to fully comprehend all aspects of business contracts and suggested that franchisee contracts were more structured and had greater levels of transparency. In comparison, all of the unsuccessful franchisees commented that they did not have a process of contractual stipulations in place. Many commented that the franchisee agreement did not provide a true rep - resentation of what was expected and involved in operating their fran - chise, for example, TB who withdrew from a three year old franchise admitted that he made a mistake due to being distracted by superficial motivations: “ There was a great PowerPoint presentation that [franchisor brand name] presented to me on a number of occasions. It says the best and lowest possible price for franchisees. I thought that the agreement re - flected this. I focused too much on how it was a lifestyle choice. None of us has a lifestyle, we are not getting the lowest price, it seems like a bunch of lies. ” (TB, FeU, Food and beverage) In terms of the performative aspect, assessing a business also takes place through attending formal meetings as well as impromptu discus - sion with other business owners, which does not follow formal rules or meeting protocols. In this case, information about business opportu - nities is transferred between individual business owners. This was observed in all of the interviewee cohorts, although the amount of effort exerted in the process and level of information access were different amongst unsuccessful and successful groups. Pre-purchase assessments of independent businesses were often limited to the information ob - tained in one-to-one interactions with vendors, providing the potential for withholding full information and this pre-purchase deficit of infor - mation continued to affect the SMEs well beyond the purchasing deci - sion. A majority of the cohort BFE suggested that the quality of information available to prospective franchisees was superior to that available to independent SMEs. Successful franchisees also considered that they had access to more quality information than did franchisees within the unsuccessful cohort. For example, BR, a franchisee in a food and beverage franchise mentioned that apart from organizing formal meetings, he also engaged in an informal conversation with other cur - rent franchisees. “ [I went and saw] two formally and a couple of others we just chatted to as we were buying a coffee in store ” (BR, FeS, Food and beverage). Another successful franchisee commented: “ I had a look at [franchise brand name] for a couple of years. I consulted with lawyers and accountants but thought that they were a little blas é about it all. So I went and talked to some other franchisees in the system. Got all the information and went ahead. ” (PH, FeS, Food and beverage) Successful franchisees took considerable time and assumed personal responsibility for assessing the likely viability of the franchise during and after the business evaluation stages through both formal and informal channels. This helped them to better realize the opportunities and threats in the market in a timely manner. In comparison, unsuc - cessful franchisees appeared to focus on the projected turnover of the franchise unit. Several suggested that they should have investigated the intricacies of the franchise system further prior to signing the franchise agreement. For example, “ It comes to a point where it is a leap of faith in any business. You can ’ t guarantee that a successful business is going to be successful tomorrow. But I should have spent more time understanding all that ’ s involved. ” (GP, FeU, Weight loss and health care) Unsuccessful independent business owners who were interviewed had also exerted less effort in evaluating their business opportunity, and a majority of this cohort recounted difficulties in conducting an adequate investigation, “ I just couldn ’ t get accurate figures from the pre - vious owners ” (JS, IU, Awnings, blinds, shades). Lack of information as well as an inability to manage capital had resulted in JS ’ s ineffective long hours of working and eventually business failure. Sufficient levels of due diligence in the pre-purchase phase for all SMEs are seen to be critical to long-term survival, including responding to changes in a turbulent market during a GFC. However, the quality of due diligence completed is primarily a function of the effort that the SME entrant is willing to exert. 4.4.1.2. Ongoing information acquisition and market monitoring. The acquisition of knowledge, as well as market watch, can be completed through the business network. The relationship with strategic business partners emerged as a salient factor in SME survival. Therefore, the ostensive routine aspect is reflected in the business relationship man - agement rules and systems such as prescribed participation at profes - sional conferences and workshops, and formal involvement in industry bodies where information or opportunities on how to improve opera - tional management capabilities can be identified. These organizational policies not only developed networking opportunities, but also facili - tated the generation of insights about new market trends for successful SMEs. In comparison to the franchisees, only performative aspects were evident among successful independent business owners who would often obtain information from informal (and recurring) participation in industry events and through personal networks such as at social gatherings. On the other hand, successful franchisees took advantage of the S. Weaven et al. Journal of Business Research 128 (2021) 109–123 118 relationship with their franchisors through formal engagement with assistance packages which were designed for struggling franchisees and developed and utilized in-house educational programs. BR, who deployed this capability enjoyed the resultant benefits of being able to access topical, up-to-date information: “We participated in all supporting programs and workshops orga - nized by the franchisors as well as National Franchise Convention by Franchise Council of Australia. We regularly went to meetings, training, conferences and similar stuff to keep up to date with what’s happening and how things are moving.” (BR, FeS, Food and beverage) The performative aspect of this sensing routine takes the form of the frequency and communications styles that individual franchisees use with their franchisor and other franchisees. Within the franchising context, wherein the relationship between a franchisor and a franchisee is, to a degree, interdependent, how franchisors and franchisees managed the business relationship either promoted or inhibited mutual feelings of trust, respect, and commitment which (in turn) affected the flow of information. JH, a successful franchisee, shared: “You’ve got to have an open relationship with the franchisor. I would speak to [the franchisor’s representative] probably three or four times a week, and it’s just to touch base, it might be a question I’m asking business-wise, or job wise, or I just ring to touch base, and there are guys out there that don’t talk to him. You’ve got to do that.” (JH, FeS, Automobile services) Moreover, in an economic downturn, some franchisees may deplete their resources or find that resources are no longer relevant as market conditions change (Battisti & Deakins, 2017). Successful franchisees were able to use their networks, in particular, the franchisor and other franchisees, to help them access information (Ambrosini, Bowman, & Collier, 2009). This is summarised by an observation from one of the business experts: “A lot comes down to how well franchisees communicate with each other as they are really good innovators in what works and what will increase sales. They can also then see what the franchisor is doing for other franchisees and ask for the same things for themselves. And sharing experiences and getting more knowledge of the market as well as ways to do business effectively.” (AH, BFE) In contrast, this capability was not clearly observed among inde - pendent business owners as they were unable to extract consistent value from their exchange partners. For example, ‘We should have developed our relationships more, maybe then we could have ‘locked-in’ to some of the resellers.’ (PH, IU, Food and beverage) A majority of unsuccessful inde - pendent business owners perceived that their relationships with contractual partners, such as suppliers, were unsupportive. Both cohorts of independent business owners did not view their business relationships with contractual partnerships as being a major determinant of survival. Customers represent another prominent source of information for business owners, demonstrating the performative routine aspect for both franchisees and independent business owners. One of the successful business owners in the beauty industry, PD, shared that her market in - sights were gathered from her clients who were from various business areas. She was able to access information from the customers’ point of view and from different industries, which enabled her to develop a more holistic view of current market conditions and changes. “A lot of my clients have many different businesses, and this is great because they keep feeding you so much information.” (PD, IS, Hair and Beauty) 4.4.2. Seizing Seizing refers to SMEs’ capability of deploying resources to create effective responses to turbulent market conditions which represent threats as well as emerging opportunities (Teece, 2012). When it comes to making a decision to take advantage of an opportunity to change operational capabilities or resources, the process of ‘seizing’ occurs. It comprises product portfolio decisions and investments in technological and human resources. 4.4.2.1. Product portfolio and market decisions. Product portfolio de - cisions are an independent business-specific factor as franchisees are often dependent on franchisors for product portfolios and target market strategies. On account of the small size of the management of small businesses, the portfolio management and market decisions were solely made by business owners without any standardized rules or systems, demonstrating the performative aspects. Their decisions were based on the knowledge and information obtained from sensing. Some indepen - dent SMEs in this research were able to survive and thrive in the recession by entering a niche industry or market segment of an industry such as tree surgery, organic grain grocery and the manufacture of a unique food product. Niche industries may be less susceptible to economic volatility and still enjoy growth despite economic turbulence. Independent SMEs are more suited to niche industries than franchises as these markets are difficult to replicate on a large scale (Laskovaia et al., 2018). In our sample, there were no franchise systems operating in these particular industries. These businesses indicated they had not been affected much by the economic downturn. The tree surgeon had plans to expand, and the other two operators were satisfied with their current growth out - comes. SH, the food product manufacturer, took advantage of infor - mation obtained from various sources such as his clients, to manage his product portfolios and identify his optimal target markets. He was in the enviable position of being able to ‘knock back clients’. For instance, he commented: “I’m not feeling any downturn ... all I’m feeling is our business has been established, and we’re on a growth pattern. We don’t feel the knocks and bumps that others would.” (SH, IS, Manufacturing) 4.4.2.2. Investing in new technologies and human resources. Evidence of the ostensive aspects was found among successful independent business owners who determined to invest heavily in the particular technologies when the opportunity arose, even though getting ahead required sig - nificant up-front investment. SH, the independent manufacturer, “sensed” a market opportunity to supply a new formula to a new market based on a thorough business assessment, constant streams of informa - tion and market monitoring. Accordingly, SH decided to “seize” this business opportunity. It was a structured decision-making approach with clear protocols requiring formal reports and written justifications from his production manager and consultants. The performative aspect is reflected in how the business owner made the decision to invest, which was predominantly based on his intuition and industry experience. “I bought all the new machinery and equipment, I bought every - thing. There is a machine that I’m busting to get now, I paid a $50,000 deposit, and I owe another $240,000, and I said “Keep it, and I’ll keep on paying it off. [How long did you spend doing research and thinking about it before you started setting it up?] Oh, about ten minutes, once I decided to do it I just did it.” (SH, IS, Manufacturing) The performative aspect is also evident in the successful franchisee cohort. This is demonstrated in the case of BR, a food and beverage retailer, who invested in communications technologies including social media and digital platforms, which were relatively new at the time. Throughout this process, there were tried and tested informal steps which were gradually modified and adapted to match changes in market conditions and promote connections with their customers. “Oh yeah, well, of course, the use of social media is quite a thing... so we are embracing Facebook, Twitter, and then we get this classic thing, small businesses need to become better with social media. I mean I’m on Facebook, and we innovated that quite a lot, with one of my staff, she’s very good at it. On Facebook, the shop has its own persona, it’s actually a person.” (BR, FeS, Food and beverage) Furthermore, successful SMEs reported that an emphasis on the customer was a focal part of their business strategy and as such, appropriate staff recruitment, training and performance systems were integral elements of their approaches towards innovation. These were S. Weaven et al. Journal of Business Research 128 (2021) 109–123 119 often implemented informally on an ongoing basis, reflecting the routinized performative aspect. DH, a successful franchisee who assumed ownership of (and revived) a struggling franchised store confirmed that staff training was key in winning-back customers. This was the result of her ability to “ sense ” the market, recognizing current and emergent challenges and opportunities under adverse conditions. She started training her staff in the very early days of the business and even provided constant support for their formal qualifications in retailing and hospitality. “ Certainly there is a feeling out there that we really need to do more to attract customers into our business. I could see with a business like this you need to be very wise with your staff and if you can avail yourself of things like traineeships and skill-based traineeships. You have to be there with them. You can ’ t just train them for two months and leave them to it. So I also developed and implemented a reward system for my staff performance ” . (DH, FeS, Food and beverage) Both unsuccessful franchisees and independent business owners did not demonstrate this capability. These business owners were struggling financially and could not see value in spending extra money on in - vestments, especially when they were unable to predict future revenue streams. 4.4.3. Reconfiguring Reconfiguring indicates firms ’ capability to continuously re- configure resources and organizational structures as the enterprise grows, and as markets and technologies change ( Biesenthal et al., 2018 ). The interviews revealed three main themes in this category, namely innovation, decentralization and knowledge management. 4.4.3.1. Innovation. The role of innovation in business development emerged as central to SME survival, particularly in periods of economic uncertainty which is consistent with previous research ( Zouaghi, S ánchez, & Martínez, 2018; Martinez et al., 2018 ). The franchisees ’ innovation capability involves formal documentation and process on new product development, reflecting an ostensive routine aspect. This is on account of the restrictions in the franchise agreement and strict reporting procedures that franchisees are required to adhere to ( Quach et al., 2019 ). Although being innovative and successful with many ex - periments in his stores, BR revealed: “ For us, we have to report all our experimentation, all innovation to the franchisor. ” (BR, FeS, Food and beverage). In relation to independent SMEs, the ostensive routine aspects manifested via the process of ‘benchmarking ’ their performance within the industry, national and international contexts. This was done peri - odically and more often during the economic downturn. In addition, the product development process followed by the most successful inde - pendent businesses often involved a systematic approach from idea generation to market testing, documentation of effects and product adaptation. Many of the successful SMEs reported conducting surveys or informal discussions with their customers to test the market and modify their offerings, demonstrating the performative routine aspect. However, it was observed that the capabilities to adapt quickly to changes appeared to be more easily achieved by independent SMEs than fran - chisees. Nimble responses to economic conditions proved crucial for some SMEs. Whereas franchisees were bound by the system and the franchisor ’ s strategies, independent SMEs were free to make key in - novations within relatively short time-frames. One franchisee likened a franchise to a ‘ship that turns slowly ’ (GF, FeS), which contrasts to inde - pendent SMEs that are generally small and involve only one or two owners, affording greater opportunity to be agile, and quickly adapt to exploit opportunities in the prevailing market conditions. Moreover, independent SMEs enjoy a higher degree of decision- making control over most aspects of their business ( Quach et al., 2019 ). The performative routine aspect is reflected in the management ’ s decision to try new (or alternative) ideas and demonstrate more market- oriented capabilities such as expanding an existing product line, tailoring product offerings and changing promotional mixes to appeal to a new target segment(s) or to create trends in the market. This ability to adapt and innovate is less accessible in franchise operations. For instance, the owners of an independent restaurant responded to wors - ening economic conditions by experimenting with a variety of approaches. “ We have what we call our lunchtime special - it is only $7.95 with some cost-effective specially designed options. No one ever did that in our area. It is quite a good meal, so to attract people on fixed incomes who are suffering from the GFC and all that would come for the $7.95 meal, and it works. You ’ ve just got to try anything and everything ... . ...” (DS, IS, Grocery) On the other hand, the performative aspects of innovation are also reflected in the ability of franchisees to maintain a balance between innovation and compliance in the franchise system. Business experts suggested that franchisees played a significant role in innovation in franchising systems, however, it was also reliant upon how franchisors fostered innovation, “ In systems where the franchisor has a bunker men - tality, and the franchisee doesn ’ t like we are seeing huge compliance issues. Franchisees are doing what they believe is right. If there is no leadership, they are forced to do something themselves ... be innovative in their role. ” (TB, FBE). As a franchisor, GF observed: “ I think a good franchisee, has to know how to listen and take di - rection. Follow the plan, as in the franchise model to a T, on some good points and some not so good points and also be open to change, and just understand that the franchisor has been there and done that, that is why they built the system. ” (GF, Fo) In contrast, unsuccessful franchisees mentioned little in relation to their role in the business innovation process. Some suggested that this the franchisor ’ s responsibility, while others believed that the nature of the franchise agreement curtailed any potential for them to engage in innovative behaviors. Furthermore, although both independent business owner cohorts were observed as adopting some proactive and innovative behaviors in managing their businesses, successful independent business owners were often more willing to try novel approaches to capture new customers and retain existing clients. A majority of unsuccessful inde - pendent business owners tended to focus on the detrimental impact of external conditions on their business operations and appeared to perceive their business in a negative light. Individuals in this cohort reported that many innovations did not result in expected outcomes and considered that success or failure in business was largely due to eco - nomic conditions, rising competition, inhibitive regulation and inherent problems with their business model. For instance, one participant commented: “ Changed marketing, created a brand, changed the name of the shop to [independent business brand] and remade website and events. It ’ s a ‘big ship ’ with a small rudder. Everything takes too long. ” (KH, IU, Food and beverage) 4.4.3.2. Decentralization. The interview results show that in an eco - nomic downturn, power was partially delegated to local managers. This was evident in some businesses in the successful cohort but was not observed in the unsuccessful SMEs group. In relation to successful in - dependent SMEs, ostensive aspects manifested in formal instructions from the owners to grant their senior managers additional flexibility to operate the stores. Noticing the importance of customer orientation and rapid market changes, especially in the niche industry, SH had imple - mented a decentralized management structure in his business but ensured that performance was then updated via informal discussion or meetings and assessed by the business owner: “ We have a staff meeting, and I don ’ t normally go because I find it inhibits people but I just pop in once a month and then I might have one on ones with the senior managers but they have to talk about all these things together and learn to debate these things, and if they ’ ve got problems then they come to me after it. Then I will say if it is a yes or no S. Weaven et al. Journal of Business Research 128 (2021) 109–123 120 to proceed with changes and then every stage we reflect on everything and move on to the next step.” (SH, IS, Manufacturing) Franchisees also permitted their store managers to make some in - dependent decisions such as increasing local marketing promotions by being more involved in the community and managing customer re - lationships. Such approaches are indicative of the performative aspect of the reconfiguration routine. DH, a franchisee who invested heavily in her staff training and development realized this way of structuring enhanced flexibility and responsibility and helped the business adapt to the local context: “Those staffs have been with me for two or two and a half years, so they really know the business and the local customers. They have become like team leaders for me .... because they are fabulous staff and I just leave them to run the business.” (DH, FeS, Food and beverage) 4.4.3.3. Knowledge management. Knowledge transfer is another impor - tant capability for multi-unit franchise owners and independent business owners who operate multiple stores. Information and know-how were formally documented and shared internally amongst staff and between different units, indicating ostensive aspects. Combining this knowledge with local learning, each unit can be regarded as a center of excellence as it maintains a closer presence with local consumers and markets. This is reflected in the following excerpt by BR, a successful franchisee who operated two food and beverage franchise units in two locations. This provided him with the advantages of being able to replicate successful practices and transfer knowledge such as innovation and know-how across these stores, while acknowledging the differences between them. “We have two shops in two locations. One is quite successful, and we learned how to create a sense of community from it by training the staff etcetera. We then need to transfer what we know to the second store. The crew in another store needed to realize the benefits of why we do things the way we do. I have always had this view that if you just say to someone you must comply it won’t work, but if you have a clear document and reporting system explaining the why and the how not just the what, but actually give them the context to it, they usually can see it and say ok, now I understand why I have to wash my hands before I touch the food. You know this is just an example. But you make me wash my hands ten times a day, but there is a reason for doing that. Things like we rotate the food the way we do, why it is important to understand what’s on a plate and how long it has been there and when it’s used by date is.” (BR, FeS, Food and beverage) In addition, many successful franchises and independent business owners also collaborated with universities/research institutes in the region whereas unsuccessful cohorts were unable or unwilling to reach out to these parties. The connections were often formed through in - dustry organizations such as the Franchise Council of Australia or the Council for Small Business Organizations of Australia or through informal networks, reflecting the performative aspects. Therefore, knowledge not only flows internally but also externally. SM, childcare business owners, worked with a university partner in developing a new education methodology which not only benefits the business but also has wider implications on industry practice. “We have industry partners and also a collaboration with researchers sometimes in formal projects and sometimes just informal relationships. But it is good because we get the academic side of things and they get our practice side of what we are doing. It is a win–win situation. We make some innovative changes and also discuss the bigger economic pictures and see what is coming so overall it is very useful.” (SM, IS, Childcare) 5. Discussion and implications This research seeks to address a gap in the entrepreneurship litera - ture by investigating SME survival mechanisms in turbulent market environments. Although the dynamic capabilities literature has pro - gressed in recent years, especially on account of a series of studies conducted by Teece and colleagues (1994, 1997, 2012), there remains a paucity of research examining both franchisees and independent busi - nesses in this context. This study utilized a qualitative approach to examine the dynamic capabilities of both franchised and independent SMEs in an economic downturn. Our findings have significant implica - tions for SME stakeholders within the GFC or other forthcoming periods of localized, national or global economic downturn. Economic growth has been observed to be cyclical, and it is therefore critically important to examine periods of the economic downturn in the certain knowledge that they will return, whether on an industry, local, regional, national or global scale. Based on the findings of the current research, we developed a framework of SMEs’ success in an economic downturn through the lens of dynamic capabilities (Fig. 1). This enables an SME to analyze its dy - namic capabilities in a turbulent environment and provide valuable input for policymakers to encourage policy development recognizing the degree to which the related factors optimize small business perfor - mance, survival, and success. Furthermore, and apart from identifying general factors of success, the framework also reveals specific capabil - ities together with their ostensive and performative aspects for fran - chisees and independent business owners, indicating a different set of strategic activities applicable for different types of SMEs. The dynamic capabilities contributing to SME survival in an economic downturn are all associated with actions that can increase, or decrease, the chances of survival. Furthermore, franchisor support, franchisor-franchisee re - lationships and positive knowledge-sharing and integration are three refined factors bearing testament to the core reasons for choosing the franchise SME model. On the other hand, independent SMEs can maxi - mize the advantages of innovation, adaptability, and exploitation of niche markets. 5.1. Business owner characteristics Our research found that business characteristics, namely business experience, motivation and attitude, affect the development of firms’ capabilities, highlighting the important role that managers hold in the deployment of resources and how perceptions of environmental vola - tility impact their judgment (Battisti & Deakins, 2017). This supports previous research which argues that dynamic capabilities lie within the firm’s core management (Ambrosini et al., 2009; Helfat & Martin, 2015; Helfat and Peteraf, 2015; Teece, 2007). Hence, similar firms might be able to deploy different dynamic capabilities because of differences in how managers perceived environmental uncertainties (Aragon-Correa and Sharma, 2003). In the context of small firms, this demonstrates the importance of business owner characteristics in the recognition and exploitation of opportunities in an economic crisis (Battisti & Deakins, 2017). The need to adopt a positive and proactive stance to SME man - agement in times of economic downturn is predicated on the findings of this research. This can be achieved, irrespective of the personalities of the owner or owners of the SME, by actively maintaining positive atti - tudes and motivations through interactions and networking with opti - mistic individuals and groups within the franchise, industry or locality where the SME is located. Individuals and organizations that promote such positive and proactive management behavior are ubiquitous. This also reduces the cognitive limitations and framing biases which hinder innovation capabilities (Teece, 2007) and counteracts a tendency to adopt the “bunker mentality” observed in some of the SMEs who did not survive or were struggling to sustain business operations. 5.2. Operating resources While responding to the volatile environment, SMEs should be capable of obtaining and allocating financial resources and their time. This is supported by Smallbone et al. (2012) who indicates that the method of financing can have an impact on business responses to the recession. Successful franchisees maintained their ability to finance S. Weaven et al. Journal of Business Research 128 (2021) 109–123 121 through formal processes for monitoring, reporting and documenting their capital movement. This is a distinct difference between franchisees and independent business owners as the latter were more likely to reduce dependence on external finance and rely more on personal loans. However, successful independent business owners were able to allocate their capital more effectively thanks to their flexibility in operations (Reid, 2007), and not being bound by any rules and obligations when compared to franchisees. In order to be able to maintain capital flow, the majority of the small business owners had to sacrifice their work-life balance and spend extra time on their business. However, this was done deliberately by the successful business owners with a clear vision of when they should restore their work-life balance. In contrast, unsuccessful cohorts suffered from the long-term consequences of adaptation strategies that involve substituting labor (personal and family) for capital. This is referred to as personal conflict which is defined as the interference of work and family roles that become a significant source of psychological distress for the individual (Cegarra-Leiva et al., 2012). This, in turn, leads to their inability to formulate an effective response to the critical conditions of a financial crisis. 5.3. Dynamic capabilities The dynamic capabilities important to SMEs’ survival during an economic crisis were discussed according to Teece (2012) three cate - gories: sensing, seizing and reconfiguring. This study also set out to explain how ostensive and performative aspects of dynamic capabilities work, following Biesenthal et al. (2018). With this consideration, we find that dynamic capabilities and their ostensive and performative routine aspects differ between unsuccessful and successful cohorts and between independent business owners and franchisees. Firstly, it is important for SMEs to be able to sense market conditions through business assessment and ongoing information acquisition and market monitoring in order to respond to threats, seize opportunities and reconfigure in response to turbulent changes (Cao, 2011). Although all of the franchisees and independent business owners engaged in formal meetings and ad hoc discussions with other business owners, only the successful cohorts formalized business appraisal processes and developed standardized and structured contracts. This helped them develop a systematic understanding of the economic conditions and provided them with the ability to constantly monitor changes in the market, enabling the next step which is to seize opportunities. Second, responding to the volatile environment means SMEs should be capable of addressing threats and seizing new opportunities. Although economic crises present major threats to firm survival and performance, they also come with potential opportunities (Bao et al., 2011). Should small firms be able to capitalize on new and emerging opportunities, they will be able to drive growth (Baker & Sinkula, 2009). Although all informants in this study did not report a formal process in place to manage product portfolios and target markets, the performative aspect was evident among successful independent business owners. While a franchisee is more dependent on the franchisor and is subject to contractual stipulations, the independent SME has the capacity to leverage the flexibility of their business model and pro-actively and positively combine available resources to determine their product portfolio and enter niche markets in response to unpredictable envi - ronmental changes (Laskovaia et al., 2018). Furthermore, exploring opportunities in an economic crisis requires investment in new technologies and human resources, which was practiced by successful cohorts. This enabled them to more effectively address changing customer preferences and market conditions. In contrast, the unsuccessful cohorts were unwilling to spend money on investment due to perceived risks attached to a prolonged recession and a lack of internal financial resources during the economic crisis (Mar - tinez et al., 2018). The last category of dynamic capabilities is reconfiguring. This includes innovation, decentralization and knowledge management. These themes are in-line with Teece (2018) and Cao (2011). Previous research demonstrates that firms are able to cope better during recession periods by performing research and development activities (Zouaghi et al., 2018; Martinez et al., 2018). Although both successful franchisees and independent business owners engaged in innovation using both formal and informal procedures, independent businesses conducted benchmarking as part of their routine whilst franchisees focused more on balancing between innovation and compliance with the legal terms and conditions specified in the contract with their franchisor. Moreover, while decentralization was executed by the successful cohorts, the opposite was observed in the unsuccessful businesses. This may be because unsuccessful business owners often try to minimize labor during the economic downturn by replacing senior staff with ju - nior staff and as such, have to operate the business by themselves. This is evident in their experience in working long hours and sacrificing any balance between work and life, as detailed in the previous section. Finally, ostensive routine aspects related to knowledge management were only evident among successful franchisees and independent busi - ness owners who operated multiple business units. Utilizing formal documentation of knowledge, they were able to transfer knowledge between different units. Performative routine aspects were observed in both successful cohorts through their participation in business networking at an industry, local and national level. Notably, unsuc - cessful cohorts found difficulty in connecting with external partners. In general, flexible performative routine deployment of dynamic capabilities enables speedy decision-making and responses while the ostensive aspects enhance formality and standardization in some dy - namic capabilities (Biesenthal et al., 2018). Though ostensive and performative routine aspects were evident in each category of dynamic capabilities, the findings demonstrate that the performative evidence was more pronounced. This can be explained by the fact that SMEs often has a simple organizational structure with few internal borders, increasing flexibility, direct ownership involvement and low formal - ization (Borch & Madsen, 2007). In short, dynamic capabilities among SMEs are context-specific and often follow flexible courses of action and behaviors. However, the use of ostensive routine aspects could be beneficial as small firms could embed standardized rules and systems in their operations for the consistent deployment of dynamic capabilities. This would be particularly useful when the business owners operate a number of different units. Moreover, it is also recommended that firms increase their investment in technologies and human resources to overcome the challenges of operating in a slowing economy (Archibugi, Filippetti, & Frenz, 2013). 6. Conclusion, limitations and future research directions In conclusion, both independent SMEs and franchises need to be able to develop and deploy specific dynamic capabilities when confronted by an economic crisis. By including ostensive and performative aspects into the discussion of dynamic capabilities, this study was able to advance a more comprehensive knowledge of the purpose for the deployment of dynamic capabilities and the context in which they are deployed. The proposed framework can also be used by SMEs to devise strategies to survive and thrive in turbulent market conditions. In conducting exploratory research using qualitative methods of in - quiry, rich data was accessed, but the ability to generalize from the findings beyond the participants to the wider small business community might be constrained by the limited size and representativeness of the sample. The framework developed in this study would benefit from further academic scrutiny and studies involving a quantitative research design. Such a quantitative approach could validate the findings and increase the practical utility of this research. Furthermore, our investi - gation focuses on the survival mechanisms of SMEs following an eco - nomic crisis. However, the implications of these mechanisms might vary over the longer-term. Thus, more longitudinal studies of the same S. Weaven et al. Journal of Business Research 128 (2021) 109–123 122 phenomenon could prove beneficial. Moreover, the nature of a crisis can determine a firm ’ s response strategy. For example, the COVID-19 pandemic is a complex blend of a health disaster, socio-political crisis, and an economic crisis. Future research can compare the different im - pacts and examine strategies based on crisis and disaster typologies. Finally, as culture plays an important role in business, future research could be undertaken in other turbulent markets in different countries heavily affected by economic downturns. Dynamic capabilities reconfigure existing asset positions and create organizational renewal. We contend that higher performance outcomes can be achieved when dynamic capabilities interact with operational-level changes (i.e., changes in management and practices or changes in used technologies and target markets). The present study explores different pathways of dynamic capabilities and operational-level changes for performance success in a media industry context (i.e., magazines). Due to the digitalization of its business, the media industry has undergone significant changes the past years. We use a set-theoretic approach with fsQCA and data from 78 magazines to test our conceptualization. Ourfindings contribute to the literature of dynamic capabilities by providing empirical evidence on the relationship between dynamic capabilities, operational changes, and performance. 1. Introduction Companies operating in dynamic business environments are constantly challenged to adapt to changing conditions. Technological advancements, regulatory changes, shifts in customer needs/preferences, and competitive moves shape the business landscape and challenge the competitive status quo of modern firms. Under such circumstances, firms seek a balance between continuity and efficiency— to ensure sustained profitability— and exploration and adaptation— to achieve new competitive positions (Maijanen & Virta, 2017; O'Reilly III & Tushman, 2013). To meet this dual challenge,firms need to purposefully create, extend, and/or modify their existing resources and competences (Capron & Hulland, 1999). 1 Drawing on the resource-based view and the dynamic capabilities approach, a firm's dynamic capabilities (i.e., sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring) are central in its efforts to address changing business conditions (Teece, 2007). These capabilities are considered dynamic when they enable afirm to formulate and realize new strategies to reflect changing market conditions by modifying its resource base and/or combining and transforming available resources in new and different ways (Morgan, 2012). Recent studies,(e.g., Fainshmidt, Pezeshkan, Frazier, Nair, & Markowski, 2016), stress that dynamic capabilities alone are not sufficient predictors of success in increasingly changing environments. Other scholars (e.g.,Karna, Richter, & Riesenkampff, 2016) argue that dynamic capabilities should align with operational-level changes, such as changes in managerial practices, technologies used, and targeted markets, to achieve success. Nevertheless, there is little empirical evidence showing how dynamic capabilities and operational changes align for greater levels of organizational performance. Furthermore, scholars such as Jantunen, Ellonen, and Johansson (2012), contend that the contribution of dynamic capabilities on performance outcomes may bemultiply realizable. No one-size-fits-all approach exists for all firms and business conditions; on the contrary, there are several ways to operate efficiently and multiple ways dynamic capabilities can lead to enhanced performance in an operating business environment. Therefore, a morefine-grained analysis is needed to uncover the performance consequences of different combinations of dynamic capabilities. Our study attempts to explore the notion of multiple realizability and provide evidence of how dynamic capabilities and operational changes align for success. Theoretical background In this section of the manuscript wefirst present the concept of dynamic capabilities, and then discuss how it is associated with operational-level changes and performance outcomes. 2.1. Dynamic capabilities Drawing on the dynamic capability view of the firm, dynamic capabilities refer to the firm's capacity to “integrate, build and reconfigure internal and external competences to address rapidly changing environments” (Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997: 516). Dynamic capabilities are considered higher-level capabilities that: (a) enable organizational learning; (b) create new combinations of assets; and (3) renew operational (or ordinary) capabilities (Helfat & Winter, 2011; Winter, 2003). 2 This theoretical paradigm puts forward three dimensions of dynamic capabilities:sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring (Teece et al., 1997). All three facets of dynamic capabilities are essential to the organizational adaptation process; however, the domain and role of each facet differs substantially. Sensing capabilities represent thefirm's activities and processes for scanning the external environment, interpreting information, and searching and identifying market opportunities.Seizing capabilities relate to afirm's attempts to capture value from market opportunities and make decisions on strategic investments and business models and how to manage value chains and ecosystems (Teece, 2007). Reconfiguring capabilities represent a firm's ability to orchestrate its asset base, transform resources and processes to new valuable combinations, and build new capabilities through learning ( Jantunen, Puumalainen, Saarenketo, & Kyläheiko, 2005). Collectively, these three dimensions establish the ability of an organization to achieve strategic change and renewal in dynamic operating environments. 2.2. Dynamic capabilities and performance The dynamic capability view of thefirm consists of one of the most central and influential theoretical paradigms in strategic management research (Teece, 2007). Despite its significant growth, systematic reviews and meta-analysis studies (see Di Stefano, Peteraf, & Verona, 2010; Eriksson, 2014; Peteraf, Di Stefano, & Verona, 2013; Vogel & Güttel, 2013) highlight that this research stream lacks conceptual consensus and robust empirical evidence that accurately validate its theoretical propositions. The key tenet of the dynamic capability view is that dynamic capabilities are positively associated with afirm's competitive advantage and performance success (Barreto, 2010). However, this association is complex. Even though current empirical studies (e.g.,Fainshmidt et al., 2016; Pezeshkan, Fainshmidt, Nair, Frazier, & Markowski, 2016 ) highlight the positive association between dynamic capabilities and performance outcomes, it is not clear under which conditions and through which mechanisms these positive effects are realized. Further, it is not clear to what extent these positive effects are mediated by the improvement of lower-level ordinary capabilities and/or operational activities (seeKarna et al., 2016). Furthermore, research (e.g.,Wilhelm, Schlömer, & Maurer, 2015) suggests that despite the positive contribution of dynamic capabilities to organizational adaptability and organizational performance, dynamic capabilities are also associated with highly developing and sustaining costs. Hence, in the context of the relative stability of business environments, the benefits dynamic capabilities offer may be overturned by the costs required to develop and maintain such competences. Recent studies (e.g.,Fainshmidt et al., 2016; Pezeshkan et al., 2016) provide support for the positive association between dynamic capabilities and performance. However,Fainshmidt et al. (2016)argue that the relationship between dynamic capabilities and performance is more nuanced. Specifically, it is highlighted that this association is contingent upon contextual factors. Further, theory (e.g., Girod & Whittington, 2017) debates whether dynamic capabilities are more conducive to competitive advantages and higher performance levels in stable or dynamic operating environments. Some studies, (e.g.,Teece, 2007; Teece et al., 1997), emphasize that dynamic capabilities are needed especially in rapidly changing environments, whereas others argue that this association is not so monotonic. Consequently, a morefine-grained analysis is needed to uncover the performance consequences of dynamic capabilities on performance outcomes. To this extent, the present study adopts a set-theoretic approach with fsQCA to provide further insights into how higher-level dynamic capabilities (i.e., sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring) relate to organizational performance outcomes in highly dynamic and changing operating environments. 3. Data collection and measures This section presents the methodological procedures used for data collection, and the measures applied to capture the study's phenomena. 3.1. Research context The research context of the study is the media industry, which has undergone significant changes (e.g., rapid technological development, changing market needs, and increased competition) due to the digitalization of its business in recent years. The digitalization of multiple media sectors has disrupted traditional business practices and changed customer behaviors (e.g., individualizing media usage) (Casero-Ripollés & Izquierdo-Castillo, 2015 ). Such industry-related challenges have compelled media companies to seek new business models, renew innate capabilities, and adjust operations to meet the challenges of the digital business environment (Maijanen & Virta, 2017). Accordingly, the media sector is an excellent example of an industry that is being subjected to rapidly changing operating conditions. Thus, the present study focuses on the magazine publishing industry. Traditionally, this industry was based on print-related products however, the past years the magazine publishing industry have faced the pressure to renew its resources and capabilities, innovate its products, and build new business (i.e., digital) channels (Ellonen, Wikström, & Johansson, 2015). 3.2. Sampling Data were collected from two Nordic countries, Finland and Sweden. The Finnish sampling frame was drawn from the Finnish Periodical Publishers' Association (FPPA) members listing from 2011. We incorporated only Finnish consumer magazines in the sampling frame; trade and organizational magazines were excluded. When comparing the number of FPPA consumer magazine members to those listed by the Finnish Audit Bureau of Circulation, the population is well presented in the sample: a circulation audit from 2010 included information from 140 magazines. The survey questionnaire, with a cover letter describing the purpose and objective of the research, was emailed to 126 chief editors in early spring 2012. Forty-one responses were received, yielding a response rate of 32.5% (41/126). The Swedish sample (n = 253) was acquired from Jönköping International Business School (Media Management and Transformation Centre). A total of 37 responses was received, yielding a response rate of 14.6%, (37/253). Thus, the combined dataset consists of 78 magazines, of which 41 are from Finland and 37 from Sweden. In the Finnish sample, key informants had an average 23.9 years of experience in the media industry, and 19 in the Swedish sample (seeTable 1). On average, the key informants had been in their current position (i.e., editor-in-chief) for 6.1 and 5 years in the Finnish and Swedish sample, respectively. The average proportion of subscribers per circulation was 82.5 and 59.6 in the Finnish and Swedish samples, respectively. In both samples,‘lifestyle’ is the largest magazine category, followed by ‘living,’ and ‘housing and gardening’ (see Table 2). 3.3. Measures A multi-item measure for three dimensions of dynamic capabilities (i.e., sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring) was developed for the purposes of this study. The measurement items for the sensing dimension incorporate activities for knowledge and resource acquisition (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000; Zahra & George, 2002) and identifying opportunities (Teece, 2007). The measurement items for the seizing dimension comprise activities of patching (Eisenhardt & Brown, 1999; Teece, 2007), investing in research and development (Katkalo, Pitelis, & Teece, 2010), building competencies (Katkalo et al., 2010), and implementing changes (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000). The items for the reconfiguring facet of dynamic capabilities represent activities of knowledge, leadership, and human resource management ( Ellonen, Jantunen, & Kuivalainen, 2011; Jantunen et al., 2012), as well as reallocating resources and assets (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000). Due to the small sample size, the items for the three dimensions of dynamic capabilities were first subjected to principal component analysis with varimax rotation, in order to screen the items with highest internal consistency. The domain-specific measures for operational-level changes and performance were developed based on qualitative interviews conducted in Finland, Russia, the Netherlands, and Hungary as part of a larger industry-related research project (seeLUT, 2013). These measurement items were also subjected to principal component analysis with varimax rotation. As a result, two composite measures for operational-level changes were identified and labeled as: (1) changes in technology and markets; and (2) changes in management and practices. Also, two composite measures for performance outcomes were extracted and identified as: (1) performance in the traditional business model, and (2) performance in the new channels (i.e., contemporary business model). Measure validation In order to validate the measures, we ran an overall measurement model using Maximum Likelihood in LISREL, and used covariance matrix as input data. We assessed all measures through confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Each item was restricted to load on its a priori specified factor, and the underlying factors were permitted to correlate (Anderson & Gerbing, 1988). Analysis This section presents the analytical technique used for testing our theoretical assumptions. We provide an overview of fsQCA, and explicate how it was implemented for the purposes of our study. We then present ourfindings. 4.1. Overview of fsQCA To test our assumptions, we applied a set-theoretic analytical approach with fsQCA. Compared to alternative analytical correlationalbased methods, fsQCA is considered superior since it accounts for: (1) asymmetry, (2) equifinality, and (3) causal complexity (see Chari, Tarkiainen, & Salojärvi, 2016). fsQCA is an analytical tool that uses a holistic perspective to explore similarities and differences across cases (Rihoux & Ragin, 2009). Essentially, fsQCA is an analysis of a set of relationships; it conceptualizes cases as unique combinations of characteristics and draws comparisons between all the predictors (i.e., antecedents) and the outcome of interest ( Haumann, Güntürkün, Schons, & Wieseke, 2015). fsQCA provides combinations of causal conditions and multiple solution pathways that can lead to the same outcome (Schneider, Schulze-Bentrop, & Paunescu, 2010). To interpret cause–effect relationships among predictors and the outcome of interest, fsQCA identifies conditions that are necessary (i.e., produce the outcome but, by themselves, may not be enough) and/or sufficient (i.e., they always lead to the outcome). Depending on the counterfactual analysis of causes, fsQCA distinguishes between core (i.e., essential elements that have a strong causal relationship to the outcome of interest) andperipheral (i.e., expendable or exchangeable elements that have a weaker causal relationship to the outcome of interest) causal conditions (Fiss, 2011). Thus, fsQCA provides novel insights into the ‘predictor-outcome’ association (Fiss, 2011; Skarmeas, Leonidou, & Saridakis, 2014). Table 2 Magazine categories (%). Implementing fsQCA When performing fsQCA, thefirst step is to calibrate all the involved variables into sets; these represent the degree of membership a particular variable takes in a specific category (Woodside & Zhang, 2013). For the purposes of this study, we calibrated all the variables involved into fuzzy sets and used three threshold breakpoints for set calibration: 0.05 for full non-membership, 0.50 as the crossover point of maximum ambiguity, and 0.95 for full membership (Ragin, 2008). Next, we constructed the truth table to identify cause and effect combinations of the predictor variables with the outcome of interest (Crilly, 2011). The truth table consists of 2 k rows; k represents the number of causal conditions used in the analysis. Thus, in our study, the truth table consisted of2 5 possible combinations. Rows on the truth table reflect specific combinations of causes with the outcome; the entire table corresponds to all the possible combinations that may exist (Ragin, 2008). Subsequently we identified relevant cause– effect combinations that are associated with at least one observation between the predictors and the outcome used in our study. The next step involved reducing the number of rows of the truth table. This step was conducted on the basis of: (a) minimum number of cases needed for a solution to be deliberated, and (b) the minimum consistency levels needed ( Ragin, 2000). Consistency and coverage statistics were employed to assess the derived solution pathways.4 4.2.1. Pathways to high performance for the traditional and contemporary business models Table 5 presents the derived complex solutions for high performance for the traditional and contemporary business models. For the traditional model of business ourfindings indicate three pathways for high performance. Thefirst highlights a combination of high sensing, seizing, and changes in management and practices and low degrees of changes in technology and markets. The second combines high levels of sensing, reconfiguring, and changes in management and practices and low degrees of changes in technology and markets. The third pathway reveals high degrees of seizing, reconfiguring, and changes in management and practices and low degrees of changes in technology and markets. Lower changes in technology and markets and higher changes in management and practices are sufficient for higher organizational performance in the traditional model of business; in other words, these conditions of operational-level changes are essential elements that demonstrate a strong cause–effect relationship with performance outcomes. In the traditional business model, however, the three dimensions of dynamic capabilities are necessary but not sufficient on their own. Sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring capabilities are peripheral to organizational performance, as their cause –effect associations with performance are weak. For the contemporary model of business, fsQCA suggests one pathway solution with four necessary conditions for high performance memberships. Specifically, the pathway indicates high levels of sensing, low levels of seizing, high degrees of re-configuring capabilities, high changes in management and practices, and high changes in used technologies and target markets. All solutions collectively and individually exhibit acceptable consistency (i.e.,≥.75) and explain a satisfactory amount of cases (i.e.,≥.25 coverage≤.65) in high-performance outcome. Discussion and conclusions In this paper we have explored how different configurations of dynamic capabilities and operational-level changes are related to performance outcomes in a media-industry context. This study contributes to the literature of dynamic capabilities by empirically assessing possible ways to achieve high degrees of performance. The notion of multiple realizability of dynamic capabilities can be found mainly in conceptual studies; yet empirical evidence on this stream of research is scarce. Hence, our study builds a base for empirically supporting this notion. Our research question is how different combinations of dynamic capabilities and operational changes relate to performance. When exploring performance outcomes, we identified two types of organizational performance: outcomes in the traditional (printed magazine) business and in the new digital channels. We argue that performance outcomes in the printed magazine model relate to short-term adaptation to external environmental changes; whereas performance in the digitalized channels reflects radical renewal. In terms of operationallevel changes, we identify two parameters of change: changes in management and practices and in technology and markets. We argue that changes in management and practices reflect changes that are internal to the organization, whereas changes in technology and markets happen in relation to the external environment of the organization. These three con figurations are characterized by changes in management and practices and by the absence of changes in technology and markets. Thus, in the absence of external environmental changes, internal changes (i.e., in management and practices) are necessary for achieving high performance in the traditional business model. According to Eurofound (2012) and the working conditions survey, compared to other European countries, Finland and Sweden are characterized by a greater amount of organizational change, which means Finnish and Swedish organizations have a strong focus on organizational change. Our findings suggest that such internal changes aim to improve performance outcomes while maintaining the traditional business model. Understandably, the three dimensions of dynamic capabilities appear to be peripheral for success in the traditional model of business. Thisfinding is well in line with the existing body of knowledge, which suggests that dynamic capabilities are more effective in changing business conditions ( Teece, 2007). Furthermore, these findings empirically support the notion of multiple realizability of dynamic capabilities (Jantunen et al., 2012). Our study demonstrates that there are several ways to operate efficiently and various ways high levels of performance can be achieved. Interestingly, we did not observe multiple realizability in the contemporary business model. Ourfindings point to only one configuration of dynamic capabilities and operational changes for success. This is characterized by high levels of operational changes (i.e., changes in management and practices and changes in technologies and markets), high levels of sensing and reconfiguration capabilities, and low degrees of seizing capabilities. This demonstrates thatfirms with the capacity to identify opportunities (i.e., through sensing activities) and to coordinate resources (i.e., by reconfiguring competences) can renew their business model and succeed in changing the business environment. However, this is not sufficient on its own; for optimal performance outcomes, significant operational changes in the external environment (i.e., changes in technologies and markets) must be matched with compatible inter-organizational changes (i.e., changes in management and practices). Contrary to sensing and reconfiguring dynamic capabilities, low levels of seizing (i.e., opportunity-utilizing activities) are necessary for success in the context of new digital channels. The implications for management are that organizations operating in dynamic environments can successfully adapt their existing business model with different combinations of dynamic capabilities and internal changes. According to ourfindings, there are multiple ways in which combinations of dynamic capabilities, together with internal changes, can lead to high performance in the existing business model. However, in order to radically and successfully renew their business models, managers should put more emphasis on sensing (i.e., scanning the external environment and interpreting the information received as well as searching and identifying market opportunities) and reconfiguring activities (i.e., transforming resources and processes into new valuable combinations), alongside operational level changes that match internal practices with external changing conditions. Interestingly, ourfindings show that direct attempts to capture market value by seizing capabilities should be avoided if one seeks higher degrees of performance in the digitalized channels. This study has limitations that may provide promising avenues for future research. The study sample is relatively small; therefore, the measure validation is somewhat limited. The lack of control variables limits the possibility of generalizing the results in other contexts. Future research is necessary to validate the results obtained in the present study. In addition, more attention should be directed to contextual factors such as environmental dynamism and turbulence. This also requires the development of more generalizable measures for operationallevel changes, so that companies from di fferent industries can be compared. References Amit, R., & Schoemaker, P. J. Introduction During the last several decades, dynamic capabilities have received widespread attention in management research. Environmental dynamism influences the fit of current operative routines and capabilities in organizations. The latter require dynamic capabilities to deal with this issue (Teece et al. , 1997). Thus, dynamic capabilities enable organizations to adapt operative routines and capabilities to dynamic environments, which is a key concern in contemporary organizations (Zollo and Winter, 2002; Winter, 2003). However, the nature of dynamic capabilities remains ambiguous. Some scholars regard dynamic capabilities as sets of organizational routines (e.g. Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000; Zollo and Winter, 2002). However, because routines are phenomena that develop within specific trajectories (Vergne and Durand, 2011) the question remains how do they enable “dynamic” adaptation and change. First, it contributes to research that elaborates on the nature of dynamic capabilities (Schreyögg and Kliesch-Eberl, 2007). Many scholars define dynamic capabilities as high level routines that shape operational routines (Winter, 2003; Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000). However, Teece, (2012, 2014, 2016) argues that routines are not the only components that constitute dynamic capabilities and that entrepreneurial behavior of individuals should also be considered. We develop this insight by outlining the mechanisms by which entrepreneurial initiatives might constitute a microfoundation of dynamic capabilities. We believe that two aspects have to be considered in order to understand this tension between entrepreneurship and routinization. First, applying a microfoundations lens shows that entrepreneurial initiatives might reside on the individual and group level. As indicated in our model, the mechanism of how dynamic capabilities exert their entrepreneurial effect resides on those levels. Moreover, we provide an alternative approach to this tension than prior research. Wohlgemuth and Wenzel (2015), for instance, find that higher routinization occurs at strategic levels whereas operational levels are less routinized. Thus, behavior is a vital element that should gain more attention in microfoundations research (Salvato and Rerup, 2011). Finally, prior research on the microfoundations of dynamic capabilities has largely focused on top management as “lonely heroes” shaping capabilities (Adner and Helfat, 2003; Helfat and Martin, 2015). By contrast, research on corporate entrepreneurship has also highlighted the role of middle managers that act in an entrepreneurial way and fundamentally change organizations (Kuratko et al. , 2005; Kuratko et al. , 2015). Thus, by examining entrepreneurial initiatives in organizations, we not only consider top management as influencers of dynamic capabilities, but extend microfoundations research to other managers and employees (Wooldridge et al. , 2008; Renzl et al. , 2013). This extension shifts the role of top management from “lonely heroes” to inspiring leaders that shape the corporate context within which capability-building occurs (Di Stefano et al. , 2014). Third, this paper contributes to research on corporate entrepreneurship. Kuratko et al. (2005), for instance, claims that research should elaborate how middle managers’ entrepreneurial behavior influences organizational outcomes. We provide a model of how those entrepreneurial initiatives are embedded in the larger organizational context.
