Integration capability Integration capability has been identi fied as one of the three classes of managerial functions, i.e. integration, guided learning, and reconfiguration/transformation, which are relevant to dynamic capabilities (Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997). Coase (1937) pointed out that the most obvious cost of organizing production through the marker mechanism is that of discovering what the relevant prices are, and these transaction costs make it more efficient to organize an activity within the firm. Therefore, the Coasian view of thefirms believes that afirm should minimize the internal transaction cost (Coase, 1937). Following this logic, centralized R&D could generate innovations that have a larger and broader impact on subsequent technological evolution by reducing the internal transaction costs associated with R&D coordination across units in the organization (Argyres & Silverman, 2004). However, in order to keepflexibility and responsiveness, resources should be decentralized while the firm is growing. Therefore, structural complexity and the amount of organizational units will be increased. It leads to the increase of transactional cost across organizational units (Teece, 2007). The dynamic capability focuses more on the efficient and effective transfer of technology/information between and among the various organizational units of afirm. It is believed that resource integrating capability could helpfirms to connect separate organizational units because it can help easing potential contractual problems. Moreover, integration also opens pathways to learning, sharing of know-how, and expertise through transfer of technology and know-how within afirm (Teece, 2014a). Integration capability does not only include internal coordination, i.e. the capability for extensive coordination between different specialized subunits within an organization, but also include the capacity to integrate external resources. For instance, typical external integration activities include integrating market and customer knowledge and integrating knowledge of emerging technologies (Iansiti & Clark, 1994). To some extent, integration capability enablesfirms to transform and convert resources into innovative outputs (Dutta, Narasimhan, & Rajiv, 2005). We expect that integration capability could both increase technological innovation and market innovation. In terms of technological innovation, external integration capability could helpfirms to adopt technology from different areas while internal integration capability could facilitatefirms to share knowledge internally. When a firm enters a new technological niche, it can divert free resources toward integrating new technological knowledge with existing technological knowledge repositories to increase innovative output (Kotha, Zheng, & George, 2011). Therefore,firms need to build logics for vertical integration, outsourcing, and R&D strategies to integrate both internal and external resources (Prencipe, 1997). They also need to maintain a thorough understanding of the contracted out technologies to be able to integrate them into the system and ‘control’ their evolution over time (Prencipe, 1997). Through the effective integration of internal and external technological knowledge, afirm is more likely to incorporate the characteristics necessary for success into the new products (Marsh & Stock, 2006). On the other hand, both internal and external integration capability can help transferring market information across the organizational units. Reconfiguration capability In order to sustain profitable growth, it is important for a company to recombine and to reconfigure assets and organizational structures when markets and technologies change. Knowledge and resources may depreciate over time, and it may lead to the lack of cumulative benefits from prior experiences (Sampson, 2005). Reconfiguration capability does not only supportfirms to maintain evolutionary fitness but also provide the possibility for them to escape from unfavorable path dependencies when it is necessary (Teece, 2007). Reconfiguration capability includes activities in whichfirms engage when adding, redeploying, recombining, or divesting resources or business units (Karim & Capron, 2016). Organizational reconfiguration capability facilitates continuous evolution and can also become a mechanism for firms to obtain novel resources and capture innovation benefits. We believe that organizational reconfiguration capability could enhance both technology innovation and market innovation. In terms of the technological innovation, the intra-organizational knowledge exchange could be stimulated and the existing tacit knowledge could be externalized and distributed in the company via redeploying human resources and restructuring business units (Nonaka, 1994). Galunic and Rodan (1998) have pointed out that knowledge tacitness and context specificity have important consequences on the likelihoods of innovation. It is also proved that the deployment offirm-specific knowledge requires specific settings. Employees who hold the key knowledge may be reluctant to make specialized human capital investments when they are deployed inappropriately (Wang, He, & Mahoney, 2009). METHODOLOGY Measurement Most of our measurement scales were adopted from or developed based on the previous studies. In the following measurement details, unless specified otherwise, all of the variables were measured using 7-point Likert-type scales ranging from 1= ‘strongly disagree’ to 7 = ‘strongly agree.’ In terms of dynamic capabilities, as Danneels (2016: 2175) most recently noted that‘as a relatively young area of strategic management research, the area of dynamic capabilities lacks generally accepted approaches to measure its key constructs. Measuring dynamic capabilities is challenging.’ Consequently, we have searched literature extensively to identify relevant items, which could help to assure content validity. Specifically, we adopted and integrated the arguments of dynamic capacity (Teece, 2000, 2007), and measured three dimensions of sensing, integration, and reconfiguration. In terms of the measurement of sensing capability, we adopted and developed measurement items based on Teece (2000, 2007) and O’Reilly and Tushman (2008). The items include investment in research activities with the aim of probing technological possibilities, probing and reproving the existing or potential customer demand, closely observing competitors and suppliers’ innovation activities, following the frontier research in science and technology, and identifying the industrial development trends through various mechanisms. We adopted and integrated concepts and ideas in previous studies (Cepeda & Vera, 2007; Wang & Ahmed, 2007) to measure integration capability. We used three items such as adopting different areas of technological knowledge, sharing new knowledge across the organization internally, and transferring industrial information or market information across the organization internally. The measurement items of reconfiguration were adopted from Prieto, Revilla, and Rodríguez-Prado (2009) and Teece (2007). The items include the flexibility to reconfigure organizational structures, the autonomy of decision-making power of organizational departments, proper redesign of the existing working process and procedures, proper redesign of the existing tasks and functions of organizational departments, proper reconfiguration of the internal and external networks and communication mechanism, and capability to dispose the outdated resource or knowledge. We usedfive items to measure technological innovation(Utterback, 1986; Anderson & Tushman, 1990; Subramaniam & Youndt, 2005): adopting new knowledge or technology in the process of innovation, innovations that make your existing production processes or equipment outdated, innovations that fundamentally change your current products/services, innovations that make your existing expertise or knowledge in current products/services outdated, and innovations that make new products/services replacing the existing ones. Three items were used to measure market innovation (Zhou, Yim & Tse, 2005): our product concept is difficult for existing customers to evaluate or understand, our product involves high switching costs for existing customer, and the use of our product requires a major learning effort by existing customers. We usedfive items to measure thefinancial performance offirms based on Dyer and Reeves (1995) and Zahra and Bogner (2000): high ROI (return on investment), high ROA (return on assets), high increase rate of sales, high rate of sales profit, and high market share. Data collection China is an active player in the global economy and it was chosen as the empirical setting of this study. The development of dynamic capabilities could be contingent on the dynamics of the environment (Day & Wensley, 1988). However, limited research has included such contingencies in emerging economies (Kirca, Jayachandran, & Bearden, 2005). China offers a rich context to test dynamic capability because its complex, fast-changing nature makes it critical forfirms to survive and prosper in this country (Zhou & Li, 2012). In other words, it is essential for Chinesefirms to develop their dynamic capability to achieve and sustain superior performance over time in thechanging business environment with economic transformation and upgrading, expansion of domestic consumption, growing of international markets, and advancement of the new type of industrialization. The infusion of new information from the emerging market in China also encourages companies to generate new ideas for innovations (Laursen & Salter, 2006). The Chinesefirms need to integrate knowledge from the potential markets in China, detect market trends, and invest accordingly to explore them (Zhou & Li, 2012). Furthermore, the dramatic technological progress in China also requires companiesto strongly pursue dynamic capacity to adapt to the environment with quick development of innovation, multiple sources of innovation, and different types of technological innovation (Zhang, Li, Li, & Zhou, 2010). Therefore, the rapid changing and competitive business and technological environment makes China an appropriate context for testingfirm’sd y n a m i c capability empirically. As the world’s largest emerging economy, China shares many characteristics and similarities with other emerging economies (Peng, 2003). This makes China an appropriate representative context of emerging economies and thereforefindings from this research could provide implications for firms operating in other emerging economies. Second, we also conveyed to respondents that the purpose of this survey is only for academic research, and there is no‘right’or ‘wrong’answers for the questions. Finally, we conducted Harman singlefactor test (Podsakoff & Organ, 1986) by loading all the measures into an exploratory factor analysis with the assumption that the presence of CMV is indicated by the emergence of either a single factor or a general factor accounting for the majority of covariance among measures (Podsakoff et al., 2003). Data analysis We used PLS-SEM as our multivariate statistical technique that allowed us to analyze multiple variables and multiple equations simultaneously. It has been popularly used in articles in top-tier journals. The estimation procedure of PLS is an ordinary least squares regression-based method rather than minimizing the error terms of the endogenous constructs to estimate the path relationships in the model (Hair, Ringle, & Sarstedt, 2011, 2013). Theoretical and managerial implications This article makes several contributions to the dynamic capabilities literature. First, we provide a more nuanced understanding about the effects of dynamic capabilities onfirm performance by empirically enhancing the arguments that the impacts of various dimensions of dynamic capabilities are not identical, which also helps to overcome the criticism of dynamic capabilities for being tautological (Barreto, 2010). Our research provides empirical support for the notion that different dimensions ‘describe significantly different dynamic capability process categories’(Wilden et al., 2013: 79), and that they do not only necessarily covary with each other, but also with different consequences (Barreto, 2010; Wilden et al., 2013). Rather than treat dynamic capabilities as a whole, we decompose dynamic capabilities into three dimensions and examine the effects of each dimension. Ourfindings suggest that unlike sensing capability and reconfiguration capability, integration capability does not have positive impact on innovation activities. We thus provide a more nuanced understanding about the effects of dynamic capabilities and thus is more appropriate than that of Protogerou, Caloghirou, and Lioukas (2012), which limited dynamic capabilities to only those cases where high levels of all dimensions are evident. The distinct effect of the three dimensions of dynamic capabilities demonstrated in this study can also address the tautology problem of the concept of dynamic capabilities in that different dimensions of dynamic capabilities are linked tofirm performance in different way. Second, this article proposes and empirically validates innovation activities as mechanisms through which dynamic capabilities influence firm performance. The question of whether and how dynamic capabilities affect performance is still open and remain a source of debates (Helfat et al., 2009; Schilke, 2014). To reconcile these debates, we need a thorough understanding of the associated mediating mechanisms, which help us better understand how and why dynamic capabilities improvefirm performance. This approach is also consistent with an‘indirect link’approach which has been considered as the most promising one (Barreto, 2010). Our study is a direct response to Barreto’s (2010: 275–276) call for future research that‘should continue to explore these relationships between dynamic capabilities and intermediate outcomes, on one hand, and between intermediate outcomes and performance, on the other hand, to better assess which dynamic capabilities and intermediate outcomes deserve more attention.’Our findings enable us to conclude that dynamic capabilities could influence firm performance through innovation activities, especially technological innovation, despite some subtle differences existing among various dimensions of dynamic capabilities. Only after we have a clear understanding of the mediating mechanisms of dynamic capabilities effects can we explore further its boundary conditions by testing a set of moderating effects. Third, this article contributes to reducing the relative scarcity of empirical research on the performance implications of dynamic capabilities, particularly on the mediating mechanisms of dynamic capabilities effects. Without empirical studies, scholars may be trapped by endless arguing and debating with each other, and therefore research on dynamic capabilities would not progress as much as it could do. In terms of managerial implications, our results provide guidance for managers on how to build and leverage dynamic capabilities, which has been a too vague and elusive concept (Kraatz & Zajac, 2001) for managers to execute, in order to improve firm performance. First, given that our findings demonstrate that one of the three dimensions of dynamic capabilities: integration capability, does not have significant effects on two types of innovation, managers should place more emphasis on reconfiguration capability and sensing capability instead of integration capability. For example, managers need to pay special attention to industry trend and adopt best practice, however, the coordination and integration of activities inside the firm is not as important. Such suggestions may point to the importance of a loosely coupled structure within thefirm. Second, dynamic capabilities must be leveraged in aid of a good strategy to be effective (Teece, 2014b). Given that ourfindings which demonstrate that technological innovation activities serve as a significant mediating mechanism between dynamic capabilities andfirm performance, the key for a good strategy is to use dynamic capabilities to facilitate innovation activities, especially technological innovation activities. Dynamic capabilities can serve a variety of purposes, including the creation, extension, and modification of resources (Stadler, Helfat, & Verona, 2013). Focusing on innovation purpose could be effective as our findings suggest that innovation, especially technological innovation, should be present for superior performance achievement. For example, managers should allocate more resources to technological innovation activities rather than other domains, particularly when they face a situation of very limited resources. This suggestion is a reflection of the fact that bottleneck of the Chinesefirms is technological innovation instead of market innovation, which needs to be overcome using dynamic capabilities. Limitations and future research Our study has some limitations that offer avenues for further research. First, our data are cross-sectional in nature which does not allow us to examine the influence of dynamic capabilities on innovation activities and firm performance over time and therefore could not definitively establish causality. Second, we assume a dynamic environment as a condition under which dynamic capabilities are relevant to improve firm performance. However, scholars (e.g., Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000) also contend that dynamic capabilities may prove less effective in highly dynamic environments. Therefore, a potential extension of this research would be to employ a longitudinal study design to empirically confirm causality and assess innovation andfirm performance outcomes over time. Future research could also examine the roles of environment dynamism in the relationship among dynamic capabilities, innovation activities, andfirm performance. Besides, despite the positive effect of dynamic capabilities on innovation activities andfirm performance, building and maintaining dynamic capabilities involves substantial cost, which should be explicitly taken into account in future research. Finally, dynamic capabilities may reside in large measure with the enterprise’s top management team (Teece, 2007), which is also termed dynamic managerial capabilities (Helfat and Martin, 2015), therefore, it might also be interesting to conduct multilevel research in the future, which provides a means to explore the micro-foundations of dynamic capabilities. However, more recent research ascribes the routines that constitute ordinary capabilities the ability to evolve endogenously. This study aims to develop dynamic capability research by increasing our understanding of the relations between and the roles played by ordinary and dynamic capabilities in producing purposeful responses to environmental dynamism. Drawing on longitudinal, qualitative data, we show how ordinary capabilities make important contributions to organizational responses to dynamic environments. Our findings pose challenges to key assumptions of extant dynamic capabilities research and allow us to explicate new roles for ordinary and dynamic capabilities, thus advancing the understanding of the relation between dynamic and ordinary capabilities and advancing understanding of one of the central issues in dynamic capabilities research: firms' capacity to respond to changing environments. 1. Introduction What explains a firm’s ability to respond to dynamism in the competitive environment? This question has received increasing attention in strategic management research, and the concept of dynamic capabilities has evolved as a forceful explanation (Barreto, 2010; Fainshmidt, Pezeshkan, Frazier, Nair, & Markowski, 2016; Vogel & Güttel, 2013). Arguing that dynamism challenges established competitive advantages, this theory holds that the capacity to renew relevant firm competencies in response to rapid environmental transformation depends on dynamic capabilities (Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997; Winter, 2003; Newey, Verreynne, & Griffith, 2012; Ambrosini & Bowman, 2009). Applied in various organizational contexts (Danneels, 2011; Helfat & Martin, 2015) and different degrees of dynamism (Helfat & Winter, 2011), dynamic capabilities research has grown into one of the central streams in current strategy research. Journal Pre-proof 2 Central to this theory is the view that firm success and failure in dynamic environments is best understood by addressing capabilities at different conceptual levels, each of which has distinct functions (Teece et al., 1997; Teece, 2007). The current theory holds that while ordinary capabilities allow firms to keep up with their competitors, these capabilities are efficiency seeking and static; thus, dynamic capabilities are necessary to leverage, create, access, and release ordinary capabilities in purposeful response to environmental dynamism (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000, Danneels, 2011). However, because the theory primarily focuses on the dynamic capabilities concept itself (Di Stefano, Peteraf, & Verona, 2014; Helfat & Peteraf, 2009) and how these capabilities relate to external environments (Ambrosini, Bowman & Collier, 2009; Barreto, 2010; Karna, Richter & Riesenkampff, 2015; Schilke, 2014a, Schilke, 2014b), it has focused less on how dynamic capabilities relate to ordinary capabilities. As an exception and questioning a unilateral influence on static ordinary capabilities, Newey and Zahra (2009) suggest that dynamic capabilities can be influenced by ordinary capability learning; findings also echoed by Newey and colleagues (2012). Illuminating constructs and the relationships between constructs is key to theory development (Suddaby, 2010), and clarifying dynamic and ordinary capabilities and the relation between them could advance one of the central issues in dynamic capabilities research, namely, explaining firms’ capacity to respond to changing environments. This study aims to develop dynamic capability research by increasing our understanding of the roles played by and the relations between ordinary and dynamic capabilities in producing purposeful responses to environmental dynamism. This study takes its starting point in established theory that considers dynamic and ordinary capabilities conceptually distinct (Teece, 2007; Teece, 2014; Teece, 2017) and adds two important insights: first, that routines constituting capabilities can evolve endogenously (Pentland & Feldman, 2005), and second, that they can do Journal Pre-proof 3 so purposefully in relation to external dynamism influenced by actively aware actors (Salvato, 2009). Empirically, our study builds on longitudinal, qualitative in-depth data with a focus on a product development project. Product development has been identified as central to firm competitiveness (Clausen, Pohjola, Sapprasert, & Verspagen, 2011), ability to respond to environmental dynamism (Teece, 2007), and re-establish evolutionary fitness (Helfat et al., 2007). We elaborate the idea of ordinary capabilities as evolving mindfully, which contrasts against the connotations of ordinary capability change as driven primarily by routines “slipping” in unwanted and unaware ways, and we thus modify key assumptions underpinning dynamic capabilities research. Our study also nuances the roles that the currently dominating theory ascribes to ordinary capabilities regarding their ability to respond to external dynamism. Lastly, we complement the roles generally ascribed to dynamic capabilities as associated foremost with initiating change in ordinary capabilities (Danneels, 2011). Together, this work advances the theoretical understanding of dynamic capabilities with regard to its central issue: explaining how firms adjust to environmental dynamism. 2. Dynamic and ordinary capabilities Dynamic capabilities research is still evolving and hence encompasses a variety of views (Barreto, 2010). A useful formal definition is offered by Teece (2017: 698), who states that “dynamic capabilities help enable an enterprise to profitably build and renew resources, reconfiguring them as needed to innovate and respond to (or bring about) changes in the market and in the business environment more generally.” To qualify as dynamic capabilities, this adaptation needs to be purposeful in terms of a firm’s situation in shifting environments (Helfat & Winter, 2011) and dynamic capabilities are ascribed the roles of accessing, integrating, leveraging, and releasing ordinary capabilities including firm resources (Eisenhardt & Martin, Journal Pre-proof 4 2000; Danneels, 2011). Because this often requires mandates to allocate substantial resources and alter the strategic direction of the firm, established dynamic capabilities research argues that dynamic capabilities are typically found in, but not necessarily limited to, a firm’s top management team (Helfat & Martin, 2015; Teece, 2007). More fundamentally, the need for dynamic capabilities emanates from a view in which organizational capabilities function at different conceptual levels (Collis, 1994) and in which different capacities for change are ascribed to dynamic and ordinary capabilities (Teece et al., 1997; Teece, 2007). Teece (2017: 696) defines ordinary capabilities as making a firm “...capable of producing and selling a defined (and hence static) set of products and services using known technologies.” More specifically, the literature describes ordinary capabilities as efficiencyfocused processes that occur as part of the ongoing activity of an organization (Newey et al., 2012). Although the ordinary capabilities may change, they suffer from path dependency (Schreyögg & Kliesch-Eberl, 2007) and are associated with organizational inertia (Lieberman & Montgomery, 1988). In short, ordinary capabilities are often described as essentially stable (Barreto, 2010), static (Leonard-Barton, 1992), and “non-change focused” (Hine, Parker, Pregelj, & Verreynne, 2014: 1302). Consequently, they are seen as unable to adapt to dynamic environments (Drnevich & Kriauciunas, 2011; Leonard-Barton, 1992; Zahra et al., 2006). This conceptualization of ordinary capabilities as static is in turn related to the dominating view in dynamic capabilities research of the routines that underpin capabilities. The almost unmatched influence of evolutionary economics on dynamic capabilities research (Di Stefano et al., 2014) suggests that routines are “regular and predictable” patterns (Nelson & Winter, 1982: 15, italics in original). Routines are also often described as skill-based, automatized, and repeatable collective processes or organizational routines (Felin et al., 2012; Zahra, Sapienza & Journal Pre-proof 5 Davidsson, 2006) and as unitary and often gene-like (Rerup & Feldman, 2011). Even if the ability of routines to change has not gone unnoticed in dynamic capabilities research, such change has mainly been associated with either luck or clearly negative connotations. Nelson and Winter (1982: 108) note that "routine operation is consistent with routinely occurring laxity, slippage, rule-breaking, defiance, and even sabotage.” Others explain routine variation with routines being “contaminated” by extraneous, historically specific, and arbitrary components (Cohen & Bacdayan, 1994: 556); others still with unintentional “slipping” or “mindlessness” and consequent inattention to changes in the task environment (Howard-Grenville, 2005: 620). In short, these views of routine change do not suggest that ordinary capabilities are well equipped for theorizing firms’ ability to purposefully adjust to rapid environmental shifts. In contrast, recent research into the “black box” of routines (Parmigiani & HowardGrenville, 2011) suggests a different, more dynamic picture. The basic argument is that “there is no such thing as perfect replication” of social systems (Gupta, Smith, & Shalley, 2006: 694). Friction among artifacts, rules, technology, accounts of routines, and the actions taken in each situation leads to the gradual evolution of routines (Becker, 2005; Feldman & Pentland, 2003; Howard-Grenville, 2005; Pentland & Feldman, 2005; Rerup & Feldman, 2011). Feldman and Pentland (2003) consider routines a source of change and state that performing a routine “brings the routine to life and hence the performance may be novel each time” (Feldman and Pentland, 2003: 101). Consequently, variation in routines can be a source of dynamism (Salvato & Rerup, 2017). Moreover, complementing connotations of lacking intention, we draw on research suggesting that routine change can be deliberate and attentive to context. Such routine change has been described as mindful, denoting “a state of active awareness characterized by the Journal Pre-proof 6 continual creation and refinement of categories, an openness to new information, and a willingness to view contexts from multiple perspectives” (Levinthal & Rerup, 2006: 502, building on Langer [1989]). Mindful routine change thus takes a position between blind routinefollowing, on the one hand, and unintended routine change (or slipping), on the other hand, and it has been used in previous capabilities research (Laamanen & Brauer, 2014). For instance, Salvato (2009) demonstrates how individual attentiveness allows changing ways of working (Georges et al., 2010; Salvato & Rerup, 2017). The combined implication is that ordinary capabilities might take on qualities that in research are generally restricted to dynamic capabilities by showing purposeful adaptation (Helfat et al., 2007) or “a minimal degree of intentionality” (Helfat & Peteraf, 2009: 95). In sum, despite its breadth, influential parts of dynamic capabilities research build on a view of ordinary capabilities as consisting of stable, or at best, gradually evolving routines. We argue that drawing on recent theoretical advances concerning evolving, mindful routines offers the prospect of a better understanding of ordinary capabilities. The conceptual unshackling of ordinary capabilities from their ascribed stability does not imply that dynamic capabilities necessarily become redundant; instead, a deeper understanding of the relation between dynamic and ordinary capabilities may offer the potential for outlining new roles for ordinary and dynamic capabilities in producing purposeful responses to environmental dynamism. 3. Materials and methods This study, which was designed as a longitudinal case study, is based on qualitative data from a larger research program focusing on the phenomenon of a firm repeatedly defending its position through at least minimally successful organizational adaptation to significant market Journal Pre-proof 7 transformation, especially purposeful product development; in short, a fruitful case for studying how dynamic capabilities adjust firms to shifting environments (e.g., Helfat & Winter, 2011). We designed this study in response to calls for more in-depth case studies of dynamic capabilities (Teece, 2014), which are useful for emerging research themes (e.g., Eisenhardt & Graebner, 2007) and when a focal phenomenon is inherently intertwined with its context (Langley, Smallman, Tsoukas, & Van de Ven, 2013). Additionally, the usefulness of case studies of organizational routines and dynamic capabilities has been demonstrated in earlier research (e.g., Manning, Hutzschenreuter, & Strathmann, 2012; Newey et al., 2012). 3.1 Research setting Here, we report on a study of Paper&Pulp (fictional name), the largely independent tissue paper division of the Paper&Pulp Group. Paper&Pulp, a globally dispersed firm, has a main development site with some 500 employees at its main plant in Scandinavia; it develops and markets costly and highly complex machines largely by drawing on already established engineering skills. This firm was selected for its dynamic capabilities in accordance with two criteria suggested by Helfat et al. (2007): one criterion is a firm achieves, defends, or reestablishes a leading position and the other is the relevant environment is transforming rapidly. With a share of approximately one-third of the total market, Paper&Pulp was known for both its advanced technology and its quality. Whereas many of the traditional methods for making tissue paper required a simpler DCT (“dry crepe tissue”) technology, Paper&Pulp positioned itself with a more upmarket technology, TAD (“through air drying”), a technology that produces a softer and more absorbent tissue but has higher energy consumption. As one Journal Pre-proof 8 senior engineer described the self-perceived market position of Paper&Pulp, “Our customers expect us to be a leader in terms of technology, to be the spearhead of innovation.” However, from a successful upmarket position, Paper&Pulp found itself facing a market undergoing substantial transformation. Financial turmoil reduced overall demand, and when demand resumed, it was directed primarily toward basic, proven technology rather than toward Paper&Pulp’s TAD machines. Increasing energy prices made the TAD technology relatively less attractive than producers of less energy-consuming technologies, putting Paper&Pulp at a disadvantage. Demand also shifted almost exclusively from Europe and North America to the Asian market. These new customers required less state-of-the-art technology and instead wanted more robust and cheaper ways of producing tissue. An additional complexity of the growing Asian market was its limited attention to patent rights; as a result, copying threatened firms investing heavily innovation, such as Paper&Pulp. Lastly, in a challenge to the upmarket segment typical of mature, technology-intensive markets (Bergek, Tell, Berggren, & Watson, 2008), the main competitor openly declared its ambition to challenge Paper&Pulp’s position as a high-end market leader through new technology. Recognizing that the market had transformed significantly, Paper&Pulp’s main response was a new product development project with an aim to develop a new method for producing tissue paper (a new “concept” or “technology”, as described by the interviewees). We considered the new technology a success according to the definitions provided by our informants (cf. Brown & Eisenhardt, 1997) and the successful product, which was launched three years later, reestablished Paper&Pulp as a market leader at the technological forefront of the industry. Regarding this as an example of adapting firm resources to a sensed environmental change (Teece, 2007) similar to examples described in earlier studies (Leiponen & Helfat, 2010; Newey Journal Pre-proof 9 et al., 2012), we focused empirically on the development project (hereafter referred to as the “RIT” project, Revolutionary Innovative Technology) and its relevant organizational context in our analysis of the ordinary and dynamic capabilities at play. 3.2 Material This study is based primarily on interview data. All interview recordings were transcribed completely. As suggested by Eisenhardt and Graebner (2007), the first step in our empirical analysis involved writing a case description of some 50 pages that covered all of the data that were gathered. This developed our understanding of the firm, its operations, and its context, as well as of the RIT product development project in terms of a channeling of the main response efforts to radical environmental change. Qualitative research has the unique potential to nuance traditional, reductionist theory by illuminating “how individual components interact to become systems whose nature cannot be completely understood from looking only at the sum of the parts” (Burgelman, 2011: 594). This requires careful analysis. Inspired by Rerup and Feldman (2011), we used two techniques to ensure that our findings were grounded in data. A natural division of work evolved whereby the second author asked critical questions about data interpretation, suggested alternatives, and identified potential areas for strengthening the connections between the data and the theory, thereby acting as a “devil’s advocate” (Nemeth, Brown, & Rogers, 2001). However, contrasting against what might be expected based on extant dynamic capabilities theory (Teece, 2007), our curiosity soon was aroused by data suggesting that purposeful organizational responses to environmental dynamism occurred before top management had intervened. For instance, interviewees were reluctant to depict the project solely as the result of managerial intervention or unique resource orchestration processes, which are signals that dynamic capabilities are at play (Teece, 2017). Rather, they maintained that resource decisions played the role of supporting processes that has already been ongoing in the organization. An important part of the managerial intervention was thus more about framing ongoing change and less about initiating change in static resources and capabilities (Teece, 2017). We therefore directed our analysis toward ordinary capabilities, or the ongoing, collective, ordinary development work at the project level, outwardly efficiency seeking and without formal responsibility for sensing, seizing, and adjusting to external dynamism (Teece, 2007). More formally, we regarded ordinary capabilities as those used “for the day-to-day operations and the Journal Pre-proof 12 routine; they help ensure that the enterprise is technically fit” (Teece, 2007, p. 1346). We noted that these capabilities played important roles related to adjustment to environmental shifts. Intrigued by an appearing mismatch with current dynamic capabilities research, we paid specific attention to how such change was directed in a purposeful manner to adjust to external events. Concretely, we organized accounts of processes constituting parts of the project, and we coded and structured all of the relevant data under inductive labels, displaying emerging changes in the day-to-day development work (Feldman, 2000; Pentland & Feldman, 2005). These data were then combined into second-order constructs that appeared in the data as repeated behaviors or routines, all of which played a role in the project. Lastly, these constructs were combined into two overarching aggregate themes. The first represented evolving ordinary capabilities and “...attentiveness of individuals and their ability to respond flexibly to contextual cues,” or mindful action (Salvato, 2009: 385), producing outcomes typically ascribed to dynamic capabilities. The second theme complemented traditional accounts of dynamic capabilities as initiating change in ordinary capabilities (Danneels, 2011) and instead represented new roles of dynamic capabilities in relation to such endogenously evolving ordinary capabilities. 4. Results 4.1 An innovative technology in response to environmental changes The decision by Paper&Pulp’s division manager to launch the development of a new technology, the RIT, in response to the transforming market expressed goals initially perceived by engineers as almost unachievable. Making a tissue softer and more absorbent than was possible with the upmarket TAD technology while using less pulp fiber, water, and energy than Journal Pre-proof 13 the traditional DCT technology, in essence reducing energy consumption by some 30%, challenged what the engineers considered possible. A Concept Steering Committee was formed, involved mainly in the early stages. Responsibility to oversee and advise the project instead fell upon a Core Team of seven people, comprising mostly senior engineers, in turn, appointing a project manager responsible for the project. At its height, approximately 20 employees from different branches of the company, including marketing and sales, worked part-time on the project. The much-celebrated launch of the RIT occurred in September, three years after the initiation of the project. Although this project built largely on “producing and selling a defined (and hence static) set of products and services using known technologies” which, in research, is recognized as an ordinary capability (Teece, 2017: 696), a closer look into the RIT project offers new insights into the contributions of such ordinary capabilities to firms’ adjustment to environmental dynamism. 4.2 Evolving ordinary capabilities The formal initiation of the RIT project was not the beginning of Paper&Pulp’s adjustment to the transformation of the paper machine market. Instead, our data reveal important contributions from already ongoing adjustment efforts that do not reflect the definition of dynamic capabilities but instead reflect ordinary capabilities as these were defined by Teece (2007; 2017). In other words, although also traditional, episodic dynamic capability interventions took place, such as a substantial investment in a test facility, the successful response to industry transformation presumed processes and routines that were already in development. The formal project therefore partially represents the creation of a formal project structure for changes that were already in progress. Our data reveal several processes amounting to three significant Journal Pre-proof 14 routines in the evolution of ordinary capabilities: accumulating engineering and managerial experience, continuous technical refinement, and self-guided interaction. These processes are explained below. 4.2.1 Accumulating engineering and managerial experience Similar to Newey and Zahra’s (2009) findings, organizational experience, i.e., development and knowledge sharing within the organization regarding how to develop components that interact in complex ways, played a central role in our case company’s project. The interviewees stressed that at the surface level, paper making had not essentially changed much over decades; nevertheless, it was a highly complex process that is difficult to perfectly reflect or predict in mathematical calculations. Hence, personal experience was crucial. One engineer, who began as a welder and later took on a variety of roles in the construction unit, expressed the importance of seeking this type of experience: “I actively look for those who have been long in the company to benefit from their experience. They’ll tell you ‘We tried that, it didn’t work.’” Accordingly, although the RIT technology was new in its combination of various elements, many of the roots of the project could be traced back decades, as could the engineering ability to develop products for similar conditions. One engineer expressed this as follows: “You have to regard this organization as a condensation of experience of how to run a [tissue paper] machine. If you have a lot of knowledge about a machine like this and how it works, then much of that process can be transferred to another process.” According to the interviewees, the fundamental uncertainty in developing these products always centered on whether a new concept could consistently produce good tissue (i.e., technical Journal Pre-proof 15 feasibility) without interruptions (i.e., runnability). In addition to varying temperatures, levels of vibration, and humidity, the technology also depended on a new type of pulp chemical and, adding to the uncertainty, a conveyor belt developed by a supplier. The effects of this combination of factors are impossible to calculate using computers and require engineering experience from past projects. There were several candidate technologies, so one of the first tasks of the Concept Steering Committee was selecting a fundamental outline of the new technology. An inventory of existing ideas was presented at the second Committee meeting, approximately one month into the project, and at the third meeting, approximately 15 ideas were evaluated. Experience was critical to evaluating how a yet non-existing technology would work under real-life conditions. To increase transparency and impartiality, a formalized system was established wherein each idea was graded along a number of predefined and weighted dimensions. Although one highly innovative technology received the highest grade, the committee agreed on another, less radical technology. As expressed by a senior R&D engineer: “The winning technology was perceived as too radical; its technology was not familiar enough.” Thus, the technology later to become the RIT was selected because it was more in line with existing experience and appeared more feasible within the chosen timeframe. 4.2.2 Continuous technical refinement Once the technology was selected, responsibility for running the RIT project was cascaded to a project manager. Despite its much-increased efficiency in producing paper, the RIT primarily drew on previously developed technology. Although the formal project start-up involved efforts to develop the technology, the RIT built largely on continuous technical Journal Pre-proof 16 refinement resulting from continuous efforts to refine the technology, and this refinement occurred before the project was initiated. Using the famous building block toy as a metaphor, one engineering manager explained the following: “If you look at the RIT technology, we had all the ‘Lego’ parts already. What we did was assemble them in a new way.” The novelty of the technology even appeared difficult to separate from previous solutions, and it appeared in unexpected places. A senior engineer came up with the main idea for the technology, sketched it on a piece of paper, and physically handed it to the project manager. In essence, the idea consisted of significantly improving the technology by taking one of the machine’s main components and turning it upside down, which required an adjustment of the interfaces but only limited technical alterations to the remainder of the product layout. Despite the new solution provided by the RIT, several interviewees considered its technical novelty to be modest. As described by one senior engineer, “So we used components that we already had when we developed it [the RIT], and said: now let’s run it this way, and this aspect we need to develop to make it work.” Thus, although the capacity of the new technology was revolutionary, coming up with the idea was regarded by the senior engineer as a modest achievement, as the part itself already existed, described by the engineer as follows: “The RIT is nothing unique. We’ve used and moved existing parts a bit and it’s become a new process, as simple as that.” The use of existing technology, which had already been developed, was also evident in the use of old ideas and patents. Development work regularly produced ideas that were further developed and, in some instances, patented. Thereby, the firm deliberately drew on patents and Journal Pre-proof 17 experience representing an organizational memory and repository of the past (Becker, Lazaric, Nelson, & Winter, 2005). Having grown increasingly wary of patents, which offer little protection in markets of increasing importance while explicating ideas to competitors, Paper&Pulp developed a sophisticated strategy of weighing the pros and cons before applying for individual patents. In this way, the RIT technology involved both old patented and unpatented advancements and, importantly, old patents that had hitherto remained unused. Although some of the patents were nearly 10 years old, illustrating how the RIT was the result of a long period of refining existing technical refinements, they still made important contributions to the project and, in turn, to meeting the new market conditions. 4.2.3 Self-guiding interaction It is clear that the engineers were given freedom to experiment; one engineer described testing new ideas as the “lifeblood” of engineers and as the reason many had chosen that profession in the first place. Without exerting formal control, Paper&Pulp’s culture allowed the pursuit of ideas. However, the work leading to the RIT did not appear to be random or haphazard, as suggested in some views of routine change (Levinthal & Rerup, 2006); thus, it was far from “mindlessness and consequent inattention to changes in the task environment” (HowardGrenville, 2005: 620). Instead, the development of product technology and knowledge in the RIT project benefited from ongoing internal and external contacts that ensured a fit between development and specific, and sometimes changing, customer demands. This can be described as self-guidance, a condition in which ideas are born and developed collectively through engineers’ knowledge. The engineers particularly stressed the importance of informal face-to-face meetings that took place in the hallways, at lunch, or during coffee breaks. As explained by an engineering Journal Pre-proof 18 manager, “[Informal meetings] is where you get the best ideas, the real novelty and solutions to problems.” This ongoing development was far from detached research for its own sake. Instead, development was directed toward fluctuating market needs. Gradual involvement of the customers’ views was integral to the project and occurred through various channels. Formal intelligence reports on customer, consumer, and competitor trends were regularly produced inhouse and sourced from consultants. Customers also regularly rented Pulp&Paper’s test facilities, creating vast amounts of data and revealing their preferences, but importantly, Paper&Pulp employees developed important contacts to customers. As explained by an R&D manager: “Product managers have a lot of contact with customers and spend lots of time at customer sites. They receive as many signals as our external sales personnel about where the needs are. Product managers have a background in the early research or construction unit and have extensive experience of the tissue process and can easily talk to customers about the [tissue] production process.” Customer contact played other fundamental roles in the project. As part of their initial apprentice-like training, junior engineers at Paper&Pulp were assigned to start-up projects, visiting customer sites for up to nine months. In addition to paving the way for a deeper understanding of the complex conditions on site, attending start-ups provided important information about customers and their needs, technical preferences, and future investments. As explained by an engineering manager: Journal Pre-proof 19 “All our construction engineers spend time at customer sites. Attending a number of start-ups is scheduled, and everyone does it, and quite early [after starting at Paper&Pulp].” Importantly, it created personal contacts to customers, invaluable in later development work. The ability to self-govern development was also related to managerial competence in the actual project. Several engineers characterized the experience as the result of a very open, professional culture. Hierarchical status was ascribed little importance compared to technical expertise. Importantly, employees customarily moved from positions as engineers to positions as team managers, only to step back into the engineering role a few years later to get closer to the development work that originally motivated them to join the firm. A senior engineer describes the situation as follows: “I was a project manager for many years, but I wanted to get back and work in product development; I mean, that’s why I took the job in the first place. So now I’m ‘Senior Engineer’.” Therefore, important technological know-how and managerial or administrative tasks did not compete. Instead, technological development experience and managerial perspectives were naturally interwoven in day-to-day development work, thus avoiding developing technology for its own sake but keeping a close eye on the strategic aim of the project. Overall, our data show how ordinary capabilities made important contributions to the development of Paper&Pulp’s RIT. Accumulating existing experience and ongoing product development processes representing ordinary capabilities (Teece, 2017) were central in producing a response to market transformation. Further, the project continuously drew on interactions with suppliers and customers as a means of both developing technological Journal Pre-proof 20 knowledge and staying in line with customer demand. Together, this suggests that ordinary capabilities played roles different from those that are usually described in dynamic capabilities research. 4.3 Control of mindfully evolving ordinary capabilities The data presented above show that ordinary capabilities associated with known technologies (Teece, 2017: 696) actively contributed to much of the adaptation to the significant market transformation surrounding Pulp&Paper. An important part of this adaptation was “attentiveness by individuals and their ability to respond flexibly” (Salvato, 2009: 385), allowing engineers to respond actively to, e.g., customer demand. Although dynamic capabilities also appeared in traditional roles, our data reveal additional roles for dynamic capabilities. The data show how dynamic capabilities, no longer needed only to initiate change, mapped ongoing development, established a shared view, and set boundaries for developing ordinary capabilities, as explained in the next section. 4.3.1 Progress mapping Successful dynamic capabilities intervention in ordinary capabilities requires sufficient cospecialization between the two forms of capabilities (Newey et al., 2012). However, the continuous technical refinement described above implied the RIT developed largely separate from top management intervention. Furthered by engineers’ personal interest in pursuing development beyond commercial considerations or formal development planning, the higher echelons were left with a less up-to-date status of the development. In this light, several early efforts associated with the RIT project stand out as aiming to create a coherent view of an Journal Pre-proof 21 organization in flux. Concretely, the inventory of the Concept Steering Committee appears as taking stock of ongoing projects and existing but fluctuating development. This mapping of ongoing development played an even more important role, as development also occurred at research sites in Italy and in the US. Therefore, important development variables were mapped, as described by a leading senior engineer: “We started brainstorming to really penetrate the ideas [ongoing technological development] that might exist... we evaluated formally in a table: product quality, runnability and energy consumption; the central parameters; and the likelihood of succeeding.” Moreover, significant leeway was given to the relatively junior managers and engineers responsible for the ongoing development in the project. These met several times per week and naturally focused on technology; however, the following was witnessed by participants: “We pay more and more attention to customers and strategy.” As these meetings evolved, another slightly different aspect of this mapping was the clarification of the timeframe, as well as of the likelihood that the project would achieve the anticipated results (cf. Danneels, 2011). Already early in the project, this typically required various competencies with very hands-on knowledge. This was solved by bringing in concrete and up-to-date knowledge from the operational level, often from the workshop floor. A manager responsible for incremental development stated the following: “We often involve someone from Construction and from Manufacturing [in our meetings] – workshop employees such as a good welder – to make sure early that we can actually assemble the product and to help the constructing engineer making the blueprints.” Journal Pre-proof 22 As expected, because managers typically had technical backgrounds and were interested in development work, there were also informal meetings, e.g., in the corridor, that contributed to updating the map of ongoing development. In sum, the managers were aware of and valued the fact that development tended to grow out of engineer curiosity and at paces and in directions not always initiated or controlled by management. Efforts were made to avoid hampering or halting such development. Still, higher echelon managers recognized a need to form an understanding of the development work. Thus, rather than exerting complete control (potentially at the expense of creativity and gradually evolving technologies), efforts were made to map ongoing development. 4.3.2 Establishing a shared view A related but separate effort involved ensuring that the mapping became a shared view of the internal reality among the involved employees. Several interviewees stressed that engineers at different levels and organizational locations had, for quite some time, considered a need for developing a new technology to increase Paper&Pulp’s competitive edge. An R&D manager expressed that “many felt the need to do something” if the firm was to survive but stated that this feeling lacked direction. Therefore, this manager welcomed the RIT project as a means of creating shared direction and common purpose. Spread both formally and informally, the project disseminated a shared view of the direction the organization needed to take. A research and development engineer explained the following: “There has been ongoing research in the organization, so in a sense the idea to develop a new technology was not new. But it was a really good thing that the division manager made the decision to unite us in what we should do. It was a really good thing.” Journal Pre-proof 23 Similarly, a large part of the work on the project aimed to ensure a shared view of the final product and of the path to develop it. Much effort went into coordinating those directly and indirectly involved in the project, e.g., regarding developments with potential consequences for the entire machine and thus for other parts of the development organization. This was channeled informally through meetings and coffee-break talks as well as through formal reporting. Describing this in the form of a “ladder,” a manager responsible for the gradual improvement work explained the following: “Decisions on the ‘nuts and bolt’ level are made locally, otherwise passed on using e-mail or personal communication upwards to team managers meeting every third week; or higher, to the Concept Steering Committee.” In short, although the engineers appreciated the formal initiation of the RIT project by the division manager, it was as much a promise for the future as an acknowledgment of work that was already being initiated. Against this background, much of the out-of-the-ordinary work revolved around creating a shared view of the direction and pace of the ongoing development. 4.3.3 Boundary-setting Several of the interventions arising from dynamic capability in our data appear as the setting of boundaries or as a reduction in the leeway of ongoing technology development. The division manager signaled that efforts should be concentrated on the RIT project by communicating that the RIT project was a priority. This meant reducing leeway for other development efforts. Concretely, this involved scrapping six of ten ongoing research projects that were considered insufficiently relevant to the RIT project and focusing resources on accelerating the progress of Journal Pre-proof 24 the RIT project. In turn, engineering time, test runs, and external cooperation with the belt provider and the chemicals providers were steered to the RIT project. In addition, other interventions aimed to reduce the leeway for development work while avoiding unnecessarily hampering ongoing development efforts within the project. One person was assigned the role of ensuring that ongoing development was kept within reasonable boundaries, and a new product framework was introduced to define the scope for future product generations. For instance, a higher level of standardization was introduced. This was inspired by visiting and learning from a truck producer who was considered skilled in modularizing. This meant furthering development within while “locking” interfaces between the different elements of the machine. While this setting of boundaries could be interpreted as hampering creativity, several engineers perceived the contrary, arguing resources could be used more efficiently in a more streamlined process, as explained by one engineer “It means that we have fixed limits within which to concentrate the development work. Previously, we had gradually drifting development, where we sometimes ended up with segments of delivery projects [sold but not yet manufactured machines] requiring urgent and costly adjustment.” This statement illustrates that the ongoing development necessary for the success of the RIT technology, which was rooted in engineering work and technologies that already existed at the formal initiation of the project, was not left without influence from dynamic capabilities. Contradicting a view in which dynamic capabilities are primarily concentrated in early development phases (Newey et al., 2012), interventions from outside the ordinary capabilities ensured continued development but channeled ongoing efforts in the desired directions within certain boundaries. Journal Pre-proof 25 5. Discussion Dynamic capabilities research identifies product development as one key for adapting to dynamic environments. Our study of a product development project initiated by Paper&Pulp to adapt to a period of market transformation illustrates this point and offers new insights regarding dynamic capabilities. Our findings show that the evolving nature of ordinary capabilities made important contributions to the success of the RIT project and hence to Paper&Pulp’s adaptation to the market transformation. Moreover, whereas our data include clear instances in which dynamic capabilities orchestrate ordinary resources in the traditional sense, e.g., through investments (Teece, 2007), they also show new ways in which dynamic capabilities interact with endogenously evolving ordinary capabilities. The contrast between the emerging view of ordinary and dynamic capabilities developed in our study and traditional views is summarized in Table 3 and discussed in the next section. * * * insert Table 3 about here * * * 5.1 Mindful and endogenously evolving ordinary capabilities Dynamic capabilities research rests on the assumption that dynamic capabilities are needed for firms to adjust to environmental dynamism. In turn, this view builds on the idea that there is a strict conceptual division between capacity for change among ordinary and dynamic capabilities (Collis, 1994; Teece, 2007). In this view, ordinary capabilities are traditionally associated with the inability to adjust to sudden events in a meaningful way unless change is initiated from dynamic capabilities. Taken together, the Paper&Pulp case does not support this traditional view. Instead, our findings indicate that engineers used existing knowledge associated with “producing Journal Pre-proof 26 and selling a defined (and hence static) set of products and services using known technologies” (Teece, 2017: 696) to contribute to adjustments to environmental dynamism. More specifically, our findings pinpoint the evolution of routines that allow certain ordinary capabilities to adjust to environmental dynamism rather than remaining stable (Barreto, 2010), static, or “non-change focused” (Hine et al., 2014: 1302). An important implication for the understanding of ordinary capabilities is that this continuous evolution did not appear as luck, slipping, or mutating (Nelson & Winter, 1982). Rather, our data demonstrate how ordinary capabilities progressed deliberately in relation to environmental dynamism in ways that have been described as mindful (Salvato, 2009; Levinthal & Rerup, 2006), out of an awareness for context and deliberate actions to adjust ongoing development in light of external dynamism. While echoing the findings of earlier capabilities research, we also extend this view. Laamanen and Brauer (2014) used the term “mindful” to indicate that cognitive efforts to re-establish routines evolve after significant interruptions (Gersick, 1991); however, these efforts are not observed empirically. Our in-depth data illustrate this cognitive, mindful effort in the context of actively aware, ongoing, deliberate adjustment to environmental dynamism through accumulating engineering and managerial experience, continuous technical refinement, and self-guiding interaction. Specifically, this finding complements earlier research demonstrating that ordinary capabilities may provide opportunities for learning, although primarily at the dynamic capabilities level (Newey & Zahra, 2009). Moreover, this finding challenges a view in which the relation between dynamic and ordinary capabilities is mainly sequential, where dynamic capabilities set the direction for subsequent ordinary capabilities (Newey et al., 2012). Instead, continuously evolving ordinary capabilities fruitfully can be considered to play an important role Journal Pre-proof 27 throughout ongoing adjustments to dynamic environments. While they may not be sufficient to ensure firm survival and performance in dynamic environments, and thus not replacing dynamic capabilities, our findings demonstrate that ordinary capabilities offered crucial contributions to the case firm’s before and during adjusting to environmental dynamism. They did so in a purposeful manner traditionally restricted to dynamic capabilities (Helfat et al., 2007), thus complementing prior theoretical understanding of ordinary capabilities. Taken together, our findings also complement traditional views of dynamic capabilities in which the sensing of new business opportunities is regarded as concentrated within top management, and where ordinary capabilities associated with lower management are unable to adjust to external dynamism because they are not “typically expected to discover the need for and to design new enterprise-wide operating routines, as this constitutes evolutionary fitness" (Teece, 2007: 1346).” Our data suggest that at least under certain conditions, both sensing and seizing can occur at both organizational levels, whereas seizing of ordinary capabilities can be associated with endogenously evolving routines. Our findings thereby suggest a new role for ordinary capabilities, that of evolving purposefully in relation to and contributing to a firm’s response to environmental dynamism. 5.2 Control of evolving ordinary capabilities Attention to endogenously and mindfully evolving capabilities at Pulp&Paper also draws attention to the ways in which dynamic capabilities intervene in ordinary capabilities. Traditionally, dynamic capabilities intervention assumes the initiation of change by configuring and deploying (Helfat et al., 2007), releasing (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000), and leveraging of static ordinary capabilities (Danneels, 2011). Although such interventions necessary to the focal Journal Pre-proof 28 project were visible in our data, e.g., the managerial decision to invest resources in a test facility, our findings broaden the repertoire of dynamic capabilities to theorize their role in managing endogenously and mindfully evolving ordinary capabilities. Extant research acknowledges that a condition for successful dynamic capability intervention in ordinary capabilities is that the latter must be correctly assessed or monitored; otherwise, firms will be unable to reallocate ordinary capabilities with sufficient efficiency (Danneels, 2011). In its focus on static ordinary capabilities, however, current theorizing has largely overlooked the risk of failure of a firm’s adjustment to a dynamic environment because of obsolete perceptions of dynamic ordinary capabilities; both what ordinary capabilities are available and at what level of development. Important roles therefore can be added to those typically ascribed to dynamic capabilities. We suggested the terms “mapping” and “creating a shared view” to denote the activity, whereby continuously evolving ordinary capabilities are identified as such and allocating or otherwise influencing them by dynamic capabilities is made possible. Moreover, as a complement to the need to initiate change in inert ordinary capabilities (Teece, 2007), boundary setting appeared in our data as a role through which dynamic capabilities could (e.g., through modularization) reduce the scope for change or variance while not impeding the evolution of ordinary capabilities. This was important in our data, as the endogenously evolving ordinary capabilities were recognized as central to competitiveness, and too heavy-handed intervention with dynamic capabilities could risk interfering with ordinary capabilities. Thus, the repertoire of dynamic capabilities of accessing, integrating, leveraging, and releasing (e.g., Danneels, 2011) can be expanded with new roles: mapping, creating a shared view, and boundary setting. Conclusion Dynamic capabilities research is concerned with explaining firms’ adaptation to dynamic environments, with particular emphasis on rapid and flexible product development (Barreto, 2010; Helfat & Peteraf, 2009; Teece et al., 1997), however, paying limited empirical attention to the central issue of how dynamic capabilities relate to ordinary capabilities. Our starting point was recent research indicating that change in ordinary capabilities may be inevitable (Rerup & Feldman, 2011) and can evolve through mindful individuals (Salvato, 2009). Our focus on the relation between dynamic and ordinary capabilities allows advancing extant theoretical understanding of dynamic capabilities, especially challenging the traditional binary attribution of change only to dynamic capabilities, and embracing the dynamism of ordinary capabilities. Our study allows us to make three contributions to the theoretical understanding of dynamic capabilities. First, this study contributes to dynamic capabilities research by elaborating mindful and evolving quality of ordinary capabilities. Our findings show different ways in which mindfully evolving ordinary capabilities contribute to firm adaptation, including drawing on evolving engineering knowledge and experience and on network relationships. Ordinary capabilities are not restricted to remain static or change through unintended slipping or mutating. Our study thereby contributes to the extant theoretical understanding of dynamic capabilities by modifying key assumptions underpinning dynamic capabilities research. Second, at an aggregate level, our in-depth, longitudinal approach has allowed us to extend existing dynamic capabilities research that previously has been dominated by distanced, reductionist approaches (cf. Burgelman, 2011). Replacing a strict conceptual separation Journal Pre-proof 30 regarding the capacity for change and adjustment between dynamic and ordinary capabilities, this study contributes with new roles to ordinary capabilities. Our case data do not demonstrate that ordinary capabilities are sufficient to complete large-scale resource investments typically associated with dynamic capabilities (Helfat & Martin, 2015), but we demonstrate they can make important contributions to firms responding to environmental dynamism, a role that previous theory has restricted only to dynamic capabilities and suggesting a more nuanced relation between ordinary and dynamic capabilities. Consequently, and finally, our study also contributes to dynamic capabilities research by complementing the currently dominating role of dynamic capabilities. Prior theory ascribes dynamic capabilities strategic value by initiating dynamism through actions such as reconfiguring and leveraging. We expand the repertoire through which dynamic capabilities intervene in ordinary capabilities to account for endogenous dynamism in the latter, suggesting mapping, creating a shared view and boundary setting, and, eventually, nurturing endogenously and mindfully evolving ordinary capabilities. Together, this study poses challenges to key conceptual assumptions underpinning traditional dynamic capabilities research and replaces them with empirically founded roles and relations between key constructs and thus advances and nuances the understanding of what is arguably the central issue in dynamic capabilities research: how firms adjust to dynamic environments. Like all studies, this study has limitations that offer possibilities for future studies. Because our study prioritized depth, our data were limited to one case in a Scandinavian context that featured an egalitarian culture; this limitation may place boundary conditions on the applicability of our findings to other, more hierarchical contexts. Moreover, our study focused on a mature industry that was able to rely on existing processes and old patents, which can be expected to Journal Pre-proof 31 create boundary conditions for the generalizability of our conclusions. For instance, more dynamic environments could have furthered the development of dynamic capabilities. Future studies could compare the organizational ability of old and newly founded business ventures to respond to environmental dynamism, an ability that may depend on access to experienced staff. Additionally, the conclusions suggested here invite a further delineation of the role of dynamic capabilities by comparing organizational responsiveness in, on the one hand, industries in which technological achievements are quickly copied or surpassed by radically new technologies and, on the other hand, industries in which intellectual property offers advantages. Last but not least, future dynamic capabilities research could build on the findings from this study and draw on longitudinal approaches to trace adjusting efforts that have yet to receive more formal recognition, as well as uncover the paths regarding how ordinary capabilities evolve into dynamic capabilities. We suggest that practitioners consider the mindful evolution of ordinary capabilities in product development and, elsewhere, a potentially important source of responsiveness to dynamic environments; however, this should not come at the expense of attention to developing dynamic capabilities. In addition to their traditional roles in integrating, leveraging, and acquiring static ordinary capabilities, dynamic capabilities can play important roles in relation to endogenously evolving, and hence nonstatic, ordinary capabilities. Email:jjmf@ubi.pt (Received 9 October 2018; accepted 25 November 2019) Abstract The contribution of dynamic capabilities (DCs) to firm performance remains unclear and at the centre of debate. Based on a systematic literature review of 92 quantitative articles, the purpose is to explore how the DC– performance relationship have and should be assessed in the future. The most promising approach seems to be indirect, as it appears that DCs primarily causes change and intermediate outcomes, though far from being the most hypothesized relationship. Moreover, investigations employ a continuum of conceptualizations, ranging from very specific DCs to generic sets with theoretical divergences and overlapping. The same applies to the varied performance measures adopted, evidencing that the literature still has a long way to go. Based on a structured synthesis and analysis of existing studies, a conceptual model, recommendations and future avenues are proposed, along with areas of attention, which have both managerial and practical relevance, contributing to advancement within this research stream. Key words: systematic literature review; dynamic capabilities; performance; DC– performance relationship Introduction The dynamic capability view (DCV) is currently considered one of the most promising frameworks in the strategy agenda, aimed at identifying drivers of long-term firm survival and growth (e.g., Barrales-Molina, Martínez-López, & Gázquez-Abad,2014; Laaksonen & Peltoniemi,2016). In fact, research on dynamic capabilities (DCs) stands amongst the most prolific streams of research within the field of management for the last two decades (Albort-Morant, Leal-Rodríguez, Fernández-Rodríguez, & Ariza-Montes,2018), since the two seminal works by Teece, Pisano, and Shuen (1997) and Eisenhardt and Martin (2000) (Burisch & Wohlgemuth, 2016). Although the concept has been widely explored with recent efforts to consolidate both definitional and theoretical divergences (e.g., Eriksson,2014; Laaksonen & Peltoniemi,2016; Schilke, Hu, & Helfat,2018; Wilden, Devinney, & Dowling,2016), the literature remains fragmented, disparate and equivocal (Pezeshkan, Fainshmidt, Nair, Lance Frazier, & Markowski, 2016). Inconsistency between definitions, conceptualizations and measurements of key constructs and variables, along with tested relationships prevails. Perhaps, the most important relationship within this field of research is the one between DCs and performance (Barreto,2010). Yet, how the nature of such should be quantitatively assessed remains somewhat unclear and deserves attention (e.g., Di Stefano, Peteraf, & Verona,2014; Wilden, Devinney, & Dowling,2016), representing a literature gap.
