From contemporary political speeches to scholarly publications, the traditional responsibilities of higher education are typically defined as teaching, research, and service (Bok, 2003). However, within these broad, directional missions, colleges and universities are also expected to respond to societal changes, shouldering relatively new responsibilities such as skills training among older workers, improving education attainment levels among disadvantaged populations, and spurring economic development and innovation (Lumina Foundation, 2013, 2015; NGA, 2007; Zemsky, 2010). Colleges and universities receive many valuable privileges from local and national governments in support of the aforementioned social responsibilities. Most higher education institutions are designated as non-profit organizations and enjoy exemptions from income, property, and sales taxes; tax-exempt debt or bond authority (depending on the state); preferred eligibility for federal grants and contracts; favorable treatment of charitable giving; and—in the case of public universities—regular (albeit declining) state subsidies (Cahoy, 2015). Colleges and universities can also often benefit private interests through income-enhancing skills and credentials, televised and widely attended sporting events, licensable technologies, for-profit spinoff companies, and luxurious student amenities that provide revenues important to the operations of these institutions. Given these potential benefits and declining public investments, higher education institutions have become increasingly entrepreneurial, often pursuing income-generating opportunities while eschewing activities that may produce social benefits. The trend toward “academic capitalism” (Slaughter and Rhoades, 2004), “privatization and accountability” (Hearn et al., 2016), and “higher education-as industry” behavior (Gumport, 2000) has raised the ire of critics who contend that the confluence of declining public funding, entrepreneurial behavior, and increasing regulation have led to diminished social contributions from colleges and universities. Recent editorials and policy-focused technical reports show, for example, that as states continue to cut higher education funding, costs have skyrocketed as has student debt, degree completion and graduation rates have declined, and valuable technologies sit on the shelves of research universities. Perhaps more importantly, critics contend that both higher education institutions and the policy infrastructure that undergird their performance have changed little with regard to how social responsibilities are viewed and delivered (Lumina Foundation, 2013, 2015; NGA, 2007; Zemsky, 2010). Given the nature of higher education institutions, generating social impact must be the primary responsibility rather than the pursuit of private market opportunities. In fact, some revenue-generating activities such as Division I college sports may even pose serious operational and reputational risks to colleges and universities. However, perceptions of “unresponsiveness” in higher education should not necessarily be attributed to intransigence or greed but may instead be illustrative of the lack of understanding of how constructive change occurs within colleges and universities as well as the paucity of management frameworks that constructively guide change within academic environments (Kezar and Eckel, 2002b; Tierney, 1999). We seek to contribute to discussions of productive change within higher education by drawing from two streams of literature within the management disciplines. First, we draw from the voluminous corporate social responsibility (CSR) literature that discusses management issues attributed to tensions between the profit-generation mission of industry and its obligations to society (Crane et al., 2008; McWilliams and Siegel, 2001, 2011). We contend that colleges and universities face analogous tensions though their responsibilities are reversed; higher education institutions, so long as they are instruments of society, cannot allow revenue-generating activities to distract from their social contributions and must instead systematically find synergies between the two. Following Siegel (2009), we contend that a strategic perspective is critical not only for realizing social impact but also balancing social responsibilities with revenue-generating activities among colleges and universities. To this end, we introduce a strategic social responsibility (SSR) framework for higher education based on a dynamic capabilities perspective (Helfat et al., 2007; Teece, 2007, 2012, 2014; Teece et al., 1997). We derive our framework from the dynamic capabilities literature in direct response to Kezar and Eckel’s (2002b) plea for change-oriented management approaches that recognize the unique culture and organization of higher education institutions. As higher education institutions have become more entrepreneurial, so too have administrators looked to rationalist management strategies to drive organizational change, all-the-while employing an industry-like lexicon using efficiency, customer satisfaction, and market responsiveness in support of their efforts (Gumport, 2000). Kezar and Eckel (2002a) posit that management practices based on rationalist, universal principles not only drive institutional isomorphism among vastly different higher education institutions, they also violate their cultural norms typically thwarting substantive change (Eckel et al., 1998; Morphew and Eckel, 2009). Adapting a dynamic capabilities approach to higher education offers a promising alternative. According to Teece et al. (1997), dynamic capabilities are an organization’s “ability to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external competencies to address rapidly changing environments” (p. 516). Dynamic capabilities are focused on strategic change and a voluminous literature applies the concept to for-profit enterprises. Helfat et al. (2007) posit that a dynamic capabilities approach is also well-suited to non-profit organizations, such as colleges and universities, given that all organizations initiate change and must adapt to a rapidly changing society. Dynamic capabilities are outcomes-focused and may include the production of both public and private benefits. This flexibility allows us to create a derivative framework that prioritizes the fulfillment of higher education social responsibilities while also accounting for increasingly entrepreneurial behavior. We thus draw substantially on the emergent change-in-higher education literature to appropriately guide our conceptualizations of relevant strategy (Hearn, 1996; Kezar and Eckel, 2002a, 2002b; Kezar and Lester, 2009; Sporn, 1999). These institutions are outwardly social instruments, the purpose of which is to improve the intellectual and skill-based capabilities of students, provide knowledge important for addressing society’s greatest challenges, and engage communities in outreach that improves agriculture and social services (Erlich, 2000). To conceptualize social responsibility within in a higher education context, we draw from the voluminous CSR management literature. McWilliams and Siegel (2001) define CSR as “actions that appear to further some social good, beyond the interests of the firm and that which is required by law” (p. 117). Research has sought to understand how social responsibility relates to sustainable competitive advantage among firms (Husted and Salazar, 2006; McWilliams and Siegel, 2011). Cutting edge CSR concepts seek to integrate core business functions with their potential for positive social impact, a situation in which both society and the business can benefit (Husted, 2000). Furthermore, recent scholarship posits that CSR-related activities, such as green management strategies, should be viewed strategically and thus adopted only if these practices advance an organization’s value-creation goals (Siegel, 2009). Although social responsibility in higher education may share the same public value goals of CSR, the different context influences how one defines and measures responsibilities. In essence, it is fair to say that social responsibility in higher education is about balancing public interests and conflicting economic interests to ensure that social responsibilities—alternatively termed public good (Kezar et al., 2005) or public interest (Thelin, 2004)—are fulfilled in the course of carrying out core college and university missions. Our review finds that the extant literature related to social responsibilities within higher education focuses on specific obligations. The specific social responsibilities of institutions depend on their nature and mission. A research university of large size will have different responsibilities than a small liberal arts college. Colleges and universities must continuously pursue and secure resources in order to fulfill their missions: “no margin, no mission” (Weisbrod et al., 2008: 5). However, Weisbrod et al. (2008) also posit, “the pursuit of revenue is a double-edged sword—indispensible for financing the social mission [of colleges and universities] but a danger to the mission at the same time” (p. 8). The limited nature of society’s resources also spurs competition among higher education institutions for donations, research grants, licensable technologies, research stars, students, and athletes and coaches. It is within this increasingly competitive, revenue-driven environment that a strategy is necessary to ensure higher education institutions maintain focus on their social responsibilities (Geiger, 2004). While scholars have long applied strategy concepts to higher education (e.g. Keller, 1983; Morrill, 2010; Rowley, 1997)—and in contrast to the extant for-profit management literature (e.g. Siegel, 2009)—prior conceptualizations did not reconcile the primary social contributions of colleges and universities with emergent revenue-producing activities. To be clear, scholars have articulated the need for practical, management-focused frameworks to drive constructive change within higher education institutions and systems (e.g. Hearn, 1996; Kezar and Eckel, 2002a) and, within the public management literature, scholars have discussed the opportunities and challenges of strategic planning within non-profit organizations (Bryson, 2010). Critics nonetheless contend that robust strategic management frameworks have yet to emerge that would move higher education institutions away from reactionary and revenue-centric management decisions toward a more proactive emphasis on organizational sustainability and social impact (Albrecht et al., 2007; Barth et al., 2011; Longanecker, 2005; Van Ginkel, 2002; V otruba, 1996; Zemsky, 2010). Many contemporary higher education practices emulate scientific or rationalist views drawn from the for-profit management literature emphasizing productivity, accountability, efficiency, and cost control (Kezar and Eckel, 2002b; Longanecker, 2005; Zemsky, 2010). Constructive change within higher education In contrast to the aforementioned rational management approaches, constructive change within higher education is a 10- to 15-year undertaking and must account for the unique academic culture of colleges and universities (Kezar and Eckel, 2002a, 2002b). Unlike hierarchical organizations with multiple levels of management, colleges and universities are exceptionally decentralized. The governance of higher education institutions has traditionally been a shared model whereby faculty are responsible for curricula, student education and mentoring, and faculty promotion and hiring, with administrators—often drawn from faculty ranks—responsible for financial management, regulatory compliance, and internal and external policy issues. Several trends have eroded the shared governance model within the context of an increasingly hostile policy environment. First, the ranks of non-tenured faculty, such as teaching adjuncts and research faculty, have grown dramatically while the hiring of tenure-track faculty has declined (Hearn et al., 2016; Kezar and Gehrke, 2014). Second, the administrative staff of colleges and universities have grown, mirroring the expansion of various higher education programs and compliance functions. Finally, tenured and tenure-track faculty face ever-increasing expectations to publish, teach, engage in communities, and pursue extramural research grants, which hamper their capability to contribute to campus leadership (Kezar and Lester, 2009; Schuster and Finkelstein, 2006; Sorcinelli, 2007; Sorcinelli et al., 2006). These trends mean that the traditional academic core is increasingly disconnected from other, emergent higher policy policies and functions, such as technology transfer and regulatory compliance. Kezar and Eckel (2002a, 2002b) find that constructive change is dependent on how well managerial action fits the traditional mission and culture of individual higher education institutions. Specifically, constructive change relies upon grassroots initiatives and leadership, shared governance among faculty and staff, and the coordination of different actions to create awareness and build scale. Kezar and Lester (2009) recommend that higher education institutions not only reemphasize the role of core faculty in governance, but also that change-oriented decisions and initiatives include other academic personnel. The ultimate goal, according to Kezar and Eckel (2002b), is the creation of a sustainable culture of change and supportive processes for achieving this goal within disparate higher education institutions. A dynamic capabilities view While most change-oriented actions within higher education emulate rationalist, efficiency-seeking approaches, we look to a well-explored alternative within the management literature to conceptualize constructive change mechanisms among higher education institutions. Specifically, we draw from the deep management literature on dynamic capabilities (Helfat et al., 2007; Teece, 2007, 2012, 2014; Teece et al., 1997). According to Teece et al. (1997), dynamic capabilities are an organization’s “ability to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external competencies to address rapidly changing environments” (p. 516). In other words, dynamic capabilities are an organization’s capacities and processes to undertake constructive change. While change occurs slowly within higher education, we posit that the structural components of entrepreneurial management, including (1) strategy, (2) capabilities, and (3) resources in support of strategy and capabilities, are applicable to all organizations, including not-for-profit colleges and universities (Helfat et al., 2007). Strategy is “a coherent set of analyses, concepts, policies, arguments and actions that respond to challenges” (Rumelt, 2011: 6). Teece posits that strategy and capabilities are symbiotic: organizational focus relies upon what is it capable of achieving or its ability to build capabilities to do so. While colleges and universities may have become adept at creating organizational priorities through strategic planning, effective management frameworks must also focus on its implementation and continual renewal (Teece, 2012). A capability is the ability to perform a particular task or activity that has evolved through organizational learning, resources, and history (Helfat et al., 2007; Teece, 2012). Teece (2014) articulates two types of capability: ordinary and dynamic. Ordinary capabilities involve the basic administrative, operational, and governance-related elements of an organization. The performance of ordinary capabilities depends on skilled personnel, facilities and equipment, organizational routines, and administrative coordination. The improvement of ordinary capabilities is typically incremental, valuing productivity, efficiency, speed, and quality. Teece (2014) posits that ordinary capabilities are easily replicated and that organizations guide their understanding of ordinary capabilities by seeking out “best practices.” As mentioned earlier, best practice approaches can lead to institutional isomorphism and a diminished ability to differentiate (DiMaggio and Powell, 1983). Within higher education institutions, the capacity to teach in-person undergraduate classes exemplifies an ordinary capability, a capability possessed by nearly all colleges and universities. Incremental change is reflected in increasing class sizes, use of technology, and use of non-permanent teaching staff (Kezar and Gehrke, 2014; Lohmann, 2005; Zemsky, 2010). Furthermore, competition among higher education institutions is manifest in an “arms race” to attract talented faculty and students, as well as build specialized programs and facilities in hopes of capturing additional resources and prestige (Weisbrod et al., 2008). These competitive tactics are not only similar—isomorphic—among many colleges and universities, they also overlook organizational processes and capacities to undertake constructive change as ways to better fulfill social responsibilities and differentiate competitively. As discussed, dynamic capabilities are an organization’s capacity to respond to outside environments and affect constructive change. Teece (2012) posits that dynamic capabilities can be broken into three elements: (1) sensing—the identification and assessment of threats and opportunities, (2) seizing—the mobilization of resources to address threats and opportunities and to capture value, and (3) transforming—the reconfiguration and modifying of existing assets. Organizational effectiveness is dependent on mobilization, what Teece et al. (1997) terms “asset orchestration.” This is a core aspect of dynamic capabilities that involves asset identification and investment within internal, non-market contexts, then configuration and deployment to support productive, synergistic goals (Helfat et al., 2007; Hitt, 2015). Teece (2012) views dynamic capabilities as embedded within the senior leadership of an organization as well as within what he terms change routines. He goes on to discuss the risk to organizations “... if the sensing, creative, interpretive, and learning functions are left to the cognitive capacities of a few individuals.” Within higher education, Kezar and Eckel (2002a, 2002b) similarly find that change initiatives within colleges and universities cannot only depend on administrators who will soon move on to their next assignment nor can change only be driven by a small group of senior faculty; change initiatives must include all faculty ranks and other higher education personnel as well as robust processes for discussing and implementing change. Toward SSR The framework We introduce the SSR framework, the goal of which is to serve as a conceptual guide for the fulfillment of social responsibilities of colleges and universities. SSR embraces Teece’s (2012) emphasis on entrepreneurial management that views change not in terms of rational approaches that emphasize standardized analysis and optimization but instead as deliberative, non-linear processes that generate long-term social impact and reinforce a change-oriented culture. To be clear, change-oriented—entrepreneurial—activities within the context of SSR differ substantially from the aforementioned concepts of academic capitalism (Rhoades and Slaughter, 2004) or higher education-as-industry views (Gumport, 2000) in which change-oriented activities are viewed primarily negatively and in terms of revenue generation. Instead, we assume that the primary change-oriented responsibilities of colleges and universities should relate to their public missions and are critical to their impact. We assume that the missions of higher education—teaching, research, and outreach as well as the more recent views on economic development and technology commercialization and sustainability—are slow to change (if at all), while specific social responsibilities Figure 1. Strategy While higher education institutions have become adept at engaging stakeholders in strategic planning processes, less emphasis is often placed on the organizational systems or culture (Kezar and Eckel, 2002b). Thus, the implementation of these plans does not occur as strategies are quickly rendered obsolete by changing political or social trends. Furthermore, contemporary strategies often prioritize revenue-producing activities that may (or may not) be aligned with higher education social responsibilities (Zemsky, 2010). In contrast, we believe that strategy within the higher education context is akin to Rumelt’s (2011) holistic view of organizational activities that respond to challenges, articulate forward-looking organizational priorities, and take into consideration exactly how strategies will be implemented. Of course, this does not diminish the importance of strategies themselves. Thornton and Jaeger (2007), for example, note the importance of organizational strategies among colleges and universities that can be “cited by biology professors, groundskeepers, and athletic directors alike,” not to mention policymakers and the general public (p. 994). Importantly, adopting an evolutionary view of strategy associated with dynamic capabilities allows colleges and universities to choose what responsibilities they will not fulfill over time, a critical component for maximizing impact (Porter, 1996). Furthermore, some colleges and universities may—together with other stakeholders—reconsider various organizational missions, reframe them under other mission areas, or choose to partner with other organizations to fulfill them. For example, our review of the higher education literature found that the so-called economic development mission of higher education institutions is frequently viewed in terms of the formal technology transfer role of research universities along with its associated revenue-generating benefits. Formal technology transfer includes the disclosure, evaluation, and patenting (or not) of technologies derived from university research (Phan and Siegel, 2006; Rothaermel et al., 2007; Shane, 2004). Recent commentary, however, finds that current policies and practices related to formal technology transfer may have a detrimental impact on other higher education social responsibilities, such as the rapid dissemination of new knowledge and suboptimal economic development and technology commercialization outcomes (Bradley et al., 2013a; Hayter, 2016a). This assumption is supported in the higher education literature, which shows constructive change rarely occurs in colleges and universities without grassroots leadership from a broad range of academic staff (Kezar and Lester, 2009, 2011). Many colleges and universities already possess these elements but rarely have they been conceptualized strategically and in direct support of social responsibilities. The sections below provide additional detail for each component of a robust orchestration infrastructure. Sensing opportunities and threats related to social responsibility. First, following Teece (2012), internal and external “sensing” is critical to understand opportunities and threats for higher education institutions. Internal sensing is the capacity to understand potential and existing efforts relevant to the social responsibilities of a college or university. Internal sensing mechanisms can be informal, such as periodic conversations among faculty and staff over coffee or lunch—or more formal through regularly scheduled meetings, online tools, and individuals dedicated to facilitating understanding of ongoing efforts. Internal sensing is not only important for cataloging myriad activities within higher education, it is necessary to identify individuals and their respective activity areas that may align with the interests of others on (or off) campus and making connections among them. Furthermore (and discussed below), sensing provides faculty and staff with an understanding of how their ongoing activities and ideas relate to broader institutional priorities—or might lead to new priorities. External sensing includes systematic efforts to understand trends, threats, and opportunities outside of higher education organizations. External sensing might create a better understanding of political dynamics and how they relate to, for example, annual higher education appropriations within a specific state and what these mean to specific organizational functions or organizational priorities. External sensing can also be forward looking focusing, for example, on emerging research grant opportunities from the federal government or from a specific industry. In both examples, sensing provides valuable information inputs important for orchestration: should resources be mobilized, relative to other priorities, in order to take advantage of potential opportunities or to mitigate various threats? Critical to sensing is how knowledge is communicated and how individuals with areas of common interest are connected. Kezar and Eckel (2002b) find that colleges and universities use a variety of internal communication vehicles, such as newsletters, emails, dedicated websites, and periodic reports for this purpose. The authors also find that even more important are individuals whose specific purpose is to identify and match similar efforts across campus (e.g. vice president for transformation) as well as cross-campus networking events that enable individuals who share common interests to connect. In-person networking also allows for the identification of individuals who may potentially lead new initiatives on campus. The communication of evolving organizational strategic goals and activities to the general public and other stakeholders is also critical. Media, public, and government relations, personnel “embedded” in mainstream activities within a college or university, have traditionally supported outside communications. Research shows, however, that academic knowledge is best exchanged through boundary-spanning intermediaries. Contemporary examples include education outreach personnel, agriculture extension agents, and industry liaisons (McDowell, 2001; Wagner, 1993; Walshok, 1995). Scholars further recommend that colleges and universities go beyond discrete programs (e.g. agriculture extension) and build cross-organizational boundary-spanning capabilities (Boyer, 1991; Kantanen, 2005; McDowell, 2001; Nowotny et al., 2001; Strand et al., 2003). Such a function could support the strategic direction of higher education organizations. Seizing opportunities. As mentioned, constructive change within the SSR framework hinges on enabling and scaling the entrepreneurial actions of individual faculty , students, and staff. Colleges and universities thus require the capacity to determine the aforementioned strategic direction of the organization as well as how to best realize this direction within the context of their unique organizational culture. While decision-making infrastructure should include faculty, Kezar and Eckel (2002a, 2002b) recommend that it also include other higher education personnel and, when appropriate, outside stakeholders. Faculty (among others) must first be involved in determining the social responsibilities of organizations in collaboration with internal and external stakeholders. Emphasis should be placed on strategies that prioritize scalable goals and impact—in support of well-accepted institutional missions. Furthermore, decision-making bodies should be charged with determining the extent to which ongoing higher education activities support or detract from the ability of colleges and universities to fulfill their respective mission(s). Importantly, the ability to determine strategies should be intimately linked with the orchestration capability acknowledging that specific mechanisms will differ by higher education institution. For higher education institutions with a relatively focused mission (e.g. education within community colleges), emphasis may be on inclusion supported by, for example, broadly available micro grants to individuals working collaboratively to advance education-related social responsibilities writ large. In contrast, large research universities may choose to prioritize a specific social responsibility (e.g. undergraduate, community-based research) and competitively award packages that include program funds as well as coordinating personnel to support this purpose. Regardless, the availability of resources (discussed below) should follow well-structured, transparent processes designed by respective decision-making bodies. Transforming assets to fulfill social responsibilities. Perhaps the most dif ficult part of a dynamic capabilities–focused strategy for social responsibility in the context of higher education is the willingness to transform resources. The ability to transform defines, to a great extent, whether an organization can make use of dynamic capabilities (Teece, 2014). Firm assets have a tendency to ossify after a period of time and it can be difficult to change course quickly or abandon investments in people and programs. Ossification is even more common in public and non-profit bureaucracies; similar to government programs, higher education initiatives are difficult to cancel or redirect long after they are created (Zemsky, 2010). Thus, as Teece (2014) notes, transformative capabilities must be exercised periodically within higher education to “soften the rigidities” that accumulate over time. Dynamic capabilities focus on the transformation of assets that underlie both ordinary and dynamic capabilities. Colleges and universities possess numerous assets that might support the strategic renewal of, for example, their teaching responsibilities, including faculty, facilities, and information technology (IT). Effective renewal, however, depends on the extent to which asset transformation is guided by strategy: assets must be orchestrated for the purpose of fulfilling specific social responsibilities. For example, many higher education institutions have responded to growing student enrollment and mounting costs by rapidly increasing the number of adjunct or “faculty associates” who teach within their institutions (Jacoby, 2006; Kezar and Gehrke, 2014; Kirk and Spector, 2009). In this way, assets have been allocated to bolster higher education teaching capabilities in a way that emphasizes cost reduction and flexibility, reflecting a rationalist management approach. However, the growth of temporary instructor pools has been associated with a decline in student learning and, perhaps more importantly, a diminished strategic emphasis on teaching. Emerging social responsibilities associated with teaching, such as enabling individuals from disadvantaged backgrounds to afford and successfully complete a higher education degree, are increasingly disconnected from other missions, such as research and outreach (Jacoby, 2006; Kirk and Spector, 2009; Zemsky, 2010). Perhaps more troubling is that the failure to conceptualize teaching capabilities strategically will likely result in a diminished ability for higher education institutions to respond to the future learning needs of society while further isolating teaching from other social responsibilities within colleges and universities. A dynamic capabilities perspective emphasizes the continual transformation of assets in support of overall organizational performance. In the example above, adjunct hiring is often reactionary with little attention paid to individual teaching quality (though the same often holds true for tenuretrack faculty). However, dynamic capabilities approach to transformation might include the development of a professional cadre of capable, clinical instructors who specialize in how different populations learn and the efficacy of corresponding pedagogical approaches. Additionally, such an approach could employ a flexible vision of technology use, moving beyond the cost saving perspective of online education to contexts that enhance education experienced beyond that provided by in-person instruction (Duderstadt et al., 2005; Lohmann, 2005). Colleges and universities could also use aforementioned sensing mechanisms to understand the shifting learning needs of different populations and articulate associated learning objectives—and how these change over time. Furthermore, a dynamic capabilities approach would ensure that the transformation of assets supporting teaching-related capabilities is aligned with the transformation of assets supporting other capabilities. For example, the original intent behind the establishment of research universities was to continuously inform curriculum with the latest findings from research (Thelin, 2004), a practice that rarely happens systematically within higher education institutions today. However, effective orchestration of co-specialized teaching and research assets within a dynamic capabilities framework would help ensure that these objectives align thus helping to fulfill social responsibilities. Legal education is a good example whereby the inability to transform assets in terms of redeploying faculty or embracing new types of students leads to higher education functions that are not only largely disconnected from the needs of society, they are also resistant to change. Despite the shock of dramatically declining interest from both students and employers, law schools have had difficulty modifying a high-tuition-based funding model (Campos, 2012). There is even strong evidence of the need to pivot to take advantage of the social responsibility opportunities in serving lower income and other vulnerable populations. However, schools are saddled with a decades-old system that has not provided incentives for change, as well as high-cost employees and dedicated physical assets, all of which limit transformational capabilities. Those who might participate in the transformation have little incentive to do so, as the consequences of failing to respond to changing condition—namely, job loss—tend to arise only when an institution is in truly dire straits (Mangan, 2016). The inability to orchestrate teaching capabilities to respond to a changing environment likely means that law schools will continue to serve a smaller and smaller population and at the same time dwindle in their ability to fulfill social responsibilities. Perhaps the best-known example of the inability to transform assets within higher education is the current tenure and promotion system. Tenure—in its current form—is essentially a job protection system that limits an institution’s ability to modify responsibilities because of the long-term institutional commitment without significant administrative oversight or performance review. Of course, the original purpose of tenure was as a mechanism to protect academic freedom (Thelin, 2004; Zemsky, 2010). An SSR approach would not lead to an arbitrary elimination of tenure—as many rationalist critics have suggested—but rather it would emphasize the transformation of (in this case) processes and other human resource–related assets in a way that protects academic freedom while providing organizational flexibility to adapt to changes in society. Absent the ability to adapt, we are likely to see the continuing growth of a “two-tier” system between dwindling ranks of tenured and tenure-track faculty and a rapidly growing temporary workforce, largely to the detriment of higher education missions. Finally, assets underlying dynamic capabilities—embodied in an orchestration infrastructure— must themselves be renewed. In practice, renewal might focus on the extent to which an orchestration infrastructure must co-evolve with strategy to reflect the changing needs of society. For example, sensing and project management processes themselves can be revised in response to changing conditions. Existing self-regulatory mechanisms that inhibit those needed to seize opportunities should be revised and any new mechanisms should be subject to revision. It is important to keep in mind that not only should the assets and existing operations be subject to transformation, but the dynamic processes themselves. Supporting resources and policy According to Teece (2012), resources should support symbiosis between strategy and capabilities in fulfillment of specific actions. SSR is focused on improving the impact of higher education social responsibilities so resources should be deployed in a way that will enable faculty and staff to initiate and scale associated efforts. Financial resources can be used to fund infrastructural elements mentioned above, such as communication platforms, facilitated meetings, and outside evaluation. Perhaps more important, however, are human resources that directly support the initiation and growth of change-oriented initiatives. First, colleges and universities could provide faculty with course buy-outs as well as student and administrative support. Second, training, conference support, and travel grants—seed grants—could be made available in areas of relevant interest. Finally, colleges and universities could recruit support staff (and/or consultants) with complementary, functional skills important for the development of emerging projects. Depending of the potential scale of the project, staff might support problem-specific priorities, such as the development and commercialization of engineering software, or cross-functional capabilities areas such as project management, facilitation, or IT. Such hiring happens often, but if the aforementioned orchestration infrastructure exists, then higher education institutions can begin to explore opportunities to build robust “matrix” functions that cut across multiple colleges and departments (Geiger and Sá, 2008; Warshaw, 2016). Policy is another important consideration within the SSR framework. Internal policies should be designed that will support the goals of enabling entrepreneurial behavior in support of social responsibilities as well as their scaling. In many cases, individuals may not be aware of policy challenges that exist to entrepreneurship-minded faculty and staff. Colleges and universities might consider creating a “tiger team” that would be responsible for understanding and then facilitating the removal of policy-related challenges that might be associated with entrepreneurial behavior. Tenure and promotion policies notoriously preference research and publishing with little room made for community impact or change-oriented initiatives within colleges or universities. Furthermore, while faculty are typically evaluated based on service, this is often defined in terms of committees and curricular and/or hiring efforts. Colleges and universities could explore ways that would allow more differentiation among tenure-track faculty, especially at large research universities, based on prioritized social responsibilities. Furthermore, colleges and universities could create differentiated career paths for different higher education staff as opposed to the reactionary hiring of adjuncts each year, who may lack the pedagogical experience, institutional commitment, and compensation-based incentives of full-time faculty (Moser, 2014). Furthermore, higher education institutions must fulfill their missions within the context of disjointed political systems, declining public funding, and ever-increasing expectations to serve myriad public interests at the lowest cost possible. The social responsibilities of higher education serve as the foundation for their existence so we assume that the managerial actions of colleges and universities must reflect this priority. To this end, colleges and universities have added online degree programs, financial aid initiatives, offices of equity and inclusion, and programs to encourage and support environmental sustainability. Furthermore, higher education institutions have established entrepreneurship and commercialization initiatives, technology licensing offices, industry research institutes, new sports programs, and numerous student-centered services and facilities to generate revenue in support of these myriad activities. Yet, with the explosion of online and campus-based activity nonetheless comes the sense that colleges and universities can contribute more to society. Furthermore, revenue-generating activities may, according to Weisbrod et al. (2008), endanger the very missions they are meant to support by prioritizing private interests over public. We contend that these deficiencies have little to do with bad intentions or lack of effort but are, instead, symptomatic of the need for organizational management tools analogous to for-profit or public management frameworks, yet tailored to the unique social missions and impacts of colleges and universities. Managerial action must be strategic within the context of an increasingly hostile policy and funding environment—and an increasingly uncertain world. In response, we introduce an SSR framework based on the emergent concept of dynamic capabilities (Helfat et al., 2007; Teece, 2007, 2012, 2014; Teece et al., 1997). Strategic thinking is applied in the context of the private sector as a means for firms to obtain a sustained competitive advantage. But while colleges and universities compete for limited resources, this in no ways diminishes their responsibilities to society. In fact, higher education institutions have an obligation to maximize the public benefits of their missions thus creating an organizational need to identify challenges, marshal resources, and initiate and sustain responses. SSR focuses on the articulation and prioritization of higher education strategies—reflecting evolving social responsibilities—among stakeholders, internal and external, the creation and continual renewal of underlying assets, as well as the deliberate deployment and alignment of higher education resources. SSR necessitates a deliberate response to changing demands within a diverse society guided by the mission-driven imperative to maximize social impact. SSR also provides an important advantage over rationalist management approaches increasingly employed by colleges and universities. Not only do rationalist approach view change as incremental, emphasizing productivity and efficiency, they do not recognize the unique culture and organizational requirements for productive change within higher education. On the other hand, SSR seeks to foster culture and processes that can foster the kind of decentralized, yet coordinated response necessary to respond to the needs of a rapidly evolving society and achieve scale critical to impact, especially among incredibly diverse higher education institutions (Helfat et al., 2007; Kezar and Eckel, 2002a, 2002b; Kezar and Lester, 2009). Our focus here has been on individual higher education institutions; yet, following a vibrant management literature (Teece, 2014), SSR is likely to be useful at multiple levels of observation including, for example, an individual department or large public university system level, or among disparate regionally based institutions. Galway, Ireland denis.dennehy@nuigalway.ie Prof. John Krogstie (Norwegian University of Science and Technology) Høgskoleringen 1, 7491 Trondheim, Norway john.krogstie@ntnu.no ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT 3 Abstract: While the topic of analytics is rapidly growing in popularity across various domains, there is s till a relatively low amount of empirical work in the field of operations research. While studies of various technical and business aspects of analytics are emerging in OR, little has been done to address how the OR community can leverage business analytic s in dynamic and uncertain environments – the very place where OR is supposed to play a key role. To address this gap, this study draws on the dynamic capabilities view of the firm and builds on eight selected case studies of operations research activity i n large organisations, each of whom have invested significantly in analytics technology and implementation. The study identifies fourteen analytics -enabled microfoundations of dynamic capabilities, essentially highlighting how organisations can use analyt ics to manage and enhance their OR activities in dynamic and uncertain environments. This study also identifies six key cross - cutting propositions emerging from the data and develops a roadmap for future OR researchers to address these issues and improve the use and value of analytics as enablers of organisational dynamic capabilities. Keywords: analytics, dynamic capabilities, agility, operations research 1. Introduction The popularity of analytics increased tremendously in the last decade, ‘rocketing’ to the top of the corporate agenda, with claims that “data is the new oil” to be “refined” to extract unprecedented value (Brown et al., 2011) . In the business world, the data deluge has sparked the interest of almost every industry to develop capabilities to extract insightful knowledge from data and achieve a competitive advantage (Provost & Fawcett, 2013) . Nevertheless, these new data sources are often too large, too complex, and are generated a nd become obsolete at such a speed that renders traditional analytics methods as ineffective in extracting any meaningful insight (Delen & Zolbanin, 2018). In response to these issues, novel methodologies and processing techniques have given rise to a new era in business decision making, referred to as the business analytics period (Mortenson, 2015). Business analytics is concerned with the context in which these tech niques are applied on big data1 to make sounder, more evidence-based business decisions (Seddon, Constantinidis, & Dod, 2012) . As a result , business analytics can enable descriptive, predictive, and prescriptive model building using diverse, re al-time, and “big” data sources (Duan, Cao, & Edwards, 2018; Hindle & Vidgen, 2018). Many in the operations research (OR2) community have cited the prominence of business analytics as an opportunity that could “promote the [ . . . ] profession and expand its reach” (Liberatore & Luo, 2010) and improve the prevalence an d effectiveness of OR activity in enhancing business value (Mortenson, Doherty, & Robinson, 2015; Vidgen, Shaw, & Grant, 2017). While there is a growing body of literature, on the value of business analytics in other domains such as information systems research (Abbasi, Sarker, & Chiang, 2016; Côrte -Real, Oliveira, & Ruivo, 2017; Seddon & Currie, 2017; Shanks, Bekmamedov, & Sharma, 2011; Shanks & Sharma, 1 In this study we base our definition of big data on having three main characteristics. These i nclude 1) volume - referring to the large amount of data, 2) velocity – referring to the speed that data is generated and processed, and 3) variety - referring to the multitude of sources and formats that the data include. Nevertheless, we also acknowledge that this data can be described by additional characteristics in accordance with relevant recent literature. 2 While there are numerous definitions of OR we, like many, adopt the Operational Research Society’s (2016) definition as “the discipline of applying advanced analytical methods to help make better decisions”. Specifically, however, we were guided by previous seminal studies such as the ten most prevalent OR techniques identified by Ranyard et al (2015), O’Brien et al (2011) and others. These are: spreadsheets (basic and advanced), statistics (basic and advanced), optimisation, strategic planning tools, simulation, forecasting, scheduling and decision support systems. Ranyard et al. (2015) refer to business analytics as a means to extend the scope of OR practice, but the exact relationship between business analytics and OR remains a topic of much debate (Duan et al., 2018; Royston, 2013). The body of work in this stream of business analytics research has also been criticised for an absence of theoretical grounding, for lacking clarity of de finition and scope, and represents “a noticeable resistance from the traditional OR community to the need to respond to the distinctive features of analytics” (Ranyard et al., 2015). Recent research has now started to address this gap, highlighting key OR challenges in eliciting value from business analytics (Vidgen et al., 2017), or providing frameworks for the deployment of OR analytics (Hindle & Vidgen, 2018). While it is encouraging to see this emerging stream of research, the extant literature to date has not specifically examined how organi sations leverage these technologies under conditions of turbulence and uncertainty to address emerging opportunities and threats (Mikalef, Pappas, Krogstie, & Giannakos, 2017). This is surprising for several reasons: (i) OR activities often become more valuable or indeed critical in highly uncertain, turbulent and dynamic environments (Constantiou & Kallinikos, 2015) . There is a rarely questioned assumption that our ‘now’ is more ephemeral, evanescent than ever before, and that any organisation's use of technology must help them su rvive and thrive in the seemingly never - ending change (Kavanagh, Lightfoot, & Lilley, 2007). (ii) Information is not static; hence, there is no option but for business analytics to handle ‘data in motion’, as the desired patterns and insights are a moving target (Abbasi et al., 2016). (iii) OR activities and analytics data typically have a time value (Grover et al., 2018) , and therefore, the speed with which OR activities can draw on business analytics to add va lue affects the value of that activity . For example, an analysis report five minutes before a meeting or before a share price announcement may be incredibly valuable; one second after that meeting or announcement, the value may drop to zero. (iv) Even in the unlikely event that the value of analytics data remains constant, the fundamental nature of that data changes over time. Such issues include the growing diversity of such data, the frequency by which it is updated, and the speed by which it grows (Davenport, 2014). As a result, failure of OR activities to incorporate such changes in nature reduce the value of the analytics function (Constantiou & Kallinikos, 2015). Given these reasons, managing this dynamic, changing nature of data necessitates that firms form an analytics-specific governance plan to elicit and maximise value that can be derived through business ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT 5 analytics. Notably, Mortenson et al. We address this call by adopting a dynamic capabilities perspective (Schilke, 2014a; Teece, 2007) to examine the use of business analytics in eight ‘revelato ry’ case studies of analytics -enabled OR activities. Theoretical Background 2.1 Dynamic Capabilities The Dynamic Capabilities View (DCV) has emerged as one of the most influential theoretical perspectives in the study of strategic management over the past decade (Schilke, 2014a). Grounded on the Schumpeterian logic of crea tive destruction, dynamic capabilities enable firms to sense and seize emerging business opportunities, and to transform their operations in order to adapt to changing market conditions (Teece, 2007). Despite considerable variation in definitions, there is increasing convergence on the idea that dynamic capabilities are purposefully developed and are comprised of a set of identifiable an d specific routines (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000) . These routines are commonly understood as learned, highly patterned, and repetitious, directed towards independent corporate actions (Winter, 2003). A key reason for much research attention on the notion of dynamic capabilities has been their proposed influence on important outcome variables (Schilke, Hu, & Helfat, 2018). Dynamic capabilities effectuate systematic change, by enabling renewal of operational capabilities and increased flexibility in response to market changes (Pezeshkan, Fainshmidt, Nair, Frazier, & Marko wski, 2016). These represent key areas in the attainment of a sustained competitive advantage (Teece, 2007). ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT 6 Dynamic capabilities hav e been disaggregated into three types of activities oriented toward strategic change, namely sensing new opportunities and threats, seizing new opportunities through business model design and strategic investments, and transforming or reconfiguring existin g business models and strategies (Helfat & Raubitschek, 2018; Teece, 2007) . Teece (2007) notes that sensing involves analytical systems of scanning, search and exploration activities across markets and technologies. Seizing on the other hand entails evaluation of existing and emerging capabilities, and possible investments in relevant designs and technologies that are most likely to achieve marketplace acceptance (Wilden, Gudergan, Nielsen, & Lings, 2013) . Finally, transforming includes continuous alignment and realignment of spe cific tangible and intangible assets (Katkalo, Pitelis, & Teece, 2010) . While prior empirical research has predominantly examined the outcomes of dynamic capabilities (Drnevich & Kriauciunas, 2011; Protogerou, Caloghirou, & Lioukas, 2011) there have been sev eral studies looking into the enablers of their formation (Capron & Mitchell, 2009) . Such investigations have looked at antecedents at different levels of analysis, including the organisational (Eisenhardt, Furr, & Bingham, 2010) , individual (Hsu & Sabherwal, 2012) , and environmental levels (Killen, Jugdev, Drouin, & Petit, 2012) , to isolate factors that either enable or hinder the formation of dynamic capabilities. Nevertheless, there is, to the best of our knowledge, no research that examines the impact of business analytics on the creation of dynamic capabilities, and particularly on each of the underlying types of activities that comprise them (see Table 1). Erevelles, Fukawa, and Swayne (2016) put forth a conceptual framework which suggests that business analytics can enable the generation and use of consumer insights to enhance dynamic capabilities of sensing and transforming. A particularly critical e nabler of processes underpinning dynamic capabilities is argued to be the data itself (Conboy, Dennehy, & O'Connor, 2018; Vidgen et al., 2017). Vidgen et al. (2017) find through a Delphi study that in realising business value the veracity of data is the number one concern for managers, followed by availability and access to data sou rces, and security and privacy. Follow on cases, showed that data veracity was a primary concern amongst managers. This finding denotes that the characteristics of the data, significantly influences reaction time, a key component of a firm’s dynamic capabi lities. In a recent study, Côrte-Real, Ruivo, and Oliveira (2019) show that attributes of the data along with the organisational structure built around leveraging such data has a direct influence on the formation of dynamic capabilities. Nevertheless, there are still some major gaps regarding the effect that business analytics and the supporting data may have on enabling a firm’s dynamic capabilities (Mikalef, Boura, Lekakos, & Krogstie, 2019a). This study addresses some of these key gaps. First, while there is a nascent stream of research examining the role of business analytics within OR activities, there are strikingly few papers examining the business value of business analytics in such activities (Hindle & Vidgen, 2018; Vidgen et al., 2017). The few papers dealing with this topic either outline core aspects that require consideration by managers when delving into business analytics for OR activities (Duan et al., 2018; Vidgen et al., 2017), or describe the frameworks for guiding practitioners with activities pertinent to analytics ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT 10 deployments (Hindle & Vidgen, 2018) . Despite the value of these studies, it is critical to explore the multitude of ways through which business analytics can support dynamic capabilities in OR activities and ultimately lead to business value. Second, despite many calls i n OR analytics research, there has been a lack of theoretical grounding of studies compared to other fields such as IS, and in particular in examining practice through the prism of theory (Ranyard et al., 2015) . This lack of theory -based research has been explicitly pronounced in the area of business value of business analytics -driven OR activities (Duan et al., 2018). Third, while research in other domains has started to e xamine the impact of analytics on business value adopting a dynamic capabilities perspective, such effects are either examined and described at a higher, aggregate level (Wamba et al., 2017) or for isolated dimensions (Torres et al., 2018) . In addition, the vast majority of such studies assumes causality of analytics through quantitative associations, therefore not exploring how busi ness analytics feed into the underlying processes that comprise a firm’s dynamic capabilities (Côrte-Real et al., 2017; Mikalef, Krogstie, Pappas, & Pavlou, 2019c). The present study aims to extend current knowledge by unearthing the micro -foundations of sensing, seizing and transforming, and delineating the complex role of business analytics in enabling dynamic capabilities in OR activities. Fourth, the predominant view in examining business value of analytics has been based on a perspective of limited heterogeneity in capturing such effects (Gupta & George, 2016). The vast majority of research has assumed that effects of business analytics on underlying dimensions of dynamic capabilities do not vary greatly, and that a largely uniform set of aspects contributes to business value (Günther, Mehrizi, Huysman, & Feldberg, 2017) . In this study we build on the premise that micro -foundations of dynamic capabilities in OR activities can be enhanced through different ways, and that there can be many alternatives to analytically enhance dynamic capabilities. Data Collection and Analysis Data were collected over an 18 -month period from January 2017 to May 2018. Data collection was primarily personal face -to-face interviews, a technique well suited to case study data collection, and particularly for exploratory research such as this, as it allows real -time clarification, expansive discussions which illuminate factors of importance (Oppenheim, 2000; Yin, 2009) , and reflexivity (Rubin & Rubin, 2011; Wengraf, 2001) by allowing the researcher to follow up on insights uncovered mid-interview and adjust the interview content and schedule accordingly. Interviews lasted between 40 and 120 minutes. The interview protocol was based on the three dynamic capabilities and six ‘V’s of ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT 14 analytics (Fig. 1). In this study, semi -structured interviewees with 26 key decision-makers at the cases studied who rely on OR techniques and analytic capabilities for the purpose of strategic and operational planning. Interviewees were selected using role -based sampling (Ikonen, Kettunen, Oza, & Abrahamsson, 2010) and their role, industry experience and knowledge of business ana lytics varied across the cases. To aid analysis of the data after the interviews, all were recorded with each interviewee’s consent, and were subsequently transcribed, proof-read and annotated by the researchers. In cases of ambiguity, clarification was so ught from the corresponding interviewee, either via telephone or e-mail. This approach afforded rich access to multiple data sources (Coghlan & Brannick, 2014) that are pertinent for longitudinal studies and it provided opportunities to obtain a detailed understanding of the empirical setting (Adler & Adler, 1994) . This data was supported by supplementary data sources that included analytics screenshots and reports, associated meeting minutes, and relevant e -mail communications. These sources were used to add context to the analysis of the cases studied and were analysed using the open and axial coding techniques. Data analysis: This was conducted through a number of steps. Each of the data sources was analysed using open and axial coding techniques proposed by Strauss and Corbin (1998) (see examples in Appendix A and B) . Coding began by looking for evidence of the constructs identified by dynamic capabilities (e.g. sensing, seizing, transforming) and the characteristics of big data (e.g. 6 Vs). The authors jointly coded the interview data to identify emerging novel themes and axial codes. Open Coding: Open coding is ‘the process of breaking down, examining, comparing, conceptualising, and categorising data’ (Strauss & Corbin, 1998) . Glaser (1992) argues that codes and categories should emerge from the data, while with Strauss and Corbin (1998) these are selected prior to analysis. The approach adopted in this study is more akin to the latter, where the data sources and subsequent analysis was based on the dynamic capabilities/6 V’s model (Fig. 1), and specifically the constructs underlying each (e.g. sensing, seizing, transforming). These provided a list of ‘seed categories’ (Miles, Huberman, & Saldana, 2013b) to structure data collection and the open coding stage of data analysis. Axial coding: Axial coding is defined by Strauss and Corbin (1998) as a set of procedures whereby data are put back together in new ways after open coding; whereas open coding fractures the data into categories, axial coding puts the data back together by making connections between the categories and sub -categories. As the data were coded, theoretical questions, propositions and code summaries arose. These were documented in ana lytic memos (Miles, Huberman, & Saldana, 2013a) to aid understanding of the concepts being studied and to refine further data collection. Memos can take many forms (e.g. diagrams, text narrative, propositions) and act as the pivital point for comparison and emergence, through which constant comparison is achieved (Charmaz, 2006; Glaser & Strauss, 2017) . Constant comparison was used to analyse data from different standpoints (Birks, Fernandez, Levina, & Nasirin, 2013), from which a number of analytics micro -foundations were identified for each construct ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT 15 (e.g. sensing, seizing, transforming), followed by the eme rgence of six propositions. Miles et al. (2013a) offer advice on effective analytic memos, and these practices were followed where possible. As categories emerged follow -up interviews were arranged with all the original interviewees to elicit further, richer, more focused information. This was done to confi rm, extend, and sharpen the evolving list of categories. As categories became integrated, further data collection did not tend to cause any additional categories to emerge, but rather reinforced those already in existence. At this point, the categories were deemed to be ‘theoretically saturated’ (Strauss & Corbin, 1998) , and data collection ended. Across all phases, to improve the re liability and repeatability of the research, an, ‘audit trail’ was sought from data collection through to the drawing of conclusions. Venting was used, whereby results and interpretations are discussed with professional colleagues to avoid the problem of w hat Kaplan and Duchon (1988) call multiple realities. 4. Propositions In this section we provide six propositions based on a cross case and cross theme analysis (sense, seize, transform). The propositions demonstrate that business analytics have different levels of relevance for companies when developing dynamic analytic capabilities to sense, seize, and transform opportunities. Proposition 1: Vs need to be adjusted across sensing, seizing and transforming to maximi se value . Previous research generally tends to analyse the value of a particular V. However, this study shows that a particular V may add more or less value as one moves from examining sensing to seizing to transforming in a particular context. For example, ITSolutions teams draw on large volumes of data from a variety o f sources such as Instant Messaging (IM) and digital Kanban boards to sense opportunities related to software quality (defects). Project managers respond to between 30 and 40 IMs during an 8-hour shift. The volume of text in an IM can range from a 10 to 10 0 lines, depending on the ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT 24 urgency and complexity of the request. However, when seizing these opportunities, the volume and variety of data was at times, overwhelming for teams (specifically during a major release) to process and identify root causes of def ects. As a result, teams missed defects, or misunderstood the severity of the defect. Similar issues were noted in LinkOne, where the large volume of data received from the networked devices was a core enabler of their sensing capability in identifying no des with a high probability of failure. However, the same volume proved to be a hindrance when the company tried to develop analytics to rank nodes according to their future risk of failure depending on weather forecasts. LinkOne initially faced the problem of a lack of human resources capable of conducting such analytics on large volumes of data, and insufficient processing power to accommodate such analyses. These circumstances led the company to seek guidance from experienced analysts at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, who were also able to provide the necessary hardware infrastructure and processing power to execute such analyses. This proposition therefore suggests that, in order to maximise value, organisations need to adjust the Vs when moving from sensing to seizing to transforming an opportunity. SoftCo’s dev eloper platform illustrated this, where developer teams can customise the platform to slow down the speed of data or turn on and off selected data sources as and when these Vs detract from value. Proposition 2: Siloing or lack of alignment between OR tools or techniques and Vs can affect overall value of analytics. As data was collected for this study, it became apparent that those collecting the data and those being interviewe d often talked about analytics generally. For example, many interviewed in SoftCo referred to “the team facing high volumes of real -time defect data” or there is a real focus of high veracity data in SoftCo. However, it became apparent that various OR tool s may exhibit very different characteristics, which often restricted or reduced the possible value from micro -foundations. As can be seen across the three sets of micro -foundations (Tables 5, 6, and 7), one micro -foundation was often supported by only one OR tool in each case, and so, while the overall volume, velocity or other may have been high in that case generally, the specific OR tool may not. Further, different OR tools are used in the same case across the sensing, seizing and transforming capabiliti es, and there was evidence to show that value may be lost if there is a disconnect between the OR techniques across these capabilities. Interviewees across all cases talked about their use of OR tools as separate tools rather than a collective suite of int erlinked tools. It emerged that OR tools were frequently used in isolation from other tools and techniques, which did affect the overall value of analytics within each case studied. Evidence of siloed thinking and siloed usage occurred within and across functions, which limited the value of analytics. For example, at ITSolutions, quality control charts are used to determine if a process (production line) requires calibration in order to ensure variations in the outcome do not occur. Historically, these char ts were manually created using spreadsheets for a specific function, did not provide root cause information, and were vulnerable to human error. Using powerful real -time analytical tools such as Tableau provide a single point of truth for teams across functions.
