Prior research shows that by adopting digital technologies, firms can contribute to their long- term success (Bharadwaj, 2000; George et al., 2020) and create competitive advantage (Nambisan et al., 2017; Pavlou & El Sawy, 2010), for instance, by penetrating a new market through digital distribution channels. To increase the entrepreneurial value of digital technologies and commercialize them, firms require an appropriate business model (Chesbrough, 2010). More specifically, to cope with the changes induced by digital technologies, firms need to engage in digital business model innovation (BMI; Teece, 2010, 2018b), which in accordance with Fichman et al. (2014, p. 335), we define as a “significantly new way of creating and capturing business value that is embodied in or enabled” by digital technologies and in which digital technologies are an essential element of the generated business value. One example of an established firm developing digital BMI is V oith, a traditional machine and plant manufacturer owned by fifth- generation family members, offering a vehicle communication platform that connects on- board systems in public transportation with several cloud- based functionalities (V oith Group, 2020). This example highlights the importance of digital BMI “being data driven,” and the relevant differences compared to conventional, nondigital BMI (Sorescu, 2017). While research generally agrees on the relevance of digital BMI, we still lack knowledge on how family influence, defined as the impact of the owning family’s decision- making “exercised through ownership and sometimes through the participation of family members in management” (Davis, 1983, p. 47), affects the firm’s digital BMI. This is important because family- influenced firms differ from other firms regarding innovation, for instance, due to their strong attachment between the family and the business (Chirico & Salvato, 2016; De Massis et al., 2016), their distinctive knowledge management mechanisms (Chirico & Nordqvist, 2010; Chirico & Salvato, 2008, 2016), and the concentration of the family’s wealth in the business, often accompanied by risk aversion (Chrisman et al., 2015; Kotlar et al., 2020). Although research has addressed family firm innovation (Duran et al., 2016; König et al., 2013), extant knowledge might not be easily transferred to the digital context given the complexity of digital BMI—for example, complex data processing, risk management, addressing new stakeholders, continuous innovation without a predefined end (De Massis, Di Minin, et al., 2015; Nambisan et al., 2017; Yoo et al., 2010)— and the potentially different drivers of digital innovation (Soluk & Kammerlander, 2021). As digital BMI is important for long- term business success (Remane et al., 2017; Sorescu, 2017; Teece, 2018b), family- influenced firms, known for their long- term perspective (Diaz- Moriana et al., 2020; Lumpkin & Brigham, 2011), need to especially focus on digital BMI. We propose that dynamic capabilities (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000; Teece et al., 1997) constitute an appropriate theoretical framework to understand the relationship between the level of family influence and digital BMI, as previous studies suggest that surviving in the digital era might require an adapted set of capabilities (Nambisan, 2017; Sambamurthy et al., 2003; Teece, 2018b). However, knowledge of how and which specific dynamic capabilities affect digital BMI is still lacking (Teece, 2018b). We assume that the level of family influence might affect the dynamic capabilities (more specifically, knowledge exploitation, risk management, and marketing capa - bilities) developed in the firm, and hence the level of digital BMI. Moreover, the impact of family influence might critically depend on how dynamic the environment is (Chirico & Baù, 2014; Wirtz et al., 2010), which could easily affect the development of new capabilities (Teece et al., 1997). This leads us to the following research questions: (1) What is the role of dynamic capabilities in the relationship between level of family influence and digital BMI? (2) How is this relationship affected by environmental dynamism? Answering these questions is important for several reasons. First, knowledge on the relationship between level of family influence and digital BMI is needed to advance our theoretical understanding of family firm idiosyncrasies regarding digital innovation (Kammerlander et al., 2018), which might differ from incremental process and product innovation (e.g., Classen et al., Soluk et al. 3 2014; De Massis, Frattini, et al., 2015). Second, focusing on dynamic capabilities will help explain the mechanisms through which family influence affects digital BMI, thus contributing to a more nuanced theoretical understanding of family firm innovation (Duran et al., 2016; König et al., 2013). To answer our research questions, we propose a set of hypotheses based on dynamic capabilities theory (Teece, 2018b; Teece et al., 1997) and test these on survey responses from 1,444 German firms with varying levels of family influence (including nonfamily firms). We make at least three contributions to the literature. First, by revealing a positive relation between family influence and digital BMI, we challenge prior research highlighting family firms’ difficulties in adopting more radical or discontinuous innovation (König et al., 2013; Patel & Chrisman, 2014). Accordingly, our study contributes to the family business innovation literature by highlighting the role of dynamic capabilities and the environmental context, two aspects that have not received sufficient scholarly attention so far (Chirico & Nordqvist, 2010; Reisinger & Lehner, 2015). Second, we contribute to research on digital BMI (Sorescu, 2017; Teece, 2018b; Zott et al., 2011) by providing theoretical and empirical insights into dynamic capabilities as antecedents of digital BMI and a nuanced explanation of the mechanisms leading to digital BMI. Third, we reveal insights into the role of specific dynamic capabilities for digital BMI, thus contributing to research on dynamic capabilities theory (Teece, 2018b; Teece et al., 1997) and dynamic capabilities in the digital economy (Karimi & Walter, 2015; Yeow et al., 2018). By revealing which dynamic capabilities are the most influential for digital BMI, we also provide relevant insights for management practice, especially for owners, managers, and advisors of family- influenced firms. Theoretical Background Our study builds on two literature streams: family firm innovation and digital BMI research. To combine these two research streams, we use the theoretical lens of dynamic capabilities. Innovation and (Digital) BMI in Family-Influenced Firms Continuous renewal through innovation is an essential requirement for an organization’s long- term success (Schumpeter, 1934), including family- influenced firms. Prior family firm research shows that product (De Massis, Frattini, et al., 2015) and process innovation activities (Classen et al., 2014) substantially differ from comparable innovation attempts in nonfamily firms due to the specific resources (Chirico et al., 2011) and often nonfinancial goals of family firms (Gómez- Mejía et al., 2007). In addition to product and process innovation, continuous renewal can also be achieved through BMI (Zott et al., 2011),1 defined as “designed, novel, nontrivial changes to the key elements of a firm’s business model and/or the architecture linking these elements” (Foss & Saebi, 2018, p. 201). Indeed, a growing body of research highlights the important role of BMI for long- term competitive advantage and survival, referring to the architecture of an organiza - tion’s value creation, delivery, and capture mechanisms (Foss & Saebi, 2018; Teece, 2010), and as such, the “core” of the business and its innovation processes. In particular, the emergence of digital technologies prompts firms to innovate their business models (Amit & Zott, 2001; Sorescu, 2017; Zott et al., 2011). Previous studies argue that digital technologies offer potential cost reductions (e.g., through automation; Bharadwaj, 2000) and the exploitation of new entrepreneurial opportunities (e.g., reaching new customers through novel functionalities; Nambisan, 2017; Soluk & Kammerlander, 2021). However, the opportunities inherent in digital technology adoption might only be fully realized if commercialized via BMI (Chesbrough, 2010; Hedman et al., 2016). Prior research labels the combination of BMI with digital technology adoption as digital BMI (e.g., Fichman et al., 2014; Remane et al., 2017).2 Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice 00(0)4 While family firm innovation is increasingly studied (Duran et al., 2016), there is still a lack of both theoretical and empirical research on how family- influenced firms deal with (digital) BMI. This is surprising given that the idiosyncrasies of family firms— such as the family’s strong attachment to the business (Chirico & Salvato, 2016; De Massis et al., 2016), distinctive learning and knowledge management mechanisms induced by their specific goals and resources (Chirico & Nordqvist, 2010; Chirico & Salvato, 2008), and risk aversion due to the concentration of family wealth in the firm (Chrisman et al., 2015; Kotlar et al., 2020)—may have a critical impact on how they engage in digital BMI. More specifically, the strong attachment between the family and the business fosters a control- oriented mindset in family- influenced firms (Chrisman & Patel, 2012), which might help them develop the capabilities needed for digital BMI initiatives more efficiently (Duran et al., 2016) and with more stamina (König et al., 2013). Moreover, with their distinctive learning and knowledge management mechanisms (Chirico & Nordqvist, 2010; Chirico & Salvato, 2008), family- influenced firms might also be particularly suited to developing digital BMI, which is characterized by knowledge intensity (Nambisan, 2017). Although there are only few studies on BMI in family- influenced firms in general, the initial insights tend to support the importance of BMI for long- term success. For instance, De Massis, Di Minin, et al. (2015, p. 12) argue that BMI is “a very powerful source of competitive advantage” in family firms, but they also point to the associated challenges, such as the “deeper changes to established routines and mental models” compared with product or process innovation. The Role of Dynamic Capabilities in (Digital) BMI Although digital BMI opens up entrepreneurial opportunities (Nambisan, 2017; Sorescu, 2017; Teece, 2018b), it is also particularly difficult to achieve (Correani et al., 2020; Nambisan et al., 2017) due to the reprogrammable and distributed nature of digital technologies inherent in digital BMI (Nambisan et al., 2017). To cope with the challenges of digital BMI (Veit et al., 2014), firms can build on their dynamic capabilities (Soluk & Kammerlander, 2021; Teece, 2018b). Dynamic capabilities are defined as a firm’s ability “to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external competences to address rapidly changing environments” (Teece et al., 1997, p. 516), hence distinguished from ordinary capabilities3 helping organizations manage their day- to- day routine activities and basic administration (Teece, 2014). Among the various dynamic capabilities that exist, three specific dynamic capabilities may be particularly important in the context of digital BMI (Easterby- Smith & Prieto, 2008; Teece, 2018a, 2018b; Troilo et al., 2017). First, knowledge exploitation capabilities, namely the recognition, internalization, and exploitation of internal and external knowledge (Easterby- Smith & Prieto, 2008; Martinez- Conesa et al., 2017; McKelvie & Davidsson, 2009), given the substantially different knowledge and technologies underlying digital versus nondigital business models (Bhatt & Grover, 2005; Ebel et al., 2016). Second, risk management capabilities (Arena et al., 2013; Teece, 2018a), which empower firms to manage the threats and uncertainties inherent in new digital technology adoption and related BMI (Teece, 2007), particularly cyber risks and protecting intellectual property, key aspects in the digital age (Greenstein et al., 2013; Teece, 2018a). Third, marketing capabilities, which provide firms with insights into (new) markets, (re) positioning the firm’s brand, and dealing with new customers or changing customer needs (Fang & Zou, 2009; Helfat & Winter, 2011). These dynamic capabilities are especially useful in times of digital change (Abrell et al., 2016), as they help firms establish novel customer- centric business models, thereby fostering competitive advantage. While research on conventional BMI has focused on dynamic capabilities, such as the identification of opportunities, commitment of resources, and realignment of structures (Teece, 2018b), we propose that the aforementioned three dynamic capabilities are particularly relevant for Soluk et al. 5 digital BMI for the following reasons. First, digital BMI is frequently described as much more complex than conventional BMI (Nambisan et al., 2017; Sorescu, 2017). While conventional BMI results in business models that usually remain in place for several years, digital BMI is often continuously developed further. The constantly changing nature of digital technologies inherent in digital BMI engenders repeated cycles of experimentation and implementation, making it unclear when a specific innovation process starts/ends or when an innovation outcome is “final” (Nambisan et al., 2017). This higher complexity compared to conventional BMI makes digital BMI particularly knowledge intense, and thus dependent on the firm’s knowledge exploitation capabilities. The higher complexity of digital BMI is also rooted in the fact that the inherent digital technologies are associated with higher risk. For instance, digital technologies make digital BMI increasingly vulnerable to cyber attacks and (data) privacy concerns (Nambisan et al., 2019). Additionally, the regular involvement of loosely organized crowds and other new external parties in the development of digital BMI challenges the prevailing liability norms and protec - tion of intellectual property (Faraj et al., 2011; Greenstein et al., 2013; Teece, 2018a; Yoo et al., 2012). This distributed nature of digital BMI, and the possibility for external parties to exploit at least some elements thereof, raises additional concerns, making digital BMI particularly dependent on risk management capabilities . Last, digital BMI is also associated with more rapidly changing customer needs and market developments compared to conventional BMI (Soluk & Kammerlander, 2021; Sorescu, 2017). As firms often address completely new customer segments and markets with digital BMI (compared to conventional BMI), they have to accumulate new in- depth insights on how these new customers and digital markets function (Fang & Zou, 2009; Helfat & Winter, 2011; Morgan et al., 2009). Moreover, advanced insights on digital markets and new customers might also help in coordinating complex external relationships in distributed settings (e.g., ecosystems) where digital BMI often emerges (Cennamo, 2020; Faraj et al., 2011). Consequently, the development of digital BMI is particularly dependent on marketing capabilities. While prior research has repeatedly conceptualized and studied these three dynamic capabilities (e.g., Easterby- Smith & Prieto, 2008; Morgan et al., 2009; Sen et al., 2020), and there are good reasons to assume they may enable digital BMI, we lack a systematic theoretical and empirical study on this relationship. Moreover, it is unclear how family- influenced firms perform with regard to digital BMI and how their idiosyncrasies may also affect the development of dynamic capabilities. Given that dynamic capabilities tend to be developed in governance structures with close social ties between individuals or groups and their repeated interactions, prior research views family businesses as a very relevant environment to study (Chirico et al., 2012). The intimate linkages between the family and the business, as well as their intergenerational traditions, suggest that family- influenced firms can internalize and reinterpret knowledge to help them develop dynamic capabilities (De Massis et al., 2016). Hypotheses Development In the following (Figure 1 for an overview), we theorize how increasing levels of family influence affect dynamic capabilities and how they in turn impact digital BMI. Furthermore, we argue a moderating effect of the environment, specifically environmental dynamism, as this contextual factor can affect organizations in their endeavors to develop dynamic capabilities (Teece et al., 1997). Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice 00(0)6 The Relationship Between Family Influence and Dynamic Capabilities With increasing levels of family influence, the often long- lasting links between the owning family and the business become more intimate, fostering the development of a shared tradition among family members (De Massis et al., 2016). This shared tradition involves high levels of trust, reciprocity, and proximity that family members develop and cultivate over time (Chirico & Salvato, 2016; Lumpkin et al., 2008), and ultimately high attachment of the family to the business (De Massis et al., 2016). This particularly strong attachment, which grows with increasing levels of family influence, results in the desire to create economic and social value across generations (Chirico & Nordqvist, 2010; Habbershon et al., 2003). Specifically, prior research emphasizes that strong attachment is accompanied by the ambition to integrate knowledge (Chirico & Salvato, 2008, 2016), as family members care even more about the firm and tend to contribute their expertise to further develop the business (De Massis et al., 2016). This is why strong attachment and high levels of trust and proximity enhance knowledge flows among family members (Chirico & Salvato, 2016). As a consequence, distinctive learning and knowledge management mechanisms increase with increasing family influence (Brinkerink, 2018; Chirico & Nordqvist, 2010). In particular, the heterogeneous experiences and knowledge rooted in the complementary perspectives of family members (Chirico et al., 2011; Kellermanns & Eddleston, 2006; Kotlar & De Massis, 2013), who might or might not be family firm managers with different educational and professional backgrounds, can lead to the productive orchestration of knowledge (Chirico, 2008). These complementary perspectives facilitate the exploitation of knowledge within family- influenced firms, and through their complementarity, raise awareness of relevant knowledge (potentially outside the firm and its industry), spawning paths to interpret and respond to this knowledge (Chirico et al., 2011). We argue that these distinctive learning and knowledge management patterns foster knowledge exploitation capabilities, which specifically depend on how well an organization performs in terms of accessing and rearranging knowledge. Thus, we assume that increased levels of family influence are positively associated with knowledge exploitation capabilities. In addition, as family influence increases, firms tend to become more long term (Lumpkin & Brigham, 2011) and control oriented (Chrisman & Patel, 2012) due to the increased focus on their financial and socioemotional endowments. This long- term orientation often motivates the family to cultivate harmony (Chrisman et al., 2012), a respected public perception (Dyer & Whetten, 2006), and the desire to transfer the firm to a family successor (Gimenez- Jimenez et al., Figure 1. Theoretical model illustrating the hypothesized effects. Soluk et al. 7 2020). The family’s aims to retain control over the firm is particularly reflected in the ambition to remain independent (Gómez- Mejía et al., 2007; Tagiuri & Davis, 1992) and reduce business risks (Gómez- Mejía et al., 2010; Kempers et al., 2019). These idiosyncrasies imply that increased levels of family influence are associated with careful risk assessment (Chrisman & Patel, 2012; Gómez- Mejía et al., 2007; Jones et al., 2008; Naldi et al., 2007), as lavish business risks might endanger their financial and nonfinancial endowments (Gómez- Mejía et al., 2007). To counter these potential business risks, increasing family influence may be accompanied by the family’s strengthened involvement in assessing such risks. This risk evaluation process is again supported by the broad and complementary experiences of various family members (Kammerlander et al., 2020; Kotlar et al., 2020), who may turn this evaluation into a collective learning process (Lumpkin & Lichtenstein, 2005). We argue that the risk- related learning mechanisms and accumulated expertise of families in how to deal with risk over time foster the development of risk management capabilities (Arena et al., 2013; Teece, 2018a). In other words, the accumulated knowledge of risk that builds with increasing family influence, aiming to control the situation now but also in the future, allows preserving the family’s financial and nonfinancial endowments, and utilizing complementary expertise in evaluating critical business decisions. Hence, we propose that increasing levels of family influence are positively associated with risk management capabilities. Moreover, due to their strong focus on tradition (De Massis et al., 2016) and sustaining steady and long- term partnerships (Lumpkin & Brigham, 2011), firms with increased levels of family influence are particularly associated with nurturing trustful network ties with customers and other established business partners (Duran et al., 2016). As increased levels of family influence are also related to business control (Salvato & Melin, 2008) and power- centricity in the hands of family owners (De Massis et al., 2021; König et al., 2013), the owning family is in the position to decide with which business partners to cooperate. When the owning family sees collaborations as useful to its financial and nonfinancial endowments, it is more able and willing to engage in such partnerships (Chrisman et al., 2015). Thus, for the owning family, not only the revenue generated, but also the firm’s reputation or “desire to make a mark” and its legacy are important (Diaz- Moriana et al., 2020, p. 10). This might be particularly true for long- standing and proven relationships with customers and business partners (Duran et al., 2016), but also for other relationships, for example, with online communities and loosely organized crowds (Boudreau et al., 2011; Mollick, 2014). In view of their less bureaucratic decision- making, firms with increased levels of family influence might have fewer formalization- related obstacles to engage in new collaborations (Chrisman et al., 2015; De Massis, Frattini, et al., 2015), and due to their efficient implementation structures, might have more stamina in perpetuating them (König et al., 2013). Thus, increased levels of family influence induce firms to align their external ties with their family objectives (De Massis, Audretsch, et al., 2018; Duran et al., 2016). Accordingly, we argue that increased levels of family influence and efficient decision- making also lead to a very conscious selection of market activities. Stronger interactions with customers are found in firms with higher levels of family influence (Duran et al., 2016). Therefore, we argue that the greater efficiency and customer focus implied by increased levels of family influence are especially important when developing marketing capabilities, since they allow quickly reacting and addressing changing market conditions based on the expertise deriving from former customer interactions. Accordingly, we expect that increased levels of family influence are positively associated with marketing capabilities. In sum, we argue that increased levels of family influence are associated with a higher degree of knowledge exploitation capabilities (as family influence is related to complementary perspectives), a higher degree of risk management capabilities (due to their long- term and control focus), and a higher degree of marketing capabilities (due to their customer focus and decision- making efficiency). Thus, we hypothesize: Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice 00(0)8 H1a: Increased levels of family influence are positively related to dynamic capabilities. The Relationship Between Dynamic Capabilities and Digital BMI Next, we examine the effect of dynamic capabilities on digital BMI, focusing on the three specific dynamic capabilities introduced above. Knowledge exploitation capabilities enable firms to access and recombine knowledge, manage learning mechanisms, and leverage new knowledge for the creation of business value (Easterby- Smith & Prieto, 2008; Forsman, 2011; Paarup Nielsen, 2006). We argue that these dynamic capabilities are particularly relevant for digital BMI. Previous studies highlight that digital BMI is complex (Nambisan et al., 2017; Sorescu, 2017), since the digital components are often “reprogrammable” to “perform a wide array of functions” (Yoo et al., 2010, p. 726), ultimately leading to an ongoing innovation process (Müller et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2010). While conventional BMI is usually developed for several years, digital BMI is often continuously developed further (Nambisan et al., 2017). These characteristics make knowledge exploitation capabilities particularly important in the context of digital BMI. Moreover, knowledge exploitation capabilities enable firms to deal with uncertainty (Easterby- Smith & Prieto, 2008; Martinez- Conesa et al., 2017), particularly prevalent when pursuing digital BMI due to its often discontinuous nature (Vial, 2019). The uncertainty associated with digital BMI is especially rooted in the novelty or even immaturity of some related technologies (Ceipek et al., 2021), the uncertain outcomes of business processes needed to develop digital BMI (Nambisan et al., 2017), and the partial lack of knowledge of stakeholders involved in the development of digital BMI (e.g., in case of anonymous, large- scale open innovation and crowdsourcing campaigns; Boudreau et al., 2011; Mollick, 2014; Nambisan, 2017). Furthermore, prior research also highlights the role of knowledge exploitation capabilities in coping with information overload (Ceipek et al., 2021; Yoo et al., 2010, 2012), specifically “technostress,” caused by digitalization overstraining organizations and their decision- makers (Tarafdar et al., 2010, 2015). Based on the complexity, high uncertainty, and discontinuous nature, and hence the need for expertise to handle digital BMI, we propose that the degree of digital BMI achieved in an organization is highly dependent on the knowledge and learning mechanisms. Thus, we expect that knowledge exploitation capabilities are positively associated with digital BMI. Prior studies emphasize the role of risk management capabilities to identify and evaluate business risks triggered by uncertainty in the firm’s environment (Arena et al., 2013; Teece, 2007). Digital BMI is often characterized by the involvement of distributed actors, such as external stakeholders (e.g., customers) and loosely organized crowds (e.g., in new markets), contributing to developing digital BMI (Faraj et al., 2011; George et al., 2020; Yoo et al., 2010). This distributed nature, uncertainty, and complexity inherent in digital BMI challenge the prevailing liability norms and protection of intellectual property (Greenstein et al., 2013; Teece, 2018a; Yoo et al., 2012). In particular, when developing digital BMI through online communities (Faraj et al., 2011) or digital ecosystems (Cennamo, 2020), risk expertise allows evaluating uncertain - ties and dealing with the lack of formal intellectual property agreements. We argue that risk management capabilities enable firms to deal with these digital BMI- related challenges. Moreover, prior research finds that digital BMI often entails strong privacy and cybersecurity concerns (Nambisan et al., 2019). Lacking distinctive expertise for dealing with security risks might severely constrain or even discourage firms in their digital BMI activities (Ceipek et al., 2021). Hence, we argue that to achieve digital BMI, firms are highly dependent on their capability to cope with these new business risks. Thus, we expect that risk management capabilities are positively related to digital BMI. Soluk et al. 9 Marketing capabilities facilitate the accumulation of deep insights on how markets and customers function (Fang & Zou, 2009; Helfat & Winter, 2011; Morgan et al., 2009). Due to the repeated cycles of experimentation and the reprogrammable nature of digital BMI, firms are more likely to face “receding boundaries” between innovation processes and outcomes. In other words, when pursuing digital BMI, it is less clear when a specific innovation process starts/ends and when an innovation outcome is “final” (Nambisan et al., 2017). We argue that these blurred boundaries lead to an increasing need to integrate customer and market expertise to better anticipate the success of digital BMI. To cope with the distributed configuration of digital BMI (Faraj et al., 2011; George et al., 2020; Yoo et al., 2010), marketing capabilities are deemed crucial (Troilo et al., 2017), enabling firms to manage multilayered and complex relations with external individuals (particularly customers), and anticipating how loosely organized crowds behave (Cennamo, 2020; Morgan et al., 2009). We therefore assume that digital BMI, due to its receding boundaries, decentralized, and distributed nature (George et al., 2020; Yoo et al., 2010), is highly dependent on customer and market insights, and the inflow of expertise on how digital markets function. Thus, we expect a positive relationship between marketing capabilitie s and digital BMI. Taken together, we argue that digital BMI is fostered by dynamic capabilities. Specifically, knowledge exploitation capabilities allow dealing with uncertainty, risk management capabili - ties allow firms to manage the new ownership, liability, and (cyber) security issues, while mar - keting capabilities support firms in utilizing distributed insights on new customers and digital markets accompanying digital BMI. Hence, we assume: H1b: Dynamic capabilities are positively related to digital BMI. The Mediating Effect of Dynamic Capabilities Based on our argumentation leading to H1a and H1b, we expect that dynamic capabilities mediate the relationship between level of family influence and digital BMI. The idiosyncrasies of family influence, such as distinctive learning patterns, high degree of control, and efficient decision- making, are positively associated with the degree of dynamic capabilities, specifically knowledge exploitation, risk management, and marketing capabilities, as argued above. Moreover, a higher degree of dynamic capabilities enables firms to cope with complex business challenges, manage the discontinuity of digital technologies, exploit external ties with customers and markets, and deal with the expiring ownership and liability norms, protection of intellectual property, and cybersecurity. Hence, we propose they are positively associated with digital BMI. In this mediation model, dynamic capabilities are closely tied to the idiosyncrasies of family influence, bundling and orchestrating these characteristics to achieve business value through digital BMI (Soluk & Kammerlander, 2021). While we identified several characteristics accompanying the increased levels of family influence in the theoretical background section, prior research reveals that these attributes do not necessarily lead to business value per se, but need to be reconfigured appropriately (Chirico et al., 2012; Teece et al., 1997). More specifically, this relationship could be more complex than previously thought (Chrisman et al., 2015; Kellermanns et al., 2012; König et al., 2013), as family firm characteristics entail a plethora of different consequences. Thus, we argue that we need to closely understand the mechanisms that link family influence and digital BMI as value- related outcomes. Dynamic capabilities fulfill this facilitating function, as they “integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external competences to address rapidly changing environments” (Teece et al., 1997, p. 516). This is the case because knowledge exploitation (Easterby- Smith & Prieto, 2008; Paarup Nielsen, 2006), risk management (Arena Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice 00(0)10 et al., 2013; Teece, 2018a), and marketing capabilities (Fang & Zou, 2009; Morgan et al., 2009) reflect three of the most crucial facets in the integration and reconfiguration of competences needed for digital BMI. Moreover, as noted, increased levels of family influence induce knowledge and learning mechanisms (Chirico & Nordqvist, 2010; Chirico & Salvato, 2008), a more attentive evaluation of business risks (Chrisman et al., 2015; Gómez- Mejía et al., 2007), strong ties to customers, and market insights (König et al., 2013). Therefore, we expect that increased levels of family influence may not necessarily be directly related to digital BMI, ultimately depending on the firm’s knowledge exploitation (Foss & Saebi, 2017), risk management (Teece, 2018a), and marketing capabilities (Sorescu, 2017). In summary, we argue that dynamic capabilities—in particular, knowledge exploitation, risk management, and marketing capabilities—are a mechanism through which increased levels of family influence lead to a higher degree of digital BMI. Thus, we expect dynamic capabilities to act as mediator in the relationship between family influence and digital BMI. H1c: Dynamic capabilities mediate the positive relationship between family influence and digital BMI. The Moderating Effect of Environmental Dynamism When firms are under environmental pressure, they are forced to develop dynamic capabilities to keep up with rapidly changing developments (Teece et al., 1997). As argued, family influence fosters the development of knowledge exploitation capabilities due to the family’s complementary perspectives (Chirico & Nordqvist, 2010; De Massis et al., 2016). We suggest that given their aim to sustain long- term business success, high environmental dynamism encourages especially family- influenced firms to put extra efforts into developing knowledge exploitation capabilities that might help them deal with uncertain times. In other words, the higher the family influence, the higher the perceived need to develop knowledge exploitation capabilities under high environmental dynamism. To develop these capabilities under high levels of environmental dynamism, family- influenced firms draw even more on the family’s internal, readily accessible expertise and complementary competences (that increase with higher levels of family influence), thus configuring their activities. Hence, we expect that the relationship between level of family influence and knowledge exploitation capabilities is positively moderated by environmental dynamism as a result of the perceived need to invest even more time and energy into capability development in rapidly changing times. As environmental dynamism “concerns the amount of uncertainty, complexity, and change emanating from the external environment” (Chirico & Baù, 2014, p. 212), it may generally increase the firm’s awareness of critical business situations and associated business risks (Bettis & Hitt, 1995), especially for firms with family influence. The higher the level of family influence, the more the family’s wealth is linked to the firm’s prosperity, resulting in a particular strong desire to survive (Anderson & Reeb, 2004; Chrisman et al., 2015; De Massis et al., 2016). High environmental dynamism thus further encourages firms to build their risk management capabilities. We argue that in family- influenced firms, this encouragement grows with increasing family influence due to the growing sensitivity to firm survival. As argued above, increased levels of family influence lead to strengthened ties between family members, intensifying their interactions, and bringing together the complementary expertise of the broader family to address the risks that threaten the business (Cruz & Nordqvist, 2012; Kammerlander, Patzelt, et al., 2020; Kotlar et al., 2020). In turn, the more dynamic the business environment, the more effort the owning family might invest in accumulating risk management expertise (Chirico & Baù, 2014). Soluk et al. 11 Thus, we argue that environmental dynamism forces firms with increased levels of family influence to put more emphasis on risk management efforts to meet their strong desire for survival and long- term success. Hence, we expect the relationship between family influence and risk management capabilities to be strengthened by environmental dynamism. In periods of environmental dynamism, market and customer needs change, hence enforcing the need to build the related dynamic capabilities (Fang & Zou, 2009; Helfat & Winter, 2011). In particular, business- owning families are willing and able to go “the extra mile” with increasing environmental pressure (Ramos et al., 2014) to preserve their financial and socioemotional endowments (Gómez- Mejía et al., 2007). Under environmental dynamism, this extra mile might manifest in the mobilization of relationships with often long- standing customers and other market participants (Duran et al., 2016). In addition, the increased complexity associated with environmental dynamism might trigger firms with increased levels of family influence to also rely on the expertise of external stakeholders, such as loosely organized crowds or online communities, which might thus far have been outside the firm’s focus. We hence argue that environmental dynamism motivates family- influenced firms to invest even more in the exploitation of connections with customers, and that this relationship intensifies with increasing family influence due to the owning families’ idiosyncratic goals and relationships. Thus, we expect the association between family influence and marketing capabilities to be strengthened by environmental dynamism. In summary, we expect environmental dynamism to strengthen the effect of family influence on dynamic capabilities, in particular, knowledge exploitation, risk management, and marketing capabilities. We argue that environmental dynamism puts extra pressure on family- influenced firms to develop such capabilities. Hence, we hypothesize: H2: The relationship between family influence and dynamic capabilities is strengthened by environmental dynamism. Methods To test our hypotheses, we used unique survey data from German firms, as there is no available database with comprehensive information on the digital BMI of firms with varying levels of family influence. We chose Germany as our research context given the relevance of family- influenced firms (De Massis, Audretsch, et al., 2018). Moreover, the innovativeness, increasing competition, and transformational challenges of key industries in Germany make this country an ideal context to study digital BMI and the role of environmental dynamism (De Massis, Audretsch, et al., 2018; De Massis, Di Minin, et al., 2015; Leal et al., 2019). Data Collection Our data collection focused on German firms with varying degrees of family influence (including family and nonfamily firms) starting with all active firms listed in the Amadeus database (Bureau van Dijk). We excluded micro- and small- sized enterprises with fewer than 50 employees due to their characteristics (e.g., lack of formalization) that might distort digital BMI engagement (König et al., 2013; Mallett & Wapshott, 2014). Furthermore, we excluded firms with headquarters outside Germany, municipalities, and religious institutions, leaving a population of 72,840 firms. We were able to obtain contact information for 14,260 firms varying in size, industry, and family influence. Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice 00(0)12 We first contacted these firms with an email explaining the purpose of the study and clarifying that our survey targets CEOs, executive- level managers, and senior executives responsible for innovation or (digital) technology. To implement the survey, we used the EFS Survey software of QuestBack. Before sending the survey link to the potential study participants, we piloted (Andrews et al., 2003; Collins, 2003) and pretested the survey (Kriauciunas et al., 2011). The pretesting consisted of two phases: (1) face- to- face interviews with five academics and four practitioners using a protocol method where the participants thought aloud while filling in the questionnaire (Hunt et al., 1982); and (2) sending the web survey to another 25 business practice participants to assess the survey structure, wording, and overall length, thus following previous survey- based research (e.g., Obal, 2017). The two pretesting phases led to small adaptations in our wording. The survey was open from May 23, 2018 to October 31, 2018, and after two reminders, a total of 1992 questionnaires were returned, thus resulting in an overall response rate of 13.97%, in line with comparable studies in the family business literature (e.g., De Massis et al., 2021; Garcés- Galdeano et al., 2017; Poterba & Summers, 1995; Schulze et al., 2003; Simsek, 2007; van Doorn et al., 2017; Zellweger et al., 2012). Of the returned responses, 1444 provided complete information (dropouts were most likely due to the sensitive nature of some of the survey questions) that we used for our analyses. Variables When developing the questionnaire, we mainly built on validated constructs (Table 1 for an overview of the questionnaire items). To ensure that the original meaning of these items was preserved, we carefully translated them into German and then back- translated them into English (Dillman, 2007; Kriauciunas et al., 2011). Moreover, we followed Dillman’s (2007) principles of constructing web surveys, thus ensuring maximum usability for respondents and avoiding potential biases from the beginning. Dependent Variable To capture digital BMI, we adapted the BMI measures used in prior research (Guo et al., 2016; Zott & Amit, 2007, 2010; Zott et al., 2011) to the digital innovation context (Nambisan et al., 2017; Yoo et al., 2012) (Table 1). The respondents had to rate the observed degree of digital innovation in their firm’s business model on a five- point Likert- type scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree). We conducted a principal component factor analysis (PCFA; using varimax rotation) on the nine items (Cronbach’s α = .89), which allowed us to find interrelationships between the items and reduce them into a unifying variable(s) (Jolliffe, 2011). The PCFA revealed one factor (with an eigenvalue exceeding the conventional threshold of 1) that explains 54% of total variance. Independent Variable To capture the influence of the family on the business, we used a proxy of the continuous family ownership stake variable (ranging from 0 to 100), following prior research (Fernández & Nieto, 2006; Miller et al., 2010; Miroshnychenko, Strobl, et al., 2020; Sciascia et al., 2015; see also Boling et al., 2016; Sirmon et al., 2008). Specifically, the respondents stated the percentage of firm shares owned by the family. We ran several robustness tests on alternative operationaliza - tions of the independent variable (see the Robustness Tests section). Mediating Variable Given that firms likely require heterogeneous capabilities to successfully implement digital BMI, we constructed the dynamic capabilities variable measuring the degree to which firms developed Soluk et al. 13 knowledge exploitation, risk management, and marketing capabilities, in line with extant theory and our argumentation presented above (Easterby- Smith & Prieto, 2008; Fang & Zou, 2009; Schilke et al., 2018; Sen et al., 2020). We thus followed the approach of Forsman (2011), asserting that these dynamic capabilities are particularly relevant for firms to innovate. We carefully adapted Forsman’s (2011) constructs in terms of the exclusion of the “risk assessment” item in the risk management capabilities measure (to ensure scale reliability with an increasing Cronbach’s α from 0.54 to 0.82). Control Variables We included several firm- and industry- level control variables in our analyses. Given that firms with superior financial performance are likely to have more resources available to pursue BMI (Aspara et al., 2010), we controlled for the firm’s financial performance (respondents were asked to indicate how successful in terms of ROA their company has been over the last 3 years on a five- point scale: 1 = very unsuccessful; 5 = very successful). In addition, liquidity concerns may also play an important role in shaping a firm’s digital BMI. Therefore, we included the firm’s financial health (respondents were asked to indicate whether bankruptcy is a realistic scenario on a five- point scale: 1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree) as an additional control variable. It is also plausible that resources invested in R&D can determine a firm’s propensity to develop digital BMI (Spieth et al., 2014). Our sample is dominated by firms from manufacturing industries that often invest between 15% and 18% of their annual revenues in R&D (Commission of Experts for Research and Innovation [EFI], 2016; Germany Trade & Invest [GTAI], 2019). Therefore, we included the firm’s R&D intensity following prior research (De Massis, Chirico, et al., 2014; Miroshnychenko, Barontini, et al., 2020). Specifically, respondents were asked to indicate the intensity of the firm’s R&D investments per revenue in the last 3 years. We constructed a dummy variable equal to 1 if a firm’s R&D intensity is equal to or above 15%, 0 otherwise.5 Furthermore, recent work suggests that BMI can be affected by the firm’s degree of interna - tionalization (Onetti et al., 2012). Following Clercq et al. (2005), we captured internationalization by asking respondents to indicate how intensively their firm conducts business abroad on a five- point scale (1 = none; 5 = very intense). We also controlled for firm size (natural logarithm of the firm’s number of employees) and firm age (natural logarithm of the number of years the firm has existed; De Massis et al., 2012; Kotey & Folker, 2007). In addition, we included 28 industry dummies (see Supplemental Table S1 in the Supplementary Document) to capture differences in the technological trajectories between manufacturing and service firms (Miroshnychenko et al., 2019). Econometric Model To test the moderated mediation model, we applied ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions with the Huber–White sandwich estimator to correct for heteroscedasticity (Long & Ervin, 2000), following the widely acknowledged procedure outlined in Muller et al. (2005). 6 We adopted OLS as the main estimator in our analysis in accordance with common practice in the Soluk et al. 15 field (Batt & Colvin, 2011; De Clercq et al., 2013; Heimeriks et al., 2012), and structural equation modeling (SEM) and 2SLS estimators in the robustness tests as additional checks, accounting for possible measurement errors, omitted variables, and simultaneity issues. Results Descriptive Results Forty- six percent of the sample can be classified as family- influenced firms (based on at least a 5% family ownership stake). The breakdown by industry (see Supplemental Table S1) shows a relatively widespread distribution of firms across sectors. The most commonly represented industries are information and communication technology (ICT) and machine construction (20.50% of the sample). The agriculture, forestry, and fishing sector has the smallest number of firms in our sample (approximately 0.14% of the sample). Table 2 reports the descriptive statistics and correlations for the whole sample. The median age of firms in our sample is 45 years, and median size is 260 employees. Family- influenced firms (above a threshold of 5% family ownership) have higher levels of dynamic capabilities than their nonfamily- influenced counterparts (t = 4.830; p < .001). Family- influenced firms score higher on financial performance (t = 1.708; p < .10) and internationalization (t = 3.988; p < .001) than nonfamily- influenced firms. Additionally, they exhibit lower levels of R&D intensity (t = −3.617; p < .001) than nonfamily- influenced firms. There are also differences between the two groups with respect to firm size and age, as family- influenced firms are on average smaller (t = −4.988; p < .001) and older (t = 6.278; p < .001). All the variance inflation factors are below 3, suggesting that multicollinearity does not significantly affect our regression estimates (O’brien, 2007). Regression Results Table 3 presents the results of the OLS estimations with heteroscedasticity- consistent (HEC) standard errors. As Model (1) and all the subsequent specifications show, the firm age variable has a negative effect on digital BMI (β = −0.167; p < .001), while the firm size variable is positively related to the level of digital BMI (β = .048; p < .001). This suggests that older and smaller firms have lower levels of digital BMI than younger and larger firms, in line with prior innovation research (e.g., Huergo & Jaumandreu, 2004). In addition, the regression coefficient of the financial performance variable is positive and statistically significant in Model (1) (β = .223; p < .001), and across all other models. The Wald tests of the joint significance of industry dummies are highly significant (p < .001) in all specifications, justifying their inclusion in our model. H1a proposes that family influence is positively related to dynamic capabilities. In Model (3), the regression coefficient of the family influence variable on dynamic capabilities is positive and statistically significant (β = .002, p < .001). Thus, we find full support for H1a. H1b posits that dynamic capabilities are positively associated with digital BMI. In Model (5), the regression coefficient of the dynamic capabilities variable is positive and statistically significant (β = .474, p < .001). Thus, we also find empirical evidence for H1b. H1c proposes that dynamic capabilities mediate the positive relationship between family influence and digital BMI. When considering family influence as our main variable of interest, dynamic capabilities as the mediator variable, and digital BMI as the outcome variable in Model (5), we find that the effect of family influence on digital BMI is no longer statistically significant (β = .000, n.s.), thus indicating full mediation. Put differently, there is a significant indirect effect of family influence on digital BMI through dynamic capabilities, supporting H1c. Robustness Tests To scrutinize the sensitivity of our findings to alternative variable definitions and estimation techniques, we conducted several additional checks. The results of all the robustness tests are reported in Supplemental Tables S2- S7 in the Supplementary Document. Alternative Variable Definitions To verify the robustness of our main findings, and due to the lack of consensus on how to mea - sure family influence (Boling et al., 2016; Chrisman et al., 2009; Kellermanns et al., 2012), we first re- ran our analyses with alternative family influence variables. First, we used a family influence dummy variable equal to 1 if a family owns more than 50% of the firm, 0 otherwise (Amore et al., 2011). The respective regression results (see Supplemental Table S2) are fully in line with our main findings. Next, we used a family influence dummy variable equal to 1 if a family has more than 50% ownership and at least one family member is involved in management (Amore et al., 2014), 0 otherwise (see Supplemental Table S3). Again, the results of this robustness check confirm our main results. Next, we built on the established family influence construct of Craig et al. (2014; see also Smyrnios et al., 1998). For this variable, the respondents had to rate their degree of approval of four statements (the family influences the hiring processes of managers; the family is involved in everyday business; members of the family are employed by the firm; and the business is to be handed over to the next generation), building on a five- point Likert- type scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree). The composite scale of this variable is reliable (Cronbach’s α = .69) and explains 53% of total variance. For all those firms that consider themselves a family business (based on self- perception; Chua et al., 1999), this variable reports the degree of family influence on the firm’s decision- making processes, while for nonfamily firms, this variable is equal to 0. The use of this variable leads to similar results as those reported in Table 3 (see Supplemental Table S4). Endogeneity Check An additional data quality check relates to endogeneity, which is a major concern in family business research (De Massis, Frattini, et al., 2018). As it is conceivable that firms develop more dynamic capabilities as a result of digital BMI, which raises concerns about the hypothesized direction of the study’s results, endogeneity needs to be addressed to mitigate biased estimations (Hamilton & Nickerson, 2003). To account for the possible endogeneity problem between digital BMI and dynamic capabilities deriving from omitted variable problems, measurement errors, or the aforementioned reverse causality issues, we adopted the 2SLS estimator (Bascle, 2008). This method addresses the endogeneity concern when dynamic capabilities and an instrumental variable are continuous variables, and when the instrumental variable is related to dynamic capabilities but not to digital BMI. We employed two external instrumental variables, namely long- term Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice 00(0)22 orientation capturing the time horizons of firm management (Narver & Slater, 1990), and variability risk capturing systematic and unsystematic risk components (Kempers et al., 2019). Firms with a distinctive long- term orientation accumulate knowledge by interpreting, valuing, and acting on information (Lumpkin & Brigham, 2011). Prior research explains long- term orientation as a dominant logic closely connected with problem- solving and organizational learning (Lumpkin & Brigham, 2011; Prahalad & Bettis, 1986). Due to the fact that dynamic capabilities are developed simultaneously to knowledge accumulation and organizational learning (Teece et al., 1997; Zollo & Winter, 2002), we assume that long- term orientation and the development of dynamic capabilities can occur simultaneously (Lumpkin & Brigham, 2011; Teece et al., 1997). Moreover, similar arguments related to the knowledge accumulation and organizational learning processes apply to firms exposed to variability risk (Kempers et al., 2019). Exposure to the variability risk expands the firm’s expertise across disciplines, thus allowing the simultane - ous development of dynamic capabilities (Arena et al., 2013). However, this instantaneous relationship does not exist between long- term orientation or variability risk and digital BMI, as there is likely a multi- year time lag before long- term orientation or variability risk causally lead to digital BMI (Foss & Mahnke, 2002). One reason for this are “time- to- market lags” that occur between a firm’s long- term orientation respective variability risk and achieving digital BMI and other forms of innovation (Palmié et al., 2016; Zollo & Winter, 2002). Thus, the adoption of digital BMI in a given year is likely not connected to the firm’s long- term orientation or variability risk in the same and previous year. Therefore, we argue that the instrumental variables influence digital BMI only via their effects on dynamic capabilities. Our 2SLS regression estimations include two stages. In the first stage, the dynamic capabilities variable is regressed against our instrumental variables along with controls (same variables as in the main explanatory model). In the second stage, we obtained the regression estimates by regressing digital BMI on the predicted values of dynamic capabilities, computed using the parameters from the first- stage regression. Given that in the second- stage regression we omit the dynamic capabilities part that is endogenous to digital BMI, the parameters are now consistently estimated. The instrumental variables are significantly correlated with the dynamic capabilities meeting the relevance criteria, as suggested by the Kleibergen- Paap rk LM statistic (Model 5 = .000; Model 6 = .000; Model 7 = .000). Moreover, the results of the Kleibergen- Paap rk Wald F statistic (Model 5 = .000; Model 6 = .000; Model 7 = .000) are far above the Stock–Yogo critical values, indicating that our instrumental variables are sufficiently strong. In addition, the Hansen J statistic (Model 5 = .442; Model 6 = .360; Model 7 = .333) suggests that our instrumental variables meet the exclusion criteria, implying they are not related to digital BMI. Hence, we do not find any empirical support for underidentification, weak identification, or overidentification of our model. Therefore, after accounting for the endogeneity problem, all our hypotheses are empirically supported (see Supplemental Table S6). Common Method Bias With regard to common method bias, we used several ex ante and post hoc measures to mitigate and analyze the risk of common method bias (Podsakoff et al., 2003, 2012). First, survey participants were assured that their data were only processed anonymously and that confidentiality was guaranteed, thereby decreasing the risk of social desirability bias. Second, we arranged the questions in the survey in such a way that participants would not notice any direct connection between the constructs. Third, we performed a Harman’s single- factor test loading all survey items into one single factor. We extracted eight factors with an eigenvalue greater than 1. The total variance of the first unrotated factor in the sample was approximately 22%, while the remaining seven factors accounted for an additional 38% of total variance. Finally, we re- estimated our explanatory model using the instrumental variable estimator (2SLS), the best possible solution to account Soluk et al. 23 for potential common method bias according to Antonakis et al. (2010) (see Supplemental Table S6). Overall, all the aforementioned checks suggest that common method bias is not a problem in our study. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) We also re- estimated our moderated mediation model using the SEM approach following Hayes (2013) and Preacher et al. (2007). SEM allows simultaneously analyzing all the variables in our model and controlling for measurement errors so that they are not aggregated in the residual term (Tarka, 2018). The results of this analysis are presented in Panel A of Supplemental Table S7. Our model exhibits good fit according to the results of the goodness- of- fit statistics (X 2 = 1167.911 [DF = 75]; CFI = .978; RMSEA = .104; SRMR = .004). The SEM estimates, based on 5000 bootstrap runs, support our main findings. We further tested the significance of the standardized indirect effect of family influence on digital BMI via dynamic capabilities using three different tests: the Delta method, Sobel’s test, and Monte Carlo simulations (5000 replications). Panel B of Supplemental Table S7 shows that all these tests are statistically significant at the 1% level, confirming the presence of the indirect effect of family influence on digital BMI via dynamic capabilities in our model. As the standardized effect of family influence on digital BMI is not different from zero (n.s.), while the indirect effect derived from the Monte Carlo simulations is statistically significant (β = .060, p < .001), we have a full mediation model (Zhao et al., 2010). Discussion Our study theorized and tested a moderated mediation model linking dynamic capabilities to digital BMI in a sample of 1444 German firms with varying levels of family influence. We find that increased levels of family influence are positively related to digital BMI, and this relation - ship is mediated by dynamic capabilities, specifically knowledge exploitation, risk management, and marketing capabilities. Surprisingly, and contrary to our hypothesis, the relationship between level of family influence and dynamic capabilities is weakened by environmental dynamism. A more nuanced analysis reveals that environmental dynamism interacts only with family influence when studying marketing capabilities, but not knowledge exploitation and risk management capabilities. Our findings are robust to alternate variable and model specifications as well as endogeneity issues. Theoretical Contributions First, our study adds to the literature on family firm innovation. While prior research has documented that family influence is a significant determinant of R&D investments (Chrisman et al., 2015), patent activities (Kotlar et al., 2013), and innovation in general (Duran et al., 2016), how family influence shapes digital BMI has not been examined to date. In particular, we reveal that the pessimistic view of discontinuous or radical innovation in family- influenced firms (König et al., 2013; Nieto et al., 2015) does not apply to digital BMI. In contrast, we show that family firm idiosyncrasies, such as their distinctive knowledge management mechanisms (Chirico, 2008; Chirico & Nordqvist, 2010; Chirico & Salvato, 2008), strong attachment between the family and the business (Chirico & Salvato, 2016; De Massis et al., 2016), and specific resources (De Massis, Audretsch, et al., 2018), equip these firms for the challenges and opportunities associated with the digital economy, thus considerably extending the insights provided by the few studies that have researched digital innovation in family firms (e.g., Soluk & Kammerlander, 2021). With our theoretical arguments and the empirical results regarding the specific Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice 00(0)24 mechanisms that family influence provokes in organizations, and the role that dynamic capabilities play, we further extend our hitherto limited understanding of how family firms engage in digital business opportunities in general, and digital BMI in particular (Teece, 2018a). Second, our findings contribute to research on digital BMI. While other studies have focused on the performance implications rather than the antecedent conditions of digital BMI (Foss & Saebi, 2017; Sorescu, 2017; Teece, 2010), we considerably extend this view by shedding light on the mechanisms that foster digital BMI in organizations. To our best knowledge, this is the first study examining the relationship between ownership type and digital BMI, as well as introducing dynamic capabilities as a relevant but understudied mediator in this relationship. Based on our relatively large and unique sample, we theoretically and empirically reveal that the level of a firm’s digital BMI is influenced by the available dynamic capabilities, in turn affected by ownership type. Our empirical insights reveal that knowledge exploitation capabilities have the strongest effect on digital BMI, while risk management capabilities have the least. In addition, we extend prior literature on digital BMI, which is mostly conceptual (Sorescu, 2017; Teece, 2010, 2018b; Veit et al., 2014; Zott et al., 2011), by adapting an established BMI measure (Guo et al., 2016; Zott & Amit, 2007) and applying it to the digital economy context, thus contributing to empirically capturing digital BMI (Foss & Saebi, 2017). Moreover, while the BMI literature focuses on both startups and established companies (Snihur & Wiklund, 2019; Snihur & Zott, 2020), digital BMI is mostly treated as a phenomenon that occurs primarily in new ventures (Hedman et al., 2016; Sorescu, 2017; Teece, 2010). We challenge this view by extending the digital BMI investigation to incumbent organizations, thus contributing to the few studies focusing on how established firms develop digital BMI to secure long- term success (e.g., Müller et al., 2018; Remane et al., 2017). Third, our study contributes to the growing literature on dynamic capabilities (Helfat & Raubitschek, 2018; Teece, 2007; Teece et al., 1997). While confirming the relevance of dynamic capabilities for competing in the digital economy (Karimi & Walter, 2015; Soluk & Kammerlander, 2021; Yeow et al., 2018), we extend this research stream by providing a nuanced and empirically substantiated understanding of the role of dynamic capabilities in the digital BMI context (Foss & Saebi, 2017; Teece, 2018b; Zott et al., 2011). In so doing, we provide empirical evidence that knowledge exploitation, risk management, and marketing capabilities mediate the relationship between family influence and digital BMI. Hence, we advance extant knowledge on dynamic capabilities in family firms (Chirico & Nordqvist, 2010; Chirico & Salvato, 2008; Chirico et al., 2012; De Massis et al., 2016). Moreover, by showing that environmental dynamism does not moderate the relationship between increased levels of family influence and knowledge exploitation or risk management capabilities, we challenge previous assumptions that the development of dynamic capabilities in general is particularly fostered in dynamic environments (Helfat & Winter, 2011; Nayak et al., 2020; Schilke et al., 2018; Teece, 2018b; Teece et al., 1997). In contrast to our theorizing, we find a negative moderating effect of environmental dynamism on the relationship between family influence and marketing capabilities. This finding challenges extant research arguing that dynamic environments might promote the development of marketing capabilities (Fang & Zou, 2009; Morgan et al., 2009). A possible explanation for this surprising result could be the inward- oriented focus of family- influenced firms, which might induce these firms to turn to firm- internal (rather than external) practices and secure the family’s financial and nonfinancial endowments when facing uncertainty (Gómez- Mejía et al., 2007; Kotlar et al., 2013). Implications for Management Practice and Policy Making Our work also has important practical implications. Owners, managers, and advisors of firms with and without family influence are increasingly required to address management questions Soluk et al. 25 related to digital BMI (Remane et al., 2017; Sorescu, 2017). First, our empirical evidence shows that established firms can successfully engage in digital BMI. This might encourage the managers of these firms to develop strategies for how to implement digital BMI, instead of leaving this opportunity to new ventures. Second, our insights reveal the specific dynamic capabilities that firms require to excel in digital BMI. Specifically, managers need to scrutinize their firm’s knowledge exploitation, risk management, and marketing capabilities. In particular, the more dynamic the environment, the more emphasis managers need to place on knowledge exploitation capabilities. Last, family firm owners and managers should be aware that family influence can be an important driver of digital BMI. Hence, the owners and managers of such firms should critically reflect on their strengths and build their digital innovation strategy on these. Additionally, our study’s findings have strong implications for policy makers, serving as a basis for policy actions aimed at fostering the adoption of digital technologies (Helfat & Raubitschek, 2018; Teece, 2018a), considered a top priority to ensure long- term competitiveness in many countries. In this regard, our results reveal that incumbent firms—and not only startups—can engage in digital BMI and might thus require and profit from specially designed support measures, such as grants and tax incentives. This is important as family- influenced firms—given their ubiquity (Anderson & Reeb, 2003; Schmid et al., 2014)—are crucial for the development of economies across the world (De Massis, Frattini, et al., 2018). Building on our insights, policy makers might design their support programs in such a way as to lead to developing these dynamic capabilities. Policy makers might think about new forms of collaboration for family- influenced firms, such as online platforms that include startups and professional firms offering digital services. Limitations and Future Research Our study has some limitations that offer valuable opportunities for future research. As with any cross- sectional work, we have not aimed at establishing causal relationships in this study (Bascle, 2008). However, as described in the methods section, we conducted a series of robustness checks to rule out possible alternative explanations and account for the potential endogeneity problem. Further research on digital BMI using longitudinal data could help verify the validity and generalizability of our findings (Lévesque & Stephan, 2020; Miroshnychenko, De Massis, et al., 2020). Moreover, future studies, especially qualitative case- based research, could shed light on the inter- and intrafirm differences induced by varying levels of family influence, exploring how firms develop dynamic capabilities and approach digital BMI on a micro- level (Kammerlander & De Massis, 2020). Specifically, longitudinal (multiple) case studies might help explain the underlying mechanisms of the time- varying effects in developing digital BMI (De Massis & Kotlar, 2014). Furthermore, it would be interesting to understand whether our findings are applicable to other settings by expanding our approach to broader institutional contexts (Autio et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2014) with different legal regimes, cultural traditions, and developments regarding digital technologies (Gedajlovic et al., 2012). Also important to mention is that data constraints did not allow us to account for family firm heterogeneity (Chua et al., 2012), above and beyond the variance observed in the family influence variables employed. Thus, studying the effect of different types of family- related variables, such as family structures (Arregle et al., 2019), is another potential avenue for future research. Moreover, future research might address the linkages of the three dynamic capabilities to other dynamic or ordinary capabilities (e.g., absorptive capacity; Daspit et al., 2019; Zobel, 2017) and categorizations thereof (e.g., sensing, seizing, and transforming; Teece, 2014) that are outside the scope of our study. Beyond the dynamic capabilities lens, we encourage future scholarly work to adopt additional theoretical frameworks to explain how family- influenced firms develop digital Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice 00(0)26 BMI. While prospect theory might provide appropriate insights into how family members assess the risks inherent in digital BMI (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974), other promising paths are rooted in interdisciplinary theoretical lenses, such as construal level theory (Trope & Liberman, 2010). Originally developed in the psychological domain, construal level theory might explain how and why family influence affects decision- makers’ mental representation of digitalization, and thus firm- level digital BMI (Kammerlander & Breugst, 2019). In addition, stakeholder theory (Freeman, 2010) might help researchers understand how family- influenced firms involve outsiders, such as loosely organized crowds, potential new customers, long- standing customers, and suppliers, in their digital BMI development processes. Conclusions Our study bridges the literature streams on family firm innovation, digital BMI, and dynamic capabilities. We show there is a positive relationship between family influence and digital BMI, and that this relationship is mediated by dynamic capabilities, in particular, knowledge management, risk management, and marketing capabilities. Taken together, our findings emphasize the importance of dynamic capabilities for family- influenced firms, highlighting the strengths of family- influenced firms in the context of digital BMI, and opening up interesting avenues for further research. Ayalac, Antonio Ghezzid a Organizational Engineering Group (Núcleo de Engenharia Organizacional– NEO), Department of Industrial Engineering, Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil b Departament of Industrial Engineering, Universidade Federal de São Carlos, Brazil c G-SCOP Laboratory, Grenoble Institute of Technology (INPG), France d Department of Management, Economics and Industrial Engineering, Politecnico di Milano, Italy ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Servitization Industry 4.0 Digitization Digital transformation Digital innovation business model innovation ABSTRACT Servitization and Industry 4.0 are considered two of the most recent trends transforming industrial companies. Servitization is mainly focused on adding value to the customer (demand-pull) while Industry 4.0 is frequently related to adding value to manufacturing process (technology-push). Although some scholars address them as complementary concepts, the literature lacks evidences about what are the interfaces and connection between the two trends. Thus, we aim to develop a conceptual framework that connects Servitization and Industry 4.0 concepts from a business model innovation (BMI) perspective. Our framework is based on three Servitization levels (i.e. smoothing, adapting and substituting) and three levels of digitization (i.e. low, moderate and high levels). We show that matching these levels results in nine possible configurations classified in manual, digital and industry 4.0-related services, which can focus on smoothing, adapting or substituting services. We use reported cases from the literature to support and illustrate these configurations. We also discuss different levels of complexity for the implementation of these configurations. The study hence provides a foundation for the growing research on the interface between Servitization and Industry 4.0. 1. Introduction Industries have been facing many transformations in the last decade, dramatically changing the way companies are doing business with their customers as well as how products are developed, manufactured and delivered (Gersch and Goeke, 2007). Two recent macrophenomena and trends are specifically challenging the business models (BMs) of productfirms: Servitization and Industry 4.0. The first phenomenon – Servitization – is predominantly related to the demand-pull innovation trajectory (Dosi, 1982). Since the market has been changing from product consumption to result-oriented demand, customers are expecting to receive additional services to improve the experience they make when getting in touch with such products (Enkel and Gassmann, 2010); or, in some cases, instead of affording the cost of the product itself, customers want to receive only the value inherently offered by the product use, thus consuming it as a service (Tukker, 2004, 2015). This change resulted in the Servitization strategy of productfirms, which consists in a transformation journey of product-centered firms towards product-service systems (PSS) (Kowalkowski et al., 2017;Martinez et al., 2017). Such transformation is so deeply rooted in the productfirms' value architecture– composed by value creation, delivery and capture mechanisms and complementarities (Teece, 2010), and acting as a manifestation of thefirm's business strategy (Cortimiglia et al., 2016) – that is considered a business model innovation (BMI) of productfirms themselves (Ayala et al., 2017; Kastalli and Van Looy, 2013), which can happen at different stages of the industry evolution (Cusumano et al., 2015). A second recent industrial macro-trend affecting productfirms is the so-called Industry 4.0 phenomenon (Liao et al., 2017; Reischauer, 2018; Yin et al., 2017). It is considered a new industrial scenario in which the convergence of different emerging technologies strengthen by the Internet of things (IoT) results in cyber-physical and intelligent systems that can create value for the industrial activities (Frank et al., 2019; Müller et al., 2018; Liao et al., 2017).
