Knowledge management and dynamic capabilities Downloaded by Tulane University At 11:12 05 December 2018 (PT) So how do we manage and achieve the goals of these institutions in their current uncertain and rapid development contexts? Thus, due to the risks acquired since its initial conception, the conditions of uncertainty and rapid evolution they are subjected to, new untapped challenges are presented to the startuppers (Blank, 2013; Giardinoet al., 2014; Ries, 2012), requiring rapid transformations in their business models as a response to pressures and tensions caused by internal and external processes. Thus, although in the business environment and history it is common for managers to be challenged to produce results in a context of risks and uncertainties, in addition to delivering them, the management must also be concerned to produce them under a larger context of uncertainty and rapid technological and social changes and to use these rapid changes in favor of their businesses, minimizing transaction costs and maximizing transaction value (Felipeet al., 2016; Schotteret al., 2017; Teeceet al., 2016; Thomson, 1998; Hwang and Gaur, 2009). From this perspective, therefore, in order to achieve its objectives successfully, a startup needs to develop individual and organizational learning capacities during the process of business development (Sosnaet al., 2010) and management models that seek to integrate different management approaches that meet the specificities of managing their context and minimize the chances of failure. Thus, given the lack of market mechanisms that protect entrepreneurial innovation from the uncertainties associated with the reception of an opportunity ( Janeway, 2012), agility seems to be an important attribute or organizational capability to be developed by current organizations seeking sustainable development (Baskarada and Koronios, 2018; Felipeet al., 2016; Ries, 2012; Singh et al., 2013; Teece et al., 2016), considering the increase in the organization’s ability to proactively respond to unexpected environmental changes, developed by agility (Appelbaumet al., 2017). Therefore, the companies that have achieved success are those that, in addition to meeting latent demands at the right time, are fast and flexible enough in terms of innovation (Teece et al., 1997), supported by the foreknowledge capability (prescience), and by the tools used to find out which parts of the business plans are misguided, in order to adapt the strategies accordingly (Ries, 2012). And it is in this context that some recently popular and promising methods have emerged and promised to increase agility and reduce risks in the decision-making process and to achieve the business objectives in uncertain environments (Blank, 2013; Blank and Dorf, 2014; Ries, 2012; Teeceet al., 2016). Thus, the agility required and inherent to these methods contributes and makes easy the search and the retrieval of relevant knowledge, allowing companies to rapidly apply such knowledge to develop high-quality solutions or react to the emergence of new competitors (Cegarra-Navarro et al., 2016). However, despite the innumerable success stories associated with agile development, a number of barriers, ranging from technical to perceptual barriers related to the process of implementing agile development, reveal the importance of the management commitment in the process of providing the necessary objectives and support aiming at the successful development of such a process (Boehm and Turner, 2003; Pikkarainen et al., 2012) as well as the need for a tailor-made, risk-oriented approach so that projects take advantage of the planned benefits of agile methods while mitigating some of their disadvantages (Boehm and Turner, 2003). Being so, strong dynamic capabilities are critical for a company to promote organizational agility required to operate in an environment of uncertainty, since they are the ones that define the company’s ability to innovate, adapt and create changes that are favorable to the consumer market and unfavorable to competitors (Teeceet al., 2016). However, the development of dynamic capabilities depends heavily on the organization’s knowledge and learning (Easterby‐Smith and Prieto, 2008), which, in turn, is strongly MD Downloaded by Tulane University At 11:12 05 December 2018 (PT) related to the role that key individuals play in the process of knowledge development within an organization (Nuruzzaman, Gaur and Sambharya, 2018). For this reason, knowledge management must be a practice developed in organizational processes and widely stimulated by governance, in order to take its effectiveness and facilitate its transfer (Anderson et al., 2015), thus improving organizational processes continuously. In this way, the knowledge management expands the competitive capacities of the organizations (Anderson et al., 2015; Nuruzzaman, Gaur and Sambharya, 2018; Nuruzzaman, Singh and Pattnaik, 2018) and contributes to the achievement of the organizational objectives or results and value creation potential (Mukherjee et al. , 2018; Mukherjee, Gaur and Datta, 2013), also being measured as an organizational performance measure (Oliva, 2014; Qi and Chau, 2018). Despite these developments and the set of pragmatic methods based on lean and agile principles recently proposed to support entrepreneurs in the evolution and innovation of their business models, little has been investigated on the theoretical and practical relationship between these management practices and the evolution and innovation of these business in dynamic environments, especially under the support and integration of some traditional and recent approaches to business administration (Ghezzi and Cavallo, 2018; Oliva et al., 2011). From this perspective, the objective of the present paper is to describe and analyze how the integration between knowledge management and dynamic capabilities in contexts of agile organizational development contributes to the management by objectives. 2. Theoretical framework 2.1 Management by objectives The entrepreneur must understand quite clearly his objectives in order to keep an organization focused on them (Picken, 2016). Thus, initially developed by Peter Drucker in 1954, the approach known as management by objectives has been used in different ways since then, in order to assist management team in the process of defining and orienting the specific objectives to be achieved. Besides Drucker, this approach has also been developed by many other management theorists, including Douglas McGregor, George Odiorne and John Humble, in which, in essence, who enshrine the process designed to jointly set specific goals to be accomplished within a defined deadline and followed by the definition of the responsibilities aiming at reaching the agreed targets and analyzing the process performance (Campbell, 2015; Thomson, 1998). At this level, the collaborative participation is still low. (3) The oriented level not only refers to a profile of companies equal to the previous level, but also presents an orientation for the creation and use of knowledge to boost the business, in addition to an organizational culture oriented toward innovation. (4) The last level, integrative, indicates high concern, organization and transparency regarding knowledge management. Furthermore, in order to move toward its objectives, a startup still needs to develop a proactive risk management system, since fast-growing companies are particularly vulnerable to risk sources (Picken, 2016). These loads of evidence, therefore, draw up the company’s behavior and show how goal-oriented management of a startup can be adapted to the dynamic context of startups and strengthened by the agility in the planning process by the dynamic capabilities in the organization process, by the knowledge management in the execution process and by the performance assessment processes and ERM in the control process (Figure 3). This model is also able to demonstrate in theory how the cycle developed by Eric Ries (2012), known as build-measure-learn, is managerially structured in startups. 5. Conclusions 5.1 Attendance the research objectives In general, as well as in corporations, the organizational objectives of a startup vary in the course of its evolution. This variation describes the business orientation to the solution of MD Downloaded by Tulane University At 11:12 05 December 2018 (PT) the main operational and management challenges inherent to a particular time of the business development. Thus, the objectives of a startup not only make up its organizational trajectory but also guide the activities and processes to be developed by it, and therefore, the way the company is conducted, the measure that shapes its activities and priorities, as well as directs the necessary resources and efforts. In addition, the development of a startup is an experimental and iterative process, and therefore, during its history, the startup empirically develops its own routines and organizational processes, according to the learning it acquires from its mistakes and successes and the established objectives. So, therefore, the learning generated by a startup is a set of knowledge and capabilities that enable the business to reach its established objectives with the agility required in the dynamic context in which it is inserted, reducing risks and preserving scarce resources. In this sense, the objective of describing and analyzing how the integration between knowledge management and dynamic capacities incontexts of agile organizational development contributes to the management by objectives was care, by presenting from the empirical evidences the way in which the management approaches proposed by the study are integrated. 5.2 Attendance to methodological procedures The methodological procedures were met by integrating the qualitative approach of the study to the single case study method and the content analysis technique for data analysis. In addition, the semi-structured script of the interview was based on the literature review in management by objectives, agile organization, dynamic capabilities, knowledge management, performance assessment and ERM, and the five participating executives were selected according to their experiences and perceptions of the phenomenon analyzed. In this special issue introductory article, we take stock of the robust multi-faceted nature of research and practice at the intersection of social media (SM) and innovation. We introduce the nine papers included in this special issue and highlight the rich variety of their contribution with reference to our organising framework. Diagnosing from a strategic perspective, we position SM strategy in and for innovation as an overlapping interaction between dynamic capabilities (sensing, seizing, reconfiguration) and the level of stakeholder engagement (macro, meso, micro). We explain how each interaction holds distinctive synergy in an open and collaborative innovation process. This organising framework shows how the malleable nature of SM creates opportunities forfirms to engage widely distributed knowledge sources, enhance innovation capabilities and empower internal human resources towards an open and collaborative culture. Yet, we warn that all is not as rosy as it seems and a purposeful and coherent strategy that delivers distinctive‘co-ownership’experiences is quintessential ingredient to realise profits from SM use in innovation. 1. Introduction It is no denying that social media (SM) are an element of our daily lives. Through SM, we are all connected– organisations, users, customers and the society. Increasingly over the last decade (and since the advent of LinkedIn, Skype and Facebook) SM have been used byfirms for new ways to connect, communicate and engage with a wide range of stakeholders. We posit that three levels of stakeholder engagement at which the utility of SM for innovation unfolds can be observed, namely the “micro” level (individuals andfirms from the innovation community itself), the“meso” level (customers) and the“macro” level (society and citizens). The premise being that SM allows for socialisation, externalisation, combination and internalisation of collective knowledge (Muninger et al., 2019). SM tools backed by the information and communication technologies (ICTs) relay information to and from active and passive audience, breaking free of traditional communication boundaries. SM thus create new channels of information exchange between stakeholders and have the potential to facilitate innovation efforts in an open and collaborative environment. It is not surprising that some firms have attempted to take up SM as the tool to enable various open innovation processes (Mount and Martinez, 2014). In particular, the adoption of SM has shaped the wayfirms communicate, collaborate and innovate, both using internal and external sources of knowledge. Concurrently, the uptake of those technologies has influenced organisational processes as well as it has triggered the identification and development of new skills and capabilities. To realise the benefits, scholars have called for firms to adopt a purposeful SM strategy (Dutta, 2010;Kietzmann et al., 2011). Evidence highlights SM use for strategic sense-making (Hill et al., 2006;Trusov et al., 2010), sense-giving across firm's operational levels (Benbya and Van Alstyne, 2010) and reconfiguration of ways to innovate by redefining co-creation (Mangold and Faulds, 2009;Zwass, 2010) and learning (Peppler and Solomou, 2011). Notwithstanding, what has been seen is barely scratching the surface of what might be possible, with significant opportunities ahead for research exploring and examining the SM and innovation interactions. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.techfore.2019.03.003 ⁎ Corresponding author at: RMIT University, Room 33, Level 9, Building 80 (Swanston Academic Building), 445 Swanston Street, Melbourne, Vic 3000, Australia. In a set of papers published inInformation Systems Research, they explore the topic of SM and business transformation. More recently, a special issue positioning SM as a revolution in communication edited by Papagiannidis and Bourlakis (2015) in Technological Forecasting and Social Changehighlighted how SM is being used as a means of broadcasting information and the relational influence of user perceptions on its utility in practice. All three attempts point to the strategic and malleable nature of SM use in public and private sector, yet neither draw attention to its interactions and applications in the innovation process. Thus, this special issue was conceptualised and designed to stimulate the investigations of SM in innovation processes. In borrowing from Teece (2007), SM tools are positioned here as influencers of the focal firm's dynamic capabilities for sensing, seizing and reconfi guring knowledge in the process of innovation. The cross-disciplinary and multi-faceted nature of the nine papers included in this special issue suggests that the topic of SM and innovation has far-reaching implications for studies in social sciences (economics, marketing, human resources, strategy... ) and computer science. Accordingly, instead of trying to establish new definitions or trend based disciplinary classifications, the approach in this issue has been to highlight the strategic perspectives at the intersection of SM and innovation, capturing the relevance and value of SM use in innovation across three strategic levels - micro (e.g. innovation community),meso (e.g. co-creation) and macrolevel (society and citizens). More specifically, it highlights the multifaceted perspective on use of SM in and for innovation as social and complex decision that calls for purposeful strategic management. In this view, a three-stage process is suggested: (1) building organisational capabilities; (2) developing strategic network capabilities (Hagedoorn et al., 2006) innovation; and (3) using SM for innovation adoption. This integrative framework aims at simultaneously identifying the relevance, value, benefits and challenges related to the adoption and exploitation of SM in and for innovation. The organising framework makes sense of the strategic SM use in innovation initiatives, by showing how they relate to strategic capabilities (sensing, seizing and reconfiguring) at various levels of stakeholder engagement (micro,meso and macro). The intentional approach adopted in this introductory article and this issue is to guide the strategic decision-making process of SM adoption and extension of its use, in and for innovation. This article is structured as follows. The next section describes an organising framework for research at the intersection of SM and innovation. This is followed by a review previous research addressing the use of SM for innovation to depict the currents limits and challenges associated in practice. This leads to an overview of the suggested threestage process of adopting and extending the use of SM in practice from a strategic perspective, each stage detailed based on current knowledge and articles included in this special issue. Lastly, the article highlights the need for integrated strategic actions to curate and create information exchange strategies in the increasingly open and collaborative innovation environment. 2. An organising framework for research on social media in and for innovation The proposed framework, which is used to systematically and logically sorts the papers included in this special issue, is intended to aid research endeavours at the intersection of SM and innovation across SM types and its strategic applications, taking into account the distinct, yet overlapping units of analysis and value perspectives. The reason for keeping the concepts and framework sufficiently broad is to invite cross-disciplinary investigations in keeping with the multi-faceted malleable nature of SM tools. A deliberate strategic lens to view SM and innovation interactions is guided by three main understandings– 1) that open and collaborative innovations are driven by top-down business strategy (Gassmann et al., 2010), 2) SM are increasingly seen as part of a firm's communication and business strategy (Hitchen et al., 2017), and 3) a focus on SM strategy is likely to contribute directly to the extent of its use and Return On Investment (ROI) (Heller Barid and Parasnis, 2010). To drive innovation performance, leaders must think deeply and coherently about ways to source, create and integrate knowledge from widely distributed sources and embed SM use in and for innovation in the fabric of thefirm. Without a clear strategic lens, the firm may not be able to harness thefinancial and competitive advantages afforded by SM's reach and capacity to assimilate information from a large group of producers and consumers in the process of innovation. To aid the decision-making process, the SM and innovation landscape can be conceptualised as an interaction betweenstrategic capabilities (sensing, seizing, reconfiguring) that decision-makers of afirm may focus on at various stages of the innovation process and thelevel of stakeholder engagement (micro, meso and macro) at which the utility of SM for innovation actually takes place. Thestrategic actions are influenced by the social engagement activities that the creators and users of SM can undertake. Simply adopting SM to engage various stakeholders does not guarantee ROI on SM use for innovation. The level of sophistication (i.e. the strategic actions and the behaviour it guides) influences the output (Bochenek and Blili, 2014). The organising framework in Table 1 provides a point of reference for strategic decisionmakers towards an integrated SM and innovation strategy: Sensing capabilities comprise ofactivities that help thefirm to learn, sense, filter and shape opportunities. These activities include trend and preference assessments, technological forecasting, business roadmapping and gathering information through user and citizen reports. Seizing capabilities include those activities that facilitate development of new product, processes and service from the‘sensed’ opportunities. Thus, it typically would include purposeful knowledge exchange, strategic signalling to right stakeholders, creation of new intellectual capital and catalysing dialogue through word-of-mouth communication during innovation commercialisation. Reconfiguration includes activities that combine and integratefirm's internal processes, values and culture to match ‘seized’ opportunities. Communities of practice, sense of co-ownership as well as creation and constraining of behaviour would characterise a strategic focus to reconfigure the firm around SM strategy for innovation. In that sense, reconfiguration is enabled by the use of social media to develop strategic network capabilities. Social media and (open) innovation Chesbrough (2003, 2006) re-ignited and emphasised the need for firms to engage with internal and external stakeholders in the process of innovation. Around the same time frame, ICTs went through breakthrough innovation cycles accelerating from the launch of LinkedIn in 2003 to Facebook in 2004, YouTube in 2005 and Twitter in 2006. The notion of communication as it was once practiced changed forever, with blogs, hashtags and video chats emulating traditional ways of exchanging information via print media. SM by its very nature offered a cheaper and faster alternative to printingflyers, posters and adverts, with a capability to cross regional and national boundaries. Today we have an entire batch of high school students (i.e. future producers, users, developers, and innovators) who in their living days have not experienced life or work without SM. Firms have already realised the potential for SM use in engaging wider audience for promotion of products and services. More recently this realisation is seen to be seeping intofirm's processes for‘open innovation’, albeit progressively (Barlatier and Josserand, 2018). Open innovation which is described as the purposely managed knowledgeflows across organisational boundaries (Chesbrough and Bogers, 2014) is a pertinent (if not perfect) companion of SM which are widely described as ICT tools that facilitate creation and exchange of information amongst its users (Kaplan and Haenlein, 2010). In an open and collaborative innovation process enabled by SM, innovation andfirm's dynamic capabilities co-evolve such that knowledge creation and transfer become integrated part of the process (Castellacci and Natera, 2013). In this view, scholars have drawn attention to the developments of SM technologies that enable firms to connect with dispersed sources of knowledge in an effective and efficient manner (Palacios-Marqués et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016). Growing stream of research on this discourse is urgingfirms to embrace the full extent of SM technologies to create, process and integrate knowledge from internal and external sources in the process of innovation, developing customer insights, accessing knowledge, cocreating ideas and concepts with users, and supporting new product launches (Roberts and Piller, 2016). Despite, increasingly number of cases presented of in academic literature, the view still is that most firms lack a coherent SM strategy for innovation (Roberts and Piller, 2016). Some scholars have attributed this to limited know-how of SM's use in innovation processes (Marion et al., 2014). To note is that SM includes not only mainstream social networking websites such as LinkedIn, Facebook and Twitter, but also applications that permit fast and/or short multi-directional interactions (e.g. RSS) and exchange of information between individuals and groups (e.g. blogs and wikis). From an internal knowledge capital perspective, SM's specific attributes (social-orientation, ease-of-use, and open infrastructure) favour a firm's employees' knowledge creation potential (Bebensee et al., 2012) by facilitating collaboration and creation of valuable user generated content (Levy, 2009; Razmerita et al., 2009; Von Krogh, 2012). Further, from an external dialogue and collaboration perspective SM affords innovation capabilities by allowing firms to extend their reach to widely distributed knowledge regardless of their location, domain-specificities and size (Martini et al., 2014). SM use in the innovation process has transformed the role of those traditionally distant from R&D (e.g. suppliers, customers, non-R&D departments) by providing a mechanism for inclusion. Adoption of SM has been acknowledged to facilitate expression of ideas, opinions, judgements, evaluations and eventual adoption of new product, services and practices (Papa et al., 2018;Scuotto et al., 2017), for incremental or radical developments (Sigala and Chalkiti, 2007). However, in the absence of a well-considered strategy for using SM for innovation, challenges emerge that threaten the privacy of individuals, intellectual capital and competitive advantage of the firm resulting from breaches in confidentiality, spillover effects and release of critical propriety information (Marabelli and Newell, 2012; Trkman and Desouza, 2012). The view here is not to reiterate the recognised risks and barriers of ICTs, rather emphasis the need for decision-makers to remain vigilant when considering use of SM in innovation process. Furthermore, favouring extreme risk aversion to SM surely would limit thefirm's capabilities to exploit available resources to improve innovation behaviour and performance. In practice, there appears to be two main strategic approaches to SM use for innovation amongst today'sfirms. Formative approach tends to replicate ‘brainstorming’ at scale. Firms adopting a formative strategy tend to use publicly available SM for macro level engagement, listening for trends, forecasts and citizen reports on the one hand and broadcasting information on the other hand ( Nambisan and Nambisan, 2008). At ameso level formative strategies tend to involve innovation intermediaries (e.g. Innoget) to connect with external sources in the process of idea formation and open innovation coordination (Katzy et al., 2013). Firms adopting more advanced SM strategies for innovation tend to integrate SM use across channels and organisational levels. Some firms at this advanced level, have developed company-built SM (e.g. IBM's“Innovation Jam”) as a crowdsourcing solution for product, process and service innovations alongside SM to facilitate prompt identification of experts and solicitation from the innovation community (e.g. IBM's “Beehive”)( Turban et al., 2011). If successful cases presented above are encouraging,firms still need to develop their understanding of the impact of SM usage and the associated behavioural changes to integrate it to their innovation dynamics. 3.1. Sensing opportunities and threats The sensing of opportunities and threats when powered by SM in innovation seeks to harmonise the trends and‘voices’of target audience with firm's innovation priorities and capabilities. This is thefirst and most basic step wherefirms can apply and benefit from SM's specific features to generate knowledge from a wide range of stakeholders. Knowledge creation in this respect involves audience feedback, participation and two-way conversations to identify trends, preferences and innovation ideas. At an operational level, SM use in sensing for innovation facilitates the process of continuous experimentation, where firms can leverage fast and incessant information to augment innovation efforts. Thefirm benefits by gaining new facts or information that can help in managing business risk and volatility in development and delivery of innovations (Franklin et al., 2014). However, to realise this benefit, decision-makersfirst need a typology (i.e. reference classification) of various SM types, the benefits they offer, their knowledge value and the inherent challenges of implementation. To this end,Marion et al. (2014), through their exploratory study about the use of SM for new product development (NPD), have identified four main categories of ICT tools used for NPD: (1) new media tools (e.g., project wikis and cloud-basedfile sharing), (2) social networking tools (e.g., Facebook, weblogs, and Twitter), (3) traditional IT tools (e.g., e-mail and CAD), and (4) process management tools (e.g., PLM systems and dedicated intranet sites). Bhimani, Mention and Barlatier (in this issue) through a systematic review of literature at the intersection of SM and innovation notice a diversity of SM tools used in and for innovation. They identity four distinct categories including Public SM (Facebook, LinkedIn, Twitter), Company-built SM (e.g. NASA@work, IBM Jam), Company-licensed SM (e.g. MS 365 Yammer) and innovation intermediary SM (e.g. Innocentive) as those prevalent in practice. Their review positions SM as thedriver and enabler of innovation, as distinct from SM media as a mere tool to facilitate communication and interaction. At a meso-level, the functionalities of SM can drive the search for new ideas and assessments of preferences by enabling customers to offer feedback and engage in two-way conversations on products and services. It can also enable crowdsourcing of ideas as well as opinions and judgments to critique or improve upon suggested ideas. Drawing on the features of SM, social commerce enables customers to express their experiences with products and services. Social commerce in this view is defined as “a new form of SM–mediated commerce that allows customers to participate actively in the marketing and selling of products in online marketplaces.” (Li, 2018, p XXX, in this issue). Yet, despite its positive effect on social interactions, Li (in this issue) finds no significant influences of social commerce on customer's social shopping intention. However, the author observes that in the complex social commerce process, familiarity and closeness with the recommending customer plays a crucial role in the level of trust in the product recommendation, ultimately influencing social shopping intentions. Indeed, simply using SM as means to craft a conversation with customers does not create loyalty and continuous engagement in firm's innovation e fforts (Bochenek and Blili, 2014). In consequence, a clear strategic direction fostering purposeful “story-telling” conversations (Salmon, 2007) can contribute to building trust in SM's use for innovation, therein enhancing firm's sensing capabilities through rich information exchange. Social media use as part of internal communications strategy can transform how employees and experts within thefirm participate in innovation efforts (see the case of Sun Microsystems inBarker, 2008). The features of SM allow for creation of personal profiles highlighting expertise, experience and areas of interest amongst other menu options. Thus, the use of SM in innovation brings together different “voices” to facilitate idea generation and hosting of conversations, both ad-hoc and purposeful. While, SM use for innovation at macro and meso-levels tends to highlight interactions with societal and end-user, at a microlevel the focus is often on innovation communities. Often managed by the firm's central innovation office, innovation communities are created to leverage internal and external knowledge sources and facilitate collaboration amongst experts, innovators, employees, partners and suppliers (e.g. BMW's“RedSquare”). However forging convenor-ship is not an easy task and organisation's internal openness tends to play a crucial role in actual SM behavior (Heinonen, 2011). Extending on the logic of strategic sensing for knowledge generation, Richey and Ravishankar (in this issue)o ffer an original cultural perspective on the development of innovation oriented networks through SM. Seizing ‘sensed’ opportunities and threats Social media can also contribute to the ultimate aim of innovation, that is to sayfinding a market for the innovative product or service. Recently Bashir et al. (2017)explored the role of SM in new product development (NPD) amongst multinational firms in the fast moving consuming goods (FMCG) sector. They found that whilefirms generally adopted SM for communication purposes, they lacked a purposeful strategy to harness its potential in NPD processes, relying instead on internal R&D departments. Zahay et al. (2018) highlighted that integrating wisdom of the crowd into NPD is difficult for decision-makers tasked with the challenge. They found that information gathered internally tends to support the early fuzzy stages of the NPD while externally generated ideas are more likely to be accepted at the later commercialisation stage. The scholars further suggest that disparity in SM use across innovation stages is explained by thefirm's lack of formal processes and alignment between managerial responsibilities, crowdsourcing efforts and strategic budgetary allocations. Ogink and Dong (in this issue) further explore the question of how to create a purposeful dynamic of innovation in an open setting with user communities. The question of how to trigger further engagement of users is central to SM enabled innovation. Specifically, their paper through a longitudinal analysis focuses on micro-interactions between users and how users' feedback can stimulate contribution of a focal user. They use the uses and gratification framework to study the impact of three types of benefits associated with user feed-back: the cognitive, integrative and affective benefits. They show how their results can be used to improve interactions through concrete design recommendations. Of course, SM use in innovation processes has been shown to support intellectual property by way of new ideas and patent parts, an important constituent of value creation and NPD at least in manufacturing firms (Chirumalla et al., 2018). 3.3. Reconfiguration Beyond the creative process of innovation, leveraging user communities is essential to foster the adoption of innovation. Notably, people interact in SM as individuals, often aligning the interests to form affiliations in new or existing interactions (Hitchen et al., 2017). Often the firm's brand service propositions define the reach and richness of their SM use for innovation. This logic explains why firms multinationals in the FMCG sector tend to employ multiple SM channels at various stages and facets of engagement while incumbentfinancial institutions tend to rely on their established Company-built or Companylicensed SM (Greffe and Sonnac, 2008 ). Whether large or smallfirm, to gain a competitive advantage and profit from SM use,firms need to organise for innovation. At a macro-level reconfiguration may involve sophisticated SM strategy for innovation to create and constrain behaviour such as the recent use of SM for idea generation in e-government (Konsti-Laakso, 2017) and the more established SM use for promotion of sustainable innovations through corporate social responsibility (CSR) programs (Waddock and McIntosh, 2011). At the meso-level, SM use include signalling strategies in brand operations (Briggs, 2010), B2B knowledge transfer through targeted stakeholder engagement strategies (Sharma et al., 2011) and development of a sense ofco-ownership. At the micro-level, a sense of co-ownership when coupled with a clear strategy fosters an open innovation enabling culture where an individual's willingness and ‘open’ mindset translates to organisation-wide shared values towards open and collaborative innovation processes (Leidner et al., 2018; see also Go Pro's exemplary case inShorty Awards, 2016). In the co-ownership paradigm, SM affordances extend the role of users beyond being customers to include alternating role of being cocreators through provision of resources and service production. The question of innovation adoption is thus not so much a question of ‘selling’ the service but rather one of engaging with the community of users that will deliver and use this service. Examining the success story of BlaBlaCar, Casprini, Di Minin and Paraboschi (in this issue) show how SM can support the development, consolidation and expansion of such a community of users to include the society. They described the process through which the start-upfirm mobilised seven building blocks of SM (Kietzmann et al., 2011) to lock-in its community. In particular, they explore the importance of the sharing identity to create and strengthen the community. In doing so they define not only a pathway towards the successful adoption of an innovative service by a community of users but also provide an explanation of how the SM building blocks can be operationalised to create new behaviours through innovations. Besides, from an operational perspective, crowdsourcing mechanisms are where SM can contribute to innovation (de Mattos et al., 2018; Martinez, 2017) by helping organisation find innovative solution to problems and leading to both product or service innovation. A proverbial question is what types of SM are best suited for crowdsourcing, taking into account the context, openness and intermediary features. The paper by Schenk, Guittard and Pénin (in this issue) further deepens our understanding of which tool is best suited by focussing on the arbitration between open or proprietary platforms for crowdsourcing. The authors provide a solid conceptual base drawing from transaction cost theories, network externalities and internal competencies. The result is a decision-making model that has important implications for theory and practice. Indeed, building the technical capabilities appears as thefirst building block of the capabilities that can support the use of SM for innovation, a feat beset with managerial and executive challenges (Zahay et al., 2018). Thus to create profit from SM use in innovation (and crowdsourcing) requires managers to engage in continuous-beta through debate and discourse, developing interdependent capabilities to drive usage intention by way of cohesion and sharing of best practices within thefirm (Dobni and Sand, 2018). Hew, Leong, Tan, Ooi, and Lee (in this issue) explore the matter by examining resistance to social commerce in the case where it is mediated by mobile phone. Interestingly, they find that resistances are not necessarily associated with a lack of usage intention. Again, this casts a new light on the complexity of innovation adoption in general and in particular on the role of SM in these complex dynamics. Thesefindings can help develop and improve existing commercialization strategies aimed at catalysing SM users' adoption decisions. Just as technical capabilities are important, softer capabilities are also highly relevant for organisational innovation to benefit from SM. Indeed, the literature has exposed the strategic relevance of delivering ‘open’ innovation promises through use of SM tools (Barlatier and Josserand, 2018). More specifically, the paper by de Zubielqui, Fryges and Jones (in this issue) demonstrates the importance of what they call modern HRM. The authors show howmodern HRM moderates the relationship between how market-based actors source knowledge on the one hand and innovation performance of thefirm on the other hand. These modern HRM practices include “intensive levels of vertical and lateral communication, provide rewards for employee acquisition and sharing of knowledge, and delegate decision rights.” (p. XX). By demonstrating the importance of such practices, the authors highlight that the impact of SM use and firm performance shouldn't be taken for granted and that technologic capabilities are not by themselves sufficient. Considering the broad spectrum covered by the modern HRM capabilities presented, some organisations will have to consider a comprehensive change program if they want the introduction of SM to lead to innovation and performance improvements. They show how strategies to combine user-led innovation with crowdfunding can lead to a new entrepreneurial model. Such a combination expands open innovation from problem solving to co-funding of innovation, where users are not only part of the discovery process but also bring financial resources that can support the innovation. The model which the authors label‘crowdfunding-enabled user innovation’mobilises SM to enhance firm's dynamic capabilities and offers a promising new perspective on SM and open innovation. 4. The contribution of the special issue The scholarly work at the intersection of SM and (open) innovation is fast evolving. Through this special issue the aim is to contribute to the growing academic debate and suggest ways in whichfirms can harness the use of SM in and for innovation. At a glance, the titles and abstracts of the articles give an impression of the extent and richness of SM and innovation interactions. This introductory article adopts a strategic lens organising the thought across dynamic capabilities to guide top-down decision-making. The central tenet of dynamic capabilities is to address the ‘how might’ questions, in that how mightfirms organise to attain competitive advantage (Teece et al., 1997). Of course, SM are multifaceted and thus other lens (e.g. process, affordance, network, tactical) can also provide nuances to current approach to SM use in practice. “One size doesn'tfit all” when adopting SM strategy for innovation. At the juncture of strategic capability development, managers need to afford attention to the level of stakeholder engagement where by sophistication process can influence value creation efforts (Bochenek and Blili, 2014). Thus, managers need to be aware of the typology of SM, their affordances at various stages of innovation and desired strategic integration (formative, advanced). The first two papers are subjectively classi fied under the macrolevel. Bhimani et al. (in this issue) undertake a systematic review to identify a SM typology and the need to harness the full potential classification of SM as driver and enabler of innovation, guiding researchers withfive clear propositions to advance the knowledge in the area. Casprini et al. (in this issue) explore a real-life case to demonstrate how SM features can be leveraged to manage user communities in the process of innovation. At the meso-level, the contribution of this special issue is the strongest withfive of the nine papers identified as those exploring and explaining the role of customers (or end-users) in the crowdsourcing and co-creation process enabled by SM. In the third paper Li (in this issue) draw attention to social commerce's impact to cognitive and affective social interactions, suggesting ways in which firms can leverage SM to make sense of customer's purchasing decisions to inform innovation efforts. In the fourth paper, Ognink and Dong (in this issue) highlight the multi-faceted benefits of stimulating innovation via SM, explaining how cognitive, integrative and affective benefits jointly influence end-user's idea and comment contribution towards innovation efforts. This leads to paper by Schenk et al. (in this issue) which explore the suitability of crowdsourcing platform for innovation, proposing a decision-making model to guide open v proprietary dilemma in choosing SM for innovation. In the same vein, the sixth paper by Hew et al. (in this issue) addresses the resistances to usage intention through an artificial neural network (ANN) analysis. At micro-level, Richey and Ravishankar (in this issue) challenge the SM use for innovation by highlighting that SM enabled innovation relies on new connections, which are hard to establish. They draw managerial attention to micro-level processes affecting framing which guide selection of cultural tools, ultimately helping to turn mental maps into action. Likewise in the eighth paper, de Zubielqui, Fryges and Jones (in this issue) explores the effects of knowledge created via SM on innovation and productivity, highlighting the moderating role of ‘modern’ HRM practices. Finally, the sequence concludes with the paper by Brem et al. (in this issue) who conduct three case studies ranging from low-tohigh-tech crowdfunding campaigns and argue that SM use in crowdfunding may give rise to user entrepreneurs, redefining how firms create and commercialise new products and services. Taken together, the contribution of this special issue also suggest a process approach through which organisations can foster the contribution of social media to innovation and innovation adoption (see Fig. 1). This three-stage approach encompasses organisational capability building, developing communities for innovation and social commerce for innovation adoption. We present bellow this integrated process before presenting a consolidated research agenda stemming from the papers of this special issue. A step in the right direction towards harnessing the potential of SM for innovation is to build dynamic capabilities. The combination of the articles of this special issue dealing with organisational capabilities is an incentive to look beyond the mere technical abilities and integrate a broader spectrum of capabilities and resources (seeTable 2 for paper classification). Capability building is captured mainly by thefirst three papers (Schenk, Guittard & Pénin; de Zubielqui, Fryges & Jones; Brem, Bilgram & Marchuk). Yet, while capability building, for instance by choosing the right combination of platforms or adapting the organisation, is important in order to leverage SM for innovation, this is only a first step that corresponds mainly to sensing and seizing activities. A second step in the process is that of engaging users and other actors in the innovation process, indeed, it is the engagement and the quality of contributions that can actually make a difference to the innovation process. It is mainly at that stage that strategic network capabilities can be fostered and support the reconfiguration process. Two papers of this special issue make significant contributions to some of the key leverages to develop user communities and networks for innovation (Richey & Ravishankar; Ogink & Qi Dong). Beyond the creative process of innovation, the third step is focusses on putting together or leveraging user communities in order to foster the adoption of innovation. The three final papers in this special issue cast a new eye on the contribution of social media to such adoption by facilitating seizing in the sense that they help the organisation yield the benefit of the previous stage. 5. Conclusion To conclude, this special issue and the organising framework proposed here contribute to develop both theoretical and managerial knowledge on how to strategically use SM to leverage dynamic capabilities – the strategic capacity for re-innovation of thefirm's business model and services to maintain external or evolutionaryfitness in line with the changing customer needs (Teece, 2007). This helpsfirms to be able to leverage SM to detect changing stakeholder's expectations and interests from their business ecosystem, such as customer behaviours A.-L. Mention, et al. Technological Forecasting & Social Change xxx (xxxx) xxx–xxx 7 and demands for thefirm's services, and accordingly reconfigure the firm's business processes and the underlying infrastructure resources to build the correspondent digital-oriented organisational capabilities to co-create value with customers and other stakeholders. From a strategic perspective, we concur withOestreicher-Singer and Zalmanson (2013) and suggest that to profit from SM use in and for innovation,firms need a clear purpose, integration of ICTs into innovation processes to create co-ownership experiences that are difficult to imitate or replicate. SM users collaborate for many reasons, from free expression of opinions to participation in co-creation activities to realising a need for‘outside’ help in conceptualising, developing and realising the innovation efforts. Viewing from this lens, collaborative tools such as SM that foster commonality-based trust can help firms achieve incremental change through continuous experimentation, and at times lead to breakthrough innovations. However, there is scarcity of knowledge as to what dynamic capabilities are comprised of, and of the role of SM therein necessary for firm to remain aligned with the changing customer needs and/or other stakeholder's focus. The contributions of this special issue highlight many relevant future research questions and present a rich variety of thought leadership on the SM and innovation interactions, both conceptually and empirically. Through the content analysis of presidential speeches and the exploratory case studies of high-speed rail and semiconductor industries in China, we clarify the role of the government as an orchestrator of open innovation and developing dynamic capabilities. State-owned enterprises, privately-owned companies, and foreign firms differentially affect the innova - tion performance of these industries, and the latter kinds of firms need greater support to implement the stated goals for open innovation in Chinese presidential speeches effectively. 1. Introduction F irms are increasingly exploring the resources of external sources as new ways to identify innovative ideas and solutions. This open innovation (OI) paradigm has gained much popularity (Chesbrough, 2003, 2017; Gassmann, 2006). Although companies are embedded in different contexts, existing OI literature has focused largely on firm-level analyses (e.g., Chesbrough, 2003; Dodgson et al., 2006), paying less attention to the context within which OI occurs and the constraints associated with particular contexts. In certain con - texts, such as China, companies are much more exposed to the external environment and must take account of a wide range of stakeholder interests. Failure to pay attention to these constituents may pose risks for the companies. In addition, external stakeholders may evaluate the results of OI quite differently, often reaching conclusions that are dif - ficult to reconcile with the goals of the companies. If the field of OI is to continue to evolve beyond the study of corporate level strategy, it clearly requires the development of models with more general applicability in different institutional contexts. In this paper, we offer a novel combination of innovation theory that is illustrated through strategic management frameworks (i.e., the dynamic capabil - ities perspectives and OI strategy). In doing so, we generate policy insights that are different from those derived from more policy-oriented disciplines. The dynamic capabilities (DC) framework is concerned about how to create and sustain competitive advan - tage in a rapidly changing environment. This lens will extend the existing research in industry policy by explaining the conditions under which industrial © 2020 RADMA and John Wiley & Sons Ltd Henry Chesbrough, Sohvi Heaton and Liang Mei 2 R&D Management 2020 policy leads to competitive advantage (Teece et al., 2016). Our research highlights the importance of coherence between DC and OI strategy. We apply this novel approach to the context of China where innovation success varies across industries. Therefore, our main research question is determining the conditions under which policy makers can realize innovation success through open innovation. Engaging in policy debates will also contribute to the fields of OI and DC by enabling these theories to become more widely applied and tested. We first explicate ‘open innovation with Chinese characteristics’, and then, we interrogate this approach by examining Chinese innovation across two different industries: high-speed rail (HSR) and semiconductors. We conclude by considering what this perspective can contribute back to the concepts of DC and OI, respectively. 2. Theoretical and empirical background 2.1. Open innovation with Chinese characteristics At its most fundamental level, open innovation is embedded in the notion that the sources of knowledge for innovation are widely distributed in the economy. When Chesbrough (2003) inaugurated the term, OI described a phenomenon of companies making greater use of external ideas and technologies in their own business, and letting unused internal ideas and technologies go outside for others. His original definition, ‘purposive inflows and outflows of knowledge’, hearkened back to a vibrant economic literature on spillovers that arise from the firm’s investment in R&D. Because firms cannot fully specify the outcomes of this investment in advance, R&D inevitably produces outcomes that were not expected ex ante. These outcomes spill over beyond the ability of the investing firm to benefit from them, hence, the term ‘spillovers’. Nelson (1959) observed basic research generated many such spillovers, and that firms who funded this research had only limited ability to appropriate value from these spillovers. Arrow (1962) also took note of this spillover problem, recognizing these spillovers meant the social return to R&D investment exceeded that of the private return to the firm undertaking the investment. Hence, he reasoned, private firms will underinvest in R&D from a social perspective. Cohen and Levinthal (1990) in turn wrote about the impor - tance of investing in internal research in order to be able to utilize external technology, an ability they termed ‘absorptive capacity’. Rosenberg (1990) asked the related question, ‘Why do firms conduct basic research with their own money?’, with the answer enhancing the firm’s ability using external knowledge. Throughout this literature, however, spillovers are deemed a cost to the focal firm of doing business in R&D and are judged to be essentially unmanageable. OI, by contrast, proposes that R&D spillovers can be transformed into inflows and outflows of knowledge that can be purposively managed. Firms can develop processes to seek out and transfer external knowledge into their own innovation activities, and also create channels to move unutilized internal knowledge from inside the firm out to other organizations in the surrounding environment. China provides a unique business environment for R&D spillovers, suggesting that existing theories may not be readily applicable to the context of Chinese innovations. The Chinese domestic market is so large that domestic companies have little incentive to commercialize their successful innovations for sale abroad (Orr and Roth, 2012). As a socialist market economy, the Chinese government has often taken an active role in the innovation process, driving a considerable portion of R&D and domestic firm innovations (Guan and Yam, 2015). . It now seems clear that China’s path to prosperity is unlikely to converge on a Western model of a limited role for the government, with strong private property rights. All these factors suggest that we need a new perspective, in order to understand and interpret the approach to innovation in China. More recently, Chinese leaders themselves have begun to articulate a new approach to innovation. Xi Jingping thought 1 suggests that the Chinese government has changed its role to one facilitating innovation, but this role is sometimes incoherent with market roles. Throughout the speech, we identify a central tension: Xi’s thought proclaims a commitment to supply-side industrial reforms, and giving play to the ‘decisive role’ of market forces in resource allocation, on the one hand, while the Party exercises overall leadership over all areas of endeavor in every part of the country, on the other. Here are Xi’s remarks on the role of the market: We must see that the market plays the decisive role in resource allocation, the government plays its role better, and new industrialization, IT application, urbanization, and agricultural modernization go hand in hand. (Xi’s speech at the 19ths national congress) In another part of Xi’s speech to the 19th Party Congress, the role of openness was also quite salient. Openness brings progress, while self-seclusion leaves one behind. China will not close its door © 2020 RADMA and John Wiley & Sons Ltd Open innovation with Chinese characteristics R&D Management 2020 3 to the world, we will only become more and more open. We should pursue the Belt and Road Initiative as a priority, give equal emphasis to ‘bringing in’ and ‘going global,’ follow the principle of achieving shared growth through discussion and collaboration, and increase openness and cooperation in building innovation capacity. It does not require much imagination to interpret Xi’s remarks on openness through the lens of OI as characterized in its definition above. ‘Bringing in’ connects well to outside-in knowledge flows in OI (Chesbrough, 2003). These flows not only include foreign direct investment, but also includes accessing external knowledge through university-based research collaborations, inward licensing of technology, Chinese venture capital investment in startup ventures outside China, reverse engineering of externally developed products, and following the technical literature. ‘Going global’ refers to the inside-out knowledge flows in OI (Chesbrough, 2003), involving exports of indigenously developed technologies from China-based companies. But it can also include external licensing of Chinese technologies, spin-offs of Chinese companies, and Chinese venture capital investment in China-based startups that export outside of China. The Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) can be understood as a country-level policy of Inside-Out open innovation. And both the high-speed rail industry and semiconductor industry figure importantly in the implementation of the BRI. The resulting perspective from Xi’s speech is a unique blend of innovation policies that we term ‘OI with Chinese characteristics’. China is with a rapidly growing industrial base and a similarly evolving technological capability (Fu, 2015), achieving its tremendously large domestic economy that has become the seedbed for substantial indigenous innovation. Also of great interest is the leading role of the Chinese government in directing the future direction of the Chinese innovation system, something that is completely new to OI in both theory and practice. The Chinese government seeks to obtain the many benefits of OI, while guiding the economy forward at the same time. This introduces tensions between the government, on the one hand, and the market, on the other, which we consider from the DC perspective. 2.2. Dynamic capabilities DC are higher-level capabilities to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external resources/ competences to address, and possibly shape, rapidly changing business environments (Teece et al., 1997; Teece, 2007). Strong DC are critical to success, especially for pioneering a market or a new product category of an innovating firm (Teece, 2012a, p. 1,396). DC can be thought of as consisting of three clusters of activities: (1) identification and assessment of an opportunity (sensing), (2) mobilization of resources to address an opportunity and to capture value from doing so (seizing), and (3) continued renewal to execute and sustain the innovation at scale (transforming). These activities must be per - formed expertly if the firm is to remain relevant as markets and technologies change (Teece, 2012a, p. 1,396). Organizations that possess stronger DC perform better, and are more adapted to their environment. However, performance effects of DC vary in different environmental contexts. Conducive governance conditions inside the firm might allow organizations to ‘pivot’ decisively when the situation demands it (Helfat et al., 2007). Institutional obstacles can curtail the effectiveness of an organization’s DC. Regulatory restrictions placed on a university, for example, can undermine the ability of managers to improve that university’s fortunes (Heaton et al., 2016). 2.3. Dynamic capabilities and open innovation strategy A strategy that is consistent, coherent, and accommodating toward innovation is just as vital as DC to achieving competitive advantage. While strategy and capabilities can be analytically separated, as a practical matter they need to be developed and implemented together (Teece et al., 2016). The two concepts are distinct but interrelated and interdependent. DC propounds that, in regimes of deep uncertainty such as those which characterize sectors of the economy experiencing rapid change, management must prime the organization for sensing, seizing, and transforming, and marry the right strategy to the firm’s capacity to be agile (Teece et al., 2016, p. 32). As innovation increasingly involves communities, ecosystems, and networks, an open strategy is necessary. Chesbrough and Appleyard (2007, p. 57) define open strategy as a firm’s justification for participating in an open initiative, including its ability to capture value from the initiative. An open initiative is characterized by a) the reliance on assets outside of the firm’s boundaries (inclusion), and © 2020 RADMA and John Wiley & Sons Ltd Henry Chesbrough, Sohvi Heaton and Liang Mei 4 R&D Management 2020 b) the (free) access to project results by outsiders (transparency) (Appleyard and Chesbrough, 2017, p. 310–311). Open strategy also requires DC. Appleyard and Chesbrough (2017, p. 318) argue that to capture value created in an open initiative, having competencies spanning technology prowess and open-supporting organizational processes is important. Therefore, we conjecture that the relationship between DC and OI strategy is complementary. 2 Teece (2015) alludes to this by arguing that: the OI framework can enhance DC (with respect to all three classes of micro-foundations) through explicit recognition that sensing and seizing can be extended to external stakeholders and also to members of crowds. 3. Methods 3.1. Research approach We employed a qualitative research approach. Data were obtained through primary interviews and combined with secondary data (presidential speeches). We used presidential speeches because leaders use these speeches to send important signals to various stakeholders when articulating a vision and proposing a new initiative. These signals help align the interests and activities of these stakeholders. In particular, a case study methodology is appropriate for exploratory studies because it allows arriving at findings inductively derived from the data rather than testing predetermined hypotheses and addresses the ‘how’ and ‘why’ questions (Yin, 1989). Moreover, the case study approach has often been used in innovation policy studies (e.g., Nelson, 1993), demonstrated applicable to analyzing shift in innovation policy in China (Chen and Naughton, 2016). Our approach entailed computerized content analysis techniques and dictionaries to measure OI strategy. There are some key requirements for conducting computerized textual analysis: collecting a corpus of documents, running a computer application to generate a score for each document, and developing a data dictionary for each construct (Short et al., 2010; Pandey et al., 2017). In collecting documents, we made sure that there is thematic similarity (innovation, industrial policy) across documents. For the second requirement, we used Nvivo 11. With regards to the data dictionary requirement, Nvivo 11 not only provides built-in dictionaries, but we also added user-generated data dictionaries. To develop customized data dictionaries, we ran the software on each document and extracted the phrases in each document. The list of phrases extracted from the documents was carefully reviewed. Coders reviewed each phrase and coded it as an indicator of OI according to their judgment. Initial inter-coder reliability was approximately 50%. The two coders went through additional coding iteration until inter-coder agreement was achieved regarding phrases reflecting OI (see Table 1). Following Pandey et al. (2017), we used phrase-level as well as word-level dictionaries. Single words like ‘open’ and ‘technology’ when decontextualized can fail as stand-alone words to convey the intended meaning as in ‘open innovation’. It is recommended that researchers conduct validity tests for measures derived through content analysis (e.g., Short et al., 2010). To ensure content validity, Short et al. (2010) recommended that researchers solicit reviews by content experts to judge whether the coding dictionary contents adequately represents the construct. To conduct validity tests, two experts in our research identified phrases that indicate OI, which is used as an expert dictionary. We found a moderate to high overlap between phrases in the two dictionaries. This is because the expert dictionary is likely to be more aspirational and better attuned to what is considered OI in theory. The customized dictionary is closer to what is actually being practiced and emphasized in the real world. 3.2. The research setting Data are from two industries: the high-speed rail (HSR) and semiconductor industries. The primary sources of data are key presidential speeches (over 250,000 words in total) and industry reports. The data collected through interviews with organizations were used to supplement these sources and examine the effects in specific industries. In selecting cases, we utilized a maximum variation strategy, a purposeful sampling strategy to ensure that the selected cases would reflect the representation of industrial innovations in China. One potential concern is that selecting cases that are different can be a problem, but this feature can also help increase the strength of the results. Patton (1990, p. 172) argues that ‘any common patterns that emerge from great variation are of particular interest and value in capturing the core experiences and central, shared aspects’ of a case. Our two cases involve different industries, and thus, different key actors in the industries. We aimed to identify emerging patterns that cut across the two cases despite how different they may be. © 2020 RADMA and John Wiley & Sons Ltd Open innovation with Chinese characteristics R&D Management 2020 5 Our criteria were to include cases that (1) receive equal attention from the government (so that we control for the level of government support) (2) differ in terms of performance. We sought industries that appeared to be of strategic importance to the country, but the performance of which varied as a result of differences in open strategy. The importance of these two chosen industries to the country is similar. Those industries we selected met the first condition because they were identified by the government as key sectors to achieve its ‘Made in China 2025’ strategy. China’s integrated-circuits deficit has become China’s biggest import item since 2005. Thus, the government has made it a priority to catch up and forge ahead in this strategic industry (Ernst, 2016, p. 3). Since 2010, the government has given priority to the development of the HSR as a new strategic industry. The domestic Railway Corporation proudly announced that China’s world-leading HSR industry is the only strategic industry in China that has surpassed its international competitors (Yan, 2019). HSR figures prominently in the BRI, with high-speed rail projects often comprising important early initiatives for the countries embracing the BRI. While the government has prioritized these sectors given the strategic importance, variation in state strategy, and the different roles of consumers led to very different outcomes in each sector. The HSR was considered a success while the semiconductor is less successful, which we discuss in detail below. 4. Results 4.1. Analysis of the high-speed rail industry Although the HSR has become globally competitive, in early years, foreign companies held substantial technological advantages over domestic firms, and domestic HSR designs were commercially unsuccessful (Wang, 2016; Mei, 2017). This all changed starting in 2004, when the Ministry of Railways (MoR) transformed its industrial development direction to ‘introduction, absorption, and re-innovation’. A key policy was China’s commitment to the ‘four vertical and four horizontal’ high-speed railway network planning roadmap in 2004. This policy clearly stated the intention to construct a 12,000 kilometers high-speed railway network throughout the country. This was roughly equivalent to all of the HSR lines that had been installed in the rest of the world to that point in time. To achieve this vision, China needed the best of foreign technology, and planned to develop an effective domestic supply base in HSR. It also utilized open innovation extensively to strengthen the domestic capability of the HSR industry in China. The SOEs developed an indigenous high-speed train the CRH380A, and did so by linking with 25 universities, 11 research institutes, major government agencies such as MoR and Ministry of Science and Technology and 51 national-level laboratories and engineering centers (Gao et al., 2016). This extensive research and technology infrastructure for HSR helps to explain why Chinese companies developed the absorptive capacity (Cohen and Levinthal, 1990) that they previously lacked (Mei, 2017). By seizing technological capabilities transferred by foreign companies, the SOEs achieved the best practice by successfully developing an indigenous high-speed train (e.g., the CRH380A at the 300 ~ 350 km/hr speed level). By promoting technology introduction through outside-in OI, the MoR facilitated technology absorption by the domestic suppliers, created the market, raised money, and set unified technical standards (Wang, 2016). Further, by forcing the merger of the two SOE providers – CSR and CNR – into the CRRC, the MoR achieved both technology leadership and tremendous scale economies in both HSR and its complementary assets such as railway construction. The government further promoted the outbound OI of China’s HSR through policies such as One Belt One Road and Made in China 2025 (Mei, 2017). The CRRC holds a greater global market share than the previous leaders Siemens and Alstom did combined (Atkinson and Foote, 2019). 4.2. Analysis of the semiconductor industry China has become the largest market for semiconductors in terms of consumption in the world (VerWey, 2019, p. 6). So the scale advantage of HSR is becoming a possible driver for the semiconductor industry as well. However, despite decades and billions of dollars of state-led investment, China’s domestic production of semiconductors covers less than 13% of the country’s demand (IC Insights, 2016). As a result, China’s trade deficit in semiconductors has been increasing (Figure 1). This is a marked contrast to the situation in HSR. Figure 1. China semiconductor trade deficit, 2011–2017. One segment is focused on the large domestic market in China, while the other is anchored in extensive international supply chains, and exports most of its output. While chip design companies have growth potential, Chinese domestic semiconductor manufacturing technology and capabilities have failed to meet the country’s demand (Ernst, 2016). In both segments, since the late 1980s, the Chinese government has tried to raise the industrial capabilities through joint ventures between large SOEs and foreign companies such as Lucent Technologies, ITT, and Phillips. None of them succeeded (Oktay, 2018). The SOEs provide the bulk of sales and employment in the industry, and virtually all of this output is consumed domestically. The SOEs lag the state of the art in the industry by 2–3 generations of technology (Ting-Fang, 2018), as measured by the line-width of the chip designs manufactured in the chips. Chinese SOEs today are building and shipping products with line-widths that were shipped by foreign companies 3–5 years ago. The state has played an active role including mobilizing capital to invest, which initiated the restructuring of SOEs, actions that mirror the successful management of the HSR industry. Li (2016) argued that the lack of strategic control on their own prevented these companies from developing organizational capabilities needed to compete. With the rise of the non-state sector, the state transferred its finance role to lower-level governments, but the structure of capital provision did not match the needs of the industry very well as it requires large economies of scale (Li, 2016). This activity has been focused primarily upon the segment serving the Chinese domestic market. There is a second segment in the Chinese semiconductor industry, though, that is shipping products of the same line-widths as the global leaders. This segment consists of the privately-owned companies (POCs) in semiconductors. Most of the output from the POCs is exported outside of China to international customers, as part of the global supply chains used by these customers. The POCs in the Chinese semiconductor industry have been the primary source of introducing new technological innovations into China (Chesbrough and Liang, 2008). These POCs are led by the decisive role of the mar - ket, and are more distant from the leading role of the Party. There is a further segmentation in semiconductors between firms designing chips (design houses), and firms building those designs (manufacturers, or ‘fabs’). Integrated circuit design continues to be the fastest growing segment of China’s semiconductor industry, with an annual growth of 23% in 2018 (Chou and Hou, 2019) (see Figure 2). The design segment is driven by creativity, with lower capital requirements, and a premium for clever design and fast turnaround. There are many hundreds of these companies (see Table 2) in China such as Spreadtrum and RDA, none of whom are SOEs. Their success was due to self-generated technology, evidenced in their large number of patents (Oktay, 2018). Put differently, these companies were able to succeed far more than their SOE counterparts, because their strategic direction was led by experienced expatriate professionals (Li, 2016, p. 16). They were led by the decisive role of the (international) markets, rather than the leading role of the Party. Figure 2. IC design enterprises in China. But even here, POCs have made strong inroads, and have been faster to adopt the latest technologies, in comparison to the SOEs (Clarke, 2017). The domestic demand structure for semiconductors is quite heterogeneous, and quite different from demand in HSR. The top players in the industry earn most of the economic profit, while other competitors lose money (Thomas, 2015). Deficiencies in the technologies of Chinese SOE manufacturers have also limited their ability to export. The Chinese POCs, by contrast, export the majority of their output outside of China (Chesbrough and Teece, 2005). Discussion Applying OI perspective to public policy, we aimed to identify contingencies under which industrial innovation policy may succeed or cause tension with market forces. In doing so, we clarified the government role as an orchestrator of both inbound and outbound open innovation, and developing DC and found that OI policy positively influences the relationship between DC and industrial innovation performance. 5.1. Theoretical contributions Our research is one of the first studies to apply DC and OI to the context of public policy in emerging markets like China. These concepts can not only help individual firms advance their innovative potential, but also they can provide new insights into the way that institutional contexts and public policy impact on industrial innovation performance for the nation state as well. Our study also contributes to the growing liter - ature on OI and public policy (e.g., Bogers et al., 2018; Chesbrough and Vanhaverbeke, 2018). Previous studies have begun to discuss possible applications of OI in the policy arena, but they often remain theoretical without considering specific characteristic of the institutional context. Beyond the existing research at the firm level, our study provides empirical analyses and sheds some light on industrial innovation policy issues. Outside the traditional domain of R&D, governments can support infrastructure such as technology platforms that facilitate the flow of ideas and resources and also that identify social problems and source effective solutions, which in turn helps develop the DC of the government. The main focus in the literature is to explain why some states are successful at developing institutions that help take on an effective coordination role while others are not (Evans, 2012). It also emphasizes the interaction of countries’ heterogeneous factor endowments with their industries’ heterogeneous characteristics but generally ignores the role of firms. Our analysis above examines three types of firms (former SOEs, POCs, and foreign companies) in two contrasting industries. Our more granular context allows the roles of open innovation and dynamic capabilities to be more visible, relative to earlier policy studies. 5.2. Two industries We discussed above how DC and OI strategy inter - act in relation to industrial innovation in these two different industries. Xi Jinping thought aligns well with the situation in the HSR. This market is driven by infrastructure development, where governments play a critical role in authorizing, funding, and sometimes operating the HSR systems. The market can be thought of not only as a business-to-government market, but also as a government-to-government business. Here, the role of the government is well suited to guide the market, since the market is constituted by other governments seeking the benefits of HSR 3. However, the innovation record in the semiconductor industry is more mixed. The high degree of capital intensity enables the government to guide and direct the development of manufacturing facilities. The design segment, by contrast, receives little attention and no government funding. This latter segment has been more agile and more adaptive, and has a much higher degree of exports. The structure of demand for semiconductors is more heterogeneous, involving the decisions of thousands of firms, rather than a handful of governments as in HSR. This greater degree of decentralized decision-making urges us to pay more attention to the POCs’ role played in China. POCs are the unsung heroes of innovation in China, contributing almost two-thirds of China’s growth and nine-tenths of new jobs in the industry 4. In semiconductors, POCs like SMIF and the many design houses in Shanghai and Shenzhen are well ahead of SOEs. We constructed Table 4 to represent the market share by ownership in HSR and semiconductors to highlight this contrast in demand structure. Outside of our two industries, the pattern of strong POCs outperforming weaker SOEs continues. Full or partial POCs such as Alibaba, Baidu, Huawei, and Tencent dominate the Chinese tech sector. The government’s level of involvement varies from company to company, often in inverse proportion to a firm’s capabilities (Bey, 2017). China’s biggest tech POCs have demonstrated increased prowess in leveraging China’s market scale and their own R&D to produce innovation-led growth. In doing so, they have developed DC to adapt continuously to stay on top of their competition. Alibaba, for example, ranked seventh among the world’s most innovative companies in a recent KPMG survey, beating even Samsung Electronics (Bey, 2017). The government aligns well with SOEs, but poorly with POCs and foreign companies, in seeking to balance the decisive role of the market with the leading role of the Party.
