Policy and managerial implications Similar to the way many Japanese firms experienced rapid growth during the 1980s (Teece, 2012b), Chinese companies rose to significance in many industries on the strength of their ordinary capabilities, developed by employing learning processes that resulted in operational excellence. However, ordinary capabilities are about doing things right, not about doing the right things, and they are imitable. Teece (2012b) argued that much of Japan’s economic weakness since the 1990s can be traced to a weakness in DC. Similarly, one of the tasks of renewal that China faces as it moves forward is to strengthen its DC. Achieving and sustaining DC across major Chinese markets will require much more than managing the SOEs. If the government persists in playing a very strong role, this will advantage certain industries with concentrated demand like HSR, but may disadvantage many more Chinese industries with decentralized demand, where POCs and foreign firms provide critical contributions to innovation. However, there is another path available to the government in these kinds of industries: embrace and promote OI strategy within and outside the country. As discussed above, openness is indeed useful particularly for certain sectors such as biotechnology where firms need to be connected to globally distributed knowledge networks complementing local sources of technological knowledge. Such a policy will increase the sources of useful knowledge available to innovative organizations like POCs in China. It may also help strong POCs increase exports to other countries, deepening the expertise of these firms, strengthening their positions in global supply chains, and increasing their economies of scale. Such a policy, though, would require the Party to look beyond their strong relations with the SOEs, so that sufficient resources are available to POCs to realize this result. Our research also provides some deductive guidance for managers. Firms should recognize that the nature of industrial policy varies considerably across sectors, which means that companies should think carefully about which industry offers the best vantage point to target the broad Chinese market. Firms should discriminate between SOEs and POCs, for they are structured differently, and play different roles in the Chinese innovation system. Firms should also examine the implications of such policy differences on their competitive advantage (e.g., capabilities and cost structure) prior to committing to the market. Moreover, firms could develop capabilities to influence policies through collaborations with a wide range of partners for innovation. For example, companies might forge a partnership with a top university in China. This could deepen ties to important sources of knowledge inside China, and provide a pipeline of talented individuals who might later work at the foreign company. It may even help influence Table 4. Future studies Our study has many limitations. China’s economy is far more complex than what we observe in two industries. Our account of innovation in each of these two industries, in turn, is necessarily limited in scope as well. One question that might arise is how this approach can work when the domestic market is small (e.g., in Israel or Finland). We tested the framework in the context of a large domestic market that allows participants to exploit scale economies in most industries. Firms and governments might need to pursue a very different strategy when the domestic market is small. Further research exploring industrial policy through the perspectives of DC and OI in smaller market contexts (e.g., Vietnam or Malaysia) would be an important avenue for future research. In turn, DC and OI need to reckon more directly with governmental actors in their roles for shaping the context for innovation in particular countries. His research, training and cons ulting activities cover strategi c change and leadership. 1 Introduction The strategic management of technological change in turbulent t imes is one of the most central managerial tasks in ensuring organisational success and even survival. An analysis of the history of established, reputable firms shows that some of them are able to adapt to changes in their environment or even to proactively st imulate change and prosper, while others are not able to change and therefore fail . The business press as well as management journals are full of examples and case studies of more (e.g. IBM; Mergenthaler Linotype) and less (e.g. Polaroid; Pan-Am) adaptive firms (e.g. Tripsas and Gavetti, 2000; Probst and Raisch, 2005; O’Reilly and Tushman, 2008). While some firms have managed to continuously initiate frame-breaking technologi cal change (e.g. Apple), other firms were unable to keep pace with technological developments (e.g. Kodak). In search of an explanation of adaptive firm behaviour, researc hers in the tradition of the resource-based view (RBV) of the firm have developed the co ncept of dynamic capabilities (Teece et al., 1997) as “the capacity of an organization to purposefully create, extend or modify its resource base” [Helfat et al., (2007), p.4 ]. During the past two decades, the dynamic capabilities vi ew (DCV) has taken centre s tage in explaining organisational adaptation. Building and using dynamic capabilit ies has become the default answer to the question as to what enables firms to deal with technological change (for some valuable reviews of the DCV, see e.g. Wang and Ahmed, 2007; Ambrosini and Bowman, 2009; Easterby-Smith et al., 2009; Barreto, 2010; Giudi ci and Reinmoeller, 2012; Eriksson, 2014). Vogel and Güttel’s (2013) meta-analysis even identified responding to environmental change via technological innovation and adaptation as one of the most dominant themes in dynamic capabilities research. However, capturing the nature of dynamic capabilities still pos es an exacting challenge (e.g. Arend and Bromiley, 2009; Schreyögg and Kliesch -Eberl, 2007; DiStefano et al., 2010; Petera f et al., 2013). Additionally, th e question of how dynamic capabilities actually lead to change has yet to be answered. Ac cordingly, research needs further elaborations on how dynamic capabilities facilitate ada ptation whenever new technological trajectories emerge . Therefore, we aim at buildin g an integrative framework that shows how dynamic capabilities contribute to man aging technological change. Our paper aims at complementing existing reviews of the DCV by systematically reviewing the widespread and heterogeneous literature on dynami c capabilities with particular emphasis on their function of enabling firms to cope with or even induce technological change. As a result o f o u r r e v i e w , w e f o c u s o n t he role of absorptive capacity, ambidexterity and techno logy management ‘as dynamic c apabilities’ and we elucidate their contribution to explaining processes of technol ogical innovation and change in firms. Our synthesis extends current knowledge by int egrating the core subprocesses of these concepts into one framework. Finally, on the basis of our review 190 S. Konlechner et al. and framework we develop a research agenda, in which we pinpoint some open questions and promising fields in dynamic capabilities research. In order to identify core papers for analysis, we conducted a s ystematic literature review (Tranfield et al., 2003) in the ISI web of science. For our literature review, we searched for papers published between 1990 and 2014 with ‘dynam ic capabilit*’ in their title and ‘technolog*’ as a topic (223 results). We excluded pr oceedings papers and book chapters and analysed the remain ing 143 results according to th eir contribution to the topics of dynamic capabilities and technology management. Based on our analysis of the papers, we excluded those papers that did not focus on dynamic capabilities and technology management, technological change or technological innovation. Additionally, we undertook forward and backward searches to ensure that all important contributions to the topic were covered (e.g. papers at the core of the ‘Technol ogical Innovation & Adaptation’ cluster in Vogel and Güttel’s bibliographic analysi s of the DCV, 2013). Overall, following this procedure resulted in a sample of 86 pa pers analysing the link between dynamic capabilities and technological change. For buil ding our framework, as presented in the third part of this paper, our literature revie w enabled us to identify ambidexterity, absorptive capac ity and technology management as three theoretical lenses that provide insights into how dynamic capabilities facilitate purposeful adaptation to technological change. Thus, we focused our analysis on the c ore contributions that integrated the issues of dynamic capabilities and ambidexterity (O’Reilly and Tushman, 2008), absorptive capacity (Zahra and George, 2002) and technol ogy management (Cetindamar et al., 2009), respectively. The remainder of the paper is st ructured as follows: in the sec ond section of this paper we review the concept of dynamic capabilities with partic ular emphasis on their role in faciliating technological change. In section three, we develop a framework of dynamic capabilities-driven change based on established constru cts. In doing so, we aim at showing how dynamic capabilities for managing technological change actually unfold their impact. Finally, in the fourth section, we propose an age nda for further research to deepen knowledge of dynamic capabilities for managing technological change. 2 Dynamic capabilities for managing technological change: a rev iew Technological change is a main trigger of innovation and reconf iguration processes in organisations. New technologies such as microelectronics, minia turisation, supply chains with their underlying ICT-systems, cyber-physical systems or so cial media applications shape economies and societies. Firms are increasingly under pre ssure to deal with discontinuities, complexity and dynamics in order to remain com petitive. Thus, developing and maintaining capabilities for governing change an d adaptation become important requirements for organisations. The DCV focuses on how firms can change their value-creating re sources over time. Indeed, dynamic capabilities are fundamental means of coping with technological change in the environment or to even inducing such change. However, de spite the enormous practical relevance of dynamic capabilities, there is still liv ely discussion regarding the question as to how they actually work (DiStefano et al., 2014). This section synthesises the key findings with regard to the essential characteristics o f dynamic capabilities and highlights some important empirical findings regarding the role of dynamic capabilities in coping with technological change. We acknowledge that differ ent conceptualisations A dynamic capabilities perspective on managing technological change 191 of dynamic capabilities can currently be found in the literatur e (for some overviews see Schreyögg and Kliesch-Eberl, 200 7; DiStefano et al., 2010; Pete raf et al., 2013). 1 O u r analysis focuses on key features that have been addressed from various perspectives. It follows the logic of describing the nature of dynamic capabilit ies, influence factors on their creation and shape, their individual components and underlying processes, as well as their performance implications. 2.1 Dynamic capabilities facilitate the dynamic adaptation of a firm’s resource base Dynamic capabilities are referred to as dynamic capabilities because they facilitate the development of a firm’s resource base (cf. Teece et al., 1997; Ambrosini and Bowman, 2009; Stadler et al., 2013). Building on RBV theorising (e.g. B arney, 1991; Peteraf, 1993), organisational resources such as operational capabilitie s are the basis of a firm’s economic activity (e.g. production processes, marketing and sal es, etc.) and the foundation of a firm’s competitive advantage (Mahoney and Pandi an, 1992; Amit and Schoemaker, 1993). N onetheless, a changing environment necessit ates the continuous development of operational capabilities. Sustaining competitive ness might therefore require firms to alter the ways by which they earn a living (Wi nter, 2003). Dynamic capabilities serve this purpose (Zahra et al., 2006; Helfat et al., 2007). Given that the differentiation between operational and dynamic capabilities focuses only on the purpose for which the capability is deployed, some capabilities might e ven be dual-purpose capabilities that allow firms to concurrently earn a living in the present and alter the ways by which they earn a living in future (Helfat and Winter, 2011). Overall, DCV serves the purpose of providing the somewhat ‘stat ic’ RBV with a dynamic perspective (Teece et al ., 1997; Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000; Ambrosini and Bowman, 2009). While the strateg y concept of the RBV can be sum marised as a “quest for Ricardian-Rents through the accumulation and deployment of non-imitable resources” [Foss et al., (1995), p.10], the DCV serves to explain how firm s may advance and reconfigure their resource base to sustain competitive advantag e, especially in hypercompetitive markets and high-velocity environments (Teece et al., 1997; Makadok, 2001). As a consequence, dynamic capabilities play a major role for incumbents facing technological change (Lavie, 2006), for coping with crises (Makkonen et al., 2014) or for preserving strategic flexibility (Singh et al., 2013). 2.2 Dynamic capabilities facilitate routinised and purposeful change Not every adaptation of a firm’s resource base is based on dyna mic capabilities. The DCV is a particularly useful conceptual lens in management research to examine purposeful and routinised adaptation processes (e.g. Ambrosini and Bowman, 2009; Easterby-Smith et al., 2009; Barreto, 2010). However, ‘dynamic capabilities-driven change’ has to be clearly distinguished from other forms of cha nge [see also Helfat et al. (2007), Ambrosini and Bowman (2009, p.33) as well as Barreto (2 010, p.264)]. In contrast to dynamic capabilities-driven change, ‘ad-hoc problem -solving’ (Winter, 2003) is not routinised and the ‘endogenous drift’ associated with th e continuous enactment (Feldman, 2000) of operational capabilities is not purposeful. Routinisation requires a starting point. According to Zollo and Winter (2002), ad-hoc problem solving is often the first step for firms in creating d ynamic capabilities by 192 S. Konlechner et al. facilitating experience accumulation. The next steps are the ar ticulation and the codification of knowledge. Therefore, the creation of dynamic c apabilities is based on deliberate efforts (Kale, 2010; Zo llo and Winter, 2002). Once t hey have been created, dynamic capabilities can be practiced through repetition [e.g. Eisenhardt and Martin, (2000), p.1114]. Research in this context shows that continuous learning and innovation efforts, in particular, enable firms to accumulate new resources (D’Este, 2 002; Figueiredo, 2003; Shang et al., 2010) and to cope with discontinuous challenges ( Bessant et al., 2011). By contrast, the non-execution of a (dynamic) capability over a lo nger period of time can cause the knowledge about the concrete performance of the capab ility to sink into oblivion. As Helfat and Peteraf (2009, p.94) put it: “It is tru e, however, that capabilities (including dynamic ones) embody past learning and therefore may depreciate if unused for a long time [...] if you don’t use it, you may lose it”. Research indicates that there is a broad range of contingency f actors that affect the creation and also the shape of dynamic capabilities. Firm-specific contingency factors on dynamic capability creation and shape range from managerial att ention (Laamanen and Wallin, 2009; Newey and Zahra, 2009; Barrales-Molina et al., 20 10; Gärtner, 2011; Eggers and Kaplan, 2013) and a firm’s strategic orientation (Sl ater et al., 2006; Zhou and Li, 2010) to issues of organisational context (Prieto et al., 2 009; Kay, 2010) and culture (Chen and Jaw, 2009; Liu et al., 2009; Hung et al., 2010) and e ven to human capital and resources (Doving and Gooderham, 2008; McKelvie and Davidsson, 2009). Additionally, the process of sourcing resources for founding a firm is often already a matter of dynamic capabilities (Newbert, 2005; Wu, 2007). With regard to the crea tion of dynamic technological capabilities, Liu et al. (2006), for example, ide ntified various distinctive patterns of dynamic capability creation. These patterns include the import of technology, co-innovation and in-house R&D. Research on external contingency factors of dynamic capability creation and shape has particularly emphasised the relationship between dynamic ca pabilities and market dynamics (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000; Aragón-Correa and Sharma , 2003). In seminal works, Eisenhardt and her colleagues have primarily analysed th e role of managerial decision-making by simple rules and decision heuristics (e.g. E isenhardt and Sull, 2001; Davis et al., 2009; Eisenhardt et al., 2010; Bingham and Eisenh ardt, 2011). Further empirical research on market-specific contingencies of dynamic capabilities suggests that the importance of dynamic capabilities vis-à-vis operational (o r ‘ordinary’) capabilities increases with market dynamics (Drnevich and Kriauciunas, 2011; Jiao et al., 2013). Moreover, studies show that governmental regulations play an im portant role in determining the framework for innovation and technology diffusion (Athreye et al., 2009; Lin, 2009) and consequently inf luence the pace of change. Resea rch also indicates that the life-cycle stage of an indus try has an influence on a firm’ s dynamic capabilities. Bergek et al. (2008), for example, showed that capabilities for sourcing and integrating new technology lead to a superior performance in mature industries. 2.3 Dynamic capabilities comprise a manag erial and an organisational aspect The successful application of d ynamic capabilities requires bot h “good strategizing as well as good execution” [Teece, (2012), p.1397]. Thus, making u se of dynamic capabilities requires managers to engage in strategic decision- making and in implementing the necessary decisions to drive change (Rosenbloo m, 2000; Hodgkinson A dynamic capabilities perspective on managing technological change 193 and Healey, 2011). Dynamic capabilities, as a consequence, comp rise a managerial aspect that focuses on manageria l cognition and decision-making , as well as an organisational aspect that is concerned with the execution of c apabilities (as change-oriented organisational routines) for the purpose of adapting the resource base. Investigations of the managerial aspects of dynamic capabilities explore the behavioural and psychological foundations of capability perform ance and pave the way for a more thorough integration of agency aspects into the DCV (Adner and Helfat, 2003; O’Reilly and Tushman, 2008; Kor and Mesko, 2013; Helfat and Mar tin, 2015). Managerial aspects of dynamic capabilities support decision-mak i n g i n t e r m s o f h o w firms should allocate their resources between capability explor ation and exploitation (Maritan, 2001; Lazonick and Prencipe, 2005; Soosay and Hyland, 2008), which markets firms should target (Macpherson et al., 2004) or which resource s they should release and when (Moliterno and Wiersema, 2007). Managerial cognition a nd strategic decision-making are major factor s in understanding why incumben t s m a y r e s p o n d differently to technological change (e.g. Bititci et al., 2011; Danneels, 2011). In a seminal empirical work linking cognitions with capabilitie s, Tripsas and Gavetti (2000) demonstrate how cognition determines initiatives for cap ability building and how adhering to an outdated business model ultimately paved Polaroi d’s way into a competence trap. Similarly, in th eir study of communications-te chnology firms entering the fiber-optics product market, Eggers and Kaplan (2009) show that managerial attention to emerging technologies greatly influences whether and when fi rms engage in strategic renewal activities. In her studies on incumbent responses to ra dical technological change, Benner (e.g. 2007, 2010) focuses on the influence of external i nstitutions on managerial cognition and strategic decisions. In particular, she shows tha t securities analysts are more positively disposed toward strategies that fit the existin g valuation models of incumbent firms than toward strategies that respond directly to the new technology (Benner, 2010) and that firms which invest in new technologies despite negative recommendations by analysts need t o m a k e i n c r e a s e d e f f o r t s t o signal their alignment with the shareholders’ interests (Benner and Ranganathan, 2012). The organisational aspects of dynamic capabilities refer to concrete change practices and processes and serve the purpose of changing operational capabilities in organisations. Such organisational aspects of dynamic capabilities become visi ble during the execution of organisational routines that are intended to adapt the resou rce base. In particular, projects have been identified as architectures that operational ly support change within firms. Research in this vein shows that setting up projects is a fundamental means of coping with technological change (Holbrook et al., 2000) and of pursuing radical innovation (O’Connor and MacDermott, 2004). Managing a broad portfolio of projects or innovations can also facilitate adaptation to technological cha nge (Daniel et al., 2014; Sicotte et al., 2014). Accordingly, successful adaptations of a firm’s resource base always require the interplay of manager ial decision-making and reconfi guration (Teece, 2007; Ellonen et al., 2009; Park and Kim, 2013). 2.4 Dynamic capabilities can rely on various organisational processes Researchers have dealt with very diverse organisational process es under the header of dynamic capabilities. Examples include R&D and new product deve lopment (Danneels, 2002; Verona and Ravasi, 2003; Lee and Kelley, 2008; Weerd-Nede rhof et al., 2008; Salvato, 2009), knowledge creation (Bueno et al., 2008) and int egration (Petroni, 1998), 194 S. Konlechner et al. restructuring (Karim and Mitchell, 2000; Galunic and Eisenhardt , 2001), patching (Eisenhardt and Brown, 1999), corporate venturing (Keil, 2004; Collinson and Wilson, 2006), continuous morphing (Rindova and Kotha, 2001), acqui-hir ing (Chatterji and Patro, 2014), building strategic alliances (Anand et al., 2010; H e i m e r i k s a n d D u y s t e r s , 2007; Rothaermel and Deeds, 2006) and post-merger integration (Szulanski, 2002). An important stream of research also focuses on the role of dyn amic capabilities in governing relations with external stakeholders and partners. St udies in this stream show, for example, that strategic supply chain management has a posit ive effect with regard to developing an innovation capability (Storer and Hyland, 2011; C heng et al., 2014) and organisational flexibility (Vanpoucke et al., 2014), that dynam ic capabilities facilitate successful participation in knowl edge networks (Gruenberg-Bocha rd and Kreis-Hoyer, 2009) and that the reconfigurati on of cooperation mechanisms st rengthens technological progress (Cai et al., 2014). A further stream of research with particular emphasis on technology management elucidates the tight interconnectedness b etween knowledge management and dynamic capabilities (Prieto and Easterby-Smith, 2006; Easterby-Smith and Prieto, 2008) and conceptualises systematic knowledge manag ement as a fundamental enabler of dynamic capabilities (Sher and Lee, 2004 ; Wilkens et al., 2004; Marsh and Stock, 2006; Cepeda and Vera, 2007; Filippini et al., 2012; Ravishankar and Pan, 2013). 2.5 Dynamic capabilities-driven change might succeed or fail A further heavily discussed issue in resea rc h is how dyna m ic capabilities are linked to firm performance. Reflecting on the consequences of dynamic cap ability deployment is crucial because not every purposeful change process is necessarily successful. Even firms that have proven to be highly ada ptive in the past are far from immune to failure (Zott, 2003). In fact, many firms tha t have successfully utilised dynamic capabilities in the past are struggling at present or may even fail in the future, despi te actually ‘having’ dynamic capabilities. A look at examples of firms that have been identi fied as possessing dynamic capabilities in the literature corroborates this effect. Firms such as Enron (Eisenhardt and Sull, 2001), Yahoo! (Rindova and Kotha, 2001), or Nokia (Doz and Kosonen, 2008) have (for one reason or another) lost their leading positions, in sp ite of having been identified as good practice examples in dynamic capabilities research (see also Arend and Bromiley, 2009 for a similar argumentation). To define measures for evaluating dynamic capability performanc e, Helfat et al. (2007, p.7) proposed their concepts of evolutionary and technic al fitness. Specifically, they argue that “evolutionary fitness refers to how well a dyna mic capability enables an organisation to make a living by creating, extending, or modify ing its resource base. [...] The term ‘technical fitness’ is introduced to denote how effect ively a capability performs its intended function”. This conceptualisation facilitates the decoupling of dynamic capabilities and competitive advantage by stating that technica l fitness does not automatically lead to evolutionary fitness. 2.5.1 Proactive change vs. reactive adaptation Research on the functions and outcomes of dynamic capabilities shows that they enable firms to drive the market proactively or to just react to the i ntroduction of new technologies. Firms can thus use dynamic capabilities to in itiate processes of A dynamic capabilities perspective on managing technological change 195 creative destruction (Schumpeter, 1935) and to proactively stim ulate market change (Aragón-Correa and Sha rma, 2003) or to react to environmental p ressure and technological change. Firms lik e Apple, Google, or Facebook, fo r instance, have dominated their markets in recent years by proactively driving their markets. In his studies on the fibre-optics industry, Cattani demonstrat es how technological preadaptation, i.e. the proactive development of technology wit hout anticipation of subsequent use, enabled pre-adapted firms to achieve higher lev els of performance (Cattani, 2005) and to foster in-house R&D competences in order to cope with upcoming technological developments (Cattani, 2006). Forbes and Wield (2 008) emphasise the potential of dynamic capabilitie s to facilitate successful reac tions to other firms by showing how dynamic capabilities allowed firms in developing countries to drive innovation in such a way as to catch up with some of the world’s leading technology-driven firms. 2.5.2 Radical change vs. incremental change Organisations may employ dynamic capabilities to bring about in cremental change and alignment or radical change and transformation. Structures for incremental innovation can be adapted continuously or in semi-continuous steps (e.g. c ontinuous improvement programs). Other dynamic capabilities-driven change processes that are more radical will require completely revamping th e organisation (Teece, 2007) and setting up particular structures that nurture radical innovation (O’Connor and DeMart ino, 2006; O’Connor et al., 2008; Tripsas, 1997). In this vein, Ambrosini et al. (2 009) distinguished between ‘incremental’ dynamic capabilities, that for instance facilitate the gradual improvement of operational processes and ‘renewing’ capabilities that enable f irms to adapt even to radical technological change and that “are concerned with modif ying the resource stock in such a way that its utility is altered so that rent generati on is sustained” [Ambrosini et al., (2009), p.15]. 3 Dynamic capabilities for managing technological change: a fra mework Adapting to technological change is essential for firm success or even survival. Researchers are well aware that e specially “dynamic and unpredi ctable environments require flexible, innovative and creative organisations, which can easily adapt quickly to the changing rules of the competitive arena” [Biedenbach and Söderholm, (2008), p.123]. How firms manage such adaptation by deploying dynamic capabilit ies, however, is still a broad field for further investigation. Research shows that scho lars may apply various conceptual lenses to examine the processes behind capability-dr iven change: absorptive capacity as a dynamic capability (cf. e.g. Zahra and George, 2002; Todorova and Durisin, 2007), ambidexterity as a dynamic capability (cf. e.g. O’Reilly and Tushman, 2008; Gilbert, 2006; Güttel and Konl echner, 2009; Teece, 2014) and te chnology management as a dynamic capability (cf. e.g. Cetindamar et al., 2009). The se lenses shed light on different aspects of dynamic capability-driven change processes as identified in the review. Although the literature within the fields of absorptive capacit y, ambidexterity and technology management focuses on different capabilities and pra ctices, all of the concepts are linked to the question of how firms can suitably a dapt to environmental 196 S. Konlechner et al. changes by applying dynamic capabilities. Absorptive capacity c an be defined as “the ability of a firm to recognize the value of new, external infor mation, assimilate it and apply it to commercial ends” [Cohen and Levinthal, (1990), p.12 8]. Accordingly, absorptive capacity is a dynamic capability that affects the cr eation of technological knowledge, as well as its utilisation for innovation in order t o enhance a firm’s ability to gain and sustain competitive advantage (Zahra and George, 2002; Wang and Ahmed, 2007). The notion of ambidexterity as a dynamic capability refers to t he contribution of dynamic capabilities for the purpose of facilitating the explor ation and exploitation of technology, capabilities and knowledge. According to O’Reilly a nd Tushman (2008, p.200), ambidexterity as a dynamic capability facilitates new r esource configurations that can offer a competitive advantage. Conceptualising ambidexterit y a s a d y n a m i c capability is thus a dynamic approach that aims at exploring ho w firms recombine and integrate their resources to adapt to market and technological changes. The final lens that we integrate into our framework is technolo gy management as a dynamic capability. Technology management can be defined as “a process, which includes planning, directing, control and coordination of the d evelopment and implementation of technological capabilities to shape and accom plish the strategic and operational objectives of an organization” [NRC, 1987, cited in Cetindamar et al., (2009), p.237]. Technology management serves as a dynamic capability by enabling firms to make effective use of technical knowledge and skills (cf. e.g. Jin and von Zedtwitz, 2008), thereby combining aspects of technology as well as the p rocess of facilitating its effective application and implementation. This process includes planning, directing and coordination of technological capabilities to shape and accompl ish strategic and operational objectives of an organisation (Cetindamar et al., 2 009). The continuous observation of the external environme n t l e a d s t o t h e recognition of new paths and represents the necessary first step of purpos eful and routinised adaptation. This process is referred to as sensing ( Teece, 2007; O’Reilly and Tushman, 2008), recognition of value (Cohen and Levinthal, 1990 ; Zahra and George, 2002) or identification (Cetindamar et al., 2009). The absorptive-capacity lens par ticularly emphasises the role o f prior related knowledge – such as basic skills, shared language and knowledge a b o u t s c i e n t i f i c o r technological developments – that facilitates recognition processes (Cohen and Levinthal, 1990). With regard to ambidexterity, O’Reilly and Tushman (2008 ) argue that sensing activities require a senior management that facilitates learnin g, challenges the status quo and accepts failure. The literature on technology management as a dynamic capability conceptualises the identification of technologies (and market c hanges in general) that are important to the business as a first step for adaptation [e.g. Centindamar et al., (2009), p.242]. In order to deliberately initiate change, organisational decisi on-makers, usually (top) managers, also need to evaluate a l a r g e v a r i e t y o f o p t i o n s t o c h a n g e a n d l e a r n . Subsequently, organisational decision-makers make selections among a variety of change A dynamic capabilities perspective on managing technological change 199 options. Seizing opportunities and making deliberate choices (s elections) for or against development options in an environment of uncertainty (Ocasio, 1 997; Pandza and T h o r p e , 2 0 0 9 ) a r e c e n t r a l m a n a g e r i a l t a s k s . H e n c e , d e v e l o p i n g a consensus among the senior team about the strategic direction is a fundamental prer equisite for avoiding decision traps and for acting on any sensed opportunities and t hreats in a timely manner [O’Reilly and Tushman, (2008), p.191]. Psychological (Hodgkinso n and Healey, 2011) and cognitive underpinnings (e. g. Gavetti, 2005; Teece, 2007; H elfat and Peteraf, 2015) of strategic managerial decision-making play a central role during this phase (Sirmon and Hitt, 2009; Martin, 2011; Beck and Wiersema, 2013). The selection of development options is necessarily based on pr ior experience and already indicates the organisational boundaries of strategic ch ange (Schreyögg and Sydow, 2010). As a result, change and learning initiatives have a higher probability of realisation if they fit established managerial decision-making patterns (Schreyögg and Sydow, 2011; Vergne and Durand, 2011). Such patterns, however, h a v e a p a r a d o x i c a l effect on firm adaptation. On the one hand, relying on prior ex perience enables managers to deal with complexity and to make quick decisions, especially in fast-paced environments. On the other hand, patterned decision-making may prevent out-of-the-box thinking, lead to a perpetuation of firm-idiosyncratic activity patterns, impede reflection on strategic decision-making and therefore prevent organisational learning. 3.2 Transformation – acquiring, reconfiguring and implementing The phase of ‘transformation’ is characterised by the realisati on of change or – put differently – by the introduction of something new (e.g. a new technology, new knowledge or a new capability) into the organisation. Absorptiv e capacity research emphasises the importance of acquiring new knowledge from external sources (Cohen and Levinthal, 1990; Zahra and George, 2002; Müller-Seitz and G üttel, 2014). Similarly, Cetindamar et al. (2009) highlight the acquisition of selected technologies – either via internal development or via external acquisition – as a core su bprocess of technology management as a dynamic capability. The introduction of new tec hnologies requires or facilitates asset reconfiguration efforts. From an ambidexterit y perspective, O’Reilly and Tushman (2008) refer to Teece (2007) by emphasising the pivotal role of reconfiguring assets and structures in the face of changing markets as the ke y to success. Transformation is a particularly critical phase for change, bec ause managing transformation successfully requires firms to solve any conflic ts that arise from tensions between the old and the new. As a consequence, firms need to cr eate a context that facilitates change and contributes to reducing such conflicts b efore anything new can actually be implemented throughout the organisation. Change architectures serve as context, where capabilities for r esource creation, extension or modification can unfold (Narayanan et al., 2009). Extant research has identified projects as a core change architecture that supports the organisational processes behind driving technological innovation (e.g. Danneels, 2002; O’Connor and McDermott, 2004; Harreld et al., 2007; Cetindamar et al., 2009). Change ar chitectures serve the purposes of: 1 developing alternatives to the current status quo within a pr edefined context and 2 providing a structure that emb eds previous experience in dealing with change. 200 S. Konlechner et al. They comprise experience-based kn owledge about the ‘what’ (meth odological level), ‘when’ (time level) and ‘who’ (social level) of change. On the methodological level (‘what’), change architectures define methods, techniques and p rocedures, e.g. portfolio analysis, SWOT analysis, scenar io techniques or survey feedback methods, for the change process in question (e.g. Ambrosini et al., 1998; Harris on, 2005; Palmer et al., 2008). On the time level (‘when ’), change architectures define relevant milestones, timetables and deadlines, e.g., schedules for a new product dev elopment project. On the social level (‘who’), change arc hitectures define the social se tting and specify roles, e.g., project team, R&D departm ents and steering committee. Fin ally, experience as to how to conduct change (on the me thodological, time and social l evels) is either documented in reports, manuals, standard operating procedures a nd so on, or stored as implicit knowledge in individual actors. While reconfiguration requires managerial planning and decision -making in particular, implementation requires all involved actors to actu ally support the reconfiguration. As a consequence, implementation is a challenging endeavour. However, dynamic capabilities research hardly addresses difficulties tha t may arise during the implementation process and how such difficulties could be tackl ed (cf. e.g. Arend and Bromiley, 2009). As soon as reso urce reconfiguration affects th e fundamental informal structure of a firm and challenge s existing expectations and ru les, firms need to develop strategies that enable them to break down organisational defenc es (Argyris, 1990), to prevent ‘not-invented-here’ syndromes (Katz and Allen, 1982) an d to overcome general resistance to change. Although resistance to change, in particu l a r , h a s e m e r g e d a s a fundamental topic in change management literature (cf. e.g. Den t and Goldberg, 1999; Ford et al., 2008; Konlechner et al., 2016), it has been widely neglected, surprisingly, in the context of dynamic capabilities. Some notable exceptions ca n be found in the works of O’Connor and McDermott (2004) and Narayanan et al. (2009). O ’Connor and McDermott (2004) argue that organisations should foster intrapr eneurship to overcome resistance to radical innovation. Narayanan et al. (2009) show that negotiating resistance is necessary during the development of dynamic capabilities. Su staining change, however, requires firms not only to govern resource reconfigura tion processes but also to deal with resistance that arises from the transformation of an old system into a new one. 3.3 Application – exploiting, protecting and learning Overcoming difficulties and resolving tensions are essential fo r successful implementation of new technolog ies. The re-stabilisation of a f irm during and after implementation processes is important for the subsequent applic ation of new knowledge or capabilities. The exploitation of newly acquired and developed knowledge reflect a firm’s ability to harvest and incorporate new practices into ex isting operations (Todorova and Durisin, 2007). According to Cetindamar et al. (2009), expl oitation refers to the commercialisation of new technolo gies as well as to incremental developments. Following the logic of ambidexterity as a dynamic capability (O ’Reilly and Tushman, 2008), sensing, seizing and asset reconfiguration are activitie s that support the dynamic development of a firm, while exploitation refers to utilising a nd applying these newly developed capabilities. In addition to exploitation, activities t o protect the expertise A dynamic capabilities perspective on managing technological change 201 embedded in products and manufacturing systems through patentin g or staff retention is important (Cetindamar et al., 2009). Finally, by reflecting on how th ey accomplish change, organisat i o n s t r i g g e r a learning process, with the goal of improvi ng their approaches to accompl ishing change. However, firms need ways of retaining experience to make them o pen to further change endeavours (cf. Zollo and Winter, 2002; Romme et al., 2010). De -briefing workshops or lessons learned facilitate the reflection on how dynamic capabi lities work in organisations. The ability to reflect on change processes is of fundamental value for firms, because it enables them to broaden their search focus fo r future change initiatives via creative search (Pandza and Thorpe, 2009) and facilitates t he refinement of existing capabilities that help firms to identify new knowledge (Capron and Mitchell, 2009). Finally, learning also requires attention to knowledge transfer for disseminating newly created solutions (e.g. new production technologies) throughout relevant organisational units to profit from novelties (Garaus et al., 2016). To conclude , our framework shows that strategic decisions, primarily at th e senior executive level of the firm, determine the organisational devel opment. How firms recognise, evaluate and select new technologies plays a major r ole in explaining why some firms are able to shape their environments, while others o nly adapt to new industry standards. Ultimately, firms need to transform their resource b ase to profit from new technologies. The acquisition of new technologies as well as th e reconfiguration and subsequent implementation of new and existing resources are bas ic elements of such transformation processes. Finally, firms need to exploit and pr otect new technologies and might also use them to stimulate organisational learning (see Figure 1). However, more re search on dynamic capabilities is still needed to substantiate and extend our kno wledge of routinised adaptation processes. We argue th at focusing on the processes b ehind dynamic capabilities facilitates analyses that show how dynamic capabil ities actually unfold their impact. Based on the framework developed in this paper, we iden tify several important blindspots that require further attention and research in the following section. 202 S. Konlechner et al. 4.1 Dynamic capabilities consist of interrelated processes In their synthesis of dynamic capabilities research, Ambrosini and Bowman (2009, p.40) have already stated that “maybe some dynamic capabilities can b e ‘stored’, for instance, the ability to reconfigure, whereas others must continually be performed, e.g. R&D”. Our framework seizes and further develops this idea by showing that dynamic capability-driven change comprises various interrelated process es, some of which are continuous, while others are performed temporarily. Observing t echnological trends and maintaining alliances in order to gain access to recent technol ogies are rather continuous processes, whereas radical shift s to new technologies often req uire formalised and substantial transformation projects. Future research could furt her investigate the interfaces between these interrelated processes more closely to develop a better understanding of the interplay between more continuous and more episodic activities underlying technological change. 4.2 Dynamic capabilities’ subsets are interrelated Some firms may have more than one capability that enables them to create, extend or modify their resource base. Research has only started to invest igate the consequences of having various subsets of dynamic capabilities. Colpan and Hiki no (2005), for example, show that combining capabilities for technological innovation a nd for related diversification increases profitability. Song et al. (2005) dem onstrate that combining technology-driven dynamic capabilities for innovation and dynam ic capabilities for marketing is important in high velocity markets. However, the q uestion of how various subprocesses, such as, for instance, decision-making and selection, contribute to different subsets of dynamic capabilities concurrently, has not received sufficient attention so far. Analysing how firms orchestrate such dynamic capabilities and a llocate resources towards them could thus be a further direction for future research. 4.3 Dynamic capabilities require observation, reflection and learning Our review and framework suggest that observation of a firm’s e xternal environment, as well as its internal development, plays a crucial role as a fun ction that has to be executed in a continuous manner. Schreyögg and Kliesch-Eberl (2007) alre ady emphasised the crucial role of capability monitoring in firm adaptation. Howev er, while they introduced the concept of capability monitoring as an alternative to dynam ic capabilities, we argue that future research should investigate in more detail how dyna mic capabilities, observation and decision-making patterns are interlinked. 4.4 Dynamic capabilities-driven change requires subsequent stabilisation In recent decades, research has increasingly investigated how m anagerial perception, cognitions, decisions and actions facilitate purposeful adaptat ion to technological change. This line of research has considerably expanded our kno wledge of the pre-reconfiguration phase of adaptation. Significantly less res earch, however, has been devoted to the post-reconfiguration phase of adaptation. We ass ume that this lack of research results from the common assumption that successful rec onfiguration quasi-automatically leads to successful implementation and subsequent application. A dynamic capabilities perspective on managing technological change 203 Against the backdrop of empirical evidence that demonstrates th e high failure rate of organisational change processes [Beer and Nohria (2000) suggest that it is as high as 70% for organisational change initiatives in general], we think tha t further research regarding the stabilisation of reconfiguration represents a major avenue for future study. Integrating the dynamic-capabilities view with existing change management knowledge (as called for by Arend and Bromiley, 2009) and addressing phenomena such as organisational defence or resistance to change could consequently result in valuable contributions. 4.5 Dynamic capabilities do not guarantee success or survival Research on the performance implications of dynamic capabilitie s has hitherto either investigated dynamic capabilities as a general organisational a bility to manage change (e.g. Luo, 2002) or shows with single case studies how firms ha ve used dynamic capabilities in the past to achieve adaptation (e.g. Rindova an d Kotha, 2001; Lazonic and Prencipe, 2005). The introduction of performance yardsticks, te chnical fitness and evolutionary fitness (Helfat et al., 2007), however, also allows researchers to analyse how firms might fail, despite having dynamic capabilities. Instead of performing ex post analyses of successful applications of dynamic capabilities, us ing a process perspective can contribute to the execution of such studies and identificat ion of how separate processes affect technical and evolutionary fitness. Finally, m ore research on the proactive or reactive use of dynamic capabilities could also en hance our knowledge of how firms initiate or deal with technological change. 5 Concluding remarks This paper has synthesised conceptual and empirical findings to develop a framework for a dynamic-capabilities perspective on technological innovation and adaptation. Our framework pushes the dynamic capabilities agenda forward. Based on our elaborations, we have identified some fields of further research to better un derstand the role of dynamic capabilities in managing technological change. We concl ude that further research could help to advance our understanding of strategic d ecision-making patterns, transformation processes and implementation activities. Researc h on decision-making heuristics (e.g. Bingham and Eisenhardt, 2011; Sull and Eisenha rdt, 2015) and dynamic managerial capabilities (e.g. Adner and Helfat, 2003; Kor and M esko, 2013; Helfat and Martin, 2015) has shown that these are promising ways of explaining differences in terms of how firms and their senior executives deal with technologica l opportunities and threats. Integrating concepts such as resistance to change (For d et al., 2008; Konlechner et al., 2016) or organisational defence (Argyris, 1990) into th e dynamic-capabilities approach can help to illuminate the difficulties of overcoming established pathways. Implementing new technologies is often a difficult endeavour. H ow dynamic capabilities enable firms to accelerate the p ace of organisational learning represents a promising approach for revealing how firms may exploit new technologies f or gaining and sustaining competitive advantage. Based on our analysis we can a lso identify practical recommendations for each phase of our framework. First, firms need to reflect carefully on their dynamic capabilities to observe technological trends and d evelopments in a routinised m a n n e r . T h e u s e o f alliances and attention paid by employees on all levels to iden tify hidden or tacit 204 S. Konlechner et al. developments with regard to new technologies can complement the structured approaches that top-management teams and R&D departments follow. Firms sho uld also reflect on the appropriateness of their decision-making behaviour with regard to the critical balance of exploiting existing technologies and exploring new technolog ies because, as always, short-term efficiency needs to be accompanied by the facilitati on of innovation for longterm survival. Second, the review of previous projects for implementing technologica l change, as well as the implementation of routinised lessons-lea rned procedures after completing change projects, can s erve as learning mechanisms fo r continuously improving dynamic capabilities for managing technological chang e. Third, firms could examine their ability to continuously improve technologies duri ng application and to quickly exploit new or newly improved technologies company-wide by enhancing knowledge transfer and replication in diverse domains. Finally, reflecting on how a firm currently deals with technological opportunities and threats, a s well as how the organisation manages technological development and transformati on internally, might serve as important steps in further advancing its competitive p osition by reacting to external change or by initiating technological developments in ways to even drive such change. Previous research shows that the interaction of these two organizational capabilities and the multidimensional configuration of DCs. However, little is known about how CCs and DCs arejointly configured within PSFs and how trade-offs between these distinct capabilities relate to service provision and performance across different firms. This study explores the path dependent nature of higher- and lower- order capabilities and uses data from 279 marketing advisoryfirms to investigate how different configurations of higher-order CCs and DCs are associated with lower-order service provision capabilities (SPCs) and similar or different performance. Wefind that CCs can substitute for DCs, and that DCs and CCs can compensate for SPCs in achieving higher levels of customer-based performance. However, the same does not apply forfinancial performance in which CCs do not appear to overcome deficiencies in DCs and SPCs. Also,firms can have similar SPCs and experience similar financial performance while emphasizing the use of either DCs or CCs; suggesting DCs and CCs may substitute for each other. 1. Introduction Professional service firms (PSFs) leverage the resources and knowledge of clients ( Aarikka-Stenroos & Jaakkola, 2012 ; Heirati, O'Cass, Schoefer, & Siahtiri, 2016) through the development and deployment of cocreation capabilities (CCs)– i.e., processes that enable close interaction with clients (Karpen, Bove, Lukas, & Zyphur, 2015). Thus, “clients play a critical role in helping [PSFs] to cocreate or‘coproduce’the knowledge-based service solution” (Bettencourt, Ostrom, Brown, & Roundtree, 2002, p. 100). Although CCs enable a PSF to form and maintain relationships with clients, the joint development of a client's value proposition ultimately occurs through the PSF's service provision capabilities (SPCs)– i.e., processes that enable direct provision of service. However, the extent to which CCs are a basis forfirms to better provide service is conditional upon their dynamic capabilities (DCs) – i.e., processes that facilitate the identification of and response to market opportunities (Danneels, 2010; Fischer, Gebauer, Gregory, Ren, & Fleisch, 2010; Kindström, Kowalkowski, & Sandberg, 2013; Storbacka, 2011; Wilden & Gudergan, 2017). Although prior research provides evidence that CCs and DCs interact and thatfirms, in general, differ in how their multifaceted DCs are configured (Gelhard, Von Delft, & Gudergan, 2016), we do not yet understand how a PSF's DCs and CCs are jointly configured. Furthermore, research is needed to investigate whether different configurations of DCs and CCs are associated with differences in SPCs and/or differ infirm performance. Following a configurational logic, we argue that PSFs are “best understood in terms of overall patterns [that capture jointly their multifaceted DCs and CCs] rather than in terms of analyses of narrowly drawn sets of organizational properties” (Meyer, Tsui, & Hinings, 1993, p. 1181). A PSF's ability to develop value propositions with and for clients requires interaction and transfer of knowledge as well as an ability to adapt to change (Wagner, Hoisl, & Thoma, 2014). Thus, a PSF's use of CCstogether withits DCs is especially critical as professional service-based industries shift and change (Aarikka-Stenroos & Jaakkola, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indmarman.2018.06.008 Received 1 March 2017; Received in revised form 27 May 2018; Accepted 11 June 2018 ⁎ Corresponding author. A more holistic understanding of how DCs and CCs characterize PSFs, therefore, cannot rest on capturing only the universal and individual roles of these capabilities. Rather, researchers and managers must consider the interconnected nature of the individual capabilities that make up DCs and CCs to understand how different PSFs are composed of unique patterns of these capabilities and come with certain SPCs and performance attainments. In this study, we explore (i) differences among PSFs based on their configurations of DCs and CCs, to reveal the interconnected nature of these two sets of capabilities and their trade-offs; and (ii) how PSFs characterized by these configurations can be further described according to their SPCs and similarities and differences in performance. We draw on recent research that has clarified the interconnected nature of DCs and CCs as two higher-order capabilities (Karpen et al., 2015; Wilden & Gudergan, 2017) and recognized the path dependence of lower-order capabilities, such as SPCs (Vergne & Durand, 2011). The configurations that we examine combine the multiple capabilities that make up DCs and CCs and are defined by the magnitude of as well as the interconnections among these capabilities. In this sense, these configurations represent gestalts thatVenkatraman (1989, p. 432)defines as the“degree of internal coherence among a set of theoretical attributes.” Rather than assuming linear associations between attributes, such as those of DCs and CCs, attributes in a gestalt form a holistic pattern that reflects a higher-order configuration of capabilities (Miller & Friesen, 1977). Thus, to develop a holistic view of the role of CCs and DCs in service provision andfirm performance, we explore higher-order capability configurations of DCs and CCs and describe their association with lower-order SPCs and performance. We investigate configurations of these higher-order capabilities by drawing on data from a sample of 279 marketing advisoryfirms because the marketing advisory industry is made up of PSFs that work closely with their clients and is faced with significant changes (Heirati et al., 2016). The study of capability configurations requires an approach that differs from marketing strategy and service research that uses variance-based arguments and analyses ( Karpen et al., 2015; Wilden & Gudergan, 2015). Configurational studies underscore the importance of investigating configurations of capabilities rather than their individual causal e ffects ( Gruber, Heinemann, Brettel, & Hungeling, 2010). Although variance-based studies are well-suited for explaining levels of outcomes of predictor variables, a configurational approach is more appropriate for establishing differences among PSFs in terms of their configurations of DCs and CCs and for describing PSFs based on their SPCs and performance (Doty, Glick, & Huber, 1993;Fiss, 2007; Meyer et al., 1993; Meyer, Gaba, & Colwell, 2005). Moreover, this approach allows exploring whether PSFs, operating in the same dynamic service ecosystem, can attain similar or different performance outcomes by making trade-offs between CCs and DCs (Fiss, 2011). We contribute to the understanding of capabilities relevant to PSFs in several ways. First, we advance a stronger integration of resource and capability thinking into service-ecosystems literature (Wilden, Akaka, Karpen, & Hohberger, 2017) by empirically studying how PSFs can be distinguished based on differences in their configurations of DCs and CCs, and how these higher-order capability configurations are accompanied by SPCs, which support PSF performance. Second, we contribute to value cocreation literature by explaining that accounting for the hierarchy of operant resources clarifies how cocreation of value occurs in different ways. Third, we add to the capability literature by discovering how different higher-order capability configurations can yield different but also similar performance outcomes; supporting the notion of path-dependent developments of capabilities along firm-specific trajectories within the DC view that come with their unique performance attainments. This will allow researchers, as well as managers of PSFs, to understand the trade-offs among the higher-order DCs and CCs, in consideration of related SPCs, and gain a deeper understanding of how different types of capabilities are associated with value creation and firm performance (Madhavaram & Hunt, 2008). 2. Background Strategy research has acknowledged the di fferentiation of capabilities into higher-order and lower-order capabilities (Collis, 1994; Danneels, 2008; Winter, 2003). Higher-order capabilities are defined as capabilities “that allowfirms to overcome the path dependence that led to the inimitability of the lower-order capabilities” (Collis, 1994,p . 149). Lower-order capabilities represent the firm's ability to perform a coordinated set of everyday tasks on an ongoing basis“using more or less the same techniques on the same scale to support existing products and services for the same customer population” (Helfat et al., 2007,p . 1244). Thus, they support thefirm to run their core operations (as in the case of PSFs is service provision) (Amit & Schoemaker, 1993; Helfat & Peteraf, 2003) and enable thefirm to make a living in the present (Winter, 2003). Following this logic, higher-order capabilities (DCs and CCs) shape the path dependency of PSFs by conditioning lower-order capabilities (in our case SPCs) andfirm performance. Ngo and O'Cass (2009, p. 45)recognize the importance of understanding how value is created through organizational capabilities and argue that “surprisingly little theory exists and few studies have been done to examine the role of firm capabilities and their differential contribution to customer value as perceived by management in strategic marketing.” To begin to address this gap, the authors propose the concept “operant resource-based capabilities”by integrating a resourcebased view (Barney, 1991) and a service-dominant logic (Vargo & Lusch, 2011) perspective. Elaborating the role of resources,Ngo and O'Cass (2009, p. 47) argue that “capabilities possess operant characteristics as they act on both operand and operant resources to produce effects, but they are not operant resources.” In this view, different operant resources enable organizations to have different types of capabilities. PSFs, as any other type of industrialfirm, typically face resource constraints that require them to make trade-offs in resource investments and thus capability development, which ultimately leads to PSFs' capabilities developing alongfirm-specific (path dependent) trajectories. Resulting capability configurations may represent either a sustained source of uniqueness that is valuable in the long term (Vergne & Durand, 2011 ) or, a source of organizational rigidity ( Amit & Schoemaker, 1993). Within service-dominant literature (e.g., Vargo & Lusch, 2011) different tiers of higher and lower-order capabilities (Collis, 1994) are supported by a hierarchy of afirm's operant resources– those that act upon other resources to create value (Madhavaram & Hunt, 2008). The hierarchy of basic, composite and interconnected operant resources (Madhavaram & Hunt, 2008) indicates that the ability forfirms to deliver service requires a portfolio of higher- and lower-order capabilities. Basic operant resources, include the individual skills and knowledge of each employee; composite operant resources comprise two or more basic operant resources and allow afirm to produce service offerings both efficiently and effectively (this represents what we call‘SPCs’); interconnected operant resources, exhibit high interactivity between its underlying basic operant resources. Building on this classi fication, Madhavaram and Hunt (2008) stress the importance interconnected operant resources, such as market relating (which are relevant to what we label CCs) and organizational learning, knowledge creation and entrepreneurial capabilities (which facilitate carrying out processes relevant to DCs). This hierarchy of operant resources framework is helpful for understanding the path-dependent role of DCs and CCs because these higher-order capabilities can be classified as interconnected operant resources. In other words, unlike composite operant resources, which include combinations of task-specific knowledge and practices needed to provide a specific service (e.g., writing an advertising slogan), the knowledge and practices that enable afirm to sustain in changing environments and develop and leverage relationships cannot be easily separated. Notwithstanding the importance of DCs and CCs as higher-order capabilities, the consideration of additional lower-order capabilities is needed to understand the relationship among capabilities and firm performance. SPCs are lower-order capabilities (composed of composite operant resources), which can be applied relatively independently in the development of value propositions. However, we lack a detailed understanding of how DCs and CCs interconnect and provide a basis on which SPCs andfirm performance rest. Higher order CCs and DCs in a PSF may create path dependent sustainable competitive advantage by fostering its SPCs in unique ways (Collis, 1994; Vergne & Durand, 2011); however, path dependencies may also weaken competitive advantage when firms experience lock-in and are resistant to change. In other words, if lower-order SPCs become stale the higher-order capabilities that enable afirm to develop and sustain relationships, as well as adapt and change become crucial. The consideration of higher- and lower-order capabilities in PSFs indicates DCs are higher-order capabilities ( Fischer et al., 2010; Kindström et al., 2013; Storbacka, 2011) through which a PSF aligns lower-order capabilities (in our study SPCs) with changes in the environment. This is done by breaking the rigidities resulting from path dependencies at lower levels, and thus represent higher-order capabilities that may lead to internal recon figuration within the PSF (Collis, 1994; Vergne & Durand, 2011). CCs are higher-order capabilities that shape the way in which a PSF interacts with its clients (Karpen et al., 2015) when deploying its SPCs. This, in turn, will enable a PSF to utilize SPCs in a more or less client-focused fashion. Resourcebased theories suggest that a given set of a PSF's lower-order capabilities (i.e., SPCs) at a given time is the result of a PSF's position and path dependencies (Barney, 1991;Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997). Cocreation capabilities Cocreation is recognized as an important strategic process for creating value with customers ( Prahalad & Ramaswamy, 2004b; Stokburger-Sauer, Scholl-Grissemann, Teichmann, & Wetzels, 2016). This process of engagement has been studied across a variety of service settings, including healthcare ( McColl-Kennedy, Vargo, Dagger, Sweeney, & van Kasteren, 2012), as well as other knowledge-intensive business industries ( Aarikka-Stenroos & Jaakkola, 2012 ). Conceptualizations of cocreation vary from speci fic dyadic encounters (Grönroos, 2011) to broad social and cultural processes (Akaka, Vargo, & Lusch, 2013;Vargo & Lusch, 2011) and include (direct or indirect) interaction between two or more individuals or organizations that potentially lead to a positive outcome for one or more parties. Value cocreation is the driving force of service ecosystems (Vargo & Lusch, 2011), which emerge and evolve through interactions among a multitude of actors and their social and economic exchange. Karpen, Bove, and Lukas (2012); Karpen et al. (2015)propose a set of six capabilities (relational, ethical, individuated, empowered, developmental, and concerted inter-action) that are based on interconnected operant resources (Madhavaram & Hunt, 2008) and, in combination, represent afirm's capacity to cocreate value with others. These higher-order capabilities enable firms to engage in different forms of interaction independent of any speci fic service episode, thereby enabling ongoing and potentially long-lasting relationships (Karpen et al., 2012). Importantly, CCs are critical for PSFs' performance because“such capabilities provide the foundation for competing on service” and thereby guide the development of related lower-order industry specific SPCs. Consequently, building on the conceptual understanding introduced by Karpen et al. (2012, 2015), we view the higher-order CCs as a portfolio of six capabilities that facilitate and enhance interactions with clients. SeeTable 1for the definitions of the respective capabilities. A PSF's ability to ensure a deep connection with customers relies on three interconnected CCs: individuated, relational, and ethical. These higher-order capabilities enable firms to engage directly with their clients by understanding their needs and establishing a relationship that is built on trust. PSFs that develop ongoing dialogue, provide access to information, are transparent about business practices, and are likely to help increase value for customers (Prahalad & Ramaswamy, 2004a). This is why relational and ethical interaction capabilities play such an important role in the overall CCs of afirm and its lower-order capabilities, such as SPCs. Furthermore, a PSFs ability to assist clients in creating value for themselves involves several enabling capabilities as well: developmental, empowered, and concerted. These capabilities, in turn, allow PSFs to use SPCs that enable critical thinking and contribute to the development of solutions as part of the knowledge creation and transfer process, which is common across professional service industries. Together, these CCs represent a PSF's potential for client engagement and interaction, which can support more effective use of SPCs. From a strategic perspective, the goal is to understand the PSF's role in a customer's value creation process (Grönroos, 2011) so that SPCs that can contribute to the development of value propositions. 2.2. Dynamic capabilities Dynamic capabilities are higher-order capabilities that enable afirm to sense opportunities, design different lower-order capability specifications, and modify these capabilities in order to match market requirements and deviate from an existing path and thus reduce path dependencies (Danneels, 2008; Teece et al., 1997). Effective lowerorder capabilities (i.e., SPCs) rely on DCs when service ecosystems change (Vargo & Lusch, 2011). Thus, like CCs, DCs differ from SPCs, which support thefirm in the present (Winter, 2003). DCs comprise the firm's sensing capability, seizing capability, and reconfiguring capability (Teece, 2007). Sensing capability comprises the scanning, search, and exploration processes deployed to generate knowledge about the PSF's internal operations, clients, markets, the competitive landscape and the general environment (Augier & Teece, 2009). It enables the PSF to recognize gaps in their SPCs— these gaps grow with increasing changes in environments, in which the provision of certain professional services becomes essential to compete, and to understand ensuing opportunities. Thus, PSFs that engage in sensing and proactively scanning the environment gain greater understanding of changes and their ensuing implications, such that ultimately they understand which capabilities are necessary for effective adaptation in dynamic markets (Castanias & Helfat, 2001). For example, in marketing advisory PSFs clients may demand more than marketing strategy advice and require complementary creative advice. Understanding the necessary capabilities to provide this advice can enable the effective provision of services that complement clients' internal capabilities. In turn, a PSF's better understanding of client needs concerning new service opportunities allows it to offer better advice to customers. Gaining understanding of suitable capabilities, which are foundations for offering professional services (i.e., developing compelling value propositions) to clients, thus is essential to leveraging new opportunities (Casson & Wadeson, 2007). Because sensing allows PSFs to recognize and understand (1) service provision opportunities; (2) gaps in their existing capabilities; and (3) possible SPCs that mightfill such gaps, the quality of PSFs' SPCs should be better. Service provision capabilities Prior studies have shown that collaboration is critical for PSFs, but the effectiveness of collaboration rests on afirm's ability to respond to market turbulence and to develop long-term relationships, rather than striving for short-term outcomes (Heirati et al., 2016). Hence, the consideration of CCs and DCs is important for PSFs that are striving to establish effective SPCs that rest on lasting relationships with customers and continually cocreate value in rapidly changing industries. These higher-order capabilities are associated with a PSFs ability to provide service and work closely with clients in developing value propositions. Although cocreation is recognized as a driver of collaboration (Karpen et al., 2015), they are not necessarily the same. In their study of PSFs, Heirati et al. (2016, p. 51)define interfirm collaboration as“the degree to which a PSF engages with two or more independent partners (e.g., suppliers, customers) to jointly develop and provide professional services.” This collaborative effort is a narrower type of cocreation, one that requires direct engagement and joint development of a value proposition. Because the main role of a PSF is to establish itself as a knowledge repository forfirms (Wagner et al., 2014), a critical aspect of the service these firms provide is the transfer and integration of knowledge from a PSF to a client. PSFs extend the boundaries of a client by allowing clients to leverage the knowledge and skills of a PSF in the development of their own value propositions (Wagner et al., 2014). Because PSFs provide high levels of knowledge in specialized areas, such as legal, marketing, accounting, and human resources, clients rely on the PSF's SPCs for developing their own products and managing their internal processes and external communications as well. In other words, PSFs connect and enable clients to create value on a general level through interaction and CCs, but also require a specialized set of lower-order capabilities related to the joint development of clients' specific value propositions. Akaka and Chandler (2011, p. 255 emphasis in original)distinguish between value cocreation and the joint development of a value proposition (also referred to as coproduction). This distinction suggests that the higher-order conceptualization of value cocreation involves the “integration and application of resources... that contribute to thecreation and determination of phenomenological value,” which aligns with the study of CCs and capabilities associated with interaction and resource integration via relationships. In this view, the lower-order, more direct collaboration between a service provider and its clients contributes more specifically to the“development of potential exchangeable resources” or a value proposition. In this way, the direct development of a value proposition involves particular lower-order capabilities that draw on different operant resources (from those that underlie CCs), such as SPCs (Akaka & Chandler, 2011). In the case of marketing advisoryfirms, SPCs contribute to the joint development of a client's value proposition by helping to manage a client's customer relationships, communications and brand image. 2.4. Performance As a PSF's configuration of DCs and CCs characterizes its path-dependent SPCs and performance, its higher-order capabilities should not be considered in isolation. CCs help align PSFs with client requirements in a way that engaging and connecting with clients comes with an effective set of SPCs that provide professional services that are connecting and enabling. While DCs allow PSFs to have in place SPCs that are relevant in changing environments, SPCs themselves are associated with the accomplishment of certain operational objectives (e.g., providing valuable services) and the PSF'sfinancial performance (Helfat et al., 2007). Although a PSF's configuration of CCs and DCs provide a means for long-term growth, its path-dependent SPCs permit thefirm to execute various business activities, and coproduce and deliver the professional services that we have outlined above. These SPCs should come, in turn, with achievement of certain performance goals, such as attainment of financial performance by o ffering advisory services through which it can generate income (cfDi Benedetto, DeSarbo, & Song, 2008). SPCs thus enable a PSF to implement a professional services strategy and meet its operational performance goals (Penrose, 1959). Therefore, as in industrialfirms performance is a reflection of industrial service capabilities (Böhm, Eggert, & Thiesbrummel, 2017; Eggert, Hogreve, Ulaga, & Muenkho ff, 2011; Raddats, Burton, & Ashman, 2015), PSF performance should reflect the firm's SPCs. Performance of SPCs, similar to performance in any operational domain, then should be associated with the PSF's overall performance (Helfat et al., 2007;Penrose, 1959). Thus, and in line with works of authors such as Eggert, Hogreve, Ulaga, and Muenkhoff (2014) and Oliva, Gebauer, and Brann (2012), a PSF's performance should mirror its SPCs. 3. Research setting and data It is important to note that PSFs integrate a variety of capabilities for a given episode of service exchange (Vargo & Lusch 2004; Vargo, Maglio, & Akaka, 2008; Vargo & Lusch, 2011). Thus, a configurational approach is used here to uncover the designs and combinations of system elements (e.g., in the context of this study: DCs and CCs) and how they, as configurations, are associated with path-dependent lowerorder SPCs as well asfirm performance. Three assumptions underlie the configurational logic and align with a service ecosystems perspective. First, single factors rarely fully explain outcomes of interest. Second, multiple factors rarely function in isolation and the configurations of these factors act as gestalts. Third, the strength and direction of effects of individual factors may differ depending on the context (Greckhamer, Misangyi, Elms, & Lacey, 2007) such that different configurations exist. Importantly, different configurations can associate with similar outcomes; that is, different configurations can relate to the same outcomes (Fiss, 2011). Organizational configurations can be both empirically or conceptually driven (Cardinal, Sitkin, & Long, 2010), with previous research differentiating between typologies (conceptual frameworks that are hard to test) and taxonomies (empirically driven but lacking underlying theory). In this study, we use an inductive approach to derive configurations (i.e., taxonomy); that is, wefirst theoretically specify the interconnected role of higher-order CCs and DCs, based on the hierarchy of operant resources and extant classifications of capabilities, and then use clustering techniques on these to derive configurations of these. Although the configurations are empirically driven, previous research has stressed the importance of such an approach for“the development of valid and precise frameworks for describing organizations and explaining their performance differences” (Ketchen Jr., Thomas, & Snow, 1993, p. 1306). Following Cardinal et al. (2010) we apply a configuration approach with the understanding that is both theorydriven and empirically testable. R. Wilden et al.
