Among them, some studies taking the technology perspective elucidate that AI can acquire new knowledge to support managers’ rational decision-making, improve resource utilization efficiency, and reduce environmental pollution, thus enhancing SBMI (Bag et al., 2021a; Di Vaio et al., 2020). However, scholars taking the capability perspective hold that artificial intelligence capabilities (AIC), rather than AI technology, perform well in guaranteeing sustainable competitive advantages (Mikalef and Gupta, 2021), which should also be true for SBMI. Some studies have introduced the notion of AIC, arguing that AIC can help firms continuously sense opportunities across different markets and technologies, thereby driving performance (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024), innovation (Sahoo et al., 2024), and servitization (Abou-Foul et al., 2023). However, the role of AIC in enhancing SBMI has not been analyzed with empirical evidence. Furthermore, the dynamic capabilities theory (DCT) has been widely used to explain the relationship between digital technology capabilities and sustainable innovation (Wang et al., 2023), which is appropriate but has not yet been used to explain the relationship between AIC and SBMI. To fill this gap, this study considers AIC as dynamic capabilities to explore whether they can help firms to enhance SBMI by rapidly acquiring and using information to sense opportunities (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). Even though AIC can be used to sense opportunities for enhancing SBMI, the pathway may not be so straightforward but rely on some intermediatory processes, which has not been addressed in previous studies. According to the process view of DCT, namely “sensingseizing-reconfiguring” capabilities, the opportunities sensed by AIC should be seized and reconfigured effectively to enhance SBMI (Teece et al., 1997). Strategic agility (SA) can be conceptualized as such a capability, which can swiftly respond to market changes and adjust strategies to accommodate environmental shifts (Clauss et al., 2021; Demir et al., 2021). Theoretically, AIC can help firms to improve the accuracy and efficiency of information exchange and integration to sense opportunities, thus enhancing SA (Fosso Wamba, 2022). In turn, SA can help firms dynamically deploy strategies, resources, and capabilities to enable constant upgrading in products, processes, and services, thus facilitating SBMI (Clauss et al., 2021; Turi et al., 2023). Practically, for example, Tesla utilizes AIC to sense the opportunity in new energy vehicles field by analyzing market data and consumer behavior; in turn, SA can be helpful for it in reallocating resources and capabilities to seize the opportunity; finally, it can release new energy electric vehicles faster to achieve high SBMI. As such, it is reasonable to hold that AIC can enhance SBMI indirectly via SA. However, existing studies have not empirically investigated how SA mediates between AIC and SBMI, even though they investigate the mediating roles of SA in the relationship between absorptive capacity and firm performance (Kale et al., 2019) and the relationship between organizational culture and business model innovation propensity (Hock et al., 2016). To fill this gap, this study intends to examine the mediating role of SA in the AIC-SBMI link. Furthermore, the existing literature employs qualitative methods to analyze the impact of a single capability on SBMI, without providing a comprehensive analysis of various capability configurations (Oliveira-Dias et al., 2022). This study employs fsQCA method to investigate different configurations of AIC and SA that achieve SBMI. Additionally, the contingency view of DCT posits that the opportunity “sensing-seizing” process must align with environmental dynamism (ED) since it makes the process of seizing opportunities more difficult (Arroyabe et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024). Theoretically, previous research has suggested that ED affects the process of capability construction and the response to market changes (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). Delving deeper into the causes of ED, we find that diverse customer needs, rapid technological changes, and regulatory pressures related to society can increase potential opportunities. Meanwhile, they also increase the requirements of sensing opportunities (Teece et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2023). In this case, firms with high AIC are equipped with high opportunity sense capabilities through rapid information processing, which in turn promotes their ability to seize opportunities to gain a sustainable BPMJ 31,7 3004 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/bpmj/article-pdf/31/7/3003/10428460/bpmj-11-2024-1045en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 competitive advantage (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). Practically, in high ED, firms are generally facing high green and social responsibility-taking pressures, as well as varied and customized market needs. In such context, to release new energy vehicle, Xiaomi corporation utilizes AIC to sense “next-generation” opportunities, and in turn utilizes SA to seize opportunities by reallocating resources and capabilities. As such, it is reasonable to hold that the relationship between AIC and SA can be moderated by ED. However, existing studies have not investigated the moderating effect of ED on the relationship between AIC and SA, even though they explore how ED moderates the link between AIC and innovation (Sahoo et al., 2024), as well as the link between AIC and market change response (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). To fill this gap, this study considers that the opportunity “sensing-seizing” process is moderated by ED. All in all, this study aims to address the following research questions: RQ1. What is the relationship between AIC and SBMI? RQ2. What is the role of SA in the relationship between AIC and SBMI? RQ3. How does ED influence the impact of AIC on SA? This study employs DCT to address above research questions. It examines how AIC influences SBMI from the process view of DCT. Specifically, this study considers AIC as “opportunity sensing capabilities”, further describing how AIC enables SBMI through SA being taking as the “opportunity seizing capabilities”. Additionally, drawing from the contingency view of DCT, this study examines how ED conditionally affects the link between AIC and SA. To evaluate the research model, we conducted an empirical analysis utilizing data from 337 Chinese firms. As the world’s second-largest economy and a key emerging market, China’s practices in leveraging AI for sustainable development can offer theoretical guidance for firms in developing countries, less developed regions, and even developed countries (Lin et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023b). The contributions of this study are as follows. First, this study takes the capability perspective of AI to examine the role of AIC in enhancing SBMI based on DCT, expanding the existing technology perspective of the relationship between them. Second, this study reveals the inner mechanisms between AIC and SBMI by investigating the mediating role of SA, deepening understanding of the opportunity “sensing-seizing-reconfiguring” process. Third, based on the contingency view of DCT, this study elucidates the boundary conditions for the AIC-SA link by examining the moderating role of ED. Theory and hypotheses 2.1 Dynamic capabilities theory To rapidly align with the changing external business environment, DCT is proposed by Teece et al. (1997) and dynamic capabilities can be divided into three capabilities: (1) sensing opportunities, (2) seizing opportunities, and (3) reconfiguring opportunities (Bashir et al., 2022). Specifically, sensing opportunities involves scanning activities; seizing opportunities involves agile investment in commercialization activities; reconfiguring opportunities involves breaking the unfavorable path dependencies that hinder the sustainable development (Bashir et al., 2022). For instance, Huawei corporation senses a novel opportunity in the realm of low-light photography for mobile phones; to effectively seize this opportunity, the firm reallocates both internal and external resources; finally, the firm launches the Huawei P series, representing a reconfiguration of opportunity. This can be understood as the process view of DCT. Moreover, the prominent feature of DCT is the emphases on ED and Business Process Management Journal 3005 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/bpmj/article-pdf/31/7/3003/10428460/bpmj-11-2024-1045en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 organizational adaptability (Sahoo et al., 2024), which indicates that the outcomes of dynamic capabilities can be dependent on ED, namely the contingency view of DCT. Recently, DCT has been widely used in the research on digital capabilities and innovation (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024; Wang et al., 2023). Specifically, Sullivan and Fosso Wamba (2024) studied how three AI-powered capabilities can seize opportunities through responses to market changes, resulting in firm performance and innovation. Wang et al. (2023) examined how digital platform capabilities can seize opportunities through inbound and outbound open innovation, thereby promoting sustainability-oriented innovation performance. Existing research has also shown that DCT can provide a reasonable framework to study how AIC influences SBMI. Therefore, we utilize the process and contingency views of DCT to explain the impact of AIC on SBMI. From the process view of DCT, AIC, which can obtain existing information through various channels and generate new information and knowledge, can be regarded as the capability to sense opportunities (Abou-Foul et al., 2023). SA, which involves quickly investing in products and services to gain market acceptance once opportunities are sensed, can be considered as the capability to seize opportunities (Kale et al., 2019; Shams et al., 2021). SBMI, which breaks the routine path by sensing and seizing opportunities, can be regarded as the capability to reconfigure opportunities to take environmental and social responsibilities (Broccardo et al., 2023; Di Vaio et al., 2020). Moreover, the contingency view of DCT holds that the construction of an organization’s dynamic capabilities is influenced by the level of ED (Arroyabe et al., 2024). Specifically, organizations seize the sensed opportunities by investing in commercialization activities (Ciampi et al., 2021). However, we find that ED may increase the requirements of sensing opportunities (Wang et al., 2023). That is to say, ED may affect the process of opportunity “sensing-seizing”. Therefore, we consider ED as a moderator of the relationship between AIC and SA. Based on the above analysis, it is reasonable for this study to use DCT to explain the research model. 2.2 An overview of artificial intelligence capabilities and sustainable business model innovation SBMI considers economic, social, and environmental values in a broader sense and shifts the focus from customers and shareholders to multiple stakeholders (Baiocco and Paniccia, 2023; Bashir et al., 2022). Although scholars have a wide range of interests, the field of SBMI remains in its infancy. Some scholars provide definitions and classifications of SBMI (Bocken et al., 2014; Geissdoerfer et al., 2018). Additionally, some scholars explore the outcomes and drivers of SBMI. Regarding outcomes, they find the significant positive effects of SBMI on both SME performance and competitive advantage based on DCT (Bashir et al., 2022). Regarding driving factors, scholars theoretically argue that creating shared value (Bocken et al., 2014), dynamic capabilities (Oliveira-Dias et al., 2022), stakeholder management and dynamic capabilities (Guo et al., 2022), blockchain (Mas et al., 2020), and digitalization (Broccardo et al., 2023) are significant drivers of SBMI. Recently, some scholars regard AI technology as the driver of SBMI (Di Vaio et al., 2020; Jorzik et al., 2024). However, these studies are qualitative and have not yet been supported by empirical evidence, even though there are empirical studies investigating both AI-driven business model innovation (Kanungo et al., 2024) and sustainability strategies (Liang et al., 2024; Siddik et al., 2025). Furthermore, scholars taking the capability perspective hold that AIC, rather than AI technology, performs well in guaranteeing sustainable competitive advantages (Mikalef and Gupta, 2021), which should also be true for SBMI. AIC has a positive impact on SBMI. 2.4 The mediating role of strategic agility According to the process view of DCT, seizing opportunity is the intermediate process of opportunity “sensing – reconfiguring” (Lin et al., 2024). SA can be served as such a capability for seizing opportunities, characterized by the firm’s ability to continuously rejuvenate itself and maintain flexibility while preserving efficiency (Clauss et al., 2021). For instance, in a turbulent international scenario, where globalization affects consumer behavior and markets are impacted by continuous change, international firms continuously reallocate their resources and capabilities in response to consumer behavior and market changes, which is SA (Demir et al., 2021). Some scholars have delineated SA within a structure that is centered on three meta-capabilities: strategic sensitivity (STS), resource fluidity (REF) and collective commitment (COC) (Hock et al., 2016). STS emphasizes the organization’s ability to perceive risks and opportunities; REF emphasizes the strategic allocation of resources; COC emphasizes cognitive consistency among organizational members (Hock et al., 2016; Kale et al., 2019). This study will explore the roles of the three meta-capabilities of SA as mediators between AIC and SBMI. (1) The mediating role of STS. AIC can help firms enhance STS by the integration of internal and external information to seize opportunities (Ahmed et al., 2022; Sahoo et al., 2024). First, AIC can enable the integration of external information by analyzing large volumes of structured and unstructured data (Chen et al., 2023; Sahoo et al., 2024). This allows firms to swiftly carry out their strategic decisions and initiatives, which can help them seize market opportunities (Ahmed et al., 2022). This helps firms seize internal resource optimization opportunities and revenue growth opportunities (Demir et al., 2021; Shams et al., 2021). In turn, STS can reconfigure the opportunities it seizes by implementing forward-looking strategies to achieve SBMI (Clauss et al., 2021). First, STS identifies unmet needs and create new needs, which can reconfigure market opportunities to promote SBMI (Kale et al., 2019). Second, STS enables firms to become aware of the new capabilities, technologies and processes needed to produce sustainable products, which can reconfigure opportunities for optimizing internal resources to promote SBMI (Ahammad et al., 2021). Third, STS helps firms offer new products or services, which can reconfigure revenue growth opportunities to promote SBMI (Fosso Wamba, 2022). AIC can help firms promote REF by the exchange of inter-firm, internal and external information to seize opportunities (Bag et al., 2021b; Sahoo et al., 2024). First, AIC can facilitate collaboration across technological and organizational boundaries, enabling efficient exchange of information between firms (Sahoo et al., 2024). This facilitates REF of inter-firm and seize market opportunities (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). Second, AIC can improve internal information exchange by effective communication between different functions within a firm (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). This promotes REF of internal and seize internal resource optimization opportunities (Dubey et al., 2020). Third, AIC can enable the exchange of external information through customer service systems (Zhang et al., 2024). This facilitates REF of external and revenue growth opportunities (Sahoo et al., 2024). In turn, REF can reconfigure the opportunities it seizes by modularizing and integrating interfirm, internal and external resources to achieve SBMI (Broccardo et al., 2023; Clauss et al., 2021). First, REF enables firms to modularize inter-firm resources during product and service development, so that they can more accurately fulfill market needs (Clauss et al., 2021). This enhances SBMI by reconfiguring market opportunities (Broccardo et al., 2023; Sj€odin et al., 2023). Second, REF enables firms improve resource utilization efficiency and reduce resource use cost by integrating internal and external resources (Clauss et al., 2021; Hock et al., 2016). This facilitates SBMI by reconfiguring opportunities to optimize internal resources and revenue growth (Geissdoerfer et al., 2018; Sj€odin et al., 2023). From the analysis above, the following hypothesis is proposed: H2b. The influence of AIC on SBMI is mediated by REF. (3) The mediating role of COC. First, AIC can enhance COC by improving the accuracy of information integration (Bag et al., 2021a). Specifically, AIC can reduce information integration errors through human-machine collaboration, which can fulfill COC to seize opportunities more accurately (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). Second, AIC can enhance COC by improving the efficiency of information integration (Dwivedi et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2018). ED refers to the unpredictability and extent of change in the external environment, encompassing dynamic shifts driven by technological advancements, fluctuations in market demand, and alterations in regulatory pressures (Sahoo et al., 2024). For example, manufacturing firms in an industrial setting have shorter product life cycles due to frequent changes in market demand (Ahmed et al., 2022), and such changes in production and regulation are associated with a higher degree of ED (Yuan et al., 2021). We contend that the impact of ED on the relationship between AIC and SA is manifested in the following aspects. (1) ED increases the demand for opportunities sensing (Chen et al., 2022). In this case, AIC can assist firms in analyzing data from diverse sources and deriving new insights to discern market trends and forecast risks, thus enhancing their STS (Duan et al., 2019). Therefore, when the ED is high, AIC can result in a higher level of STS. (2) ED presents a potential threat of rapid resource obsolescence (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). In this case, AIC can enhance willingness to share resources by fostering long-term external partnerships and building trust, thus promoting REF (Hock et al., 2016; Sahoo et al., 2024). Therefore, when the ED is high, AIC can result in a higher level of REF. (3) ED affects the efficiency and quality of senior managers’ decision-making to a certain extent (Chen et al., 2022). In this case, AIC can enhance COC by enabling more rational decision-making through vast amounts of data analysis (Fosso Wamba, 2022; Zhang et al., 2023). Therefore, when the ED is high, AIC can result in a higher level of COC. From the analysis above, the following hypotheses are proposed: H3a. ED strengthens the connection between AIC and STS. H3b. Research design 3.1 Sampling and data collection This study used a questionnaire to collect data from the sample. It considered three factors in selecting Chinese firms as research samples. First, according to the Global Digital Economy White Paper (2023) released by the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, China’s AI industry has ushered in rapid development. In the third quarter of 2023, there were a total of 29,542 AI firms worldwide, and China accounted for a quarter of them. Second, resource scarcity and environmental pollution have further strained the relationship between firms and the environment, and Chinese firms are more aware of the crucial role of sustainability in business activities (Lin et al., 2024). Therefore, they have a strong incentive and institutional pressure to adopt AI for sustainable development (Wang et al., 2023). Third, as the world’s second largest economy and a key emerging market, China’s practices in leveraging AI for sustainable development can provide theoretical guidance for firms in developing countries, less-developed regions, and even developed countries (Lin et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023b). Although our study only involves samples from China, the issues of AI and sustainable development are widespread globally. In addition, our samples are drawn from different regions of China, covering various levels of economic development. Therefore, it is reasonable to hold that the research findings of this study can be generalized. A pretest with 30 MBA students assessed the survey’s clarity and understandability, yielding no negative feedback due to validated scales (Wang et al., 2023b). We employed a consulting firm to conduct a formal survey in two phases, and targeted middle and senior managers for this study on firm strategy, as they are key informants for assessing strategic orientation and SBMI (Wang et al., 2023b). The PLS-SEM was employed for its capability to measure causal relationships between multiple independent and dependent variables simultaneously (Marzi et al., 2023). This regression-based method utilizes a net effect approach to examine the influence between variables. But the covariance between variables in the model reveals that the presence or absence of one variable can affect the effects of other variables and the expected outcomes, which highlights the importance of configurational analysis (Kolagar et al., 2024). Therefore, to obtain richer results beyond traditional regression techniques, we further employed the fsQCA method. The fsQCA is a set-theoretic method for causal analysis that assumes outcomes are often caused by multiple factors rather than any single factor, which aims to identify all the combinations of causal conditions that potentially lead to a certain result (Fiss, 2011). First, AIC has a positive impact on SBMI. This implies that firms with AIC can sense opportunities through information integration, thus achieving SBMI (Abou-Foul et al., 2023). Our results are consistent with previous studies by Sullivan and Fosso Wamba (2024), who pointed out that AIC can respond to market changes through information integration, thus promoting innovation. Notably, we further validated this mechanism in the context of SBMI. Furthermore, our results confirm the findings of Di Vaio et al. (2020), who contended that AI technology plays a significant role in SBMI but lacked empirical evidence. Second, SA including STS, REF, and COC, plays a positive mediating role between AIC and SBMI. This indicates that ED allows AIC to sense opportunities by reducing the threat of rapid resource obsolescence (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). In turn, AIC can enhance willingness to share resources by fostering long-term external partnerships and building trust, thus promoting REF (Hock et al., 2016; Sahoo et al., 2024). Finally, the fsQCA analysis identified six configurations, all of which relate to SBMI and complement the previous PLS-SEM analysis results. The “Synergy – co-creation” configuration emphasizes the importance of AIC and COC in firms, which further confirms that achieving SBMI necessitates not only AIC for sensing opportunities but also SA for seizing them (Broccardo et al., 2023; Geissdoerfer et al., 2018). The “Aggregation – breakthrough” configuration highlights the critical roles of COC and REF, while the “Ambidexterity – efficiency” configuration emphasizes the importance of STS and REF. This suggests that SA can also sense opportunities in addition to AIC, and then to seize these opportunities effectively. These findings support previous research by Clauss et al. (2021) that SA is a dynamic capability to sense and seize opportunities, ultimately enhancing business model innovation. 5.2 Theoretical implications This study provides threefold contributions to existing literature. First, this study takes the capability perspective of AI to examine the role of AIC in enhancing SBMI based on DCT, which expands the existing technology perspective of the relationship between them. Existing studies have discussed from the technical perspective that AI can acquire new knowledge to support managers’ rational decision-making, improve resource utilization efficiency, and reduce environmental pollution, thus enhancing SBMI (Bag et al., 2021a; Di Vaio et al., 2020). However, these studies are qualitative and have not yet been supported by empirical evidence. This study empirically tested the relationship between them, confirming scholars’ hypotheses that AI is beneficial for SBMI. Additionally, AI can constitute a distinctive and valuable capability that requires emerging literature to explore its impact on SBMI (Sj€odin et al., 2023). In response to this call, this study establishes a research model of AIC and SBMI based on DCT. We contend that AIC can sense market opportunities, internal resource optimization opportunities and revenue growth opportunities by integrating inter-firm, internal and external information, thereby facilitating SBMI (Di Vaio et al., 2020; Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). Therefore, the conclusions of this study not only enrich the body of knowledge on AIC but also shed new light on the factors propelling SBMI. Second, this study reveals the inner mechanisms between AIC and SBMI by investigating the mediating role of SA, which further deepens understanding of the opportunity “sensingseizing-reconfiguring” process. Although many firms have deployed AIC to sense opportunities for enhancing SBMI (Broccardo et al., 2023; Sj€odin et al., 2023), the pathway through which the opportunities sensed by AIC translate into SBMI remains unclear. Based on the “sensing-seizing-reconfiguring” framework of DCT (Teece et al., 1997), this study clarifies the theoretical mechanisms by which AIC facilitates SA to improve SBMI. AIC can enhance STS and REF to seize opportunities by the integration and exchange of inter-firm, internal and external information (Sahoo et al., 2024; Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). Further, SA promotes SBMI by reconfiguring seized opportunities (Baiocco and Paniccia, 2023). Additionally, the fsQCA method was employed to comprehensively analyze all combinations of AIC and SA to achieve SBMI, which extends the methodological exploration of the internal mechanisms between AIC and SBMI (Wang et al., 2023b). Thus, this study facilitates the opening of the black box of the mechanism between AIC and SBMI within the framework of opportunity “sensingseizing-reconfiguring”. Third, based on the contingency view of DCT, this study elucidates the boundary conditions for the AIC-SA link by examining the moderating role of ED. Existing research has explored how ED moderates the link between AIC and open innovation (Sahoo et al., 2024), and further research has discussed its moderating role between AIC and market change response (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). However, there are no empirical studies that demonstrate the role of ED in the relationship between AIC and SA. To fill this gap, this study considers that the opportunity “sensing-seizing” process will be moderated by ED. We contend that ED increases the demand for opportunities sensing (Chen et al., 2022), presents a potential threat of rapid resource obsolescence (Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024), and affects the efficiency and quality of senior managers’ decision-making (Chen et al., 2022). In this case, AIC can enhance the ability to sense opportunities, strengthen the willingness to share resources, and facilitate rational decision-making (Duan et al., 2019; Sullivan and Fosso Wamba, 2024). Thereby, firms improve STS, REF, and COC to greater degree through the adaptation between AIC and ED (Ahmed et al., 2022). Thus, this study investigates the contingent role of ED in the relationship between AIC and SA, as well as reveals the boundary conditions for firms to utilize AIC for strategic deployment. 5.3 Practical implications First, managers should prioritize enhancing AIC and leverage its role in sensing market, internal resource optimization and revenue growth opportunities to better achieve SBMI. The findings show that AIC can positively impact SBMI by sensing new opportunities through inter-firm, external and internal information integration. Therefore, it is necessary for managers to increase their investment in AI research and commercialization. For example, firms can allocate a certain percentage of funds annually for the development and improvement of AIC and its infrastructure. Meanwhile, managers should also intensify the training for relevant personnel to effectively absorb and utilize new knowledge and technologies, thereby enhancing AIC. For example, firms can collaborate with professional AI training institutions, rotating professional technical personnel to participate in training programs focused on relevant technical knowledge and operational skills. Second, managers should pay attention to improving SA if they rely on AIC to further enhance SBMI. The findings reveal that the influence of AIC on SBMI is mediated by SA. SA allows firms to swiftly seize market, internal resource optimization and revenue growth opportunities. In this way, it can adjust resources and capabilities to innovate products and services, meet diverse customer needs, and reconfigure the cost and revenue structure, thus achieving SBMI more effectively. Therefore, it is imperative for managers to consider SA as a fundamental capability. For instance, managers can maintain close communication with suppliers and implement jointly associated information systems. When firms sense new opportunities, they can fully leverage the resources provided by suppliers to update or create new products and services, thereby seizing the opportunities and achieving SBMI. Third, managers need to closely monitor the level of ED and flexibly adjust their decisions regarding AIC and SA based on it. The findings show that ED enhances the link between AIC and REF, yet it does not notably influence the connections between AIC and STS or COC. ED increases the demand for opportunities sensing, compelling firms to utilize AIC to enhance their opportunity-sensing capabilities, thus enhancing REF. For example, firms can design a set of processes and mechanisms to collect information on industry development policies, technological development levels, and competitors. This enables firms to promptly capture changes in both internal and external environments. Moreover, this study can provide suggestions for government and scientific research institutions. For one thing, the government can encourage firms that utilize AIC for achieving SBMI by offering them financial incentives, subsidies, and tax reductions. For instance, the government offers subsidies to high-tech firms that engage in research and development of AIdriven sustainable technologies, such as energy optimization, carbon footprint tracking, and circular economy modeling. These subsidies cover a specified percentage of the associated research and development costs, typically ranging from 30% to 50%. For another, scientific research institutions can collaborate with firms to develop AIC training programs. These training programs can include and update the courses related to “AIC and SBMI”, as well as the analysis of case studies and hands-on exercises, to enhance employees’ abilities in utilizing AI technologies and enhancing SBMI. For instance, firms within the information technology service sector may establish AI laboratories in collaboration with universities to concentrate on research and training in AI technologies, as exemplified by Baidu’s partnership with Tsinghua University. 5.4 Limitation and future research This study presents several limitations. First, this study relies on self-reported data from questionnaires. The findings may be affected by the respondents’ subjective feelings and biases. To improve the external validity of the findings, future research can collect more objective and longitudinal data. Meanwhile, future research can collect cross-country and regional data to increase the universality of research results. This study draws on the results of sample analyses from Chinese firms, it is reasonable to posit that our findings may also be applicable to firms in developing countries, less developed regions, and even developed countries where AI is extensively utilized to address sustainable development challenges. However, further validation is required to confirm this inference. Second, this study examines the effect of AIC on SBMI. Future research can explore the impact of other digital capabilities on SBMI, such as digital platform capabilities and big data capabilities. Third, this study reveals the inner mechanism between AIC and SBMI in terms of SA. Future research can reveal their inner mechanisms in other respects, such as intellectual capital, ambidextrous learning, and network alliances. Fourth, this study posits that organizational culture and AI aversion could potentially account for why the moderating effects of ED on the relationships between AIC and STS/COC are not supported. Dynamic capability of the firm: analysis of the impact of internationalisation on SME performance in an emerging economy Mahfuzur Rahman Lincoln International Business School, University of Lincoln, Lincoln, UK Dieu Hack-Polay University of Lincoln, Lincoln, UK Sujana Shafique Leeds Beckett University, Leeds, UK, and Paul Agu Igwe University of Lincoln, Lincoln, UK Abstract Purpose – Internationalisation is considered as a key strategy for the growth of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs). The purpose of this paper is to examine the relationship between dynamic capability, SMEs internationalisation and firm performance in the context of emerging economies and to evaluate the impact of financial, asset and market expansion on internationalisation of SMEs. Design/methodology/approach – Using primary data from 212 SMEs from Bangladesh, structural equation modelling and mathematical (hierarchical reflective) model, the analysis enabled the measurement of the casual relationship on the impacts of internationalisation. Findings – The results revealed that internationalisation of SMEs has significant impact on both financial and non-financial performance of SMEs in an em erging economy- Bangladesh. The paper found internationalisation impacts on two dimensions (financial and non-financial) with eight defined indicators– higher sales, higher profit, assets maximisation, market expansion, competitive advantage, better reputation, better customer service and added knowledge. Originality/value – Despite several studies that examine the relationship between SME internationalisation and firm performance, limited research exists on emerging economies. This is contrary to the fact that SMEs are one of the main vehicles for growth in those economies such as Bangladesh. In this research, the authors use the theories of dynamic capabilities to conceptualise how internationalisation becomes a core SME capability for SMEs in an emerging economy. Keywords Internationalization, SMEs, Dynamic capabilities, Firm performance, Small emerging country Paper typeResearch paper 1. Introduction The contribution of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to economic development has been widely recognised in business and economic literature. These firms are more productive than larger firms and ensure efficiency, productivity, innovation, and employment within economy (Cravo et al., 2012; Gkypali et al., 2021). However, financial markets and other institutional failures in the home country may prevent the development of SMEs. Internationalisation presents itself as a novel way for SMEs to grow (Mendy et al., 2020) and circumvent financial and institutional barriers (Filatotchev et al., 2009; Ganotakis and Love, 2012; Gashi et al., 2014). By examining the dynamic capabilities, the financial and non-financial impact of internationalisation on firm’s performance, this article contributes to knowledge in several ways. First, we contribute to identifying issues and conditions under which SMEs in emerging economy such as Bangladesh develop dynamic capabilities, performance, market agility and sustainable competitive advantage. There is no significant research on marketing agility, how marketing agility could be developed and sustained in emerging markets such as Bangladesh (Osei et al., 2019). Secondly, we clarify and analyse financial and non-financial impacts variables that impact on SMEs internationalisation. It has been revealed that international expansion is an important decision for SMEs, which traditionally face financial constraints (Pacheco, 2019). This article extends the literature on this topic since it is focused on SMEs in developing country context with unique environmental, market and business factors. The second section then outlines the methodology while the third presents and discuss the finding. The final section summarises the research and considers its implications. 2. Literature review and hypothesis development 2.1 Resource-based theory and dynamic capabilities The theory of resource-based view (RBV) has become one of the most influential and cited theories (Kraaijenbrink et al., 2010). RBV emphasises that the accumulation of valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable (VRIN) resources by firms (Lin and Wu, 2014). Lin and Wu (2014) maintain that dynamic-capability view (DCV) have been used to extend RBV to analyse the influences of dynamic markets, the important role of capabilities to build, integrate and reconfigure resources to cope with the highly volatile environment. Consequently, Teece’s (2011) theory of dynamic capabilities has been used to inform this investigation. The theory projects a strategic approach to seeing the organisation ’s competitive strategy. Internationalisation has long been regarded as one of the most effective ways to ensure sales growth of firms (Singh et al., 2009; Park and Jang, 2010). Despite this important relationship between sales growth and SME internationalisation, literature is still short of a consensual state. While some of the studies (Rahman et al., 2020; Moen et al., 2016; Lages and Lages, 2004) identify higher sales as an important outcome of internationalisation, other studies (Albaum and Tse, 2001; Ling-yee and Ogunmokun, 2001; Lu and Beamish, 2006) do not support that positive impact. Considering this debate over the nature of relationship between higher sales and SME internationalisation, the following hypothesis is proposed: H1a. Higher sales as a factor of financial impact and internationalisation of SMEs will not be independent from each other. Internationalisation strategies are often motivated by the higher profit expectation (Pangarkar, 2008). Although increased turnover/sales can contribute to profitability, this study keeps higher sales as a separate variable. While, it is a significant and important panacea for profitability, it does not always automatically happen particularly in SMEs. Internationalisation of SMEs can lead to higher profit because of higher revenue (Lu and Beamish, 2006), cheap labour (Pangarkar, 2008), production efficiency (Thomas and Eden, 2004), lower taxes (Pangarkar, 2008) and/or the possibility of arbitrage (Allen and Pantzalis, 1996). However,Lu and Beamish (2006)pointed out that continued foreign expansion would be accompanied by decelerating profit growth and negative marginal returns beyond some optimal level.Vuorio et al. (2020)do not consider higher profit a result of internationalisation alone but more critically of SME innovation. Therefore, the findings related to higher profit as an important impact of internationalisation are still inconclusive. Based on the above discussions, it has been hypothesised that: H1b. Higher profit as a factor of financial impacts and internationalisation of SMEs will not be independent from each other. It has been argued that internationalisation enables the SMEs to access complementary assets-based resources (Estrin et al., 2017; George et al., 2001; Lavie and Miller, 2008). In fact, internationalisation of firms may facilitate the bundling of resources that owners or managers use to create value, i.e. to increase assets firms’ assets (Javalgi and Todd, 2011). A number of studies suggest that internationalisation has a positive impact on the growth of a firm’s assets (Mudalige et al., 2019; Ling-yee and Ogunmokun, 2001; Lages and Lages, 2004; Dynamic capability of the firm 2385 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijoem/article-pdf/18/9/2383/3319916/ijoem-02-2021-0236.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 Chelliah et al., 2010). However, authors such asHoang (1998), Wolff and Pett (2000)and Shoham et al. (2002) did not find any positive impact. Therefore, the findings related to increase in assets as an important impact of internationalisation are not consistent. On the basis of the above discussions, it has been hypothesised that: H1c. Increase in assets as a factor of financial impacts and internationalisation of SMEs will not be independent from each other. Cadogan et al. (1999) considered market expansion as an outcome of internationalisation strategy. Although larger firms are at the forefront of international market expansion, SMEs are also coming forward to expand the market internationally (Mendy et al., 2020; Pangarka, 2008) and earning more revenue from international market than local market (Chelliah et al., 2010). Some studies find positive relationships between internationalisation and market expansion such asDhanaraj and Beamish (2003), Akyol and Akehurst (2003), Morgan et al. (2004) and Smolarski and Kut (2011). However,Kwon and Hu (1995), Armario et al.(2008) and Kirca et al. (2009) did not find a positive relationship between market expansion and internationalisation. On the basis of above discussions, the following hypothesis is proposed: H1d. Market expansion as a factor of financial impact and internationalisation of SMEs will not be independent from each other. Competitive advantage is an important outcome of internationalisation (Hsu et al., 2013). Although competitive advantage is important for both large and small firms, it is more important for smaller firms because of the resource constraints (Bell et al., 2004; Bonaccorsi, 1992; Ghauri and Herbern, 1994). While large firms are financially capable to develop product diversity, market or even skills, SMEs are more dependent on comparatively low cost and high value business strategies. According toHsu et al. (2013), internationalisation assists these firms to achieve competitive advantage particularly for the firms which have limited home market opportunities. Other studies that support a positive impact of internationalisation on attaining competitive advantage include research byAlbaum and Tse (2001), Cadogan et al.(2003), Rose and Shoham (2002), Balabanis and Katsikea (2003), Akyol and Akehurst (2003), Morgan et al.(2004) and Chelliah et al.(2010). However,Lu and Beamish (2006)could not find any such relationship. On the basis of above discussions, the following hypothesis is proposed: H2a. Competitive advantages as a factor of non-financial impact and internationalisation of SMEs will not be independent from each other. Firm reputation plays an important role in attracting the target customers. It is generally agreed that large firms have more resources to manage reputation. In contrast, SMEs build their reputation in the long run based on the quality of products or services, values and networks. Lu and Beamish (2006)stated that SMEs can build reputation by pursuing an internationalisation strategy as it helps to improve product quality and increase their networks. Studies that support positive relationship between enhanced reputation and internationalisation include those by Morgan et al. (2004), Ruzzier et al. (2007), Lu and Beamish (2006) and Pangankar (2008). However, Hoang (1998), Francis and Collins-Dodd (2000) and Wolff and Pett (2000) did not find reputation to be an outcome of internationalisation. Consequently, the following hypothesis is proposed: H2b. Better reputation as a factor of non-financial impact and internationalisation of SMEs will not be independent from each other. It has been argued that success of SMEs is partly dependent on the skills of the owners and managers (Hack-Polay et al., 2020b; Bryan, 2006). Internationalisation is a source for accumulating business skills that augment the organisation’s capabilities as suggested byMudalige et al.(2019); Morgan et al. (2004), Aspelund and Moen (2005), Knight and Cavusgil (2004). However, Hoang (1998), Francis and Collins-Dodd (2000)and Wolff and Pett (2000)could not agree on the role of internationalisation in enhancing business skills. On the basis of above discussions, the following hypothesis is proposed: H2c. Skills development as a factor of non-financial impact and internationalisation of SMEs will not be independent from each other. Knowledge is one of the most important success factors of business process management (Trkman, 2010; Mahmoud et al., 2018). While larger firms can improve knowledgebase through hiring staffs, SMEs cannot do the same for resource limitations. Internationalisation could be a good source of knowledge accumulation for the SMEs asAutio et al.(2000) pointed out that firms may enjoy learning advantages from newness. While studies byZahra and Hayton (2008)and Bradley and O’Reagain (2001)consider new knowledge as an important outcome of internationalisation, others such asHoang’s (1998), Francis and Collins-Dodd’s (2000) and Wolff and Pett’s (2000)investigations did not arrive at the same conclusion. On the basis of above discussions, the following hypothesis is proposed: H2d. New knowledge as a factor of non-financial impact and internationalisation of SMEs will not be independent from each other. 2.3 Conceptual model Based on the theory of dynamic capabilities and the extant literature on internationalisation of SMEs, this paper proposes the research model illustrated inFigure 1. Methodology 3.1 The Bangladeshi context SMEs are considered as the engine to employment generation and economic growth particularly for the developing countries. Although SMEs are significant both for all types of economies, emerging economies are more dependent to these smaller firms. On the other hand, many SMEs struggle to survive in the long run (Mendy et al., 2020). While this is a significant issue for entrepreneurship research, the number of studies on the internationalisation of SMEs is very limited. Therefore, this study focuses on the internationalisation of SMEs from Bangladesh perspective whose economy is significantly dependent on the performance of SMEs (Mendy et al., 2020). Bangladesh is a leading developing country and where both SMEs and internationalisation count as a significant part of the country’s major economic activities. This study developed and validated a partial least squares based SEM (PLS-SEM) on the impacts of internationalisation for SMEs where it formulates a theory that is empirically testable and“law-like generalisations” (Orlikowski and Baroudi, 1991; Henseler et al., 2009). As this study proposed a mathematical (hierarchical reflective) model on the impact of internationalisation for Bangladeshi SMEs and formulates a theory that is empirically testable, the research philosophy reflected in this study is positivistic in nature. The purpose for using the empirical survey was to measure a casual network relationship on the impacts of internationalisation for SMEs. To carry on the empirical investigation, cross-sectional survey technique was applied to extract views from the respondents only once (Malhotra et al., 2006). To achieve the maximum response rate from a developing country perspective, standard mail out procedure was applied rather than a home, telephone or online survey (Dillman, 1978). This study developed hypotheses on the basis of relevant literature review to propose hierarchical reflective models. To validate the model, an empirical survey was carried out which followed deductive research approach. Data were collectedfrom four major divisions of Bangladesh– Dhaka, Khulna, Chittagong and Rajshahi from July 2011 till September 2011. A total of 1,000 questionnaires were distributed among these four divisions (250 questionnaires each) following the cluster sampling technique. To ensure equal selection opportunities, a systematic random sampling technique was applied. The population for the survey was defined as the SMEs doing international business, i.e. interacting or trading with other businesses and customers across borders. Non-internationalised firms were excluded as the dynamics of local firms are very different than the internationalised SMEs (Mendy et al., 2020). Out of 1,000 questionnaires, 219 responses were received. Among the 219 returns, 7 were unusable due to excessive missing data. Finally, the data from 212 questionnaires were analysed. The PLS-SEM model is based on hierarchical construct which is defined with multiple dimensions at several hierarchies to capture an overall latent variable (Akter et al., 2010; Wetzels et al., 2009). This is supported by many studies which show that the hierarchical construct is effective in reducing model complexity and increasing theoretical discretion (MacKenzie et al., 2005; Reinartz et al., 2009; Roldan and SanchezFranco, 2012). Another key advantage of using the hierarchical construct is related to the level of abstraction for predictor and criterion variables (Chin and Gopal, 1995). Although there are many advantages, PLS-SEM is critiqued as it is unable to consistently estimate factor models (Henseler, 2012). This paper aims to identify the impacts of internationalisation on performance of SMEs from the Bangladesh perspective. It specifies the impacts of internationalisation on performance of Bangladeshi SMEs as a hierarchical reflective model with two reflective constructs (Figure 1) – financial impacts of internationalisation and nonfinancial impacts of internationalisation. Both of these constructs share a common theme which is the overall impact of internationalisation on the performance of Bangladeshi SMEs. According toBollen and Lennox (1991), the correlation between two measures is supposed to be highly positive for a reflective construct.Akter et al.(2010) and Petter et al. (2007)further explained that internal consistency is one of the most important elements of reflective constructs. Besides, the undimensional nature of the reflective measures assists to get rid of individual measures for the purpose of improving construct validity with no effect on content validity (Petter et al., 2007). Conclusion 5.1 Summary One of the key objectives within this study was to identify the impacts of internationalisation on the performance of Bangladeshi SMEs. To fulfil this objective, this study has developed and validated a structural model on the impact of an internationalisation model that is able to explain the key impacts of internationalisation on performance of Bangladeshi SMEs. This study also contributes by extending our knowledge on the impacts of internationalisation as a dynamic capability for SMEs from Bangladesh by categorising internationalisation impacts in two dimensions (financial impacts and non-financial impacts) with eight indicators (higher sales, higher profit, assets maximisation, market expansion, competitive advantage, better reputation, better customer service, added knowledge).Denrell and Powell (2016) contend that the firm’s internal dynamic capabilities are important in embarking on the internationalisation journey. However, these capabilities will remain dormant, thus, not useful (or dynamic) if they do not interact effectively with the institutional dynamics (culture, legal frameworks, networks, etc.) within the international markets. In this perspective, we IJOEM 18,9 2394 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijoem/article-pdf/18/9/2383/3319916/ijoem-02-2021-0236.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 conceptualise internationalisation itself as an external dynamic capability that can reinforce and give competitive meaning to SME internal capabilities. It has effectively enclosed impacts of internationalisation as a dynamic capability on the performance of SMEs in a second order reflective model where both two dimensions reflect overall impacts of internationalisation on the performance of SMEs. Hence, it complements to theoretical support for studies ofTeece (2011)and Pangarka (2008). It also provides further support for Mudalige et al. (2019) perspectives about the criticality of the deployment of institutional dynamic capabilities in SMEs are to make effective use of the opportunities in the international environment. In general, the financial impacts of the effective deployment of internationalisation as dynamic capability seem to be most influential impacts on performance as it explains 80% of overall variance followed by the non-financial impacts (75%) because it augments the learning that organisational members use in both operational and strategic formulation (Mudalige et al., 2019). Even though the ranking has been done on the basis of the explanatory power of individual constructs, the magnitude of difference is relatively small. Thus, it can be suggested that all these constructs should be given equal attention. 5.2 Limitations and further research The main limitation of the study centres of its geo-cultural coverage. Though Bangladeshi is credited with more SMEs in South Asia, limiting the study in this sphere restricts generalisability because economies and cultures in South Asia present some particularities. In the light of the limitation of the findings of this research, we suggest that future investigations consider a more systematic and in-depth examination what learning sits in the international environment that is critical for developing country SME to internalise and appropriate, then how to deploy them. Such an approach will help theorise internationalisation not as a mere external factor impacting SMEs but as part of the critical capabilities for growth. Future studies could also consider a wider developing world context by collecting data in several countries in order to derive some useful comparisons according to the level of economic development and cultural systems. The interplay of integration, flexibility and coordination: a dynamic capability view to responding environmental uncertainty Attique ur Rehman and Muhammad Shakeel Sadiq Jajja Suleman Dawood School of Business, Lahore University of Management Sciences, Lahore, Pakistan Abstract Purpose – Supply chain literature highlights that environmental uncertainty (EU) encourages firms to integrate their business strategies and develop strategic flexibility (SF). The authors’ use the dynamic capability view (DCV) to explain why the EU motivates firms to develop SF and integrate business strategies for better supply chain coordination (SCC) and enhanced performance. This study tests the role of SCC as a mediator between (1) business strategy integration (BSI) and operational performance, and (2) SF and operational performance. The study also measures the contingent effect of structural constructs on the relationship between EU, BSI and SF. Design/methodology/approach – Data of 356 firms drawn from the continuous innovation network (CINet) are used in this paper. Structural equation modeling (SEM) is used to test the direct, indirect and moderation hypotheses. Findings – The paper finds that EU enhances SF and BSI. Further, BSI has a significant positive impact on SCC that drives operational performance. The paper also finds that SF has no direct impact on SCC rather it affects SCC through BSI. SCC mediates the relationship between (1) SF and operational performance, and (2) BSI and operational performance. The organization ’s structural factors including connectedness and formalization moderate the effect of EU on BSI and SF. Originality/value – The paper extends debate at the interface of supply chain risk and strategy literature and provides a specific understanding of the“external-internal-external” mechanism in the context of the turbulent business environment. This mechanism helps to understand why and under what structural conditions EU (external) leads to BSI and SF (internal). Further, BSI and SF (internal) help firms to manage SCC (external) effectively that in turn improve operational performance. Keywords Business strategy integration, Strategic flexibility, Supply chain coordination, Operational performance, CINet, Dynamic capability Paper typeResearch paper 1. Introduction The emergence of technological advancements, globalization, disruptive business models and increased competition has substantially amplified the complexities and uncertainties of businesses (Grant, 2003; Burton, 2013; Haarhaus and Liening, 2020). The world has further witnessed significant environmental and supply chain challenges aggravated by the uncertainties associated with the COVID-19 pandemic (Dai et al., 2018; Ivanov, 2021). Environmental uncertainty (EU), explained as an inability of an organization to predict future events or determine the results of an action (Hernandez and Kreye, 2021; Pennings, 1975), encourages firms to build strategic flexibility (SF) in their processes (Zhou and Wu, 2010; Miroshnychenko et al., 2021) and develop business strategy integration (BSI) (Swink et al., 2005) for responding to these unprecedented changes in the environment. SF argues that firms commit superior resources to enhance their ability minimize the impact of environmental changes, and promptly act when there is a need to halt or reverse these resource commitments (Shimizu and Hitt, 2004; Haarhaus and Liening, 2020). SF has become an area of importance in supply chain as it is referred to as a dynamic capability that firms develop to respond to the uncertainties in the environment (Sanchez, 1995). Further, the developments and changes in supply chain-related processes associated with SF are supplemented by appropriate decision-making structure, communication channels and alignment among various business functions– referred to as BSI (Donaldson, 2001; Prajogo et al., 2017). BSI is the intra-organizational interaction that makes its objectives consistent with internal and external requirements (Swink et al., 2005). The effectiveness of the business strategy is characterized by the synchronization of crucial decision areas in an organization such as production, marketing and product development. The extent to which firms establish this synchronization depends upon the degree to which actions taken in one business area are aligned with the other business areas (Miles et al., 1978; Miller and Friesen, 1978). The integration of one functional unit with other functions has been identified as a means to achieve strategic nexus (Wheelwright, 1984). The roles of SF and BSI are entrenched in supply chain literature as dynamic capabilities concerning changes in product design, developing supply chain agility, enhancing logistics management, encouraging innovation, inter-departmental coordination and value creation across different functions (Sanchez, 2004; Chen et al., 2007; Vickery et al., 2013; Umam and Sommanawat, 2019). Despite the significance of SF and BSI as the core dynamic capabilities of the firms in today’s turbulent era, there is hardly any research that examines the role of SF and BSI as a response to EU and an enabler of performance. Building flexibility in supply chain operations and developing strategy integration enhance firms ’ abilities to coordinate their supply chain activities under turbulent technological, market and competitive situations ( Li et al., 2019; Dubey et al., 2019; Srinivasan and Swink, 2018) that may result in improved performance. Supply chain coordination (SCC) is the degree to which a firm share resources, information and develop alignment in its processes with key supply chain members such as customers and suppliers (Yu et al., 2007; Sreedevi and Saranga, 2017; Ivanov et al., 2018). Extending the discussion on the ways firms handle EU, current literature has studied the role of SF (Prajogo et al., 2017; Ouakouak and Ammar, 2015) and BSI (J€uttner et al., 2010; Swink et al., 2005) toward firm performance and some broader supply chain strategies, and strategic and logistics relationships in silos. Similarly, empirical studies, though limited in this stream, have proposed that BSI helps firm strengthen their supply chain capabilities and processes such as supply chain responsiveness, supply chain integration and supply chain agility (Yusuf et al., 2004; Rajaguru and Matanda, 2013; Brusset and Teller, 2017). Yet, the turbulence in the environment warrants the need to study the impact of SF and BSI on SCC as there is a lack of understanding of the empirical role of SF and BSI toward SCC that improves operational performance. Based on this gap, the first research question, this study intends to answer is, RQ1. What is the impact of SF and BSI on SCC under EU that drive performance? The resource-based view of firm contends that firms make use of superior resources to develop capabilities either as a reaction to uncertainty or as a proactive approach to exploit opportunities (Jajja et al., 2018) that help the firms to achieve competitive advantage (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000). Further, the notion of resources is not confined to tangible or physical resources, in fact, the resources include knowledge, skills and know-how of key processes (Wamba-Taguimdje et al., 2020; Votto et al., 2021; ur Rehman et al., 2022) that result in either resource-driven or process-driven IJOPM 43,6 918 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijopm/article-pdf/43/6/916/975321/ijopm-11-2021-0708.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 capabilities. Firms address environmental rigor by configuration, reconfiguration and integration of resources that drive positive performance (Teece et al., 1997). We contend SF and BSI as resource-driven dynamic capabilities that lead SCC, a process-driven dynamic capability, to achieve superior performance and enhanced competitive advantage. 2.2 Contingency theory Contingency theory emphasizes the impo rtance of situational factors in the way organizations are managed and questions the existence of a single best way to manage or organize a corporation (Tosi and Slocum, 1984; Donaldson, 2001). Firms develop and use appropriate strategies, such as integration, flexibility, contextual and structured strategies based on the characteristics of the situation (Burns, 1961; Chang et al., 2015). In the supply chain context, the literature has provided evidence of inferior firm performance resulting due to mismatch between structural dimensions, strategic approaches and environmental characteristics (Fisher, 1997; Randall et al., 2002). Using contingency theory as a lens toward theoretical development, we also argue that the degree of formalization and connectedness affects the ability of firms to develop dynamic capabilities of SF and BSI as key responses toward EU. 2.3 Environmental uncertainty, business strategy integration and strategic flexibility Environmental uncertainties are characterized by a change in technologies, variations in customers’preferences (Dess and Beard, 1984) and increased competition (Werner et al., 1996). Technological context refers to the unpredictable and rapid change in technology and is considered an essential factor to determine EU (Jaworski and Kohli, 1993; Im and Workman, 2004). Similarly, market context explains the degree to which customer preferences changes in terms of new product and service demands (Jansen et al., 2009). Also, it refers to the overall growth in the market in terms of increased demand for goods and services. Competition refers to the number of organizations competing in the same industry. A higher level of competition indicates a high degree of uncertainty in the environment as competitors continuously focus on low-price strategies and new competitive moves (Menguc and Auh, 2008). Prior studies have revealed that environmental uncertainties affect the business strategy deployment and alignment of firms’ operations (Tjahjadi, 2011; K€oseoglu et al., 2013). Grounded in DCV, the firms build integration capabilities at their functional level strategies triggered by degree of EU they are exposed to because a fit is required between environment and strategy for firms to stay competitive (Miles et al., 1978; Defee and Stank, 2005). The conceptualization of strategy integration has been argued at the business unit level (Dedinak et al., 2003; Hong et al., 2015) and functional level (Moenaert et al., 1994; Gatignon and Xuereb, 1997 ; Troy et al., 2008). There is dearth of literature that precisely defines the concept of BSI. For the purpose of this study, we define BSI as an“inter-departmental effort to align functional strategies such as marketing, production, procurement, and research and development to achieve organizational objectives. ” Bauer (2001) assessed the role of technological advancements toward business functional integration such as research and development, marketing, pr oduct development and production. It is argued that technological turbulences compel business organizations to align and integrate their strategies at the functional level (Silvius, 2013). Rapid changes in market and customer demands also push organizations to enhance their product development capabilities. The continuous emergence of knowledge from the market drives organizations to share information about customers, suppliers and competitors to adjust to any anticipated change and serve the market better. To achieve quality, cost, delivery and positioning competitiveness, firms need to integrate business functions through effective coordination and knowledge sharing. A fit is required among firms’strategy, structure and performance (Defee and Stank, 2005). Drawing on contingency theory, we study the effect of two structural constructs as moderators, i.e. connectedness and formalization on the relationships of EU→BSI and EU→SF, respectively. Firms need to exhibit connectedness to stay competitive (Kao et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2020) because connectedness enhances the firms’ ability to share information, develop functional level liaises and support collective decisionmaking. Our results showed that connectedness positively moderates the relationship between EU and BSI which means the firm will be able to enhance its BSI when faced with EU if information flows are not restricted, and departmental managers can openly communicate with each other. Similarly, we also checked for the negative moderation effect of formalization on the relationship between EU→ SF. We argue that the higher the degree of formalization in a firm’s operations, the lesser would be their ability to develop SF when encountered with EU. It is argued that firms’strategies become rigid when there exists a high degree of formalization among intra-organizational relationships (Lichtarski et al., 2019). Reed and Blunsdon (1998) developed a typology highlighting that organizations’SF is contingent upon rule-governed and formalized mechanisms. Our result empirically supports this argument by signifying the negative moderation of formalization between EU and SF. 5.5 Theoretical implications EU has become an issue of importance among supply chain scholars (Lee, 2002; Prater, 2005; Moscoso et al., 2010; Wang, 2018) as it has strong implications for supply chain risk, business strategy and firm performance (Wang, 2018). Simangunsong et al. (2012) have identified various strategies, such as flexibility, collaboration, structural redesign and configuration, used by companies for reducing and coping with uncertainty. The impact of such strategies on firm performance has been measured empirically to some extent (Yusuf et al., 2004; Rajaguru and Matanda, 2013; Brusset and Teller, 2017). Also, other studies elaborate on the role of EU toward BSI and SF (Ashenbaum et al., 2020; Haarhaus and Liening, 2020; Huang et al., 2020), but what is missing is a clear articulation of BSI and SF as a response toward EU and an enabler of SCC. Further, our results divulge that SCC fully mediates the relationship between BSI and firm performance. Developing functional integration at the strategy level will not help in improved performance unless these strategies are aligned with supplier and customer coordination. Integration and coordination can be seen as dynamic capabilities that will help managers enhance operational performance. From a managerial point of view, these findings may not come as a surprise; however, previous studies have not integrated such strategic and supply chain level factors toward enhanced performance. We provide an overarching view to the managers and business decisionmakers to line up their resource-driven and process-driven dynamic capabilities with the degree of change in environmental factors such as technology, competition and the market. The emergence of online business activities and changes in the ways firm manage their supply chains contain ample evidence of SF and BSI. Additionally, there is a need to consider the organizational factors by managers to ensure that developing strategy-level integration and flexibility will help them achieve the desired level of coordination among supply chain partners. 6. Conclusion and future research directions This paper uses DCV to argue for the relationship between EU, BSI, SF, SCC and firm operational performance. We argue that firms try to integrate their functional-level business strategies and build SF when faced with uncertainty in technological, competition and market contexts. These strategic level efforts enhance SCC of firms in terms of integration and collaboration among suppliers and customers that drive superior firm performance. Our study revealed exciting insights. Based on the data from the third CINet survey from 356 companies in eleven countries, our findings show that EU significantly sensitizes the firms to develop BSI and SF. These strategic efforts significantly drive SCC and firm performance. Our mediation analyses unearth interesting insights into the relationship between EU, strategy integration, SF and SCC. We also tested for the moderation of organizational level variables such as connectedness and formalization on the relationship between EU– strategy integration and EU– SF. Though measurement and structural models were ensured to be rigorous, we do acknowledge a few limitations. We draw the sample from the CINet survey that restricts the data under a limited number of industries, so our results can only be generalized to those industries. Further, the data regarding the total number of companies contacted in eleven countries was not available, thus response rate cannot be determined for the purpose of this study. Sodhi Bayes Business School, City University London, London, UK Abstract Purpose – This study aims to answer the question: What dynamic capabilities do diverse humanitarian organizations have? Design/methodology/approach – We examine this question through the lens of dynamic capabilities with sensing, seizing and reconfiguring capacities. The research team interviewed 15 individuals from 12 humanitarian organizations that had (a) different geographic scopes (global versus local) and (b) different missions (emergency response versus long-term development aid). We also gathered data from secondary sources, including standard operating procedures, company websites, and news databases (Factiva, Reuters and Bloomberg). Findings – The findings identify the operational and dynamic capabilities of global and local humanitarian organizations while distinguishing between their mission to provide long-term development aid or emergency relief. (1) The global organizations, with their beneficiary responsiveness, reconfigured their sensing and seizing capacities throughout the COVID-19 pandemic by pivoting quickly to local procurement or regional supply chains. The long-term development organizations pivoted to multi-year supplier agreements with fixed pricing to counter price uncertainty and accessed social capital with government bodies. In contrast, emergency response organizations developed end-to-end supply chain visibility to sense changes in supply and demand. (2) Local humanitarian organizations developed the capacity to sense demand and supply changes to reconfigure based on their experiential learning working with the local community. The long-termdevelopment local organizations used un-owned and scalable relief infrastructure to seize opportunities to rebuild affected areas. In contrast, emergency response organizations developed their capacity to seize opportunities to provide aid stemming from their decentralized decision-making, a lack of structured procedures, and the authority for increased expenditure. Originality/value – We propose a theoretical framework to identify humanitarian organizations’operational and dynamic capabilities, distinguishing between global and local organizations and their emergency response and long-term aid missions.
