Underlying theory 2.1 Dynamic capabilities The resource-based view (RBV) is used extensively as a theoretical lens to understand heterogeneity in firm performance ( Vanpoucke et al.,2 0 1 4). The RBV explains how organizations can bundle and deploy valuable, rare, inimitable and non-imitable (VRIN) resources to achieve competitive advantage ( Barney, 2001). However, maintaining a competitive advantage is challenging in highly dynamic environments (Helfat and Winter, 2011; Vanpoucke et al.,2 0 1 4; Zott, 2003). The dynamic capabilities view complements the RBV by explaining how firms integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external competencies to respond effectively to rapidly changing environments ( Teece, 2007). Dynamic capabilities differ from operational capabilities because they guide the evolution of how firms achieve competitive survival in turbulent environments, going above and beyond the standard operating procedures that maintain the status quo (Vanpoucke et al.,2 0 1 4; Zollo and Winter, 2002). Operational capabilities refer to organizations’abilities to“make a living” and maintain the status quo in the short term (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000; Winter, 2003). The impact of dynamic capabilities on a firm’s performance is indirect, shaped by transforming operational capabilities and the bundling and deployment of VRIN resources (Zott, 2003; Helfat and Peteraf, 2009). Some commonly cited examples of dynamic capabilities are a firm’s ability to develop innovative products (Winter, 2003) and successfully carry out mergers and acquisitions (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000). In operations and SCM, the use of dynamic capabilities as a theoretical lens (Aslam et al., 2018) aids our understanding of how firms achieve supplier integration capabilities ( Vanpoucke et al. ,2 0 1 4), continuous improvement capabilities (Anand et al., 2009), and strategic flexibility (Kortmann et al., 2014). Dynamic capabilities comprise threefold capacities: (1) to sense and shape opportunities and threats, (2) to seize opportunities and (3) to enhance, combine, protect and reconfigure the enterprise’s resources (Teece, 2007). We must also be mindful of whether the capabilities are operational for day-to-day business or truly dynamic in response to external threats or changes. 2.1.1 Sensing. An organization’s “sensing” capacity enables it to scan the business environment continually to identify opportunities and threats (Teece, 2007). Studies on the sensing capacities are typically related to how for-profit firms use deliberative learning strategies and knowledge-management techniques to sense (and shape) market opportunities and enhance a firm’s competitive advantage (Anand et al., 2009; Schilke et al., 2018; Zollo and Winter, 2002). Like for-profit firms, humanitarian organizations need to sense threats and opportunities when faced with severe supply and demand shocks. In a supply chain risk context,“sensing”refers to an organization’s capacity to regularly monitor vulnerabilities and threats of disruptions in its supply chain (Ambulkar et al., 2015), Dynamic capabilities in humanitarian ops 3 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijopm/article-pdf/45/1/1/9696550/ijopm-12-2022-0778.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 with visibility across the various parts of the supply chain as a critical capability (Christopher and Peck, 2004). Organizations can achieve visibility by using information technology to gather real-time information on the location of supplies, labor, and supply chain assets (Tukamuhabwa et al., 2015). During continuous long-term supply and demand disruptions, such as those seen during the COVID-19 pandemic, organizations seek to enhance visibility in their supply chains by involving a range of supply chain actors in collective sense-making to assess the nature and severity of disruptive events (Johnson et al., 2013; Krause et al., 2007; Olcott and Oliver, 2014). 2.1.2 Seizing. A “seizing” capacity allows a firm to act quickly on the identified opportunities and threats (Teece, 2007). In terms of supply chain risk, a seizing capacity responds to impending threats to the smooth flow of materials and services across each tier of the supply chain (Chowdhury and Quaddus, 2017) by establishing new redundancies and preparing to use pre-established redundancies such as backup suppliers (Lomi and Pattison, 2006 ; Sheffi and Rice, 2005 ), just-in-case inventory and excess capacity (Christopher and Peck, 2004 ; Tukamuhabwa et al.,2 0 1 5). Seizing capacity can be operational or dynamic. As an operational capability, redundancy absorbs low-level demand and supply risk from normal day-to-day operations by acting as a buffer to absorb shocks (Lomi and Pattison, 2006; Sheffi and Rice, 2005; Chopra and Sodhi, 2004). However, supply chain responsiveness is adynamic capability (Chopra et al., 2021; Sodhi and Tang, 2021; Chopra and Sodhi, 2004; Upton, 1995). Acting quickly in response to a sensed disruption in the supply chain often requires flexibility and redundancy through wellpositioned inventory at various tiers. Organizations can extend flexibility across the supply chain by swapping production volumes between regional manufacturing hubs, postponement strategies, and rapidly switching make-buy decisions (Brusset and Teller, 2017; Tukamuhabwa et al., 2015). Organizations also needcoordination capabilities across multiple supply chain actors at short notice to best utilize flexibility and redundancies (Johnson et al., 2013; Krause et al., 2007; Mascaritolo and Holcomb, 2008; Olcott and Oliver, 2014; Scholten et al., 2014). 2.1.3 Reconfiguring. Reconfiguration refers to a firm ’s ability to recombine and reconfigure its resources and operational capabilities to respond to external change and uncertainty (Teece, 2007; Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000 ). The heightened uncertainty associated with prolonged supply chain disruptions, such as during the COVID-19 pandemic, creates ambiguity about the value and utility of existing planned responses that comprise operational capabilities and related resources (Ambulkar et al., 2015). The firm may need to redesign the supply chain for long-term disruptions ( Roscoe et al. , 2022 ). Such reconfigurations require an organizational mindset open to new ideas and working methods, including continuous improvement (Son et al., 2021) and other transformations that support the emergence of reconfiguration in the supply chain (Aslam et al., 2018). 2.2 Research gap The dynamic capability view examines how for-profit firms respond to disrupted environments, but researchers have only recently applied it to the humanitarian relief domain (Polater, 2021). The scholars who have applied a dynamic capability lens to humanitarian response have done so only to identify isolated capacities and their enablers for sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring. A handful of humanitarian supply chain studies discuss the sensing capacity, which includes demand forecasting (Tabaklar et al., 2021), dynamic perception (Gralla et al., 2016) and continual identification of operational improvement opportunities (Mishra et al., 2022). Seizing has been studied in terms of enablers such as agility (Altay et al., 2018; L’Hermitte et al., 2015), collaboration (Gabler et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2019; Mishra et al., 2022; Polater, 2021), redundancy (Tabaklar et al., 2021) and flexibility IJOPM 45,1 4 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/ijopm/article-pdf/45/1/1/9696550/ijopm-12-2022-0778.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 (Altay et al., 2018; Polater, 2021). However, thereconfiguration capacity of humanitarian organizations is rarely mentioned (Vaillancourt, 2017). Overall, there is a threefoldresearch gapthat we seek to narrow: (1) While these studies shed some light on the antecedents of sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring capacities in isolation, there is limited empirical evidence on how humanitarian organizations develop the three capacities holistically. (2) Existing humanitarian operations studies have yet to distinguish operational capabilities from dynamic ones. (3) There is no distinction between the dynamic capabilities of different types of humanitarian organizations, whether by geographical scope (local vs global) or mission (emergency response vs long-term aid). Narrowing this research gap is important because humanitarian organizations must build dynamic capabilities to operate in disrupted environments and situations of extreme uncertainty (Fikar et al., 2018). Methodology 3.1 Research design The rapid spread of COVID-19 around the globe complicated an already unpredictable operating environment for humanitarian organizations delivering emergency relief and longterm aid. At the same time, the pandemic also created a unique research opportunity to gather real-time information on how global and local humanitarian organizations respond to the same compounding crisis. Our research design is an inductive, theory-building approach using Gioia’s (2013)systematic method of concept development. We aimed to elaborate on the dynamic capabilities view by examining the context of humanitarian organizations providing long-term aid during the successive supply and demand shocks caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Within this context, we were able to isolate how global and local humanitarian organizations reconfigured their resource endowments and operational capabilities to build dynamic capabilities. Throughout the data collection and analysis process, we remained open to new and emerging concepts not yet addressed in the existing literature. We sought theoretical insights to build on the dynamic capabilities view whenever we identified novel constructs. 3.2 Data collection The study uses a multiple case study design, which allows for a comparison between organizations that share similar features (within group comparison) as well as a comparison between organizations with very different features (across group comparison) (Eisenhardt, 1989). Our sampling method was to designate organizations first according to their geographic scope – the number of countries/regions where aid is provided (global versus local), and second, by theirthematic scope or mission– the type of humanitarian relief the organization typically provides (emergency response vs long-term aid). We also collected secondary information from organizational websites and news databases (Factiva, Reuters, Bloomberg), as well as operational procedures and protocols provided by interviewees, to determine the resource endowments of the sampled organizations. Geographic scope: Geographic scope refers to a global organization providing aid to multiple countries and regions or a local organization near the epicenter of an event giving aid to victims affected by that crisis. Geographic scope was considered an essential criterion in case selection because it correlates with resource availability and scarcity (Shaheen et al., 2022). Findings Analyzing primary data helped us identify the organizations’ operational and dynamic capabilities using the 23 2 categorization of global and local humanitarian organizations with long-term development or emergency response missions. A capability was categorized as operational if it enabled an organization to carry out its core relief activities– emergency response or long-term development– in an operating environment with relatively predictable supply and demand. Analysis of the interview data also provided insights into when a capability could be considered dynamic. Interviewees explained how their organization required additional and new capabilities to manage the severe disruptions caused to the supply of medicines and materials and to address the surges in demand seen during the first and second waves of COVID-19. These capabilities were categorized as dynamic when deployed to manage highly unpredictable swings in supply and demand, above and beyond what was required to manage the changing daily field operations. We also used secondary data to identify the resource endowments. For many of the organizations in our study, demand surges and supply disruptions during the first two waves of the pandemic went well beyond disruptions experienced in day-to-day operations, rendering existing operational capabilities insufficient. By exploring their responses, we could examine their dynamic capabilities, described below, in terms of sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring capacities. 4.1 Global humanitarian organizations The global organizations in our sample – with differences between long-term aid and emergency response organizations– had the sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring dynamic capabilities described below, along with the underlying operational capabilities and resource endowments. 4.1.1 Sensing: implementing end-to-end supply chain surveillance systems (emergency response). We saw a clear link between a global organization’s level of supply chain visibility and how it responded to COVID-19-related supply chain disruptions. Emergency response organizations prioritized end-to-end supply chain visibility and real-time monitoring of their staff and supplies. These organizations quickly increased supply chain surveillance efforts as early as February 2020. Despite having robust IT systems and extensive networks of field operators raising alarms, long-term development organizations took significantly longer to set up their supply chain surveillance systems, typically after the second wave of the pandemic, thus curbing their sensing capacity. During the first wave of the pandemic, development organizations prioritized setting up long-term agreements (LTA) with multiple suppliers, which forecasted but did not require the relief items to be purchased annually with the agreed price per item. Importantly, these contracts did not include a commitment to buy, only a longterm guarantee on price. Long-term development organizations thus gained sensing capacity as they had visibility of the supplier’s available stock and a pre-agreed price for products, even when markets fluctuated wildly. An interviewee from UNICEF Middle East/North Africa (MENA) explained how these pre-agreed contracts proved extremely useful during the first wave of the pandemic when prices for personal protective equipment (PPE) skyrocketed on global markets: We may have signed LTAs with ten suppliers for masks, but we only buy from one. At least with LTAs, we know they have enough products, and at the fixed price we agreed, they can produce the needed amounts of products for us. (UNICEF MENA) Similarly, an interviewee from Care International explained that maintaining a pool of preapproved backup suppliers helped to maintain supply continuity during the initial stages of the pandemic: We are now trying to assign as many LTAs as possible with our suppliers. Ensuring the quality of the items and signing the LTA doesn’t mean we have to buy from them, but at least LTAs set a standard, so if the supplier meets the standards, we can buy from them. Under the United Nations umbrella, organizations pooled their PPE stocks and other COVID-19-related medical and relief supplies as strategic buffers in UN Humanitarian Response Depots (UNHRD) in regional hubs worldwide. The WFP manages these depots for all UN agencies, serving 86 partners, including government and non-governmental organizations (NGOs). An interviewee from WFP Africa explained the importance of the hubs during the initial COVID19 wave in early 2020: It was challenging initially, but we have UNHRD, our savior, as it had all the emergency stocks we needed. (WFP Africa). Emergency response organizations such as MSF deployed rapid response kits to regional hubs worldwide, including water and sanitation equipment, tarps, rope and medicines. An interviewee at MSF explained how his organization pre-positioned rapid response kits in Jordan to deliver supplies to disaster zones around the Middle East quickly. It is difficult to forecast all the needs accurately, so we pre-position critical items before natural disasters and humanitarian crises and forecast based on experience. It is not always 100% accurate, but we try our best to pre-position critical materials inventory near the locations we consider strategic. At the end of the pandemic, we learned that it’s all about pre-positioning critical material! This is something that we could have done better at the beginning. (MSF) By pre-positioning rapid response kits, emergency relief organizations did not have to purchase goods on international markets, thereby avoiding the supply shortages, excessive price hikes and currency fluctuations seen during the initial waves of the pandemic. The global organizations in our study had IT systems of varying degrees of sophistication in place before the first wave of the pandemic. The WHO, WFP and ACF had made significant investments in enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems that provided visibility of the movement of staff and supplies to in-country distribution hubs. Other global organizations, such as M/C19edecins Sans Fronti/C18eres (MSF), used SAP-enabled systems to track stock from global suppliers to their distribution centers located around the globe. With IT infrastructure, these global organizations could manage standard operational deployments of materials and staff to disaster zones. An interviewee at ACF Middle East explained the level of visibility provided by their ERP systems as follows: We have a supply chain ERP system. This system records, monitors, and shows all the steps and possible actions. Nothing can be done without including all the data and the decision process inside the system. Future studies should examine more humanitarian organizations to further build theory and test it. The scope of the studies needs to be widened, too. An important aspect is preparation. Existing frameworks for managing risk in humanitarian settings focus on the capabilities for managing the aftermath of a particular disaster (Jahre, 2017; Shaheen et al., 2021) rather than preparing for future disasters. The need for preparation is not just for rapid onslaught disasters like earthquakes but also for those foreseen or already unfolding, as with long-term crises. For example, the UNRWA’s Commissioner-General, Philippe Lazzarini, notes that“the plight of Palestine refugees remains the longest unresolved refugee crisis in the world”(UN, 2023), with 700,000 Palestinians permanently displaced in 1948 and another 2 million displaced in 2023 with little hope of settlement anywhere. We also face the almost certain permanent displacement of millions of people in low-lying areas caused by rising ocean waters in the coming years (as of writing) as the ice caps continue to melt. Researchers need to study how national and supranational humanitarian organizations (and countries) develop the three capacities to respond to such impending disasters with high certainty, longevity and impact, in contrast to those with high uncertainty. Our work has implications for extending the dynamic-capabilities view, which focuses on profit-seeking organizations. Sensing, seizing and reconfiguring apply to profit-making organizations for which the dynamic-capabilities view seeks to develop a competitive advantage in line with RBV. The implication of our work is not only how these commercial organizations develop these capacities buthow the development of these capacitiesdepends on the nature of the organization. So, we need to identify the features of commercial organizations for classification just as we have the geographic scope and mission of humanitarian organizations. Moreover, rather than a focus on competitive advantage for profit-seeking organizations, perhaps RBV and dynamics capability literature need a more general view of the organization and its purpose to subsume humanitarian and commercial organizations, possibly using the notion of hybrid organizations and supply chains in development settings (Sodhi and Knuckles, 2021). Another implication is understanding the essential– and potentially narrow– difference between profit-seeking and humanitarian organizations regarding dynamic capabilities. Instead of profit-seeking organizations developing dynamic capabilities to seek competitive advantage in turbulent environments (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000), our work shows that humanitarian organizations do so to seek the continuity of supply to beneficiaries during compounding crises. The resources and operational capabilities may be identical in both commercial and humanitarian organizations. For instance, flexible decision-making structures and localized procurement can help maintain supply, benefiting from local knowledge, regardless of whether the organization seeks profits or humanitarian relief. Yet, theraison d’^etre for commercial organizations differs fundamentally from humanitarian ones. 5.3 Managerial implications Managers of humanitarian organizations can apply our frameworks to identify critical resources and operational capabilities needed to support dynamic capability development depending on their organization’s geographic scope and mission. Contingency planning is limited against rare and high-impact events such as the COVID-19 pandemic because of high uncertainty, leaving the development of dynamic capabilities as the only practical means of tackling future events. Our proposed framing highlights the importance of resources and capabilities such as flat organizational structures and decision-making decentralized to local organizations during extreme supply and demand shocks. A responsiveness culture coupled with enacting emergency guidelines allows global humanitarian organizations to reconfigure their standard operating routines (and operational capabilities) during severe disruptions. Local procurement allowed these organizations to avoid currency fluctuations and extreme price hikes on international markets while enabling local businesses to stay solvent throughout the pandemic. Organizations that pivoted from global to local procurement helped build more resilient communities to withstand the subsequent supply and demand shocks that accompanied the second and third waves of the COVID-19 pandemic. To conclude, our study offers a framework showing the dynamic capabilities of different types of humanitarian organizations and how these build on the different resources and operational capabilities of the different types of such organizations. Our findings show how the geographic (global versus local) and the thematic scope ofhumanitarian operations (emergency response versus long-term development)lead to distinct combinations of operational and dynamic capabilities. Future studies can provide field practitioners and their organizations with more comprehensive frameworks to prepare for future disasters and disruptions by better understanding the mechanisms by which humanitarian organizations develop and deploy dynamic capabilities. A dynamic capability perspective on the impact of big data analytics and enterprise architecture on innovation: an empirical study Sunil Pathak NCDOE, SVKM’s Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies Deemed to be University, Mumbai, India and Information Technology and Systems Area, Indian Institute of Management Kashipur, Kashipur, India, and Venkataraghavan Krishnaswamy and Mayank Sharma Information Technology and Systems Area, Indian Institute of Management Kashipur, Kashipur, India Abstract Purpose – The prevailing conceptualization of information system (IS) capabilities, rooted in the resourcebased view (RBV) framework, tends to focus on unique firm resources. In the digital age, as emphasized by dynamic capabilities (DC), resource reconfiguration is critical in maintaining strategic advantage. This paper focuses on big data analytics capabilities (BDAC) from a DC perspective to present a novel conceptualization of BDAC–DC. We examine its effects on product, business model and business process innovation, including the effects of enterprise architecture (EA) on the BDAC business model innovation relationship. Design/methodology/approach – This research presents a novel DC-based BDAC conceptualization, operationalized as a hierarchical construct. A survey-based approach is used for data collection and data analysis is done using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings – The novel conceptualization and the effects of BDAC DC on BDA sensing-seizing and reconfiguration capacities support BDAC’s functional and evolutionary roleplay. Empirical results confirm the positive effects of BDAC–DC on first-order value targets (innovation) and the moderating effects of EA. Research limitations/implications – The novel BDAC–DC conceptualization has several implications for BDAC, DC, EA and business value research. Practicing managers must adopt a multifaceted approach to BDAC development by considering non-technical and organizational factors, collaborate with their business counterparts to explore unique big data ideas, initiate proof-of-concept projects to secure support and allocate resources synchronously, considering a multidimensional view of the process, product and business model innovation. Practical implications – Practicing managers must adopt a multifaceted approach to BDAC development by considering non-technical and organizational factors, collaborate with their business counterparts to explore unique big data ideas, initiate proof-of-concept projects to secure support and allocate resources synchronously, considering a multidimensional view of the process, product and business model innovation for synergistic outcomes. Originality/value – To the best of our knowledge, this research is the first attempt toward DC-based BDAC conceptualization, empirical validation of first-order effects on various forms of innovation and the oftenoverlooked role of critical EA capability. Despite substantial investment in big data capabilities, numerous initiatives face challenges in realizing their intended business benefits (Andrew, 2019). Big data capability such as BDAC is the firm’s ability to leverage big data created by people, tools, and machines to gain strategic and operational insights on its consumers, products, and performance (Akter et al., 2016; Kiron, 2014). The conceptualization of BDAC in extant research is centered around the resource-based view (RBV) theory (Barney, 1991) and IS capabilities (Bharadwaj, 2000). RBV based conceptualization of BDAC presents few challenges in dynamic business contexts. First, the RBV viewpoint posits that firms gain strategic advantage by exploiting VRIN (valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable) resources. In dynamic business contexts, competitive advantage and resource uniqueness is often temporary. Further, RBV focusses on mere existence of resources and fails to explain how firms adapt and change to create new resources and capabilities, a fundamental requirement in dynamic business contexts. Second, from a capability standpoint, BDAC is often regarded as a typical IS capability that carries out information processing function (Pathak et al., 2021), thus reducing it to a functional role. While the strategic and transformation role of BDAC is widely acknowledged (Garmaki et al., 2023; Statista, 2023), especially in dynamic business contexts, RBV-based functional perspective is limiting. Bharadwaj et al. (2013) note that the data and information-centric business ecosystems have hastened the need for the information systems (IS) strategy to shed its functional role in favor of strategic role by leveraging digital resources (such as data) to create differential value. In this context, the dynamic capability framework (DCF) (Teece et al., 1997) offers a promising lens to investigate IS-centric digital capabilities such as BDAC. DCF, as an extension of RBV (Barney, 1991), emphasizes on managerial processes, continuous innovation, adaptation, and reconfiguration of resources in response to changing business environments, where flexibility and adaptability are critical to long-term success. While the importance of newage technology capabilities such as BDAC and AI, often termed as GPTs in the DCF context, has been highlighted (Teece, 2018), more work is needed from a DC perspective (Vartiainen and Hansen, 2019). Despite their relevance, DCs face criticism due to abstract nature, identification of underlying micro-foundations (Easterby-Smith et al., 2009), and lack of empirical validation. Further, technology-driven capabilities such as BDAC are essential across various business functions, their widespread application often leads to accountability and management challenges, potentially compromising desired outcomes (The Open Group, 2018). Although Enterprise Architecture (EA) is designed to provide a framework for addressing these issues by defining an organization’s current and future states (Ross et al., 2006), the specific role of EA in optimizing BDAC outcomes remains underexplored. The above research gaps can be summarized as (1) Lack of DC-based conceptualization of BDAC, (2) Lack of an integrative BDAC perspective covering BDAC’s functional and evolutionary role-play, (3) empirical validation of BDAC-DC and its effects on business value, (4) the role of EA. We address these gaps by proposing a DC-based framing of the BDAC, and by examining the path to business value through BDA sensing, seizing, and reconfiguration capacities, and by investigating the role of EA use (EAUse). In doing so, we address the following research questions: (1) How do firms create business value from BDAC DC? (2) What is the relationship between BDAC DC and various forms of innovation? (3) How do BDAC DC and EA capability affect indirect business value? The next section covers literature review, followed by hypothesis and model development. Literature review 2.1 BDAC BDAC research is an emerging and vibrant research field within the larger IS capabilities research. Initial works by Chen and Zhang (2014) and Davenport (2012) called for a focus on BDAC phenomena to expand the research agenda. BDAC’s conceptualization by scholars such as Wamba et al. (2017), Wang et al. (2018), Akter et al. (2016), Gupta and George (2016) paved way for BDAC investigation and its effects on firm performance. BDAC research, like other IS capabilities, is heavily influenced by RBV, and recent studies, following RBV logic, position BDAC as a functional capability (Pathak et al., 2021). In line with IS capabilities research, many authors have focused on its effects on direct performance relationships at firm and process levels (Garmaki et al., 2023) primarily focusing on firm performance (Wamba et al., 2017); supply chain performance (Cetindamar et al., 2021), manufacturing performance (Dubey et al., 2018), innovation, and strategic value (Mikalef et al., 2019, 2020). Torres et al. (2018) consider BDAC as a DC, albeit with limited research scope. 2.2 Dynamic capabilities DC is defined as an organizational capability that enables a firm to efficiently integrate, construct, and reconfigure its internal and external capabilities in response to the rapid changes in its business environment (Teece et al., 1997). DCs pertain to the firm’s processes for the assimilation, reconfiguration, acquisition, and deployment of resources (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000), a set of operational activities through which the firm generates and adjusts its operational routines (Zollo and Winter, 2002), and the ability to generate, extend, or modify its resource base (Helfat and Peteraf, 2009). Literature identifies three categories of DCs: (1) specific DCs, such as marketing, supply chain, and technology; (2) generic DCs, such as coordination, knowledge-based, and learning (Ba � ıa and Ferreira, 2024); and (3) dual-purpose DCs (Helfat and Winter, 2011). Beyond their direct effects, DCs influence change, agility, and innovation (Ba � ıa and Ferreira, 2024). Despite recent investigations into BDAC’s influence on strategy, learning, agility, and innovation, it is predominantly viewed as an IS functional capability grounded in RBV (Pathak et al., 2021). The call for inclusion of DC perspective in BDAC research is growing (Garmaki et al., 2023), including investigating indirect value-creation mechanisms and first-order effects (Grover et al., 2018; Steininger et al., 2022) underscoring a significant research void. 2.2.1 Functional and evolutionary fitness. The DC literature highlights two key capability dimensions of (1) functional fitness, focused on “doing things right,” and (2) evolutionary fitness, centered around “doing the right things” (Teece, 2014). Functional or ordinary capabilities focus on functional fitness and comprise personnel, technology infrastructure, management skills, and coordination to drive task excellence. In the BDAC context, generic IS infrastructure falls short of handling diverse data sources, requiring specific BDA resources to address the big data challenges. These resources lack VRIN properties and can be easily acquired through consultancy, hiring, or training (Teece, 2014). In rapidly changing business landscape characterized by shifting market dynamics, customer preferences, and product demands, companies must continuously acquire new knowledge and adapt their capabilities to remain competitive. The “data as strategy” and “data as industry” perspectives (Mazzei and Noble, 2017) emphasize the evolutionary fitness perspectives, highlighting the importance of evolving capabilities in response to changing environments. Innovation, generates strategic value by transforming products, processes, and business models. In response to this requirement, BDAC serves the dual role of information processing (functional) and business change (evolutionary) (Helfat and Peteraf, 2009) as demonstrated by companies such as Amazon, Netflix, and Google. Despite substantial investments in BDAC development (Andrew, 2019), two critical issues persist. First, advanced digital capabilities such as BDAC manifest value differently (Schryen, 2013), and authors call for a focus on intermediate outcomes, which are valid proxies for business value creation (Grover et al., 2018). While some studies have examined indirect measures such as agility and innovation in BDAC (Mikalef et al., 2019), further research is necessary (Grover et al., 2018). Second, given the low success rates of analytic projects (Andrew, 2019), alternative perspectives such as DCF with a focus on microfoundations, examining effects through indirect and first-order effects, and value linkages are crucial for understanding business value creation (Ba � ıa and Ferreira, 2024). Finally, from business value standpoint, innovation serves as a proxy for BDAC value creation, generating both first-order and second-order effects (Grover et al., 2018; Vial, 2019; Steininger et al., 2022). First-order effects, such as cost leadership, market expansion, and revenue growth, stem from innovation’s impact business processes, product/services and business models. In this context, innovation literature suggests two perspectives: (1) innovation process or capability (Markides, 1998) and (2) specific value outcomes, such as products, business process innovation. 2.3.1 Product and service innovation. Product and service innovations (PSI) describe how a firm changes its product or service offerings to meet user requirements. Since PSIs are market and customer-driven (Utterback and Abernathy, 1975), they provide strategic value by supporting a differentiation strategy to achieve superior product performance (Butler, 1988). Digital imperatives demand servitization, enabling firms to shift from traditional product-centric models to product-service-oriented approaches, creating smarter, connected products that deliver greater value to customers (Paiola and Gebauer, 2020). Information and knowledge for PSI can come from customer data, product/service feedback, buying behavior, user-generated reviews, and competitor product information from various digital channels. Often, this information results in new data-based products (e.g. Nike’s data-driven fitness service), monetization/trading of data (Google/Facebook advertising revenue from network data), enhancement of customer experiences through new value propositions (e.g. the New York Times data platform to enhance readers’ engagement), or even movement into new industry contexts. 2.3.2 Business process innovation. BPI transforms a firm’s production or business processes (Damanpour and Gopalakrishnan, 2001) by changing existing processes, tools, and knowledge inputs. BPI stresses on efficiency (Utterback and Abernathy, 1975) and cost reduction (Schilling, 2020), thus requiring internal, systematic, and tacit information (Gopalakrishnan et al., 1999). Such information is often challenging to comprehend and therefore, it is difficult to imitate BPI, making it an effective approach for competitive advantage. A classic example of BPI is Amazon.com’s product review feature, which hinges on user data for product purchase suggestions to boost sales. Digital capabilities incorporate technology into existing business processes to improve business process management, and are considered crucial enablers of transformation (Annarelli et al., 2021). Further, BPI, in the digital context, involves leveraging digital technologies to facilitate servitization, enabling firms to shift from traditional product-centric models to service-oriented approaches for maximizing value creation. Product-service integration requires an intricate interplay of products, services, and business processes, suggesting that business process innovation can Journal of Enterprise Information Management 535 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/jeim/article-pdf/38/2/532/9669760/jeim-01-2024-0059.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 often drive PSI and BMI (Foss and Saebi, 2016) thus impacting value proposition, value creation, and value appropriation dimensions. 2.3.3 Business model innovation. A business model explains how a firm creates and captures value to remain competitive (Teece, 2014). BMI relates to how a business model is renewed to develop and sustain competitive advantage. BMI is defined as “designed, novel, nontrivial changes to the key elements of a firm’s business model or the architecture linking these elements” (Foss and Saebi, 2016), suggesting that BMI is an important phenomenon that needs to be independently conceptualized and theorized. From a value triad (proposition, creation and capture) perspective, BMI positively impacts value creation, value appropriation, or value delivery aspects to transform a firm’s value proposition. It differs from PSI and BPI as it is a complementary form of innovation for building competitive advantage and reshaping the industry (Zott and Amit, 2007). As a better business model often beats a better technology (Chesbrough, 2007), the role of BMI becomes critical. Digital capabilities such as BDAC are argued to play a positive effect on BMI (Xie et al., 2022). 2.3.4 Enterprise architecture. EA, according to the eGovernment Act of 2002 (Public Law (PL) 107–347), is defined as “(A) means- (1) a strategic information asset base, which defines the mission; (2) the information necessary to perform the mission; (3) the technologies necessary to perform the mission; and (4) the transitional processes for implementing new technologies in response to changing needs; and (B) includes- (1) a baseline architecture; (2) a target architecture; and (3) a sequencing plan” (Hagan, 2004). EA is a high-level model of the entire organization (Lankhorst, 2013; Ross et al., 2006) that covers strategy, processes, information systems, applications, and technology and is practiced as EA frameworks (EAFs). The notable EAFs within the IS domain include the Zachman framework, the Open Group Architecture Framework (TOGAF) (The Open Group, 2018), and the Department of Defense Architecture Framework (DoDAF). Though prevalent in industry, EA has received limited attention in research. Romero and Vernadat (2016) advocate for further research into EA’s contribution to enterprise and digital transformation initiatives. 3. Model development The DC literature highlights two key capability dimensions of (1) functional fitness, focused on “doing things right,” and (2) evolutionary fitness, centered around “doing the right things” (Teece, 2014). This research conceptualizes BDAC as a DC encompassing functional and evolutionary fitness perspectives using DCF micro-foundations (Teece, 2007). DCs can be broken down into sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring capacities (Teece, 2007). Sensing refers to identifying and assessing opportunities to capture value related to customers, competitors, processes, and products (Day, 1994). Seizing focuses on resource mobilization to capitalize on identified opportunities, and included design, planning, and development activities. Reconfiguration capacity is the ability to recombine and reconfigure resources, to exploit seized opportunities. In BDAC context, we define BDA sensing, seizing (BDA-SS) as the capacity to learn, process, and analyze information about customers, competitors, methods, and products from internal and external sources to sense and seize new opportunities using BDA. Similarly, BDA reconfiguration (BDA-RECNFG) is defined as the capacity to reconfigure capabilities by dynamically informing and updating an organization’s internal and external processes, systems, and capabilities using BDA. BDAC’s lower-order capabilities (micro-foundations) support evolutionary and functional fitness objectives, to enhance BDA sensing, seizing, and reconfiguration capacities. As for the performance impacts of BDAC, it is argued that firms make strategic choices that help them seize opportunities, and each strategic choice (such as differentiation or low-cost strategy) requires intermediate mechanisms to generate value. This indirect value creation is manifested in various forms of innovation, such as PSI, BMI, and BPI. Rapidly changing environments, coupled with structural inertia and core rigidity, can deplete key competencies, causing strengths to become weaknesses. This requires sustained investment and capability renewal to maintain competitiveness. A key to exploiting innovations is reconfiguring assets and organizational structures as markets and technologies change (Teece, 2014). Research suggests that firms achieve capability reconfigurations in two ways (Girod and Whittington, 2016): (1) Capability evolution, which entails the continual refinement of specific routines. Capability substitution requires firms to evaluate their existing capabilities and decide to retain, eliminate, or acquire new ones. This is achieved through mergers, learning, joint ventures, and recruitment. Ex ante, we applied procedural remedies suggested by Podsakoff et al. (2003). These remedies included improving the questionnaire’s readability, using simple language, eliminating jargon, and providing adequate description wherever required. Ex-post, the absence of CMB was confirmed using Harman’s single-factor test. Variance for a single factor (47.7%) was less than the threshold (50%), confirming the absence of CMB. In addition, a full collinearity assessment test (Kock, 2015) using an unrelated marker variable was also conducted. The test confirmed that all VIF values of inner model constructs were less than the threshold of 2.8 (Kock, 2015), confirming the absence of CMB. 4.4 Non-response bias To minimize informant bias, early and late responses were compared to confirm invariance between early and late responders (Bethlehem, 2010). To test non-response bias, the sample was divided into two groups of early responders (first six weeks) and late responders, with 119 and 83 cases, respectively. We used MICOM (Measurement invariance of composite models) and PLS multi-group analysis (PLS-MGA) to analyze invariances between the two groups (Henseler et al., 2016; Hair et al., 2018). PLS-MGA results (Annexure 9) reported invariance in path coefficients, confirming the absence of non-response bias due to early and late responses. 5. We also analyze the effects of EAUse on BDAC-SS, BDA-RECNFG on BMI. The findings support the proposed BDAC DC fitness framework confirming the positive effects on BDAC’s functional and evolutionary capabilities on BDA-SS and BDA-RECNFG capacities. Diverging from the present-day discourse of RBV based positioning, this research is the first attempt to conceptualize BDAC as a DC, identification of BDAC DC micro-foundations, and its effects. For practitioners, the findings underscore the strategic importance of developing robust BDAC capabilities and leveraging BDAC to support agility and innovation. By conceptualizing and operationalizing BDAC as a dynamic capability, these findings not only provide a solid foundation for future BDAC research using DCF, the approach can be extended to examine other digital capabilities. Second, we focus on indirect and first order effects of BDAC(DC)instead of direct effects such as firm performance. Our findings suggest that BDAC(DC) impacts various forms of innovation except for the BDA-SS and BPI relationship. A plausible explanation for this finding is that conventionally, the sensing-seizing focus is to support growth objectives (PI, BMI) as opposed to BPI, suggesting a lack of integrated perspective of innovation targets. Consideration of an integrated perspective is critical in digital business environments. A strong effect of BDA-RECNFG (R 2 5 44.9%, f 2 5 0.154)) on BPI indirectly supports this observation. Third, the insignificant moderating effects of EAUse on the BDA-RECNFG → BMI relationship could be attributed to EA’s IT centricity, lack of business engagement, and internal focus (Dang and Pekkola, 2017). EA is often perceived as an IT-centric supporting capability for decision inputs (indicated by significant moderating effects on BDA-SS and BMI relationship) instead of changing the business architecture (absence of moderating effects on BDA-RECNFG → BMI relationship). This finding alludes to the potential challenges in EA adoption in enterprises, specifically as a business change agent. 5.3 Implications 5.3.1 Implications for research. Despite the popularity of DCF in strategy research, DC-based framing of advanced digital capabilities and their empirical validation remains nascent. Past research has typically examined BDAC as a functional capability through RBV lens and often positioned it as an antecedent to other DCs (Mikalef et al., 2019; Wamba et al., 2017). To the best of our knowledge, this research is a first attempt to model and investigate BDAC as a DC on its own and has critical implications for BDAC research. Second, it is suggested to examine the path to business value through first level effects (Steininger et al., 2022); and at the process level (Grover et al., 2018; Schryen, 2013) specifically in DC context. By adopting an indirect approach (Grover et al., 2018). to assess business value, our study uses comprehensive innovation metrics as proxies for these effects. By dissecting innovation processes, our work significantly contributes to BDAC research on business value and innovation. Third, EAF’s practical prevalence contrasts with the need for more EAF research discourse, signaling a perplexing gap in the literature. While we respond to the author’s (Grave and Kusters, 2024) call for attention on EA research, our findings on the relatively weaker effect size of BDA sensing-seizing and lack of support for BDA-RECNFG in changing business models suggests challenges around EA business engagement, technology JEIM 38,2 546 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/jeim/article-pdf/38/2/532/9669760/jeim-01-2024-0059.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 inclination. These findings highlight that BDA and EA interventions may not have uniform effects across contexts. Such nuances highlight the potential challenges inherent to EA application, specifically in relation to organizational-technology engagements. Researchers can continue to expand this perspective into the lesser-explored facets of EA to advance theoretical constructs while simultaneously enhancing the real-world applicability of EA. Finally, the proposed approach of conceptualizing and operationalizing BDAC as a DC extends its applicability beyond IS research, specifically in digital capabilities research. Our research is also a novel attempt to represent the concept of dual-purpose or integrative DC (Helfat and Winter, 2011) and IT-embedded DCs (Steininger et al., 2022). The artifacts and findings can be extended to expand the growing body of literature on digital capabilities and strategic IS research. 5.3.2 Implications for practice. Despite the strategic significance of BDA, and massive investments (Statista, 2023), in BDAC development, numerous initiatives are projected to falter due to insufficiently developed BDAC and recognition of the BDA organizational context (Andrew, 2019). Further, Sivarajah et al. (2017) suggest that firms should first recognize the BDA landscape and the context instead of investing in costly big data technologies. In response to these obstacles, managers should implement a comprehensive strategy by identifying and addressing non-technical organizational factors to address capability gaps. The approach necessitates evaluating micro-foundations and customizing strategies to align with the firm’s unique context to maximize value realization. Additionally, managers must weigh in both tangible and intangible benefits from BDAC investments, business case justification, and assessing project successes (or failures). In digital business context, PI, BPI, and BMI are interconnected, necessitating an integrated perspective to increase efficiency, revenue growth, and market expansion while avoiding the pitfalls of singular focus on one type of innovation. For instance, BPI, as a result of innovative processes, can trigger product innovations, new features, new services and support new business models with new pricing strategies or innovative delivery methods. Further, as firms move towards servitization, where the line between products and services is blurred, it is critical for managers to take an integrated and synchronous resource allocation approach for investments across all innovation dimensions. BDA and EA capabilities, are too often misconstrued as mere derivatives of established IS constructs. This oversimplification belies their distinctive strategic advantage, thereby necessitating a reevaluation. Our study underscores the imperative for a collaborative, and integrative endeavor to drive synergies between BDA, EA, and business constituents, to substantiate the latent strategic value inherent within BDAC. This research also advocates for a recalibration of EA practice towards enhancing business-centric strategies, fostering agility within development processes, and promoting an EA lexicon that is both accessible and comprehensible to stakeholders. 5.3.3 Limitations and conclusions. We acknowledge that our study has limitations, some of which open avenues for future research. First limitation is related to the generalizability of our findings. Using the proposed DC-based framing, future research can extend our work by adopting a qualitative, longitudinal approach. Second, while our sample covers diverse industries and regions to increase generalizability, several factors were omitted. Further investigation could focus on these factors, which can be governance and decision-making mechanisms (formal/informal), leadership style, culture, data quality, user engagement, training, and other related factors. Researchers can also examine the model across various sectors or industries using multigroup analysis techniques. These insights will be critical in alleviating the concerns around BDA failures (Andrew, 2019). Finally, researchers can expand on the intricate nature of the value creation process, by focusing on the second-order business benefits resulting from each innovation type or their unique combinations. Linking green intellectual capital to sustainability and sustainable business model innovation in manufacturing SMEs: the role of green dynamic capability Maqsood Ahmad and Qiang Wu Faculty of Business, School of Accounting and Finance, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Kowloon, Hong Kong, and Muhammad Sualeh Khattak Division of Business and Hospitality Management, College of Professional and Continuing Education, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Kowloon, Hong Kong Abstract Purpose – This study investigates the impact of green intellectual capital (IC) on the economic, social, and environmental sustainability performance of manufacturing small-and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Pakistan– an emerging Asian economy–and the mediating effect of sustainable business model innovation (SBMI). It also examines the moderating effect of green dynamic capability (GDC) on the relationship between green IC and SBMI. Design/methodology/approach – Data were collected through a survey completed by 324 owners and top managers of manufacturing SMEs in four Pakistani cities. A purposive and snowball sampling approach was used to gather the data. A dual-stage methodological approach (a combination of PLS-SEM and artificial neural networks) was applied to capture both linear connections and complex, hidden, nonlinear patterns between variables. Regression analysis was used to verify the results. Findings – The findings indicate that green IC positively contributes to manufacturing SMEs’ economic sustainability performance (ECSP), social sustainability performance (SSP), and environmental sustainability performance (ESP) in an emerging Asian economy. SBMI appears to mediate these relationships. Furthermore, GDC strengthens green IC’s positive effect on SBMI adoption. The artificial neural network results indicate that green human capital has the highest positive influence on ECSP and SSP, suggesting its pivotal role in achieving SMEs’ economic and social sustainability goals. However, green relational capital was identified as having the strongest effect on ESP, indicating its crucial role in driving environmental sustainability in SMEs. Originality/value – The present study is a pioneering effort because, to the best of our knowledge, green IC, SBMI, and GDC have never been systematically tested with the ECSP, SSP and ESP of manufacturing SMEs, nor has their predictive ability been analyzed in an emerging Asian economy. Second, this study divulges the mediating role of SBMI in the relationship between green IC and sustainability performance in an emerging market. Third, it adds to the literature by examining the moderating role of GDC in the link between green IC and SBMI and provides valuable insights into how green IC and GDC interact to foster SBMI adoption. Fourth, the study enriches the resource-based view literature by integrating green IC, SBMI, GDC and sustainability performance. Finally, the study is unique in its use of a dual-stage methodological approach consisting of structural equation modeling and artificial neural networks to capture both linear connections and complicated, hidden, nonlinear patterns that conventional statistical approaches might overlook. No study had analytically assessed how the dimensions of green IC affect the ECSP, SSP and ESP of SMEs by employing this hybrid approach so far. Introduction Sustainability has become a vital component of contemporary business strategies and denotes a delicate balance between economic prosperity, environmental stewardship, and social responsibility (Sheehy and Farneti, 2021). In the business context, sustainability refers to balancing profit-making activities with activities that benefit society and the environment in the long term (Bansal and DesJardine, 2014). Companies are increasingly recognizing that their long-term success is inextricably linked to their ability to address and mitigate their adverse impact on both communities and the environment. Thus, companies are now integrating sustainable practices into various aspects of business processes, from logistics management to product development and stakeholder engagement (Savitz, 2013). Implementing sustainable business strategies requires a comprehensive approach addressing the environmental, social, and economic sustainability pillars (Purvis et al., 2019). The environmental pillar concerns reducing ecological degradation, minimizing material wastage, and reducing power consumption and the occurrence of environmental disasters (Schwarz-Herion, 2015); the social pillar encompasses the benefits that firms contribute to communities, such as improving their health, safety, and welfare (Wang and Dai, 2018); lastly, the economic pillar ensures that sustainable business operations are financially worthwhile, generate positive returns, and contribute to longterm profitability (Kramer and Porter, 2011; Eltayeb, 2011). Business organizations globally are struggling to reach a balance between the three pillars of sustainability, particularly in emerging markets. Due to their size, abundant resource availability, and formal policies, large businesses are in a better position to implement sustainability practices than small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs; Rashid et al., 2024). SMEs face resource constraints, limited access to advanced technologies, and insufficient regulatory frameworks guiding sustainable business practices (Ahmad et al., 2024). Manufacturing SMEs, particularly in emerging economies, are under growing pressure to align their processes with sustainable development goals for two main reasons (Khattak et al., 2024a, b, c). First, customers increasingly prefer ecologically friendly goods and are thus eager to pay more for sustainable products (Kumar et al., 2021). Second, pressure from local communities has pushed firms to adopt sustainable business operations to maintain their competitive long-term market position (Zhou et al., 2022). As a result, SMEs have attracted the attention of policymakers and stakeholders. They are appreciated for their considerable role in economic development (accounting for 90% of enterprises), their contribution to the national gross domestic product (GDP; more than 40%), and the fact that they generate one-third of the country’s total exports and two-thirds of the labor force (World Bank, 2022; Pakistan Today, 2024). Many SMEs remain ignorant about the ecological impact of their business operations and uncommitted to sustainable practices even though their collective influence on sustainability outcomes is more substantial than large firms (Eweje, 2020; Smith et al., 2022). Manufacturing SMEs are collectively responsible for over 70% of global waste and industrial pollution, 60–80% of CO 2 emissions, and more than 70% of marine industrial waste discharge (Chen et al., 2017; Mitra, 2022). In Pakistan, industrial waste and carbon emissions released by manufacturing enterprises are the main contributors to air pollution and result from weak control by environmental regulatory authorities and the government (Afridi, 2025). Consequently, SMEs should adopt sustainable practices to overcome ecological, social, and economic concerns in the long run. Achieving sustainability in these dimensions is essential for SMEs’ long-term competitiveness, especially as the global business environment becomes increasingly complex and dynamic (Lee et al., 2024). As part of this shift, firms increasingly recognize the strategic importance of leveraging their intellectual capital (IC), particularly in the form of green IC, to drive sustainability initiatives and foster innovation. Green IC, which encompasses a firm’s knowledge, skills, and capabilities related to environmental sustainability, is an emerging concept in the literature on sustainability and innovation and plays a critical role in enabling firms to address environmental challenges while also enhancing their business performance (Wei et al., 2024). Nonetheless, our understanding of how green IC influences sustainability performance across economic sustainability performance (ECSP), social sustainability performance (SSP), and environmental sustainability performance (ESP) dimensions remains limited, particularly in the context of SMEs in emerging markets. Literature review 2.1 Theoretical framework We analyzed the intricate relationship between green IC, SBMI, GDC, and sustainability performance based on the RBV theory paradigm. This theory was originally proposed by Barney in 1991 and suggests that firms with valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable (VRIN) resources outperform their rivals in a competitive market. RBV theory has been extensively corroborated in the business literature, which has established a link between valuable intangible resources and firm success (Ahmad et al., 2024; Oprean-Stan et al., 2020). Enterprises enjoy a superior monopoly over their rivals in a competitive market by implementing and cultivating an effective combination of resources and capabilities with VRIN characteristics (Barney, 1991). However, the utilization of intangible resources alone is not always productive for businesses, particularly small ones. Combining resources and capabilities enables an enterprise to design and carry out business operations more effectively than other enterprises because current or emerging peers lack similar resources and capabilities to execute business activities (Barney, 1991). Initially, RBV theory was primarily associated with organizational outcomes such as competitive advantage (Mohammad Shafiee, 2022), performance (Ahmad et al., 2023), business reputation (Anser et al., 2024), venture success (Anwar et al., 2018), and sales growth (Lu et al., 2021). More recently, environmental scholars have expanded its scope to encompass environmental and social outcomes and showed that firms with a combination of intangible resources and capabilities are more likely to engage in social activities, which improve their environmental performance. Environmental scholars have mainly used RBV frameworks to understand the role of green intangible resources in green performance (Shehzad et al., 2023), green process innovation (Jirakraisiri et al., 2021), environmental performance (Asiaei et al., 2022), green competitive advantage (Li et al., 2024a, b), social performance (AgyabengMensah and Tang, 2021), and business reputation (Anser et al., 2024). Enterprises must leverage green IC and implement GDC to build SBMI and enhance their sustainability performance. RBV theory is particularly pertinent to GDC because it emphasizes the role of heterogeneous resources in escalating GDC to achieve a long-lasting sustainable edge over rivals. Applying the tenets of RBV, researchers have suggested that SBMI might enhance an enterprise’s sustainability and competitiveness (Le et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024), although it also requires intangible resources and green organizational capabilities (Bashir and Naqshbandi, 2024). Furthermore, Bhatti et al. (2024) posit that green intangible resources are indispensable for manufacturing firms in developing SBMI, but few studies have considered green IC, SBMI, and GDC together to assess the three aspects of sustainability performance through the lens of RBV. We argue that green intangible resources (green IC) and GDC assist SMEs in fostering SBMI to cope with the dynamic environment while achieving ESP, SSP, and ESP. Our research enriches the scope and knowledge of RBV theory under the umbrella of green IC, SBMI, GDC, and sustainability performance in manufacturing SMEs. Additionally, based on RBV theory, its insights contribute to scholarship on how the interaction of green IC and GDC can influence SBMI and lead to improved sustainability performance. 2.2 Sustainable performance Sustainability, defined as “development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs” (WCED, 1987, p. 43), is receiving growing attention from scholars globally. These are collectively described as the “triple bottom line” and affect stakeholders’ actions (Elkington, 1998). Achieving an optimal trade-off between the three is a pressing goal of modern-day businesses (Brenner and Hartl, 2021). We argue that firms with GDC recognize and respond more quickly to market demands than their rivals and can apply these skills along with green IC to facilitate SBMI adoption. 2.8 Moderating role of green dynamic capability We posited that GDC enhances an enterprise’s capacity to sense, grab, and alter resources in response to environmental challenges and fosters the impact of green IC on SBMI. In the presence of GDC, green intangible resources significantly improve the organization’s innovative green practices (Joshi and Dhar, 2020). Conversely, enterprises with poor or no GDC may be unable to develop sustainable innovative practices (Chotia et al., 2024). Firms with both green IC and robust GDC can effectively adopt SBMI. Notably, firms with good GDC can accomplish superior sustainability outcomes through SBMI than those with poor GDC. Thus, GDC magnifies the positive effects of green IC, leading to more significant improvements in SBMI. Accordingly, researchers describe GDC as a moderator in the link between green business strategy and green process innovation (Chotia et al., 2024). Feng et al. (2024) found that GDC amplifies the link between digital capabilities and green innovation, although the role of GDC in the association between green IC and SBMI remains overlooked. GDC may act as a crucial moderator intensifying the positive impact of green IC on SBMI. Therefore, we hypothesize that GDC strengthens the nexus between green IC and SBMI. H7. The positive relationship between green IC and SBMI is more pronounced in the presence of high GDC. 2.9 Conceptual model Figure 1 displays the conceptual model for the study. The proposed framework demonstrates the role of green IC in the ECSP, SSP, and ESP of manufacturing SMEs in Pakistan and the mediating effect of SBMI. The study also analyzes the moderating role of GDC in the link between green IC and SBMI. 3. Methodology 3.1 Sample and research design To test the hypothesized relationship (see Figure 1), we gathered empirical data through a quantitative survey approach from manufacturing SMEs working in Pakistan, specifically in Lahore, Rawalpindi, Peshawar, and Islamabad, which have the highest percentage of manufacturing firms, most of which have their center of operations in these cities. In the Pakistani context, the classification of manufacturing enterprises follows the state bank’s definition as firms with between 20 and 250 employees operating in the manufacturing sector. For the pilot test, 80 questionnaires were disseminated, and 64 were returned, of which 47 were considered suitable (an effective response rate of 58.75%). To choose the appropriate sample size, we relied on the criteria proposed by Osborne (2008), who outlined a sample size selection procedure based on the ratio of the number of participants to the number of items. According to this method (which calls for eight participants per item), 300 was considered the minimum suitable size for the sample. The number of questionnaires was increased to 600 to mitigate sample size error and deal with non-response concerns (Hair et al., 2012). Subsequently, 450 questionnaires were distributed in hard copy format and 250 via online platforms to SME managers. A total of 398 responses were returned in the allocated time (two months). However, only 324 of these were appropriate for further investigation, and the remaining 74 were discarded due to deceptive data. Consequently, the data comprised 60 online responses (24.01% response rate) and 264 responses in hard copy (58.66% response rate), resulting in a total of 324 responses (54.0% response rate), which is considered adequate for a survey study (Bashir and Naqshbandi, 2024). This hybrid approach offers both explanatory insights and predictive accuracy, thereby addressing the complex nature of the framework. In the first stage, we employed PLS-SEM, which is particularly suited to exploratory studies involving complex models with multiple constructs, to assess the linear relationships between our variables (Sarstedt et al., 2021). PLS-SEM allows the evaluation of measurement reliability, validity, and structural paths. We opted for it because of its multifaceted nature and the need to assess the causal links between green IC, SBMI, GDC, and the three dimensions of sustainability performance (ECSP, SSP, and ESP). However, PLS-SEM is limited in its ability to capture nonlinear relationships and rank predictors based on their relative importance (Baig et al., 2023). To address these limitations, we turned to ANNs in the second stage of the analysis. An ANN is a machine-learning technique capable of detecting both linear and complex nonlinear patterns that traditional statistical methods may overlook (Yadegaridehkordi et al., 2023). Their use thus enhances the predictive relevance of a model and complements SEM results by validating and extending their implications (Khan et al., 2022). ANNs also demonstrate robustness in handling multicollinearity, non-normal data distributions, missing values, and small sample sizes, which are common challenges in behavioral research (Rehman et al., 2024). Specifically, the model relied on two hidden layers, striking an optimal balance between model complexity and performance during preliminary testing. The first hidden layer contained 16 neurons, and the second had eight. These values were determined through a grid search approach and k-fold cross-validation (k 5 10), which helped identify the configuration yielding the lowest prediction error. The model was trained using the Adam optimizer because of its faster convergence and handling of sparse gradients. To avoid overfitting, we implemented a 10-fold cross-validation approach, with the dataset split into 70% for training and 30% for testing (Ashaari et al., 2021). Model accuracy was assessed using the root mean square error (RMSE) and the sum of squares error (SSE) during both the training and testing phases (Rehman et al., 2024). Finally, we conducted a sensitivity analysis to determine the relative importance of each predictor variable in explaining ECSP, SSP, and ESP. This hybrid SEM-ANN methodology not only improves the robustness and predictive power of the analysis but also aligns with recent best practices in sustainability and green IC research (Khattak et al., 2024a, b, c; Khan et al., 2022; Ur Rahman et al., 2024). We proposed a model built based on the existing scholarship and substantiated via the PLS-structural algorithm method in the SmartPLS-04 graphical version. Figures 3 and 4 offer a snapshot of the results of the structural model. Following RBV theory, H1, H2, and H3 predicted a positive impact of green IC on the ECSP, SSP, and ESP of SMEs. Our results support this theory and confirm that green IC (e.g. intangible resources) significantly positively contributes to ECSP, SSP, and ESP in SMEs, thus corroborating H1, H2, and H3. This suggests that green IC significantly promotes the ECSP, SSP, and ESP of manufacturing SMEs. Our findings partially align with prior studies in developing economies, such as Yusliza et al.’s (2020), who posited that green IC has a more significant influence on the social performance of enterprises than other sustainability matrices. Furthermore, our conclusions match those of Suki et al. (2023) and Yusoff et al. (2019), who revealed that green IC is a significant determinant of corporate sustainability. These findings are also in keeping with the work of Khan et al. (2023a, b) and Wang and Juo (2021), which showed that green IC leads to better environmental performance and provides guidelines for implementing sustainability initiatives. Focusing on SMEs in Malaysia’s developing economy, Hina et al. (2024) revealed that sustainable performance within an organization can be accomplished by leveraging the dimensions of green IC. However, these studies predominantly used a single PLS-SEM model. In contrast, our study employed a hybrid methodological approach combining PLS-SEM and ANN to examine the role of green IC dimensions on each pillar of sustainability performance (ECSP, ESP, and SSP) in Pakistani manufacturing SMEs. H4, H5, and H6 suggested that SBMI plays a mediating role in the nexus between green IC and ECSP, SSP, and ESP in SMEs. Our results indicate that SBMI partially mediates these relationships. This suggests that green IC and SBMI are equally decisive for boosting the ECSP, SSP, and ESP of manufacturing SMEs. Our empirical study was a unique endeavor to illuminate the intervening role of SBMI in the green IC–sustainability performance relationship in an emerging market. It is a novel effort to elucidate SBMI as an intervening mechanism between the green IC–sustainability performance relationship in the context of manufacturing SMEs, which makes it difficult to directly compare its findings with those of earlier works. However, research has proven that intangible resources play a crucial role in developing SBMI (Bashir and Naqshbandi, 2024; Bhatti et al., 2024; Vasylieva et al., 2020) and SBMI, which in turn promote sustainability initiatives (Rosati et al., 2023; Schl€uter et al., 2023). Our findings add to the literature by demonstrating that green IC alone may not directly boost ECSP, SSP, and ESP in SMEs but instead requires the mediation of SBMI. Researchers have highlighted the mediating role of green competencies (Khan et al., 2023a, b), green innovation (Shehzad et al., 2023), green performance (Hoang et al., 2024), and the green workforce (Mansoor et al., 2021), but no study had used SBMI as a conduit to link green IC to sustainability performance before ours. In addition, few studies have focused on SBMI in SMEs, particularly in Asia (Bashir and Naqshbandi, 2024), where SMEs are considered the backbone of the industrial sector and account for more than 90% of all business activities. SMEs may not be able to beat their rivals in a continuously shifting environment without robust SBMI, which is why they nurture sustainable innovative practices. H7 predicted that GDC moderates the link between green IC and SBMI. The results suggest that GDC indeed strengthens the impact of green IC on SBMI, possibly because GDC is crucial for achieving SBMI. GDC can therefore be leveraged to restructure and reconfigure resources to capture and create value while adhering to environmental ethics (Sui et al., 2024). These findings suggest that enterprises with robust GDC are in a better position to amplify the positive effects of green IC on SBMI. In SMEs with strong GDC, green IC can promote the effective adoption of SBMI. No study so far had focused on the role of GDC as a moderator between green IC and SBMI. Ours thus offers new insights into the green IC and GDC of SMEs. The study’s overall conclusions are coherent with the RBV hypothesis, according to which a firm’s intangible capabilities and resources are essential to sustainability performance (Ahmad et al., 2024).
