Conclusion and implications This study aimed to determine how green IC influences ECSP, SSP, and ESP in manufacturing SMEs in Pakistan through the mediation of SBMI and examine the moderating role of GDC in the relationship between green IC and SBMI. We collected data through a survey completed by 324 owners and top managers in manufacturing SMEs in four Pakistani cities. We employed a hybrid approach to assess both the linear connections and the complex hidden nonlinear patterns between the variables. The results were confirmed by a regression analysis. Our findings indicate that green IC positively contributes to ECSP, SSP, and ESP in the manufacturing SMEs of this emerging Asian economy, and SBMI appears to mediate these relationships. This means that green IC influences sustainability performance both directly and indirectly through its impact on SBMI. Firms with stronger green IC are more likely to develop and adopt innovative sustainability-oriented business models, which improve their sustainability performance. This mediating effect of SBMI points to the essential role of innovation as a channel through which intangible resources translate into tangible outcomes. Notably, we found that GDC moderates the relationship between green IC and SBMI, strengthening it. The positive effect of green IC on SBMI adoption is thus enhanced when a firm has higher levels of GDC. This is because GDC enables firms to reconfigure, adapt, and integrate their green resources more effectively, thereby facilitating the translation of green IC into innovative business practices. Together, these findings shed light on a dual mechanism in which green IC influences sustainability performance directly and indirectly via SBMI, and the strength of the green IC– SBMI link depends on GDC. This integrated model contributes to theory by revealing not only that green IC matters but also how and in which conditions it drives sustainability in SMEs. In addition, our ANN results show that GHC has the highest predictive power on both ECSP and SSP. This implies that internal employee skills, knowledge, and eco-conscious culture are fundamental to achieving SMEs’ economic and social sustainability goals. However, GRC emerged as the strongest predictor of ESP, underscoring the crucial role of external stakeholder relationships, customer trust, and environmental legitimacy. This illustrates why different types of green IC lead to different sustainability outcomes: internal human capital may enhance innovation, operational efficiency, and internal capability development, which in turn enhance ECSP and SSP, while GRC strengthens external collaboration, trust, and legitimacy, which are essential for achieving environmental goals. These insights from ANN go beyond linear models and suggest that firms should strategically develop and leverage different types of green IC based on their sustainability priorities. 6.1 Theoretical implications Our study enhances the understanding of green IC, SBMI, GDC, and sustainability performance in SMEs in several ways. First, we used RBV theory to spotlight the importance of leveraging intangible resources such as green IC, SBMI, and GDC, which support SMEs in accomplishing ECSP, SSP, and ESP. RBV theory has been extensively corroborated in the business literature, which has demonstrated the link between valuable intangible resources and sustainable outcomes (Ahmad et al., 2024; Oprean-Stan et al., 2020), indicating that enterprises with VRIN resources enjoy superior social and ecological performance in a competitive market. However, the use of conventional resources alone is insufficient for businesses; small businesses in particular should utilize green resources and capabilities to achieve highly sustainable outcomes. RBV theory has been overlooked in establishing the associations between green IC, SBMI, GDC, and SMEs’ sustainability outcomes (i.e., ECSP, SSP, and ESP). Our study fills this gap by developing a new, comprehensive model. Building on RBV theory, the findings of this empirical study enrich our view of green IC and its influence on the ECSP, SSP, and ESP of SMEs through SBMI and GDC, especially in emerging economies. Second, by examining the impact of green IC on SBMI, our work expands the green IC and SBMI literature. Our findings contradict prior research that found that green IC affects business model innovation in large manufacturing firms in Australia (Roos, 2013). This dual strategy offers a deeper and more nuanced understanding of the most critical predictors of SME sustainability. The combination of PLS-SEM and ANN is a pioneering analytical framework capable of uncovering both linear and nonlinear relationships and revealing hidden patterns among latent constructs in complex models. The findings extend previous research on developing economies (e.g. Hina et al., 2024; Yusliza et al., 2020; Yusoff et al., 2019) by demonstrating the value of ANN in ranking the predictive power of green IC dimensions (i.e., GHC, GSC, and GRC) in achieving sustainability goals. Limitations and directions for future research This empirical study’s limitations should be considered by scholars in future research. First, our study utilized a cross-sectional research design for data collection, which may have generated a CMB issue. Therefore, a longitudinal method should be utilized in future research to examine this model. Second, the study relied only on a quantitative method (i.e., a survey approach), potentially overlooking qualitative data that may provide a comprehensive view of the issues faced by small business industries in integrating green IC, GDC, and SBMI. Exploring qualitative data techniques such as case studies or semi-structured interviews could thus produce useful findings. Third, our study focused exclusively on manufacturing SMEs, and future researchers should target large firms and other industries that establish a high configuration with green practices. Fourth, we only examined SBMI as an intervening mechanism, but other constructs such as environmental management accounting, bricolage, and AI green business strategy may be considered as mediating variables to provide more nuanced insights and enhance the practical understanding of the hypothesized relationship. University of Athens; cUniversity of California; dYunnan University of Finance and Economics ABSTRACT Global strategy cannot be fully understood without consideration of dynamic capabilities (DCs). This is because the three key constituents of DCs – the sensing and seizing of opportunities and the reconfiguration of the resource base – are essential preconditions for strategy development, within nations and cross-border. We investigate the aspects of DCs that are most suitable for global strategy and those that need to be revisited and developed. We discuss theory and evidence on DCs and global strategy , present a systematic literature review , compare theory and evidence, and identify gaps between the two as well as opportunities to align them more closely and to develop both. To help guide future research, we develop a novel conceptual framework and provide suggestions for more theory-congruent empirical research. Keywords: dynamic capabilities, multinational enterprise, global strategy , empirical evidence, novel conceptual framework INTRODUCTION As described in Chandler’s (1962) classic book, business strategy details a company’s objectives and how and by when the company intends to achieve them. The how and by when regards where the company wants to be in terms of its activities and locations, its value proposition, its business model, the resources and capabilities it needs, its approach towards competition and cooperation, and any contingency plans it puts in place. Global strategy is business strategy applied at the international level. Global strategy without DCs is Hamlet without the prince of Denmark. This is because the answer to the question of where a company chooses to operate requires sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring (SSR) the organizational resource base to align with and facilitate the sensing and seizing of opportunities. Global strategy also involves shaping the context within which companies operate to the extent that it is possible. This includes the creation, co-creation, and orchestration of markets, business ecosystems, and institutions. Co-creation and orchestration opportunities pre - suppose SSR (Pitelis and Teece, 2010, 2019). The modern theory of the multinational enterprise (MNE) is rooted in the microeconomic theory of the firm and industrial organization (Horst, 1972; Hymer, 1960/1976). It has featured seminal contributions from Buckley and Casson (1976), Dunning (1980), Teece (1977, 1986), Williamson (1981), Hennart (1982) and Kogut and Zander (1993), among others (see Dunning and Lundan, 2008; Dunning and Pitelis, 2008, 2010). The theory has delved into the question of how and why MNEs differ from markets, and the modality they adopt when they enter a foreign market. Since Coase’s (1937) classic article, the first question is also known as the nature of the firm and hence the MNE. It relates to the reasons why in an economy that is based on voluntary exchanges between transactors in markets, hierarchical organizations such as firms that are based on fiat should exist. The modality of cross-border operations is closely linked to the question of the nature of the MNE, because some modalities of entry , such as licensing, are more market-based, while others, such as foreign direct investment (FDI), are more hierarchical (firm)-based. In this context, in the traditional literature of the MNE, the decision to adopt FDI and hence to internalize a cross-border activity within organizational boundaries defines the MNE (Dunning and Pitelis, 2008, 2010). The question of cross-border modalities assumes that the MNE has already decided which cross-border activities to conduct and in which locations/countries it will oper - ate. These are important, usually prior questions, and require the ability of MNEs to sense and seize cross-border opportunities and reconfigure their resource bases to better achieve their purposes. Hence, it requires the MNE to possess DCs. While the internalization of activities and markets is an important part of the wider MNE global strat - egy , global strategy incorporates several elements that go beyond internalization. These wider considerations of global strategy and the MNE’s capabilities to implement it have been largely missing from the early theoretical and empirical literature on MNEs in international business (IB) scholarship. These are the limitations and gaps that we seek to fill in this paper. More specifically , while global strategy is a key area of application for DCs, the extant conceptual and empirical literature has paid limited attention to it. A way to understand and address the gaps and to orient future research is to undertake a thorough review of the extant empirical and conceptual literature. By comparing the two, we expect to identify and explain gaps and disjuncts and propose ways forward. A keyway to guide future research is to draw on theory and evidence to develop a more comprehensive conceptual framework that permits a better understanding of the concepts and relationships under consideration. THE DYNAMIC CAPABILITIES VIEW (DCV) AND MNE GLOBAL STRATEGY The dynamic capabilities view (DCV) of the firm and the MNE was developed by David Teece and associates (Petricevic and Teece, 2019; Pitelis and Teece, 2010, 2018; Teece, 2014; Teece et al., 1997). The DCV is built upon the resource-based view (RBV), according to which a key source of sustainable competitive advantage (SCA) is derived from firm-specific resources, capabilities, practices, and processes that are valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable (VRIN) (Barney , 1991; Penrose, 1959). It is also built upon the evolutionary theory of Nelson and Winter (1982), which emphasized evolutionary processes and the role of organizational capabilities and routines, namely collective, patterned, and recurrent organizational acts (Pitelis and Wagner, 2019). Routines are the intersection between evolutionary economics and the capabilities literature and constitute ordinary organizational capabilities (Winter, 2000). While the evolutionary approach indicates that routine-based capabilities by themselves can explain differences in companies’ performance, DCs emphasize the importance of entrepreneurial decision making, which is beyond the scope of ordinary capabilities (Katkalo et al., 2010; Teece et al., 2021). The DCV emphasizes human, notably managerial and entrepre - neurial traits, that operate within a cohesive organizational shell, as well as the ways in which these are embedded within organizations (Jones and Pitelis, 2015; Pandza and Thorpe, 2009; Teece, 2014). Teece, Pisano and Shuen (1997, p. 516) originally expressed DCs in terms of the organizational and managerial capacity to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external resources and competencies to address rapidly changing environments. Eisenhardt and Martin (2000) identified several specific processes, such as product development, alliances, and decision making, and added the shaping of the internal and external environment. In Teece et al. (1997), DCs referred to processes, positions, and paths. Sensing refers to the identification and creation of opportunities and the mitigation of threats. Seizing refers to the requisite steps and actions to take advantage of these opportunities. Reconfiguring refers to adjusting the resource base so that it remains VRIN and relevant. It is aligned with and enables the continuation of sensing and seizing. In the DCV , ‘ordinary’ capabilities (OCs) refer to the enterprise doing things right, while dynamic capabilities (DCs) refer to doing the right things at the right time. OCs support technical fitness, while DCs support evolutionary fitness. DCs rely on good/ best practices as well as ‘signature’ practices, meaning practices that are firm-specific and proprietary . Additionally , DCs require astute managerial orchestration guided by what Rumelt (2011) termed ‘good strategy’. Signature processes and business models include the firm’s history , experience, culture, and creativity (Gratton and Ghoshal, 2005). These are hard to copy and can confer lasting advantages. Besides the tacit nature of their knowledge base, and in part because of it, DCs are characterized by ‘uncertain imitability’ (Lippman and Rumelt, 1982). Creating signature problem-solving processes and business models entails learning, problem recognition and solving through continuous experimentation (Rosenberg, 1992). In summary , DCs reside in and are the outcome of the skills of the top management team (TMT), as well as how and the extent to which these are embedded within the organization (Pitelis and Teece, 2018; Pitelis and Wagner, 2019). They help explain how an enterprise can align its business processes and models with the external environment and, to the extent possible, help shape the environment to its advantage (Pitelis and Teece, 2010). While all three DCs are important for global strategy , reconfiguration is derivative of sensing and seizing, especially sensing. Sensing and the need to seize inform reconfiguration both during and prior to cross-border expansion. Once informed by sensing and seizing, however, reconfiguration becomes the essence of implementation (Pitelis, 2022). Entrepreneurship within and outside of firms permits SSR and is underpinned by cognitive elements, such as entrepreneurial orientation, perception, vision and global mindset (Autio et al., 2011; García-Cabrera and Durán-Herrera, 2016; Jafari-Sadeghi et al., 2021) and imagination (Jones and Pitelis, 2015). Entrepreneurial action has been largely missing from the traditional economic theory of the MNE and FDI. More recent international entrepreneurship (IE) literature has emphasized proactiveness, risk-taking and innovativeness (Covin and Slevin, 1988). In IE, the concept of entrepreneurial orientation (EO) has become popular. EO can affect DCs as well as firms’ international behaviours; for example, it can enhance firms’ opportunity recognition and exploitation for global expansion (Buccieri et al., 2020; Eriksson et al., 2014). Entrepreneurial imagination is absent from the economics-based rational choice approach to the MNE. Loasby (2001) argued that the creation of new patterns rests on imagination, not logic, and it is typically stimulated by a perceived inadequacy in established patterns. Imaginative efforts can draw upon prior experiences, learning, and insights. Entrepreneurs with experience in a particular context, such as their home country , can ‘imagine’ a situation in which suitably modified, and appropriately adapted conditions can be created cross-border. In such cases, imagined entrepreneurial realities that draw upon their experiences can help motivate decisions and actions that create and co-create a desired context for their intended operations at home and cross-border (Jones and Pitelis, 2015). This renders imagination an important aspect of the sensing part of DCs. Accordingly , both EO and entrepreneurial imagination can support SSR (Teece, 2014). These actions are partly endogenous to the actions of the MNE and partly dependent on the actions of the market’s co-creators, which are often unknown or unpredictable. Put differently , much of the extant economic theory of the MNE and FDI assumes prior knowledge of the organizational internal and external environment and the opportunities it presents. For the DVC, all of these are co-created and co-evolving. The business ecosystem concept relates to work on clusters (Pitelis, 2012; Porter, 1990). In the DCV cross-border market, cluster and business ecosystem co-creation are important reasons for the existence and global strategy of the MNE. The capability to orchestrate and leverage co-specialized and complementary assets across multiple jurisdictions to help co-create cross-border markets and business ecosystems is an important reason for the spectacular advances of internationalization (Pitelis and Teece, 2010). Several scholars have reviewed the DCV literature and provided clarification and boundary conditions for the research area (i.e., Easterby-Smith et al., 2009; Fainshmidt et al., 2016; Pitelis and Wang, 2019; Schilke et al., 2018; Wang and Ahmed, 2007). Critical surveys have been used to assess the state of play so far and have proposed ways forward (Laaksonen and Peltoniemi, 2018; Schilke et al., 2018). However, the application of DCs to global strategy remains in its infancy . This is a major limitation in that DCs are of the essence in the semi-globalized, knowledge-based economic environment we live in. MNEs operate in jurisdictions that involve sovereign actors with a legal monopoly of force and often unique identities. This renders the MNE conceptually more ‘interesting’ and general than the domestic firm and, accordingly , a challenge to model and manage. DCs are important in sensing this and informing MNE global strategy . As noted, IB theory focuses on the nature of the MNE and modalities of entry . Extant theories, such as John Dunning’s ownership, location, internalization (OLI), and the country-specific advantages (CSA)/firm-specific advantages (FSA) framework of Rugman and V erbeke (2000), assume the existence of CSAs. DCs help explain the often prior question of where an MNE should be in terms of activities and locations. They can help companies sense CSA and seize opportunities that arise from cross-border locations and activities. They help identify , co-create, and align the FSAs and the CSAs. In IB scholarship, the DCV has received comparatively limited, albeit growing, attention (Luo, 2000; Pitelis, 2022; Schilke et al., 2018; Zahra et al., 2022). Studies on the role of DCs in the cross-border expansion of firms, such as Pitelis and Teece (2010, 2018), Prange and V erdier (2011), Teece (2014), Grøgaard et al. (2019) and Zahra et al. (2022), have not made an explicit link to the wider issues of global strategy . An exception, albeit a limited one, is the role of DCs in the market, ecosystem, and more widely , context creation, co-creation, and orchestration. This is receiving growing attention in conceptual papers (Pitelis, 2022; Pitelis and Teece, 2010, 2018; Teece, 2014; Zahra et al., 2022). While considerations of global strategy are critical for organizational performance, they remain poorly understood and tested in extant empirical research. In part, this is because of the lack of a comprehensive conceptual framework (Pitelis, 2022; Pitelis and Teece, 2019; Teece, 2014; Teece and Petricevic, 2021; Zahra et al., 2022). SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW Method To conduct a systematic review of DCs, the MNE and global strategy literature, we employed content analysis (Drisko and Maschi, 2016; Krippendorff, 2004). Content analysis is suitable for identifying and summarizing trends in the extant literature and dealing with a large volume of unstructured data, such as text. It is also appropriate for qualitative and quantitative data analysis. It helps identify both manifest and latent content and enables the development of important themes from the literature (Duriau et al., 2007; Gaur and Kumar, 2018). To conduct our systematic review , we followed the six-step process suggested by Gaur and Kumar (2018). This entails selecting the appropriate database, selecting the sample literature with criteria that serve the pur - pose of the review and ensuring the reliability of this process, creating the coding scheme, coding the content of the sample, analysing the coding accuracy and testing the reliability , and summarizing and providing an interpretation of the coded content. We elaborate on these below . Sample Selection Our starting point is to search for sample literature. We focused on full-length, empirical, and conceptual peer-reviewed articles published between 1997 and 2021. The starting date was the seminal paper of Teece et al. (1997) on DCs, which also anticipated the development of DCV in the MNE context. To ensure the relevance and rigour of the sample literature, we set various criteria for identifying appropriate journals and articles. First, we investigated different indexes of journal rankings, including Thompson Reuters’ 2020 Journal Citation Report, Chartered Association of Business Schools’ (CABS) Academic Journal Guide 2021, Australian Business Deans Council’s (ABDC) Journal Quality List and Leiden University’s Centre for Science and Technology Studies (CWTS) Journal Indicators. The selected journals needed to satisfy at least two of the following four criteria: minimum 1.0 of 5-year citation impact factors, CABS 3 and above, ABDC B and above, and minimum 1.0 of source normalized impact per paper (SNIP). We did this to add diversity in designing the criteria and to avoid missing relevant journals (even when the journals were relatively young) while ensuring a minimum quality threshold. Search Method We investigated different ranking systems and league tables, and selected target jour - nals (Table II). To identify relevant articles, we implemented a keyword search across journals’ home pages through different databases (e.g., Scopus, JSTOR, Emerald and Science Direct). Specifically , we searched for articles that contained words such as ‘dynamic capabilit*’ or ‘dynamic* capabilit*’ (the DCs set of keywords), and ‘MNE’, ‘global’ and ‘internationalization’ (the IB set of keywords). We mixed and matched the two sets of keywords in the initial search. Following that, we read the search results one by one, including the abstract, keywords and main text of the articles, to evaluate whether they fit the criteria. These criteria included articles that (1) specifically used the term ‘dynamic capabilities/capability’ as the core of the study; or (2) explicitly categorized the capability/capabilities studied as a type of DC or highlighted their dynamic nature; or (3) adopted the DC perspective as the theoretical lens. As such, we have avoided distinguishing whether the capabilities studied in the sample articles are ‘dynamic’ or ‘ordinary’, an ongoing concern of DCV scholarship (see Fainshmidt et al., 2016; Laaksonen and Peltoniemi, 2018; Pitelis, 2022; Schilke et al., 2018). RESULTS The literature we examined has witnessed fluctuating growth; the booming years were 2016, 2018, 2019 and 2020, with 18, 21, 26 and 21 articles published, respectively (Figure 1). Figure 2 shows examples of key authors and co-authorships in this area. Several clusters can be identified, such as the Augier–Teece–Pitelis cluster, which highlights the entrepreneurial perspective and orchestration aspects of DCs; the Khan– Kuivalainen–Larimo cluster, which employs DCs to explore features of firms from de - veloped and emerging economies; and the Murray–Kotabe–Malik cluster, which focuses on the role of knowledge. Of the 196 studies in our sample, 60 were conceptual articles and 136 were empirical (Figure 3). Among the empirical studies, the most popular method employed was quantitative analysis (71 articles) based on surveys (51 articles). Most of the 61 qualitative studies (49 articles) adopted the case study method, including cross-sectional, longitudinal, single and multiple cases. A handful of studies (four articles) combined quantitative and qualitative analysis using mixed data sources. In what follows, we look at the extant literature in more detail, particularly the common terms used for DCs, paying attention to the MNE context and the empirical mea - sures and proxies used. Another observation from the extant literature is that DCs and OCs are barely differentiated in empirical research. While conceptual studies have highlighted the importance of distinguishing DCs and OCs and investigating the relationships between them, only a small number of empirical studies have addressed this issue. For example, Michailova and Zhan (2015) conceptualized organizational and strategic routines as first-order DCs; generative, sourcing and integrative capabilities as second-order DCs; and dynamic knowledge capabilities as third-order DCs. Similarly , the R&D expenditures and technology diversification of firms are considered first-order DCs, while firms’ dynamic technological capabilities are higher-order DCs; the former are typically organizational routines, and the latter are higher-order organizational heuristics that are harder to imitate (Li-Ying et al., 2016). The global strategy of the MNE is not only about entry modalities but is also related to the alignment with and shaping of the external environment within which firms operate. In such a context, orchestration skills and capabilities are key . In the scholarly literature, orchestration often refers to assets. However, it can be broader and can refer to the creation, co-creation and management of organizations, markets and business ecosystems, including global value chains (GVCs) and clusters/local production systems (Katkalo et al., 2010; Pitelis and Teece, 2019; Teece, 2014). Orchestration includes market and ecosystem co-creation (Pitelis and Teece, 2018). Cross-border market and business ecosystem creation and co-creation essentially require entrepreneurial managers (Jones and Pitelis, 2015; Pitelis and Teece, 2010). Orchestration capabilities become more important in the context of open team production, where team players are both internal and external to the firm (Berti and Pitelis, 2022). However, market and ecosystem co-creation (5.1 per cent) showed a relatively low frequency of appearance compared to other External Environment factors. The process of creation and co-creation of cross-border markets and ecosystems is facilitated by entrepreneurial imagination, which is appropriability-informed and legacy-shaped (Jones and Pitelis, 2015). Imagination, alongside vision, perception, creativity , etc., are cognitive elements/capabilities that can underpin the SSR of dynamic capabilities (Giudici et al., 2018; Helfat and Peteraf, 2015). Despite their importance in conceptual studies of DCs, entrepreneurial cognitive elements have received limited attention. This is especially true for the imagination subtheme under the Entrepreneurship theme (3.1 per cent). Co-specialization is a stronger version of complementarity and can be viewed as complementarity exclusive to two assets: activities and/or parties. Co-specialized assets have limited value outside the relevant area of application and hence are non-priced, meaning there is no market in which they can be readily bought and sold. This helps explain why it is often beneficial to bring together FSAs and CSAs in setting up an organization cross-border. Co-specialization challenges and opportunities are often discovered during cross-border activities. When internalization is deemed a preferable means of capturing value from such opportunities, the undertaking of activity inside the firm is chosen over market-based transactions. Hence, the nature of the organization (designing and setting up an organization) and the essence (employing strategy and a business model to help capture value) are co-determined. They are linked to asset co-specialization and the DCs required for orchestrating such assets. Like imagination, cross-border co-specialization of assets appeared with a frequency of only 7.7 per cent, which is the lowest among the subthemes of Resources. A glaring omission in the literature refers to key issues of global strategy , such as where MNEs want to be in terms of locations and activities, products and services. As already noted, the OLI and the FSA CSA frameworks assume that there are pre-existing CSAs and FSAs that are clearly identifiable. The DCV is about seeing these and/or creating them and aligning the FSAs with CSAs. There is very little work on this in the literature, and this is a major area for development. Figure 4. To summarize, global strategy entails more than internalization and includes the requisite agents, resources and capabilities and the shaping, co-creation and orchestration of the context within which MNEs operate. DCs are implicated in both developing and implementing a good strategy . They are more relevant for MNEs than national firms because of the added dimensions and layers implicated in addressing the key questions in a multinational context. This includes national borders and hence politics and geopolitics. However, while the relevance of the DCV to global strategy has been conceptualized, it has been poorly tested in a theory-congruent way . Moreover, a comprehensive conceptual framework has not been developed to help guide it. In the next section, we take stock of our findings, highlight the poorly tested/potential variables and relationships, and develop a novel, more comprehensive framework for studying DCs in MNE global strategy . Antecedents Factors identified as antecedents for the development of DCs include human capital, organizational structures, strategies, governance, and resource base. Human capital, such as the CEO’s age and experience, are considered micro-level sources of DCs (Rodenbach and Brettel, 2013). DC development is associated with entrepreneurship, especially managerial orchestration, and entrepreneurial cognition. Entrepreneurs’ or - chestration of external complementary resources can feed the seizing of opportunities (Ma et al., 2015), while ‘open-system’ orchestration can enhance a firm’s sensing capabilities through co-creation with members across the network (Giudici et al., 2018). Features of DCs, such as the integration and coordination of assets, require the alignment of organizational structure and strategies (Donada et al., 2016). Flexible organizational structures facilitate knowledge transfer and innovativeness, which contribute to creating DCs (Kapoor and Aggarwal, 2021). Structures, processes, routines, and skills are identified as cross-functional microfoundations of DCs, which may either positively or negatively influence synergies at product and market levels (Haapanen et al., 2019). For example, Riviere and Bass (2019) found that dimensions of internationalization (depth, breadth and speed) have different impacts on MNEs’ renewal capabilities. Dependent Variables Several variables have been used as dependent variables. These include financial indicators for performance, such as sales, profitability and return on investment, as well as non-financial indicators, such as competitiveness, reputation and achievement of stra - tegic goals. (Wang, 2020; Zeng and Glaister, 2016; Zhan and Chen, 2013; Zhan and Luo, 2008). For example, managerial and network capabilities were found to positively affect MNEs’ performance (including financial performance and market performance) in highly turbulent environments (Srećković, 2018). Some studies focused on value cre - ation as the dependent variable (De Silva et al., 2021; Matarazzo et al., 2021) and found a positive relationship. Another important dependent variable for DCs is SCA. Although various empirical studies have found a positive relationship between DCs (i.e., exploitative capabilities, explorative capabilities and flexibility) and SCA (Anning-Dorson, 2019; Ferreira et al., 2020; Zeng and Glaister, 2016), inconsistencies and some confusion remain. For instance, several scholars argued that DCs might be a necessary but insufficient determinant of SCA (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000; Fainshmidt et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2020). Besides performance, other potential dependent variables include ordinary capability , modality (make/buy/ally), resource base, context and cross-border modalities (FDI, international strategic alliances, international joint ventures) (Pitelis, 2022). From these, the modality and cross-border modalities as dependent variables of DCs have received some attention. DCs can explain organizational forms, FDI activities and international commitment according to empirical studies (Bell and Cooper, 2018; Vahlne and Bhatti, 2019; Yang et al., 2014). For example, absorptive capabilities can encourage a firm’s asset-seeking FDI activities to acquire or create new resources (Yang et al., 2014). There is some empirical evidence that DCs can determine the foreign market entry mode of MNEs and eventually influence international perfor - mance (Blesa and Ripollés, 2008). Despite its conceptual importance, context creation by DCs is missing in most empirical articles. While the impact of DCs on performance indirectly affects the context within which firms operate, it would be important to test directly whether, for example, they help create a new market through diversification. Independent Variable According to the theory , the key independent variable in the DCV is DCs, which have been measured in different ways that are not always congruent with theory . The theory entails the identification of human and non-human organizational attributes and their linkages. Most empirical work has focused on the former, and more work is required on organizational DCs and their interactions with human DCs. A notable one is the re - source base and its relationship to human DCs, which remains underexplored. Mediators Mediators between the chosen dependent variable and the DCs include a firm’s re - source base, ordinary capabilities, and modality (make/buy/ally). The empirical evidence mainly focused on the make/buy/ally modality . For example, entry modes such as joint ventures, strategic alliances, acquisitions and greenfield investments can mediate the relationship between dynamic managerial capabilities and firm perfor - mance, alongside the geographic dispersion of assets (Tasheva and Nielsen, 2020). Blesa and Ripollés (2008) found that international commitment and level of direct investment can mediate the relationship between marketing capabilities and international performance. However, the mediating effect of static/ordinary capabilities is underexplored. Firms need DCs to modify or reconfigure their resource base to build competitive advantages or enhance performance; the resource base includes both human and non-human ele - ments as well as social capital (Helfat et al., 2007; Pitelis, 2022; Pitelis and Wagner, 2019). Furthermore, empirical studies in the sample paid relatively little attention to the potential mediating role of resource base on the relationship between DCs’ and MNEs’ performance/SCA. Intangible resources such as knowledge, organizational culture and reputation were more frequently studied than tangible resources (Bell and Cooper, 2018; Wan et al., 2015). RESEARCH OPPORTUNITIES AND POLICY IMPLICATIONS Our key purpose was to compare theory and evidence to develop a novel conceptual framework to help guide future research. By critically assessing and extending the theory and evidence of the DCV of the MNE and global strategy , we identified disjuncts and gaps that helped us develop novel conceptual insights to guide further empirical research. These include the need to clearly identify , separate and proxy antecedents, dependent and independent and control variables, moderators and mediators and account for the several potential simultaneities. Several key aspects were found to be under- or unexplored. Arguably , more is required to fully develop this framework, and this is an opportunity for further research. Our arrows in Figure 5 are intended to show the key directions of the relationships. Feedback loops are shown with dotted lines. For instance, the choice of modality can depend on MNEs’ perceptions of their abilities to shape the context. In such a case, instead of a causal relationship, we would have a simultaneous relationship. Empirical testing in such cases can be challenging. These challenges in accounting for causality and simultaneities remain a limitation and challenge of the empirical literature (Pitelis, 2022). Our key advice for future research is to focus on a particular relationship and analyse it in depth, theoretically and empirically , including the control variables, mediators, and moderators. DCs should be both human and organizational. Adding to the SSR should be done with care, as most proposed additions can arguably be seen as subsets of the three (Pitelis, 2022). The distinction between OCs and DCs should always be kept clear, and both should be proxied appropriately . The set of potential dependent variables can be expanded to include modalities, ordinary capabilities and the external context. In the case of the MNE, it is a paradox that the canonical relationship between DCs and FDI remains underexplored. Global strategy should go beyond modalities of entry and even context co-creation and orchestration to addressing issues of where, when, how , and at what scale and speed. Simultaneities should be acknowledged, and in the case of econometric studies, accounted for, for instance, by using instrumental variables. The DCV remains rather new and requires further conceptual and empirical analysis. As contributors to the field, we acknowledge a degree of confusion. This is in part be - cause of the integrative nature of the framework that draws upon pre-existing ideas and concepts, places them in a dynamic setting, develops them, and helps make them more applicable in practice, while also adding new concepts, such as SSR, co-specialization and context co-creation and orchestration. This is a taller order than testing, for example, the relationship between asset specificity and vertical integration in TCE, as challenging as that was (Monteverde and Teece, 1982). Our work has important managerial implications. Good global strategy is arguably the holy grail of MNE, in that when successful, it helps the MNE acquire and sustain a competitive advantage, but when unsuccessful, it can lead to failure and even extinction. Our paper suggests that MNEs should choose a particular cross-border activity employing DCs to SSR based on the congruence between what they envision and what they can expect to achieve, and how and when it can be achieved through requisite resources and capabilities. Importantly , our research emphasizes that what MNEs can envision is based on the strength of their DCs. Moreover, the successful implementation of their plans depends on the MNE’s ability to shape the context within which they choose/plan to operate. This also entails consideration of non-market strategies to include international business diplomacy (Doh et al., 2022). Hence, it also has implications for public policy . The latter is beyond the scope of this paper and represents an exciting future research opportunity . Revisiting the idea of knowledge-based dynamic capabilities for digital transformation Gioconda Mele, Guido Capaldo, Giustina Secundoand Vincenzo Corvello Abstract Purpose – In the landscape created by digital transformation, developing the ability to adapt and innovate by absorbing and generating new knowledge has become a strategic priority for organizations. The theory of dynamic capabilities, especially from a knowledge-based perspective, has proven particularly useful in studying the phenomena of transformation and change. Moving from this premise, this paper aims to map the state of research and to define guidelines for the actualization of dynamic capabilities theory in the digital transformation era. Design/methodology/approach – A structured literature review of 75 papers, using descriptive, bibliographic and content analysis, was performed to analyze the evolution of dynamic capabilities in the context of digital transformation. Findings – Studies concerning knowledge-based dynamic capabilities for digital transformation have been clustered into five main research areas: the micro-foundation of dynamic capabilities for digital transformation; dynamic capabilities for value creation in digital transformation; dynamic capabilities for digital transition in specific industries; dynamic capabilities for ‘‘data-driven organizations’’; and dynamic capabilities for digital transformation in SMEs and family firms. A future research agenda for scholars in strategic management is presented. Practical implications – A conceptual framework and a future research agenda are presented to highlight directions for this promising research field concerning the renewal of dynamic capabilities in the context of digital transformation. Originality/value – The originality of the paper lies in the conceptual framework aiming to systematize current research on knowledge-based dynamic capabilities for digital transformation and to provide a new conceptualization of digital dynamic capabilities, clarifying how organizations create and share knowledge in the era of digitalization. Keywords Digital transformation, Dynamic capabilities, Digital transition, Value creation, Structured literature review, Knowledge creation, Knowledge sharing Paper typeLiterature review 1. Introduction Digital transformation is causing changes in society, as well as at the organization level, owing to the disruptive role played by the convergence of digital technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), additive manufacturing, big data, artificial intelligence, cloud computing and augmented and virtual reality ( Cappa et al.,2 0 2 1; Del Giudice et al., 2021a; Li et al., 2022; Papa et al., 2020; Sousa-Zomer et al., 2020). According to Verhoef et al. (2021 , p. 889), digital transformation is “a change in how a firm employs digital technologies to develop a new digital business model that helps to create and appropriate more value for the firm.” Digital transformation supports enterprises in the achievement of sustainable development ( Ardito et al., 2021; Chin et al., 2021; Del Giudice et al., 2021b). In such a context of transformation, companies are obliged to continuously improve their competences, by absorbing and generating new knowledge, to gain and maintain a competitive advantage (Ghasemzadeh et al., 2021). Since the first definition byTeece et al. (1997, p. 156), dynamic capabilities have been considered as “the firm’s ability to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external competences to address rapidly changing environments.” Later, leading scholars defined a dynamic capability in general terms, i.e. “the capacity of an organization to purposefully create, extend, and modify its resource base” ( Helfat et al.,2 0 0 9, p. 4).Teece (2007, 2014) suggested that dynamic capabilities could be disaggregated into three broad capacities (sensing, seizing and transforming) that operate through specific organizational actions working together to generate and sustain change ( Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000; Teece, 2023). Dynamic capabilities are necessary to successfully implement the changes characterizing digital transformation ( Ellstro ̈ me t al.,2 0 2 1) and to generate new knowledge for digital transformation ( Zheng et al. , 2011 ). From a theoretical perspective, they represent a fundamental framework to study digital transformation processes ( Annarelli et al., 2021). Some authors have investigated the link between dynamic capabilities and digital transformation, using a literature review approach. Among these, Ciampi et al. (2022) reviewed the literature on digitalization and organizational agility (conceived as a dynamic capability). Vial (2019) reviewed the literature on digital transformation in general, considering dynamic capabilities as central aspect in this phenomenon. Other authors have focused on defining, again based on reviews of the literature, the concept of “digitalization capabilities.” Chang and Lin (2021), for example, analyzed the literature to identify the digitalization capabilities needed by IT organizational units to support digital transformation. Annarelli et al.(2021) argued that digitalization capabilities are a precondition for sustaining a competitive advantage and lie within the intersection between the fields of information systems, innovation and knowledge management. Digitalization capabilities were defined in their study as organizational capabilities that combine firms’ digital assets and business resources by leveraging digital networks with the aim of producing innovation in terms of products, services and processes for “[... ] organizational learning and customer value creation and to manage innovation for ensuring sustained competitive advantage” ( Annarelli et al., 2021,p .8 ) .Bereznoy et al. (2021) defined the concept of “dynamic digitalization capabilities” that sustain knowledge exchange and knowledge creation through the use of digital technologies. Based on the theoretical framework of Teece (1997, 2014), Ghosh et al.(2021) defined the capabilities necessary for organizations to compete in high-velocity environments as “digital transformative capabilities” (DTCs), which are capabilities useful in readjusting business processes, both internally and externally, in a digital transformation era. DTCs represent the ability of a firm to systematically identify and develop core capabilities for digital transformation ( Chaudhuri et al.,2 0 2 2; Ghosh et al., 2021). Cordeiro et al.(2022) focused on how dynamic capabilities contribute to innovation, defining the “knowledge-based dynamic capabilities” (skills, processes, procedures and routines) that drive transformation (see also Faccin et al., 2019). Overall, when analyzing dynamic capabilities in the context of digital transformation, these studies underline the following aspects related to knowledge creation and management: digital sensing requires specific knowledge and practical wisdom ( Nonaka and Toyama, 2007) for the identification and development of technological opportunities; digital seizing includes the development and management of knowledge to seize opportunities; and digital transforming implies a reconfiguration of resources including organizational knowledge ( Hsu et al. ,2 0 1 8; Sousa-Zomer et al.,2 0 2 0). Examples of these capabilities include: digital scouting and digital scenario planning; digital sensing capabilities; digital mindset crafting; rapid prototyping; strategic agility; balancing digital portfolios; navigating innovation ecosystems; redesigning internal structures; and improving digital maturity ( Sousa-Zomer et al.,2 0 2 0). Despite the increasing number of studies published in recent years, the existing research on digital transformation and dynamic capabilities does not yet provide a clear and complete picture of the domain. To date, there has not been adequate theoretical and conceptual development in the dynamic capabilities literature in the emerging context of digital transformation ( Annarelli et al., 2021; Gong et al., 2022). In particular, the nexus between dynamic capabilities and knowledge dynamics in the context of digital transformation has been rarely investigated and is poorly understood. How can we redefine knowledge-based dynamic capabilities in the digital transformation era? RQ3. Based on the analysis and discussion of these clusters, a conceptualization of knowledgebased digital dynamic capabilities is provided in terms of context-dependent and higherorder capabilities, the development of which requires interaction both between the elements of the organizational system (strategy, structure, processes, culture and people) and with external actors (customers, suppliers and the innovation ecosystem). A conceptual framework thus is derived, describing dynamic capabilities for digital transformation. Finally, implications for theory and practice conclude the paper. 2. Research methods 2.1 Question formulation To address the research questions of the study, a SLR was performed on the topic of dynamic capabilities and digital transformation. This methodology has the advantages, underlined in literature, of categorizing/classifying and synthesizing the state of the art on a given topic (Christofi et al., 2019; Danese et al.,2 0 1 8; Nofal et al.,2 0 1 8; Tranfield et al., 2003; Vrontis and Christofi, 2021; Vrontis et al.,2 0 2 1; Wang and Chugh, 2014). A SLR is particularly appropriate for studying phenomena that have been considered in many studies, such as the relationship between the process of digital transformation and the theoretical framework of dynamic capabilities. Moreover, it enables defining a future research agenda, as well as implications both for theory and practice ( Kraus et al.,2 0 2 2). The methodology starts with the definition of research questions to increase the SLR’s reliability and validity (Leonidou et al.,2 0 2 0; Massaro et al.,2 0 1 6; Nguyen et al.,2 0 1 8; Petticrew and Roberts, 2006; Tranfield et al., 2003) and to identify the significant research papers to be included in the study sample. The result of this initial step was the three research questions presented in Section 1. 2.2 Search strategy and synthesis A set of inclusion and exclusion criteria was defined. The inclusion criteria refer to the search query, as well as time search boundaries ( Wang and Chugh, 2014 ). Using the keywords “dynamic capabilit/C3 ,” “digital transformation” or “digital technolog/C3 ” in the title, abstracts and keyword, 89 research papers were extracted from the Scopus database within the timeframe 2009–2022 (no paper published before 2009 was found in the sample). Scopus is one of the most comprehensive databases and includes a larger number of paper than, for example, Web of Science (WoS) (Thelwall, 2018). Moreover, most (97%) of the papers indexed in WoS are included in Scopus (Christofi et al.,2 0 1 9; Snyder, 2019; Waltman, 2016). The exclusion criteria were defined to effectively address the study aims and research questions. In particular, unlike previous studies, not only articles in the “business and management” disciplinary field were considered but rather, considering the interdisciplinary nature of the phenomenon, studies in all areas. The initial sample was further analyzed to reduce false negatives and increase false positives ( Petticrew and Roberts, 2006) through a further abstract reading. The exclusion criteria were based on the coherence with the research topics, publication type and language (Crossan and Apaydin, 2010; Follmer and Jones, 2018; Kauppi et al.,2 0 1 8; Nguyen et al.,2 0 1 8). Discussion, implications and a future research agenda 4.1 A synthesis of the literature on dynamic capabilities and digital transformation The aim of this section is to discuss the main findings, starting withRQ1 (What is the state of the art of the literature on dynamic capabilities in the digital transformation era?). Our review covers 14 years of publications, starting in 2009, on the topic of dynamic capabilities and digital transformation. The literature in this domain has constantly grown, with a notable acceleration observed from 2021. The amount of literature has stimulated several reviews dealing with adjacent topics ( Kraus et al., 2021). The distribution of articles in a large number of different journals underscores the importance of the topic across different research communities, confirming that the issue of digital transformation concerns many research areas. Accordingly, the dynamic capabilities framework can be useful in different research fields, including knowledge management, innovation management, business performance and value creation. The analysis of citations by article highlights that the most cited articles are a literature review article ( Vial, 2019), a conceptual article (El Sawyet al.,2 0 1 0) and a qualitative article (Warner and Wag̈er, 2019). The impact of these kinds of articles [in particular with regard to the last two, since the high number of citations forVial (2019)is certainly also due to the fact that it is a review article and reviews tend to attract more citations] seems to reflect a need for greater clarity and a better definition of the constructs used. All three articles, in fact, aim to clarify concepts that are evolving and that are not treated in an univocal way in the scientific community. The average number of citations of the articles analyzed is 26.4, which is rather high compared to other fields analyzed in literature reviews ( Lim et al., 2022), demonstrating that this research field is rapidly consolidating. Our analysis of the literature identified the ten most influential articles, helping to clarify which are the mainstream and minority approaches (which are perhaps even more worthy of further study). The analysis based on the geographical area shows a prevalence of scientific production from Western countries. Contributions from Asia and Africa are fewer. The analysis of the research published on dynamic capabilities and digital transformation highlighted five clusters founded on the knowledge-based perspective: 1. the micro-foundation of dynamic capabilities for digital transformation; 2. dynamic capabilities for value creation in digital transformation; 3. dynamic capabilities for “data-driven organizations”; 4. dynamic capabilities for “data-driven organizations”; and 5. dynamic capabilities for digital transformation in SMEs and family firms. The first three clusters highlight issues to which the literature on digital transformation is particularly sensitive and for which it finds the concept of dynamic capabilities a useful theoretical framework. The second cluster, in fact, comprises articles analyzing new ways of creating value in a context that has been digitally transformed or that is in the process of digital transformation. From this point of view, the studies analyzed highlight the existence of a double context in which companies operate: digital; and physical ( Koch and Windsperger, 2017). In terms of dynamic capabilities, the impact of digital transformation is twofold: it requires the development of new capabilities, which we can call “digitalization capabilities,” both to adapt rapidly to changes in the digital context (Annarelli et al.,2 0 2 1) and to create new knowledge (Ghasemzadeh et al.,2 0 2 1). The third cluster focuses on a specific aspect of digital technologies, namely, the ability to collect, organize and analyze data, which can contribute to enhancing sensing capabilities (Sultana et al., 2021). This stream of literature strongly focuses on technology (Felsberger et al.,2 0 2 0; Lambourdiere and Corbin, 2020). Meanwhile, the first cluster analyzes areas complementary to the technological one, i.e. the organizational dimension (Vial, 2019) and human factors ( Warner and Wag̈er, 2019), necessary to effectively acquire dynamic skills in a hybrid digital/physical context. The last two clusters highlight the importance of the context in which both the theme of digital transformation and that of dynamic capabilities are considered. Variables such as business sector (Aghimien et al., 2021; El Sawy et al.,2 0 1 0; Rubbio et al.,2 0 2 0)o r company size (Garbellano and Da Veiga, 2019; Soluk and Kammerlander, 2021) require specific approaches and equally specific in-depth analysis of the issues highlighted by Clusters 2 and 3. The analysis of these clusters is relevant for future research, for at least three reasons: to position and locate the contributions and to investigate specific aspects of the individual topics; to highlight the specificities of the domain with respect to the research areas that generated it (answering the question of how the concept of dynamic capabilities changes in a digitized context); and to identify gaps and lines of future research. 4.2 Redefining the concept of knowledge-based dynamic capabilities In this section, we provide a response toRQ2 (How can we redefine knowledge-based dynamic capabilities in the digital transformation era?). One of the reasons justifying our review of the literature is the assumption that the new context brought about by digital transformation requires a redefinition of the concept of dynamic capabilities, in particular with reference to knowledge creation and management. (1997) and as it has been used in recent decades (Chatfield and Reddick, 2019; Matarazzo et al.,2 0 2 1; Tortora et al.,2 0 2 1), most have tried to expand or adapt the concept to a changed context of digitally transformed organizations ( Annarelli et al.,2 0 2 1; Sousa-Zomer et al.,2 0 2 0; Warner and Wag̈er, 2019). To achieve this, some scholars have pointed out the need to reconcile technology with human and organizational aspects (Vial, 2019; Warner and Wag̈er, 2019). Others have underlined the importance of managing environmental uncertainty and dynamism (Soluk et al.,2 0 2 1). One quite innovative aspect is that digital transformation has brought about the need to manage contemporarily two tightly intertwined levels in the external and internal environment of organization: the digital level; and the material level ( Koch and Windsperger, 2017). Considering that these issues that have emerged from the analysis of the literature, we propose the following definition of knowledge-based dynamic capabilities in a digitally transformed context: Definition: knowledge-based dynamic capabilities in a digitally transformed era are contextdependent and higher-order capabilities that enable a firm to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external knowledge and digital or material resources, as well as lower-order capabilities, in order to rapidly address changes related to the digital transition. Their development requires interaction both between the elements of a firm’s organizational system (strategy, structure, processes, culture and people) and between a firm and its customers, suppliers and the innovation ecosystem. Knowledge-based dynamic capabilities allow firms to realize an ongoing process of strategic renewal based on the advancements in digital technologies, to replace an organization’s business model, to develop innovation in products, services and processes, and to generate new knowledge to achieve value creation and improve firms’ performance. Since the effectiveness of this process is strictly dependent both on the interactions within the organizational system and on those between the organizational system and the external environment, dynamic capabilities must be defined and described using a holistic approach. The context-dependent nature of dynamic capabilities for digital transformation is due to the fact that the same digital capability that may be operational or ordinary in one firm may be a dynamic capability for another firm in a different context. 4.3 Implications for theory: a conceptual framework Based on our findings, this section aims to present the implications for theory, responding to RQ3 (What are the implications for the redefinition of the knowledge-based dynamic capabilities concept in the digital transformation era?). Initially, we present a conceptual framework derived from the literature review, followed by a future research agenda to highlight the novel research directions for this promising research field regarding the renewal of dynamic capabilities in the digital transformation era (seeFigure 9 ). With the exception of Chirumalla (2021), who focused on industry-level antecedents, all studies in the clusters identified organizational factors that represent antecedents of dynamic capabilities, such as exploring the digitalization vision, sensing and responding ( Annarelli et al.,2 0 2 1; Tajudeen et al., 2021). Dynamic capabilities for digital transformation are essential and strategic for SMEs as they allow the entrepreneur and her/his collaborators to develop the mindset change and knowledge base necessary to achieve successful digital transformation. In some cases, entrepreneurs and their closest collaborators have the capabilities to search and select the right sources of digital knowledge; in other cases, the executive team has the capabilities to seize and orchestrate internal and external resources ( Garbellano and Da Veiga, 2019). However, capabilities such as an entrepreneurial mindset, knowledge resources, an innovative ecosystem, strategic partnerships and cooperation are fundamental for this kind of organization ( Soluk and Kammerlander, 2021). The development of dynamic capabilities requires a “change-oriented culture” but, at the same time, they are rooted in the resource base of the company. This is extremely important, both in order not to create excessive discontinuity in the organizational transformation of the company and not to cause excessive resistance to change. Moreover, dynamic capabilities in SMEs allow firms to successfully adopt digital technologies while preserving their strategic and operational flexibility, and they can also help entrepreneurs to face crises through the adoption and reconfiguration of new resources. A strong and positive relationship between digital dynamic capabilities and strategic flexibility has been identified in SMEs. Conclusions and limitations In the conclusion of our paper, it is important to recall that the aim of our research was to contribute to theoretical and conceptual development of dynamic capabilities for digital transformation, from a knowledge-based perspective. Our research has focused on the origins and meaning of the dynamic capabilities necessary for organizations to adapt and compete in the digital transformation era. Today, business scenarios characterized by highvelocity changes due to the rapid development of digital technologies require the development of dynamic capabilities that include “knowledge acquisition,” “knowledge generation creation” and “knowledge combination” since “knowledge” constitutes the basis of competitive advantage (Beuter J/C19unior et al.,2 0 1 9; Zheng et al.,2 0 1 1). This study has aimed to investigate, from a knowledge-based managerial perspective, how organizations could implement digital innovation to achieve a competitive advantage by exploring the main critical knowledge-based dynamic capabilities to support firms’ innovation processes. In this specific regard, to date, the contributions of the literature are quite limited. Our contribution is provided through a SLR, focusing on the specific topic of dynamic capabilities in the digital transformation era, that addresses three research questions, as detailed below. Based on the analysis of the literature, we provide three key theoretical contributions to the emerging literature on dynamic capabilities for digital transformation. First, we contribute to the dynamic capabilities literature by providing insights into the typologies of specific knowledge-based dynamic capabilities that are required for digital transformation. In the past decade, disruptive digital technologies, unexpected consumer behaviors and disruptive competition have accelerated an unprecedented level of change for incumbents, as well as for SMEs and family business. In line with the literature, our findings underline that, to sustain the digital transition, all firms (regardless of the industry) need to implement changes both at the organizational and technological level by developing knowledgebased dynamic capabilities, which are defined as the “ability to acquire, generate and combine internal and external knowledge resources to sense, explore and address environment dynamics” ( Zheng et al., 2011, p. 1037). These kinds of dynamic capabilities are necessary for all organizations. Consequently, companies need to be fully equipped with dynamic capabilities for digital transformation to allow them to realize an ongoing process of strategic renewal based on advancements in knowledge suitable for digital technologies, to replace the organization’s business model; to capture customer knowledge; to generate market knowledge; to develop innovation in products, services and processes; and to achieve value creation and improve firm performance. Third, in response to RQ3, we have developed a theoretical framework of dynamic capabilities for digitally transformed organizations, comprising the main pillars that reveal the external drivers of digitalization transformation that act as antecedents and underscore the very concept of digital dynamic capabilities and the internal triggers to sustain these transformations. At the core of this framework, we have the micro-foundations of dynamic capabilities, for which we were able to identify first-order capabilities [digital scouting, digital sensing (that requires specific knowledge) and digital savvy skills]. The second component of the framework mostly concerns competitive advantage and value cocreation issues, especially for customer knowledge generation, business model innovation and digital products and services enhanced by renewed dynamic capabilities. The last three components of the framework highlight the context-dependent nature of dynamic capabilities and investigate the dynamic capabilities required to successfully start the process of digital transformation in a specific industry, with a focus on data-driven organizations and SMEs and family firms. All the components enabled redefining the concept of dynamic capabilities in a digitally transformed era, through the lens of the knowledge-based perspective. The fundamental aspect to highlight is coherent with Velu’s (2017)research since we identified several typologies of capabilities that, in isolation, could apply to nondigital-based change but that, as a system of capabilities, reflect the current industry view regarding what types of dynamic capabilities are needed to pursue digital transformation. In line with the findings of Tortora et al. (2021), the proposed framework underlines that knowledge management is a common element in all the components and represents a tool to analyze how digital transformation presents challenges for all kinds of organizations in terms of reorganizing their existing structure and resources to develop and implement process and product innovations. Consequently, knowledge-based dynamic capabilities represent an important source of innovation ( Teece, 2007; Zollo and Winter, 2002). 6.1 Limitations The present study contributes by applying a SLR for the period 2009 –2022 as a methodology to investigate the research topic in the management literature, which may be used a reference for scholars aiming to deepen understanding of this multifaceted phenomenon and represents a first attempt to provide an organic view of the literature on the topic of dynamic capabilities for digital transformation. However, some limitations must be acknowledged. The first limitation of the study is the manual approach used in the analysis of abstracts, keywords and titles, due to the lower costs and greater flexibility. Examining the impact of artificial intelligence capability on dynamic capabilities, organizational creativity and organization performance in public organizations Hamad Mohamed Almheiri Management Department, College of Business, Abu Dhabi University, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates Syed Zamberi Ahmad Department of Management, Abu Dhabi University, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates and School of Management, Canadian University Dubai, Dubai, United Arab Emirates Khalizani Khalid Dubai Business School, University of Dubai, Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Abdul Hafaz Ngah Department of Management and Marketing, Faculty of Business Economy and Social Development, Universiti Malaysia Terengganu, Kuala Terengganu, Malaysia Abstract Purpose – This study aims to evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI) capability scale using resource-based theory and tests its impact on dynamic capabilities and organizational creativity to influence the performance of public organizations. Design/methodology/approach – The study used qualitative and quantitative methods to develop and validate an AI capability scale using an integrative psychometric approach. An initial set of 26 items was selected from the literature for qualitative analysis. Self-reported data from 344 public managers in United Arab Emirates public organizations were used for scale refinement and validation. Hypotheses were tested against theoretically related constructs for nomological validation. Findings – A 23-item AI capability scale was developed. Nomological testing confirmed that AI capability positively and significantly enhances dynamic capabilities, which in turn boosts organizational creativity and improves organizational performance. Originality/value – Previous information system literature has not sufficiently addressed the importance of organizational-level complementary resources in developing distinctive capabilities within public organizations. Grounded in resource-based theory and recent AI research, this study provides a framework for public sector organizations to assess their AI capabilities. Thefindings empirically support the proposed theoretical framework, showing that AI capability increases dynamic capabilities, organizational creativity and performance. Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) has recently become a top technological priority for public organizations, driven by the need to digitally transform operations and deliver quality services to residents and stakeholders ( Mikalef et al., 2023). AI could enhance public organizations’ ability to respond to rapidly changing environments and improve service quality and speed (Rana et al., 2022; Madan and Ashok, 2023). AI adoption has surged by 270% in the past four years, tripling in the last year alone (Gerner, 2020). Despite the excitement surrounding AI’s potential, many public organizations struggle to leverage AI solutions effectively, leaving questions about how to optimize AI investments for improved organizational performance (Gesk and Leyer, 2022; Mikalef et al., 2023). Gartner (2021) reports that, although AI investments are increasing, key deployment challenges remain. In information systems (IS) literature, it is well established that organizational competitiveness arises from unique, hard-to-imitate capabilities built through the combination of complementary resources ( Karanja et al.,2 0 2 1; Madan and Ashok, 2023). This raises the question of how AI applications can enhance organizational performance, making it critical to understand the complementary resources required for this purpose (Rana et al., 2022; Mikalef et al., 2023). Research indicates that many public organizations face challenges in deploying AI because of a lack of resources or other organizational barriers (Dwivedi et al., 2021). Although some successful cases highlight important organizational factors, there remains limited theoretically grounded knowledge on building AI capability in public organizations (Priyono et al.,2 0 2 1; Giest and Klievink, 2022). The understanding of how to foster AI capability for organizational performance is still developing. This study uses resource-based theory (RBT) and dynamic capabilities (DC) to explore the resources needed for AI capability in public organizations in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Previous research suggests that dynamic capabilities complement RBT, making them a suitable theoretical lens for dynamic, turbulent environments, particularly when resource complementarity is essential ( Al Dhaheriet al., 2024; Mikalef et al., 2023). The study hypothesizes that AI capability indirectly affects organizational performance by enhancing dynamic capabilities, which in turn influence creativity and performance. It contributes to the literature by identifying the key aspects public organizations need to develop to benefit from AI and by empirically demonstrating how these improvements can be achieved. It also provides practitioners with guidance on approaching new digital technologies such as AI and highlights areas for AI initiatives. The current study develops survey instruments to quantify organizational resources and measure AI capability, following established IS literature guidelines (Mikalef and Gupta, 2021). Content validity was ensured through expert panel reviews, and psychometric properties were tested using a self-reported sample of 344 public sector employees with AI knowledge from various UAE departments. The AI capability nomological test was evaluated alongside dynamic capabilities, organizational creativity and performance. To test the research model and hypotheses, partial least squares-structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was used. The study addresses the following research questions: RQ1. What is the effect of AI capability on organizational performance? RQ2. What are the effects of AI capability on dynamic capabilities, organizational capabilities and organizational performance? Section 3 presents the research model and hypotheses, followed by a description of the methodology in Section 4. Background 2.1 Resource-based theory and dynamic capabilities The RBT, a fundamental strategic management framework, is widely used in IS literature to explore information technology (IT)-business value ( Bharadwaj, 2000; Freeman et al., 2021). Public organizations manage significant societal resources, including workforce, land, buildings and infrastructure (Clausen et al., 2019; Harvey et al., 2010). Unlike these resources, organizational capabilities– such as business capabilities, enterprise systems, processes and culture– are designed to maximize resource value (Muneeb et al., 2023; Priyono et al.,2 0 2 1). However, organizational inertia, marked by routine rigidity, impedes change and capability development (Madan and Ashok, 2023; Mariani et al., 2023). Mikalef et al.(2022) argue that AI adoption can strengthen an organization’s dynamic capabilities. Environmental turbulence and the demand for public value necessitate robust internal knowledge processes to overcome inertia (Madan and Ashok, 2023). Public managers must cultivate dynamic capabilities to integrate and restructure resources, enhancing competitive advantage (Kump et al., 2019; Teece, 2007). Rooted in RBV , dynamic capabilities are crucial for both public and private sectors, enabling the renewal of core capabilities to meet policy and service demands (Abou-Foul et al., 2023). These capabilities are categorized into sensing, seizing and reconfiguring, each essential for strategic change (Wirtz et al.,2 0 2 1). Sensing identifies market and technical needs (Wirtz and Müller, 2019), seizing evaluates capabilities (Kump et al., 2019) and reconfiguring aligns assets continuously (Matarazzo et al., 2021). Mikalef et al.(2022) highlight AI-driven activities that enhance organizational outcomes in line with these dynamic capability processes. Public organizations’ performance depends on overcoming inertia by effectively leveraging resources and capabilities (Singh et al., 2022). Dynamic capabilities in public organizations focus on integrating and reconfiguring skills and resources for improved performance (Mikalef et al., 2021; Muneeb et al.,2 0 2 3). Identifying these capabilities, especially in human resources, is crucial for knowledge creation, social integration and organizational reconfiguration, all of which are vital for public sector performance (Apascaritei and Elvira, 2022). 2.2 Artificial intelligence capability in the public sector AI technologies stand out from other advancements because of their ability to mimic cognitive functions, perform tasks in a human-like manner and learn and self-correct (Choung et al., 2022). They have diverse applications, including process automation, virtual agents, predictive analytics, recommendation systems and speech analytics (van Noordt and Misuraca, 2022), all of which can benefit public services by offering free resources, improving accuracy and reducing costs (Andersson et al., 2022). While AI adoption in government organizations is growing, it remains in the early stages (van Noordt and Misuraca, 2022). Initial research on AI adoption in the public sector has focused on factors that drive or hinder AI use, such as political, legal and policy issues (Dwivedi et al., 2021), but there is a lack of studies on how different public sector organizations can better use these technologies to enhance performance (Madan and Ashok, 2023; Mikalef and Gupta, 2021). Some research has shown that AI applications in public administration can improve perceived public service value (Gesk and Leyer, 2022), decision-making processes (van Noordt and Misuraca, 2022) and resource allocation (Mikalef et al., 2023), leading to greater effectiveness, efficiency and convenience for citizens (Martins and Picoto, 2020).
