A key reason for this is insufficient AI capability, which hinders organizations from identifying, implementing and effectively using appropriate AI technologies. Developing AI capabilities could improve organizational performance (Mikalef and Gupta, 2021). Mikalef and Gupta (2021,p .2 )d efine AI capability as“the ability of afirm to select, orchestrate, and leverage its AI-specific resources.” This suggests that organizations with robust AI capabilities can effectively use various AI technologies to create value. This concept is grounded in the RBT, which explains the link between organizational resources and performance. RBT-based studies often categorize resources into tangible, human and intangible assets in the context of capabilities (Mikalef and Gupta, 2021; Mikalef et al., 2023). Accordingly, this study considers organizational AI capability to consist of these three types of resources. Tangible AI capability resources include physical assets such as equipment and data essential for running AI applications, as well as other basic resources necessary for maintaining these applications (Madan and Ashok, 2023; Mikalef et al.,2 0 2 3; Wirtz and Müller, 2019). Human-related resources refer to the skills needed to develop and train AI applications, as well as the ability to recognize the potential of AI technologies in various business contexts (Apascaritei and Elvira, 2022). This encompasses both technical skills for handling vast data and implementing AI technologies and managerial skills for understanding the potential applications of different AI technologies (Dwivedi et al., 2021). Intangible resources related to AI capability include interdepartmental coordination and the organizational ability to initiate and implement change (Andersson et al.,2 0 2 2; Madan and Ashok, 2023). These resources should be used together to effectively measure an organization’s AI capability (Mikalef and Gupta, 2021). 2.3 Artificial intelligence capability and organizational performance Recent scholars have emphasized AI’s potential to enhance organizational performance (Mikalef et al., 2023; Olan et al., 2022; Wang, 2022). (2022) argue that AI capability necessitates dynamic capabilities across all technological environments to handle turbulence. Several studies link AI capability to improved organizational creativity and performance. Despite these promisingfindings, much of the current research is based on single cases or remains conceptual, often overlooking the concurrent mechanisms of value generation. As a result, determining how public organizations should organize around AI to maximize its impact on performance remains challenging. The literature suggests that building organization-wide AI capabilities can enable public organizations to deploy various AI applications, thereby enhancing performance ( Mikalef and Gupta, 2021). AI capability allows public organizations to move beyond isolated applications, driving digital transformation and overall performance improvements. Dynamic capabilities positively impact organizational performance. 3.2 Dynamic capabilities, organizational creativity and organizational performance Fetratiet al.(2022)define creativity as the ability to generate unconventional ideas by applying prior knowledge in novel ways. Creative problem-solving combines knowledge and experience, facilitated by divergent thinking, which generates multiple potential solutions (Pinkow, 2022). Public managers may approach problems differently, adjusting strategies to enhance public organization performance. While creativity can be individual or organizational (Fetrati et al., 2022), this study focuses on organizational creativity, which is supported by dynamic capabilities and organizational performance. Organizational creativity involves generating value through products, services, ideas, routines and processes, fostering entrepreneurial abilities within a complex social system to navigate dynamic environments (de Vasconcelloset al., 2019). Organizational creativity adds value by developing unique, rare and inimitable capabilities and resources (Fetrati et al.,2 0 2 2), driving innovation and leading to competitive advantage (Ameen et al.,2 0 2 2). In the dynamic environment of public organizations, creativity is crucial for responding to changing trends and gaining a competitive edge (Houtgraaf, 2022). Discussion and implications 6.1 Discussion This study examined AI use in public organizations through the RBT, a framework valuable for understanding IT-organization value in the IS domain (Bharadwaj, 2000). The goal was to identify the organizational resources necessary to leverage AI technologies for performance improvement. Findings emphasize AI capability’s critical role in enhancing organizational performance, both directly and indirectly, through dynamic capabilities and organizational creativity. The study confirmed the hypothesized relationships between AI capability, dynamic capabilities, creativity and performance. Mediation analysis showed dynamic capabilities significantly mediate the link between AI capability and both creativity and performance, whereas organizational creativity mediates the relationship between dynamic capabilities and performance. These results align withMikalef et al. (2023) and Ameen et al. (2022), highlighting AI’s role in fostering dynamic capabilities that drive innovation and performance. Despite AI’s potential, many studies lack a theoretical framework explaining how organizations should structure themselves to use AI effectively. IS literature often focuses on AI’s technical aspects, neglecting the challenge of aligning AI with organizational goals. This study contributes by empirically validating the interconnectedness of AI capability, dynamic capabilities and organizational creativity and underscores the need to understand the resources that enable public organizations to deploy AI, enhancing public service value, decision-making and resource allocation (Gesk and Leyer, 2022; van Noordt and Misuraca, 2022; Mikalef et al., 2023). 6.2 Theoretical implications This study contributes to AI literature in public organizations in three keyways. First, it presents a theoretical framework for AI capability, covering both technical and non-technical resources. Prior research has shown that emerging technologies create unique organizational needs ( Mikalef and Gupta, 2021; Mikalef et al., 2023). Expert panel evaluations and input from 30 public managers refined thesefindings, identifying key resources constituting AI capability. Second, the study develops an empirical construct to assess AI capabilities in public organizations, differentiating AI capability from other digital constructs such as IT capabilities. Following MacKenzieet al.’s (2011) guidelines, the instrument focuses on AI-specific technologies, skills and intangible resources, offering new insights into AI usage. Reliability and validity were confirmed through empirical research, addressing calls to define organizational capacity for leveraging AI (Bharadwaj, 2000; Mikalef et al., 2023; Mikalef et al., 2021). Finally, this study shows how AI capability impacts organizational resources, particularly its role in enhancing dynamic capabilities, creativity and performance. While previous studies noted AI’s importance in organizations (Madan and Ashok, 2023; Mariani et al., 2023; Mikalef et al.,2 0 2 0; Mikalef et al., 2021; Wamba et al.,2 0 1 7), few have empirically linked AI to key outcomes. This study demonstrates that AI capability development enables organizations to use dynamic capabilities to boost creativity and performance. It underscores that focusing solely on data and technology is insuf ficient for signi ficant results. Additionally, AI capability directly improves organizational creativity, which enhances performance, supporting the idea that strategic IT use fosters new capabilities, especially in the public sector. This study extends IS research by applying RBT to AI and identifying the resources necessary to unlock AI value. It follows Wade and Hulland’s (2004) argument that RBT enhances IS literature by specifying organizational resources and testing their relationship with performance outcomes. 6.3 Managerial implications This study emphasizes the importance of incorporating“soft” factors, such as human skills and intangible resources, in AI deployment strategies. While much literature focuses on data and infrastructure for AI implementation (e.g. Lee et al., 2021), this study highlights the critical role of intangible aspects. Technical solutions alone are insufficient for significant performance gains. Policymakers should create structures and cultures that support AI value generation, such as fostering interdepartmental coordination for smooth dataflow and AI alignment with business needs. Unlike many IT solutions, AI demands training, calibration and adaptation to new data sources, requiring a culture of collaboration across departments, aligning with calls to prioritize people and processes in AI research (Chowdhury et al., 2023). Developing an AI orientation is essential for successful deployment. The study also stresses the role of dynamic capabilities in mobilizing AI within organizations. Government sectors should prioritize both technical AI skills and managerial competencies to direct AI initiatives toward public service value. This requires training staff in emerging AI techniques and offering online resources for continuous learning. AI demands a different skill set from other IT solutions, so training and recruitment must be adapted accordingly. Furthermore, the study advocates for an ambidextrous culture that embraces risk-taking, particularly in high-potential but uncertain AI projects (Ahmad and Khalid, 2017; Ekaabi et al.,2 0 2 0; Hujran et al., 2023). Many government organizations are risk-averse when adopting new IT solutions. Becoming AI-ready involves developing AI-savvy human capital and self-assessing organizational strengths and weaknesses. The survey instrument developed in this study can help public managers identify areas needing improvement, such as technical skills or resource availability, and spot disconnected or underemphasized units, guiding resource allocation and enhancing value generation with lower costs. Some applications automate tasks, while others enhance creativity, and the derived value depends on both the technology and its implementation. Finally, from a policy perspective, public organizations can regulate AI through legal frameworks to improve public service value. Developing a talent management strategy that rewards key AI talent with recognition beyond monetary rewards ( Pereira et al., 2023) could help motivate public managers to extract discretionary efforts, linking recognition to broader reward programs. 6.4 Limitations and future directions This study has limitations. First, while the study provides a foundational understanding of the resources needed to develop AI capabilities, future research should explore context-specific resources across diverse public sector settings. Factors such as sector, organization size, AI application types and geography, which influence the resources required for successful AI implementation, should be considered. Second, future research should adopt a process-based perspective to better understand the complexities of AI deployment in public organizations. An interpretivist approach could reveal nuanced dynamics, such as stakeholder tensions, governance challenges and decision-making processes that influence AI outcomes ( Mikalef et al., 2023). This would offer deeper insights into organizational pathways and barriers, enriching our understanding of AI’s role in public sector innovation. Third, given the study’s focus on UAE public organizations, future research could explore AI capability development across regions and stages of technological adoption. Comparative studies involving organizations with differentfinancial capacities, technological sophistication and regional contexts could provide tailored strategies for AI implementation, contributing to a global understanding of AI in public administration. Finally, the reliance on self-reported data from single respondents per organization introduces bias, highlighting the need for multirespondent surveys or triangulation with objective performance metrics. Time-stamped, objective indicators before and after AI deployment would strengthen evidence of AI’s impact, enhancing the reliability offindings and allowing for more precise models of AI’s value in public organizations. 7. Conclusion This study developed and validated an AI capability scale within the RBT framework to assess its impact on dynamic capabilities, organizational creativity and performance in public organizations. Using psychometric methods, the initial 26-item scale was refined to 23 items, based on data from 344 public managers in the UAE. Hypothesis testing confirmed that AI capability significantly enhances dynamic capabilities, which in turn boosts organizational creativity and performance. The study highlights AI capability’sr o l ei n improving decision-making and problem-solving, enabling better organizational outcomes. It fills a gap in IS literature by emphasizing the importance of complementary resources for developing unique capabilities in public organizations. Grounded in RBT and AI advancements, the research offers a solid framework for evaluating and enhancing AI capabilities in the public sector. The results confirm that AI capability is crucial for driving dynamic capabilities, creativity and performance, providing valuable insights for both researchers and practitioners. Pharmaceutical supply chains are essential to health-care systems, contributing to living quality and shorter hospital stays. This study aims to examine the role of multiple integrations on business performance (BP) through supply chain flexibility (SCF) and supply chain agility (SCA). Design/methodology/approach – Data was collected from 198 supply chain professionals in the pharmaceutical sector of the developing economy of Pakistan. The sample was collected based on a nonprobability purposive sampling approach. A five-point Likert-scale survey was used and analyzed with the PLS-SEM technique using SmartPLS 4. Findings – This study found that process integration (PI) does not affect SCA, whereas relationship integration and measurement integration positively affect SCA. SCA positively impacts BP. In contrast, all integrations significantly influenced supply flexibility and BP except for PI. Finally, SCF significantly mediates the relationship between all integrations and BP. Originality/value – This study examined the relationships of multiple integrations on BP, directly and indirectly, through SCF and agility. The theory of dynamic capabilities has been applied and extended to increase the comprehensiveness of the findings. As a result of globalization, technological advancements, shorter product lifecycles, declining margins, downsized economic markets and increasingly well-informed customers with specialized and rapidly changing needs, businesses face an aggressively competitive environment (Asif, 2022). The main objective of most companies is to maximize the stakeholder’s wealth, which is largely a result of continuously increasing sales (Zhang et al., 2022). To support such growth, the timely delivery of products and services to customers is essential (Ardito et al., 2018). Pre-internet era, supply chain management depended on physical communication between parties; more recently, technology has been used to manage supply chains for optimal utilization of valuable resources (Ali et al., 2022), and more researchers and practitioners are focusing on supply chain integration (SCI) (Braunscheidel and Suresh, 2009; Flynn et al., 2010). This has necessitated increased cooperation and collaboration to improve interorganizational processes (Lambert and Cooper, 2000; Zhao et al., 2008). Globalization has resulted in challenges for firms and an increased reliance on academic and industrial researchers to contribute to the firm’s success and growth (Bildirici and Gökmenoğlu, 2017; Shen et al., 2017). Many of these challenges are related to global uncertainties driven by rapid technological and environmental changes, accompanied by changing consumer demand trends, including those related to the COVID pandemic (Brintrup et al., 2020; Cadden et al., 2020). To improve business performance (BP), companies recognize the importance of SCI (Chaudhuri et al., 2018). SCA can be a powerful tool with which to respond to these challenges (Do et al., 2021), as SCA enhances the firm’s ability to react quickly to uncertain situations (Dubey et al., 2021). Müller et al. (2022) suggest that an agile supply chain has the capacity to meet demands during periods of economic or logistic disruption. In emerging economies, the pharmaceutical industry faces several serious challenges, including those related to the supply chain (Hashmi et al., 2021); however, pharmaceuticals are a vital component of the health-care sector, contributing to improved living quality and shortened hospital stays (Hashmi et al., 2020a, 2020b). Millions of people die every year due to a lack of medicine availability or lack of access to basic medications, especially in low-income countries. According to World Health Organization estimates, 50% of the populations of some Asian and African countries lack access to life-saving pharmaceuticals, compared to the worldwide average of 30% (Saffell-Clemmer, 2021). In Pakistan, the pharmaceutical sector generated US$212m in export revenue between 2014 and 2015 (Fida et al., 2022), which is low compared to other Asian countries. Researchers and practitioners have shown an increased focus on SCA as a vital part of meeting market demands in recent years. Research on SCF and SCA has often presented the two as interrelated (Aityassine et al., 2022; Shukor et al., 2021). While such integration aims to coordinate information, resources and process flow from supplier to the end user, the result is a fundamental enabling of SCF and SCA (Khan and Wisner, 2019; Shukor et al., 2021). Thus, this research examines the mediating role of SCA and SCF between multiple integrations and a firm’s performance in the pharmaceutical industry. The novelty of this study lies in its application of the dynamic capability (DC) perspective to the supply chain context, emphasizing the importance of developing capabilities that enable organizations to respond effectively to uncertain environments, especially in the pharmaceutical industry. The study highlights the role of SCI s as a DC that facilitates new value-creation methods in unforeseen situations. It underscores the significance of both internal and external integration in enhancing SCA, positively affecting BP. Focusing on the nexus between SCA and flexibility, the study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding how these elements interact to improve organizational outcomes. Theoretical foundation 2.1 Dynamic capability view According to Teece et al. (1997), DC is a firm’s ability to integrate, build and reconfigure internal and external competencies to handle quickly changing surroundings. It is possible to distinguish between operational or “ordinary” capabilities, concerned with an organization’s existing operations and DCs. Alternatively, “the capacity of an organization to actively generate, extend, or adjust its resource base” is referred to as “dynamic capacities” (Steininger et al., 2022). The fundamental premise of the framework for DCs is that core competencies should be applied to alter short-term competitive situations, which can then be used to create a competitive advantage. Multiple dynamic abilities are needed to address new or emerging issues. Organizations and their employees need competencies that enable them to learn new skills and create strategic assets. Companies must incorporate new strategic resources, such as capability, technology and client input (Santa-Maria et al., 2022). Ultimately, it is necessary to configure or transform the current strategic assets so they better address changes in market conditions. Teece’s notion of dynamic capacities holds that what counts for business is corporate agility or the capacity to recognize and shape opportunities and threats, take chances and retain competitiveness. In doing so, the commercial enterprise’s intangible and tangible holdings that are important for business will be maximized, combined, safeguarded and, where required, reconfigured to achieve the DC and the ensuing commercial success (Bianchi et al., 2022). 2.2 Literature review 2.2.1 Integration. Organizations capitalize on their resources to enhance BP by using their capabilities (Zhang et al., 2022). Those capabilities improve their BP through collaboration (Gavronski et al., 2011). Strategic collaboration and coordination in the organizational processes are known as SCI (Donkor et al., 2021), one of the most effective strategies for firms during periods of disruption (Siagian et al., 2021). Furthermore, to survive in today’s comparative digital era, SC integrations are required (Awad and Nassar, 2010). These integrations may include process integration (PI), relationship integration (RI) and measurement integration (MI). PI is the DC that allows a firm to use its value chain partners’ assets and skills to maximize operational efficiency and develop SCA (Benzidia et al., 2021). PI includes a range of tasks, such as customer services, demand forecasting, inventory planning and logistics integration (Moody et al., 2022). PI focuses on how well organizations collaborate with their channel partners to plan and implement integrations. PI increases adaptability and flexibility to enhance responsiveness (Velvizhi et al., 2022). MI positively influences SCF. 2.2.2 Supply chain agility. SCA refers to the aspect of a firm’s operational strategy that focuses on quick response to changes in market conditions (Dhaigude and Kapoor, 2017; Yildiz and Çetindaş, 2020). According to Sharma et al. (2017), SCA is the capacity of a firm that enables it to survive during uncertain times through adaptation. SCA boosts performance by optimizing operational efficiency and reducing cost (Wu et al., 2017), thereby increasing the firm’s competitive advantage through supply chain efficiency (Cao and Zhang, 2011). Prior studies have examined how SCA affects BP, including operational and financial performance, and how its enablers, such as SC integration, might help (Junaid et al., 2022). Existing literature provides evidence for the positive influence of SCA on BP. A study emphasizes the direct and positive impact of the degree of flexibility present in the pharmaceutical industry on SCA, which influences BP. In addition, research by Deloitte Insights highlights the importance of agile supply chain organizations in improving supply chain resilience and BP, especially in the face of increasing disruptions and changes in the business environment of the pharma industry (Deloitte, 2022). Furthermore, a study by Aldhaheri and Ahmad (2023) explores the factors affecting organizations’ agility and competitive capability. This indicates that firms can enhance their competitive capabilities through agile supply chain operations, positively influencing BP at pharmaceutical manufacturing. Therefore, the existing literature consistently demonstrates the positive influence of SCA on BP. Hence, the following hypotheses are put forth for testing: H7. SCA positively influences BP. 2.2.3 Supply chain flexibility. The ability of a company to modify operational activities in response to internal and external market situations is known as supply flexibility. This study concentrates on the pharmaceutical supply-side flexibility (i.e. volume and mix). Mix flexibility (MF) has been described as “the ability of an organization to manufacture a combination of products efficiently” (Wei et al., 2021). However, volume flexibility (VF) is the ability of a business to function at various output levels without sacrificing the quality of its goods and services (Benzidia et al., 2021). Previous literature suggests that SCF improves the BP of pharmaceutical manufacturers by reconfiguring the volume and mix (Benzidia and Makaoui, 2020). According to García-Alcaraz et al. (2020), SCF helps build trust between buyers and suppliers, enabling them to adjust to product mix or volume changes. In essence, SCF refers to the capacity to anticipate shifting client demands and modify internal processes accordingly. Pharmaceutical companies deal with short lead times and constrained production schedules and may fulfil deadlines and enhance customer response through SCF (i.e. volume and mix) (Sood and Jain, 2022). Research implications 6.1 Theoretical implications The theoretical implications of the current study are significant in the context of DCV theory and supply chain management. The study emphasizes the importance of relationship and MI as important variables that significantly impact SCF. It also adds to the knowledge on DCV in three key ways. First, the study connects DCs (capability of integrations) with operational capabilities (SCF and SCA) in a developing economy to address supply chain challenges. This highlights the relevance of DCV in different economic contexts and its application to specific industry challenges. Second, the study integrates DCV into research on SCF and agility in a mediated framework. This novel approach to studying DCS and their impact on BP provides valuable insights into the contingent effects of various factors. The study demonstrates that SCA and SCF mediate multiple integrations and BP. This highlights the complex interplay between different variables in the supply chain and their impact on overall BP. The study’s focus on the pharmaceutical industry adds valuable information to the literature, as most studies are conducted in product manufacturing firms. This industry- specific focus provides insights directly relevant to the challenges and dynamics of the pharmaceutical supply chain. Overall, the theoretical implications of the study underscore the importance of DCs in addressing supply chain challenges and the need to consider the specific context and industry dynamics in the study of supply chain management. 6.2 Managerial implications The study’s findings have several managerial and societal implications for supply chain management in developing economies. The study suggests that businesses in developing economies could benefit from establishing sourcing connections with peers in surrounding Asian nations and joining forces with distinctive product offers. A multi-firm supply chain with effective multiple integrations (PI, RI and MI) can help achieve this. In addition, to address the volatility in demand and supply caused by supply chain complexity, pharmaceuticals should improve integration techniques and build SCF, which includes volume and mix. By using multiple integrations, businesses may grow their capacity for learning and market orientation while also managing volume and mix to cope with shifting market demands. From a managerial perspective, the study’s findings highlight the importance of strong cooperation and resource integration between buyers and suppliers to introduce new goods effectively. It also emphasizes the need for continuous monitoring of processes through multiple integrations to achieve flexibility and SCA. This suggests that SC practitioners must strategically plan their thinking to compete internationally and offer distinctive value propositions through multiple integrations. Limitations and future research This research has some limitations, including the fact that the study gathered data from a developing country (Pakistan), which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Hence, future researchers could gather similar sample data from a developed country and examine the variables, possibly identifying a contextual and methodology gap. Moreover, this study collected data from SC experts and executives from pharmaceutical companies, and future studies could collect data from other types of manufacturing firms. This study is cross- sectional; a similar study could be conducted with longitudinal data, which might produce interesting findings. The conceptual framework was based on DC theory; therefore, future researchers may include other underpinning theories. Finally, future research could include higher-order constructs with artificial intelligence as a moderator and supply chain performance as an endogenous variable to validate its significance for a business. A dynamic capability perspective on digital transformation: drivers, the process and consequences Chengli Shu and Keeratinun Srimuang School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, China Abstract Purpose – Despite wide awareness of the importance of digital transformation (DT) for emerging market firms, we have limited understanding of the drivers, the process or the outcomes of DT in emerging market firms. Design/methodology/approach – We conducted a qualitative study on 24 case companies in Thailand and embraced thematic analysis to generate our research findings. Findings – The framework shows that the DT process in emerging market firms proceeds over three stages— market-opportunity sensing, digital technology acquisition and leading DT—which are driven by technological dynamism, business ties and institutional support. Once DT is successfully implemented, emerging market firms can improve their operational efficiency, customer relationship management, business model innovation and human resources management. Originality/value – This study thus contributes to the DT literature by offering a three-stage model of DT and identifying important antecedents and consequences of DT, which together specify how emerging market firms transform themselves digitally. Keywords Digital transformation, Dynamic capability, Emerging market firms, Qualitative study Paper type Research paper 1. Introduction Digital transformation (DT) involves strategic and disruptive changes brought by digital technologies to a company’s business model, operational processes, products and organizational structures (Browder et al., 2024; Hess et al., 2016) and it becomes an important source of competitive advantage as digital technologies enable companies to renovate and enhance their value creation, delivery and capture (Hanelt et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2023; Vial, 2019). Although several recent literature reviews (Kraus et al., 2022; Nadkarni and Pr€ugl, 2021; Plekhanov et al., 2023; R^ego et al., 2022) indicate that scholarly attention to DT has been rising significantly in recent years, they also suggest that relatively few studies on DT in emerging markets have been published. For instance, in the four abovementioned literature reviews, only one study (Jin et al., 2020) pays attention to DT in emerging market firms (EMFs). Given the fact that EMFs lack the necessary technological basis, skilled employees, experienced managers, well-known brands and mature market–supporting mechanisms (Hitt et al., 2000; Khuntia et al., 2019), it is unclear how EMFs transform themselves digitally. More specifically, what is surprisingly lacking in the current DT literature is a comprehensive framework that depicts the processes involved, the important antecedents and the consequences of DT for EMFs. This study, therefore, aims to answer three research questions: 1) What are the drivers of DT in EMFs? 2) What are the critical stages through which EMFs progress to transform themselves digitally? 3) What are the benefits that EMFs can gain from embracing DT? In the emerging literature, dynamic capability theory has become an important lens through which to study DT. Dubey et al. (2023) suggest that digital adaptability is an important dynamic capability as it assists firms in building supply chain resilience. It is also suggested that dynamic digital capabilities become microfoundations on which to develop and introduce digital products and services (Chirumalla et al., 2023). In addition, as an important dynamic capability, strategic flexibility aids firms in leveraging digital platform capability in order to achieve greater innovation ambidexterity (Li et al., 2025). The specific stages of the DT process in EMFs remain unclear; however, as the DT literature is still evolving and there does not exist a unanimous “best practice” for all companies (Chen and Tian, 2022; Simsek et al., 2024; Volberda et al., 2021). In addition, as emerging economies differ greatly from developed ones (Anand et al., 2021; Khuntia et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2023), the DT process in EMFs might be driven by distinct factors and might have outcomes that differ from those experienced by companies that operate in developed countries. As such, it is imperative to examine important drivers and consequences of DT in EMFs. More specifically, anchored by the dynamic capability perspective, we conducted 24 case studies on EMFs in an emerging market, Thailand. We selected Thailand as the empirical site based on several considerations. First, Thailand is an emerging economy with the potential to thrive. Before the COVID-19 outbreak, Thailand’s foreign direct investment inflows increased by about 62% in 2019, a growth rate that was highest among Association of South East Asian Nations countries (United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, 2019). Second, serving as a manufacturing base for global brands in the production of subcontracted parts, especially for the automotive, electronics and electrical industries (Hobday and Rush, 2007; Laosirihongthong and Dangayach, 2005), Thai companies need to keep up with the DT requirements of their partners from more fully developed countries. Finally, the Thai government has recently announced its Thailand 4.0 policy (Chiengkul, 2019) which has a strong and clear focus on DT. Our 24 case-study companies vary in size, industry, industrial technological base, and, more importantly, their motivation and practices deployed in embracing DT. This variety provides a rich background against which to understand the DT process with practical representativeness and theoretical generalizability in accordance with the multi-case study method (Eisenhardt, 1989; Eisenhardt and Graebner, 2007). We recruited new case companies until newly added cases could no longer offer novel insights, satisfying the saturation requirement for case studies (Eisenhardt, 1989). Our research suggests that the DT process in which EMFs engage involves three important stages—market-opportunity sensing, digital technology acquisition and leading DT—that have strong theoretical anchors in dynamic capability theory in that these stages correspond to the sensing, seizing and reconfiguring elements of dynamic capabilities (Helfat and Peteraf, 2015; Teece, 2007; Teece et al., 1997). In addition, the DT process is driven by technological dynamism, business ties and institutional support. EMFs that have successfully implemented DT are relatively superior in operational efficiency, customer relationship management, business model innovation and human resources management. Therefore, this study develops a comprehensive framework which details the drivers of, processes involved in, and outcomes of DT in EMFs. By doing so, we make important theoretical contributions to the literature. First, the insights gleaned from the 24 case companies allow us to develop a dynamic capability–based view of DT that depicts how EMFs implement DT from a dynamic capability perspective and helps us identify important drivers and consequences. This process-oriented DT model contributes to the DT literature by revealing that the DT process in EMFs progresses over three important stages which flesh out the sensing, seizing and reconfiguring elements of dynamic capabilities. As such, our study offers a highly comprehensive understanding of DT in EMFs. Second, this study contributes to the dynamic capabilities literature by suggesting that DT in EMFs could be regarded as an important type of dynamic capability and that dynamic capabilities may include novel Management Decision 747 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/md/article-pdf/64/3/746/11236229/md-06-2023-1077en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 elements in the context of DT. Theoretical background 2.1 Digital transformation in emerging market firms Compared with companies that operate in developed countries, EMFs must engage in the DT process with limited resource endowments and in less advanced task environments. EMFs tend to rely on generic resources to obtain raw materials, low-cost labor and homogeneous manufacturing technologies and to offer products that are usually economically competitive, whereas companies in developed countries compete with value-added and technologyenabled products (Hitt et al., 2000; Hoskisson et al., 2000; Sheth, 2011). Moreover, EMFs suffer from deficiencies in resources, knowledge, essential capabilities (such as marketing capabilities, managerial capabilities and technological capabilities) and digital infrastructure which are critical for DT (Khuntia et al., 2019). New digital technologies such as the IoT, big data, AI and cloud computing require high-quality network infrastructure to support highspeed data transmission (Constantinides et al., 2018; F€urstenau et al., 2019; Nambisan et al., 2019). Indeed, digital infrastructure cannot be made possible solely through investment from the private sector, so it also requires government investment and support. A country-level digital infrastructure is an essential mechanism that enables entrepreneurial action (Schade and Schuhmacher, 2022). In addition, technologies such as AI and big data analytics require large pools of data and business intelligence that can be systematically managed and smoothly transferred for accurate data analysis and real-time decision-making. In fact, EMFs are relatively deficient in these areas as opposed to their counterparts in developed economies. Moreover, as EMFs are net technology receivers, they lack qualified talents and the technical know-how needed to empower creativity, which is the key to driving DT (Foo et al., 2020; Shankar and Narang, 2020). As a result, EMFs are not technologically independent because they need to rely on outsourced high-tech skills and knowledge transfer from developed economies. Although corporate innovations can be engendered by technology policies that attract entrepreneurs with incentives and promising business opportunities (Holmes et al., 2016), EMFs may also encounter turbulence in political environments as well as political interruptions and policy discontinuations (Karna et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2023; Sheng et al., 2011). Furthermore, companies in developed economies are more proficient in market competition based on experienced management teams, high-quality human resources and standardized operating procedures, making them better prepared to adopt and more competent in transforming digitally than EMFs. Although scholarly investigations of DT in EMFs have been rare, with only a few exceptions (Jin et al., 2020; Lee and Roh, 2023), DT might represent a promising avenue for EMFs seeking to reap the benefits of digital technology and catch up with their counterparts in developed countries (Khuntia et al., 2019; Lee and Roh, 2023). According to the United Nation’s World Economic Situation Prospects 2021; United Nations (2021), the rising trend toward a service economy caused by digitalization contributed, between 2005 and 2017, to a significant (greater than 10%) increase in the share of global trade in the service sector captured by developing economies through structural transformation and business diversification. This circumstance demonstrates that EMFs should enjoy promising opportunities to grasp and investigate how they could achieve DT to supply new products and services to satisfy global demand. For these reasons, we hope that an in-depth examination of DT in EMFs based on dynamic capability theory might create novel understandings that could complement prior studies conducted in other settings. Eisenhardt and Martin (2000) describe dynamic capabilities as organizational processes through which firms engage in resource utilization through strategic routines to develop new models of resource configuration in the context of changing market conditions. Zollo and Winter (2002) propose that dynamic capabilities arise from three mechanisms of organizational learning—experience accumulation, knowledge articulation and knowledge codification—that indirectly demonstrate the distinction between dynamic capabilities and operational capabilities. Dynamic capabilities help companies cope with and benefit from environmental dynamism. Such learning-to-learn skills are classified as higher-order capabilities because they permit companies to advance beyond path dependence supported by lower-order capabilities (Collis, 1994). Eisenhardt and Martin (2000) propose that dynamic capabilities benefit their possessors differently across distinct levels of market dynamism. In our case, DT creates market dynamism and companies that are accompanied by dynamic capabilities may gain the most from such dynamism. Teece (2000, 2007) has specifically emphasized that sensing and seizing opportunities related to resource configuration requires core dynamic capabilities because a company needs to build sensing and seizing abilities to be aware of and astutely exploit business opportunities in a timely fashion. A highly developed sensing capability supports information acquisition and processing in the task environment and opportunities derived from sensing must be seized by responding to competitive moves and/or developing novel innovations to solve customer problems (Teece, 2007). Reconfiguration of a company’s tangible and intangible assets helps to maintain congruency and co-evolve with the changing environment while breaking free of unfavorable path dependencies (Teece, 2007). A series of studies support the view that dynamic capabilities can be better understood by reference to a process consisting of three steps—sensing opportunities, seizing opportunities and resource (re)configuration (Teece, 2007, 2012; Teece et al., 1997)—and we focus on this process as a theoretical anchor for our investigation of the DT process in EMFs. The above discussion suggests that dynamic capability theory should provide an effective theoretical lens through which to understand DT in EMFs based on the following considerations. First, dynamic capabilities are often recognized as the groundwork for obtaining competitive advantages, particularly in technologically dynamic contexts (Brock and Hitt, 2024; Peteraf et al., 2013; Teece, 2007), while DT substantially alters and upgrades companies’ technological bases, paths and structures (Gong and Ribiere, 2021; Hanelt et al., 2021). For example, Felin and Powell (2016) explain that internet-based technologies have shifted the competitive landscape and made industries more volatile than in the past, requiring higher-order capabilities to make it possible to anticipate, shape and sustain innovation. Indeed, Karimi and Walter (2015) emphasize dynamic capabilities that are generated by organizational adaptation of resources, processes and values that impact the ability to counter digital disruptions. As such, digital adaptability as an important driver of supply chain resilience (Dubey et al., 2023) and digitally enabled dynamic capabilities are microfoundations of servitization in firms (Chirumalla et al., 2023). Second, dynamic capabilities and the DT process share a common linkage with market dynamism (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000; Gong and Ribiere, 2021). Digital technologies yield substantial information flow between customers and firms and between customers, which accelerates market changes and innovations as well as customer preferences and market trends (Guo et al., 2019b; Li et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2020). Guo et al. (2019b) reveal that Huawei, as a latecomer in the global market, explores windows of opportunity after fostering strategies in technology-building and market-seeking. Thus, DT can be regarded as a strategic response to market challenges and the DT process itself can generate dynamics for companies in response to market challenges and opportunities (Gong and Ribiere, 2021; Hanelt et al., 2021). Finally, emerging markets feature dramatic market dynamics (e.g. customer demand and competitive moves) and unpredictable regulatory changes (Hitt et al., 2000; Karna et al., 2022; Khuntia et al., 2019), making them an ideal context in which to demonstrate the explanatory power of dynamic capability theory and show how it can help EMFs catch up with or surpass their counterparts in developed counties through embracing DT. Methodology We conducted a qualitative study and our empirical data were collected through multiple case studies (Eisenhardt, 1989; Eisenhardt and Graebner, 2007; Yin, 2014). We argue that this qualitative study method matches our research objectives based on three key considerations. First, since the current literature lacks an in-depth understanding of DT in EMFs, case studies which can offer broad insights permit us to gather a more expansive view concerning the antecedents of, processes involved in and consequences of DT without limiting informants within a discriminative response structure. Case studies can also help us delve into underlying evidence of relationships suggested by the “why” question (Eisenhardt, 1989). Second, we can draw novel insights or new concepts from informants’ reflective views based on their individual scenarios and experiences that are not likely to be revealed through statistical or quantitative information (Gioia et al., 2013; Magnani and Gioia, 2023), especially when there is little existing prior theoretical guidance. Lastly, we can compare field data with the extant literature to develop a more comprehensive framework which has strong robustness and generalizability (Eisenhardt and Graebner, 2007). Since we applied the standard of saturation in the sampling process, we were able to glean broadly insightful views from managers working in a range of industries. In summary, we followed a standard procedure to conduct the qualitative study and our case companies provide relevant data that reflect actual business criteria and evidence that allowed us to answer our research questions. 3.1 Research setting and case selection The theoretical sampling procedure we employed was designed to enable us to acquire the most in-depth data possible, because this technique allows researchers to access relevant empirical data when a selected sample consists of actual players in a real context. As a result, our case companies were not limited to specific industries, so we were able to obtain observations of DT in various types of businesses (e.g. the automotive, electronics and food industries as well as IT, retail and insurance services) and sizes (ranging from five to 62,556 employees) in Thailand, enabling us to explore the DT process from multiple angles. Having done so, we believe that the commonalities and differences between companies we observed can provide us with novel and insightful perspectives. To access appropriate cases, interview participants were chosen after consulting with related government and non-government agencies that were familiar with DT embracers in multiple sectors and noting personal recommendations from interviewees. The sampling process was terminated when no novel insights were forthcoming from interviewees (Charmaz, 2006), suggesting that we had achieved robustness in the saturated data. The selected 24 case companies are actual DT practitioners that demonstrated diverse stages of DT, allowing us to explore multiple angles on DT in multiple backgrounds. The interviews were conducted according to the Eisenhardt’s (1989) procedure. Open-ended questions permitted us to explore informants’ perspectives to better understand the detailed scenarios that each company faces in the DT process. In accordance with Gioia et al. (2013), semi-structured interviews allowed experienced participants to contemplate differences between retrospective and actual time in the interest of theoretical comprehensiveness. The interview structure incorporated three main elements. The first element focused on attributes of informants and firms such as job positions, duties and industries. The second element focused on DT concepts, including participants’ understanding of DT including key approaches, challenges and factors contributing to success or failure and an overview of changes that have occurred. The third element combined informants’ opinions and explanations with the extant literature, which informed the coding procedure. This helped us connect and cross-check emerging codes with relevant DT conceptualization through symbolic interaction to reach grounded theoretical insights (Charmaz, 2006). During a four-month period of data collection in 2021, we gathered interview data from 24 case companies. All interviews were conducted in face-to-face fashion. The respondents were restricted to managerial positions or higher because the questions were designed to acquire management perspectives and capabilities as well as a holistic view of how organizations have implemented DT. The diversity of the interview participants in their management positions offered us the opportunity to understand a wide range of managerial capabilities and working experience with DT. Each interview took about one hour to twoand-a-half hours. All interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed and translated from Thai into English, with a total interview time of 34 h 46 min, producing and a total of 187 transcribed pages. 3.3 Data analysis The data analysis process started after all interview data were gathered and sorted to estimate similarities and differences between DT processes in EMFs as well as their drivers and consequences. To maintain the reliability and validity of our findings, we followed the Gioia methodology (Gioia et al., 2013) as a rigorous systematic qualitative approach to evaluate correlations between the data and theories as well as the viability of the results. More specifically, data were gathered to develop first-order concepts and second-order themes for data rendition to aggregate concepts to further establish a framework for the data structure (Gioia et al., 2013). First, reflective perceptions regarding various aspects of DT were grouped according to the informants’ business environments. A set of relevant perceptions were aggregated, from which we selected representative quotes as our zero concepts. We then conducted data coding to frame the consolidation of the first-order concepts that were aggregated from the informants’ concepts. This stage was carried out through evaluating interview transcripts to nominate informants’ quotes that could draw out common understandings. Second, we analyzed the first-order coding data, which represented the informants’ perceptions of particular factors, to identify broader themes that the first-order concepts represented. This stage was developed through intensive comparison with relevant theories and helped foster symbolic interactions with theoretical implications (Charmaz, 2006). According to Gioia et al. (2013), second-order themes are theoretical domains where emerging phenomena are identified. DT may require firms to acquire new technical skills and knowledge from external sources, especially EMFs, which are inferior in technological know-how (Grimpe et al., 2023; Khuntia et al., 2019). This helps firms explore available technologies to foster internal knowledge management. However, EMFs usually lack the resources and capabilities that are needed to operate the new systems or machines enabled by digital technologies (Khuntia et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2023). The founder of SI-Rbot1 and the managing director of Drone9 noted, respectively: This is because if we want to provide DT services, we need to attain knowledge as well as have DT implemented throughout the organization. We acquire know-how from international research while accessing academic laboratories provides high-tech testing tools and consistent results. Many informants, such as those from PartSup2, Autosteer5, Aeropart8, Drone9, Autopart17 and SmartDC18, also reported that their knowledge was acquired from other sources such as business networks, supply chain ecosystems and international research. This is consistent with current understanding that external technological knowledge is a critical source for companies seeking to develop their own competencies (Awate et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2019b). Researchers (Monteiro and Birkinshaw, 2017) explain that more successful firms in this respect possess three essential characteristics: absorptive capability, external networks and boundary-spanning, which extend organizational potential by broadening organizational knowledge and competency boundaries. The personal level relates to senior managers’ personal relationships with their networks of entrepreneurs and managers (Peng and Luo, 2000; Sheng et al., 2011; Shu et al., 2012). Managerial ties determine the familiarity and similarity of cultural bonds between business leaders, impacting cooperation and information-sharing (Gao et al., 2008, 2017; Shu et al., 2012). The role of government is principally to stimulate a country’s economic growth (Anand et al., 2021; Lazzarini, 2015). The Thai government has offered strong concrete support for DT since 2016 (Desatova, 2018; Jones and Pimdee, 2017). As a result, this policy change encourages companies to emphasize advanced technologies and embrace DT. When a policy is introduced, the government may initiate policy stimulators such as tax and non-tax incentives, measures, awards and budgetary support to bring companies on board. As EMFs are not technology-independent, their capacity to sense and seize new business opportunities as well as reconfigure routines indicate their readiness to conform with DT requirements. Such readiness includes budgeting, knowledge and infrastructure for building digital ecosystems because DT requires firms to reinvent, reinvest and restructure both structural-based and knowledge-based assets. Among the 24 case studies, the greatest gains have been achieved by firms that attain greater readiness to respond to changes in the market, especially incumbent firms that upgrade their information systems continually and have larger IT investment budgets. According to their business models, firms that rely heavily on the accuracy of their information databases that are larger and have built customer bases, such as SI-Rbot1, Electro14 and Retail16, are better able to adjust their business models to satisfy customer needs through digital technologies. As a result, they are keen to invest in cutting-edge digital technologies and compatible digital infrastructure as they swiftly fine-tune their vital resources, including human resources, to efficiently operate advanced systems. This trend can be observed in the diversity of their technology usage and flexibility in business operations. For instance, these firms they can effortlessly work off-site and on-site or modify production customization to suit exquisitely detailed requirements. Discussion and conclusion Based on dynamic capability theory, we examine 24 companies for a case study and develop a more comprehensive framework which details the DT process and its important drivers and consequences in EMFs. We find that the DT process in EMFs includes three stages—marketopportunity sensing, digital technology acquisition and leading DT—and this process is driven by technological dynamism, business ties and institutional support. Once EMFs successfully implement DT, they enhance their operational efficiency, customer relationship management, business model innovation and human resources management. 5.1 Theoretical contributions This qualitative study contributes to the literatures on DT and dynamic capabilities in several ways. First, we contribute to the DT literature by developing a dynamic capability–based framework for the DT process in the context of EMFs. Mapping the three elements (sensing, seizing and reconfiguring; Teece, 2007, 2012; Teece et al., 1997) of dynamic capabilities onto the DT process, we find that the development of a market-sensing capability initiates the DT process as it helps companies implement DT at a level such that their strategic planning outcomes meet their targeted business positions. As emerging economies usually lack robust digital infrastructure and EMFs lag behind companies in developed countries in advanced digital technologies (Khuntia et al., 2019), the second stage of the DT process in EMFs involves acquisition of digital technology. Our research also shows that the conduits that EMFs use to acquire digital technologies vary significantly. Finally, leading DT is the final stage, where leadership determination, organizational persistency and managerial capabilities are the key ingredients. The DT process generates substantial rents only when companies capitalize on market opportunities by exploiting the acquired digital technologies. As such, our research contributes to the DT literature by opening up the “black box” of the DT process and thereby adding to what prior studies have found regarding the conceptualization of DT and its antecedents and consequences (Gong and Ribiere, 2021; Hanelt et al., 2021). By doing so, our research enriches dynamic capability theory in that it fleshes out the sensing, seizing and reconfiguring elements of dynamic capabilities through the corresponding three stages of DT in EMFs: market-opportunity sensing, digital technology acquisition and leading DT. Second, we expand the DT literature by identifying important drivers and consequences of the DT process in EMFs. We reveal that technological dynamism is the primary trigger of DT. Technologies have evolved at an unprecedented pace in recent decades, and EMFs have to embrace DT through adopting advanced digital technologies to remain competitive rather than being disrupted by these technologies (Chan et al., 2019). Moreover, our study demonstrates that business ties are a critical channel through which firms acquire resources, knowledge and business opportunities, aiding their DT process. This finding is consistent with the proposition that senior managers’ personal linkages with other business leaders are important to their businesses in emerging economies (Peng and Luo, 2000; Sheng et al., 2011; Shu et al., 2012), but our study is among the first to find evidence that business ties are also important for DT in EMFs. Additionally, we discover that governmental and institutional support can significantly influence the DT process in EMFs. As such, governments and related institutions should help EMFs along with the DT process, which is time-and resource-consuming. Finally, our study also reveals that, once EMFs have successfully adopted DT, they enhance their operational efficiency, customer relationship management, business model innovation and human Management Decision 769 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/md/article-pdf/64/3/746/11236229/md-06-2023-1077en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 resources management. These findings from EMFs add to prior insights that have largely involved firms that operate in developed countries (Hanelt et al., 2021). Third, we enrich the current DT literature by substantiating the importance of the emerging market context. Since EMFs may lag behind their counterparts in more developed countries in digital infrastructure, technologies, mindset and skills (Schade and Schuhmacher, 2022; Shankar and Narang, 2020), their DT process may indeed be different (Kraus et al., 2022; Plekhanov et al., 2023; R^ego et al., 2022). On the one hand, the three-stage model (marketopportunity sensing, digital technology acquisition and leading digital transformation) of DT in EMFs explicitly maps onto the three components of dynamic capabilities (Teece, 2007, 2012; Teece et al., 1997). As such, our model has a strong theoretical anchor as the process of DT in EMFs is consistent with dynamic capability theory and this theory can also reflect the dynamic environments where EMFs digitally transform themselves. On the other hand, our three-stage model of DT in EMFs combines both technological and human aspects of the DT process, which is consistent with a recent review of DT (Nadkarni and Pr€ugl, 2021). Our findings support the idea that the “digital transformation needs both technology and people” (Nadkarni and Pr€ugl, 2021, p. 234) and thus provide a more comprehensive understanding of DT in EMFs. Finally, we contribute to the dynamic capability literature by suggesting that DT is an important dynamic capability in EMFs. As dynamic capability theory highlights the essence of asset orchestration in dynamic environments (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000; Teece, 2007; Teece et al., 1997), DT becomes an important conduit through which companies can co-evolve with changing environments given that DT helps in maintaining synergy between a company and its volatile environment through resource orchestration (Chen and Tian, 2022). Although recent studies show that digital adaptability (Dubey et al., 2023) and strategic flexibility (Li et al., 2025) are important dynamic capabilities, it is still unclear whether DT could be an important dynamic capability as this is also evidenced in a recent systematic review of the dynamic capability literature (Brock and Hitt, 2024). This systematic review summarizes that there are six meta-dynamic capabilities (agility, building/upgrading, leveraging, reconfiguring/transforming, seizing and sensing) and six strategic dynamic capabilities (ambidexterity, asset/resource management/orchestration, entrepreneurship, innovation/new product development, knowledge creation and localization/adaptation), but DT is not mentioned in connection with these capabilities. Our case studies show that DT has become an essential tool that cannot only link entire internal operational systems in EMFs but also enable them to integrate their supply chain partners to establish a digital ecosystem. Thus, DTcould be considered an important dynamic capability for companies, especially EMFs. Therefore, this study adds a new form of dynamic capabilities (i.e. DT) beyond those included in the recent review (Brock and Hitt, 2024). 5.2 Managerial and policy implications Our major findings provide several implications for managers and policymakers. First, our identification of the three important stages of the DT process offers managers a hands-on guide for how to pursue DT. To initiate the DT process, managers need to identify market opportunities, understand how technologies impact their business operations and customer behaviors, and evaluate the advantages and disadvantages that DT might bring. For the digital technology acquisition stage, our research suggests that managers can rely on business collaborations, academic institutions and personal networks. As such, managers need to participate in a variety of industrial organizations, business networks and personal social activities to be actively and deeply involved in diverse networks. Our study also shows that partners in a company’s supply chain can offer opportunities for sharing knowledge and orchestrating resources, thereby enhancing digital technology acquisition. Lastly, the leading DT stage highlights the leadership and managerial capabilities that are needed to manage the entire DT process. Second, we recommend that managers pay close attention to technological dynamism, business ties and institutional support when boosting their DT efforts. Technologies are shaping every element of business, including products, processes and customers. To embrace rather than avoid technological trends, managers need to, for example, integrate their operations into the IoT using machines that offer remote service, use e-commerce to expand their markets, install robots and automation in high-risk areas and choose social media to foster customer relationships. Moreover, managers can rely on personal ties when seeking assistance, support and resolutions for DT. Managers also need to develop and expand their business ties with government agencies and industrial associations to gain institutional support and to maintain good rapport with partners who have finished their DTs. Moreover, companies can collaborate with academic institutions in joint R&D efforts to develop innovation and recruit talents. Finally, governmental and non-governmental institutions, such as research institutes and industrial associations, need to offer generous support to encourage DT in EMFs. The government can offer budgetary support, rewards and other incentives such as tax-reduction policies to establish a pro-DT environment. Our case studies reveal that institutional support considerably influences DT in EMFs. To support EMFs pragmatically as they seek to complete their DTs, the government should emphasize both output-based and input-based measures to establish a virtuous cycle. As the DT process consists of important stages, the government should introduce stage-specific policies and incentives to help EMFs initiate, evolve and implement DT. For example, exhibitions, networking and company visits could be organized by the government or industrial associations in the initial stages of DT (sensing market opportunities); policy measures and incentives that promote inter-organizational and international collaborations should be issued at the stage of acquiring digital technologies; and finally output-based incentives such as tax reduction and rewards could be offered based on the degree to which companies have achieved DT. 5.3 Limitations and future research Although we have followed widely accepted procedures to conduct this qualitative study, our research may be subject to limitations while also suggesting possibilities for future investigations. First, although the objectives of theoretical sampling in selecting cases can expand the boundaries of emergent theory (Eisenhardt, 1989), we did not select our case companies randomly. Fortunately, our case companies are experienced and knowledgeable in the area of study (i.e. DT), which may successfully address the limitation associated with purposeful sampling. In addition, as our case companies are located in areas close to highways, airports and deep-sea ports for convenient transportation, this might limit the variety of data collected regarding company locations. Future studies could sample companies in more remote areas as such companies may face additional pressures and pursue unique purposes for undertaking DT. In so doing, scholars might be able to paint a different picture of DT. At the same time, future research is needed to examine the mechanisms underpinning the influence of drivers of DT in EMFs. Because our research is qualitative in nature, we cannot quantity the impacts of the identified antecedents of DT, which future studies are welcome to examine. Second, we selected Thailand as our data-collection site for several good reasons, but this country is more likely a technology-receiver than a technology-developer. Previous studies have shown that technological infrastructure is important for DT (Hanelt et al., 2021; Lyytinen et al., 2016), and as digital infrastructure drives technology usage that satisfies societal demand (Constantinides et al., 2018; Malik et al., 2024; Senyo et al., 2023), future explorations could consider other, more highly developed, emerging economies such as China Management Decision 771 Downloaded from www.emerald.com/md/article-pdf/64/3/746/11236229/md-06-2023-1077en.pdf by Tongji University user on 23 September 2026 and India. For instance, China and India have established a strong basis for the software industry, which is an important facilitator of digital technologies. Moreover, businesses nowadays can access much cheaper open-source software and platforms that can be easily scalable, such as Google Cloud and Microsoft Teams, which help firms optimize their service designs for targeted markets (Gomber et al., 2018). As such, future studies could replicate our study in other emerging markets. Moreover, future studies are also needed to conduct cross-country comparisons to understand how, when and why companies pursue DT. Third, future studies could employ large-scale surveys or secondary data to validate, test and enrich our conceptual model. Although our 24 case companies provide rich experiencebased evidence regarding the DT process and its antecedents and consequences, the detailed relationships between constructs in our conceptual framework cannot be verified using case studies. To corroborate our framework and offer a more fine-tuned understanding of how EMFs pursue DT and how this could influence their performance outcomes, we need to rely on large-scale surveys or secondary data. Finally, research topics such as the social and environmental aspects of DT are emerging in the DT literature, so future studies are needed to explore how DT in EMFs can enhance or hurt social welfare, justice and fairness in these countries. For example, it is promising and important to examine whether DT in EMFs can lead to wage divides or payment unfairness because some types of labor would be replaced by robots. In addition, scholars could develop and examine some novel constructs such as responsible DT, green DT and ethical DT by conducting qualitative studies followed by quantitative studies if relevant data are available. Veiga5,6 · Luís Farinha6,7 Received: 20 May 2021 / Accepted: 21 June 2022 / Published online: 18 July 2022 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2022 Abstract Dynamic capabilities (DCs) are a growing field of research within the scope of theoretical structures based on resource and strategic management. Given the demonstrated impact of DCs on company performance, it is important to study the effects of DCs on small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs) within the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. Hence, this research evaluates the role of DCs during the pandemic and its impact on the performance levels of SMEs. Analysing the responses of 209 SMEs using a structural equations model, we report that DCs positively affect company performance both prior to and during the pandemic. However, we also verify that while prior to the pandemic companies placed greater emphasis on the search for new opportunities, following the onset of the pandemic the focus shifted to getting their products to the market. These results contribute to the literature on strategic management and the DC based approach during periods of turbulence and pandemics. Keywords Dynamic capabilities · SME · Performance · COVID-19 pandemic JEL Classification M10 · L10 1 Introduction Between 2007 and 2013, the world experienced one of the most severe economic recessions since the Great Depression of the 1930s. The peripheral countries of Europe—Portugal, Italy, Ireland, Greece and Spain—ranked among those most severely affected.
