Irrespective of the economic recov - ery that came about, with the difficulties inherent to each respective country, 2020 brought another major crisis, entirely unprecedented and unpredictable, namely the COVID-19 pandemic (Clark et al., 2020; Clauss et al, 2021; Breier et al, 2021). The economic and social restrictions implemented to contain global crises inevitably caused major disruptions for companies. Within such an environment, the secret to untying this gordian knot arises from the development of dynamic capabilities (DCs) (Fainshmidt et al, 2017). Thus, deploying DCs serves to enhance the likelihood of organisational success within the currently prevailing context (Bailey and Breslin, 2020). Eisenhardt and Martin (2000) define DCs as the organisational and strategic routines by which companies obtain new configurations of resources in keeping with how markets emerge, collide, divide, evolve and die. Hence, DCs affect company performance to the extent that it changes the package of resources, operational routines, and competences that, in turn, shape the firm’s economic performance (Helfat and Raubitschek, 2000; Zollo and Winter, 2002). Teece et al. (1997) defend how companies need to apply specific abilities to be able to effectively integrate, create, and reconfigure the internal and external competences necessary to their adaptation to rapidly changing environments. Various authors not only point out the need to study DCs but also to understand how these affect organisational performance in both internal and external environments (Wang and Ahmed, 2007; Ambrosini and Bowman, 2009; Helfat et al., 2009; Stoyanova, 2018; Grigoriou and Rothaermel, 2017; Zhang and Wu, 2017; Teece, 2018). This indicates that DCs are essential when engaging in substantial and significant operations in globally competitive environments (Galbreath, 2005; Ahn and York, 2011). In this context, we propose that the performance of SMEs during the different phases of global crises (like COVID-19, for example) stems from the extent to which the SMEs are able to create, expand, or deliberately modify their resource bases (Helfat et al. 2007), hence, their DCs (Eikelenboom and Jong 2018). The distribution of DCs attains a heterogeneous incidence in companies given that they require high management and operating costs as well as high levels of managerial involvement (Ambrosini and Bowman, 2009). Therefore, the existing literature recognises the sweet-and-sour nature of social capital (Gao et al., 2017), proposing it as a facilitator and/or inhibitor of DCs depending on the surrounding external environment (Yeniaras et al., 2020). Various researchers focus on the characteristics of the behaviours that enable SMEs to deal with diverse and different challenges as well as to improve their per - formance vis-à-vis large companies (Brouthers et al., 2009; Oura et al., 2016; Lobo et al., 2018; Nakos et al., 2018). However, instability arises in different ways in market environments, with the meaning and relevance of DCs varying in accordance to the nature of the respective prevailing instabilities. Our study approaches the relationship between DCs and SME performance within an unstable environment of crisis; in this case, the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore, this study addresses the following research question: How do DCs affect SME performance during the COVID-19 pandemic crisis? Our research seeks to cast light on the ways in which DCs shape and influence the performance of SMEs during crises. However, we are aware that companies also 1705 1 3 The impact of dynamic capabilities on SME performance during... differ in the way they deal with crises: some suffer considerably, others avoid the worst effects, while still others detect business opportunities. Thus, this study makes various contributions to the literature. First, it contributes to the literature by testing for the direct effects of DCs on the performance of SMEs during a pandemic. Studying the ways in which companies adapt and implement their DCs fosters a better understanding of this multidimensional construct as well as the ongoing relationships among its respective different aggregating subdimensions. Economic downturns normally trigger profound industrial changes due to the fact that demand becomes so much more volatile. DCs may help companies get through these turbulent periods and, potentially, identify new business opportunities. Secondly, it provides new lines for future research on the role of DCs in the per - formance of SMEs in times of crisis. Considering how the dynamism of companies is frequently assumed to be a defining condition for the capability-performance relationship (Peteraf et al., 2013), we demonstrate that DCs perform a fundamental role in the survival and competitiveness of firms facing adverse environments (Wang and Ahmed, 2007). Furthermore, and thirdly, there is a lack of research studying the relationship between DCs and the performance of SMEs within the framework of global crises like a global pandemic (Makkonen et al., 2014; Fainshmidt et al, 2017). Finally, this study also provides important implications for managers of SMEs. The conclusions convey how those SMEs that deploy/apply their DCs are able to ensure higher levels of performance in periods of crisis through their greater capacity to optimise their resource utilisation and capabilities in keeping with the appropriate deployment of their distinctive competences. The remainder of this paper is organised as follows: in Sect. 2, we set out the theoretical underpinnings; Sect. 3 presents hypothesis development and conceptual model; Sect. 4 details the methodology, while Sect. 5 outlines the results and Sect. 6 provides the discussion of their implications, conclusions, limitations and future lines of research. 2 Theoretical underpinnings As an offshoot of the resource based view (RBV), DCs emerged as an approach for understanding strategic changes (Teece et al., 1997), seeking to provide a structure for how companies develop and maintain competitive advantages in turbulent environments within the scope of identifying the determinants underlining long term success (Wilden et al., 2016; Alves & Galina, 2020). Over the years, this definition has been revised and expanded, resulting in various conceptualisations. Furthermore, the descriptions of DCs frequently define them as company processes that consume resources, specifically the processes for integrating, reconfiguring, obtaining, and releasing resources to keep up with or even to create changes in the marketplace. Hence, perceptions of DCs may also encapsulate the organisational and strategic routines and processes through which companies lever - age new configurations of their resources in keeping with how markets emerge, collide, divide, evolve, and die (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000; Ahmed et al. 2019). 1706 M. Dejardin et al. 1 3 Frequently, the operational implementation of DCs involves a set of distinctive groups of activities to explain how they function and thus to operationally apply them. According to Barrales-Molina et al. (2014), these groups generally divide up into the characteristics broadly accepted for such DC processes, such as reconfiguration, leveraging, learning, integration and coordination (Teece et al., 1997; Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000; Dabić, et al. 2019). Thus, the DC approach appears to be one of the most popular in the field of strategic management (Arend, 2014). Teece et al. (1997) put forward the first comprehensive approach to DCs in the scientific literature. Subsequently, hundreds of articles and studies conceptually approach this topic (Di Stefano et al., 2014; Fernandes et al., 2017; Vlačić, et al. 2019). The swift growth of the DCs literature includes a broad theoretical variety and considerable methodological scope, thus rendering it difficult, but not impossible, to maintain close control over the directions this research field takes. Various studies establish the intellectual foundations of the DC approach, not just summarising the definitions, but also discussing the respective components, determinants, obstacles, key empirical results, as well as identifying the conceptual shortcomings and the difficulties arising from its empirical applications (Zahra et al., 2006; Schreyögg and Kliesch-Eberl, 2007; Wang and Ahmed, 2007; Ambrosini and Bowman, 2009; Helfat and Peteraf, 2009; Barreto 2010; Fernandes et al., 2017; Hock-Doepgen, et al. 2021). An additional problem stems from the increasing proliferation of relevant publications. This is reflected in the considerable differences across the multiple perspectives regarding the perceptions and applications of DCs as well as on their varying influences on the development of strategic management. Arend (2014) concludes that this only somewhat vague or inconsistent theoretical justification places the DC approach at a disadvantage to other strategic management approaches. The same author is also critical of how this concept generally underutilises organisational theory and, more specifically, organisational change concepts like "absorption capacity", "organisational learning", and "change management". In contrast, Helfat and Peteraf (2009) respond by arguing that the terminological and conceptual variety simply reflect the complexity of the phenomena under study and that it inherently requires multiple theoretical visions. These authors maintain that the continued exploration of fundamental research issues and the lack of empirical validation are characteristics of any field of research in its adolescent phase of development. Thus, the relevance of research focusing on DCs remains. DCs enable prospecting for new opportunities in business environments and converting organisational resources into assets as well as tangible and intangible capacities (Easterby-Smith et al., 2009; Lucianetti, et al. 2018; Lövingsson, et al. 2000). The value creation processes explore these opportunities through the efficient and effective development of new products and services. Consequently, these dynamic resources reflect the capacities of organisations to create, extend, and intentionally modify their existing resource base. Thus, these resources facilitate change and renewal, ultimately fostering innovation that achieves a better adaptation to the sur - rounding environment (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000; Zollo and Winter, 2002; Winter, 2003; Zahra et al., 2006; Helfat et al., 2007; Dabić et al. 2013). 1707 1 3 The impact of dynamic capabilities on SME performance during... Hence, there are different conceptions regarding whether dynamic capabilities may inherently represent a source of increased performance (Baia et al., 2020; Wilden et al., 2016; Vrontis, et al. 2020). An initial phase in the approach to dynamic capabilities postulated a direct relationship between company DCs and their later performance (Makadok, 2001; Teece et al., 1997; Maley et al. 2020). Teece et al. (1997) share assumptions with the RBV that stipulates how resources are valuable, rare, difficult to imitate, and organisational (the VRIO model). Therefore, whenever DCs attain such characteristics, they may become a direct source of sustainable competitive advantages and, therefore, drivers of better performance (Barney, 1991; Ferreira and Fernandes, 2017; Singh et al. 2019). Not every company experiences the consequences of a crisis in the same fashion (understandable, as companies are financially and intangibly differ - ently endowed); companies also benefit differently from the government policies designed to recover from a crisis. Should we adopt the theories of cognitive behaviour and planning from the mid-1990s, then entrepreneurship becomes conceived as a process involving both perceptions of opportunities and the subsequent actions leading to the launching of new companies (Krueger, 1993; Busenitz et al., 2000). During turbulent periods, sporadic shocks in the business cycle affect not only labour markets but also individuals launching new companies (Audretsch and Acs, 1994; Highfield and Smiley, 1987). Hence, theories on company life cycles maintain that economic shocks may produce ambiguous effects (Parker, 2011; Fairlie, 2013). Such shocks may enable individuals to detect and explore new entrepreneurial opportunities arising from the recessionary context or, alternatively, such uncertainties may dissuade individuals from searching for and detecting new business opportunities due to their innate pessimistic growth expectations (González-Pernía et al., 2018). Correspondingly, the interrelationship between the organisation and its operational environment, in conjunction with the respective impact on company per - formance, make up central research themes and remain a focus of debate among management theoretical specialists (Makkonen et al., 2014; Santos et al., 2020). This has led to the identification of certain processes and organisational capacities as more specific DCs, including dynamic marketing resources, dynamic management resources, specific supply chain resources, and alliances. The discussion on the nature of the relationship between the DCs and company performance emerged at roughly the same time as the concept itself. The question of how DCs really shape and affect company performance remains unknown, very much at the centre of debate (Pezeshkan et al., 2016). Further - more, other authors express less confidence in any necessary and direct inter - relationships (Barreto, 2010). Eisenhardt and Martin (2000), for example, reinforce the idea that DCs are, in fact, necessary, but insufficient, for generating competitive advantage. Within the framework of this vision, competitive advantage and long term performance do not depend on the DCs themselves but rather on their configurations and the effects of change (Barreto, 2010). 1708 M. Dejardin et al. 1 3 3 Hypothesis development and conceptual model As of 2022, the world is in crisis, experiencing unprecedented economic disruption, because COVID-19 not just affects societies but also companies, especially if not handled appropriately (Pedersen et al., 2020; Cortez and Johnston, 2020; Obal and Gao, 2020; Zafari et al., 2020; Wenzel et al., 2021; Harms et al. 2021). Despite unprecedented levels of state support, estimates of the global economic contractions range from 6.1% in the United States, 9.1% in the Eurozone, and 7.2% in Latin America and the Caribbean to low growth of 0.5% in East Asia and the Pacific (World Bank, 2020). SMEs appear to be more vulnerable to exter - nal shocks due to their limited safety networks, access to credit, and social capital (Menguc and Dayan, 2020; Yeniaras et al. 2020). Furthermore, although a United Nations for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR, 2019) report identifies a growing number of global high risk events, the dynamic capacities literature has not noticeably focused on crisis management. Capacities involve the abilities of organisations to deploy their specific and idiosyncratic permutations of resources in conjunction with processes to modify, integrate, and renew their existing organisational skills and competences. Thus, DCs may represent a means of sur - viving this pandemic period (Kaur, 2020a). Several authors use dimensions like sensing, conceptualizing, coproducing, orchestrating, scaling, and stretching to measure the impact of DC on company performance (Leifer et al., 2000; O’Connor, 2008; Jansen et al., 2015; Vahlne and Jonsson, 2017; Baden-Fuller and Teece, 2020). 3.1 Sensing Sensing is related to the scope for producing a new range of products or ser - vices. This category breaks down into two (sub)capabilities related to supply and demand, corresponding to the orientation toward the client and the orientation toward the competition. Jansen et al. (2015) intend to analyse the detection capacity of companies in this construct, trying to understand if companies systematically observe and assess customer needs as well as the actual use of their services or products. The key problem facing most organisations is not economic, in the sense of more or diverse resources and capabilities, or even more loyal customers; rather, it is cognitive, perhaps even emotional (Porac, 1989). The cognitive side of competitive dynamics is completely omitted from traditional neoclassical economics, also given scant attention in the resource-based view. It is the capacity of established firms (and new ones too) to see possibilities that others have not seen and the capacity to inspire and mobilise both employees and strategic partners to commit resources in an effort to exploit the perceived opportunities that are the core of competitive dynamics (Baden-Fuller and Teece, 2020). H1 Sensing (dynamic capability) has a positive effect on performance. 1709 1 3 The impact of dynamic capabilities on SME performance during... 3.2 Conceptualizing Within DCs, conceptualizing is the essential capability to select and develop an idea. In this construct, Jansen et al. (2015) intend to assess the greater or lesser ease of conceptualising their services or products. They assess whether companies are innovative in presenting or experimenting with new concepts or ideas for new service or product concepts. The innovation literature explores radical innovation (Leifer et al., 2000), breakthrough innovation (O’Connor, 2008), discontinuous innovation (Kaplan et al., 2003), and disruptive innovation (Christensen, 1997), offering both theoretical and practical pointers for transforming strategies in large corporations to advance technologies and create new markets. Kodama (2017) argues that the ability to conceptualize and develop new ideas, turning them into innovations, is a dynamic capability crucial for the performance of companies. H2 Conceptualizing (dynamic capability) has a positive effect on performance. 3.3 Coproducing and orchestrating The coproducing and orchestrating construct is interrelated with the partnerships established to retail the new products/services. With this construct, Jansen et al. (2015) want to assess the firm’s ability to maintain partnerships and initiate new ones; they also want to check whether cooperation with other organizations allows them to improve or introduce new services or products. Thus, this identifies if they have an organization that can help them coordinate innovation activities that involve multiple parties. To build dynamic capability for coping with global marketing turbulence, the companies must flexibly reconfigure their organizational structure, hiring employ - ees with a wide variety of skills. These employees then, based on the company’s vision and goals, cooperate with upstream companies and downstream partners to seek compatible goals that promote flexible strategic actions (Vahlne and Jonsson, 2017). Organizational goals that guide strategies and activities provide the basis of goal interdependence that affects the interaction patterns between organizations and, in turn, determines companies’ outcomes, including business development, organizational competence, and performance (Wong et al., 2012; Yang and Gan, 2021). H3 Coproducing and orchestrating (dynamic capabilities) have a positive effect on performance. 3.4 Scaling and stretching Scaling and stretching incorporate those efforts required to get a new product/ser - vice to the market. With this construct, authors intend that in the case of a successful product or service, companies will be able to extend it to the entire organization (Jansen et al., 2015). A spearhead for communicating, embodying, and orchestrating 1710 M. Brands also can address cultural anxieties and contradictions (Kadirov et al., 2016), which may entail institutional change for social issues unrelated to direct business operations (Kemper and Ballantine 2019). Although brands may participate in efforts toward the betterment of society due to a perceived responsibility to do so (Moorman 2020), an understanding of how branding may orchestrate social change needs greater attention (Conejo and Wooliscroft 2015; Spry et al., 2021). Realizing whether branding strategies are considered in developing new products or services as well as the existence of a marketing plan is also an object of analysis in this dimension. Finally, the authors intend to understand if companies are actively involved in promoting their new products or services (Jansen et al., 2015). H4 Scaling and stretching (dynamic capabilities) have a positive effect on performance. DCs may play crucial roles during the crisis, especially for SMEs that are par - ticularly exposed. Global crisis are difficult for SMEs (Eggers, 2020), in particular, COVID-19. Crises may bring opportunities within the scope of pre-crisis normality, the occurrence of the emergency, the post-crisis period, and the post-crisis normality (Pedersen et al. 2020; Wendt et al. 2021). But, taking into account the limitations of SMEs (Freeman et al., 1983), they may not always hold the resources necessary to identify market opportunities and threats, whether for exploring or for neutralising (Ambrosini and Bowman, 2009; Hoskisson et al., 2011). This questionnaire contained two sections, the first for characterising the companies and the second containing measurement scales for items depicting the attitudes and opinions of the respondents about the DCs of their companies. To provide an empirical context within which a market oriented economy renders DCs relevant for organisational success, the sur - vey targeted Portuguese SMEs. This study highlights the benefits of applying partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) to empirical research on strategic management, which commonly requires the modelling of latent constructs, in this case the DCs, and testing for complex relationships in small samples (Hair et al., 2019; Hulland, 1999). Furthermore, our study demonstrates the worth of applying PLS-SEM to the model’s latent, second order construct (Sarstedt et al., 2019). The application of PLS-SEM as an alternative to covariance based SEMs (CBSEM) arises from the items not following normal distribution, an assumption for the data distribution in CB-SEM, and alongside some variables included in the model being ordinal qualitative variables (Hair et al., 2019, 2020). To confirm the factorial structure of the instrument, there is a need to examine the reliability and validity of the indicators deployed to represent and measure the theoretical concepts (Hair et al., 2019, 2020; Sarstedt et al., 2019). As there is no single test that best evaluates the reliability and validity of the constructs, various measures serve to evaluate the quality of the adjustment. Composite reliability (CR) and Cronbach’s Alpha (Alpha) serve to estimate the internal consistency and reliability of the reflexive items of the factor or construct (CR and Alpha ≥ 0.7). As regards the validity of the instrument, there are three measures for application: (1) factorial validity; (2) convergent validity; and (3) discriminant validity (Hair et al., 2019, 2020; Sarstedt et al., 2019). Factorial validity derives from evaluating the standardised factorial weightings of each item in relation to the construct (Hair et al., 2010). In turn, the evaluation of convergent validity takes place through the average variance extracted (AVE) of the construct (Hair et al., 2010) while analysis of discriminant validity follows the criteria stipulated by Fornell and Larcker (1981). As for the perception of performance variation, in industry 57.8% of respondents perceived a reduction in turnover in 2020, with this proportion being 51.4% in services, 56.5% in micro-firms, and 52.4% in companies with at least 10 employees (Table 6). 6 Discussion and conclusion The ways in which companies are able to maintain their levels of performance and innovation during a global crisis, specifically throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, is a question requiring the application of new concepts and structures that may differ from more traditional concepts. While theoretical research on the impact of the dynamic capabilities of companies on performance and innovation provide alternative conceptual structures, empirical research returns only dispersed and frequently difficult to compare results (Beliaeva et al, 2020; Kraus et al, 2020; Wenzel et al, 2021). Our research contributes to overcoming this shortcoming in the literature by providing a basis for empirically measuring the strength of the DC effect on assisting SMEs to maintain their performance. While the pandemic difficulties are generalised in scope, by developing their DCs, companies gain a greater likelihood of being able to cope with their impact (Obal and Gao, 2020; Zafari et al., 2020). Thus, we demonstrate how the means for untying this gordian knot stem precisely from the DCs (Fainshmidt et al, 2017). These greater competences boost the likelihood of organisational success in the current period (Bailey and Breslin, 2020). This emerges through the relevance of the Conceptualizing construct conveying the essential capabilities of companies to select and develop an idea, and the Coproducing and Orchestrating construct that encapsulates efforts to get new products to market; these jointly enable companies to maintain their performance levels. Therefore, DCs represent the abilities of organisations to apply their idiosyncratic permutations of resources effectively as processes for modifying, integrating, and renewing their existing organisational competences (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000; Teece et al., 1997). Organisations worldwide need to undergo a paradigm shift, not only to survive the current crisis but also to prosper in a post-Covid-19 recessionary environment—a totally new world in which clients concerned with costs continually seek greater value for less expenditure (Pedersen et al., 2020; Cortez and Johnston, 2020). Within this framework, we verify the changes that companies are able to process in terms of their dynamic capabilities. If, before the pandemic broke out, Sensing constituted a priority, thus the search for opportunities to come up with new products and services with a client oriented focus, when companies are in the “eye of the hurricane”, they engage in a transition to Coproducing and orchestrating. This becomes possible in keeping with how companies have already been able to develop, and continue to maintain, their focus on Conceptualizing. 1722 M. Dejardin et al. 1 3 The coronavirus pandemic wreaked havoc on the business environment, not only in terms of the availability of certain resources but also due to the general scarcity of many other resources. Even in such times, we still must note that having less does not necessarily mean doing less. In situations when organisations need flexibility in their existing resources, members of staff face the challenge of moving on from a shortage focused mentality in order to take advantage of the resources existing to thereby guarantee the optimal application of the organisation’s respective resources (Zafari et al., 2020). In this context, the development of creative attitudes to overcome the prevailing challenges may drive industry toward untying this gordian knot (Conceptualizing and Coproducing and orchestrating). Indeed, in times of frugality, organisations compensate for the lack of resources by turning strongly toward their internal and external stocks of knowledge as well as their respective learning capacities (Hossain, 2021; Kaur, 2020b). During the Covid-19 pandemic, these problems essentially all deepen, hence the utilisation of DCs emerged as a solution to the pandemic while simultaneously equipping organisations with the capabilities of ensuring instantaneous responses to the ongoing dynamism in the surrounding environment (Yeniaras et al. 2020). In fact, the DC may flourish as it remains necessary to be at the top, even dur - ing the pandemic. This ambidextrous approach contains the scope for producing synergies, thereby methodically transforming them into a magic formula that grants frugal organisations some advantages. Such advantages may help organisations not only coping with the COVID-19 crisis but also with building a COVID-19 legacy deeply sustained by the dynamic resources based on internal knowledge (Eggers, 2020; Meyer et al, 2022). Our research brings has important implications for research into dynamic capabilities. The first relates to strategic management theory. In approaching the resilience of companies through recourse to their DCs in periods of crisis, such as the COVID-19 pandemic (Obal and Gao, 2020; Zafari et al., 2020), we demonstrate the importance of this tool to company performance and their overcoming such adverse periods. Furthermore, because we analyse the impact of DC before and during the pandemic, our results may facilitate understanding the impacts of pre-crisis DCs and the consequences of their application during the pandemic. According to our results, we may state that the strong management of these assets, especially of capacities, may represent the secret to the survival of organisations during such turbulent periods. The environments surrounding dynamic tasks lead companies to develop the capabilities essential for dealing with change even though preparations for one type of change may not necessarily generalize to those required for other types. According to Linnenluecke et al. (2011), organisations that are highly optimised to deal with certain surrounding conditions are more prone to experience a lack of resilience against unexpected shocks. Hence, we provide new conceptual insights into the resilience of SMEs, highlighting the importance of DCs for their performance. Secondly, we generate new knowledge for the dynamic resource vision. The evolutionary nature and DC dependent approach, as management capability 1723 1 3 The impact of dynamic capabilities on SME performance during... assets, may make them less effective whenever SMEs encounter unforeseen events (Schilke, 2014), which managers have difficulty in identifying and creating packages of productive resources (Ambrosini and Bowman, 2009). DCs do not always represent the most appropriate means of change even if there is a significant need for resource configuration. Our research demonstrates that the surrounding environment within which DCs evolve may determine the effectiveness of their approaches to less typical types of change, like a global economic recession triggered by a global public health issue. Thus, DCs stand out as potential proxies for resilience. These capabilities may contribute to the resilience of SMEs, depending on the context prevailing around these capabilities. Thus, we may infer how the general efficiency and effectiveness of DCs is influence by the ways in which SMEs interact with their surrounding environments over the course of time. This process deserves far greater attention within the framework of DC research to better understand the performance results of such capabilities. Finally, we contribute to research on the fungibility of resources. Within this scope, while organisations may boost their fungibility, thereby gaining a greater range of strategic options, fungibility inherently depends on the context just as resilience may take on various forms, holding different requirements in different environments. In environments displaying a shortage of resources, for example, earlier research indicates that resilience to crises may deepen through the development of close networks and personalised strategies. In face of the COVID-19 pandemic and its serious health consequences, manifesting in high death rates and high risk of infection, the authorities stipulated strict isolation and social distancing measures, negatively impacting economic activities and, consequently, on the financial positions of companies (Ataguba and Ataguba, 2020). In this context, one hope arises from developing DCs (Fainshmidt et al., 2017); and so doing, boosting the likelihood of company survival and success (Bailey and Breslin, 2020). In keeping with the set research question—What role do DCs play in SMEs performance during the COVID-19 pandemic crisis?—we note that DCs effectively perform a fundamental role in the SME response to the emer - gency circumstances of the pandemic. However, and through the application of the constructs incorporated into the research model, we may verify that not all DCs contain the same influence before and during the pandemic. In this pandemic period, companies focus greater efforts on getting their products to the market than in the eventual production of something new. Company DCs associated with decision-making that involve a combination of abilities, processes, and routines foster growth in organisational knowledge, thus enabling an appropriate response to the crisis situation. Within this framework, our study further demonstrates how DCs facilitate company performance during periods of crisis. Through developing their DCs, companies gain a greater probability of overcoming their impacts through deploying higher levels of competences and skills. These distinctive capacities endow the organisation with a greater capability to optimise the application of its resources and capacities, not just guaranteeing greater efficiency in the development of new processes but also 1724 M. Dejardin et al. 1 3 for optimising those processes that require adaptation to the new contexts emerging in the surrounding environment. Our research displays certain limitations that may themselves provide fruitful avenues for future research. Our research took place during a crisis, focusing on the implications of the effects of DCs on company performance standards. In periods of great turbulence, the results may be subject to extreme volatility. Our sample contained only SMEs: examination of a different company sample, for example made up of born global firms, which can emerge from within such crisis contexts, may provide different and additional perceptions. Another issue can be identified in that DCs and performance variation are self-report metrics. There are also recommendations for other future lines of research, targeting SMEs with operations ongoing in international markets, their network capability, and establishing terms of comparison for their performance levels in periods of pandemic crisis against other SMEs without such international operations. Despite the proposition of DCs as able to generate sustainable competitive advantages (Helfat and Martin, 2014; Teece, 2007), the study of this may require greater nuance, especially when approaching contexts of unforeseen change, like crises. There is also a need for research to identify contingencies within the ongoing dynamic relationship between resources and performance so as to advance toward the construction of a more robust and complete theory regarding the role of DCs in management. However, resource depletion, ecological degradation, and climate change are major environmen - tal concerns of industrialization [ 1]. Manufacturers are under pressure to incorporate sustainability into their business strategies as environmental awareness grows [ 2]. Current business practices require environmental compliance and sustainability values in corporate cultures [3]. By using smart resource capabilities, manufacturers must balance short-term operational efficiency and long-term environmental responsibility [ 3]. Green development violations harm the environment, reputation, consumer trust, and brand loyalty [4]. Thus, manufacturers must develop internal competencies that promote sus - tainable innovation and green production. GDC—a firm’s ability to adapt to changing environmental demands through resource reconfiguration and innovation—has become a key driver of sustainable competitive advantage [ 1, 4]. GDC helps firms adopt green Discover Sustainability Abstract This study investigates the influence of green dynamic capability on sustainability performance through the mediating role of green innovation and the moderating role of green sustainability pressure among manufacturing firms in Ghana. By employing a survey questionnaire, data was collected from 325 companies in Accra Metropolitan Area in the Greater Accra Region of Ghana. Data was analysed using structural equation modelling using Amos 24. Findings from the study indicate that green dynamic capability innovation influences both product and process dimensions of green innovation. However, only the process dimension of green innovation impacted positively on all three dimensions of sustainability performance. Additionally, the findings of this study revealed that green dynamic innovation impacts sustainability performance through the mediating role of green innovation. Furthermore, the study found that sustainability pressure moderates the relationship between green innovation and sustainability performance. In today’s competitive market, manufacturers that incorporate green innovation can reduce envi - ronmental harm and increase profits and legitimacy [ 5, 6]. Green innovations reduce environmental impact and improve resource efficiency [5]. These innovations allow firms to meet global sustainability goals and local regulatory and market demands [ 6]. Green innovation improves environmental performance, job creation, and corporate perfor - mance [7]. Thus, green innovation links dynamic capabilities to sustainable results. There are several drivers and outcomes of green innovation, but stakeholder pressure’s impact on sustainability trajectories is unknown. Customers, regulators, suppliers, and communities pressure firms to adopt sustainable practices like recycling, eco-design, emission control, and clean energy transitions [8–10]. With more companies investing in socially responsible and environmentally friendly strategies, their influence is clear [ 11]. Studies show that stakeholder engagement significantly impacts firms’ ability to inno - vate sustainably and stay competitive [ 12, 13]. The direct impact of stakeholder pres - sure on green dynamic capabilities and sustainability performance is still unclear [ 11, 14]. Although some scholars have examined stakeholder influence on risk management and green practices [ 15], few have examined how these pressures interact with internal capabilities to shape sustainability outcomes. This highlights a policy and theoretical gap in understanding how stakeholder influence can improve green performance. Strategic management and innovation literature has extensively studied dynamic capabilities, but their integration with green strategies is largely unexplored. Green dynamic capabilities’ dimensions and causes are debated, especially in emerging markets [ 4]. Some research has linked green dynamic capabilities to competitiveness and sustainability [ 16], green innovation and financial performance [ 17, 18], but little has examined their long-term sustainability effects. Additionally, stakeholder-driven sustainability discourse has mostly focused on external pressure, with little attention paid to how it moderates or mediates the relationship between green dynamic capability and sustainability perfor - mance. Thus, to improve manufacturing sustainability, internal and external dynamics must be studied. Future research should consider multidimensional models that account for these complexities to provide policymakers and corporate leaders with more action - able insights. The literature also lacks research on green innovation as a mediator between strategic drivers like stakeholder pressure and dynamic capability and sustainability performance. Green innovation has been shown to directly affect environmental outcomes [ 5, 19], but how it links antecedents to sustainability achievements is unclear. Weng [ 20] identified stakeholder behavior and government regulations as antecedents to green innovation, but the study did not examine how green innovation moderates stakeholder pressure and environmental performance. Huang and Li [ 5] found that dynamic capability drives green innovation but did not examine the sustainability performance-dynamic capability chain. This is a major theoretical gap because green innovation’s mediating and moderating roles could illuminate how firms can structure their sustainability strategies. To bet - ter understand manufacturing sustainability performance, future research must examine these complex relationships. Current scholarship neglects the contextual relevance of these dynamics in developing economies, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa. Stud - ies have focused on developed nations, but Ghana, where manufacturing is crucial to national development, has received little attention. Ghana’s manufacturing sector added Page 3 of 28 Asiedu et al. Discover Sustainability (2025) 6:961 GHS 4.34 billion to the economy in the fourth quarter of 2020 and attracted US$1.27 billion in foreign direct investment (Ministry of Finance, 2021). There are few empiri - cal studies on how green dynamic capabilities, stakeholder pressure, and green innova - tion affect sustainability in Ghanaian manufacturing, despite its economic importance. Understanding these relationships is essential for creating environmentally responsible industrial growth policies. Bridge these gaps to enrich sustainability and innovation research and guide firms and policymakers seeking long-term viability in a resourceconstrained but opportunity-rich environment. This study aims to fill gaps in the literature by investigating the link between green dynamic capability and manufacturing firm sustainability performance in Ghana’s Greater Accra Region, with a particular emphasis on the facilitating role of green inno - vation and the moderating factor of green sustainability pressure. The research objec - tives of this study include the following: (1) to investigate the link between green dynamic capability and green innovation among industrial enterprises in Ghana; (2) to examine the link between green innovation and sustainability performance across industrial enterprises in Ghana; (3) to examine how green sustainability pressure moderates the relationship between green dynamic capability and green sustainability performance in Ghana’s Greater Accra Region’s industrial companies; and (4) to determine the role of green innovation mediating the link between green dynamic capability and sustainability performance throughout Ghana’s Greater Accra Region’s industrial enterprises. 2 Literature review and hypotheses development 2.1 Green dynamic capabilities Green dynamic capability is described as a corporation’s ability to use its possessions and expertise to recommence and enhance its green capabilities in response to changing market conditions [ 21]. Green dynamic capability refers to a company’s ability to inte - grate, grow, and restructure internal and external competencies to achieve conditions and green product design [ 6]. As stated by Amaranti et al. [ 1], green dynthe amic capa - bility is described as an organization’s capability to modify all corporation processes and practices to be greener, which could then contribute to reducing the adverse effects of the organization’s processes on the environment. Furthermore, green dynamic capability has been defined as a strengthening and extension of the notion of self-motivated capa - bilities, which comprises organizations’ high-level capability to achieve sustainable and green progress in an ever-changing environment [4]. Rodrigo-Alarcón et al. (explain that green dynamic capability is also defined as a company’s ability to integrate resources to achieve sustainability and a green environment through its operations. Green dynamic capabilities have been conceptualized as a multidimensional construct with dimen - sions or sub-constructs. Qiu et al. [ 4] elucidate that green dynamic capability is a threedimensional construct that includes resource integration, resource reconfiguration, and environmental understanding. Internal and external resources are both integrated in the capacity to integrate resources [4]. Internal resource integration comprises the exchange and addition of internal environmental information and cocompetencieshighlighting the need of collaborating with other divisions and the capacity to incorporate sustainability knowledge and skills into business operations [ 22]. According to Verona [23], the ability of a corporation to absorb knowledge from external sources, as well as to communicate, collaborate, and transfer knowledge across diverse external stakeholders, is emphasized. Page 4 of 28 Asiedu et al. Discover Sustainability (2025) 6:961 These stakeholders include customers, suppliers, shareholders, special interest groups, research institutes, local governments, and environmental non-governmental organiza - tions. The capacity to efficiently attract personnel with environmental skills and expe - rience is also part of external resource integration [ 22]. The ability to construct and reconfigure resources is referred to as resource reconfiguration capability, whereas the ability of enterprises to collect and use environmental information in a market context to identify opportunities or dangers and to reflect the sensitivity of enterprises to envi - ronmental changes is referred to as environmental insight capability [4]. According to Zhang et al. [ 24], environmental sensing, resource seizing, and resource reconfiguration are all capabilities that are part of the green dynamic capabilities’ framework. Environmental sensing capability is a company’s capacity to use intelligence to detect future development patterns in their business environment [ 25], where client green preferences, market demand, and the growth of new technology are all part of the intelligence gathering process [ 16]. Resource seizing capability refers to an organiza - tion’s ability to absorb information about green development and use it for technologi - cal commercialization events. In contrast, resource reconfiguring capability refers to the adoption of alternative business development modes when obstacles arise, allowing the organization to remain flexible in the external business environment [16]. 2.2 Green innovation According to Weng et al. [ 20], green innovation can be defined from two perspectives: first, in terms of a company’s capabilities, and second, in relation to an organization’s environmental practices. Green innovation is defined as the development of hardware or software that is linked to green products or processes when applied to a company’s activities [ 26]. Green innovation, according to this definition, entails technological breakthroughs or fresh managerial processes that enhance an organization’s environ - mental performance and competitive edge. Green innovation is a dynamic process that is designed to meet several demands and address a variety of technological, economic, and environmental challenges [ 27], and it is instrumental in helping companies achieve sustainable development by meeting consumer requirements, enhancing critical com - petitive advantage, and attaining sustainable growth [ 28]. Green innovation is also more indefinite and high-risk than traditional innovation because of their high investment costs and imprecise returns [ 29]. Green innovation refers to technologies designed to reduce waste, global warming, water consumption, air pollution, and the use of coal, oil, and power, while promoting energy conservation [ 30]. It also encompasses industries’ creative efforts to transform existing processes into more sustainable ones [31]. 2.2.1 Green innovation dimensions Green innovation has two main dimensions: green product and green process innova - tion [5, 32]. 2.2.1.1 Green innovation product The process of developing new green products, or improving existing ones, with the goal of minimizing environmental consequences over the product’s life cycle while meeting market needs, is known as green innovation [ 32]. Green product innovation has been one of the most important components in achiev - ing growth and environmental sustainability in recent years [ 22]. Experiments in green Page 5 of 28 Asiedu et al. Discover Sustainability (2025) 6:961 product creation can help businesses avoid environmental issues and regulatory penal - ties while enabling them to explore new market opportunities and achieve success with green products [ 33, 34]. Furthermore, increasing green expertise, boosting a company’s green reputation, and increasing financial performance are all dependent on green product innovation [6, 35]. Green product innovation is measured by how much new products reduce pollution and energy consumption, though green process innovation is described as how much new processes reduce pollution and energy consumption [20]. For instance, green product innovation refers to the creation of new products or services that have no or less environmental impact than existing products or competitors’ products [36]. 2.2.1.2 Green innovation process Green innovation process, on the other hand, refers to the addition of more environmentally friendly technology to existing production pro - cesses in order to create things and deliver services that have little or no negative effect on the environment [36]. Green process innovation is concerned with industrial processes and can be used to reduce environmental risk, pollutant emissions, and other negative repercussions [ 37]. The green innovation process focuses on a company’s capacity to improve existing processes while also developing new ones, leading to energy savings, pollution prevention, resource recycling, and increased production [5]. Green innovation has been demonstrated to provide organizations with long-term advantages [ 37]. It also contributes positively to technical performance and organizational learning [38]. 2.3 Sustainability pressure Companies generally do not volunteer to implement green practices if left to their own initiatives. Objectives such as increasing employment, exports and protecting strate - gically important industries have traditionally enjoyed a greater political priority than environmental protection [ 14, 39]. Organisations’ perceptions of stakeholder pressure on sustainability are crucial because they impact their reactions [ 40, 41]. Some pres - sure groups, however, force companies to be more sensitive to environmental issues. According to Lin and Chen [ 6], government influence is the most significant factor driving corporations to implement green practices. For example, competition and gov - ernment pressure, as well as employee behaviour, have been demonstrated to have sub - stantial and beneficial influence on green innovation practices [ 20], as well as the green dynamic capabilities of organizations [ 18]. As a result, it is reasonable to conclude that stakeholder demand for sustainability has driven companies to develop and offer envi - ronmentally welcoming goods [ 42] as well as using new green practices in the products and services they create [ 43, 44]. Stakeholder influence has an effect on a company’s environmental approach [ 45]. It compels firms to participate in continuous integration and resource reconfiguration in order to obtain a competitive advantage [ 46]. Firms responding to the demands of stakeholders which include institutions, organizations, communities, and individuals that may influence or be affected by specific organizations [11] allow corporations to build strategic alliances with stakeholders while encouraging the development of specialized environmental and social capabilities [47]. Pressure from stakeholders supports initiatives in understanding stakeholder preferences regarding sustainability [48]. Page 6 of 28 Asiedu et al. Discover Sustainability (2025) 6:961 2.4 Sustainability performance Elkington [49] coined the phrase “sustainability. ” It is described as the broadening of a company’s vision to include environmental, social, and economic considerations [2]. The concept of sustainability shapes organizational planning and success measurement [ 50]. Accordingly, an organization’s success is determined by the quality of its products and its environmental and social characteristics [ 51]. The changing nature of sustainability has prompted a global shift in thinking, pushing executives to reconsider the breadth of green creative activities and their influence on the long- term viability of sustainable businesses [ 52]. Three essential concepts underpin the execution of the notion of sus - tainability: environmental dignity, social justice, and prosperity. The performance of a company in terms of the environment and society has been termed as sustainability per - formance [53]. The notion of sustainability performance argues that a company should evaluate the impression of its activities on all investors, together with the society, com - munity, and the environment, in addition to achieving short-term shareholder profit [54]. The extent to which a company integrates financial, environmental, social, and governance considerations into its operations reflects the impact these factors have on both the company and society [ 55]. Furthermore, sustainability performance indicates the corporations’ hard work and accomplishments concerning sustainability [56]. 2.4.1 Dimensions of sustainability performance Sustainability performance has been conceptualized as a multi- dimensional concept [57] with different dimensions. However, there are three main dimensions of sustain - ability performance that has been espoused by most scholars. These dimensions include environmental, economic, and social performance [ 2]. These dimensions have been referred to as the “three pillars of sustainability” [ 57]. In this study, only economic and environmental performance will be discussed. 2.4.1.1 Economic performance How successfully a country expands while also safe - guarding the environment and enhancing people’s quality of life is a measure of eco - nomic success [ 2]; therefore, the utilization of well-organized and cleaner maintainable energy supplies is critical in this dimension [ 2]. Indeed, according to Yang et al. [ 58], environmental performance that imitates energy competence has a beneficial impres - sion on financial performance. The economic dimension of sustainability performance is categorized into three components: direct economic value created, market presence, and indirect economic impacts [59]. 2.4.1.2 Environmental performance The environmental component encompasses materials, energy, water, biodiversity, emissions, waste, products and services, compliance with environmental standards, product transportation, and the overall environmental protection measures adopted by a corporation [ 59]. Environmental performance, according to King and Lenox [60], entails increased compliance with requirements. 2.5 Theoretical underpinning This research is founded on the Institution-Based Perspective (IBP) and the firm’s Resource- Based View (RBV). Discover Sustainability (2025) 6:961 2.5.1 Institution-based perspective for corporate sustainability The institution-based perspective insists that failure to react to this systemic demand for sustainability endangers the firm’s legitimacy and existence, as governments, customers, public media, and society as a whole are growing increasingly interested in sustainability matters [61]. In contrast, active stakeholder engagement, used as a tool to identify and manage potential negative social and environmental impacts, not only reduces a com - pany’s ethical and ecological vulnerabilities but also grants access to valuable resources while enhancing its popularity and reputation among stakeholders [ 61]. Regardless, the external pressures for sustainability that firms confront are coming from many of com - peting interest groups with diverging priorities [ 62]. This complicated and contextual circumstances seriously challenge the traditional management approach of the firm in three ways. Firstly, a firm with constrained and limited resources is unable to satisfy all the sustainability needs from a wide variety of stakeholders at the very same time. They have to choose and satisfy what is most pressing and is being perceived legitimate first [63]. Companies used to adhere to social and environmental norms enforced by public reg - ulators [64]. Regrettably, companies frequently face difficulties in rapidly detecting and adequately managing these new concerns because they often lack more direct communication channels with these purported indirect stakeholders [64]. Second, the institutional push for sustainability is not understood as a set of accepted and agreed on schemas, norms and rules. Rather, it is a complex process full of contra - dictory opinions and interests [ 62, 65]. The different stakeholders might construe sus - tainability with different forms on the basis of their specific needs. Thus, sustainability is not a pre-established objective, but the result of negotiations between different stake - holders [22]. Stakeholders, including regulators, customers, members of the community and companies play a well-defined role in delineating what sustainability means and how it should be navigated [ 65]. Finally, companies that are incorporated in different regula - tory environments in distinctive institutional settings may encounter differing sustain - ability deployment pressures [63]. 2.5.2 Resource-based view perspective for corporate sustainability The resource-based approach sees corporate sustainability as a continuous, nonlinear trip directed at the crossroads of environmental, social and economic capabilities [ 64, 66]. The resource-based view theories that organizations can obtain a modest advantage by improving competences and competences from either the “steady state” or “dynamic capabilities” viewpoints. To react to the altering environment and take advantage of accessible chances, a company can either acquire design innovation using the steady state strategy or develop competences using the dynamic capabilities approach. For businesses to acquire a competitive advantage in the market, they must have strong but consistent capabilities. Thus, workers’ knowledge, beliefs, exercise programs, and lively skills can be renewed and updated, resulting in inspired behaviour and environmental novelty [59]. Firstly, it is simple for firms to identify cheaper ways to cut waste and attain immense cost savings by improving internal processes and innovating. When these alleged “lowhanging fruits” are dried up, then further gains will become difficult to attain through simply improving the efficiencies of the existing business processes and practices and Page 8 of 28 Asiedu et al. Discover Sustainability (2025) 6:961 their patterns. It will take massive capital investment and significant changes in orga - nizational strategy and technology [ 67]. According to Hart et al [ 64] and Darnall [ 68], the various proficiencies described are essential at different stages of sustainable growth. Therefore, concentrating on the present ability and capacity of the company is essen - tial, but not sufficient, and it only guarantees provisional success. Long-term strategic competitive edge will soon necessitate that firms exploit and employ new capabilities in response to the significant and discrete shifts that are occurring with increasing fre - quency in the social, environmental, technological and regulatory domain [ 67]. Nonetheless, firms that are currently outperforming are more expected to hold on to their present capabilities [2, 64]. As outlined by the Resource-Based View (RBV) [69], a corporation’s unique capabilities are self-reinforcing and cultivated through the accumulation of a structured and relevant set of skills, expertise, and knowledge [ 70, 71]. They repre - sent behaviour that is stabilized by the accumulation of specialized skills, expertise, and know-how [70, 71]. This will leave organizations unable to adapt their well-established “ways” in a volatile environment where the rules of the competitive game are constantly evolving [ 72]. This “capability trap” can result from the input into sustainability efforts [73], which will become prominent when the firm is not precise about its returns. As an outcome, firms face a contradictory situation: on the one hand, excellent capabilities that are the foundation of a valuable, rare, one-of-a-kind, and non-substitutional form of a firm’s strategic strength and competitive advantage; on the other hand, the actual com - petences confine the suppleness and receptiveness of the organisation in the direction of the emerging sustainability challenge. Obviously, companies will have to discover new habits to crack this and other dilemmas. In summary, together, the IBP and RBV provide a comprehensive lens for under - standing the study’s conceptual framework. Institution-Based Perspective explains the external institutional pressures that necessitate the development of green dynamic capabilities and stakeholder-responsive innovation. Resource-Based View highlights the internal mechanisms—specifically green dynamic capabilities—that drive green innova - tion, which subsequently leads to improved economic and environmental performance (Fig. 1). [ 88] quantitative studies are geared to answer the ‘who’ and ‘what’ of a research issue, but they do not adequately address the ‘why’ of a phenomenon or event attribute. As a result, for numerical data, the quantitative approach relies on tools such as questionnaires, surveys, and/ or historical data [ 89] and then uses statistical analyses to obtain their findings [ 90]. Furthermore, the survey strategy enables researchers to answer questions such as ‘who’ , ‘what’ , ‘how much’ , and ‘to what extent’ [91]. We chose a quantitative approach because it allows us to test the relationships between variables such as green dynamic capability, green innovation, and sustainability pressure. Survey research was favoured over experi - mental research because it provides a numerical representation of trends, attitudes, or opinions within a population by analysing a sample and using questionnaires to gather primary data [92]. 3.1.1 Population The target population for this study comprises all full-time employees of selected man - ufacturing enterprises located in the Accra Metropolitan Area. Accra was chosen due to its status as Ghana’s industrial and economic hub, hosting a high concentration of formal manufacturing firms. This region offers a diverse and representative workforce, making it ideal for exploring green innovation practices. This study employed a nonprobability sampling strategy, specifically convenience sampling, in which participants were recruited based on practical criteria such as ease of accessibility, geographic prox - imity, availability at a given time, or willingness to participate [ 93]. The minimum selection size which is satisfactory for analysis was employed. The current research makes use of structural equation modelling (SEM), and the sample size was calculated employing the minimal accepted sample size for SEM [94]. There are divergent views on the sample size recommended for SEM. Some academics advocate for a minimum of five respon - dents per variable, while others suggest that a ratio of ten respondents per variable is more appropriate [95]. According to Martínez‐López et al. [96], a critical sample size for SEM is 200 representations. Any number larger than 200 is considered to give appropri - ate statistical power for data processing [ 94]. Iacobucci [ 97], however, argued that this is a “conservative” and “simplistic” rule of thumb, suggesting that SEM models can per - form well even with small sample sizes of 50–100 individuals. According to experts, a sample size of at least 300–500 individuals provide sufficient statistical power for SEM analysis [98, 99]. The sample size in this study was 325, which is sufficient according to the recommended number for SEM. 3.1.2 Data collection Primary data for testing the hypotheses was collected via self-administered question - naires from employees of the listed manufacturing firms in the Accra Metropolitan Area, and secondary data included information retrieved from databases and publica - tions. Different technologies or tactics are available for data collection. Interviews, Page 12 of 28 Asiedu et al. Discover Sustainability (2025) 6:961 questionnaires, and observations are all common tools. Questionnaires were utilized to collect data for this investigation on the green capabilities, green innovation, sustain - ability performance, sustainability as well as respondent profiles. Questionnaires are generally affordable and have the potential to describe huge populations’ features. Sustainability performance was defined as a multidimensional construct that included economic, environmental, and social performance. This observation of the study’s finding is similar to the result obtained by Singh et al. [ 18] as well as that of Yousuf et al. [ 73] who discovered that green dynamic skills have a favourable and considerable impact on organizations’ green innovation, by gender [130]. This observation suggests that green dynamic capabilities is an impor - tant corporate asset that has significant influence on how firms churn out process and product innovations. This finding supports the study by Qiu et al. [ 4] and Cobinah et al. [131]. Green dynamic capabilities, in particular, had a significant impact on product and process innovation, which is consistent with earlier research [132]. This implies that businesses with green dynamic skills would have the capabilities to create innovative products and innovative processes that would propel businesses to assist them in using their current expertise and resources in order to create and expand their green organizational skills and remain competitive in a volatile market. 5.2 Relationship between green innovation and sustainability performance The study’s findings yielded conflicting results in terms of the association between green innovation and sustainability performance. 5.2.1 Green product innovation and sustainability performance According to the data, product innovation had no effect on all three criteria of sustain - ability performance. This sug - gests that process innovation is an important contributor to sustainability performance of firms. 5.3 The moderating role of sustainability pressure on the relationship between green innovation and sustainability performance The findings further indicated that sustainability pressure played a moderating role on the product innovation- economic performance relationship by attenuating the rela - tionship. As the previous result indicated, there was a negative significant relationship between product innovation and sustainability performance, this implies that sustain - ability pressure is driving firms to develop green innovation products. Therefore, pres - sure from stakeholders towards the production of “green” products is key in achieving economic sustainability. Similarly, this study found that there was a significant interaction that was produced between the product innovation-environmental performance links by also damping that relationship. This also implies that sustainability demands play a significant part in the development of green innovative goods in order for businesses to meet their sus - tainability goals. The results for the moderation effect of sustainability pressure on the link between process innovation and sustainability performance were similar to those obtained for the link between product innovation and sustainability performance, indi - cating that sustainability pressure moderated the relationships between process innova - tion and economic performance as well as the relationship between process innovation and environmental performance. 5.4 The mediating role of green innovation Green innovation was discovered to be a mediating factor between green dynamic capa - bilities and the three sustainability performance characteristics. Product innovation acted as a full mediator between green dynamic capabilities and economic performance, as well as between green dynamic capabilities and environmental performance. It was also proven that process innovation has a mediating function in the interaction between green dynamic capabilities and sustainability performance. The findings also showed that process innovation acted as a complete mediator between green dynamic capabilities Page 23 of 28 Asiedu et al. Discover Sustainability (2025) 6:961 and environmental performance. These results suggest that the employment of green dynamic capabilities lead to the deployment of green processes and the production of green innovation products which in turn positively impact firm’s sustainability performance. This finding can be better understood through the lens of the Resource-Based View, which suggests that firms gain sustainable competitive advantages by continuously improving and adapting their internal processes. In Ghana’s resource-constrained busi - ness context, process innovations—such as reducing energy consumption or stream - lining resource use—are often more cost-effective and immediately impactful than investing in new green products. From the Institution-Based Perspective, the result also reflects how external institutional pressures (e.g., regulatory mandates, public expec - tations) might compel firms to demonstrate operational efficiency and compliance before pursuing more advanced or customer-facing sustainability initiatives. Hence, firms prioritize process improvements to meet compliance demands and stakeholder expectations. 5.5 Theoretical implications This research contributes to theory in several important ways which extends the Resource-Based View by emphasizing how green dynamic capabilities act as a bridge between internal competence and sustainability-driven innovation. It advances the Institution-Based Perspective by showing how diverse stakeholder pressures shape firms’ strategic priorities, especially in developing regions. Most notably, the study adds novel insight into the relative impact of green process vs. product innovation, which has received limited attention in the African context. This study’s conclusions have some theoretical ramifications. In the context of indus - trial companies in Ghana’s Greater Accra Region, the current study attempted to iden - tify how green dynamic skills contribute to the promotion of sustainable performance. Despite the fact that past research has shown a correlation between green dynamic skills and green innovation, Studies on how green innovation affects green dynamic capacities and sustainability performance are few and far between. As a result, this research adds to our knowledge of how green dynamic capabilities affect sustainability performance. Furthermore, by assessing the role of sustainability in modulating the relationship between green innovation and sustainability performance, this study contributes to the current body of literature on green dynamic capacities, green innovation, and sustainability per - formance. The findings add to the little literature on the moderating influence of sustainability pressure and broaden the theoretical knowledge of the circumstances in which green innovation might improve sustainability performance. The empirical evidence from a developing nation environment in Sub-Saharan Africa adds to the study’s contri - bution. The current study’s literature review highlights that most existing publications are concentrated in emerging countries and underrepresented regions, with only limited studies from Africa. Consequently, there is a notable scarcity of evidence from develop - ing economies. This research addresses this gap and contributes to filling the contextual void in the literature. Strengthen institutional alignment across ministries and agencies to reduce fragmented sustainability mandates. Promote public–private partnerships that encourage shared sustainability agendas and innovation ecosystems. 5.7 Limitation of the research There were a few flaws in this study that should be noted. First, this research was limited to a single industry, i.e., the manufacturing sectors. In addition, this study was limited to Ghana, an emerging economy with unique socio- cultural dynamics Therefore, the findings may not be reflective of other sectors and other economies. Moreover, this study considered only product and process innovation dimensions of green innovation. Despite the fact that the chances of shared technique bias influencing the outcomes were low, data was collected at the same time. This study’s cross-sectional research methodology makes it impossible to prove causation between the investigated variables. 5.8 Contributions of the research This study contributes to the body of literature in several ways. First, it extends the existing research on green dynamic capability, a subject with limited exploration [4], by examining its influence on sustainability performance—an area that remains largely unexplored. Second, by including stakeholder pressure into the green dynamic capability- sustainable performance relationship, this investigation leads to a deeper understanding of the function of green dynamic capability. Furthermore, this study provides a unique context by examining the influence of green dynamic capability within an emerging economy context. This study will, therefore, further our understanding of green dynamic capability as this context offers a unique opportunity to contribute to the development of theories and inspire new knowledge. For marketing practitioners, this study offers a better understanding of the factors that drive sustainability performance and offers avenues to formulate strategies to sustain competitive advantage. It is also crucial to investigate the link between green dynamic capability and sustainability performance, as well as the supportive function of green innovation. 5.9 Directions for future research The findings of this study, as well as the limitations listed above, point to the need for more research in the area under consideration. First, future studies can be conducted in other countries to confirm the results obtained from this study as the developmental level in terms of technological advancement and education may influence the results. In addition, further studies may replicate this study in other sectors as the results may not be applicable to other industries and especially to the service sector. In addition, the direct impact of sustainability pressure on sustainability performance was not explored in this study, therefore future research might expand the framework employed. Longitudinal studies could be conducted to establish causal relationships between the variables examined. Such studies would enhance our understanding of the causal links between the constructs while also reducing common method bias. Future research should apply the model across different sectors such as agriculture and services to explore how industry-specific dynamics influence green innovation and sustainability outcomes. Additionally, adopting longitudinal study designs will help establish causal relationships and capture the evolving nature of green dynamic capabilities over time. Vanvitelli, Italy ABSTRACT The purpose of this editorial is threefold. First, the framework of dynamic capabilities—DCs, proposed and embedded in the field of management, is recalled and the state-of-the-art of research on it is reconstructed and clarified. Second, the results obtained are questioned in an attempt to apply the framework to entrepreneurship. Appropriate evaluations are performed to pave the way for the concept of dynamic capabilities in entre - preneurship—DyCE. Third, a call is made for future research that can offer new perspectives, reveal new insights, and advance research on DyCE among scholars interested in this new domain. KEYWORDS entrepreneurship; dynamic capabilities Introduction Research on entrepreneurship is developed along four main lines, which concern the aim, individual characteristics, context, and network (Matricano, 2015 , 2025a ). In terms of the aim, scholars arrive at a sequential reading of entrepreneur - ial opportunities and the creation of new businesses. Entrepreneurs work on entrepreneurial opportunities and can exploit them in different ways, so the creation of new businesses is only one alternative. In terms of individual characteristics, it is not possible to identify a clear entrepreneurial profile. Scholars have enlisted a large set of individual characteristics that change over time. In terms of the context, favorable or hostile, its influence on entrepre - neurial actions is indisputable. However, scholars note that it is not influential in itself. It exerts a positive or negative impact based on the reactions of individuals. Finally, in terms of networks, there is no ideal configuration since they change over time according to the emerging needs of entrepreneurs. The four lines of research cannot be read separately, they must be read as a whole. In fact, individual characteristics, which influence the creation and management of entrepreneurial networks, are linked to the aim pursued and influenced by the context. If one variable changes, all the others change CONTACT Diego Matricano diego.matricano@unicampania.it Department of Management, Università Degli Studi della Campania L.
