Theoretical framework The DCV highlights the importance of cultivating and employing firms’ resources to attain sus - tained competitive advantage (Junaid et al. 2023 ). The DCV focuses on a firm’s capacity to incor - porate, shape, and reconfigure its fundamental capabilities to address various complex tasks in a continuously evolving environment, hence improving supply chain effectiveness and efficiency to enhance GSCM (Dubey et al. 2024 ; Dubey, Gunasekaran, and Papadopoulos 2024 ; Lu, Zhao, and Liu 2022 ; Mohaghegh, Åhlström, and Blasi 2023 ). This theory encompasses the capability to sense opportunities, seise resources and reconfigure operations from various perspectives (Dubey, Bryde, et al. 2024 ; Dubey, Gunasekaran, and Papadopoulos 2024 ; Feng et al. 2024 ). The DCV has been implemented by firms to enhance supply chain integration and operational efficiency, enabling transformation toward a more environmentally friendly supply chain configur - ation (Chaudhuri et al. 2024 ; Gruchmann and Seuring 2018 ). The three perspectives of sensing, seising and reconfiguring capabilities are relevant in the context of generative AI for green inno - vation, thereby providing a suitable framework of generative AI capabilities in terms of improving GSCM. However, the traditional DCV is not sufficient to address the present dynamic environ - mental requirements of the supply chain, requiring a continuous learning process for new knowl - edge and innovation. The DCV encompasses attributes pertinent to the capabilities of monitoring the environment, capitalising identified opportunities, and reconfiguring resources for improved GSCM; however, this emphasis on the capabilities to integrate, develop, and reorganise internal and external resources neglects the fundamental learning processes that drive these capabilities, thereby con - straining the development and creation of innovative firm capabilities in response to swift environ - mental changes and technological advancements (Song et al. 2024 ; Souza and Takahashi 2019 ). In the context of generative AI, the learning capabilities that comprise the capacity to acquire new knowledge and reassessing existing information for enhanced supply chain data analysis as well as adapt and evolve in dynamic and immediate circumstances, which can facilitate successful GSCM operations, are still unclear (Benzidia, Makaoui, and Bentahar 2021 ; Ghobakhloo et al. 2024 ). In addressing these challenges, the OLT is proficient in elucidating the generative AI’s learn - ing capabilities necessary for assessing current knowledge, discovering new knowledge, and proces - sing data and information obtained from these knowledges to enhance industry’s operations and GSCM development (Junaid et al. 2023 ; Ritala et al. 2024 ). Hence, the DCV must be combined with OLT to enhance and attain complete generative AI capabilities for GSCM enhancement. Jack - son et al. ( 2024 ) argued that OLT, which can be represented by generative AI learning capabilities, potentially transforms firms by improving their forecasting, analysis and decision-making pro - cesses, thus facilitating the successful implementation of innovative practices that reduce the environmental impact of supply chain operations. Ghobakhloo et al. ( 2024 ) emphasised that gen - erative AI, with its learning and adaptive capabilities, can enhance operations, mitigate negative environmental impacts, improve overall supply chain efficiency, and offer dynamic and adjustable capabilities to address unique supply chain process issues. In an integrated DCV and OLT, the sen - sing capabilities of generative AI must incorporate learning processes to foster better seising and reconfiguring capabilities for improved GSCM. The attributes of the integrated DCV and OLT relevant to generative AI capabilities for enhan - cing GSCM require the incorporation of learning processes from the following three perspectives: sensing, seising and reconfiguring (Ghobakhloo et al. 2024 ; Jackson et al. 2024 ). Consequently, this study expands existing DCV perspectives by including organisations’ learning processes to harness advanced generative AI capabilities for GSCM. In this context, Junaid et al. ( 2023 ) emphasised that the integrated DCV and OLT must integrate the sensing and learning capabilities of generative AI to develop improved supply chain operations and services that meet emerging environmental requirements. By incorporating sensing and learning capabilities, firms develop innovative and adaptable strategies for SCM, enabling them to swiftly recognise and address shifting market 608 T. Generative AI capabilities Generative AI capabilities are employed to drive ongoing enhancement and innovation throughout the SCM process, emphasising the capacity of generative AI to autonomously produce innovative ideas, designs, and solutions, thereby transforming product development, manufacturing, and operational management for improved SCM (Akhtar et al. 2024 ; Al-Khatib, Al-Shboul, and Khattab 2024 ; Ooi et al. 2023 ). Li et al. ( 2024 ) and Ochieng, Ominde, and Zuofa ( 2024 ) highlighted that gen - erative AI, which incorporates the capabilities to sense and seise new information and scenarios, has the potential to revolutionise supply chain operations by facilitating enhanced simulations and fore - casting abilities. Furthermore, Rana et al. ( 2024 ) emphasised that generative AI possesses the capa - bilities to reconfigure the manner in which businesses operate and collaborate with stakeholders across the supply chain for improved operations. Jackson et al. ( 2024 ) argued that generative AI capabilities encompass an array of perspectives, with a particular emphasis on the necessity of lever - aging sensing capabilities to improve supply chain visibility and the need of seising capabilities to provide more appropriate supply chain process reconfiguration. Prior studies have concentrated on generative AI capabilities in dynamic SCM; yet, multi-attribute investigations that integrate learn - ing processes to enhance other capabilities and dynamically adapt to supply chain operations in response to environmental changes remain lacking. Consequently, prior studies have recognised substantial theoretical and practical constraints associated with illustrating operational circum - stances and investigating approaches that are capable of incorporating learning capabilities into fundamental sensing, seising and reconfiguring capabilities to enhance firms’ generative AI capa - bilities for SCM. Firms’ generative AI learning capabilities are needed to enhance all other types of capabilities, including sensing, seising and reconfiguring capabilities (Jackson et al. 2024 ; Khan et al. 2024 ; Li et al. 2024 ). Li et al. ( 2024 ) emphasised that the learning capabilities of generative AI are required for improving predictive quality analytics, enabling firms to sense and resolve possible supply chain problems before they intensify. Khan et al. ( 2024 ) posited that the learning capabilities of generative AI potentially encourage and provide the ability to seise identified opportunities, thus fostering more effective and efficient supply chain operations. Ghobakhloo et al. ( 2024 ) reported that the learning capability of generative AI can continuously update firms’ knowledge bases, thereby facilitating the continuous adaptation and reconfiguration of supply chain oper - ations in accordance with the needs of stakeholders and customers and product development. In addition, Jackson et al. ( 2024 ) concluded that the learning capabilities of generative AI are necessary for sensing data and information, seising opportunities from the identified information and enhancing the decision-making process for enhanced supply chain operation reconfiguration. Therefore, it is imperative to cultivate and integrate learning capabilities to improve supply chain processes. In summary, this study addresses the need for multi-attribute exploration by structuring an inte - grated perspective of the sensing, seising and reconfiguring capabilities of generative AI to improve SCM. Nevertheless, learning capability integration is indispensable for ensuring appropriate supply chain operations and improvements. This study proposes implementing an integrated DCV and OLT as the structural foundation to enhance and attain complete generative AI capabilities for improved SCM. Generative AI capabilities for GSCM In the GSCM context, generative AI capabilities exhibit remarkable capacity in analyzing extensive sets of information to discern trends and patterns, thereby generating innovative ideas and approaches that may facilitate more environmentally friendly supply chain operations (Al-Khatib, Al-Shboul, and Khattab 2024 ; Bolón-Canedo et al. 2024 ; Ghobakhloo et al. 2024 ). Akhtar et al. ( 2024 ) and Wang and Zhang ( 2024 ) argued that generative AI capabilities can transform traditional products and production design processes by providing an intelligent assistant that generates numerous possible designs with regard to specified parameters, leading to an expedited design pro - cess, diminished material waste, and frequently better-performing products and processes for enhanced GSCM which may not have been conceived through traditional AI approaches. More - over, Dubey, Bryde, et al. ( 2024 ) and Dubey, Gunasekaran, and Papadopoulos ( 2024 ) and Li et al. ( 2024 ) highlighted that generative AI capabilities can enhance inter-firm relationships within the supply chain through analyzing communication patterns to pinpoint potential areas of friction or misunderstanding, developing tailored recommendations for enhanced communication approaches, and enabling real-time transcription and language translation. This enables enhanced objective alignment, collaborative problem-solving and resource sharing among firms globally, ulti - mately leading to improved supply chain coordination aimed at achieving environmental objectives and improved GSCM. Wamba et al. and Ochieng, Ominde, and Zuofa ( 2024 ) emphasised that gen - erative AI capabilities substantially transform supply chain environmental performance by provid - ing numerous advantages, such as improved evaluation of supplier environmental impacts for preferred selection, enhanced prediction of potential disruptions and generation of appropriate contingency plans, as well as better demand forecasting to avert overstocking and enhance inven - tory management, resulting in more sustainable and ethically responsible operations. Hence, iden - tifying and enhancing generative AI capabilities are indispensable for enhancing GSCM. Generative AI capabilities concentrate on sensing and analyzing supply chain information to provide enhanced opportunities for seising, resulting in the reconfiguration of entire supply chain operations to achieve GSCM (Khan et al. 2024 ; Rana et al. 2024 ). Meier, Gruchmann, and Ivanov ( 2023 ) and Ghobakhloo et al. ( 2024 ) argued that the sensing capabilities of generative AI, exemplified by reflexive control and measurement capabilities, can assist firms in both internal and external comparisons and evaluations of supply chain functionality, thereby facilitating strategy development and execution for improved GSCM. Li et al. ( 2024 ) and Lu, Zhao, and Liu ( 2022 ) high - lighted that augmenting sensing capabilities can further enhance seising capabilities, leading to improved supply chain partner development and co-evolution capabilities for strengthened collab - oration and relationships among supply chain members and advancing supply chain members in fulfilling their environmental responsibilities for GSCM improvement. Additionally, Akhtar et al. ( 2024 ) and Feng et al. ( 2024 ) noted that the integrated sensing and seising capabilities of generative AI can augment flexibility and adaptive capabilities, as well as eco-dynamic capabilities, to facilitate green innovation and swiftly reconfigure supply chain approaches and procedures with respect to environmental challenges. Generative AI capabilities prioritise the analysis, development, and readjustment of supply chain processes to enhance GSCM; however, the indispensable learning processes that are capable of linking and enhancing all of these capabilities have been overlooked (Jackson et al. 2024 ; Song et al. 2024 ; Souza and Taka - hashi 2019 ). Chaudhuri et al. ( 2024 ) and Jackson et al. ( 2024 ) posited that dynamic knowledge and innovative learning capabilities are required for transforming obtained knowledge and information into innovations that enhance services, products, and procedures, hence improving firms’ GSCM. Therefore, generative AI capabilities that incorporate learning processes into sensing, seising and reconfiguring capabilities are required for enhancing GSCM. Essentially, sensing, seising and reconfiguring capabilities are fundamental components of gen - erative AI for enhancing GSCM. Additionally, it is imperative to incorporate the learning process into these capabilities to improve performance. Through the continuous learning of evolving 610 T. Methods This section elaborates on the data collection procedure, FDM, FSE-DEMATEL approach, and pro - posed analytical procedures. 3.1. Data collection A total of 30 experienced respondents, possessing an average of 10 years’ experience in green supply chain management and proficiency in utilising generative AI for problem solving in the Indonesian automotive industry, participated in the FDM and FSE-DEMATEL analyses to guarantee the val - idity of the findings. This panel of experts were selected using purposive sampling technique and consisted of 10 academic experts, 15 professionals from automotive firms, and five government representatives. The respondents participated in-person interviews. The sample size was deemed enough for conducting the specified analyses, considering the data collecting methods and meth - odologies used (Bui et al. 2023 ). Appendix 1 provides specific demographic details for those experts participated. 3.2. FDM The FDM is an integrated method that amalgamates fuzzy logic with the Delphi methodology to assess and eliminate criteria deemed less significant and invalid (Ishikawa et al. 1993 ; Tsai et al. 2024 ). Within this study, the FDM is utilised to enhance questionnaire design while addressing the limitations of the experts’ reference base (Bui et al. 2024 ; Ishikawa et al. 1993 ). This method also used to effectively address the vagueness and uncertainty inherent in qualitative data associ - ated with dynamic supply chain environments (Tsai et al. 2024 ; Tseng et al. 2023 ). FDM relies on professional judgment and linguistic assessment to validate initial criteria collection. Hence, this study used FDM to eliminate superfluous and invalid criteria from six aspects identified based on expert evaluations. In addition, this method reduces the data collection time due to the relatively small number of respondents needed (Bui et al. 2024 ; Tsai et al. 2024 ; Tseng et al. 2023 ). FSE is recognised as a classification in fuzzy set theory that offers an approach for addressing issues that are characterised by nondeterministic features, specifically expert judgment and the intricate interrelationships linked to generative AI capabilities in dynamic supply chain contexts. The FSE method addresses uncertainties, integrates measurements, and provides an overall index for each component level (Islam, Tseng, and Karia 2019 ; Kurrahman et al. 2024 ). This method uses membership grade theory to transform linguistic scales into quantitative data, producing precise outcomes (Kurrahman et al. 2024 ; Wu et al. 2024 ). Consequently, FSE is necessary to convert professional perceptions into quantitative data and provide a synthetic assessment of the attributes for achieving a specific objec - tive associated with uncertain circumstances and involving multicriteria decision-making. Further - more, the FSE-DEMATEL approach is used to ascertain the interrelationships among attributes, as well as to construct and illustrate the causal model of generative AI capabilities for GSCM improve - ment, hence assisting decision-makers in identifying essential attributes (Islam, Tseng, and Karia 2019 ; Wu et al. 2024 ). 3.3.1. Discussion This section discusses the theoretical and managerial implications of this study in the context of prioritising generative AI capabilities for enhancing GSCM. 5.1. Theoretical implications The incorporation of the DCV and OLT provides a profound understanding of generative AI’s capability to assess dynamic supply chain data, hence improving learning processes for enhanced supply chain reconfiguration that optimises GSCM. The integration of the DCV with OLT amplifies the generative AI capabilities for the advancement of GSCM. This study addresses the inadequacy in integrating essential learning processes that act as sources and catalysts for generative AI dynamic capabilities, thereby improving the development and enhancement of innovative firm capabilities in response to swift environmental changes and technological advancements (Gho - bakhloo et al. 2024 ; Jackson et al. 2024 ). This study offers an approach that signifies the sensing, seising and reconfiguring capabilities of the DCV while elucidating the mechanisms by which these capabilities are perpetually produced and maintained over time. The amalgamation of the DCV and OLT provides an indispensable approach to sustaining generative AI dynamic capabilities for enhancing GSCM. Generative AI capabilities for GSCM enhancement integrate learning processes within the per - spectives of sensing capabilities, seising capabilities and reconfiguring capabilities on the basis of DCV-OLT integration. Within this integration, the results of this study indicate that the dynamic knowledge and innovative learning capabilities (A1) and reflexive control and measurement capa - bilities (A2) incorporated into the sensing capabilities perspective, as well as the co-evolution Figure 4. According to the sensing capabilities perspective, the dynamic knowledge and innovative learn - ing capabilities of generative AI were found to be fundamentally causative for GSCM enhancement. This result corresponds with prior studies asserting that dynamic knowledge and innovative learn - ing capabilities improve the identification and acquisition of new knowledge and information, as well as the evaluation of existing knowledge by all stakeholders in the supply chain, to promote eco-dynamic innovation that enhances services, products, and processes, thereby improving firms’ environmental performance within the supply chain (Gruchmann and Seuring 2018 ; Meier, Gruchmann, and Ivanov 2023 ). Enhancing these capabilities can improve flexibility and adaptive capabilities, thereby supporting innovations and technological adoption that foster new idea creation and the emergence of business opportunities aligned with supply chain environmental objectives for enhancing GSCM. Furthermore, dynamic knowledge and innovative learning capa - bilities are essential for successfully converting resources and capacities into green innovation, hence producing effective sustainable solutions (Feng et al. 2024 ). As emphasised by Meier, Gruch - mann, and Ivanov ( 2023 ) and Chaudhuri et al. ( 2024 ), these capabilities may enhance data analysis of production processes, hence maximising resource use, refining procedures, and upgrading sys - tems to promote GSCM. The incorporation of dynamic knowledge and innovative aptitude for learning is crucial for the advancement of generative AI in GSCM improvement. Reflexive control and measurement capabilities include the acquisition of information to assess, compare, and evaluate supply chain performance in favour of GSCM requirements. In this study, these capabilities found to assist firms monitor progress toward environmental objectives, pinpoint areas for improvement and enhancing eco-dynamic capabilities for better adherence to environ - mental standards. This findings regarding reflexive control and measurement capabilities are con - sistent with prior studies that has emphasised its capacity to monitor both internal and external operations, as well as to facilitate strategic planning and decision-making to enhance environmental performance across the supply chains of firms (Gruchmann and Seuring 2018 ; Lu, Zhao, and Liu 2022 ; Meier, Gruchmann, and Ivanov 2023 ). For example, firms may implement data monitoring and analysis to evaluate the risks and threats associated with their green supply chains. This approach offers the requisite insights to modify strategies and operations in response to these threats, thereby preserving the flexibility and control necessary for GSCM enhancement (Javaid, Haleem, and Singh 2023 ; Kosasih et al. 2023 ). Additionally, reflexive control and measurement capabilities can continuously collect data on suppliers’ carbon footprints, waste management strat - egies, and energy usage to ensure their compliance with GSCM standards. Emphasising reflexive control and measurement capabilities is vital for enhanced GSCM. The co-evolution capabilities within the seising capabilities perspective aim to strengthen relationships among supply chain members, thereby promoting enhanced partnership and collab - oration for the continuous creation of innovative capabilities and resources to advance GSCM (Gruchmann and Seuring 2018 ; Lu, Zhao, and Liu 2022 ). These capabilities found to be effective in transcending the mere development and introduction of innovative services and products by integrating market dynamics into the firm’s environment within an interorganizational evolution - ary process. Co-evolution capabilities may facilitate knowledge transfer and the learning processes essential for supply chain partner development, hence improving eco-dynamic capabilities for gra - dual enhancement of current operating procedures to advance GSCM. Prior studies corroborate these findings, asserting that such initiatives can assist firms in establishing and sustaining success - ful collaboration with suppliers and customers to promote GSCM (Belhadi et al. 2022 ; Lu, Zhao, and Liu 2022 ; Meier, Gruchmann, and Ivanov 2023 ). Firms across the supply chain may enhance their GSCM strategies by means of horizontal and vertical collaboration. Therefore, co-evolution capabilities are essential for improving GSCM. In summary, this study makes a significant contribution to the existing literature on generative AI for GSCM, particularly in regards to the integrated application of DCV and OLT. This study 622 T. KURRAHMAN ET AL. notably integrates DCV and OLT to elucidate how firms cultivate and use dynamic capabilities for environmentally friendly efforts through the learning process, in contrast to prior studies that examined these theories independently. This integrated theories and point of views offers a more refined comprehension of the dynamic interaction among firms’ resources and capabili - ties, learning processes, and environmental performance. Within these integrated theories, the dynamic knowledge and innovative learning capabilities, reflexive control and measurement capabilities and co-evolution capabilities of generative AI must be prioritised to enhance GSCM. Within the context of generative AI for GSCM improvement, the significance of these aspects lies in the ability of generative AI to promote flexibility and adaptive capabilities and supply chain partner development capabilities to achieve enhanced eco-dynamic capabilities. Firms may focus on enhancing all three of these aspects to increase generative AI capabilities for GSCM development. 5.2. Managerial implications This study presents generative AI capabilities for enhancing GSCM in the Indonesian automotive industry. These criteria include data gathering and analysis for predictive maintenance improve - ment (C5), sales and operations strategy identification (C6), high-quality and consistent data gath - ering (C1), data-driven production insight analysis (C2) and production strategy identification (C3). These criteria must be enhanced to facilitate GSCM improvement. Data gathering and analysis for predictive maintenance improvement leverage generative AI’s ability to foresee needed maintenance, detect all possible problems prior to their escalation, and enhance operations utilising these insights to improve supply chain environmental performance. This capability may be employed in the automotive industry to oversee and maintain manufactur - ing machinery, hence ensuring efficient and ecologically sustainable production processes. Data gathering and analysis for predictive maintenance improvement extend the lifespan of machinery and equipment by facilitating prompt and highly accurate maintenance while also reducing the number of superfluous repairs, hence minimising the waste of materials and resources across the automotive industry supply chain. Moreover, optimised and more efficient maintenance pro - cedures provide greater energy efficiency and decreased emissions, thus promoting an environmen - tally friendly supply chain. Additionally, to improve data collection and analysis for predictive maintenance, the automotive industry can integrate generative AI with Internet-of-Things sensors and devices that proficiently capture real-time data from diverse sources within the supply chain, including vehicles (engine temperature, fluid level, tire pressure), machinery (machine temperature, vibration, output), and environmental (temperature, climate, humidity) sensors for enhanced GSCM. Sales and operations strategy identification is the capacity to discern and assess market possibi - lities and risks to guide practical decisions that ensure the successful alignment of sales and envir - onmentally friendly operations. In this context, generative AI employs precise market patterns and customer demand data to formulate proactive sales and operational strategies. By employing and evaluating these data, generative AI may develop personalised marketing strategies, thus enhancing engagement and increasing revenue. The utilisation of market data and forecasts may lead to opti - mum inventory levels, hence reducing surplus stock and minimising waste for GSCM improve - ment. Moreover, operational data may be used by generative AI to detect inefficiencies in manufacturing processes and supply chain activities, suggesting strategies that minimise waste and improve sustainability. Consequently, the sales and operations strategy identification capabili - ties provided by generative AI enable the automotive industry to acquire insightful knowledge regarding customer preferences, market trends, and the competitive landscape, thus facilitating the development of a comprehensive strategy that enhances sales while also promoting environ - mentally sustainable practices for the improvement in GSCM. To improve the identification of sales and operations strategies, generative AI may be integrated with other AI processes, such as INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF LOGISTICS RESEARCH AND APPLICATIONS 623 reinforcement and machine learning, to maximise these strategies via experimentation in a simu - lated environment, hence increasing efficiency and GSCM. High-quality and consistent data gathering includes obtaining reliable information to identify opportunities and risks accurately, hence improving decision-making processes for strengthening supply chain environmental performance. Augmented data ensure that generative AI delivers accu - rate and reliable insights, leading to improved decision-making. Consistent data collection guaran - tees comprehensive and current information, enhancing strategy development. In the automotive industry, higher-quality and dependable data enable generative AI to identify opportunities for improvement and promote more sustainable practices. Furthermore, the continuous gathering of data may increase the efficiency of logistics and transportation routes, hence reducing consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, which contributes to advancements in GSCM. Moreover, the collec - tion of high-quality and consistent data enables the monitoring of the effects of improvements in environmentally sustainable practices, facilitating ongoing GSCM enhancement. In addition, to enhance high-quality and consistent data gathering, generative AI could potentially be integrated with the Internet of Things and computer vision to detect irregularities, patterns, and trends in con - tinuous real-time data. By guaranteeing high-quality and consistent data collection, generative AI may markedly enhance the efficiency and continuity of the automotive industry’s GSCM, resulting in a more robust competitive advantage for the industry. Data-driven production insight analysis includes detecting or forecasting environmental advantages and hazards through the collection and examination of data from production pro - cesses. Through the analysis of production process data, generative AI may detect inefficiencies and propose optimizations that increase workflows, decrease energy consumption, and reduce waste for GSCM improvement. This approach can assist firms in controlling their raw resources, leading to a reduction in the negative environmental effects of industrial activities. This feature allows for the continuous monitoring of production processes, identifying the causes of and suggesting ways in which to reduce waste creation. Furthermore, the data-driven analysis of pro - duction insights may foster the development of innovative and sustainable production pro - cedures. Thus, data-driven production insight analysis generates actionable outcomes, supporting decision-makers in developing informed plans for production and operational improvements to improve GSCM. To improve data-driven production insight analysis, generative AI can integrate data from all pertinent sources, including enterprise resource planning, manu - facturing execution systems, Internet of Things sensors, ecological data, and other information regarding the supply chain, to achieve a more comprehensive data representation and enhanced insights for GSCM. Production strategy identification entails the use of generative AI to develop and enhance plans that augment efficiency, environmentally friendly practices, and overall effectiveness throughout the production process inside the supply chain. The generative AI capability in for - mulating improved production plans facilitates the optimal allocation of resources, ensuring the efficient utilisation of materials and energy while concurrently reducing waste for GSCM enhancement. The use of generative AI to identify improved production processes enables firms to anticipate market demands and strengthen their competitive edge. Moreover, generative AI may assist firms in forecasting possible challenges or complexities in the manufacturing pro - cess, enabling proactive production strategies, improved problem resolution, and enhanced oper - ational efficiency. The use of generative AI in production strategy identification is essential for firms aiming to optimise their processes and enhance their GSCM. Furthermore, in order to improve the identification of production strategies for enhanced GSCM, generative AI can be integrated with digital twins that can visually represent physical production systems. This inte - gration will facilitate the simulation of numerous production scenarios and the assessment of the potential effects of different decisions toward environment prior to their implementation in a real-world setting. 624 T. Conclusions This study strives to assess the judgments of experts and professionals in the field to determine the complete, valid, and imperative attributes of generative AI capabilities for GSCM in the automotive industry. Generative AI capability assessment has garnered considerable attention and evaluation in recent years, driven by the growing acknowledgment across supply chain members regarding the need for generative AI to formulate strategies that mitigate the notable environmental repercus - sions stemming from the insufficient end-of-life management of vehicles and automotive com - ponents, as well as the escalating air pollution levels due to production processes that intensify environmental consequences. Nonetheless, despite numerous efforts to improve generative AI capabilities, our understanding of the valid and thorough attributes of generative AI for enhancing GSCM remains limited, particularly with respect to learning capabilities that can augment sensing, seising, and reconfiguring capabilities to meet the dynamic environmental demands of the supply chain. Consequently, this study offers useful recommendations by integrating the DCV with OLT. This study presents an approach for constructing a solid theoretical or hierarchical structure that offers extensive guidance to facilitate practical advancement. This study’s findings are pertinent to the indispensable attributes of generative AI capabilities for GSCM, as they reveal the causal interrelationships among these attributes, which are used to determine and prioritise the most essential attributes for future assessments and decision-making. This study provides a more clear and complete comprehension of generative AI’s capabilities in augmenting GSCM through the integration of DCV and OLT. In accordance with the necessity for OLT to be integrated with DCV, the findings indicate an imperative emphasis on the dynamic knowledge and innovative learning capabilities and reflexive control and measurement capabilities incorporated into the perspective of sensing capabilities and the co-evolution capabilities incorpor - ated into the perspective of seising capabilities, which are the key aspects in the structure. All of these aspects have the potential to enhance supply chain partner development capabilities, flexibility and adaptive capabilities and eco-dynamic capabilities, hence improving generative AI capabilities for GSCM improvement. Furthermore, the findings identify practical guidelines for the automotive industry, including those related to data gathering and analysis for predictive maintenance improvement, sales and operations strategy identification, high-quality and consistent data gather - ing, data-driven production insight analysis and production strategy identification. High-quality and consistent data collection for real-time production insight analysis and long-term strategic planning can improve data-driven decision-making throughout the production lifecycle, encom - passing predictive maintenance enhancement, sales and operations strategy formulation, and pro - duction strategy development, eventually resulting in enhanced resource utilisation and a diminished environmental impact. Hence, these criteria must be prioritised in efforts aimed at enhancing the automotive industry’s generative AI capabilities for GSCM improvement. Practical guidance derived from these criteria offers practitioners explicit directives for improving decision- making processes and cultivating generative AI capabilities to improve GSCM. This study significantly contributes to the literature on generative AI and GSCM by establishing a valid hierarchical structure and highlighting key aspects of generative AI capabilities that should be prioritised for enhancing GSCM. This study further provides significant insights for decision- makers through determining essential criteria and analyzing the causal linkages among them. Moreover, previous studies have shown an insufficient ability to incorporate the learning process into the hierarchical structure. This study rectifies the identified gap by integrating OLT into this structure to enhance the pertinent DCV of sensing, seising, and reconfiguring capabilities. The need for dynamic knowledge and innovative learning capabilities and reflexive control and measurement capabilities that are incorporated into the perspective of sensing capabilities and co-evolution capabilities that are included in the perspective of seising capabilities are highlighted in terms of their ability to enhance generative AI capabilities for GSCM improvement. In addition, this study presents the interrelationships among the criteria and transforms them into INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF LOGISTICS RESEARCH AND APPLICATIONS 625 recommendations that can be implemented by practitioners and decision-makers to improve the decision-making process. Practical guidance offers recommendations pertaining to data gathering and analysis for predictive maintenance improvement, sales and operations strategy identification, high-quality and consistent data gathering, data-driven production insight analysis and production strategy identification. There are several limitations associated with this study that may be addressed in future studies. First, it is imperative to recognise the potential constraints of this study in terms of the extensive - ness of the structure, as the attributes employed in this study are derived from the literature. Further research is necessary to broaden and refine the measurements to improve the structure. Moreover, this study only focuses on the automotive industry in Indonesia. Future study may explore the gen - erative AI attributes of different countries and industries to augment the understanding of appro - priate enhancements in GSCM. Future research could also examine comparisons across geographical areas. In addition, the methodologies implemented in this study are subject to certain constraints. The total number of experts and professionals is limited owing to the study’s require - ments for expertise, proficiency, and industry knowledge. Furthermore, the uneven allocation of academia, professional, and government, along with an evaluation process that based on pro - fessional experience, knowledge and subjectivity, can contribute to bias stemming from pro - fessionals’ familiarity with the industry. Future research is essential to address these issues by increasing the number of experts participating, integrating more cross-sectional experts, and acquiring a more balanced sample for enhanced generalizability. Additionally, the methodology employed in this study has the potential to be applied to other disciplines to extend the literature. We also hypothesize that organizations with a stronger innovation culture, where employees share a common understanding of the value and importance of innovation, will be better able to convert capabilities into innovation performance. We test our hypotheses using time-lagged, multisource data from 173 companies in the Iranian pharmaceutical industry, a knowledge-intensive, high-velocity environment highly dependent on HRs to innovate. Our results show that the relationship between HPWS and innovation performance is mediated by dynamic capabilities (DCs). Further, alongside finding support for the moderating effect of innovation cul - ture in the relationship between DCs and innovation per - formance, we find that innovation culture moderates the indirect effect of HPWS on innovation performance via DCs such that innovation culture strengthens the mediated rela - tionship. The theoretical and practical implications of our findings are discussed. The resource-based view (RBV) of the firm argues that employees are an important resource that enable organizations to adapt in dynamic environments and achieve a competitive advantage (Barney, 1991 ; Barney et al., 2001). Indeed, extensive research confirms that the stra - tegic use of HRs such as high-performance work systems (HPWS) positively contribute to an organization’s ability to achieve a competitive advantage. HPWS are defined as bundles of HR practices designed to enhance the abilities, motivation, and opportunities of an organization’s workforce (Boxall, 2012; Hung et al., 2010; Ogbonnaya & Valizade, 2018; Way et al., 2015). While several mechanisms have been proposed linking HPWS to organizational performance in general and innovation in particular (Gahan et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2012; Wei & Lau, 2010), researchers continue to call for additional theoretical development and empirical evidence, particularly with the specific outcomes studied (Saridakis et al., 2017). In response to these calls, researchers have linked HPWS to organizational outcomes through various types of organizational capa - bilities, such as learning (Jerez-Gómez et al., 2019), ambidexterity (Patel et al., 2013), adaptive capability (Wei & Lau, 2010), and absorptive capacity (Soo et al., 2017). These studies have operationalized organi - zational capabilities from different views and in different contexts in terms of industry type and environmental conditions, leading to tenuous conclusions. Consequently, this area remains somewhat fragmented in terms of the types of capabilities developed by HPWS and how those capabilities link to innovation performance, highlighting the need for more research on how HPWS contribute to innovation performance through organizational capabilities (Shipton et al., 2006, 2017). In the current study, we posit that HPWS foster organizational inno - vation in part through the development of dynamic capabilities (DCs). Dynamic capabilities are defined as ‘a firm’s ability to integrate, build and reconfigure internal and external competencies to address rapidly changing environments’ (Teece et al., 1997, p. 516). While DCs are viewed as an important source of innovation and value creation in dynamic environments, the understanding of how organizations develop DCs is less clear. In this regard, we argue that HPWS, consisting of HR practices designed to enhance employees’ abilities, motivation, and opportunity (AMO) (Appelbaum et al., 2000), help build the three core dimensions of DCs (i.e. learning, integration, and reconfiguration capa - bilities), which in turn enable firms to learn from within and outside the firm, integrate acquired resources, and properly reconfigure them - selves in response to external changes. Although previous research THE INTERNATIONAL JOuRNAL OF HuMAN RESOuRCE MANAGEMENT 3557 recognizes that HR systems are related to the development of capabilities (e.g. Lin & Wu, 2014; Wei & Lau, 2010), we propose that DCs are a more robust, yet parsimonious, mechanism for understanding the link between HPWS and innovation performance. In addition to examining the mediating role of DCs between HPWS and innovation performance, we also consider how the organizational context influences the ability of firms to translate HPWS and DCs into innovation performance. The organizational context influences how employees interpret and perceive phenomena in organizations, which in turn, affect attitudes and behaviours (Ferris et al., 1998; Johns, 2006). When a workforce has a common understanding of the purpose and practices associated with HR systems, it can strengthen the relationship between the system and firm outcomes (Bowen & Ostroff, 2004). Although a wide range of contextual factors potentially link HPWS, capabilities, and innovation performance such as psychological safety (Rasheed et al., 2017), voice opportunity (Shahzad et al., 2019), orga - nizational engagement (Gahan et al., 2021), and transformational lead - ership (Chen et al., 2012), innovation culture is a broader contextual factor addressing both an organization’s infrastructure conducive for innovation, as well as the goals and values oriented towards creativity and innovation (Martín-de Castro et al., 2013). A firm’s innovation culture shapes the mindset of a workforce and directs employees’ efforts, behaviours, and interactions towards the common goal of innovation performance (Dodge et al., 2017). Hence, we examine how an organi - zation’s innovation culture fosters an organization’s activities and capa - bilities towards the introduction of new ideas, processes, or products. Overall, the current study makes several contributions to the literature. First, there is both theoretical and practical value in examining how DCs, as firm-level capabilities, link HPWS to innovation performance. Although some researchers have assumed such a relationship exists or test only one type of capability, we provide empirical evidence of the role of HPWS in building DCs (i.e. learning, integration, and reconfig - uration) and, in turn, increased innovation performance. Second, we examine how a firm’s innovation culture affects the ability of firms to direct DCs towards innovation performance. When firms develop a culture in which employees can safely express new ideas, offer construc - tive feedback on others’ ideas, and take risks without fear of punishment, the organization will be more likely to translate its resources and capa - bilities into innovation. Further, we explore whether innovation culture moderates the indirect effect of HPWS on innovation performance through DCs. This approach adds new insights on the importance of innovation culture in understanding how HPWS convert resources into capabilities for innovation. 3558 G. MEHRALIAN ET AL. Finally, we test our model in a knowledge-intensive, high-velocity environment (i.e. Iranian pharmaceutical industry) that is highly depen - dent on HRs to innovate (Farzaneh et al., 2021) and achieve organiza - tional outcomes (Hess & Rothaermel, 2011). This setting is novel to the HPWS literature and particularly relevant to DCs and innovation (Tasavori et al., 2021). Iranian firms face numerous unexpected envi - ronmental changes due to economic sanctions against the country, and they inevitably struggle to procure needed materials and maintain oper - ations (Mehralian et al., 2017). HPWS provide a more flexible approach to HRM than control-based approaches, enabling firms to reconfigure existing resources in the face of environmental constraints. Hence, we extend the generalisability and applicability of SHRM theories to a Middle Eastern country marked by political and economic uncertainty. Theory and hypothesis development Over the last several decades, the RBV has been used as a foundation to explain how HR practices can be a source of competitive advantage and innovation performance. This theory conceptualizes firms as bundles of resources and suggests that the possession of inimitable resources can facilitate the achievement of competitive advantages, leading to outstanding performance. Drawing on the RBV , scholars have emphasized the role of HPWS in creating organizational-level capabilities, such as DCs, and their contribution to organizational performance (Beltrán-Martín et al., 2008; Chadwick & Flinchbaugh, 2021; Seeck & Diehl, 2017). The DCs perspective, as an extension of the RBV , emphasizes that the evo - lution, reconfiguration, and renewal of the firm’s resources and capa - bilities must occur for firms to survive in dynamic environments (Baía & Ferreira, 2019; Farzaneh et al., 2022). More specifically, DCs are highly patterned, repetitive organizational routines that lead to changes in the firm’s available resource base (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000; Teece et al., 1997), and consist of three activities/routines for generating innovation and sustaining competitiveness: learning, integration, and reconfiguration (Teece, 2007). Consequently, as displayed in Figure 1 , we argue that DCs (i.e. learning, integration, and reconfiguration capabilities) mediate the relationship between HPWS and innovation performance at the organization level of analysis. HPWS and dynamic capabilities HPWS involve a set of HR practices that exhibit interrelationships and mutual reinforcement (Kehoe & Wright, 2013), and when aligned, they form HPWS (Jiang et al., 2012 ; Lepak et al., 2006 ). While each THE INTERNATIONAL JOuRNAL OF HuMAN RESOuRCE MANAGEMENT 3559 individual HR practice targets a specific aspect of the individual or team experience, it is widely recognized that bundles of practices create a stronger HR system that builds synergies within an organization and can accumulate to influence organizational effectiveness (Bowen & Ostroff, 2004). For example, some researchers view HPWS as having three main dimensions, namely practices that enhance employees’ abil - ities, motivation, and opportunities (AMO) (Appelbaum et al., 2000; Boxall & Macky, 2009; Lepak et al., 2006). Ability-enhancing practices are designed to improve employees’ knowledge, skills, and abilities (KSAs) through activities such as rigorous recruitment and selection processes, and training (Obeidat et al., 2016). Motivational practices , such as linking performance with appraisal systems and rewards, help increase employee motivation and performance management (Katou & Budhwar, 2010 ). Finally, opportunity-enhancing practices emphasize employee involvement and collaboration through a wide range of activ - ities such as flexible workplace design and work schedules, team-based work, information sharing, and employee participation in decision-making (Jiang et al., 2012). In this paper, we use the AMO framework to under - stand how organizations build the three dimensions of DCs: learning, integration, and reconfiguration. Of the three dimensions of DCs, learning capabilities have been most closely linked to HR practices. Learning capabilities help organizations avoid repeating mistakes from past experiences (Y alcinkaya et al., 2007) and are necessary for organizations to respond to rapid changes in the marketplace. Learning capabilities depend on the organization’s ability to accumulate experience, as well as the development of knowledge articulation and codification activities (Zollo & Winter, 2002). In terms of the accumulation of experience, HPWS help manage the inflow of new knowledge both by attracting and selecting employees who bring in distinct KSAs (Kang et al., 2007; Wang & Zatzick, 2019), and by supporting and encouraging learning via extensive training. Indeed, researchers report that HPWS have a significant impact on Figure 1. Theoretical model. 3560 G. Further, HPWS enhance knowledge articulation and cod - ification through opportunity-enhancing practices designed to increase communication, transparency, and employee involvement (Mehralian et al., 2021). Therefore, we propose: Hypothesis 1 : HPWS are positively related to learning capabilities. Integration capabilities refer to how well a firm integrates external and internal resources to provide a comprehensive and coordinated approach to resource utilization (Porrini, 2004). From a microfoundations perspective, integration capabilities involve both the collective behaviour of employees as well as the associated routines, work patterns, and daily activities that allow organizations to integrate diverse resources (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000; Zollo & Winter, 2002). Microfoundations can be viewed as the underlying actions at the individual and group levels that shape strategies, organizations, and, from a general perspective, DCs; and these microfoundations lead to the emergence of superior organizational-level performance (Eisenhardt et al., 2010). That is, DCs, as organizational-level strategic capabilities, are supported by key procedures, activities, and behaviours whose systematic design and adoption in organizations help foster and sustain the innovation behaviours of employees (Wilden et al., 2016). In line with the microfoundations view of strategic HRM practices, we argue that HPWS build the necessary routines and work activities needed for the development of collective knowledge at the organizational level, leading to integration capabilities (Minbaeva, 2013). For example, HPWS use teams and information sharing to build intra-organizational networks, which enable organizations to connect diverse knowledge and experiences across its workforce (Hansen & Nohria, 2004; Lin & Chen, 2006; Song et al., 2018). Team-based work also strengthens relationships between employees, which further contributes to the development of integration capabilities within an organization (Dixon et al., 2014). Finally, opportunity-enhancing practices allow employees to engage in decision-making and problem-solving, which can improve the flow of information and increase collaboration, both of which are needed for integration (Bowen & Ostroff, 2004). Taken together, HPWS help orga - nizations improve their ability to integrate internal and external knowl - edge (Minbaeva, 2005). Therefore, we hypothesize: Hypothesis 2 : HPWS are positively related to integration capabilities. Reconfiguration capabilities enable organizations to recombine and modify existing resources in response to dynamic environments (Teece, THE INTERNATIONAL JOuRNAL OF HuMAN RESOuRCE MANAGEMENT 3561 2007). In a rapidly changing market, organizations need to continuously find new ways to use existing resources more efficiently and effectively (Zhou & Wu, 2009). HPWS help firms develop reconfiguration capa - bilities in several ways. For instance, job rotation, which is often included in HPWS, enables employees to develop knowledge of multiple processes within and between departments. When employees accumulate knowl - edge of diverse processes, organizations are better positioned to recon - figure resources in response to external changes. Further, the use of teams and open communication at all levels of the organization increases an organization’s flexibility in responding to external changes. Finally, HPWS offer reward and recognition policies linked to team and orga - nizational goals (Gahan et al., 2021), which can unite employees around a common organizational purpose such that reconfiguring activities and processes to meet the environmental changes is understood and sup - ported by employees (O’Reilly & Tushman, 2008). In summary, HPWS not only help organizations learn from both inside and outside the organization and integrate newly acquired knowl - edge with existing knowledge, but they also help organizations recon - figure themselves in response to changing external conditions (Lin & Wu, 2014). Therefore, we posit the following hypothesis: Hypothesis 3 : HPWS are positively related to reconfiguration capabilities. Linking HPWS to innovation performance through DCs Prior research identifies HPWS as an important factor influencing orga - nizational innovation. HPWS build employee KSAs, encourage collabo - ration, and create opportunities for employee involvement, all of which contribute to employee creativity and, in turn, organizational innovation (Camps & Luna-Arocas, 2012; Sung & Choi, 2018). Further, HPWS focus on the enrichment of work by increasing the skill variety, auton - omy, and responsibility in jobs, all of which increase internal work motivation, an important precursor of employee creativity (Hackman & Oldham, 1976). Finally, when organizations have open communication and provide team-based compensation, the generation, development, and implementation of innovative ideas is more likely (De Spiegelaere et al., 2018). Hence, prior research argues that HPWS help build a sustainable competitive advantage for organizations, in part through the ability to innovate. It is widely discussed, however, that HR practices do not directly lead to organizational innovation, but are first converted to organizational capabilities to give organizations more opportunities to meet market needs effectively (Lin & Wu, 2014; Shahzad et al., 2019). With respect to DCs, innovation requires active resource orchestration via high-level 3562 G. MEHRALIAN ET AL. routines. The role of employees is central to the DCs viewpoint, as much of the DCs literature is concerned with changing behaviour, as well as with building and reconfiguring internal and external compe - tencies (Teece et al., 1997). As Zollo and Winter ( 2002) note, a funda - mental challenge in building DCs involves changing the resource base (Helfat & Peteraf, 2009), as well as the routines, behaviours, and work patterns (Eisenhardt & Martin, 2000; Zollo & Winter, 2002). Consequently, we argue that the relationship between HPWS and innovation performance develops through DCs. Prior research is sug - gestive of this mediated relationship in various contexts. For example, Patel et al. ( 2013) report that HPWS generate flexibility in the form of ‘organizational ambidexterity’ , which allows organizations to adapt and innovate in response to environmental changes. In addition, Zahra and George ( 2002) found that, when properly developed, integration capa - bilities can enable firms to combine new and existing knowledge to generate new ideas. Likewise, Wei and Lau ( 2010) reported that adapt - ability mediates the relationship between HPWS and organizational innovation performance. Finally, research has shown that the develop - ment of DCs can improve radical innovation in established firms (Chiu et al., 2016). The underlying rationale of these studies is that DCs are an important mechanism that explains how organizational resources are translated to innovation performance. Moreover, in the context of our study, organizations in developing economies and knowledge-based industries rely more heavily on DCs than organizations in other contexts due to rapidly changing environmental conditions (Fainshmidt et al., 2016). Therefore, we hypothesize: Hypothesis 4 : The positive relationship between HPWS and innovation perfor - mance is mediated by DCs. The moderating role of innovation culture From a social context perspective, an organization’s environment is critical for understanding the effect of HR practices on the organizational outcomes (Ferris et al., 1998). One overarching aspect of the social context is an organization’s culture, which encompasses the shared values, beliefs, and assumptions of organizational members, and offers the guid - ing principles that direct behaviours towards achieving organizational goals. In particular, an organization’s innovation culture is viewed as an important contextual factor capable of influencing innovation perfor - mance (Martín-de Castro et al., 2013). An innovation-oriented culture values open-mindedness, learning, and creativity such that employees share an understanding of how HR practices work together towards a firms’ innovation goals (Tian et al., 2018). A stronger innovation culture THE INTERNATIONAL JOuRNAL OF HuMAN RESOuRCE MANAGEMENT 3563 develops when organizations encourage employees to take more risks, increase the psychological safety for employees to express new ideas, and provide resources to increase employees’ willingness to embrace new challenges (Ireland et al., 2003; Van Esch et al., 2018). Therefore, innovation culture shapes employees’ mindset and behaviour as they participate in and carryout the activities within an organization. In the current study, we argue that a strong innovation culture helps translate organizational capabilities towards innovation performance (Ali & Park, 2016; Chen et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2018). Although DCs alone can increase innovation performance, we expect organizations with a stronger innovation culture will be better able to direct DCs towards innovation performance. In a strong innovation culture, the routines and activities associated with DCs will be carried out by employees who hold a common understanding that new and creative ideas are valued and taking risks towards this goal is supported (Shalley & Gilson, 2004). For example, while an organization’s reconfiguration capabilities inher - ently involve routines and activities that make it possible to combine diverse resources, a stronger innovation culture will provide a strategic focus and frame of reference supportive of creativity and innovation. In contrast, in organizations with weaker innovation cultures, employees carrying out these activities may be concerned about taking risks or offering new ideas beyond organizationally sanctioned approaches to the reconfiguration process. Furthermore, when an organization’s culture is oriented towards other outcomes such as efficiency, employees may carry out the activities around integration or reconfiguration with the express intent of finding savings rather than on developing new and/or improved products. Thus, when DCs operate in an organizational context that encourages and supports innovation, the positive effect of DCs on innovation performance will be enhanced. In formal terms, we predict: Hypothesis 5 : The positive relationship between DCs and innovation performance is stronger in organizations with a stronger, as compared to a weaker, innovation culture. Method Research setting The data for the present study were collected from organizations in the Iranian pharmaceutical industry. The pharmaceutical industry has grown rapidly in recent decades in terms of market value and the number of new products launched. Approximately 75% of the market value belongs to local manufacturing firms, most of which are involved in international collaborations with foreign firms for co-development and co-marketing of products (Ghasemzadeh et al., 2021). The pharmaceutical industry 3564 G. MEHRALIAN ET AL. is well suited to test our hypotheses for several reasons. First, as illus - trated by the COVID-19 pandemic, firms in this industry must respond quickly to market needs, be able to reconfigure internal resources, and be responsive to social concerns (Droppert & Bennett, 2015). Secondly, they are not only competing with leading pharmaceutical companies but also with companies that produce generic drugs around the world. Thus, they have to meet both local and international standards and regulations in order to obtain marketing approval (Khanna, 2012). This creates a dynamic and competitive environment where innovation is critical. Finally, given the central role of HR in the pharmaceutical industry (Hess & Rothaermel, 2011), most firms invest in HRM practices and are concerned about the extent to which these practices affect their business performance. Sample and procedure The Iranian pharmaceutical industry consists of approximately 200 com - panies that produce finished drugs, active pharmaceutical components, and pharmaceutical grade packaging. The study spanned two years between September 2015 and September 2017. Because HPWS take several years to develop (Patel et al., 2013), we first invited those firms with at least three years of experience to participate in our study. To this end, we sent an email to the CEO of each company explaining the main research objectives and ethical considerations. A total of 183 companies agreed to participate in our study. To reduce concerns about common method bias, data were collected from multiple respondents. In addition, to control for cross-sectional biases, innovation performance was assessed with objective data collected approximately one year after the survey. At time 1, three different sources were used to collect data: senior HR managers (one per company) reported on HPWS, CEOs assessed dynamic capabilities, and middle managers (approximately 4 per company) reported on innovation culture. A total of 176, 184, and 671 completed questionnaires were provided by CEOs, HR managers, and middle managers, respectively, representing a response rate of approximately 88%. A face-to-face survey was con - ducted with the CEOs to increase the accuracy of the responses, whereas the remaining surveys were distributed via email. Finally, we collected objective data in 2017 (described below) regarding innovation perfor - mance from government records. After data cleaning and matching, we received completed questionnaires from 173 firms, representing a response rate of 85%. Approximately 88% of the respondents reported having a master’s degree and the other 12% a doctorate. This shows that most of the respondents were highly skilled workers who were in THE INTERNATIONAL JOuRNAL OF HuMAN RESOuRCE MANAGEMENT 3565 a good position to report on our key variables. The average tenure of the respondents was 7.5 years. The age of the firm ranged from 5 to 63 years, and the firm’s size ranged from 60 to 1200 employees. Data analysis A second-order factor analysis was conducted for the measures of HPWS and dynamic capabilities. The criteria used to select the factors were in accordance with those proposed by Kaiser ( 1958), including an eigen - value >1 along with an absolute loading factor value >0.5. As shown in Table 1, Cronbach’s alpha coefficients for all the variables are above the acceptable value of 0.7, which supports the reliability of our constructs (Hahn, 1962; Kaiser, 1958). Convergent validity is achieved through high scores of factor loading and average variance extracted (Fornell & Larcker, 1981). According to Table 1 , all scores of average variance extracted are greater than 0.5, and all factor loadings are equal and greater than 0.63, reaching the acceptable level (Marin-Garcia & Tomas, 2016). Discriminant validity was evaluated using Fornell and Larcker’s approach (1981). The results showed discriminant validity across all latent variables. We then used AMOS maximum likelihood estimation (Arbuckle & Wothke, 1999) to establish the measurement properties of the latent variables. We tested a series of CFA models. As Table 2 shows, to test the goodness-of-fit of the measurement model, we first analyzed a three-factor CFA model in which HPWS, DCs, and innovation culture were entered to ensure that sufficient con - vergent and discriminant validity existed between all the constructs. The model provided an acceptable fit to the data: χ 2 (165) = 745.814, p < 0.001; THE INTERNATIONAL JOuRNAL OF HuMAN RESOuRCE MANAGEMENT 3569 RMSEA = 0.06; CFI = 0.93 (Browne & Cudeck, 1992). Several two-factor models also were conducted where we combined two of the factors (e.g. HPWS and DCs) as one factor along with a third factor (e.g. innovation culture). For the one-factor model, all three constructs were combined. By comparing the three-factor model with the two- and one-factor models, we found that the three-factor model has a better fit than the alternative models, resulting in sufficient discriminant validity of the constructs. Discussion Given the central role of HRM practices in achieving organizational outcomes, this study developed and empirically tested a conceptual model of how HPWS influence firms’ innovation through the development of dynamic capabilities. We provide arguments for how HPWS build the dynamic capabilities of learning, integration, and reconfiguration towards improved innovation performance. HPWS encompass practices that allow organizations to acquire and develop a highly skilled workforce, ensure open communication both horizontally and vertically to share knowledge, and provide autonomy and decision-making opportunities (Jiang et al., 2012). Further, we propose and find evidence that an organization’s innovation culture can direct DCs towards innovation performance. A strong innovation culture ensures that employees have a common under - standing that creativity and innovation are valued and expected, which helps firms translate HPWS into DCs and, in turn, innovation perfor - mance. The implications of these findings are discussed below. Implications for research Our study makes several contributions to the literature. First, this study builds on the DCs view of the firm (Teece et al., 1997) by proposing and empirically validating HPWS as a means for organizations to shape their HRs to meet the challenges of a dynamic environment through the dynamic capabilities of learning, integration, and reconfiguration. In dynamic environments, timely recognition and response to opportu - nities and changes are paramount to remaining competitive (Teece et al., 2016). While prior studies have proposed various organizational capa - bilities resulting from HPWS including, ambidexterity (e.g. Patel et al., 2013), adaptability (Wei & Lau, 2010), and absorptive capacity (Soo et al., 2017), we propose that DCs provide a more robust framework for understanding how HPWS contribute to an organization’s competitive advantage when operating in a dynamic environment. Therefore, we provide theory and empirical evidence for the relationship between HPWS and the three dimensions of DCs. Second, this study underscores the role of innovation culture as a facilitator in converting HPWS and dynamic capabilities into innovation performance (e.g. Shipton et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2011). Although some studies view HPWS and DCs as direct catalysts for innovation perfor - mance, we provide support for the idea that firms also need to create a context conducive to employees’ creativity in order to fully capture the benefits of both HPWS and dynamic capabilities. This is consistent with the social context theory of HRM (Ferris et al., 1998) where the THE INTERNATIONAL JOuRNAL OF HuMAN RESOuRCE MANAGEMENT 3575 shared understanding of the HR system influences a firm’s ability to translate HR practices and subsequent developed capabilities into per - formance (Bowen & Ostroff, 2004; Van Esch et al., 2018). Our findings, both hypothesized and exploratory, augment social context theory by showing that innovation culture, as a contextual factor, can indirectly facilitate the effect of HR systems and organizational capabilities on innovation performance. Likewise, the inclusion of innovation culture into dynamic capabilities research suggests some future research direc - tions. For example, recent studies emphasizing how dynamic capabilities interact with business strategies in general, and entrepreneurial activities more specifically (Teece, 2018; Teece et al., 2016) may benefit from understanding a firm’s innovation culture as well. When employees share a common mindset around innovation, they will likely view organiza - tional strategies and goals through a similar lens, and therefore may understand and implement the strategy in a way that enhances both capability development and innovation performance. Third, as ample evidence in the literature suggests, HR practices should first be transformed into organizational-level capabilities like organizational ambidexterity to improve organizational performance (Collins & Smith, 2006; Lin & Wu, 2014; Wei & Lau, 2010; Wu, 2007). The results of this study confirm that HPWS play a key role in the formation and development of DCs at the organizational level, which in turn leads to higher innovation performance. Therefore, our results support the theory that by implementing HPWS, organizations can transform organizational resources into DCs to improve innovation performance. As future research continues to explore the ‘black box’ between HPWS and organizational outcomes the role of DCs will move from a theoretical perspective to become more prominent in the empir - ical tests of these relationships. Implications for practice Our findings have important implications for managers in general and those working in pharmaceutical companies, in particular. In the face of frequent regulatory and technological changes (Narayanan et al., 2009), as well as environmental shocks (e.g. Covid-19 pandemic) and demands from multiple stakeholders (e.g. patients, regulators, shareholders, etc...), pharmaceutical firms need to develop capabilities that allow them to access and absorb external knowledge, as well as integrate it with existing knowl - edge. In this vein, our findings provide insights for pharmaceutical man - agers to direct investments beyond only R&D to benefit from their HR systems, thereby developing DCs and improving innovation. HPWS provide a more flexible approach to HRM than control-based approaches, enabling 3576 G. MEHRALIAN ET AL. firms to reconfigure existing resources in the face of environmental con - straints. Hence, managers working in contexts similar to those examined in this study should consider how their HR systems support the devel - opment of organizational capabilities. In addition, the development of a stronger innovation culture facili - tates the activities needed for innovation within an organization. Managers should promote an organizational culture that fits its goals and meets the demands of the organization’s competitive environment. When innovation performance is imperative to the organization, suc - cessful firms enact cultural norms to strengthen their innovation capa - bility (Boada-Cuerva et al., 2019). Leaders can develop a strong innovation culture by encouraging risk-taking within a psychologically safe envi - ronment where employees feel comfortable offering new ideas and giving and receiving constructive feedback. Constructive dialogue within teams would assist individuals in integrating different pools of knowledge in search of innovative solutions (Park et al., 2019). Given the dynamic nature of the pharmaceutical industry (Min et al., 2017), creating a collaborative atmosphere can be extremely influential in motivating employees to generate new ideas and be more creative. Limitations This study has several limitations that warrant additional discussion. First, although we assessed the perceptions of executives and managers, we did not measure lower-level employees’ perspectives on the effective - ness of HPWS. Therefore, a potential area for future research may be to examine employees’ perceptions of HPWS, and how such perceptions relate to DCs within different organizational cultures. Second, we tested our hypotheses in the Iranian pharmaceutical industry. To increase the generalizability of the results, future studies could be conducted in other settings. For example, the highly skilled workforce in these firms can be a good fit for the implementation of HPWS. Future studies should examine the value of HPWS in organizations that rely more on efficiency and less on innovation to survive, such as companies in more stable industries. It is unclear whether the value of DCs translates in industries that are less volatile. Third, future research is needed to understand how the interconnectedness of learning, integration, and reconfiguration capa - bilities influences organizational outcomes. This is particularly important in relation to innovation, as many empirical studies utilizing dynamic capabilities theory have examined only one type of capability, and it would be valuable to understand whether these capabilities are not only distinct but also potentially substitutable for one another. Finally, this study occurred in the context of significant political and economic THE INTERNATIONAL JOuRNAL OF HuMAN RESOuRCE MANAGEMENT 3577 instability within Iran. While this context is certainly appropriate for testing the development and value of dynamic capabilities towards inno - vation performance, future research is needed to confirm our findings in other contexts not hampered by such instability. Conclusion Despite the existing literature on HRM and organizational outcomes, few studies have analyzed how HPWS, as a bundle of ability-, motiva - tion-, and opportunity-enhancing practices, can improve organizational innovation performance. This study integrates the DCs perspective to discern how HR practices influence innovation performance in a knowledge-based environment. Further, this study highlights the con - tribution of innovation culture as a contextual factor that influence the links between HPWS, DCs, and innovation performance. Our results highlight the importance of having a shared understanding that supports how HR policies and practices are implemented toward the development of capabilities and innovation goals, and may explain why some firms outperform their peers in terms of innovation performance. Finally, this study provides insights into the role of HRM in the knowledge-intensive context of the pharmaceutical industry. Notes 1. RESEARCH ARTICLE Developing dynamic capabilities for the circular economy in the textile and clothing industry in Italy: A natural-resourcebased view Carla Coppola1 | Agostino Vollero 2 | Alfonso Siano 2 1Department of Economics and Statistics, University of Salerno, Salerno, Italy 2Department of Political and Communication Sciences (POLICOM), University of Salerno, Salerno, Italy Correspondence Agostino Vollero, Department of Political and Communication Sciences (POLICOM), University of Salerno, via Giovanni Paolo II, 132, Fisciano, Salerno 84084, Italy. Email: avollero@unisa.it Abstract Implementing the circular economy (CE) through the design of a restorative industrial system is a major challenge. This study investigates the capabilities that underpin the circular competitive advantages of firms in the textile and clothing industry in Italy, which is one of the country's most polluting sectors. We have developed a framework of dynamic capabilities needed for circular transition, using the theoretical lenses of a natural-resource-based view. Using a multiple-case study, the strategies of pollution prevention, product stewardship, and sustainable development and the associated capabilities of sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring are investigated. Internal practices, the role of the downstream actors in the supply chain, co-creation dynamics with external actors, and the social potential of the CE emerge as key factors. Managers may also benefit from our recommendations aimed at increasing the environmental performance of their firms and scaling up their born-circular businesses. KEYWORDS circular economy, circular transition, dynamic capabilities, natural-resource-based view, textile and clothing industry 1 | INTRODUCTION The circular economy (CE) is considered the most effective way to achieve global sustainability (Murray et al.,2017). The European Environment Agency (EEA, 2015) highlights that the CE focuses on the efficiency of material resources, involving both waste management and waste prevention. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation (EMF,2013) describes the CE as an industrial system that is restorative and regenerative by design. The CE represents a market opportunity for the textiles and clothing sectors (T&C), which are simultaneously one of the most polluting and resource intensive industries (Elf et al., 2022) and a strategic asset for some countries. As reported by the EEA (2019), clothing, footwear, and household textiles are the fourth highest pressure category for the use of primary raw materials, the second highest for land use, and the fifth highest for greenhouse gas emissions. The intensive use of resources (Paras & Curteza, 2018) and the creation of waste (Koszewska, 2018) are exacerbated by the fast-changing dynamics of the fashion industry, which involves the rapid acquisition and disposal of produced items. While the CE is considered as one way of achieving sustainability in this industry, the T&C sector still seems unfamiliar with it (Elf et al., 2022; Saha et al.,2021).
