In the fashion industry, technological limitations are a key obstacle to achieving a fully closed loop, due to the difficulty of recycling and separating garments made of mixed fibers (Pal & Gander, 2018). The development of technologies has been discussed for mechanical, chemical, and biological recycling in closed-loop textile recycling (Ribul et al.,2021); however, the capabilities that support the transition to the CE of companies seem to be under-investigated. Both in the strategic management (Centobelli et al.,2020; Khan et al.,2020; Urbinati et al.,2017) and sustainable entrepreneurship literature (Santini, 2017), opportunities/challenges have been explored (Aakko & Koskennurmi-Sivonen,2013; Franco,2017) by emphasizing the need for further analysis of the capabilities concerning the CE at a microlevel. The gap in developing these capabilities thus seems to be the greatest challenge to jumpstarting the CE (Panwar & Niesten, 2022) and to unleashing the full potential of reuse and recycling along the value chain in order to generate a competitive edge and development local creative industries (Baruque-Ramos et al.,2017; EMF,2017; Elf et al.,2022). This paper therefore aims to expand knowledge of CE implementation at the microlevel by addressing the following research question:“What capabilities can support a transition to the CE in the T&C industry in Italy?,” Italy being one of the most significant players in the global textile market. This research aim is uniquely addressed by combining the naturalresource-based view (NRBV) with the dynamic capabilities framework. On the one hand, the NRBV connects the competitive advantage to the environment by offering specific strategies as categories of analysis (pollution prevention, product stewardship, clean technology, and base of the pyramid). On the other, the dynamic capabilities framework focuses on specific categories (sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring) for capability development. We conducted a multiple-case study combined with a constructivist grounded theory approach for data analysis on the T&C industry in Italy. This qualitative study sheds light on key issues of the CE in the sector, such as internal practices, supply chain management to implement a closed loop, and interactions with external actors for developing both clean technology and exposing the social potential of CE. The paper adds empirical evidence of the manifestation of the four NRBV strategies, addressing a claim made in previous research (Hart & Dowell, 2011; McDougall et al.,2019). In addition, the circular economy offers an appropriate context to examine the presence of NRBV strategies, due to their close relationship with natural resources (Kusumowardani & Tjahjono, 2020; Mishra et al., 2021). The paper thus contributes to both circular economy and strategic management literature, by exploring how to implement circularity through NRBVbased dynamic capabilities and how T&C firms can enhance their competitive edge and promote a shift toward circular business models. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the main issues involved in the circular transition and the role of the two main market players (growing-circular and born-circular firms). The theoretical background is then introduced by combining the NRBV with the dynamic capability framework (Section 3). Section 4 describes the methodology, by illustrating the research context, the selection of cases, and data collection and analysis. The findings are reported in Section 5, by proposing an NRBV-based dynamic capabilities framework, and then discussed in Section6. Section7 concludes by addressing the implications, limitations, and directions for future research. 2 | TOWARD CIRCULAR ECONOMY The transition from a linear (take–make–dispose) to a circular economy is identified as a solution to the unavailability of resources and environmental negative impacts (Lieder & Rashid,2016). The original principles of the circular economy— reduce, reuse, and recycle— can be used as guidelines in business models for achieving sustainability (Murray et al.,2017), thus creating both environmental and economic value (Frishammar & Parida,2019; Henry et al.,2020). These principles are incorporated into the business model innovation process (Geissdoerfer et al.,2018). In the product–service system model, this takes place through a transition from selling to leasing and sharing services and therefore from ownership of an asset to its use, thus encouraging the company's investments in the durability of products (Mont & Tukker, 2006). On these lines, Urbinati et al. (2017) distinguish between upstream, downstream, and full circular business models depending on the position of innovation for circularity within the value chain of goods or services. The actual implementation of CE depends on how a firm is structured. In fact, sustainable entrepreneurship studies have analyzed the exploitation of CE opportunities by both growing-circular firms (longstanding and large ones moving toward CE) and born-circular firms (generally start-ups, hence, small and young firms) (Zucchella & Urban, 2019). The interaction between different types of players in the sustainability transition has also been recognized from a multilevel perspective (Hörisch, 2015), for example, by theorizing that start-ups should adopt push strategies to disseminate their products and solutions in the mass market. Established firms are considered to give sustainability a lower priority than economic objectives (Hockerts & Wüstenhagen, 2010), while, in contrast, born-circular firms seem to integrate the social and environmental aspects (the so-called social CE; Soufani et al., 2018). Nevertheless, competences are not given enough attention (Santini, 2017), despite their importance to value (co)creation and competitive success. The centrality of competences in CE has been recognized also in the field of strategic management (Centobelli et al.,2020; Urbinati et al., 2017). Several contributions (Barreiro-Gen & Lozano, 2020; Franco, 2017) suggest that microlevel studies are needed since the transformation of individual firms is a prerequisite for the CE transition of the entire industry to which they belong. As a fundamental dimension of the CE, innovations in products, processes, and organizations require specific resources and competencies (Suchek et al., 2021). Developing circular business models thus requires a wide range of capabilities, in order to achieve environmentally sustainable economic activities. 3 | NATURAL-RESOURCE-BASED VIEW AND DYNAMIC CAPABILITIES AS A FRAMEWORK FOR IMPLEMENTING CE The NRBV is a theoretical framework that examines the connection between an organization and the natural environment (Hart,1995; Hart & Dowell,2011). Kusumowardani and Tjahjono (2020) state that NRBV is“one of the roots of CE” (p. 46), and Mishra et al. (2021) propose this perspective as a path for the CE transition. NRBV focuses on how business models can be transformed at the microlevel and states that the competitive advantage is“rooted” in rare, tacit, and socially complex “capabilities that facilitate environmentally sustainable economic activity” (Hart, 1995, p. 991). Pollution prevention, product stewardship, and sustainable development are the three key strategies identified by Hart (1995), which have been indicated as crucial to achieving circularity in the T&C industry (Jia et al.,2020). Pollution prevention concerns the upstream reduction of emissions and effluents during manufacturing and not only controlling it at the “end-of-pipe.” This means adopting intraorganizational environmental practices, that is, acting proactively with respect to the consumption of resources (energy, materials, and water), in addition to emissions and waste, in the firm's internal processes through continuous improvements and voluntary standards (Shi et al., 2012). Preventing pollution (toxic chemicals effluents and greenhouse gases emission prevention) is considered an antecedent of CE (Kusumowardani & Tjahjono, 2020; Sikdar, 2019), whereas efficient use resources as the minimization of losses is a key issue in CE (Van Ewijk, 2018). Product stewardship concerns the reduction of the environmental impacts throughout the entire product lifecycle, from the choice of raw materials and product design to the disposal of used materials. Green purchasing, design for the environment, and green distribution have been reported as being related practices (Shi et al., 2012). Supplier selection criteria (Münch et al.,2022) are a topic investigated in the circular supply chain studies for purchasing environmentally friendly materials, such as renewable or recyclable materials. In addition to product design, the creation of closed-loop processes in the supply chain, where the products return upstream to recover their value, has been proposed (Miemczyk et al., 2016), also for clothing firms (Ashby,2018), as part of a green distribution. However, González-Torre et al. (2010) argued that environmentally oriented reverse logistics require the development of internal capabilities to enable firms to achieve a real competitive advantage. Moreover, product stewardship entails stakeholder engagement so that networks can be created to preempt competition (Hart, 1995). The third strategy was originally sustainable development (Hart, 1995), later referred to as clean technologies (Hart,1997) and the base of the pyramid (Hart & Christensen,2002). Clean technologies do not reduce the negative effects but create positive outcomes through lower consumption and are not related to current products and processes (as are the first two strategies) but future technologies capable of revolutionizing an industry (Hart, 1997). In the automobile industry, for example, the difference between product stewardship and clean technology has been addressed in terms of incremental versus radical technology innovation (De Stefano et al.,2016). Considering the research gap concerning the link between CE and clean technology, Mishra et al. (2021) propose the adoption of NRBV to understand how to achieve circular benefits through clean technologies. Finally, the base of the pyramid represents the social dimension of sustainable development (Hart et al., 2016) and should be aimed at testing innovations by entering new emerging markets (London & Hart, 2004). Kusumowardani et al. (2022) empirically investigated the social dimension of sustainable development highlighting the role of collaboration with social enterprises as enabler of social responsibility in CE. On the other hand, the integration of base of the pyramid with CE principles remains underexplored. Various studies have proposed other strategies, such as local philanthropy, that is, supporting social issues in local communities (McDougall et al., 2016, 2019). It has also been shown that NRBV strategies can be implemented in any order as there is no set hierarchy of stages. It is therefore critical to explore NRBV resources in practice and specifically concerning the context of specific firms (McDougall et al., 2019). Dynamic capabilities are a key aspect of NRBV, since they provide a more complete understanding of how firms support environmental strategies (Hart & Dowell, 2011).1 The reason is that dynamic capabilities framework is based on the ability to adapt to changing markets. According to Hart and Dowell ( 2011), unavailability of resources and environmental issues accelerate such complex markets, threatening the survival of firms. In addition, it has been argued that dynamic capabilities are essential to achieving sustainability (Wu et al., 2013; Zahoor & Lew,2022). Panwar and Niesten (2022) state that dynamic capabilities are necessary to the first step to diffusing and sustaining the CE of the firm, as they facilitate the firms' engagement with supply chain partners, customers, local communities, and regulators. Miemczyk et al. ( 2016) underlined that there is scant research integrating dynamic capabilities and environmental strategy together, including pollution prevention, product stewardship, clean technology, and base of the pyramid (McDougall et al., 2022). With the extensive environmental problems in the T&C sector and the acknowledged need to adjust the circularity of the players through the development of specific capabilities, a theoretical framework combining NRBV and dynamic capabilities seems appropriate. Furthermore, because NRBV emphasizes the importance of achieving complementary economic and environmental performance, it seems applicable to different configurations of firms, specifically both borncircular and growing-circular firms. 4 | METHODS A qualitative multiple-case study design was adopted to address the research question, in line with similar studies on business cases of circular economy (Khan et al.,2020; Marrucci et al., 2022). The case study is a method to investigate contemporary phenomena in-depth, within their real-world context, relying on multiple sources of evidence (Yin, 2018). Using the theoretical lenses of NRBV and dynamic capabilities, a qualitative case study approach can also reveal tacit capabilities that are not readily apparent, which would have been more difficult to achieve through quantitative measures (Marrucci et al., 2022). A multiple-case study also produces more robust conclusions by reducing the level of uncertainty regarding outcomes than a single-case study (Yin, 2018). Constructivist grounded theory for data analysis was used. A constructivist grounded theory approach recognizes multiple realities within a social context and“the mutual creation of knowledge by the viewer and the viewed, and aims toward interpretive understanding of subjects' meanings” (Charmaz, 2000, p. 509). Unlike conventional grounded theory (Glaser & Strauss, 1967), constructivist grounded theory is situated between postmodernism and positivism and stresses the importance of knowledge that is realistically situated and context-specific approached (Charmaz, 2017; Charmaz & Belgrave, 2012). This approach was selected for the present study to provide an in-depth understanding of different managers' perspectives on specific themes, which are grounded in the experiences of the people involved in circular processes within the firms, whose perceptions are generally not taken into account in the literature or in official documents. 4.1 | Research context The textile, clothing, and fashion sector is one of the most strategic sectors in Italy: 45,000 companies with approximately 398,000 employees and a turnover of 55 billion euros in 2018, which represents 30.9% of the European textile, clothing, and fashion sector (Confindustria Moda, 2019). In Italy, this sector has a networking nature and many firms tend to be located in the same area: ideal elements for implementing CE (Mazzoni,2020). Also, the implementation of CE in this context could be stimulated by strong competition from recently industrialized countries, which has also generated the relocation of production activities and a reduction in employment levels (ICESP, 2020). The recent EU directive 2018/851, which encourages such CE practices, is also gradually having an impact on all European manufacturing. Other factors, such as the nondirect availability of natural fibers, which are almost always imported from foreign producers, and the increase in textile waste due to fast fashion dynamics highlight the potential for the recovery of textile products (ICESP, 2020). 4.2 | Case selection A purposive sampling strategy was needed to identify those firms which would be able to provide rich data to answer the research question. Sustainability managers were preferred as interviewees. When not available, CEOs and Founders were chosen as they could provide information on the implementation of CE strategies based on their extensive knowledge of the company. The interviews took place between June 2020 and December 2021, were nonstructured (only an interview protocol was followed), and generally lasted from 30 to 80 min. All interviews were carried out via videoconferencing and were recorded and transcribed. For the purposes of the study, interview guidelines were designed. Interviewees were asked to discuss subjects along lines that touched on different facets of the research question in order to obtain insights into the strategies and dynamic capabilities needed for CE transition. The interview guidelines facilitated interviewers in ensuring that all significant areas were covered. These included general questions about the company's core business and position in the textile/ fashion supply chain and interviewees' experience in sustainability and circular economy processes. There were also specific questions about defining risks and opportunities related to the company's strategies and practices to prevent pollution, in designing and developing products for circularity and in adopting“clean” technologies and initiatives to develop the social potential of the environmental/circular improvements. The guidelines also covered topics related to future scenarios (including the rise of startups in the market in the case of growingcircular firms), especially by trying to understand which additional competences companies need in order to complete their transition to circular business models. Understanding such mechanisms is crucial in order to advance and substantiate our knowledge about transition toward CE. Our framework highlights how the NRBV-based dynamic capabilities not only minimize resource input and waste, emission, and energy leakage but also help to develop new business practices and strategic collaborations with different stakeholders. They also reshape organizational structures and identity, based on a strong commitment to sustainable development. The paper addresses the lack of knowledge on the role these firms play in developing the four NRBV strategies, in particular, clean technology and BoP strategies (Hart & Dowell, 2011). In addition, by “building on the central role of capabilities in NRBV” (McDougall et al., 2022, p. 24), the paper also contributes by empirically investigating the presence of NRBV strategies, while generally previous research has been prevalently theory-based with very few studies that explain how the four strategies tend to be manifested (Hart & Dowell, 2011; McDougall et al.,2019). The paper also sheds light on the dynamic capabilities needed in the T&C sector for CE transition, by considering not only growingcircular firms (as in Khan et al.,2020) but also start-ups and born circular firms. In line with McDougall et al. (2016, 2022), the paper describes dynamic capabilities for each of the four environmental strategies in CE context, by presenting the application of the three core elements of dynamic capabilities (sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring), thus suggesting an evolutionary path that underpins the competitive advantage under the lens of NRBV. In addition, the paper substantiates the fact that NRBV involves internal and external levels, as suggested in Martín-de Castro et al. ( 2016), and intraorganizational and interorganizational practices, as suggested by Shi et al. (2012). Our results confirm that dynamic capabilities are key to promoting the CE, as they stimulate firms' engagement with stakeholders (Panwar & Niesten, 2022). In line with Karagouni and Protogerou (2015), the development of dynamic capabilities facilitates value co-creation processes, or rather, these processes are the result of dynamic capabilities. Sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring co-specialized and complementary resources allow different actors to create value together. Furthermore, firms' engagement with stakeholders in T&C industry (Ki et al., 2020) seems to be crucial for the adoption of NRBV strategies. These strategies require the development of relationships with several different stakeholders, including supply chain partners, customers, research centers, competitors, and local communities. Specifically, regarding product stewardship, the findings show the importance of developing listening skills by engaging with the downstream actors of the supply chain, who carry out pull strategies toward the upstream actors. The inputs generally start with the clothing manufacturers (or the “brands”) as they need both to cocreate with customers, to demonstrate their transparency, and therefore, to be able to trace the final product back to the raw materials used. In line with Jia et al. ( 2020), consumers seem to be one of the main drivers of the CE in the T&C sector. Changes to consumer culture, regarding the awareness of environmental issues, have a corresponding impact on the demand for environmentally friendly products (Siemieniuch et al., 2015). Consumers are interested not only in buying more eco-friendly products but also in having a more active role in determining the firms' offerings. Consequently, circular business models of sustainable fashion firms depend on the increasingly relevant role of end consumers (Elf et al., 2022). In line with previous studies, the engagement of the consumer in the reversal loop (from user to manufacturer) can be decisive in both achieving a closed-loop supply chain (Jia et al., 2020) and increasing the firms' competitiveness (Musova et al.,2021). Closed-loop supply chains emerge as a vital part of product stewardship, as also highlighted by Miemczyk et al. (2016) and Ashby (2018). This approach involves managing both upstream and downstream relationships, which foster trust and mutual goals within the supply chain (van Bommel,2011). These relational resources can be a competitive edge and difficult to imitate (Ashby,2018), even more if they are developed in collaboration with local suppliers, which can help narrow material and energy loops in a unique way. On the same lines, traceability systems and certifications seem to promote transparency and, hence, trust along the T&C supply chain. In this sense, the acquisition of digital technology is recognized as a reconfiguring resource activity that improves traceability and transparency, thus substantiating digitalization as an enabler of the CE (Antikainen et al., 2018). However, a few initial steps toward a mutual evolution are evident. In fact, start-ups use established firms' know-how to add quality to the circularity, and in their turn, established firms use start-ups' innovative ideas to cultivate and develop. In contrast to Hörisch ( 2015), start-ups do not employ push strategies to spread their product to the mass market. The role of born-sustainable firms in the sustainability transition is traditionally associated with product innovation (Hockerts & Wüstenhagen, 2010) and with the development of clean technologies. In our cases, it appears that circular start-ups develop product stewardship competences for supply chain management from a closed-loop perspective, also by delegating manufacturing to companies specialized in using second raw materials and guaranteeing associated certifications. Even the growing-circular firms, typically devoted to “weak sustainability” (Schaltegger et al., 2016), seem more committed to innovation. Clean technologies seem to be driven by firms envisioning their future position (Hart & Dowell, 2011) in the T&C industry. Growing-circular firms consider both disruptive process innovation and product innovation with a low level of novelty as a way of promoting circular best practices downstream, since they do not require change to other actors. Business customers can continue to use yarns/fabrics with the same production facilities, and the end consumer can use garments with the same consumption behavior. Similarly, one of the elements that differentiates the clean technology of a product from the innovation of product stewardship, namely, a radical from an incremental innovation, is the change in behavior that it entails for the consumer (Danneels & Kleinschmidtb, 2001; Gerrard & Kandlikar, 2007). Radical innovation thus concerns discontinuous product innovation, such as the ability to fully implement take-back programs to close the loop. In our cases, the discontinuity refers to unprecedented consumption behavior that comprises the end stage of consumption (postconsumer waste), as well as the associated active behaviors necessary to close the loop. Born-circular firms, unlike their larger counterparts, appear not only to close the loop (by engaging partners and customers in takeback programs) but to restrict it to 0-km fashion, as well as to slow it down by implementing different strategies for product life cycle extension (e.g., reuse and secondhand sales by engaging social cooperatives). On the other hand, the crucial role of stakeholder engagement in supporting circular transition of fashion industry is confirmed (Ki et al., 2020) where growing-circular firms engage with different stakeholder groups (suppliers, customers, research centers, competitors in consortia, and local communities), while born-circular ones are more focused on building relationships with local communities. Regarding the BoP category, none of the investigated firms seems to have developed competences aimed at“real” strategies from Hart's perspective (development of the social potential of environmental improvements, on a global level). In line with McDougall et al. ( 2016, 2019), the results show a greater attention to social issues at the local level. This suggests a gradual adoption of BoP strategies, from those closest to the NRBV to those closest to local philanthropy (McDougall et al., 2019). According to Soufani et al. (2018), the social dimension seems to be linked to circularity, so that the phenomenon of benefit corporations (certifications), already detected in born-circular firms (Zucchella & Urban,2019), also emerges in the T&C sector, and particularly in growing-circular firms, where they represent an evolution of CSR management.2 7 | IMPLICATIONS, LIMITATIONS, AND DIRECTIONS FOR FUTURE RESEARCH The study provides an NRBV-based dynamic capabilities framework aimed at advancing our knowledge of circular transition in the T&C industry. Despite the isolated initiatives of some firms, the drivers of CE implementation are supported by different strategies and come from various types of stakeholders. To encourage a more rapid transition of the whole T&C sector, firms need to shift their focus from linear, extractive business models to more integrated and regenerative models that prioritize material selection (i.e., both environmentally friendly fibers and recyclable/recycled technical materials), collaborative product design, integrated supply chains with distributors, and a strong engagement with their customers. Overall, the transition to a circular economy could lead to a fundamental shift in the way firms in the T&C think about their resources and capabilities and, in turn, their identities. While our findings offer useful insights into T&C industry, future research could extend the geographical and sectoral scope, also from a comparative perspective. Further studies could also consider firms that deal with other man-made and organic fibers, such as cotton, which were not included in the firms analyzed and which could have developed different types of CE competencies. The same applies to the inclusion of different types of participants who could extend the view on the CE transition, as suggested by Khan et al. ( 2020). Future studies could further explore the specific capabilities developed by born- and growing-circular firms from a longitudinal perspective, to understand the way in which the competences of these two types of players have evolved and are evolving over time. Lastly, it would be interesting to understand the role of focal firms in the sector dynamics, as the results of recent empirical studies seem to downplay this leading role, by suggesting that the diffusion of CE practices remains primarily within the company rather than being spread throughout the supply chain (Masi et al., 2018). This resonates with Zwass ( 2010) and his“sponsored cocreation,” namely, the activities conducted by consumers in value creation, generated on behalf of firms. Thus, firms not only can communicate the adoption of circular principles to their end customers (Urbinati et al., 2017) and facilitate environmentally friendly selfproduction (Coppola et al.,2021) but also, in this case, firms can also involve consumers in firms' CE practices. Clothing manufacturers encourage the consumer to be greener with take-back programs, and conversely, these programs are implemented to match the growing consumer demand for engagement and more sustainable products. In addition, in line with Elf et al. ( 2022), it seems co-creation can reduce the market risk for micro, small, and medium fashion firms as it improves customer loyalty. Similarly, mutual co-creation dynamics occur throughout the supply chain, also between suppliers and business customers, where there is a “joint value creation process” (Grönroos, 2011). Finding partners and interacting with them thus become important. The business customer can then invite the supplier to cocreate, providing insights concerning green consumers, thus leading to new successful solutions. Both business customers and suppliers could become a service provider (and not only a product provider). This would ensure continuous flows of return materials/products, as suggested by Ashby ( 2018). Our research also reveals that circular economy must be addressed in a proactive manner. Firms that want to pursue CE opportunities should build a CE culture that starts with including it in the organizational structure (Khan et al., 2020) through an additional unit, specialized human resources, and a clear vision. Another implication is that the four NRBV strategies are not sequential, and not every organization develops clean technologies (McDougall et al., 2019). Nevertheless, a holistic approach to CE cannot separate product stewardship from pollution prevention without creating a trade-off between circularity, that is, a closedloop approach, and environmental sustainability. The development or adoption of clean technologies, as well as circularity-oriented practices, should be encouraged by policy makers through adequate policies and funding. Lastly, in line with Panwar and Niesten's ( 2022) assertion, jump-starting the circular economy at the exemplar firms' level favors the adoption of CE practices and develops dynamic capabilities at the“group efforts” level, by cultivating an ecosystem approach, also by encouraging the coevolution between borncircular and growing-circular firms. Local and regional institutions should contribute identifying new trajectories in CE, mobilizing resources and consensus, and incentivizing them (Bressanelli et al., 2022). This could promote not only technological ecoinnovation but also the birth of new circular start-ups, creating fertile ground for their scaling up. A rich environment of dynamic small firms can favor not only philanthropic initiatives with local suppliers but also can lead in the long term to a benefit corporation approach for circular firms, thus supporting a more global perspective in the circularity transition.
